I haven't played for nearly enough time given the calibre of this game, but I have so much love for Gloomhaven that I just wanted to write a quick review of my experiences thus far. 

Firstly, I like to consider myself a fairly seasoned Gloomhaven player. I have a couple hundred hours in both the online and physical copy of the game. I have never played Frosthaven prior to this. And for the first couple hours, I just couldn't get into this game. I found it way too overwhelming character wise and the missions were way too hard for us to complete. 

So right off the bat, if you are new to the franchise, I would not start with Frosthaven. It is noticeably the more difficult of the two games, even for someone who knows the basics. Gloomhaven does a much better job at easing you into the game mechanics and the character decks and synergies are much easier to grasp. 

After picking it up and putting it back down multiple times, I have found that changing the difficulty and only picking one character to start off with while learning their deck has been the best way to ease into this game. My duo and I are starting to genuinely enjoy this game (whilst appreciating the complexity) and cannot wait to unlock new characters to work with. 

If you have never played a game in this series before, essentially you pick a preset character and deck. You select a personal mission for the campaign that your character solely works towards. You complete quests and while doing so, you unlock more of the map and story. Along the way, you unlock new cards and gear to personalize your experience. You also meet up and unlock new characters as you progress and can retire your character and start with a new one. 

This is a great group game because you actually have to sit and plan out your plays with your teammates. There are certain objectives within the scenarios that need to be met or the mission is failed. I also love how there are little encounters as your heroes journey throughout the map and they require you to make decisions as a group (with actual consequences, both good and bad). 

It is still in EA, but so far we have not encountered any problems. They have improved the interface in this game. The game looks more polished to me. I am appreciating some of the smaller details, like the art on the player cards and the addition of voice acting incorporated into the game. My favourite tho, is the base camp town. You now collect resources instead of gold. You use these resources to build up your town to unlock more perks to improve your party. Feels more active outside of just missions. 

Would def recommend this game to seasoned players, but maybe just take it at a slower pace than Gloomhaven. Just don't give up!! It gets better and I cannot wait to see what this game grows into ^_^

I'd hold off on this for now until the developers fix more bugs.

The blinkblade, one of the six starting classes, is basically unplayable. Firstly, the cards are literally not represented correctly, so it is not actually possible to understand how the class works without referencing the cards from the board game. In the board game there are base parts of the card with slow and fast modifiers - the video game doesn't work like this at all and it has a slow half and a fast half. While that sounds ok on paper, it's actually unusable because other cards say things like "ignore the slow modifiers only" and there's no actual way to figure this out with the information the video game gives you. 

On top of the visual unplayability (I am literally playing with a PDF of the class cards open), the blinkblade seems to have constant desync issues as the Fast/Slow tokens get into weird states. I've had several games where I chose Slow and had no Fast tokens available and when my turn came up my cards acted like they were in the Fast mode. The UI ends up bugged in this state and frequently it crashes multiplayer.

The game is in EA but I don't think this class should have been included yet, especially as a starting class - it's a huge problem. If you do play the game now I strongly recommend you do not choose it and basically treat it as not implemented yet because that's what it is. Guessing dev's shoved in anything they could in order to meet a milestone target and the quality shows as it's a miserable experience.

There are a few other bugs in the game as well that makes me feel like most are better holding off, but they're more manageable / annoying to me rather than making the game unplayable with the core UI.

[h1] Эталон разработки и игра с душой [/h1]

Накануне релиза решила написать этот отзыв, чтобы выразить свою любовь к Timberborn и неустанное восхищение командой Mechanistry. От всей души поздравляю всех с этим долгожданным событием!

Я приобрела игру еще в 2022 году, и с тех пор Mechanistry стали для меня эталонным примером того, как нужно подходить к разработке. Это трудолюбивые, увлеченные своим делом люди, которые с невероятным вниманием относятся к деталям и к своему сообществу. 

Наблюдать за тем, как игра с каждым обновлением становилась глубже, сложнее и отполированнее, было захватывающим удовольствием. За все два года я практически не сталкивалась с багами — разве это не лучшее доказательство качества их работы?

Timberborn — это уникальный, живой, продуманный до мелочей мир. Я уверена, что этой игре суждено процветать и стать классикой жанра.

[h2]Что делает Timberborn по-настоящему особенной?[/h2]

[list]
    [*]Уникальные фракции. Это совершенно разные виды бобров со своей философией и подходом к выживанию.
    [*]Глубокое управление водой. Строительство дамб, плотин, шлюзов и акведуков — это не просто задача, а целое инженерное искусство.
    [*]Многоуровневое строительство — вы можете комбинировать здания друг с другом и даже создавать "небоскребы".
    [*]Масштабное терраформирование. Отдельная моя любовь — это возможность перекроить всю карту с помощью динамита и кучи земли.
    [*]Производственные цепочки и фермерство сложны, увлекательны и многообразны. Они заставляют подумать над выбором места, логистикой, количеством рабочих, снабжением энергией.
    [*]Самая удобная система распределения ресурсов из всех, что я видела в похожих играх.
    [*]А чего стоит система транспорта? Когда у Железных Зубов появились туннели, я буквально построила метро!
[/list]

И это далеко не всё! Я уже не говорю о таких милых деталях, как бассейны и дискотеки для счастья маленьких бобров.


[h2]Сообщество[/h2]

И отдельный восторг, что разработчики с самого начала растили вокруг игры живое сообщество. Возможность создавать свои карты и активно обсуждать идеи на форуме, полноценная поддержка модов — всё это создает уникальную связь между игроками и миром Timberborn.

Это проект, в котором к игрокам действительно прислушивались все эти годы. Проект, который постоянно кропотливо улучшали. И на протяжении всего этого пути Timberborn приносила мне огромную радость.

Очень надеюсь, что история Timberborn не закончится. Мне бы хотелось увидеть в будущем DLC: новые фракции, дожди и... зимнюю карту с замерзающей водой.

Reviewing (mostly) every game (or DLC) in my library, part 454:

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️☆ (9/10)

[i]Contraband Police[/i] really shouldn't be so good as it is. I mean, a traffic simulator? Doing the worst job ever invented (paperwork)? But somehow! It’s a tense, morally engaging exercise in law, logic, and human error. On the surface, you play as a border officer checking papers and scanning cars, but underneath, it’s a meditation on power, trust, and the gray spaces between legality and conscience. The comparison to [i] Papers, Please[/i] is low-hanging fruit, but whatever, I'll always grab whatever fruit I can see.

🚥 [b] Pros:[/b]
[list]
[*] Tense, methodical gameplay. Every car, every bag, every ID can hide secrets. You'll have to spot inconsestities: a shade of paper too light, a wrong letter on a passport, an expired date. You'll use a UV flashlight, as well, to check for contraband. And somehow, it stays fun? You can go as serious or funny as you want, and yes, you can take bribes.

[*] Morality in miniature. You can write someone off for lying—or give them a chance and risk smuggling getting through. The game forces you to weigh procedure against humanity. For me, I did not care. If you didn't have the EXACT paperwork, you're getting denied. Sob stories do not work on me. How do I know you're not lying?

[*] Atmosphere. A dreary border post, a gray, rain-soaked world, and the sense that everything is slightly off. The music, the environments, the weary NPCs—it all builds a feeling of being trapped between bureaucracy and chaos. But on one random day, an alarm can go off and bandits from the woods swarm to attack your post. And just like that, the grim atmosphere shifts to some wacky FPS gameplay.

[*] Side content. The gameplay loop doesn't just involve paperwork. You can drive vehicles into town to buy weapons or trading supplies; drive prisoners to their new home (some kind of mining depot); and explore other areas. You can also hunt down fleeing criminals and defend your base from rebel scum. The shooting is surprisingly smooth, no complaints from me.

[*] Humor and absurdity. Between the grim stakes, the game sprinkles moments of dark comedy: a smug smuggler, ridiculous contraband, or an NPC’s bizarre excuse. It reminds you that life at the border is sometimes tragic, sometimes absurd, and often both.
[/list]

⛕[b] Cons:[/b]
[list]
[* ] Repetitive pacing. The basic loop of checking papers, scanning luggage, and issuing rejections can feel a bit samey over long sessions. The tension is excellent in bursts, but the routine can become grindy.

[*] Occasional mechanical opacity. Sometimes it’s unclear why your answer is marked wrong. I wish there was a highlighted example of the mistake you didn't catch.

[*] I wish there were more ways to find contraband than the snake symbol. It got very same-y.

[*] Steep learning curve for the details. IDs, stamps, and procedures require careful attention. You'll have multiple mistakes in one interaction late-game.
[/list]

One of the best feeling Metroidvanias available on the market, in my opinion. I ended up playing it way after release with a discount, but even at full-price I think it's very worth it. I will say to take some things with a bit of salt as I've seen people's reviews calling the game hard, but I didn't struggle all that much. Might've just clicked with this game uber hard.

Comparatively it's rather short for what one would expect from a Metroidvania (it took me 15 hours to 100% the game), but I think that's part of the strength of Worldless. It doesn't overstay its welcome and instead garnishes you with an amazing and very, very unique feeling combat style with a wonderfully cozy artstyle and beautiful soundtrack. There's even a very decent and healthy sprinkling of secrets for the more explorational types and a couple extra challenges, including a special hidden fight that took me I want to say over an hour to finish. The story itself is also rather intriguing even if left (intentionally) vague as to how things in this world works. Nothing ground-breaking, but it's enough that it added to me getting the "damn, what do I do now?" pit anyone gets after finishing an amazing game.

The rest is rather self-explanatory, but what's the deal with the combat? 
The closest comparison I can think of is Expedition 33's combat which has real-time sections mixed into its turn-based combat, or Child of Light which is turn-based combat on a more free-flowing timeline. 
The best way to describe how it actually *feels* is that it's a fighting game/beat-em-up put on a turn timer. You have a set amount of time to beat up your opponent, with a few means of further extending your turn by exploiting your target's weaknesses, before it shifts to the opponent's turn and you have to block, parry and dodge attacks. It's very fast-paced with you gradually unlocking more options through finding new tools and absorbing your opponents - speaking of which, killing your opponents isn't even the main point a lot of the time. You will generally need to fill out their separate absorption meter to a high enough level to make an attempt in the first place, which is followed by a quick time event. Depending on how much is filled is how many of the button presses you actually know. This is one of your main ways of gaining upgrades, outside of absorbing corpses, so you are encouraged to be strategic in the middle of combat and mix high damage attacks with lower damage ones that fill out the absorption meter.

Overall, amazing game that's worth the full price tag. It goes on a 50% sale rather often, though, so if you see it on that sale (like right now, as I'm typing this)... go buy the game and check it out. It's really, really worth it.

Dead Reset is a horror FMV game. The main character, Cole Mason, is a surgeon who wakes up in some kind of science lab with no memories of where he is, and is ordered to save the life of a woman who is infected with some kind of parasite. But when the surgery goes wrong, Cole finds himself trapped in a Groundhog Day style time loop.

This is basically an interactive movie, so gameplay consists of watching the FMV scenes, and occasionally making a choice to influence the story. The story and the acting are fairly good. The monster looks a bit like a Resident Evil boss, and some of the deaths are entertainingly gorey.

However, the weakest part of the game is the time loop mechanic, which is extremely under used. I’ve seen many episodes of Sci Fi TV shows where a character is stuck in a time loop, so I was expecting this game to have a kind of trial and error, puzzle type progression, where I would need to figure out the correct sequence of events necessary to break the loop.
 
Other than the first chapter, Dead Reset is disappointingly linear. While some choices can put you onto a different story path, other than specific scenes where you encounter the monster, there’s almost no looping back. Its just a glorified respawn mechanic. Even the monster fights are fairly basic. You’ll get a couple of choices, attack or evade, run or hide, and if you make the wrong choice you die. Then you reset and Cole automatically makes the other choice, and you live.

The story is divided into several short chapters, and the restart point will move to the start of each chapter, so its not like you get to the end of the day, fail to break the loop and then wake up back at the very start, ready to try again armed with the knowledge gained from the previous attempt. Other than the monster fights, every choice you make is permanent (unless you start a new game). No looping back to undo mistakes, no gathering intel and then looping back to unlock new choices.

My 5.3 hours playing time represents two full playthroughs. I replayed, made different choices, and got slightly different versions of the same scenes in the same locations with the same characters. Only the final chapter and the ending were significantly different.

Dead Reset isn’t a bad game, its worth playing if you like horror movies. But its just not what I expected it to be.

Total War: Shogun 2 remains one of my all-time favorite strategy games, transporting players back to the turbulent Sengoku period of feudal Japan. I first dove into it during my college days, and it provided endless hours of engaging gameplay that made those stressful study sessions feel a world away. The real-time strategy (RTS) elements were top-notch for its time, blending large-scale battles with deep campaign management in a way that felt innovative and immersive.
One of the standout features is the graphics, which still hold up remarkably well even years later. The depictions of samurai warriors charging into battle, with detailed armor, flowing banners, and dynamic weather effects on the battlefield, create a visually stunning experience. Watching armies clash amid cherry blossoms or misty mountains captures the essence of historical Japan beautifully, making every skirmish feel epic and cinematic.
That said, the game isn't without its limitations. The playable clans are somewhat restricted, which can feel confining after multiple playthroughs, as you cycle through the same factions without much variety. Additionally, the historical figures and characters based on real events are quite minimal, which dilutes the sense of authenticity for history buffs. It focuses more on broad strategy than on fleshed-out personalities or intricate storylines tied to specific historical events.
It's a shame there haven't been any significant updates to refresh the experience, or better yet, a Shogun 3 with a modern engine that could enhance the visuals, AI, and overall polish. I'd love to see expanded campaign modes that follow historical accuracy more closely or offer branching alternative histories for replayability. Even more exciting would be a new feature or mode where you start as a lowly soldier and rise through the ranks to become a general, complete with robust character customization options. The idea of embodying your own created character—customizing their appearance, skills, and backstory—would add a personal touch and make the journey feel even more rewarding and immersive.
Overall, Total War: Shogun 2 is a classic that defined the RTS genre in its era, and revisiting it always brings back fond memories. If you're a fan of strategic depth wrapped in historical flair, it's still worth playing today—though I can't help but wish for a sequel to build on its strong foundation.

If Runescape is like addicting cigarettes, Melvor Idle is like vaping. You have similar dopamine hits, but instead of sitting there all day jumping from rooftop or rooftop, clicking on regenerating trees over and over, or moving periodically so the crabs can continue beating on you and you don't get caught by the AFK timer, you can simply let Melvor Idle run in the background. So it's a lot less destructive to your actual time and maybe even your health.

If you're a fan of the Idle genre, just know that this isn't a traditional idle game. There isn't a huge progression curve where numbers grow outrageously out of control. Or prestige mechanics. etc. Basically this game is exactly how it is advertised: a distillation of Runescape down to its core elements. 

I'm enjoying my playthrough so far. I highly recommend the Ancients Relic mode that comes with one of the DLC, as it's the kind of gameplay mode that offers extra challenge (the skill cap), but you end up with better rewards (the relics). You can't just over train everything, the mode forces you to engage with the game mechanics and systems and gives you actual walls to overcome. In compensation you get crazy good bonuses you wouldn't be able to get if you played it in normal mode.

My only criticism of the game 400 hours in, is that inventory space and gold gate the early game too much. I feel like early-game you are too limited by inventory space and the gold costs of everything. And then suddenly when you get your thieving system setup in the right way, that problem literally can disappear overnight, as you find yourself with hundreds of millions... even billions of gold and are buying inventory upgrades at cap price like your daily morning Starbucks coffee.

The game is very well tuned. Getting +50 HP when you have like 800, or an extra 3% damage reduction doesn't seem like much, especially if you are used to other Idle games prostituting exponential and and multiplicative increases to you. But it DOES makes a difference and sometimes that difference means being able to idle a dungeon with no effort to franctically sitting there for 12 minutes clicking on your food like a sweaty gamer exactly the moment your auto attack timer rolls over. I always appreciate when a game is tuned so that small upgrades can make the world of difference.

I do think skills like Astrology and Cartography should have been passive skills like township and farming, as these are both things that take incredibly amounts of time, offer very little game play other than waiting for the skill to train, yet are necessary because they tie into so much other stuff. 

Just my two cents. Melvor Idle 2 is coming out, so I'm interested to see how the dev iterated on the systems they put in place here.

Some tips from a min-maxer who got 100% achievements:
Start your controller before you start the game.
Alt+Enter to fix full screen mode.
There is never a need to actively stock up on wood, Stone, or coin (leaflets).

Wait until you have finished Summer Bar for the remaining tips:
Some orbs require a charged attack, others require you to bait a rot over and make them hit it.
Dowsing rod events have more challenge for rarer items: 3 cards for yellow shell, 5 cards for blue, and 10 for red.  If you only want red shells right now, you can intentionally fail by spamming other directions, exit the screen, and come back to try again. 
Goldie is in a hidden screen to the east of The Riverway in Spring Hamlet, you have to break the orb first. Finish their quests and then visit daily for free stuff.
Instead of going to sleep, check memories to improve your stats... you can even see what to do to unlock more memories.  Stack luck to nearly guarantee things like glass lenses when you break jars.
You carry a jar for each season, and can switch from the inventory menu.  You have to fill them separately too, but dont give up hope in a dungeon when you can just swap.
Putting chests everywhere you can is worth it.  You need sap to make chests.  Sap can be farmed from the Spring library dungeon or by getting a special dew and using it on dry stumps to convert them into leafy stumps.
The game maxes out at stacks of 35 in your bank, but you'll never need more than 25 items at a time.
Tools max out at level 5, but aside from your base sword and dowsing rod it's not worth it except for fun.
Towns max out at level 5, but by the end it's not worth doing it.  Check the stores during the day if there's anything still locked and pursue only the color you need for it.
Benches can fast forward up to a quarter of your day, but then you have to change screens.
It seems like certain towns grow things better (multiple results instead of one at a time).  Autumn town for cobblestone (cobble piece), Winter Glade for chick peas (porcelain shells), think it's jelly beans (bioluminescent pods) in Summer Bar, and Kukui nuts in Spring Hamlet (but might have that reversed with Summer Bar).
Charming story, art music, and a fun gameplay loop!

Yes, I've tried it multiple times, but unfortunately, I still cannot recommend the game.

The developer asked for feedback twice, which was provided, but he clearly isn't listening.

When I bought the game back in 2021, it at least had a map where you could build properly, find resources from the start, and the "gameplay" (if you can even call it that) was much more intuitive.

Now, the map feels empty despite the POIs. These POIs look different but contain exactly the same loot. Buildings are repetitive and set up the same way everywhere.
There are giant rocks and boulders that simply block your path, and you cannot use them in any way.
Orientation is a pain—you always have to check the map because there are no visible landmarks or anything distinctive; everything looks the same. And it rains constantly, which makes visibility even worse.

Lakes and rivers are essentially obsolete—you don't need them anymore. There's no visible life left. I think you can still go fishing, but again, it's not necessary and no fun. (Throwing a fishing rod into an empty lake!?)

You have to walk (!) with your cart across the huge map while having almost no stamina. Even if you set food consumption to low in the settings, it's annoying to constantly monitor your vitamin, health, stamina, and thirst bars. The character consumes water like a camel in the desert.
So much micromanagement!

When it comes to blueprints... man! I'm glad I've known the game for so long; otherwise, I'd have lost interest much earlier.
You now need blueprints for simple and essential items like a drying rack. If you're lucky, you find them quickly—only if you're lucky! It's a gamble throughout. As a beginner, you have no clue what to unlock first or what you need to make progress. Like I said, I'm glad I already know the items—it makes it easier for me, but for new players... no!

Overall, development is extremely slow because the single developer doesn't seem to ask for help.
Progress in development, proper gameplay elements, interesting POIs and maps, as well as taking feedback more seriously would make the product so much better.

This War of Mine doesn’t reward you with achievements or glory. It rewards you with understanding.
It makes you feel something real.

I love this game deeply, painfully, honestly.

This game is essentially trying to be Left 4 Dead in VR, but sadly it comes across as little more than a cringeworthy bargain bin bastardisation of Left 4 Dead rather than a successful VR adaptation of the Left 4 Dead formula.

To start with, the gameplay is extremely shallow. You kill zombies whilst walking from point A to point B. You loot buildings for weapons and ammo. You get to a safe room which functions as a checkpoint, and then you immediately set off for the next safe room. Throw in some uninspired fetch quests between safehouses, and that's pretty much the extent of the entire gameplay loop. Sounds just like Left 4 Dead, right? Except;

-The guns suck, the aiming physics feel off, weapons feel floaty and weightless, the firing sounds don't match their caliber of weapon, and melee attacks lack any impact or feedback.

-The zombies are barely a threat, you can avoid most attacks by simply backpedalling slowly. As far as I've seen there are only two enemy types; zombie and zombie that runs. [i]What a concept.[/i]

-This game markets itself as survival, but aside from finding ammo, there's no point to exploring the map or looting buildings. There's no reason to find shelter, your character has no needs to upkeep, and there's nothing in the sense of player progression.

-Aside from a couple of radio lines from the only other npc in the game, the story is almost nonexistent. You're just some guy in a zombie apocalypse, following instructions from some other guy on the other end of a radio, collecting inconsequential things and finding keys to open locked doors.

But the most disappointing thing, something that seems to be the norm in a lot of VR games, is how cheap and half baked the game feels. Every model, texture, animation, sound effect, music track etc, seem to have been bought straight from an asset store. I've seen these character models, building prefabs, and weapon models before.

This game is probably fun if you're 12 years old, but for me it has no lasting appeal. It's too shallow, too lazy, too boring, and costs too much money relative to what little entertainment value you can siphon from it.

Valkyria Chronicles is a tactical role-playing game that combines turn-based strategy with real-time control, creating a distinctive and memorable combat system. Set in a fictional version of Europe during a massive continental war, the game follows the story of Welkin Gunther and Squad 7 as they defend their homeland from invasion. Its hand-drawn, watercolor-inspired visuals make every battlefield look like a living illustration, giving it a timeless aesthetic that sets it apart from other war games.

The gameplay revolves around the BLiTZ system, which merges strategic planning with direct character control. You move soldiers individually, aim manually, and make every shot count. This approach makes combat more dynamic than traditional grid-based tactics. Terrain, unit class, and line of sight all influence success, rewarding careful positioning and tactical foresight. Each mission feels like a puzzle that can be solved in multiple ways, depending on your preferred playstyle.

Beyond the combat, Valkyria Chronicles shines through its cast of characters. Every squad member has unique traits, personalities, and relationships that affect performance on the battlefield. These small details humanize the soldiers and give emotional weight to each mission. The story blends heroism, tragedy, and moral reflection on the cost of war, maintaining a tone that’s serious but not hopeless.

Technically, the game runs smoothly and still looks impressive thanks to the CANVAS engine’s art direction. The orchestral soundtrack heightens both the tension of battle and the poignancy of the story’s quieter moments. Voice acting is strong, particularly in the English localization, giving life to characters who might otherwise fit simple archetypes.

There are a few rough edges. The AI can be inconsistent, and some missions demand trial and error to overcome. Yet these flaws rarely overshadow the strategic depth and narrative heart that make the game so memorable. Valkyria Chronicles remains one of Sega’s finest works—an inventive mix of art, tactics, and storytelling that still feels fresh and emotionally resonant years after release.

Дэвид Шимански снова сделал гнетущую, неуютную игру про сектантов и всякую жесть.

Обшарпанные притоны, клаустрофобные подземные лабиринты, сельские домики и сараи посреди лесов вечной ночи, сеттинговая связь с The Pony Factory — вылезти могут не только поехавшие отбросы, маньяки-сектанты, производители снаффа, но и, как кажется, сами адские существа. А мы босиком, повсюду стекло, и драться приходится подручных средствами: досками, трубами, молотками и топорами, канцелярскими ножами.

Здесь необычная система сохранения: через запись на найденные кассеты, которые также дают бонусы персонажу. И всё же пренебрегать сохранением не стоит. Вот оружие сломалось, а маньячины обступили со всех сторон и замесили. Если не сохранялись, то начинайте сначала, либо перезапускайте главу из меню.

Ещё необычнее способ восстановления здоровья: мы находим расчленёнку и кровь на стенах и фотографируем её. Кровать может появиться и во время столкновения с врагами, когда мощно вдарим орудием по черепушке супостата — осталось быстренько взять в руки фотоаппарат и сфотографировать, пока пятна не впитались в стены. А ведь частенько только что пущенная врагу кровь может спасти вам жизнь — важно успеть запечатлеть. Такой подход к восстановлению здоровья здорово влияет на геймплей и даже на сами сражения, делая их интереснее и напряжённее, ведь приходится отвлекаться от битвы на фотографирование, пока гад грозит расправиться с тобой.

Увы, игре не хватает всего двух вещей. Во-первых, большего разнообразия вражеских криков: кажется, в Condemned: Criminal Origins, которым вдохновлён Butcher's Creek, враги реагировали на встречу с героем чуточку разнообразнее. Во-вторых, финал хоть и логичен, но всё равно идёт разочаровать отсутствием боссфайта. А ведь перед финалом даже отсыпят кассет — будто бы чтобы подготовить к эпическому махачу. Но нет. Butchers Creek is as better at being Condemned than Condemned and is significantly better than Bloodshot.

You play as a guy best described as "troubled" who ends up getting nabbed by a cult composed entirely of what appears to be serial killers, guys who watch/make torture porn, and general violent weirdos. The game in general is very dark and violent and the plot reflects this (if you choose to engage with it, its entirely through notes). I'm not going to spoil anything, just know that this game goes into some uncomfortable stuff so it's probably better if you go in knowing that.

The gameplay is a very clear send up of the Condemned system of melee hobo combat, with weapons having distinct stats for damage and speed, and having a timed block and kick at your disposal. Butchers Creek changes up the formula in a couple ways: there's no taser to cheese out the combat, you have a stamina meter (that can be refilled instantly on timing a block) forcing you to be smart about how and when you swing so you don't run out of gas in the middle of a fight, and you can kick objects into enemies or enemies into environmental hazards. There's not a single gun in the game, if you want to hurt someone you either gotta get in close, kick something at them, or start chucking weapons in their direction. Overall, I think it's better than Condemned in this regard.

You can tell that its going for a VHS style for the visuals, it's very gritty. However I never had a problems being able to distinguish anything or spot something in the environment, in terms of gameplay readability its still clear. Where Condemned had you walking around abandoned buildings, Butcher's Creek has you mostly stumbling through basements in dilapidated backwoods factories, but there are a couple other notable locations as well, so it doesn't end up being too samey. The audio is great. Impacts sound like they hurt, the background ambiance is unnerving, and the music is surprisingly good and fits whats happening in game.

Butcher's Creek is a well put together game that I can see a lot of people bouncing off of, so I'm giving it a tentative recommendation. If you like bloody horror movies, or kicking teeth out of heads, go for it.

This game feels like one of those forgotten PS3 titles. Especially visually, yes, but also narratively and mechanically. Even the font choice is reminiscent of PS3 (and some PS2) cult classics.

It's a very slow-paced game filled with dreamlike environments, wistful piano melodies, and cryptic but sentimental letters. Some might find the pace frustrating (especially with how slowly you move and how much backtracking there is), while others might enjoy taking in the atmosphere. The imagery and symbolism are quite on-the-nose yet effective, and the stories will stick with me for a while.

I would describe it as an atmospheric adventure game rather than a horror game, although one of its subnarratives is mechanically and aesthetically more akin to a horror title (think Clock Tower). So if you're expecting a true horror game, it might be too little for you, but if you're averse to horror, it might be too much. And just like with those PS3 cult classics, you need a certain tolerance to general jank to be able to get through it. If you don't mind that -- and I certainly don't -- it's a worthwhile experience.

The first hour of this game is genuinely exciting and gets your ready for a solidly crafted dungeon crawling RPG experience. However, every minute past that one hour mark exposes more and more problems, a lack of care from the developers, and the idea that this game is just another piece of bloatware for VR catalogs. 
 The Swordplay/melee combat in this game is atrocious. Enemies attacks are wild, fast, and often pass through any attempt to guard as their model awkwardly pushes into yours and damages you from behind. Parrying, although in the tutorial shows that it can temporarily stun the target if done correctly, often does nothing but stop their swing just so they can immediately take another from a completely different angle. As someone who has played games like "Blade and Sorcery" or "Legendary Tales" this was massively dissapointing to me.
 Now speaking of parrying not working, there are a number of bosses in this game that are just the most miserable experience I think I've ever had the displeasure of encountering. Every boss I've encountered are MASSIVE  damage sponges. I'm talking like killing the boss took about the same amount of time as exploring the entire rest of the dungeon. And partly due to the fact, I'm sure, that melee combat is just utterly pointless when it comes to these bosses. Their attacks are literally unblockable altogether, and some of them just fly in the air forever and range is your only option anyway. Back pedaling for 10 minutes and spamming ranged attacks is not an enjoyable boss fight. It's uninteresting and unrewarding.
 Not to mention the RPG elements, or the "exosuit" is so embarassingly bland and practically nonexistant it often doesn't even feel worth it to do the boring crystal hunt game mode which is the only way to gain skill points for it. You have four slots, each dedicated to "Head, Chest, Arms, and Legs" and each category has it's own tree with unique abilities. But every ability is nothing more than a small, do nothing percentage boost. Things like "Do 10% more melee damage" "Take 20% less magic damage" I've never seen an rpg with a skill tree like this get praised, and I do not think just because this game is VR it should get a pass.
 All of this comes together with the fact that there are four different biomes, and they feel largely like simple recolors of eachother rather than distinct environments. The enemies that spawn are largely the same save the "critters", the rooms and dungeon layout are largely the same with some minor differences in decor.
 Ultimately I think I wouldn't be as hard on this game if it weren't for the fact that Legendary Tales didn't already exist, which is a VR hack and slash RPG with much deeper combat, far more interesting skill trees which actually change how you play, and bosses with mechanics who you can also safely engage at melee range if you're good at blocking. All in all I can't recommend this game and seriously do not think it's worth your time or money.

I first discovered this game back in 2017 and... at the time it was rough. Very obviously a pre-alpha indie title. It had good bones, but there just wasn't enough there yet to make it a *game* you could *play*. 

I've been playing a LOT of Valheim recently (and loving every minute of it), but I've been pushing up against its limitations. Not enough wildlife, not enough build piece diversity, too many mobs interrupting my homesteading, too few environmental hazards. So I asked AI for a suggestion that might fill those gaps and it suggested Rising World. 

A LOT HAS CHANGED SINCE 2017!!! 
The Good:
- More wildlife
- More construction/building diversity
- More chill (seriously, this game has ALL of the chill)
- More smooth jazz
- OH MY GAWD IT'S SO PRETTY

The Bad:
- Confusing tech tree
- QOL issues
- Overly granular crafting/building 

The Ugly:
- OMG THIS GAME IS SO PRETTY that even the max view distance isn't max enough :(
- It's still a pre-release indie title so be ready for bugs 
- Just figuring out what to do when you first start playing is ROUGH, even with the help "Journal"
- Despite having more of some things, it has less of others - your clothing and cooking options are still fairly nonexistent

The tech tree is less of a tree and more of a ficus: it's somewhat nonlinear, very confusing, overwhelming, and lacks the structure that Valheim and other titles provide that could balance its complexity. It lacks any kind of theme to give it cohesion. It's really just a jumble of seemingly random anachronistic tools and items, and the utility of any given thing you might craft is hard to pin down without watching a youtube video to explain it - and there aren't a lot of youtube videos out there for Rising World just yet. The core gameplay would improve DRAMATICALLY if it had a clear, linear tech progression that provided a short list of clear farming/crafting/homesteading goals for each tier. 

There are a LOT of quality-of-life issues with the UI, interactions with the world, and the core mechanics of the game. 
Input: Every other video game uses E as the main "Interact" key, but Rising World chooses F for some reason. Every other game users Left-click for placing objects/build pieces but Rising World chooses Right-click for some reason. You can rebind keys, of course, but there are still shortcomings in what each input option does so keybinding is only part of the problem. I think the entire input system needs an overhaul. 
UI/Menus: The crafting UI lacks any detail on what the "stats" of any particular object are, so you don't know how one pair of shoes will impact your gameplay over another without crafting both of them. There are stats, only visible if you hover over a crafted item in your inventory. 

Crafting is monotonous bordering on torturous. Some people really go for that "high fidelity" "realism" in survival crafting games, I don't. I'm actually not a fan of the entire survival crafting genre, mostly because I hate having to micromanage every single task. I have enough trouble remembering to eat and drink in real life, much less in a game. And other tasks, like harvesting a crop, just take too long. As an acute example, spinning yarn requires holding down a mouse button and a keyboard button and then just sitting there. You spend more time *watching* the game than *playing* it. If that's your idea of fun, more power to you, but If I stop playing Rising World it'll be because I got bored watching a spinning wheel spin while giving myself carpal tunnel. 

The build system is VERY flexible, but it's also so complex that it's intimidating. I played for 10 hours yesterday with all my crafting stations out in the open before I finally had enough wherewithal to face the building system. More structure in the tech tree to limit your build options so there's less overwhelm would help, but also the game needs more prefab build pieces that you don't have to "pick a shape" or "resize" to use. A handful of prefab wall/floor/ceiling/roof pieces that you could quickly drop in the world and arrange to make a simple "first shelter" would go a long way to helping new players feel less intimidated by the more advanced construction tools (which should probably be introduced later anyway, after players have gotten familiar with the rest of the game and are ready for something more complicated and flexible). On a related note - building that first rudimentary shelter had way too many prerequisites and did not feel intuitive at all. You mean I have to build medieval-level of tech tree crafting stations before I can build a stick lean-to? (Only a *slight* exaggeration.)

I know this is long so I'll cut to the chase: Overall this game is fun and engaging, and it *does* qualify as a *game* now. But it's got a lot of rough edges. It will be confusing and intimidating for new players, especially casual players who are attracted to it for the chill vibes. The core gameplay lacks cohesiveness and doesn't have enough meat to keep players engaged long-term. And the cludgy UI and pedantic level of crafting minutia will limit the game's appeal to a small niche of gamers. 

If you're into survival crafting games and want something that's environmentally chill and cinematic, and also like games that feel like real-life chores, then you'll love Rising World. And I expect it will only get better, especially when I see how far it's come since I first tried it way back when.

If I had a “maybe” option for a recommendation, I’d check it. After about ten hours in, I’ve been pulled in by what Mirthwood could be—and frustrated by where it falls short.

Let’s start with the high-points. The music and voice-overs set an atmospheric tone so strong I kept pausing just to take a moment and listen. The graphics are storybook-beautiful, charming in a way that whispers “cozy medieval fantasy” but with a bit of grit. I’ve been waiting for a grimdark lifelike farming sim—“a harvest-moon meets middle-ages” kind of game—and Mirthwood is fulfilling that fantasy.
The crafting loop is deep and fun: gathering, refining, building, outfitting—there’s real joy in mixing and matching furniture, walls, floors, and even tailoring your character’s look with armor, greaves, helmets and under-armor. On those fronts: 10/10.

But... here’s where the cracks show. The systems I love are stellar, but others—including ones I care deeply about—just don’t land.

Relationships and NPCs. I think many devs chasing the success of something like Stardew Valley underestimate how much we care about characters. In Stardew we know each villager, their quirks, their arc. In Mirthwood the folks feel like walking text-boxes: no personality, no heart. I don’t care about them. A weak social system is especially glaring when the game teases NPC death mechanics (coming in an update) but I’m hardly invested enough to care when the mechanic triggers. That disconnect is echoed across several reviews. 

Combat. It’s clunky. Moving a 2D‐style character in a 3D space, fighting, especially with a bow—just feels awkward. I roll past an enemy, swing the wrong way, miss entirely. Based on external reviews:

“enemies constantly jump backwards to avoid attacks… you can only perform combat actions while facing left or right” 
CGMagazine

“archery… tricky to use… precision feels nearly impossible” 
Gamerheads Podcast

Yes, melee feels okay, but the lack of a proper lock-on system like classic titles (e.g., The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time) makes fights frustrating rather than fun.

Farming & loop issues. On the upside, you can play in a “build up your homestead” mode, which I love. But some systems drag: seeds are costly; upgrades require massive material investment; and there’s a sense of going in circles. One reviewer said:

“My character still hasn’t managed more than one tool upgrade after 20 hours.” 
PC Gamer (someone doesent know how to grind like a pro lol)

And others point to performance problems—frame rate drops, stutters—which hamper immersion. 

Overall? Yes—you should play Mirthwood. It is absolutely worth your time if you’re drawn to its artistic vision, the sandbox-life chase, the crafting aesthetic. But go in knowing it’s a “beautifully imperfect” piece right now. It’s as much about promise as it is about present execution. If you’re someone who cares most about character heart, super tight combat, or ultra-polished systems—I’d wait for the next major update. But if you’re happy wandering, building, crafting, and immersing in mood, you’re in for a treat.

[h1]圧倒的な自由度で殴り合うモンスター育成ゲーム[/h1]
モンスター育成成分が不足していたので、セール中に購入。
序盤でなかなかハマらずに少し積んでいましたが、舐めてました。面白すぎました。
実績コンプリート済み、途中放置して他の事をしていた時間もあるのでプレイ時間は参考にならないと思います。

簡単にまとめると、
[b]・戦術の自由度が高いので組むのが楽しい。
・個体値や努力値が無いのでずっと使い続けられる。
・クリア後はやり込み要素の強いハクスラに。
・序盤は様々な面でやや難ありか。[/b]

[h2]良かったところ[/h2]
[h3]◆高い自由度で中盤以降はやりたい放題できる[/h3]
PvPがメインじゃないのもあって、かなり好き放題戦術を組めます。
先制で全体催眠、先制で高火力ぶっぱでオーバーキルなどやりたい放題です。
それに対し、相手も先制技を跳ね返してきたり、一部のタイプに強力な耐性を組んでいたりと一強の戦術は組ませてくれないため、こちら有利のバランスでありながら偏った戦術だけでは勝ちづらい良い調整になっています。
[h3]◆クリア後はハクスラでさらに強くなれる[/h3]
レア効果を収集して合成してステッカーを作るのが楽しすぎます。
レア効果もブートレグ（色違いみたいなもの）を多く編成すれば結構手に入るので、バンバン強くなっていくのが気持ち良いです。
[h3]◆個体値や努力値といった数値が無い[/h3]
知ってしまうとどうしても意識したり、やりこみ時に旅パから切り替えたりしないといけなくなるシステムですが、こういったものが存在しないため、ずっと使い続ける事ができます。
途中でキャラクターの能力を振り分けるシステムが追加されますが、それもデメリット無しで何度も振り直せるため阻害しません。
[h3]◆個体数に限りのあるモンスターがいない[/h3]
伝説や準伝や幻といった、1体限りのモンスターはいません。
御三家…御二家？も低確率で出現したりレートは高いものの交換したりできますし、その他一度しか戦えないように見える相手も後々野生で普通に出現するようになります。
[h3]◆ローカライズがしっかりしている[/h3]
文脈やフォントなども違和感がなく、きちんとローカライズできていると感じました。
ただ、表現や文化的な価値観などはやっぱり海外のゲームだなと感じたので、その辺りは合う合わないがあるかもです。
[h3]◆ボーカルありなしが状況で切り替わるBGM[/h3]
このゲームの特徴とも言えますが、フュージョンした際、もしくは相手がフュージョンした際などにインストからボーカル曲に自然と切り替わるのが熱い。
しかも全部？の戦闘曲が対応していて素晴らしいです。

[h2]気になったところ[/h2]
[h3]◆基本ダブルバトルなので雑魚戦でもテンポが悪くなりがち[/h3]
序盤はステッカーが少なく、APが無いと満足に戦えないので雑魚戦でも時間がかかります。
中盤以降は一気にサクサク進行できるようになるものの、終盤はパッシブ発動を増やさないと手強くなるので再びやや時間がかかるようになります。
せめてエフェクトやモーションのOFF設定ができれば改善されるのですが…（MODならできるらしいです）
[h3]◆序盤は消耗戦が多く帰還が増えがち[/h3]
火力を出せないので何度かダメージを受けてしまうのと、回避を織り交ぜても運によっては被弾が増えるので、数回の戦闘で帰還やキャンプまで戻らざるを得ない状態になります。
ただ、中盤以降はこの点も改善されるので、全体的にテンポの悪い序盤をどう乗り切るかが大事かなと思います。
[h3]◆ステッカーのUIが使いづらい[/h3]
良さげな効果を見つけてもどのモンスターが装備可能なのかが分かりづらく、やり込み段階になったら英語のWiki片手にプレイしないとやりづらいです。
レア効果付きは同じレア効果でもスタックされずにかさばっていくのもマイナスポイント。

[h2]まとめ[/h2]
総合的にとても完成度が高く、面白いゲームだなと感じました。
モンスターのデザインもやや癖があるものの、幅が広く親しみやすいのもいるので、好みのが見つかると思います。
[strike]というより最近は走りであり代表でもある某ゲームのがキャラデザや個性付けや顔芸やメ〇シンカが奇抜になりすぎて苦手[/strike]

Rock of Ages 2: Bigger & Boulder is a physics-driven action game that combines tower defense and racing. The player controls a giant rolling boulder and must navigate obstacle courses while defending their own base. The structure alternates between planning defenses and attacking enemy gates.

The core loop emphasizes momentum. Steering is sensitive, and the level designs include jumps, hazards, and enemy traps. Losing speed reduces damage on impact, so route efficiency matters. Physics interactions can feel chaotic but create surprising moments.

Defense building uses units like catapults, walls, and explosives. Placement directs or stalls incoming boulders. Resource limits create tradeoffs between density and coverage. The balance improves as new defenses unlock through campaign progress.

Art style draws heavily from art history. Characters and environments parody famous paintings and sculptures. Visual humor keeps tone light. Cutscenes use paper-doll animation that exaggerates expressions for comedic effect.

Multiplayer adds depth. Racing against other players increases tension, and meta strategy becomes important. Competitive matches are fast and reward map knowledge and trap placement. Stability is consistent, though matchmaking can vary in population.

Sound design supports comedic presentation. Music adapts classical themes into playful arrangements. Impact effects are sharp and communicate damage clearly. Voice acting is minimal and leans on slapstick delivery.

Rock of Ages 2: Bigger & Boulder targets players who enjoy physics chaos and creative tower defense. It may feel unpredictable to those who prefer precise control. Fans will find replay value in multiplayer, humor, and varied stage design.

ACE Team’s brand of historical absurdity returns with Rock of Ages II: Bigger & Boulder, a sequel that gleefully doubles down on everything ridiculous, creative and chaotic about the original, and mostly succeeds. If the first Rock of Ages was a strange experiment that somehow worked, this follow-up feels like the studio saying, “You thought that was weird? Hold my boulder.”

Once again, you roll a massive stone through handcrafted stages, smashing through enemy defenses and castles while building your own fortifications in return. But Bigger & Boulder polishes and expands on the formula in all the right ways. The physics are tighter, the level design more ambitious and the roster of boulders (yes, each with different stats and special abilities) adds a welcome layer of strategic depth. The environments - inspired by different art movements and mythologies - are more vibrant, detailed and surreal than ever, turning every match into a moving museum of chaos.

The game’s sense of humor is as sharp and absurd as always. Its cutscenes, rendered in that distinctive paper-cutout style, parody everything from Romanticism to modern pop culture with deadpan brilliance. The soundtrack - a reimagining of classical compositions - keeps the energy high, while the pacing between offense and defense feels smoother and more refined this time around.

On the downside, the game’s online mode can be inconsistent, with occasional lag and matchmaking hiccups, and the AI still struggles to pose much of a challenge. But the improvements in visuals, variety and overall flow make this a clear evolution over its predecessor.

Rock of Ages II: Bigger & Boulder is funnier, sharper and better balanced than the original; it's a joyful, artistic descent into madness that somehow turns rolling rocks into one of gaming’s most eccentric pleasures.

Higurashi When They Cry Hou – Ch.5 Meakashi retells the events of the previous arc from Shion’s perspective and exposes the hidden logic behind several long-running mysteries. It is a turning point in the series because it reframes familiar scenes with direct access to Shion’s motives, impulses, and errors. The result is a clearer picture of how the tragedy unfolds.

The narrative is defined by escalation. Shion’s emotional volatility, loyalty, and fixation drive every decision. The chapter tracks her gradual slide from frustration into obsession and then into catastrophic action. The writing avoids sensationalism and instead focuses on methodical cause-and-effect.

As a perspective arc, Meakashi explains contradictions from earlier chapters. Moments that once appeared supernatural now read as misunderstandings or deliberate misinterpretations. This strengthens the series’ central theme: human choices often produce outcomes that feel supernatural only because observers lack full context.

Interactivity remains minimal. This is a linear kinetic novel without branching paths. The value comes from piecing together narrative threads across chapters, not influencing outcomes. Meakashi’s structure rewards readers who track timelines and character relationships closely.

Presentation aligns with the Hou releases. Visual assets are simple, but the soundtrack carries emotional weight and marks each psychological shift. Tension builds through music and pacing rather than animation or visual flourish.

Thematically, Meakashi explores jealousy, pressure, and the collapse of judgment under stress. It addresses how personal grievances scale into irreversible harm. The arc is heavier and more direct than earlier entries, making it one of the darker structural pillars of the series.

Higurashi When They Cry Hou – Ch.5 Meakashi delivers critical narrative clarity and psychological focus. It resolves earlier ambiguities, deepens character understanding, and sets the foundation for later arcs. It works as one of the most important and most intense chapters in the entire sequence.

1.游戏tag写着推理，推理在哪？推理成分不到10%吧。如果把同为韩国游戏的异能缉凶作为参照，假设异能缉凶的推理成分是10，那么本游戏大约是1。
2.游戏中85%以上成分都是解谜小游戏，可以认为是低配版锈湖。之所以说是低配，是因为这些解谜小游戏和游戏主题没有任何关系。制作组想让你在这里修管子你就得修管子，想让你弹钢琴你就得弹钢琴，即使目前正在追查在逃的凶手你也得玩这些幽默小游戏。
3.说到弹钢琴，默认玩家必须看得懂五线谱才能完成解谜，写出这种设计案的关卡策划也是这辈子有了。
4.而且根本不给出「之前通过这条路的角色」到底是怎么在「没有解谜的情况下通过的」或「通过之后将谜题复原了」的解释。反正主角来的时候人不见了，而一切东西都得你从犄角旮旯里找出来重新拼好。
5.女主角莫名其妙就从侦探爱好者jk变成能不带任何表情在凶案现场验尸的神秘武装jk了，一点角色成长的弧光都没有。这在剧情的人物设计上也算得上是败笔。
6.简体中文翻译有很多错别字，「河谷镇」的相关译名也没有统一，让给人的感觉是找了个暑期大学生做的简单翻译。虽然除了最后的选词填空（由于翻译的词语词性导致的问题）以外基本不影响游戏进程，但还是有点不爽。
7.不过，本作的美术还是比较在线的，尤其是街景的设计——虽然我严重怀疑大量霓虹灯布置的商店街在1960年是否可能存在，但那句话怎么说的来着，「二次元的事你少管」。

如果把tag里的推理改成解谜，我或许会打好评……不过也可能根本不会买就是了。总之，如果你只喜欢推理游戏而对纯解谜游戏不感冒，我不建议你玩这个游戏。

It is really, really, REALLY irritating to me that I like this game, because I have some major gripes with it.

I wanna get the stuff I really like out of the way first. It was obviously made by someone with a strong passion for Weird Fiction who gets it in a way that the developers of DREDGE do not (the fact that there's a reference to "The Shunned House" instead of just the standard "hurr durr Colour Out of Space Shadow Over Innsmouth Call of Cthulhu" stuff you get in these types of games is awesome. The only way you could demonstrate a better familiarity with Lovecraft is if you referenced something insane like "The Beast in the Cave" or "Beyond the Wall of Sleep", things practically nobody has read). The idea of being able to play an Arkham Horror-style board game by myself is very appealing, since Arkham Horror takes two cumulative days to set up, play and dissassemble, and I think for the most part the execution is very cool in a way that made me want to keep playing until I 100 percented it.

Now comes the serious issue I have with this game, which is that after a couple of runs it just doesn't feel fun or interesting to play anymore. Once you realize how to get the best endings for every Mystery there's no real reason to play them any other way (and a lot of Mysteries aren't actually that deep, having an investigation along the lines of "kill the boss" or "make a single choice at the end", and they railroad you into a bad ending unless you do a lot of planning beforehand). The combat feels floaty and lifeless, as it's just clicking buttons on a static image while your health decreases each turn. I'm not saying every game has to be gorgeously animated, but I think RPG Maker games (e.g. Look Outside, especially relevant to this example) have proven that you can make very static turn-based combat more engaging than this. The art in this game is wildly inconsistent; I get that they're going for a low-poly look but there are a handful of sprites and drawings here and there that look weirdly proportioned or like rough sketches. Maybe it's unfair, but i feel like if you're deliberately aping the artstyle of Junji Ito, a guy who is a superhuman at drawing, then I expect the artwork to at least try to match his quality (an admittedly far-fetched task, so again this is perhaps unfair).

That brings me to my biggest overall gripe with this game, which is that it just feels unfinished. Even after deliberately waiting years for this game to come out of Early Access before touching it, it's still missing several features and doesn't have that rewarding of a gameplay loop. Why doesn't this game have Steam achievements? Why does the game just anticlimactically end with a series of boring skill checks? Why are there a bunch of features that presumably involve the upcoming "scenario mode" that don't currently do anything, like the VHS player in your apartment? I want to err on the side of good faith and not be a conspiracist who says that the dev dragged out the development process for as long as he could in order to provide a sustainable source of income, but it is confusing nonetheless when he will disappear for years at a time without providing any updates on new content or estimates for its arrival. Not to lean too heavily on one comparison here, but Look Outside was a game that was blatantly, self-admittedly, OBVIOUSLY incomplete at launch and yet still felt like more of a finished product than this, not to mention that Coloumbe has been pumping out updates to re-add back in all the stuff that was cut for time during development over the past year.

I dunno. Would I recommend this game? I guess I'd have to say yes. It very much appeals to my sensibilities and was made by someone who understands the inspirational material they were working with, and those first few runs where you're constantly discovering new events and mysteries are genuinely exciting. But I can't help but feel that even discounted at 17 bucks this game was a tad overpriced. It might end up resonating more with other players than it did with me, so caveat emptor.

I have been following the series ever since the first game released in 2008, and it has always been a franchise I truly enjoyed. GRID Legends is easily one of the best racing games I have played recently. The graphics are stunning. The cars and their details, the environments, and everything you look at are genuinely eye pleasing. Especially during night races or in foggy conditions, the atmosphere becomes absolutely captivating. The soundtrack is far better than what you would normally expect from a racing title, featuring several adrenaline-inducing pieces of music that elevate the overall experience. In a racing game, the most important element is the driving feel, and GRID Legends truly excels here. When you switch from one car to another, the difference is immediately noticeable. You have to quickly adapt to each vehicle's speed, grip, and handling characteristics. There is a wide variety of cars, and I genuinely enjoyed driving every single one of them. The tracks are just as impressive, with the developers crafting fast, intense, adrenaline-filled circuits that keep the excitement high. The story mode is decent, but I did not enjoy feeling like a robot simply watching events unfold. It would have been much better if the main character had taken a more active role and actually participated in the narrative with dialogue and real involvement. In general, it's good, but it could have benefitted from a bit more depth. The career mode, on the other hand, is incredible. There is an enormous amount of content. You can unlock new events, acquire new cars, and even complete sponsor challenges that open up special races and unique vehicles. The career mode never seems to run out of things to do, making it one of the strongest parts of the game. As much as I love the main game, I cannot say the same for the DLC. Story mode for the DLC is especially disappointing, filled with awkward cutscenes and uninspired maps. I completed all of them, and compared to the base game, they all feel mediocre at best. In summary, GRID Legends is an amazing racing game, whether you are a longtime fan of the genre or completely new to it. Its stunning graphics, energetic soundtrack, and excellent gameplay come together to create a memorable and thrilling experience

Геймплейно — просто царство. Уровни стали огромными, с кучей этажей и комнат. Да, иногда из-за этого можно застрять и поймать пулю из-за угла, которую не видно- это бесит. Но когда запоминаешь расположение врагов и выстраиваешь свою кровавую цепочку — чувствуешь себя богом.
А сколько всего нового! Арсенал просто огонь — от подручного хлама до серьезной артиллерии. И враги теперь не лыком шиты — некоторые носят бронежилеты, и их сходу не возьмешь.

Что касается ачивок — это отдельный хардкор. Чтобы выбить все, нужно быть настоящим маньяком: пройти уровни с высшими оценками, найти все секреты и не сломать при этом мышь. Это вызов для самых упертых фанатов, но чувство выполненного долга того стоит.
Короче, если первая часть была гениальным наброском, то вторая — это уже полноценная картина, написанная кровью и неоном. Игра сложнее, длиннее и безумнее. Иногда даже слишком, но оторваться невозможно. Маст-хэв для всех, у кого есть нервы и жажда адреналина. Рекомендую всем!

[h1]Beyond hope[/h1]
I came across this title in the same way I imagine most people did – by watching the game’s neat trailer, showcasing a haunted London with a sprinkle of sci-fi. Drawn in by the appeal of the setting, I opted to give Beyond Hanwell a try, knowing full well that a horror game by unknown developer will likely need to be taken with a grain of salt. For now, let’s just say that the first-hand experience has exceeded my wildest expectations. Nonetheless, the game’s selling point is stellar – located in Westminster district of London, the surroundings are stylish, atmospheric and a treat to look at. It’s a shame that precious little else about this title matches the quality of its visuals.

[b]City of the damned[/b]
Let’s start off on a good note, the protagonist arrives to the city via underground tunnel, dug underneath the wall, which otherwise separates the entire district form the outside world. After a short tutorial section, the game gives a pointer on where to start, but otherwise leaves the player to explore the district at their own pace. Beyond Hanwell has a small, albeit open world, allowing free exploration of Westminster streets in search of points of interest. Such locations can be easily divided between major story-related locations and optional set pieces, often rewarding exploration with a handy upgrade.
[url]https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3590595953[/url]
I strongly recommend following the game’s advice to begin at New Lyceum Theater, as this is possibly the best location of the title and, at least to me, the most cohesive one. Half-derelict and abandoned, save for a massive number of mannequins, the place has an effective ‘haunted house’ feel to it. Furthermore, the location does well to introduce the player to further game mechanics – the plain combat system and somewhat slap-dash crafting, giving an incentive to gather pieces of junk strewn across shelves and cupboards of the city. Theater tour concludes with a confrontation at the main scene, amped up by excellent musical track first heard in the main menu, delivering possibly the best sequence of the game. With interest thus piqued, I embarked on a vague quest to gather 4 governmental ID badges. And then the rest of the game happened, to be blunt, it only goes downhill from here.

[b]Know you’re anomolies[/b]
Let’s begin with the narrative. You may ask yourself a question of “why am I the only breathing person in the entire district of London” – at face value, the situation is explained by rampant anomalous activity (if you’ve heard of SCP foundation before, you will know exactly what kind of anomalies), which ominous governmental body “the Ministry” held back at first, only to abandon Westminster as social order inevitably collapsed. On paper, this is a fairly compelling post-apocalyptic setup. Unfortunately, the longer you spend exploring and reading numerous notes with bits of exposition, the less coherent Beyond Hanwell’s setting becomes. Say, anomalies at first appear to be a recent occurrence, which has caused the world to collapse. However, there is a bloody Museum of Anomalies, which outright states the supernatural to have been a known phenomenon for centuries and that concepts such as parallel dimensions are apparently a thing. I can appreciate that developers had a wellspring of ideas for the game, but perhaps some of them should’ve been scrapped along the way, especially that from the gameplay perspective, London has been struck by half-baked zombie apocalypse.
[url]https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3590596711[/url]
Enemy variety and by extension, the combat altogether are arguably the lowest point of Beyond Hanwell. Despite the potential for infinite variety the game’s lore hints at (the story takes place in the future on top of everything else going on), the opposition primarily takes form of several types of similar, emaciated corpses and giant spiders. To be frank, the enemy roster seems so out of place at times, that you can get an impression the zombies were copied straight out of generic asset package. Simply put, disparity of quality between the enemies and the environment is striking. Worse yet, the combat is riddled with bugs. Cinematic follow-ups of melee look well during the trailer, however the fights often take place in narrow spaces, wherein the enemy and the player partially sink into the wall, making the ordeal a mess of clipping issues. Other notable bugs involve pathfinding, which causes the enemies to stop at certain doorways and don’t you dare shoot the spiders with a pistol. The critter will sink into the ground and continue clipping around the player throughout the entire location, while also making insufferable noises as it attempts to strike from underneath the floor. On the sidenote, the spelling mistakes in subheader of this section are quoted from the posters found throughout the game, which is made more confounding by the fact Steel Arts Software is apparently a British company.
[url]https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3590596972[/url]
[b]London bridge is falling down[/b]
Unfortunately, Beyond Hanwell’s shenanigans don’t end there. Westminster’s landscape is powered by Unreal Engine 5, meaning you need some serious hardware for the game to run as expected. Especially taking into account it only does so on “ultra” setting. Truth be told, this title has one of the most bizarre graphics settings I’ve ever encountered, with some of the features outright shutting down at “medium” (I dread to think what “low” does) and notably, entire chunks of terrain turning invisible. FPS drops I was hoping to tweak with thus reduced settings, were not affected. Just weird.

All things considered, I believe the point has been made thoroughly enough at this stage – essentially every aspect of the game comes with a number of caveats, including the visuals which are Beyond Hanwell’s only strength. Despite all of my reservations, there is a glimmer of potential here, highlighted by the game’s strong opening section. Unfortunately, it is essentially a trick to elevate the player’s expectations, which is ultimately a disservice, as the rest of this title has no hope of keeping up. To my eyes, the game would greatly benefit from trimming down some of its more outlandish ideas in order to deliver a more focused and cohesive experience. Many of the smaller side-locations in Beyond Hanwell highlight this notion well, as a bite-sized sections such as haunted pub, snuff film studio or twisted carnival genuinely work as an indie horror set pieces.

Ultimately, I struggle to recommend this game at all, especially at full price. Should you happen to come across it at a hefty discount, perhaps an indie horror veteran, accustomed to quirks often involved with the genre may find it approachable. Similarly, if the Union Jack happens to be your banner, Beyond Hanwell’s interpretation of historical district of London just might be the saving grace to make the experience worthwhile. Otherwise, if you were hoping to find a hidden gem here, just heed my advice and go dig somewhere else.

一周した感想。

アトリエシリーズ、名前だけは知っていたのですが、やったこともゲーム内容も知らず、プレイしました。

オリジナル版をやって絶望し挫折、リメイク版をやりました。

アトリエって、錬金術のゲームだったんですね。

なぜかほぼフルボイス
どうして？　純粋に驚いた。モブにも割と声があるのにも驚き。

ゲームシステム
よくも悪くもリミットがあるのが、緊張感と、時間配分を考えるというのが楽しいですね。
伝説へとなれたのは何気嬉しかった。

わりとイベント見逃しちゃったのは残念。あと、複数エンド見るために０から周回は正直面倒ですね。
ただ、一周は割とそこまで時間かからないですね。私の場合１日とちょっとでクリアしました。後半はほとんどやることがなくなるのも正直欠点かな。日付だけ気を付ける日々。かといって、キャラ育成するには時間が足りないというね。

イベントのタイミングが何年目のみとかも多く、取り逃したらもう一周するか、ロードしかないというのも残念。

ただ、完璧を目指さなくても、伝説エンディングは普通に行けますし、十分満足できました。

最大の欠点は、２，３がリメイクされていないこと。ＰＳ持ってないよｗ

総評としては面白い作品でした。
