Before you play there is a mental switch you need to make.  

In this game you do not collect a team of cute pets to face the world.  

In this game you gather disposable minions you throw at problems often intentionally sacrificing them for a chance at a stronger new minion.  

The second you stop thinking about your cute little pets as your companion and see them as the disposable slaves they are the game stops being impossibly hard and the whole game opens up with wide tactical choices every battle.  


Without this mental switch well, you get some of the negative reviews here complaining about how hard the game is.  

If you use a taming item to heal with instead, that's 99% of the time a mistake. Healing that weak minion could also have been used to tame a stronger minion instead.  

This game is great IF you're willing to make that switch in how you see your pets. 

They are disposable slaves, use them as such.  

The game is great, very unique as this is not how pet games  or deck builders are generally done. It's fresh, unique and the art is just gorgeous. Absolutely amazing work.

看到游戏的好评率一路走低，有点难过，来说点好话吧。

老卡牌玩家。
游戏时长36.2小时（有挂机的时间实际上可能20多吧）
已通过全部地图的极难，真结局以及收集了全部故事书页。
没有尝试无尽等特殊模式（个人游戏审美，对无尽以及各种变体玩法没什么兴趣）。


【玩法】：
不断驯服怪物，优化配队，融合调试出强力怪物，努力活下去。

虽然大家可能都会戏称是类宝可梦，“宝克梦”游戏。
但实际上，游戏理念和宝可梦相差甚远。

怪物拥有生命和速度两个属性。
每个怪物有着若干技能和天赋。伤害主要依靠技能的数值以及各种buff。
几乎所有技能和天赋都可以用针管抽出，注射到其他怪物体内，自己搭配融合各种强力怪物。
（这方面比邪恶冥刻有点像，但更加自由）

游戏的上手难度非常高。玩家需要对战斗内的结算有非常清晰的理解，否则会迅速被战损所击垮。
大部分情况下，你抓的怪物都是为了度过当前的困境。

一开始，我没熟悉玩法之前，还带着其他卡牌游戏的思维，总是想去救下自己的怪。结果被打的鼻青脸肿。
后面理解了游戏本质后，游戏的难度直线下降。（已经可以任意地图极难连胜，但需要SL）
它们只是工具，素材库，用完就丢的弃子。
唯一能让早期怪再后期有用武之地的设计是金甲虫和银甲虫。可以让初阶怪进化，一跃变成4阶/5阶的强力大哥。
也许是为了迎合虚构层上营造的世界观氛围————这个设计不是常驻机制，而是一个随机事件。


【美术&音乐】
游戏有着优质的美术和音乐。卡面的画风和质感都有万智牌的风格（让我想起了很早以前玩的旅法师对决2014？）。
图鉴和世界观的融合做的很好。是以主角的视角所写下的深渊冒险日记。

音乐并不多，没到怪物火车那个地步，但是和世界观的结合恰到好处，有代入感。可以随时回想起几个旋律。

能看到自己遇到，抓到过的怪物的背景信息。带着胜利过的怪还可以解锁一个豆知识。
（很抽象，从游戏性的角度出发，终盘时所有的初级怪基本都没有意义）。

也许是为了真实感，这个图鉴与其说是游戏里的图鉴，不如说真的是个日志。
它根本没有提供怪物的任何游戏性信息（怪物的攻防，技能组等），只有背景内容。
据说或许会更新这一部分。怎么说呢，好像破坏了一点意境，但可能还是必要的吧。

每次打完都会解锁一些进度，可以解锁更多日记章节。笔者后面每次胜利好像能解锁2章。一共25章。


【设定&剧情&世界观】
据说和《来自深渊》类似（我没看过）。

世界观的设定也丰富有趣，让我非常有动力打完故事书页。
玩家需要扮演一个生物学家，不断向深渊探索。（很全能的主角，会驯兽懂生物还会画画拼图鉴写日志......）

图鉴里虽然没有怪物的游戏性信息，但是真的很像一个真正的日志。
每个怪物都有一段栩栩如生的背景描述，拼贴的照片，以及主角的手绘画。
非常有沉浸感。

剧情不多剧透，大概讲述的就是一个人逐渐步入深渊的心路历程（物理和精神的双重意义上）。
因为笔者今年家里的猫去世了。一些剧情让我挺意难平的。

真结局最后一场战斗，颠覆了怪物先手，玩家后手的设计。
看到有玩家说，这是否意味着主角也从人变成了怪物呢？


【一些可以改进的地方】：

1. 战斗计算复杂度在同类游戏里极高。
强烈建议出类似于怪物火车的伤害预览模式。可以得知按下回合结束后的战斗结果。

游戏和尖塔一样可以回主菜单SL，在战斗内也可以和怪物火车一样回到上一个回合。
我不太理解的是...可以回主菜单SL，但战斗内的撤回却有次数限制，并且难度越高越少，直至完全没有。
和怪物火车2似乎是反过来的（怪物火车类似于，大方向的战略不能反悔，战斗内可以无限重开优化）。
而驯牌师的SL可以回到路线选择前，战斗内却处处限制。

2. 前期体验。
实话说游戏的残酷风格做的很好。笔者玩的时候沉浸感很强。
但从大众反馈来看，显然很多玩家都无法接受这个难度曲线。

平心而论，游戏的难度曲线确实过于陡峭。
这个游戏的可操作空间非常大，玩家实际上需要很多时间来适应和理解各个机制。
由于并不像尖塔，火车等游戏，用流派来区分的卡池，玩家在短时间内需要学习和理解大量词条，机制。
并且可能会陷入不知道怎么搭配各个词条的情况。

比如说，尖塔里，战士会聚焦护甲力量烧牌，贼会聚焦敏捷弃牌毒；
火车里，有的氏族注重护甲狂怒，有的注重再生等等。
而驯牌师里所有的机制都是同时交给玩家的。信息量比较大。内容消耗速度也变相加快了。

3. UI预览。
战斗内希望可以查看地图，有的时候会忘记打完之后的奖励是什么，这可能会影响食物使用的决策，要牺牲谁等等。

4. 放生（删卡）
虽然有点残忍，但可以考虑和八方旅人的猎人一样，让玩家可以把不要的怪做成肉？
可能可以缓解很多玩家反应的生存压力过大的问题。


【一些新手可能不知道的小诀窍 / 技巧】：
1. 战斗内，事件内，都可以随时用针管抽和植入天赋/技能，可操作空间极高。
2. 只从胜利角度出发，不要有救怪情节，该兑子就兑子。尤其是中期，经常会出现大量兑子来去抓敌人核心怪的情况。
3. 中后期开始应当保持牌库精简，很多时候5只就可以。（保证开局全上手）
4. 模仿者天赋模仿的技能也可以被抽取。
5. 鲸鱼，进化/飞升类的流派相对来说最轮椅，完全不需要思考组合。其他流派在中期都可能需要变阵。
6. 有的时候可以只上一只弃子，结束回合，让对方的攻击轮空打空气，躲一些aoe和麻烦的debuff。


推荐玩家群体：
1. 什么都玩的卡牌重度爱好者。
2. 抖M。喜欢在脑力上虐受苦的。
3. 对深渊世界观有兴趣的。
4. 喜欢抓宠玩法的。（比起宝可梦，更像真女神转生，Persona系列的风格）

不推荐玩家：
1. 为了爽的。这游戏并不是爽游。
2. 不喜欢算数的。比炉石复杂
3. 喜欢玩无尽模式的。目前无尽的体验看起来一般，性能优化上也有很大问题。



结语：

可以感受到这个作品是作者用心去制作的游戏。
每一只怪都有完善的设定。看到一些玩家说怪的数量太少，其实是有点寒心的。
（当然，多出点怪吧，我也想看到更多的怪）。

与其说是游戏，不如说更像是一个艺术品。
作者明显有一些自己的坚持在。
当然，这也付出了一些代价。毕竟游戏除了是艺术，也是商品。
无法否认游戏有着许多体验上的问题。

真心期待作品后续的更新。

Synergy is a great example of how a cool initial idea is completely ruined by undercooked execution.
[list]
    [*] Visual design. As you can see from the screenshots - the game looks kinda neat and unique. Here is the problem though: with this drawn design the developers did not draw every facing of a building - so not only you can’t rotate most of the buildings properly (most only have 2 options), but you are also unable to rotate the map. Considering that this game has some big buildings that can completely obscure buildings behind (making them unselectable) - the process of building near such tall structures quickly becomes irritating.
    [*] Sound design. There is none. Even after I increased volume 3 times the norm I could barely hear some completely generic BGM. Sounds of a busy, working city? None. Sounds of alarms and notifications? Almost inaudible. To put it simply - if you turn off the sound completely you would not feel the difference. In a fully released game made in 2025 this is just ridiculous.
    [*] Exploration. There are two kinds - learning the effects of the plants on your current map and going to expeditions. Both kinds are bad. The first one is completely meta-dependent: there is no randomization, so once you encounter the plants and memorize their effects - exploring your local map turns into a tedious process that you have to endure. Expeditions are the most basic and bare bones implementation of what you could see in Frostpunk, Endzone and other games. You send your teams to grab some stuff, but here are the problems: you do not control what you take in case you don’t have enough carry space to grab everything - so I lost precious resources while picking up garbage. Also, apart from the early game and 3 resources that are unobtainable by any other means - the rewards for the event are useless - getting 20 tools for a 2 month long expedition when you are producing 20 tools in 3 days is a joke. The writing of the events isn’t impressive and, what is the worst part, there aren’t enough events to keep them unique in ONE run - so you will run into repeated ones even in one scenario, and you are required to go through six.
    [*] Tech tree. To put it simply, from 5 tiers of science you will not get to anything interesting until you hit 4th tier - the time before it is just a dull grind/padding that you have to “survive” through just to get to the actual gameplay. There is a good reason why frostpunk mostly upgraded the existing building or used extremely limited resource, because this game gives you new buildings that make all of the previous tiers of water/food/housing completely useless, as lower-tier buildings are just temporary placeholders that can’t last you through the game even if you try. And every new tier of said things either has its own building requirements or sizes, so you can’t plan your city properly before you hit T4-T5. Also the tech tree is so poorly structured that prerequisite technologies are not always shown and you have to find that a completely separate, unlinked node is actually required to get the tech you want.
    [*] Biomes/plants. The idea of planting stuff that changes the properties of the land around you is great, but once again, the execution is extremely lacking. First, you will unlock the tech only on T3, but will be unable to use it properly till you get to T4 and set a proper resource gathering, as this thing is extremely pricey. Second, you can’t just select a zone and tell your people to plant - nope, you have to plant each and every plant BY HAND. Do I need to say that making a corn field clicking 30 times is extremely dull? Third, while you can find plants in expeditions - by the time you do it you have already made a big enough farm of whatever you had, so there is simply no point in replanting everything just to get a small increase that will not even pay for itself before the game ends.
    [*] Districts. Basically you have a central building for each district where you need to place your buildings. Since the space in said districts is limited and you aren’t even getting all of them til you get to T5 - you guessed it, for 70% of time your city will be a temporary setup that works but looks ugly. As soon as you hit T5 - your cities will become carbon copies of each other - because you have to build houses for 30+ people per district and need to cover all of the houses with a stupid amount of zone-projecting buildings. And while lower tier buildings will only require the building cost, T3 and further also have a significant upkeep - so you either place them in the most efficient, optimized and soulless way - or your city will be unable to keep those buildings working.
    [*] Quests. Or I’d rather call them “punishments for success”. Because every time you upgrade your district you are punished by a quest that requires you to upgrade the satisfaction of your citizens. If you don’t have technology for that and can’t complete it till the timer runs out -  you are punished so hard that it even lowers your score. If you waited and prepared for that quest beforehand - you are punished for completing it by getting more people than you have houses and/or food production (because in that game as soon as you have empty houses your citizens start to procreate fast to fill each free slot). So no matter if you win or lose - you are getting a negative result, great game design.
    [*] Scenarios. There are 6 of them, they are exactly the same. Sure, the map is different, but this is the only difference. There ARE objectives here, sure, but they all end with something on T5 - so every time I just didn’t even look at objectives getting my city to the ideal state and after that watching how tasks complete themselves one after another. Those scenarios are just sandbox maps with extra annoyance. 
    [*] UI. Just to be bored from the start: you have to manually set the limits for production and gathering every single scenario, there is no save option. The resource panel on top is a dropdown, so you will not see that you are running out of something if the other stuff in that category is going up. There are no good production breakdowns, there are no consumption graphs, there is almost nothing in terms of UI you could expect from a city builder.
    [*] Logistics. While at the start it works fine, when you are getting to a fully grown city, 180 population, you have to employ around 80 people just to move resources - because at this point the AI of citizens breaks, they start ignoring some buildings entirely, forget about priorities and move erratically, that leads to goods not moving and people starving despite all of the food warehouses being full. It should not be a problem in a fully released game.
[/list]
All of this leads to one conclusion - the game becomes a boring grind, first to get through the tech tree to be allowed to finally build good buildings - only to grind resources to build the only working layout of the city in each and every scenario. It was interesting for exactly one scenario - where everything was new and I was experimenting with what works and what doesn’t. After that it is just extremely slow repetition of a working formula.

[h3] 雰囲気と目の付け所が素晴らしいゲーム。
言い換えるとそれ以外、ゲーム性やリプレイ性には難があると言わざるを得ない。
まあ値段分は楽しめたからオススメできるとしておくが、正直かなりギリギリの所なのは否定出来ない。[/h3]

このゲームの良い所はまず雰囲気だ。
砂漠の惑星で水に悩みながら地元の植物と格闘し、滅びた技術を求め探索隊を派遣し、乾季に苦しむ。この素晴らしい没入感の高さは面白さにつながる。
植生に目をつけたのも良い。〇〇は△△と相性が良く、この地形では▢▢が適していて、✕✕の繁殖をせき止める為に他の植物や環境変化を使う。
このパズル的ゲーム性はなかなかに面白く、ゲーム進行とともに植物の特徴が明らかになるにつれて戦略の余地が広まっていく体験は非常に興味深かった。

[b] だからこそ植物の特徴を知ってしまった初回以降のプレイは楽しみが大きく削がれてしまう。[/b]
開始シナリオによって地形も配置植物も違いその分は再プレイを楽しめるが、せいぜい2、3回のプレイで全部の植物を知れてしまい、適した組み合わせを編み出してしまった後は一気にゲームが色褪せてしまう。

[b] また、ゲームデザインそのものが特定の技術の研究、特定の建造物の建造を強要するようになっている事もリプレイ性欠如の要因となっている。[/b]
このゲームは、区域を建設し、区域を特定分野に特化し、特化分野に関連した建物を区域内に建てる事で区域を強化し、都市全体への恩恵を得ていくというのがプレイの根幹となっているのだが、[b]建物による区域強化は建物の種類ごとに上限がある。これ自体は良いのだが調理の仕方がまずい。[/b]
初期から作れる製材所を立てまくって産業区域を無限にレベルアップ出来ないのはバランス上当然だが、逆に言うと建物を建てる為の技術の大部分を[b]絶対に研究しなくてはならない[/b]し、[b]絶対に建てなくてはならない。[/b]
後半の技術は400、500の研究ポイントの貯蓄・消費を要求してくるが、研究ポイントは300が上限。上限を上げるには区域のレベルアップが必須。そしてレベルアップに必要なポイントの要求値は高く、[b]建てなくていい建物は僅かしかない。[/b]
しかもほぼ全ての建物は特定の区域にしかボーナスを与えられないので、〇〇を✕✕区域に建てる事まで必須だ。

また、建物や資材に使われる原料は代替がほぼ認められていないのも良くない。
〇〇を建てるにはレンガが必須、レンガを作るには道具が必須……というように特定の資材が連鎖的に必須になっているせいで[b]プレイする度に同じような生産ラインを作らされ、しかもその原料の連鎖的必要性によって研究の順序さえある程度束縛されてしまう。[/b]

また、住居の近くに建造物を建てる事で生活環境を改善しボーナスを得るシステムによって効率的なレイアウトも必要になる。
上位ボーナスを得る為の建物は維持費がかかるし、時間が経っても上位ボーナスを得ていないとバッドイベントが起こるし、更に生活環境は市民の知的水準でもある為に探索の結果が悪くなるからだ。

[b]住環境への範囲ボーナス目当てで効率的に敷き詰められた都市には、このゲームに期待した広漠と閑散とした静かな砂漠で逞しく生きる人々の雰囲気は微塵もない。
そして雰囲気重視で非効率に走る事は輸送コストと恐るべき乾季が許さないのだ。[/b]


[b]最序盤は割と自由度があるのは間違いない。[/b]
食料の供給を野菜にするかベリーにするか種子をオートミールに加工するか、道具を木材で作るか石で作るかといった自由度だ。
しかしそれも現地で採集できる素材により大きく制限されるので、最適解を見つけ出すパズルとしての要素が強いものだ。

[b]結果このゲームはプレイすればするほど、最序盤を凌いだ瞬間に既視感と退屈が強く浮き出てくる。
多くのシナリオがあり、それらを差別化するストーリー・イベントもあるのは確かだ。
だが、根本の都市建設の部分に本質的な自由度や意外性が存在していない為に2,3回遊ぶとゲーム開始と同時に今回のプレイが最初から最後までどういったものになるか遊ぶまでもなくわかってしまう。
このゲームは本質的な部分で開発者の想定した一本道を辿る事しか出来ないのだ。[/b]

There are things I really like about this game, and I really want to continue to play it, but there are some quality of life changes that need to be made. First off, I really like the concept of this game, and the kind of cyberpunk-ish universe and world-building with [spoiler ]1984 [/spoiler] themes. 

Issues:
1) I am missing game content/dialogue all the time because the dialogue auto scrolls way too fast. I get through about 75% of the text before it moves on to the next part of the dialogue, and this is especially frustrating when I am trying to read the text from the news on the tv. I am still getting used to the universe, and all of it's unique jargon like "fixies," "fixers," "floaters," etc. And now I'm on day 6, and I just missed some event about [spoiler] some new tax now being at 10% [/spoiler], but I looked away for a second to look something up and I lost all context for what was going on. I don't even know at this point if this event is going to affect the way you run the shop. I didn't pause at the time, because I saw something on one of the discussion posts on here that I can go back and look at the log to see the dialogue again. But... 
2) The dialogue in the log CLEARS after this point on day 6, and I noticed that the log actually clears pretty often. I genuinely don't know why. If there is a log, why doesn't it show either all dialogue history in the game, or all dialogue history for the day? Either of those options would be fine. 
3) This goes along with the text going too fast thing, but the HUE robot who acts as your guide- when he is trying to show you how to use a new tool, if you are sitting for too long, even if its because you are actively referencing the manual, or in your showcase, he pings you I SWEAR EVERY 5 SECONDS. Saying "come on, figure out the material [you dumbass]." Not only is it super annoying, but hearing the text sound effect while I'm trying to identify things is distracting me from *identifying it.* 
4) One last thing, I also find it very strange that you cannot haggle when customers offer to buy something but want a lower price. If they can negotiate for a lower price, I should be able to counter.

TLDR: Dialogue goes too fast and I'm missing shit. I would love to play this game in the future if the following things are implemented: 1) OPTIONS for autoscroll or click to continue dialogue, and allowing us to choose the speed of autocscroll 2) the "log" including all dialogue, or dialogue from the day, 3) HUE being *less effing annoying* when trying to teach you something and 4) allowing us to counter buyer negotiations as well as sellers'.

TRIANGLE STRATEGY is a tactical RPG developed by Artdink and published by Square Enix, following the legacy of classics like Final Fantasy Tactics and Tactics Ogre. It combines grid-based strategy combat with a complex, choice-driven political narrative set in the war-torn continent of Norzelia. The game’s strength lies in its layered decision-making, both on and off the battlefield.

Combat is deliberate and methodical. Positioning, terrain elevation, and unit synergy are critical. Each character has fixed abilities and roles—archers excel at height advantage, mages manipulate terrain with elemental magic, and melee fighters control space. The balance between offense, defense, and support creates a consistent tactical rhythm. Mistakes are costly but fair, encouraging planning over improvisation.

Outside battle, the “Scales of Conviction” system defines the story’s branching structure. Key decisions are voted on by party members, and persuasion determines outcomes. These choices affect alliances, character recruitment, and even major story routes. The moral ambiguity of war and governance is central, avoiding simplistic good-versus-evil framing.

Visually, TRIANGLE STRATEGY employs the “HD-2D” style—pixel art characters on 3D environments with cinematic lighting. It’s visually distinct, combining nostalgia with modern polish. The orchestral soundtrack reinforces tension and gravitas, shifting seamlessly between calm diplomacy and large-scale warfare.

Narratively, it’s dense and politically charged. Dialogue-heavy sections slow the pace, but they enrich the world’s lore and ethical complexity. The writing aims for mature realism—decisions carry real weight, often with no ideal outcome. Voice acting and localization are solid, though some scenes lean verbose.

Overall, TRIANGLE STRATEGY is a precise, intellectually driven tactics game. It values foresight, consistency, and moral complexity over spectacle. A standout title for players who enjoy strategy depth and narrative consequence in equal measure.

I feel like the score for this game is misleading.

I mean, it's a deeply flawed one, but it's genuinely a decent game (with a good game hiding underneath some issues).

What is it? It's a choices matter walking simiulator combined with essentially resource managment focused on dialogue and investigation. It's focused on political plays of the vampire court and the secrets everyone keeps. If you do not like these types of games, it's not for you. If you've played The Council you have a good idea of how it feels to play.

And the story is genuinely well done. You have three characters whose stories intertwine and they are genuinely all rather well done, they feel distinct in tone and character. The investigation and sweeping of all floors for secrets hits a decent balance between challenging and fun. The game manages to hit a few truly satysfying moments where you truly feel the power you have as a vampire. Since you have three different vampire archetypes, there is a high chance one of them fits what you enjoy at least. I certainly had fun.

Now, the faults. This is a falwed game and I'm not talking about the animation (you get used to it and the environments look pretty nice actually). Main one is that its skill progression is not well done and there are some skills without which you cannot get certain outcomes (the game will not tell you that) - do yourself a favour and look up an "Anti-anxiety safe sailing, a spoiler-free guide to the swansong" which gives pointers on that front without giving spoilers if you don't want to do multiple playthroughs/restart scenes.
Some quality of life things are also missing - manual saves are a prime example. But you can skip through the dialogue if you wish.

Is it a great game? No, too much holds it back. But it did scratch that "vampire game" itch and I think it's genuinely pretty good at what it attempts to do (it's just that it's formula is not as universally liked by all, not everyone likes walking similuator/detective type games).

First of all, I must precise that I've been studying linguistics for 5 years and that I've been learning German since 2012. And so I picked "German" as my chosen language for my walkthrough. With that in mind, here's my review:
NounTown is a good game! The idea of turning the most boring and tedious task that comes with language learning (a.k.a learning vocabulary) into a game is truly a good idea. And it works! I was quite amazed at seeing how well I could remember the few words that I did not know (or had learned but ended up forgetting throughout the years). I got the 100% in one sitting ('cause I like to suffer, I guess?) and still those new words were printed in my brain with permanent ink. This was quite impressive to me because I usually have to read countless times my lists of words in order for some of them to remain in my brain. However because of its fun vibes or because some Steam Achievements could be unlocked this way, I just learned them and still remember them to this day. So just for this, congrats to the dev' team!

Now that are a few things that I must point-out (regarding the German version of the game): some terms are wrongly chosen. As someone who has German-speaking family and who has lived in German-speaking countries for a while, some words portrayed in the game are just not used during every-day talks. "Unterhemd" (=shirt) for example is just not something that I heard any German say, to talk about a shirt people would simply say "Hemd". 
Also some words portrayed there are just so rare that it seems very pointless to teach 'em to beginners "river dolphins" for example is such a niche and unusual word to know. Whereas some very useful terms are just not present like "fridge", "washing machine" or "sink". 

In conclusion, NounTown is a very great game for a very specific audience: people who already know a bit about a language and who want to work on their vocabulary. If you do not know anything about a language you'd like to learn, do not use NounTown as your base because it's not gonna be very useful to you. NounTown doesn't teach you the rules of grammar nor syntax of the language you're tryin' to learn but it can sure help ya work revise and improve your vocabulary.

P.S.: adding body parts, more pieces of furniture, more plants/trees/crops, basic car/truck names, basic mechanical parts, some dishes, some country names, some job names and parts of the house (roof, stairs, floor etc.) to the word lists would be a great addition in my opinion.

Noun Town has been super fun to play! It’s incredibly educational and really helps with reading and vocabulary. I can’t wait to see the updates that come in the future. The graphics are right up my alley — there’s something about that low-poly style that feels so cozy and welcoming.

I do hope that in future updates, we’ll be able to customize our avatars or even create our own. I’d also love to see more conversational actions — there are some already, but I just want more!

If you’re looking for a fun, relaxing game that helps you learn the basics of a language, this is the game for you. 🎮💬

Magicka 2 continues the series’ focus on chaotic spellcasting and cooperative play. The core mechanics revolve around combining elemental inputs to create custom spells, and this system remains both deep and unpredictable. The game expects players to experiment, and as a result, no two encounters feel identical.

Combat is fast and often unforgiving. Mastery requires remembering elemental combinations under pressure while dodging enemy attacks. Friendly fire is always on, which can lead to accidental disasters. This mechanic may frustrate some players but also creates memorable moments when coordination works or collapses spectacularly.

The campaign offers a mix of linear levels and varied environments. Each stage introduces new enemy types, hazards, and small puzzles to solve using magic. While the story is relatively light, its humor fits the tone. Dialogue and visual jokes target fantasy tropes, keeping the experience playful rather than serious.

Co-op is the strongest part of the game. Local and online modes let teams coordinate spells or sabotage each other unintentionally. The difficulty curve feels tuned for groups, and playing solo can be noticeably tougher. Communication improves survival dramatically, as synchronized strategies make a difference in later encounters.

Progression is customization-focused. Robes, staffs, and artifacts modify spell effects and passive bonuses. These options encourage experimentation and replay value. Different loadouts can shift your role from offense to support or crowd control, depending on the situation.

Visually, the game uses a clean art style with vibrant spell effects. Sound cues for different elements provide clarity during chaotic fights, helping players track what is happening. Performance is stable, and load times are short on modern hardware.

Overall, Magicka 2 succeeds when players embrace its playful chaos. It rewards skill and experimentation but can punish disorganization. It is best enjoyed with friends who are willing to learn the system and laugh through the inevitable magical accidents.

I am writing this review through nostalgia goggles, however I can confidently say that this game is phenomenal. If you played this in the 90s/early 2000s pick this up on sale for a couple of quid/dollars. You're getting two games. The one we remember and its upgraded version. I was often flitting between both modes for that nostalgic hit. But be under no illusion this is a point and click game from the 90s wearing a pretty coat. 

Graphics - Most things look far better no matter what anyone says beauty is in the eye of the beholder and any negative reviews complaining about that should be disregarded as you can revert it back to its original art style through one button click. I will concede that they have twinkified our main man but I can look past that.

Voice acting - Yes it's a nice addition but again it's a point and click adventure game from the 90s if you can't read you probably shouldn't be playing puzzle games that rely heavily on your reading comprehension. 

Difficulty - I've seen several negative reviews about how this game is abstract and doesn't hold your hand. THAT'S THE POINT! with a guide you can sail through this game and get change out of 3 hours but that's on you. There are written guides, videos guides and community guides that will hold your hand through this but i think most people leaving negative reviews because they 'had too look up a guide' missed the point and then blame the game. They've also missed a huge QOL improvement. Press H and the game will physically tell you the answers to the puzzles and even show  physical arrow pointing you where to go. 

A lot of the negative reviews are from people who expected this 30 year old game with a nice coat to play like a modern indie. It doesn't. They've ignored the help the game gives you and then blamed the game. 

If you're sitting on the fence just buy it. If nothing else then to see where puzzle games started and appreciate where they've gone.

When The Secret of Monkey Island: Special Edition arrived in 2009, it wasn’t just a remaster, it was a resurrection. LucasArts’ beloved 1990 classic, reborn with hand painted visuals, full voice acting and a new orchestral score, managed to capture the original’s anarchic humor while gently polishing it for a new generation. It’s the rare remake that honors nostalgia without embalming it.

At its heart, Monkey Island remains one of the funniest, sharpest adventure games ever made. You play as Guybrush Threepwood, an ambitious but utterly inept would-be pirate who somehow bumbles his way through sword fights, voodoo curses and ghostly villains; all in pursuit of fame, fortune and love! The writing, courtesy of Ron Gilbert, Tim Schafer and Dave Grossman, hasn’t aged a day: the jokes land, the absurd logic puzzles still amuse and the dialogue’s timing is impeccable.

The Special Edition overlays this brilliance with loving care. The new art style is bright and painterly, if a little too glossy at times, and the voice cast (headed by Dominic Armato’s perfectly clueless Guybrush) breathes new life into familiar lines. The remastered music adds depth without drowning out the original’s whimsy. Best of all, the ability to swap instantly between the remaster and the 1990 version is a masterstroke, a reminder of just how well the old design holds up.

If there’s a weakness, it’s that some purists may find the updated visuals a touch sterile compared to the pixel-perfect charm of the original. But it’s hard to fault a remake that treats its source material with such respect and affection.

In the end, The Secret of Monkey Island: Special Edition isn’t just a nostalgic return; it’s a reminder of how timeless great writing and personality can be. After all these years, Guybrush Threepwood still makes us laugh and that’s treasure enough.

No More Heroes 3 is the culmination of Grasshopper Manufacture’s long-running saga about Travis Touchdown, the foul-mouthed, lightsaber-wielding otaku whose journey from underground assassin to reluctant hero has always mixed stylish violence with bizarre satire. Developed under the vision of Suda51, the game marks a chaotic return to the series’ over-the-top roots while experimenting with new ideas—some that elevate the experience and others that stumble in execution. Set several years after the previous entries, Travis finds himself drawn into yet another deadly competition, this time against an extraterrestrial invader named FU and his gang of intergalactic assassins. The narrative setup feels larger than life even by the series’ standards, pitting Travis against cosmic-level threats while grounding the story in his trademark absurd humor and pop-culture-laden self-awareness.

From the start, the game wastes no time establishing its wild tone. The world of Santa Destroy and its surrounding islands serves as the backdrop for a gauntlet of ranked duels, blending science fiction, anime homages, and fourth-wall-breaking comedy into one outrageous mix. What sets No More Heroes 3 apart from its predecessors is its scale. The game expands its scope with semi-open-world exploration, letting players roam freely between missions, take on side activities, and engage with quirky minigames such as garbage collection, lawn mowing, or battle challenges. While this broader structure gives the game variety, it also highlights its uneven pacing. The open world feels sparse, with long stretches of travel that sometimes interrupt the high-energy rhythm that defines the series’ combat. Yet even within this looseness, there’s an undeniable charm to the world—its deliberately empty spaces, ridiculous side objectives, and tongue-in-cheek parody of open-world conventions make it feel like a deliberate joke about modern game design.

The heart of No More Heroes 3, as always, lies in its combat. Travis’s beam katana fights have never felt more responsive or kinetic. The gameplay blends light and heavy attacks, wrestling-inspired grapples, and flashy finishers with the addition of new Death Glove abilities, which grant explosive powers like telekinetic throws and area attacks. Each encounter is a burst of spectacle, punctuated by comic book effects, neon explosions, and a frenetic soundtrack that turns every fight into a performance. Boss battles remain the series’ crown jewel—each one uniquely designed, filled with personality, and accompanied by Suda51’s signature eccentric direction. Whether you’re clashing with alien warlords or deranged bounty hunters, every fight feels like a self-contained vignette that pushes creativity to the forefront. These moments showcase the game at its best: wild, unpredictable, and unashamedly self-indulgent in its own style.

Narratively, the game oscillates between satire and sincerity, often blurring the line between parody and genuine emotion. Travis, once portrayed as an arrogant slacker, has evolved into a strangely introspective antihero—a man aware of his legacy, yet trapped in the absurdity of his own story. The writing leans heavily on meta-commentary, poking fun at tropes of sequels, fandom culture, and even the video game industry itself. The frequent tonal shifts—from comedic anime-style cutscenes to dark, quiet monologues—are jarring but intentional, reinforcing the idea that the game itself is a collage of media chaos. While this approach will delight long-time fans who understand Suda’s surreal storytelling, it can feel alienating for newcomers seeking coherence. Still, beneath the absurdity lies a surprising sense of melancholy, as Travis’s world of constant violence and fame begins to show cracks of emptiness and reflection.

Visually, No More Heroes 3 embodies the punk aesthetic that defines Grasshopper Manufacture’s work. The art direction mixes cel-shaded character models with vibrant color palettes and comic-inspired effects, creating an exaggerated visual identity that feels both retro and futuristic. On higher-end platforms, textures and lighting have been refined from the original Switch version, giving the game a more polished presentation without losing its hand-crafted charm. The soundtrack, composed by Nobuaki Kaneko and other contributors, is another highlight—an eclectic mix of rock, electronic, and experimental tracks that shift dynamically with the action. Combined with strong voice performances from returning cast members, including Robin Atkin Downes as Travis, the audiovisual design reinforces the game’s surreal, cinematic energy.

Despite its stylistic brilliance, the game’s technical execution isn’t flawless. The open-world segments, though conceptually interesting, suffer from performance inconsistencies and design repetition. Side missions can feel more like obligatory chores than meaningful diversions, and the world’s emptiness sometimes contrasts too sharply with the intensity of the core missions. These flaws, however, are part of the No More Heroes identity—intentional or not, they contribute to the game’s rebellious, unpolished charm. It’s a title that mocks both itself and the conventions it’s built upon, wearing its rough edges as a badge of artistic defiance. For every frustrating stretch of traversal or frame drop, there’s a boss fight or cutscene so strange and stylish that it makes you forget about the imperfections.

No More Heroes 3 ultimately feels like a celebration of Suda51’s entire creative philosophy: a messy, heartfelt, wildly entertaining explosion of ideas that defies convention at every turn. It’s a game that thrives on excess—too loud, too strange, and too self-aware to ever be mistaken for anything else. For fans of the series, it serves as a fitting conclusion to Travis Touchdown’s saga, offering closure wrapped in chaos and sincerity. For newcomers, it’s an invitation into one of gaming’s most eccentric worlds, though one that demands a taste for surreal humor and experimental storytelling. While its pacing and technical issues hold it back from greatness, its fearless personality and energetic combat ensure it stands as a memorable, if flawed, masterpiece of punk game design. No More Heroes 3 may not be perfect, but it’s unapologetically itself—and that’s exactly what makes it so captivating.

Cogmind is an extremely well designed and detailed traditional roguelike.  Unlike most traditional roguelikes, where you level up a fantasy character, you are instead a robot that attaches parts.  As you explore the complex you'll come across better parts with a higher rating, so you're constantly adjusting and tuning your build accordingly.  

One of my favourite aspects of the game is the lore.  The 'Complex' has a rich story, told by the other robots you run into as well as from chunks of lore from the terminals that you hack into.  You can also align yourself with several different factions. Each has their own special aspect that either changes the normal mechanics of the game or introduces new mechanics.  Some of them also have a 'quest', where you will meet them on one of the later harder levels and they will help you out.  This game is not an RPG though - 99.9% of your interactions are as a 'silent observer', with binary decisions often made by moving into a piece of machinery.  Or if you're feeling powerful you could just blast them to bits, which may have its own ramifications...any character and nearly all objects besides the stairways can be killed in this game.

There's many different tactics you can use in this game.  You can equip flight units and hacking suites and be a really stealthy guy that can hack terminals and slip past the enemies.  Or you can equip treads and blow up anything you come across.  Each tactic has been carefully curated by the developer so that nothing is too powerful and everything has ramifications - if you are tanky your parts last longer, but if you blow up too much, your 'alert' goes up and more and more nasty bots come after you, eventually overwhelming you.  If you are a stealthy flight hacker, it is much easier to deal with 'alert', but you are very vulnerable and cannot take many hits.  

Like many traditional roguelikes, the game has a steep learning curve.  There's so many small but important details you have to know to get good at the game.  Compared to other traditional roguelikes I'd say the UI is generally excellent - once you learn the basic keys to play (fire, move, pick up parts) and the basic mouse commands (drag and drop parts from inventory to your slots) then you're off.  

A few things I don't like so much about the game - there's a bit of meta-progression knowledge, some which I don't entirely agree with, the biggest one being the manual hacks - manual hacks are such an important part of the game, and they are available to everyone no matter what lore you have uncovered about them, but you can only do them by hitting 'z' in a terminal and typing stuff out manually, and typing hints don't appear until you've used them the first time.  I guess it was done this way so that new players aren't utterly overwhelmed, which is maybe a good thing.  However I have had to set up Automapper hotkeys to save the poor fingers from all this manual typing, since manual hacking is something you do a lot of, especially once you get better at the game and know what you're doing.  

Another thing I don't like is that some of the mechanics are non-obvious until you go on the wiki (search 'cogminder' on google) and read up about it, then it becomes an 'aha! of course!' moment.  An example is the random chance that being in Heavy sensor range sends reinforcements after you - Cutters if you're a flight build, or Specialists if you're a tank build.  I think I was already hundreds of hours in the game without knowing this, and only by actually reading it in the wiki did it all make sense.

Another common complaint is that there's a lot of content that is only accessible to the 1% of very skilled players.  This is a true statement to an extent - even with 500 hours I am not skilled enough to take on the hardest content.  However the game does have 3 difficulty levels.  On Rogue (the default) I'm at the point now where I can get a basic win fairly consistently, and one of the minor harder wins every so often.  On Explorer (the easiest) I've experienced a few of the really difficult endings that I could never do on Rogue.

Overall the game is incredible.  If you have any interest in roguelikes at all then buying it is a no-brainer.  I highly recommend it.  Development is still ongoing and the solo developer keeps on adding great new content with each 'beta' release (though I would not consider this in any way a beta - it really is a fully-fledged game right now).

Когда весной 2022 года я решил залететь в Snowrunner, это было прекрасное время, чтобы ознакомиться с игрой. У игры на тот момент было два Season pass и хорошие скидки. А после сырых Spintires и Mudrunner геймплей был более цельным и осмысленным. Начинал я играть с другом, и о тех временах очень приятные воспоминания. Помню, как мы страдали на Мичигане - ехали куда-то не туда, переворачивались, застревали, вытаскивали друг друга, подвозили топливо. Это были увлекательные 100 часов. Я играл на руле с педалями от первого лица, и это было весьма атмосферно. Правда, не хватало поддержки trackir, чтобы пользоваться зеркалами заднего вида. 

Помимо Мичигана, в базовой игре есть еще две карты - Аляска и Таймыр. Открыты они с самого начала, но проходить рекомендуется попорядку. В принципе, базовой игры вам хватит, чтобы поиграть 200-250 часов и познать дзен. После идут 16 (на данный момент) сезонов для самых отбитых. За 3,5 года я только завершаю второй сезон, так что не спешите покупать их все.

Что понравилось. Графический стиль. Физика грязи с поддержкой мультиплеера. Система прогресии и экономики. Чувство превозмогания. Чувство удовлетворения, когда восстановил регион. Исследование карты, поиск апгрейдов. 

Что не понравилось. Однообразие. Душный гринд (в DLC картах). 

А теперь о том, стоит ли это покупать. Обязательно стоит, игра офигенная. Базовой игры вам хватит за глаза. Now that I've "finished" the game I'd like to write out some of my thoughts as part review and some things I'd like to see in the future.

As a game trying to capture the classic MMO feel I think it really hits it out of the park. World, dungeon and encounter design felt authentic to the source materials. 

The out door zones all felt unique from one another with plenty of places to level up in. I appreciated that you would sometimes have to watch your back because even in a lower leveled area you might get ambushed by something much stronger. Most areas were of course safe but it was a nice touch. There weren't a ton of quests in the outdoor areas but the ones around were worth doing. There are enough different areas to level up that you could do a dozen play throughs and take some what different paths each time. 

My only real critique here is that while there all of these different spots to grind at you realistically just wouldn't do them because there were no loot drops. So they kind of just exist as window dressing currently. Old school MMOs had a ton of these kinds of camps and they existed as places to go because everything else was taken. It would be nice to see sim players at these types of places just to fill out the game world with more 'players'. Like it would be nice to see 1 or 2 groups at the Ogre camps in Soluna's Landing as an example.

As far as the dungeon I was really happy with the layouts. They were all unique and had their own vibes. I liked that CC is required in this game and that you have to be mindful when it comes to pulling and respawn timers. If you aren't careful its pretty easy to get overwhelmed and sent back to the well. As long as you understand the spawns and mechanics you can pretty much chain pull from level 1 to about 28ish. It wasn't until about then that I started having difficulty with mana management on my Paladin to keep up with all the taunting/debuffing. This was later remedied by a single Aura item. The enemies and bosses were fine. Not a ton of unique abilities but there was some add management needed and spells that needed to be interrupted. This isn't really a negative as its pretty standard for the old school MMO to be more about "tank and spank" style encounters. There were also bosses that that mechanics that required moving the boss around, trying to kill multiple targets around the same time, bosses that would spawn something that would either heal them or summon more adds that needed to be dealt with, bosses with massive AoEs that require you to think more about your resistances, a boss that splits into smaller versions of itself multiple times, bosses that requires you to complete zone objectives in order to summon them or weaken them. It was a nice mix of that older classic styles fights with some "newer" things thrown in as well.

My critique of dungeons is going to be pretty similar to my one about the open world camps. Where are the sim players? During a few of the first dungeons you see sim players running around. I would see the occasional one in the third dungeon (Krakengard) but after that it felt like I was running instances in WoW and not running dungeons in an old school open world MMO. I would sometimes see sims standing outside a dungeon later on but they seemingly never went in. I also see them selling a lot of loot from these places that they never venture into. 

This combined with the open world made it feel like I started off in an MMO but then veered into a single player RPG. Of course it is a single player game but the vibe is supposed to lean more into the MMO realm and the things that come with that. 

In the future I'd like to see the Sims more around the world and in dungeons. I'd also like to see them actually hold down camps so that it didn't feel like you could just walk into any dungeon you wanted and head to whatever boss you needed for a drop with 0 competition. Player competition was a big part of early MMOs, even on pve servers. On that note I'd also like to see there be something like a Need/Greed system. The party sims are happy enough to say they need something but thats pretty much it. Being out rolled on gear is also part of the MMO experience. And yeah having a party at the camp you want and losing gear sucks but its that dealing with the 'human' element that was a big part of MMOs. The game would do well with some drama between the sims and the player IMO.

Some other random thoughts I had written down that I wanted to touch on. 

1. Mobs don't flee and I think that is a mistake. There are several items in the game that root or slow down mobs but they feel pretty useless. Having to snare and root runners was a skill expression back in the day and even letting just 1 mob run out of the room could pull an entire train on the group. 

2. There are a couple items that are too good and unrealistic to exist in an MMO without being hit by a nerf hammer. 

a)The Forest Pendant is incredible for something you could get at like lvl 8. It will easily last you for like 20 levels if not more. I think I worse it on my Paladin until around level 32. 

b) Diamondine Mace. This has to be one of the most OP leveling weapons I've ever used in an MMO. I used it from around lvl 17/18 until my early 30s. You go from doing like 30 DPS to doing several hundred. Its like adding an additional DPS class to the party and outclasses and just invalidates any other Paladin weapon the entire time you use it. I don't think 2H weapons even out damage it for quite awhile especially when you also factor in the Diamondine Shield. The 90% proc chance combined with double attack is just too much. Again this is looking at it from MMO design. 

c) Sage's Trinket. This one item made the game go from worrying about mana management in the later stages to not having a single care. And that small window where I had to worry about my mana probably wouldn't have even existed had I known about it earlier. Complete game changer and probably the most powerful Aura in the game and something easily obtainable around lvl 24ish.

d) Eon, Blade of Time. A truly disgusting weapon combined with high Resonance and Triple Attack. Fighting Astra was about 50/50 due to the AoE wiping my sims until Eon dropped and without changing another piece of gear I never had another group death. All of Astra's drops are good but none of the other weapons are going to warp the game as much. Its one of those weapons where encounters will need to be designed with it mind for the foreseeable future.

3. I really feel like Resonance either needs a much lower cap or drastically reduced on items and unaffected by upgrading. It feels a lot like Spell Crit % in other games with the addition that it also works with Heals and Procs. It just feels like its way too easy to stack and really lets you steam roll over everything. My paladin is mostly in blue gear using Eon (20k HP, 1750 AC), with 0 purple, and my sims have 1 to 2 blues each and I can do 0 stone Eldoth with no issues. A boss that can max hit me for around 14k. I think a big part of that is just how good Resonance is (and also Eon). It also makes every other stat on the item meaningless up to a certain point. When looking at upgrades nothing else, outside of worn/special effects, really matters. It feels like a stat that pre-raid we should only be hitting around 15-20% at max. 

4. The music is really good imo. 

5. I'm really enjoying the lore. I honestly didn't pay much attention for the first while but then started reading the random lore pages and item descriptions and was pretty impressed by the world building. I'm excited to see how teaming up with Ripper is going to work out. 

tl:dr

Very good game. Captures classic MMO vibe with a lot of love and respect for the source materials. Some MMO elements need turned up and some potential nerfs/adjustments for future design sake.

Looking forward to future updates and seeing where the game goes.

I played this game on PS5 when it first came out and loved it back then but after reading the mixed reviews, I was on the fence on buying it again on steam after reading that CO-OP was disabled. 
Luckily, it's back on and running again so my friend and I can play together!
This game is a very cute cozy farming fae game with different elements to it that you can choose to focus on or jump to which is great for our ADHD. 

All in all- the game does have bugs and some issues that could be worked on for better QOL.

This is a cute and enjoyable game, but there is definitely room for improvement.

The dialogue for characters is incredibly lifeless and repetitive. Although there's some that you are introduced to in quests, most don't have any unique dialogue even when meeting for the first time or just between other NPCs. It wouldn't be such an annoyance if there wasn't a relationship measure implemented into the game. You can even get married, but only to a very small selection of characters.

While farming sims are grind-y by nature, I felt a greater push to progress more quickly through the main quest rather than relax and freely enjoy separate components (mining, fishing, farming, decorating, etc.) as I pleased. Though it's natural to have upgrades you need to unlock over time, I found that I continued to be blocked by not having access to later game materials at every turn. I couldn't craft the majority of recipe scrolls for furniture that I picked up at the very start of the game until I was significantly through the main chapters, and so I had no interest in decorating. Teleports for early game locations also required material from much later on (Why does the Stay-A-While Bay need emerald from the Floating Ruins?). I wanted to change my wings from the default and also could not do so without more "undiscovered" materials. And so on.

Despite the title, you are not a fae, and much of the fae content comes a few chapters into the story. Instead, you unlock large jumps, which felt rather hard to control--especially in the Floating Ruins where you frequently have to bounce off of jumping pads. And for a game that seemingly had such nice QoL components, like not having tools get damaged, it was a bit annoying to keep crafting potions to explore the area and have different items to replenish HP, energy, and mana.

My final gripe is with the map. There's no minimap, and the main map is not very detailed, so I found myself getting a bit lost from time to time. You can't unlock teleports for all of the listed locations either, which was also a bit disappointing and contributed to the grindiness I felt.

Overall, I've enjoyed the art style, fantasy atmosphere, and story so far, but I don't think I'll play much after I finish the main quest nor buy the DLCs. I'm glad I got this one on sale because the standard price is a bit too high when there are better options out there for solo-players. It would probably be very fun to play with friends, though I would be a bit worried about the option getting removed again, seeing as it's apparently already happened once.

I've seen this in game before - just a little world-crafting for a loading screen. whatever. cute. 

but then I realized I could ZOOM IN and actually read the text ... and there was a lot. fake ads for places I'm sure you go in the game later (detox facility? demolished little girls' lemonade stand??) ... really cool. I love stuff like that. 

then I started reading the actual article (noticing how the font was formatted quite like a newspaper would be - tiny detail nailed), assuming it was gonna be all about how terrible this asshole was, blah blah, the world's better for being rid of him (so the player doesn't feel bad after). but no, the article's actually in FAVOR of the guy I killed. and not only that, it details the incident itself, providing statistics for kills, shots hit, shots missed, etc. all while reading like an actual article would - seamless. 

they just don't DO stuff like that anymore for even major games. those tiniest of details is mostly just Rockstar (RDR2 has dozens of editions of papers, though I bet they don't detail the player's actual choices like this one did!)

my thoughts on the game are that it doesn't play great these days, but must've been unbelievable when it came out. I'll take Hitman 2 or 3 for sure ... but the detail of the paper is something I've legitimately never seen - it's so, so cool how they give it to you to see, then give you a full rundown while staying in character as a paper article IF you decide to actually look at it. I love, love, love that. 

what a great idea, concept and execution [hah]. top-tier Hitman.

Так что же это за зверь такой – Toribash? По сути говоря, это файтинг, но файтинг весьма своеобразный, можно даже сказать, исключительный. В качестве героев выступают собранные из шариков и кубиков куклы, поначалу находящиеся в статичном режиме. Целью игры является нанесение как можно большего урона противнику посредством выбора удачной комбинации движений. Игроки самостоятельно решают, как именно они будут действовать в отдельно взятом раунде. Куклы могут драться руками, ногами и головой, совершать прыжки и уклонения – все зависит от манеры поведения самих геймеров. Кажется, что все весьма просто, но это не так. Чтобы исполнить мало-мальски удобоваримое комбо, нужно учесть множество факторов (Toribash базируется на чистой физике), а на выполнение красивой и продуманной атаки и вовсе придется затратить уйму времени и сил. Почему? Все дело в этих самых шариках и кубиках, из которых состоят куклы. Если просто-напросто ткнуть на активные точки-фигуры, не проведя никаких вычислений, то кукла, скорее всего, грохнется на пол, ни капельки не повредив оппоненту. 

Залог победы в Toribash – тщательный и скрупулезный анализ своих действий. Нужно учитывать, в какой позе находится боец, какое у него состояние: напряженное или расслабленное, куда он отклоняется в процессе битвы и так далее. Да, все это достаточно сложно, но куда труднее было бы, если поединки в Toribash проходили в режиме реального времени. Но в Toribash реализован пошаговый режим, благодаря которому игроки могут более-менее адекватно контролировать своих подопечных, хотя и это не является панацеей. Конечно, особенно сильно страдают новички, столкнувшиеся с Toribash впервые, но даже они, при должной доле усидчивости, могут поднатореть в драках за пару-тройку деньков, а за неделю – достичь по-настоящему серьезных успехов. Но стать мастеровитым “сенсеем” все равно не выйдет ни за две недели, ни за три – тут уже потребуется месяц серьезнейших тренировок.

Это не просто очередная глава, это настоящий мультимедийный перфоманс, который стирает грань между игрой, кино и головоломкой.

Вы просыпаетесь в странной, классической для Rusty Lake комнате. Вы - Дейл Вандермер, и вам нужно вспомнить, кто вы и как сюда попали. Знакомо? Да, но в этот раз всё иначе. Игра была выпущена вместе с полноценным короткометражным фильмом с живыми актерами. Просмотр фильма не просто дополняет игру - он является ключом к её пониманию.

Комната, в которой вы заперты, - это один большой пазл. Головоломки здесь не просто логичные, они - сюжетные. Каждое ваше действие, каждая найденная вещь - это кусочек истории Дейла, его памяти и его связи с Ржавым Озером.

Некоторые загадки в игре можно решить, только внимательно посмотрев фильм. Это не спойлеры, а часть игровой механики. Вы постоянно переключаетесь между экранами, чувствуя себя настоящим детективом.

В игре есть две главы, и прохождение первой открывает вторую, с абсолютно новым набором головоломок. Это два разных испытания в одной комнате.

Для фанатов серии здесь просто рай. Игра отвечает на старые вопросы и задает новые, плотно связывая историю Дейла с общей мифологией.

Атмосфера Parodox - это квинтэссенция всего Rusty Lake. Мрачная, давящая, но при этом с оттенком абсурдного юмора (куда же без ворона?). А благодаря фильму атмосфера приобретает новое, осязаемое измерение.

Cube Escape: Paradox -  это не просто "еще одна точка-и-клик адвенчура", это смелый эксперимент, который удался на все 100%.
是逃脫方塊系列中最有挑戰性的，好玩。

Перепройти первые части игры я хотел еще до прохождения BG3, чтобы освежить в памяти события. Однако друзья затащили проходить новую игру в коопе. В процессе игры я был неким "лормастером", потому что, как оказалось, даже спустя годы довольно хорошо помнил персонажей и важные события, периодически пересказывая их товарищам.
Забавно, но игра в моей памяти была значительно лучше, чем она есть на самом деле. Сразу же извиняюсь перед теми, кого не отпускает синдром утенка.  BG1, даже в Enhanced Edition, очень сильно устарела. 
Разумеется, важно понимать, что именно Baldurs Gate положила начало всему жанру изометрических RPG и заложила ключевые основы. Но в то же время игра полна "детских" ошибок и проблем, повторять которые считается моветоном. Жанр CRPG, вопреки расхожему утверждению, не стоит на месте и постоянно развивается. 

У игры очень странный пейсинг. Игрока выбрасывают на глобальную карту и говорят "ну как нибудь сам перебором локаций пойми куда тебе надо попасть". Фанатами игры принято нахваливать "открытый" мир и свободу действий, хотя фактический геймплей представляет собой поэтапный переход между маленькими локациями на глобальной карте с последующей их зачисткой - открытием тумана войны из угла в угол. При этом игроку предстоит действовать исключительно методом тыка - где находятся точки интереса практически никогда не рассказывают, а переходить между дальними локациями можно только найдя путь до них через промежуточные зоны.
Стандартная ситуация в игре: игрок натыкается на какого-то NPC на одной из локаций. Он оказывается потенциальным спутником и предлагает бродить вместе, но хочет, чтобы ему помогли кому-то отомстить. Где именно цель мести находится он не знает. Но если игрок не найдет эту цель через N-цать игровых дней, то он обидится и уйдет навсегда, либо вовсе нападет на игрока. Ситуация становится абсурднее, когда таких требовательных спутников становится несколько.

В BG1 нулевая волнообразность. Нет ни моментов расслабления, нет каких-то челленджевых эпизодов. Сложность в игре на постоянном уровне.

Локации абсолютно плоские, без тактических перепадов высот и без сложных закоулков, где игрок находился бы в уязвимом положении. Буквально все стычки можно пройти подсвечивая зону вором в невидимости и закидывая врагов АОЕ-уроном.

На локациях нет интерактивных объектов. Отсутствуют небоевые способности, чтобы решать какие-то проблемы или преодолевать препятствия или находить какие-то секреты. 

В свое время появление в игре спутников стало чем-то уникальным. Но если разбираться...
20 бесполезных компаньонов, чьи личные задания ограничены тем, что нужно за определенное время найти локацию, где убить кого-то или найти кого-то. Менеджмент спутников отсутствует напрочь. 
Игроку на старте буквально навязываются две пары спутников, которых не разъединить. И практически сразу же, в пределах еще 2-3 локаций, появляется возможность взять еще 6 (!). При этом взаимодействие с персонажами либо одноразовое (отказался при первом разговоре принять в группу - прощай), либо персонажи при отсоединении уходят навсегда. 
Нет возможности сделать квест персонажа и вернуться к нему. Он обязательно должен быть в пачке, иначе квест просто ломается. Получается замкнутый круг.
Нет возможности даже попробовать различные варианты. Даже нет возможности до присоединения персонажа понять кто он по классу и что он умеет.
Реакция спутников на выполнение сюжетных заданий минимальна. А та что есть - абсурдна. Пример: на рандомной локации на корову нападали монстры. За их убийство дали +1 репутации. После этого из группы сразу же ушла Викония, заявив, что ей противно путешествовать с добрым персонажем.

В игре очень фрустрирующая система глав. Она формирует у игрока обоснованный страх перед переходом в новую главу. Потому что обычно это значит потерю связанных квестов и изменение в локациях, приход/уход NPC. Здесь игроку буквально за первые пару часов предлагается перейти к 3 главе, хотя остается куча побочных квестов. Смену главы вызывает определенное сюжетное событие. Поэтому могут быть главы практически без дополнительных квестов.
Важно отметить, что некоторые переходы между главами ДЕЙСТВИТЕЛЬНО делают невозможным выполнение каких-то заданий. Но игроку об этом не говорят.

BG1 это приключение для небольших уровней. Богоподобия здесь достичь невозможно.
А первые уровни - это классическое DnD мучение. Персонажи с 4 хп, отлетающие от одной тычки гоблина. Драки, где 10 тушек стоят и машут палками, будучи не в состоянии попасть друг по другу.
Правилом хорошего тона давно уже является небоевой левелинг, направленный на знакомство с миром и на квесты-расследования или подай-принеси, т.к боевка на первых уровнях это что-то невразумительное и скучное.

У аддона Siege of Dragonspear смешанные отзывы, но как бы это больно не звучало для фанатов классики, он превосходит оригинал по всем пунктам.

Играть в BG1 в 2025 году всё еще можно, но рекомендовать через эту игру знакомиться с жанром точно не стоит. 
Но минус великой классике я, конечно же, ставить не буду.

30$ for a queue simulator where people are very, very clearly playing, but matchmaking just seems to not want to work at all. You can see everyone running around the plaza, see them running into the queue area, then you do so yourself and get an empty queue forever, even when you try to Quickplay or intentionally click the "popular"/individual league(s). Maybe everyone's only queuing with their friends and completely missing out on the intended mayhem aspect of the game. I don't know, but the game is definitely suffering because of it, people are thinking the game is dead when it really isn't.

Yes, there are singleplayer solo campaigns, but they're pretty boring (or long and annoying, which is the end levels of the first three campaigns and seemingly all of the last one) and not really the main focus of the game.

The art style's fine, the combat's not too bad, the cutscenes have a weird off-putting edging-adult-humor-quality, but conversations with each character don't and are actually engaging and normal. The platforming's just basic and the drop shadow's not quite dark enough. Again, the main focus is the multiplayer chaos, but you can't really random-queue for it right now, so...

...ultimately, I have to say to not buy this until they fix matchmaking or disable being able to play privately. 90% of the game takes place in the matchmade leagues but you usually can't even actually get a match in it currently, so, what's the point?
Too expensive for a game that's supposed to be free to play. Completely dead and without players.

The Evil Within is a horror survival game that is about an investigation of what seems to be mass homocide at Beacon Mental Hospital in Krimson City, but things turn out to be much more deep and sinister than what all of this comes across at the beginning. 

First off, the protagonist of this game, Detective Sebastian Castellanos is a very emotionless, stale and boring person who doesn't seem to get affected by anything, even though he had endure things that would drive a normal person to madness i.e. fighting monsters countless times, waking up inside a nightmare world that he would go on to visit lots of times via a portal and so on. Not even a single time he seem like he was on the brink of completely losing it, which doesn't make any sense whatsoever.

Lots of interiors in this game are very grimy, full of looming shadows, artistically designed buildings and ominous escape routes. All of that combined created a frightening mood of expectation. Sometimes you even confused your own shadow with the one of an enemy, all of which created a massively immersive and compelling experience.

When it comes to the antagonists, bosses and villains you come across, it has to be poined out that they are just so unpredictable, smart and hard-to-trick. They would eventually get weirder the more you progress, but still are inventive creations. 
Their names are as follows: 
Ruvik, a brilliant neuroscientist who created the STEM system to achieve his goal of rebuilding the world to bring back his deceased sister.
The Kepper, a big, masked figure with a safe, with wrapped barbed around it with, on his head, who loves to wield a large hammer and keeps respawning after dying.
Laura, who is an extremely fast and powerful creature, who can only be hurt and killed with fire.
The Sadist, a chainsaw-wielding lunatic who serves as a recurring antagonist.
Valerio Jimenez, a deranged hospital orderly acting as an antagonist aand various sections of the game.
Shigyo, a grotesque, multi-limbed creature

The weaponry you receive are modest and well-balanced - a pistol, shotgun, sniper rifle, greande and a crossbow, which caters to a variety of special attacks (freeze, electrocute, harpoon, explosive etc.) Managing the usage of your arsenal is crucial, as there's only little available and to be found, very similar to the Resident Evil Games. Sebastian runs out of stamina so quickly, tho. Yes you can actually upgrade that along with other abilities, the stock, your weapons and so on, but at the very beginning his lack of stamina is frustrating as hell. Checkpoints are scarce, so surviving and not dying repeatedly and stupidly is very, very important, which makes for such an exhilarating expierience no matter whether you decide to flee from an enemy or fight it. Making extremely calculated moves is absolutely key.

Playing the stealth route is possible and not a bad decision, but still it somehow feels like that, whether you plan on throwing a bottle at an enemy or sneak up behind it, they somehow still manage to detect you shortly before you could go for it. That playstyle was, for me at least, not the most accessible gameplay style to adopt.

You're not entirely powerless tho, One of EW's most enjoyable mechanics is its very simple upgrade system. "Green gel" is the resource you need to use in order to improve your attributes in the nightmare world accessible via a portal in the form of a broken mirror, which partially breaks as soon as you approach it and can be heard with a very distinct music. It is spread across the entire map, which make it worth to explore every possible inch and corner. Cashing in the points you obtain by collecting the green gel allows you to shape your own gameplay style. For instance, if you're more like an aggressive player, it makes sense to value upgrading the damage, accuracy and reload time of your weapons, rather than the ability to run for longer. And if you're a player preferring the stealth playstyle, the other way around makes the most sense.

Conclusion: The Evil Within is a vicious, barbaric, challenging and overall very fun game. Its eerie world and imaginative, creative and unique enemies are genuinely frightening and smart. The lack of resources you got makes it even more challenging than already to defeat them. All of which makes it seem like the odds are against you, whilst they're not as soon as you keep a cool head and don't start panicking.

If you can get the game discounted in a sale it is a pleasant experience, however at full price it is nto worth it. It has very basic platforming and puzzle mechanics and relies heavily on its castle in the sky aesthetic to carry it as a visual experience.
Its only 4 hours long and sadly spends the first 2 hours introducing very simple mechanics and not really doing much. It would have been vastly improved if it had implemented more puzzle mechanics at a faster rate, as it is, it's a very barebones experience from a gameplay standpoint.

I’d like to thank the developers of Icarus.

I was looking for a survival game with an open world that truly challenges the player.
As an adult, I don’t have endless hours to spend grinding — which is unfortunately the norm in this kind of games. The sense of progression and character development in Icarus is a masterpiece.
The fact that the game offers a skill tree providing meaningful support for a solo players is something truly special. It’s not overcomplicated, rather subtle and perfectly balanced.
You don’t suddenly become a superhero, but you do feel well and fair treated if you play solo. 

The atmosphere of the world is outstanding.
That first dusk on the planet, the distant sounds, the whispering wind, and the echoes of unknown creatures - all of it creates a powerful sense of isolation. You genuinely feel surrounded by something unknown and unpredictable.

The planet doesn’t make survival easy — the environment is harsh, and the wildlife can be hostile.
Get too close, and you’ll be attacked. Yet those same creatures can also be tamed, becoming your companions as you venture farther from the safety of your base.

From a crouched, frightened survivor clutching a wooden spear, you evolve into an explorer whom planning, logistics, and resource management become essential.

The lore and the world itself form a cohesive whole — every anomaly and strange occurrence simply fits.

It’s a wonderful adventure that can fill many evenings.

Once again, a big thank you to the developers. I wholeheartedly recommend Icarus to anyone seeking an open-world survival experience that is unpredictable, genuinely challenging, yet ultimately fulfilling and rewarding.

GON takes a very different approach compared to what you might expect from a game inspired by Fire Emblem. I'm only on the 9th chapter (but about 6+ chapters  more than that played since there are many side quests) and I already have many items and skills with very unique effects. It's very critical that you pay attention to what your units and the enemy possess at all times if you desire strategic success. This is a very engaging system, and I've been surprised (but not unfairly) by plays enemies have made several times with their item and skill combinations. For example, I currently possess an item that increases a unit's HP by 25, but sets their defense to 0, making for some interesting considerations.

The game also doesn't slack when it comes to character variety. Compared to some modern AAA strategy games where you'll see the same bosses over and over again, every location, even side quests, are brimming with unique characters and bosses with their own stories and charm. That's not even to mention your own army, which also has a great variety. I just got a pirate that can spawn a little squid in water. Cinema.

There's also great customization so every type of player can enjoy the game. If you're not a fan of RNG level ups, you can turn on fixed growths, to remove that stress. If you want mechanics from the games that inspired it, such as the weapon triangle, you can turn those on too. If you don't want much of a challenge, you can save at the start of every turn. Your experience is your own. I believe other negative reviews that say things like "rng level ups should be BURIED" lack proper reading comprehension, as they're the ones who chose to have those settings on in the first place.

I won't comment on the story, as I'd like to see how it plays out, but I do enjoy the most of the character dynamics so far. Most of the characters have good chemistry with each other, and I'm interested in seeing how their lives play out.

However, there are some areas that I believe could be improved. Rather than a list showing all the items in your army's possession, you have to manually go to each one, or the convoy, if you'd like to get a specific item from a specific place. This can lead to spending more time in battle preparations than needed, and I've lost track of some of the items I possess a few times. I also find the progress story hard to follow at times. The characters will say "we're going to (INSERT LOCATION HERE)", but I don't know what that location is or where it is relative to everything else.  If the characters have spent a few chapters trying to get somewhere, how close are they to it? This is probably a nitpick, but I think a world map or glossary of some sort could help in this area.

Those are just a few negatives in a game that is overflowing with passion and creativity. If you like strategy games, I'd highly recommend picking up this unique entry in the genre.

Great strategy / tactics RPG with plenty of content and replayability, especially for the price. I just finished my first play-through of the story and it took me over 100 hours, though I did spend entirely too much time checking all my items between missions, considering what moves to make, etc.

As some other reviews have stated, playable units are fairly unique and there are plenty to choose from. It doesn't take long at all before you have more than you can deploy to a mission, and by late game you have more than double the deployable number. Enemy units are fairly straightforward, but mixed up well enough that you typically must respect their strengths and especially defense / resist stats.

The game does a good job of not tossing you into unfair situations. There are a handful of missions in which you must prevent enemy units from reaching target points, on top of the typical "slay enemy leader" objective, and many similar games will have sneaky units spawn on a very tight path / window to catch them. Gales of Nayeli units will often spawn in a variety of places throughout missions, but they feel appropriate and give you time to respond. They are also typically marked by fortresses, monster lairs, or roads, so you can purposely leave units on top of them to prevent the spawns if desired.

Another aspect I liked vs. similar games (especially in the second half) is that enemy units are aggressive and most of them will come to you. It avoids the awkward waiting that can occur of having to put certain units 1 or 2 tiles into attackable range to draw units out - which is still necessary, occasionally.

One aspect I truly did not enjoy was weapon proficiency, which dictates what items a unit can use and equip. The concept is good, especially for weapon classes in general, but the issue with Gales is that it takes an excessive amount of encounters to raise ranks. I had 4 or 5 "main" units that did heavy lifting in every mission, starting from when they were first recruited, and they still just barely hit S rank (to use all weapons) by the last couple of missions. By that point the game was over. A couple of others hit max level, used only one weapon type, and still could not wield weapons I had found 5 chapters ago.

The romance / support options between characters was also initially a bit lacking, but the developer(s) just pushed a patch with a bunch more!

Overall, I would certainly recommend this game unless you dislike the strategy / tactics RPG genre entirely.

[b]Gedanken zum Spiel[/b]

Müsste ich eine Computerspielreihe nennen, die mir am tiefsten ins Gedächtnis gebrannt wurde, so wäre es Tomb Raider. Ich möchte gar keine Superlative behaupten, es sei die beste oder so, aber bei mir  war es das Gefühl, [i]so[/i] soll computerspielen sein.

Heute kann ich manches kritischer betrachten, und auch die Schwächen ausmachen, die ich damals nicht als solche sah oder ausblendete. Etwa eine krude Geschichte einer Grabräuberin mit Indiana-Jones-Attitüte, einem überaus simplen Kampfsystem und vielen (nur beim ersten Mal) überraschenden Todesfallen.

Aber es machte auch so viel richtig nach meinem Dafürhalten und vieles davon so gut, dass ich es auch heute noch nicht nur als Meilenstein der Computerspiele sehe sondern auch noch mit Genuß spielen kann.

Was hat mir damals oder heute so gut gefallen? Es war eine 3D-Welt, in der man Gefahren meistern und Geheimnisse lüften musste. Die Hürden waren oft komplexe Rätsel, die mehr im Levelaufbau versteckt waren, als offen zutage lagen. Eine versperrte Tür braucht einen Schlüssel, den zu finden man die Umgebung absuchen musste; man sucht, findet es nicht, findet etwas anderes oder entdeckt einen geheimen Zugang zu einem Secret; man hat ein Objekt, aber keine Ahnung, wo man dies verwendet; man muss Jump&Run-Passagen meistern, die manchmal wirklich schwer waren.

Und man macht es einfach. Kletterpassagen, die ewig dauern, Rätsel und Labyrinthe, die verwirren, Levelenden, die anzeigen, dass man nur 1 von 5 Geheimnissen gefunden hat. Selbstauferlegte Challenges in einer Zeit, als es noch keine Errungenschaften gab. Keine Ahnung, wie viele Stunden ich damit verbracht habe, aber es waren sehr, sehr viele. Selbst nun in diesem Remastered sind es wieder unglaublich viele Stunden geworden.

Inhaltlich sind die Spiele, so scheint mir, unverändert. Woran ich mich nicht erinnern kann, aber hier jetzt vorhanden ist, ist eine New Game+ Möglichkeit, bei der die Gegner schwerer sind und man nur an den Stellen automatisch speichern kann, wo "Diamanten" im Level sind (wohl wie in der damaligen Konsolenversion). Dieser Spielmodus, war mir aber an einigen Stellen zu schwer.

[b]Technik[/b]

Technisch gut. Nie abgestürzt. Bugs, also solche, die stören, habe ich keine gefunden. Es gibt aber ein paar Bugs (oder sie sehen jedenfalls so aus), ohne die man manche optionalen Dinge schwerlich oder nicht erreicht.

Die Grafik ist toll, gemessen an der Verbesserung zum Original. Schon allein Lara, die man ja ständig in der Third-Person-Sicht sieht, sieht gut aus und auch die Umgebung ist angemessen aufgehübscht worden, ohne die Geometrie der Level zu ändern. Per Knopfdruck kann man während des Spieles zwischen moderner und alter Grafik umschalten.

Der Ton blieb, so hörte ich, unverändert. Man kann die Dialoge auf Deutsch genießen. Die klassischen musikalischen Einlagen, wenn Lara insbesondere bestimmte Bereiche betritt und für mich sehr prägend waren und sich gut anhören, sind auch mit dabei.

Bei der Steuerung gibt es die klassische und eine moderne. Die klassische ist die sogenannte Tank-Control, die ich zumindest immer mit Tastatur spiel(t)e. Vielleicht ist sie heute ungewohnt, aber für mich ist sie genau die Steuerung, mit der ich bestens in diesen Spielen zurecht komme.

Die neu spendierte "moderne" Steuerung, die vorzugsweise für den Controller gedacht ist, konnte mich nicht überzeugen, obwohl ich eigentlich zuerst damit die Remastered-Version spielen wollte. Es ist definitiv nicht die Steuerung, mit der moderne Spiele ihre Figuren steuern, denn damit komme ich ja klar. Bei meinen Versuchen lief Lara nie dahin, wo ich hin wollte. Wenn man Let's Plays anschaut (von Leuten, die die Steuerung beherrschen) sieht man, dass Lara oft im Kreis geführt wird, ehe sie den angepeilten Sprung macht, weil sie sonst eben nicht so springt, wie man es will, sondern in eine falsche Richtung.

Der Vorteil dieser Steuerung ist, dass damit Sprünge möglich sind, die mit der traditionellen Steuerung nicht oder nur sehr schwer möglich sind ("Bananensprünge" oder weite Sprünge ohne viel Anlauf), so dass man Ziele erreicht, die vorher (fast) unerreichbar waren, was für manche Errungenschaften und Abkürzungen hilfreich bzw. nötig sind.

Ich habe es also so gehalten, die moderne Steuerung nur für ganz bestimmte solche Zwecke einzusetzen und blieb ansonsten bei der traditionellen Steuerung.
