The Game of Life, developed and published by Marmalade Game Studio Ltd, is a vibrant digital reimagining of Hasbro’s timeless board game that invites players to spin the wheel and chart the unpredictable course of their virtual lives. Designed as a faithful yet visually enhanced adaptation of the original, it transforms the tabletop experience into an interactive 3D environment filled with charm, color, and accessibility. Players begin by choosing a life path—either attending college for future opportunities or jumping straight into a career—and from there, every spin of the wheel propels them through the major milestones and setbacks of life. Whether buying a house, getting married, having children, or dealing with unexpected financial twists, the game maintains its core philosophy: life is a combination of luck, choice, and the occasional surprise that changes everything.

From a visual and technical standpoint, Marmalade’s adaptation succeeds in translating the nostalgic charm of the original into a lively digital experience. The environments are bright and cartoonish, with cheerful animations that bring the game board to life. Each turn feels like a small vignette, accompanied by colorful characters, whimsical vehicles, and celebratory effects that make even simple spins entertaining to watch. The developers have clearly aimed to capture the fun, family-friendly tone of the classic board game rather than reinvent it, and the result is a polished experience that’s easy to jump into and suitable for all ages. The 3D presentation adds movement and energy that keep sessions engaging, while the playful soundtrack enhances the mood without becoming intrusive. This accessible and polished approach makes it a strong choice for casual players and families looking for a relaxing group game without the need to manage physical pieces or setup time.

In terms of structure, The Game of Life remains almost identical to its physical counterpart, preserving the mix of luck-based progression and light decision-making that defines the original. Each player takes turns spinning the wheel to move along the board, stopping at spaces that trigger key life events such as career changes, weddings, taxes, or random fortune cards. The decisions offered—such as whether to go to college, which career to pursue, or whether to take a risky investment—add just enough choice to make each playthrough feel slightly personal, but the game is still driven primarily by chance. This reliance on randomness is part of its enduring appeal; it mirrors the unpredictable nature of life itself, where success or failure often feels like the result of circumstance rather than strategy. Yet, it also limits the game’s depth, ensuring that sessions are lighthearted rather than competitive or tactical.

One of the digital version’s greatest advantages lies in its convenience. The game automatically handles all of the scoring, money management, and rule enforcement, which keeps the flow fast and eliminates the bookkeeping that can slow down a physical game. This simplicity makes it perfect for quick sessions, especially in multiplayer mode, where up to four players can compete locally or online. The addition of online play allows friends and families to connect from different locations, while the AI opponents provide an alternative for solo play. These modes extend its accessibility, but the core experience remains the same—an easygoing, luck-driven ride that encourages laughter and social interaction rather than deep competition. For families or casual gamers, this makes The Game of Life a reliable go-to for game nights and online gatherings.

Despite its appealing presentation and faithful recreation, the digital version’s limitations become apparent after several sessions. Because it adheres so closely to the original mechanics, it lacks the variety or progression that might keep players engaged over the long term. The absence of new gameplay systems or dynamic events means that each playthrough feels similar to the last, with only the outcomes of the wheel spins providing variation. Some players may also find that the dominance of luck can feel frustrating, as strategy rarely outweighs randomness. Once you’ve experienced the joy of seeing the digital world unfold a few times, the novelty tends to fade, especially without meaningful unlockables or progression incentives. Furthermore, while the online multiplayer mode is functional, it doesn’t offer the depth of matchmaking or long-term community engagement found in more competitive digital board games.

Still, these drawbacks are largely balanced by the game’s accessibility and family appeal. The Game of Life isn’t designed to be a deep or strategic experience—it’s meant to be lighthearted, spontaneous, and easy to enjoy regardless of age or skill level. In this sense, Marmalade Game Studio accomplishes its goal admirably. The user interface is clean, intuitive, and colorful, allowing even younger players to understand the flow without confusion. The pace of play is steady, and the auto-saving and quick-play features make it ideal for casual gaming sessions. The game captures the same feelings of laughter, frustration, and surprise that make the physical version a family staple, while adding the benefits of modern convenience and lively presentation.

Ultimately, The Game of Life by Marmalade Game Studio offers a faithful, accessible, and visually appealing recreation of a board game classic. It delivers exactly what it promises—a cheerful digital adaptation that captures the charm and unpredictability of life’s journey, complete with whimsical turns of fate and light decision-making. It’s the kind of game best enjoyed in short bursts, especially with friends or family, where the focus is less on competition and more on sharing the experience. While it doesn’t expand on the original’s mechanics or offer much in the way of long-term depth, it succeeds in providing an easy, relaxing, and joyful way to experience a beloved board game in digital form. For fans of the original or those seeking a casual, family-friendly game that’s simple to play yet full of personality, The Game of Life remains a solid and endearing choice.

This game is really fantastic.  The crafting survival genre is my favorite and Dawn of Defiance checks all the boxes.  Systematically it is quite similar to Valheim, which is a fantastic game as well.  The developers have taken some of the best ideas from that game and implemented them here, but they've done it in a way that is better.

Visually, Dawn of Defiance is a gem.  Probably one of the most visually impressive crafting survival games I've played.  It's just beautiful.  The nights are DARK and in some zones you can't see shit all.  There's weather rotations which add flavor.

Environmental sound design is incredible and makes hunting one of the most enjoyable things you can do in this game.  I really like the 1-3 star system based off a critical hitbox.  Sneaking and being able to amplify sounds around you is so great.  I have done everything there is to do in the game at about 35 hours playtime and I am still going to go hunting all the time because it is just so damn fun.

Combat is also a major strength.  Combat is fast paced, crisp movement, different moves for each weapon type - combat is just really fulfilling and hits all the right highs.  Building is really great as well.  All the pieces snap together easily and build options are fairly robust.  I have rebuilt my base 2-3 times now and each time there's just more and more options to implement as you progress through the game.

The game client itself is very reliable.  I have completed the game and never crashed once.  At this time, I only ever encountered a single in-game bug (which was my cooking spit freezing up) but I was able to work around it and keep going.  Honestly, a remarkable achievement these days.  I did play solo so I cannot testify to the multiplayer experience.  However, the fact that there is one already is really great and I plan on playing it again with friends/family.  Dawn of Defiance has a "save anywhere and at any time" feature that is fantastic for busy people who can't devote hours at a time to playing - definitely a big plus.  In solo, there is also a pause feature which is great when you need to get up and do something for whatever reason and not get merked by enemies for being AFK.

The game is early access but devs have a robust public roadmap and they are working their way through their goals.  The map is incomplete at the moment, but you can really get a feel for what it will be like when they are done, because two mid-game zones are already really robust experiences so I'm looking forward to what they do with the other 3-5 zones.  Their first raid dungeon was a really cool experience and vastly different from the open world.  Great loot that justifies re-completing the dungeon. Assault Spy is a high-energy, anime-inspired action game developed by Wazen and published by NIS America, Inc., that combines slick, combo-heavy combat with a tongue-in-cheek corporate espionage story. It follows two protagonists—Asaru, a freelance spy who wields a briefcase as his weapon of choice, and Amelia, a fierce CIA operative with a more direct and brutal fighting style. The game’s narrative centers around the mysterious Negabot Corporation, which has been taken over by rogue AI and mercenaries, forcing both agents to infiltrate the company for their own reasons. Rather than delivering a deeply layered plot, the story thrives on its eccentric characters, fast pacing, and over-the-top humor, often parodying both spy fiction and Japanese corporate culture. Its tone feels closer to a quirky anime episode than a traditional action thriller, and that’s precisely what gives the game its personality.

At the core of Assault Spy lies a fast and fluid combat system reminiscent of classics like Devil May Cry or Bayonetta, though with a smaller indie scope. Every encounter is built around chaining together elaborate combos, juggling enemies, and maintaining momentum. Asaru’s fighting style is acrobatic and flashy, combining quick melee strikes with ranged attacks using his “explosive business cards,” while Amelia focuses on heavy hits, ground slams, and close-quarters grappling. Both characters offer a distinct rhythm of play, giving the game a strong sense of variety. The dodge, dash, and combo-cancel mechanics keep battles smooth and reactive, rewarding players who learn to master timing and positioning. When the systems click, combat feels exhilarating—fast, stylish, and satisfyingly chaotic. It’s a kind of rhythm-action flow that becomes deeply rewarding once you learn how to chain moves seamlessly and avoid getting hit.

The presentation is one of the game’s most striking features, leaning heavily into a minimalistic but energetic anime aesthetic. The characters are sleekly designed, the animations exaggerated, and the story sequences unfold in visual-novel-like cutscenes complete with expressive 2D portraits and fully voiced Japanese dialogue. The art direction fits the tone perfectly, emphasizing humor and exaggeration rather than realism. Unfortunately, the environments don’t share that same level of vibrancy. Much of the game takes place in repetitive corporate settings—sterile offices, industrial corridors, and empty warehouses—that lack visual diversity. While this minimalist design helps maintain a high frame rate during intense battles, it also makes exploration feel visually bland at times. The music, on the other hand, is a highlight: an energetic blend of electronic beats and rock guitar riffs that keeps the tempo high and matches the intensity of the action.

Despite its strong combat mechanics, Assault Spy’s rough edges are impossible to ignore. The camera is often one of the biggest challenges—its positioning and lock-on behavior can become erratic during hectic fights, occasionally obscuring the player’s view of enemies. The platforming segments also feel less refined, with clunky jumps and awkward level geometry that can disrupt the otherwise smooth pacing. Enemy variety is another area where the game shows its limitations; while the bosses are flashy and entertaining, many standard foes share similar attack patterns, making extended play sessions feel repetitive. These shortcomings don’t ruin the experience, but they do remind you that this is a lower-budget indie project that can’t quite match the polish of the genre’s heavyweights.

What keeps Assault Spy engaging is its sense of momentum and replayability. Each of the two campaigns offers a different perspective, with unique cutscenes, dialogue, and fighting styles. Playing through both gives a fuller picture of the game’s world and allows players to experiment with alternate approaches to combat. The short runtime—roughly six to eight hours combined—works to its advantage, ensuring the experience doesn’t overstay its welcome. For players seeking additional challenges, there are unlockable difficulty levels, a boss rush mode, and performance ranking systems that encourage mastery and replay. While it lacks deep narrative complexity, its combat loop is strong enough to sustain multiple playthroughs, particularly for players who enjoy refining combos and chasing high scores.

Technically, the game runs well, with smooth performance and quick load times, though it bears the hallmarks of a small-scale project. Some animations and visual effects can appear rough around the edges, and occasional bugs or clipping issues can break immersion. Still, the overall responsiveness of the controls and the consistency of the frame rate make it a joy to play once you adjust to its quirks. It’s the kind of game that values feel over flash, emphasizing responsiveness and flow over technical spectacle. The end result is an experience that might not look as polished as big-budget action games but manages to capture their spirit through mechanical precision and enthusiasm.

Assault Spy is best described as a love letter to the character-action genre—a fast, stylish, and slightly unpolished gem made by a small team with big ambitions. It’s a game that lives and dies by its combat system, delivering a satisfying rush of speed, flair, and control that rivals much larger productions. Its lighthearted tone, distinct dual protagonists, and anime-inspired charm give it personality, even when its environments and systems occasionally falter. For fans of stylish action who value mechanics over production scale, it’s a refreshing and underrated entry that rewards mastery and persistence. It may not reach the refined heights of its inspirations, but it has the heart and energy of a game made by someone who truly understands what makes the genre fun.

Huh.  For a free game I'm actually thoroughly impressed.  I picked this up thinking it would be the dumb usual shovelware for Vive, but considering it's free, it's not bad.  Having taken only 15 minutes to beat, I definitely wouldn't pay more than 2$ for it.  However, the gameplay is surprisingly solid enough that if it were more than an hour long, I'd actually pay upwards of 5-10$ or so for it, which really isn't bad.  The game runs remarkably smoothly compared to many worse-looking VR titles, the action is nice and responsive, and I felt immersed in the action.  
The game plays almost exactly like a classic arcade shooter.  And I don't mean "arcade" like a steam "arcade" game- I mean this actually feels like one of the classic rail shooters that you play with friends at an arcade, paying tokens and being rewarded tickets.  Surprisingly, very (VERY) few VR games actually take advantage of this type of game mechanic, clearly making the false assumption that it's not worth making it less immersive.  The action makes you feel badass enough that it's borderline silly (similar to arcades- as long as you have good aim, you can see all the opponents collapse in almost an instant).  Between the aesthetics, music, and action, this game feels *exactly* like a traditionalistic early 1980's sci-fi classic vibe.  
There are only two cons that I'd say are substantial:
1.  There are things that appear as fun, intimidating boss battles, of two kinds: A giant exosuit, and a powerful shielded knight.  Apparently, the giant exosuit isn't implemented in the game yet, since shooting it immediately brings you to the next area without any fight.  Although the shield knights would otherwise be badass, they go down in almost a single hit.
2.  The reloading system feels a bit dumb.  It's interesting- when you run out of ammo, a clip automatically appears in your non-dominant hand and you have to slap it into the gun.  This actually feels pretty cool.  However, seeing as how bare-bones it is, I'd rather just press a button.  I like it when vive games let you use only one controller.  In this game, you need to use the second controller, but solely for this one purpose that isn't even necessary.  

Overall, I've gone on too long seeing as this is a free game.  I'd say it's 1000% worth downloading and playing.  It's not spam, and I promise that it actually gave me a wholeheartedly FUN experience for a solid 20 minutes or so.  It doesn't even take up too much disc space.

After over 200 solid grinding hours on this game, I feel I can finally weigh in on it.

Let's start with the basics: EYE: Divine Cybermancy is, on the surface, a sci-fi role-playing game which puts you in the shoes of an elite cyborg member of an Inquisition-like organisation called EYE, which is meant to fight aliens, pirates and literal demons (more on them later) in space for a galactic human government called the Federation. Over the course of the story, besides the aforementioned enemies, your order will find itself stuck within tensions with the Federation as well as internal ones.

Okay: those are the generic lines which should (I hope!) draw you into the game. 

In practice, this game is a mess. Players have compared it to playing GMOD whilst spawning hundreds of NPCs and fighting them with a combat mod, and honestly that's a great description. 
There are elements of a stealth game, a tactical game, and a spell-casting swordfighting fantasy game all mashed into lightning-fast combat which is bound to catch you off guard the first time you play.
And, of course, throughout this game the story doesn't make much sense, but as you can tell from the very beginning, you're supposed to mistrust what you see. 
You instantly understand that something is not quite right with you, your character, and what's happened to him. It's your job to navigate the strangeness (as well as the actual ragebait moments) within this game to understand what's "actually going on". 
For now, all I can say is: if you really wanna figure out the plot, read one of the guides on how to get the "true ending". There are four endings in the game, all determined by choices you make at certain points.

Now for pros: the combat and atmosphere in this game are amazing. You do need to invest in the RPG level ups to feel it, which often needs a bit of grinding, but really nothing stops you from becoming any combination of an elite spell caster, an invisible sniper, a peerless swordsman cyborg or anything else you may desire. You can become really OP. The guns are punchy and few enemies can really tank them, same for the melee weapons which really allow you to rip and tear. With time, you will unlock weapons at the Armory that will make you effectively invincible. 
You can use both ordinary level-ups as well as the ingame currency, Brouzoufs, to both upgrade your cyber body parts as well as to launch research projects (which you can loot from enemies) to unlock various upgrades.
You can buy new weapons, implants, as well as psi-abilities (basically spells) from vendors in the Temple.
There are penalties for going down too many times, called Wounds, but with the right research not only will you make yourself more powerful, but you will eventually be able to gain immunity to these permanent wounds. From there, you really get no penalties from dying and the game becomes carefree.
You can finetune your own experience in the options tab: you can rig the AI like a horde shooter, or tune it more towards stealth. This all makes it so that each playthrough is unique.

Cons: the combat will be a turn off at first. The NPC's, especially the literal space demons I mentioned before, will respawn endlessly kinda like Nightmare mode in OG Doom. Most enemies can and will kill you quite easily if you're not careful at first. Many enemies are meant to be incredibly OP, such as the higher level demons and the gunships. The upside is that these enemies drop massive amounts of brouzouf and XP, and in Co-op they're easier to deal with.
I mentioned that each playthrough is unique, but unfortunately there are some tools you just need, period. The Bear Killer revolver, which you can unlock at the weapon vendor, is essential for destroying the stronger enemies. You kind of need to grind some research to stand a real chance, too. All these things do make it so that some options are more like mandatory steps.

All these dynamics apply to multiplayer: you can play both the campaign as well as bonus maps with your own avatar along with your friends' avatars.

In summary: grind your own post-apocalyptic cyber-wizard-knight and let it play with your friends' cyber-wizard-knights to smash all the evil alien demons in space. Now, with dream sequences!

I hate that I gotta give this one a non-recommended but it's simply not there for a full release game. There's a ton of fun elements to the game but it's missing a lot to be considered a 1.0. It's a 0.6 or 0.7 at best. 

Sailing ships, building bases, exploring, it's all super fun and something I love and have been craving in some survival games, I was hoping this one would scratch that itch, but it's missing a lot. The promo videos and images are not at all what is in the game. 

I'll say this, sailing is fun, exploring is fun, building decently cool bases great. Chasing down ships that steal your cargo great. Even blasting a kraken. But that's about where it ends. 

Graphics are decent at first, however, there's lots of glitching, clipping through walls, the storm that appears has no depth as to where it is, you just get this black glow on part of the screen that suddenly you're in the storm. Draw distances are horrible, I was building a guard ship at the crew haven island and I could see the flashes from the hammers of the people building it from miles away but the ship didn't appear until I was right next to the dock. 

Combat is super clunky on land, I'll swing right at an enemy five times, three will hit, one will say it missed and one just swings aimlessly. But then they won't even swing and I'll start losing life. Another time I was taking on the merchant ship, kept running to heal up and was a decent challenge until I finally boarded a third time, and the captain just froze, the rest of his crew wandered around didn't notice me and I could just hit the captain over and over until he died. Went from a challenging fight I needed to bounce away from a few times to a cake walk in seconds. 

Ship combat is no better. It's fun to blast a ship away but it's beyond easy. I've yet to face any other ship besides the ghost ships that have been a major challenge to even the basic warboat. It's just point and click and attack. But honestly my biggest gripe with the ship combat is the types of ships even available. I've played 20 hours. Start with the raft and then the warboat, not bad. Then you get the sloop for free, which gives you some broad sides. It's not really a spoiler cause it happens pretty quick. But then the next boat you can reasonable afford is 2500 gold and looks great until you realize it only has a rear facing cannon. I ended up losing my sloop due to not realizing the storm was damaging me cause I was fighting ships and lost my sloop which you can't get back, and now only have a small warboat which is roughly same strength but super slow, or this new providence boat which is fast but any ship i want to attack I have to pass then shoot from behind. I try to do a cargo mission where you're facing cargo stealers who ram you and take your stuff then flee the other direction and I can't do anything about it cause to get your stuff back you gotta sink them, but that means I gotta do a full 180, while they're just darting off cause somehow they can flip around completely in one go, then chase past them or get along side and then turn my back to them and fire from my rear deck. Makes it completely useless, even going to sink ships to get treasure takes 3 times the time since there's no good positioning. There's one boat above that in the base options that I've seen so far and it's 4 times the price. At the rate of accumulating gold it'll take another 20 hours of play to get that if not more cause I don't have a good fighting ship to down enemy ships, I'm level 42 but can't even take on bigger ships cause the tactics suck. 

As for challenges with the ship battles, there is none other than positioning. You can blast them from miles away and they rarely shoot at you. Even taking on forts, and watchtowers, they barely scratch you while you're blasting them. 

Building is clunky, the UI and controls are horrible in my opinion, there's no fast attaching things to the hotbar, using anything requires bringing up a menu or adding it to the hotbar so to use a single piece of food you gotta click and drag it to the hotbar then press the button or click it in the inventory, open a window and click use. If you got a nice setup on your hotbar already it's very inconvenient. No option to just select half a stack of items, want to take half gotta click the item, then click withdraw from another pop up menu, then type your quantity, no buttons to select 10, 100, half, etc. Just makes it clunky and time consuming. 

Questing is also another thing that's clunky, your list of quests fills up the side of your screen, miss a quest at the time and gotta redo all parts. I once did the quest that needed to buy the cartography blueprint and something else. I bought the blueprint, built the table, then did the other part (I forget exactly what it was) but because I no longer had the cartography blueprint in my possession because I already used it, I had to go get it again wasting gold just so I could have both items in my possession. Another one I failed cause cargo stealers took my loot and I couldn't catch them both and didn't make it to the trader in time, the crew haven no longer sold that item so now I have 4 crates of porcelain that I can't sell, wasted 400 gold on, and the quest for it is stuck on the side of my screen cause it wasn't completed. That was around hour 10, still there, still no sign of being able to complete it. 

Playing solo is also a drag with the randomly changing islands and timers. Quests appear for things that you can't get to, and since it's seemingly random, literally just have to wander around for 30-60min for the next event. I can see that being a bit better with other people but the game is so small I can't see much being gained from playing with others. It's on par with Sunkenland for size and while that too is a multiplayer game, it has a lot more fleshed out factions, raids, action, crafting, and things going on even between islands to make it's size seem more filled. Here it's just a lot of empty space. I've on multiple occasions, just hit numlock to continuous sail and then pulled out my phone and played a game or watched a youtube video while waiting to get to a location. 

For all the bad, it really does have a great structure, it really does have some amazing potential, and if it was still early access, version 0.6 or 0.7 I could absolutely give it a recommend right now in it's current state. But because it's already put out as a fully fleshed game, and from experience that usually means roadmap ahead is going to be a lot of minor tweaks not major changes to improve, I can't give it the thumbs up.

Absolutely fucking brilliant. Purely as a work of art, this is the best video game I have played in my entire life, and it's not even finished yet. I will always, always have so much respect for a dev who actually has something of substance to say, who is brutally sincere in their work - especially in this very superficial profit/clout-driven industry, where people are constantly afraid of alienating potential customers. Having a theoretical underpinning is so incredibly rare to see in the medium on any level, let alone a very polemic political one. That said, it doesn't gloat or parade its own intelligence or insight - it will happily bounce between fringe 20th century psychoanalysis and the most low brow bodily fluid humour, seemingly at random. It takes the moral and ethical implications of its subjects deathly seriously, but finds humour in their absurdity.

Improves, develops, and expands on everything that Cruelty Squad was going for, but it is very much its own beast. The writing is genuinely literary, the level design is superb, and the integration of gameplay into narrative is so cohesive that there basically isn't a distinction. It is a masterpiece of diffused satire - at a point, you are just as desensitised to all of this as the main character, with only brief, stunted moments of reflection. The last few quests in the current version genuinely made me feel disgusted with myself in a way that no binary moral choice ('do you kill the people or not kill the people???') ever could.

This is an absurdly ambitious project in terms of scope, but Ville Kallio is an absolute genius - I have no doubt that he'll be able to pull it off. It almost works as a full game already (as is, it's probably the same length as Cruelty Squad), and I'm so excited to see it develop.

(Also, it's fucking hilarious, and I think the player character is legitimately one of the most interesting and well-written protagonists I've ever played as in a game.)

"To boldly go where no man has gone before." – Captain James T. Kirk

FTL manages to immerse you in a brand new story every single time you set out in a shiny new ship. As you’ve probably gathered from other reviews, you will die often and spectacularly. Your crew will suffocate to death, be eaten by giant mutant space spiders, get beaten to death by rock aliens or mantises, burn up while flying too close to a sun, or be wiped out by a virus. Over and over again. FTL is brutally hard, and that’s exactly where its beauty lies. Your ship and crew improve gradually, and every loss hurts. When a beloved slugman, human, or android gets sucked into the cold abyss of space, it stings every time. Few games manage to create such an intricate, random, and volatile universe as FTL does. The tactical sacrifices you’ll be forced to make will make you cringe, curse your luck, and swear vengeance on the rebel fleet all while pushing you to keep going for just one more run.

The combat system is deep enough to deserve its own Wikipedia page. Every weapon, ship upgrade, character ability, and subsystem has its own strengths and weaknesses, and understanding them along with those of your enemies is key to survival. Balancing your ship’s limited power between weapons, shields, and other systems is one of the most brilliant mechanics ever designed. You never know what the next FTL jump will bring, so every decision feels like a gamble whether you’re spending scrap to upgrade your shields, repair your hull, hire new crew, or buy a beam drone. The game is smart, punishing, and completely engrossing.

[h1]Identity crisis at its worst.[/h1]

5k is a [b]sad game[/b]. I'm gonna address something that usually gets ignored, but this [i]"tactical shooter"[/i] aspect falls apart [b]relatively quickly[/b]. Gameplay loop [b]does not require planning or positioning[/b] because NPCs just run at you and damage you or sometimes shoot you. They don't try to hide or flank or group up or form a defensive position. Due to their high quantity individually they can't deal too much damage and their time to kill is low, therefore it provides [b]almost no risks[/b] beyond accidentally dying due to being cornered or having a bad weapon for crowd control and realising it loads on a checkpoint that was [b]15-20 minutes away[/b]. [b]You have infinite stamina[/b] and your movement speed is high enough you can outrun most enemies. Ammo and medical equipment is abundant, so you don't have to worry about that. You can't utilize the environment to gain an advantage (ala elevation, darkness, destructable surfaces, hazards like fire or electricity, traps) and there is no stealth.

I'm not gonna claim false advertising because due to game's early access nature they can still steer it in proper direction. [b]But you must know[/b] that this is a pretty basic horde shooter with horror elements, closer to something like Left 4 Dead than say Ready or Not.

After around 3-4 years of development (depending if you start counting from Kickstarter goal reach or Steam Early Access release) we have a game that has so many different things it's honestly [u]baffling[/u]. For some reason they spent precious development time and resources on:

• Main Campaign (still in development).
• Fully developed Bonus Chapter.
• Simple Wave Survival as Foundation personnel.
• Complicated Wave Survival as D-Class with unique maps, narration, challenges and even an ending.
• PVP.

And the only two thing truly worth talking about right now are guns and bonus chapter.

[b]Shooting[/b] in the game is very satyisfying, animations are fluid and detailed, sound design is fine with questionable decisions here and there and gun variety is delicious. The thing that kept me hooked the most is [u]finding new guns to try out[/u]. It's truly a highlight of this game.

Another highlight is [b]Bonus chapter[/b] that imho serves as [b]"Look at what we can cook if we lock in"[/b] type of addition. It has proper story, dialogues, suspense, tension, unique enemies, couple of great set pieces, lore, it's just fun. Unfortunately its ~ one hour long. 

Everything else is very raw, underdeveloped and at this stage of the game quite [u]unnecessary[/u]. Because in order for everything to work and be fun you need to make sure [b]the foundation[/b] (pun intended) is properly developed. 

What's the point of wave game modes if enemies have no proper AI, no variety in tactics, they don't interact with one another and humans with guns possess more anomalous properties than SCPs due to their unpredictable pathing and rare ability to instakill you from seemingly any distance. 

What's the point of PVP when average online according to SteamDB is around 150 people and there are better games like Insurgency or Arma that provide more tactical gameplay loop. Not even mentioning the fact that people are interested in the campaign.

What's the point of main campaign when bonus chapter is 100 times more engaging, unique and properly developed. Why not make small independent chapters from the perspective of different groups interacting with Foundation's atrocities while highlighting each group's unique approach. [b]Hilariously[/b], due to this lack of focus, [u]3 years later main campaign has only 3 chapters[/u] with relatively simple gimmicks, no plot and protagonist just runs around, shoots stuff and presses buttons/throws switches. For ~20 bucks I'd expect that amount on launch.

I really want to see this game succeed. I want them to finally focus on what's important and stop ADHDing all around the place. Idk if I'll live to see the day though. We are on version 0.17 guys. How much longer do we have to wait?

A great pick for anyone who enjoys narrative-based life or raising sims. I’ve played through a few generations now, and while there are things that could be refined in a sequel, overall it’s a thoughtful and fun game - especially for the price.

Visuals & Music
The art style is honestly one of the best in the genre. It’s warm, expressive, and fits perfectly with the story’s tone. The soundtrack also deserves praise - chill, nostalgic, and really sets the mood.

Customisation
Being able to customise your character is a nice touch, though I wish there were a few more options to make each generation look more distinct.

Tone & Story
The writing is emotional and often relatable, but it leans heavily on sad or serious storylines. I found myself playing therapist to my friends more often than expected! A few more lighthearted or uplifting moments would help balance things out.

Friendships
Friendships are a big focus, but they sometimes feel one-sided - you spend a lot of time helping others through tough times without much in return. A bit more mutual growth or fun in these relationships would make them feel more rewarding.

Skills & Choices
The skill system is enjoyable, but some paths seem to matter more than others (sports in particular). I also didn’t always feel like my choices had much impact on how the story played out, which made some playthroughs feel similar.

Parents & Mental Health
Balancing your mental health with parental expectations can feel harsh - simple leisure activities can tank your relationship points fast. It’d be nice if there were more positive interactions or family moments to offset that.

Exams
Exams are presented as a mini-game, which is fine, but a little underwhelming after all the skill-building. Something that ties more directly into your progress could make it more satisfying.

Overall
I really enjoyed Growing Up, even if it can feel emotionally heavy at times. There’s a lot of heart and nostalgia in it, and you can tell the devs put personal experience into the story. It’s a unique, touching take on growing up - I just wish it had a few more bright and playful moments along the way.

I played 3 hours so far and gonna grind a bit more, but I am a veteran player when it comes to arpgs , survival games and so on. So even though I do recommend this game I have to warn that the game is very bare bones still, but it had potential. 
POSITIVES : 
  Fun game play loop and with more content it should be even better.
  Crafting is simple and not tedious. 
  Very good Stash implementation, you basically can upgrade one Stash to fit most of your stuff. People who like having many stashes with different types of material in all of them could not be as happy, but that can be done too.
  Combat is decent , still feels very much early access, but that is not a bad thing if it will be improved later on.
Gear is quite simplistic but feels impactful. 
 Building is quite good, it is simple and it does the job, I don't think it needs to be as complex as Valheim.
NEGATIVES/ FEEDBACK the more important stuff at the moment : 
  Leveling doesn't feel exciting at all, you just get skill points to open skill/glyph slots and that's it. I feel that this should be improved a lot, leveling is one of the dopamine hits in arpg, you have to feel it , maybe get stat points, maybe some talent trees or what not, a lot of option can be explored here.
  Classless doesn't feel that great, you have no need at all to create new character apart from the fact that maybe map is gonna be a bit different. Only few games do classless very good but in my opinion classes are cool and fun, there should be some way to specialize your character that is somewhat permanent or requires a lot to change so you have incentive to make different character. I think doing some kind of classes that maybe have different talent trees that give thematic passive and skill modifying options, but still letting you be whatever you want with those specializations would be awesome.
 Combat doesn't feel punchy enough , but that I would assume should be better with time.
 Map needs a lot of work, you should be able to place markers and some other stuff, maybe see level of zones that you visited when you mouse over that area.
 Left click is melee , right click is ranged or wand attack, honestly I really hate this , even if you just wanna play bow or mage you still have a melee attack on left click, it feels weird having two buttons for basically same purpose. I think if you wanna mix range with melee you should just use skills for melee attacks or the other way around if you are more focused melee.

Game is worth a try, I will be spending more time with it and see where I can leave more feedback, I think it had great potential if it gets frequent updates.

[b]Scars Above[/b] es un shooter en tercera persona con algunos componentes soul-like en un mundo de ciencia ficción que tiene algunas reminiscencias de Mass Effect. Todo esto puede sonar un poco rebuscado, pero está implementado de una forma tan precisa que el juego es gratificante en cada apartado planteado. 

El argumento es interesante e invita a continuar jugando hasta el final. Los diálogos y textos tienen mucha presencia en cada escena y son indispensables para comprender la historia. Es posible poner las voces y textos en español, aunque en lo personal, siempre me gustó jugar en su lenguaje original con subtítulos, que sea de paso, se pueden ajustar en tamaño (lo más viejos agradecemos esto).

Gráficamente hablando es muy bueno y goza de una excelente optimización que permite verlo en su calidad máxima sin caídas de frames. El sonido está bien y aunque tiene alguna que otra musiquita agradable, termina quedando en segundo plano al punto que actualmente no recuerdo ninguna melodía.

A nivel jugable es donde nos encontramos los componentes soul-like con la clásica barra de “stamina”, la posibilidad de esquivar ataques haciendo un “roll” y recuperación de energía a través de consumibles recargables en cada monolito (equivalente a las hogueras). Sin embargo tiene una dificultad apta para todo público con posibilidad de ajustarla durante la partida y escenarios lineales. También tiene un componente RPG que nos permite mejorar al personaje a través de “información” encontrada en los niveles o escaneando enemigos por primera vez. La dificultad de los jefes es un acierto sin ser ninguno de ellos un dolor de cabeza, pero no se regalan en su primer encuentro y hay que saber encontrarles la vuelta.

A todo esto, [b]Scars Above[/b] tiene una duración media de 7 a 8 horas y es posible obtener todos sus logros en una única run. Es imposible quedarse atascado y se juega realmente bien con gamepad. A lo largo de todo el juego no encontré bugs, pero algunos usuarios han reportado problemas en ciertas zonas. Para suerte de todos, esta pequeña joyita suele tener descuentos de hasta 90% y marida muy bien con una copa de cabernet sauvignon por las noches. Sin miedo al exceso, que es posible habilitar la asistencia de apuntado.

I give a 4 out of 5 Stars ★ for Middle-earth™: Shadow of Mordor™

I just completed the 100% Steam achievements with a play time of about 60 hours and here is my review. 

Shadow of Mordor was released in 2014, a tricky time for game developers as it was a transition between Playstation 3 to 4 and Xbox 360 to One. I had 2 copies 1 for PS3 and another for PC to test it and just ran through the Campaign and completed it in about 15 hours. I never liked the combat back then, found the nemesis system interesting but the lore was a big disappointment for many LOTR Fans. I remember this game was criticised for being a copycat of Assassin's creed free running at the time of its release including the air assassinations but it actually plays out differently. Its basically Arkham series style rhythm-based combat with excellent crowd control and fluidity. 

Fast forward to 2025 considering the quality of games these days, this game feels like a gem to play. I needed some marathon single player game for Halloween and Shadow of Mordor became my go to choice. Despite a boring routine revenge main story and a lack of memorable characters beyond Talion and Celebrimbor, the developers made an excellent compensation with the much loved Nemesis system which gives the Orcs a lot of personality making an individual gamer's experience totally random and unique. 

The Orcs are the real stars of the game and the reason one would love to play the game and with the Nemesis system you can play this forever if you want as there is no ending as an Orc can become a Captain and then a War-Chief for Talion to defeat. 

Overall Middle-earth™: Shadow of Mordor™ has very good Nostalgia factor. It does have outdated graphics for new gamers but it has an enjoyable combat system with Nemesis. The campaign and boss battles are pretty bad but the funny Orcs and their non stop banter and complaints of just about everything will keep anyone engaged. If you got bored simply go any stronghold and listen to the Orcs talk to themselves and you will be entertained.

Cheers! Have Fun!

Finished first story playthrough on Hard, around 30 hours.

Absolutely amazing Action RPG, even as a non-FF fan.  The action system is incredibly interactive and consistent, the RPG elements are super varied and fun to experiment, music is great from start to finish, and the story, despite the memes and all, was a fun campy and sincere tale of an adventure, with terrific voice acting and all.  Like all modern Team Ninja offerings, the game showers you with loot, but this game lets you completely ignore it with the "Optimize" option, even on Hard.  Understanding and exploiting the action system mattered way more in my view, though I hear the DLCs are a different beast in that regard.

And boy, the action.  While built on Team Ninja's Nioh format, there's so much [i]interaction[/i] happening that it was a completely different experience.  This interactivity works on one hand in how you mix jobs and abilities, but more importantly how you interact with enemies, mobs and bosses a like.  You can manipulate enemies from flinching to launching, or hard knockbacks resulting in wallslam, or triggering something in the environment.  On top of that, you have 3 defensive options (guard, dodge, a "parry") at any given time, while good ol' positioning also works really well.  Even though Jack has less moveset than William or Hide, the sense of expansive options and freedom was definitely there.  This isn't a discount Nioh by any means.

Further expanding this interactiveness is how the Soul Shield - the "parry" - works.  Blocking an attack with SS gives you MP, which are resources to use various active skills.  There are some enemy attacks you can "steal" by doing SS and then turn it right back at them.  It's not really a universal defense though, as SS will always cost Break Gauge, a stamina/posture resource.  So the game never felt like a Simon Says simulator of pressing the universal defense button at the right timing, and it required a fair bit of quick, on-the-spot decision making.

What's amazing is that this action interactivity was incredibly consistent.  Whether facing mobs, elites, or bosses, all of this basic architecture applied (well, minus the launching and knockbacks, but that's minor).  The bosses honestly deserve a special shoutout, as they were consistently great to fight.  A lot of the so-called Stylish Action or "CAG" titles have really elaborate combat system, but often have a hit-and-miss track record with bosses, whether Devil May Cry or Ninja Gaiden.  The consistent quality of bosses here, and how they complement the combat system, definitely deserves praise.

The game isn't without fault (no game is), but SoP's faults are more obvious.  First, it's clear this is a budget title in many ways: maps both in terms of visual and level design leaves a lot to be desired, enemies' visual variety is low (mechanically good though), gears visual variety is also low, and there's some finicky performance issues, like the fog/particles suddenly tanking my FPS.  

The bigger fault is the loot - I essentially did not interact with it [i]at all[/i] in this playthrough.  I'm not sure if I could have either, since the next mission will probably give loot that will automatically invalidate anything you tried to "build" anyway.  Team Ninja really need to cut back on their lootosexual fetish, the spam email folder clearing gets old.  Maybe cut down the amount of loot drop by 50% for the first playthrough or something?

All in all, a great Action RPG with very distinct identity, beyond the KILL CHAOS meme.  Not sure if I'd recommend at full price, but do consider it at some degree of discount.  You're in for a pretty wild ride!

This is one of those times where I wish Steam had a sideways thumb for reviews instead of just up or down. Personally, I err on the side of not recommending this game, but it definitely still has a lot of merit and I think a certain type of person will still enjoy it enough.

For the most part, I actually was really enjoying this game and getting super interested in the setting and story. I found myself hardly being able to wait to play it again. The lead up to the ending though is abysmal. The story throws so many twists at you so quickly while also turning back in on itself like some sort of drug addled ouroboros that I just completely stopped caring. I'm sure there is a lot of symbolism and stuff but it ended up feeling just way too pretentious and strange for me to actually get into it versus what had started as a pretty grounded game. It gets really immersive, potentially too immersive at times honestly, but then throws away what seemed like such a carefully and intricately crafted narrative at the finish line.

On top of that, the game still has plenty of bugs in it and doesn't run very well at all. You can break out of the map, get stuck, see things that aren't supposed to happen yet, break quests and puzzles... all while the game comes apart at the seams with awful auto exposure and stuttering from just standing still and moving the camera around.

As far as the "horror" aspect goes, there was one part that genuinely scared me and that's about it. Most of its horror is either shock horror or simply macabre. Shock horror is great when you do it right and this game does have its infamous "face peeling" moment done very well. However, pretty much everything else just had me thinking it was more stupid than scary.

This is a real shame because, like I said, the game DID have me hooked for most of the run time, minus a few issues here and there like any other game. It wasn't exactly what I expected, but after adjusting to what the game actually was I was liking it quite a lot. The massive problem was just the ending and the lead up to it. The game felt like it lost all of the identity it had built up and just derailed entirely.

I've played walking sims and puzzle adventure games just like this one with far better, more cohesive stories and gameplay structures. If you're looking at this thinking it might be interesting to you because of the horror aspects, you'll be disappointed. If you're looking at this thinking you might really enjoy the setting of Italy during WW2, you'll like the beginning but hate the ending. If you're looking at this thinking you might enjoy a story told through the environment with little interactive bits here and there... go play What Remains of Edith Finch instead.

Kao the Kangaroo is a mixed bag. It's very close to being a great game but the bugs, jankiness, and general lack of polish in several areas brings the experience down. Regardless I think there's enough to enjoy here that I do recommend it overall.

In a lot of ways, this is the best game in the Kao series. It's got the best hub worlds by a long-shot, there's more things to do within them and more reason to explore than ever with costumes and health upgrades to buy. I think the game is GORGEOUS, it's on par with Spyro Reignited if not even better looking, the game has some really nice looking levels and speaking of levels - this game has some bangers. I think they are well designed and have fun gimmicks involving your boxing gloves, Elemental effects can be applied to them and used for puzzles and platforming which is neat. I think this game controls really good and the combat here is genuinely some of the best combat I've seen in a 3D platformer, it's nothing complex or crazy but it's perfect for this kind of game. It's a satisfying pacebreaker for the platforming that doesn't go on too long, it's really fun to punch dudes in this game and build up to a big take-down to wipe out a bunch of guys at once.

All of this sounds great right? and it is. It's a really solid platformer but the thing is this game is JANK as hell. It's a lot of little things, boxes disappearing instead of breaking when you hit them, hitboxes of certain enemy types are weirdly small, the way Kao picks up items looks really awkward because he tries to face the camera but doesn't track to face it so he just looks off in a random direction. The audio mixing here is really bad too, sometimes music just turns off and the level is silent for the rest of the level or some things within the game seem like they'd make a sound but just don't. This entire game screams that it was rushed out because there's just a general lack of polish in a lot of different places. 

One of the worst things I ran into was that the grapple points were just not working, Kao would just fling off in a random direction and I couldn't figure out why. I messed with the settings and it turns out if you have FPS higher than 60 they literally don't work. If the physics don't work beyond 60fps, there shouldn't even be an option for any FPS higher than that. There was another time I got sort-of softlocked where a flame powerup for my gloves didn't spawn where it was supposed to and I had to die and re-load to get it to spawn again. It wasn't horrible, but annoying. 

As for actual negatives with the game itself, I think the voice acting is pretty bad. I understand they wanted to get Polish voice actors because Kao as a franchise originates there but man these actors just do not do a good job. I also am not a huge fan of Kao's new design, it's not the worst redesign I've ever seen for a platformer character but the old one was much better, and it is here as a costume which you can get pretty early on which is cool. It doesn't stay for cutscenes though which is a shame.

If I could, I'd give this game a "mixed" review because it really is a good game hidden beneath jank and bugs that easily could have been patched out but never were. I did have fun playing it but it's got issues, maybe you won't mind the problems as much as me though.

Итак, в самом начале вы выберете компанию за жизнь или смерть.
Пожалуй начнём с жизни, где вы постараетесь спасти пациента, но для начала рекомендую пройти обучение, чтобы разобраться что к чему. А то будете лечить всех подорожником.
И скажу сразу, у кого вид внутренних органов вызывает неприязнь или ухудшение самочувствия, то вам не стоит в это играть.

Сама компания делится на несколько уровней от мединститута до отделения реанимации. А для их разблокировки вам потребуется уверено и верно провести лечение пациентов до того как станет слишком поздно. И каждый уровень делится на дополнительные подуровни. И начнете вы с интернатуры. Попыток может быть сколько угодно, к счастью пациенты только виртуальные.

Сначала вы дадите имя пациенту ну или оставите стандартное. Кстати также можете выбрать кого-то из предложенных известных личностей, как например Трампа и полечить его.
Выберете пол пациента, для игры это имеет значение, так как мужские и женские заболевания могут быть разными.
Ну и конечно выберете сложность. Для знакомства я бы рекомендовал начать с уровня мягкий.
Далее по мере прохождения у вас будет возможность выбрать одно или несколько усилений, которые дадут бонус при лечении. Так что стоит хорошо подумать какой взять.

После запуска перед вами предстанет пациент. Точнее вы увидите его или её насквозь, а точнее посмотрите на систему кровообращения, органы дыхания, пищеварения, скелет, нервную систему, почки, иммунную систему и мышечные ткани. Прям как из учебника по анатомии. У каждой систему будут свои жизненные показатели, а у пациента отдельный общий показатель, но зависящий от остальных.

Чтобы проводить какие либо действия по проведению диагностики вам потребуется собирать био очки, они выглядят вы виде красных кровяных тел или белков и соответственно имеют разную стоимость в очках. На дальнейших этапах вам откроется авто-сбор, но а пока придется поднапрячься со сбором вручную.

После того как соберёте достаточное количество очков, откроете био карту, где будут указаны симптомы на что жалуется пациент. Симптомов может быть множество, от серьезных до малозначительных. Каждый симптом может иметь связь с одной или несколькими системами органов, что иногда может привести к ошибочным диагнозам.

Выбрав симптом вы увидите возможные причины его появления, а выбрав заболевание прочитаете его описание и список потенциальных симптомов. Далее вы назначите диагностику для подтверждения наличия заболевания. Кстати каждая диагностика также имеет описание, так что узнаете, для чего они нужны в реальности. В случае, если тест будет положительным, назначите лечение. На выбор всегда будет несколько вариантов с разной стоимостью по очкам, с разной эффективностью и продолжительностью курса. И также будет прилагаться описание, в чем заключается лечение.

Игра проходит в реальном времени, но вы всегда можете поставить ее на паузу, чтобы подумать. Ваша цель это достичь показателя восстановление до 100% до того как у пациента откажут органы. 

Чтобы например замедлить ухудшение состояния определенных систем внутренних органов мы можете улучшить образ жизни пациента, например, назначить курс занятия аэробикой, чтобы улучшить систему кровообращения и органов дыхания. Или назначить медитацию для повышения иммунитета и улучшения нервной системы. всего 16 различных способов улучшения образа жизни.

Когда уровень здоровья одной из систем опустится ниже 20%, станет доступна интенсивная терапия для более существенного восстановления, чтобы замедлить наступление критического момента. Как например шунтирование желудка повысит систему пищеварения на 15%.

Также при достижении определенных требований можно улучшить сбор ресурсов.

В случае успеха в лечении пациента в окне статистики вы увидите, сколько времени ушло на лечение, медицинское заключение, количество полученных очков, эффективность поставленных диагнозов и вылеченных заболеваний.

А теперь перейдем к компании за смерть, где вам предстоит сделать всё ровным счетом наоборот и добиться смерти пациента до того как его вылечат.
Если в компании за жизнь всё начиналось с интернатуры, то в компании за смерть, вы начнете с морга.

Также вам будут доступны слоты усиления, но в этот раз не для лечения.
Сбор био очков будет проводится также, но собирать вы будете различные вирусы. А набрав достаточно, перейдете в био карту, где будут представлены все системы органов. Можете выбрать любую какую захотите, и назначить развитие какого-нибудь заболевания. Все также будет сопровождаться описаниями, так что прочитав их, думаю вам захочется побеспокоится о своем здоровье.
 
С каждым развитым недугом, жизненные показатели органов пациента будут снижаться. Дойдя до определенного уровня, пациент захочет пойти в больницу, но этот момент также можно отсрочить, например привив пациенту страх похода к врачу. Также в разделе факторы риска можно развить и другие страхи и вредные привычки, как например курение или избыточный вес. А еще есть интересный фактор нимфомания, если его активировать, то периодически во время игры будет появляться рулетка, крутанув которую с определенной вероятностью наградите пациента каким-нибудь венерическим заболеванием, что с точки зрения игры в компанию за смерть, приблизит вас к победе.

Кстати, как только пациент обратится к врачу, ему назначат лечение, так что вы можете и проиграть, если не ускорите разрушение организма.

А еще в игру можно поиграть и вдвоем, как соревнование. Один лечит, другой калечит.

И в заключение. 
Визуальная и звуковая составляющая выполнена, как мне кажется на все 100%, вспоминаются уроки анатомии. И это довольно интересный медицинский симулятор, где вы познакомитесь с большим разнообразием заболеваний, симптомов, о методах лечения и улучшении здоровья. А игра на высокой сложности заставит вас напрячься.

It's an interesting campaign with some cool battles and good voice-acting, but shipping a game without a campaign for both factions is a major flaw. You can play as the tyranids in an endless hordes mode, and in a non-story "planetary dominance" campaign.
There are also just two factions for non-story gaming, you can meet other factions as enemies, but you can't play them without buying DLC. The DLC also don't have more campaign content, it just unlocks factions that are ALREADY in the game, since you can fight against them, just not as them.
If you buy it at a discount, the game is fun enough with just the one campaign. Do not buy the DLC unless they are at a deep discount.

Star Knightess Aura is a corruption h-game about a classic conundrum: do you solve your problems the easy way, or the right way? Picture this: you bump into your mother's favorite vase, smashing it to pieces. She's not going to be happy. It's not the only one of its kind, though. After some online sleuthing, turns out it's available for same-day order. Do you meticulously glue it back together, or just buy the new one? The glue is a lot cheaper, and if you really try your best, she won't be able to tell. But is it worth the hours of effort? This is a game about that choice, Aura's corruption dictated by how many shortcuts she's willing to take in her quest.

Aura is not your typical student. She's smarter than you, for one. What really sets her apart though, are her dreams. At night, Aura finds herself in a fantastical land of Heroes and Demon Kings, goblins and magic, sword-wielding warriors and spellcasting priests. In this land, Aura is in fact THE Hero, the titular Star Knightess. It's an isekai-style story, something I personally am incredibly exhausted of. However its spin, while not unique, is interesting: Aura is able to freely pass between Earth and this fantasy world, bound only by the clock.

To speak further of the plot would do a disservice of its twists and turns. The demo is sufficient to get a feel for the story. The writing, while occasionally long-winded, I found perfect. A lot of the prose, particularly the back-and-forth screaming between opposing characters, felt reminiscent of Umineko (and if you think THAT story has bad writing, you're beyond help). Emubi's art is fine, middling at worst.

The CGs and h-scenes are at times unrewarding given the amount of effort required to access them, and the script could have used a spellchecker. Both of these things are being addressed in game updates, with more h-content to balance the scales and copious amounts of typo correction. I reported an obscure combat bug and it was fixed it within a day. I really can't find much to complain about.

In all my time playing, I've only finished one route. I intend to continue.

This game is sort of a middle ground between Trailmakers, which I feel is quite simplistic in vehicle design, and GearBlocks, which is very advanced. Screw Drivers strikes a great balance between extensive customization and creativity but not requiring an engineering degree to make a basic vehicle.

The building system is very much like playing with Lego Technic, and in a good way. There are some restrictions as blocks can usually only be attached to on one side, so getting the correct combinations of 90 degree joints can be a bit of a finagle, but in my mind this increases the diversity of builds vs just simple boxes slapped together.

This game gives me serious flashbacks to Lego Racers 2 in particular, it's only missing powerups and AI players to zap with powerups.

Definitely recommend this game to anyone who thinks the trailers look fun. The game is in early access, but it's easily worth the $5 for the supporter pack already. I put about 9 hours into the Demo and had plenty of fun there. I look forward to the future of Screw Drivers

Feedback for the Devs:
-I like the separation to air controls vs driving. I see that people with 10-keyless keyboards are upset, maybe controls could be set to IJKL or a toggle in the menu to put them back where they were, I'm not sure
-Air Brakes. I think the air controls really needs this. in numpad controls "5" should dampen/stop car's rotation and slow it down while mid air. 
-I don't like the way the motors "clunk" into reverse. If I'm driving the half-pipe and come down facing backwards, it seems reasonable that I should be able to continue driving in reverse. As it is the car has to come to a complete stop before starting accelerating in reverse which doesn't make sense to me.
-Some courses really struggle with blind corners, You can't see them as you are climbing or there's a rock or otherwise. There needs to be some sort of Arrow signs before/behind more than a few corners throughout the campaign to indicate upcoming corners.
-I know there is only so much you can do about the dreaded Unity Bounce(tm), but it is a real problem sometimes. Getting gold on Hill Climb is difficult because even with the long travel suspension there is almost no hope of making it through the terrain at the speeds required without getting yeeted (or suddenly slammed to a stop) by the tiniest bumps.
-When pressing "r" to rebuild during a race, obviously resetting speed to 0 makes sense. Holding me in the air for 2 seconds is punishing enough, but more than a few times I am reset FACING BACKWARDS to the track. This is NOT OKAY.  I'm not sure whether resetting facing the checkpoint is the right idea or what, but there's gotta be a fix for this.

Giving a review for this game in 2025 might seem a bit odd, but I just wanted to share my feelings about it. I’m so happy that I played The Cat Lady. It’s definitely one of my favorite games ever.
I liked it from the very beginning — maybe because I’m close to the themes this game explores. I don’t really know, but it comforted me from the start.

From my personal experience I’m really glad to see a game that shows the mentality of people who have depression and survived clinical death for $u!c!de attempt. I feel very close to Susan; somehow, we’re very alike. At first, I didn’t like her. I liked Mitzi more, but over time, as Susan changed, I realized that I didn’t hate her anymore — and that was a big step for me. Because I saw so much of myself in her, it was easy to hate her but in the end, I want to be like her. I want to recover and learn to like myself. I want to change — and seeing a character so similar to me doing that gives me hope every time I play this game.

I love that The Cat Lady talks about rebirth, $u!c!de, hope, sadness, and spreads awareness about depression. I love the plot, the twists, and the surreal scenes and characters. I love how well it’s made — it still feels amazing to play, even 13 years after its release.

In the end, I just want to say: play this game. It’s a masterpiece with a deep story and so many things to think about. It gives you something that opens your eyes. I love this game, and I love Susan, Mitzi, and so many other characters :)

If you’re sensitive to the game’s trigger warnings, maybe avoid it — it can be difficult to play. But I highly recommend this beautiful game, especially if you want to understand the subjects I mentioned before.

Have a good day or night, everyone who read this! 💙

as a new player, this is what it felt like playing BDO in 2025

The combat is nice.
The classes are awesome.
The main quest, which includes the story of the world, is also nice. You’ll finish it in about 30 hours.

Then the horror starts.
You have no idea where to move or what to do. The world is open and fun to explore, until you realize you need good gear to stand a chance against the monsters in the new areas.

You grind for hours to gather materials to upgrade your weapons and gear. You click enhance, but the higher your gear level goes, the higher the fail chance becomes. When you fail the enhancement, your weapon or gear durability drops significantly, and you lose the materials for the upgrade.

So you keep trying to enhance. You keep failing because the RNG angels hate you. Your gear becomes damaged and needs another type of material to repair, so you go grind.
Then you grind again for enhancement materials.

All that effort just to face the RNG angels once more when you click enhance… whether you succeed or fail, you keep repeating the horror cycle for eternity.

And just when you think you might get ahead, you realize there are no guides or in-game help. Some detailed functions require you to go and search for answers yourself. If you turn to YouTube, prepare for burnout from the flood of information they dump into your head.
If you ask the community, some people will try to help, but others just laugh at you. So now it's another round of RNG, only this time, it's human-based.

P.S. Even if you get an item that lets you gain EXP to level your character, you have to go AFK because your character trains in real time. Depending on your item choice, it can take 1 hour or even 10 hours. You can watch your character train tho,  or you can grind more to get almost 0.001% EXP per monster, depending on the level. I’m not kidding.

REVISION: After more than 30 hours, I have finally won my first game. But did my opinions change about it? Not really. The game somehow got its claws in me, and I could not stop playing it. But that does not excuse many of its shortcomings. If you are looking to play this game, feel free to play blind up until you have a solid grasp of the basics, and then do not be afraid to wiki things. Without looking up what and how you need to win, you'll be left in the dark, and will likely DNF. 

ORIGINAL REVIEW:

The game is an overcomplicated mess of moving timers, where progress is always brought on by tedious, luck-based strategies. I spent hours grinding away at the end game trying to get lucky, and lost because I accidentally clicked the wrong card, ending my multiple day lasting session. 

Although the lore and style might be enjoyable, the game mechanics are the definition of time wasters, with no tutorials, obtuse hints, and an annoying interfaces that requires YOU to put in the work that the devs should have from the get go. 

If you prefer this writing but want something much, much better, go and play the Sunless games. Your time is much better spent elsewhere.

A cult classic entry into the survival horror psx style genre. My hype surrounding this release had been in full swing for 6+ months from the time I heard about it. Puppet Combo/Torture Star/Dread XP type games are my warm blanket and the types of experiences I can consistently rely on for quality entertainment. Similarities to the above begin and end with the art style/aesthetic, The Lacerator does enough gameplay wise to stand on its own and justify the $9.99 ($8.99 intro offer) price tag. 

If you enjoy losing limbs the way Ubisoft loses player trust, you're in the right spot. Gameplay is affected by the loss of limbs in tangible ways that I haven't seen many games do quite this well. One minute Max is an 80's corn star with all appendages and before 2 shakes of a lamb's tail you're a single armed bandit with the aim of Shaq at the free throw line. There's a strong blend of humor and horror in the game that fits the 80's theme perfectly. Navigating the claustrophobic and foreign spaces is intense and unsettling, never quite knowing what will be waiting around the next corner. Enemy design is quite ghoulish and eerie, but the run ins with the Lacerator are the star of the show. During these sequences the intensity is turned up a level as it's a fight for limb or death. Fair warning, the game is short, but what adds to the experience is the plethora of secrets, puzzles, and multiple endings!

For as much as I adore this game there are 2 HUGE downsides for me personally that may be deal breakers for some. For starters there is NO 1440P Support. How? Why? Either you're playing this one in 720p, 1080p, or 4k... leading to my other disappointment, no way to disable the visual filter. While the effect does well in immersion I would have appreciated the ability to toggle this off like similar games in the genre. Aside from these points of contention there are some minor grievances a la lacking enemy variety. 

While $9.99 usd may not be a lot of money to many of us, I am of the philosophy that a game has to earn player time and money regardless of the price tag. I can confidently say The Lacerator is worth the investment. [spoiler]8/10 would replace Max's third leg for a drill again.[/spoiler]

I really want to like Cairn--it's clear that a lot of love went into its design--but the way it's balanced right now isn't fun. Each encounter carries out like a small boss battle where you really have to be judicious with your healing items and spells. There are several spots early on where you can easily soft lock the game because you've run out of healing items and are unable to reach a shop or a healing spot. This means you have to carefully pick-and-choose which battles you do engage in. In Chapter 3, items and spells start becoming underpowered relative to how hard the enemies hit. So you end up relying on chance to not throw more at you than you can heal from in battle, even when you do have adequate items and spells. It's stressful.

One other thing I feel should be mentioned is that I wouldn't call Cairn an Earthbound-like, except in the characters' visual design. I played both Earthbound and Mother 3 in the month prior to this, so they're fresher in my mind. The overarching story could possibly be found in an Earthbound game, but the way the characters interact and the world itself lack the levity you'd find in an Earthbound game. Sure, you fight furniture and other weird whatnots, but the characters remark on how strange this is rather than simply accepting it as part of the implicit strangeness of the world they're in.

In that regard, if you view Cairn as a more traditional RPG set in modern day, it feels better. Characters are all fairly realistic and self-serious. There are some attempts at humor but they're incidental and, I found, somewhat unnecessary. For example, the animals all have their various chirps and squeaks and meows translated into English. The cat is always preoccupied with food, isn't that funny?

So I went into Cairn with expectations, and that was partially my fault. But the dungeon design and soft locking are still major issues. Much of this could be fixed with future updates. And I hope they are, I feel like there's a heartfelt story here just begging to be told.

First of all... I dont usually leave reviews on games but this one was a HUGE EXCEPTION.

I don’t even know where to begin. THIS GAME, was a massive experience. It’s heartfelt, quiet, and deeply emotional in a way that sneaks up on you. The story, the people, and the atmosphere of it feels alive, I can tell that the developer really put as much care into the game as possible. As someone who grew up with a lot of RPG games (especially loving earthbound), this game hit me in the same place those did. That strange mix of magic spells, skills... Including those moments where every smile hides a little sadness, and every quiet moment feels important. Cairn gave me that same feeling again, and I honestly wasn’t expecting it.

[b]Basic Breakdown[/b]: Off-Peak, a game developed by [b]Cosmo D[/b] and published by [b]Cosmo D Studios[/b] is basically a fancy surreal experience/walking simulator. The game takes about half an hour to complete and has 2 slightly different endings depending on your actions towards merchants within the station that you explore.

Off-Peak at it's core is a trippy dream like land that seems to follow it's own rules, and it's own narrative that has this strange leader whose name is peppered through conversations of the inhabitants within the world.

At the start of the game a person named [b]Luuke[/b] sends you out to find the pieces of ticket that he misplaced. You have 8 pieces to collect as you traverse through this wonderfully detailed station, speak with merchants and others who seem to inhabit this place.

The game is very deliberate in avoiding what the fate all of these people have, their motives for being there and even what Marcus's deal is, it's however done in a way that keeps you engaged. It's such an in-depth world with many people to interact with and it's worth going that extra way even once you've put your ticket together to see what random inhabitants have to say. 
 
[b]Graphics[/b]: Looks like a bit of an acid trip, but the detail to the art which it contains is amazing. Textures are very polished, character design is really good and it's just an all round pretty game. 

[b]Soundtrack[/b]: The music to this is by far one of my favourite things to this game. It's the perfect addition to it giving you that trippy atmospheric immersion. Thanks [b]Archie Pelago[/b]!!  

[b]Menu[/b]: Text built into the start of the game to give you a rundown of it's basic controls and it works wonderfully to just throw you straight in. 

[b]Final Conclusion[/b]: I absolutely love this game. It's kind of like a fancy walking simulator but doesn't feel like one at the end of it all. The music ties perfectly with the atmosphere, the art is incredible and the polished pretty graphics help it be just that little bit extra. 

During the game, you tend to find putting the ticket together is a bit of an afterthought as you lose yourself in exploring your surroundings. Once you have completed your ticket, it's almost sad that you don't have anymore of the world to delve into. 

It gives you a trippy dream like experience in which nothing feels real, nothing fully makes sense and even at the end of it all you have many unanswered questions.

It's very much worth a look at and play through. The developers clearly put a lot of thought and detail into this creation - it pays off and it shows. Very keen for the sequel called The Norwood Suite hopefully making it's way to steam greenlight soon!
