Embora muitos o considerem um dos títulos mais fracos da franquia, pessoalmente, tenho um grande carinho por Final Fantasy VIII. Sua história, mesmo com suas fragilidades, me agrada bastante. Os personagens são marcantes, ainda que alguns deles poderiam ter sido mais bem explorados. A trilha sonora é icónica e, para a época, a façanha da Square de integrar sequências onde podemos controlar o personagem em meio a uma animações CGI era simplesmente de explodir a cabeça.

O sistema de Junction e de magias com quantidade limitada permanece um dos aspetos mais questionados do jogo. Trata-se de um mecanismo complexo que, na minha opinião, é fantástico e radicalmente diferente de tudo o que a série já tinha apresentado até então. Embora exija um tempo para ser compreendido e dominado, no final, é um esquema que maximiza a personalização de builds, tornando qualquer personagem versátil. Com isso, o limit break acaba por se tornar o único diferencial real entre eles, um aspeto que pode ser visto como positivo ou negativo, dependendo da perspetiva de cada jogador.

Quanto a esta versão Remastered, ela concede uma sobrevida ao jogo, com gráficos ligeiramente melhorados e a inclusão de funcionalidades muito úteis para jogadores com menos tempo disponível. No entanto, esta edição está muito longe do esperado.

Veredito Final: Nota 9 para o jogo original, nota 3 para o remaster.

Es fällt mir schwer Hell is Us richtig zu bewerten. Ich wünschte Steam würde einen "Neutral"-Daumen einführen.
Warum?

Pros: 
Die Vertonung der Charaktere. 
Egal, ob es ein kleines verzweifeltes Mädchen oder aufatmende Rentner im Flüchtlingslager sind. Man kauft ihnen ihre Umwelt und Erlebnisse ab. Man hört die Angst, Verzweiflung, Hoffnung wirklich heraus, was dem Spiel enorme Immersion gibt.

Die Rätsel
Manchmal für mich etwas zu schwer oder nicht ganz logisch, sind sie doch zu größten Teilen mit etwas Gehirnschmalz zu lösen und dabei teilweise wirklich gut durchdacht.

Die Nebenquest
Klar. Oft sind es nur verwinkelte "Hol-Bring-Such" Quest, aber man freut sich auch, wenn man tatsächlich mal eine Quest erledigen kann, weil man alle dazugehörigen Puzzlestücke gefunden hat.

Die Atmosphäre
Wie schon vorher erwähnt gänzt das Spiel teilweise durch gute Immersion. Der Krieg, Hass und Misstrauen zwischen den zwei Völkern ist an allen Ecken und Enden zu sehen und zu spüren. Was wirklich gut umgesetzt worden ist.

Neutral:

Die Welt: 
Auf der einen Seite empfinde ich die Gebiete als schön abwechslungsreich und in den verschiedenen Ecken wird gutes Umschauen auch durchaus belohnt. Auf der anderen Seite wirken manche Gebiete einfach nur groß und relativ leer.

Der Kampf:
Auf der einen Seite wirkt er flott und die FInisher sind ganz cool und auf der anderen Seite nutzt er sich eben auch nach und nach ab. Immerhin sorgen die Skills für etwas Abwechslung

Negativ:
Der Hauptcharakter. 
Der interessiert mich mal so gar nicht. Wirkt auch nicht sympathisch oder wie jmd mit dem man sich identifizieren möchte.

Rüstung
Rein kosmetisch. brauch ich persönlich nicht

Das Menü
echt unübersichtlich. Ich glaube dazu muss ich wirklich nicht viel sagen.

Die Gegner
Der Faktor, der den Daumen nach unten hervorbringt. Alter Schwede. Wie kann man das Spiel rausbringen und der Überzeugung sein, dass dieser Punkt nicht nochmal überarbeitet werden sollte?! Es gibt quasi nur einen Gegnertyp, der immer mal wieder bisschen abgewandelt auftaucht. Schlussendlich sorgt es aber dafür, dass kämpfen nur als sehr lästige Pflichtaufgabe angesehen wird und in mir immer größeres Augenrollen hervorgebracht hat. Ganz ganz schlecht.


Ich möchte Hell is Us wirklich mögen, gerade wegen seinen unweigerlichen Stärken, die es hat. Aber die Gegner, die Kämpfe und der unsympathische Hauptcharakter machen es mir SEHR schwer das Spiel überhaupt beenden zu wollen. Es fühlt sich teilweise an wie ein vermeintlich leckeres Steak auf dem Teller, dass man aber eeewig kauen muss. Am Anfang sagt man sich noch, dass das nicht so schlimm ist, Hauptsache es schmeckt. Aber nach dem dritten oder vierten Bissen hat man keine Lust mehr ewig zu kauen. Sehr schade.

- Music for the most part is creepy, but I suppose it was done on purpose.
- Enemy variety is poor.

Positives:

+ Locations design and lore are pretty decent.
+ Cool looking journal, with interesting investigation mechanics.
+ Haven't encountered any bugs.

I will say, as a fan of the original 20XX, this is definitely a worthy sequel, that builds on the first while offering its own features & flavor. The worlds it builds are now more varied, with a broader range of shooting, platforming, and avoidance challenges. The pixel art adds a more genuine look and feel to the game, compared to 20XX's smoother, less retro art style. The variety of builds possible is deceptively complex, and each character plays differently enough to make a switch seem like a different game entirely.

The narrative is, as in 20XX, more implied than explicit, although it does try to pick up the slack with discoverable lore nuggets, and the late game seems to [i]think[/i] it's telling an epic story about the end of days or... something. But really, it has as much story as a game like this needs. What I do enjoy is the low-key morbid messages that appear whenever you find & loot the body of a previous Contractor (the game refers to the protags as "Contractors" for reason I still haven't quite worked out). Mechanically, it's little more than another item chest, but the little random messages that briefly arise manage, in a fashion Hemmingway might be impressed with, to convey a sense of confused hopelessness unique to the X0XX series. It was my favorite little narrative touch in 20XX as well.

There are bits I don't particularly care for, but I hesitate to complain about them because they're clearly carry-overs from the Megaman games which inspire it. The only one I'll really cite is that the Leg Cores, which grant air movement abilities such as doube jumps, hover jets, & air dashes, often wreak havok on my muscle memory. A lot of my untimely deaths simply come around to me twitch-responding as if I have a double jump, only to stop dead in the air because I have hover. I realize part of the strategy is to deactivate cores that you aren't using (and in fact I started doing a lot better once I made liberal use of core-changing mid-run) but pausing to make build-adjustments (not to mention having to re-learn your basic movement every run) is a flow-breaker for such a fast-paced and action oriented game.

Wow, is that really the worst thing I can complain about? Not really, I think the big one's gonna be that I still haven't gotten the 30XX Maker feature functioning. You need a 3rd party account to make it work and it has not even once connected to the server properly. As a fan of making & playing community content, I do find that bit annoying, if only because it cuts me off from an advertised feature. But I also have to confess I'd have bought this game even if it was never offered, so, eh, we'll call that one "minor" as well.

But yeah, if you like difficult-but-not-impossible 2D platformers, this will keep you nice and engaged for quite some time. I'd say you get more out of the experience if you played 20XX, especially in the late game when the callbacks are at their most blatant, but it's not really required.

It took a long time for this series to click for me. I would lose territory as fast as I could take it, and it always felt Sisyphean. Once I started bolster every area with standby forces, I understood that every inch of ground gained was precious. The income from resources going un-interrupted is absolutely worth protecting, but this can also vary with the settlement in question. There is a tradeoff in that. There is also a trade-off in choosing to focus on building up defenses at all.

What I just described might work for some, but not all, of the widely variant classes in this game. Each one really is it's own playstyle. Some classes excel at building defenses in their territories, but others have very different focuses. If you dislike one class, play another and see how the game balance changes completely for you.

More than anything, I don't often experience drama arising from mechanics in a game, unless it's D&D. In this game, every session feels like a drama; cultists opening up a demon gate to hell is cause for all the players to call a truce until Elysium is protected again. The same goes if you see a queen ant. I've had a port city fend off armies of undead, only for there to be a lone survivor, who inherited a wizard hat from some dead commander. The next time the city was seiged, there was another lone survivor, this time not the same guy, who likewise inherited that hat.

This game is just so engaging once you settle into it, in all kinds of ways. And I haven't even touched on multiplayer.

Arma: Cold War Assault stands as one of the most influential military simulators ever released, not because of modern polish or cinematic presentation, but because of how boldly it redefined what a tactical shooter could be. Developed and published by Bohemia Interactive, the game—originally known as Operation Flashpoint: Cold War Crisis—places players in the middle of a fictional conflict between NATO and Soviet forces at the height of late-Cold War tension. Rather than funneling you through scripted corridors, it drops you into sprawling island battlefields where the terrain is vast, the stakes are high, and every mission feels like a small piece of a larger, unpredictable war.

The campaign offers a wide variety of roles, putting players in the boots of infantrymen, behind the controls of tanks, and even inside military helicopters. Each mission unfolds across kilometers of open countryside, forests, coastal villages, and mountain roads, making navigation, positioning, and awareness just as important as marksmanship. What sets Cold War Assault apart is its demand for patience and tactical thinking: firefights happen at long distances, ambushes are genuinely dangerous, and vehicles do not feel like flashy power-ups but essential tools to survive and maneuver in the field. The game’s emphasis on “combined arms” warfare—blending infantry, armor, and air support—was groundbreaking for its time and remains a core identity of the Arma series today.

The sense of realism extends beyond weapon handling and large maps. The game’s pacing is intentionally slower, favoring methodical progression over instant gratification. Missions rarely rely on predictable waves of enemies; instead, threats can emerge naturally from the world, elevating tension as you scan distant tree lines or listen for the rumble of approaching engines. The story, while understated, gains power through this grounded approach. The campaign’s protagonists feel like ordinary soldiers thrust into extraordinary circumstances, and the narrative—especially when paired with the Resistance expansion—captures the desperation, uncertainty, and sacrifice of war without melodrama.

Despite its enduring legacy, Cold War Assault does show its age. The interface and controls can feel stiff and unintuitive compared to modern shooters, and the animations and textures reflect the technical limitations of early 2000s hardware. The AI, though ambitious for its time, can behave erratically, causing moments of immersion to clash with moments of frustration. Close-quarters combat especially highlights these limitations, with movement and aiming feeling noticeably clunky. However, players willing to adjust to the older design will find a depth of simulation that few newer titles attempt, making its quirks more a matter of adaptation than deal-breakers.

One of the most impressive aspects of the game’s legacy is its mission editor and modding support. Even at release, Cold War Assault came with robust tools that allowed players to design entire scenarios, craft custom campaigns, and create new gameplay systems. This openness fostered a passionate community that extended the life of the game for years, contributing thousands of user-made missions and modifications. Many hallmarks of the modern Arma experience—sandbox scenarios, realism mods, experimental units—were shaped here, turning Cold War Assault into both a beloved game and a creative platform.

Arma: Cold War Assault remains a historic milestone in tactical gaming. It is not a title meant for players seeking fast, arcade-style action or modern production values. Instead, it rewards those who embrace slow, strategic gameplay and appreciate simulations that strive for authenticity over spectacle. Its vast environments, immersive atmosphere, and uncompromising design philosophy still resonate today, offering an experience that feels raw, deliberate, and surprisingly timeless. For fans of military strategy or anyone interested in the roots of the Arma series, Cold War Assault is more than a classic—it’s a foundational chapter in the evolution of realistic shooters.

[h1]Trois époques, et une mémoire en ruine[/h1]

Je ne sais pas exactement quand Lorelei and the Laser Eyes a cessé d’être un simple puzzle game pour devenir une sorte de rêve éveillé.
Peut-être quand j’ai commencé à douter du temps, ou quand j’ai réalisé que l’hôtel dans lequel j’errais n’était pas fait de murs, mais de regrets.

Le jeu ne prend pas ton poignet pour t’expliquer quoi que ce soit. Il t’enferme doucement, te teste, te frustre, puis te récompense par ces instants de clarté absolue où tout s’aligne ; chiffres, symboles, souvenirs..
Chaque énigme, chaque date, chaque note semble appartenir à une même pulsation : celle d’une mémoire qui cherche à se réconcilier avec elle-même.

Visuellement, c’est très intéressant. Ce noir et blanc presque clinique, ces éclats de rouge, ces couloirs où le silence pèse lourd.
On sent la main d’artistes obsédés par la forme, mais surtout par le sens. Rien n’est gratuit. L’inconfort est voulu, même le flou est un message.
Et puis il y a Lorelei : artiste, mais aussi témoin, victime d’un drame qui se rejoue encore et encore.
On ne sait plus si on la guide ou si on marche dans ses pas. Peut-être un peu des deux.

Ce n’est pas un jeu que je recommanderais à tout le monde (ou peut-être bien que si). 
Il demande de la patience, de la curiosité, et un goût pour les énigmes qui parlent autant à la tête qu’au cœur.
Alors, si vous aimez les œuvres qui ne vous expliquent rien et vous laissent tout ressentir, Lorelei and the Laser Eyes est une expérience pour vous ! (;

之前我解谜解到红温，差点弃坑，但是最近实在没啥东西耍，在攻略的辅助下，游玩体验无限良好。那就说明游戏没问题，是我的问题。
美术精致合理，细节丰富，营造出了相当出色的氛围，表现手法新颖，很见匠心。叙事节奏相当不错，先碎片再收束，非常经典的悬疑游戏&沙盒游戏叙事思路，但和独具一格的表现手法搭配，就很令人印象深刻了。而且伏笔埋得很好。流程设计也没什么冲突的地方，比较严谨。
游戏时长至少10小时，量还是很大的。总体推荐喜欢做《挑战你的大脑！聪明人都在做的益智谜题500例》的人游玩。开玩笑的，适合重度解谜玩家，而且不是锈湖那类“拿到东西，想想在哪用、怎么用”的密室逃脱解谜，是解密码的那种解谜。
优点叙述完毕，接下来是想吐槽的部分，也不完全能算缺点。无剧透。
——————————————————
猜思路其实是这个游戏最难的部分，也是这个游戏最大的问题，我甚至可以说这是硬伤。因为这游戏谜题太多，解谜的文本和剧情文本杂糅，再加上有些东西会重复用，所以拿到谜题方向太多，不知道该如何做，不知道信息是否足够；而且这游戏沙盒的形式，会让大量谜题混在一个环境中，这就更无法分辨哪些谜题是可解的，哪些是暂时不能解的。我无法确定当我的尝试得到否定时，是因为信息不够，还是方向错误。为什么我会说这是硬伤，因为这不太符合游戏的奖赏机制，记住更多的游戏文本、思考的更细致反而会被惩罚，这是什么道理？
这游戏在这个基础上，还非常恰当的弄了一些纯场景解谜，而且基本都是非常重要的节点。你一个玩密码的游戏，突然插一个场景解谜，说句难听的不就是藏比吗？被藏比一卡卡半天，关键是我只会觉得是有密码可解了但我没解开，继续在那些谜题上钻牛角尖，结果一看攻略，藏比，血压直接上来了。建议游戏里也别设置没用的体温和压力值了，干脆连个血压计，实时监测玩家血压。

当你经过大量的谜题后，就可以归纳出：其实这游戏的谜题和答案大多情况下都是在同一个房间，比较复杂的多房间谜题一般都设计的很花哨，大概能猜到现在解不开。当你体会到这一层之后，这游戏的难度就下来很多。不过我还是持原有的观点，这游戏的玩法基本是纯机关盒，如果你抱着很高的预期，觉得他有什么很吊炸天的解谜的话，那1000%失望。他的解谜大概就是那种中游2D小游戏水平，也有不少是益智读物like，总体低于机械迷城。知道这一点会对游玩很有帮助，至少不会因为想太多而卡关——我不知道有多少次实在想不出来看攻略，结果气笑了的经历。

The game starts strong, has nice visuals and sound for people who are into pixel graphics, nostalgia is properly invoked. After a short while, slowly the frustration is creeping in because basically you just run around with WASD and try to find a bunch of items that synergize well. You try to finish the challenges but very often that is absolutely not possible, especially on hard or very hard because the runs are also just too short and you have literally no influence over anything. You cant reroll (only banish a minor amount of items in the vast pool of random items). Sometimes on top of that the boss just has a random setup which you just can't anticipate with the RNG. 

So you just start over. Again and again and again until the RNG is merciful. Then every tenth run you are a bit lucky and gather some working setup. Maybe you get a mythical item (but again you need lots of luck to get a properly fitting one). Then sometimes, when you expect it the least, you find a few broken items (like Royal Scepter) you just steamroll over everything and barely know why.  There are a lot of possibilities in the game, but because of the nature of VERY short runs and luck dependency you barely see them. 

That said, the game has a stupidly negative progression that feels anything but rewarding. The more you play the more items you will unlock with completing the challenges. This dilutes the item pool to the point that it is even harder to get the fitting items that you are looking for, no matter how hard you try because you don't get an expanded choice of items in the chests. Most items are niche additions to certain builds but require a lot of other niche items to work together. If you don't a proper items and pick the niche item at start you might not kill even the first boss, but if you don't get it you might miss the item later because you will not see it again.

The other part is that it feels frustrating to always have to choose for "the lowest amount of downside" rather than choosing items for their benefit. You have 4 equipment slots and want to merge something. Better hope to find golems and second items. Ditch other good items in the meanwhile. Didn't work out? Alright, start over the game. Try and hope again. 

All in all: WASD, gambling with zero influence to find items that are not stupid, start over. It is like a slot machine where you pull the lever and hope for a nice outcome. Not worth 15€, maybe 5€ but in the end it will still waste your time without giving you a rewarding feeling. It is not thought through properly.

The only way to fix the game is to have a solid meta concept (like Path of Achra), where the game gets harder but you get more skill points etc., which makes you feel like you progress something.

[h1][b] TLDR: An overall chill and zen experience. I found the simplicity too simple and the advanced scoring too involved. [/b] [/h1]

[h1]PROS: [/h1]
➕Relaxing vibe
➕Chill music


[h1]CONS: [/h1]
➖I wish the game would tell you why you can’t place a tile in a specific place
➖Not a lot of depth/Heavy RNG based
➖Feels a little pointless
➖Objectives, like flags and boundaries, are too hard to see

[h1] [b] Content (Game world/Narrative) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
The game world starts off with a blank slate of nothingness with a single hexagon tile in the middle. You then create the game world through hexagons with different layouts like forests, farms, houses, and water. The world has no interactivity whatsoever aside from placing tiles in certain directions. 

There is no plot. 

[h1][b] Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The mechanics are deceptively simple - you get a random tile, and you place it on a map in a strategic position. The goal is to place tiles in a manner that completes the random quests that the game gives you. Things like having tiles with x attached houses or farms, or forests and also some small variants like not exceeding a specific amount so you can’t take advantage of a previous group of tiles, or things like closing off a section of tiles. Each completed quest then gives you more tiles so you can keep going for a bigger area and a higher score. 
To me, the gameplay loop almost felt like a simplified version of Tetris. Imagine if you had 5 shapes. Your goal here would be to combine the shapes into groups. Aaand that’s….kinda it. I think that while the quests and the pieces themselves offer some much-needed diversity in the gameplay through RNG, I felt there wasn’t a lot of meaningful interaction with the mechanics. 

As for the difficulty, this is generally a relaxing and chill game. Only when you care about getting higher scores can it become a test of patience as you realize you shouldn’t have placed that tile in that spot 5 turns ago. 

[h1] [b] Graphics (Quality/Technical) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Simple and rudimentary. There’s not much here with graphics, each tile contains only a few variations of the same couple of biomes, so you’ll basically be seeing tiles with a combination of houses, forests, railroads, water, and farms, with the occasional special tile sprinkled in. Each tile doesn’t have enough detail for this the graphics to be good. 

On the technical side, I noticed no issues or bugs. The game ran smooth. 
i9-13900KF | RTX 4090 | 64GB RAM | 1440p @ 240hz | Windows 11 installed on SSD 

[h1] [b] Audio – [7/10] [/b] [/h1]
A great mix of relaxing and chill music to hex-out to. I thoroughly enjoyed how relaxing the music was. 

There is no voice acting. 

[h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
I think the replay factor is there, but I can also see how it can be a tough sell. Yes, there are multiple game modes and the native RNG is actually a positive part of the game, but on the other hand, after only two or three games played I felt like I had pretty much seen all there was to see. The few games I played after that just felt repetitive. 

[h1] [b] Final Verdict – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Dorfromantik is a charming puzzle game that caters to two very different play styles - a casual and relaxing vibe, and a hardcore score-chasing alternative. I think it meshes these two types of play styles pretty well, but I find myself being stuck in the middle. I like the relaxing vibe the game has, but its repetition has me bored. Meanwhile, I don’t want to invest dozens of hours learning the nuances just to compete on the leaderboards. It’s a strange feeling for such a chill feeling game. It’s almost like if Stardew Valley had a competitive MLG mode. Odd, right? 

Above in the mechanics section, I made the comparison to this game being kind of like Tetris, and I think it's a solid equivalency to both the strengths and weaknesses of this game. Like Tetris, the pieces you get are random, and you must fit them into a specific slot for max effectiveness. Also like Tetris, after playing only a couple of games, you’ve already seen pretty much everything the game has to offer from a gameplay standpoint. And also like Tetris, its simplicity is also its complexity as the skill floor is in the basement and the skill ceiling is ten stories high. 

Ultimately, do I recommend Dorfromantik? I think it’s a great game for mindless relaxing, but the game’s “mindless” aspect is incredibly boring to me. It’s like it pushes me into wanting to learn more and be better, when I find the core gameplay to be rather simple and repetitive. 
As you can probably tell, I’m a bit conflicted, and when I feel like smack in the middle, it's a solid 5 rating. In the end, I’m going to go with a recommendation because the casual approachableness of the game is worthy of checking out.

Review after playing through the game, which took about 10 hours.  This is a remaster of a game from the NES in 1988.  This game is worth playing for JRPG and Final Fantasy fans, other folks should give it a pass.  It is pretty dated, so for folks looking to get more of a introduction to the series I would point them more toward 6 or 4.  In this one they tried some new things out that they ultimately decided not to go forward with, so its an odd entry.  I have started this a few times in different versions (and not finished it), and this is without a doubt the best version of this game available.

So in Q&A form:
- Does this game hold up?  Yes, though it is nothing groundbreaking.  I think it would fit in with some of the more barebones indie games of today.
- Why do you recommend it?  For a FF fan its a requirement as one of the full numbered entries in the series.  It also has a plot revolving around the 'Wild Rose Rebellion' against the empire, and the plot is alright.  These days the story is pretty trope-y, but that may be because this game helped make those tropes.  This version of the game features a bunch of quality of life improvements that make the more dated aspects better and helps the game not overstay its welcome.

Birth is a short, eerie, and oddly tender puzzle game where you collect bones and organs to assemble yourself a little companion. It sounds morbid, and it is, but in the most delicate, cozy way possible. Think melancholy meets comfort, wrapped in a pastel graveyard hug.

Each puzzle is simple and intuitive, making it accessible to absolutely anyone. It’s 100% playable on Steam Deck, saves perfectly, and even the achievements are easy to snag if you’re chasing that 100%. The hand-drawn art and soft soundtrack create a peaceful yet unsettling vibe that’s impossible not to love. There are even small side quests to find coins and trinkets along the way, giving you reasons to explore every eerie little nook.

The only real downside? It’s short. You can finish everything in around 2 hours, so the price might sting a bit at full cost, but on sale, it’s an absolute must-play.

Overall, Birth is a beautifully macabre gem, perfect for cozy gamers who love their calm moments served with a sprinkle of morbidity. It’s gentle and quietly unforgettable, the kind of game that lingers long after it’s over.

**Dragonkin: The Banished – My Thoughts So Far**

I went in without big expectations. I’ve got thousands of hours in different ARPGs, so I expected something in the range of *Wolcen*… but ended up getting something better than *Last Epoch*.

There’s a lot of potential here. Sure, there are bugs and moments of tedium — some quests involve a bit too much walking, and you’ll hit the occasional frustrating spot — but the positives gradually outweigh the negatives. Once your city starts to grow, everything clicks. Your character feels stronger, progression feels meaningful, and the game really starts to reward your time.

The biggest strength, in my opinion, is **build customization**. I love when an ARPG lets me shape a unique playstyle, and *Dragonkin* already shows promise in this department. I went in blind with a *Thorns Barbarian* idea — just saw the stat and went for it — and the game gave me enough tools to make it work. No guides, just experimentation, and it felt great.

Now, the one major downside for me: **the Fragment system**.
I know it’s a core mechanic, but honestly, it ends up being more frustrating than fun. Rearranging fragments to trigger symbiosis, managing rarity types, juggling active vs. passive vs. wyrmling skills — it turns into downtime rather than gameplay. Every time I got new fragments, I had to stop and reshuffle things instead of just diving back in. It’s overwhelming, and I think this alone could limit the game’s broader appeal.

If fragments are here to stay, I’d love to see a full **UX overhaul**. Simplify it:

* Let players select a few actives and wyrmlings.
* Show which support fragments can attach to which actives.
* Give each active a “fragment capacity” and each fragment a “cost.”
  This would keep depth without drowning the player in busywork.

If you can look past the fragment system and the usual Early Access quirks, *Dragonkin: The Banished* is absolutely worth checking out. Just don’t go in expecting *PoE*, *GD*, or *D2*. Go in open-minded — and you might be pleasantly surprised.

If you’re looking for a game that delivers relentless action, razor-sharp combat, and an atmosphere drenched in cosmic horror, look no further than Katanaut. From its very opening moments, the game plunges you into a space station rife with mutations and menace—every corridor hums with dread and every swing of the blade feels meaningful. 

Katanaut's  combat is a standout: fluid, responsive, and satisfying. The katana feels weighty yet agile, the guns provide great complement for ranged threats, and the dodge/slash rhythm genuinely makes you feel like you’re mastering something. 

Katanaut's roguelite progression is nicely tuned; you’re rewarded for each death with more knowledge, more build options, more freedom to experiment. The memory-fragment upgrade system ensures that each run matters. The pixel-art design is rich and moody, the environment evokes a dilapidated space station in collapse, and the sound / synthwave soundtrack give the whole experience a strong identity. Whether you prefer rushing in with the blade, picking off from range, or mixing abilities and implants, the game offers enough toys to keep you invested and exploring different styles. 

If you’ve enjoyed games like Dead Cells, Katana Zero or other tight-action roguelites, Katanaut hits that sweet spot of difficulty + reward. The thrill of chaining kills, dodging at the last moment, exploring the next section of the station—it all adds up to a very satisfying loop. It’s also refreshing to see a strong indie title that combines melee and ranged so effectively while keeping things fast-paced.

Plus, the setting gives it more flavour than many generic action games—there’s a cosmic horror twist, an underlying narrative of a station gone wrong and twisted creatures lurking in the dark. I'd give Katanaut a solid 8.5/10.

I’m a regular player with some experience in games like Dead Cells (didn’t finish it) and Hades (completed it), and I really enjoyed this one. The movement feels smooth, the katana slashes are incredibly satisfying, and the impact sounds make every hit feel powerful.

The setting is intriguing - kind of a cosmic cyberpunk vibe - and there’s an impressive variety of unique enemies to fight.

On the downside, I’m not a fan of the save/load system, as it feels a bit too casual. The game could also use some balance tuning: for example, once I find two skills that fit my playstyle, I end up skipping a lot of spells just to look for upgrades.

Overall, the game has a lot of potential, delivers great gameplay, and is definitely worth the price! 

And a special thanks for adding the Ukrainian localization!

OPINION SUR LA PHASE 1 de l'EARLY ACCES

Le jeu est intéressant, l'artwork est vraiment joli et le concept général derrière le jeu fonctionne. Les développeurs ont visiblement passé beaucoup de temps à essayer de créer un environnement où dès la première run, le jeu est engageant et offre une vaste gamme d'options - incluant un aspect RNG qui aide à donner de la rejouabilité. La prise en main est agréable et finir une run ne nécessite pas plusieurs runs de gathering pour obtenir des mobs et des capacités.

Néanmoins, c'est aussi un peu le problème du jeu dans sa forme "Early Acces" - le manque de progression. Il existe actuellement un système de progression des monstres, mais ce dernier reste limité - 3 bonus permanents. Le personnage incarné ne possède pas de skill tree pour son développement personnel et le contenu déblocable au moyen des points de néant influence relativement peu la progression. Le "end-game" ressemble donc davantage à un jeu Pokemon où le but est de débloquer tous les éléments du jeu qu'à un Monster Train 2 où l'objectif est de finir les 10 niveaux de difficulté.

Actuellement, le jeu manque donc encore de personnalité puisqu'on ressent l'envie d'en faire un jeu à forte rejouabilité. Toutefois, l'aspect narratif des runs est encore trop faible pour en faire un jeu chill où l'on découvre progressivement l'histoire - ce qui en soi est dommage. Le jeu pourrait nommément avoir des runs narratives (dans l'environnement autogénéré) où certains des monstres/composantes seraient fixes et permettraient de au joueur de suivre l'histoire du monde en s'aventurant dans des scénarios rejouables, avec différents modes de difficulté, à l'image d'un mode mission. 

De l'autre, l'aspect progression dans l'aventure est encore trop faible pour vraiment rendre le jeu extrêmement rejouable pour un fan de Roguelike. Le système de progression étant conçu actuellement pluis pour les complétistes que pour les gens qui souhaitent réellement gagner en puissance et retenter l'aventure. On regrette également la présence de mode défi, et la durée des runs qui est en effet légèrement trop importante pour un pur rogue-like,

Au final, nous en sommes encore au tout début de la période d'early access et ayant énormément apprécié "Monster Sanctuary",  je demeure super content de mon acquisition (en duopack avec "Monster Sanctuary" que je n'avais que grâce au gamepass). Le early acces démontre clairement qu'il y a de la place pour ce type de jeu. Il ne reste plus qu'au développeur à clarifier un peu la proposition de gameplay pour que le jeu trouve véritablement sa niche :).

As it exists I cant give it a thumbs up. I want to, but I can't because Its terribly imbalanced. I love the concept and the direction its going, especially the vast array of aesthetic additions available for you. But functionally there are problems and I'm still very early into the game which does not bode well for later on. 

One example is how slowly citizens age. Unlike other similar games, it does not seem that building up your town attracts any new citizens outside of the occasional migration of people. This would be fine normally, however when your citizens have kids, it takes what seems like a realistic number of years in game for them to grow up which creates a problem because overall, the needs of your people stack up WAY faster than your number of citizens so you can VERY quickly go from being a successful settlement one year, to a starving one the next. 

Another imbalance is the amount of certain resources you gain from things like felling trees. There is a forester hut that is supposed to provide a steady flow of lumber and replant trees (provided you have enough laborers working there) but again, with how quickly the game makes you try to grow, you would either have to have at least 3-4 people working there to keep up with a small town of maybe 10 homes, or have more than 1 forester. Which isn't feasible when you account for all the other things you need people for early on.

Then other things like tools and iron gathering are imbalanced in the other direction entirely. For example. I put up a forester and a mine for iron. Both were running at the same time. After a couple years, my forester struggles  intensely to keep up with wood demand while the iron is just stacking up like crazy! 

Now a lot of this is due to the fact that most construction requires wood, on top of needing it for fuel to keep homes warm, while less things require iron in the beginning but still. I chop down what I would estimate are 20-25 trees and I get maybe 70-80 wood which trust me is NOTHING. The average home costs something like 20 or 25 lumber to build. That's 1/4 of what I got from 20-25 trees. That's insane.

Finally the clinic.... Healing is insanely slow. When people are sick the clinics are decent and fixing that problem fairly quickly if you have the needed items on hand. But a physical injury? Nah.... that person is basically out of commission for a couple years. Which is again way too punishing for something you didnt do wrong and just happens as a form of challenge. 

I think this game has a LOT of potential, but again, it just is in terrible need of some balance before I can give it a thumbs up.

[h2]Sinopsis[/h2]
Kathy Rain: Director’s Cut es la versión ampliada de una clásica aventura Point & Click detectivesca ambientada en los 90. La protagonista es Kathy, una joven de actitud rebelde y descarada, que regresa a su pueblo natal, Conwell, para acudir al entierro de su abuelo. Con un padre que se desentendió de ella y una madre con problemas mentales, Kathy tuvo que apañárselas por su cuenta desde muy joven, escapando de su pueblo y desentendiéndose del mundo. Sin embargo, al regresar, descubre que su abuelo guardaba un peligroso y turbio secreto que despertará su curiosidad y la arrastrará a lo más profundo de su mente. A lomos de su moto y con ayuda de algunas personas del pueblo, Kathy se propone llevar a cabo una minuciosa investigación, removiendo cielo y tierra hasta dar con el secreto que su abuelo guardaba tan celosamente.

[h2]Jugabilidad / Apartado técnico[/h2]
Kathy Rain sigue la dinámica de los clásicos Point & Click, proponiéndonos una aventura donde iremos visitando diferentes enclaves del pueblo y sus alrededores a medida que vamos tirando del hilo que nos conecta con el pasado de nuestro abuelo. En cada zona podremos usar la barra espaciadora para revelar todos los elementos interactivos, facilitando mucho la investigación e identificación de objetos. Por supuesto, dispondremos de un inventario donde ir almacenando cada nuevo ítem que encontremos, así como una pequeña libreta donde anotaremos cada pista que vayamos rebelando. Esta libreta es muy importante, ya que, a la hora de conversar con otros personajes podremos preguntarles directamente sobre las anotaciones que hayamos registrado, una mecánica clave para ir progresando en nuestra investigación. A medida que avancemos en la trama iremos desbloqueando nuevas localizaciones visitables, y por supuesto, podremos regresar a lugares ya conocidos, desplazándonos de un lugar a otro gracias a nuestra moto. En general, resulta sencillo ir atando cabos y decidir cual será el siguiente paso, con quién hablar, qué objeto utilizar, etc., y por supuesto, la investigación irá salpicada de pequeños y entretenidos rompecabezas que amenizarán el juego, como hackear un ordenador, burlar a la poli o manipular cintas de audio.

[h2]Valoración[/h2]
Aparte de su llamativo pixel art, Kathy Rain es un juego realmente bueno para tener tantos años y la versión Director’s Cut lo hace aún más accesible, ampliando la historia en ciertos puntos, añadiendo nuevos diálogos y skins para la moto de Kathy y mejorando los controles, gráficos y animaciones. Esta aventura nos mete de lleno en una trama de investigación realmente interesante, con toques sobrenaturales; la protagonista es carismática y su pasado juega un papel crucial en su carácter; las conversaciones son entretenidas y contamos con múltiples líneas de diálogo y opciones multirrespuesta y los puzzles son asequibles y satisfactorios de resolver, con un nivel de dificultad relativamente sencillo. Todo ello queda adornado con situaciones y mecánicas diferentes, que saben romper la monotonía en los momentos adecuados, dando como resultado una obra bastante bien pulida y divertida de jugar. Como la mayoría de Point & Click, es un juego algo lento en su desarrollo y mecánicas, pero si te gusta el género y disfrutas con los pixel art, Kathy Rain es un título indispensable en tu biblioteca. Personalmente recomiendo la versión Director’s Cut, por todos sus extras y mejoras, pero la versión básica seguro que también cumple tus expectativas si prefieres ahorrar.

✔️ [b]Positivo[/b]:[list]
[*]Trama interesante, con toques sobrenaturales, que sabe desarrollarse de una forma adictiva y entretenida, ofreciendo numerosas mecánicas que nos harán sentir verdaderos detectives.
[*]A pesar de ser una aventura lineal, donde cada parte de nuestra investigación debe darse en un orden y secuencia concretos, el juego sabe hacernos sentir que tenemos cierta libertad, permitiéndonos revisitar varios lugares, con múltiples personajes a los que entrevistar, tomando notas y resolviendo diversos rompecabezas. 
[*]Personalmente me agrada mucho el diseño gráfico del juego, apostando por un pixel art algo grueso, pero suficientemente detallado para ser vistoso y colorido. [/list]
❌ [b]Negativo[/b]:[list]
[*]Como muchas otras aventuras gráficas, el desplazamiento y animaciones se sienten algo lentos en ocasiones, pudiendo llegar a ser tedioso en algunas secuencias concretas. Aunque esto se alivia un poco al permitirnos el desplazamiento rápido a las salidas de los escenarios con un doble click. 
[*]La gestión del inventario en horizontal es algo incómoda, ya que se irán acumulando numerosos objetos (muchos de los cuales no usamos más que un par de veces). 
[*]Aunque no es un problema importante, a nivel de diseño gráfico, a veces falla a la hora de conseguir la sensación de “profundidad” entre el escenario y los objetos/personajes ubicados en él, dando un resultado poco natural. [/list]

I want to start of by saying that for a pixel game the art style was beautiful and the cut scenes and animations were very well done. Last Report is a well made game, though maybe a little short in regards to it being a full game as this more just feels like a lengthy demo in my opinion. I completed the game in just over an hour and that includes getting all 9 achievements. 

For me, the pros for this game would mainly be the art style. I loved how tense the atmosphere felt and the jumpscares were on the spooky side, (ive played a lot of horror games at this point so the effect kind of wears off when it comes to jumpscares for me). I loved the little human verification puzzles, although easy and repetitive they still made my brain tingle with each one i did and didnt find myself getting bored of them. The music and sound effects were also nice, I definitely recommend playing with headphones. 

For the cons the main issue for me would be the plot. I found it very lacking and there was many build ups and lore dumping of characters and events that seemingly lead nowhere. Despite being given choices in game they change nothing and the outcome is always the same which was very disappointing. Because of this there is also zero replayability, despite enjoying the game its not something i think i could go back and play multiple times due to there being no different routes to take. Another couple things would be, theres no punishment system in place, having a report tracker seems a little pointless in game to me when getting reports wrong have no effect on the story or outcome, though it may just be there as an immersive feature, i just find it a missed opportunity to add more content to the game. And I was also confused why when picking the walkie talkie up you have the option to call one of the four workers youre introduced to but you are never once able to contact them yourself, even when theres in game dialogue saying 'i should contact this person' but again, it could be there for purely immersive reasons and im simply nitpicking but was something i wanted to mention.

Overall for just under 5 buckaroos i would say this game was still worth the price tag. I did enjoy playing it despite the cons listed. I do hope for maybe a dlc or even a second game that is set in the same universe cause the lore and story has so much potential. If you dont think the price is justifiable i would 100% recommend getting it if its discounted at any point in the future.

I've played Warframe for over 4,000 hours. I supported the game financially, bought cosmetics, and genuinely enjoyed the grind, the builds, the boss fights, and the community. But over the past 3 years, things have gone seriously downhill.

The devs introduced damage attenuation, a system that basically nerfs your DPS into the ground. Even in this update, there are still 5 viable one-shot builds (one using the Tornado augment), but generally, your 500 million damage build gets reduced to 50,000 against certain bosses. Why? Because they don’t want players one-shotting bosses.

Fine—but if you’re going to prevent us from nuking bosses, at least design bosses that are actually fun to fight. Not these dull bullet sponges with 1.5 predictable attacks and no unique mechanics.
There are great bosses in Warframe—Ropalolyst, Profit-Taker, Exploiter Orb, and Jackal. They have mechanics, phases, movement. But these new ones? Just health bars with legs.

The In-Game Economy Is a Joke Now
In just 2.5 years, Arcane Energize plummeted from 2,000 platinum to around 220. Inflation is bad enough in real life—I don’t want to see it in my escape too. Thank you, yearly Jade  update and event,

They’ve Killed Entire Activities:
Eidolon Hunting? Dead. (Yes, macros were a problem—but punishing the whole community wasn't the answer.)
Steel Path Disruption? Dead.
Void Cascade? Still alive, but a buggy mess + inflation = nope .

Warframe used to reward farming, improving, optimizing.  None of that really matters now . With damage attenuation, someone using an under-modded weapon can do similar damage to someone who spent hours fine-tuning their gear.

Yes, there are still 4–5 one-shot boss-killing builds that work.  Enjoy 4-player squads with random loadouts in Deep Archimedea taking forever to clear a boss—unless you happen to have that one friend with a cheese build to carry the run ( now you have to carry him for another Deep Archimedea  round ).

Instead of balancing or refreshing old content, DE keeps adding trash-tier weapons just to pad the Mastery Rank system. It feels like everything is catered to new players, while veterans are being pushed aside.

I never minded the grind. I liked it. Farming rivens, arcanes, or new skins just to kill things 0.1 seconds faster—that was the fun. But now? That motivation is gone.
I even built a big clan with an active Discord back in 2023. Now? No one wants to play anymore—including me.
DE chose to treat their long-time players like this. And I’ve made my choice too: I’m done.

Several levels are still bugged so certain areas become unsolvable e.g. you're supposed to be able to push a slider but it doesn't slide. Cross checking against walkthroughs show that it is my game that's bugged and not working as intended. 

Regarding skills, the game only lets you complete all skill trees right before the final fight. On top of that, it feels like there are TOO many skills that each character has to the point where trying to switch between each becomes confusing as hell as you try to remember who can do what in order to solve puzzles. Song Of Horror starts off very strongly, with the most interesting chapter in the whole game in my opinion.
The whole setting in this big, creepy, dark mansion, some unknown entity lurking around every corner, hiding behind every door, puzzles and the fact you can forever lose your characters. This sounds to me like a mixture for a good horror game.

I enjoyed how mysterious The Presence was for the majority of the game. I absolutely loved the subtle little scares, there's hardly any real jumpscares in the game, and a lot of it (especially the amazing 1st episode) are a lot more subtle, maybe a figure appears somewhere, not really announcing itself, and then you look again and it silently disappeared, maybe a door closes itself around the corner. I feel like later in the game those particular, subtle events don't really happen anymore, and just resort to the more generic ones that can happen basically anywhere, but they still get the job done.
I also find certain events that I'm pretty sure can kill your character if you wander into them (I can't really confirm this because if I enter a room that changed into an impossibly long corridor and wandering into it makes my vision blurry, I'm getting the f outta there, never to see the event ever again xd) very interesting, and I find that the game even upon loading - would not repeat same events and surprise me with a new one on a different occasion. 

The game uses some insta-kill spots too, but I will say - they don't feel cheap at all. They all really do make sense if you take the time to analyse the circumstances and the information at hand, and other times The Presence really does try and trick you very sneakily.
Also, I have to compliment the usage of characters that you lose! They may appear again in the chapter, actually - and they may pose a new threat themselves, or they may not. I thought it very creepy and very much in theme with the game.
Each episode the game introduces a new threat. What that means is basically [b] how [/b] you would defend yourself against it. And no - there is [b] no [/b] combat in the game, you have to run and hide which adds to the tension, really making you feel like a powerless little bi*ch stacked against impossible odds.
Every new encounter basically means a different minigame, from "go hide and hold your breath" to "hold the door down" etc.

The controls may require more modern audience to get used to it, but if you're a little older, I don't think you should have a problem with tank control system. The only issue I had with it personally is when the camera angle changes as you're holding the button, adding another input or letting it go for split second will reset the orientation which can end up making your character spin in a circle when you [b] really [/b] don't want to spin in a circle, just a mild annoyance really, very easy to get used to.
Oh, and sometimes it feels like the camera angle should change a little bit quicker, like at times where it want's you to go to the end of the big room from one end to the other, you're meant to look at the items at the end there but the camera happily hangs in the opposite corner, not allowing you to see where you're going or what you're looking at. Doesn't happen very often but there were instances where it did happen.

Graphically, I must say the game looks stunning, and the atmosphere is so thick you could slice it with a knife.
Also, worth noting - the game only plays up to 60fps, can't go above that (maybe with some tinkering in the config apparently) but in all honesty - somehow I could barely even notice it, and I puke when I see games locked to 60fps normally.
Audio is really creepy as well. Hardly any music really, but all the sounds mask up the lack of it. I could often hear floorboards creak behind me, something that sounded like footsteps would approach from behind every now and then, doors knocking and stuff like that.

I feared a lot that the longer the game went on the less scary it would be, maybe the threat from The Presence is more trivial later on or something?
Nope. Throughout the whole game I felt just as vulnerable.
Similarly, I felt perhaps the levels would get a lot worse after the amazing mansion in the 1st episode?
Well, at certain points I felt like it wasn't the same anymore, but honestly, there was not a single location I disliked. Well, apart from the library, which is a short section only thankfully.
I had the same exact concern (once again) in regards of the "monster". Will the devs dumb it down at some point and turn this mysterious being into a dumb zombie or something?
Well, once again in the library there was a part involving The Presence that made it seem really dumb to me. Like all the mystery was gone and it was just this stupid monster thing, but thankfully that came and went, and the game continued on being creepy. I think the very next level actually, involved something that looked like a zombie, and I fully expected the game to take a turn here and present me with Resident Evil-like creatures (hey, I love RE, but that's not what I wanted from this game) alas, I misjudged the game once again, and it managed to avoid slip-up. 

One actual issue I had were some of the puzzles. Most of them are perfectly fine! They can be fairly easy, others you're going to have to sit down and read what information you have, decipher this and that and it's really good, everything makes sense and everyone's happy. Then other times the puzzles feel so ridiculously obscure, even with a guide on the side (yes, some puzzles had me stomped to the point where I just looked them up to avoid frustration) and if my life depended on it - I could not tell you how the weight of the sun = the wind blows at 12,4mp/h in South Africa so therefore 13x4 = Eagle if you turn it upside down and count backwards.
Seriously, some of the puzzles drained me like Sasha Grey drained you know what.


Overall though, I really, really enjoyed the premise of the game, the setting, the atmosphere - all phenomenal, despite difficulties and a bit of frustration with certain puzzles.

Always had a soft spot for this one. Tried playing it at launch back in '16 but had to shelve it owing to the flashy 14 fps I got out of it with my laptop. Not quite since Mafia 3 has a repetition problem.   Mafia 3 is severely repetitive with its mission design but I don't think it's as soul-lessly repetitive as something like ubisoft's latest installments. 
These Racket missions all have you running around and causing a specified amount of damage/loss to take down the businesses. It being grindy and repetitive is an understatement but the thing is a lot of the level design seem distinct enough, the set pieces all look pretty unique from eachother most of the time and the shooting mechanics is crisp af with stealth being viable as well, so ultimately, the pacing of the narrative throughout these missions is what made it a slog to get through for the better part of the game. I found it extremely annoying when the game forces you to revisit the same locations you’d already been to earlier just to kill or recruit one of the racket bosses. They shouldn't have opted the ubislop route of not just having a kill list but also making it grindy af to the likes of something like Wildlands or Odyssey. It might be a better experience to play the game slowly and avoid the repetitiveness get to you, but it's a Mafia game, you play it solely for the narrative.
Rockstar has the same tedious mission design of moving from A to B to kill someone. But what makes their games stand out is that the focus on narrative is never lost, they keep expanding and developing on their characters and plot, so it makes these repetitive ass missions playable to a great degree which is something that Mafia 3 forgets to do. And the thing with M3 is that you know where the plot is heading towards right at the start of it all, so it has no reason to stretch itself like it did, there was no gotcha moment at the end, Lincoln accomplishes exactly what he sets out to do and his character barely changes during it. Now the execution of Sal and Giorgi's ending was amazing but not sure if it was worth all the grindy parts of it preceding that. All the character bio was so nicely written, just hope they had infused all that into the story in the form of cutscenes/driving conversations. I say this as someone who loves third person shooters the most out of all genres, TPS has gotten stale and monotonous, so you need to make it linear and have a neat narrative tied along with it. There's a reason why no one else attempts to do a full fledged open world TPS other than rockstar nowadays. So yeah it was a poor decision on hangar 13's part to bury a decent story under all that repetitiveness when they could have gone the same route as the previous games or paced the story well to fit the open world. I like how you get benefits out of all the racketeering that are actually pretty helpful when it comes to gameplay. Really wish they hadn't abandoned some of the mechanics introduced here in Mafia Old Country. The driving felt really good but the pedestrians resembled those from GTA 3 where they dive into the car to kill themselves instead of just walking like a normal human being 😭. Also I found the driving to be disgusting when I first picked it up but that was all because of the performance. And to think of it narratively it makes absolutely no sense why THREE underbosses would uselessly and shamelessly depend on a single guy to toss all the districts and rackets to them and be ungrateful pricks about it. Speaking of it, I really hoped Vito would have had a bigger presence in the story instead of being one of these obnoxious underbosses I mentioned. Also I don't think they should've teased Joe like that in the ending, kinda removes the impact and ambiguity of the 2nd game's ending. Overall the endings were neat tho some where outright hilarious like the one where father james randomly plants a bomb under Lincoln's car. M3 had it all,  be it the amazing driving mechanics, satisfying gunplay, a stellar soundtrack or a captivating premise but it all gets buried under a grindy mission design and a few game breaking glitches here and there. Might check out the dlcs soon enough.

If you’ve made it this far, my sincerest of apologies to all the non-existent readers for my repetitive use of the word “repetitive.” 🙏🏼

Pros
- Visceral combat. Both you and enemies go down fast, making for some intense gunplay, kills aren't always clean too, with enemies lying wounded, begging for their lives or groaning, emphasising the brutality, though for you you do get adrenaline shots you can use to recover from near-death and buff your health back, but that only goes a little towards making you less squishy until you get late game upgrades for it.
- Memorable setting and story. A Southern US city with French influence, diverse range of gangs (Hillbillies, KKK, Mafiosi, Haitians, Irish), and easily hateable racist scumbags trying to hold back the march of the civil rights era, and a narrative told in several formats, the 60s, which acts as your character's present, and flashforwards in some cutscenes to 2 different forms, a 1970s Senate hearing and a 2010s documentary, speaking about your crime spree in past tense with the characters reflecting on it, those characters are certainly interesting too, both friends and enemies, well voice acted with excellently mocapped cutscenes. Plus the radio music rules.
- Sit Down system. Mafia 3 is all about conquering the city, the basic gameplay loop is this, you have 9 districts to take over by killing their bosses, each district has its boss (representing the whole district) and 2 underlings (representing its 2 rackets/businesses), the first 3 districts are automatically assigned to your 3 different ally gangs, but after that you get to decide who gets what, earning cash and unique perks from the allies you provide for, each offering 4 district’s worth of perks and 3 district's worth of loyalty missions which add a little extra story at the end of the chain. First you can decide rackets individually, but once you kill the boss you assign the district as a whole, giving all of its rackets to your chosen ally. Each ally always wants the turf, but their hunger for it will be impacted by 2 things, whether you already gave them rackets in that turf, and their overall loyalty (based on if you give them turfs previously, or did post-turf loyalty missions for them), you can keep them all happy and make lots of cash together if you play your cards right, but if you don't they'll ditch you and become a problem to be dealt with and a hole in your wallet. The only real flaw it has is there’s no real reason to assign any rackets to a boss you don’t plan to give the turf to, as it just pisses them off with no benefits, making that choice basically irrelevant.
- Quality DLCs. The DLC missions, included free in this edition, are great fun with proper plotlines and unique missions, best played in between waves of district conquering to break up their monotony.
- Smoother controls driving. Taking an even further step in this direction from M2 the driving is fast and it’s easy to make turns, making for really nice cruising round the city that only really is lost if you pick a really shit vehicle or it gets so shot to bits you don’t have any tires left to cruise with. On foot it’s easier to snap in and out of cover too.

Cons
- Repetitive gameplay loop. To draw out a district boss you have to kill their underlings and to draw out the underlings you have to meddle with their rackets, you do that by doing assassinations, interrogations (just a takedown where you hold instead of press the button), thefts, property destruction and the occasional hostage rescue, these get very repetitive very fast. That gets added to once districts are taken over, where you have delivery jobs to do to increase their income and the loyalty missions (which include more collectathons and assassination jobs), although those are at least optional. These generic, repetitive, plot lite, bite sized jobs make up the vast majority of missions, with only the Prologue, District Bosses*, Finale and DLC content including unique encounters.
- Wonky takedown system. Takedowns can either be lethal or non lethal, but rather than being 2 different keybinds or a press/hold distinction, lethality has to be toggled in the options menu, underling bosses can also only be spared if you do the arbitrary extra step of wiretapping their area, otherwise Lincoln will automatically kill them.
- Occasional tanky enemies. In general combat is fast paced, but some enemies have artificially buffed health, being able to take dozens of Tommy Gun rounds to the chest with nothing but a generic shirt on and still turn round and blast you as you reload, not fun. This becomes a non issue around half way through the game, when upgrades to your health restoring Adrenaline make you the tanky one.
- Lacking interactivity. Except for car shops all of the game's stores can't be bought from, with resources instead handled through mobile dealers you can call, although those dealers make for great convenience the lack of stores, makes the city feel pretty barren of things to do. You just have the car dealerships, mission content, planting wiretaps and robbery, a step down from M2.
- Mission bugs. Sometimes missions don't appear when they're supposed to, forcing a restart to get them to appear, and sometimes icons for them can show up on the map when they're not actually available, leading you towards red herrings.
- Lacking faction variety. The early game gives the impression you’ll be up against a variety of factions, introducing the Haitians and Dixie Mafia as early rivals, but in reality almost the whole game has you fighting against the Mafia, with the Haitians joining you and Dixie only appearing in filler missions after the prologue. Though you do face the KKK styled Southern Union in select other encounters.
- Loss of collectivity. In M1 you were part of a gang, very frequently working with other mobsters like Paulie and Sam as well as regular goons, in 2 you swapped from family to family but were constantly with your buddy Joe and sometimes others like Henry and Tony, in 3 there’s almost none of that except for the prologue, where you work with several allies to rob the Federal Reserve. After that Lincoln has people in a support role like the 3 allied gang bosses and their associates, plus his spook ally Donovan, but the actual dirty work is done by him on his own, even though it’s his crime family. His own gang he was part of before, the Black Mob, is also completely forgotten about after the prologue. A nearly entirely one man war, Rambo style, is a departure from the series that just makes the immersion harder to maintain.
- Simplified police system. Cops don’t try to arrest you anymore, they either ignore your shit or shoot, and they don’t enforce most traffic laws unlike M1 and 2 where they’d try to fine or arrest you for speeding or running red lights, I don’t mind not being harassed by that given how much driving there is to do, but the option would be cool, especially for this setting where these racist cops would pull you over for any little thing irl, they also don't remember you/your vehicle’s look after being wanted.
- Outfit choice not respected. Because most cutscenes are pre-rendered, Lincoln will always appear in cutscenes in his veteran jacket, rather than what you chose to wear.

*District Bosses are usually 1 mission, but the last set of bosses have 2 missions, having you take down an accomplice of theirs too

For much of my first 9 hours with the game (where I conquered the first 3 districts) I really hated it, drained by its constant repetition, but after playing one of the DLCs, getting a breather, when I came back to the main game I found I wasn’t bothered as much, since the combat and driving is a solid core, in the end enjoying the game despite its faults, especially since more weapon and vehicle unlocks sped up those repetitive rackets, letting me get to the more substantial parts faster.

The fact that they barely bothered to include proper missions really keeps it down, leaving it as just good, rather than truly great, but on balance, I’d say it's worth a play.

Let’s start with the good stuff, because The Quarry does have some solid points. The visuals are honestly great - the characters look just like their real actors, and the motion capture is top-notch. (except Emma, whose expressions look like they’ve been turned up to 200% for some reason). Technically, the game runs fine too - it only crashed once during my entire playthrough, which is impressive these days. There are also a few genuinely cool moments, like the scrapyard sequence or the chase on the island. The story itself, despite some silly moments, is actually decent. It’s got potential and a few scenes that pull you in.
But most of the characters are unbearable. Out of the whole cast, maybe two are actually interesting, and the rest are just annoying stereotypes who never stop making dumb jokes. They’re not just unfunny - they’re straight-up unpleasant people. At one point, they literally break into a store to steal alcohol and a gun. When told to stay put and wait until morning, they wander off like clueless kids. The “wise old fortune teller” lady between chapters is another irritation - I started skipping tarot cards on purpose just to see how mad she’d get. Ironically, I still got an ending where she was completely satisfied.
The pacing is rough. The walking sections are painfully slow - seriously, how hard would it have been to add a run button? And the first two chapters (plus the prologue) are so boring they feel endless. It’s just a bunch of clumsy tutorial moments like “catch these keys” or “don’t trip over a stick,” while we play as idiots tossing stuff to each other.
Then there’s the writing. The story concept is fine, but the dialogue is pure millennial cringe. Everyone’s constantly trying to sound witty or funny, and it just doesn’t work. It’s like two different writers worked on this - one who wanted to tell a good story, and another who thought they were writing Guardians of the Galaxy. The result is painful to listen to.
Some characters barely get screen time at all. Lin Shaye screams for five minutes and disappears, while Lance Henriksen shows up at the very end, says about five lines, and that’s it. Totally wasted talent.
And let’s talk about decisions - or the illusion of them. The game tries to sell you on “choices that matter,” but most of them don’t. I spent the whole game being a jerk to one character, and when he finally had a gun pointed at the other in the finale, I thought my choices would pay off. Nope. Nothing mattered. Just scripted fluff.
Breathing sequences could’ve been intense, but instead, they’re boring - the game literally tells you when to release the button by showing red fluff. Why not use the controller’s mic for that? Missed opportunity. Same with cutscenes: you can’t skip them. In a game that encourages multiple playthroughs, not being able to skip scenes is just insane.
Music? Total mismatch. They tried that cliché “happy song in a dark moments” thing, but it’s been done to death - and here it just feels tone-deaf and out of place.
And Jake spends half the game running around naked for no reason. I have no idea why. 
All the time when the characters should be hiding and staying quiet together to survive, they suddenly decide to split again and again. It’s the most classic horror-movie stupidity possible. 
The ending credits are consistent - you can’t skip those either.
In conclusion, I simply don't recommend PLAYING this game. It has a good story, so watch a walkthrough on YouTube; it's free and less annoying.

Если вы ждали от A Machine for Pigs прямого продолжения The Dark Descent с его механиками выживания, то вас, скорее всего, ждёт разочарование. Но если подойти к ней как к отдельной, самостоятельной истории, то это незаурядный и очень мощный опыт, который глубже и философичнее первой части.

Атмосфера здесь совершенно иная. Это не готический ужас в замке, а индустриальный кошмар. Вместо склепов и подземелий - бесконечные цеха, скрипящие конвейеры, дымящие трубы и лабиринты грязных улиц. Звуковая дорожка, как и в первой части, просто шедевральна: грохот машин, пронзительные скрипы и жуткая музыка создают невероятное чувство тревоги и подавленности.

Самое главное отличие - геймплей стал значительно проще. Здесь почти нет головоломок в привычном понимании. Вам не нужно собирать трутницы и масло, чтобы поддерживать свет; ваша лампа работает вечно. Из-за этого исчезает чувство нехватки ресурсов и управления рисками.

По сути, A Machine for Pigs - это интерактивная история-прогулка с элементами стелса. Ваша главная задача - идти вперед, погружаться в атмосферу, слушать аудиодневники и читать записки, которые складываются в душераздирающую и шокирующую картину. Сюжет здесь выходит на первый план, и он невероятно сильный. Это мрачная притча о жертвах прогресса, одержимости, отцовской любви и цене, которую человечество платит за свои амбиции. История Манделя и его "Машины" останется с вами надолго.

Что касается ужаса, то он здесь больше психологический и атмосферный. Монстры-"свинолюди" выглядят жутко. Страх рождается не от самой погони, а от осознания того, что именно представляет собой эта чудовищная "Машина" и для чего она была создана. Финал игры - это абсолютно сюрреалистичный и оглушительный аккорд, который ставит всё на свои места.

Кому стоит играть?
Тем, кто ценит атмосферу и сюжет. Это сильнейшая сторона игры.
Любителям индустриальной эстетики и викторианской Англии.
Тем, кто хочет глубокой, философской притчи.

Кому может не понравиться?
Фанатам первой части, ожидающим сложного геймплея выживания.
Тем, кто ищет хоррор-экшен и сложные головоломки.
Игрокам, которые не любят формат "прогулка" с минимумом интерактива.

Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs - это не столько классический хоррор, сколько мрачная, поэтичная и безумно атмосферная история. Это скорее духовный наследник Dear Esther, чем The Dark Descent. Она не столько пугает скримерами, сколько заставляет чувствовать себя неуютно, грустить и задумываться.

>> Ну вот, я наконец-то прошел Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs. Я знаю, что среди фанатов первой части мнения разделились, и многие недовольны, но мне, как человеку, который любит именно атмосферное погружение и историю, эта игра зашла просто отлично!

Да, это действительно больше похоже на симулятор ходьбы (и это комплимент, не ругательство!). Если вы ждёте постоянно убегать от монстров и искать спички, как в Dark Descent, то да, вы будете разочарованы. The Chinese Room (разработчики, которые делали Dear Esther и Everybody's Gone to the Rapture) полностью сфокусировались на повествовании и атмосфере.

>> И знаете, атмосфера здесь — это нечто. Викторианский особняк, потом эти индустриальные, живые, мерзкие и пугающие цеха... Всё пропитано копотью, ржавчиной, и каким-то болезненным механическим гудением. Ощущение, что само здание — это живой, больной организм. Звуковой дизайн просто гениален! Эти свиные визги, скрежет, тишина, которая постоянно вот-вот взорвется.

Сюжет про Освальда Мандуса – это мощная, философская притча. Она пугает не скримерами, а идеями. Это ужас от масштаба безумия, от осознания того, на что способен человек. Я буквально шёл по игре, как по интерактивной книге, слушая эти пронзительные монологи главного героя. История очень цельная, трагичная и очень умная, что редкость для хорроров.

>> Мне понравилось, что они убрали полоску рассудка и бесконечное масло для лампы. Это позволило мне спокойно вникать в детали, читать записки, смотреть на окружение, не отвлекаясь на менеджмент ресурсов.

В общем, моё мнение: если вы ищете адреналин и хардкорный стелс-хоррор, то, возможно, вам не сюда. Но если вы цените глубокую, мрачную историю, философский подтекст и великолепную, осязаемую атмосферу, то Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs — это просто шикарный, недооценённый проект. Всем любителям мрачных "симуляторов ходьбы" и историй-притч — очень советую!

Ce jeu constitue une manière intéressante de replonger les fans dans l'univers de l'excellente série [i]The Expanse[/i], hélas éteinte aussi prématurément que maladroitement par Amazon. Il y a de quoi se réjouir, tout y est scrupuleusement respecté : musique officielle du générique, voix des acteurs (à quelques exceptions près) et tous les codes propres à cette humanité lointaine, en proie aux luttes de pouvoir entre Mars, la Terre et la Ceinture. Ces mêmes aficionados sauront sans doute fermer les yeux sur le manque d'audace du scénario, l'intrigue effaçant même toute la dimension politique qui fait pourtant le sel de la série. 

Le jeu alterne entre phases de QTE, choix plus ou moins déterminants (les décisions véritablement importantes étant immanquables) et séquences d'exploration pour notamment collecter les divers items disséminés au fil des cinq épisodes. La durée de vie de l'ensemble reste limitée et la rejouabilité relative : le rythme, assez lent, aura tendance à décourager l'entame d'une nouvelle partie.

Sur le plan technique, l'Unreal Engine 5 met solidement en musique une direction artistique intéressante, quoique surprenante s'agissant du [i]character design[/i]. On regrettera au passage que le jeu soit limité au 16/9, là où l'on aurait espéré une expérience plus cinématographique, donc adaptée aux écrans larges.

S'agissant du DLC [i]Archangel[/i], il se révèle parfaitement dispensable, sauf si passer trois quarts d'heure dans le bureau de Chrisjen, à lire des messages et répondre à des appels, correspond à votre conception d'un jeu vidéo.

Pour résumer, [i]The Expanse: A Telltale Series[/i] ne se destine qu'aux fans de la série, lesquels se montreront probablement plus conciliants envers une offre vidéoludique somme toute limitée. À acquérir lors des soldes, à moins de dix euros par exemple.

This game fits the vibe of The Expanse, the vastness of space, the political intrigue, etc. But as a Telltale game, it's lacking. It's certainly not Wolf Among Us or TftB. The main mechanic is exploration, so it's more of a walking simulator. The QTEs are silly, and the story is equally strange.

To get a "good ending", even the *tiniest, most insignificant* decisions are important. Literally any choice could cause a companion death in later chapters. [spoiler] If you didn't find that medical chip in Ch1, then your medic will have a panic attack in Ch5, unrelated to the chip, because he "doesn't trust you enough". If you don't break up a play fight between two brothers [i]IN THE VERY FIRST CHOICE OF THE GAME[/i], then one of your other companions will straight up die because he thinks you like to see him bullied.[/spoiler]

I highly recommend the first two Telltale games I mentioned in this review. Please give them a try.

[H1]The coziest breakdown you’ll ever experience. Bring tissues (and maybe a hug)[/H1]

I’ve apparently entered my “games that make me cry” era, and As Long As You’re Here hit especially close to home. Having grown up surrounded by loved ones battling dementia and Alzheimer’s, this game felt like watching a slow echo of my own fears play out, and yet, it’s done with such care, empathy, and quiet grace that I couldn’t help but call it a gem.

It’s deceptively cozy at first. You tend your plants (all charmingly named), knit whenever you please, and move through peaceful daily routines. But soon, that calm starts slipping. Tasks become confusing, memory blurs, and you feel yourself unraveling, not through jump scares or shock, but through subtle, masterful design. You know where it’s heading, but not how fast, and that’s what makes it so powerful.

The writing and mechanics mirror real-life caregiving with painful accuracy. It’s short (about an hour), but that’s almost a mercy: I don’t think I could’ve endured much longer emotionally. There are small hiccups, like the lack of scene selection to replay certain parts, slow text display from time to time, and some slightly dizzying morning animations, but none of it dims the final impact.

This isn’t an easy experience, but it’s a meaningful one. Take the trigger warnings seriously. If you can handle it, As Long As You’re Here is a beautifully designed, heartbreakingly human story that lingers long after the screen fades to black.
