There are two kinds of people who should play Freedom Wars: those who played the original over a decade ago and don't want to fish out their Vita for a second play-through, and those who have played every other hunting game worth playing and are desperate for something a little different.

That's not to say Freedom Wars is BAD, it's not, but it's not GREAT either, and a lot of its value comes from the novelty of its setting (which disappears over time), and the very specific era it released in (when Monster Hunter was completely absent and competitors were ass).

As a reference point, Freedom Wars is somewhat akin to God Eater (though a little less chuuni in tone, and a little less floaty). Combat focuses on using two weapons (usually a melee and ranged weapon) to clunkily grapple through the environment and dismember large enemies through button mashing prompts. It sounds reductive, and it is, but not nearly as much as you'd hope. There isn't much variety in the enemies you fight, or the maps you fight in - and when variety technically starts to appear, you're still approaching the fights the same way you always have and always will, so it amounts to a new coat of paint at best. 

What makes the game worthwhile is the setting. You exist in an oppressive post apocalyptic society that fights other equally awful societies in a fight for resources. Each society (called panopticons, which are effectively regional mega-prisons) constantly use giant robots to steal resources back and forth from each other, like metal scraps, ice cream, and math nerds. 

Narratively it's all played very straight, but mechanically it feels very tongue-in-cheek. As an example, you're labelled a "sinner" (a prisoner/ slave) that has a 1 million year prison sentence to work off, and without warning you can be penalized for all sorts of things (like sleeping sideways, walking too fast, talking to NPC's, etc) and you have to buy the right to do the simplest of tasks you'd otherwise take for granted. As you play, you replace the constant robotic wardens (intentionally voiced with shoddy TTS, not AI) with a large cast of surface-level characters, and replace the navigation of oppressive rules with a by-the-book mystery and themes. This means as you progress through the game (by buying privileges, learning more about the world, and streamlining repetitive combat), it's novelty falls to the wayside leaving a bland experience you may not have the heart to finish despite its short length.

It's not worth $50. It might be worth $30 if you're someone who values novelty, doesn't value your time or money that much, and wants to have some fresh talking points to bring up with other videogame weirdos. I'm in the latter camp so I've enjoyed my time with it, but Freedom Wars is a relic out of time and not for everyone. There's a reason it was remade, a reason it has a cult following, a reason I've put the time and effort to re-experience it, and a reason it's flopped yet again a decade after its original release.

In regard to the game itself:
If you enjoy playing an isometric perspective and enjoy gameplay based around scavenging, exploration, and weapon customization, go for it! There's plenty to do and I'm not even halfway through the currently available maps. There's tons of weapon variety and each weapon has like 11 or 12 potential parts to be swapped out to preference.

The game also gets updated regularly and is steadily growing.

In regard to the early access development:
I encountered a pretty big bug that resulted in a weapon I'd spent a lot of time collecting attachments for being stuck as a UI element that couldn't be interacted with. Luckily, I had the wherewithal to grab a backup of my save off the Steam Cloud before closing the game.

I went to the Discord to report the bug and upload my log, and the Dev responded immediately. He pushed out a fix very quickly and even offered to drop me the weapon I'd lost to make things right. Thankfully I had the backup save and was able to, with his help, transfer the weapon from my backup to my current save so I wouldn't lose any progress.

The Dev, Sean_G, went above and beyond my expectations and I figure leaving a positive review was the least I could do. I know these early access indie games can make potential players a bit nervous about taking the leap, so I'd like to assure you that this is one of the good ones. I play a lot of early access games and bugs happen, its just the way of things, but usually the most you can expect from development is a nod of acknowledgement towards the existence of the bug and an apology for the inconvenience. Developers who actually put the effort into making things right are a rare breed and deserve all the support we can give them.

This is a UFO in 4X games.

A foreword for those of you who cannot play a top notch graphic game : just stop reading. This game is not about good graphics (although they are adequate and do the job), but about content.

The setting is unusual. Imagine you're in Star Wars (well that's not that, but close enough). The republic & empire have been crumbling. Core planets may still be working together, but your planet, a fringe planet that had loose ties to the civilization, your planet is cut out, causing internal strife to control meager resources, and a return to basic civilization. You start there, with a small setthment that is still working, has access to basic technology (trucks is the most advanced tech), and has grabbed some old, high tech weaponry. That weaponry will give you a small edge while you're trying (and you're not alone) to reunite the planet to ensure the rise of a new civilization and possibly reconnexion to whatever remains of the old empire/republic.

Given that background, the map on which you'll be playing is as varied as is possible, including lush planets with a lot of water, trees and wild lfe, to barren and hostile. No other game gives you that range of possibilites. 

When exploring with your units, you'll be expanding you borders. However, usually you never really know what resources you have. Mines are discovered later (they will be discovered by unseen prospectors), and interestingly, they have a limited amount to deliver! Once depleted, you have to find other sources. These should not be too far away from your cities (this strains your administrators and gives huges production penalties). You will however find some perks, such as that derelict ship from which your scientists will be able to produce an influx of research, or that old, hidden, but still working computer that will help your governor.

The question is, what this game has not ? I wonder. The economic system is one of the most complex around, in the good sense. It is merged with a logistic system that, in such games, is a revolution. No, you're not goinf to send a unit around the world, because very soon it will dissolve for lack of resources to survive. That mountian range, well, it's mostly impassable. Not that you cannot cross it, but your supplies won't be following.  To achieve any of these, you will have to expand your logistic system, which is not that difficult ; however, this consumes industrial resources that you might want to use in a better way... And it also uses resources (such as oil) ; so in the end, expanding is possible, but your economy will be the limiting factor.

The economic system itself is based on a few resources : metal, rare earth, basic industry, worker. Using that, you'll create power plants, farms, water extractors (where water is a rare resource) , roads, railways... The trick is that everything is tightly knitted together, and you cannot run in one direction only because you're going to unbalance you economy (you may even wreck it). Even if you could, it is pointless to build too many buildings, because you wouldn't have enough workers to man them, or you would be producing enough electricity etc... This is really different of what you see in other games because you really have to be carefull and everything you do can and will have real consequences on your economy.

To add to this , you also have to care about the morale of your workforce & population (dissattisfaied workers will leave your assets which will stop producing, eh!) and also the major leaders of your state. Because, yes, you'll also have to deal with internal politics, say twenty people, and having powerful individuals turn sour on you may well cause an armed revolution. Not that you really need that with enemies around and an hostile world ready to eat you.

To top it all, you'll have regular events, such as strikes, for which you have usually two, three or four ways to deal with. Some of these implies to use cash (do you have enough ?), and all of them are either backed or opposed by the powerful guys behind you. Some events are nasty, such as the slaver raid that will destroy part od your population and workforce if you fail to deal with it (once your choice is selected, it is usually solved by using a roll based on your councilors). So sometimes the question will be : do I nominate people who think more or less like me (unlikely to revolt) or do I choose the competent one (who might soon become grumpy) ?

And last, to help you deal with all that, you can use polical strategies, which cover a lot of fields, from diplomacy to military postures, dealing with the civil economy (not your's -the government- but that of the normal people), or dealing with your populace or councilors... These assets are regularlly handed to you as "cards", which you decide to play when you see fit.

Resaerch is a two step process : first find the idea, then produce the prototype. If the research involved a building, you can then contruct it. If it involved military units (say Medium Aircraft), then you'll have to create an appropriate blueprint to create a real model (what engines, what wingspan, what role...), which will have to pass through your military administration for "validation". Only then wil you be able to build some..

Units are organized along a NATO schema, under a HQ which will provide some benefits (you can have units running without HQ -using the high command-) but they'll be less efficient. This is just the tip of the iceberg ; needless to say, your units and your opponent units may look alike (say infantry), but your own unit might be 1000 soldiers where your opponent might be fielding an additionnal 200 machineguns and 30 bugguies ; you would end up mowed...

All in all, this system is very well thought and rich ; you really feel you are running a country and people. 
I could go on and on, but I think you now have an idea of the game. Be warned that the learning curve is hard, but you have a rare thing for these times : a manual! Read it, you'll need it, especially to grasp the logistics.

If you're keen on a system that makes you think instead of just catching your eyes, this is your game!

PS: what you won't see in this game
- other major country units running around in you territory (not possible because of logistical constraints)
- city spamming (building a city from scratch involves economic efforts from your whole economy, not just a basic "settler")
- mushroom ciry : you cannot "rush" building, and you barely control your population who may well choose to ignore, or even run out of your new city
- rush construction (buildings/units) ; everything is built at its pace, using your industrial base production
- oversized army : due to many constraints (logistical on the map, resources for building), your (and your opponents) army will have to stay in line of your economy

If you’ve ever wanted to command dragons, undead accountants, and elves with better hair than shampoo commercials, this is your game.

I’ve sunk more hours into this than I care to admit (my coffee mug now has diplomatic immunity). The strategic depth is fantastic — every move feels like a chess match where your knight is actually a vampire and your pawns are angry dwarves with axes.

The graphics? For its time, they were like a Renaissance painting had a baby with a fantasy novel. The music? Epic enough to make brushing your teeth feel like preparing for battle.

Sure, the AI sometimes makes decisions that suggest it’s been sniffing too much mana dust, and the campaign difficulty curve occasionally resembles a cliff... but hey, that’s part of the charm. You don’t play HoMM V for mercy — you play it to conquer, cackle, and reload your save file for the 17th time.

Multiplayer? A glorious test of patience and friendship. Nothing says bonding like a six-hour hotseat match and passive-aggressive castle sieges.

Final verdict: 10/10 would lose sleep over again. If you love strategy, fantasy, and yelling “NOOOO!” when your hero steps into a trap, this game’s for you.

[h2]かなりお勧めのお手軽RTS+ローグライク[/h2]

現時点の最高難易度をクリアしたのでレビューしました。

わらわらユニットがいるタイプのRTSに、
みんな大好きスキルツリー形式のローグライク要素がついたゲーム。
知っていればPlanetary Annihilation: TITANSの惑星を1つにしてローグライク要素が
入った感じが一番わかりやすいかも。

9面あり自分のプレイスタイルでは大体1時間30分くらいで一周が終わる感じでした。
大きな流れとしてはゲーム開始時に自機であるエンジニア、採掘ユニットのハーベスター、強力なスキル持ちユニットのスペシャリストを何種類からか選びます。
マップが始まるとユニットを選びながら全体バフのハック、ユニットごとに2つけられるアップグレード、使用スキルのドロップを選びながらクリアを目指します。
それに加えてユニットごとのパッシブ・アクティブスキルがあるので組み合わせの自由度が非常に高く。

資源は1種類なのでRTS部分はそこまで複雑ではなく、どのユニットを選ぶか・どのアップグレードやハックをつけるかが戦略のカギになる印象でした。

個人的には編成の要になるスペシャリストを事前に決めることができるため、
ローグライクにありがちな似たような構成になりがち問題を回避しやすく
それが非常に好印象でした。
まだまだ早期アクセスの段階で今後のアップデートも非常に楽しみです。
ユニット動かすタイプのRTSが好きなら間違いなくお勧めします。

以下細かい話になるので興味があれば見てください。

スタート前に決める要素
・エンジニア
　自機。ライフが3つあり、0になるとゲームオーバー。
　スタンダード、戦闘用、索敵用などの種類がある。
・ハーベスター
　建設・ユニット生産の資源（クリスタル）を採掘できるユニット。
　これも採掘特化の物や戦闘もできるものなど種類がある。
・スペシャリスト
　スタート前に一番大事な要素。一般ユニットと比べ強力なスキルを持っている。
　ダメージ軽減や回復をするタンクや、戦闘力が高いカマキリメカ、
　ミニオンを召喚するクモメカなどその周回の戦略の要になる。
　ほかにもいるが特にタンクとクモメカが強いと思いました。

ゲーム中の強化要素
・ハック
　全体に適応されるパッシブスキル。移動速度アップやコストダウン、デバフ（火、スロー、
　スタン、フィアーなど）の時間・ダメージ延長など種類が豊富。
　構成とかみ合うと非常に強力。
・アップグレード
　ユニットにつき2個まで付けられる強化要素。ステータス強化や、ヒット時に〇％の
　確率でデバフ付与や、死亡時にバフ・デバフをまいたりこちらも種類が豊富。
・ドロップ
　各マップに1回使用可能なアクティブスキル。範囲内を爆撃したり、
　味方へのバフ・ヒールなどがある。
　強力ではあるものの個人的には重要度は低い印象でした。

もし攻略に詰まったら攻撃レートの早い低コストユニットにバウンティ（ヒット時10％の確率で防御ダウン+撃破時クリスタルをドロップ）をつけることをお勧めします。
味方の火力を上げつつ生産力を上げられるので、どんな構成でもとりあえず入れておくと安定します。

Внезапно, загорелся идеей пройти всех Шерлоков и всех Пуаро. На несколько неплохих игр попадается и вот такая серия из двух игр Hercule Poirot "The first case" и "The London case".

Поиграл в первую часть, прошёл быстро, не особенно пожалел. В 2023г., аж спустя пару лет после выхода предыдущей "The first case", выходит вот это. То есть было два года чтобы допилить первую часть, но разрабы сделали даже ещё хуже, хотя такое казалось невозможным... Ну дорисуйте анимаций, сделайте хоть какую-то вариативность сюжета и было бы более-менее видно что хотели сделать лучше. Вместо этого, породили какого-то совершенно изометрического линейного монстра:

1. Теперь локации обязательно надо крутить, чтобы увидеть каждую стенку. Я бы смирился, окей, новая фича с окружением, но крутить можно и нужно только помещения, и то не все. Вышел на улицу, пытаешься крутить локацию, выскакивает уродливый запрещающий аларм. Хотели в 3D локации, но не смогли.

2. Появились квесты с "протыкиванием" предметов на статичной картинке. Кам он, вы всерьёз используете механики игр 2001 года? Мало того, что это совершенно древняя механика, так ещё и выполнена она здесь ужасно. Кликать надо на самую маленькую точечку-область на предмете. Кликнул на том же предмете чуть левее/правее/и тд. и никакой реакции. Естественно, такие "интерактивные" элементы никак не выделяются визуально. В результате, ты иногда просто тыкаешь буквально построчно всю картинку. И таких "увлекательнейших" квестов иногда бывает до 3-4 в одном помещении.

3. Взаимосвязь фактов и умозаключений окончательно перестали быть понятными. Люди так не строят мысли, это была проблема ещё в предыдущей части, но теперь она возведена в абсолют. Логика вышла из чата. Формула подсказок хотя бы осталась прежней - три раза не угадал, подсветится вариант

4. Интерфейс инвентаря и умозаключений стал ещё хуже, да ещё и медленнее. Срабатывание ответного действия от "меню" Пуаро хуже чем можно было даже представить. Такое впечатление, что моё действие сначала улетает в 19-20 век, а потом обратно приходит ответ. Как можно так добить инпут от клика, я не представляю. Допустим,  ответил я неверно, кликаю другой вариант, но... неееееет, ты сначала дождись музыкального и текстового аларма, потом уже опять заработают кнопки действий. Так ещё и "меню" дополнительно утяжелили элементами и переходами. Стало ещё неудобнее разбираться с уликами и фактами. 

5. Несколько существенных выводов Пуаро почему-то делал буквально на ходу и сам, без какой-либо моей помощи. Вот, только что я собирал улики, что-то там сопоставлял ради какого-то умозаключения... и вот в диалоге Пуаро уже сыпет инфой, которой у нас не было. Он почему-то догадался об этом и без меня.

Если бы эта игра выходила во времена первой Сиберии, ну или первых MYST, я бы конечно же не хейтил так сильно. Но сейчас примеров детективных квестов овермного и делать такое в 2023г, это странно.

Я знаю, что буквально уже следующая игра серии вышла нормальной, адекватной и получила отличные отзывы. Как закончу этот мрак, начну её.

Voidwrought is a dark and evocative Metroidvania that draws its strength from atmosphere, movement, and its stark, oppressive sense of worldbuilding. Developed by Powersnake and published by Kwalee, the game opens with a haunting premise: a cosmic event known as the Red Star awakens a Simulacrum—an artificial being created to carry out a grim task. As this construct, you traverse desolate ruins, ancient laboratories, and decayed biomes in search of Ichor, the lifeblood of long-slumbering gods. This blend of cosmic horror and decaying high fantasy sets the tone immediately. The environments feel oppressive yet beautiful, bathed in heavy shadows, twisted organic shapes, and eerie lighting that accentuate the game’s brooding tone. Voidwrought’s hand-drawn visuals do an impressive amount of narrative work without relying on long text boxes or explicit exposition.

The moment you take control, it becomes clear that movement is one of Voidwrought’s strongest features. Jumping, dashing, wall-climbing, and aerial transitions feel exceptionally smooth, giving the game a distinct kinetic rhythm. Combat is grounded in close-range melee exchanges that reward timing and spatial awareness. Early on, your kit is deliberately sparse, which gives the game’s opening hours a sense of vulnerability. As you progress, new movement-based abilities open previously inaccessible paths, lending a satisfying sense of discovery as you loop back through old areas and uncover secrets with a renewed sense of power. The design emphasizes precision: enemies hit hard, hazards punish missteps, and mastering the controls becomes essential for navigating later zones that combine platforming and combat pressures seamlessly.

The structure of exploration reinforces the feeling of entering a hostile, ancient world whose secrets are not meant to be easily revealed. Each biome—ranging from rusted mechanical caverns to corrupted biological pits—feels distinct, both visually and mechanically. Hidden alcoves, concealed walls, and branching tunnels encourage deliberate exploration rather than brute-forcing your way forward. Voidwrought often expects the player to read the environment carefully, watching for subtle visual cues rather than relying on map markers or overly explicit guidance. While this design philosophy rewards attentive players and creates the thrill of personal discovery, it can also become a point of friction. Without clear direction, some sections risk feeling obscure, particularly when progression hinges on spotting deceptively hidden passages.

Combat escalates as the world grows more unforgiving. Enemies exhibit varied patterns, and bosses are striking in both appearance and attack design. The game’s grotesque creature concepts make each encounter feel like a clash against something ancient and unknowable rather than a mere obstacle. When the combat system comes together—precise dodge timings, planned aggression, and confident use of aerial movement—it feels exhilarating. However, Voidwrought’s approach to combat progression leans more toward refinement than expansion. Most upgrades reinforce what you already possess—stronger stats, enhanced mobility, better survivability—rather than dramatically changing playstyle. This can lead to a sense that the combat toolkit plateaus before the game itself concludes, which may leave players wishing for more variety in weapons or transformative abilities.

Despite its limited weapon variety, Voidwrought maintains a strong sense of progression through world expansion and ability-based growth. The Shrine system, where you channel Ichor to awaken upgrades and advance your capabilities, acts as a narrative and mechanical anchor. Each upgrade feels like peeling back another layer of the Simulacrum’s potential, even if the upgrades are more practical than flashy. The story itself unfolds in subtle ways through environmental clues, cryptic encounters, and the steadily escalating presence of cosmic forces. Rather than offering a heavily scripted narrative, the game opts for mood, implication, and sensory storytelling—allowing players to piece together the broader mythos at their own pace.

In terms of scope, Voidwrought delivers a focused and tightly crafted adventure rather than a sprawling epic. Most players will complete the main journey within ten hours, with additional time required for discovering secrets and optional areas. While the length is modest compared to some genre giants, the concentrated design ensures that the experience rarely drags. Performance is stable, the animations are fluid, and the art direction elevates every moment of traversal and combat. Where the game may fall short for some players is in sheer content breadth: it doesn’t aim to overwhelm with dozens of areas, weapons, or builds, and those seeking a massive, long-term Metroidvania may find the adventure more compact than expected.

Voidwrought ultimately succeeds by delivering a cohesive and visually striking blend of cosmic horror and precision platforming. Its world is memorable, its movement satisfying, and its atmosphere thick with dread and mystery. While it stops short of redefining the genre or offering extensive combat customization, it excels in presenting a refined, atmospheric, and engaging journey through a world teetering on the edge of divine collapse. Players who value meticulous world design, challenging traversal, and the eerie pleasure of uncovering ancient secrets will find much to appreciate in Voidwrought’s focused and haunting vision.

[b]Strateji ve Eğlencenin Kusursuz Karışımı: Mushiverse

Mushiverse, hem masa oyunları severlerin hem de strateji tutkunlarının kesinlikle göz atması gereken bir yapım. Oyun, klasik masa oyunlarının temel unsurlarını modern grafiklerle birleştirerek, çevrimiçi bir dünyada bizlere sunuyor. İlk bakışta oldukça sevimli görünen mantar temalı dünyası, aslında derin stratejiler ve zekâ gerektiren hamlelerle dolu.

Mushiverse, oyunculara çeşitli oyun modları ve haritalar sunarak, her seferinde farklı bir deneyim yaşatıyor. Aarkadaşlarla oynandığında, oyun tam bir strateji şölenine dönüşüyor. Haritalar her biri farklı dinamikler sunan çeşitli zorluklarla dolu, bu da her hamlenizi dikkatlice planlamanızı gerektiriyor. Mantarlarla bezeli bu evrende başarılı olmak için sadece hızlı düşünmek yetmez; aynı zamanda rakiplerinizin hamlelerini önceden tahmin etmek de büyük bir önem taşıyor.

Oyunun grafikleri ve animasyonları, son derece akıcı ve estetik bir yapıya sahip. Mantarların sevimli tasarımları ve haritaların detayları göz alıcı. Her şey bir araya geldiğinde, atmosfer tam anlamıyla içine çekiyor. Ayrıca ses tasarımı da bu atmosferi destekliyor, her hamlede duyulan efektler oyuna ekstra bir canlılık katıyor.

This is the most frustrating game I'll ever recommend. Gameplay is difficult, made more so by the amount of stuff that you need to know which the tutorials don't address. The single player campaign requires tremendous amounts of grinding, because your overall strength is limited by how much cash you make, and that's limited by what levels you can play on in what difficulties, so there's a fairly linear grind that has you replaying these same, circular little levels that do nothing and go nowhere (the singleplayer experience of this game), as you try desperately to keep the number of creeps below 100 (the unstated lose condition for the game, though you figure it out quick; there's also a nice visual effect that makes it clear you're boned as the creep number climbs up).

But it's a lot of fun. Seriously, give it a try. Funstrating. There are deep mechanics to this simple looking game. It's compelling to try to get further. Levels are unforgiving, even brutal, as a lot of the difficulty ends up being down to not allowing exponential increases in the enemies on screen... Balance seems to be 1. good, and 2. absent, in that 1. you'll find levels get progressively harder and you'll enjoy being challenged, but 2. there is no real effort made to ensure the player progresses at any given speed - you just slam into a brick wall of unsurpassable difficulty, or the level is easy and you can do it fine. Either you're over the hump and can do more damage than the enemies can take hit points, or you're not and you have to replay earlier levels more.

There are a number of improvements possible for this game, but it's already a quixotic, charming, maddening, enjoyable title. Hopefully the designers will continue to improve it. But I can recommend it as an enjoyable and even somewhat innovative Tower Defense title right now, as long as you're willing to lose quite a lot if you're trying to progress through the levels too quickly, and don't mind a total lack of hand-holding past a few basic tutorials.

[h1] A Sea of Regrets: Edward Kenway's Unlikely Redemption [/h1] 
Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag is a masterpiece of pirate fantasy that often feels like it transcends its own franchise. It delivers an unforgettable adventure on the high seas, even if it can't fully escape the series' most tedious traditions.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3480966131
The game's greatest strength is its surprisingly heartfelt story. Following Edward Kenway, a brash privateer out for glory, you witness a raw and personal journey of greed, loss, and redemption. It's a deeply human tale set against the romanticized Golden Age of Piracy, far removed from the convoluted ancient conspiracies. This fresh perspective allows you to meet legendary figures like Blackbeard and Charles Vane not as historical caricatures, but as flawed, living men.

Of course, the star of the show is the thrilling naval combat. Sailing your ship, the Jackdaw, across the vibrant Caribbean is pure joy. Chasing Spanish galleons, boarding man-o'-wars, and weathering violent storms is an endlessly rewarding gameplay loop that remains arguably the best in the entire series.
https://youtu.be/fLEw9IMC2Q4
However, this paradise has its pests. To truly upgrade the Jackdaw and survive in dangerous waters, you must engage in a colossal, mind-numbing grind. Hunting whales, looting countless ships, and clearing underwater shipwrecks becomes a repetitive necessity. Furthermore, the game is plagued by the series' worst trope: an overwhelming number of tailing and eavesdropping missions. These tedious assignments brutally disrupt the pacing of an otherwise brilliant pirate epic.
 It's a journey worth taking, but you'll need patience to see it through.

The gameplay is okay, but the meta-progression is awful.

I don't know, because I haven't even come close to finishing everything, but I estimate it would take around 400+ runs to unlock everything. There are 3 characters, each with 4 variants. Each variant needs to be leveled up separately to unlock their full kit, which takes perhaps 10-15 runs to reach max level. I'm not quite sure how the XP is calculated, but I've yet to get a single variant to max level after around 20 hours of play. Multiply that by 12. Then you have to go down each path of the map with each character (or perhaps each variant), to 'unlock' the ability to know if a specific character has a unique interaction at a specific map node. Slightly cute, but time-consuming.

Then there are the 'challenges'. I would think that something called Challenges would imply some level of optionalness to them. Difficult, but optional. However, in this game, the challenge mode is just an alternative to story mode. Story mode is a static map with the same nodes, challenge mode is a random map with generated nodes. Sounds cool, except the challenge mode is a second track to unlocking your character's abilities and cards, outside of the XP mentioned earlier.

Think ascensions in Slay the Spire, or any sort of progressively more difficult mode. Except, in this game, each level you successfully complete awards your character a PERMANENT power increase, such as "Resting grants a full heal instead of a partial heal" or "you can carry +1 additional potion". Seemingly nothing too big on their own, but altogether they make up a chunk of your power.

Surprisingly, the cards you have in your deck barely seem to matter, compared to the equipment your character has. The starting deck is more than capable of achieving victory on several of the character variants, if you have good equipment. The cards you are offered within a run can sometimes be synergistic, but more often than not, they make your deck worse than just having the basic cards in them. What makes or breaks a run is if you find a good piece of equipment that *does* something. Adds strength every turn. Converts gold into armor. Converts burnt cards into block. Heals you whenever you deal damage. If you fail to get a good piece of equipment somewhat quickly, it's far more difficult than if you succeed.

Lastly, and this is more of a nitpick than anything, the enemy intents that show projected incoming damage don't reflect the ACTUAL damage incoming. If the enemy has a +50% damage buff, or you have a +50% damage taken buff, the number above the enemy still shows the baseline number, instead of adjusting. Sometimes it's simple to calculate if you're going to survive an attack, e.g. I have 50 life, the enemy is attacking me for 40, but I'm taking +50% more, so I die. Other times, it's not simple at all. I might have 76 life, 12 block, 1 evasion, and gain 15 block at the end of my turn. The enemy is attacking for 33x3 damage, and their next hit deals double (the first hit only? does my evasion block the 2x damage hit, or not?). Every time my character takes health damage, I gain 5 block, and every time the enemy deals health damage, they gain 1 strength (for each subsequent hit of the multi-attack?). I have no clue if I will live or not. No clue if I hit end turn, will my run end. Should I drink an invulnerability potion? Should I restart the entire fight, replay everything the exact same, but play 1 additional block card the turn prior? Never mind enemies changing their intents mid-turn. There was an elite enemy that summoned allies to help them. When I hit end turn, the minion had 1hp and was attacking for a small amount, whilst the boss was buffing themself and otherwise doing nothing. The enemy minion died upon attacking my character due to reflected damage. 🔨 Решта геймплею виглядає знайомо - отримуючи нові рівні ви або покращуєте свою зброю, або отримуєте ще якусь нову разом із всілякими томами посилень, котрі виступають в ролі пасивних предметів з хорошими бонусами. It occurred to me that the To the Moon series has a bit of an identity crisis.

On one hand, it seems committed to being a clean, lean, 100% story-focused experience. The gameplay is minimal, with a very light exploration purely serving the narrative, and the humor, though prominently present, exists as a contrast to the upcoming tragedy, not because it wants to become a proper comedy. "An espresso execution with zero filler", to quote the author’s own descriptions. This is how To the Moon and most of Impostor Factory went, to great success.

On the other hand, it does dabble with filler quite a lot, spending precious development resources of its small team on the most needless things. The jokes become excessive and self-indulgent, the sprites get loads of custom one-time animations, while brief yet elaborate minigames introduce new mechanics for the sake of parodying various genres. Which is not a problem per se, but the story and drama take a hit accordingly. They start feeling like a second priority, unbalanced and vague, skipping over necessary buildup straight towards a rushed conclusion.

This is what happened in Finding Paradise, which fooled around with puns and references like there’s no tomorrow, then spent half of the final act on spoof "final boss" battles instead of communicating its message clearly. And this is what’s happening again here, exacerbated by a strange decision to never make another "full-length" entry, instead ending the series with two little side projects, even though the overarching narrative feels far from finished.

So we get a "beach episode" that tries really hard to be merely a fan-service-oriented beach episode yet also acts as a finale to Eva and Neil’s story, somehow, or at least a good chunk of it. The important bit gets telegraphed within the first 15 minutes, then you spend 2-3 hours goofing around while you encounter all of the characters (a bunch of them not even from this saga but from the developer’s older work, Quintessence), interspersed with more telegraphing to make sure you don’t have too much fun.

Then the post-credits scene confirms the said bit, spends another 15 minutes on drama, and shoos the players away to connect the dots by themselves. No further character development or consistent sci-fi worldbuilding takes place, and the whole thing is extremely abrupt because, uh, real life can also be abrupt? And once you connect the dots, you can conclude that, yes, enough has been said to reveal an overarching story… that never got shown or properly told. Because the author would rather spend screen time on cameos and minigames.

And now we have [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/2664600]The Last Hour of an Epic TO THE MOON RPG[/url], yet to be released but already quite telling in its design decision to conclude the franchise while doubling as a full-blown RPG parody made in a new engine. Will it get showered with praise for making people cry in what’s outwardly presented as a joke game? You bet. Will it give the characters and players proper space to breathe and process the implied events? I seriously doubt it.

There’s a reason why visual novels and story-heavy JRPGs, which clearly served as a source of inspiration for these games, tend to have bare-bones or repetitive gameplay and lazily reuse assets left and right – it’s so they can give enough attention to the more important things. Stories need a clear direction to be impactful. They don’t have to be long, as To the Moon itself proved, but they’ve got to be focused, and they certainly shouldn’t pursue two orthogonal goals at once.

Even if your message is simple, even if you technically touched on these topics before, own it. Give it the spotlight, explain it, talk about it, make us and the characters feel it through, just like you did at the emotional heights of the previous titles. This was never a subtle series where the real drama sneakily happens behind the scenes, yet now, at the last moment, it somehow tries to be. It works as an interesting experiment, but it’s absolutely not the kind of sendoff these characters deserve. And even if the author changes his mind later, and it stops being a sendoff, we’ll still have a saga that sometimes had no idea what it was trying to do.

Maybe it really should have been just a To the Moon series beach episode.

Сразу стоит отметить плотную атмосферу, которая усиливается за счет ностальгии. Игра не слишком сильна в создании тревоги, но прекрасно справляется с формированием уютной, почти теплой обстановки.

История подается буквально из каждой детали. Листовки с пропавшими детьми, которые можно изучить, бабушка у подъезда с пачкой этих самых листовок - она рассказывает о пропаже единственного внука. Соседский мальчик упоминает, что помогал отцу другого пропавшего расклеивать объявления. За гаражами, в поисках сигареты, мы встречаем местного тридцатилетнего дурачину, который просит нас быть осторожными. Все вокруг будто кричит об опасности, но тихий дворик и знакомые лица притупляют бдительность. Что может случиться там, где, кажется, никто не способен причинить вред?

Отдельно стоит похвалить озвучку - для бытового хоррора это всегда огромный плюс. Голоса делают персонажей живыми, а вы лучше представляете, с кем беседуете, формируете эмоциональную связь и начинаете по-настоящему сопереживать или подозревать.

Хотя сама идея исследовать дом похитителя и следить за его перемещением по звукам и репликам - интересна. Она заставляет двигаться быстро, параллельно высматривая подходящее укрытие. Но сам побег ощущается вялым.

I bought this game years ago when I first saw trailers for it and though the premise might be interesting, finally got around to playing it recently (Oct 2025).

Currently I wouldn't recommend the game for two reasons.
The first is that it relies way too much on RNG, and the second is that runs take far too long.

First on the Over reliance on RNG: the upgrades you get are random, the perks your characters can get are random, the gear your town makes is random, the enemy types and their attack directions are determined at random, the heroes you start every round with are random. Etc

I found this to be very annoying, as not being able to control or predict these aspects doesn't make a game more enjoyable, it just makes the process tedious and irritating. I'd have several runs that would go well, only to not be able to repeat the process, as it would re-roll totally different characters/abilities/items the next time.

Second on each run taking far too long: This game is very difficult, often frustratingly so. It expects you to lose and die many many times so you can slowly unlock upgrades to do better in future runs. The problem with this is a full run takes at least 4-6 hours if you don't lose early. 

This frustration is compounded by flying/ghost enemies ignoring your heroes and going through the walls. Or by late game enemies, with regenerating armor bars, that require you to waste all your action points focusing them if you didn't get the correct RNG reliant upgrades.

*** (You also have to start a level completely over again any time you lose).

Essentially every time you lose (which for most people will be often) you will make you feel like you just wasted 4-6 hours. Often for rewards that are small, hard to notice, upgrades.

I feel like the high difficulty, long round time, and RNG are just there to pad the experience. The core game (without DLC's) only has 5 levels total; however, good luck actually seeing that as the difficultly spikes suddenly and will not give you much guidance at all. The game expects you to just keep bashing your head against the wall until you find something that works.

I wanted to like this game, as it has a genuinely rad soundtrack and some great art. However, I don't think it's going to be worth all the frustration and time spent just for the reward of marginal upgrades over time, and essentially repeating the same 5 levels many times over.

If you like really difficult/challenging games, this might be the game for you. 
If you're like me and only have a few hours to play games most days, then you're probably going to want to avoid "The Last Spell".

Ghost of Tsushima is one of those games that will definitely make you feel cooler than you actually are. Just a moment ago you might have been fumbling and tripping in real life, but now you are Jin Sakai, cutting down Mongols like it’s nothing, as if you've been training with a bamboo sword under a waterfall your whole life. The game is stunning, cinematic, and almost a spiritual experience... unless you take into consideration the fact that you stop during a fight to pet a fox. 

The Director’s Cut is essentially the same game, but with an amplified effect of everything, more island, more narrative, more wind dramatically blowing through your cape as you contemplate honor and trauma. The Iki Island expansion is Jin’s journey in therapy, which is cleverly disguised as a side quest. It is aesthetically pleasing and tragic at the same time, and sometimes it can be the “my dad didn’t hug me enough” energy. 

The visuals are worth discussing. This game doesn’t have graphics, it has art. Every single frame could be a piece of art that people museum it and they silently say “wow, the composition.” You might find yourself in the middle of a fight and suddenly stopping to take pictures because the sunset is just too beautiful. While you’re technically supposed to be saving Japan, you are here instead, like a feudal times influencer, adjusting filters and focal depth. 

The fight? Exquisitely sharp. It’s a combination of ballet and murder. Each stunt and every sword strike is real and believable. You’ll transition from button, mashing panic to perfect timely parry that will make you say “yes” quietly to yourself at 2 a.m. They even have a standoff mode where you can basically act as the main character of every cool samurai movie you’ve ever seen, with the difference that you are the one who doesn’t fail and misses. 

Also, the dual, audio Japanese voice acting? The best. If you opt to play in English, that’s ok but playing in Japanese and with Kurosawa mode on is an absolute vibe. Black and white, film grain, wind that is blowing dramaticaly, it really gives you the feeling that you are watching a masterpiece from the 1950s, except without the smell of the film burning. 

The Director’s Cut is not a major overhaul of the game, but a kind of a mirror polish. Emotionally, the weight comes from Iki Island and a handful of new gadgets, and on PS5, ‘blink and it’s done’ would be a pretty accurate description of the load times. It’s essentially the same game, only smoother, prettier, and slightly sadder in a good way. 

Essentially, Ghost of Tsushima: Director’s Cut is the result of art, combat and open, world design teaming up to form a boy band. It’s gorgeous, emotional, and at times, silly, in the way that only a game that lets you write haikus about death next to a waterfall can be. 

Play it. Then play it again. And don’t forget to pet every single fox, they really deserve it.

В целом игра отличная, приятных впечатлений вагон и тележка. Красивый мир, практически не наскучивающие активности, многообразные и разнообразные сюжетом миссии отлично раскрывают нам свой проницательный сюжет. Можно это назвать разным взглядом на одно и тоже, что у всех своя правда и сложно для себя решить как в итоге относиться к тому или иному персонажу, но это к концу игры сильно надоело. Хотелось чего-то более прямолинейного и без эмоциональных качелей. Например, я ожидал какое-то эпичное сражение с лучницей, предавшей свой народ, но всё оказалось намного скучнее. Также (чуть не забыл про это) в игре очень странная система поиска предметов. Вот мы пришли на очередную базу монголов для зачистки и там, помимо уничтожения врагов, надо найти знамя, но отметок где они нет и приходиться тупо бегать по всей локации и лишь изредка появляются маркеры. Это добавляет лишних действий. Тут, возможно, добавить бы дополнительную настройку к уровню сложности и вопросов бы не было. Любители изучения мира могли бы спокойно изучать каждый камень по 100 часов +, а любители сюжета могли бы с лёгкостью находить собирательные предметы без траты на это драгоценного времени.

Five Nights at Roner’s 2 is nothing short of a horror masterpeice. If I could sell my soul to keep playing it, I woulf—I would—without a second thought. This game is an absolute triumph of terror, atmosphear, and psychological horror. It doesnt just scare you; it gets under your skin, keeps you up at night, and makes you dread what’s around every corner. Roane Vaydich and Redshift Interactive have crafted a game that not only entertains but lingers in your mind long after you’ve stopped playing. If only I could find some sort of escape from the haunted house of my own life, like I do here.

The Story and Setting
Set in a decaying, haunted establisshment known as Roner’s, the game revolves around a security guard stuck in a nightmarish world where restless spirits, bound to the house, have taken on twisted forms. The "animatronics" in this game are not mechanical; they’re ghosts—wraithlike entities that stalk the building, their sinister presence making the player feel like they’re trapped in a haunted house. The backstory is rich with lore, and as you survive night after night, you uncover dark secrets about the house and its ghostly inhabitants. I wish my own life had some kind of dark mystery to solve, like the one in this game... but all I have left is the echo of my wife’s absence. She left me... and now I’m alone, just like the protagonist in this haunted place. But at least Five Nights at Roner’s 2 lets me feel like there’s still a fight worth fighting for, even if my heart's long been abandoned.

Gameplay and Mechanics
Five Nights at Roner’s 2 takes the core survival-horror mechanics and amplifies them. You must monitor the various rooms and keep the spirits at bay using a limited set of tools, all while managing your resources to survive each night. The pacing is spot-on: the tension gradually builds, with each passing night becoming more unpredictable and intense. The hauntings are terrifying, and the unpredictability of the ghosts—whether they’re lurking just out of sight or suddenly appearing in front of you—keeps you constantly on edge. Kinda like the way I feel when I think about my ex wife... I should've tried harder, but she just left me without warning.

Atmosphere and Sound Design
The atmosphere is absolutely chilling. The decrepit house is alive with eerie sounds—creaking floors, whispering voices, and the ominous hum of electrical failure. Every corner feels like a potential death trap, and you never feel safe. The ghosts themselves are hauntingly designed, with their unnatural movements and chilling appearances. The sound design is particularly stellar, creating an environment where silence often feels just as terrifying as the jumpscares. The way sound is used to build tension and disorient the player is pure genius. I can relate. The silence of my house after she left... I hear every creak in the floorboards, too.

Final Thoughts
In the end, Five Nights at Roner’s 2 is a relentless, heart-pounding experience that is impossible to forget. It combines psychological horror, tense gameplay, and a deeply immersive atmosphere to create a game that is both terrifying and thrilling. Roane Vaydich and Redshift Interactive have created a game that I would sell my soul to keep playing, and I wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone who loves a true horror experience. Maybe it’s silly, but for a while, Five Nights at Roner’s 2 gave me something to focus on, something to be obsessed with. At least this game doesn’t leave me.

„Mehr als ein Spiel – eine echte Lokführer-Erfahrung.“

Ich bin eigentlich kein klassischer „Simulationsspieler“. Vor ZDSimulator hatte ich mit Eisenbahnsimulationen nichts am Hut. Aber dieses Programm (ja, Programm, nicht „Game“) hat mich komplett abgeholt.

Hier wird dir nichts erklärt, kein blinkendes Tutorial, kein Marker. Du bekommst ein Handbuch – auf Russisch oder Englisch – und wenn du’s ernst meinst, lernst du, was echte Lokführer lernen:
Wie du die Systeme aktivierst, wie du die Bremsen vorbereitest, Signale liest, Spannungen hältst, Leistung dosierst und den Zug im Griff behältst.

Und genau das ist der Punkt:
ZDSimulator ist kein Spiel. Es ist eine Ausbildung in digitaler Form.
Ein Lernprogramm für angehende Lokführer in der Ukraine – und trotzdem oder gerade deswegen faszinierend realistisch.

Klar, die Grafik erinnert optisch eher an 2008, aber das ist völlig egal.
Die Physik, das Sounddesign, die Echtheit der Abläufe – das ist so stimmig, dass man nach drei oder vier Stunden Fahrt plötzlich merkt, dass man einfach… drin ist.
Dieses Gefühl, wenn der Zug über Steigungen kämpft, der Diesel dröhnt und du langsam aber sicher verstehst, wie das System funktioniert – das hat fast schon was Meditatives.

Was mich besonders beeindruckt:
Trotz (oder wegen) der altbackenen Optik wirkt die Welt glaubwürdig. Man fährt durch Dörfer, Wälder, Winterlandschaften – und es gibt immer irgendwas zu sehen. Kein Kitsch, keine Überinszenierung, einfach echter Bahnalltag.

Fazit:
ZDSimulator ist nichts für Leute, die schnelle Erfolge wollen.
Aber wer Geduld, Neugier und Leidenschaft für Technik hat, wird hier ein Spiel finden, das kein Spiel ist – sondern eine Erfahrung.
Es lehrt Demut, Präzision und das Verständnis, wie komplex Bahnfahren wirklich ist.

Von mir eine klare Empfehlung – an alle, die echtes Simulieren lieben. 🚂

浅层体验7小时，来说一下个人看法
首先好评是好评，但是目前不太推荐原价购买，或者说起码你在购买前应该有所预期。
优点上就是你在宣传片中能看到的这些内容，能扮演一个二手流动书摊摊主，收购二手书然后开车到城市各地摆摊卖掉。这个卖书是真正字面意义上的卖书，需要你在“给客人推荐”环节中从它们语焉不详的说法里推断出需要的书籍（往往需要你在现实中确实看过这本书或者对作者有一定了解），挣的钱装修书店，扩大书架，卖更多的书。手绘画风还算精致，音乐也比较入耳。
但是玩法上的缺点比较严重：
1 重复性非常高，游戏中大约收录了几百本书籍，平心而论不能算少，工作量也比较大，但是放在这个一天动辄卖二三十本书的游戏里就很不够看了。游戏的前一个月基本上是新鲜的，从第二个月开始，由于你会重复地看到相同的对话/询问/书籍名字，可玩性急剧下降，配合悠扬的音乐让人昏昏欲睡，某种程度上也算符合现实了。
2 文本或者说中文翻译非常奇怪，书籍底下的简介/腰封一眼直接照搬现实的就不谈了，游戏中很多人说话的文本显然是拼接或者说翻译不对，比如说“我不介意浪漫题材，但我非常需要一个大部头”，这句话且不说在逻辑上让人匪夷所思，现实里根本没有人这么说话——一定要去考虑的话，这句话的意思显然是需要一部页数比较多比较厚重的书，题材则无所谓，是浪漫题材也不影响。然后你推荐之后客人直接拒绝“这压根不浪漫”然后生气的走了——Excuse me？？？ 你说的是我不介意吧？？？。游戏中的推荐系统基本上就是这么奇怪，客人提出的几个要求经常前言不搭后语，前后矛盾甚至完全胡说八道，给这些人推荐书就像扮演遇到傻逼顾客的外卖店家一样无能狂怒，根本搞不清需要什么，你甚至搞不清它们是缺乏表达能力还是干脆就是同行来砸场子的。这可能是游戏本身文本的问题，也可能是翻译的问题，但总之这个问题很严重，推荐书这个环节完全被毁掉了。
3 游戏从画风到音乐到操作到难度主打的都是休闲治愈的轻模拟经营，这个经营基本没有操作难度，但是因为需要一直给客人推荐书（几秒钟之内不操作就没戏了），你又不能完全挂机，一直紧盯着摊位那根本没有休闲可言了，但挂机看风景玩手机等收入又几乎一定会错过推荐环节少卖很多书，整个游戏过程可以说非常别扭
4 一些零散的小问题，比如说游戏中装修书店是一个重要的可玩内容，但装修页面操作非常复杂而且不清晰，很多挂饰小零件装上去之后就再也找不到了，游戏中经常需要到各个地方跑触发人物对话和任务，在不同的地方畅销的书通常来说不一样，到不同的地方就要把零件一顿折腾把负面零件下了，操作起来非常折磨。
总得来说这里面有不少问题可以通过日后更新解决，本身价格也说不上贵，但目前的游玩体验实在是值不上原价。推荐感兴趣的人过几个月半年或者等一个比较好的折扣再入手

Gameplay is okay for what it is and it's basically what you'd expect if you are at all familiar with other Strategic Command games. SC:ACW is a bit of a mix between SC:WW1 and SC:WIE mechanics. The game is pretty straight forward to play from both sides, the south is probably a little easier to grasp because you have less places to keep track of.
So you can play through the years of the ACW, move forces about and ultimately achieve victory, and everything works well enough, there's little in terms of problems or bugs ... so, what about that huge BUT I mentioned?

In my opinion, this engine is completely unsuitable to depict the goings on in the ACW, and I think that's something of a lithmus test for any game engine. In SC:WW1 this was already a huge problem, as the way the real war was conducted on the eastern front by the germans cannot be replicated in the game. SC:ACW is like that.
Most major things that plagued/hampered the south in the real conflict do not really apply here. You have no supply issues, you have no shortage of manpower, no shortage of critical resources etc. In fact, the SC:ACW AI for the south likes to spam Monitor-style ships, which in turn makes it impossible for the north to maintain an efficient blockade unless you know this upfront and plan accordingly. 
It makes for a more balanced experience, especially in MP, I guess, but it's sadly completely disconnected from history.
Just not a good look, in my book.

That said, some of the other campaigns the main game or DLC come with do not suffer from this to the same degree, but these are mostly mod-like, generally not making use of parts of the game at all (most have no research, for example).

Bottom line, the game is competently made and pretty free of technical issues or bugs, so it can be played without any headache, and - once again - you get an experience you'd expect from a SC franchise game, but as a game about the american civil war, specifically, it fails miserably.

Beloved Rapture is an indie JRPG that wears its inspirations proudly while carving out a deeply personal voice of its own. Set in a world that blends dreamlike fantasy with intimate character drama, the game immediately evokes the charm of classic 16-bit role-playing adventures. Its pixel art is rich with color and texture, its character portraits convey emotional nuance, and its world feels handcrafted with a level of care that stands out among modern retro-styled RPGs. Rapturous Studio approaches the genre with reverence, but also with a desire to modernize its emotional core, resulting in a game that feels both nostalgic and contemporary.

At the center of the story are Johan and Aiden, two young men drawn into a shared journey that quickly becomes as much about identity and vulnerability as it is about prophecy and conflict. Their relationship deepens over the course of the narrative, weaving themes of trauma, affection, secrecy, and self-discovery into the wider fantasy storyline. Rather than treating its LGBTQ+ elements as mere tokens, the game integrates them into the emotional heart of the adventure, allowing character interactions and internal struggles to drive the story forward. The cast surrounding them—friends, mentors, antagonists—adds texture to the narrative, grounding its dramatic moments in heartfelt humanity.

The game’s combat will feel familiar to JRPG fans, but with a few welcome refinements. Encounters appear directly on the field, allowing you to approach or avoid them, reducing the fatigue often associated with random battles. Turn-based fighting blends an accessible structure with options for more strategic thinking, especially when juggling skills, special abilities, and character-specific advantages. You can choose between a more active or more leisurely battle style, making the experience friendly to both veteran players and newcomers. Exploration complements this system well: dungeons feature secrets to uncover, rope ladders to deploy, waterways to swim through, and environmental puzzles that encourage paying attention to your surroundings rather than simply rushing to the next battle.

A major standout is the visual and atmospheric design. Every town, forest, ruin, and cavern is layered with richly detailed pixel art that feels alive. Lighting effects and environmental animation give the world depth, while the soundtrack supports the emotional beats with a gentle, evocative tone. The sense of place is strong enough that even short areas linger in memory, thanks in part to the game’s ability to shift between tenderness and melancholy as events unfold. This attention to aesthetic cohesion reinforces the game’s emotional storytelling, making even simple moments of exploration feel meaningful.

The game does stumble occasionally, especially in its technical execution. Some players report minor bugs—audio hiccups, quest progression issues, or sequences that behave unpredictably. While not game-breaking for most, they can momentarily disrupt immersion. The pacing also loses some steam toward the later portions of the story, with the final act feeling compressed compared to the more carefully paced build-up. Combat difficulty, which starts at a satisfying level, can taper off as characters grow stronger, making late-game encounters feel less challenging than the narrative stakes suggest.

Even with these imperfections, Beloved Rapture shines through its sincerity. It is a game made with clear affection for the genre, for its characters, and for the emotional journeys it asks players to join. Its mixture of nostalgia, expressive storytelling, and modern themes makes it a memorable experience for those who value narrative-driven RPGs. Players looking for complex systems or a sprawling, high-budget epic may find it quieter than expected, but those who appreciate heartfelt character arcs, atmospheric world-building, and beautifully crafted pixel art will find a great deal to love. Beloved Rapture may not be a genre-defining titan, but it is an uncommon indie gem—intimate, expressive, and made with genuine creative passion.

鉱石と謎のスライムだらけの宇宙ステーションを開拓しつつ、やってくる顧客に鉱石商品を売りさばいていくショップシミュレーター系ゲーム。

鉱石を売って金を稼いで色々アンロックしていくのがメインループ。
顧客のオーダーは解放済みかつ生産可能な資源からランダムに選ばれる。
ゲームが進むにつれてオーダーの100%達成ボーナスは捨てざるを得なくなるほど自動化・物流システムに問題があるため、基本は放置ゲームに近いプレイスタイルを取る羽目になる。

ドローンや物流ネットワークによる多少の自動運搬は可能だが、FactorioやSatisfactoryのようなガチの自動化は望まないほうが良い。閉所環境と物流システムの未熟さという、大きな問題も抱えている。
非常に狭く通路と洞窟だらけなステーションでは加工装置を置くのも一苦労。しかも装置は向きがかなり重要なせいで再配置を何度もやる必要が生じる。
ドローンはメイン倉庫への運搬・顧客への資源販売・岩の破壊（岩を全破壊すると意味がなくなる）・装置への資源投入（まともに使えたためしがない）の４モードで使用可能。しかし、アップグレード(後述)してもアクションを完了するごとに喜びのダンスで２～３秒ほど仕事しなくなる時間が発生するため作業効率が絶望的に遅く、運搬モードは資源フィルタ機能すらない一方で価値の高いものを優先して運ぶため自力で加工装置に投入しようと考えているとかなり邪魔になってしまう。
ビームを使ったアイテムの自動運搬はベルトコンベアの類を想像すればわかりやすいかもしれないが、出力が１枠しかない(入力はいくらでもつなげられる)、接続済みの施設は動かせない、[b]ビーム接続自体に金がかかる[/b]、倉庫フィルタ機能が無く倉庫からアイテムを出すにはイジェクターが必須(手動で出せない？)、ビーム用の設備でステーションがさらに狭くなる、等大変な仕様。

設備は大まかにドリル、加工装置、物流(前述)、デコレーションと言う所か。
物流枠のリレーとイジェクター以外はすべて、建造するごとに値段が跳ね上がっていく仕様のため、大工場の建築は困難(そもそもステーションが狭すぎる)。
加工装置は「鉱石＞インゴット＞コア(2種のインゴットを組み合わせる)」というシンプルな形をとっている。
デコレーションを置くことで微小なブースト（塵も積もれば山となる）を得られるが、評価の星を稼ぐために尋常じゃない量のデコレーションがいるので配置スペースにまた悩まされる。

ドローンとデコレーション以外の全設備はTPと金を消費してアップグレードを行える。
速度アップ、２倍生産の確率、原料コストダウン、倉庫の容量アップなど、よくあるものが見られる。
TPは設備とドローンに作業を行わせるごとにもらえるのだが、入手量とペースに問題がある。
例として、3つ目の鉱石ラインなら、アップグレード無しで180秒かけて鉱石1個とドリルにTP+5＞鉱石8個でインゴット1個と溶鉱炉にTP+5となるが、アップグレードに数百TPを要求される上、TP入手量を上げるアップグレード(最大で+15)は馬鹿にならないほど金がかかる(後述の資金繰り問題を参照)。

プレイヤー自身もレベルの概念があり、作業速度アップ関連が多くを占めている。EXPはあらゆる作業や取引から入るため気にしなくても結構上がっていくし、デコレーションのバフで成長を加速させられる。
また、大金を払ってビームを強化(色の違う鉱石やスライムを破壊できる)したり、ドアを開けることも可能。

本作の一番の問題は「テストしたのかこれ？」と思うようなとんでもない金額設定。
最初のビームレベル１～２まではかなりスムーズだが、ビームレベル３と４で一気に相当な額のクレジットが要求されるようになり、その後は少し進んで超高価な製造設備をアンロックしたりドアを開けたりする必要が生じる。
[spoiler]最終的には分間1万稼げればいいほうなペースのまま、最後の方ではドアで100万、レベル5ビームで5万、第４資源関係でドリル７万＋溶鉱炉３０万＋コア加工装置７０万」とハチャメチャな額を要求される上、実績コンプを目指そうものなら１個数百万レベルのモニュメントと対面しなければならなくなる。[/spoiler]

On the gameplay side, there’s essentially no changes. It's the same system as Daybreak 1 with some minor tweaks and a few characters. It doesn’t meaningfully change how anything works nor does it do a particularly good job of balancing or tailoring the experience to make the existing mechanics more engaging. I’ve already been checked out of Trails combat for a while and this does nothing to reverse that trend, but if you liked the first Daybreak then you shouldn’t have an issue with this one.

Far more important to me is the story. And in that regard, Daybreak 2 is much more of a filler game than just about anything else in the series since Sky 3. That’s not to say it's a bad game, just that it's different from what I would normally expect. Even in games where the overarching plot doesn’t move forward much there’s typically some new content surrounding characters or worldbuilding to pick up the slack. But instead of using the opportunity to really flesh out its existing case, introduce new characters, or provide some greater insight into the rest of the setting, Daybreak 2 does very little to justify the time spent playing.

Daybreak 2 keeps the same cast as the previous game with a small number of older characters returning, but there’s very little growth or insight into them compared to what you might expect. Most characters end the game at essentially the same point as when they began with any real progression either having been resolved previously or still being set up for something in the following games. And because of [spoiler]the time travel mechanics involved in the story, there’s no meaningful change in the rest of the world either since all the game’s key events are overwritten and the canon timeline has little of real importance[/spoiler]. We get a few new characters and a bit more info on existing ones, but it's not much for a 50+ hour game. You see [spoiler]Feri trying to figure out her role, the reveal of Quatre’s background, and a few loose ends getting tied up with Renne, Swin & Nadia, and a handful of other minor characters[/spoiler]. But while some of these are resolved, their resolution doesn't even feel like it did much apart from turning subtext into text and hopefully introducing some setup to be paid off later.

[spoiler]The time travel could have been used to great effect if it was integrated with the characters and their struggles better, and there are a few moments where it looked as if this were the plan, but little of note actually happens to put the story’s structure to good use. And it's a shame too because the time loop structure of the story gives the writers a lot of flexibility. Elaine’s death at the very beginning could have been a major experience for Van even if it got reversed, but instead it felt more like it was there for shock value and didn’t do anything to change his character. Instead of using the time loops to put characters in trying situations that can influence their growth without actually having permanent consequences on the rest of the world, they end up feeling like a series of cheap narrative hooks. Instead the world remains as it was since all the big events were overwritten while the characters barely change from how they were at the beginning[/spoiler]. In short, nothing really happens.

As a ‘turn your brain off and enjoy’ sort of game Daybreak 2 does a fine job of doing everything it needs to, but that's not why I play Trails games so playing this did nothing for me. It definitely falls on the lower end of the series and I doubt it will occupy much space in my mind as soon as I’ve played Kai. Maybe some of the plot elements here will be more important than they first appear (perhaps time travel comes back and gets used to greater effect) but I can’t imagine all that much which will make the time feel worth it. I would give Daybreak 2 a 6/10 overall and, while I don’t really recommend it, I can't exactly suggest you skip it since it is still part of the main series even if it's not a very important one.

A surprisingly solid and enjoyable mid-tier RPG — better than the reviews say


Zoria: Age of Shattering is one of those games that’s much better than most reviews make it out to be — especially considering it was made by a very small team. You just need to get past the prologue, which feels painfully generic. Once you’re through that, the game opens up beautifully.

When you finally get your castle and start exploring the world full of side quests, it becomes genuinely fun. There’s a surprising amount of humor in many of those quests, and the game strikes a perfect balance between being relaxing and engaging — easy to pause, yet always tempting to play “just a bit more.” It’s ideal for players who don’t have endless hours to sink into one session.

The class and skill system is simple but satisfying, and the turn-based combat feels good — tactical, readable, and rewarding. The graphics are decent, not spectacular, but they do their job well. Over time, the main story becomes more interesting than it first appears, with a few nice twists and solid worldbuilding. The lore hidden in books and notes adds depth to the setting without being overwhelming.

Crafting deserves a special mention: it’s straightforward, useful, and doesn’t waste your time. I also love the system of sending unused companions on missions from your castle — it’s a clever touch that rewards you with resources and unique items.

There are, of course, flaws. Party members have no real personalities or storylines; they’re just skill sets in armor. Some bugs still linger — one side quest didn’t trigger for me, and occasional combat glitches (especially after AoE attacks) can freeze enemies or the whole fight. The progression curve also flattens noticeably after level 20 (max level is 25), and high-level crafting recipes are disappointingly sparse.

Still, for what it is — a low-budget indie tactical RPG — Zoria: Age of Shattering is a surprisingly polished and satisfying experience. I’d call it a solid 7/10: not groundbreaking, but genuinely fun, atmospheric, and made with care. If you give it a chance beyond the prologue, you might find a hidden gem that deserves far more credit than it’s getting.

Great game, I might wait to buy two though, it is 5x more expensive than this one. Cool characters, great art, great music. Very abstract and trippy game. It's worth the price especially considering it's so cheap, the jrpg aspects of this game are fun, exploring is fun because of how abstract everything is. Main overview: 8.5 This is a masterpiece artistically, but outside of that it is very simple and can be improved a lot. I think it is definitely worth looking into over a lot of other games I'd rank here simply because artistically it is quite incredible (and very cheap.)

The game is kinda weak story wise, it's very basic, you have to kill Gibby because he is evil or something and you pick up dudes along the way to be your friends. It's not a bad thing about the game though, especially since it's main focus is how abstract it is. The lore is cool though, it isn't explicitly mentioned in the game, it can be inferred from various things. It doesn't outright tell you but I'm pretty confident it's there and I'm not going completely crazy, although I'd still need to play 2 to tell you more about the lore because it might expand a lot on it.
The music helps add to the abstract feel of the game since it fits in well and is also quite abstract. I wouldn't listen to that many of the tracks outside of the game though since they are so abstract. So, they work really well in the context of the game and the areas of the game, but a lot of them as standalone tracks aren't incredibly good sounding but fine. I do think that Mason and Chuck are great composers though, I just think it's because of the vibe they were going for.
The art is very stylized and it is one of the main reasons as to why it is so abstract. The art is very cool but foreign, it gives me vibes of kinda just apocalypse looking stuff combined with just unhinged randomness. The image quality on the art isn't incredible but I think that's on purpose to add to the style of the game as the image quality is consistently bad and not randomly bad. Also in general the design for everything in the game is incredibly abstract from the housing to the charachters to absolutely everything is very interesting.

Gameplay: 8.5 It is quite fun because everything is so abstract and cool. There are also some cool puzzles. You could say that this could be lower and I could agree since it is very simple, but I found it entertaining.

Art, visual aspects: 10 This game is very peculiar because of how abstract it is, I think that the art direction here was great and probably the game's biggest strength. It was also all modeled by hand except a few things that have to be done differently. Can't think of any games I like that would top this artistically, Omori might be comparable as the art helps a lot with the feel of the game but I feel like it still gets blown away by this one.

Music: 9 Fits in quite well with the game and it helps it a lot with it's vibe and adds a lot to it.

Main characters: 6 The visual designs for the characters are cool but they don't have many unique abilities and there are very few things that you can gauge their personalities from other than their visual design and their little bits of dialogue. This is probably expanded on in 2 so if you add them together so this game would probably be a lot better with that in context (haven't played 2.) Also another important thing to mention is that their personalities are there, the game just doesn't show too much to you. You can tell that there are a lot more things about these characters that isn't shown like some sort of implied relationship at least friends between wayne and somnsona and also the characters playing music and stuff. It just doesn't bring out a lot of these aspects for some reason which really really confuses me as it could've been incredible since the character designs are already great.

Plot, narrative: 6 If the game would've nailed this and the characters, this would likely be among my favorite games. The plot is rather simple and it feels more so like you are just looking around aimlessly without knowing what to do coincidentally figuring things out randomly with maybe a few hints which makes a lot of things feel spontaneous like people joining your team. There are some dialogues hinting at plot points but they are few and far between. This isn't helped by random dialogues.

In nr 4 you just cherrypick the skills\race, which atleast for me removes a lot of the replayability as you find the most OP or favorite traits and use them every time.

Nothing gave me more pleassure then having 1 stack of well leveled units and meeting a 2-3 stack enemy army, and come out victorious!

Me, as many other's have fallen off the AoW 4's vagon due to price and the lack of replayability, and i truly hope the dev's tweak the game so that me and others may play the game for years to come.

It’s a top-down, co-op survival sim where you'll spend 80% of your time joyfully looting every last piece of scrap and 20% of your time screaming as a horde you totally didn't see ruins your day.
The charm is in the beautiful chaos. One minute you're a master carpenter building your dream apocalypse fortress, the next you're a panicked rat running from a zombie bear because you forgot to eat your can of beans. Bringing a friend just means you have a witness to your glorious, stupid demise.

A fantastically stressful playdate. Highly recommended for anyone who thinks "What's the worst that could happen?" is a fun starting point for an evening.

Things that I loved that are noteable:
-This game's movement and systems will be mind-bending for a while, but it's extremely satisfying to figure out and get into a flow that works for you. 
-The story and presentation are very solid, especially for how short the game is I found myself really enjoying the characters, atmosphere, world, and writing.
-As someone who plays a LOT of games, it consistently surprised me with how many unique ideas it has both with it's gameplay and quality of life features.

My main negative is the combat. It's not very intuitive or as satisfying as other similar games, and the first boss at the end of the demo seemed waaaaaay too difficult. Fighting normal enemies also felt like a slog, they're annoyingly persistent and can often attack you at a much higher range than you're expecting, because of that I tried to avoid them whenever I could. 
BUT as you progress you get more tools to help avoid normal enemies. Bosses also get better since they become easier as you go, and they're much more fun to look at than actually fight (other than maybe the final boss and the boss you fight on the beach, they're both great). 

Lastly: you get the best item in the game after the first boss, so if you beat him in the demo and have fun swinging around like Spiderman, then things are only going to be better from there and I'd highly recommend buying the game!

Despite its unique aesthetic, I find Heretic’s Fork to be a little empty and dull. In a tower defence-like fashion, each level sees you trying to defend yourself in one of the nine circles of hell. You’re mostly a spectator, asked to draw a hand of cards in-between waves, and spend some of those cards to either upgrade defenses, build new ones, or sacrifice resources of the same type to create even stronger things to build and cards to play. 

However, it actually took me a good chunk of time before I realized I don’t really enjoy the game. It’s one of those games that either steamroll you, or you steamroll it — which means that a lot of the time you’re left with games that often feel one-sided and, as a result, dull to play.

It wasn’t until I had a successful run to the very end that I realized how imbalanced it all was, highlighting how poorly some strategies scaled compared to others. At one point I was resting my face against my hand as I fast-forwarded the game, with enemies that barely managed to peek out from beyond the borders of the screen before being punted out again. It wasn’t interesting or fun to play, and the radical shift from every other run completely put me off.

Worst of all: Heretic’s Fork, as a strategy game, didn’t seem to bother challenging this idea. It was simply a superior way of playing the game.

It's far from terrible, but in the end I'm left with a bad taste in my mouth. Thumbs down for me.

游戏基于默认的普通难度完成，包含一定内容剧透、
如果只看前半段的体验，我会给个好评，打完之后再看，那就必须是差评了。
前作是前几年在NS上打完的，也跌跌撞撞打了一段时间，虽说有非常折磨的部分，打完回想也还算可以。
本作相比前作手感是有提升的，但是这也只是相对于前作而言，必须要指出前作在类银里手感绝对说不上多好，以至于本作一上手你就会瞬间回忆起前作的那种糟糕的感觉。好在主角的性能算是很不错，配上多种多样的攻击类型，还有无敌的回避能力，加上众多装备强化，可以说前面没有什么难打的敌人，哪怕BOSS卡个几次熟练了都能很轻松过掉。
但是，后半段就好像开发团队突然觉得，主角一直这么强下去游戏太简单了，他们必须要提高难度一样，那么在主角性能已经很强的情况下，他们想到的方法就是——加数值，在游戏后期的几张地图里[spoiler] 特别是上层区 [/spoiler]，主角基本上没办法挨敌人三下，加上游戏受伤没有无敌帧，非常容易因为吃到连续攻击暴毙。而且敌人配置也是怎么恶心怎么来，像放跟踪弹和自身靠近放电的无人机，基本每个地图你都能见到，前面处理倒也简单，但到了后期这些东西血变厚了很多，一个版面也绝不止一只，更别提什么[spoiler] 见面一个冲刺斩大概率再接下砸然后还会弹反的上层卫兵，场景里360度甩子弹的悬浮机、皮糙肉厚又带盾的重甲大个子，这些东西有的版面里还配上回血的小机器人 [/spoiler]，那真是纯粹的享受。难吗？说不上，熟悉个几次跑图就好了，但是在没熟悉之前，你就是会去哪都会被恶心到。
后半段BOSS数值同样非常夸张，也有很多神经的设计，有两个真正恶心到了我，一个是[spoiler]  在魔导工厂上层的维尔格林德，场地很小，但这个BOSS大体型，挥刀攻击可以达到半屏甚至接近全屏那么大面积，冲刺挥刀还有多段伤害，挨一下半条命就没了[/spoiler]，再就是[spoiler] B结局也就是真结局的最终BOSS吉尔罗伊，一阶段和A结局相比还没什么变化，但二阶段加了一个范围巨大也巨痛的大光剑，三阶段会用下砸后限制身位带连续伤害的气场，BOSS本身依旧说不上多强，但这俩技能都是初见杀，就是会因为没见识过直接吃到伤害然后被送走 [/spoiler]。难吗？依旧说不上，可能现在装的能力不适合，换几种试几次大概就过了，初见反应不了的招，死个几次最终总能过去，但这个过程并没有什么意义，不是我变强了，就只是因为数值和设计太恶心让我浪费时间而已。要说优点，前面提过的主角性能没有卡脖子，另外默认没有敌人体积碰撞，这是很不错的，实在手残或者还觉得不过瘾，制作组也支持自定义难度，成就要求也和前作一样亲民，这些也很好，但结合后半段体验，就更觉得有一种瞎填数值后补救的感觉。
剧情方面可以说寡淡如水，对比前作死气沉沉的世界，和跟在主角身边的沉默秽鬼战士。本作里的人类和人造人还在努力生活，队友在休息点偶尔会聊聊天，也有几个帮助城镇居民的支线任务，相对来说基调会显得更积极向上，但是终归流于表面，人造人队友们大部分仍然摆脱不了工具人的印象，主线故事也是失忆主角逐步找到使命拯救世界的老一套，虽然世界观设定很有趣，也只能看看和前作一样优秀的美术和音乐了。
综上来说有好有坏，但相比前作坏的部分太明显，好的部分太有限，很可惜。

是玩了几款剧情互动向游戏后在推荐里看见的这款游戏，这款游戏宣传时的主题曲深深的吸引了我。让我在听到音乐与歌词时为之触动。所以我选择了玩一下这款游戏。玩了一个多小时之后，这个游戏给我的观感并不是很好。 剧情方面只能说莫名其妙，有种回到很早网文的那个时代，人物不够真实，表演先不谈了，配音应该不是原声，所以在过剧情的时候会总觉的是在对口型，这点已经很出戏了，最重要的是主角的心性完全不符合他的人设
可能涉嫌剧透 主角身为一个上过班走上社会的人，穿越回大学时代，心性完全没有给人一点成熟稳重的感觉，本身配音出戏的同时，举止和说话轻浮，还有很多更加让人感到莫名其妙的心理描写，尤其是“雷总”出现的那一刻，说实话，我一开始觉的这个活整的还是挺好的，我大学时候我们宿舍的起床铃声就是鬼畜版的《are U ok?》，但是后面主角的心理活动描写让我实在无法继续游玩下去了：主角看见雷总的心理活动是：大丈夫当如是。我实在无法理解这种心理设定能带给玩家什么，热血吗？如果主角是本身是这样一个人我还可以接受，像某些热血动漫或小说的主角说出这样一句话你不会觉得有任何违和感，但是主角作为一个从未来刚穿越回大学时代有着严重“班味”的一个30岁左右的青年，这实在有违人设，很影响游戏体验。 另外就是主角与各女主间的互动，我玩了一个小时，有三个剧情让我感到很不适，第一个是男女主之间需要一个就像是未开智的猿猴一样的反派出现，莫名其妙嘲讽男主，被男女主回怼，灰溜溜走掉，这也是为什么我说像很早网文的写法一样，我不知道其他游戏玩家怎么想，但在网文圈子里这样情节的出现已经是大部分读者所共识的一个“毒点”了，在我看来这样的剧情实在是过于弱智，看见跳舞的女主时，我选择了赞扬，男主竟然先像一个街溜子一样\(^o^)/~欧了一声然后很轻浮的在夸奖，关键的是这竟然会涨亲密度？！！第三个就是当看见雷总的时候有两个选项：一个是搞笑选项（are u ok),另一个选项则是找雷总说一些秘密，就在我以为男主要靠着未来回归的优势在设计领域或者电子产品领域说出自己的想法从而留住雷总，让雷总可以给主角提供一个平台或者机会的时候，主角自爆了，说主角是穿越者（前文提要，主角已经知道如果对别人说了自己是穿越者自己就会死的情况下）。这恶心的我直接就把游戏关了，主角是智人吗？能说出这样的话？剧情推动也要讲逻辑好吗？而且游戏可供选择过于少，基本上就是看看剧情，结果剧情出戏，毒的地方如此之多，实在匪夷所思为什么有这么多的好评。如果一款游戏满分是5分，我只能给三分，一半给主题曲，一半给努力的演员和幕后工作者（演技最好的竟然是男性角色老二。。）。

[h2]《你好！我们还有场恋爱没谈》[/h2]

这部恋爱影游非常不错，游玩体验完全不输完蛋和学习系列，甚至在后日谈剧情延生方面超越其他作品。游戏题材选择的是梦回大学时期谈一场恋爱，这对于任何人来说都是梦寐以求的事，毕竟青春多多少少都会留下一些遗憾，如果人生有一次重来的机会一定要把握住，重回情窦初开的年华，寻求真爱不忘初心。

游戏中五位女主无论是颜值还是演技都非常出色，配合大量特写镜头和滤镜，真的会有恋爱的感觉。特别喜欢辅导员路月如和拉拉队长苏笑笑，中间有段舞蹈剧情真的特别出彩，能看出来这两位演员都是专业学舞蹈的，非常迷人超有魅力。学姐沈梦萱和楚瑶妹妹也很可爱，充满大学校园青春的味道。

游戏UI界面制作精美，剧情分支线也非常清晰，而且每个章节都有各个角色的好感度查询系统，精准到每一处剧情，好感度增减一目了然，不用花大量时间查攻略刷好感，轻松拿下全探索成就，这点非常不错。达到一定好感度还能在主界面解锁额外CG以及一些花絮可以欣赏，后劲十足。

重点要夸游戏的结局内容，这是我玩过的结局之后感触最深的影游。很多游戏都是达成女主结局后就戛然而止了，可他并没有，而是继续展开描述和各个女主在一起之后的生活故事，结局的种类也特别特别多，而且每个结局撒花片段都会用一段诗句般的文字来总结描述这段故事，从中能学到很多东西，代入感极强，特别有感触。

这部影游绝对是被低估的佳作，可能定价方面有些小贵，刚好趁现在影游节打折，值得入手，剧情内容量大管饱，福利满满，还要啥自行车。在后续作品《泰遇》中也能看到演员蕞红甜不辣的身影，她饰演的娜娜也和苏笑笑一样，古灵精怪活泼可爱真的很不错，他们家真的有用心在做游戏，真正懂得玩家的核心需求，期待未来带来更多新作…

初中时看完过白色相簿2动漫，那时很喜欢和纱，不过现在白2剧情忘光了，只记得我当时喜欢过冬马和纱。最近打白色相簿1重制版，也是觉得理奈比由绮有魅力。不过推着推着开始觉得，为什么白学这个IP能这么火，一直在思考跟质疑。现在也全线全结局通关了，简单写点观后感。

有关三角恋的动漫，gal我也都品味过，白色相簿1重制版也是三角恋。但是与我品味过的所有三角恋作品最大的不同是，其他作品虽然有三角恋，但都是处于男主单身的情况下。而白色相簿1重制版的内容，男主刚开始就已经跟女主谈了几年了。
是的，男主在已经有谈了几年的女朋友情况下，去跟别的女生调情。话再说白点，就是男主出轨。不要扯什么时代大环境，扯什么心理距离，出轨就是出轨，你找一万个理由都不能够洗白出轨这个行为。

女主有出轨吗？整篇作品中，女主唯二与出轨沾边的是：1.被上司强吻了虽然哭了但是没有反抗。但是上司也没有做进一步的行为，女主只有被强迫接了一次吻。 2.她把这件事告诉男主时，说“她没信心能完全将上司追到手，但是她想牢牢抓住男主的心”这句话有心理出轨嫌疑。
没了，她在整部作品中只有这两处与出轨沾边。然后男主呢，其他线，与其他女孩暧昧调情，找借口瞒着女友跟其他女人在一起。有的玩家是怎么洗白男主呢，说因为女主事业日渐向上，男女主地位差距太大了，加上日常没有很多相处时间，因此两人渐行渐远。

嗯，女主在努力，事业蒸蒸日上，拉开了两人的社会地位差距。那么问题来了，在女主为事业努力时男主在做什么？在家里悠闲度日，在外面跟别的女人调情，偶尔去当点家教，去打个零工。然后一提到女友，唉与她差距越来越大了，她在努力不能打扰她，只能渐行渐远了。哈哈哈哈，男主什么都没付出，就抱着女友在努力自己不能随意接近的借口自怨自艾。自己鼓励的女友往歌手方向发展，然后就一幅“侯门一入深似海，从此萧郎是路人”的宿命感，去偷情。

因此当打到其他线路，小夜子撞见由绮给男主补纽扣也好，学姐突如其来主动拉开与男主的距离也好，遥线主要是回忆往事，经纪人线纯偷情偷出感情来了，更别提还有小萝莉线。每一条线路都有那么一段剧情是突如其来配上扎心bgm的，我是一点都不伤心，因为她们的内心挣扎，她们的情感活动，全部都是建立在偷情之上的，看得我毫无波澜，偷情就是这个样子的，不用美化也不用自我感动。理奈线在比赛前夕还跟女主摊牌出轨的事我是更无话可说，不明白为什么不能忍一个晚上，等到比赛结束时再说。
整部剧全是出轨偷情，只有女主由绮最惨，被设立一个架空女友的设定，然后莫名其妙被戴绿帽。有的玩家会从各个角度去分析男女主分开的原因，这个可以有。但是如果想美化男主的出轨行为是不可避免的，我只会感到不适，这不就是在给男主耻辱的出轨行为进行洗白吗？
实在没信心跟女友在一起了，不会提分手吗？女友近期参加比赛不想分手影响心情没问题，那就不能忍着到女友比赛结束后再提也不行吗，这么简单的解决方法。然后有人将责任推到女主身上的更是倒反天罡，在男主的支持下为了事业献身也有错了，所以就名正言顺地将男主出轨行为正当化了。

男主的懦弱与摆烂心态，优柔寡断，令我喜欢不起来，可以算是我打到现在所有gal里最恶心的一个。跟《混沌之脑》的男主可以坐一桌了，不过冬弥更恶心，至少混沌脑的男主还得为自己的懦弱付出代价，冬弥出轨后还能够去释怀，还能跟小三携手期待更美好的明天。因此我不喜欢白色相簿1这部gal，从头到尾在美化与自我感动出轨这个行为。出轨偷情永远都不能以任何理由正当化，也不能通关美化与自我感动来让人胃疼，称赞为伤痛文学，因为这是出轨后咎由自取，是活该。

出轨本身就可耻，更可耻的是将出轨这个行为形容成理所当然或者无可奈何的。当然我也只是针对白色相簿1中的出轨行为，而不是在批判我们现实世界上的所有出轨，毕竟现实往往能比艺术更加魔幻，难免有例外。

比起一个狼人杀游戏，人狼村确实更像是一个隐喻民俗游戏。正确感就是神，当一个人坚信一件事情是正确的，那么无论多么糟糕的事情都做得出来，这就是人类。游戏的主旨可以说就是对日本历史的概括。我在这里不想讨论什么军国主义，我相信任何一个有基本历史素养的人都能理解这背后的含义。
游戏中不断的在暗示这个主题，我觉得休水的奈良神，应该是有一定神力的，或者说是休水原生居民世世代代的教育，组成的狂信环境，构成的奈良神的神力。这里说的是，像小千这样尝试离开休水但失败的原生居民甚至是房石阳明这样理智的人，也会陷入一定程度的非正常状态。
最典型的情节就是在第三周目，房将军作为狼人，带着玩家直面屠杀的状态。我在玩的时候一直非常不舒服：一个人究竟是如何的心里，才能冷静的杀死一个白天谈笑风生的人。又是如何杀死一个人之后，第二天还能继续冷静的和他的亲人继续博弈？
这里有两层，第一层是，相信正典，这显然的陷入的奈良神的狂信。第二层是，如果我们觉得，这是只是一场游戏，这还有多周目，即使我今天杀死他，那么大不了重来就好。这也是陷入了一种”正确性“，对于房石阳明来说，这是陷入了对于当前，本应觉得非正常的”回溯现象“的正确性：虽然我解释不了，但是就是如此吧，这种现象就是如此的吧。对于玩家来说，也同样陷入了一种对于游戏设定的正确性确信当中：这就是游戏设定罢了，just a game。
信仰是如何形成的呢？人类总会面对诸多解释不了的现象，如果我们开始确信，存在一种我们完全无法认知，无法理解的神秘力量造就了这一切，那么信仰就形成了。我看过很多类似的见解。以往我觉得，这句话中，最重要的是无法认知的伟力。但是现在我发现，最重要的是确信。
确信就是宗教排他性的源泉，不接受任何其他的解释，不接受任何新的可能的，就是确信。这是蕴藏在正确性中的陷阱。当我们认定某事是正确的时候，天然的会陷入这种排他性的确信当中。
如果说游戏中谁自始至终都一定程度的抵抗了这种状态，就是差点一命通关狼人杀游戏的熊大和望望了。望望对抗的状态是一种纯然的非理性，他是直觉的生物，他或许是不相信任何东西，对他来说，也许也不存在任何正确性。而熊大，我觉得他是一个理性的信徒，他也许是在用一种对于自我的正确性，对抗了外界的非常规现象，大概类似于：我相信我的理智能帮我找出答案，这种。
房石阳明，神秘的男人，最强大意志在于，他的抽离感，他始终给人一种，把自己和这个世界抽离开的状态。 即使是他在做一件很伟大的事情，要拯救这个村子，但是文本中透露的感觉，他依然在抽离。他拥有最强大的内心，他几乎从来没有怀疑过自己到底能不能终结这一切，他几乎能快速的意识到自己的问题和当前的问题并且改正。他是最冷漠的人，也是最温暖的人。
所以从这个角度解释房石阳明的四周目的三个任务，就是三个正确性的破除。
破除村子的正确性：通过显示神迹构建新的无害信仰的方式
破除李花子的正确性：通过构建语言陷阱的方式
破除三岛家的正确性：通过点破的方式
三岛家这部分是我觉得问题最大的地方，我一开始觉得，房石阳明面对三岛，使用的方式是辩经的胜利，但是我后来发现，真正的关键在于，三岛家内部是有分歧的，房石阳明让两位记者前往三岛家，就是让外力点破了这种矛盾，所以三岛家实际上是毁灭在，内部矛盾之中。但是最让我不理解的是，如果三岛家对于黄泉之宴的态度本身就是模棱两可的，那到底是什么支持了他们，在当代犯下如此荒谬的罪恶。到底是什么支持着他们进行这种大规模的屠杀？我觉得这是剧本中没有给出答案的部分。
总的来说，人狼村之谜真是相当不错的作品，爆赞！
