Hidden Gem als "Puzzle Citybuilder" mit Wuselfaktor für alle Ressourcen, Logistik- und Warenkettenenthusiasten auf begrenztem Terrain mit einem Hauch von Anno durch notwendige Befriedigung verschiedener Bedürfnisse unterschiedlicher Kasten.

Beschreibung :
Laysara Summit Kingdom lässt uns verschiedene Berge besiedeln mit dem Ziel einen Tempel auf dem jeweiligen Gipfel der Karte zu errichten. Stück für Stück arbeiten wir uns anhand kleinerer Quests von Plateau zu Plateau und versuchen dabei die Bedürfnisse unserer drei Kasten zu befriedigen, damit wir deren Häuser verbessern können um wiederum genug Arbeitskräfte (für jede Stufe erhalten wir mehr Personal aus einem Haus) für unsere Waren- und Transportketten zu erhalten. Unseren begrenzten Platz auf den Plateaus müssen wir so effizient wie möglich nutzen. Die Berücksichtigung der Reichweite von Gebäuden, das Zwischenschalten von Lagern sowie Verteilungsstationen sowie die Optimierung von Straßen ist sehr wichtig. Da wir durch das Erhalten von Forschungspunkte weitere Baumöglichkeiten erhalten und Industrien immer wieder optimieren und sehr oft auch umsetzen müssen, verbringen wir einen großen Teil damit Gebäude zu versetzen - daher erhält das Spiel seinen Puzzlecharakter.  Machen wir hier Fehler dreht unsere Finanzlage schnell ins Negative und wir verlieren das Spiel. Glücklicherweise gibt es einen Pausebutton, der uns die Möglichkeit gibt Anpassungen vorzunehmen, um wieder in die grünen Zahlen zu kommen. Drohende Lawinen die man berücksichtigen muss, machen diese Aufgabe nicht gerade leichter. 

Bewertung :

Ich habe aktuell den Tutorial sowie ein Szenario gespielt und bin schon jetzt voll auf meine Kosten gekommen. Grafisch ist das Wuseln auf dem Berg schön anzusehen. Technisch hatte ich in 16 Stunden bisher einen einzigen Crash, aber da das Spiel alle paar Minuten automatisch speichert, war das nicht so tragisch.  Das beschriebene Gameplay macht sehr viel Spaß und das Spiel fordert einen ständig heraus die eigene Infrastruktur/Industrie weiter zu verbessern, mehr Plateaus zu besiedeln (jedes Kästchen Platz ist wertvoll) und die Häuser der Kasten aufzuwerten. Dabei muss man stehts ein Auge auf die Finanzen haben.  Die Zwischenquests ziehen einen roten Faden durch das Spiel und bereiten einen auf die finale Aufgabe vor.
Das Gefühl "nur noch kurz" eine kleine Sache optimieren und zwei Stunden später immer noch vorm PC sitzen, ist mir mehr als einmal passiert. 
Negativ anzumerken ist das weder die Gebäude rotiert noch mehrere Gebäude auf einmal versetzt werden können ( zumindest konnte ich diese Funktion nicht finden) - letzteres ist eine der Hauptaufgaben und kostet oft viel unnötige Zeit und wäre meiner Meinung nach ein großes Quality of Life Update.

[h1]Pra quem não entendeu muito bem a moral do jogo, vou dar uma resumida. [/h1]

O jogo consiste em aparar barbas, basicamente só isso. Claro que temos outras coisas, como a administração do estabelecimento, a contratação de novos funcionários (É possível dando um upgrade de localização na barbearia) e a melhoria do visual comprando novos móveis e outras coisas para agradar os clientes. A cada novo cliente, você deve escolher a cor que ele deseja e o corte deve ser igual ao que ele pede, não precisa estar 100% certo por que isso seria uma tarefa impossível, basta apenas ficar parecido. O nível de satisfação do corte segue 4 escalas que mudam de acordo com o visual (tipo, médio, bom, incrível e épico) quando mais parecido com a imagem modelo, mais o cliente fica satisfeito e mais dinheiro você ganha. A cada mês que se encerra, é removido uma quantia de dinheiro simulando os gastos mensais,  e além disso acontece alguns roubos que também fazem você perder dinheiro dificultando um pouco mais o seu objetivo que é basicamente não falir. O que não gostei foi a fato de dar game over quando você perde todo o dinheiro, e seu progresso não é salvo quando fecha o jogo, fazendo com que você não se prenda a ele. Na minha opinião se fosse possível fazer empréstimos e se sua barbearia fosse fixa (sem reiniciar quando o jogo acaba) seria 100% melhor, mas mesmo assim achei o jogo excelente por trazer uma temática diferente e por ter uma trilha sonora contagiante.

或许算是蛮电波的作品，打完以后甚至一时间不知道该怎么写出我的感受。
游戏的系统很简单，操作着摩托车沿着公路漫无目的的前进，搜刮一些食材做出食物推进剧情，而游戏显然也有背包检测，会优先给你推进剧情所需要的食材。本质是一个文字游戏，实际的玩法非常单，但不知道为什么，就是很想继续开下去。
漫无目的地四处游荡，找到一些食材烹饪，天黑后赶紧找到地方过夜，就这样又度过游戏中的一天，哪怕在故事结束后，再到我完成全成就以后，我依旧不想停下来。
严格意义上，游戏并没有讲述什么故事，没有很明确的开始，也没什么很明确的结束，就如同灰炑和黑妙的旅途一般，将会一直一直持续下去。
游戏的全程平淡且温馨，文案的风格也将这种氛围营造得恰到好处。
虽然世界空无一人，但随着唯美的木吉他伴奏与摩托车的引擎声与在两个少女有一句没一句的闲聊里漫无目的沿着公路前进，在二人的旅途中还能遇到两个临时旅伴，聊着世界的现状和她们各自的故事，在一段时间的同行后简短道别，再次回到各自的旅途中去……虽说略显寂寥，在不长的这场旅途的片段中也实际有着一丝忧伤的底色，但总的来说，一切显得平静与安闲。
比较令我意外的是游戏“不在他人视线里就会消失”的设定竟然真的有一个在游戏的框架里相当自洽和严谨的解释，真的有一个经过设定的世界观，它的设定很有意思，我都快要觉得它能是半个科幻作品了。 
在游戏短暂的故事与游戏本身的设定之中，其实能朦胧地瞥见一些这部作品的创作者对世界的感受——或者说，我认为我仿佛瞥见了创作者的感受。
因为看到了同一个世界，因为认可了彼此的世界，所以才能生活在同一个世界中，因为人们之间有着连接，所以才组成了整个世界。但因为通讯的发达，人们能淡化这种链接，又因为种种原因，最终人们切断了连接，一个个消失，一个个活在自己的孤零零的世界之中。在《死亡搁浅》中，虽说我看不到任何的人，但他们留下的设施与物资告诉我，我们在一个世界上，我们连接在一起。而在本作中，即使她们能通过设备听到对方的声音，但却因为连接被切断，而被分割在两个世界。
我似乎看到了对于原子化社会的隐喻，我似乎看到了对于“人们应当实际地连接在一起”的表达，而当灰炑与黑妙各自清楚自己眼中的世界或许也存在些许差异，但依旧能与对方一同前行时，或许又是一种“即使对世界的认识不同，人们也可以彼此包容，彼此连接，组成同一个世界”的表达。
它们零零碎碎的分散在闲聊似的文本与设定之中，以至于我其实很难有一定逻辑的，一个接一个的表达出来，所以就这样吧，我就干脆直接这么列出来好了。
就如同游戏并没有再更深一步的去深入探讨一般，我也只能浅尝辄止地把我似乎看出的东西写下来而已。
不过，对于这部作品想要传达的——或者说，我眼中的这部作品想要传达的东西来说，它也并不需要深入探讨任何话题，我也并不需要在这部作品上对我看出的话题做任何探讨。
[h1]“在如今这个世界，为了动脑而停下来肯定活不了多久
“孤独、空虚、难以捉摸的现实都会把人压得喘不过气
“所以才必须驱车而行
“为了活着，也为了延续人生。”
“重要的是拥有目标，目标的内容并不重要。”

一款故事劇情大於遊戲玩法的步行模擬器遊戲。
遊戲的玩法就是在末日的世界裡開著摩托車漫遊，四處收集食材來製作料理推進劇情。
遊玩時如果選擇「STORY模式」會更加舒適，因為其他模式會讓閱讀劇情有著不通順的部分，例如劇情會斷在很懸的地方，然後你得收集食材製作指定料理才能繼續下一段劇情，這部分的體驗會很糟，所以「STORY模式」是最舒適的。

故事看似是主人翁在一個末日之後的世界裡旅行，但是很意外有著相當完整的世界觀而且還有許多有趣的設定，這些點都與故事有著絕妙的搭配，喜歡劇情向遊戲的你相當值得一玩。

Há muito tempo, entrei em contato com a desenvolvedora do jogo sem saber que eram brasileiros. Escrevi um texto bonitinho em inglês e mandei pra eles. Eles responderam humildemente em português, mas eu continuei em inglês mesmo. Joguei a beta do game e curti bastante — tinha muito potencial. Notei alguns erros na tradução para o português e enviei novamente, em inglês, os erros que encontrei. Fiz alguns vídeos e guardei tudo.

Quando o jogo foi lançado, corri pra comprar e ajudar. Do nada, comecei a ver vários tweets do desenvolvedor todo feliz com o lançamento — foi aí que caiu a ficha de que o jogo era brasileiro! Comprei e deixei guardado. Agora, com mais tempo, voltei pra jogar e destrinchar tudo por completo.

Não dá pra comparar com *Vampire Survivors* — é uma proposta diferente, algo com um “quê” a mais. Mesmo que não seja tão longo ou explorado quanto outros, é muito bom, viciante até. Joguei direto até platinar.

Dev’s, se vocês estiverem lendo isso: vocês têm ouro nas mãos!
Eu sempre falo isso quando vejo potencial em algo — e esse jogo tá incrível. Tá ótimo, tá redondinho, mas ainda dá pra ir além.

Fico imaginando as cenas de transição para os chefes... daria uma série fantástica sobre a galinha guerreira! Dentro do próprio jogo, seria muito legal ver mais galinhas, galinhas personalizáveis, armas personalizáveis... E pra quem já platinou, não seria nada mal um modo “debug”, né? Poder colocar quantas magias quiser, quantos equipamentos quiser — seria um prato cheio pra testar tudo.

Mas voltando à review: vale a pena demais. O jogo é bom, é viciante, e diferente de tudo que já tem no mercado. Você sente vontade de ir além, de chegar até o fim.

Agora que finalizei vou ficar na depressão pós finalizar

This game is brilliant. I'm going to update this review once I finish the game, but after these first few hours of playing through the main story, I'm feeling pretty confident that this game deserves a strong recommend.

The big thing they're doing absolutely right is handling progression-gating. This game has floored me with the number of abilities that it readily hands the player. And these aren't tiny abilities that only help with one or two puzzles. These are abilities that affect numerous room you have access to. The game's initially straight-forward areas keep revealing layers upon layers of things to discover.

And the best part is the game isn't stingy with these. Unlike Hollow Knight/Silksong, this game doesn't hide every interesting ability behind a giant grinding labyrinth of fighting and bosses. Sometimes you'll find an upgrade just wandering around. This is some of the most rewarding exploration I've experienced in a game. 

It helps that the game tries to be dense. Rooms/areas are centered around introducing new gimmicks. The pace at which the game varies gimmicks feels good, (so far) nothing has overstayed its welcome. The game doesn't seem interested in padding things out so it can become known for being a "big" game. Quality over quantity.

The game's overall difficulty is generally pretty easy. That definitely makes back-tracking less painful, but may also bore those looking for a challenge. Combat generally isn't really the focus of the game, but it gets enough attention that it isn't a nuisance.

* The game is also beautiful. The 2D and 3D work well together, creating a lot of really vibrant visuals and emotive interactions.
* The fan service is blatant, but doesn't feel like it gets in the way. The game doesn't waste time oggling the characters, or making awful perv jokes. The characters are pretty, and the game doesn't feel the need to justify or obsess over that.
* The game maps are connected in a very linear fashion. It would be interesting to have a more open world design, though the lack of that doesn't bother me much.
* The writing is OK. It's not as clean and tightly-focused as [i]Pirate's Curse[/i]. Some parts feel too non sequitur (i.e. things happen because the writers need it to).

They try to make him an ethical moneylender, just for him to deny his services to specifically women if they don't want to work in the sex industry. Which is just so strange. Saejima was a net zero to me. He's fine, in every sense of the word. Kiryu was cool until the last hour, where I genuinely had no idea what was going on through his head. 

Anyways, play if you plan on playing the whole series. Otherwise, the game is good because it's Yakuza and the story is kinda ass lmao

Узнал про игру из новостей, где говорилось что разработчик сам написал на свою игру обзор, так как никто в нее  не играл. 
Мне стало его немного жаль + русский язык есть и цена приемлемая, почему бы не попробовать.
И так по игре
1) Хардкорный платформер с элементами метройдвании, есть на выбор 5 уровней сложности, где сложный это третий по счету, на остальных играть нереально. По игре также открываются другие режимы усложнений, но и без них и так играть трудно. Сам проходил на сложном, пока не застрял на одном уровне, даже на легком играть стало не комфортно, поэтому игру я так и не прошел (может позже найду сил, а пока я устал от игры).
2) Необычный визуальный стиль, графика минималистичная, из цветов только белый, синий и красный, что из-за снежного сеттинга,  многие тайные проходы и нычки приходится искать тыкаясь в разные углы. Палитра цветов со временем начинает надоедать, особенно когда играешь на сложном и приходится по 20 раз перепроходить один и тот-же участок игры.
3) Хорошо проработанные враги и боссы.  Последние приходится заучивать и тренить как в каком-нибудь dark souls, и есть улучшенные их версии по ходу игры, что создает для игрока испытание. После определенного этапа игры, мир наполняется другими врагами и механиками, усложняющие игру.
4)  Сюжет повествуется из реплик и обрывках воспоминания, немного криповый, поэтому картину приходится додумывать самому, а хотелось бы побольше записок каких-нибудь и других элементов повествования.
5) Карта игры, как по мне, сильно запутанная и приходиться долго искать пропущенный тайный проход ведущий в следующую главу. Хотелось бы побольше подсказок или чтобы игра сама тебе намекнула куда идти, если ты долго стоишь на месте.
6) Технически игра сделана качественно, багов и вылетов никаких не обнаружено, монстры все озвучены и анимированы, вылетов за границу локаций тоже не нашел, хотя пытался =). Разработчику в этом плане респект.

I try not to overuse this phrase, but this is an absolute masterpiece of a game.

It's a point-and-click mystery set in a mid-90s web browser where you work as a content moderator for a Geocities-esque web space full of haphazard, often low-quality personal websites. It tells a fascinating story, but in a very roundabout way that may not appeal to casual fans of the point-and-click genre. Getting from plot point A to B is NOT the game's primary focus, nor is it just simple nostalgia for the wackiness of the 90s internet. This is a game about the joy of digging, snooping, and discovering.

The majority of the 10 hours I spent playing it was spent simply browsing these (fictional) people's websites. Not only are they hilariously accurate parodies of what kinds of pages we used to make in the 90s, they feel genuinely REAL, like each one was created by a random person logging on to the internet for the very first time, in an era before such insane concepts as social media or engagement farming. Whether I was reading a middle-aged midwestern woman's poetry, a 13-year-old's garbage MSpaint comics, reviews for (fake) obscure horror movies, or downloading bizarre wallpapers and goofy sound effect packs, the simple act of traversing through personal websites - each one unique in its poor construction and hard-to-read formatting - brought me a special, inimitable type of joy. This game truly captures the magic of the old web; the magic of DISCOVERING things, almost always by accident.

The main plot of the game moves along as you flag webpages for content violations (copyright, harassment, malware, etc), but the REAL story unfolds the more you just kinda poke around. Characters update their pages after you copyright strike them, they feud with each other and with the company that runs their communities, and they share files with each other - music, leaked chat logs, and annoying but funny viruses. Each one is living their own life and has a story to tell, and it's crucial to understand that the majority of all this is entirely skippable, missable, or completely hidden, which makes it feel that much more satisfying when you manage to catch it. Make no mistake, the story is good, but the CONTEXT of it is what makes it excellent.

Bottom line, this is a game for weirdos like me who enjoy "outdated" concepts like surfing the net, digging around in the Wayback Machine, or reading Homestuck and laughing at all its weirdly specific 90s tech jokes moreso than the trolls who said funny bad words at each other. You don't HAVE to be a tech nerd to enjoy it, but this is game aimed a very niche audience, so if you're IN that audience, this is definitely a MUST-PLAY.

Lastly, I hope this game inspires more people to consider making their own websites! It's much easier to do than it sounds, and I would LOVE to go back to spending hours surfing the REAL internet full of REAL human people's random websites, as opposed to just the ones in the game! It's something that brings me immense joy, and I was shocked at how powerfully Hypnospace Outlaw reignited that feeling inside me. If you give it an honest go, you might just find yourself agreeing!

Shelter 2 is an unforgettable experience that blends art, atmosphere, and emotion into a beautifully crafted survival adventure. Playing as a mother lynx, you’re immediately immersed in a world that feels both majestic and fragile. The game’s hand-painted visuals and hauntingly beautiful soundtrack create a sense of wonder and serenity that few games can match.

What truly makes Shelter 2 stand out is the emotional connection it builds between you and your lynx family. Watching your cubs grow, explore, and learn about the world around them feels deeply rewarding — and when danger strikes, every chase and narrow escape hits with genuine intensity.

The open-world design gives you the freedom to explore at your own pace, hunting for food, discovering hidden valleys, and surviving the changing seasons. There’s no hand-holding, and that’s part of its charm — it captures the raw, instinctive nature of survival in a beautifully poetic way.

Overall, Shelter 2 is not just a game; it’s an emotional journey about motherhood, nature, and the circle of life. It’s a short but deeply memorable experience that lingers long after the credits roll.

Shelter 2 is a quiet and contemplative survival experience that places you in the role of a mother lynx trying to raise her cubs in a vast and indifferent wilderness. Rather than framing survival as a struggle of crafting and resource meters, the game emphasizes instinct, responsibility, and the emotional weight of keeping your young alive. From the moment you give birth, the world is no longer simply a space to explore—it becomes a living environment full of subtle threats, fleeting opportunities, and moments of unexpected tenderness. The central tension of the game emerges organically: every decision you make, every path you take, and every successful or failed hunt directly affects the fate of your cubs, and the bond that forms through these simple interactions quickly becomes the game’s emotional anchor.

The visual presentation of Shelter 2 is one of its most distinctive qualities. The world is rendered in a patchwork art style that evokes watercolor illustrations and cut-paper landscapes. Trees, hills, and rivers feel stylized and almost abstract, yet still convey the essence of nature’s beauty and danger. The shifting seasons and weather effects enhance this sense of a world that is both artistic and alive. Nightfall brings an eerie stillness, snowstorms dim the horizon, and spring mornings bathe the terrain in warm colors. These stylistic choices aren’t just aesthetic—they reinforce the themes of fragility and transience. The sound design supports this with gentle ambient noises, distant animal calls, and a soft musical score that rises and falls with your journey, creating an atmosphere that is calm, reflective, and sometimes melancholic.

Gameplay revolves around a combination of exploration, hunting, and managing the needs of your cubs. You stalk prey across open landscapes, using patience and timing rather than complex mechanics, and bring food back to your litter or call them to you when danger is near. Watching them grow stronger and more independent provides a subtle sense of progression. At the same time, the world is not always forgiving. Environmental hazards, scarcity of prey, and the possibility of losing a cub create underlying tension, though the game often stops short of being truly difficult. Shelter 2’s challenge tends to lean more toward emotional stakes rather than mechanical ones, and much of its impact comes from your own desire to protect your family rather than any forced pressure from the systems themselves.

Despite its evocative presentation, Shelter 2 can feel limited in terms of depth. The world, while visually striking, can appear empty, with long stretches where little happens beyond hunting the same animals or wandering through quiet biomes. Once you learn the basic rhythms—follow trails, execute simple hunts, guide your cubs—the game’s systems reveal themselves to be relatively shallow, and the repetition may become noticeable in later hours. The expanded scale compared to the first Shelter title doesn’t always translate into increased variety, as the core activities remain mostly unchanged throughout your playthrough. This creates a tension between the promise of a large, open world and the reality that your role within it doesn’t evolve dramatically beyond ensuring your offspring are fed and safe.

Still, Shelter 2 finds meaning in the small moments. When your cubs call out for food, when they huddle close during a storm, or when they scatter in panic at a sudden threat, the game succeeds in creating a quiet emotional resonance that lingers long after its short runtime. The generational progression—allowing you to play future runs as the surviving cubs—adds a layer of continuity that makes each loss feel personal. While the gameplay loop may not hold up for those seeking extensive systems or long-term complexity, the emotional through-line remains its defining strength.

Viewed as a whole, Shelter 2 is less a traditional survival game and more an artistic meditation on parenthood, vulnerability, and the cycles of nature. It offers a gentle but poignant experience that rewards players who appreciate atmosphere and emotional storytelling over mechanical challenge. Those who enter expecting an expansive, feature-rich wilderness simulator may find it lacking, but players drawn to artistic games that explore unusual perspectives will likely find Shelter 2 to be a quiet, memorable journey through a world where survival is measured not by meters or stats, but by the small creatures who follow at your heels.

I wanted to like WoG2 more since I have fun memories of the first game, but I think I'm leaning towards a thumbs down in this case.

The good:
- New fluid mechanics add a fun twist to a lot of the levels
- New types of gooballs have fun mechanics
- Great music and ambiance

The bad:
- New gooball types are pretty underutilized
- (Without spoiling much) The experimental section of the game is overly long and not really what I wanted out of the game. I'm grateful there's an option to skip levels because I probably would have dropped the game outright at that point.
- The new level challenges feel unrewarding and too numerous. (I thought the simpler sole objective of getting a certain number of gooballs in the tube for OCD in the first game was better than having three separate challenges of time, quantity, and number of moves for each level. Plus, in the first game, all the extra gooballs you manage to get to the pipe end up being available for the freeform build mode).
- Just a general lack of QoL with the gameplay. I know part of the charm of WoG 1/2 is their relative clunkiness with regard to how you build with the gooballs, but I feel like WoG2 was a chance to improve a few elements of the first game, but it instead feels like a step backwards from it. They removed the ability to coax the gooballs to a particular part of your structure, and I frequently found it frustrating when I had to pick a particular type of gooball out from a mixed crowd of them, especially so if it was a balloon that I was trying to quickly grab to keep my structure from falling into some kind of hazard. The time bugs used to be limited per level, so it was more forgiveable to have to chase them down with your cursor and click them, but now they can be used as often as you'd like, but that means having to chase it down repeatedly if you decide you want to go back a number of steps (instead of restarting the level outright).

As this is a remake of the NES game Blaster Master, spoilers are in this review. You have been warned.

The good:

* Graphics are stellar SNES standard
* QOL improvements, such as a map and save points are quite welcome
* Remake fairly sticks to the original, but deviates in some parts for the better
* Story incorporates the original story to some extent, the world has been reshaped in places
to emphasize this, which is good, because now the story makes sense. (Which is something that irked me about the NES original) 
* Developers catered to fans of the original in wonderful ways by injecting new content as well into the game in certain points. Those of you who loved area 5, will now see it truly realized as it should have been back then. It's incredible.
* They used the Sunsoft audio libraries for the music

The bad:

* There are a few instances of the game being cheeky and obtuse about where to go, I'd wished those places didn't have tons of enemies at every turn.
* Area 8 has been turned into a forced stealth section area, which is extremely tedious to navigate. Tank navigation is bad, the dungeon sections are an annoying nightmare.
* Area 9 is a great concept, but entirely too obtuse
* Jason has always sucked at moving in this and the original game, this game has some few extremely frustrating ladder jumps, fortunately they don't show up more than a few times
* Soundtrack is a hit and miss, some themes were completely replaced with other versions which would be stellar when put into any other game than this, but since this is a remake one wonders why they weren't recreated as well? (I've never played the original Japanese version, if these themes are from that game, please consider this a moot point)

Summary:

This is a solid remake, one of the best I've played since Secret Of Mana. It adds a lot of new things, some good, some very bad. However, the overall impression of the game still stays with me because of the good new additions. These additions really are what I imagine the original devs having done if they had today's technology available. It's rare to see this in a remake, and I for one cherish it.

This game fixes most  of what was wrong with the original without really being entirely compelling on its own. It was definitely made with affection for the source material. I'll give it a weak recommend for fans of the original. (Or sufferers of the original, as it were.)

Only a few minutes in and I can already say this seems to be a quality release.

Visually speaking, it's not perfect since some artworks look a bit odd on a big screen, and the game's PSP roots do show especially in 3D models. However, assets still got an obvious upgrade and the remaster apparently targets 4K, so it looks good on modern displays. Plus actual fights are in 3D, and thankfully the internal resolution isn't locked at something that would make it blurry.

Gameplay-wise, I trust it to play the exact same as the PSP version but at 60 fps and with added features (including online with rollback netcode). Note that I haven't played the original, but this style of game seems harder to actually mess up than something like 2D fighting games that heavily rely on frame data.

Do I like the game? Kind of, as someone who has yet to play Falcom games this is more of a curiosity release than anything to me. It's pretty fun but kind of janky, and I think it's a bit expensive for the little I might end up playing it. But considering there seems to be proper care and effort in the port/remaster at all levels, it's the kind of release I want to support regardless.

作为一款银河城类平台跳跃游戏的话，人物除了跳跃以外没有任何的衍生跳跃能力，例如二段跳、蹬墙跳、加速跑等能力。
在没有衍生跳跃能力的情况下地图的复杂程度又是突然增加的，尤其是对于银河城平台跳跃游戏全收集爱好者来说是十分折磨的，本作地图难度曲线在前期的时候很普通，到了中期的时候突然变得十分复杂，到了后期又地图复杂程度又恢复成正常水平，全流程地图主打一个绕和门不能从这一侧打开。剧情流程在地图里面主要体现在通往主线的道路路线相对固定，玩家在偏离正确路线的时候经常需要绕路回到起始点继续探图，地图不能在打开地图界面的时候直接自动锁定到人物当前所在的位置，在一张地图用了很多标记的情况下很容易眼花找不到玩家目前所在的位置。本作作者还很贴心的实装了一个当前地图探索度达到90%以后装备相对应的“心得”以后能够追踪剩下10%的路径功能，这个功能如果放在其它平台跳跃游戏里面一定会起到很不错的效果，但是放在本作里，在路线相对固定，各种单向通道，绕来绕去的地图环境，又没有其它衍生的跳跃能力里面真的是有点折磨人了。
如果作为一款回合制战斗的游戏来看的话，缝合了杀戮尖塔的行动点数（决意点）和暗黑地牢的随从（姿态）和各种各样的debuff，再结合一点rpg人物养成系统里的点数分配，以上要素缝合在一起构成了本作主要战斗的玩法，所产生的问题是很高的学习成本以及轮椅是真的轮椅一旦坐上了就再也不想下来的问题。学习成本主要体现在如果玩家没有玩全缝合的那些游戏单纯的把本作当成一个回合制游戏来玩的话是完全行不通的，至少能够上手暗黑地牢里面的战斗模式才能比较快的理解本作的战斗机制，再加上本作对于“暴击率”，“回蓝速度”，“吸血”这种玩家早就达成共识，一眼就知道什么意思的词条进行了重新设定，例如“凝结值”“心流”“狂血”玩过游戏的知道这些其实就是回蓝速率，暴击率，吸血的意思，没玩过游戏的还以为这是什么小说的设定，这种大规模对游戏常识加私货的行为实在是有些画蛇添足，十分生硬地增加了玩家的学习成本。
结合以上内容，游戏大体上缝合了三大类的游戏类型，银河城平台跳跃的探索模式，回合制战斗的战斗模式，rpg人物的养成机制以及任务流程。以上要素的缝合首先没有产生奇妙的化学反应，有的只是想当割裂的游戏体验，就拿我自己来说的话我是奔着看起来像是暗黑地牢的战斗模式才打算尝试本作的，实际体验下来20多个小时里面大部分时间却全部用在了探索上面，因为本作地图路线相对固定，走错路了就需要绕，不去收集的话拿不齐装备道具，有一种上当受骗的感觉，相反的如果玩家是想体验银河城平台跳跃，那么遇见怪物以后就必须进入回合战斗，进入战斗就得掌握本作的战斗机制，造成了明明想去探索却得先学会如何进行回合制战斗的诡异情况。
从此可以看出，缝合的内容不但没有起到有效的相辅相成的效果反而互相制约，玩家玩游戏首先需要弄明白自己玩的是什么以后才能上手本作。
现在明白了为什么本作没有二段跳等跳跃的衍生能力了，因为如果本作有了二段跳的话玩家几乎可以去到任何想要去的地方，就不需要绕路开门了，也不需要必须先清掉面前的小怪才能拿到小怪身后的收集物品了，闪避就更不要多说了，如果本作有闪避玩家甚至不用战斗了。
因此，对于想要体验银河城跳跃的玩家来说是极其不推荐游玩本作的，因为暗黑地牢加杀戮尖塔的缝合是一块硬骨头要啃，对于奔着回合制战斗的玩家来说如果你对笔者提到的雷点能够接受可以考虑入手本作尝试一下，最多和自己和解一下别做什么全收集，直接战斗爽就完事了。

It's hard to overstate how much I love this game. Some of that is probably bias; when some friends of yours spend 10+ years lovingly crafting something, you have a certain amount of obligation to support it. But I've played a [i]lot[/i] of puzzle games in my time, and a lot of box-pushers in particular, and this one is easily up there with the very best. Easily 20-30 hours of playtime just to finish the main story, and probably twice that if you're aiming for all of the optional goals. A quirky, humorous story about the post-apocalypse with a lovable cast of characters. An absolute banger of a soundtrack.

One of the things that really sets Puzzle Depot apart from the standard sokoban is how organic it feels. The game leads with its story, which means that the levels are designed to feel like actual places with their own internally consistent logic, rather than simply vehicles for delivering a bunch of abstract puzzles. Baba Is You may have a world map with loosely themed areas, but each puzzle is (for the most part) self-contained, with no real connection to any other. Puzzle Depot, in contrast, might let you cleverly exfiltrate an item from one puzzle to use in another, or as part of an overarching meta-puzzle for the whole level. If anything, it's a lot more like DROD than most pure puzzlers, giant roaches and all.

Another standout feature that makes Puzzle Depot unique in the genre is how it handles difficulty scaling through the use of light RPG elements. Killing roaches and collecting items accrues points, which convert into more health each time you level up. Health can very frequently be sacrificed to skip a particularly difficult section of a puzzle, or bypass the whole thing entirely. Consumable items can restore health to give you even more opportunities to do that. And of course, many of the puzzles are entirely optional if you're just trying to finish the level. Simply [i]surviving[/i] to the end usually isn't that hard. But truly mastering each level, finding every secret, hunting down every item, squeezing the last few points out of a high score or shaving off just one more move--that can keep you occupied for hours or even days.

All in all, Puzzle Depot is a phenomenal piece of work, made even more impressive for being the product of two hobby game developers in the little free time they had, and a handful of amateur composers. It's the kind of game that seems destined to wallow in obscurity for having no name recognition at all, which is a real shame given how much love and polish has gone into it. So if you've found yourself here and think it sounds even remotely up your alley, do yourself and the devs a favor and pick it up. You won't be disappointed.

OVERVIEW: This game's description doesn't do it justice. "Sokoban" is an understatement. This is a bonkers, post-apocalyptic Sokoban-inspired dungeon crawl (with attendant light RPG elements). The number of interactions boasted in that description, however, is barely if at all an overstatement. The puzzles are devious, the art is on-point, the music is good, the plot is nifty, the characters all have their own personalities, and there's a ton of lore-text to read and even some secret lore to find if you don't have enough from just the main story.

I was involved in relatively minor fashion in its production (I'm one of two less prominently featured OST composers, so I'll talk less about that aspect.) But after being along for the ride and beta testing a few levels here and there I finally experienced the main story as a 'whole'. AND IT RULES. ALL OF IT RULES. EVEN THE SUPER FRUSTRATING PARTS, MR LAUGHING MANATEE.

(The manatee is laughing at me right now.)

THE PUZZLES:

Not only do puzzles have an ideal solution, but they also often admit subpar solutions if you're willing to sacrifice health. they're also all connected to each other somewhat like a Zelda dungeon but with more box-pushing. I've heard comparisons to Deadly Rooms of Death, but this game is the one I've played at any length.

Don't get me wrong. it's really hard. I have (somewhat performatively) teased and shouted at the devs for how stupid I felt after solving certain puzzles. BUT IT IS BRILLIANT. Ever since Otto of Laughing Manatee was working on this game's MegaZeux predecessor I have been saying (to one of the other OST guys and anyone else who'll listen) that Otto is an evil genius, and very likely you will feel it too if you play this, especially if you're trying to get at a level more efficiently than me.

THE NARRATIVE:

Apocalypses aside, the story is mostly comedic with a side of serious in tone, and as mentioned the characters are all awesome in their own way. I haven't experienced as much of the side-lore yet, but when I inevitably go back for more of the secrets, I might have more to say.

That's not to say nothing somber happens--in fact, the single saddest main-story moment is also (in my opinion) the crowning moment of funny AND crowning moment of awesome, to use the TVTropes terms. But overall things aren't TOO serious.

THE TECHNICAL:

Programming pretty on-point. Of course, this is a category where you only find things noteworthy when they're wrong, so it's noteworthy that I've been playing on PC an encountered no major issues of note for review purposes. Aside from a very minor quibble or two, the UX is also pretty much a dream. There's even an UNDO button with a very generous buffer that lasts until you load the last autosave in a room.

THE ART AND MUSIC:

Otto Germain did the art for this. Since his MegaZeux days we've all known how good he is at working with pixel art and the use of palettes and limitations to convey the world of Puzzle Depot is...Hmm. I think there's this pretentious philosophical idea that even if you portray something that is lacking a good it ought to have, or 'ugly', if you portray it well, it is still beautiful. It's cartoony, yes, but Puzzle Depot portrays a beautiful pixel-art apocalypse.

The music is pretty good if I do say so myself. Due to aforementioned involvement I won't comment too much on this, but I firmly believe we did a good job overall! And there were tracks from at least one co-composer I hadn't heard in any substance until playing through the game post-release. Every single new track in that regard was a delight.

TO SUM UP:

This game rules. This game is hard. Mind-bendingly, frustratingly hard by the end. But it's also great, funny, beautiful, even heartfelt in places. Otto, you magnificent genius, I hate you for whatever puzzle I'm stuck on now, but I love you for a great, fantastic game and the chance to contribute to it.

Tales of Arise is an RPG game se in Dahna, I initially dropped it because it felt slow and confusing, but then decided to give it another try, and I'm glad I did because this game is awesome.

It's not too easy but neither too difficult; it depends on you, because before fighting a boss you need to organize your team.

I recommend this game to everyone because I find it awesome.

+ Great Art
+ Great Music
+ Great Voice acting for main characters
+ Party Members who are interesting and show real growth (apart from the main two unfortunately).

- Terrible writing - The line by line dialogue feels like it was done by AI with characters telling you exactly how they feel or the bare minimum to keep the story going. The second and third realms you go to are the only places where the story feels polished and engaging. The villains' MO is to siphon magic from slaves and collect it for their own purposes, similar to the exspheres in Symphonia, yet as it turns out, the writers just want to one up each baddie by making the next even more evil. By the time you get to the third realm, they're just killing people rather than only enslaving them. By the time you get to the fifth realm, you see a ghost town because the Lord is so bad he's killing all of his own people, and even his guards from his home planet who work for him are all mind controlled. And beyond him are characters that just want to destroy the world. (Go big or go home.) The edginess started to make me laugh out loud when I got to it.

- Theme of coming together with the people from the other world when they are violent oppressors who are depicted as 99% pure evil. The story acts like it wants to stand against colonialism but also scolds anyone who would speak against colonizers to remind them that there is one in the party who isn't as bad. Also the usual "both sides" BS where they point to one group of the colonized people who are too uppity and bloodthirsty. Those people aren't doing rebellion correctly unlike the characters in the first realm who are objectively even more violent but are depicted as saints because they are nice to the protagonist.

- The second half of the game is poorly structured and full of filler and padding where you repeatedly just run around and do sidequests until the villains make a move. The last 4-5 hours of the game is just corridors of filler battles and standing in front of NPCs to listen to long exposition dumps. 

- The worldbuilding is trash. The game just lies to you about how everything works and then pulls twists that are like, "haha, you fell for that exposition I gave you earlier?"

- The combat has a lot of issues and is not very fun for reasons other reviewers have gone into great detail about. I can accept boring combat for a great story, but this game doesn't have that.

- I started playing the DLC Beyond the Dawn, and let's just say every problem I've listed here is even worse... Don't buy that even if it's on sale.

Katamari Damacy Reroll preserves the core structure of the original game: simple movement, clear objectives, and a steadily escalating sense of scale. The premise is direct. Roll objects, grow larger, and meet size targets within strict time limits. The clarity of goals makes each run easy to grasp.

Controls are dual-stick and require brief adjustment. Once learned, movement becomes predictable and allows smooth navigation through crowded spaces. The design emphasizes momentum and route planning instead of precision.

Levels are compact but layered. Each stage introduces new object groups and environmental boundaries that shift as the katamari grows. Early runs focus on small items, and later stages push into larger open areas that highlight the jump in scale.

Visual design is stylized and consistent. The bright palette and simple geometry keep objects readable at high speeds. Performance is stable and supports the rapid transitions between size tiers without slowdown.

The soundtrack is a major component. Tracks are energetic and define the tone of each stage. Music and movement sync well, which reinforces the game’s rhythm during time-limited challenges.

Content is concise. Reroll stays close to the original structure and avoids significant additions. This preserves pacing but may feel short to players expecting expanded features.

Overall Katamari Damacy Reroll delivers a clean and faithful update of a focused concept. It offers a tight loop built on scale, momentum, and sensory clarity, and remains effective due to its direct design.

Um dos melhores seguimentos para games de Terror são aqueles psicológicos. Aqueles que o foco não é um monstro deformado ou um fantasma na sua cola. Mas sim, a sua própria cabeça. E quando o dev sabe manipular isso, o horror consegue ser maior.
Já tive muito preconceito com games de gráfico 2D. Aos poucos fui tendo paciência para conhecer alguns, gostar de outros e hoje, eu não dispenso mais, ao testar alguma coisa de Terror, nesse gráfico. E não julgo de cara que por ser grátis (e 2D) o game deve ser em algo, ruim.

Você percorre a campanha de Nycto tentando descobrir o porque de pesadelos recorrentes, vívidos; mesmo que você tenha fugido um pouco de sua vida para um pouco de paz. Mas quando o Terror está na sua cabeça, nem o Paraíso é um lugar seguro. É o caso do personagem.

Enfim, a jogabilidade é simples. Interagir e andar, o resto o game faz sozinho, mas nem por isso ele fica em débito.
Porém, possui alguns contras: as transições para quase-cutscenes dão uma leve demorada do jogo (não chega a ser do sistema) fazendo você perder alguns minutos (contando no geral) para a ansiedade de desvendar logo a história. E infelizmente, adiantar as conversas das "cutscenes" não é possível, dando um pouco a mais de cansaço nessa adicional demora.

Um outro ponto contra que talvez use mais a paciência, do que propriamente um ponto ruim, é quando usamos a lâmpada. Às vezes topamos com momentos em que nos perdemos e que não há tasks, e até se recordar que precisamos usar esse acessório, voltar ao passado e então descobrir algo para avançar, foram mais minutos que perdemos, desnecessariamente. Mas até aí, tem um ponto interessante. A volta ao passado.
Labirinto tedioso ao começo dos dias na história, mas não há outro jeito a não ser rodar e rodar as entradas até descobrir o que se precisa.

Battery life: about 4 hours at high quality, or under 3 hours at 90 FPS.

Native controller support is included, but you must enable it manually and fix the inverted axes with a community layout. 16:9 is the correct aspect ratio - 16:10 stretches the image slightly.

For a game that was once unplayable on Deck, it’s now smooth, stylish, and fun.

Verdict: Fully playable, looks great, but drains battery fast.

This is an excellent metroidvania with a world that feels very dynamic due to the frequent infighting between different animals and a living ecosystem. You play as a caveman on a hunting trip with his family, who's attacked by a dinosaur. As you run away, you lose your family but find a baby dino companion. Your goal is to first find your wife and daughter, then find your way back home to your village... but then, a spaceship appears and aliens kill your wife and abduct your daughter!

Now you have to explore the world, hunt dinosaurs for food, and find a way into the alien ships to get your daughter back. The mix of prehistoric and sci-fi setting works really well. Most of the time you'll be exploring prehistoric jungles and mountains populated by dinosaurs, but there's a few high tech alien bases to fight your way through, too. I really enjoyed the variety of environments and enemies here, every time you enter a new area you'll encounter something new.

The variety of creatures is one of the game's greatest strengths. There are dinosaurs, birds, prehistoric fish, giant insects. You can fight (or sneak past) dangerous dinosaurs like the t-rex or spinosaurus, and you can hunt dinosaurs like stegosaurs and triceratops... or simply walk past them, as they won't attack you unless provoked.

The game somewhat simulates an ecosystem by having hunter and prey animals interact with each other. You will often come across different animals locked in a fight, or a pack of raptors picking at a freshly slain carcass. You can even use this dynamic to your advantage by luring dangerous animals towards each other so they fight. For example you can lure a big dino into the water to get piranhas to attack it and help you bring it down. Or you can lure a pack of raptors to a carcass so they get distracted by fresh meat instead of hunting you down.

Wherever you go, you'll find the wildlife interacting with each other. It's such a joy to behold and makes even backtracking through familiar areas fun, because you can always come across an interesting situation.

The game has a crafting system, and while I'm usually not a fan of crafting at all, I found it pretty decent here. Slain dinos can be harvested for meat which can be grilled at a campfire to create your most important healing item. Bone can be carved into throwing knives, wood and flint make spears. You find enough raw materials as you explore, so it's not grindy at all, and beyond the meat for healing, you can easily finish the game without crafting anything. It's just there for getting more optional tools to help you fight.

There's also a leveling up system for both your own character and your dino sidekick. You can increase health and damage, but also buy skills like double jump, or increase your breath capacity for underwater dives. It works pretty well and makes taking risks rewarding, as big dangerous dinos like the t-rex give a lot of experience.

The game's world design is very solid, with plenty of secrets to find and a great variety of different biomes. To get a map of the area you're currently in, you first have to find it in the level. In every level there's a cave wall with a map painted on it, and to read the map, you must light a torch next to it. This is a pretty cool way of filling out your map in a metroidvania. The overall world map that shows how the different levels connect to each other is a bit unclear, though, so I made my own connection map in Photoshop (you can check Steam Guides for it, I uploaded it there) to have a clearer image of how to travel between areas. I quite liked this, as it made me explore the world in an organic way, without overly relying on maps as a crutch.

Overall, this was a really great game that I enjoyed thoroughly. One of the best metroidvanias I played in a while. I really like dinosaurs and prehistoric settings so I may be a bit biased though!
But really, it's the dynamically interacting wildlife that sold it for me. Almost feels like an immersive sim. Great stuff.

Raining Blocks es un juego que sigue una mecánica tan antigua como adictiva. Hace 30 años en Amstrad ya había juegos que combinaban bloques con gravedad (Squeaker, Caverns of Death o Tower of Rubble) y aquí mismo en Steam también hay 2 o 3 más que combinan estos dos elementos. Pero Raining Blocks tiene algunas características que lo ponen por encima de otros (a mi gusto, claro está):

1. Simplicidad. El modo de esquivar bloques  únicamente me parece de  lo más adecuado, porque no se pierde en detalles que distraen la atención de lo importante, sobrevivir. 

2. Varios modos de juego diferentes para que el juego se pueda alargar más cuando uno domina la dinámica de la supervivencia.

3. Compatibilidad. Se puede jugar en cualquier plataforma, no sólo en Windows (la que más utilizo es sin duda la versión de Android)

4. Precio. El resto de juegos de esta mecánica que hay en STEAM tienen un precio bastante superior.

Hay algunas cosillas que se pueden mejorar (y que no dudo que se irán puliendo poco a poco) como el movimiento de los personajes que a veces es algo brusco y la tipografía de las pantallas ( a mí me gustan letras más ornamentales o simplemente una tipografía arcade) aunque esto son ya gustos personales.

Gran Juego, muy divertido y ameno. La música de Sergio Gordillo se sale, le da un toque de color al juego maravilloso. Gran trabajo, lo recomiendo tanto por su precio como por su jugabilidad. Esperando ansioso a ver nuevos juegos vuestros, sois la caña. :)

Amnesia: The Bunker is the latest entry in the franchise that looks to change up the formula that ultimately panned out for Frictional Games.

I’ll start by highlighting how the atmosphere is one of the best aspects, as it truly gives the eerie vibes that make players terrified throughout their journey in the bunker. This sense of helplessness is felt even more in the higher difficulties. Now, to complement the chilling atmosphere, the “Beast” is introduced as a stalker enemy that keeps the game interesting with its random behavior that will have you drop whatever you’re doing and hide. But fear not, the “Beast” only wants to give you a big hug :) One other thing is how the sound design does an amazing job of immersing players in being alert for even the subtle noises. You know horror is done right when the player is constantly watching their surroundings and slowly creeping around areas…

There are also rats and these are no ordinary rats, so this further justified my hate towards them more lol. 

Now, for the gameplay, which is another strong core, sees players manage key items and resources in their inventory to survive from the darkness within the bunker. This is what I found to be most enjoyable because it gives players freedom/choice on what to bring, including being conservative for later areas that may prove more challenging. Also, as a survival horror game, the environment may be one of the most vital elements that can help a player out in a rough situation. Always try things out, as the game encourages!

Finally, the story is definitely where this game falls short. Don’t expect a complex narrative, but that doesn’t mean it fails to deliver on what it sets out to do. You have a clear objective that is required of you. And as you scour the notes within the bunker, you learn more about what disturbing things happened. Ultimately, the story accomplishes what it strived for, and the ending is a satisfying way to conclude this chapter in the franchise

In my initial playthrough on normal, it was fun exploring the creepy bunker, all while getting lost and eventually making progress. I will say that the game is even more tense (which is good thing) when playing on higher difficulties, as your resources are much limited and the Beast is far more aggressive, which further escalates the horror. Additionally, I never felt the game was unfair, another bonus.

Closing:
Highly recommend it to those fans of survival horror! While not your usual amnesia game, you can still appreciate what the devs cooked up here and one could imagine what a amnesia title can look if it combines dark descent writing and bunker gameplay…
Best survival horror game currently available. Playing the other amnesia games is not required at all; this game is the perfect standalone horror game experience

进入游戏后，卢卡的父亲怒骂卢卡为什么要这样做？根本就不是他的儿子，根本不是卢卡。通过铁盒可以发现两人断肢的照片，这两人分别正是卢卡的妈妈和妹妹。离开房间，进入另一个房间，看到椅子中央发现卢卡16岁的生日礼物一台“拍立得相机”，用拍立得对墙壁缝隙拍照会看到电视机播放一则新闻麦迪逊黑尔（1987年连环杀人凶手）遗产拍卖，其中麦迪逊小姐最喜爱的相机就是我们手上的这台。后面经过解密会来到爷爷家，墙壁上全是关于麦迪逊事件的报道，43岁麦迪逊残忍杀害并分尸了四人，其中有她的家人。并有相机拍下分尸的尸体，完成邪教仪式。根据后面笔记（恶魔的指引）和神父指引我们会来到麦迪逊杀人藏尸的水井，通过“拍立得拍照”的媒介进入类似“里世界”麦迪逊的回忆，“麦迪逊”在杀害35岁中年女子的时候被邻居看见报警，罗素警官下入水井遇到麦迪逊警告她不要靠近警告无果后枪击。剧情经过我们会进入里世界从一处墓地来到“悲惨教堂”圣朱庇特教堂通过拍照我们可以来到三个时间线，这三个时间线分别是1987年，2022年，1951年。时间来到1987年报纸上有记载（爷爷家墙报纸），神父公开给麦迪逊棺椁守灵希望麦迪逊上天堂，引发众怒。（我觉得麦迪逊家里从电视来看资产应该受过高等教育不会在大庭广众之下杀人被发现）。通过拍照来到1951年，忏悔室里有一名信徒叫南希，觉得自己的丈夫（德国士兵）是个怪物（毒气室工作杀了很多无辜人）反杀了丈夫。后面根据剧情来到现实世界看到奶奶留下的磁带和笔记，1972年给约翰（卢卡的父亲）买了一本“青膝”故事书（里面写了关于孤独的青膝失去了双眼的故事一直找不到）自此奶奶开始生病。奶奶觉得不对劲包括自己的戒指多次丢失（奶奶后面藏起来了），发现是被“青膝”折磨，告诉爷爷觉得奶奶疯了。奶奶死后爷爷发现了“青膝”真实存在并一直试图跟死去的奶奶交流愧疚于让奶奶在折磨中过世，并试图销毁“青膝”发现无果，选择封印（井上的锁）。听到电话录音神父会告诉我们恶魔想要进行交换巫术，做完解密最开始的房间会出现一本书告诉我们巫术仪式需要的条件“七个祭品”“情感价值的物品”“两具身体：客于主”“人类骨灰”。解开封印来到里世界通过纸条会发现小时候的约翰和青膝成为了朋友，并觉得约翰眼睛好看。此时青膝已经不用受到封印的桎梏想要替代卢卡（奶奶笔记里写了怕光可以用相机拍照逼退），通过音乐拿到青膝的眼球，丢弃让青膝再也找不到。青膝震怒重伤卢卡。剧情来到最后卢卡代替父亲成为最后一个祭品。但是经过麦迪逊干扰人类骨灰变成相机拍照，最后活下来的究竟是青膝，还是卢卡？我自己的理解:时间线先来到1951年青膝附身德国士兵杀人得到祭品选择跟南希结婚想要得到具有感情物品举行仪式，但是被南希发现反杀仪式被终止。来到1951年，青膝被买回约翰家（感情物品难以获得决定先获得）杀害了奶奶得到了戒指成功了。再来到1987年青膝附身麦迪逊杀害了四个人（神父知道不是麦迪逊干的）解密有个madsion 失去了自我“i”，但是被“青膝”附身的麦迪逊被枪杀，青膝越来越虚弱只能选择养精蓄锐附身卢卡，麦迪逊死后附身到相机上，这就能说明为什么相机可以逼退青膝（麦迪逊应该知道青膝怕光）这就能解释麦迪逊一直在恐吓我们并不伤害了，时间来到22年回到最后仪式祭品全了，青膝开始想要附身卢卡但是卢卡重伤（不想要残缺的身体）（原定祭品应该是他的父亲）但是前面夸了父亲眼睛好看，不知道他到底想要附身谁，做仪式应该就是为了换一具身体从新拥有眼睛。不过后面我觉得卢卡想要代替父亲约翰上吊，自此完成巫术。

Shadowveil es un juego que está bien, aunque he de reconocer que lo compré equivocado. La base principal es que lo compré por ser de 5 Anillos, que es un universo que adoro desde hace muchísimos años y que no había visto aún adaptado a videojuego y quería apoyarlo. Y pensaba que era un deckbuilder que es un género que me gusta mucho.

Sin embargo, no es el caso. La historia está en el universo de 5 Anillos y, sin ser la gran maravilla ni mucho menos, resulta competente y cumple su función. Pero la jugabilidad no es la de un deckbuilder sino la de un autobattler, que es un género que me convence menos. Cinco clases de personajes, cada uno con su colección de habilidades y talentos, más una buena variedad de artefactos, permiten un cierto grado de personalización que está bien. Luego a colocarlos en el terreno, colocar algunas habilidades que requieren despliegue manual, y a dejarles luchar. Funciona, sobretodo como algo de segunda pantalla, no como algo a lo que de verdad prestarle atención, aunque se termina haciendo repetitivo, en buena medida porque es insuficiente en lo que a mejoras permanentes y desbloqueables se refiere con lo cual un run no difiere tanto de otro. Y el modo en que maneja las misiones secundarias deja que desear también.

Gráficamente el juego es pobre, se nota la falta de recursos con la que fue hecho, aunque captura razonablemente la estética del juego de rol/cartas sin duda no llega a alcanzar la belleza de sus imágenes. El sonido lo desactivé, no por malo ya que estaba cumpliendo con su cometido, sino que al tenerlo en segunda pantalla quería el sonido del video de youtube que estuviese viendo en ese momento. Y en mi campaña no me encontré casi ningún bug, y ninguno de importancia, lo cual siempre está bien.

Por todo ello, no es un juego espectacular e histórico pero entretiene. Un 6.

He aquí mi análisis de este juego.

Para empezar, Between the Stars es una historia donde vas a tener que tomar decisiones y, alguna vez, depender de tu suerte con los dados (son opcionales y se puede jugar sin este factor aleatorio), sin embargo, yo juego con ellas, porque así está por defecto.  

Sabiendo eso, y que va a tener que leer mucho, tome su decisión para comprarlo.

Ahora, veamos lo malo:

-. El juego te da pocas opciones para explorar y para hacer cosas fuera de la historia. De hecho, la cantidad de misiones y de eventos es escasa y repetitivo hasta hartar.
-. Conseguir ciertas naves implica que hayas tenido que pasar cierto tiempo haciendo esas misiones y consiguiendo créditos a base de destruir piratas. En algunas ocasiones, sólo se tendrá una oportunidad de comprar esas naves, así que vaya con ahorros.
-. El combate, salvo en los niveles más bajos, se vuelve casi un trámite porque las capacidades de tu personaje y la tripulación multiplica la eficacia de las diferentes armas, esto es así incluso en difícil.
-. No hay asistencia de apuntado, así que disparar desde lejos, y a veces desde cerca, con ciertas armas es más que nada un acto de fe.
-. Los misiles son tremendamente eficaces a pesar de ser armas de medio o corto alcance, debido a que el combate lejano es casi imposible de impactar, hace que estas armas, que dañan el casco de forma directa, sean mortales.
-.El combate terrestre, como es a base de dados, puede ser especialmente difícil si no te tocan buenas tiradas.
-. Que tu equipo mejore en combate terrestre es bastante difícil, además, se premia el tener un equipo grande.
-. Las armas como los sistemas son tremendamente difíciles de encontrar en las tiendas, los planos son demasiado infrecuentes, y en las tiendas están carísimos, además que algunas armas sólo te van apareciendo según subes de nivel, por lo que tienes que pasar un tiempo siempre para hacerlo y que te vayan apareciendo.
-. El equipo terrestre se consigue sólo por medio de saqueo de naves... así que, para tener buenas reservas hay que estar un rato por ahí fuera,
-. Para acceder a los sistemas estelares tienes que avanzar obligatoriamente en la historia principal. Cada vez que avanzas se desbloquean 3 sistemas estelares jugables, y un cuarto de historia donde no hay nada.
-. En los sistemas hay siempre un planeta y una estación, con varios puntos de interés que se renuevan lentamente, lo que se antoja bastante escaso.
-. Puedes hacer minería, pero que yo haya visto, es sobre un mineral nada más, y es bastante pobre la minería.
-. La historia da una sensación de urgencia que en algunas ocasiones te impide disfrutar del juego.

Lo bueno:

-. Hay variedad de armas.
-. Hay variedad de naves.
-. Hay variedad de equipo.
-. Puedes contratar ayudantes que van en sus propias naves.
-. Hay tripulantes para aburrir... y es difícil que se mueran, así que al final se empieza con unos, y salvo que cambien de estrategia, terminarán con los mismos. 
-. La historia no está del todo mal, aunque es un poco simplona y un tanto rocambolesca con tanto giro argumental.
-. Los combates espaciales, a pesar de ser fáciles, resultan interesantes.
-. Las físicas de los obstáculos y la iluminación son buenas, de lo mejorcito... párense a pegar un par de tiros a los asteroides.
-. Tiene cierta rejugabilidad porque se pueden tomar otras decisiones, variando un poco la historia.

En definitiva... aprobado por los pelos.

Me esperaba algo más del estilo de juegos de mundo abierto espacial, pero es, como digo, una historia con un poco de recolección por el camino. Pasable, pero poco más. 

Personalmente, me deja un sabor agridulce en la boca, como que podrían haber conseguido algo más con el juego, y lo dejaron así.

Are you ready for camp? No, you don't have to pack your sleeping bag and mosquito spray, this is bringing the camp to you!

Dinosaurs in space with giant guns and swords vs generic black goo alien energy thing. Hosted by what appears to be a slightly taller Vanellope von Schweetz. The dialog is... campy, the jokes are... also campy. The entire premise is campy, but if you're okay with camp, it's actually pretty solid. The VR is used in a way that really emphasize the scale of the characters and how that sense of presence comes across to the normal sized person that you are.

All said, it seems to mostly just be an advertisement for a comic book series, which looks even campier from the previews they offer, and it seems to just be a passive experience, despite pretending otherwise, but everything is polished well enough to be worth at least checking out to see what they do.

Look, while I said I'd recommend this -- just know that these games are literally all the same. While this is every single game we keep playing them? The controls are terrible, the stories are usually silly and I do not believe they are real, and yet. It's been enjoyable to play through them, though I think the fire tower one was the best (even if the mechanics of "run and hide" at the end were so silly I simply watched the end on youtube). I like the idea of these games, but in reality they're pretty much the same game with various spooky overlays. But do I enjoy my time playing them? Sure! (Except the Woodbury one, that was too unbelievable and sort of boring).

De forma resumida, esse jogo, assim como os anteriores, foi feito pro DirectX 9 e o Windows 10 e 11 não usa mais isso diretamente. Eles fazem uma espécie de emulação de API e recursos usando o WARP. Além disso, a otimização dessa trilogia é igual a de console, praticamente copiada e colada, esse jogo em específico ainda tem problema de loop single-threaded, Physics Middleware, e outras desgraças técnicas que não foram revisadas e não tem patch. 

Tem uma entrevista no GameDeveloper bem interessante de ler, aonde foi comentado várias coisas do desenvolvimento. Esse game foi feito praticamente junto com o Anniversary, com uma equipe minúscula, algumas etapas da produção foram puladas por completo, e por causa da data de lançamento, cortaram um monte de coisa, e ainda a Microsoft ainda pediu duas DLCs exclusivas pro Xbox 360, o que basicamente dividiu o tempo da equipe....

Falando do jogo em si, dá pra ver na cara que ele não foi finalizado. Os puzzles perderam totalmente o charme. Antes, nos jogos antigos, você precisava observar, raciocinar e entender o cenário pra resolver o quebra-cabeça, em Underworld, é tudo óbvio demais, e muito sobre chegar em tal lugar, puxa a alavanca, pega o item, empurra a pedra e pronto, e o pior é que isso se repete até o final do jogo, puxe alavanca X, pegue item Y, vá pro lugar Z. 

[h1] Spoilers [/h1]

E você consegue ver durante o game que os cara tinha intenção de fazer mais coisa, em certos pontos na fase do méxico, você precisa usar o gancho pra enrolar a corda em volta de objetos e depois puxar, aplicando força física de "verdade" pra mover uma pedra. Em outro momento, o jogo te faz usar o mesmo recurso pra girar um parafuso ou destravar algo com base no movimento circular da corda, fora a mecanica de dirigir a moto, esse tipo de detalhes mostra claramente que o jogo foi pensado pra ser muito mais complexo, mas o cronograma apertado e as exigências externas.

A história também tenta ser ambiciosa, mas se perde completamente. Tem tanto furo que não dá pra saber se é proposital pra ser algo fodão ou se é só bagunça mesmo. A mãe da Lara Croft aparece do nada no final, sem lógica nenhuma,  a Doppelganger que aparece o jogo inteiro e não tem explicação decente, não dizem quem ela é, de onde veio, nem por que ajuda a Lara no final. E a espada do Rei Arthur? Como ela saiu da caverna do Legend e foi parar em Atlântida? E a mansão que é destruída e não tem desfecho do que aconteceu depois, e para onde a Lara vai no final ?

O combate também é outro ponto duvidoso (pelo menos na minha experiência), eu tomava hit de inimigo e logo em seguida outro, sem tempo nem de reagir, eu morri umas 10x seguidas porque não dava pra atacar de volta. 

No fim das contas, eu não recomendo esse jogo.... Ele é bugado, preguiçoso e inacabado. Tenta focar na história, mas falha feio, desperdiçando um potencial enorme. Os puzzles não são puzzles de verdade (puzzle = quebra-cabeça, não check-list de botão), a movimentação é travada, e a câmera parece ter sido programada por um inimigo da humanidade, colide com tudo e te obriga a LUTAR com os ângulos.

Os único ponto positivo são que o jogo é o mais bonito dessa trilogia Legends, desde a água e o cenário de vegetação.

A sequel to sci-fi narrative RPG.
  The game keeps with the simple and readable interface of the predecessor. The art is generally static, but detailed and charming. Character portraits are again excellent and hint at the personality and backstory. UI for interactions is functional and readable. The music is great, moody and atmospheric. There are no voices. Most of the feedback, description and interactions is communcated through text.
  The core gameplay stays, but with modifications. Once again, each cycle the character gets a set of dice (number dependent on their health) with random values. These can be then used for interactions. Instead of separate hacking interactions that use low value dice, there is a push mechanic that allows to modify the value but casuses stress. Accumulated stress has another effects, for example deterioration of dice, that replaces stabilizer mechanic from the prequel. Push and stress management are different for each of 3 character classes, which are more different this time. The push mechanic and stress are core of the new job mechanic, with push being used only there. These are short sidequests in separate locations and they are performed with selected companions who provide their own dice (and stress gauge). These are more high stakes and require tight resource management. This is in contrast with more free and relaxed interactions in various stations. The world is also more open, with multiple stations and free travel between them (with fuel management).
  The story is set after the first game, with the new main character. Some of the characters from the prequel and notably its DLC also have a role. A lot of the new characters are now a recruitable companions who can participate on jobs, even propose new jobs as part of their side quests. There is significantly less branching in terms of multiple endings, but there are many internal branches and decisions, potentially leading to  lasting effects like loss of companions. The writing and characters are again excellent. X-COM: Terror from the Deep stands as one of the most demanding and atmospheric tactical strategy games of its era, a sequel that took the original formula of X-COM: UFO Defense and submerged it into a world of deep-sea dread. Developed by MicroProse Software and published by 2K, it places players in command of a revived X-COM organization in the year 2040, where alien forces have once again risen—this time from the ocean depths. The world’s previous defenses are rendered obsolete by the saltwater environment, forcing humanity to rebuild its arsenal from scratch while battling a new wave of aquatic invaders. The shift to underwater warfare changes not only the setting but the tone of the entire experience, trading the cosmic mystery of UFOs for the eerie silence of the abyss. The result is a game that feels both familiar and deeply unsettling, drenched in tension and uncertainty from its opening moments.

The gameplay structure remains faithful to the original X-COM’s dual-layer design, balancing high-level strategic management with turn-based tactical combat. The Geoscape mode challenges the player to manage bases, funding, research, and global defense, while the Battlescape mode tests the player’s command skills in missions that can turn disastrous with a single misstep. MicroProse, under pressure to deliver a sequel quickly, reused much of the original game’s engine and systems, which ensures a strong sense of mechanical depth but also makes the game feel punishingly rigid. Every decision carries weight—researching the wrong technology or losing a skilled aquanaut can have cascading consequences. What makes Terror from the Deep particularly notorious is its unapologetic difficulty. Unlike the first game’s accidentally lenient settings, this installment enforces its challenge with precision. Missions are longer, enemies deadlier, and resources scarcer. Even with knowledge of X-COM tactics, players often find themselves outmatched, battling both the aliens and the game’s brutal design philosophy.

What truly separates Terror from the Deep from its predecessor is its atmosphere. The ocean setting introduces a unique kind of horror—one born of isolation, pressure, and the unknown lurking in the darkness. The color palette is cooler and more muted, the soundscape more foreboding, and the sense of claustrophobia much stronger. Fighting aliens inside sunken ships, drowned colonies, and alien bases evokes a creeping dread that few strategy games have captured since. The artwork and enemy designs enhance this feeling, blending Lovecraftian influences with biomechanical nightmares that look right at home in the deep. Even though the graphics today are dated, the pixel art and limited animations manage to convey a haunting beauty that continues to impress retro fans. The eerie soundtrack, punctuated by ambient tension rather than melodic themes, adds to the sense of unease that defines the game’s identity.

However, the same complexity that gives Terror from the Deep its depth can also lead to frustration. Missions often stretch for hours, especially the two-part terror missions on cruise ships or alien colonies, where a single surviving alien can force the player to comb through massive, multi-level maps. The game’s insistence on thoroughness—searching every corner, managing every resource, planning every move—demands immense patience. Some research paths are counterintuitive, and certain technologies can only be unlocked in a strict order, leaving players trapped if they make early missteps. The interface, though functional for its time, can feel cumbersome, especially during extended engagements where micromanagement becomes exhausting. These flaws are not just minor inconveniences—they are fundamental to the game’s character, shaping it into an experience that rewards discipline, foresight, and endurance more than reflex or improvisation.

Yet beneath the difficulty lies a uniquely satisfying sense of mastery. Success in Terror from the Deep feels genuinely earned, the result of careful learning, strategic adaptation, and an understanding of how to survive in a world designed to crush you. Losing troops, bases, or missions is inevitable, but rebuilding stronger each time is what gives the game its lasting power. Its punishing nature mirrors the themes it embodies—humanity’s desperate fight for survival in an alien, unforgiving world. Every victory, no matter how small, feels monumental, and every failure teaches hard lessons that carry forward into the next attempt. For players who crave tension, depth, and consequence, Terror from the Deep offers one of the most enduringly rich tactical experiences in gaming history.

Even decades after its release, X-COM: Terror from the Deep remains a hallmark of strategy design. Its aged visuals and interface can deter newcomers, but those who persist will discover a game that combines haunting atmosphere with uncompromising strategic complexity. It stands as both a continuation and a reflection of its predecessor—a mirror image that magnifies its brilliance and its brutality. While it may not innovate drastically in mechanics, it excels in tone and challenge, embodying the spirit of old-school design where every choice matters and every mission could be your last. It is a game that does not merely test your skill but your resolve, leaving players with the lasting impression that survival, in the depths or otherwise, must always be fought for.

Of all the indies that I have had the pleasure (and the occasional displeasure) of playing, Desktop Survivors 98 has to be one of those rare few games that sells its premise more so on the immersion and atmosphere than the actual gameplay, given my own personal preference for the types of games that I tend to play purely by what I see via trailers and the likes. Since I had already bought Vampire Survivors, the most clear comparison as far as bigger titles go, a good few months now and yet I've sat on it all this time whilst I've had an urge of playing this indie that few have matched thus far.

With the recent movement led by Louis Rossman against big tech firms regarding various anti-consumer practices, one might dismiss Desktop Survivors 98 as nothing short of a veiled 'cash grab' of the sorts that borrows the iconic Clippy for its own gameplay. However, seeing as the demo for this indie was first released in December of 2024, I can put those concerns to rest as the developer behind this creative indie, Brandon Hesslau, has paid homage to the early Microsoft days in perhaps the best way possible by creating a particularly fun and engaging 'bullet hell' roguelike game that does justice to that precious late 90s era of Windows.

Though to go into what this indie entails, Desktop Survivors 98 follows a more dungeon-crawler design of exploring three floors in increasing difficulty, facing off various themed monsters that escalate in challenge the further you go down. During this, the player is encouraged to kill as efficiently as possible to quickly gain XP for more levels as each level up grants a new item or an upgrade to a current one and amassing gold, either to buy items at a store that periodically spawns inside the dungeon itself or for making minor but permanent improvements outside in the hub, whilst engaging with optional bosses who drop powerful books of code to inject enhanced stats and additional abilities into weapons.

No doubt there's a lot of ground to cover here, first and foremost being the monsters themselves as they vary in difficulty and how they threaten the player, some moving erratically whilst others advance in unique ways that can catch you off-guard when combined with other monsters. However, some of these monsters aren't just 'living bullets' in this bullet hell game but also fire projectiles at you too, some of them even having unique properties to them like summoning weak enemies or forming a chain in a breath-like attack. On top of that, each enemy has a regular and 'evolved' form that guarantees more damage dealt by them and taken in order to defeat them whilst also presenting new dangerous attacks that their regular forms don't possess, keeping even experienced players on their toes for a new run into these dungeons!

This may sound quite intimidating at first, although no rougelite or rougelike is good without a well-designed system that gives players the ability to slowly enhance their items and abilities as they make more progress into the game itself! Seeing as you'll start off with the absolute basics and nothing else, however by interacting and engaging with both friendly and aggressive NPCs (these are also faithfully designed with that Windows 98 aesthetics) throughout each run you will begin unlocking new features that allow you to gain permanent upgrades for future attempts alongside other handy features and the likes! These include a burial site that gives higher odds of buried items showing up during a run, a mining garden which successfully mining all gems in a layer from pickaxes gained randomly throughout runs giving you various small buffs that stack and even a blackjack minigame where one can bet coins for chancing their odds as a quick way of gaining or losing money!

On the note of this game's fantastic aesthetics, Desktop Survivors 98's biggest appealing factor is its visual artstyle and how pleasing it is to the eyes as far as how this game might have looked in Windows 98. Since I was still learning the early ways of life around this time, not having been introduced to the world of PCs until Windows XP was the go-to operating system, I hold no nostalgia for this era of Windows personally. And yet, in spite of it all, I can feel that love and care put into crafting such an experience where many before my time can easily be taken back down memory lane with the faithful recreation put on display here with this roguelike title.

It also helps that Desktop Survivors 98 is not one to outstay its welcome either, since it took me about 28 hours or so to get all but one achievement at what felt a reasonably decent pace. One tip I'll give right off the bat is to try out and experiment with each of the game's 'cursors', the stand-in for human characters, as the 27 cursors all feature a specific starting weapon for you to focus on whilst also having their own specific stats. To give a couple of examples here, Gills starts you off with a level 2 shield pick-up that is separate from the standard upgrades and increases reflection damage by 1% for every level you gain. Bloom, meanwhile, guarantees an additional projectile when beginning each run for all weapons on top of any upgrades whilst also recovering a quarter of your max HP for every room cleared.

What I enjoy most about this roguelike indie with bullet hell gameplay though is how it is fairly difficult when starting off, requiring you to 'lock in' as it were for a good portion of the game when starting out. However, as you unlock more programs to build your starting power up as well as influence your overall preferred playing style, it becomes more manageable and eventually reach a point in the game where it becomes a real possibility of becoming super-powerful and having the game essentially play itself in all of that spectacular power fantasy glory!

Now whilst this indie shares a lot of elements with Vampire Survivors, there are several key distinctions to be made as that game has more of an 'open field' style of arena alongside a hard limit of 30 minutes whereby survival is nigh-impossible with the grim reaper on your case unlike Desktop Survivors 98's dungeon crawler roots and much brief time limits set for each individual room. Also the item store equivalent seems to largely be for unlocking new characters and items instead of incremental improvements and the likes whilst there's more of an emphasis on keyboard controls over using a mouse.

Considering that I have next to no experience with this specific type of gameplay up until now, I'm beginning to see why there is as much widespread appeal and enjoyment to be had with such games as this and Vampire Survivors here! However, even though I don't have much criticisms outside of it becoming easy past a certain point and generally only having the one gameplay cycle to lean onto, a major issue that may arise for some players is regarding one of the collectable items which can be dropped by monsters that aid the player, including gaining a quick HP boost (biscuits) or a brief power surge in attacks from the player (batteries) among others. This specifically pertains to the iconic 'blue screen of death' item that is used to wipe all enemies currently on screen when gained, however it has also ironically posed a problem for certain users who eventually encounter it crashing the game and, more importantly, deleting all progress made until that point.

Since the developer has not made any updates since shortly after the official launch of this game, I wish to make others aware of this potential game-breaking bug even though I have never encountered it myself despite having used hundreds of this item assuming this does not get patched. Outside of this one blemish however, Desktop Survivors 98 is a fantastic roguelike to dip your toes into and experience the joys of intense combat under randomly-generated and it is one that I can fully recommend to both new fans and enthusiasts of the genre as a whole!

I've got a few comparisons to make, using Vampire Survivors as a touchstone.
- DS98 doesn't hope to match VS in terms of depth and variety, but it's not really trying to do that. DS98's satisfied with what it is. Instead of the vastly unfolding experience VS provides, you unlock "programs" as you master the game's six locations. On the whole, they mostly exist to let you spend the money you accrue between runs for a little extra utility.
- For that reason, there's a lot more to spend your money on in DS98 than there is in VS. You ever played a casual game from the 00s? It's like that. Slow, steady, perpetual upgrades, so you can expect to still have goals in front of you for a long time. Unless you wanna try and win really big at Blackjack, make a killing, and max out everything. But then I'd wager you'd spend about the same amount of time gambling for the money as you would earning it.
- DS98 has bosses as a core part of its loop. VS technically has boss fights, but they're not part of VS's identity like they are DS98's. You can expect to fight one or two bosses a run. They're each associated with one of the six areas, but if you do fight a second, that one's gonna be from a random area. They have fun bullet-hell patterns that can really catch you off guard, but they aren't that bad once you've played enough. The bosses drop programs and code injections.
- Code injections are something that don't have a VS analogue. You'll run into one to three of them every run. Each of your weapons can slot one, and they modify weapon stats in neat ways. Fully separate from corruptions, which is DS98's version of VS's awakened weapons, which you get the same way. Trade-off is you can only have five weapons and five items, compared to VS's six.
- Pretty notable one: in DS98, you play as your mouse cursor. So you have massive natural mobility compared to most games, and the enemies move in idiosyncratic patterns to compensate. Enemies and bosses can be fast as hell if they wanna be. It's fun playing keep-away once you get the hang of it.
- There's a pretty huge variety of weapons, distinct from VS's collection. They slot wonderfully into the framing of DS98 as an old operating system, plus the literal "frame" your monitor acts as.
- Huge open maps wouldn't work for something on your desktop. DS98 generates simple dungeons for you to progress through, with fights in each room broken up by shops. DS98 doesn't work on a timer like VS does. Fights last a certain amount of seconds before you're free. This has the side effect of meaning DS98 runs can last for a while if you invest heavily in clock speed decreases. I don't think this game has an analogue to Death as a run-cutoff guarantor.
