Hard as balls side-scrolling shooter with plenty of content. Loss of a life takes you back to a checkpoint, & using a 'continue' takes you all the way back to the start of the level, making death meaningful. You need to hold the button down to shoot, but there are occasionally reasons not to shoot; shooting invincible ghost-like aliens in one section of the game causes them to rush towards you, making that section of the game much harder if you are just firing indiscriminately, & a toggle fire can easily be added via Steam Input settings.

Super Hydorah is a lovingly crafted side-scrolling shoot-’em-up that wears its classic arcade inspirations openly but confidently stands on its own strengths. Developed by Locomalito with music by Gryzor87 and released by Abylight Studios, it pays tribute to genre staples like Gradius, R-Type, and Darius, but rather than simply imitating them, it refines and modernizes their ideas. From the moment your tiny starfighter launches into its first mission, the game establishes a tone of intensity and precision. Every level is designed with deliberate enemy placement, sharp pacing, and a sense of escalating danger that rewards memorization, quick reflexes, and strategic weapon choices. It is an experience built for players who appreciate disciplined design and the gratification that comes from mastering a demanding pattern-based shooter.

One of Super Hydorah’s standout qualities is its level variety. Spread across more than twenty stages, the game constantly introduces new ideas, environments, and mechanical twists. You move from claustrophobic caverns filled with biological horrors to open-space battles where swarms of enemies surround you from all directions. Many stages layer environmental hazards into the combat—rushing fluids, mechanical traps, narrow tunnels, or shifting terrain that forces you to navigate with precision while still fighting off enemy waves. The branching stage paths allow you to choose your route across the galaxy, giving the game a degree of nonlinearity rare in its genre. This design encourages replaying levels not only to improve performance but also to uncover hidden routes, optional bosses, and additional upgrades.

Combat feels crisp and responsive, thanks to tight controls and clear visual telegraphing. Your ship’s hitbox is small and fair, allowing skilled players to weave through bullet patterns that, at first glance, look impossible. Each mission provides a choice of primary, secondary, and super weapons, and although not all combinations are equally effective, part of the game’s appeal lies in experimenting to discover which loadouts suit each level’s unique patterns and bosses. These bosses are often the highlight of the game: massive screen-filling creatures, grotesque alien organisms, and mechanical monstrosities with multi-phase attacks. Every encounter feels handcrafted, requiring not only fast reactions but careful study of attack sequences and vulnerabilities.

Visually, Super Hydorah embraces a retro pixel art style, but the detail work and effects push it far beyond mere nostalgia. The color palettes shift dramatically between levels, creating moods that fit each environment—suffocating crimson caverns, icy blue voids, or neon-lit mechanical structures. The pixel animation is fluid, and explosions carry satisfying visual weight without obscuring gameplay clarity. The soundtrack, composed by Gryzor87, is a major highlight. It channels the energy of 80s and 90s arcade music with modern layering and instrumentation, giving each stage a distinct musical identity. The audio cues, from weapon fire to enemy alerts, reinforce the rhythm of combat and help the player anticipate incoming threats.

Super Hydorah’s challenge is both its defining strength and a possible barrier. The game expects commitment. Lives are precious, checkpoints are limited, and death often means replaying entire stages to try again with better understanding. While this difficulty curve will thrill genre veterans, newcomers may find it punishing. Some stages demand extreme precision, especially those with tight corridors or aggressive enemy patterns. The game is not shy about testing your limits. Despite this, the challenge feels fair more often than not—learning is always the key, and improvement is palpable. The option for local co-op also helps soften the experience, letting two players enjoy the chaos together and making the game more accessible.

Ultimately, Super Hydorah is a celebration of classic arcade shooters elevated by modern craftsmanship. It offers a long campaign, meaningful replay value through branching routes, satisfying weapon experimentation, and a steady cadence of memorable boss fights. The game respects its roots without being constrained by them, delivering a polished, intense, and thoroughly rewarding experience for anyone willing to take on its challenge. For fans of the genre, it’s a standout example of how retro design philosophies can thrive in today’s indie landscape. For newcomers, it may be demanding but remains an excellent entry point for those ready to embrace the heart-pounding rhythm of a true old-school shoot-’em-up.

Rating: 8/10

Story of Seasons (titled Bokujo Monogatari in Japan) is a beloved franchise of farming sim games that started on the Super Nintendo. The usual SoS plot aims to immerse players in a town full of lovable characters as they work to restore a neglected farm to its former glory.
Story of Seasons: A Wonderful Life (2023) is a remake of Harvest Moon: A Wonderful Life, which debuted on the Nintendo GameCube in 2003. The original was a charming experience that earned positive reviews, though some felt it offered fewer activities than expected.
I’ll admit, the original’s limited scope was always an issue for me: crops didn’t yield much profit, leaving you to spend most of your time caring for animals. While not feeling pressured to plant and harvest can be liberating, I can’t deny it took away some of the excitement. Many of us also didn’t realize that cross-breeding crops was the true way to farm profitably. In fact, when I first played, I’m not sure I even knew hybrids existed!

Mechanics

Thankfully, the remake addresses the crop concern by increasing the base profit of crops. The entire game has also been shortened and streamlined, making crossbreeding more accessible. To counter the original’s emptiness, a bulletin board now offers delivery jobs and fetch quests, filling some downtime and providing extra earnings.
Still, you might occasionally find yourself with idle in-game hours. At no point did I ever feel pressed to accomplish something rapidly. There’s little difficulty here: cows and chickens no longer get sick in the rain, and neither do pets if you neglect them. Plus, there’s no failing condition for ignoring farm upkeep, though it’s true the series has long since moved away from harsh penalties.
Mining remains a minor diversion, something BokuMono titles have never expanded deeply. But that’s arguably part of the charm: the game isn’t striving to bury you in tasks.

Where A Wonderful Life shines is in its villager interactions. You’ll find a generous number of cutscenes tied to each era of your farmer’s life, and you’ll definitely want to google gift lists to boost everyone’s affection. One slight annoyance is that some NPCs, like Gordy, won’t accept gifts while they’re busy working, meaning you’ll have to return later. It’s a mild inconvenience, but not a deal-breaker
Character designs have been tweaked, ranging from subtle changes to the complete replacement of at least one figure. While I sometimes miss the old designs, none of them drastically undermine the nostalgic feel. The marriage system returns, and this game goes a step further by letting your child grow into adulthood, choosing their future. During childhood, you can influence their interests; eventually, they settle on a path. In my playthrough, I guided my child toward the joys of farm life, and by adulthood, they were set to inherit the farm, an incredibly heartwarming twist I wish more BokuMono titles offered.

Other additions to the remake include gay marriage, a welcome trend in the more recent BokoMono games, and the ability to choose your character’s gender at creation (a feature once relegated to an entirely separate title, Harvest Moon: Another Wonderful Life). There are also helpful quality-of-life improvements, such as faster story progression (the original dragged on a bit) and a bell that automatically transports all animals in and out of the barn or coop.
Sound Design

The music is wonderfully nostalgic, though it can get repetitive. Fortunately, unlockable records allow you to swap tracks on your farm, just like in the original, helping keep the soundtrack fresh. Many menu and action sounds also return from the original—an excellent move that preserves the game’s legacy feel.
Graphics

There isn’t much to say about the visuals: they’re perfectly fine and never unpleasant, but they don’t go out of their way to wow you either. I’ll admit, a remake of a beloved classic might have been a chance to push the art style further. Still, A Wonderful Life was never about flashy visuals; it’s more about the relaxed vibe of the farm and village life.
Final Verdict

I genuinely enjoyed my time with Story of Seasons: A Wonderful Life—especially the character interactions and memorable cutscenes. Watching my in-game child grow into someone ready to continue the farm remains one of my favorite gaming memories. Though less jam-packed with activities than some other farming sims, A Wonderful Life keeps the focus on a simpler, slower pace.
If you prefer farming sims bursting with endless tasks and challenges, you might find A Wonderful Life a bit too relaxed. But if you enjoy a calmer, more personal farming experience, it offers a comforting return to the series’ roots—reminding us that sometimes, less can be more.
Finally, although comparisons between Story of Seasons and Stardew Valley are inevitable, it’s best to see them as different takes on the same genre. Stardew Valley is a phenomenon born from one dedicated creator, while BokuMono developers produce a steady line of polished farming titles within a narrower scope. If you accept A Wonderful Life for the easier, more heartfelt experience it is, you’ll likely find it a warm, nostalgic journey that doesn’t try to overshadow Stardew—and that’s perfectly okay.

In the end, Story of Seasons: A Wonderful Life remains a gentle reminder of what these games aim to provide: a cozy sanctuary from life’s hustle, where tending to animals and nurturing relationships can be enough. It may not reinvent the farming sim formula, but it successfully preserves the heart of the original while smoothing out a few rough edges. If you’re looking for a nostalgic, laid-back adventure that gently unfolds rather than races at full speed, this remake offers a truly wonderful life indeed.

Tom Clancy’s EndWar is that game I use to get obsessively into alongside ChromeHounds and other games you just remembered just now because we’re talking about them. 

Set in an alternate timeline back when Ubisoft was sort of cool, Tom Clancy’s EndWar is an amalgamation of all the plots from other TC games of the time period like Ghost Recon: Advanced Warfighter and Splinter Cell: Double Agent but everything went wrong and now World War 3 actually happens.

In the distant future of 2020, an American and European backed anti-missile orbital network called SLAMS is introduced to the world, basically nullifying the risk of full scale nuclear war. Soon after, the three big players of the world are attacked by a mysterious Terrorist organization. One misunderstanding leads to another, there’s some fingers pointed, some trigger fingers get too hot, and now you’re fighting in World War III. 

On the bright side, WW3 looks really, REALLY cool. 

Originally released in 2008, EndWar was a pretty big deal for those types of people that liked to play interesting multiplayer games. A console RTS primarily, the game had you command your own army from either the US Joint Strike Force, the European Union Enforcer Corp, and the Russian Federation Spetsnaz Guard Brigade. Each one has their own strengths and weaknesses. 

The US JSF use a mix of powered armor skeletons and cool UAV technology to support their smaller but more elite infantry. The SGB hit you with the big guns and the big tanks, and the European Union gets to your control point before you can neener neener. 

It basically comes down to how you want to play the game or what faction you’re more jingoistic for. When I was younger I always played the EUEC because I thought they had cool laser guns. 

EndWar’s big thing was the Theater of War mode, a multiplayer mode where you chose a faction and stuck to it for the duration of a war, which was basically Risk but you’re the little soldier guy the players roll dice over. You choose a map that represents an uplink sector and then you fight players from the opposite faction in a war to take said map for your faction. 
Winning battles means you gained more credits and more experience for your soldiers, which carried over from one battle to another. You could actually permanently kill an enemy and remove that battalion from any future wars, forcing the other player to spend the credits on amping up a new unit. 

Yes, it was a Dick move. Yes, I did it every chance I got. This is war, son. 

As the battle went on and became more dire, you had a thing called Defcon 1, which was basically you’re go ahead to just blow up the other guy with a WMD. Since Nukes are off the table, each faction had their own big blow up button, the Russians used Thermobaric missiles, the EU had a space laser, and the Yanks liked to just hit you with a rod from god from orbit. 

I like that idea, hey we’re not allowed to use nuclear weapons anymore, better just break the earth’s crust instead. 

How the game plays is that you see your units from either a tactical map or from a third person like camera focused on whatever unit you have selected. From there, you can command the unit to move somewhere via mouse and keyboard as well as attack and defend sectors. But the big draw was the voice commands, EndWar relies heavily on map awareness and your abilities to command units via your own voice.

You say something like “Unit 1, attack hostile 1” or “Unit 2 capture zone B” stuff like that. Back in the day I remember having a lot of problems with it, but I’m guessing just how far voice technology has come, I never had a problem with it afterwards, I could even dish out multiple orders in one go now. Its a game that really profited with age, especially with its gimmick. 

Combat is actually pretty exciting. Large rounds and explosions are booming and violent, there’s no real gore but everything blows up good. Infantry can also use cover and are really well animated during movement and fights. 

Its a Rock Paper Scissors affair, you need to keep a consistent army to deal with the enemy force. Infantry can capture points, tanks blow up light vehicles, helicopters blow up tanks, light vehicles and AA can blow up helicopters, stuff like that.

Wow, this sounds like a lot of fun, Meta games aren’t really a thing with a lot of multiplayer games these day, we’re not really going back to the Mech Assault 2 and EndWar days. So what happened?

Well, nobody bought it. From what I understand, sales were horrible even back in 2008. It had a solid playerbase, you’ll always get someone interested when you say the words “Online war”. But it wasn’t worth keeping around apparently, according to Ubisoft, and a sequel was canceled in 2010. 

The game’s official servers shut down in 2016, and I think all kinds of online support finally ended in 2022 or so, so I don’t know if you can still do just regular player matches. So now you only have single player to work with.

You have two modes outside of bot matches. Prelude to War is a series of missions where you play as all three factions and fend off terrorists as well as one another later one. Prelude leads to WW3, which is a map painter mode that’s LIKE Theater of War, but you’re conquering areas faster and a Mexican guy isn’t explaining to me how to properly make Tacos at 3 AM in 2009. 

I don’t know if there’s private servers or some kind of community for it, I hope there is. EndWar is a neat game, its one of the stronger 7/10 games out there. The presentation is nice and I liked the control and voice gimmicks. It goes on sale for, like, 2 dollars sometimes, so you can just play around with it for a bit before moving on.

Its really a shame, I used to be such a big fan of the Tom Clancy license. I used to breath the worlds of Splinter Cell, Ghost Recon, and Rainbow Six back in the day, as well as the other TC spin off games like this and HAWX. It was all a shared universe, with a good chunk of the games crossing over in one way or another (You fly escort for Ghost Recon during the Mexican Civil War in HAWX and get to see them overhead in Advanced Warfighter 2, cool stuff like that.) 

EndWar isn’t the last game in that particular timeline, there are more after it, I know Wildlands and Breakpoint still talk about the stuff that happened in earlier GR games and Scott Mitchells, who’s your commanding officer if you play the Americans in EndWar, shows up still. But it was a very interesting series of games back in the day.

EndWar itself gets 7 perma-killed units out of 10. I’d say it was an 8 if the multiplayer was still around. But I’m going to be honest, even back in the day it was sort of hard to get a game going.
A shame, really.

Fresh Start Cleaning Simulator ist Island Saver recht ähnlich, aber mit einigen bedeutenden unterschieden.

Wir haben eine Art Sauger, welcher mit einem Wassertank ausgestattet ist, mit dem wir Wasser versprühen können. Wasser ist das Wichtigste, beim ganzen, denn damit müssen die Haufen welche man in Bild 2 sieht erst mal abgetragen werden damit der Müll aufsaugbar wird. Wir haben anfangs glaube 4 Behälter welche wir mit Müll oder Items befüllen können, was später mit Erfahrungspunkten ausgebaut werden kann, aber in der Regel hat man genug. Weitere Items sind zb. Gegenstände welche man für zb. beim vorletzten Bild, den Hut der Katze, braucht oder Teile zur Reparatur von dem Bahnhof Haus. Den gesammelten Müll kann man an einem Terminal, welches man auf jeder Karte findet, abgeben und bekommt dafür Erfahrungspunkte, später wenn man es mit Erfahrungspunkten im Skilbaum freigeschalten hat wird automatisch Müll im Behälter gegen Erfahrung getauscht.

Es gibt 3 Skilbäume, mit Persönlichen, Sauger und Roboter Skils bunt gemischt. Roboter sind Stationär und können 1 Saugen der andere Wasser versprühen. Man kann sie zum auflösen der Müllberge nehmen oder zum Wässern von Bäumen und Pflanzen. Jedoch sind die Roboter erst sehr spät wirklich nützlich, da sie in den ersten 2 Skillstufen zu wenig Radius haben. Sie sind aber Teil der Errungenschaften. Das erste was man der Nutzbarkeit halber erweitern sollte wäre der Wassertank und die Anzeige wo noch Müll liegt. Es gibt auf einigen der glaube 14 Karten so was wie Physik Rätzel, welche in etwa so gehen das man einen Behälter mit Wasser füllt welcher dann einen Schalter auslöst, letztlich eher Kinderkram mit höchstens Errungenschaften Funktion, statt wirklich ernst zunehmen. Ein Teil der Aufgabe ist auch Dinge mit Wasser zu reinigen und Blumen wie Bäume zu gießen damit sie wieder Grün werden und blühen.

Errungenschaften sind denke kaum ohne Guide (gibt es) zu erspielen, schon gar nicht in überschaubarer Zeit. Fast die hälfte der Spielzeit ist bei mir nur für das Tiere streicheln Archivment drauf gegangen, weil ich ewig brauchte herauszufinden welche art ich noch nicht gestreichelt habe. Für Errungenschaften Sammler also vorher Guides lesen.

[b]Nasgatives:[/b]
[list]
  [*]Man muss jeden Dreckhaufen mit Wasser erst auflösen um dann eine kleine menge Müll, welcher wie Bauschutt aussieht zu bekommen.
  [*]Wie man in Bild 2, im Video und anderen Bildern sieht sind die Haufen einfach da, als hätte jemand die mit LKW da abgeladen, allgemein fern ab von realistisch. 
  [*]Man braucht zu viel Wasser
  [*]Die Bots werden erst in Max. Ausbaustufe brauchbar, weil vorher deren Reichweite zu begrenzt ist und bei Wasser schlicht jeder Halm den Strahl blockieren kann, wodurch man dann nacharbeiten muss.
  [*]Die Skills sind teils einfach zu teuer und teils in der Mechanik wenig hilfreich.
  [*]...
[/list]
Das Spiel hat durchaus einen gewissen wieder Spielwert, aber der ist dennoch begrenzt.

I would give this game a neutral review if I could. It's just... meh. Since Steam doesn't let us give neutral reviews, I *barely* recommend this game, with a bunch of caveats.

The gameplay loop is extremely simple and exactly the same every single day: mine, refine, sell. That's it. I kept waiting for Grandmole to reveal some weird conspiracy or for Pietro to do literally anything; I thought surely something cool or exciting was bound to happen, but nothing ever did. It's a fine game if you like what it offers, it just doesn't offer very much unfortunately. It's cute. It's pleasant. It's extremely predictable. It's a little bit stressful but also a little bit boring.

The game punishes you for having a poor short term memory. I could never remember when the loan shark was coming, but there was no way to check the calendar during the day. You can buy a TV to find out the popular gem of the day, but then there is no way to quickly see what it was, so you just have to go all the way back to the TV and check again. The controls are also a bit awkward and not thoughtfully designed. This game feels rough around the edges with many missing features that feel like low-hanging fruit.

In short, buy the game on sale, play it long enough to pay off your Grandmole's loan and get all the achievements, then that's it. Everything becomes pointless after that, and there is zero replay value. Meh.

[b]slime slam[/b] is a tetris-like where every piece has 2 halves, like a domino, and the goal is to match at least 4 of the same color to make them disappear. matches don't have to be in a straight line, as long as they're directly connected, it's fine (diagonals don't count).

the presentation is very retro, reminiscent of snes-era games. [b]nice pixel graphics[/b], there are even a bunch of level backgrounds to choose from with f12, and the music's not bad either.

keyboard, gamepad and joystick(!) are supported and [b]controls are fully rebindable[/b]. excellent news, as the defaults are pretty bad (enter for pause?) and it's important to note that [b]the accept and back buttons rotate the pieces[/b]. it's not mentioned anywhere, and for an hour I though I could only flip the two colors and everything has to be vertical for some reason.

[b]pressing esc anywhere in the menu immediately quits the game[/b], no settings saved if you were in the middle of tinkering with them and didn't manage to back out of a particular set of options. pressing esc also brings you instantly back to the menu while playing, which is a fun way to lose some progress accidentally.

since f12 is used for changing the background, [b]you can't take screenshots[/b], and more often than not the game didn't appear on my taskbar after alt+tabbing. [b]volume settings and windowed mode are available[/b], along with a few more settings, not too bad.

[b]there are 4 game modes.[/b] [u]30 challenges[/u] for single player, 5 types with 6 levels each. make combos, longer matches, clear garbage blocks, etc. I'm not a tetris expert, but I couldn't even do the first level of some, but made good progress with a few of them, until they got too fast. the name of this game mode is apt, to say the least.

[u]versus[/u] is a competitive mode for 2 local players with some customizability: speed, number of colors, matches necessary (can be as low as 2), garbage block type and strength, etc. you don't need extra controllers for multiplayer, a single keyboard works fine.

[u]arcade[/u] is for 1 or 2 players, not competitive, fixed rules, no customization, and [u]endless[/u] is somewhere in-between, for 1 or 2 players, it's customizable, but not played against each other.

all in all, [b]a worthy addition to one's tetris collection[/b], as the presentation is good, it offers multiplayer and plenty of variety and customizability, and the price was not too high either before it went free.

Firstly, this game has a great art style and music, both resulting from some big names in JRPGs, but the good stops there. As a huge SaGa fan, the gameplay loop is extremely boring and repetitive. Battles require little strategy, rather relying on you grinding, and there's no QOL improvements like fast forward, so you have to watch some frankly slow, unexciting battle animations play out repeatedly. I like the idea of exploring and mapping an uncharted island, but you'll soon realize each area is just a reskin that shares many of the same assets and gameplay. Storyline is minimal but would be serviceable if the underlying game didn't suck.

You'll also quickly notice that this port is sub-par. Some textures look good, but others are crunchy and poorly upscaled. Dialogue boxes are often cut off at the top of the screen because they weren't adjusted to the new aspect ratio, and that's visible from the very beginning of the game as you struggle decipher the less than half of letters on the top line that you can see, among other issues.

I had been waiting for a sale to pick this up as $50 is insane for what you're getting compared to the pricing of even major JRPG titles. $30 sale price is honestly still too steep but I really wanted to give this title another shot. I was quickly reminded this is a $10-15 game. I got the 3DS version used years ago for $7 and was still unhappy with my purchase. As you'll notice, many reviewers here who received the game for free are still disappointed.

Buyer beware, this game is not worth the asking price. What had amazing potential culminated in one of the simply most boring JRPGs I've ever played. At best, this game could fill some idle time, but there's so many better options out there, including the next game by the same team, The Alliance Alive, which plays much better and is priced appropriately, or any mainline SaGa title, which are much cheaper not on sale.

Edit: Pressed RB on my inventory screen looking at an item and it broke all controller input completely meaning I lost an hour of progress. Lovely.

Edit 2: Tried on PC instead of my Steam Deck. This game lacks v-sync so has horrible screen tearing. On Surface Laptop 4 (AMD), there’s no control panel to force it. Switched between fullscreen and borderless modes and it didn't make a difference. I then adjusted anti-aliasing and it literally crashed my entire computer to the point that it automatically restarted. Drivers are up to date. I'm continuing to try to play this game but it's literally fighting me every step of the way, like it really doesn't want to be played.

Edit 3: Been playing more without further crashes. Still unimpressed and stand by my review. If you, the publisher, want this game to review and sell better, you should cut the non-sale price in half. I’m sure you have money to recoup but obviously it’s not working out. This is no FF7, not even close, quit trying to price it like it is.

This is a decent game but its not really clear how to get anything other than the noob ending. 

The story did a good job of immersing me in the characters life. After the initial wave of spooks, I was very much on edge and kept thinking more was gonna happen. This didn't exactly go away when i reached the noob ending. Being met with a realization that i had missed something, I thought maybe I didn't move fast enough or just needed to let a jump-scare happen to find out.  Fortunately for me this, isn't a survival game that requires reflexes. Rather, this is a game that very much requires you to think around its limitations.

 The Pro Ending involves understanding what you can't do with the options provided to move or interact with things in the game. Then, accounting for that, (and anticipating the ending) you do something random. It was disappointing that to get the Pro Ending i had to do something that the story doesn't really sync with. Ultimately after reaching the Pro Ending (with a little help) i didn't get a satisfying extra bit of content. 

It would have made more sense in my mind to make the alternate ending something that you could have accidentally have run in to. I guess that wouldn't make sense though, given the objective was to play the game "better" and get a different outcome than before.  If it were up to me, after the story begins to add spooky stuff in your house, you would suddenly have a thematic motivation to start moving or changing things to your bedtime routine. Even after a playthough to the end, it would have made sense to take action when the nightmare turns real. 

But no, you just have to know that the end is coming and purposefully go out of your way to take advantage of a staged prompt that, if you miss, you cant remedy later.

After knowing and understanding the Pro Ending mechanics, i kind of get it. But it largely only made sense Back-to-Front, you know? Now that i know the answer i can see that i was asking the wrong questions....but the actual question is kind of a let down. 
I never would have guessed what was needed after the work done to immerse me in the story and character. Maybe if you've played a lot of these Indipendent-horror games it seems obvious, but as someone who is new to the genre i was disappointed. The grief i went through spending a few hours trying to figure it out was all due to my immersion and the spooks. If i had pulled myself out for a second and realized it was a game design decision i was trying to solve for and not a story one, i may have guessed it quicker (and without help).

All in all this game is a good try to make a quick spooky story, but it should be free considering the length and lack of reward for your effort.  
The music was cool tho and the spooky maze part was fun. If your new to the genre and need something to dip your toes into that can offer a challenge and give you a couple of spooks for the cheap, this is a good game to start with.

Joe Danger, developed and published by Hello Games, is an exuberant fusion of racing, platforming, and stunt performance that captures the essence of arcade fun while offering surprising depth beneath its colorful exterior. First released on consoles before making its way to PC via Steam, the game introduces players to the world of Joe Danger—a fearless stuntman determined to reclaim his former glory. The premise is lighthearted, but the execution is remarkably refined, blending tight controls, skill-based challenges, and an infectious sense of joy that harks back to the golden age of high-score chasing games. Rather than presenting a straightforward racing experience, Joe Danger turns every course into a playground where precision, timing, and creativity matter just as much as speed.

At its core, the game is built around a series of compact but meticulously designed stages, each offering multiple objectives. Players must guide Joe through loops, ramps, traps, and absurd hazards, collecting stars, spelling out the word “DANGER” by grabbing scattered letters, and performing daredevil stunts to rack up points. What makes the experience shine is how fluidly these elements come together. The controls are instantly responsive and intuitive—accelerate, jump, perform tricks, and land cleanly to build momentum. Yet behind this simple setup lies a deep rhythm-based challenge, where maintaining flow and chaining combos becomes a satisfying dance of reflexes and mastery. It’s a game that rewards replayability; the more you play, the more you notice nuances in timing and technique, and each successful run feels earned rather than luck-driven.

The presentation of Joe Danger is a major part of its charm. Hello Games built the world with vibrant, cartoon-inspired visuals that burst with color and personality. Each environment—from dusty desert tracks to chaotic stunt arenas—is filled with exaggerated obstacles and comical details that make the act of crashing almost as fun as landing a perfect run. Joe himself is a caricature of the classic daredevil, complete with a toothy grin and an unflappable spirit, and his animated reactions lend the game a layer of humor that keeps failure lighthearted. The soundtrack matches the energy perfectly with upbeat tunes and rhythmic sound effects that make each jump and flip feel like part of an orchestrated performance. The presentation never takes itself too seriously, but beneath its humor lies an appreciation for the craft of game design—a sense of balance that few arcade-style titles achieve so elegantly.

As players progress, the difficulty ramps up steadily, introducing new mechanics and challenges that test both dexterity and strategy. While early levels are forgiving and designed to build confidence, later ones require a near-perfect understanding of each course’s rhythm. The game cleverly encourages players to replay levels, not only to collect all the stars but also to master the flow of each stunt run. This layered approach gives Joe Danger its long-lasting appeal—it’s easy to pick up and enjoy for a few minutes, yet it also invites extended play sessions as you chase perfection. The PC version enhances this replayability through a level editor and Steam Workshop integration, allowing players to create and share their own courses. This feature adds a creative dimension that keeps the community engaged and ensures a steady stream of new challenges beyond the core campaign.

Despite its many strengths, Joe Danger isn’t without its minor shortcomings. The game’s structure, while polished, can feel repetitive over long sessions. Its variety comes from track design and secondary objectives rather than drastic mechanical evolution, so players looking for radical shifts in gameplay may find the pacing predictable. The lack of robust online multiplayer also limits the potential for competitive play, something that could have elevated the experience even further. However, these are minor blemishes in an otherwise tightly constructed and joyfully executed game. The emphasis on skill, charm, and player expression ensures that the fun rarely fades entirely, even when repetition sets in.

What makes Joe Danger so special is its understanding of pure playfulness. It’s a game that celebrates movement, rhythm, and the satisfaction of improvement without burdening the player with unnecessary complexity. It channels the same spirit that made classic arcade titles addictive but pairs it with modern polish and creativity. Whether you’re chasing high scores, experimenting with custom levels, or simply enjoying the act of pulling off ridiculous stunts, the game offers a constant sense of reward. Hello Games’ craftsmanship shines through in every detail, from the fluid animations to the intuitive feedback loops that make success feel exhilarating.

Ultimately, Joe Danger is a love letter to the kind of gaming that’s driven by enthusiasm and imagination. It proves that you don’t need realism or narrative gravitas to create something memorable—just tight mechanics, playful design, and a contagious sense of joy. Beneath its cartoonish surface lies a masterclass in game balance and pacing, where every jump, crash, and victory feels like part of a larger rhythm. It’s the type of game that can make anyone smile, whether you’re a casual player drawn to its charm or a perfectionist chasing that elusive flawless run. Joe Danger’s enduring appeal lies in its simplicity, sincerity, and the sheer delight of motion—a reminder that sometimes the best games are the ones that simply make you feel like flying.

Rating: 7/10

[H1]Perfect for when you want Halloween without the horror[/H1]

Hidden Cats in Spooky Village is the perfect Halloween comfort game: cozy, cute, and packed with purring little secrets. It’s slightly easier than previous Nukearts titles, but that actually makes it a great pick for a chill October evening (or, honestly, any cozy night in).

The first map gradually colors itself as you complete each section, which feels super rewarding. There’s a handy hint system, dark mode, adorable art, collectible cards, and even meowing cues to guide you toward any unfound cats. The soundtrack is soothing, achievements are clean and manageable, and your progress saves perfectly. It’s overflowing with charm and content, while keeping things friendly for all ages.

Of course, there are a few tiny hisses. Zoom is limited in smaller levels, the first map gets constantly interrupted by unlock pop-ups, and hints are restricted (plus, you’ll need to avoid them entirely for 100% completion). Still, none of that really overshadows the fun.

Overall, this cat search is a delightful, kid-friendly Halloween treat that perfectly balances spooky and sweet. Easy, cozy, and meowtastic. Nukearts did it again!

I would usually not do this, but upon interesting response and a longer while of thought, I have altered this review.

I played this first all the way through with a controller, giving a more mixed response to this game initially. I gave this game a positive thumb up, if more so for its soundtrack, style and the desire to see more games like this, not remarking as well upon the gameplay. 

Then I finally tried to use a mouse. 

While I’m still getting used to it, I’m understanding the zen flow and precision dance work of this game better. I still have conflicts with late-game choices regarding some overly busy and sporadic elements on screen, but for the majority of the game prior, I am being more forgiving.

This is not Thumper and will never beat it, but I still appreciate the choice to do something different and this is it entirely, regarding the way it controls as well as how it functions. 

This is quite clearly best for VR, but for lesser privileged persons as myself, mouse and controller are other options. If possible, try the mouse. While the controller/gamepad is an official setup designed for this, I believe it is the worst and most punishing method to play, particularly late-game.

The soundtrack is the game’s most absolute high and is my personal best reason as to why you should try to keep with it. 

While I still don’t think I’ll ever come back to this one as often for more professional practice like its older brother, it is worth a look and I’ll be back again within however many years it takes for Brian Gibson’s next creation. 

ETA: In response to a fellow review from Sionnach; that was just my personal experience 🤷. Glad you somehow found the controller easier for yourself.

First, DON'T GO INTO THIS EXPECTING SOMETHING LIKE THUMPER. There's a rhythm to it, but it's not a rhythm game. It also does feel like a $10 game that was originally VR, if you know what I mean. Someone else pointed out how flat it is and they're right. The aesthetics, vibe, and final level are the only things really comparable to Thumper (the last level is WAY more annoying in this though).

It took me about 4 hours to finish, with all of my first-try scores being at least a B. It's difficult and not at the same time. You feel like you want to rush way faster than you actually need to on your first play through, but once you remember that circling keeps your combo from running out and that the time limit is reset every wave, it's less stressful. I found it easier to play with a controller instead of mouse even though the mouse is definitely better for speedrunning. The power-ups are cool, but two of them feel really similar, and the bullet one is kind of difficult to control.

Considering the entire difficulty of the game comes from the time-limit, whether or not it's worth $10 will depend on how much you want to invest in that. I don't think I'll really be playing it past 10hrs, but that's only a dollar an hour, and I mainly want to support the developer to keep making games, so I'm fine with that. I already have at least a combined total of 200hrs+ on Thumper, counting on PS4. I hate that this dev is going to have Thumper following them forever, but it's for a good reason, and I hope they either go back to rhythm games or continue making new ideas... just maybe not in VR next time since it doesn't do their art style justice.

Unlike in most games there are no counterspells and no reaction phase where you can react to an enemy spellcast. Combined with the fact that Darkness for instance has really cheap "Destroy Creature" cards and by cheap I mean they are often cheaper than the creature they destroy. Yes,the enemy can instantly kill most of your creatures without you being able to keep them alive and does this with the same or fewer resources. 
Example: 
"Destroy a creature with 2 atk or less"-2 mana,level 1
My collection of ~250 DIFFERENT cards has no creature with the same or less cost that has 3 attack or more and most that have a higher manacost get destroyed by just this card as well.This game really needs to have weaker or more expensive creature shots.

I know it seems like a bad reason to not recommend something,but when you play 6-7 out of 10 games against the very same decks and basically have no chance to win unless you do it as well the whole thing becomes extremely repetitive and loses diversity.

Альбом, по словам матери, должен был лежать в старом комоде в спальне. Он открыл ящики один за другим. В верхнем обнаружил пожелтевшие письма, перевязанные лентой. В среднем – коллекцию старинных ножей, каждый из которых казался неестественно острым. В нижнем…


В нижнем лежал человеческий череп, гладко отполированный и лишенный нижней челюсти.


Андрей отшатнулся, чуть не выронив находку. В голове всплыли отрывки детских воспоминаний: приглушенный шепот взрослых, испуганные взгляды, бабушка, судорожно крестящаяся при упоминании имени деда.


В этот момент хлопнула входная дверь.


Повернувшись, Андрей увидел в проеме темную фигуру. Фигура двигалась бесшумно, и от неё исходила такая волна первобытного ужаса, что ноги Андрея приросли к полу. Это был дед. Он умер двадцать лет назад. Или нет?

Garfield Lasagna Party is a lighthearted, family-oriented party game developed by Balio Studio and published by Microids that brings the humor and laziness of everyone’s favorite orange cat into a colorful collection of mini-games. Built around the idea of a giant lasagna-themed competition, the game features Garfield and his friends—Odie, Arlene, and Nermal—as they take part in a series of silly, fast-paced challenges inspired by everyday scenes from the comic and cartoon universe. The premise is straightforward: players compete across a variety of bite-sized games, collecting points and trying to outdo one another while navigating a cheerful, board-game-style structure. It’s designed for accessible fun rather than complex gameplay, appealing primarily to families, younger audiences, or anyone looking for a casual multiplayer experience that captures the spirit of Garfield’s world.

The visual presentation is bright and welcoming, staying faithful to the familiar art style of the franchise. Every environment bursts with color, from Garfield’s cluttered house to Liz’s veterinary clinic and Jon’s kitchen, all rendered in a clean, cartoonish 3D style. The characters themselves are expressive and full of personality—Garfield with his lazy smirk, Odie with his trademark enthusiasm, and Arlene and Nermal with their own playful quirks. These details make the game immediately recognizable and appealing to fans of the comics. The animations are smooth enough for a game of this scope, and the performance is stable even on lower-end systems, reflecting its design as an accessible party title. While it doesn’t push technical boundaries, the game succeeds visually by delivering a polished, colorful experience that feels cozy and inviting.

The gameplay is structured around a combination of mini-games and a turn-based board mode. Players take turns moving across a board filled with random events, shortcuts, and power-ups, while competing in mini-games that determine who earns extra points. This structure is reminiscent of the Mario Party formula, where the joy comes less from winning and more from the chaos of unpredictable outcomes. There are thirty-two mini-games in total, each with simple controls and clear objectives, ranging from slicing pizzas and throwing snowballs to dodging obstacles or racing against the clock. These games are intentionally straightforward, designed to be instantly understandable even to new players. They emphasize quick reflexes, timing, and sometimes a touch of luck, which makes them perfect for spontaneous competition.

Beyond the main board mode, Garfield Lasagna Party offers two additional ways to play: Challenge mode and Tournament mode. Challenge mode allows players to jump directly into their favorite mini-games without the board structure, perfect for short bursts of play or focused practice. Tournament mode, on the other hand, shuffles a random selection of mini-games into a sequence, providing a faster-paced competition that eliminates downtime. Both modes ensure variety and flexibility, allowing players to tailor the experience to their group’s preferences. The inclusion of local multiplayer for up to four players makes the game ideal for gatherings, where its humor and simplicity shine brightest.

While the game’s design succeeds in capturing a fun, family-friendly tone, its simplicity also limits its depth. After a few rounds, players may notice that the mini-games begin to repeat in concept or feel similar in mechanics, which can reduce replayability over time. The physics and control responsiveness are serviceable but not as refined as in larger party game franchises, occasionally leading to moments of unintentional comedy or mild frustration. Additionally, there’s no robust single-player mode beyond competing against AI opponents, which means the experience is heavily reliant on multiplayer sessions. Online functionality is limited, and the community size is small, so most of the fun comes from gathering friends or family for local play.

Despite these constraints, Garfield Lasagna Party succeeds at what it sets out to do—it provides light entertainment wrapped in the charm of a beloved license. It doesn’t try to reinvent the party game genre but instead focuses on delivering approachable fun that can be enjoyed by players of all ages. The humor is mild and in keeping with the Garfield brand, the pacing is quick, and the overall mood is relaxed and friendly. It’s easy to pick up and play, with short, self-contained matches that make it perfect for casual gaming sessions. Fans of Garfield will appreciate the small details sprinkled throughout the game, from the character quips to the familiar backdrops that capture the essence of Jim Davis’s comic world.

Garfield Lasagna Party is ultimately a warm, uncomplicated party experience built on nostalgia and simplicity. It thrives as a local multiplayer game, the kind that’s best played on a couch with friends or family laughing at the chaos that unfolds. While it lacks the polish and depth of the genre’s biggest names, its genuine charm, accessible design, and cheerful presentation make it an enjoyable diversion for those who appreciate Garfield’s laid-back brand of humor. It’s not a game that demands long play sessions or mastery; instead, it invites players to relax, share a few laughs, and indulge in a world where competition is as silly and satisfying as a plate of lasagna.

Rating: 7/10

I want to preface my review by saying I love the concept of a horse game with a Life-is-Strange-esque vibe and story. It is a very brave decision to make a horse game targeted at a mature audience, and I cannot be more grateful for that (I think it's the first horse game I've ever played that has the f-word in it — the only other one I can think of is RDR2, which is technically not a horse game at all). 

I also understand that the game is in Early Access, and a lot of things will be (and have already been!) improved. The game has an active Discord community where the devs are communicating with players and taking players' concerns into account, which is truly amazing. 

However, there is one thing I find very strange and unsatisfying: the player character / main character approach. 

The game tells the story of Alex Evans. It would be absolutely fine if this was a single player game telling the story of a particular character. However, this game is an MMO, and you create your own character at the beginning, customizing their gender, appearance and name. You choose your own name — and then the game ignores it and calls you Alex.

This is immersion-breaking and weird, and I truly cannot understand the reasoning behind this narrartive decision (I can only think of "we want the main character to have a name in cinematics and dialogues" as the reason). When I create my character, I want to play as the character I've created, not deal with a split personality situation.

I truly hope the devs will reconsider this and find a solution that would allow us to experience the story of the character they have in mind and let players play without being called the wrong name.

Hubris is an ambitious and visually stunning virtual reality action-adventure game developed and published by Cyborn B.V., designed to showcase what immersive VR storytelling can look like when fused with high production values and physical interactivity. Set in a distant corner of space, the game places the player in the role of a recruit of the Order of Objectivity, an organization on a mission to locate a missing agent on a terraforming planet. What begins as a standard search-and-rescue mission quickly turns into an odyssey across an alien world teeming with life, danger, and mystery. Unlike many VR titles that focus on isolated gameplay systems, Hubris strives to blend traversal, shooting, exploration, and environmental interaction into one cohesive experience. The result is a title that feels both cinematic and tactile, drawing the player into its world through a combination of breathtaking visuals and physical engagement.

From the moment you don the headset, Hubris asserts itself as one of the most visually polished VR experiences to date. The environments are meticulously crafted, featuring sweeping alien vistas, vast industrial complexes, and underwater ecosystems that shimmer with vibrant detail. The level of texture work, lighting, and environmental scale is rare in VR and immediately sets a high standard for immersion. Whether you’re climbing cliffs above a turquoise sea, diving into alien waters, or exploring the interiors of metallic space installations, the world feels alive and layered. The underwater sequences, in particular, deserve praise for their fluidity and realism; swimming through submerged ruins and alien fauna while light ripples overhead is one of the most convincing and memorable experiences the medium has to offer. Every visual element, from the way your hands reflect off the water’s surface to the subtle particle effects in alien caverns, reinforces the illusion of presence that VR thrives on.

The gameplay structure of Hubris is an intricate mix of traversal, exploration, and combat. Players will climb, swim, and jump across complex environments, each interaction executed with an emphasis on physical immersion. The climbing system is smooth and natural, encouraging you to reach, pull, and balance as you navigate the terrain. Swimming uses intuitive hand motions to propel you through water, making movement feel genuinely embodied rather than simulated. These traversal mechanics, combined with a steady pacing of exploration, make simple navigation surprisingly satisfying. Combat adds another layer, equipping you with an array of firearms and tools to fend off hostile drones and alien creatures. Weapons can be crafted and upgraded using materials gathered from the environment, providing a light layer of resource management and progression. While combat isn’t as finely tuned or strategic as in traditional shooters, it fits the game’s rhythm of exploration and discovery, serving as punctuation between moments of awe and movement.

Where Hubris truly excels is in how it encourages players to engage directly with its world. There’s an inherent satisfaction in physically pulling yourself up a ledge, diving beneath the surface to locate a hidden passage, or interacting with the machinery scattered throughout the planet. The sense of touch and movement makes exploration feel personal, almost like a series of physical challenges woven into a sci-fi adventure narrative. This tactile design philosophy keeps the player grounded even when the story drifts toward familiar space-faring tropes. The world’s design is dense with small details—floating spores in the air, the hum of alien technology, and the shifting weather patterns—that make the environment itself one of the strongest characters in the game. The sound design complements this beautifully, with ambient audio that enhances immersion without overwhelming the senses.

However, Hubris is not without its flaws. While its traversal and world design are top-tier, its storytelling and combat systems fall short of that same standard. The narrative is serviceable but predictable, relying on standard sci-fi archetypes rather than breaking new ground. The dialogue and voice acting do their job but rarely rise to memorable heights, and the central mystery—though intriguing at first—unfolds in expected ways. Combat, while visually exciting, can occasionally feel shallow due to simple enemy AI and repetitive encounter design. Enemies tend to follow basic patterns, and the limited weapon variety means engagements start to blur together after several hours. The game’s linear structure also restricts player agency, giving the illusion of openness while guiding progression along tightly scripted paths. These shortcomings don’t ruin the experience but keep Hubris from reaching the level of systemic complexity that might make it a true VR classic.

Despite these limitations, Hubris remains one of the most technically impressive and immersive VR titles available. Its pacing, which balances action and exploration, allows players to absorb the environment rather than rush through it. The campaign length, averaging between six and ten hours depending on playstyle, feels well-suited to the medium—long enough to provide a satisfying arc without overstaying its welcome. The game’s performance is generally stable on high-end systems, with only occasional frame rate dips or minor bugs that rarely break immersion. When experienced on powerful hardware, the visuals and fluid controls combine to create moments that feel almost real, like standing on the edge of an alien cliff with the wind brushing past or gliding weightlessly through a submerged tunnel.

In the broader landscape of virtual reality gaming, Hubris stands as both a showcase of technological prowess and a reminder of VR’s untapped narrative potential. It demonstrates how carefully crafted motion systems and environmental design can make even familiar mechanics—climbing, shooting, swimming—feel exhilarating when tied to physical motion. Though its story and combat may lack the depth to fully match its visual grandeur, the game’s ability to immerse the player in a tangible, living world is unmatched in its category. Hubris may not redefine VR as a medium, but it elevates it through execution, proving that even straightforward ideas can feel extraordinary when brought to life with care and craftsmanship. For players seeking a breathtaking, physically engaging journey across an alien world, Hubris delivers exactly that—a visually majestic and deeply tactile experience that captures the true promise of virtual reality.

Omega Labyrinth Life, developed by Matrix and published by D3Publisher, is an unapologetically niche dungeon-crawling RPG that combines the mechanics of a roguelike adventure with the over-the-top fanservice of an anime dating sim. It continues the peculiar legacy of the Omega Labyrinth series, known for its blend of dungeon exploration, lighthearted humor, and risqué themes. Set in the idyllic Belles Fleurs Academy, the story follows a transfer student named Hinata Akatsuki, who arrives at the all-girls school only to discover that its sacred flower garden has mysteriously wilted. To restore the academy’s beauty, Hinata and her classmates must venture into the dangerous labyrinths that have appeared nearby, collecting magical seeds and facing bizarre monsters along the way. While the premise sounds whimsical and innocent, the game’s tone quickly reveals itself to be anything but, embracing absurdity and erotic comedy as core elements of its design.

The game’s visual presentation is strikingly polished, with bright, detailed character art that reflects the high production values often associated with D3Publisher’s more eccentric projects. The cast is brought to life through expressive anime-style illustrations, and each heroine is designed with a distinctive personality and aesthetic that caters to the fanservice-heavy tone. The dungeon environments, though repetitive, are vibrant and filled with colorful enemies that range from cute to grotesque. While the character designs and environments are pleasing to the eye, it’s clear that much of the development attention was lavished on the game’s more provocative features. The growth and “blooming” system, which literally causes characters’ bust sizes to increase as they grow stronger, is the game’s most notorious mechanic. It’s designed to function as a tongue-in-cheek representation of progress and empowerment, but it’s impossible to ignore how central this feature is to the overall experience. The soundtrack complements the aesthetic well, offering upbeat and occasionally serene tunes that suit both the academy’s lighthearted tone and the deeper, more dangerous dungeon sequences.

At its core, Omega Labyrinth Life is a turn-based roguelike dungeon crawler that plays much like classic titles in the Mystery Dungeon tradition. Every movement and action consumes a turn, and dungeons are procedurally generated, ensuring a slightly different layout each time. The gameplay loop revolves around exploring floors, collecting loot, defeating monsters, and managing hunger and inventory space while progressing toward deeper, more dangerous levels. Between dungeon runs, players return to the academy to plant seeds in the magical garden—a system that provides resources and contributes to the narrative theme of rejuvenation. It’s a charming addition that balances the intensity of dungeon runs with light management elements. The roguelike mechanics themselves are serviceable and satisfying, featuring solid enemy variety, useful items, and well-paced difficulty spikes. However, the gameplay rarely rises above competence, and it becomes apparent that the roguelike structure exists primarily as a framework for the game’s fanservice rather than a deeply developed system in its own right.

The game’s most distinctive, and controversial, aspect is how it ties its fanservice directly into gameplay progression. Defeating enemies and collecting items earns “Omega Power,” an energy that not only levels up characters but also triggers the infamous “chest expansion” mechanic, symbolizing the character’s growth. It’s both ridiculous and self-aware, intentionally playing into the absurdity of its concept. There are also side activities like “purification” mini-games, bathing scenes, and interaction events that push the game’s mature rating to the forefront. These moments can be awkward or humorous depending on one’s sensibilities, but they undeniably give Omega Labyrinth Life its identity. For players familiar with Japanese fanservice-heavy titles, the tone is more comedic than exploitative, though the constant reliance on sexual humor can wear thin over long sessions. For others, it might simply be too much, especially since the game rarely offers respite from its fixation on its own outrageous gimmick.

Beyond its spectacle, the game does have moments of genuine charm. The cast is likable and plays their exaggerated archetypes with a sense of self-awareness that prevents the tone from feeling mean-spirited. Hinata’s cheerful optimism, along with her interactions with the other students, creates a surprisingly wholesome counterbalance to the fanservice. The dialogue is filled with silly banter and fourth-wall-breaking humor, often poking fun at its own tropes and excesses. The overall story remains thin, serving mostly as an excuse to move from dungeon to dungeon, but it’s delivered with enough levity that it remains entertaining. What makes Omega Labyrinth Life interesting is its strange commitment to sincerity—it never feels ashamed of its outrageous premise, nor does it attempt to mask its identity as a game made for a very specific audience.

Technically, the game performs smoothly on PC, with crisp visuals, short loading times, and stable performance. The interface is intuitive, and despite its odd premise, the systems are easy to learn. The biggest downside is repetition; once you’ve experienced the core dungeon loop, much of the game’s content begins to blur together. The enemies, layouts, and objectives tend to recycle heavily, and while unlocking new characters and abilities adds variety, the sense of progression plateaus before long. The garden-building mechanic adds some longevity, as players can decorate the academy grounds and grow plants that influence gameplay bonuses, but even this system eventually becomes a background feature rather than a driving force.

In the end, Omega Labyrinth Life is a strange yet confident blend of roguelike gameplay and unabashed fanservice. It’s a game that knows exactly what it is and never pretends otherwise. For players who appreciate anime-style dungeon crawlers and don’t mind (or actively enjoy) its provocative humor, it can be an oddly endearing experience filled with charm, comedy, and simple but rewarding mechanics. For others, its overreliance on sexual themes and its limited mechanical depth may make it feel like a novelty that overstays its welcome. It’s an eccentric title best enjoyed for what it unapologetically represents: a bizarre, playful, and occasionally enjoyable fusion of dungeon crawling, character bonding, and cheeky self-parody. Omega Labyrinth Life might not appeal to everyone, but for those attuned to its blend of silliness and sensuality, it’s a rare kind of guilty pleasure that thrives precisely because it refuses to take itself too seriously.

Truck and Logistics Simulator is an open-world driving experience that blends the freedom of sandbox play with the structured discipline of a trucking career. Developed by Simula Games and published by Aerosoft GmbH, it aims to capture the full process of logistics—from loading and securing cargo to delivering it safely across diverse environments. Rather than focusing solely on long-haul trucking, the game emphasizes the entire supply chain, letting players handle forklifts, cranes, and loaders before even hitting the road. This holistic approach distinguishes it from other titles in the genre, offering a more hands-on look at the transportation business. It’s a game that thrives on the satisfaction of doing work methodically and watching a job come together piece by piece, even if it occasionally struggles with polish and realism.

The heart of Truck and Logistics Simulator lies in its sense of freedom. The world is fully open, spanning towns, industrial zones, ports, and highways that can be traversed at your own pace. You’re not limited to a single type of vehicle—there are over 20 categories, from compact vans to heavy trucks with multi-axle trailers. Each vehicle has its own personality, with handling and weight distribution that change depending on your cargo and the terrain. Before each delivery, you’ll need to physically load the cargo yourself using different equipment, which adds an extra layer of immersion. Whether you’re operating a forklift to balance pallets or securing a vehicle onto a flatbed trailer, the process feels tactile and rewarding. While this may seem like a small detail, it helps ground the experience in realism and gives the player a tangible connection to the logistics side of the business.

The driving itself is accessible and enjoyable, though it walks a fine line between realism and arcade-style handling. The physics engine provides a good sense of vehicle weight, especially when you’re hauling heavy cargo up steep inclines or braking to avoid traffic. However, the simulation isn’t as detailed or punishing as those in more hardcore titles like Euro Truck Simulator 2. The roads are wide, controls are forgiving, and the AI traffic is largely predictable, making the experience smooth but sometimes lacking in challenge. That balance works well for casual players who prefer relaxation over precision. The game rewards patience, steady driving, and attention to detail rather than split-second reactions. With a variety of mission types—from delivering construction materials to transporting luxury cars—there’s enough variety to keep the gameplay loop engaging, even if the tasks begin to blur together after many hours.

A major highlight of Truck and Logistics Simulator is its cooperative multiplayer mode, which allows up to 24 players to share the same map. This turns what might otherwise be a solitary experience into a social one, where convoys of players can coordinate deliveries, assist with loading operations, or simply drive together across the open world. It’s here that the game finds its most enjoyable rhythm. Working as part of a team to manage logistics in real time gives the gameplay a sense of purpose and camaraderie that single-player mode can’t quite replicate. The multiplayer integration is generally smooth, though some players may notice occasional bugs or synchronization issues, especially when handling heavy cargo. Still, the feature is impressive for an indie-developed simulation and adds immense replay value, transforming what could have been a quiet solo sim into a shared virtual workspace.

Visually, the game is solid but not spectacular. Vehicle models are detailed, and the interiors capture the look of real machinery with impressive authenticity. The environments, however, can feel sparse. Towns lack the density of life that makes a world feel inhabited, and traffic patterns are repetitive. Lighting and weather effects do a good job of adding atmosphere, with sunsets, fog, and rain lending a sense of realism to long drives, but the landscapes themselves occasionally feel static. Despite these shortcomings, the aesthetic is functional and clear, prioritizing readability over spectacle. The user interface follows the same philosophy—simple and clean, allowing players to focus on the task at hand without distraction. It’s a game that favors clarity and usability over artistic flair, and in the context of simulation, that’s often a smart choice.

Performance is another area where Truck and Logistics Simulator mostly holds up. The game runs smoothly even on mid-range systems, with load times kept short and optimization handled reasonably well. Physics interactions can occasionally glitch, especially when cargo is mishandled or collisions occur, but these moments are rarely game-breaking. The sound design, meanwhile, delivers the expected range of engine noises, road ambience, and machinery hums. Each vehicle type sounds distinct enough to be recognizable, though some repetition creeps in during long sessions. There’s no licensed music or dynamic radio system, but that absence helps maintain immersion—after all, this is a simulator about work and precision, not entertainment or spectacle.

As with many simulators, the longevity of Truck and Logistics Simulator depends on the player’s mindset. Those who enjoy repetition, efficiency, and the gradual mastery of systems will find it satisfying to perfect their deliveries, build their vehicle fleet, and explore every corner of the map. Others may find the game’s pace too slow or its world too quiet. The lack of deeper management elements—such as running a company, hiring drivers, or negotiating contracts—means the long-term sense of progression is somewhat limited. Once you’ve delivered enough cargo and purchased a few new vehicles, there isn’t much else to strive for beyond personal satisfaction. Still, the act of driving and working through deliveries remains calming and meditative, which is often exactly what fans of the genre are looking for.

Truck and Logistics Simulator ultimately succeeds as a grounded, approachable entry in the vehicle simulation genre. It captures the satisfaction of steady progress, from loading your first pallet to completing a flawless long-haul delivery, and it does so with an appreciation for realism that never becomes frustrating. It’s not as deep or as expansive as the giants of the genre, but it offers something they often overlook—a more intimate, hands-on depiction of the logistics profession. Whether played solo or with friends in multiplayer, it provides a relaxing and rewarding experience for those who find joy in precision and patience. For anyone looking to escape into a world of roads, machinery, and quiet purpose, Truck and Logistics Simulator is a trip well worth taking.

The game in it's current state is not worth the price. 

It has very limited features and I believe it's way overpriced for what it is.

Negatives:

- Controls often react slow.
- The ONLY way to advance with show jumping is to complete ALL objectives, that includes the often tricky, incredibly frustrating stride system, it would be better if the devs could make it a little easier to advance if you, like me. stink at completing the stride objectives.
- Show jumping is the only interesting thing to do after you complete the quests that guide you through the game. Yes you can do jobs at the other stable for money, but those are repetitive and get boring real fast.
- Terrible system for collecting loot. You have to dismount your horse and collect everything one by one. It's a tedious task which takes a lot of time, time horse girls like to spend on actually riding and caring for their horses.
- Designing the horse. I will tell more about this in my 'positives' section of this review. The designing of the horse makes it far too easy to get your dream horse right at the very start of the game. That's a pity, because if you enjoy breeding horses like me, I'm afraid this part of the game can be boring once they introduce breeding. I can be wrong on this, but so far, it's too easy to get your favorite horse.
- Every breed looks exactly the same. Arabians are my absolute favorite breed, but because every breed looks the same, it looks nowhere near an Arabian.
- I kinda wish there were more quests, not just the ones to get you started.
- Riding outside... I mean come on, we only have the camp site, which is very limited in it's diversity.

Positives:

- Designing the horse, it's very complete and you can get quite specific with it down to the little details (especially when it comes to 'purebred' horses). It's kind of comparable to the Sims 3/4, which is a nice system. It's just a little more limited than the Sims, but in turn, Unbridled's horses look more realistic.
- I like the farming system, it takes just the right amount of time.
- The feed system is good, I like that you can (eventually) produce enough feed for your horses while keeping costs relatively low.
- The quests that are available do help you get started easily.

All in all... I think this game has potential, but they truly should not have released this game (especially at this price) BEFORE having added the dressage system and a proper breeding system.

Maybe it'll be worth it in the future, but now, I can't recommend buying this game at this price.

Having spent over 200 hours on previous demo versions and waited many years for this "1.0 Release", my thoughts are varied and complex.

For starters, the final game varies significantly from the demo vision. i.e. there are more options to play as, but fewer scenario types to play in combat. It's also much shorter than I would have expected- At about 6.5 hours I've successfully completed all 3 campaigns. Though I'm nowhere near unlocking all the troops, edicts, and artifacts I feel I've seen plenty to review this game.

To be fair, I did complete each campaign on my first try on normal difficulty. That's not something everyone will be able to do, but people who are pretty good at roguelites (and people who spent over 200 hours on previous versions like I have) will find it not so difficult to "one and done" all three campaigns, with the second one (mage type) being the hardest in my opinion due to physically weaker units, and the third one (commander type) being the easiest due to a focus on tougher units. Your Threat also goes up just by wandering around through empty locations, something I think should be removed since regular gain from interacting with important nodes is already significant.

I do recommend this game, but after all the time and the changes it feels a little bit hollow. To really make it "great" the devs should add additional campaign content, ideally further chapters along the timeline of a completed initial run. For example, the conclusion of Berold's story teases the rise of a rebellion against his Crimson Empire, which could be built upon to deliver a campaign fighting for or against the rebels (or maybe options for both). 

As it is a run can be successfully completed in 1.5 to 2 hours and then say goodbye to all the stuff you worked to build up.

In closing, it's a bit of a pale shadow of what it could have been but is worth it for 10 bucks. Just don't get too attached to your individual runs or expect "iron man difficulty" except on the highest difficulty levels.

[h2]读作《Clannad》写作 人生：[/h2]

[b] 人是有限性的存在，而世界是一个充满着奇迹却又冷酷无情的世界。我们必然遭遇到不期而至的苦痛；有时候，你甚至连走出苦痛活下去都做不到——你根本没有办法面对实在界的创伤，而只能选择逃避。但是，人既不能直面现实，又不能沉溺幻想，只能在现实与幻想的夹缝中探索生存的方式。所以，我们必须从与他人一次次的相逢与祈愿中，学习足以成长下去的坚强，并且选择相信希望。生而为人，就是这样活下去的...... [/b]

《Clannad》从不是一款简单的文字冒险游戏，而是Key社用十三年光玉、无数细腻日常编织的人生史诗——它以冈崎朋也的迷茫开篇，从樱花坡道的相遇起步，串联起十余位角色的悲欢离合，最终在“家”的底色里，完成了一场关于爱、责任与救赎的闭环。通关的那一刻，指尖离开键盘，却仿佛刚从一段真实的人生中折返，屏幕里的悲欢仍在心头萦绕，现实中的羁绊更显珍贵。

游戏的叙事如涓涓细流，没有惊天动地的剧情，却在琐碎日常中藏着最动人的力量。主线里，朋也从一个逃避现实的叛逆少年，在渚的温柔陪伴下逐渐敞开心扉，学会直面生活的重量：从陪渚重建话剧社的青涩，到共同抵御疾病的坚韧；从毕业求职的碰壁，到组建家庭的担当；从失去渚后的沉沦，到与汐相依为命的觉醒——这条布满荆棘却终向光明的路，是每个普通人都会经历的成长轨迹。

而支线故事则是生活的多棱镜，每一条都折射出不同的情感维度：智代用孤勇守护珍视的事物，让我们看见“坚持”的模样；琴美在孤独中坚守与父母的约定，让我们懂得“思念”的重量；风子用海星传递祝福，让我们感受“纯粹”的温暖；春原兄妹的拌嘴与扶持，让我们明白“陪伴”的真谛……十三条光玉，十三段人生切片，有错过的遗憾，有相守的赤诚，有误解的消解，有传承的温情，它们共同构成了《Clannad》的完整世界——不回避悲伤，不夸大美好，却让每一份情绪都真实可感，每一段故事都直击人心。

Afterstory更是将这份真实推向极致：婚后的柴米油盐、育儿的手忙脚乱、失去至亲的崩溃、与家人和解的释然、直面命运的勇气……从少年到丈夫，从父亲到儿子，朋也的每一次蜕变，都让我们看到“成长”的本质——不是变得强大无坚不摧，而是学会在脆弱时坚持，在失去后珍惜。当汐在雪地里倒下，当时间回溯重获圆满，那种从绝望到希望的巨大情感冲击，早已超越了游戏本身，成为刻在记忆里的深刻体验。

关掉游戏，回到现实的喧嚣与平淡，《Clannad》带来的触动却从未消散。曾经觉得“家人的陪伴”是理所当然，如今才读懂秋生早苗对渚的呵护背后，是父母对孩子最深沉的托举；曾经对父母的唠叨满心不耐烦，如今想起朋也与父亲和解的瞬间，才明白那些看似笨拙的关心，都是藏在岁月里的爱；曾经在生活中遭遇挫折时总想逃避，如今却记得渚那句“能前进的话就要一直前进”，懂得了成长本就是在跌倒后一次次爬起。

它让我们重新审视身边的羁绊：那些日常里的拌嘴、失意时的安慰、相聚时的欢笑，都是“家”的具象化表达；它让我们学会珍惜当下：生命中的每一次相遇都是馈赠，每一段陪伴都值得感恩，不必等到失去才追悔莫及；它更让我们坦然面对悲伤：生活本就有悲欢离合，眼泪不是软弱的证明，而是释放情绪、继续前行的力量。屏幕里的朋也找到了自己的“光”，而屏幕外的我们，也在这份感动中，看清了生活的方向。

《Clannad》用整个故事，为我们上了一堂关于人生的必修课，它教会我们的，是刻进骨子里的生存智慧：

  朋也有过迷茫，渚有过脆弱，每个人都有自己的缺陷，但正是这些不完美，让彼此的陪伴更具意义，让成长更显真实
• 学会“承担责任”：从对爱人的承诺，到对孩子的守护，再到对父母的感恩，责任不是负担，而是让人生变得厚重的基石，是“家”之所以为家的核心；
• 学会“与过去和解”：朋也与父亲的隔阂、琴美对父母的思念、芳野佑介的过往遗憾，都在告诉我们，放下执念，与过去和解，才能轻装前行；
• 学会“传递温暖”：渚用温柔治愈朋也，朋也用爱守护汐，早苗用微笑传递希望，善意与温暖是会传染的，它能照亮黑暗，驱散迷茫。

If you're thinking of checking it out then perhaps start on the map I played (seed 548409612). It's huge and in total darkness. Fortunately I revealed the map and found where several of the towns are. The screenshots are in the guide below.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3596845249

There are many towns in the game but they all have the same vendors and are functionally identical. It would be great if they were unique in some way or there was a reputation system that enabled you to grind rep to earn unique gear. How they play currently is you can roll up to any town destroy everything, kill all the animals and no one reacts.  

Inventory management needs some love. There is no crafting from chests which means you need to have all materials in your inventory before you can make anything. There is quick stack to nearby chests but the range is pitiful. You need to be basically touching a chest for the quick stack to register. You can't label chests nor is there a search function across chests, so you need to remember where you've stored your items.

The other main issue with the game is how the developers have implemented multiplayer. You and your mates can play and do everything together EXCEPT the last boss. For some strange reason, the developers thought it would be a good idea in a multiplayer game to force players to fight the last boss SOLO. If your're the host and you've beaten the last boss you'll be left to twiddle your thumbs waiting until your mates are successful. This is such a dumb idea!

Other than the multiplayer quirk I enjoyed Keplerth. It's a bit rough around the edges but the gameplay is solid.
