Let me just quickly say before getting into the game itself, I played this back on release on a PC I no longer have. It ran well with some adjustments and I was able to play the game without interruption. I recently installed the game on my newer PC (the specs of which is strictly speaking better in every way) because I felt like playing it, and I found that I could not find a way to get the game to work without serious issues that prevented me from being able to enjoy the experience. So I have to stress this: If you buy the game because the actual gameplay sounds cool to you, which it should because the game itself is awesome, keep an eye on that time played because you want to be able to refund it if you find you can't fix the stuttering issues. As far as I can tell it has nothing to do with the actual ability of your hardware so it is basically luck of the draw for whether it will work for you or not.

Anyway, Wilds Hearts is to me the design philosophy of Monster Hunter: Rise, but perfected. If Rise was your favorite monster hunter game, or even if it was just something you found to be an enjoyable change of pace for MH, Wild Hearts is a game you need to check out. It is a fast paced, resource spending, somewhat arcadey version of the Monster Hunter series that just has so many little parts of the game that really build an awesome experience.

The main difference between MH and Wild Hearts is that where Monster Hunter is a position focused game, Wild hearts is more of a timing game. Monsters in MH have very little tracking, but your dodges have almost no i frames, so you can avoid most attacks by simply moving to the right place when you see an animation start, but you aren't really going to be able to reactively dodge that move. Wild Hearts is the reverse. Kemono have tons of tracking and you will basically never be able to avoid an attack by simply getting out of the way (except for when you are in the air, which can be relatively often for a lot of weapons), but instead you have access to a lot of i frame tools whether that be dodge rolls, slides, or as we will discuss certain Karakuri. MIght as well talk about those now.

Karakuri are Wild Hearts' unique mechanic that it brings to the Monster Hunting genre. Basically, you build up a resource called Threads by attacking monsters. With that resource, you can build several different Basic Karakuri. For example the simplest is just a Box that you can climb. But there is also stuff like a spring that lets you jump further and a hook thing that lets you attack it to a wall or monster to enable you to either sit on it or to boost yourself upwards. They all have value in and of themselves that you will want to use often both for exploring the maps and fighting the Kemono. For example Boxes stacked 3 high allow you to do a special jumping attack, and because you can build karakuri while in another animation (such as a long commitment from a big maul) you can build a spring at your feet to give you i frames and launch you out of the way of an incoming Kemono attack.

Not only that, but building these basic Karakuri in certain orders can create Fusion Karakuri. These are more advance contraptions that have more direct effects. The most basic is simply a Wall that enables you to do those jumping attacks, but also acts as a barrier that Kemono have trouble breaking. But there are also things such as Traps that enable you to keep a Kemono in one place for sometime (just like a MH trap), a timed bomb contraption that blows up after a few seconds, or a  diffuser that gives an AoE heal for you and any friends you are hunting with. You can think of these tools as similar in use case to special Wirebug moves from Rise. 

It is hard to really emphasize just how well this Karakuri system comes together and how amazingly well it melds with the weapons. You can really feel like every weapon was designed to work well with Karakuri. That isn't to say these weapons don't hold up without karakuri, but unlike in Rise with its Wirebug moves, Karakuri just flow into your weapon's movement and combos extremely well. 

And there is so much more to talk about. I haven't even mentioned how much you can customize the world with Dragon Karakuri and the webs of tools you can use to enable fast map traversal or ways to ambush Kemono as they cross certain areas, or even create farms. There are so many parts of Monster Hunter they Wild hearts has turned into an entire minigame, and it just adds so many layers of mechanics that are completely optional but really fun to engage with. If you want to simply just hunt the Kemono and not worry too much about the tertiary mechanics of the game, you can and you won't feel gimped by not doing so. But if you want to really dive into it, you really do feel rewarded for doing so and I love that they have really made a Monster Hunting game that feels like more than just simply a Boss Rush game in the way that Monster Hunter's tend to be.

Overall I think Wild Hearts had the potential to be a proper competitor to the Monster Hunter series if the game wasn't destroyed by a bad launch due to poor optimization that plagues the game to this day. And if you can get the game to work on your machine, it is absolutely worth playing.

本作は、運送屋シミュレータである。
開始当初は小さい運送屋営業所で、持ち込みの荷物を梱包して大手運送屋に引き継いで金を稼ぐ。
段々と自社流通の割合を増やして、最終的には100%自社流通の運送屋に育てるシミュレータ。

営業所でのタスク以外に、車を運転して配送先や街中の宅配ボックスに届けるなどのタスクも発生する。
しかしながら一日が短く、届けるほうのタスクを行うと営業時間内に営業所に戻ることは至難の業。
そのため、宅配をするならばスタッフを雇って営業所を回さなければならないが、まぁスタッフのAIが結構ひどい。
アプデで多少マシになったが、AIスタッフには窓口業務と車での宅配しかやらせてはいけない。
荷物を車に積み込んだりする業務を任せると、なぜかずっとプレイヤーに手渡してきたりする。
どんなに離れていようが超能力でプレイヤーに荷物が手渡され、プレイヤーは何度荷物を捨てても次の瞬間に荷物を持つことになる。
またAIスタッフが次に掴もうとしていた荷物をプレイヤーが横取りしてしまうとスタッフの描画がおかしくなり、人外の行動を始める。とても気持ち悪い動きで笑ってしまう。

現状、AIスタッフに任せられない、店舗内での車への荷物の積み込みをやるしかなく、それ以外の作業をAIスタッフに任せるゲームになっている。

パレットやハンドパレットが実装されており、最大のトラックを買ってパレットを用意しておけばパレットに荷物が置かれてハンドパレットで楽に積み込みができたりするのかなと思っていたが全くそんなことはない。
パレットは買うとハンドパレットでしか移動できず、ただただ邪魔なだけ。
ハンドパレットで直接パレットごとトラックへの積み込みなんかはできない。
パレットをまとめて買うと、梱包された状態で積み上がって納品されるが、これを開梱すると荷物の上で開梱されてハンドパレットを差し込むことができず、パレットを移動することができなくなり詰む。
ハンドパレットや台車などを操作しているときのプレイヤーはとんでもない怪力で、そのまま車に突っ込んだりすると車が吹っ飛ぶが、パレットは移動できない。
カートを操作している時は割と壁とかもすり抜ける。カート最強。
カートだと直接、荷物を車に全部下ろすみたいなことができるので、現状ではパレットなどは不要でカートだけあれば良い感じになっている。
棚なども設置できるが、地面置きの荷物もAIスタッフがちゃんと認識して持っていってくれるので、棚に荷物を整理する意味がない。
変にAIが優秀なせいで、最終的にプレイヤーがやることはトラックへの荷物の積み込みと、梱包資材の注文だけになってしまうのがちょっと残念。

全体的には出来が良いと思うので、今後に期待。

Изначально хотел писать любовную тираду этой игре про то, как круто тактические элементы Ready or Not стыкуются с классической формулой Hotline Miami; про замечательный редактор уровней, в котором я провозился двое суток и смастерил ОГРОМНЫЙ полицейский участок Raccoon City и всю приграничную улицу в масштабе 1 к 1; немного пожаловаться на то, что врагам в игре очень не хватает умения патрулировать (из-за чего всё действо ощущается излишне простой периодически).

Но всё омрачилось на третьи сутки, когда во время финальной полировки редактор уровней стал давать сбои. Сперва это были незначительные баги вроде дверей, которые вылетают из петель во время геймплея, если задать им отрицательный показатель поворота (я лично как раскрыл этот баг, так ещё и нашёл фикс - тестерское пособие можно прислать на карту ВТБ, если есть желание). 

Потом сюжетные объекты вроде бомб и растяжек стали периодически спавниться невидимыми или под текстурами других предметов. Для избежания оверлапинга у объектов в игре есть параметр depth. И я прекрасно осведомлен о нём. И он прекрасно работает. Когда дело касается чего угодно кроме БОМБ. Бомбы даже с глубиной -3 будут неизбежно находиться ПОД текстурой туалета с глубиной 0. Для тех кто в танке, чем меньше глубина - тем выше приоритет у предмета, и выше шанс, что он будет визуально виден на экране, так сказать. Такая, вот, проблемка. 

А у растяжек на уровне игрового движка какая-то очень странная механика, связанная с их отображением. Сама растяжка состоит из трёх частей (2 зеленых бомбочки и нить между ними), и у меня сложилось впечатление, что пока игрок ЧЁТКО и ЯСНО не увидит всех трёх частей, она не отрисовывается у него на экране В ПРИНЦИПЕ! 
И в чем нюанс: даже если 1 пиксель одной из бомбочек случайно оверлапнется другими объектами (и даже СТЕНАМИ), то растяжка будет невидимой навсегда! 

Казалось бы, это проблемы, с которыми можно работать: ну просто ставь растяжки по-человечески, без оверлапов! И бомбы клади прямо на пол, чтобы они не перекрывались столами и стульями. Да, всё так. Tetris Forever es un juego increíble. Trae versiones icónicas de Tetris que, aunque faltan las de NES y Game Boy, se compensan con otras muy buenas. Además, varias de ellas nunca habían salido de Japón, y es genial poder disfrutarlas legalmente aquí.

Técnicamente, en el modo Time Warp hay una variante que se parece bastante al Tetris de Game Boy, así que es lo más cercano que tenemos.

Me encanta poder jugar la versión de Electronika 60, creada por Alexey Pajitnov, la versión original del Tetris. Aunque claramente es una recreación fiel (porque emular una Electronika 60 sería mucho más complicado), sigue siendo una experiencia muy especial.

Y los juegos que no son Tetris… ¿qué puedo decir? Hatris es el segundo mejor juego creado por Alexey después del Tetris, sin duda uno de mis favoritos entre los que no son Tetris. También me gustó Go, lanzado por Bullet-Proof Software; una linda adición.

Ahora, sobre el documental: una maravilla. Me encantó poder profundizar más en la historia de Tetris, de Henk y Alexey, más allá de la película y del documental de la BBC.

Recomiendo totalmente la compra del juego. Sin duda, vale la pena.

As a Cricket fan, Cricket 24 is a solid step forward compared to previous Big Ant titles, but it still carries some of the old problems that cricket fans know too well. 

The Good
1. Improved graphics: Player faces, stadium lighting, and animations look noticeably better. Not perfect, but a clear upgrade.
2. Licensing: Having more official teams and leagues really adds to the immersion. Career mode feels more authentic now.
3. Batting feels smoother: Shot timing is more consistent, and playing different strokes feels satisfying, especially when timing a cover drive perfectly.
4. Atmosphere & presentation: Crowd noise, commentary, and stadium ambience genuinely improve the match experience.

The Not-So-Good
1. Bugs & glitches: Classic Big Ant issues. Weird fielding animations, sudden drops in frame rate, and players teleporting/overthrowing for no reason.
2. Fielding AI: Still the weakest part. Fielders react late or throw to the wrong end at crucial moments.
3. Career mode lacks depth: Fun at first, but progression feels slow and repetitive.
4. UI feels outdated: Menus and navigation could be much more modern and intuitive.

Overall Cricket 24 is enjoyable for fans who love cricket games, and it definitely has its moments. But it still needs patches and improvements for the experience to feel polished. If you’re already invested in Big Ant games, you’ll appreciate the upgrades. If you’re new, expect fun gameplay mixed with some frustration.

For me it mostly just came to working out two or three shots that always worked and hitting them over and over again through club, state & ultimately international level. Ultimately the experience just left me feeling kind of empty by the end as it required very little beyond the initial learning curve and no real problem solving once that way of 'winning' was worked out.

If you are a cricket fan you may enjoy this for a time as it is a functional game that works and doesn't have too many bugs but I wouldn't call it a good game, much less a great one.

A great little game that sets out to do one thing and does it perfectly.

This is a team combat racing game, that is easy to pick up and play, and difficult to master. It lets you play as the insane speed maniac orks of the WH40K setting.

The WH40K ambiance is on point and there's no orkier game around. Just hearing players scream "Waagh!" in chat will bring a smile to your face. The art direction is great, and the graphics really look like the WH40K figurines. The weapon and engine sounds in particular are superb.

The combat racing is team based, and while I generally hate multiplayer games, here even if you suck you can feel you're making a contribution, even if that's adding orky chaos to the proceedings.

There are two play modes which are quite different: one where you score points racing through several rally-style tracks and other where you deliver bombs to your opponents’ mobile fortress while avoiding your own from being bombed. Appropriately enough, you can always get points by destroying you opponents, and hunting you enemies and/or blocking their advance is a valid strategy.

The vehicles are all fun to play, easy to learn, and relevant to the gameplay. If you switch vehicles frequently, you'll notice there's rarely a moment you'll say "bummer, this one sucks". They all have their strengths and weaknesses and can play a role in all race modes and stages.

All I can add is, kudos to the developers, the game is great and deserves a bigger player base. Get krumping boyz!

历时大约四年终于第一次通关游戏，为手残的我撒花鼓励~ 

不追求全成就而是游戏体验的我来说说这款游戏的迷人之处。横向卷轴平台游戏对我来说本身自带一种怀旧，最初接触游戏的时候玩过一些，比如马里奥、超级食肉男孩、蜡笔小新等，这种熟悉感会让害怕动作类的我稍微得到些安抚吧。

游戏最核心的玩法就是三位可操作角色的切换，每一位使用不同技能，这种玩法在今天已经十分熟悉，但不得不说法师的技能让我对游戏的自由度一题在四年前有了新的认识，当然那个时候我还没有玩过塞尔达，后者是向我定义了什么是开放世界的游戏，再次刷新了我对自由度的理解。有了法师的加入，[spoiler] 或者说捣乱，我在初玩这个游戏的时候基本都不是在好好打怪过关，[/spoiler]收获了有趣过瘾的游戏体验，后期几个角色配合更多，[spoiler] 我在紧张下乱来的时机也少了[/spoiler]。个人由于手残缘故很喜欢游戏有除开技术层面的玩法，无事也会去摸索这种设计的存在，和我有相似喜好的玩家们十分推荐入手~

关卡设计上难度层层递进，又巧妙地让三位角色以不同的组合都可以过关，于是自带一层玩法上的解谜，虽然每个关卡中自身的解谜都是很经典或者说比较简单的，但两者配合起来十分有趣。相信二周目的时候，参照成就列表的一些要求，也许可以带来另一层丰富的游戏体验，手残的我大概是没有机会享受这个了，但谁又说得好玩更多动作游戏的几年以后的我会不会接下这个挑战呢？人生的广度正在于可能性与未知。

作为我喜欢的第二个动作类游戏，（第一款是《伊苏：起源》，按游玩时间而不是个人喜爱度排的这个顺序，两者相比，我更喜欢《三位一体》）接触初期就一口气打到最后一关卡住，并且卡了四年 lol 究其原因并不是最后一关有多么难，而是遇到了一个心理上难以克服的问题：倒数计时。当我能够以理性分析去安抚倒计时带给我的压力时，很多考试和死线的障碍也迎刃而解，今年再玩这个游戏时，[spoiler] 我发现与我跳跃和移动的速度相比，倒数计时可以忽略不计，[/spoiler]笑着明白了过去的自己早已轻轻穿过迷雾来到了当下。

回顾人生，许多事情都是如此，当下无法解决的事情，很多时候不是自己不够好或不够努力，而是被卡在某个无法克服的心理或认知障碍上，外因大多只是推脱或者逃避的借口。譬如我从前觉得我不适合玩游戏，《最终幻想14》的亲友们让我明白了来自伙伴们的关爱是什么，高难游戏是什么，团队合作是什么，技术提高又是什么。与大家相识一年半以后，我开始称呼自己为玩家，这是从前想也没有想过的事。

《三》里卡住的最后一关，其实前后并没有打很多次。今天通关时，就打到当日的第二遍。当我看着英雄们一个个死去，忽然发现自己的左手在发抖。这是我打游戏卡住时一个经典状态，心态有些紧绷就会反应在手指上。我深吸一口气，想到正念冥想老师Jon Kabat Zin说的接受全部的自己同时不必努力奋斗，我给了自己一个目标：我打七次，如果七次不行就关游戏，明天再来。

这样想着，英雄们又在上一个存档点刷新满血复活了。我将更为沉着的手指再次放到WASD上，一边向前，一边熟悉方向与跳跃的互相配合。对关卡的熟悉及更为冷静的操作让我在一个角色死去之后也没有慌张，而是马上熟悉用剩下的角色互相配合跳跃和战斗。终于，场景发生变化，我来到了最后的平台…

有一天，友人千山跟我说，打MMO（当然是我最喜欢的FF14啦）会紧张是因为单机打得不够多。我想了几天，决定要打通《三位一体》。原本起床后心情不大好的状态也随着投入游戏而缓解，通关的时候才知道原来游戏早已打到最后。看着片尾字幕我兴奋地鼓掌，像多年前在影院看了一场喜欢的电影后起立鼓掌一样，表达有幸接触到这个作品的欢欣及对制作者们的敬意。

+ Sidequests and random NPCs are a lot of fun.

- Small bugs still present, like getting stuck because an elevator didn't start. (reloading fixed them).
- Some of the combat is a bit messy/chaotic.
- Why do ladders not work?

A strong recommend and a very fun way to spend a few gaming sessions.

As it stands right now, if you like classic Dark Souls but with more challenge then this is the game for you. My complaints are the early game is far too limiting with point spending. Having to find new body parts that allow your stat upgrades to then be bought is a special kind of grinding/searching. Second is the bow and how difficult it is to hit enemies from afar, but at least you can recover your ammo on the ground when you miss. 
The potential is there for it to stand on its own with varying weapon types, emphasis on co-op, and, what got me interested, the robots resembling Bionicle with interchangeable body parts.

a bit of context. I have played 2 demo versions of this game. First, a while back, when it was just one large island with 3 biomes and second from the previous Steam Next Fest

Game is pretty good. I like the visuals and the vibe. Really reminds me of Dark Souls, with the decayed world and the remnants of what it was before. Performance is also pretty good - never dropping below 60fps (usually around 90 and 110+ in dungeons and other enclosed spaces) and i'm playing at 4k Epic settings (r7 5800x and rx 9070 xt). Combat feels a bit clunky as you cant animation cancel the recovery of your attacks, but that goes for the enemies as well. So you can bait their attack and counter freely. The mechanic of upgrading your character from salvaged parts is fun, as it allows you to easily respec at any Bonfire. Basic enemies have some variaty - mostly other humanoid robots with different weapons, armor and sometimes abilities - but the random drops mean that you might have to farm for a while to get a specific part. Weirdly enough i fought the First boss twice (resummoned him by mistake) and he dropped the same part (it might be fixed drop in Early Access version, but in previous demo i played it was random)
in the 10 hours i played, i have not yet completed everything, but I have found 3 bosses (excluding the tutorial Crab). The First boss is the same from the Demo that is still available (as of when this review is posted). The second boss i found is this blob creature that game me a lot of trouble in melee combat, but it was ok with a bow and the third one is this ball transformer type that is just difficult (high hp and damage) and has a dungeon without checkpoints before it.
One last thing. I found the balance of the different classes / builds is a bit off. If you build pure Wizard or Ranger you are way too fragile - the body parts with magic or dex / perception stats, dont provide any HP or armor stat, and the actual armor pieces provide very little (if any). Meanwhile Melee Strength (Torque) gets both HP and Armor stats from the body parts and even more armor stat from wearable armor pieces. What i managed to build was Wizard = 14hp, 2 armor. Warrior = 42hp, 20 armor (and even the warrior build could die easily in some situation, while wizard is one-shot from before first boss onwards to the end of the game)

Overall Very Nice Game, would recommend for both solo and co-op with friends

Wo Long: Fallen Dynasty is one of those titles that probably won't change anyone's life, but it will drag you into its world if you're foolish enough to let yourself get captured, like yours truly.
Developed by Team Ninja, the same team behind Nioh, Ninja Gaiden, and Dead or Alive, Wo Long is a game that's entirely similar to Nioh in every way, sometimes feeling like a well-crafted mod for it. If you don't know Nioh, well, it's a sort of alternative souls-like that starts from FromSoftware's formula but expands into very different territory. The loot system, storytelling, and game maps are straight out of Nioh, with the difference being that the plot—this usual mix of ancient history and legend—takes place in China during the Three Kingdoms period (184-280 AD). The differences, however, lie in the progression system, which is much simplified compared to other titles, rewarding experimentation with different builds once you understand the 5 elements system, which replaces classic RPG stats. The pace is frenetic, with combat that's less tactical than Nioh's but more oriented toward a deflection and posture-break system, similar to Sekiro's. The difficulty isn't particularly high, except for sporadic peaks, mostly in the three DLC areas and the final maps. Since many contents and some QoL features were added with the extremely expensive DLCs (which I luckily found at a bargain price), the feeling is that many of these features (including multiplayer with co-op and PvP) were added in a somewhat unorganic way, barely enriching the experience. The third DLC has more interesting endgame content, but at the end of my playthrough where I got every single trophy, I have to say that NG+ isn't exactly inviting. In conclusion, I believe Wo Long is a rock-solid action RPG with some souls-like elements (according to Team Ninja's vision) but not a particularly memorable title.
If you look past some optimization issues, Wo Long can be an interesting title for those seeking frenetic combat and respectable difficulty, but without the punitive mechanics of a true souls-like; for those who prefer simpler, more linear exploration over complicated interconnected worlds; for those who want to enjoy a story instead of groping in the dark trying to piece together events from clues.
I recommend it on sale, though.

A fun space survival game with some flaws. Want to float around breathtaking vistas filled with asteroids, crashed spaceships and space cows while investigating what caused all the mayhem? This game might be for you.


There's four main points that some people may love or hate about it:

1: The humor. To me it's hit and miss, and most of the bad jokes are frontloaded, probably because the opening section has such a buttload of them, making it feel like there's never more than a minute of quiet between the jokes, often less.

2: The speed at which you traverse. This never bothered me, yes you are quite slow, or rather, you move at a decent speed but the distances travelled are enormous and since you have finite air in your spacesuit you don't just need to go somewhere but often go back and forth multiple times. But to me complaining about this is like complaining about any other survival game mechanic like needing to eat, it just isn't for everyone, but there's nothing wrong with it.
Besides, both the speed and air tanks get upgraded throughout the game.

3: There are 4 areas to the main game, the first one which is the longest (like 4/5 of the main game's length,) is openworld while the other three are more or less linear. Once you leave the openworld part of the game you abandon whatever you had built in that first section, yes you can return to previous sections of the game but there really is no point to it. 
Since part 1 allows you to build your own space station and some people really love that sort of stuff this upsets them, completely understandable. But the space station is in all honesty a completely superfluous part of the game, you only need to build it for a single module that allows you to research items that you haven't found complete blueprints for, and as far as I know, maybe all of those actually can be found without that module anyways. I waited until the very end of the first section until I built my station and did find it a bit odd how much stuff I'd collected that could be built there yet none of it really mattered.

4: The game does not guide you much besides quest markers and the comments of your built in AI companion in your space suit when you get really close to something interesting. Some people will love this, the game does have a robust system of tabs where you can read up on all the dialog and messages you've had, as well as all items you've discovered to find out both their purpose and what sort of places to find more of it, so as long as you interact with all the games systems that shouldn't be much of a problem. However sometimes when you have a quest marker in say a crashed spaceship, the way to get into said ship may be extremely obscure and you either stumble upon the solution on how to enter it, or you have to scour every detail of the outside of it to find some tiny thing that will allow you to progress.


The game looks really good, although the indie budget does show through in a lack of animations for many regular tasks which are often just a circular loading bar on screen while you interact with something.

There are coffins with AI which you can extract encrypted tapes from, there's a reader for those in your starting location which I never realised since I never returned there once I'd left so I only got to use the tapes once I reached the end of the openworld section of the game at which time I realised they contained coordinates to points of interest... all of which I'd already discovered by just playing the game normally anyways. I guess they're there for those less adventurous that need a kick in the butt to get on with the exploring.

There were several items that you could make that just trolled you early on by making you waste resources. But also, later there were ones that I just never found a use for  like the beef grenades, Scraper, bribes, chewing gum after you'd researched it. And then there's the soil analyser which can be used in a few spots but it really never does anything, so I guess you can toss that on the troll pile maybe, unless I missed something, it was never needed to progress anyways.
There's also the kenotron which you could build which is used for one section of the space station you can build, but that section you don't even need...

While the open world section rewards exploration with either stuff that helps you or eastereggs, the more linear areas of the game for some reason do not, like at all. I even found a spot where I fell through the floor once and had to reload a save in one remote part of this section and it wasn't even through weird geometry, just a simple flat floor. (For those wondering where, it was the forest dome, and just don't go to the far back of it to avoid this.)


The DLC, Leia Center: 
Basically a completely different game where you are put into a test of surviving for 30 minutes without access to any oxygen station.
It's all about replaying the same thing over and over and memorising where stuff can be found and planning the best route to collect everything without dying from asphyxiation. When you reach certain thresholds your future runs get another starting item.

I can't say it's anything I'm interested in playing so I quit after my second attempt.

For that low price, you can't go wrong.

At the moment, I cannot recommend this game to others even though I am, for the most part, enjoying myself and think this game has some good things going for it. There are a lot of aspects of the game that feel far more polished than others, and unfortunately the structure of the game feels amateurish at this point in the game. After beating the first boss, I can say that so far it's been little more than getting keys to unlock doors that themselves contain more keys and locked doors. Beat a puzzle? You get a simple key. Beat a series of puzzle rooms with enemies sprinkled throughout? You get an emerald key that unlocks a few different emerald doors. Beat the boss? You get- hold on, you might want to sit down for this- a BIG KEY which you can use to unlock a BIG DOOR. With the lack of segmented stages, ever-growing map, and level design that are all reminiscent of Metroidvanias, why not implement the most appealing part of that design by having the keys also serve as upgrades for character growth? It helps make the world feel less repetitive and acts as a reward that will stick with the players throughout their journey instead of being forgotten as quickly as the door it was used on disappears.

The story, dialogue, and cutscenes are also too generic and exposition-heavy to enjoy. The opening cutscene, while containing nice pixel art, is the worst offender. The text moves far too fast at times to read, you are inundated with information that takes 50 words to convey what a game like Shovel Knight did in 10. What’s worse about it is that almost ALL of the information told to us in the opening is reiterated with more subtlety and investment in the opening gameplay section. We don’t need to be told that Ezra is a street urchin when not two minutes later we’re playing as him breaking into a keep for food. We don’t need to be told that the soldiers are bad news when Ezra is nearly killed by them for wanting to eat in the middle of a famine. Beyond the opening cutscene, the dialogue ranges from passable albeit trope-filled to meandering exposition dumps with no sense of weight or mystery. I might have been more interested in the story of the owl people, the human empires that came before, and the discovery of the Gnosis… if I had any say in discovering that information. Instead, a contrivance ghost ambushes me and lays it all out in painful detail, robbing what has happened or is happening of any and all intrigue. On top of that, even the technical delivery of this exposition is flawed, as the last word of a line tends to jump to the next line as it types out on screen, making it hard to read, and there are multiple points where a single idea is spread over multiple text boxes but the second box only has one or two words in them. Was *every* word in the prior text box absolutely necessary that the end of the thought had to be stapled on the back?

The manual camera barely transitions from the default view to the extended view, causing snapping and jerky motion that’s incredibly unpleasant to look at. Thankfully the manual camera isn’t needed, especially since it also prevents you from taking any other actions while using it.

The “lighting” for certain assets is out of place and distracting. The light brown platforms and ladders used throughout the tower are also used in the dimly lit keep at the start of the game. Even though the background is pitch black with a scant few candles to indicate deep shadows all around, both Ezra and the thing he’s standing on feel like they’re painted in construction yellow by comparison.

The music, while not bad, also leaves a gap in the mood that isn’t filled by anything else. The pieces are vaguely serviceable to the area, but none come to mind or invoke any particular mood aside from chip-tune dungeon crawl.

The corpse-run mechanic feels unnecessary. The upgrade material isn’t as vital as souls from the Souls games, nor is it needed in a slew of different purchases like in Silksong, so there’s less added tension and more annoyance that on top of being set back in progress I now need to get back to the place that killed me to slap a chest before I die again. Because of this game’s linearity (at least at this point in the game), there’s not even much of a risk-reward decision because the place where you died is almost certainly the only place left for you to progress.

Control in general is solid, but lacks a lot of grace other games build in. It feels like there’s no buffer system for when you input a jump when you are a few pixels off of the ground, which results in it sometimes feeling like your jump input is being ignored. Additionally, while the rest of the vertical movement is quick and snappy, the ledge get-up animation is weirdly sluggish and difficult to intuit from pressing the jump button. I want to be able to jump off of a ledge in the same way I jump off of a ladder, but instead I first need to look in the opposite direction and then jump, lest I be punished with a getup animation slower than Ganondorf's in Smash Bros

The puzzles are generally enjoyable, with a nice balance between simple pieces and multi-faceted interactions between them. My biggest gripe is the tedium of solving some puzzles, particularly the ones that involve dropping your sword at one spot to change one thing somewhere else, going back to your sword to grab it, going back to the other end of the room to change one other thing, going BACK to the first spot to drop the sword AGAIN… you get the idea.

Combat is pretty good with a strong vision about how swinging a massive sword should feel. The air attack transitioning into a down-stab is great, and it all lends into a patient playstyle that reinforces the puzzle-like approach to the entire game. My biggest gripe with it is the missed opportunity to further add to the Big-Sword-Fantasy, namely the lack of increasing damage when dropping from higher up. As far as I can tell, there’s no scaling, which is such a missed opportunity, and if that happens to be an future upgrade then my question then becomes why it wasn’t included in the base kit when apparently the sword needing to shoot laser beams at full health takes priority for Big-Sword-Fantasy.

I originally thought this would be a positive review, as I enjoyed myself and feel proven correct in how the moment-to-moment gameplay feels solid and rewarding to hone in on. The puzzles are already good and bound to get better with more complexity, and the bosses mix between fast and slow attacks to make the end-lag-heavy dodge roll more of a careful decision instead of a panic button to be spammed. However, there’s simply too many snagging details that hold it back at the moment for me to want to recommend it to others as a product. Regardless, I wish the dev the best of luck on any and all future endeavors and that these shortcomings can be an opportunity to make this game or future games even better.

This game is pretty good overall, but I wouldn't recommend playing it for the 100% like I did. 
Multiple problems arise when you start to hit the endgame : 

- The game has potential, but a lot of it is wasted by the developer's lack of vision for the game, or organisation.

- The endgame is tedious. It's just, waking up, taking scrap deals, sending your workers there, then waiting 5 minutes for the game to give you the option to sleep ("It's too early" at 10am, but 12pm is appropriate to go to bed ?)

- Despite most of the game having automation, you still have to do some things manually. The separating zone is a conveyor belt, but you can't connect it to other conveyor belts, and the materials bin aren't moved by the conveyors.

- Some things don't make sense, despite it being good like the sorting agents taking the same amount of time to order 500KG of materials than they do 10KG.

- Why a time system ? 9pm is the limit, but you can still go to scrap deals, still take orders, still do everything. The only use to changing days is updating contracts, which could have benn implemented without a day-night cycle in the first place.

- Scrap deal agents always come back later than the latest time you can send them out, which means you an only have them do one scrap deal each day, without possibility of upgrading that.

- The upgrade that gives you better worth for your star of each worker is quite messy. All you agents will be upgraded but newer ones that appear on the computer won't always spawn upgraded.

- Conveyor belts aren't explained at all. I spent 10 Hours in the game before understanding that the multi exit conveyor had multiple exits that were configurable, and thought it always had 3 exits active.

To conclude, this game is still pretty good, but the dev didn't seem to put too much mind as to how the player should progress in the game, which shows everywhere. A lot of features aren't explained, or are badly implemented. The dev should have thought how each system would integrate with each other instead of adding them all wothout much thought. I still recommend playing it but lvl 2 should be the end with how tedious finishing it is.

Journal de bord du Resolute. Me voilà enfin assignée à la section ingénierie du vaisseau. J'avoue être un peu nerveuse, n'étant pas vraiment familière avec cet environnement. Je ne connais Starfleet qu'à travers sa grande réputation au sein de la Fédération. Je me suis faite cependant accueillir chaleureusement par un collègue très motivé et j'ai entendu dire qu'une nouvelle seconde officier particulièrement talentueuse venait d'être promue, de quoi me rassurer. Notre première mission : atténuer les tensions entre deux nations au bord de la guerre. Les décisions à prendre risquent d'être difficiles... et cet orage ionique persistant ne me dit rien qui vaille. Notre unité risque d'être aussi mise à rude épreuve. Ma première expédition aura-t-elle alors un goût d'aventure ou de turbulences ?

❤ Le scénario nous embarque dès les premiers instants, en prenant le temps de poser les bases de l'univers avant de décoller peu à peu vers des scènes plus mouvementées. Il n'est pas necessaire d'être un fin connaisseur de l'univers ST pour se lancer dans cette mission. Le jeu parvient en effet à être à la fois accessible aux nouvelles recrues tout en offrant aux vétérans plusieurs références et clins d'oeil au lore de la série. Le fait d'incarner deux personnages aux rangs différents, l'un étant au poste de commandement et l'autre dans la partie technique, permet de nous faire vivre ce périple à plusieurs échelles. Et si leurs actions semblent indépendantes, on se rend vite compte à quel point chaque membre est crucial et comment toutes leurs décisions finissent par rentrer en résonance pour maintenir ce vaisseau à flot, ce qui est assez jouissif. Et on aura bien besoin que chacun fasse son travail, car au fil du chemin, les rebondissements s'enchaînent nous menant à des moments critiques qui nous gardent bien sous tension jusqu'à la fin. Après toute cette frénésie, cela donne presque envie de repartir immédiatement pour une nouvelle aventure interstellaire. 
❤ Les deux personnages jouables sont très différents tant par leur rang que par leur personnalité, mais c'est ce contraste qui les rend attachants. D'un côté, la charismatique Jara dégage une autorité naturelle et un grand professionnalisme, tandis que Carter apporte plus de chaleur et de positivité. Ainsi, même si chacun de leur choix peut jouer sur des émotions similaires, leur tempérament distinct rend chaque situation unique. Aussi, ils ont déjà un vécu qu'on nous dévoile sans grande exposition forcée, à travers quelques dialogues et détails. Cela leur confère de la profondeur et suffit à comprendre leurs aspirations. On gravite donc autour de ces deux protagonistes dont les approches opposées convergent néanmoins vers un but commun ; Jara doit prouver sa valeur auprès de son équipage afin de gagner leur confiance, et Carter cherche la reconnaissance de son supérieur. En les aidant à atteindre cet objectif, on découvre parallèlement les autres membres du vaisseau tout en se faisant petit à petit une place au sein de Starfleet, pour le meilleur ou pour le pire.

+/- Il faut l'admettre, les graphismes ne sont clairement pas le point fort du jeu. Les modèles des personnages et des décors sont plutôt quelconques, les textures manquent de relief, et les expressions faciales ainsi que les mouvements corporels sont assez rigides. Malgré cela, la direction artistique réussit à compenser ces faiblesses grace à une bonne diversité de race alien, au design des diverses technologies mais surtout au soin apporté au Resolute, dans sa conception et sa disposition. On en connaitrait quasiment chaque recoin à la fin du voyage ; d'ailleurs le jeu nous donne la possibilité de naviguer dans son intérieur depuis les bonus, une petite touche sympathique qui accentue le sentiment d'être un officier à part entière du Starfleet. 
+/- L'ambiance sonore contribue de manière efficace à l'immersion. Les bruitages nous plongent facilement dans cet univers SF, et les compositions orchestrales se déploient de manière épique digne d'un bon space opera. Le doublage anglais, quant à lui, est excellent et les acteurs parviennent à insuffler plus d'émotions à leur personnage que ne le permettent leur modèle 3D ; petite mention d'ailleurs à la voix de Spock, étonnamment proche de celle de l'acteur original. En revanche, la balance sonore manque d'équilibre : la musique prend souvent le dessus sur les dialogues, qui eux-mêmes varient d'intensité selon les scènes. Même après quelques ajustements dans les paramètres, certaines répliques ne ressortent toujours pas assez. 
+/- La trame du scénario repose principalement sur des choix que l'on effectue, et ceux ci donnent souvent lieu à des dilemmes intéressants. Ils ne sont jamais manichéens puisqu'il ne s'agit pas de décider de ce qui est le plus juste, mais de porter le poids de nos actions et d'en assumer les repercussions, qu'elles concernent la survie de notre équipage ou de nos alliances diplomatiques. Seulement, leurs conséquences ne sont pas vraiment à la hauteur. Les choix importants ont souvent un impact à court terme, et se répercutent trop peu sur la suite des évènements. Même après une seule expédition, on devine que les multiples fins sont atteignables de par nos décisions prises dans les derniers chapitres. J'ai également eu du mal avec les réactions de certains membres de l'équipe : je peux comprendre qu'ils puissent douter d'une action encore en suspens, mais lorsqu'un choix aboutit à une situation favorable et que cela provoque malgré tout des remontrances, cela donne une impression de puérilité peu crédible pour des membres censés être entrainés à ce genre de situation de crise. Pour finir, une option dans le menu promet d'accéder à une page récapitulant nos choix et leurs statistiques mais demeure inaccessible, et ce, depuis un long moment d'après le forum.
+/- Bien que le jeu soit axé sur des choix narratifs, il propose cependant des phases de gameplay variées et immersives. On retrouve évidemment les QTEs caractéristiques du genre, mais aussi des séquences d'infiltration et de tirs, sans oublier quelques scènes où l'on se glisse dans la peau d'un technicien du vaisseau ; on jongle entre paramétrages de systèmes, analyse moléculaire et même pour le plaisir, un peu de pilotage. Tout ceci rend l'ensemble plus dynamique... mais cela reste mal calibré. A la manette, la sensibilité de visée s'avère très lente malgré plusieurs réglages, rendant les phases de tir laborieuses. L'analyse de l'environnement via le tricorder manque aussi de clarté, notamment pour distinguer ce qui a déjà été scanné. Quand aux QTEs, leur simplicité et le temps de réaction trop long accordé aux joueurs réduisent fortement la tension de certaines scènes.

✖ Beaucoup trop de bugs ont perturbé la mission : crash, glitchs visuels, PNJs bloqués rendant l'infiltration impossible, ou encore mon propre perso avançant tout seul sans que je lui commande. Je ne suis qu'ingénieur novice, ces dysfonctionnements auraient dû être corrigés bien avant mon arrivée.
✖ La traduction française des sous-titres semblent très fortement issue d'un traducteur auto : on passe du vouvoiement au tutoiement sans logique, on emploie des tournures féminines pour des personnages masculins et inversement, des phrases sont traduites littéralement ("he made it!" devient "il l'a créée" au lieu de "il a réussi", ça pique un peu). Un peu plus de rigueur aurait été appréciée pour les recrues étrangères.
(x Ne pas pouvoir romancer ou même flirter avec Tylas après tous ces petits regards appuyés a été une véritable torture ><)

Malgré toutes les difficultés techniques, cette mission a été exaltante et je compte bien rester à mon poste et vivre encore plus d'aventures. Peut-être qu'un jour, je pourrais me retrouver à l'avant poste et enfin dire : en avant toute !

Ich würde Resurgence gerne weiterempfehlen. Denn die Story ist über weite Teile sehr gut. Sie hat aber auch an einigen Stellen ihre Aussetzer. Leider ist das aber auch wirklich das einzig Gute an dem Spiel.

Negativpunkte:
- Die Beziehungen zwischen den Charakteren sind sehr aufgesetzt und das Konfliktpotential ist bereits beim Kennenlernen der Charaktere klar umrissen. Die Reaktionen der Charaktere sind oft nicht nachvollziehbar. Manchmal aber schon.

- Die Technik. Katastrophal. Zu Release des Spiels hatte ich es deshalb abgebrochen. In der Zwischenzeit (Stand Oct 2025) hat sich glücklicherweise einiges getan. Aber dennoch ist die Performance mehr als fragwürdig. Auf hohen (nicht maximalen) Einstellungen habe ich etwa an einer Stelle im Spiel 180fps und wenn ich mich herumdrehe sinkt sie auf unter 50fps ab. Solche Einbrüche gibt es immer wieder.  Noch dazu gibt es zwar kein 30fps-Lock mehr, wie zu Release des Spiels, allerdings sind die Ingame-Cutscene-Bewegungen noch immer auf (vermutlich) 30fps gelockt. Und diese Ingame-Cutscenes gibt es immer und immer wieder. Und es ruckelt wie Hölle. Wer nun mit 30fps spielt wird das nicht bemerken, aber wer hohe Refreshraten gewohnt ist umso mehr. Meine Lösung war das Spiel extern auf 60fps zu locken und dann mittels Lossless Scaling auf 120fps Framgeneration zu betreiben. Das machte es erträglich ohne zu viele Artefakte zu erzeugen.

- Spielmechanik: Durch und durch Wimmelbild und Quick Time Events. Dazu extrem langsamer Cursor während den Quick Time Events und den Tricorder-Szenen. Das ist alles purer Timesink. Selbst wenn ich aus einer Cutscene heraus nur einen Knopf drücken muss um damit die nächste Cutscene einzuleiten -- und das kommt verdammt oft vor -- muss ich erst entweder 3m laufen oder mit einer viel zu langsamen Maus/Stick 5cm über den Bildschirm fahren um zu klicken. Das nervt unglaublich.

- Selbst die eingefügten Deckungsshooter-Sequenzen fühlen sich zu keinem Zeitpunkt an wie eine Deckungsshooter-Sequenz sondern wie ein weiteres Quick Time Event. Ähnliches gilt für die Schleichsequenzen bei denen man nicht entdeckt werden darf. Die Kamera ist so nah an uns dran und das Blickfeld ist so eingeschränkt, dass man das Geschehen überhaupt nicht gut überblicken kann.

- Die Gesichtsanimationen: Ich sehe was sie ausdrücken sollen. Aber sie sehen einfach völlig unnatürlich gekünstelt aus.

- Die Entscheidungen spielen quasi keine Rolle. Ob nun Charakter A oder B eine Narbe bekommt, ist egal. Viele Entscheidungen führen ohnehin zum exakt selben Ergebnis. An einigen Stellen denkt man sich auch, dass die Antwort auf meine getroffene Entscheidung viel besser auf eine andere Entscheidung von mir gepasst hätte. Und: Das Korsett ist halt so eng, dass es keine wirkliche Entscheidungsfreiheit geben kann. Ich hatte mir oft gedacht: Ne, weder noch. Ich würde gerne was anderes machen.

Fazit: Als 2h-Film wäre das eine großartige Star-Trek-Story, mit entsprechenden Anpassungen. Als Spiel versagt es aufgrund der Negativpunkte leider auf voller Linie und wirkt mit den Spielsequenzen wie ein großer Zeiträuber. Dennoch: Durch eine Episodenstruktur lässt es sich sehr schön auf mehrere Abende verteilt spielen. Abends kurz eine halbe Stunde Zeit? -> 1-2 Episoden spielen und wieder ausmachen.

[h1]Atlas Fallen: Reign of Sand[/h1]

A flawed, but ultimately enjoyable Co-op-Action-RPG - as long as you don't mind a bit of sand.

[b]Gameplay:[/b]
Atlas Fallen is fast-paced and action-heavy and tells its story between the numerous battles and exploration of its sandy world.

The bones and meat of the game are the fights, often taking a few minutes before letting you go just to fight the next sand-monster barely a minute later. And while this part isn't as polished as the common Soulslike these days, it is indeed a good system that Deck13 has built. The fights are parry-heavy and mobile, combining dodges, dashes, double-jumps and lunge-attacks with multiple enemies, constantly mashing attacks to not fall behind on DPS. While small enemies just take a few hits, bigger enemies have multiple parts that you need to wail down with their own health-bar. Sometimes fights even change their dynamic once you "disabled" a few parts of the monster you are fighting. They feel fast, challenging enough and rewarding. Unless...

Unless, well, if they don't. While most of the fights are fine and nothing special, sometimes you just get a Hit and sometimes a Miss. For every aerial-heavy fast moving "I hope you don't fall" adrenalin rush you get a "I am pretty sure I parried that" or "Why am I not seeing the attack, why is the camera where it is?". This was a common trope in the game where the quality was sometimes all over the place and (without any big spoilers) it was incredibly bad with the final boss being a pushover that just didn't feel fun to do (first try).

Going away from the fights Atlas Fallen has many, many ideas it thrown into the mix. You have an [i]incredible[/i] variety of different builds you can do with your essence stones, letting you switch from glass cannon to support to tank to momentum-generation even into self-hurting corruption builds. Being a co-op-game it was fun to see the big effect that the build actually had! While my friend went from a momentum-monster into a support build (and a shatter build very late into the game), I went glass canon. This led to me sometimes just one-shotting a whole wave of enemies but only reaching that state if he was there - before I inevitably got one-shot by an attack myself because I lowered my defense into oblivion. Sadly this level of freedom ended with the armoury and weapons. While you get three weapons to choose from, using 2 at a time, the armour system was a letdown, often forcing you to use an armour inferior for your build because every piece of new armour just was objectively better.

Other than that we have treasure hunting actually feeling treasure-hunty, boring side-quests, boring Jump'n'Runs, boring side objectives on the map (like following animals or hitting a statue) and side-fights which then again felt good, for example the Rifts. While I trash the rest of the game here, the exploration in itself actually felt nice, especially with the great mobility you got from the game, even though the world was a bit shallow. The rest served the game good enough to make you have a pause from the otherwise non-stop fighting.


[b]The story and the Writing:[/b]
The story of Atlas Fallen felt very cookie-cutter. While it wasn't bad, every twist just felt like it was done a hundred times before, no character stood particularly out and even when the game told grand stories of gods fighting for the fate of the world... I just couldn't care. This was deepened by a few choices made by the devs:

Being a Co-op-Game, you were given the freedom to free-roam, so at times one of us would finish a mission without the other one noticing. For side-missions this was fine, you would miss the dialogue but no one of us really cared. Then the main-quests happened and sometimes you could do a fight or a dialogue without the other one present. Then you needed both of the players, but at least the other could fast-travel to you. And then you had the times when the other person had to walk to you just for you to smack a chain without anything happening. It felt inconsistent and strangely limiting in an otherwise free game.

Other than that the story was told to you, not with you. You had no real choices to make, nothing to really change. Often enough the most important things happened in the past and you were just exploring them - oh, time for the next fight! The presentation was incredibly off-throwing, sometimes giving you okay-ish cut-scenes, then having you talk to an NPC where the other person would have to stand next to it to not miss anything.

All in all the story served its purpose, but its nothing I will greatly remember - or remember at all. Well, except for that one really bad moment right at the end.


[b]Music, graphic and technical stuff:[/b]
The music was good enough, the sound-design felt good (which is important in a game where you constantly sand-glide!). The graphics were mostly fine, but did have one big problem: Since the game is very focused on sand... every area just felt the same. Instead of some big twists with glass houses or sand castles as areas you often enough just left an open sand area just to be in another open sand area. The biggest groundbreak was a cave. Yea.

On the technical side the game was, just like much of the rest, Hit or Miss. while 90 - 95 % of it was a Hit, we did encounter a few too many difficulties to not mention them. Everything from frame drops when a fight ended and you got your materials over crashes, disconnects, failing auto saves, unobtainable steam achievements (because of the before-mentioned), save files being locked out of multiplayer (leading to us needing to load an earlier save) and more. While we encountered those problems just rarely, they added up over time.

Putting a small area for QoL here: While the game often did a good job marking your new things, giving you shortcuts to them, giving you the ability to teleport your friend and so on, I found it then very funny, that it disabled the ability to save manually or fast-travel to another map in Co-op. What a strange choice!


[b]Summary:[/b]
I bought Atlas Fallen (quite a few times actually!) for a simple reason - an Action-RPG built for Co-op. None of that FromSoftware-BS. An actual Co-op-Action-RPG. Without guns (nothing against Looter-Shooters, but sometimes you want something else). And that's what I got. So I can't be too mad, especially considering the price I paid for it and with its playtime of about 25-30 hours.

And to make one thing clear: I am not mad. I did enjoy the game. The fights felt distinguishable from other games, Deck13 did try to make something to stand out and I can applaud that. For every tripping-stone they encountered, I had multiple good moments having fun with a friend. And that was what I paid for.

Is this game good? Yes.
Is this game underrated? Absolutely.
Is this game GotY material? Absolutely not.
But not every game needs to be that. If you are looking for something else - this might be it. You will know this very soon (after that prolonged tutorial ended at least).

Resident Evil 0 Remaster shares the same fundamentals with the original Resident Evil, apart from the different story and some new unique gameplay aspects, however the enjoyment is dragged down by some rather idiotic decisions when it comes to game's overall difficulty increasement compared to the original.

The idea to give the player 2 characters to play as at the same time was intriguing, but has its issues. When you engage with enemies together, the AI controlled partner not always will assist you, even though you have set their behavior to aggression. The puzzle solving that requires both Billy and Rebecca to cooperate smoother. As they both get separated, you need to be extra careful as you will be facing enemies alone for a while, as well as you need to be smart about items and which character gets to have priority with them.

Item management can be a mixed bag itself. No more you need to store items in boxes at specific locations, you can just drop them around levels where ever you like it, but it does not solve the back tracking completely, as you will probably need to travel back to earlier locations to pick up items needed for progression somewhere else.

Enemy encounters are where the game lost it is footing for me. Several of the enemy designs are just dreadfully unbalanced, like the mimics, zombie monkeys, and crawlers. The mimics especially are some of the most stupidly designed enemies I have seen in any game. With their ranged attack, movement speed and grabbing, compared to the clunky and slow controls of your character, it makes these encounters utterly irritating and frustrating, not challenging.

At least the story was mostly pleasurable, as it was intriguing to experience events that led up the original game's events.[i][hr][h3]Billy and Rebecca wouldn’t be my first pick as my favorite Resident Evil duo, but I still enjoyed the dynamic and unconventional comradery between them throughout the game![/h3][/hr][/i]

El remaster del "Resident Evil Zero" fue mi primer contacto con un juego antiguo de la saga, (hasta ahora solo había jugado al RE7 en su fecha de salida), y me sorprendió bastante. Podría afirmar tranquilamente, que superó con creces mis expectativas.
Me sorprendió gratamente cómo la tensión constante de los survivals horrors clásicos convive con nosotros durante las horas de juego, casi sin parar. Desde los pasillos oscuros y claustrofóbicos del tren, hasta los laboratorios debajo de la mansión, todo está diseñado para hacernos sentir vulnerabilidad en cada momento y cada segundo. 
El sistema de manejar a dos personajes, Rebecca y Billy, introduce una mecánica brillante la cual agrega estrategia y complejidad. Podemos alternar entre ellos, compartir y administrar recursos, y resolver puzzles en equipo, además de obligarnos a administrar a ambos por separado de ser necesario.
Mencionando la complejidad, justamente, hay que pararse en este apartado un tiempo y desarrollarlo a fondo. Este juego NO te regala nada. La gestión del inventario puede ser tan desafiante como los enemigos mismos. Cada bala, cada planta curativa, cada objeto y cada espacio libre, puede salvarte la vida o condenarte completamente obligándote a estar minutos y minutos organizando los objetos, cambiándolos con el segundo personaje o dejándolos en el piso, o simplemente hacer malabares hasta dejar todo organizado. No hay baúles ni almacenamiento compartido. Si dejamos un objeto en el suelo, tendremos que recordar en que parte los dejamos. Todo esto que mencioné, más los puzzles variados, le dan al juego una dificultad justa pero muy exigente. A fin y al cabo, todo esto que mencioné, es lo que lo hace adictivo, muy tedioso por bastantes momentos, pero muy adictivo.
La ambientación, la iluminación y los sonidos, están muy bien logrados. Esa marca registrada del terror clásico, de los videojuegos de fines de los 90' y principios de los 2000', está presente siempre en este juego, gracias sobre todo a esos tres apartados que mencioné recientemente.
Respecto a lo visual, este remaster cumple bastante. Los escenarios pre-renderizados fueron restaurados con un nivel de detalle que, incluso hoy, resulta impresionante. Lo visual y lo gráfico, se mantiene muy bien incluso hasta día de hoy. Las luces parpadeantes, las sombras proyectadas y las texturas de los entornos transmiten una atmósfera opresiva e inmersiva a cada momento. Este remaster hace justicia al original; respeta su estética, la realza y la hace brillar en resoluciones modernas, sin perder en absoluto su escencia.
La historia no es especialmente profunda, pero construye bien el misterio al fin y al cabo, además de atar cabos sueltos e introducir nuevas ideas a la saga.
En resumen, este remaster del "Resident Evil Zero" es el título de entrada recomendado a la saga, (al menos si lo jugás en orden cronológico), además de ser una puerta de entrada al pasado de la saga. Difícil, tenso, atmosférico y visualmente bonito. Me encantó comprobar que ese terror, esas entregas clásicas y antiguas, todavía se pueden sentir frescos, desafiantes e inmersivos. Este título demuestra que este videojuego, a pesar de tener 23 años, sigue teniendo potencial y contenido para explotarlo por nosotros mismos, incluso en 2025, y eso es más que admirable.

DOOM 3 is such a mixed bag, there are something to love here like the atmosphere and overall gameplay/ level design, but there are also some of the worst game design choices I've ever seen in my 20 years of experience as a gamer

Let's get it out of the way: The Shotgun

I know, people are gonna say "It's fine, it has it's use, it can be fun" bla bla bla...

All of that could be true, but it does not change the fact that it's still a terrible weapon, hell it's barely a gun, it's a melee weapon with it's wild spread even at close range, some people might say "Skill issue", yeah, duh, no shit, it is exactly because the gun is bad, that's why you need to compensate with your skill, I mean I can make the shotgun fun when I get a few close range combo kill, but that doesn't change the fact that it's a terrible weapon, so stop arguing that DOOM 3 shotgun is good, IT'S BAD, just because you can make it fun doesn't make it good, and the sad thing is that the Double Barrel shotgun from ROE expansion is barely any better than the base one, sure it does more damage but the spread is still definetley in the melee weapon category, and the increase reload time diminish it's usefulness even further.

Next: No reload cancel

Oh god this is a pet peeve of mine, look I understand it's intention is for your to mind your ammunition and time your reload, ok fine, it shouldn't be the case since it's not a survival horror game but whatever.

But most of us FPS player would instinctvely press for the next weapon during reload, if you do not let me cancel the reload, at least don't switch to the next weapon after the reload is completed, why would you design this way so I have even further gap between reload and firing? You might say oh just wait for the reload to complete don't switch weapon during the animation, yeah it's easier said then done, like I said it's a FPS instinct that's been building for years, I can't just switch it around for ONE game.

The last one is a BFG edition issue

What the hell happened to the dynamic lighting when the weapon is firing? Why is it cut? It makes no sense and it really ruined the immersion for me, if it's not that I really need 120fps I would have stuck with the original DOOM3 with dhewm3 source port, always a trade off and never a perfect version, that's just annoying.

Anyway overall I still like this game, I replay it from time to time just like the original Doom 1&2, but it definitely ranks lower than every other game in the franchise

CARIMARA: Beneath the Forlorn Limbs is a short but fascinating story-driven point-and-click adventure that perfectly blends eerie charm with creative gameplay. It’s one of those games that hooks you from the first screen. It's mysterious, melancholic, and beautifully strange.

You collect cards that let you interact with your environment in unique ways, uncovering secrets and story threads as you go. The world feels alive in that quiet, unsettling way: every character oozes personality, the French voice acting is great, the art style pulls you straight into its weird beauty, and the soundtrack fits every moment like a glove. It’s dark but not grim, spooky but still cozy: the ideal Halloween mood despite not being Halloween themed at all.

The game is bursting with secrets, and the achievements cleverly guide you toward discovering them all. Everything feels intentional and meaningful, down to the quirky achievement names. The story itself is rich and layered, though one of the [spoiler]alternate endings does leave a cliffhanger[/spoiler], but it somehow works within this mysterious world.

Sure, it’s short (around an 1h30 for 100%), and the speedrun achievement cuts it close, which demanded me multiple attempts, but for what it offers, it’s perfectly paced. It’s a quick, hauntingly sweet experience that rewards curiosity and attention to detail.

Overall, CARIMARA is a little indie gem that feels handcrafted for fans of narrative and visual oddities like [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/1764390/BAD_END_THEATER/?curator_clanid=45639970]BAD END THEATER[/url] or [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/1889040/Birth/?curator_clanid=45639970]Birth[/url]. It's short, strange, and full of heart. Exactly what an autumn evening calls for.

This is going to be one of my first and only times I will give a honest review of a game because I've been following the development through the various socials of the creator since the announcement of the game closely and eagerly anticipated it's release. With that being said, before I get into the details of why I will say for the people who don't want to bother with reading this review, no, I cannot recommend the game in it's current launch state and to be quite frank, I'm left disappointed with how the state of this games launch was due to the numerous issues regarding glitches, absent QoL features, and overall gameplay choices I have encountered that I will now list below.

Issues I've encountered so far (These range from minor to drastic gameplay impairments):

The main menu breaking after trying to join a game (Just leaves a blank screen, you have to restart the game entirely to fix it)
The UI for the menus (Very simple and allows for very little customization and even somewhat confusing regarding Push to Talk)
Mission item softlock (The mission item doesn't get picked up or despawns, you actively lose a day and have to move on) 
Items not working as intended (Mainly applies to decoys)
Enemies not working as intended (Especially seen with the "weeping angel" enemy of the game, they will not stop sometimes)

These are the glitches I've encountered and had ruined my gameplay experiences and I would assume will be fixed in the next couple of weeks or hopefully sooner.

Now, the things i'm going to discuss are my pet peeves that me and my friends have encountered so far, which may or may not effect you:

Nausea due to the bitcrunch filter effect (depending how far you are from certain details or text which leaves you hugging the wall or squinting trying to read the terminal or fliers, overdone here compared to similar filters other horror games implements)
Low health effects (you get a bloody screen that is overly prominent and easily disorients you)
Spawns (either you get camped at the front door upon first entering or every enemy spawns in at once)
Inventory system
Time at which the days progress
Lack of tutorial
Random vents (please rework them)

Everything listed above could definitely be subject to change but I just wanted to point them out.

All in all, I truly wish for this project to succeed and I hope these issues get addressed in the near future. I hope this review informed you and gives you a better idea of what is expected with this beta. Let me know what you think in the comments, and point out the glitches I missed or even what should be added/changed entirely, just keep it civil!

As a game in the detective/crime investigation genre, it was FANTASTIC. This is the same game about Sherlock, which tried to create the structure of the open world, which I really couldn’t do. Much longer than other series of games, especially to solve all the side puzzles, etc.

I played it co-op and didn’t try the solo mode.

The game has a clever idea: building a mobile machine that serves as your main base. It’s a concept that stands out from most survival games. The premise has a lot of potential, but in its current state, it needs much more work to feel polished and enjoyable.

The early hours I felt the urge to explore the world and experience traveling with the machine. However, progression quickly becomes all about repetitive crafting. Almost every main quest requires crafting new tools and items from start to finish, which makes the pacing slow and sometimes tedious. This could’ve easily been simplified or front-loaded in the first hour instead of forming the backbone of the entire quest structure.

Crafting is the core of the experience, but it feels limited and lacks depth. A simple repair system for tools and weapons would help a lot instead of forcing players to rebuild everything, especially since resources aren’t always easy to find.

Player movement, controls, and combat all need improvement. Activities, environments, and even bosses repeat often. Facing the same boss multiple times gets dull, and important areas lack meaningful challenges, such as adding unique bosses that could have encouraged exploration and balanced risk versus reward.

I don't recommend the game in its current state, but I still believe the idea itself deserves more development. It has a unique core that could turn into something great if it gets the attention it needs.

As someone who's very much enjoyed Battle Chef Brigade and regularly played the daily and survival modes, I was excited for what Trinket Studios was gonna do next. The game we finally got, Battle Suit Aces, is certainly a game that plays to their strengths: A large variety of characters with clear relationships/camaraderie and excellent voice acting. I'm a sucker for good voice acting and fun character interactions.

The gameplay portion is practically a rougelite card battler, but I find it difficult to call it that when there's no real deck-building involved and no real rougelite mechanics. Cards (Suits and Drones) are added to your deck as you acquire them, with most coming from advancing Factions, and cards are modified by using mods. And that's it? Yeah, that's it. There's pros and cons to this approach that I ultimately enjoy with caveats.

At first the game feels very basic which is natural while it slowly introduces new mechanics with every fight. Most of the first act introduces something new every fight, whether it's a new color type, a new type of trigger to use/avoid, or a new buff/debuff. You get plenty of time to learn so you're not truly being overwhelmed with too many new things at once. I found that after acquiring the first two Factions, the depth starts picking up and getting actually interesting.

At this point you realize two important things: 1. There are three colors (Red Green Blue) and you have mostly Red and Blue cards, with two Green Drones. Cards can only bank and use energy of their own color, so these two Green Drones bloat your deck. 2. You cannot exclude any acquired cards! These two Green Drones only support themselves, they do nothing else but to take up space and unnecessarily limit your choices when they do come up in draws. There's no point to using Green Drones that only support themselves when you can use literally any other card that does support other cards.

This is a design choice that goes against the way the game is naturally played. You'll naturally want to focus on building towards a single color or a specific play style for the combo synergy, but you're encouraged to acquire as many Suits as possible. Each Suit comes with a pilot, which means more characters and more interactions. And more cards, more options, and potentially more bloat that you cannot remove.

But the game isn't designed for a one-size-fits-all approach. Battle Suit Aces features a large variety of triggers and mechanics to keep you on your toes: everything has counter play to get around it. Armor and Plate stacking? Damage that triggers on move and/or hit to melt it. Spread and Sweepers? Weakening and Spike to diminish and punish. Solo-color? Dampen and Chaining to negate and wipe. Big numbers? Damage limiters. If you were able to exclude cards and focus on your own play style, you could very easily find yourself in unwinnable situations from being hard-countered.

To make bloat a little easier to avoid, when you achieve a new faction level you get to pick which card or mod you acquire. You can still focus on a color or play-style by picking only the faction cards that support it, and grabbing mods when no cards are left for it. Mods can enhance a Suit or Drone's strength, add new abilities, or change how they work entirely. And the game is fairly generous with redraws, you get one every turn plus you can spend the one Command point you get every turn for a second redraw (and a third redraw for 2 more Command points), that's 6-8 cards every turn to pick which to play.  So I find it difficult to advocate for the ability to exclude cards. I just wish those Green Drones wouldn't populate if there are no Green Suits to go with them.

Ultimately I've had a lot of fun with Battle Suit Aces. But it's definitely not for everyone. Rather than being a roguelite with random elements to build with, it's a story-based card collector that encourages full-on multiple playthroughs to experience the different ways to play it. For some people that can be a tough sell, but I found it worth while once I sat down and got past the initial introductory missions.

Inside hooks you from the very first moment. Without uttering a single word, it pulls you into a bleak, mysterious world that builds tension and curiosity at every turn. The game’s atmosphere is unnerving in the best possible way, its haunting visuals, subtle sound design, and minimalist storytelling create an experience that feels both oppressive and beautiful. The puzzles are clever and well paced, challenging enough to make you think but never so difficult as to break the flow of gameplay. That said, it’s a short and fairly linear game, with limited replay value aside from the hidden secrets and alternate ending. Still, for its accessible price and the sheer quality of its design and mood, and rivals Limbo in its dark ambience and thought provoking imagery its worth a playthrough.

Немецкая компания Crytek, знакомая игрокам по серии Crysis, выпустила игру Ryse: Son of Rome в далеком 2013 году. Спустя 12 лет после релиза мне удалось до нее добраться и теперь хочется поделиться мыслями о том, как она ощущается. Это приключенческий экшен и специфика этого жанра в том, что вы будете почти безостановочно сражаться, прокачивая своего персонажа. Поэтому забудьте об открытом мире, глубоком сюжете и выборе в диалогах - вместо этого вас окунут в историю римского легионера Мария Тита, прошедшего через жерло войны Рима с варварскими племенами Британии.

[h1]Senatus Populusque Romanus (Сенат и народ Рима) [/h1]

Сеттинг Римской империи, в которой уже наметился упадок, студия Crytek выбрала и реализовала с вниманием к мельчайшим деталям. Здесь всюду проглядывается авторское стремление показать одну из самых развитых цивилизаций древнего мира во всем ее величии. И хотя повествование сюжета проходит в альтернативной вселенной, которая допускает исторические неточности – это не помешает увидеть в деле римские легионы и флот, порочных правителей, чьи решения повергали в смятение другие народы, а также грандиозные бетонные строения, устоявшие до наших дней. Игра разработана на собственном движке студии - CryEngine 4, который радует потрясающим визуальным оформлением и позволяет наслаждаться красотой локаций, архитектурой, зданиями и персонажами игры. Все это отлично передает дух того времени, пока вы будете шинковать направо и налево врагов S.P.Q.R.

[h1]Panem et circenses (Хлеба и зрелищ) [/h1]
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3585153104
Сюжет игры с самого начала забрасывает в водоворот безостановочного экшена, делая перерывы лишь на время кат-сцен. Каждая кат-сцена смотрится как фрагмент из высокобюджетного сериала, поражая безупречным качеством картинки. А технология, использовавшаяся для созданий лицевых анимаций, бросается в глаза – каждый персонаж выглядит живым и естественным, что выделяет игру 2013 года среди прочих. Сюжетный режим проходится в среднем за 6 часов. Однако его высокий и динамичный темп повествования я тоже запишу в плюс, потому что ближе к концу уже приходили мысли, что мне начинает надоедать. Это связано с тем, что боевая часть проработана не очень глубоко – я заучил всего пару комбинаций, чтобы успешно проходить каждую новую группу противников. Чаще всего достаточно вовремя парировать вражеский удар или сделать откат, а дальше вам нужно лишь как можно быстрее нашинковать супостата ударами своего гладиуса, пока не появится возможность совершить над ним казнь. To me, this is a game most reminiscent of the Twilight Zone, but with the inclusion of a Cryptid of some sort. People say it's a Wendigo, and who am I to argue? Dude definitely seemed very hungry. But the key point here is you don't really know what it is. You just know that something is definitely outside the bus. And you are inside the bus. Everything about this game revolves around that dynamic.

You, the unnamed protagonist, are taking a bus ride home after a long day, but for some reason, the bus goes way off course, driving through a forest road instead of wherever it was supposed to be going. You're exhausted and fall asleep. When you wake up, the bus has crashed and nobody else is still on the bus outside of you. A fun game that has some unfortunate flaws, likely due to its messy development. I have not played co-op, so I can't speak to how that affects the game. 

The Good:
-Core gameplay loop is fun. It's a mix of exploration in some open world zones and dungeons. The open world has different events that pop up, and a ton of loot (more on that later) so things feel fresh. The dungeons seem to have some randomized areas and events as well, but they feel pretty similar on repeat runs (also more on that later)
-The enemy variety is great. There are a ton of different enemies.
-Combat is simply but surprisingly engaging. Each character has 4 abilities that replenish via cooldowns, each weapon has a different ability, and some "echoes" (modifiers for your gear/weapons) have abilities that can be activated as well.
-Lots of build variety. There are a lot of items and armor to equip and modify with echoes, which is engaging for players interested in creating specific builds. 
-Leveling is available via experience drops for characters you never use, so if you want to try them out in later game areas, you can level them up instead of being forced to run lower level dungeons/zones. 
-No microtransactions 

The Bad: 
-Performance/optimization isn't great, and often everything runs fine until you're fighting a boss with AoE moves. Dropping down the settings from what it recommends based on your hardware helps, but there are still issues. 
-Mobile game amounts of currency.
-Crazy amounts of grinding.
-No way to affect loot drops, so be prepared to get a ton of cosmetics for characters you never use. 
- TONS of loot drops for a player home that I imagine most players never engage with (I sure haven't)
-Huge weapons imbalances. I mentioned I primarily use melee, but whenever I want to run a dungeon quickly (for the crazy amounts of grinding), I use a character with a gun build. It completely negates a lot of challenge certain enemies present. I'd be fine with that if it was a glass cannon approach, but the characters that can efficiently use ranged weapons often have great survivability/mobility options too.
-Melee requires stamina to block and roll, which is normal, but your damage is determined by a combo counter so you are always feeling the need to stay in the middle of the action. When you do have to move out of range to avoid an AoE attack, you almost always lose the full combo counter. 
-Some bosses are just not fun, and those are usually ones you need to grind for good armor (and you'll probably get the armor drops for characters you never use before anything you actually want)
-Story is a lot of two characters talking at each other for way too long. 

Overall, the game is fun. and well worth the price. There's a ton of content and I find myself putting in a few hours here and there in between other games. I do think the devs got really close to something amazing, and I hope they can continue to add on to the positives with their future releases.

Плюс до цього гра постійно кидає тобі нові сегменти:
-ганяєш на авто, розстрілюючи ворогів;
-прокрадаєшся в стелс-сцені, наче шпигун із майбутнього, в якого з озброєння тільки кухонний тесак;
-а потім стрибаєш по крилу літака і місиш ворогів в небі.
Нудьгувати нема коли.

Сюжет і персонажі

Сюжет тут для галочки. Щось про погоду, змови, магію — коротше, щоб було. Все настільки швидко відбувається, що глибину тут шукати без сенсу.
