I don't want to get into too many details here as I intend to write a more in-depth review for Buggos 2.  If you enjoyed Buggos 2 then you will enjoy Buggos and vice versa.  Some sequels change everything about the game until it's barely recognisable from the original, such as was the case with the Frostpunk series.  Buggos 2 has some differences and even a few improvements over the base game, but it still feels true to the original.

The Buggos series of games is one of those very rare 'play as the monster/villain' games where you play as the titular buggos, a very comedic version of the classic sci-fi hivemind bug swarm, as you try to conquer a human colony.  There are a few different bugs to choose from, and numerous upgrades to choose from, some that improve all buggos, others that improve only certain buggos.  With every victory you always feel like you're progressing forward, until you hit the next major challenge such as a new enemy unit or building being introduced.  The best gameplay is in the final missions when you feel like an absolute boss taking on the full might of humanity, which on the hardest difficulty is extremely challenging and unforgiving.

I've just played Buggos 2, and I'm now going back to replay the original again, it's truly a great series and the Developer is an absolute pleasure to deal with.  They're always keeping on top of any bugs 😏 or complaints, and remaining open to community feedback regarding improvements or new features, which is something that is always good to see.

This game strongly reminds me of flash games or early 2000s games, in terms of both gameplay and aesthetics.
There aren't a lot of controls. You just tell the buggos where to go and what to build, and they do the rest. Not necessarily efficiently (they meander around a lot and there is no micro that you can do), but they Swarm. They are without number. For every dead buggo, a new one is instantly born to replace them for free. You don't have to right-click every enemy unit and building because they will do it on their own, and it's so much more glorious to see it that way.
There is a huge difficulty spike come Zones 7 to 9 (the "free DLC") though. The repair bots are absolutely bullcrap because they will instantly respawn a 10,000 HP building in your swarm's face, which will then attract all your swarm's aggro while the shooters behind them massacre your swarm. But it's this sort of bullcrap that makes me think of early 2000s broken OP jank. It IS possible to overcome it, but it's a grind.

The story/humour is terrible. (Another thing that is 2000s-ish.) But luckily that doesn't impact the gameplay whatsoever.

Ultimately, this game provided some raw fun, and honestly that's what games are about.
Not sure if it's worth $15 though. Get it on a sale.
I look forward to playing Buggos 2.

Immortals of Aveum is a first-person magic shooter that tries to merge the pacing of modern action games with a fantasy setting built around spellcasting instead of guns. The premise follows Jak, a street-level thief turned battlemage, who is pulled into a large-scale conflict known as the Everwar. The narrative focuses on personal growth and political intrigue, giving the campaign a clear emotional through-line even when the worldbuilding becomes dense.

The core appeal is its spell-based combat. Instead of traditional firearms, you wield three color-coded schools of magic that fill the roles of shotgun, rifle, and rapid-fire weapons. Each school has several abilities and alternate modes that can be layered together, and the game encourages constant switching. Encounters feel fast and aggressive, with mobility and timing playing a large role.

Progression is skill-tree driven. You earn points to enhance specific spell archetypes or unlock new tactical options. The system adds variety without overwhelming you with unnecessary complexity. Gear and sigils provide additional stat tuning so you can lean into burst damage, control effects, or survivability depending on your preferred rhythm.

Level design is mostly linear, but optional rooms and traversal puzzles break up the action. These segments use magical tools gained through the story, creating Metroid-like backtracking opportunities. They are not difficult, yet they help pace the campaign and showcase the world’s visual style.

The game’s presentation is one of its strengths. Environments feature bright color palettes, crystalline structures, and sprawling battlegrounds. Spell effects are elaborate and readable, and the soundtrack reinforces the high-fantasy scale. Performance varies by platform, because the game relies heavily on visual effects, but recent patches have improved stability.

Enemy variety is adequate. You fight armored soldiers, spectral creatures, and larger bosses that require specific spell combinations to break shields or exploit weaknesses. Combat readability stays consistent, and even chaotic fights remain manageable once you understand the color-coded systems.

Immortals of Aveum succeeds when it leans into its identity as a spell-shooter with momentum-driven combat. The story is straightforward but earnest, the world is vibrant, and the progression loop is satisfying. While its linear structure and performance demands may limit its reach, the overall experience delivers a distinctive take on the first-person action genre.

Possessor(s) 는 Hyper Light Drifter 로 유명세를 다진 Heart Machine 스튜디오에서 만든 게임으로, 올해 초에 출시한 Hyper Light Breaker 가 3D 로그라이크 장르의 게임이었다면 이번 작품은 횡스크롤 메트로배니아 / 액션 어드벤처 게임이라 서로 분위기가 완전히 다르다. 게임 내적인 이야기를 더 하기 전에 외적인 걸 조금 적어 보자면, 사실 이 스튜디오는 상황이 매우 좋지는 않은데, Hyper Light Breaker 가 처참하게 망해 버리면서 여러 명의 직원들을 해고해야 했으며, 심지어 해당 게임이 얼리 엑세스로 출시 되었기 때문에 게임에 산소 호흡기를 붙이려다 돈이 또 새어 나가서, Possessor(s) 를 출시하기 전에 해당 게임의 개발에 참여한 직원 대다수가 해고되었다는 기사도 나올 정도였다. 그래서 스팀 토론에 이에 대한 말이 다소 있었는데, 결론적으로는 "퇴사한 개발자들도 수익의 일부분을 받으며, 게임이 흥행하면 재취업도 쉬워지니, 만약 게임이 마음에 들었다면 다른 사람들에게도 추천해 주고 불매운동은 하지 말아달라!" 라는 말을 해고당한 개발자가 직접 와서 말한 뒤로, 해당 이슈가 Possessor(s) 의 판매량에 부정적으로 작용하지는 않았다고 생각한다. 그래서, 솔직히 말해 Heart Machine 의 이전 게임들을 플레이 해 보지 않았는데, 이 스팀 토론을 읽고 "아, 전작이 크게 망했으니 이번 게임이 마지막 불꽃 같은 역작인가 보다." 라는 약간의 뒤틀린 생각을 가지고, 게임에 대한 소량의 기대감과, 만약 명작이라면 다른 스팀 친구들에게도 추천해 주겠다는 긍정적인 마음으로 게임을 시작하였다.

그리고 이 기대감은 나를 배신하여 플레이 중 분노로 변화하게 되었다. 이 게임의 개발에 참여한 사람들에게는 정말 미안하지만, Possessor(s) 는 정말 진부하고 지루한 메트로배니아이다. 개인적으로 메트로배니아 게임들을 그렇게 많이 해 보지는 않고 약 20개 정도 플레이를 하였는데, 흔히 사람들이 메트로배니아에 있어서 명작이라 부르는 게임들도 제대로 안 해 보고 그보다 덜 인기있는, 속된 말로 "입소문을 거의 못 탄 메트로배니아" 들을 더 많이 해왔는데도, 그런 자잘한 게임들에서 보이는 자신만의 색채가 이 게임에서는 거의 느껴지지 않았다. 왜 이렇게 느껴졌는지 단점들을 나열하기 전, 그래도 몇 안 되는 장점부터 살펴보도록 하자. 먼저, 게임 내 캐릭터 및 몬스터들의 디자인들은 잘 뽑았으며, NPC 들의 스탠딩 일러스트들 또한 나쁘지 않았다. 두 번째로, 게임 내 로딩 시간이 지역 사이를 왔다갔다 할 때만 길게 느껴져서, 로딩 면에서 답답함을 느껴지지 않았다. 세 번째로, 다른 비추천 평가들을 보면 버그에 시달리는 사람들이 보이던데, 의외로 직접 플레이하면서 치명적인 버그가 한 번도 걸리지 않았다. 단 한번 버그가 걸린 건 벽에 붙어 있었을 때 몬스터의 공격을 받아 벽 밖으로 밀려나간 경우였는데, 다행히도 게임 진행을 막아버리지 않았다. 또한 출시 하루 후에 버그 픽스 업데이트가 바로 나온 걸 보면, 버그들은 빠르게 잡아내는 것 같다.

그러면 왜 이 게임을 플레이하며 짜증을 느꼈는가? 이에 대해 설명을 해 보자면 다음과 같다:

A. 게임플레이 - 전투 편

Possessor(s) 의 전투는 플랫폼 파이터 장르에서 영향을 받았다고 스팀 페이지에 써져 있는데, 그래서 그런가 초반부의 전투는 화려하게 느껴지고, "내가 뭔가 대단한 콤보를 하고 있구나!" 라는 착각을 플레이어에게 심어준다. 게임 초반에 주인공은 채찍을 얻게 되는데, 이를 통해 공중에 날아다니는 소규모 적들을 눈 앞으로 끌고 와서 때릴 수도 있고, 이후 다른 게임에 국밥처럼 나오는 다양한 서브웨폰 / 패링 / 그로기와 공중콤보 시스템을 통해 전투를 좀 더 주도적으로 이끌 수 있다. 문제는 진짜 그게 다라는 것이다. 앞의 문장에서 이야기한 시스템 중에 혁신을 가져다 주는 건 없고, 그냥 어디서 많이 먹은 듯한 전투 양상이 게임 내내 이어지니 (그나마 자신들의 고유한 패턴이 있는) 보스전 말고는 플레이어가 흥미를 느낄 부분이 없다. 차라리 메인 웨폰이 다양해서 플레이어가 무기를 가지고 여러가지 시도해 보는 재미가 있거나, 혹은 (다른 메트로배니아처럼) 전투 양상을 다르게 바꿔볼 수 있는 스킬 및 패시브들이 점진적으로 해금되는 구조가 제대로 갖춰져 있다면, 전체적인 전투 게임플레이는 좀 밍밍하게 설계해 두되 플레이어가 자신만의 빌드를 짜면서 원하는 조미료를 첨가하는 재미를 느낄 수 있었을 것이다. 그러나 이 게임은 두 면 모두 실패하였다. 게임 내 등장하는 총 4종류의 메인 웨폰은 사거리 / 공격 속도 / 공격력의 차이밖에 없으며, 공격 모션마저도 역동적으로 차이나는 게 아니여서 뭘 들고 싸우든 전투 양상의 차이가 느껴지지 않는다. 더 경악스러운 건 게임 내 패시브나 스킬 다양성의 부재인데, 물론 장르가 메트로배니아인 만큼 주인공이 다양한 스킬을 해금하긴 하지만 (패링을 제외하고는) 탐험에 더 비중이 높은 스킬이며, 패링마저도 사용감이 매끄럽게 느껴지지 않는다. 게임 내 패시브 시스템이 존재하긴 해서 주인공을 간접적으로 강하게 만들 수는 있으나, 공격력 증가 / 서브웨폰 공격 강화 / 받는 피해 감소와 같은 심심한 패시브들밖에 없어서, 플레이어가 강해지는 기분이 전혀 들지 않는다. 그 와중에 전투마저 쉽게 느껴지니 뭔가 도전 정신을 자극할 만한 게임을 원했던 플레이어는 지루함을 느낄 수밖에 없다. 물론, 전투가 쉽다고 나쁜 겜은 아니다. 하지만 전투가 쉽다고 하더라도 자신만의 독창적인 시스템이 있었다면 플레이어가 지루함을 덜 느꼈을 것이다. 전투가 어렵지 않았던 다른 메트로배니아를 예시로 들어 보자면, Biomorph 의 경우 다양한 몬스터로 변하는 시스템을 통해 전투 + 탐험의 재미를 이색적인 맛으로 플레이어에게 소개해 주었으며, Pronty 의 경우 바다를 배경으로 하여서 주인공과 적들이 모든 방향으로 이동할 수 있다는 자유로움을 제공함과 동시에 다양한 패시브를 통해 평타 위주 혹은 스킬 (서브웨폰) 위주 전투로 극단적으로 다른 캐릭터를 만들어 갈 수 있었다. 반면에 이 게임은 전투의 참신함이나 캐릭터 육성의 재미 둘다 없으니, 때깔은 좋으나 정작 맛은 밍밍한 빵을 꾸역꾸역 먹는 기분밖에 느끼지 못하는 것이다.

솔직히 말해, 전투 시스템은 그냥 순수하게 재미가 없다 뿐이지 어떠한 하자로 인해 플레이어가 불쾌감을 느낄 부분은 거의 없었으나, 세 가지 면이 크게 마음에 들지 않았다. 먼저, 특이하게 캐릭터에게 패시브를 장착시키는 게 아니라 무기 (메인 및 서브) 의 슬롯을 늘리고 거기에다가 장착을 하는 방식인데, 새로운 시스템을 시도한 건 좋지만 그냥 다른 게임들처럼 주인공에게 패시브 슬롯을 쥐어주는 게 더 직관적이며, 무기마다 슬롯을 뚫어주는 게 생각보다 재화가 많이 들어서 불편하다. 여기에 더해, 무기의 슬롯을 늘릴려면 게임 내 곳곳에 숨겨져 있는 "크로마 보석" 이 드는데, 게임 엔딩까지 진행하는데 약 60개나 찾았을 정도로 과하게 존재하며, 막상 내가 사용하는 무기를 완전히 업그레이드하면 더 이상 찾아도 소용이 없기 때문에 수집품을 찾는 데서 느끼는 기대감을 크게 깎아 내린다. 두 번째로는, 게임 내 무적 시간이 거의 없어서 부조리한 피격을 받는 상황들이 나오는데, 예를 들어 분열되는 탄막에 직격으로 맞으면 메인 탄환 + 분열된 탄환을 한 번에 다 맞아서 즉시 사망할 수도 있다. 세 번째로는, 몬스터의 다양성이 생각보다 적어서 세상을 탐험하는 재미가 반감된다. 물론 초반부의 쉬운 적들과 후반부의 어려운 적들의 구분은 존재한다. 하지만 게임의 절반만 진행해도 새로운 몬스터가 더 이상 나오지 않으며, 극 후반부의 지역에도 8시간 전에 본 몬스터들이 그대로 나오는 걸 보면 허무감을 느낄 수 있다. 적어도 각 지역마다 2 ~ 4 종류의 고유한 몬스터는 넣어 두었어야 플레이어가 탐험하는 맛이 있었지 않을까 싶다.

B. 게임플레이 - 탐험 편

사실 Possessor(s) 를 비추천한 가장 큰 이유는 전투가 아니라 탐험 면이 더 크다. 왜냐하면 예전에 플레이 했던 전투 허접인 메트로배니아들이 그래도 탐험에 비중을 실어서 아예 어드벤처에 비중을 크게 두었거나 (예시: Teslagrad 2 는 전투보다는 퍼즐 및 플랫포밍에 비중이 더 큰 메트로배니아인데, 탐험 관련 기믹이 매우 독창적이며 몇몇 숨겨진 수집품들은 "와 이런 지역이 있었다고??" 라는 경외감이 느껴지게 만든다), 아니면 탐험에서 특출나지 않되 플레이어에게 편의성 기능들을 지원해 주어서 적어도 플레이어가 탐험을 하며 내실을 차곡차곡 쌓아감에 있어 불편함보다는 호기심을 느끼는 데 집중을 하였다면, 이 게임에서는 두 방향 모두 실패하였기 때문이다. 탐험 관련 능력이나 방 배치가 독특하다고 느껴지지 않았으며, 편의성 관련 기능은 죄다 거세해 둔 수준이라 엔딩을 보고 수집품 100% 달성하는 게 고문처럼 느껴진다. 이 두 특징들에 대해 더 자세히 서술해 보자면 다음과 같다.

> 이 게임의 장르가 메트로배니아인 만큼, 게임을 진행하다 보면 매우 익숙한 능력들이 하나씩 해금이 되며, 이를 통해 이전 지역으로 돌아가 못 가봤던 길을 뚫을 수도 있고 숨겨진 방들을 찾을 수 있다. 문제는 이 "새로운 능력" 들이 어디서 많이 본 능력들을 다 하향시킨 기분이라, 능력을 다 해금해도 경쾌하고 매끄러운 플랫포밍이 불가능하다는 점이다. 각 능력들에 대해 (위에서 말한 패링을 빼고) 간략하게 적어 보자면:

1. 채찍 날리기: 채찍으로 적을 끌어 당기는 것 말고도 특정 부위에 채찍을 걸어서 갈고리처럼 움직일 수 있는데, 채찍이 미묘하게 짧으며 채찍이 걸리는 구역에 유도 기능이 없으며 정직하게 8방향으로 플레이어가 휘둘러서 정확하게 감아야 하기 때문에 어처구니 없는 판정으로 채찍이 안 걸려 플랫포밍 구간을 다시 해야 하는 상황들이 종종 나온다. 심지어 몇몇 상황들에서는 채찍이 닿았는데도 안 감아진다!
2. 내려찍기: 바닥을 부술 수 있는 능력. 조작키가 S+shift 라 좀 불편하다는 것 말고는 단점은 없다.
3. 슬라이딩 격파: 슬라이딩으로 벽을 부술 수 있는 능력. 역시 조작키가 S+shift 라 좀 불편하다는 것 말고는 단점은 없다.
4. 벽 달리기: 벽을 탈 수 있는 능력. 문제는 대부분의 메트로배니아에서 벽타기라 하면 염소처럼 벽에 착 매달려서 무한정 매달리는 능력인데, 여기서는 일정 시간 탔다가 벽타기를 취소하고 미끄러지기 때문에 쾌적한 벽타기가 힘들다. 게다가 벽타기 판정이 "미끄러지면서 W를 눌러야 벽을 탄다" 여서 벽타기 키가 씹힐 때도 나오며, 몇몇 벽에서는 아예 벽타기가 불가능하다.
5. 수중 돌진: 물 속에서 Shift 키를 눌러 빠르게 수영하는 능력. 그나마 여기 적힌 것 중에 유일하게 단점이 느껴지지 않은 능력이다.
6. 공중 질주: 다른 게임으로 치면 극후반부에 나오는 능력이라 사실상 최강의 이동기가 되어야 하는데, 그냥 애니메이션 멋진 공중 대쉬이다. 심지어 점프 중에 Shift 키를 두 번 연속으로 눌러야 발동되어서 공중 대쉬 하향된 버전에 더 가깝다. 

눈치가 빠른 사람이라면 알겠지만, 다른 메트로배니아에 흔히 나오는 글라이딩이나 이단 점프와 같이, 탐험이 매우 편해지는 / 게임 내 세상을 한눈에 보기 편해지는 이동기를 게임 끝까지 주지 않는다. 원래 게임 엔딩 쯤 되면 그냥 날아 다니면서 수집품을 싹싹 긁어 먹어야 하는데, Possessor(s) 는 엔딩을 봐도 세상을 이곳저곳 뒤지는 게 불편하게 느껴진다. "그래도 이 정도면 플레이어에게 줄 거 다 준 거 아니냐?" 라고 생각할 수 있는데, 탐험 능력뿐만 아니라 편의성 기능이 부족하다는 것도 문제이다.

> 이어서 적어 보자면, 이 게임을 플레이하며 가장 발목을 잡는 부분은 사실 전투가 아니라, 2026년이 다 되어 가는데도 불편함을 버릴 생각 없는 게임의 구조이다. "의도적으로 불편함을 추구하는 게임이 아니냐?" 라고 생각할 수 있는데, 이러한 명제가 성립하려면 게임이 자신만의 철학이 있거나 탐험 면에서 플레이어에게 감탄을 자아내는 구간이 있어야지, 전투나 탐험 면에서 단 하나의 매력적인 면도 없으면서 탐험을 불편하게 만들어 놓으면 플레이어 입장에서는 "뭐지? 플레이타임을 억지로 늘리려는 것인가?" 라고 게임에 대한 부정적인 감정이 들 수밖에 없다. 크게 두 가지 면에서 편의성의 부재를 느꼈는데, 바로 게임의 지도와 텔레포트 면에서였다. 전자의 경우, 지도가 요즘 메트로배니아들과 비교하면 너무 허접하다. 자세한 경로 표현 없이 그냥 모든 방이 네모의 집합체로 표현되어 있으며, 숨겨진 방을 찾아도 지도에 표시되지 않아서 게임 내 방 구조를 다 외우지 않았다면 지도가 반쪽짜리 도움밖에 주지 않는다. 후자의 경우, 게임 내 세이브 포인트의 분포는 나름 잘 되어 있다만, 문제는 세이브 포인트 간 빠른 이동이 불가능하고, 지역별로 하나만 존재하는 지하철 역에서만 다른 지하철 역으로 순간이동 할 수밖에 없다. 이 때문에 안 그래도 백트래킹으로 인해 호불호가 강한 장르에서 더 백트래킹이 답답하게 느껴지고, 심지어 몇몇 지역은 지하철 역을 꽁꽁 숨겨 놓아서 처음에 못 찾는다면 이후 게임 진행이 심히 비참해질 수도 있다.

더 웃긴 건, 이 두 문제점을 따로따로 가지고 있던 게임들이 이로 인해 비추천 평가를 다소 받은 과거가 있는데, 이 두 개를 같이 결합해 놓고 좋은 평가를 받으려는 심보가 괘씸하다는 것이다. Ender Lilies 의 경우 게임플레이 면에서는 별 말이 없었으나, 게임 내 지도가 자세하지 않고 그냥 직사각형 뭉치여서 이를 싫어한 사람들이 많았다. 그런데 이 게임은 적어도 각 지역 내 구간마다 수집품을 100% 수집했는지 아닌지 알려주는 기능이 탑재되어 있었고, 이 때문에 게임 100% 달성을 자력으로 하는 게 그렇게 어렵지는 않았다. GRIME 의 경우 (게임 출시 버전 기준) 세이브 지점 사이 텔레포트를 무려 최종 보스를 잡고 나서, 즉 엔딩 보기 직전에 준다. 그 이전에는 이 게임처럼 특정 위치 간 제한된 텔레포트만 지원하며, 새로운 능력을 얻고 이전 지역을 돌아보려면 텔레포트 가능한 곳까지 직접 뛰어가야 한다. 차라리 이 게임은 엔딩 보기 직전에 주는 최소한의 배려라도 해두었지, 이 게임은 엔딩을 보고도 그런 거 주지 않는다. 더 놀라운 점은, 여기서 말한 두 게임은 Possessor(s) 와는 다르게 왜 이런 특징들이 욕을 먹는지 배우고 이를 고쳤다는 점이다. Ender Lilies 의 경우 후속작인 Ender Magnolia 에서 지도를 훨씬 보기 좋게 개선하였으며, GRIME 의 경우 대규모 업데이트 이후 게임 중반부에 세이브 포인트 간 텔레포트를 해금할 수 있도록 해 두어서 탐험이 덜 비참하게 느껴지도록 만들었다. 그런데 이 게임은 지역 간 이동이 불편함 + 지도가 상세하지 않음 + 수집품을 찾는 것 관련 편의성 기능 없음 3단 콤보를 동시에 심어 두어서, 메트로배니아 장르의 게임에서 가장 재미있게 느껴져야 할 탐험이 끔찍하게 답답하고 짜증나게 느껴진다. 

> 위에서는 적지 않았으나, 탐험 관련 심각한 단점이 하나 존재한다. 게임 내 초반 지역을 보면 세로로 서 있고 붉은색 실밥같은 게 튀어나와 있어서 딱 봐도 부술 수 있는 것 같은 벽들이 존재하는데, 게임을 플레이 하다 보면 이것들을 어떻게 부수는지 전혀 알려주지 않아서 막히는 상황에 도달할 것이다. 그럼 이들을 어떻게 부수는가? 정답은 "게임 시작 때 얻은 채찍을 튀어 나온 부분에 걸어서 고정한 다음 당겨서 부숴야 한다!" 이다. 이게 진짜 등신같은 게, 게임 내 내려찍기로 부술 수 있는 바닥과 똑같은 색으로 칠해 놓은 벽을 만들어 놓으면, 당연히 플레이어는 이를 보고 "아, 그러면 이 벽이 바닥이랑 비슷하니, 나중에 여기를 부수는 능력을 얻겠구나!" 라고 생각한다는 걸 고려조차 안했다는 것이다. 게다가 채찍으로 당길 수 있는 몇몇 구조물들은 눈에 띄게 하얀색 손잡이를 달아 두었는데, 이건 잘 해 놓고 게임 진행에 핵심적인 채찍으로 벽 부수기는 알려주지도 않는다는 게 기이하게 느껴진다. 심지어 붉은색 벽인데 하단에 존재하는 건 또 (앞의 문장처럼) 채찍으로 못 부수고 슬라이딩 격파 능력을 이용해서 파괴해야 한다! 이쯤되면 게임 내 통일성이나 디테일은 쓰레기통에 버린 수준이다.

It's 2025, everybody knows that this is Lolisouls. 
Is it hard? 
Nah, not really. Parry & just-evade are both viable to clear the game & the Trial Tower. You can clear the game without even parrying once, or you can clear the game without even evading once. But you do need either of them to survive.

How was dying?
This isn't Sekiro: Loli Die Twice. If you die, the game doesn't punish you with fewer souls. You keep the same amount upon death, so keep dying if you're too weak & level up by farming souls.

Do you need to farm/grind stuffs?
For achievements, yeah. For progress, kinda but not too demanding.

Is it cute? 
You bet, but the story is not Gochiusa-kawaii-cute. Then is the story dark? Not really too.

Is it long to beat? 
If you wanna get all achievements, then about 20+ hours. I took about 48hrs because i played blind so i needed to play NG+, and i was overthinking during the Trial Tower.

Is the Trial Tower compulsory? 
Nah it's totally optional for casuals. For achievement hunters, yes. The condition was just to beat it once for the achievement.

How was NG+? 
Enemies hit harder but you can change the difficulty setting at the start of NG+. If you're aiming for achievements, then play on the harder setting first (Advanced). In NG+ you get all your souls & spells so you're kind OP at the start.

Extras:
1. The short movies were short, cute & funny. You get them after beating the game.
2. Noel Danchou & FBK voiced two characters in the game. Didn't know that, was a pleasant surprise.

一开始进去是为了征战三国，结果玩着玩着变成到处找老婆的游戏了

挺上瘾的，从第一次开玩差不多每天都玩10小时，但还是不推荐，简而言之就是如果你喜欢《三国志13》的RPG战略玩法但又觉得不尽兴，你玩这个游戏会对上你的点，让难受并快乐着玩下去，如果你对这种类型游戏不感冒，那他就是依托答辩。
虽然这游戏到处都透着半成品的味儿，但像是UI、交互、特效、操控这类技术上的毛病就不挑了，知道国产小厂也没有那么高的技术力，凑合凑合得了，主要提一些设计层面的不推荐理由

最大的问题就是游玩时候的断点太太太太太太太踏马多了。剧情里不停地在对话和过场旁白中间切换，知道你没那个能力和资源把所有情节表现出来，但其实也不用所有东西都要交代的一清二楚，很多没用的废话旁白过场不用写玩家是可以理解和脑补出来的。进入大地图了更是重量级，武将去世、大事件、武将出仕、过季、年度大赛、孩子出生抓周成年、武将登庸、军粮不足的夺命连环催、战报，最近又新出了一个没什么卵用但是能打断你游戏进程的灾害捣乱。在战场里也是不停有消息打断，击破、支援、俘虏、技能，本来操作手感就稀烂了，一直被打断更是痛苦。关键是各信息停留时长简繁不得当，比如武将出仕我点了接受就直接关掉界面行不行？需要那个又丑又无意义的短暂动画吗？孩子成年或者抓周侍女来报，报完关了就行了需要主角再说一句“知道了”吗？反而是重要的敌军来袭的信息很容易在ESC跳过的时候一闪而过还找不到在哪儿看。
能看出来这个游戏缝了不少其他游戏进来，但设计的时候没考虑过整体只考虑各个模块，导致玩起来很多时候体感很差。如果拿文学来类比，这个游戏的气质属于网络文学，而《三国志》、《太阁》属于严肃文学，虽然三国志被人诟病的点很多，文案幼稚的像儿童向玩法简单的像少年向，但是他有一个整体的设计思路，有一个属于自己的固定风格，而这个游戏则是纯粹的娱乐性、市场导向、量大管饱，但是做事东一榔头西一棒子（那一大堆乱七八糟让玩家开关的可选项就能看出来），这属于国产游戏的通病。好的是至少这个游戏做出来了，还做出来了好玩的点，就是这样容易走不长。
总而言之问题很多很多，但也好玩，主要是很对胃口，如果能把系统和剧情断点问题优化了，我将改成好评

Cleanfall is an excellent mix of World of Goo style building in a roguelike setting, but instead of building a structure, you're building a ship to defend yourself as you dig down. While the building can be a bit clunky at times, your ship will inevitably turn into a scrappy mess after frantically repairing it, so it doesn't quite matter. The biggest problem with designing your ship is that it can feel like you're stuck with something you aren't happy with, but the game forces you to abandon it right when that starts to happen. The turret alchemy system is excellent for getting a little (or a lot) more out of your crappy little ship you made in act 2, along with greatly rewarding you if you play around the system the whole time. Generally the gameplay reminds me of Noita in a way that I can't quite describe, but that's definitely a good thing. One small mistake can completely thrash you, whether that's staying too long or positioning your ship poorly, but you get better at knowing what's a terrible idea and what to plan for as you go. 

I think this game is awesome and I cannot wait to see more from this game and the dev. Cleanfall is definitely worth checking out if you like physics based games and roguelikes.

Quite like a first-person adventure, even often relaxing when you weren't being pursued. Good logical and mostly physical puzzles. Cool screen effects when you lose sanity. The diary entries were very well written, reminded me of a novel, but they weren't too long. This first instalment of the Amnesia series made me want to play the others.

Игра отлично передаёт чувство полной беззащитности. У тебя нет оружия. Ни пистолета, ни даже дубины. Встретив монстра, ты можешь только одно - бежать и прятаться. И от этого не становится скучно.

Отдельно хочется выделить механику рассудка. Когда ты находишься в темноте или видишь что-то ужасное, твой разум начинает сдавать. Экран мутнеет, по стенам ползут тени, слышатся шепоты, а руки Даниэля трясутся. Это не просто визуальный эффект - это прямой сигнал: "Найди свет, иначе сойдешь с ума". Поиск масла для лампы или последней трутницы становится вопросом выживания.

Атмосфера в игре просто отличная. Мрачный готический замок, скрип половиц, завывание ветра в пустых залах... Звуковой дизайн здесь работает на все 100%. Иногда самый жуткий момент - это не появление монстра, а просто звук чьего-то дыхания у тебя за спиной, когда ты уверен, что вокруг никого нет.
Сюжет подается через записки и флешбэки, и тебе самому интересно собирать воедино пазл того, что же случилось с главным героем и почему он оказался в этой адской ловушке.

Недостатки? Возможно, графика по современным меркам уже не та, а некоторым финал может показаться немного скомканным. Но эти мелочи меркнут на фоне того, какой уникальный и пугающий опыт предлагает игра.
Это эталонный хоррор, который заставит вас бояться темноты по-взрослому. Это игра, которую нужно прочувствовать, а не просто пройти. После неё вы ещё долго будете с опаской смотреть на темные дверные проёмы и прислушиваться к ночным звукам.

[h1] Мемные Зомби [/h1]
Кажется, что в эту игру удачно зарядили множество пасхалок и отсылок. К тому же, это оказался шикарный шутер с богатой прокачкой.

[h1] СЮЖЕТ [/h1]
Зомби захватили мир. К счастью, у героев есть машина времени и они могут попробовать победить апокалипсис.

[h1] ГЕЙМПЛЕЙ [/h1]
Игровой процесс представляет собой шутер с серьезной прокачкой оружия и массой режимов.

После небольшого пролога герой оказывается на многофункциональной базе. Здесь несколько секретов, станция отправки дронов помощи, аппарат гэмблинга, несколько порталов на испытания, тир, торговцы и строительство глобальных объектов (машина времени и здоровая пушка).

По сути, мы можем заниматься практически всем, чем душа пожелает, чем дальше по прохождению, тем больше  возможностей.

Есть приличных размеров общая кампания. Она находится в круглом фиолетовом портале. Прямо тут же располагаются стадии испытания определённых видов оружия и уровни с бесконечными волнами атакующих врагом. Уровней и локаций тут очень много. Врагов и боссов просто море. На локациях в этом портале можно и нужно отыскивать секретики, которые обновляются раз в час.

Кроме того есть режим рогалика. Он в портале за стеклянными дверями. Тут проверяем себя  на прочность и пробуем проходить всё усложняющиеся локации. Кроме боевых испытаний тут, конечно, полно и наград. С этим режимом связаны перки оружия и возможность бафнуть свои пушки во всех режимах мощными усилениями. Наград в виде ресурсов тоже наваливают от души. Это не тот рогалик, где при смерти теряешь всё, наоборот, чем больше продвинешься, тем больше получишь ништяков. Стимулирует к превозможению. 

Чтоб войти в режим рогалика понадобятся специальные билеты. Если активно играть, то их будет в достатке.

Ещё имеется нестабильный портал. Это красный прямоугольный портал. Здесь раз в некоторое время появляются совершенно забавные уровни. Например, порубить зомби пожарным топором в горящем доме. К этому режиму подошли явно творчески. Награды хорошие, как тут и везде.

В центре хаба находится стойка постоянно идущих разнообразных соревнований и испытаний. Кто настреляет больше всего зомбаков из дробовика или из снайперки? Это регулярно выясняется. Награды в наличии.

Даже за полминуты зачётной стрельбы в тире дают немного монет и показывают рейтинг попаданий.

=======================

Очень понравились необычные шутерные механики. Во всех режимах кроме рогалика у нас бесконечные патроны. А вот в рогалике приходится экономить каждый патрон и стратегически распределять из каких стволов, кого и когда убивать. Ещё в рогалике накидывают временных пассивных усилений. 

У нашего героя будет пять типов пушек: Пистолет, Автомат, Дробовик/Снайперка, Гранатомёт/Пулемёт и холодное оружие. В каждом из пяти видов штук 20 оружек, почти к каждой пушке есть скины, которые ещё усиляют оружия. Система очень даже мощная.

Еще есть что-то типа общих усилений. Сюда относятся баррикады разной крепкости и хорошие шмотки по прибавке здоровья и брони герою.

=======================

Суперский процесс стрельбы и боя. Обычно дело происходит на архитектурно сложно устроенных локациях. Из особых входов лезут зомбаки разных видов. Кого тут только нет и чем дальше, тем враги чуднее. Например, как вам пьяные черепашки-ниндзя-зомби, которые кидаются бутылками и показывают своё кунгфу? Драки очень бодрые, напряженные. Зевать совершенно нельзя.

Рассмотрим плюсы и минусы игры, подведем итоги.

Удивили и порадовали QTE, не думал что они окажутся настолько к месту. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3598503185 В игре много смелых решений, разработчики не побоялись показать расчленение детей, каждая смерть оставляет мрачное послевкусие, и от того насколько это реалистично, от понимания жестокости мира, создается особая, непередаваемая словами атмосфера. На первый взгляд светлая сказка со временем оставляет тебя лишь с тьмой, заставляя наблюдать за повешенными жителями и их утопленными детьми - при том, что главный герой сам еще совсем мальчик. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3598503703 Отдельно хочется поговорить о боссах, сражения с ними выполнены в стандарте крупных игр, где необходимо заучивать атаки и уклоняться. И это идеально сочетается с созданием атмосферы через смерти, умирать придется в любом случае перед тем как выучить атаки. Игра бросает вызов, требует адаптации, но при этом грань сложности на оптимальном, не душном уровне. Из серьезных минусов могу отметить только кривоватое управление из-за выбранной перспективы, здесь идентичные проблемы от очевидного вдохновения Little Nightmares. Bramble: The Mountain King - это настоящий hidden gem в жанре, крайне достойный и не настолько известный, каким заслуживает быть.

Mirá, si sos de los que se manija con los juegos onda Little Nightmares pero querés una historia más cruda y ambientación que te vuela la cabeza, este juego, el Bramble, es un golazo de media cancha.

Te ponés en la piel de Olle, un pibito que sale a buscar a su hermana, Lillemor, que se la llevó un trolazo (¡posta!). Lo que arranca como una pavada en un bosque re lindo se te transforma en un cuento de hadas nórdico, pero de esos que te cuentan para que no salgas de casa, ¿viste? Acá la cosa se pone turbia, eh.

¿Por qué tenés que jugarlo? Los Pro que te parten la cabeza:
⚡ La Ambientación es un Viaje de Ida: Los escenarios son un flash, una belleza. Pasás de bosques re coloridos a lugares que son puro cachengue (quilombo/problema). Todo inspirado en la mitología sueca. Sentís que sos una hormiguita en un mundo gigante y peligroso. ¡El diseño de las criaturas es zarpado! Te da un toque de cagazo (miedo) pero no de jumpscare berreta, sino de ese terror que te da cosa.

🎶 El Sonido es Pura Melodía (y Tensión): La música es sublime, te mete de lleno en la historia. Te juro que los efectos de sonido te hacen sentir el crujido de las ramas y los pasos de esos bichos gigantes que te quieren morfar. ¡Es un festín para los oídos!

📖 La Trama es un Enganche Total: Es lineal, sí, pero la historia te atrapa. Es un cuento oscuro, lleno de emociones fuertes y te juro que tiene momentos que te dan un vuelco al estómago. Acá no te esconden nada, es gore y cruel cuando tiene que serlo. Es la aventura de Olle madurando a las piñas.

Ojo al piojo: No es un paseo por el parque. Hay partes de plataformas y persecuciones que te van a hacer transpirar la gota gorda. Pero el sistema de checkpoints es re copado, así que si palmás, volvés casi al toque sin renegar.

En resumen, Bramble no es solo un juego, es una experiencia que te queda grabada. Si te va el terror con onda, la mitología y las historias que te hacen pensar, ¡dale una oportunidad, no seas gil! Es una joyita indie que merece todo el bombo (publicidad/atención).

¡Ponelo a descargar ahora, que es un juegazo! Después contame. 😉

I'm not finished with this game, but I just had to leave a review. If you loved 8-bit Armies, then is an obvious and easy purchase. Everything is upgraded, from the visuals to game enhancements. For newcomers, this is a really fun RTS with deep unit variety and diverse missions. The game even supports different modes to keep it engaging. I love the Rogue mode, which was a free upgrade. 10 out of 10!

While it is a basic game by design, this is one of those cases where it has become too basic.

It's very clear that the only way to play the game is build wide with rapid expands, followed by blobbing the enemy since neither their units nor base defences will be enough to stop you. I don't quite know what could be done here, but there needs to be more options for economy, and something about the Rock-Paper-Scissors mechanics needs to be looked at, since certain units are clearly performing too well (Most of the tanks), even when countering with Air based Anti-Vehicle, the AI can't really answer a tank horde unless it's got one of their own.

I think there's parts of the game that are interesting, but imho given that games like Beyond All Reason exist (which is a 100% free game, no MTX, no nothing), this makes games like this a much harder sell, doubly so since C&C (Generals, Zero Hour, Red Alert 3, I mean pick your poision tbh) is still around and still plays better than this for not much more money.

The rock papers scissors element could've been interesting if the pace of the game wasn't so high, since as a player you are rarely able to pair counter unit with counter unit, so it really just comes down to numbers, production efficency and cost to win, which makes the game more simple than their competitors as well, without any tangible benefit for it.

First of all, I think it's a great game.
But there are a few annoying things that are mostly convenience/design issues that could be addressed with simple quality of life fixes (idk, maybe it was lack of budget or whatever but still).
For example, the game would've profited significantly if it had any hints on where to go next when you have multiple options of what to do and different possible locations to go, but instead you end up wandering everywhere pixel hunting. Or the fact that there's no ability to run can be annoying at times, because everything is so slow, or the part with the flashlight - the idea is good but the controls are nightmarish at times. Deduction is also a bit confusing, because some options get hidden by the new ones, then later you see some things you already know but the options are still there etc. Or having to wait after every launch of the game while it's loading a heavy scene to have a smooth transition into a new game? I get that it looks cool the first time you play it, but the game could've checked whether there are any saved games and have a different starting menu if so. And these are all really not bugs and could be fixed relatively simply - this is why it's so unfortunate to have them.
That said, the rest of the game outshines the cons - style, music, deduction, plot, mechanics, characters - all that I really liked. Also there are really some not that obvious choices that'll have consequences and some different and sometimes unexpected outcomes. One day, someone thought "what if I made a fairly laid-back, casual fishing game and used it to tell a Lovecraftian horror story?" This is the result. It's probably not for everyone, but I loved it.

The fishing isn't overcomplicated: go to the right spot and play a fairly simple minigame, then maybe do a bit of inventory management to fit the fish in your hold. There are things that want to kill you, but during the day (roughly speaking) they're limited to specific areas of the game world. At night, the monsters come! So it's up to you whether you want to play it safe and sleep through most nights safe at a harbour, or take risks to get the valuable fish that come out at night.

The ambience is interesting: a slightly unlikely mix of cozy and creepy. And the story, while light, is fun. If mild horror and fairly chilled out gameplay appeal to you, give this a try. Definitely one where I'll keep an eye on new games from this developer.

The individual sprite animations have so much life and quirkiness. For example: the sprites move across the board at different speeds depending on the unit type, so mounted skeletons advance to the next area a little faster than the walking skeletons. It shows so much love an care in it's small details that I just adored. I also loved the tailored sound design of the units. 
Other reviewers complain that the game is slow and repetitive. I can see how they had that experience but I think that's part of the genre with turn-based combat encounters and the loop-style game set up. The game was actually shorter than I expected because some reviews made it out to be endless story acts (I think it's 5 acts? I will say they are repetitive with content but with a new mini boss and enemy types added each time). If you replayed through every difficulty (I did not) you would definitely get bored. But I played through the game completely twice, not rushing, and had fun both times, then just grinded out the last couple tricky achievements.
I had fun but if you're still on the fence, on sale the game is a steal. It can be repetitive but it has a gorgeous art style, so much charm and isn't really all that long of a game. I feel like it hit a sweet spot but do see how others could not have as fun of an experience. I would still heartily recommend giving the game a go.

Wow, Streamer Life Simulator 2 — what an experience. Not the game itself, of course, but the incredible vanishing act by the developers. Seriously though, was this just a social experiment to see how long people would wait for basic bug fixes before realizing they got scammed? No updates, no patch notes, no "Hey, we're alive!"—just total radio silence. It's almost artistic how thoroughly you've ghosted your own game. We’re not even mad at the bugs anymore—we’ve formed emotional attachments to them. At least they stuck around.

Next time, maybe slap a "Now with 100% more neglect!" sticker on the store page so people know what they’re actually getting. Just a thought.

It's a really solid adventure game in the vein of King's Field, The Elder Scrolls, and Lunacid. Quite frankly, if you enjoyed Lunacid, I think you'll find yourself at home with this one.

Anyway, it's an open world adventure game. You run about and do quests. The combat is extremely simple and you could probably play the entire game without fighting at all if you were familiar enough with the game. Your deaths will likely only ever involve falling. It's just not a game focused on combat.

What really makes the game shine is that it's filled with tough choices. I often found myself not completing quests because I really just didn't like either option. I mean that entirely in a positive way. The game is just full of uncomfortable decisions and you're free to not choose. 

However, as much as I enjoyed the story and the setting, I wasn't big on the ending. The "good" ending feels out of touch with the game's narrative. The alternative ending was alright, I was expecting a bit more but I wouldn't call it "bad" either. Still, it was worth completing.

I finished this game last year in a week-long binge and I just keep thinking about how special it is. Dread Delusion is by no means perfect, and I'll get my main criticism out of the way to start - the combat and just base mechanics are incredibly basic, to the point where you're going to need to essentially be willing to overlook them to enjoy this game. They're not un-fun to engage with - it's very low friction - it's more that the game just fails to challenge you mechanically in any meaningful way. Also, there's not much music in the game - it gets real repetitive, real fast.

BUT

Pretty much everything else about the game is just fantastic. The world of Dread Delusion is one of my favorite open world RPGs I've experienced to date - the writing in this game is genuinely good, I was very invested in the worldbuilding and several of the individual characters, and each area pokes on some philosophical questions that are deep enough to not have clear, clean answers. The entire game's quests and even main storyline is wonderfully gray in a legitimately compelling way, rather than an oversimplified black and white or some arbitrary chalked-up ambiguity.

The sense of exploration in this game is really palpable - you're using your compass and map to orient, working off of landmarks, looking for hidden passages and cues. I absolutely adore the art style as well - I think it's incredibly evocative and immersive once you sink into it.

For $20, there's a ton of really high quality content here. I think this game is genuinely special; you can feel the passion from the devs come through on this one. If you're looking at this wondering if it's worth the leap, I encourage you to take it. Can't wait for their next game.

The rooms and furniture in Little Corners are seriously charming and well drawn and there are 3 hidden stickers to solve per room, which is awesome. This game is also a welcome non-pixel art addition to decorating games like Whisper of the House and Unpacked.

However, anyone who has done sticker books knows the charm comes from the precision and freedom of placement in those books, and this game really does not do those factors well (or at all).

Some serious qualms I have about the game:
- Some pieces are so tiny I have no godly idea what they are supposed to be and there is no way in this game to zoom in. Not being able to zoom in to see the pieces or to even help you precisely place pieces is a feature I think is necessary for accessibility and enjoyment. The small pieces are the best part of a sticker book so not being able zoom in to see them or to just make placement easier sucks.
- I used to do sticker books with tweezers because the pieces were so small. There are plenty of small pieces in the game, but the fat hand-shaped mouse cursor is infuriating and you can't tell where it's pointing... Good luck rearranging a sticker that you accidentally put on another sticker without the power to zoom in and with the clunky cursor.
- You can only rotate stickers horizontally and that is all?! I don't need to be able to rotate it 360 degrees, even if that would be nice and truer to a sticker book, but I NEED to at least be able to flip some stickers upside down. Like the first room has a set of utensils for the dining table, but I can't rotate them so all my utensils face the same way. Yes, it's a small detail -- but small details is the selling point of the game.
- This is a less necessary feature to the above, but I still think it would be really nice. The layering system is awesome and can be made better if the players could actually see and rearrange the layers in a list, like in a photo editing program like Photoshop.

The art that went into the game is truly charming and I would have bought the sticker sheets if they existed in real life. However, as a game trying to emulate a sticker sheet, it just lacks the precision and QOL that I would expect from any decorating game.

I will change my review to a positive one if the devs add zooming in and more ways to flip stickers than just vertically, because both features are way too essential to not exist in a game based on sticker sheets

It is always, always, always important to remember with games like these that each item that can be placed is the result of a certain amount of artistic talent that was funneled into designing pieces that can seamlessly fit with each other to make a cohesive whole no matter what. With that alone in mind, the price is a bargain and because there is no endgame the game is, in theory, infinitely replayable.

The secret sticker aspect is fun, and it's clear that a lot of thought went into what sort of designs could work in each themed room. The items all have to be placed manually, they don't 'click' even if one looks like it should seamlessly fit around another - good for creativity, bad for perfectionists. 

Pros:
- Art's cute. You're reading this, you can use your eyes. It's a sticker game, the art's cute.
- Hidden stickers are like little puzzles and I love me a funny little puzzle.
- Guys it's like five dollars, who doesn't love a bargain? For this much of a genuinely cozy game? That's borderline theft. Never mind buying it, I'd feel guilty for refunding it even if I wanted to. It's five dollars.
- Customizing is fun and you wouldn't be here if you didn't agree.

Cons:
- The game runs fine but my laptop wheezes like it's dying anyway. Some code review might be necessary, I'm not used to such a simple-looking game getting my computer to make those noises.
- I knew this from looking at the trailer, but there's a very specific overarching theme for all the rooms, and while that theme does account for some fantasy it probably won't be able to capture your specific dnd artistic vision room or what have you. Maybe in the future.
- I'm not at all opposed to the layering system, but I do wish there were a list of layers simply because scrolling through the entire list of props because you forgot to place a rug at the bottom is one of those harmless little hassles.

Anyway, good game, it's a steal, you should buy it.

The Spirit and the Mouse is a gentle, heartfelt adventure that trades tension for warmth and spectacle for charm. Set in the small French village of Sainte-et-Claire, the game casts you as Lila, an ordinary house mouse who becomes infused with electric powers after a storm. Rather than turning this premise into a tale of danger or epic quests, the developers lean fully into comfort. Lila’s new powers connect her to Lumion, a guardian spirit responsible for the happiness of the village’s residents, and together they set out to mend small disruptions in the townspeople’s lives. From its opening minutes, the game establishes a tone of kindness and curiosity, making it clear that its priority is not challenge but empathy and exploration.

The village itself is the heart of the experience. Sainte-et-Claire is lovingly crafted in miniature, with narrow cobblestone pathways, old stone buildings, cozy cafés, and laundry hanging from balconies. The environments are compact yet rich in detail, inviting players to poke into alleys, scamper across rooftops, and crawl through vents. The lighting and art direction evoke a warm, slightly magical version of Europe, and the soundtrack supports the atmosphere with soft melodies and ambient flourishes. As you explore, you encounter humans going about their daily lives—each with small troubles that Lila and Lumion take it upon themselves to solve. The stakes may be tiny, but the emotional impact comes from restoring comfort and connection to these residents one small act at a time.

Gameplay unfolds as a mix of light puzzle-solving, exploration, and platforming framed around Lila’s newfound electrical abilities. She can zip through power cables, activate switches, and channel energy to restore broken devices. These abilities open up playful traversal routes, letting you weave through the world in ways only a tiny lightning-powered mouse could. Much of the game revolves around helping Kibblins—mischievous little spirits who embody electrical energy. Individually, they each present short tasks or challenges, and gathering them becomes a central loop. While none of the puzzles are particularly taxing, they are varied enough to keep the experience engaging, relying on observation and movement rather than trial and error.

What makes the experience compelling is its rhythm. There are no enemies to defeat, no timers, no game-over screens. Instead, The Spirit and the Mouse flows at a gentle pace that encourages wandering. Each quest contributes to a larger sense of restoring harmony to the village, and your interactions with characters—whether human or spirit—carry a light emotional resonance. This is a game designed to make the player feel helpful, not heroic, and that distinction gives it a refreshing identity in a genre often dominated by action-oriented objectives.

The simplicity does come with limitations. The puzzles rarely evolve beyond basic interactions, and the structure of “talk to a villager, activate objects, return with results” can feel repetitive if played in long sessions. Some camera quirks and small UI irregularities occasionally interrupt the smoothness of the experience, and the game’s scale means that once the main story is completed—typically in five to six hours—only optional collectibles remain. For players seeking mechanical depth or narrative complexity, the game may feel more like a relaxing diversion than a fully layered adventure.

Even with these constraints, the game’s charm is undeniable. The Spirit and the Mouse succeeds precisely because it commits wholeheartedly to its cozy premise. Its world is warm and inviting, its characters feel grounded despite the magical framing, and its tone stays consistently uplifting. It offers a style of play that emphasizes connection, care, and gentle exploration in a landscape where quiet experiences are increasingly valued. For players wanting a soothing, visually appealing, and heartwarming journey, this is exactly the kind of game that leaves a lingering sense of comfort long after the credits roll.

Tempest, developed by HeroCraft and published by HeroCraft PC, is a pirate-themed action RPG that invites players to live out the age-old fantasy of commanding a ship on the high seas. The game blends open-world exploration, naval combat, and light role-playing elements into a single seafaring adventure. From the moment you set sail, the sense of freedom is striking—you can chart your own course across the ocean, take on quests, engage in trade, hunt sea monsters, or simply plunder other ships for profit. Unlike many pirate games that focus on scripted storytelling, Tempest leans heavily into player choice and open-ended discovery. Its strength lies in the feeling of captaining your own vessel through dangerous waters and watching your modest sloop gradually evolve into a fearsome warship adorned with unique upgrades and mythical enhancements.

The world of Tempest is spread across multiple regions, each dotted with ports, factions, and opportunities for wealth or trouble. The player can take contracts for various factions, engage in smuggling, or form temporary alliances—all while keeping an eye on the wind and the weather that affect how their ship handles. Trading is straightforward but rewarding: goods fluctuate in price between islands, encouraging long-distance commerce for profit. Combat, meanwhile, offers the kind of cinematic tension that makes piracy so thrilling. Ship-to-ship battles rely on positioning, timing, and cannon management, with the choice of ammunition types adding a layer of tactical decision-making. Watching cannonballs tear through enemy hulls while waves crash around your vessel is deeply satisfying, and the addition of boarding mechanics allows for close-quarters chaos when you close in for the kill.

As the journey unfolds, Tempest introduces fantastical elements that set it apart from traditional pirate simulations. Mythical creatures like the Kraken and Leviathan lurk in the deep, and players can acquire enchanted crystals that imbue their ships with supernatural powers—reflecting projectiles, boosting speed, or summoning monstrous allies. These touches of fantasy add spice to the experience, though they may not appeal to purists seeking a historically grounded pirate adventure. Still, they help keep the gameplay loop fresh by mixing seafaring realism with magical spectacle. The balance between these two tones—the historical and the mystical—is one of Tempest’s more distinctive qualities, even if it doesn’t always mesh perfectly. It’s clear that HeroCraft wanted to create a world that felt larger than life, where folklore and adventure coexist just beyond the horizon.

Visually, Tempest performs admirably for an indie project. The ocean is dynamic and beautiful, with changing lighting and weather patterns that make each voyage feel unique. Ship models are well detailed, and there’s a gratifying sense of weight to how they move across the waves. While not pushing the limits of graphical fidelity, the art direction captures the romanticism of high-seas adventure. The user interface, however, can sometimes feel dated and clunky. Navigating menus, equipping upgrades, or managing trade goods lacks the fluidity of more polished RPGs, occasionally breaking immersion. The audio design fares better, with a rousing orchestral score and the distant boom of cannons enhancing the mood. The overall presentation succeeds in drawing the player into a world that feels alive, even if it’s occasionally rough around the edges.

In terms of pacing, Tempest’s open structure can be both a blessing and a curse. The freedom to explore means you can spend hours trading and upgrading your ship before diving into combat-heavy missions. However, that same freedom can lead to repetition, as many of the game’s activities—raiding merchant convoys, collecting bounties, or escorting allies—follow similar patterns. The quest variety isn’t deep, and over time, the repetition of naval battles may diminish the sense of novelty. Yet for those who enjoy the meditative rhythm of exploration and ship management, this repetition becomes part of the charm. There’s something undeniably relaxing about sailing from port to port, selling rum and silk, then fending off a sudden pirate ambush before returning to calm seas. It captures the ebb and flow of a pirate’s life, alternating between moments of chaos and tranquility.

Tempest’s RPG systems, while not overly complex, give a sense of progression that keeps you invested. Earning gold and reputation allows you to purchase better ships, weapons, and crew members, while upgrading your vessel with mystical crystals adds strategic variety. Crew morale plays a subtle role in determining how efficiently your ship performs, reminding you that your success depends on the people who keep the cannons loaded and the sails trimmed. The game’s difficulty is forgiving enough to welcome newcomers but offers enough challenge to satisfy those who seek tactical naval combat. Despite occasional technical hiccups and a few bugs, the overall experience is stable and smooth, especially after post-launch updates that refined many of its earlier issues.

Ultimately, Tempest captures the essence of what makes pirate adventures compelling: the thrill of freedom, the danger of the unknown, and the satisfaction of building your own legend at sea. It’s not a game that tries to overwhelm with cinematic storytelling or complex systems—it’s a game that trusts the player to create their own tales of adventure. While it suffers from limited quest diversity and occasional clumsy interface design, its charm lies in the authenticity of its ambition. Sailing across the ocean, battling foes, and discovering mysterious creatures provides a sense of escapism that few pirate games manage to sustain so effectively. For players who crave an open-world experience driven by exploration, trade, and naval combat, Tempest offers a voyage worth taking. It may not reach the heights of AAA polish, but its heart, atmosphere, and spirit of adventure make it a rewarding journey for anyone who has ever dreamed of hoisting the black flag and claiming the sea as their own.

It's really funny how one's perception of a game may change over time. When I bought Who's Lila? shortly after it came out, I liked the unique gameplay concept but I quickly abandoned it, brushing it off as one of those games where you replay the same thing with minor variations everytime, to shed light on an overcomplicated and pretentious plot. And while yeah, that is partially true, there is much to love here.

Lila could be considered a strange point and click adventure game. Instead of solving puzzles through inventory items, you basically have to go to places, talk with people and think about what you could do differently. The unique gameplay hook of the game is that the protagonist, William Clarke, has to deliberately move face muscles in order to express emotions: this translates to you having to manually compose an expression by clicking and dragging each specific muscle, while also fighting against the involuntary muscle spasms that occour when William is particularly agitated. This is a neat system for different reasons: for starters, it's unique and unlike anything else I've ever played; secondly, it allows for dialogue trees of sorts while remaining unpredictable. Not every emotion gives way to unique dialogue, but many of them do, and witnessing the outcomes is one of the game's strengths. Aside from that, there aren't many traditional puzzles to solve, but there is plenty of meta-game thinking to do: Lila has strong Alternate Reality Game components, and if you want to collect its many endings you'll have to do a bit of investigating among the game files, the Steam and itch.io pages and more. Now, I usually don't really like ARGs, because most of them (at least that I know of in the indie games sphere) are hyperfocused on the community aspect, strictly requiring the collective work because the things you need to do are far too elaborate and esoteric to figure out on your own. In Lila, it's just another component to the single player game. Nothing particularly outlandish is required to get a pretty complete picture of the story, just some lateral thinking and getting into the mindset the game wants you to have. There are crazy secrets which basically require a guide, but they are just that: secrets, and while they reveal some of the most obscure facets of the plot, the story is plenty enjoyable by just achieving the 15 regular endings. If anything, the most frustrating part is that some of the endings are just slight variations of each other, and it's not always clear what exactly nets you one or the other. But it's not egregious.

The premise of the game is that a girl named Tanya Kennedy is missing, and pretty much everybody suspects the socially awkward recluse William Clarke. Now, this kind of summary is much like saying "Twin Peaks is about this Laura Palmer girl who got murdered", and I say this because Lila wears its David Lynch influences on its sleeve. Aside from the explicit homage with a poster of Blue Velvet you can find, the game is filled with the legendary director's sense of surrealism, more specifically (but not limited to) the horror-inclined surrealism of Eraserhead and Twin Peaks: The Return. What surprised me is that, while Lila is not subtle about its utter adoration for good ol' David, it still puts its own spin on things and manages to be quite the distinctive blend. Yeah, you can find familiar themes and images such as electricity gaining an almost mythical quality, or souls inhabiting machines much like Philip Jeffries in The Return, but most is contextualized within a philosophical framework, with the game asking explicit questions on the reality of things, the perspective of the beholder, one's sense of self, the life people collective "infuse" within works of art, and more. While David Lynch often just alludes, creates images and refuses to elaborate, requiring the viewer's imagination to figure out a meaning that might or might not even be there (which is something I never fully embraced), Lila requires the player's engagement to piece together what the game has to say, while also leaving them much room for reflection. The player's agency is integral to the game itself, for a storytelling that is unique to games. More and more titles, indies especially, are employing the medium's unique storytelling capabilities, and I love it.

The presentation is another thing that's unique to Lila, adopting a crunchy, "ditherpunk" visual style that makes everything hazy and surreal. Plus, the ever-present faces on the right of the screen bring to mind the Nintendo DS cult classics Hotel Dusk: Room 215 and The Secret of Cape West, which I miss very dearly. The game is also not afraid to break its own visual rules and surprise you. The soundtrack and sound design are also great, very alienating and otherwordly.

Overall, I'm really glad I gave Lila another chance, as it is one of my favourite ARG-infused experimental horrors with amazing ideas and a unique gameplay to boot.
Gimmicks aside, still genuinely a fantastic game. Love the story.

Une bonne suite pour tous ceux qui ont aimés le premier Styx, ça en reprend les principes de jeu et nous proposer à nouveau de l'infiltration dans de grandes niveaux très dense et avec beaucoup de verticalité afin de profiter de toute la panoplie de mouvements et de capacités de notre gobelin préféré.

On a ainsi à nouveau le contrôle de Styx, toujours aussi cupide, rusé et agile mais néanmoins très fragile ce qui est une bonne chose pour un jeu d'infiltration car il est tout bonnement impossible de a jouer bourrin dans ce jeu et le level design récompense la curiosité et l'exploration.
Au cours de la progression dans les différents niveaux on aura en effet l'occasion d'accomplir des objectifs annexes en écoutant des conversations qui nous renseigneront sur des trésors et opportunités ce qui aura un vrai impact sur notre façon de jouer en débloquant de nouveaux objets comme une cape d'invisibilité qui va booster le pouvoir associé ou bien une nouvelle potion pour masquer notre odeur par exemple.
On aura aussi toujours de nombreux moyens d'accéder à l'endroit désiré que ce soit par des passages dans les murs, des points d'accroches en hauteur, des lustres à escalader, des cordes tendues sur lesquelles glisser ou tout simplement des portes à ouvrir ou crocheter. Le jeu nous laisse libre de choisir le chemin par lequel passer et les cartes fourmillent de petites passages dérobés.

On a aussi un système de branches de compétences qui se débloqueront avec des points accumulés par la complétion des différents objectifs au cours des missions.

Là où le jeu est moins bon c'est que c'est une suite un peu fainéante: on a plus ou moins les mêmes capacités que dans le premier et au final pas tant d'environnements que ça car on retourne dans certains endroits déjà visités fréquemment. Il me semble que c'était déjà le cas dans le premier Styx et je m'attendais à ce qu'il fasse mieux avec la suite. Dommage.

Le scénario se termine aussi assez brusquement et appelle à une suite (elle a été annoncée depuis).

Globalement ça reste un jeu solide en particulier si comme moi vous aimez les jeux d'infiltration mais il ne faut pas s'attendre à la suite qui chamboule tout et améliore grandement la formule.

Unfortunately, most of this does not seem to present in the base game and its balance has been heavily skewed towards the melee combat which was by far the worst part of the demo. In the demo, you having to make use of your melee combat felt like a justified punishment for missing too many shots before downing an enemy - in the base game, you are practically forced to do so because your shots do basically no damage to even the base mobs and unlike in the demo where they did drop ammo, here its a crapshoot to where they will or won't and most of the times, they don't - forcing you to kite enemies around to try and melee them safely.

I still think this game's demo is absolute peak gameplay but very misleading to what the final game ended up being. 

Healing items and ammo are obscenely stingy. You can get a singular healing item by backtracking to the station hub and while the secondary healing item is purchase-able, they cost so much it's practically almost not worth doing so. You at most randomly earn $10 from random mobs whereas to replace a healing item it can cost $150 from the only item shop that you can't even use until you spend $100 prior to. I love hexagons and general deductive stuff more than I hate sudoku, so I had to try [b]hexdoku[/b] at some point.

you have to place various shapes all over the hex-based grids, without repeating them in the same line or area. no guessing necessary, one solution per level. [b]32 main levels[/b] unlocked one by one, including a tutorial and a final 'thank you' level. [b]31 bonus stages[/b] with slightly different rules are made available on separate branches when you reach them on the map (3x10 but one also has a tutorial, and they also unlock one by one).

[b]custom levels[/b] get enabled after level 7. there are only two, but this is where workshop levels would go too. the [b]level editor with workshop support[/b] appears after level 9, and the [b]random level generator[/b] after level 13. you can choose from 4, 5 or 6 shapes and even enter a seed, so generated levels can be shared easily.

[b]mouse-only controls do their job.[/b] when you click or pick a piece up, same ones on the level get highlighted. if the [i]'display affected cells'[/i] toggle is on (I really recommend it), you can right click any cell to show other cells it affects, predictably. right clicking a fillable cell lets you mark it for future reference with the shape(s) of your choice, so left click does the affected cells things there. it also works elsewhere, except on cells containing a shape placed by you. mouse wheel zooms, holding left click moves the level around, neither are really necessary. in fact, I'd like a toggle to disable board movement, as it's very easy to do that instead of whatever your intention was.

[b]mid-level progress is not saved, but no reset or penalty when you make a mistake[/b], the piece won't even fly back to the bottom, you can have them all over the screen. completion time and 'mark assignment count' are shown at the end but no visible timer, thankfully.

the [b]easy mode toggle[/b] adds an extra icon to the bottom, clicking it shows which pieces can go on which cell. it [b]doesn't adapt to changes automatically, have to click it again when you need help[/b], but it's not a mistake finder. right clicking pieces in the inventory while easy mode is enabled shows where they can go on the grid, based on the current state of the board. the eraser icon clears cells of markings, whether they're from easy mode or your own. 

the minimalist graphics serve their purpose but some of the music doesn't really fit the game, would've expected something less... noisy, I guess. windowed mode, resolutions, separate volume settings, some languages, and a toggle for the background to make bouncing balls disappear. only gameplay-related toggles and volume settings are available while playing a level.

far be it from me to toot my own horn, but I'm relatively good at this sort of puzzling, so let's blame the hot weather for draining what little patience I have and call that a reason for [b]finding this more difficult than expected[/b]. I often had a hard time deducing the next logical step, I was only done with about half the levels when I posted the review and it took many more hours and a bunch of easy mode to get through the rest. or maybe it's just more difficult, and with relatively few levels there's not much room for filler. [b]it's a challenging and enjoyable package for a good price[/b], and you can [b]try the demo[/b] on the game's [url=https://puetsua.itch.io/hexdoku]itch page[/url].

Interesting shape-based twist on the Sudoku formula. Judicious use of color makes it much more playable than other attempts to deviate from the traditional 3x3 grid. Good QoL, though some of it has to be turned on via the settings. Runs great on Steamplay.

Botany Manor is a gentle, atmospheric puzzle adventure that invites players into a meticulously crafted English estate filled with sunlight, quiet gardens, and scientific curiosity. Developed by Balloon Studios and published by Whitethorn Games, the game places you in the role of Arabella Greene, a retired botanist who has returned to her family manor in the late 19th century to complete her life’s work. Rather than relying on dialogue-heavy storytelling or dramatic plot twists, the game unfolds through exploration—every room, scrap of paper, and forgotten notebook becomes a piece of Arabella’s world, inviting you to reconstruct her research and rediscover who she was beyond the labels society imposed on her.

At its core, Botany Manor is about solving botanical puzzles, each centered around cultivating a fictional plant with unusual environmental needs. The puzzles are constructed around observation and deduction: you wander through the manor’s greenhouse, library, conservatory, and outer grounds, gathering clues in the form of notes, letters, scientific diagrams, and environmental cues. Each plant demands a specific combination of soil, temperature, light, humidity, or stimuli, and the process of deciphering its requirements feels like assembling a scientific case study. The game encourages you to pay attention rather than brute-force your way through, and when a plant finally blooms under the right conditions, the sense of accomplishment comes not from difficulty but from the satisfaction of connecting ideas.

The manor itself is a character—grand but not ostentatious, lived-in yet meticulously maintained. Every location feels curated with purpose. Sunlight streams into the conservatory at different angles, dust motes drift gently in abandoned hallways, and old photographs hint at a life once filled with travel, ambition, and struggle. The art direction embraces warmth and clarity, painting the estate in soft colors that invoke nostalgia rather than gloom. Coupled with the tranquil ambient sound of birds, rustling leaves, distant water, and calm piano notes, the game creates a soothing environment that encourages slow, thoughtful exploration. Even without puzzles, many players will find comfort simply wandering through the estate and absorbing its atmosphere.

Narratively, the game unveils Arabella’s story through environmental storytelling rather than explicit exposition. Newspaper clippings, personal correspondence, academic evaluations, and travel keepsakes reveal the challenges she faced as a woman attempting to contribute to the scientific community of her time. Her work was often dismissed, her achievements overlooked, and many opportunities denied to her, shaping a quiet undercurrent of resilience that runs through the experience. The subtlety with which the game approaches these themes is one of its strengths—nothing feels forced, yet each discovery adds depth to Arabella’s voice, allowing players to step into her perspective not through cutscenes but through the artifacts she left behind.

While the game is beautifully crafted and thoughtfully paced, it does have limitations that some players may notice. Its overall length is modest, with most finishing the experience in just a few hours. The structure is fairly linear, guiding players from one area of the manor to the next with puzzles tied to specific chapters. This makes the experience cohesive, but those seeking a sprawling or highly replayable puzzle environment might find it more contained than expected. Additionally, the clue management system can feel a bit cumbersome at times, occasionally forcing players to revisit earlier areas just to reread a document. None of these issues meaningfully disrupt the experience, but they do highlight the game's emphasis on calm storytelling over mechanical complexity.

Botany Manor ultimately succeeds because of its cohesion. Everything—from the serene visuals and quiet soundscape to the thoughtful puzzle design and understated narrative—works together to create a gentle but emotionally resonant journey. It is a puzzle game for players who enjoy contemplation rather than challenge, atmosphere rather than spectacle. Its charm lies in the quiet pleasure of tending plants, uncovering forgotten stories, and wandering through spaces that feel steeped in memory. For those seeking a peaceful, beautifully crafted escape with emotional warmth and intellectual engagement, Botany Manor is a rare and deeply satisfying experience.

Zum Preis:
Ich habe mir das game mit beiden DLC's geholt, obwohl es schon sehr frech ist am release Tag Content hinter einer Paywall zu verstecken. 
32€ sind momentan ein recht stolzer Preis auch wenn ich wirklich positiv überrascht bin. Aber wäre ich nicht so neugierig gewesen und seit Ewigkeiten auf der Suche nach einem guten Tattoo Tycoon game hätte ich wohl eher auf einen guten Rabatt gewartet.

Price point may scare some people off but personally I really like this game! But yes, I believe the 2 DLC's should have just been included with the base game.

Graphics remind me of a blend between Nintendo's Mii's and Two Point. They are very charming. 

Your character is completely customizable from facial features to hair, clothing and accessories. More goodies unlock as you progress in the game!

The Tattoo Parlor is your oyster as you decorate, furnish and tidy up to heart's content. Objects you place can actually be interacted with by your character which add for a lively world! Same as for the cosmetics; new objects become available with progress. But they still need to be unlocked with 'inspiration' points. (More on that later)

The tattoo loop goes as following: You consult with your client about their interests/dislikes/preferred tattoo style and suggest a stencil. If the consultation goes well: once at the tattooing chair you can look together for a perfect placement (higher pain levels give more $$$ but are more difficult). After choosing a position for the stencil a tattooing mini-game pops up where you have to stay as close as possible to the blue line and collect 'stars' (aka inspiration points) along the way. It doesn't have to be perfect, as long as you don't see too many ' X ' on your screen and keep your clients pain levels in check, some have a higher tolerance than others. After completion the client will show off the work you put on their bodies. If you made too many mistakes you won't get paid. I have to say the first time doing the mini-game was a bit uneasy but you really grow into it and it stars getting easier, just don't give up! It's handy to know you don't have to do the ENTIRE tattoo but just a couple of lines here and there until it completes itself. If the tattoo mini-game is not your cup of tea you can skip it entirely and choose for auto-tattoo.

Next to cash you receive a special currency called 'inspiration points' which are used to unlock various options in the game. Furniture, stencils, booster packs and a whole array of skills in different categories, depending on what you'd like to train first! 

If your business is booming, you can rely on hiring staff members, each with their own special talents! So you can let someone else do the consults and/or tattooing for you so you can focus on other things.

During your day you have random events happening and challenges you can accept.

Story and characters are fun so far. My only complaint is that there is a bug during dialogue where some of lines get skipped.

I hope this review helps to paint a better picture of the game and will help people with their decision about buying.

Besiege is a creative and physics-driven construction game that challenges players to design medieval siege engines capable of destroying fortresses, completing objectives, and solving intricate engineering puzzles. It offers a sandbox-style experience that encourages experimentation and problem-solving, making it an engaging choice for those who enjoy mechanical creativity. The game stands out for its ability to blend humour, destruction, and ingenuity into a cohesive and entertaining package.
Gameplay in Besiege revolves around constructing complex machines using a wide range of parts, from simple blocks and wheels to advanced weaponry and flight mechanisms. The intuitive building system allows for deep experimentation, rewarding players who think critically about balance, weight, and propulsion. The physics engine ensures that every success and failure feels earned, and the sheer variety of possible designs gives the gameplay remarkable depth and flexibility.
Visually, Besiege embraces a minimalist yet charming art style that complements its mechanical focus. The environments are simple but effective, allowing the player’s creations to stand out as the true visual centerpiece. The fluid destruction physics and smooth animations enhance the sense of realism, making every collapsing fortress and exploding contraption visually satisfying to watch.
Overall, Besiege delivers a highly creative and rewarding experience for those who enjoy experimentation and engineering challenges. Its blend of intuitive design, realistic physics, and open-ended gameplay ensures hours of engaging problem-solving and discovery. While it lacks a traditional story, its sandbox freedom and satisfying mechanics more than compensate for it.
Besiege gets a 7/10.

Not my vibe. I soft-locked it a few times. I was expecting this game to have more atmosphere, but it really didn't set one too well. The puzzles weren't that fun either; They didn't feel unique in any way.

The gameplay is simple: You control the little pink-haired witch and can move any distance in eight directions every turn. Your goal is to light all the magic runes on the level by moving over them, but if an enemy steps on one it will extinguish and you have to light it again.

The game is entirely confined to little 5x5 grid levels. I was skeptical at first. What kind of level design can you do on 25 tiles? As it turns out, quite a lot. The game mixes its few different enemy types plus environmental tiles (walls, teleports, death tiles) into quite a variety of levels, each of which puts a clearly formulated challenge to the player. 

Levels can be simply cleared or beaten in the minimum number of moves. Doing the former isn't too difficult until later in the game, but the latter really brings out the surprising amount of complexity in the mechanics. If you're looking for a challenge, this is it. Most levels can be cleared in around ten moves. It doesn't feel like that should be too difficult but some levels made me give up after exhausting all the ideas I could come up with (damn those cats). Of the levels where I did find the solution I can say that you often need a flash of insight revealing an unlikely move as a different, more effective strategy to beat a level.

What I want from a puzzle game is, a non-derivative set of simple mechanics that fit well together, tight and varied level design, and a bit of challenge. This game takes a place in my short list of games on steam that fit the bill.

Definitely challenging puzzle game. The constraints in design were definitely a good choice to create enough variety for the extremely simple mechanics.

Puzzle difficulty is all over the place, however. Some are easy and meant to teach you the mechanics, some are intuitive enough that you can do on your first try, but from the 3rd world onwards you start seeing puzzles that even brute-forcing them becomes complicated. Not going to lie: I did use the guide to solve some levels, or to get the optimal solution in some cases. It does help to understand that each level tries to push for a specific theme, and hence the puzzle names, and sometimes you have to "solve backwards" to be sure you can reach the end-state.

If there was literally only one thing I could change? Give each pair of teleporters unique identifiers to differentiate them upon sight; some of the latter levels' complexity stems from having to track the position of too many elements that swap positions. If there was a second change I'd love to have markers to show which pieces move in what order, given that some puzzles rely on their order of movement. But if both of these things were addressed, it would ruin the (beautiful) aesthetic of the game, probably... So hands tied, I guess?

Definitely a good puzzle game though. If you like the genre you should definitely get it.

It looks cute, and you'd think it would be cosy. Everything looks soft and cute and pretty. Characters have amazing designs and come in all shapes and sizes. The colours are soft and unassuming and makes you think it will be a nice, chill game where you can relax and wander around doing nothing but mindless exploration or being a permanent fixture in your cafe just doing menial work while your patrons visit.

Then you learn to cook. Because you have a cafe, obviously you need to make the food and drinks yourself. Sure, sounds fun.

This game has an intriguing cooking minigame, where you become a small version of yourself, walking all over your kitchen counter and using wooden spoons to catapult yourself to specific locations. There's even a small elevator so you can get into your cupboard, and a mixer so you can mix your ingredients. You also have to run in a mousewheel to bake some goods evenly, too. It's amusing and fun...

But it comes with a ridiculously short mandatory timer that barely lets you enjoy all the work you did in making your first product. (I wish it held my hand when I was just beginning, because cooking under a timer with no idea what to do stressed me out so badly. It made it an anxiety-inducing experience instead of something fun and relaxing. The game is already barebones, at least make cooking fun!)

The timer should have been optional for those who enjoy it instead of mandatory. There's no good rush from cooking when you're too slow and because your control of the character isn't good. You're trying to be faster than the timer because you want to give your future customers superb meals, but you can't do that at all. Because somehow, no matter how many shortcuts and techniques you do, the timer leaves you at bronze quality before you can get every ingredient ready. There are other better players out there who can do this game better than me, which makes this so much worse when they barely get silver and have to speedrun just to get gold star quality food.

But there's more: you can ask the game to finish it for you. Obviously, you can do that! Surely nothing will go wrong, right? 

Nope. Know that if you ask it to be finished, the product is called stale instead of ordinary, because apparently whoever helped has somehow made the ingredients age.

I am all for ordinary cooking, but stale? Who would even want to try to sell that? Why would you allow me to serve that? Where are the food inspectors when you need them to breathe down the necks of those who are trying to serve proper food at a cafe? I would ban whoever it is that helped me cook and banish them from the island. Food is sacred. Never serve stale food if you can. But in all honesty, who would even have fun cooking when you're not able to serve gold quality? Why bother at all? They made the game look "cosy" and inclusive, but that's all design. There's no accessibility option. 

TLDR; The timer sucks, period. Make it optional or extend it for far longer for those with accessibility issues. Give them fun, not stress and defeat. Tag says casual, but minigame says speedrun or feel like a failure.

As for the movements... the controls were NOT fun to do and the movements felt too slippery instead of grounded. I move just a little to the right and my character is still moving over when i reset the position of my joystick -- have tried it on keyboard and it acts similarly. It's like a permanent stick drift that aims to make your moves clumsy instead of precise. 

The world outside has shape and good scenery, but so... empty. I think it would have been more fleshed out if there was clutter, gardens, other buildings that you can visit/explore that can be filled with subtle lore. The stray animals are... stray, and there's a lack of variety of design in each region of the map. There's already good areas with good landscape, but there's something missing that can give this game greater potential for more.

But for its price, yeah, it's fine. Good-looking. Gaming, I do NOT recommend. Casual should be casual, not a stressful minigame. Also, they haven't updated the videos in their ABOUT THIS GAME. Character creation looks different.

[h3]《廢土戰爭》，搭配英特爾 Arc B570 顯示卡[/h3]

《狂怒煉獄2》的核心就是槍戰，而它確實做得非常出色。武器手感強勁且反應靈敏，每場戰鬥都充滿了爆炸、技能，以及與變種人或裝甲車隊的混戰。遊戲節奏緊湊、緊張刺激，有著源源不絕的樂趣。

我最近組裝了一台純 Intel 配置的電腦（i5-12600K 處理器搭配 Intel Arc B570 顯示卡），遊戲運行得非常順暢。在高畫質設定下，幀率達到了 165 FPS 左右，在每幀所需時間方面表現優異，動作流暢度也極其令人驚艷。以一款 2019 年推出的遊戲而言，它的最佳化做得很好，畫面依然非常出色。
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3593515943
這片廢墟充滿濃厚的《瘋狂麥斯》風格：塵土飛揚的沙漠、荒廢的建築、廢棄的車輛、掠奪者，以及怪異的變種人，共同營造出廢墟的氛圍。這是一個殘酷的世界，但在其中快速穿梭卻也充滿了樂趣。

劇情並非這款遊戲最強的優勢，但它成功地引導玩家在地圖上探索，與各個派系和角色互動，同時讓戰鬥成為遊戲的核心所在。除了視覺效果和槍戰之外，表現最為突出的是音效設計 ── 每一聲槍響、爆炸和引擎轟鳴都震撼人心。尤其是在佩戴了品質不錯的耳機時，這一切都增添了遊戲的緊張感。

整體而言，《狂怒煉獄2》完美融合了精彩的槍戰、強烈的氛圍和紮實的遊戲性能，即使在今天依舊值得一玩，特別是搭配現代的硬體設備。若你喜歡混亂刺激的槍戰、震耳欲聾的爆炸效果，以及各式各樣的裝備道具，這款遊戲絕對值得推薦給你。
