It has come to my attention that the dev has no interest in my thoughts on how to make this program user accessible. A few of the negative points I addressed were resolved, which is good, but Clip Studio can't hold a candle to the likes of Daz Studio. Sure Daz studio is daunting with DLC, but this is slowly becoming just as bad, with the minor exception that it's super difficult to get user content into Clip studio.
This will be my last review update. 
I cannot recommend Clip Studio, and will not be returning to it. 
I would love to be proven wrong in the future, but until I see software reviewers showering Clip Studio with praise, I'm out. 

TLDR version: 5/10*, Needs vast improvements
*: Only with nude/sex DLCs, otherwise 4/10 (It DOES function as a recording studio).
- Just wait for me to come back and change my review before you buy this. Get and learn Daz instead. 

The long read:
1. The UI is horrendous. It desperately needs a quality of life overhaul. It might look alright when you're not trying to make a scene with it, but as soon as you want to actually DO things with this program you very quickly realise just how un-intuitive things are.
2. The lag is gone! I can run scenes at the built in cap of 99fps and my PC only gives off a light whir. It has regained some functionality.
3. Building a scene is STILL pointless. If you take the time to go through all the steps to build your own good looking scene, it's going to take a very long time (Level designers, back me up). Then you save... and the only things that are saved are the positions and the timeline. NONE OF THE PROPS, CHARACTERS, ANIMATIONS, OR ANYTHING ELSE SAVES! You have to go through every single chunk of your timeline, search for what you used, and re-activate all of it piece by piece. What do the Devs expect? For us to power through a 40 hour long design session in one go, leave the program running while we nap, then start working on our actual scene recording... All while praying to the dark gods of computers that updates don't happen, or power doesn't go out.
The Dev has indicated she has no intention of fixing the issues. The current save system is fine in her books. Ergo as of this final review Clip Studio is asset flips and model posing. 
4. OMG the asset flips! So I bought a few DLCs, and I get it, they're not "expensive per-say" But the pre-made scenes in a lot of the things you can pick from are just ripped whole-hog from Humble Bundle packs, and possibly even Unreal Engine giveaways, with NO MODIFICATION to the sample scenes that come with them. The worst offenders are the Synty packs for sure. I'd almost go so far as to say the depths of "Just copy/paste that free asset we got" goes far enough to break the EULA of said packs.
5. Bad representation of the product. Every video shows the dev clicking effortlessly through all these options to change things, sometimes clicking buttons that don't even exist in the base product, all without mentioning that the buttons they're using are part of DLC packs. Asking the Dev where that button is gets "Watch this video" as a response, and give you a link to their entire library of videos (not the one that tells you that you have to buy the DLC to use those one or 2 buttons).
6. Clothing is fixed. Even though the models are basically all about the same general size and shape (give or take a breast slider) and the clothes seem to be weighted in a way that they LOOK like they could work on any character, THEY DON'T. You get ONE outfit option per character with a shader to change it's color... that's it. You can take the layers of clothes off, and put them back on, but you can't mix and match to at least TRY to make your scene a little different from every other person who uses this product. 
7. There is now a boob slider! However boobs only get bigger (No small tiddied girls for me :( )) The inflation looks a bit unnatural, and comedic. 
8. Character preview exists now, but the pictures used in the preview don't do the models any justice. They look far better than the previews indicate. 

The program is not worth your time or investment. Get Daz Studio instead, and spend a few bucks on a couple models, and hunt down the legitimate free Daz download sites.

This program is average at best. If you're a lazy Dev who doesn't care that their scenes look exactly the same as anyone else who uses Clip Maker, then this is for you. If you want to make projects that aren't asset flips, find something else.

This program went from "So bad I wrote what I spent on it off as a loss and learned Daz instead" to "Yeah, you can try it,at your own risk."

It's free now. Get it, try it out. It might work for what you want to do with it. It might not.

I still don't plan to use it the way I thought I would when I bought it. There are just better options out there. 

I will never update this review again.

Создатели этой игры, похоже, не очень старались сделать её хорошей. Их главная цель была быстро заработать деньги. Многие независимые разработчики сейчас не хотят тратить много времени и сил на свою работу. Рынок таких игр стал очень большим: каждую неделю выходит много новых проектов, и всем приходится конкурировать друг с другом. Раньше считалось удачей продать 30 тысяч копий игры, а сейчас — если хотя бы три тысячи.

Кому нужно хорошее качество? Давайте сделаем игру за полгода, выпустим её такой, какая она есть, и будем исправлять ошибки потом, если она станет популярной. Не будем долго думать над сюжетом и механиками. Подумаем, что сейчас интересно, но непонятно, и сделаем что-то похожее, только проще.

В оригинальной игре был охранник, а у нас — детектив, который задержался на работе. Вместо пиццерии — полицейский участок. Но это не важно, потому что мы снова будем прятаться от больших нелепых кукол в полутёмных местах, которые хотят нас съесть. Мы даже не придумали им название! В оригинале это были аниматроники, и в нашей игре они тоже будут. Напишем это слово в названии, и фанаты «Five Nights» скажут, что это часть вселенной или неофициальный спин-офф.

Сюжет игры получился запутанным и плохо продуманным. Понимаю, что в хоррорах глубокий сюжет не всегда важен, но разрозненные факты создают ощущение хуже, чем полное его отсутствие. Наш мозг старается сложить все кусочки информации в логическую цепочку. Если не получается, мы чувствуем дискомфорт.

Например, почему по офису разбросаны анонимные записки с непонятной предысторией? Они не проясняют ситуацию, а только сбивают с толку. Создаётся впечатление, что их добавили, чтобы игроки не скучали, блуждая по коридорам и прячась под столами.

Главная идея игры — какой-то сумасшедший мстит вам через телефон, запуская смертоносных роботов. Но как он пронёс их в полицейский участок? Как всё это организовал? Почему месть такая сложная? Очень жаль, что разработчики не добавили немного юмора или не заставили главного героя повторять одну и ту же фразу: «Что за ерунда!»

Свет выключился? Что за ерунда! Телефон зазвонил? Что за ерунда! В камере трясётся коробка? Что за ерунда! В офисе бродят роботы-коты? Что за ерунда! У одного из роботов к спине привязан ключ от входной двери? Что за ерунда!

Эту фразу повторяют очень часто. Её говорят и персонажи в игре, и сами игроки. Каждые две минуты один и тот же текст появляется на экране. Если играть без перерывов, за час можно услышать её больше 30 раз!

Несмотря на все проблемы, первые десять минут игры могут напугать. Потом это чувство проходит. Если аниматроники не стоят на месте, они нападают быстро и неожиданно — это может испугать даже тех, кто не боится громких звуков.

This game has an incredible progression system. Starting off slow and then maintaining a steady pass through my entire play through. As I bought tools it felt less like upgrades and more like alternative ways to play. I stated with a pick and shovel than moved into a drill, then a gun, then explosives, and finally back to the drill. And what felt impressive about this game is that all tool options felt viable. It was more about how I wanted to play. It was also impressive that I would be using my new expensive drill and for a duration I would decide to go back to my lower cost drill. All the tools are useful for your entire play through. What you're really buying aren't upgrades, they're tools that are good at doing different things, with  some exceptions like the wooden shovel and pick.  
To accompany this many styles of play based on your tools they also have a fantastic gear system. I found myself constantly changing my gear to fit the environment and tool I was using. Like the drill.

Later I swapped my gear again and found a way to power my drill with another mining tool that makes power on hit, so instead I spec'ed my gear for agility.
This game is a master at progression design and I'm very excited to see what this creator does as they continue to develop this game.

I've been playing Wadjet Eye games since Blackwell: Legacy. Every one has been a treat in a completely different way, not least because it's so rare to see a developer go from strength to strength like this. Going in, I know that all of their games will have something special that will leave me raving about them to my friends after the fact, but even so, I wasn't prepared for everything that Old Skies had to offer.

So with that said, this is perhaps my favorite of Dave Gilbert's games so far. It builds on ideas and mechanics explored in past games, with a high level of polish and absolutely beautiful art. I wasn't initially sold on the move away from pixel art, but I can't argue with the results - it looks great. The voice acting is superb, with several Wadjet Eye mainstays returning, but it's Sally Beaumont as Fia who carries the game, with her initial cool professionalism revealing hidden vulnerabilities. She's by turns diplomatic, indignant, and adorably flustered.

The main plot feels like a slow burn, and I felt the opening chapters were carried more on the strength of their puzzles, but once it gets going, it really is something special. Old Skies is, as with many of Gilbert's projects, a meditation on human connection, on the strange convergences that bind people together - and on the ways that someone might stand apart from the rest of humanity. For Fia, it's her role as a ChronoZen employee, walking an ever-changing timeline while leaving no footprints of her own, and it's her struggle with this that captured me. Again, this won't be anything new to people familiar with this studio's work, but the game's tone straddles a careful balance, acknowledging tragedy and impermanence without feeling as though it wallows in it. There's a rare humor and heart present throughout, a sincerity that never feels saccharine. It's a game that is honest about the uncertainty and sadness of life: everything you love could be taken away, but to live in fear of losing everything is no life at all.

This game is a particular treat to longtime Wadjet Eye fans, with wonderful callbacks to past games. I was delighted to see [spoiler]Vicki Santini herself[/spoiler], as well as spotting cameo appearances from [spoiler]Lauren Blackwell[/spoiler]. Gilbert's New York City has an incredible richness to it, a sense of place and presence that most games can only hope to achieve, and much of this lies in the continuity he's developed across his games.

[h1][b]Office Simulator : De Stagiaire à PDG, une ascension exigeante [/b][/h1]

[h2][b]Introduction - Qu'est-ce que Office Simulator ?[/b][/h2]
Office Simulator est une simulation d'entreprise complète et immersive vous plongeant dans le monde de l'entreprise. Le but est simple : commencer en tant que stagiaire, gravir les échelons en complétant des tâches quotidiennes, gérer vos propres besoins (et ceux de vos collègues), obtenir des promotions, et éventuellement, lancer et diriger votre propre société.

[h2]🎨 Graphismes et Ambiance[/h2]
Le jeu utilise des visuels 3D stylisés qui offrent un look moderne et épuré, adapté au thème du bureau. L'environnement est interactif, avec des objets comme des imprimantes, des archives et la machine à café. L'ambiance se veut réaliste et axée sur la productivité, mais certains avis notent que l'immersion peut être limitée par l'absence remarquée de Musique de Fond (BGM) et d'Effets Sonores (SFX), laissant parfois l'environnement de bureau un peu trop calme.

[h2]🕹️ Gameplay et Mécaniques[/h2]
Le cœur du jeu est la gestion du temps et l'exécution de micro-tâches, le tout combiné à une progression de carrière structurée :
[list]
[] [b]Le Cycle de Travail :[/b] Chaque journée est rythmée par des tâches spécifiques (classer des fichiers, imprimer des documents, répondre à des e-mails, planifier des réunions). Ces tâches doivent souvent être accomplies dans un temps limité, ajoutant une pression de gestion du temps.
[] [b]L'Auto-Gestion :[/b] Deux jauges cruciales doivent être surveillées : le niveau de café/fatigue et le besoin d'aller aux toilettes. Négliger ces besoins impacte la productivité, forçant le joueur à intégrer des pauses rapides dans son emploi du temps chargé.
[] [b]Progression et Promotions :[/b] L'accomplissement des tâches rapporte de l'expérience et du prestige. Atteindre certains seuils (niveau + prestige) permet d'accéder à des postes supérieurs (Spécialiste, Chef d'Équipe, etc.), débloquant de nouvelles responsabilités, y compris la gestion d'employés et l'achat d'améliorations de bureau (postes de travail, décorations).
[] [b]Création d'Entreprise :[/b] Le point culminant est la création de votre propre société. Vous gérez alors un bureau complet, recrutez des employés et décrochez des contrats, passant du micro-gestionnaire au PDG.
[/list]

[h2]📖 Histoire et Narration[/h2]
L'histoire principale est votre propre parcours professionnel. Le jeu n'a pas une narration profonde basée sur des PNJ ou des événements scénarisés, mais se concentre sur la progression personnelle. Chaque promotion est une étape narrative, et les dialogues se limitent principalement aux exigences professionnelles et aux interactions basiques avec les employés. Le voyage d'intern à entrepreneur est le moteur de l'expérience.

[h2]✅ Points Positifs (Synthèse)[/h2]
[list]
[] [b]Concept Solide :[/b] Le parcours de carrière est addictif et bien structuré.
[] [b]Simulation Détaillée :[/b] La gestion des micro-tâches et des besoins personnels rend l'expérience réaliste.
[] [b]Haut Potentiel :[/b] Le mode de création d'entreprise offre une rejouabilité immense après avoir gravi les échelons.
[] [b]Très Positif (Steam) :[/b] Le taux d'approbation élevé montre une base de fans satisfaite de la boucle de jeu.
[/list]

[h2]❌ Points Négatifs (Synthèse)[/h2]
[list]
[] [b]Accès Anticipé :[/b] Présence de bugs (tâches qui ne se terminent pas, problèmes de saisie de texte dans les e-mails).
[] [b]Manque de Finition :[/b] Absence de Musique de Fond (BGM) et d'Effets Sonores, réduisant l'ambiance.
[] [b]Microgestion Frustrante :[/b] Certaines mécaniques de gestion d'équipe ou de bureau (comme l'assignation de tâches aux assistants) sont incomplètes ou buguées dans la version actuelle.
[] [b]Répétitif :[/b] La phase de stagiaire/débutant peut devenir répétitive avant d'atteindre les niveaux de gestion plus avancés.
[/list]

[h2]🎯 Conclusion et Verdict[/h2]
[spoiler]Office Simulator est déjà un excellent jeu de simulation d'entreprise malgré son statut d'Accès Anticipé. Il réussit à transformer les tâches de bureau en un défi de gestion du temps et de progression. Si vous aimez les jeux de simulation 3D qui nécessitent de l'organisation et une progression claire, et que vous êtes prêt à composer avec quelques bugs de jeunesse, ce titre est fait pour vous. Le potentiel de la phase PDG est immense et promet de belles heures de jeu.

[b]Verdict :[/b] Une simulation de carrière très prometteuse, déjà très appréciée par la communauté.
[/spoiler]

Let's say dodged the bite, then the dog would continue on it's path and might bite someone else, which means that someone else could blame you for it and then he can sue you.

Let's say you did a pre-emptive kick to the dog, then the police would come to you and you would be known as an animal abuser for the rest of the game.

But it gets deeper, what if while walking around with a bite on your arm a lady approaches you and tells you she has medicine.

Maybe you take the medicine, maybe it makes you grow an extra leg, now the serious game you were playing turns into an altogether comedy because now everyone is going to notice you have a 3rd leg.

The game can go on and on and on like this. As far as making stories go with some meaning to it, it's kind of perfect, but maybe I haven't hit any limitations so I wouldn't know.

進行要素として新規パワーアップやアップグレードが解禁され、戦略性や生存性を向上させます。これにより中期的な目標設定が成立し、アンロック速度は適度に調整されています。

ビジュアルはレトロ調のピクセルアートとグリッチ演出を組み合わせ、腐食範囲の拡大に伴い画面は暗転しますが、視認性は維持されています。サウンドキューは脅威および強化状態を明確に通知します。

本作は短時間のハイスコアセッションを志向するユーザーに適合します。深度はパターン認識とパワーアップの使用タイミングに集約されており、現代的な変動要素を伴うアーケード的緊張感を提供します。

...Now, that being said, if you aren't a fan of early access, you might want to wait until this game is out of early access.

I understand that game development, especially solo gamedev, takes a long, long time. Video games like this do not grow on trees, it requires a lot of long, substantial effort! I certainly commend the devs at Semag Games on their efforts. However, I think a lot of the development time gets muffled in re-iteration. Now, of course, game development is also an iterative process! Things change a lot as games progress, but I think Vibrant Venture has a problem where the devs seemingly want to fluff everything up rather than focusing on the substantial meat and bones of the game's A to B.

It took 4 years for World 3 to be complete, with the boss fight for the world releasing later this year. I think this is great, this is a huge milestone! But it also makes me wonder if development time is being focused on the right things? They've introduced a full level editor, redone character sprites and tilesets multiple times, added a ton of extra story content, and introduced extra hard challenge levels for every world. This is all cool, don't get me wrong!... But the game still isn't finished.

Based on the opening cutscene, I'm assuming that the game has five worlds, and currently the progress of the game's main story has been stalled on the third one for most of the time I've had it in my steam library. Again, I don't want to throw shade on the devs at all, I think the work they've done on Vibrant Venture is very impressive and I'm very eager to play the game once it's complete! But... I sorta wonder if the game will ever be finished at this rate? (I'm no longer in the game's discord so I don't know what's being shared in there.)

I want to start off by saying I do think this is a good game, and a puzzle game, but if you are coming solely for logic based puzzles you may come away frustrated. I think this is more accurately a Discovery game with puzzle elements. The crux of the game is experimentation, trying different combinations until something new happens, then using that new info to solve puzzles and progress. While there is logic in that (and again, there are puzzles) it can be difficult if you miss a single interaction, or make incorrect assumptions. While this is true in a lot of puzzle games, the scope and size of the singular level and the finality of it all (you have to reset everything if you make a mistake, which in the story is appropriate, but setting things up many times over just to try one new thing takes time and effort that can feel taxing.) I strongly recommend the guides for this game that nudge you instead of out-right telling you. I found in my playthrough that the times when I was stuck, looking at the hints and then solution always left me feeling like "I don't think I'd ever had gotten that." That's partly my own fault and my own assumptions. 

The game is entirely knowledge locked, which I like, but which also means that if you knew everything you could complete the game in a minute (literally, WR is 1:04).  I think the fun is talking to Zero and  getting the rules naturally through exploration and trial and error. Overall it is cool to explore and poke around this world/level and I think there were some cool moments. I still recommend it, just don't come in expecting logic puzzles as the defining genre.

tl;dr - This game WANTS to be Super Metroid *so* badly. Too bad it only apes each aspect of it while failing at every conceivable turn in the process. If I still could, I'd ask for a refund.

This game is *so* close to being a fun game like one of its big influences, Super Metroid. Like, you can see where early designs must've been taking it. with the exploration and huge, almost sprawling map. Unfortunately, instead of letting players play the game the way *they* want to play it, it seems the game devs favored a "Git gud and play it *right*, newb!" sort of mindset. Needless precision platforming with a game style, controller scheme, and loose controls that simply *are NOT* made for it make just getting around an exercise in frustration and bullshit gotcha moments. The boss fights are incredibly boring, with each encounter, each *attack*, having a clearly singular "right" way to go about things that gets enforced by needless restrictions on weapons like extreme short ranges, an auto-targeting system that seems OBSESSED with pointing at the ground, but ONLY when you're trying to hit an incoming enemy, and boss rooms that are incredibly small with areas that you clearly MUST stand in or be annihilated. Deviation from this poorly illuminated method will result dying just this side of instantly. There's no dodging, there's no moving, there's no actual strategy besides the exact one the devs decided you MUST follow. 

Nothing about ANY of this game feels organic, like you're actually exploring the map and making your way through things on your own. Instead, it feels like you're being forcibly walked through the game and made to feel like an idiot every time some bullshit landmine or un-dodge-able enemy suddenly evaporates what little health you have. When a simple boss fight takes 16 tries to beat because the game literally only showed you that you had to use a brand new mechanic in an ENTIRELY unused way, you've probably fucked up that boss fight. When just getting through a simple screen just to get to one of the sparse save points takes 8 tries because the thing calls for precision platforming that the whole damn game was CLEARLY never built to provide and near super human precognition to dodge all the conveniently placed enemies that can ALWAYS shoot where you're GOING? You know you've made a bad game.

And devs, you KNOW you made a bad game.

[h1] 于是，我把这个混账游戏全收集了 [/h1]

玩永恒之夜的动机其实是我把锈苔dlc打完了，然后自认为没啥银河城的跳跳乐能让我破防了，正好群友又一直在给我推，于是决定挑战一下。
结果是这游戏就成了我玩的银河城里最难最混账之一了。

省流：量大管饱，跳跳乐水平优秀，但是跳跳乐极多，还有逆天地图，非跳跳乐高手不建议玩困难模式。

说它难，倒也不算太难，个人感觉它所有关卡的难度其实都还没红丝绒高，更何况它有个三段跳和传送箭时缓的宝石，第一次带时缓宝石去跳跳乐的时候我一直在笑，然后感慨以前过的什么苦日子啊。
但它还是很难，如果一般的银河城玩家想不开来玩的话，真的建议不要在乎成就直接开普通模式（毕竟恒夜有每个boss的无伤成就，有竞速成就，有付费dlc成就，正常来说困难模式通关也拿不到一半的成就），因为打简单模式都有可能会破防。

这个游戏前期的跳跳乐虽然也不少，但在有跳跳乐基础的情况下算不上很难，而当你拿到传送箭离开西墙后，才是出新手村了。

中期的每一张地图都是重量寄。以下会包含一部分的关卡剧透，但我觉得这玩意剧透了也没什么。

最简单的梦境，核心设计是隐形墙，你看到的墙和地刺不一定是真的墙和地刺，而你要想分辨出路在哪只能用传送箭，传送箭会有一个小范围揭示真假的效果。并且梦境的房间的入口和出口并非在地图上是联通的，你进一个房间右下角的门可能会从左上角出来，所以每个房间的联通关系只能自己试出来，那我为什么说这个地方简单呢，因为它本身的设计更接近于解谜，所以没有过于逆天的跳跳乐，和后面几个图比起来算是纯良的。
然后是海底要塞和深渊，海底要塞简单一点，抛开跳跳乐不谈，它最大的特点是有岔路口，其中一条路会给你能推进主线的道具，而另一条路只有漫长的跳跳乐和尽头的收集品，以及一个你第一次来大概率拿不到的主线道具，因为你要先拿前面那个主线道具然后开启机关后才能回来拿这个主线道具，而且这段的跳跳乐比较长，这就导致了如果你想全收集至少得跳两边这里。
深渊要更难一点，而在深渊你可以拿到最后一个能力，又称黑暗国王在黑暗中会被限制能力，具体说来就是没这个能力你碰到黑暗区域会受伤，有这个能力你可以进黑暗区域了，但是在里面没法使用传送箭。显然，这种限制就是为后面更难的跳跳乐所用的。
接下来是宇宙，这个图是整个游戏里最恶心的一张图，难倒不难，但是有个混账的反重力设计。一般的游戏设计重力反转，要么是你视角转操作不转，要么是视角不转操作转，只有你恒夜，是视角不转操作也不转。这也就意味着当你站在星球上时，角色的上下左右和操作的上下左右是不一样的，这就导致了宇宙跑起来及其反直觉，而且四元素的收集得一遍跳跳乐一遍克服它的反直觉，甚至最恶心的地方要你绕整整两圈，还限制传送箭（哈哈，这就是前面深渊给的能力啊），在你推完这张图的主线后，恭喜你，还有场逃脱战等着你呢。我的两位群友都是在这个b图破防退坑的。
大后期的两张图没什么好讲的，纯毕业考试，在前面的基础上虽然没有过于逆天设计，但是综合性更强，难度更高。

关于它银河城方面的地图设计，以我个人的感受来说算不上是很好，虽然它有很多的收集品，但它的地图更大，这导致了在没有跳跳乐的地方就显得很空，但是它跳跳乐多啊，九成的地图都是跳跳乐，尽管剩下一成会显得又大又空，但是绝大多数时间玩家还是能够激情跳跳乐的。

当然，这个b游戏我还是想推荐的，一是本着苦不能只有我吃的伟大精神，我还是希望更多人来玩然后破防；二是这个游戏跳跳乐质量是真的好还量大管饱，除了宇宙以外我几乎没什么怨言了，绝大多数时候跳跳乐都是又痛苦又爽的。

It's easy to judge this game early due to how simple it is, but you haven't really played this game if you haven't cleared the game at least once. 

This used to sit in my library for years after feeling underwhelmed at the initial playthrough, but when I decided to come back to actually beat it, everything clicked. I hated the format back then, but now I think this format gives more action and experimentation, and I'm even starting to think I might prefer this over Hotline Miami. 

I don't even consider this a rouguelite because ability to clear comes from how much drinks you drank, not what drinks you get, and that's determined by how much money you earned by scoring, not by RNG. [spoiler]You can completely bypass drink RNG by abusing quit restart as well (not that you'd need it to beat the game). You can also use it to reset and practice boss fights.[/spoiler] Maps aren't procedurally generated either, so I think it's more of an arcade-like than rougue.

Experimenting with guns is where this game shines the most, and makes it replayable even if you went through it once. I tried sawed-off-only run not expecting to clear, but the game balances itself by making enemies equip the weapon you want to bring so it was surprisingly doable, and managed to bring this unserious attempt to a clear.

If you don't know what to do to clear the game, I recommend going for unlocking all drinks/guns before attempting a full-run. Sure later levels/bosses are impossible with you spending most of your cash on unlocks, but aiming to score for cash will help you train for the real runs.

[h1][b] TLDR: Average in all aspects except music. The focus point seems to be on the game world and plot over gameplay, but everything ends up being mediocre. [/b] [/h1]

[h1]PROS: [/h1]
➕Music

[h1]NEUTRALS: [/h1]
🔹Steeped in real life political drama

[h1]CONS: [/h1]
➖Controls
➖Poor hub with merchant NPCs spread out everywhere
➖Can be difficult to see where crosshair is amidst chaos

[h1] [b] Content (Game world/Narrative) – [4/10] [/b] [/h1]
The game world consists of a hub that you return to between levels, and multiple stages of randomly-generated areas. The stages are all contain the same general layout of platforms and rooms with the only thing changing is backgrounds. There is not much interaction with the world aside from destructible items. I unfortunately found no secrets or anything cool, 

I found the narrative to be a bit mediocre. You play as a member of an underground resistance trying to save the country of “Europa” from an oppressive regime trying to control its citizens. There isn’t really any sort of plot events other than “Kill the next boss “. While there are some funny memes and references to things like Evil Dead, I didn’t find any NPCs or dialog to be memorable. 

[h1][b] Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
The mechanics I found were average at best. I was met with an immediate issue upon playing - controls. With KBM, the aiming is good, but the platforming and movement feels off. When I tried the controller, the platforming is better, but the aiming is poor and the controls are unable to be rebound. Having dodge as the trigger is just plain awful and led me to go back to KBM. 
Aside from the controls, it plays like a fairly traditional roguelite. You have persistent upgrades that carry over between deaths, but you lose everything else. You have a wide selection of weapons, passives, and companions to assist you. The companions are basically passive entities that sometimes have an activated effect. 

The difficulty is fairly hard until you get some upgrades. Once you get some health, armor, and enough items to form a defensive wall, you can quickly snowball your power into turning the game into easy mode. In my playtime, I beat the game once. After dying around 3-4 times, I had enough upgrades to carry me through. 

[h1] [b] Graphics (Quality/Technical) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Fairly standard 2D platformer with an optional retro aesthetic. I didn’t find anything really noteworthy here graphically. 

On the technical side, the game ran fine and I encountered no bugs. 
i9-13900KF | RTX 4090 | 64GB RAM | 1440p @ 240hz | Windows 11 installed on SSD 

[h1] [b] Audio – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
Good music, I felt like this is probably the high point of the game. There are two forms of music - your basic music and the combat music. The basic music is some decent background music, like the rest of the game its just mid, but once you get into combat the music adds some additional layers that easily gets the blood pumping. Again, nothing significant here, but I felt the music was by far the standout part of the game. 

There isn’t much voice acting, just small parts said by bosses. 

[h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [4/10] [/b] [/h1]
It’s a roguelite, so there is some good replay value here, however, I felt the way the game presented its mechanics leave a lot to be desired. There are much better roguelites out there from a mechanical perspective that will last you much longer than this game (Dead Cells comes to mind). 

[h1] [b] Final Verdict – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
The Great Rebellion (TGR) is a roguelite that relies on its tone, messaging, and plot instead of gameplay, to provide an experience and considering how the roguelite genre is, none of that generally matters if the gameplay isn’t good. And to be fair here, I wouldn’t necessarily say the gameplay is [i]bad[/i], more that its just the shining example of mediocrity. 

There is nothing, aside from the music, that stands out to me with TGR. The guns/weapons, the skills/passives, the progression, are all “Typical roguelike experience 101”, and again while this isn’t terrible, its the same thing I’ve done before while having these systems implemented better. 

Lastly, I also want to address the elephant in the room: the political drama aspect and claims of white supremacy/anti-DEI. This is one of those games that I bought where I didn’t know there was a controversy surrounding it at the time (Looking at you, Heartbound). After playing and beating the game, yes, TGR has some obvious and intentional design decisions that promote the devs point of view. Do I agree with it? No. Is it offensive? Maybe. Is this factored into my scored review? No. I am a believer of satire, and a meme-y game with a differing point of view is simply someone I don’t agree with expressing their point of view that they have every right to. 

Overall, I do not recommend TGR. I consider it to be an average roguelite at best and then with the additional layer of drama surrounding it, it's not something I would recommend to others. 

If you want any example of a roguelite that I do recommend, and is actually very similar, yet superior mechanically, to TGR, check out my review on [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/Synikx/recommended/588650?snr=1_5_9__402]Dead Cells[/url].

Can’t wait to see how many jesters a negative review will get me. Give me points, snowflakes :P

First review of this game :). This game is a one man passion project by a friend of mine. He designed the entire game by himself from the ground up, which is an impressive feat. That, combined with the fact this game is only $2 almost negates it from any criticism. However, I'm still going to genuinely talk about the game to give my experience.

Gameplay - The game has good foundational. The combat is enjoyable and can be fast paced depending on the situation. Different enemies throw different attacks at you, and there is some strategy in the mix with what weapons/character you are going in with. Zarus and Greugus, the main characters of the game play differently, and the varying weapons swap up different playstyles. Sometimes it's easier to play one over the other, though you can certainly brute force it as one.

Difficulty - I feel like I need to make a statement on this. This game is really difficult. Like VERY difficult. I get that the developer intends for it to be difficult, but the spike in difficulty is pretty intense, and I feel that people who are willing to give this a shot might drop out at this point. If you are someone who likes challenge, you may enjoy this game.

Soundtrack - The soundtrack is interesting. The SFX is good and feels nice, so that's great. The background tracks are interesting, and interesting is probably a good word for it. It's good, yes, but given the difficulty of the game, listening to the ost continously as you try a level over and over can get a little grating. Still, it's overall a solid soundtrack.

Art - Art is subjective, I can't say I am smitten with the art in the game, but I can say this: the developer made all of the art in this game. That is impressive.

Overall, I think this is a fantastic first game. While there are a lot of flaws that can jump out, the fact of it being a one man's first game, that he made on his own, is an impressive feat. Combine that with the inoffensive price tag, and I think the game is worth a look. While the difficulty can be overwhelming at first, the gameplay is solid and enjoyable enough that you can get better and overcome.

X-Blades, developed by Gaijin Entertainment and published by TopWare Interactive, is a fast-paced hack-and-slash adventure that embraces the energy and excess of late-2000s action games. It stars Ayumi, a confident and impulsive treasure hunter armed with twin gunblades, who finds herself entangled in an ancient curse after seeking out a legendary artifact. The story begins as a classic quest for fortune but quickly spirals into a struggle between light and darkness, forcing Ayumi to confront mystical forces far beyond her control. It’s a familiar fantasy setup, but one told through a colorful and stylized lens that reflects the game’s anime-inspired roots. Rather than relying on deep character writing or intricate storytelling, X-Blades leans heavily on visual spectacle, kinetic combat, and a sense of unrelenting momentum that defines its entire experience.

At its core, X-Blades is about constant motion and flashy combat. Each stage throws hordes of enemies at the player, ranging from demonic beasts to monstrous constructs, and the goal is usually simple—defeat everything that moves and move on. Ayumi’s dual blades can switch seamlessly between melee and ranged attacks, allowing for both close-quarters slashing and stylish shooting combos. The system encourages chaining attacks together for high scores and more powerful magic, creating an almost arcade-like rhythm where efficiency and aggression are rewarded. As you progress, you collect souls that function as both currency and experience, which can be used to unlock new skills and spells. These magical abilities add variety to combat, letting you unleash elemental attacks, summon energy blasts, or briefly empower Ayumi’s blades with devastating effects. The fluidity of switching between swordplay, gunfire, and magic gives combat a satisfying flow, especially when facing large waves of enemies that fill the screen with chaos.

Visually, X-Blades makes a strong impression with its bright color palette and elaborate art direction. The environments—ancient ruins, sunlit temples, shadowy catacombs—are expansive and filled with glowing architecture that suits the game’s mythical tone. The cel-shaded character models and exaggerated animations complement its anime aesthetic, giving it a distinctive look that separates it from the more realistic action games of its time. Ayumi herself is the focal point of the visual design: energetic, stylized, and designed to stand out, both for her combat agility and for the obvious fanservice built into her appearance. The presentation aims for spectacle, not subtlety, and while it succeeds in creating a visually striking world, it can sometimes feel repetitive as later levels reuse similar structures and textures. The soundtrack matches the high-energy tone, with orchestral and electronic themes that rise and fall with the intensity of battle, enhancing the game’s sense of flow and motion.

Despite its visual flair, X-Blades struggles with repetition. The combat, though flashy, doesn’t evolve significantly as the game progresses. Most encounters rely on the same formula: destroy enemy generators, wipe out waves of foes, collect the spoils, and move forward. While the magic system offers a wide range of powers, many of them feel redundant, and the limited enemy variety means you’ll often rely on the same handful of strategies. The bosses are designed to provide moments of scale and tension, but they often feel drawn out and lack the mechanical complexity that could make them memorable. The camera can also be a persistent annoyance, occasionally losing track of enemies during chaotic battles or obstructing the view in confined areas. These issues don’t ruin the experience but highlight the game’s focus on style over refinement. It’s a spectacle-driven experience that values adrenaline and speed more than precision or variety.

Narratively, X-Blades keeps things simple. The story revolves around Ayumi’s struggle to overcome the darkness that infects her after touching the forbidden artifact. Along the way, she discovers the truth about the curse and the fate of the world she has inadvertently endangered. The plot is presented through brief cutscenes and narration, offering just enough to connect the action sequences without bogging the player down with exposition. Ayumi herself is more of an archetype than a complex protagonist—brash, fearless, and somewhat naive, acting as a vessel for the game’s over-the-top energy rather than a deeply developed character. While her personality suits the game’s pulpy tone, the lack of emotional depth means the story serves mostly as a backdrop to the combat and exploration. Still, there’s a certain charm in its simplicity; it’s the kind of unapologetic, straightforward adventure that thrives on enthusiasm rather than sophistication.

Technically, the game runs smoothly and remains easy to access even on modern systems thanks to its modest requirements. Its control scheme is intuitive, with quick inputs for switching between attacks and spells, though the targeting system can feel imprecise in crowded encounters. The upgrade and progression system is straightforward, making it easy for players to experiment with different abilities without being overwhelmed by complex menus or branching skill trees. That accessibility is one of X-Blades’ enduring strengths—it’s designed to be picked up and enjoyed in short bursts, delivering immediate action without demanding mastery. However, this same accessibility limits its long-term depth, as veterans of the genre may find the mechanics too shallow to sustain engagement beyond the first playthrough.

In the end, X-Blades is a relic of its time—a game built on the promise of pure, unfiltered action and eye-catching design rather than nuanced storytelling or innovative mechanics. It’s loud, colorful, and confident in its identity, even when that identity borders on camp. While its repetition and lack of depth prevent it from standing among the genre’s best, it succeeds as a fun, fast-paced experience for players who appreciate simple, stylish combat and a dose of nostalgic flair. Ayumi’s journey through temples and tombs might not offer much in the way of surprises, but the game’s enthusiasm for its own world and mechanics gives it a charm that lingers. For fans of hack-and-slash games who value spectacle over substance, X-Blades remains an energetic, if imperfect, adventure worth revisiting.

Давайте сразу уточню: почти все игры MDickie — это без пяти минут скам. Вы, вероятно, впервые слышите его никнейм, но чел реально звезда трэшового геймдева. Беркан Денизарян со своим Hunt Down the Freeman прославился на весь интернет, но, если подумать, сколько он выпустил игр? Одну. А сколько игр на счету у Мэта Дикки? Больше двадцати.

И они все — пиздец.

Начать стоит с того, что творческая фишка MDickie — это игры про рестлинг (Wrestling MPire) и игры про библию (The You Testament). Все его проекты — комбинация этих двух тем в разных пропорциях, иногда с примесью новых идей. The You Testament — буквально игра о том, как случайный библейский (или не очень) персонаж ходит по Назарету и кидает с прогиба римлян, евреев и даже Иешуа Га-Ноцри. По крайней мере, пытается.

…потому что вторая характерная черта игр MDickie — отсутствие каких-либо внятных внутриигровых инструкций и отвратительное управление. Нужно приложить усилие, чтобы понять, как в игре что работает даже на базовом уровне. Например, чтобы использовать предмет вроде аптечки, нужно взять её с пола и крутануть правый стик в любую сторону. Невероятные инновации, сделанные хер пойми зачем. Вероятно, причина таких костылей в том, что большинство игр Мэта — по сути порт с мобильников, а значит, адаптированы под тачскрин.

Цели игры никто никогда не объясняет. Игрока просто выбрасывают в песочницу, предлагая развлекать себя самому. Например, взяв лежащий на полу металлический стул и приложив им первого проходящего мимо персонажа. Просто так, чисто по фану, по причине «почему бы и нет».

И тут выясняется, что игры MDickie — по сути социальные сэндбоксы. Персонажи реагируют на действия игрока. Втащив кому-нибудь стулом, можно нажить себе кровного врага. Подарив аптечку или помогая в бою, можно заработать верного союзника. С кем-то можно подружиться, кто-то будет нападать без предупреждения, кто-то попытается переманить вашего персонажа в свою социальную клику. Локаций в игре много, и они даже не совсем хаотичны: на военной базе полно оружия, в кафетерии — еды, в храме живут мирные люди, которые не хотят участвовать в происходящем хаосе.

Я бы сказал, что с этим миром интересно взаимодействовать. Для дешёвых, кривых, уродливых игр, собранных на одном и том же движке, в них вложено на удивление много усилий. Эдакий неогранённый алмаз F-tier геймдева, вытащенный из китайского баттплага.

К сожалению, до звания хотя бы «окнорм» ни одна из игр Мэта не дотягивает, потому что у социальной песочницы его игр на удивление нет никаких социальных трекеров, чтобы хотя бы понять, где находятся дружественные персонажи, или хотя бы список друзей ГГ посмотреть. Да, вот до такой степени всё плохо.

Ну и да, искусственный интеллект заточен только на то, чтобы беситься, как обезьяна, и кидаться говном. Локации только создают атмосферу, а не эмулируют жизнь: это просто набор статистов и лежащего на полу оружия, которое эти статисты очень скоро начнут активно использовать, потому что им тоже хочется бить случайных прохожих металлическим стулом ради рофлов. Буквально через минуту после того, как игрок входит в помещение, боты начинают крушить всё вокруг.

I've been playing Nancy Drew games with my family since 2003, still play them as an adult, and have completed all 34 plus the dossiers; this is the closest we've gotten to a True Nancy Drew game since Sea of Darkness. Art of Deceit is a game that wholly understands the ND formula, down to the details of having a kooky phone character to consult on an edutainment topic, fastidiously avoiding Penelope's reflection, and letting you die in ways both horrifying and ridiculous. In fact, it's such a good successor that I found myself going "oh my [i]god[/i], Nancy" whenever an insensitive dialogue option would pop-up, and then remember oh, wait, it's Penelope.

I never write reviews, but I'm trying to manifest as much cash as possible for Default Cube so that we get more of these. This feels like the start of something new. I think we're just like one major Nancy Drew streamer away from seeing a huge spike.

There *are* some growing pains here: a bit too much talking, starting with an opening five-minute unskippable monologue overlain on one static visual of a typewriter, after which you're launched into a ten-minute phone call. Small quality-of-life complaints, like when you order pizza, you have to sit around doing nothing for 30 in-game minutes, which translates to 3 agonizingly long minutes of real time. Or, you can pick up some objects immediately and others only after you have reason to. (Why did she steal a random spray bottle on sight but wait to pick up a box of screws?) Lots of little hitches like that. Sometimes the game was really good about anticipating my next thought (like when Penelope's next question for a suspect was also mine), and sometimes I felt like I was being arbitrarily held back (like when I couldn't fix an arcade game until another NPC told me to do what I already wanted to do). I got stuck for upwards of an hour at least twice, once because it let me cross off a task that I hadn't actually finished doing. ([spoiler] I didn't realize that you could interact with one of the bootprints at the cliffs, which you have to do to trigger the next sequence, and I had already crossed off exploring the cliffs on my checklist. [/spoiler])

But here's how I think about it: Art of Deceit is objectively a much (much!) better first entry for an IP than Secrets Can Kill. And I had a great time with it. There are all the classic puzzles you know and love, plus a crazy secret passageway you won't want to miss. (There's one part of it that's so freaky-cool it made me pause and make the @_@ face for a solid thirty seconds.) Also, if you're somehow still not convinced, Default Cube gets away with using all sorts of words that HerInteractive could never, like "heterosexual" and "methhead", which should give any ND vet a shiver of forbidden delight. Who could ask for anything more?

If I wasn't a mega fan of Paul Wang's work before, now I am.[i] Lords of Infinity[/i] is a monster of ambition, an epic, sprawling saga that blends deep political intrigue, moral complexity, and the relentless weight of legacy into one of the most ambitious text-based experiences I’ve played. Actually, one of the most ambitious games, period. This is the third book in the [i]Infinity[/i] series, and it is a step up from the two previous books in so many ways. You were once a soldier, once an officer, and now you're a lord of a small barony. Of course, you can't spend your time happily growing cultivating your land; a bitter political battle between two factions drags you to the Capitol. Not to mention the empires with their eyes on your little nation. You have the power to change history. What will you do?

🏰[b] Pros:[/b]
[list]
[*] Writing. Again, Wang's writing is terrific. Not only does he manage to track your idealism or ruthlessness, both flavor traits have just beautiful monologues on power, or honor, or duty. His writing is more elegant, the characters vivid, and the setting rich with detail.

[*] Choices that actually matter. Gosh. Your choices will literally make or break a nation. You can side with an upstart Duke trying to reform the kingdom or the young Queen, the first female ruler. And if you side with one side, you can also act as a spy and betray them. The text always reacts to your choices, big or small. You can even decide which club to join in your free time, or what skills to improve, which leads to great replay value. 

[*] Moral complexity. Just because you side with the Duke or Queen doesn't mean you have to agree with them. Each side has its good and bad points. Every decision feels like a test of your principles. You can fight for justice and still commit atrocities, or uphold the system only to realize how rotten it is. The game never flatters you with “good” or “evil” choices—it forces you to live with the fallout of your ambition, compassion, or cowardice. It’s rare to find a story this unflinching about the costs of leadership. You just have to do the best you can.

[*] Worldbuilding. There's a timeline history, maps, and character indexes in the Stats Sheet. And in-game, there's more on society's view on baneless and women, a lot of political and economic talk, etc. You actually feel like a lord living in this universe, trying to survive. 

[*] Writer's passion. You can tell Wang cares about the content he puts out. He's also active on the game's forum and doesn't lock a lot of content behind his Patreon. 

[*] More romance! There's more romance scenes, including an arranged marriage, and you can even choose to have a romance with a man (though it's not very long). It's still a slow burn for Katerina and Welles, but for Welles, you can confess, at least. And you get very affectionate letters from them :P

[*] New gameplay mechanic: house debt/estate management. This builds off the debt mechanic from the last book. If you choose the Estate path, you'll have to balance your expenses, estate upgrades, tenant loyalty, tenant contentment, and tenant rent. It's super cool.
[/list]

🛤️ [b] Cons:[/b]
[list]
[*] Too much branching? I can't believe I'm saying this, but I feel like there's too much branching. For example, early on, you have to choose between managing your estate or going to the city. It's pretty much a given you should go to the city: all the political threads are there, all the important characters are there, you can get wealthy there, etc. But you'll be missing out on quite a lot of the estate management content, and vice versa. I don't see why we couldn't spend summers at the estate or something.

[*] Super slow burn romance. I'm going to be so real, half the reason I'm so invested is because I'm waiting for my marriage and children to Katarina. Even though romance is not a main part of the story, there's just a lot of longingly gazing into each other's eyes.

[*] It's gonna be a hell of a wait for the next book.
[/list]

Dead Island Retro Revenge, developed by Empty Clip Studios and published by Deep Silver, is a tongue-in-cheek spin-off from the well-known zombie franchise that trades its open-world survival horror roots for a fast-paced, retro-styled beat ‘em up. Released as a companion piece to the Dead Island: Definitive Collection, this game embraces a different tone entirely—it’s not about scavenging for supplies or surviving on a tropical island but about unleashing chaos in a neon-soaked, side-scrolling world filled with undead enemies. What it lacks in depth, it makes up for with energy, humor, and an old-school arcade flair that captures the spirit of 16-bit brawlers while still paying homage to its zombie lineage.

The game follows a hilariously simple premise: Max, a rugged anti-hero with a knack for violence, has his beloved cat Rick Furry kidnapped in the middle of a zombie apocalypse. Driven by fury and feline loyalty, Max sets off on a road of blood, metal, and retribution across California, taking down waves of zombies, criminals, and military thugs along the way. The story, though paper-thin, is perfectly aware of its absurdity. It leans into parody, blending B-movie melodrama and self-aware humor that suits the 16-bit presentation. The writing doesn’t take itself seriously, and neither should the player—it’s the kind of game where the plot exists merely to justify the mayhem.

Gameplay is structured around an endless runner-style combat system combined with lane-based beat ’em up mechanics. Each stage scrolls automatically, and Max can move between three lanes while punching, kicking, and slashing his way through enemies. Timing and reflexes are key as players must dodge projectiles, counter incoming attacks, and chain combos to maximize their score. While the controls are simple, the game demands precision, especially at higher levels where the screen fills with hazards. Power-ups and special weapons—ranging from explosive attacks to magic-like abilities—add variety to combat, while collectible upgrades and score multipliers reward skillful play. The flow of combat feels frantic and satisfying in short bursts, and pulling off a chain of perfectly timed attacks can feel exhilarating. However, the repetitiveness of the mechanics and the lack of real progression become apparent after extended play sessions, as the limited move set doesn’t evolve much over time.

Visually, Dead Island Retro Revenge achieves exactly what it sets out to do. The pixel art is vibrant and detailed, capturing the essence of 1990s arcade games with exaggerated animations and gory effects that feel both nostalgic and over-the-top. The color palette bursts with neon hues and fiery explosions, while the pixelated blood splatter and decapitation effects add a comedic edge to the carnage. The environments—ranging from city streets to desert highways and military zones—are richly layered with background details that give a sense of place despite the linear gameplay. The soundtrack, a mix of energetic rock and synth-inspired beats, complements the action perfectly, pumping adrenaline into every encounter. Together, the visuals and music create an atmosphere that’s both ridiculous and oddly charming, proving that the developers understood exactly the kind of game they were making.

Despite its strengths in style and presentation, the game’s limitations are hard to ignore. Its structure, though engaging at first, quickly becomes repetitive due to its limited mechanics and recycled enemy patterns. There are no checkpoints within levels, meaning that dying forces players to restart the entire stage, which can be frustrating in longer runs. The difficulty curve spikes abruptly, and while this encourages mastery, it can also feel punishing for casual players. Furthermore, the game offers little incentive for replay beyond chasing high scores or leaderboard rankings. There’s no narrative branching, character progression, or unlockable modes that might have added depth. The result is an experience that’s best enjoyed in short, nostalgic bursts rather than as a sustained campaign. It feels like a tribute to old-school arcade frustration—both its glory and its grind.

Still, Dead Island Retro Revenge succeeds in one very specific way: it’s fun when taken on its own terms. The controls are responsive, the visuals are striking, and the absurd premise keeps it entertaining even as repetition sets in. The humor and retro charm are its strongest assets, and for players who grew up with classic side-scrollers like Streets of Rage or Final Fight, there’s a nostalgic satisfaction in its simplicity. The addition of leaderboards and combo systems gives competitive players a reason to refine their runs, and the overall polish in its presentation demonstrates that the developers poured genuine affection into what could have easily been a throwaway spin-off.

In the end, Dead Island Retro Revenge is a playful detour from the gritty realism of its parent franchise—a game that embraces silliness, gore, and nostalgia in equal measure. It’s short, it’s simple, and it doesn’t pretend to be anything more than a stylish, tongue-in-cheek distraction. While it won’t appeal to everyone, especially those looking for depth or innovation, it captures the essence of arcade fun: quick reflexes, flashy visuals, and unrelenting action. For fans of retro aesthetics and zombie-smashing chaos, it’s a lighthearted romp worth revisiting when you need a dose of pixelated carnage and humor.

Rating: 6/10

I still recommend Dead Island: Retro Revenge if you are someone who:

enjoys retro arcade-styled games with a clear completionist goal

doesn’t need a massive active online community

is okay with a short-ish playtime

likes the mix of fun + challenge and quirky tone

However, temper expectations: it may not offer the large community or endlessly deep game world of big multiplayer titles. But for your stated likes — achievement hunting, fun style, manageable game — it ticks many boxes.

Guilty Gear Isuka is an experimental spin-off in the Guilty Gear series by Arc System Works. Released after Guilty Gear XX #Reload, it attempted to add cooperative and four-player competitive gameplay to the traditional 2D fighter format. The result is ambitious but flawed—an intriguing idea that sacrifices precision and balance for chaotic multiplayer.

The core gameplay builds on the classic Guilty Gear foundation: fast, technical combat with complex systems like Roman Cancels and Tension management. However, Isuka introduces a manual turn button that players must press to face opponents, breaking the natural flow of combat. This single change disrupts the rhythm that defines the series, leading to frustration and awkward inputs.

Multiplayer was the main selling point. Up to four players can fight simultaneously, turning matches into frantic brawls. While chaotic fun with friends, it lacks the structure and clarity of traditional duels. The camera struggles to track action, and visual clutter makes it difficult to read attacks or spacing—key elements in competitive fighting.

The roster is generous, including fan favorites like Sol, Ky, Millia, and new additions such as A.B.A. and Robo-Ky II. The characters retain their distinct move sets and personality, but the game’s mechanics often prevent them from being used effectively. Balancing multiple players on-screen comes at the cost of fine-tuned design.

Presentation remains strong. The 2D sprite art and animation are top-notch for their era—vibrant, expressive, and fluid. The soundtrack, composed by Daisuke Ishiwatari, delivers the same high-energy metal sound that defines the series. Despite its gameplay missteps, Isuka still looks and sounds like a Guilty Gear game.

The game includes a side-scrolling beat ‘em up mode called GG Boost, where players fight waves of enemies instead of dueling opponents. It’s a creative bonus but quickly becomes repetitive and shallow. Customization elements, such as the character color editor, add minor replay value but don’t fix the core design issues.

Overall, Guilty Gear Isuka is a bold but unsuccessful experiment. Its multiplayer focus and directional control system clash with the precise mechanics that made the series great. While visually and musically impressive, it remains a curiosity for collectors and die-hard fans rather than a must-play entry. For serious fighters, it’s an interesting detour—not the real road.

At a basic level it's fun. "Weapons" have different moves so at first it's random but later, as enemies get more complex (range, shielded, deadly shielded etc.) you need to choose the right tool to deal with them. I was surprised how varied the challenges were making the whole game feel a bit more than just running and smacking things. Most section also have more than one way to deal with them. Finding secret wolves was super fun as reaching them was always a dexterity puzzle.

Things that keeps the game from being truly amazing is slight inconsistency in attacks. There's an auto-lock mechanism and it feels like all attacks are checking for that and not physical contact. In other words sometimes it feels you should hit but you don't. It's maybe 4% of all actions in the game but in such a fast game where you die instantly it can become annoying. Not to the point you want to stop playing but still. Another thing is the camera. Sometimes it zooms out too much or angle is weird and "platforming" feels more complicated than actually is as it's hard to understand the space you are in. The last thing is the addition of some out of place/time elements that are fun to use but break immersion. For such a cartoony game story is pretty grim and hits some serious tones and those items just trivialize it a bit too much for my taste.

To sum it up it's an interesting take on "one hit" game and if some of the fiddlyness would be ironed out it could become a classic in my book. But it's not so it's "just" a good game that I can recommend if you’re looking for a fast game that won’t feel repetitive even if you get stuck in some area.

Ten Dates, developed by Wales Interactive in partnership with Good Gate Media, is an engaging continuation of the studio’s interactive film series that examines love, chemistry, and the unpredictable nature of human connection in the modern age. As the successor to Five Dates, it expands on the concept of digital romance by trading video calls for in-person encounters, following two protagonists—Misha and Ryan—as they each navigate five potential romantic interests. The game’s structure allows players to step into either character’s shoes, offering a perspective on both sides of the dating world while maintaining the signature full-motion video format that Wales Interactive is known for. What emerges is a vibrant, dialogue-driven experience that sits somewhere between an interactive movie, a dating sim, and a social experiment.

The narrative unfolds through a series of speed-dating sessions and follow-up encounters, where every conversation choice shapes how the relationship progresses. Each of the ten potential dates has a distinct personality, worldview, and dynamic that demands different approaches. Some are lighthearted and flirty, others intense or introspective, and part of the fun lies in learning to read each person’s cues and reacting appropriately. These interactions feel organic thanks to the cast’s strong performances, with each actor embodying their character in a believable and natural way. The dialogue often feels spontaneous rather than scripted, with enough emotional nuance to make even short exchanges meaningful. While the game’s scenarios are often humorous or awkward in the best possible way, there’s also a sincere exploration of how people present themselves when searching for connection, making the experience feel both entertaining and surprisingly genuine.

From a production standpoint, Ten Dates is one of Wales Interactive’s most polished FMV projects to date. The cinematography is sleek and confident, using warm lighting and close framing to create a sense of intimacy that mirrors the tension of real-life dating. The locations—trendy bars, cozy restaurants, and other London hotspots—add visual flair and realism, grounding the story in a believable setting. The user interface is smooth and intuitive, fading seamlessly into the live-action footage so that the player’s input never breaks immersion. The fast-paced editing and responsive choice system keep scenes dynamic, with decisions needing to be made quickly to simulate the conversational flow of real-life exchanges. It’s this immediacy that makes the experience engaging; the player doesn’t have time to overthink, just as in real social interactions.

Ten Dates also deserves credit for the diversity of its cast and relationships. Players can pursue both heterosexual and same-sex options, with different romantic arcs depending on which protagonist is chosen. Each potential partner offers a distinct emotional tone—from witty banter to more heartfelt vulnerability—and the range of backgrounds and personalities gives each route its own flavor. This diversity extends beyond romance; the writing touches on contemporary themes such as online identity, emotional intelligence, career ambition, and the anxieties of post-pandemic dating. These discussions feel modern without being preachy, and they add an unexpected layer of authenticity to what could easily have been a lighthearted dating simulation.

That said, Ten Dates isn’t without its limitations. While player choice is central to the experience, the branching narrative structure remains relatively constrained. Dialogue options often lead to slightly altered scenes rather than drastically different outcomes, and the illusion of control can fade on subsequent playthroughs when players realize how tightly scripted the game truly is. Some exchanges also suffer from tonal inconsistency, with certain lines feeling forced or mismatched with the character’s demeanor. The short runtime—each playthrough lasting around two to three hours—means that relationships sometimes progress too quickly, and emotional depth can feel compressed into brief conversations. While the replay value is enhanced by the number of possible dates, repetition becomes noticeable when revisiting similar scenes or topics across multiple routes.

Despite these drawbacks, Ten Dates succeeds in what it sets out to do: create a charming, human-centered exploration of love and vulnerability in the digital era. Its strength lies not in complexity but in relatability. The experience captures both the excitement and awkwardness of meeting someone new—the pauses, the glances, the small talk that either fizzles or sparks something genuine. The performances make these moments come alive, and the direction gives each date an identity strong enough to make players curious about every possible outcome. Wales Interactive and Good Gate Media have built a niche for themselves in the interactive film genre, and Ten Dates stands as one of their most accessible and emotionally grounded efforts to date.

In the end, Ten Dates is less about winning the perfect romance and more about understanding the imperfect nature of human connection. It’s a short, sincere, and highly watchable story that balances humor and heart with modern sensibility. While it doesn’t reinvent the FMV format or the dating sim genre, it refines both, delivering a thoughtful and enjoyable experience that feels at once playful and authentic. For players who appreciate interactive storytelling, strong acting, and the unpredictable dance of dating, Ten Dates is an experience worth revisiting—one that reminds us that every connection, no matter how brief, tells a story of its own.

Rating: 7/10

I would like to say I preferred Five Dates, mainly because of the casting — and casting is a big part of this kind of game. Still, Ten Dates is a unique experience. The script is really well written: it manages to be cringe when it needs to be, caring and passionate when there’s genuine chemistry between characters. All of that works thanks to a strong scenario.

I don’t want to spoil anything, but with the male character I found most dates a bit disappointing — maybe intentionally, to reflect how difficult it can be for men to find the “perfect fit”? Still, there are some deep thoughts behind the scenes. Some characters only reveal who they truly are if you’re kind and tolerant, and the writing is so good that if you don’t listen to your heart you can end up disliking the wrong people.

In the end, the game shows how simple love should be: when you trust and stop blaming/complaining, everything becomes smoother and more natural, almost like gender barriers don’t exist. Bash, in particular, shows how problems can be solved with humor: even when you mess up, your partner still smiles and cares.

Some situations feel exaggerated, some connections happen a bit too fast, but I understand the game lasts barely one hour and has to condense a huge amount of scenes. Editing must have been a nightmare.

Of course I wish we had access to more profiles — choosing between only five partners makes things harder. Sometimes the decision timer starts before the narrator even finishes the sentence, so you don’t always get the context. And when English isn’t your first language and you need time to read, it goes a bit too fast. Having only two choices also leads to lucky guesses; maybe more branches and fewer filler conversations would improve the flow.

Overall it’s a cool and cozy experience when you’re alone at your PC with all those charismatic characters for company. I know it’s not an 18+ game, but in a romance game you expect at least some erotic tension — maybe more kisses, more flirt, more “heat”. It’s definitely too soft for a romance story. Please don’t make 2025 more politically flat than it already is.

Não costumo dizer que um jogo mudou minha vida, mas este mudou — não pelo que acontece na tela, e sim pelo que aconteceu fora dela. Sem perceber, ele se tornou uma ponte entre mim e meu pai, algo que não conseguíamos construir há anos.

Começamos a jogar juntos de maneira casual, quase por acaso. Mas, com o tempo, aquela experiência virou nosso espaço seguro: um lugar onde conseguíamos rir, cooperar e conversar sem a pressão das conversas “sérias” que sempre travavam entre nós. Pelos personagens, pelas missões e pelas pequenas vitórias compartilhadas, fomos retomando uma intimidade que parecia perdida.

O mais surpreendente foi ver meu pai se abrindo — primeiro comentando sobre o jogo, depois sobre a vida. Eu também fui me permitindo estar mais presente, escutar mais, falar mais. Era como se aquele universo virtual nos desse a chance de reconstruir tudo o que, na correria do mundo real, deixamos escapar.

Não avalio esse jogo apenas pelos gráficos, pela jogabilidade ou pela história. Avalio pelo que ele nos devolveu: tempo juntos, conversas naturais e uma sensação de proximidade que eu achava que não voltaria.

No fim, ele não mudou só meu jeito de jogar — mudou meu jeito de viver ao lado do meu pai.

Founders’ Fortune is a colony simulation that blends settlement-building, life management, and light survival elements into a charming but surprisingly layered experience. Developed and published by Dionic Software, the game starts small: two settlers, a few tools, and a patch of land filled with promise. What unfolds from there is a steadily growing village shaped not just by resource flow and buildings, but by the desires, fears, personalities, and relationships of the colonists themselves. From the outset, the game signals that it cares as much about the inner lives of its characters as it does about construction efficiency, making your colony feel more like a living community than a series of production chains.

The heart of Founders’ Fortune lies in the settlers. Each villager comes with traits, ambitions, quirks, and emotional needs that must be tended to if you want a productive, harmonious settlement. Happiness isn’t cosmetic—it dictates how well they work, how cooperative they become, and even whether they spiral into tantrums or breakdowns. As the village expands, settlers form friendships, rivalries, and families, age into adulthood, grow old, and eventually pass away, leaving behind children who inherit their place. This life-cycle system gives the colony a tangible sense of history, something many city-builders lack. Managing emotional wellbeing becomes just as important as managing food stores or construction materials, and this balance lends the game a personal touch that resonates long after the first few hours.

Resource management and construction follow classic colony-builder conventions but offer enough flexibility to keep things engaging. Players gather wood, stone, and ore, develop farms, craft tools, and research technologies to push the settlement into new eras. The building system is intuitive and genuinely fun to experiment with, allowing for fully customized houses rather than preset templates. Decorating interiors, laying out workshops, and expanding fortifications bring a creative satisfaction that complements the strategic aspects. Seasonal changes add urgency—winter is harsh, and failing to prepare crops or secure food can doom a settlement quickly. Early decisions carry real consequences, giving the opening hours a sense of purpose and tension that hooks you in.

As your settlement grows, new systems open up to expand the experience. Diplomacy with neighboring goblin tribes introduces a layer of negotiation and occasional conflict. Visitors and traders arrive with opportunities or demands. Raids and threats force you to consider defensive strategies, though combat itself remains one of the simpler mechanics in the game. Research trees, crafting chains, and skill progression push the colony forward, but the late game can begin to feel repetitive as advancement slows and the variety of challenges tapers off. While there’s plenty to do, some players may find that the sense of novelty diminishes once a stable, self-sufficient colony is established.

The game’s presentation is cheerful and visually appealing. It adopts a stylized, bright aesthetic that gives its world a friendly, approachable charm. Animations are expressive enough to convey settler emotions, and the overall art direction helps the village feel warm and lived-in. The interface is clean, though some menu layouts and controls can feel slightly clunky at times. Still, the game maintains a pleasant atmosphere, making it easy to sink into long play sessions without feeling overwhelmed or pressured.

Founders’ Fortune’s weaknesses mostly stem from its scope and balance. Certain late-game tasks take considerably longer to complete, creating pacing dips. Combat, while functional, lacks depth and can feel somewhat detached from the otherwise strong systems of village simulation. A handful of mechanics, such as goblin diplomacy or advanced research, might benefit from additional complexity. Yet these shortcomings never fundamentally undermine the experience—they simply highlight areas where the game prioritizes accessibility and charm over depth.

Ultimately, Founders’ Fortune thrives by focusing on humanity rather than scale. It’s not the largest or most complex settlement sim on the market, but it excels at making your villagers feel alive, giving every house built, every meal cooked, and every relationship formed a sense of importance. It’s a game where the story is written through the daily routines of its characters, where triumphs and failures belong not just to the player but to the community they shape. For fans of relaxed but thoughtful colony-builders—especially those who enjoy games with personality and emotional depth—Founders’ Fortune offers a warm, engaging, and memorable experience.

Rating: 8/10

If you enjoy base-building, resource management, and colony simulation games, Founder’s Fortune is a hidden gem that deserves your attention. It combines the charm of games like The Sims with the strategic depth of RimWorld, but with a more cheerful, approachable art style. You’ll guide a small band of settlers as they construct homes, farms, workshops, and defenses, all while managing moods, relationships, and the occasional goblin raid. Each colonist has unique needs and ambitions that affect productivity and morale, giving every decision personal weight. The progression feels rewarding, the AI is quirky and full of personality, and the sense of growth from a fragile camp to a thriving settlement is deeply satisfying. It’s an ideal pick for players who love creativity, problem-solving, and watching a tiny world come alive under their care.
