Time Lock VR 1, developed by WR-VRG and published by Whale Rock Games, is a virtual reality adventure that blends science fiction storytelling with puzzle-solving and light action elements. It casts players as a time agent trapped in an unstable timeline, navigating through distorted environments where the laws of time and space no longer behave as expected. The concept is immediately appealing—a blend of temporal manipulation, environmental exploration, and first-person interactivity designed to make full use of VR immersion. Set within laboratories, corridors, and alien-like ruins, the game invites you to experiment with the flow of time itself to solve puzzles, unlock doors, and escape mysterious confines. It’s a title that leans heavily on atmosphere and conceptual intrigue, presenting an experience that feels simultaneously experimental and cinematic.

From the opening moments, Time Lock VR 1 makes a strong impression with its aesthetic and spatial design. The environments are constructed with a clean, futuristic visual language—metallic halls, floating platforms, and glowing machinery that reinforce the sensation of being inside a fractured reality. The sense of scale and physicality afforded by VR is one of the game’s biggest strengths. You can reach out to grab objects, manipulate levers, and physically peer around corners, which helps ground the player in its surreal world. The sound design adds to the immersion, with echoing footsteps, humming energy fields, and environmental cues that shift as you tamper with time. The overall tone is one of solitude and quiet discovery, as though you’re exploring an experiment gone wrong, a place built by a civilization—or laboratory—that has long since ceased to exist. In these moments, Time Lock VR 1 captures the magic that virtual reality can deliver: the thrill of physically existing inside a mystery.

At its core, the game’s central mechanic revolves around the manipulation of time. You have the ability to slow, stop, and rewind temporal flow, and these powers are integrated into the puzzle structure. Some rooms require freezing moving platforms to cross gaps, others demand rewinding falling debris or repositioning objects across different points in time to open pathways. The satisfaction of these puzzles lies in the tactile engagement—rather than simply pressing a button, you physically control time and interact with objects in three-dimensional space. When these systems click, they create moments of real delight, forcing players to think spatially and causally, as though rearranging reality itself. Unfortunately, this core mechanic is not as fully realized as it could have been. Many puzzles rely on simple object manipulation rather than creative temporal logic, and some of the advertised abilities, such as freezing or rewinding time, are underutilized or appear in only a few sequences. The potential for deeper complexity is clear, but it often feels like a proof of concept rather than a fully developed system.

The gameplay alternates between puzzling and light action sequences. At times, players will encounter small combat segments, wielding weapons or tools against automated defenses or environmental hazards. These moments add variety, but they rarely feel as polished or satisfying as the puzzle design. The shooting mechanics are functional but basic, with little depth beyond point-and-shoot interactions. Still, they serve as brief diversions that break up the pacing, preventing the experience from becoming too repetitive. Movement, handled through teleportation or limited free locomotion depending on the hardware, is smooth and accessible, though some players may find the controls a bit finicky in tight spaces. The physics interactions are another mixed bag—grabbing and throwing objects can feel imprecise, and small inconsistencies in how the environment reacts to your inputs occasionally disrupt immersion.

Visually, Time Lock VR 1 makes good use of lighting and color to differentiate areas and signal progress. Brightly lit corridors give way to darker, more mysterious chambers where glowing elements hint at interactivity. While not graphically advanced by modern standards, the art direction compensates with clarity and atmosphere. The game’s simplicity works in its favor, keeping environments readable and avoiding unnecessary clutter that might overwhelm players in VR. The soundtrack, composed of ambient sci-fi tones and subtle electronic layers, complements the aesthetic well. It reinforces the feeling of isolation and experimentation, enhancing the sensation that you’re tampering with forces beyond human understanding. The pacing, however, is inconsistent. Some sequences flow naturally from one challenge to the next, while others feel disjointed, with transitions that abruptly break immersion or undercut the tension the game builds.

Time Lock VR 1’s greatest strength lies in its immersive premise and its ability to make players feel like active participants in a temporal experiment. It’s easy to see the ambition behind its design—the desire to merge the physical engagement of VR with the cerebral satisfaction of time-based puzzles. However, the experience is notably brief. Many players report completing it in under an hour, which limits its impact and replay value. The short runtime could have been excusable if every moment felt essential, but the uneven pacing and occasional mechanical underuse leave the impression of an unfinished idea. There’s also a lack of narrative framing; while hints of story exist through environmental clues and subtle visual motifs, the absence of meaningful context can make the world feel hollow. The setting begs for a greater sense of mystery or discovery—a deeper explanation of who you are, what went wrong, and why time itself is breaking apart.

Despite these shortcomings, Time Lock VR 1 remains an interesting showcase of VR’s potential for spatial puzzles and conceptual storytelling. Its interactive mechanics, though limited, deliver moments of genuine immersion that only virtual reality can provide. It invites players to physically engage with its world, to move, reach, and think in three dimensions, which makes even its simpler challenges feel more tactile and personal. As a short, experimental experience, it succeeds in evoking curiosity and wonder, even if it falls short of being a fully realized game. For newcomers to VR or players seeking a compact session that demonstrates the medium’s strengths, Time Lock VR 1 offers a satisfying, albeit fleeting, glimpse into what time manipulation can feel like when placed directly in your hands.

Ultimately, Time Lock VR 1 is a creative but imperfect experiment—a puzzle-adventure that shines in concept and atmosphere but stumbles in execution. It delivers an enjoyable hour of exploration and interactivity, supported by intriguing ideas and strong environmental design. However, its limited depth and brief runtime prevent it from achieving the same level of impact as more polished VR titles. It’s a game that feels like a prototype for something greater, a foundation upon which future entries could build richer mechanics and storytelling. For players who appreciate inventive VR design and are willing to overlook its rough edges, Time Lock VR 1 is a small but memorable journey into the strange beauty of broken time.

本作最快的通关方式需要两个东西：
1.到达T6一星解锁电玩店
2.一个能正常运作的手柄，然后进入电玩厅剪刀石头布刷积分：
手柄快速按下Y+A，此时AI出的牌会是上一次出的牌的下一张。例如第一次对局的结果AI出石头，快速按下Y+A之后AI会出剪刀，我们只需要确保有足够的代币就能一直刷分了。

刷出来的电玩积分可以拿来买好感度礼物，也可以买工具书直接把所有属性升满。天赋主升右上黄色，点满买彩票打折
然后在小天商店找下面三张卡：
1.全属性等级上限提高到120级
2.刮彩票幸运提高平均等级*0.8%增益
3.每装备一张赌博卡，彩票收益提高9%
这样操作之后每次刮彩票稳赚不赔

然后是战斗，这个游戏的战斗只需要用到1张因果牌：消耗5张废票（蓝色强化后是2张）将选中的手牌替换为最接近的顺子或者对子。找两张这个因果牌，这样每次对局每个回合几乎都能出豹子，而有豹子就意味着开牌输不了+结算分数x2，升级巨快

基本上玩到这个阶段就是随意升级随意花钱了。由于有二周目加点的存在，本作大部分的因果牌都没什么用（毕竟经济压力还是比较小的，在电玩店刷分也不需要去图书馆健身房学习锻炼）。
——————————————————————————————————————————————
总体游玩下来体验还是非常好的。
随着市民等级的提升，玩家赚钱方式和生活方式（养成节奏）也相应发生了改变：一开始玩家靠打工掏垃圾过活，琐碎的，重复性的体验很多，也需要很频繁地与NPC交流对话+打牌获取金钱积分。进入游戏中期，玩家刮彩票开始不断赢钱，也从此时逐渐开始出老千，因果牌构筑也逐渐从单一走向多元：不仅仅是战斗，就连生活/送礼/刮奖都能开挂，各个因果牌之间的联动让各项数值开始起飞，所谓的概率游戏炸金花在千术加持之下也不过是点两下鼠标就能赢钱的东西，这种全维度的构筑+剧情推动塑造的“咸鱼翻身感”确实很爽。
而进入T3之后由于钱实在是太多了，各种高端消费也层出不穷。
富豪消费确实给足了情绪价值，却也逐渐让升级之路变得空虚：高等级NPC的减少导致每天只能去找那几个T2T3打牌升级，所谓的“豪车美食生活”其实就是天天刮不一样的彩票，实际也带不来多少的数值提升；每天两点一线穿梭于彩票中心和床上的生活本质上和T9苦苦求生的生活别无二致，玩家却越来越不屑于与T7T8T9的底层穷人打牌。这种市民等级制度下的所谓的“富豪生活”因为缺少了人情烟火而显得苍白又干枯。从另一个角度来看，这些所谓的江城富豪又何尝不是被等级制度囚禁在富人区的傀儡？
这些设计似乎也是作者有意为之的结果，kksk。

When I purchased this game I loved it.  The difficulty setting seemed fair and the puzzles were solvable.  As you move forward the levels get tougher.  Then you hit the wall.  A really tough level.  You sleep on it and the next day you come back and solve it and feel like you really accomplished something.  The trouble is, the next five levels are so easy you just cruise through them.  
Then you hit another clanger.  You sleep on it again, and the next day you solve it and then move ahead another bunch of levels.  This continues ad infinitum until you hit level 38.  
After you spend ages on it, you suddenly realize it's not about solving the problem in the most efficient way, it's about solving the problem according to the mind of someone who really doesn't want you to win.  This is the point of the game when I decided I'd had enough.  I don't have ESP.  I'm not a mind reader.  I'm not wasting any more time on this.
Even though beating those "hit the wall" levels is so satisfying, I can't recommend this.  
The puzzles are in the most bizarre order.  Multiple easy levels followed by one super hard level, followed by multiple easy levels again.
You are provided with the amount of moves the programmer decided were adequate to solve the puzzle.  Sometimes I used less moves which made me wonder what his end game was (because the idea is to use the exact amount of moves to solve the puzzle), then, when I hit level 38, I questioned the movement/direction count and was told it was correct.  I can solve it if one arrow direction is changed.  I plodded on but after 5 days I gave up.
I hope you can get past level 38 and enjoy the rest of the game but sadly level 38 has destroyed my desire to continue and I've lost all passion in playing this.

Necrosmith is an inventive blend of light strategy, roguelite progression, and chaotic minion management wrapped in a tongue-in-cheek necromancy theme. Developed and published by Alawar, it places you in the role of a reclusive necromancer who sits inside a magically fortified tower while assembling an army of stitched-together undead creatures. On the surface, the game appears simple—build units, send them out, survive as long as possible—but the appeal lies in the constant experimentation with bizarre combinations of limbs, cores, and weapons. The game’s pixel-art presentation and humorous tone make it approachable, while the underlying mechanics create a satisfying loop of discovery and incremental advancement.

At its heart, Necrosmith revolves around constructing minions from a growing catalogue of body parts harvested from fallen enemies or unlocked through upgrades. Each limb influences the resulting creature’s stats—speed, strength, armor, magic ability—while special cores grant tactical advantages, such as elemental attacks or increased resilience. The joy of creation is central to the experience: every run invites experimentation, and odd combinations often lead to unexpectedly powerful or hilarious results. Once your undead troops are assembled, they roam semi-autonomously across a procedurally generated world, uncovering resources, battling enemies, claiming structures, and spreading your influence outward from the tower.

The tower itself functions as the hub of progression and survival. As your units explore and gather materials, you funnel those resources into strengthening your magical base—unlocking new laboratories, boosting defenses, crafting modules that accelerate part generation, or learning spells that can aid your roaming undead. Each decision affects both short-term survival and long-term success, especially since enemy attacks grow stronger and more frequent as time passes. The roguelite structure ensures that, even when you fail, upgrades carry over into the next attempt, gradually broadening your roster of parts and increasing your potential for deep runs. This gradual expansion of possibilities fuels a compelling “just one more run” rhythm.

While the game’s concept is strong, its limitations become more noticeable during extended play. Unit AI is intentionally simple, leading to amusing but sometimes frustrating situations where minions wander off in odd directions or prioritize irrelevant targets. You can directly control units one at a time, but broader troop management is limited, preventing more sophisticated strategies from emerging. As you progress, repetition in map layouts and enemy encounters becomes more apparent, and once you have unlocked many upgrades, later runs can feel like variations on a familiar routine. The challenge persists, but the sense of discovery that defines the early hours gradually tapers off.

Despite this, Necrosmith remains engaging because its core loop is well-tuned and easy to enjoy in short sessions. The lightweight design makes it accessible to players who may be intimidated by heavier RTS titles, while the fast pace and cheeky humor keep the tone breezy rather than oppressive. The game never takes itself too seriously, and its compact scope works in its favor—offering quick bursts of creativity and strategy without demanding long commitments. The pixel-art visuals, quirky animations, and simple interface support this accessible approach, giving the game a charming personality that fits its playful necromantic theme.

Ultimately, Necrosmith succeeds as a compact, addictive sandbox where necromancy becomes a puzzle of resource management, experimentation, and tactical improvisation. It may not offer deep narrative arcs or complex strategic layers, but it excels within its chosen niche by presenting a steady cycle of creation, exploration, and incremental improvement. For players who enjoy building strange creatures, watching emergent chaos unfold, and gradually powering up through repeated runs, Necrosmith offers a surprisingly engaging—and often humorous—take on the RTS and roguelite fusion. It’s a small game with big charm, best enjoyed as a creative playground rather than a grand tactical challenge.

Sora is only technically a shoot 'em up. The player does the usual dodge enemy bullets and can shoot to destroy them. Where the game differs is the player's avatar stops to shoot. Complete wrecking one of my favorite things about playing STGs: the flow. Instead, Sora wants the player to plan their position then fire either a weak regular shot, charge up a power shot or fire a solid projectile. None feel especially powerful save the charged shot. Unfortunately, for me, I hate shumps that use charged shots being from the school of ABS (Always Be Shooting). 

However, not all is lost. Sora also features a melee attack. Which feels like the games real way to combat enemies. But like the STG Sol Divide demonstrated, melee doesn't often work well in a shooter. Especially if the game is stiff. Which Sora basically is with the stop and go flow. No, what Sora seems to want the player to do is dodge dash in and out of melee. And the way it is done here just isn't satisfying in anyway to me. Well beyond the rather steep learning curve the game wants from the player to use well.

The story is a bland. You are the next gen model of android combat little girl that is completely clueless and the previous gen combat girlies are jealous or whatever. I tried to skip the dialogue as much as possible. I can play cute 'em ups, which Sora really isn't, if the game is good. But Sora isn't. And I play shumps to mostly avoid story. If it doesn't get in the way or is mildly interesting it is usually a non-issue. Sora is mostly out of the way, but the fact that I even know what I do, shows the dialogue boxes don't go away fast enough.

I really tried to get to an hour before writing a review. But even a couple of minutes was soul draining for me. If Sora happens to click for a player, it might be a good game. As said, it doesn't technically do anything wrong. It is just on the opposite end of the shoot 'em up spectrum for my preferences. Everything it does irritates my sense of what I want in a shooter. It has a novel, if slow/deliberate, game play loop that probably works well for the player that can manage it.

So I saw a friend buy this game and I was intrigued. I like turn based tactical games, and it had a lot of neat things going for it in the trailers and the tutorials. Unfortunately the game isn't that deep and its design made it frustrating. The campaign is non-existent military jargon being thrown around while they pretend these string of missions are all connected. There are basically three mission types, eliminate the target, exfil the target, or escape from a hostile area. I played for little over an hour and felt I had experienced everything the game had to offer and it got very repetitive very quickly. Stealth is actually enjoyable enough, but the missions lack depth. While going loud is not enjoyable at all. Unlike games such as XCOM or Mechanicus which is a more apt comparison, there is no way to even the playing field in action economy. While you do get an extra action when compromised and a drone strike, the drone strike is a one time use and by design you are supposed to be out action economied. But I think its just handled in a shitty way. The fundamental problem with loud missions is that you might be able to clear a group of enemies but that uses all of your action points, only for new guys to spawn in and shoot your guys to bits. Or more likely clog up the narrow corridors you need to progress. Flanking doesn't really work either as some paths just lead to dead ends and ultimately you need to push to the exit but cannot because your path is blocked. Protracted fire fights are miserable and will usually end up in a squad wipe. 

Now that is in line with their design, which thematically isn't bad but if going loud is going to be certain death then they shouldn't have loud missions and that should be considered a near fail state like for stealth missions. I also find some of the tactical elements to be shallow as everyone has the same loadout, Breaching is down to sneak in or flash band and no real options for dealing with groups of enemies like grenades, or suppressing fire. your support options are limited in scope and use. No alternative loadouts like shotguns or machineguns. It just makes the experience too shallow and repetitive for an asking price of $20. If you are initerested get it on sale, but otherwise pass. There are better games out there. 

As for positives I do like the sprite work, and the music. It is a very atmospheric game and you do feel like a bunch of prowlers stalking the back streets of a Yemeni city. The music is also decent too.

Get this while it's on sale, which will only save you 5 dollars.

Nintendo64やPS1の時代を思い出させるオールドスクールなストーリーベースのFPS。
Godotエンジン製の2.5D的なグラフィックで、ゴールデンアイやパーフェクトダークで育ったおっさん世代のゲーマーは懐かしさに歓喜。
あくまでもタスクをこなすのがメインで、脱出シューター/ルーターシューターとしての完成度は他作品と比べるとお世辞にも良いとは言えず、フレーバー程度の要素としてそれらが存在する作品だと思ってプレイすべし。
この手の作品に慣れたゲーマーなら10時間以内にクリア可能なボリューム。

●脱出/ルーターシューター要素
Zero Sievert等の同ジャンルや、オープンワールドサバイバルゲームに慣れているゲーマーからすると正直かなり物足りない。
漁れる箱は武器箱/弾薬箱/医療クレート/ゴミ箱/ロッカーの主に5種。
1stステージの間はある程度戦利品システムが機能するが…2ndステージ以降の調整はかなり大雑把で、獲得可能な戦利品が主に脱出便利アイテムに絞られ、その2種アイテムの売値が高い故にインフレの如き金策が出来てしまう。
武器種はAR3種/SG1種/HG2種/GL1種の計7種。SMG/SR等は無し。
武器カスタム要素として一部武器にスコープが付けられる。
AK/マカロフ/モシンを担いだ敵PMCが登場するが、彼らを倒しても落とすのはAK/マカロフと弾薬だけ。
ダメージがAKの2倍で唯一ACOG的な倍率スコープが付けられるSCARがずば抜けて強力だが、武器箱からの低確率ランダム入手でしか手に入らない。しかし運が良ければ1stステージで容易に入手出来てしまう。2nd/3rdステージでのみ排出しやすくするのはどうだろうか？ゲーム終盤でAKやマカロフが武器箱に置かれてるのを何度も観るのはあまり良い心地がしなかったが、エンドゲームで相応しい武器を入手出来るとゲーム体験はより良いものになるだろう。
最初から最期まで特定の武器が一強で使えてしまう調整はゲームをつまらないものにしてしまう。用途に応じて銃を使い分ける楽しみが主体のこの手のジャンルとしては致命的だ。
総じて、これらの要素"だけ"を求めるプレイヤーには到底オススメ出来ない。

●シューターとしての完成度
敵PMCは視野内に入ると超反応で精確にタップ撃ちしてくる。
弾速が遅めなので遠距離なら横移動で避けられるのだが、近距離では視界に入る前に先手を撃たない限り被弾不可避。
近くの遮蔽にダッシュで逃げようとすれば、その間ももれなく全弾ヒットさせてくるエイムボットクオリティ。
難易度を変えてもエイム精度や反応速度が変わったりするわけでもないので、ステルススナイプ有利or回復ガブ飲み撃ち合いゲー感は否めない。

もしこれがSyntyアセットのいつものUnity/UE製ポリゴン脱出シューターだったら間違いなくクソゲー認定していただろうが、

This one flew under EVERYBODY'S radar but I'm really glad I somehow caught notice of it because Kiss/OFF was a total blast start to finish. This is one of the best western visual novels I've ever played -- every character is fantastic and there's a ton of alternate paths based on how well or badly you treat them.

The only downside is after a few runs, it can get a bit repetitive going through the motions with each character to find all the endings. Even so, whenever the game branches from its base storyline -- which happens more often than you'd think -- it's extremely entertaining, and the true ending in particular was a blast to run through after what it took to get there.

The artwork and music are top tier throughout and it had me constantly guessing what was going to happen next. This one's an absolute hidden gem and I had a fantastic time.

The game feels well polished and I personally have not been affected by and game breaking bugs in my 90 minutes of game time. The sound effects, music, graphics, dialogue and story all feel original, which is hard to find these days. However, the game play, mechanics and obstacles feel similar to other games I have played in the past (Mario is the big name that comes to mind), and this is hard to shake when this comparison has been established. The game play elements are well introduced, so that the player knows what he will need to deal with in future chapters of the story. The majority of boss fights I have played are diverse, fun and challenging, however, the spaceship boss fight has twitchy controls, and as I found pretty quickly, you can just press the up arrow after evading the rockets to beat the boss. One negative to all boss fights is the lack of communication to the player saying which controls he needs to use (in some cases the mouse and in others the keyboard, which might not be a problem on a controller).
My main worry with this game is that it targeting the wrong audience. This game has simple mechanics, a small download size and is kid friendly, which could be a great game for a mobile game audience.
Big kudos to the game developer who has clearly put a lot of thought into this game. It is hard to believe that a single person is behind the entire game due to its execution and originality. I look forward to finishing the game.

So this was my first Lu Game. After seeing a few of them around on Steam, I decided it was about time to sate my curiosity surrounding them and... well, this is a strange game, but honestly, i'm charmed by it.

This is a completely wordless game, aside from the title card. The blurb of the game basically gives you all the context you're going to get and you have to figure the rest out yourself based on the environment.

Essentially this is a resource management sim. You have to keep the titular Megadeka from destroying your buildings, but you also need to manage your own stress, keep her placated and also manage your own funds. You only have a limited amount of time in the day and every night, Megadeka will randomly do something.

You can finish this in about an hour on the normal difficulty, but Hard difficulty is another story entirely. I still haven't managed to get through a full run yet, because juggling things gets super tricky.

It's a very cheaply made game but honestly that doesn't really matter too much. The intrigue behind just, dropping a player in a bizarre scenario and letting them figure it out is really appealing and carries it. It's easy enough to figure out, even it in its ambiguity and makes for a rather unique experience that is worth trying out if it seems like your kind of thing.

Reflex is often highlighted as one of, if not, THE best motocross games of all time. This title marked a huge change for the series in many ways. It introduced dual inputs for not only the bike but also the bike, which gave players access to much more expression both on track and in the air. With it was the reflex system, which would be used on subsequent games, as a way to possibly save a bad landing from becoming a crash. And it also was one of the first games to bring terrain deformation, giving each lap a new look as players could build up racing lines. The environments still hold up today, and I think the track layouts themselves are fun and creative, especially the supercross tracks that go up into the stands. I always remember that being one of my favorite layouts.

Replaying this game from my early adolescence was a lot of fun, and while the game has mostly held up there are a few glaring issues when viewed from a 2025 perspective. The handling model is very responsive, but you might find yourself careening in a weird direction every now and then, seemingly from nothing. The computer players are pretty easy beat, as there's no difficulty setting. And the tracklist does leave a lot to be desired, especially since you'll probably enjoy riding the bikes the most. Any events outside of the MX or ATV vehicles are super repetitive, but it was kinda expected that these were included. Oh, last big thing, the engine sounds get old so fast. I remember even being annoyed by them back in the day.

All in all this is still a good game to play if you're a fan of motocross, racing, or just want to play one of the greats.

I bought MX vs ATV Reflex about ten years ago for two euros and never played it until a few days ago. I finally gave it a go, and honestly, it was a nice surprise. It feels like stepping straight back into the early 2010s. The menus, the soundtrack, the bright bloom effects, and the style of the tracks all scream that era. There is something comforting about it. Games back then had a kind of raw energy that did not try too hard, and Reflex fits that perfectly.

For a game from 2010, the graphics are still impressive. It is full of bloom, reflections, and exaggerated lighting, but it works. It gives the game that over-the-top look that defined so many games of the time. What really stands out though is the physics. The terrain deformation is incredible. Mud, sand, and dirt actually move and change as you race. It makes every lap feel slightly different and adds a lot of depth to the handling.

The Reflex control system is brilliant. The left stick controls the bike, and the right stick controls the rider. It sounds simple, but it gives you much more control than you would expect. You lean into corners, shift your weight mid-jump, and save yourself from bad landings by reacting fast. Tricks are easy to pull off with a combination of the stick and a button, and the small quick-time events to avoid crashes work surprisingly well..

The career mode is basic. You just race, win, and move on to the next event. There are a few disciplines like Omnicross, Freeride, Waypoint Racing, Champion Sport Track, and Freestyle Motocross. They are simple but fun. Some of the buggy and truck races even reminded me of MotorStorm, which was another great game from that time. The online part is dead, so it is best enjoyed as a single-player game.

MX vs ATV Reflex is not deep, but it is a fun and nostalgic experience. The physics and controls still hold up, and the atmosphere brings back that 2010 feeling in the best way. My teenage self would have loved it even more, but for a few evenings of light racing fun, it does its job very well.

This is a very wholesome exploration game as you play as Pilo, a fennec fox apprentice explorer travelling with his beloved Professor.  They decide to explore a system called XOP-642 which consists of 4 major planets.  These planets have completely different environments from desert, marsh, water and a broken planet with a substance like tar.
The Professor creates a Holobook to get Pilo working.  He is usually searching for a hidden cookie jar to raid!!!  This Holobook records and details everything Pilo sees through camera like lens, so it creates an encyclopaedia of knowledge about each planet.  As Pilo captures an object, it creates a sticker in his Holobook and each planet has a set number of stickers to collect.
Graphics are hand drawn and are very cute and colourful.  There is a cartoonish feel to the graphics, but done in a delightful way.  Music is subtle but playful.
If I had to dislike anything about this game, it is that it lacks directions.  The desert secrets were particularly hard to find.  Other reviewers have stated that some hints are needed.  I was just going around and round in circles not knowing what to do at one stage, so had to resort to video playthrough to get some guidance.
There is some light puzzling which is pretty easy.  You do meet some quirky and delightful characters and you learn the story about what happened to the people of this solar system.  
However, having to catalogue every single item on every planet did get tedious for me in the end.  Even children may lose interest despite the stickers being very colourful.  The Holobook gets upgraded which means that you have to visit each planet multiple times to catalogue missing objects.
There are a few time sensitive achievements to get.  You need to round up the electric sheep under 30 seconds and catch the flying fish under 40 seconds.  I managed to get them after a few attempts and I'm on keyboard and mouse.  You able to go back after completing the game to find missing achievements.  I had to chase the sheep!
This is a game that children may enjoy, but with assistance.  There is no violence or anything bad, but there are adult themes about the demise of the solar system.  There is both sadness and joy in this story.
Most people finished this around the 4 hour mark.  I recommend playing the demo to see if you like doing this sort of thing as I haven't seen this style of game before.  Recommended.  7.5/10

Doraemon Story of Seasons vereint das ruhige Landleben der Story of Seasons-Reihe mit der Wärme und Fantasie des Doraemon-Universums. Das Ergebnis ist eine friedliche, nostalgische Farmsimulation, in der man Feldfrüchte anbaut, Tiere versorgt und Freundschaften in einer wunderschön illustrierten Welt pflegt.

Man spielt als Nobita, der zusammen mit Doraemon und seinen Freunden in die friedliche Stadt Natura gelangt. Ohne futuristische Gadgets muss die Gruppe lernen, einfach zu leben und auf eigene Anstrengung zu vertrauen. Diese Ausgangslage verleiht der Geschichte einen bodenständigen Ton über Selbstständigkeit, Freundlichkeit und die Freude am Alltäglichen.

Die Landwirtschaft steht im Mittelpunkt. Obwohl die Mechaniken für Genre-Fans vertraut sind, bringen Doraemons verspielte Gadgets einen Hauch von Fantasie hinein. Sie können Arbeiten automatisieren oder bestimmte Aufgaben beschleunigen, ohne das Gleichgewicht zu stören, und machen den Tagesablauf abwechslungsreicher und unterhaltsamer.

Das Spiel legt zudem großen Wert auf Gemeinschaft und Beziehungen. Jeder Dorfbewohner hat eine eigene Persönlichkeit, und durch regelmäßige Interaktionen schaltet man neue Dialoge und Ereignisse frei, die sich aufrichtig und herzlich anfühlen. Der Ton bleibt stets sanft, mit einem Fokus auf Freundschaft, Empathie und Zugehörigkeit statt auf Wettbewerb oder Konflikt.

Der Aquarell-Stil ist beeindruckend, mit weichem Licht und natürlichen Details, die jede Szene wie ein lebendiges Gemälde wirken lassen. Zusammen mit der beruhigenden Musik und den Umgebungsgeräuschen entsteht eine Atmosphäre der Ruhe und des Eintauchens, die perfekt zum gemächlichen Rhythmus des Spiels passt.

Das langsame Tempo mag für einige Spieler ungewohnt sein, ist jedoch Teil seines Charmes. Das Spiel fördert Geduld und Achtsamkeit und belohnt Beständigkeit statt Eile. Es ist ein entspannendes Erlebnis für alle, die stille Zufriedenheit einem ständigen Aktionstempo vorziehen.

Letztlich geht es in Doraemon Story of Seasons darum, das Tempo zu drosseln, kleine Momente zu schätzen und Trost in der Routine zu finden. Es ist ein herzerwärmendes und visuell wunderschönes Erlebnis, das den Geist von Doraemon und Story of Seasons in einem friedlichen, unvergesslichen Paket vereint.

Toki Tori is one of those deceptively cute puzzle games that lures you in with soft edges, bright colors and a chirpy bird protagonist, only to reveal - puzzle by puzzle - that it fully intends to scramble your brain. Two Tribes’ classic remains a remarkably well designed exercise in logical clarity: no filler, no gimmicks, just tight, disciplined puzzle construction that rewards foresight and punishes impulsiveness.

Each level is essentially a self contained brainteaser. You’re given a limited set of abilities (bridges, teleports, freezes...) and must figure out the exact sequence of actions needed to reach each egg. There’s no wiggle room; Toki Tori is engineered with the precision of a Swiss watch. When you finally crack a particularly thorny solution, the satisfaction is real, earned through genuine reasoning rather than trial-and-error thrashing.

Its charm helps enormously. The presentation is clean and warm, with cheerful animations and a gentle soundtrack that encourages patience rather than frustration. The difficulty curve is generally well judged, though later stages spike abruptly and demand a kind of meticulous planning that can feel more exhausting than enjoyable if you tackle too many in a row.

Still, the game’s design philosophy - clarity over chaos, logic over luck - makes it stand out in a genre that often leans on trickery or reflexes. Toki Tori respects the player’s intelligence and that respect is reciprocated in the pleasure of solving its most elegantly constructed challenges.

It’s not flashy, extremely long or narratively ambitious. What it is, however, is pure, focused puzzle craftsmanship wrapped in a wonderfully disarming package. For anyone who savors thoughtful, methodical problem solving, Toki Tori remains a small but polished gem.

This is an interesting experiment. The engine is extremely capable in a great many ways, and it is extremely easy to give a scenario to the prompt and a whole world is created.  This is particularly intersting when you task the engine with recreating a scenario (I tried being a cook on the Edmund Fitzgerald and another where I was a warrior of the Dakota tribe in the US/Dakota war 1862).  While my experimentation is limited here, I have no doubt of the engine's capability to create and deliver fantastical settings.

As the player, you are able to attempt to do anything and only the logic of the world that has been created by the system will limit your actions.

But it's not all roses here.  It's heavily LLM-based, and the kind of issues that arrive with LLM-based solutions also appear here.  For example, places are created but they do not logically interconnect - they're just created.  Quests are created as a means to drive the plot forward, but the LLM doesn't truly care if you've completed them or not. The engines "DM" feels a bit like having the attention spam of a squirrel; while my playtime is extremely limited, I have not yet witnessed or played through a scenario where there felt like there was an overarching plot story, just interconnected 'ideas' created on a whim by an LLM that has difficulty peicing the logic together in a humanistic way.

Graphics are created and that's awesome.  Yet, the graphics created are 'just a bit off' - like, in the Fitzgerald I was cook, but the galley looked like a house kitchen.  Or how seemingly straightforward paths are obscurely hidden in weird ways.  

Actions are slow.  That is, it takes a noticeable amount of time for the engine to process your action and determine the result.  There's a speech-to-text thing that happens and it's cool, but the voices are strange and weirdly paced.   Some text is also missing in the presentation.

Some people have obviously had a lot of fun with this tool, and so therefore it goes without saying that some people will very much enjoy the many options that are available to the player.  AI Roguelite is literally a pandora's box of quests, but like Pandora's box, once you've opened it you may not really like what's inside.  

I recommend this to those select few of us who enjoy text adventure games, are extremely creative, patient with plot holes (think swiss cheese), and enjoy tinkering with their game systems.   AI Roguelike provides players with an uncanny ability to experience all manner of RPG worlds, but unfortunatley it also provides players with an uncanny valley of human expectation.

It's not... bad. The bones of a merged RTS / Roguelike / TRPG are here! From what I've played (admittedly not much) it's smooth, there's minor jank, and it's competent enough... 

So what is the problem?

This game did NOT sell well upon entering Early Access. They had some pretty big plans but after ~80 reviews within 6 months of release, and only 107 on full release, it's unlikely the game will see any updates moving forward. I don't blame the devs for this - with the priormentioned review #'s there's NO WAY this was profitable. You can't expect any size team to keep working on a project that is literally NOT selling. My heart goes out to them because I think they started this with the best intentions.. 

So what was the problem for sales?

Well, for starters, the art style is INSANELY off putting. It makes your eyes bleed with how washed out it is. It's just not.. clear? Sharp? It's like they maxed out the fuzzy. Second, the voice acting is just atrocious. It's like the devs brought their youngest family members in and just handed them a set of lines. In a more story-oriented roguelike, this was a killer. Third, the lore dump is overwhelming. Bizarre names and factions are thrown around like candy, and this whole 'world' with all its rules / lore you're just expected to know. It's a lot for new players to digest. Finally, the game is structured as a Rogue-Like that leans toward 'Fail, Fail, Fail' and build up meta currency until you eventually can win, vs. player capability being strong enough upon starting to win a run. You're essentially soft-locked from winning until you acquire enough meta-progression from within the runs themselves. (And these are often rewarded vs. in-run upgrades, which further prolongues the grind). 

You can decide if those issues prevent you from enjoying the game. I think it's worth $20, as you'll get 10-15 hours out of it, but don't expect anything else from it. Again, I feel bad for the dev team. So much slop is released everyday on Steam while *potential* gems like this get buried, never to be heard of again. I hope their next project goes well.

Finnish Cabin Mayhem, developed and published by Sophisticated Keppana Enjoyers, is a chaotic and irreverent indie brawler that captures the spirit of wild, drunken Finnish countryside weekends with an unapologetically over-the-top dose of absurd humor and physics-based violence. Set in a series of rural cabins, forest clearings, and lakeside saunas, the game invites players into a gleeful mess of alcohol-fueled combat where everything becomes a weapon and nothing is sacred. It’s a celebration of both Finnish stereotypes and classic party-game sensibilities, merging slapstick action with cultural in-jokes about beer, summer cabins, and the kind of mayhem that erupts when good friends and bad decisions collide.

The core of Finnish Cabin Mayhem is built around fast-paced melee combat that prioritizes spontaneity and chaos over precision. You pick up whatever objects happen to be nearby—beer bottles, axes, sausages, rifles, even chunks of furniture—and use them to pummel opponents in small, destructible arenas. The gameplay thrives on physics-based interactions, where the hilarity often comes not from planned strategies but from unintentional disasters: a misplaced swing that sends both players tumbling into a sauna fire, or a beer-fueled brawl that ends with someone flying off a jet ski. The controls are intentionally loose and comical, designed to enhance the unpredictability rather than offer rigid mastery. It’s not about finesse; it’s about letting the chaos unfold naturally. Every encounter feels like a drunken bar fight filmed in a rural cabin, which, in the world of this game, is exactly the point.

The game’s tone is its strongest feature. It embraces its identity as a ridiculous, unapologetically Finnish comedy of violence and excess. The atmosphere is pure countryside absurdity, where heavy metal riffs, the crackle of campfires, and the buzz of mosquitoes accompany the sound of breaking bottles and guttural laughter. The developers clearly understand the humor in exaggerating national clichés—characters who drink too much, fight over trivialities, and express themselves through primal brawls behind saunas and on frozen lakes. Rather than feeling mean-spirited, it’s endearing in its self-awareness, and that authenticity makes it all the more entertaining. The visual style reinforces this tone with simple but expressive graphics, colorful lighting, and a cartoonish exaggeration that fits perfectly with the game’s personality.

Multiplayer is where Finnish Cabin Mayhem truly shines. The game supports both local and online play, allowing groups of friends to dive into the madness together. In these sessions, the game transforms into a festival of laughter and destruction, where teamwork often dissolves into betrayal and chaos. The different arenas, ranging from cramped wooden cabins to open outdoor settings, keep matches varied and dynamic. Every environment is designed for maximum absurdity, filled with objects to throw, destroy, or ride into battle. Bicycles, snowmobiles, and other improvised vehicles appear as tools of both mobility and comedic disaster, often leading to slapstick outcomes that feel straight out of a Finnish cult film. It’s the kind of game that flourishes when played with others, where the unpredictability of human reactions enhances the experience far more than any AI opponent could.

Despite its strengths, Finnish Cabin Mayhem is not without its limitations. Its content is designed for short bursts of play rather than long sessions, and players looking for a structured single-player campaign or narrative progression will find little here beyond the raw fun of combat. The mechanics, while intentionally simplistic, can feel repetitive after extended play, especially when solo. Some may also find the controls unwieldy or the physics inconsistent, though those very quirks often add to the comedic unpredictability that defines the game’s charm. Visually, it carries the look of a low-budget indie title—functional rather than refined—but the art direction’s personality more than compensates for the lack of polish. What might be seen as rough edges in other games feel here like part of the deliberate absurdity.

Technically, the game performs well on modest hardware, reflecting its indie roots and accessibility. It runs smoothly, loads quickly, and its environments, though small, are packed with interactive elements that invite experimentation. The sound design complements the gameplay perfectly—rowdy shouting, crunching impacts, and a raucous soundtrack that feels like it belongs blasting from a cabin stereo at 3 a.m. after too many beers. The developers have infused every aspect of the experience with an understanding of its own ridiculousness, turning what could have been a throwaway gimmick into something oddly memorable.

In the end, Finnish Cabin Mayhem succeeds because it knows exactly what it wants to be: a loud, unrestrained, and hilarious party game that thrives on chaos. It’s not trying to deliver a deep combat system or emotional storytelling—it’s about cracking open a beer, inviting a few friends, and letting digital insanity unfold in the most Finnish way imaginable. It stands proudly alongside cult indie titles that favor personality over polish, and its unique cultural flavor gives it an identity all its own. For players who appreciate absurd humor, unpredictable multiplayer brawls, and a healthy dose of cultural satire, Finnish Cabin Mayhem offers a chaotic, beer-soaked experience that’s as messy and unforgettable as a real night at a cabin deep in the woods.

Conflict: Desert Storm occupies a distinct place in early 2000s tactical shooters, representing a moment when developers were beginning to merge squad-based strategy with more traditional third-person action. Developed by Pivotal Games and published by Square Enix, it attempts to provide a grounded depiction of special forces operations during the Gulf War. Rather than casting players as a lone super-soldier, it hands them command of a four-man squad drawn from either the British SAS or U.S. Delta Force, emphasizing cooperation, positioning, and complementary skills. The game’s campaign follows a loosely historical structure, taking the squad across fortified cities, mine-ridden deserts, military compounds, and war-torn industrial zones, always placing them at the center of high-risk military intervention.

One of the game’s most memorable strengths lies in how it builds identity within the squad. Each soldier has a defined specialization—sniper, engineer, heavy weapons expert, medic—and the ability to switch between them at any moment gives players full tactical control. Missions often require all roles to contribute, whether planting explosives, disabling anti-air batteries, providing long-range overwatch, or patching up injured teammates under fire. As campaign progression unfolds, soldiers gain experience that improves their accuracy, stamina, or technical skills. This light RPG-style system not only rewards careful play but gives long-term investment to characters who might otherwise feel interchangeable. When a soldier goes down, the motivation to revive him isn’t just mechanical—it’s tied to the advancement you’ve earned over hours of gameplay.

Mission design was ambitious for its time, aiming for variety rather than repetition. Some operations revolve around stealth infiltrations, requiring players to move slowly, avoid detection, and quietly disable threats. Others focus on explosive assaults, tank escorts, or wide-scale battlefield engagements. Environmental elements—such as shifting winds, long sightlines, trench networks, and narrow canyon passes—shape how encounters play out. The game occasionally creates tense, cinematic moments, like storming a bridge under artillery fire or fleeing a collapsing bunker. These set pieces give the campaign a sense of momentum and evolving conflict rather than a flat series of disconnected firefights.

However, the execution doesn’t always match the ambition. The control scheme, particularly by modern standards, can feel cumbersome. Cycling between squad members, issuing movement commands, or managing inventory in the heat of combat sometimes works against the player rather than empowering them. The interface demands more attention than it should, which occasionally leads to deaths that feel unfair rather than tactical missteps. Enemy AI varies significantly—some foes behave intelligently, taking cover and coordinating attacks, while others stand exposed or detect the squad instantly regardless of stealth approach. This inconsistency can make stealth missions feel unpredictable in ways that diminish player agency.

Visually, the game reflects its era. Its sandy color palette and harsh lighting successfully evoke the dryness and desolation of Middle Eastern warzones, but environments can become repetitive, with similar rock formations and corridor-like desert paths. Textures and animations were already aging by the time of its PC release, and today they read as noticeably stiff and simplistic. That said, the atmosphere still carries weight through audio design—distant explosions, radio chatter, helicopter blades, and echoing gunfire contribute to an immersive wartime tension, even when the visuals show their age. The soundtrack complements the pacing rather than overwhelming it, maintaining a tone of militaristic urgency.

The cooperative element was a significant attraction on consoles, allowing multiple players to control different squad members locally. In this format, many of the interface frustrations fade, replaced by organic teamwork and communication. Alone, the game can feel like an ambitious tactical experiment limited by technical constraints; with others, it becomes a shared strategic puzzle where success feels collaborative and earned. Unfortunately, the PC version lacks online features that might have preserved this appeal for modern players.

Conflict: Desert Storm remains a product of a transitional design period. It gestures toward tactical realism, squad coordination, and grounded military storytelling, yet remains tethered to the era’s clunkier control philosophies and limited processing power. For players revisiting it with nostalgia—those who grew up with early military shooters—it still offers engaging mission structures, distinct personalities within the squad, and a style of accessible tactical gameplay that has largely vanished. For newcomers, expectations must be adjusted: the game’s core ideas remain compelling, but the execution shows clear signs of age.

Despite its flaws, the game deserves recognition for attempting something more thoughtful than a simple action shooter. It encouraged players to slow down, assess the battlefield, use cover, and consider squad composition. That foundation eventually led to sequels and successors that refined the formula. Today, Conflict: Desert Storm stands as a snapshot of its era—a mixture of ambition, innovation, and rough edges. With patience and an appreciation for older design sensibilities, it can still provide a satisfying campaign filled with tense firefights and strategic decision-making, especially for players seeking an early blueprint for modern squad-based shooters.

Niplheim’s Hunter – Branded Azel, developed by Black Train and published by Kagura Games, is an adult-oriented action RPG that blends traditional monster-hunting mechanics with character-driven storytelling and a light crafting system. Set in the frontier region of Niplheim, the game follows Azel, a young huntress who bears a mysterious brand inflicted by a powerful beast. Her journey becomes one of survival, revenge, and self-discovery as she navigates dangerous wildernesses, hunts monstrous creatures, and seeks to unravel the secret behind her curse. What begins as a simple tale of vengeance slowly unfolds into a story about resilience and identity, wrapped in a gameplay structure that combines exploration, combat, and collection with sensual undertones characteristic of Kagura’s catalogue.

The presentation immediately distinguishes Niplheim’s Hunter from many of its contemporaries. Its vibrant pixel art is cleanly animated, and its character illustrations—especially during story and event sequences—are polished and expressive. The side-view combat system gives the game a slightly more dynamic feel than typical top-down RPG Maker titles. Azel’s animations, enemy designs, and attack effects are smooth, and the transitions between combat and exploration feel natural and well-paced. The world of Niplheim, though small in scope, is beautifully detailed in its simplicity. From lush forests and caves to ruined villages, each area is drawn with an appealing level of color and atmosphere. The soundtrack supports this aesthetic with relaxing themes during exploration and energetic compositions during battle, grounding the game’s pacing with a sense of rhythm and tone that keeps it engaging despite its compact scale.

Gameplay revolves around a simple but satisfying loop: hunt monsters, gather resources, craft better equipment, and take on progressively stronger enemies. The game’s structure is mission-based, with quests given by the Hunter’s Guild serving as the central progression path. Combat is turn-based and fairly accessible, focusing more on strategy and preparation than on difficulty or grind. Azel’s progression depends on materials harvested from slain monsters, which can be used to forge weapons, armor, and accessories. Crafting plays an important role not only in upgrading her abilities but also in customizing her appearance through unlockable outfits and gear. The game’s resource management system, while not deep, adds a sense of continuity and reward for players who enjoy collecting and building. This gameplay loop encourages exploration without overwhelming the player with systems, keeping things focused and rewarding within its limited but well-defined parameters.

Azel herself is the heart of the experience. She’s a capable and confident protagonist whose journey is as much about reclaiming her strength as it is about survival. The brand she carries symbolizes both physical power and personal struggle, and her interactions with the supporting cast reveal a blend of humor, determination, and vulnerability that makes her compelling. The writing, while not elaborate, manages to give the world a sense of personality. The townsfolk, guild members, and even minor NPCs contribute flavor and charm, adding levity to the darker themes. Dialogue is localized with care, capturing both the emotional tone and the lighthearted moments without losing nuance or awkward phrasing. Kagura Games’ translation is notably smooth compared to earlier adult localizations, and it helps the game feel more professional and immersive.

The adult elements, while central to the game’s identity, are integrated in a way that complements rather than overpowers the experience. The erotic scenes are tied to story progression and character development rather than being tacked on as random fanservice. These moments explore Azel’s emotional and physical transformation while maintaining the tone established by the narrative. The artwork during these scenes is highly detailed and well-illustrated, a signature strength of Black Train’s design team. The mature themes do, however, limit the game’s audience—those uninterested in adult content may find the focus distracting, while fans of the genre will appreciate the balance between gameplay and sensual storytelling.

Where Niplheim’s Hunter begins to show its limits is in its simplicity. While the combat and crafting systems are functional, they lack complexity and can feel repetitive after extended play. The game’s short length—averaging around six to eight hours for full completion—means it ends before its systems can evolve into something deeper. The limited variety of monsters and quests contributes to a sense of repetition, particularly in the later stages. However, this brevity also works in its favor for players seeking a focused, self-contained experience without excessive grinding. Its accessibility and pacing make it easy to pick up and complete without the time investment typical of larger RPGs.

Despite these constraints, the game’s charm and craftsmanship shine through. It demonstrates a thoughtful balance between style and substance, ensuring that every part of its design serves its atmosphere. The combination of sleek visuals, satisfying progression, and mature storytelling creates an experience that feels polished and cohesive. While it may not reach the complexity of full-scale RPGs or the narrative depth of story-driven visual novels, it succeeds at delivering exactly what it intends: an intimate, well-crafted, and aesthetically pleasing adventure that respects the player’s time and attention.

Niplheim’s Hunter – Branded Azel is ultimately a compact yet satisfying RPG experience built around strong art direction, engaging presentation, and a simple but addictive gameplay loop. It captures the spirit of monster-hunting adventure with an adult twist, providing both entertainment and atmosphere in a concise package. For fans of Kagura’s catalog or those seeking a short, polished RPG with beautiful art and accessible mechanics, it delivers on its promises. It is not a sprawling epic, but a focused, well-realized story that blends sensuality and strength, and it succeeds in offering a distinct identity within the crowded field of indie RPGs.

Faire une review de Soul Hackers 2 est quelque chose de très important pour moi... Bon, peut-être que j'abuse un peu, certes, mais ce jeu mérite justice.

J'ai pu lire pas mal d'avis sur ce titre un peu partout sur la toile, notamment sur Steam, et je suis confus.

Je trouve que les gens ont été extrêmement sévères avec ce Soul Hackers 2. À en lire certains, on aurait presque pu croire que c'est une bouse monumentale, alors que pas du tout.

Mais avant de donner mon avis, je vais d'abord poser les bases.

Tout d'abord, Soul Hackers 2 a été développé par Atlus, à qui l'on doit notamment les Shin Megami Tensei, qui est leur série principale.

Et au vu de leurs succès, les SMT ont eu droit à de nombreux spin-off, dont les célèbres Persona que l'on ne présente plus, mais également les Devil Summoner. Et le quatrième opus des Devil Summoner est justement Soul Hackers, originellement sorti sur Saturn en 1997.

Et donc en 2022, soit 25 ans plus tard, sort enfin Soul Hackers 2 avec de nouveaux personnages et de nouveaux enjeux, mais toujours dans le même univers !

Voilà pour l'introduction. C'est bon ? Vous arrivez à suivre ? Passons maintenant au vif du sujet.

L'histoire se déroule dans un Tokyo futuriste où la technologie et le surnaturel coexistent, car parmi toute la population, de rares humains possèdent la capacité d'invoquer des démons afin d'y faire le bien ou le mal selon le "camp" qu'ils ont choisis.

Et en plus de cette société se trouve également Aion, une conscience informatique cachée dans un complexe qui a commencé à naître à partir des données que les humains génèrent sur les réseaux numériques.

Aion possédant donc des milliards d'informations et de données en temps réel sur l'humanité, elle va finir par prédire un enchaînement d'événements venant de certains invocateurs de démons qui finira par déclencher la fin du monde.

Et donc, afin d'éviter cette catastrophe, Aion va créer et envoyer deux IA, Ringo et Figue, qui vont prendre forme humaine et partir en mission dans la société afin d'empêcher la fin du monde de se produire.

Les personnages sont excellents et bien écrits, surtout l'héroïne que l'on incarne, Ringo. Les conversations sont beaucoup plus profondes et touchantes qu'un Persona, ce qui m'a surpris. Il y a beaucoup de réflexion sur le monde et sur soi-même à travers les dialogues, et ce d'une manière subtile. J'ai vraiment été conquis, même si pour être honnête, je n'ai pas du tout aimé le début du jeu.

En effet, la présentation de l'intrigue est très bâclée et la manière dont les personnages principaux sont introduits accentue ce sentiment de médiocrité que j'ai pu ressentir à l'introduction. Donc oui, les premières heures ne sont pas terribles et j'ai failli croire que ce jeu était bel et bien une bouse.

Sauf qu'après que l'univers et les personnages sont en place, la magie opère et l'âme qui se dégage du jeu se dévoile enfin. Ce jeu a une atmosphère propre à lui-même et j'ai fini par beaucoup accrocher malgré mes réticences au début. De plus, la bande-son est excellente !

Soul Hackers 2 est un JRPG classique, on est vraiment sur une formule simple qui se concentre sur l'essentiel, et c'est franchement agréable. 

Il est donc important de préciser pour ceux et celles qui s'attendent à quelque chose du même niveau qu'un Persona, que vous serez sûrement déçus. Soul Hackers 2 n'est pas ambitieux et n'invente rien, mais est très plaisant quand même. Mettez-vous cela en tête avant de potentiellement tenter l'expérience.

Pour ce qui est des combats, on est sur du tour par tour classique, avec un système de combo qui s'accumule en touchant les faiblesses des ennemis afin de déclencher une attaque ultime à chaque tour. C'est une excellente idée qu'il n'y a pas dans les Persona et qui apporte ce petit plus au jeu.

Tout ça, c'était pour les points positifs, passons maintenant au négatif :

- Les donjons : J'ai vu beaucoup de gens dire que les donjons étaient répétitifs et je suis assez d'accord mais il y a une nuance. Ce n'est pas leur architecture et leur direction artistique qui sont répétitives, mais plutôt le principe même des explorations avec notamment l'apparition des ennemis qui est toujours aléatoire. Mais malgré cela, j'ai vraiment pris du plaisir à les explorer, contrairement à ceux de Persona 3 où pour le coup je me suis beaucoup plus ennuyé.

- Le DLC : Il ne vaut clairement pas son prix. Alors oui, l'histoire est sympathique et le personnage supplémentaire est réussi, mais ça se résume à des requêtes disséminées dans tout le jeu et à un donjon bonus qui lui est vraiment mauvais. Ce ne sont que des enchaînements d'étages qui se ressemblent et qu'il faut faire à la chaîne. Donc je ne le recommande pas, à moins qu'il soit en promotion, à la limite.

- Le manque de budget : Même si le jeu reste agréable, il y a vraiment un côté cheap que l'on ressent durant toute l'aventure, que cela soit à travers la mise en scène ou les animations des personnages et ça donne au jeu un côté brouillon dont on aurait pu se passer. Même techniquement c'est compliqué, le jeu tourne très bien et consomme peu de ressources mais il y a énormément d'aliasing, ce qui fait que les personnages sont pixelisés quand ils sont trop éloignés de la caméra.

Tout ça pour dire que même si le jeu n'a pas eu droit à d'autant d'amour, de budget et de temps qu'un Persona de la part d'Atlus, cela reste tout de même une expérience à part entière, que je recommande malgré ses défauts.

Ma note : 7/10. Et oui, c'est aussi la note que j'ai donné à Persona 3 Reload, j'en suis moi-même étonné. 

Mais encore une fois, j'ai été conquis par l'univers et les personnages et je ne me suis pas ennuyé une seule fois dans les donjons, donc pour moi Soul Hackers 2 mérite amplement sa note, même si les Persona resteront toujours la référence.

C'est tout pour moi, merci de m'avoir lu et je vous souhaite de bons hacks !

[h1]👨‍⚖️ Verdict? Guilty of counter-revolution propaganda! 👨‍⚖️[/h1]
"We. The Revolution" tries to sell itself as a tense moral and political drama set during the French Revolution, but it never decides what it actually is. The result is a confused mix of pseudo-historical grimdark, opaque mechanics, arbitrary punishments, and a moral message so heavy-handed it could have been delivered with a guillotine blade.

The game never explains clearly its systems. The tutorial is a sequence of tooltips that dumps vocabulary on you without showing how anything fits together. The core mechanic – linking elements of a case file to abstract judicial categories to unlock questions – is often unclear, and persuasion scenes are even worse. You don’t learn the system, you simply poke at it until the machine accepts something.

I pushed through the initial fog because I genuinely care about justice and family in narrative games. That was a mistake. The moment you invest emotionally, the game punishes you. Trials force you to condemn or acquit people based on faction preference ; the story unrealistically kills characters for narrative convenience; and the family arc is quickly weaponized against you. What remains is not a judicial drama, but a faction-meter simulator where emotional involvement guarantees failure.

None of this would matter as much if the historical setting were remotely coherent, but it isn’t. The game treats the entire French Revolution as a chaotic street circus where judges are assassinated every other night, random citizens get the death penalty for petty disputes, and factions stalk you like jealous exes. In reality, judges of the Revolutionary Tribunal were high-ranking state officials, not pizza couriers wandering through a Bronx cosplay of 1793. The game conflates decades of history, distorts the period’s political logic, and uses the Revolution only as a backdrop for a modern “violence is always bad” fable. That moral could be interesting if the world were consistent. Here, it’s just preachy and disconnected.

My suspension of disbelief didn’t survive Act I. If any fragment had somehow made it to Act III, the late meta twists and Game-of-Thrones-style antagonist would have shred it to pieces instantly.

If you enjoy juggling faction meters and don’t mind that your decisions barely matter except as fuel for the next punishment, maybe this will work for you. If you hoped for a political, historical, or even structurally coherent experience, prepare to be disappointed.

[h1]💖 Pros 💖[/h1]
-    Attractive art style
-    The atmosphere (before everything collapse on itself)
-    The idea of judging trials in revolutionary France was really promising

[h1]💀 Cons 💀[/h1]
-    Historically incoherent from top to bottom
-    Opaque core mechanics with poor explanations
-    Emotional involvement is punished instead of rewarded
-    Faction system dominates everything and feels artificial
-    Family arc is used as a blunt instrument, not a narrative thread
-    Late-game twists that bring the circus to another level
-    Decisions often feel meaningless beyond shifting meters

メトロイドヴァニア要素とドット絵に惹かれてプレイしたが、挑戦的なシステムが残念ながら肌に合わず、プレイを断念。
Steam Deck でプレイ。（Proton にしないとプレイできなかったので注意！）

良かった点

・ドット絵。キャラクターの細かい動きやステージの背景など、非常に凝っていて最高。

・パズル要素。意外な能力の使い方が必要になったり、強引に突破したりと、ステージギミックは面白い。

・ボス戦。まともな攻撃手段があまりないゲームなので、ボス戦は工夫を凝らして倒すことになる。かなり手強いが、リトライはしやすい配置になっていて良かった。

残念だった点

・キャラクター切り替え。珍しいタイプのシステムなので最初は楽しくプレイできていたのだが、キャラクター数が増えてくるとキャラ切り替え操作が煩雑になり、障害を乗り越えるためにいちいち対象キャラへと切り替えるのがすぐに面倒に感じるようになる。メトロイドヴァニアの表現（能力を獲得して行動範囲が広がる）という点ではシンプルに相性が悪いように思える。

・同じステージを何度も周回が必須。多少アイテムやキャラの配置が変わっても、ステージの構造自体は変わらず、さすがに2〜3周で飽きてくる。アイテム持ち越しがあるとはいえ、一回解いたギミックを何度もやらされたり、探索状況がリセットされてマップ開放しなおしが必要だったり、キャラ加入をし直さないといけなかったり、とにかく同じ事の繰り返しが求められる。探索すればするほど、リセットで巻き戻るのが非常にストレス。

・目標設定。時間制限内に目標金額を集める、という目標設定は、目標金額を集め終わると意味のないものになってしまう。通常のメトロイドヴァニアなら、苦労してボスに勝利したら探索範囲が広がるアイテムや能力をGET、というのが定番の流れだが、このゲームではアイテムや能力（キャラ加入）は通常の探索によって見つかるもので、ボス戦はまとまった金がもらえるだけ（だからボス戦はしなくてもよい！）。しかも、その金をいくら集めても次の周回ではリセットされてしまう…　達成感がスポイルされまくっている。大目標も周回しまくってストーリーを進めるだけなので、なんのためにプレイしてるんだっけ、という気分になってくる。

総評

メトロイドヴァニアとしては、かなり挑戦的なシステムを導入している。
最初の数周は楽しめるが、最後までのプレイは自分には無理だった。
周回プレイやスピードランが好きな人には良いかも。

Ще з моменту анонсу я вважав що після Call of Duty WWII тематика театра Другої Світової Війни розквітне новими фарбами, особливо коли на анонсі гри було зрозуміло що на відмінну від тієї ж WWII де був лише один протагоніст, то в Vanguard їх декілька, і це мені нагадало часи перших двух частин де ми грали за американця, британця та радянського бійця, плюсом того що покажуть різні місця битв, Європа, Африка, Тихоокеанський театр та ін., але нажаль бачивши що як попередні частини в плані сюжету були такими собі, то я не чекав в цій частині чогось неймовірного, а лише чекав гру заради зомбі режиму та частково мультиплеєру. 

І так воно й сталося, скільки пропусків, анахронізмів, та іншого я не бачив мабуть ще з часів Black Ops I, історія головних героїв не до кінця зрозуміла, їхнє минуле та то як ці люди різної національності та характеру зустрілися та стали загоном який й зветься як сама гра, не кажучи вже за те що кожного протагоніста є здібності. 

Зброя часів Другої Світової пророблена непогано але те що деяка з’являється в часі коли її ще не існувало та ще з різними модулями це дуже дивно, я розумію що хотіли зробити різноманітність, але не так.

Геймплей та механіка залишилася на тому самому рівні що в ребуті Modern Warfare 19-го року, бої виглядають більше менш не такими аркадними які ми бачили в Black Ops II, але щодо ШІ союзників та ворогів є питання, перші куди стріляють а другі дуже чуткі стрільці що можуть миттєво вбити, рівні хоч й мають невеликі вузькі проходи але все рівно вони короткі, збір боєприпасів змінився тільки в тому що треба натиснути певну клавішу щоб поповнити запас, система зайняття укриття під час прицілювання непогана, але в сюжеті безнадійне а стрілянина на осліп це щось в дусі Far Cry. 

За мультиплеєр нічого сказати, все те саме що в ребуті Modern Warfare 19-го року, хіба що тіки атмосфера Другої Світової Війни а так все те саме, починаючи з підбору зброї, перків, спорядження, та серії вбиств/смертей.

Зомбі режим який мені подобається більше ніж сам сюжет та мультиплеєр, непоганий але виявився на слабшим що нехай краще я ще раз побігаю в цей режим у Black Ops Cold War або в Black Ops III де кастомні мапи можна завантажити через Workshop, сюжета як такого майже нема, пасхалки пророблені неідеально.

Тому з вище описаного мною я дійшов висновку що Sledgehammer Games перевищили свої можливості, та в них була чудова можливість зробити цю частину дійсно неймовірною, але вийшло не те щоб погано а більш всього недоробленою. Ну хоча б саундтрек до гри проробили непоганий завдяки композитору який поставив музику до гри God of War. Як графіка та саундтрек чудово вийшли, як геймплей без змін, як сценарій незрозумілий.

It's a neat premise, and I do like it for the fact that it helped me learn JS a bit, which is a language I haven't messed with (though I know many others). 

However, the gameplay leaves a lot to be desired.  Maybe it's just not my style, but I don't think that's it. 
 I play idle games, and enjoy them usually.  And this is essentially an idle game, since you're using code to control your character automatically.  But I don't like this game's progression for a few reasons.  

1.  Way too grindy from the getgo.  I don't have the kind of weeks this game would require.  Your character will be extremely weak for a very long time until you manage to get lucky enough to get the right items.  You can't buy anything but the weakest items in this game, so everything has to be found, which isn't bad on its own, except that all the players are camping the same mobs, which means high-level players are in the newbie areas constantly spamming all the monsters to death from a huge range and with 5 simultaneous targets, while you're limited to walking extremely slowly and attacking them one at a time, meaning you don't get ANY.  
2.  No real progression.  There are no skills in the traditional sense, you don't level up any abilities and you don't learn any new abilities.  There's no skill tree, and no stat points to distribute.  You also can't power up your character at all with leveling, as leveling seems to do absolutely nothing except extend your HP and MP pools.  Your stat changes seem to make no difference at all in combat.  It never took me less hits to kill a monster between level 1 and advancing to level 40.  So the only way to increase your strength is to upgrade your items, and this is done at the forge, randomly.  Failing means you lose the item entirely (always a horrible mechanic in games where every item has to be obtained as a drop).  I would never risk upgrading any item other than the base ones as a result.  It would just be a huge waste after the many hours it would take to get one of these extremely rare drops.
3.  Monsters level up if left alone for a while, meaning even weak monsters become extremely strong and take forever to kill.  I think this mechanic is supposed to increase your item luck, but it doesn't seem to.  You do, at least, get more XP.
4.  There's an achievements system that's locked behind quests that will be impossible in your first few weeks, and this achievement system is the main source of stat upgrades (not leveling up). The mobs chosen to give you the item that unlocks this system are always the strongest on the server, which means you will never kill them as anything but a veteran.  Stuuu-pid.
5.  I kind of assumed there would be some kind of story or something but there doesn't seem to be.  Just kill mobs, level up, get items.  Which isn't necessarily bad, but since I can't seem to advance at all...it's just boring.  

Maybe I'll leave it running for a few weeks so I can move into the 2nd area though. I don't know; I'm not really into it.

However, I will leave a few tips behind for those who do pick up this game.

First thing you should do is make your own version of the use_hp_or_mp function that comments out or deletes the last two "else ifs," otherwise your character will use a potion anytime they lose a single point in either stat.  Huge waste.  Then replace the "use_hp_or_mp" line with your new function.

Second thing to do is remove the "|| character.isMoving" or whatever it says in the conditions for the if that cancels the loop.  You don't want the character to stop processing targeting just because they are moving.  By removing this, your character will be able to retarget while still moving before they've reached their destination if the target is no longer available.

Anyway, hopefully the game will get better.

I'm somewhat obsessed with all the Spiderweb Software game series, and of late, Queen's Wish has been on the top of my list of their games. 

There's everything here I've been looking for in a good RPG for years now. It has excellent writing and a compelling story with amazing world building, which is my personal biggest driver (and is true for all of their other franchises), and the game loop is just right. Tactical combat is turn based and fast paced with reasonable depth and no extraneous elements. Exploration is satisfying and the world is large and feels very lived in (and the fast travel option becomes more and more useful as the game progresses). There is a lot of content, yet none of it feels like it's there just as filler (there is some repetition in mine-cleansing quests, but it's not too problematic).

What I also like is that character progression and equipment procurement is meaningful. Each level brings much needed ability increases, and 1 added level might make a difference between a quest being possible to complete or not just yet. Equipment is rare and relatively expensive, so there's no meaningless looting here - every find is useful.

Base and kingdom building adds one more layer, and is well integrated with the questing and exploration aspects of the game. There's an interdependence between personal quests and the state of your colonies that feels natural and adds to the overall experience in a way which makes it larger than the sum of its parts. Evolving familial and personal connections are a cherry on top.

There's also an elephant in the room with these games. For what it is, I find the graphics quite compelling though. Queen's Wish doesn't try to be flashy (on the contrary, it embraces its scrappiness), but I find the graphics appealing nevertheless, and they are very readable and quite varied. No sprite or character portrait here will win an art contest, but there's many little details scattered throughout the world, and each tells a story, which to me is, again, the most important thing in a game like this.

Finally, I'll add that I'm playing this mostly on the Steam Deck, and it's great! Almost all game text is presented in dialog boxes that take a relatively small central portion of the screen, which works great with Steam Deck's ability to toggle zoom in and out on a mappable key press. I set the display zoom to 220% is settings which allows me to instantly zoom into the text portion for dialogs and for reading tool tips on the small screen. I mapped the left trackpad to an on-screen menu with numbers 1 through 6 which I also positioned centrally, so it appears overlayed on top of text popups for choosing dialog options. Loaded up with all Spiderweb games, my Steam Deck is almost like a specialized ebook reader for choose-your-own-adventure books filled with tight tactical combat. I love it!

To me, these games are like cozy adventure books with surprisingly compelling, deep and multifaceted stories, and Queen's Wish is unique among them.
