Но все же мне как обывателю представляется, что галактика и есть скопищем относительно похожих друг на друга кусков камня и газовых гигантов, и на этом фоне разнообразие ивентов можно считать, хм, типа как реалистичным. К тому же, временами вы будете находить и разные формы жизни, и заброшенные космические корабли древних, и даже живые цивилизации. Все же интересно, что там под очередным скучно описанным камушком; иногда встречаются неожиданности.

Члены экипажа прокачиваются, что дает улучшение к вероятности успеха в ивентах. Корабль апгрейдится, но не совсем очевидно - апгрейды надо добывать как раз "броском кубиков" в ивентах. В целом игра кажется довольно короткой и не такой уж сложной, когда поймешь, что именно надо делать. Небольшой проект для тех, кто обладает хорошей фантазией и интересом к исследованиям. Из чего-то схожего можно рекомендовать Colony Prospector (менее научная и более странная).

Pixel Ripped 1978: An Atari Adventure, developed by ARVORE and published by Atari, is a nostalgic, time-bending VR journey that blends classic game design with modern immersive storytelling. It stands as the third major entry in the Pixel Ripped series, but its partnership with Atari gives this installment a distinctly celebratory tone—one steeped in the culture, creativity, and quirky energy of early video game development. From the opening scene, the game positions you inside the shoes of Bug, a passionate Atari programmer who is developing a world inhabited by the series’ long-running heroine, Dot. This dual perspective immediately gives the experience a unique charm: you are both creator and hero, both in the real world and inside the game world that your character is building. It’s a delightful framing device that lets the game explore nostalgia without becoming stale or overly derivative.

Much of the appeal lies in the interplay between Bug’s office environment and Dot’s in-game adventures. In VR, you sit at Bug’s cluttered 1970s-style workstation—complete with chunky CRT displays, piles of cartridges, and Atari paraphernalia that lovingly re-create the era’s aesthetics. The nostalgic details are precise enough to feel lived-in rather than merely decorative. As you debug code or test new levels, you slip into Dot’s 2D platforming worlds, which unfold as colorful, retro-inspired stages that pay tribute to Atari classics without reproducing them wholesale. These segments shift between pixel-platforming and more three-dimensional VR interactions, creating a layered experience where your actions in one world meaningfully resonate in the other. This back-and-forth structure keeps the pacing lively and gives the game a tangible sense of evolution.

When playing as Dot, the game delights in merging retro influences with modern VR freedom. The platforming sequences echo classics of the era with simple jumps, enemy patterns, and collectible items, but often explode into creative 3D moments where the VR perspective lets you interact with the world in surprising ways—shooting enemies from a distance, manipulating objects directly, or helping Dot overcome obstacles from outside the platform. ARVORE’s playful approach ensures that each new stage brings a twist. The game makes the most of VR’s immersive strengths, especially in humor and visual spectacle, even if some segments feel mechanically looser than others. Combat, for instance, can be enjoyable in concept but occasionally lacks the crisp responsiveness found in more refined VR action titles.

The aesthetic presentation is one of the game’s biggest triumphs. Pixel Ripped 1978 succeeds not only because it references retro visuals, but because it celebrates them with sincerity. The recreated Atari office is full of character, and its blend of browns, oranges, and neon highlights instantly evokes the late ’70s without turning into caricature. Dot’s worlds, meanwhile, are vibrant mosaics of pixel art and neon vectors, mixing eras of game design into something vibrant rather than merely nostalgic. The soundtrack reinforces this duality, alternating between chiptune pulses and airy VR ambience, constantly reminding you that you are straddling two realities at once. It is an audiovisual homage that feels assembled by developers who genuinely love the era they are celebrating.

Despite its creative strengths, the game is not without shortcomings. The VR segments—especially those involving first-person combat or movement—are sometimes less polished, featuring moments of awkward tracking or imprecise interaction. The difficulty curve is fairly light, and experienced players may find the overall challenge modest. The campaign is also on the shorter side, typically lasting only a few hours, which makes the experience feel more like a compact, curated adventure than a sprawling journey. While the Atari branding is present and charming, some players may feel the licensed IP integration could have been pushed further, incorporating more iconic references or deeper mechanical riffs on the company’s classic catalog.

Still, what Pixel Ripped 1978 delivers is something genuinely memorable: a playful VR adventure that blends humor, nostalgia, and inventive design without relying solely on retro novelty. ARVORE’s affection for gaming history is evident in every corner of the experience, and Atari’s involvement gives it a sense of authenticity that enriches the world rather than overshadowing it. For fans of VR, retro games, or meta-narratives about game development, this title offers a warm, spirited journey through the early days of the medium. Although its short length and occasional rough edges keep it from achieving perfection, Pixel Ripped 1978 succeeds as a heartfelt tribute to an era of creativity and experimentation—and as an experience that bridges gaming’s past with its technologically ambitious present.

I had hopes for this one, as even if it isn't quite there, it felt like it had a vision of a Battle Network spinoff.  ...But, I think it has kind of missed the 'point' of an idle game.  The amount of mechanically impactful goals feels like it dries out quickly, and the autobattling nature limits how exciting trying to strategize your arsenal can be. Any semblance of greater story or worldbuilding to discover (which could've been a cool alternative), is so brief as to be weightless and basically relies on familiarity with what it's aping.

To boot, there's just a ton of playability stuff that feels off, in ways that were off months ago in demos and leave me wondering how they stayed a problem.  The desktop companion style design is a neat idea, but suffers from a ton of things (like the scaling either meaning things are too small, too big for a constant overlay, or stretched in ugly ways).  Navigating menus is an active pain, often giving way too little information (eg missions not informing you where they're taking place), and having your attacks come from little wandering monsters is a cute idea until you need to actually manage them to try out new abilities, nevermind the incredibly messy chip encyclopedia and an inventory with only manual sorting that quickly becomes a nightmare.  Display settings have to be reconfigured each time I start it up.  There's bugs with terrain display desynchronizing in navigation, or the chip load system half breaking, all just the sort of thing that make me wonder how they made it past the months and months thsi game has spent in development.

I want to love it.  I'll keep an eye on it and keep giving it a chance, and maybe someday this will become a thumbs up.  Idle games don't really demand much to keep up with, after all.  But man, for all the love I can tell was put into parts of this project (like the music and art), and for how long I followed it, a lot of it just leaves me thuroughly like "oh, that's it?"

Fairy Bloom Freesia is a 2D action brawler developed by Edelweiss, best known for its fast, combo-driven gameplay and anime-inspired visuals. It combines arena combat with light RPG elements, offering a short but intense experience focused on mechanical skill and progression.

Gameplay centers on controlling Freesia, a forest fairy defending her home from waves of invading creatures. Combat takes place in small arenas where movement, timing, and juggling enemies are key. The system rewards chaining attacks, air combos, and knockbacks, giving it a rhythm similar to fighting games.

Between battles, players earn experience and mana crystals to unlock and upgrade new abilities. The skill tree allows customization of playstyle—offensive magic, defensive counters, or crowd-control options. While progression is straightforward, experimenting with move combinations adds replay value.

Visually, the game uses clean, vibrant 2D sprites and smooth animation. Attacks are flashy but readable, and the backgrounds, though simple, match the tone of a small-scale fantasy story. The effects and camera shake during combat emphasize speed and impact effectively.

The soundtrack, composed by Masaru Yokoyama, complements the action with energetic, melodic tracks. Audio cues are clear and responsive, making combat feedback immediate. The overall sound design keeps momentum without overwhelming the player.

Performance is excellent on all systems due to its lightweight engine. Controls are responsive whether using keyboard or controller, and input timing feels precise. The limited screen size and small arenas make it ideal for short, focused sessions rather than extended play.

Overall, Fairy Bloom Freesia delivers polished, arcade-style combat in a compact package. It’s fast, satisfying, and mechanically tight, offering a surprising amount of depth for its scale. For players who enjoy combo-based action games like Devil May Cry or Melty Blood in a 2D format, it’s a concise and rewarding experience.

Sooo... At first, I was rather sceptical about whole game. The story of a girl who moved from small town to a bigger one, looking for her place in life was a bit of cliche... until we start to get some more info along with some cutscenes and story progression. Already telling you - it's not a kind of game that will tell you most of its story in less than 30 minutes, if you don't feel it or like it. Of course, the progression is highly dependant of how well we play some parts. But as much as I delved into the story - I've found it quite therapeutical for myself, in a way.

Concept of fighting and gathering 'awake-world' resources while dreaming - nothing new, but gives a lot of place and opportunity for interesting solutions. Also, mechanics are rather forgiving for newcomers to roguelikes, adding fast-travel between already discovered rooms (including boss room), pickups don't disappear after leaving the room, etc. Makes you want to speedrun this game or at least try to get your own best strat to do stuff as you want.

As for graphics, characters are simple in design, but that is not the 'meat' of this part - the devil is in the details around. Detailed surroundings, especially in further stages of runs, give out how much can be taken from 'dream-fighting' concept. Many of weapons used by protagonist have interesting animations, similarily the enemies designs are something that we can't get bored with, even if mindlessly tearing through them during another run on higher difficulty. Not to mention how awesome is the design of bosses, along with their cutscenes. Especially the latter is worth to look at, instead of skipping every time.

In my opinion, soundtrack is a must-have in collection. Beautiful, soft, orchestral sounds, emphasizing emotions that might 'spill out' from our protagonist accidentaly - a bit of melancholy on early stages, slowly turning into a fight for survival in her own nightmares and symbolic depictions of her past experiences. Even if the tracks are looped for each stage, they are long enough and constructed in a way that doesn't annoy or make you bored.

All in all, Dreamscaper has this special little place in my heart, as I like to come back to this game and play again. And again. And again. And... well, you know the drill. I've enjoyed the story, despite how slowly it might unwind at first. Came in sceptical, but stayed because I've found some reflections of things in myself while playing and fighting through nightmares. Fell in love with music, enjoy the art after getting comfortable with the concept and, well... it's a kind of game that will be enjoyed by more 'artsy-fartsy' people. Including me in this bunch.

Когда мурда исчезает, мы впервые слышим пустоту. И пустота звучит громче, чем мурда мурда. Ты можешь мурдить вечно, но мурда тоже умирает, даже петухи это знают, а ты все еще сомневаешься. Смех превращается в жвачку, жвачка превращается в привычку, привычка превращает тебя в свинью. А интернет всегда подскажет: "Жди следующего брата". Но он не придет. И мурда не появится. Это не брат. Это не мурда. Это знак, что мурда закончилась. Что ждать больше нечего. Мурда была мурдой - мы ее мурдили и смеялись. Но мурду можно не только мурдить, мурду можно замурдовать, и тогда получится не мурда, а МУРДА, а МУРДОЙ можно осчастливить уже не просто человека, а даже целого ЧЕЛОВЕКА. Это только начало.

Despite recommending this game, I feel it's only fair to point out this game's negatives, as I do have some complaints. I'm not exactly sure why I feel the need to list my complaints like this but I do and so I will.

1: The controls are clunky. In the early game you won't notice this too much, but later on it becomes very hard to tell if you'll make a jump because depth gauging is hard and because the hit marker for the frogun will sometimes just lie to you. It will turn red, meaning you can fire and it will grab the enemy or latch onto the wall, but it seems to do this when you are slightly too high for it to hit or when you aren't at a good angle. It didn't have me losing my mind but it was definitely frustrating at times.

2: There are a lot of invisible walls. There were times I totally could've lowered my time for a level for the time trial if the game didn't kill you at that point. It is very frustrating and this seems to be random. And if I was wrong about that gap being doable, let me find out for myself.

3: Enemies often behaved strangely. Sometimes they'd walk in a cycle, obeying the laws of physics, other times they'd teleport back to their starting position. This often varied on the exact same enemy. This can be annoying if say, you are trying to make a jump and an enemy teleports in your path, making you grab them instead of the wall, making you fall to your death, They also spawned weirdly sometimes. They'd like, have to walk to their actual starting position from somewhere else when you spawned in.

4: If you are a completionist, you will have to grind for coins for at least a couple hours at the end of the game. Even after you have 100%ed every level.

Even with those problems though the game is great fun! The music is nice, the retro-stylization is fun, and while clunky, the gameplay feels rewarding. There's plenty of variety in the levels and bosses as well! I'm excited to play the sequel.

Игра меня привлекла своими яркими и красочными 2d модельками. Но увы, разочаровала своей бессмысленностью, однообразием и скукой. 

Итак, чем же нас может развлечь ангельская пыль? В основном, двумя вещами - истреблением врагов и строительством. 

Врагов в игре видов 10, но каждый вид имеет большое количество реколоров. Половина врагов новорит чем-то плюнуть, чаще всего кислотой. В начале может показаться, что дальше ждёт огромный мир с кучей разнообразных существ, но по итогу те же самые (но другого цвета) обезьяны, скорпионы, лошади и волки заебут весьма скоро. Боевая система не очень хороша: персонаж медленный, двигается будто бы в желе. Не знаю, как у других классов, но у лучницы есть только один навык - ловушка с паутиной, все (ну и закликивание). Еще такой неприятный момент в бою: враги очень жирные, иногда их нужно бить чуть ли не минуту реального времени. Сомнительное удовольствие. А, главное, ради чего? Ради несчастных 20-40 монет? 

Строительство просто не имеет смысла. База не нужна. Ну построите вы красивый дом/замок/конуру, а зачем? Просто чтоб было. 

В игре даже нет квестов, хотя бы минимальных, вроде убей 10 крыс или принеси 5 грибов... 

Чтобы получить предмет для приручения животных - нужно на стриме разраба выиграть в розыгрыше. Замечательно просто (нет). 

Не рекомендую даже по скидке, 1/10 (1 балл только за 2d модели).

Oyun Minecraft, Portal Knights, Creativerse oyunlarında olduğu gibi tamamen deforme edilebilir bir dünya üzerine inşa edilmiş ve bu oyunların bir MMO versiyonu gibidir. Oyunda her yeri kazabiliyor veya doldurabiliyorsunuz, tamamen ortama şekil verebiliyorsunuz. Dokusu Minecraft gibi kübik yapıda değil, daha yuvarlatılmış köşeli olmayan parçalardan oluşuyor. Grafikler çizgi film tadında, oldukça renkli ve sevimli. Yaratık çeşitliliği de epey fazla. İçinde birbirinden farklı biyomlar var ve bu biyomlardaki tüm yaratıklar, bitki örtüsü, yapılar, doğal zenginlikler o biyoma özel olarak oluşturulmuş. Kar biyomunda kutup ayıları geliyorken, çöl biyomunda akrep ve yılan, bataklık biyomunda timsah geliyor. Oyunda büyücü, şövalye, okcu gibi farklı tipte karekter seçebiliyorsunuz. Her karekterin kendine ait yetenekleri ve silahları oluyor. Oyunda ev kurabiliyor ve içini istediğiniz gibi restore edebiliyorsunuz. At, ayı, ejderha gibi hayvanlara binebiliyorsunuz. Öldürdüğünüz yaratıklardan paralar ve deneyim puanları geliyor. Bu puanlarla level atlıyorsunuz. Paralarla da oyun içinden item alabiliyorsunuz. Etraftaki sandıklardan itemler elde edebiliyorsunuz. Oyunda pvp alanları var. Buralar arena olarak geçiyor ve herkes burada kapışıyor. Belirli zamanlarda random questler oluyor. Buralara giden oyuncular görevi yapmaya çalışıyorlar. Oyun içinde her yerde evler, kaleler, şatolar, tarlalar var. Herkes bir yere kurulmuş ve yayılmış, kendi alanını belirlemiş. Sonra da oyunu terketmiş. Oyun ölü bir şehir gibi. Boş yapılarla dolu. Koskoca evrende 4-5 oyuncu var. Onlara rastlamak zor. Oyunda single yapılabilecek bir quest sistemi yok, herşey oyuncu katılımına bağlı. Bu tarz oyunların evrenleri oyuncu kitlesinin kalabalık olacağı hesap edilerek geniş hazırlanıyor. Oyuncu az olunca da bu geniş oyun alanında kendinizi yalnız hissediyorsunuz. Oyuna içerik eklenmesi, hikaye eklenmesi, oyuncuyu kendine bağlayacak dinamikler konulması gerekirdi. Ama bunlar yok. Çok güzel düşünülmüş ama devamı getirilememiş bir oyun. Geleceği çok parlak iken ölü doğmuş bir bebek.... Tavsiye etmiyorum. Bu tarz oyunları sevenlere şiddetle Portal Knights öneririm.

ARCADE GAME SERIES: Ms. PAC-MAN, developed by BANDAI NAMCO Studios Inc. and published by BANDAI NAMCO Entertainment, is a faithful preservation of one of the most iconic arcade experiences of all time. Originally released in 1981 as an unofficial but soon fully embraced sequel to the legendary Pac-Man, Ms. PAC-MAN took everything that made the original great and refined it into a tighter, more dynamic, and ultimately more engaging formula. The Steam version retains the same gameplay that has captivated players for more than four decades, offering a pure and undiluted slice of arcade history. With its simple yet endlessly compelling design, it continues to prove that good gameplay needs neither elaborate graphics nor complex mechanics to endure across generations.

At its heart, Ms. PAC-MAN is about rhythm, instinct, and precision. The rules are timelessly simple: guide Ms. PAC-MAN through a series of mazes filled with pellets, fruits, and ghosts, clearing every dot on the board to advance to the next stage. What sets this game apart from its predecessor is its evolution in design. Instead of the single, repeating maze from the original Pac-Man, Ms. PAC-MAN introduces multiple mazes that change color and layout as you progress, each with its own twists and pacing. The ghost AI is also more sophisticated, moving less predictably and forcing players to rely on quick thinking rather than memorized patterns. Power Pellets remain the ultimate equalizer, giving you the brief satisfaction of turning the tables on your pursuers, but timing their use becomes a delicate balance between survival and score maximization. The gameplay loop is so elegantly crafted that even in its repetition, it never loses its tension or momentum.

The presentation captures the magic of the arcade era perfectly. The pixel art remains clean and immediately recognizable, with each maze glowing in bright neon hues and every ghost exuding personality through simple animation. Ms. PAC-MAN herself, with her trademark bow and lipstick, brings a bit of playful charm to the familiar formula. The audio is equally iconic, with the rhythmic “waka-waka” of pellet eating, the frantic tones of ghost pursuit, and the cheerful jingles between stages. There’s something hypnotic about the combination of visuals and sound—a sensory loop that evokes both nostalgia and focus, as every movement and sound cue reinforces the tight feedback loop between player and game. Even after all these years, the sensory precision of Ms. PAC-MAN remains unmatched in its ability to draw players into the flow of play.

The Steam version does little to modernize or embellish this classic, and that is both its greatest strength and its most noticeable limitation. It preserves the original gameplay exactly as it was, which means it’s best appreciated as a piece of gaming history rather than as a reinvented experience. There are no major graphical overhauls, new modes, or added progression systems—only the pure arcade challenge that defined early gaming. For purists, this is ideal; it captures the exact feel of the cabinet version with minimal input lag and crisp controls, allowing players to relive or discover the authentic arcade experience. For others accustomed to modern quality-of-life enhancements, the lack of features such as leaderboards, customizable controls, or visual scaling options may feel dated. However, its simplicity is part of its enduring charm—it’s a game that asks for nothing but your focus and rewards you entirely with your own skill.

Beyond the nostalgia, Ms. PAC-MAN holds up as a masterclass in elegant game design. Every mechanic exists for a reason, and every mistake is your own. There is no randomness that feels unfair, only patterns waiting to be understood. The increasing speed of later levels turns the game into a dance between instinct and calculation, where a single mistimed turn can lead to disaster. This tension, balanced perfectly between control and chaos, is why the game remains captivating even decades later. It’s easy to play but nearly impossible to truly master, and that eternal pursuit of perfection is what defines its replay value. Whether you are chasing a high score or simply trying to clear one more level, the urge to press “restart” after every loss is irresistible.

In the broader landscape of modern gaming, Ms. PAC-MAN stands as a reminder of where the medium began. It embodies a purity of design that many contemporary titles, with all their complexity and visual grandeur, sometimes overlook. The Steam release, though barebones, performs the essential function of keeping this classic accessible and playable in the modern era without diluting what made it special. It remains fast, challenging, and satisfying in a way few games can replicate. For newcomers, it’s a crash course in timeless game logic; for veterans, it’s a trip down memory lane that feels as fresh as ever.

Ultimately, ARCADE GAME SERIES: Ms. PAC-MAN is more than a nostalgic curiosity—it’s a living piece of game design history that continues to demonstrate the universal appeal of simplicity and skill. It doesn’t need elaborate storytelling or modern enhancements to entertain; its tight mechanics and addictive rhythm do all the work. Whether you’re a long-time fan of the arcade era or a new player curious about gaming’s roots, Ms. PAC-MAN remains an essential experience—proof that a great game, no matter how old, never truly loses its spark.

Store page says "Cronenberg-inspired". As someone so obsessed with Cronenberg that my biggest achievement in life is HUGGING CRONENBERG AND SOBBING IN HIS ARMS - I tell you this game is not Cronenberg by any means. Right from the beginning it's clear the entity is supernatural/occult. My disappointment was immeasurable. I was about to look up where the dev lives and sprinkle his bedroom full of legos to step on. But then I gave up on my cartoon villain plans because this story turned out to be amazing.

I am hard to entertain and this game entertained me so much that I spent 4 hours on it in one day. First normal playthru - I got the bad ending, I was naive! Second playthru, strictly aiming to get the good ending - I got the good ending.
An absolute mindfxck of a story in the best possible way. In fact, now that I've played it, I feel like I want more. I need more of this lore. I am mad that this isn't a novel already!! The bad ending calls for a continuation.
I don't even know how could I describe it without spoiling. If you're thinking about getting this game, then I can assure you it's well worth the price and the short time to play through.
My only gripe is that the store page description is very misleading. It's just way too simple of a mechanic to call it "virtual pet elements" and "Cronenberg-inspired" made me think this would be about a human being going through some transformation or violation or something among his materialistic themes of human condition or something more philosophical. Definitely not this. So overall I feel I was misled, BUT I am not mad in the end since I got an amazing story that I didn't regret for a second. 
Congrats to the dev Yames for creating such an amazing art piece. It was beautiful.

Kukoro: Stream Chat Games, developed and published by HeyNau, is a distinctive and inventive title that redefines how games can interact with livestreaming communities. It is not a traditional single-player or even a typical multiplayer experience, but rather a social platform disguised as a collection of interactive mini-games. Designed primarily for Twitch streamers and their audiences, it blurs the boundary between spectator and participant by allowing viewers to directly influence the game in real time through chat commands. The result is a dynamic, community-driven experience that transforms passive watching into active engagement, giving both streamers and their followers a way to share the spotlight in unpredictable and hilarious ways.

At its core, Kukoro functions as a collection of over twenty mini-games that range across genres such as action, strategy, role-playing, and cooperation. Each one is built with one goal in mind—to create fun, chaotic, and interactive moments that the entire stream can take part in. A simple shooter might turn into a frantic race as dozens of chat participants flood the game with commands, while a strategy or investigation mini-game might require collective decision-making as viewers vote or contribute to solving puzzles. Every game feels like an event rather than a round of gameplay, because what matters most is not who wins, but how the group interacts. This interactivity is what sets Kukoro apart; it doesn’t just entertain the streamer’s audience, it gives them agency. Each viewer becomes a player, a participant in the chaos, shaping the outcome through messages typed into the chat window.

From the streamer’s perspective, Kukoro is more than just a novelty—it is a powerful tool for engagement. Livestreaming thrives on interaction, and this game amplifies that dynamic by turning every viewer into a potential co-conspirator. When a streamer launches Kukoro, the chat immediately springs to life, filled with viewers eager to join the game, earn rewards, and see their input reflected on screen. The sense of community it builds is tangible. Streamers benefit not just from the entertainment value but also from the increased chat activity, viewer retention, and overall energy that Kukoro naturally generates. The game’s integration is seamless, requiring little setup beyond linking a Twitch account, making it accessible even for smaller streamers who want to experiment with audience participation.

For viewers, the experience is equally rewarding. Instead of sitting back and passively consuming content, they become part of the show. Participation is simple—they type commands or responses directly into chat to control their avatars, perform actions, or make strategic choices. The game rewards active viewers with experience points, cosmetic items, and persistent progression across sessions, creating a sense of investment that keeps them returning. Even those who join a stream for the first time can immediately get involved without needing to download anything, which makes the game inclusive and welcoming. This design philosophy—treating viewers as essential participants rather than background noise—sets Kukoro apart from most other Twitch-oriented tools or overlays.

The variety of games within Kukoro is one of its main strengths. Some are fast-paced and competitive, others are cooperative or purely for fun. Each mode has a different rhythm and tone, ensuring that streams stay fresh and unpredictable. The art style is bright and charming, with simple but expressive visuals that make the action easy to follow even when dozens of avatars crowd the screen. The humor and energy that arise from chat-driven gameplay are where the game shines most; the blend of human unpredictability and lighthearted design ensures that every session feels different. It’s a kind of entertainment that only works in a live setting, where spontaneity and social connection drive the fun more than mechanics or skill.

That being said, Kukoro is a game built for a very specific context. Without a livestream audience or an active Twitch chat, its appeal drops considerably. While it can technically be played offline or used in a small private setting, the true magic happens when dozens or even hundreds of viewers participate at once. The mini-games themselves, while varied, are intentionally simple and not meant to stand alone as deep gameplay experiences. They function more like interactive toys designed to enhance a broadcast rather than replace traditional gaming sessions. For this reason, players seeking single-player depth or narrative content may find Kukoro limited. However, this design choice is deliberate—the simplicity allows everyone to join in instantly, even those unfamiliar with gaming conventions.

Technically, the game is well-optimized and user-friendly. It runs smoothly on most systems, with minimal hardware requirements, making it accessible to streamers regardless of their setup. The interface is clean, and the integration with Twitch is stable and intuitive. The developer’s continued support is evident through frequent updates and community interaction, which have helped maintain a positive reputation among players. Reviews on Steam overwhelmingly praise its functionality, humor, and ability to transform an ordinary livestream into something unforgettable. Many streamers report noticeable improvements in community engagement and viewer participation after incorporating it into their streams.

Kukoro: Stream Chat Games stands as a testament to how creativity and technology can redefine entertainment in the streaming era. It’s less a traditional game and more a social experiment—a playground for connection, laughter, and chaos. For streamers, it offers an innovative way to engage audiences and create moments that feel organic and collaborative. For viewers, it provides an opportunity to be more than spectators, turning passive entertainment into an active shared experience. It’s a title that thrives on community energy and creativity, delivering an experience that’s as unique as the people playing it. For anyone looking to elevate their Twitch channel or simply experience gaming in a fresh, participatory way, Kukoro is a charming, lively, and endlessly entertaining addition that transforms every stream into a party.

After Us erfordert nicht die ausgefeiltesten Skills, jedoch verlangt die verschachtelte 3D-Welt Orientierungssinn und Beharrlichkeit. Spannung hält das Spiel durch gelegentliche Kämpfe gegen entseelte Verschlinger und Jagden aufrecht. Kern sind aber nicht Motorik und Skills, sondern Bildsprache und Wahrnehmung.

Was das Spiel erfordert, sind ein offenes Auge und ein offenes Herz. Die Bildsprache ist eindringlich und beklemmend, grausam und schön zugleich. Sie urteilt nicht, sie zeigt: eine dystopische Welt, verstummte Lebensräume, unmissverständliche Hinweise auf die Vorgeschichte und das Leiden, das Opfer und Täter verbindet. Leid und Angst werden spürbar, wenn du versuchst, den Scheinwerfern und Schnappfallen der Jagd oder den Walfang-Harpunen auszuweichen. Wenn du deinen Weg suchst durch die nackten Betongänge der Schlachthäuser oder über schier endlose verseuchte Geröllhalden. Wenn du die krummen Rücken der Versteinerten siehst. In dieser Welt ist Gaia damit beauftragt, das Leben zu finden und zurückzubringen, was ihr – entsprechende Ausdauer der Spieler vorausgesetzt – auch gelingt. Der Lohn sind ein Samen der Hoffnung und ein Anstoß zu Reflexion und Mitgefühl. Ich bin dankbar, dass ich dieses Spiel gefunden habe.

*****

After Us doesn’t require the most advanced skills, yet its intricate 3D world demands a sense of orientation and perseverance. The game maintains suspense through occasional encounters with soulless Devourers and through its chase sequences. But the true core isn’t motor skills or gameplay mechanics. It is the imagery and what the player perceives.

What the game demands is a watchful eye and an open heart. Its imagery is haunting and unsettling, cruel and beautiful at the same time. It doesn’t judge, it simply shows: a dystopian world, silenced habitats, unmistakable traces of what happened before, and the suffering that ties victims and perpetrators together. Fear and pain become tangible when you try to evade the searching spotlights and snapping traps, or the whaling harpoons. When you navigate the bare concrete corridors of slaughterhouses or trek across endless contaminated debris fields. When you see the hunched backs of the petrified. In this world, Gaia is tasked with finding life and bringing it back, which she accomplishes — provided the player’s endurance holds out. The reward is a seed of hope and an invitation to reflection and compassion. I am grateful that I discovered this game.

Yield! Fall of Rome offers a refreshing twist on the 4X formula by narrowing its focus to shorter, more intense campaigns set during one of history’s most turbulent eras. Instead of presenting a sprawling empire builder where hundreds of turns pass before anything meaningful happens, the game emphasizes urgency. You are thrust into the chaotic world of 401 AD, a time when Rome’s stability is crumbling and surrounding factions are circling like wolves. This backdrop gives every decision immediate weight. Resources are limited, opportunities are fleeting, and neighboring powers grow quickly if left unchecked. The result is a strategy experience that feels compact yet consequential, appealing to players who love the genre but prefer campaigns that move at a brisker pace.

The mechanics reinforce this sense of focus. Rather than juggling several resources, Yield! simplifies your economy so that gold serves as the backbone of nearly every strategic choice. This makes the flow of each run more transparent and removes the need for the kind of micromanagement that often bogs down larger 4X games. Investing in new technologies, constructing buildings, fielding armies, and reinforcing your borders all draw from the same pool, forcing you to weigh trade-offs constantly. The research system in particular stands out for its efficiency: instead of unlocking deep, branching tech trees, you simply direct your wealth into incremental upgrades that support your current priorities. This eliminates downtime and keeps the game moving forward with purpose.

The playable factions enrich the experience with distinct styles, units, and strategic advantages. Whether commanding a barbarian tribe taking advantage of Rome’s weakness, a desert kingdom leveraging unique light cavalry, or a remnant Roman successor determined to hold the frontier, each campaign feels different enough to encourage replay. Heroes further personalize your forces, gaining experience across battles and shaping the identity of your army. Because maps are smaller and the timeframe condensed, every faction sits in threatening proximity to its rivals, amplifying tension and encouraging bold, calculated expansion.

Combat mirrors the game’s broader philosophy: concise, meaningful, and dependent on correct positioning rather than overwhelming numbers. Engagements hinge on terrain, unit type, and tactical foresight. Charging blindly into enemy lines or relying purely on quantity is rarely effective; the system rewards careful advance, flanking, and using the environment to your advantage. These battles retain the essence of turn-based tactics without becoming overly granular, which suits the game’s bite-sized structure. Even in defeat, the quick pace encourages you to jump back in and try a different approach.

Despite its strengths, Yield! Fall of Rome has shortcomings that reflect its streamlined nature. The diplomacy system is sparse, offering only a handful of interactions compared to the complex webs found in more ambitious 4X titles. Cultural nuance is minimal, and long-term internal development is limited. Players who enjoy deep nation-building or intricate political maneuvering may find the game’s strategic layers thinner than expected. There are also moments where scenarios feel uneven or rushed, with some missions ending abruptly due to the crown-based victory system. Minor technical issues and occasional balance quirks further remind you that the game leans toward indie scale rather than grand strategy depth.

Still, these limitations don’t overshadow what the game does well. Yield! Fall of Rome convincingly carves out a niche between traditional 4X sprawl and fast-paced strategy skirmishes. It delivers the satisfaction of expansion, conquest, and tactical problem solving without demanding dozens of hours to resolve a single campaign. The streamlined systems, varied factions, and high-stakes historical setting combine to create a uniquely digestible strategy experience. For players who appreciate the genre but struggle to find time for longer sessions, it is especially appealing.

In the end, Yield! Fall of Rome succeeds by embracing a smaller, sharper vision of empire building. It may not offer the depth or density of the genre’s giants, but it delivers a focused, engaging, and often tense strategic adventure rooted in one of history’s most dramatic turning points. For anyone seeking a strategy game that is easy to learn, relatively quick to play, and grounded in a compelling historical collapse, it stands as a distinctive and satisfying option.

Battle Chasers: Nightwar is a delightful return to the golden age of classic Japanese Role-Playing Games (JRPGs), executed with a distinct Western charm and modern sensibilities. Based on the popular comic book series by Joe Madureira, the game wins players over with its stunning visual style, deep combat system, and engaging dungeon exploration.

Key Highlights:

- Stunning Visual Style and Atmosphere. The game looks like a comic book brought to life. Detailed characters, vibrant locations, and gorgeous animations (including spectacular "Burst" attacks) create an unparalleled atmosphere. Even the loading screens are works of art.

- Deep and Tactically Rich Combat System. The turn-based battles are the heart of the game. The "Overdrive" system adds tactical depth, allowing you to generate bonus mana with basic attacks and use it for more powerful skills without depleting your main resource. The variety of enemies and their abilities demands constant strategic adjustments and party composition experimentation.

- Engaging Dungeon Exploration. Dungeons are procedurally generated, ensuring high replayability. They are filled with traps, puzzles, secrets, and formidable bosses, rather than just being arenas for random encounters.

- Diverse Characters. Each available party member has unique skills, perks, and a specific role in combat, allowing players to customize their team to fit their playstyle.

- Rich Supplementary Content. Beyond the main story, the game offers numerous side quests, a robust crafting system, fishing, and other activities that reward curious players and help them dive deeper into the game's world.

- Excellent Soundtrack and Sound Design. The musical score sets the perfect mood, and the sound effects—such as the impact of attacks in combat—feel substantial and satisfying.

Battle Chasers: Nightwar is a must-play for all fans of classic RPGs. It successfully combines nostalgic elements with modern mechanics, offering an exciting and beautiful adventure that can keep you hooked for many hours.

Kill The Clock is SO GOOD. I honestly didn’t expect to enjoy it this much, but wow! I was completely hooked and left hanging at the end! 😭

From the very start, the story just pulled me in. The mystery, the time-loop concept, the choices, and everything that will make an impact to the playthrough. everything feels so well-thought-out. You’re stuck reliving the same week where a murder happens, and every decision you make can change how things unfold. It’s both exciting and stressful in the best way possible. I really love the mix of dialogue choices, stat checks, and dice rolls <3 it makes every outcome feel unpredictable and alive... it gives that feeling of “oh no, please let this succeed” every time.

The art style is simple but fits the atmosphere perfectly. The writing kept me curious and emotionally INVESTED the whole time. You can tell it’s still in Early Access, but even now it feels so solid and well-made. The only problem? It’s not finished yet. Only two chapters are out right now, and when I reached the end I was like, “HUH? THAT’S IT???” 😭😭 I wanted more!!

I seriously can’t wait for the next updates. It’s such a promising game!! the story, the tension, and the feeling that your choices actually matter make it unforgettable.

⭐ Rating: 9/10 for now (definitely 10/10 once it’s complete!)
🎲 Best part: The thrill of not knowing what will change each loop
🕐 Worst part: Having to wait because I was totally left hanging

IN CONCLUSION: Kill The Clock is one of those rare indie games that truly surprises you. It’s clever, mysterious, and full of replay value. Even though it’s still incomplete, it already feels so immersive and unique. I genuinely loved every minute of it <3 the only problem is that there weren’t enough minutes! 😭

If you enjoy story-driven games, time loops, and decision-making with real consequences, this one is ABSOLUTELY worth your time. I’ll definitely be waiting (impatiently!) for the next chapters.

P.S: I REALLY LIKED the journal concept where we can just freely put our detective notes on there. It just adds up to the immersion :3 luv it!!

It's catastrophe realism and it's gritty opressive athmosphere even if raw are some of the most convincing ones that i've encountered in many years in this hobby, the agressiveness and darkness that oozes from every encounter you have, wheter it's with a gang, some lone wolf, or simply someone scavenging to survive is something you remember long after the credits roll, as well as the other people you can help, condemn or simply leave, rewards are not guaranteed

The gunplay is barebones but it serves well the theme of the game and is very unique: draw the gun, and the encounter is halted, bullets in the chamber or not, aim for too long, and enemies will build courage against you, that is... until you shoot, a single bullet can stall the encounter for a long time since fear is what drives npc AI and what dictates the flow of combat, at least if no other npc has a firearm, in which case the balance shifts

Parkour is the other half of the game, climbing, sliding... always keeping an eye on your energy meter that will deplete PERMANENTLY if you are not careful, with checkpoints that do not forgive if you fall to your death because of a miscalculated jump

Nowadays even if not labelled as a cult classic it can definitely feel like one, and it's an experience worth a playthrough at the very least, and a game to keep in your memory at best

Possibly the most uncomfortable social VR hub I've visted. Compared to the simplistic style of Altspace and RecRoom, SurrealVR is head and shoulders above in terms of graphical complexity, yet despite this there is not a single clothing or model combination for your avatar that doesn't come across looking like a complete and utter d-bag, including the female avatars. Everything about the style and events makes it feel like it is specifically catering towards "mature audiences" as some sort of VR Second Life, but it winds up coming across rather seedy.

This might be why the place is so empty. Though I haven't played extensively, the only person I've ever bumped into was apparently away from their headset at the time. Alternatively, it might just be because there's not really much of a quick start option so you can get into the meat of the content before deciding if you want to invest in the trouble of actually creating an avatar that suits your tastes.

Despite this, there are still interesting areas to explore and different VR tools/toys to play with. I don't know if people are ready for adult oriented social VR interactions, but it's entirely dependent on the people who actually try this app and continue to use it that will decide what type of attitude will foster and thrive there. If a bunch of creeps (or just people who feel this is a good place to do creeping) then it could turn toxic very quickly, but if mature people actually go there to meet people and have real talk conversations, it could wind up filling a very important niche in the VR community.

I recommend trying this at least for a few minutes each day over the course of a week. If you can actually find anyone real to talk to, it could be worth while.

Holo Hidden is a delightful and relaxing hidden-object game developed by toMoMI Games and published by holo Indie, offering players an endearing experience built around charm, fan appreciation, and detail. It is a love letter to both the hidden-object genre and the passionate Hololive community that inspired its design. Rather than relying on difficulty or mechanical complexity, it focuses on warmth, comfort, and the joy of discovery. Each level is filled with tiny treasures, familiar references, and lovingly hand-drawn illustrations that invite you to slow down, explore, and simply enjoy the process of finding what’s hidden in plain sight. It’s a game that understands that not every puzzle needs to be taxing; sometimes, satisfaction comes from noticing the small things.

The premise of Holo Hidden is as straightforward as it is inviting. Players are presented with a series of beautifully drawn environments—ranging from cozy living spaces and bustling cafés to vibrant fan meetups—each packed with objects and references tied to Hololive talents and their fandom culture. The goal is to find a series of hidden fans or items within each scene, checking them off one by one as you progress. The game’s design emphasizes observation and attention to visual cues rather than speed, creating a relaxing flow that encourages players to take their time. There are no punishing timers or harsh penalties for mistakes; instead, each stage feels like an invitation to take in the scenery and appreciate the artistry behind it. The result is a quietly satisfying experience where every click feels rewarding, not stressful.

Visually, Holo Hidden stands out through its distinctive, hand-drawn aesthetic. Every scene bursts with color and character, layered with delightful details that make the world feel alive. Fans of Hololive will recognize subtle nods to familiar personalities and inside jokes, from character mascots tucked into background corners to themed props that evoke specific stream moments or fan-made creations. Each environment feels crafted with affection, blending everyday warmth with playful imagination. The game also features additional modes like a coloring option and a photo mode, allowing players to interact with the artwork beyond the standard hidden-object format. These creative touches show that Holo Hidden isn’t merely about puzzle-solving—it’s about celebrating a community and its shared enthusiasm through art and interactivity.

The gameplay itself is designed to be intuitive, making it accessible for players of all ages and experience levels. The interface is clean, with item lists that update smoothly and a responsive click system that makes exploring each scene enjoyable. The progression through the eleven main levels, plus an additional bonus stage, feels natural, and the variety of environments keeps things from growing repetitive. Each level has its own identity, whether it’s a sunlit kitchen, a crowded festival, or a quiet fan’s bedroom. While the core mechanics remain consistent throughout, the sheer amount of visual variety and the clever placement of objects keep the hunt fresh. Finding that one cleverly hidden object often brings the same rush of satisfaction as solving a tough riddle, even without the pressure of competition or complex mechanics.

While Holo Hidden’s charm is undeniable, it is also a modest game in scope. The campaign can be completed relatively quickly, and once you’ve memorized where the hidden objects are, there’s little incentive to replay levels beyond enjoying the visuals again. Some players might wish for a greater level of challenge or more dynamic mechanics to sustain long-term engagement. That said, this simplicity feels intentional. The game isn’t trying to be a brain-burning puzzle title—it’s designed to be a cozy, casual experience. Its strength lies in how approachable and stress-free it is, offering a rare space in gaming for relaxation and lighthearted engagement. The experience is further enhanced by its polished presentation and subtle music cues, which create a calming rhythm that pairs perfectly with its visual serenity.

For fans of Hololive, the game is more than a hidden-object collection—it’s a celebration of a community. Each scene feels like a tribute to the VTuber phenomenon and the shared joy between creators and their audiences. The developers clearly understand the cultural touchstones that make Hololive special, infusing the environments with references that longtime followers will immediately recognize. Yet, even for players who have never watched a stream, Holo Hidden remains enjoyable as a cozy and visually appealing hidden-object adventure. It balances fan service with accessibility, ensuring that newcomers can appreciate its artistry without needing to know every reference.

In the end, Holo Hidden succeeds by being exactly what it sets out to be: a relaxing, lovingly made hidden-object game that radiates positivity and appreciation. Its inviting visuals, gentle pacing, and heartfelt design make it ideal for short play sessions or quiet evenings when you want something calm and engaging. It may not have the depth or length of more complex puzzle games, but it doesn’t need to. Instead, it thrives on simplicity, creativity, and emotional connection. For Hololive fans, it’s a treasure trove of visual tributes; for everyone else, it’s a charming reminder of the joy found in small discoveries. Holo Hidden is a warm, comforting experience that encourages players to slow down, smile, and take pleasure in the little things hidden all around them.

Rating: 8/10

Missile Command Delta is a combination of the tactical gameplay you'll see in the trailer (with light deckbuilding elements) and an exploration game with light visual novel elements. My opinion of the tactical gameplay is reasonably good, 7-ish out of ten, probably scratches a specific niche few mainstream titles do.

I'm generally ambivalent or disappointed with everything that *isn't* that tactical gameplay.

This sounds fairly harsh. But a lot of the game's quality, I feel, is kind of front-loaded. And a lot of the misgivings I had didn't really become apparent to me until about halfway through my playthrough. The more I played this game, the more comparisons I drew to Dangagnronpa, which is a game I think is arguably best-in-slot for a lot of the areas that this one flounders in.

My first gripe regarding this turn-based tactics, choose-your-own-adventure, exploration game is the exploration. A lot of this game's environments are very samey. Very similary floorplans, very similar color pallet, lots of confined spaces and hallways. This sounds like a knitpick, but a core premise of the game is starting in a relatively confined space, unlocking new areas, and progressing deeper in this underground missile bunker you've found. 

This is kind of a bigger problem than you might think, because you'll be running around that small area a lot looking for clues and solving puzzles. You sprint fairly slowly, and you retrace the same ground a lot, and it all kinda blends together for me. Clover Pit, buckshot roulette,  and Inscription are three games that take place almost entirely in a single room. But they're visually interesting and are built around maximizing the effect of that confined space. Danganronpa, like this game, starts in a fairly confined part of a building and slowly opens up. But each new area is visually distinct, which lends itself to a sense of progression solely through the environment.

Missile Command doesn't feel like it tries to do either of this to me. The level design feels like it's solely there to break up the puzzles and the tactical gameplay. This would be fine if the game didn't make me spend so much time in it. We do finally start seeing some more interesting spaces in the climax of the game, but the other 95% of the time you're running through three floors that are remarkably similar or crawling through air vents. The game tries to amend this somewhat by having you move through those rooms with no power, or after they've been damaged, but it doesn't feel enough to make discovering new areas feel exciting to me. The third level has some elements of the environment tied to its puzzles, but it also makes you run around so much in that otherwise-samey area that the main character lampshades it.

Level *transitions*, admittedly, are done reasonably well. There's multiple ways to traverse levels, and the game's plot makes you use different ones. 

I think puzzles are overused. There's a couple unique ones, but there's also two that I felt like repeated enough that it became annoying.

The pacing for this game feels really weird to me. The beginning third feels like it had the most variety of puzzles, exploration, and things to do. Then it starts feeling like it's getting more dynamic and might be building up to something before absolutely dragging along. Then the climax comes and it's fun and somewhat intense again out of seemingly nowhere. Like, I didn't know I was about to enter the climax until the game explicitly told me this was the point of no return, because it didn't feel like I was building towards anything emotionally for me.

Characters feel really weak. I'm honestly kind of surprised they included them at all. The storytelling is done through a combination of character dialogue, flashbacks/dream sequences, and random notes you find lying around (similar to the voicemail system in FEAR). I got an achievement for maxing the relationship with my goth-trans-girl best friend and the only thing I really knew about her by the end was that she was trans, had issues with her dad, and liked music. It's fine for characters to just be there as quest-givers, but the game tries to pretend like they aren't with these dialogue branches where you get to pick sides when they fight. There's a lot of these Evangelion-esque dream montages where the game tries to leverage some emotional weight, but it all feels really goofy and unearned to me. I was learning about who my friends were through a flashback montage at the end of the game, which feels like an unusual choice. 

The notes and such feel weird too. Like, not that they're purposely self-aware, but like the writers know there's supposed to be a story in the game so they're making game prose rather than creating breadcrumbs for an organic narrative. 

Music during setpiece moments is pretty good. Music during spooky moments is pretty good. Music during everything else is just okay. You spend a sizeable chunk of the game during 'everything else'.

Outside a few brief segments, I never felt like there were any stakes in this game, or any real motivation to explore deeper, until the climax. Like, one moment you're sneaking around this guy's back because you think he's dangerous and the next moment you're opening an air vent and crawling into it right in front of him. One moment a suspected murder is freaking out at you calling you a traitor and the next you end the dialogue tree and just walk away. You're going to be playing training simulations around 4x as often as real missions, because that's what unlocks all your doors for some reason, so most of the combat has no real stakes. 

There's a mystery. I didn't find it very well-developed. I feel like I was kind of just told there was a mystery and was expected to speculate about it without any real interplay with the gameplay. The saucy elements I did like were resolved about halfway into my playthrough and was something of a letdown. There was a strong opportunity for a System Shock-style character deception or plot interplay with the fact that you're informed early on in the game that you're under surveillance, but the execution feels 'meh' to me. 

I got the true ending. The climax segment and the ending path I chose was fairly enjoyable, and the music and plot twist felt like it was an okay emotional resolution. It also felt kind of silly though once I stopped to think about it.

I only encountered one bug during my playthrough. It didn't effect gameplay. This is praiseworthy.

All told, I think i'd rate the tactical portion of the game 6-7/10, the puzzle elements 5/10, the exploration 4/10, and the plot 3-4/10. For a combined overall weighted score of about 5/10. I absolutely think credit should be awarded for trying to mix genres like this into something cohesive. I don't feel scammed or ripped off. But having finished my playthrough, I don't think I'll have a strong desire to play it again or get different endings, and I would have enjoyed playing something else more.

Enemy Front, developed and published by CI Games, is a World War II first-person shooter that aimed to reintroduce players to the classic atmosphere of the genre while focusing on a rarely depicted setting—the Warsaw Uprising. Released in 2014, the game follows American war correspondent Robert Hawkins, who finds himself drawn into the chaos of occupied Europe, documenting and fighting alongside resistance forces across various countries. Built on the CryEngine 3, Enemy Front was envisioned as a flexible shooter that blended stealth, sniping, and open-ended combat into an experience that gave players freedom in how they approached missions. Unfortunately, while the ambition behind the project is evident, its execution is inconsistent, resulting in a game that alternates between moments of excitement and long stretches of unfulfilled potential.

The strongest aspect of Enemy Front lies in its concept and presentation of the Warsaw Uprising, an event rarely explored in video games. By placing players in the heart of Poland’s resistance movement, the game distinguishes itself from the countless shooters centered on the beaches of Normandy or the ruins of Berlin. The narrative occasionally captures the grim heroism of underground fighters and the desperation of ordinary people taking up arms against an overwhelming enemy. The variety of missions—spanning occupied Poland, France, and Norway—provides a good range of environments, and the art direction gives each theater of war its own distinct tone. While not cutting-edge visually, the game’s use of lighting, destructible environments, and period design helps it evoke the right atmosphere for a World War II setting.

The gameplay structure combines elements of open combat and stealth, giving players the choice to approach situations quietly or with all guns blazing. At times, this flexibility works well. Sniper missions, in particular, are tense and satisfying, offering expansive maps and multiple vantage points that allow for creative problem-solving. When the shooting mechanics click, Enemy Front feels like a nostalgic return to the more straightforward, objective-driven war games of the early 2000s. The CryEngine foundation gives it enough power to render explosions and physics effects competently, making firefights occasionally thrilling. However, these moments of enjoyment are undermined by erratic design and technical flaws that consistently disrupt immersion.

One of the most persistent issues is the game’s artificial intelligence. Enemy soldiers often behave erratically—sometimes spotting the player from impossible distances, while other times ignoring them completely even when gunfire erupts nearby. This inconsistency affects both the stealth and action elements, making it difficult to rely on any particular strategy. The stealth mechanics themselves are simplistic, relying heavily on line-of-sight and noise detection that feel underdeveloped. Enemies rarely patrol logically or respond in coordinated ways, and the game’s attempts to offer “multiple paths” through missions often boil down to choosing between two corridors that lead to the same encounter. The design intention of giving the player freedom is admirable, but the shallow implementation makes missions feel linear despite the illusion of choice.

Technically, the game suffers from several noticeable shortcomings. Frame rate drops, stuttering, and animation bugs are common, and interactions with the environment can be clunky. The controls feel slightly off, especially during close-quarters combat where the hit detection and melee animations lack precision. Even with its relatively simple mechanics, the game manages to feel uneven in its responsiveness, which can make intense firefights frustrating. The level design occasionally redeems these flaws with its use of verticality and open sightlines, but the pacing suffers due to the uneven enemy behavior and repetitive mission objectives. What should have been an empowering blend of tactical options too often feels like a struggle against the game’s systems rather than its enemies.

The multiplayer mode was a missed opportunity that further limited the game’s longevity. Featuring only a handful of modes—such as standard deathmatch and team-based variants—it quickly lost player engagement due to its lack of variety, matchmaking issues, and general instability. Without a steady community or meaningful progression system, the online component felt like an afterthought. In contrast, the single-player campaign, while flawed, at least carried the spirit of the developers’ ambition to explore an underrepresented piece of wartime history.

Despite its technical and design flaws, Enemy Front does manage to carve out a niche for itself through its subject matter and occasional flashes of strong atmosphere. When the music swells, the ruins of Warsaw burn around you, and the resistance fighters shout in Polish as the city collapses, the game achieves something memorable. It reminds players that World War II was not fought only by massive armies but also by civilians, journalists, and partisans who risked everything for freedom. It’s in these moments that the game’s emotional core shines through, even as the mechanics stumble.

In the end, Enemy Front stands as an ambitious but uneven entry in the World War II shooter genre. It tries to merge classic FPS gameplay with modern flexibility and succeeds only partially. Its technical execution and inconsistent design prevent it from being the revitalizing return to form it could have been, but its thematic focus and flashes of sincerity give it some merit. For those who appreciate the history it represents or crave a nostalgic, slightly rough-edged shooter experience, it may still hold appeal. However, for players seeking tight mechanics, deep tactical design, or refined production values, Enemy Front feels more like a missed opportunity—a game with heart and vision that ultimately falls short of its potential.

Хотите стать огромным осьминогом и разрушать всё вокруг? Тогда это не та игра. Тут мы огромный осьминог-творец в мире VR.

Конечно, вы можете переворачивать всё вверх дном и разрушать некоторые объекты, но цель игры: что-то строить, склеивать, возводить, примагничивать и так далее. Вся фишка игры даже больше в песочнице, где можно строить города, ставить дороги, населять жителями и так далее.

Для пополнения песочницы есть сюжетная кампания  и побочные задания. Все они работают для большего понимания, как всё работает, плюс открываются новые вещи для песочницы. У меня же стояла другая цель - пройти сюжет и все побочные задания.

Так вот, вы огромный осьминог и у вас в распоряжении две руки, вернее, два щупальца. На каждом щупальце множество присосок, которые могут хватать предметы. Сделано это вполне удобно и не кажется симулятором хлеба или Octodad. Важно какими именно присосками вы хватаетесь. Ближайшие к нашему туловищу логично сильнее, чем в области “пальцев”.

Физически у вас существуют только щупальца и вы вольны перемещаться по обозначенной зоне. Можно опускаться и подниматься, будто мы в полёте, как в креативном режиме Minecraft. Кстати, вы можете погладить собачек!

В заданиях чаще всего вас будут просить поставить ключевые предметы. Вы будете видеть силуэт предмета, а вокруг пустота. И вот вам выдают балки, составные зданий, магниты и так далее. Можно назвать игру головоломкой с возможностью креатива. Игра хорошо дружит с физикой (но в редких случаях не очень), поэтому всё нужно ставить по уму и учитывать вес. Если вы поставите всё на один край, то всё упадёт. В школе ненавидел физику, но здесь можно наглядно на неё посмотреть и это правда увлекательно.

Чаще всего от вас будут просить использовать магниты. Это разнообразные шарики и не только. Новые виды будут открываться по ходу прохождения. Помимо обычных магнитов мы будем использовать более крепкие, вращающиеся (например, для колеса обозрения), магниты-рогатки, и так далее. 

Чем дальше прохождение, тем труднее будут побочные задания, которые раскрывают игру в полной мере. Сильно попотеть заставляли задания, где нужно аккуратно расставить маленькие объекты или сделать идеальное равновесие, чтобы контейнер стоял под наклоном. На такие задания у меня спокойно могло уйти по 30+ минут.

Ракеты тут играют не последнюю роль. С их помощью можно высоко запустить что угодно. Или можно хитрым образом расставить ракеты в разных направлениях, чтобы раскрутить предметы.

Ещё вы можете зайти в пользовательские миры, чтобы посмотреть, кто что создал с нуля. Строят замки, города, фестивали, гоночные трассы, ракетные комплексы. После прохождения игры решил туда заглянуть и всё разрушить, так как всё время только создавал. Было приятно сравнять всё с землёй!

Каждый уровень и побочное задание можно пройти заново в специальном разделе, где житель признаётся, что наш фанат и делает игру про нас. А перепроходить стоит, если вы хотите получить все достижения, особенно за испытания на время. Времени даётся крайне мало, поэтому могу только пожелать вам удачи в этом!

Если вы творческий человек, то вы можете засесть тут надолго. Вы можете создавать ландшафт, простраивать маршрут дорог, выставлять пешеходные зоны, ставить разнообразные здания, построить “кукольный” домик, сделать пляж и ещё много-много всего. Предметов сумасшедшее количество и инструментов для создания объектов предостаточно. В первую очередь для творческих людей горячая рекомендация. Увы, я не в их числе, но мне было весело и интересно во всём это возиться, пускай и только в рамках сюжета и побочек.

Выглядит игра приятно, мультяшно и местами пиксельно. Фотореалзим тут и не нужен.

История проста, но интересна. Мы гигантский осьминог и люди действительно неоднозначно на нас реагируют, удивляются, боятся и так далее. Раньше мы не выходили в люди, но как только появились - сразу начали работать на благо общества, помогая что-то достать, построить, починить. Один из влиятельных и богатых жителей восхищался нами и просил испытывать его ракеты. От этого персонажа сразу веяло чем-то злодейским и вам не показалось. Также частыми персонажами будут наша “сестра”, мэр, профессор. Ещё окажется, что мы немного не из этого мира и вокруг начали появляться кристаллы, которые вырабатывают много энергии. Но они имеют негативный эффект: при контакте резко хочется во что-то вложиться, делать деньги и прочее финансовое. Юмор здесь хороший и добрый.

Музыка есть и она нормальная, ни больше, ни меньше.

Судя по всему, игра не очень хорошо продалась и не нашла должного внимания. Признаться честно, вряд ли бы я обратил внимание на Tentacular без Devolver Digital. Игра заточена на творческих людей и предлагает созидать, а не разрушать. Мало кому такое нужно, а если и нужно, то отсутствует VR-гарнитура. Судя по достижениям в Steam, уже до одного из первых уровней с появлением магнитов дошли только 17% игроков. Большая часть людей если и играла, то даже не дошла до основной фишки.

Мне для общего развития зашло, но больше нравится махать руками для разрушительных последствий.

Devolver Digital фигни не издают, даже если игра не получила должного внимания =(

Picorinne (a developer that is mostly a single person) already showed a lot of promise with Battle Crust but this far surpasses it, while staying true to the principle of maintaining old shoot-em-up design.

Right from the 4:3 aspect ratio and the intro, Infinos Gaiden looks like something you'd see run on MAME, precisely from the 1993-95 timeframe. Compared to Battle Crust which could be even a little drab at times, this game is much more colorful and sports some top-notch spaceship and mecha designs. Even better than the graphics is the amazing soundtrack, once again a collaboration with composer Hyakutaro Tsukumo; I especially love the tracks of levels 3 and 6, but also the tense boss theme.

Don't go in expecting your ship to become some death machine: the power-ups are in fact quite "modest", as they consist of two small pods for additional fire, with extra colored pickups for some more "specialized" shots. The only function of the second button is to move the pods so to get a wider (or rear, in the case of one of those shots) or more concentrated fire. It may feel too "essential" even if you are a fan of the genre but on the other hand this sensation of being never powered enough helps with the vibe of being an ace pilot in a desperate struggle against a whole army.
Although I have cursed a lot for the rare sections where the scrolling becomes vertical, as they seem especially designed to hopelessly take as many lives and credits from you as they can, I appreciated the design of obstacles and enemy waves. It definitely requires quite a bit of memorization. Levels feature several classic "biomes" but are no less pleasant to look at. For example level 3 is a desert with even a sandstorm blowing for a while, while level 6 starts above earth's surface and then takes to space, with even a dramatic shot of the light of the Sun before the boss battle.
Bosses range from good to great, and a few also feature nice entries before the battle; for example, after the first level is spent flying over a city under an orbital attack, the satelite responsible for it descends from the clouds.

My Little Pony: A Zephyr Heights Mystery is a lighthearted, cheerful adventure game that embraces the bright energy of the My Little Pony franchise while presenting a gentle mystery suitable for younger players. Developed by Drakhar Studios and published by Outright Games Ltd., the game transports fans to the glittering cloud city of Zephyr Heights, where strange magical disturbances begin to cause chaos. Objects behave unpredictably, gravity itself seems confused, and the citizens are growing increasingly uneasy. Against this backdrop, the familiar cast—Sunny, Izzy, Hitch, Zipp, Pipp, and Misty—take center stage as they work together to uncover the source of the magical mischief and restore harmony to the city.

The game’s presentation is highly appealing, especially for its intended audience. Zephyr Heights is recreated with vibrant colors, inviting architecture, and smooth character animations that faithfully mirror the style of the My Little Pony: Make Your Mark series. Each playable pony has expressive mannerisms and a warm, approachable personality, supported by upbeat music and charming voice performances. The visual polish helps carry the adventure even in its simpler moments, making the world feel friendly, safe, and fun to explore. The city’s areas—cafés, plazas, studios, and airy walkways—feel cohesive and lively, creating an inviting playground for younger players to wander through.

Gameplay is straightforward and intentionally accessible. Players can switch between multiple ponies, each offering small differences in interactions and abilities. Missions revolve around light puzzle-solving, simple platforming, delivery tasks, collect-a-thons, and various mini-games such as dance challenges, photography activities, or smoothie-making sequences. The structure is closer to a collection of bite-sized adventures than a deeply interconnected storyline, which works well for a younger audience with shorter attention spans. The quest objectives are easy to follow, navigation is forgiving, and visual prompts clearly guide players from one activity to the next. Cooperative local play adds another layer of enjoyment, allowing siblings or friends to join in on the fun and solve the mystery together.

The narrative itself is intentionally simple. A series of magical anomalies disrupt daily life in Zephyr Heights, and the Mane Six must track clues, talk to residents, and examine affected areas to figure out what is causing the instability. The mystery unfolds gently, ensuring that nothing feels frightening or heavy. Dialogue is friendly and humorous, and each step of the quest emphasizes teamwork, kindness, and curiosity—values strongly tied to the MLP brand. While older players might find the plot predictable, younger fans will likely enjoy seeing their favorite characters take the lead in a new story.

However, My Little Pony: A Zephyr Heights Mystery is not without limitations. Its simplicity, while perfect for children, means the game offers little depth for older or more experienced players. The missions follow familiar patterns and rarely evolve into more complex mechanics. Once the main story and side quests are completed, there is limited replay value beyond enjoying mini-games or experimenting with cosmetic outfits. Some of the controls and platforming sequences also feel a bit loose, though never to a degree that disrupts play significantly. Because the game is designed first and foremost as a family-friendly introduction to adventure mechanics, these shortcomings are expected, but they do limit its broader appeal.

Despite these constraints, the game successfully delivers a wholesome, approachable experience tailored to young gamers and dedicated fans of the franchise. It captures the heart and optimism of My Little Pony through kindness-focused storytelling, vibrant art direction, and playful activities. It is easy to pick up, forgiving in its challenges, and structured to make children feel capable and engaged. For families looking for a cooperative adventure, or for younger players eager to spend time in the world of Zephyr Heights, My Little Pony: A Zephyr Heights Mystery is a delightful and welcoming game that emphasizes joy over complexity.
