[h2]Introduction[/h2]
In Grimtale Island, you play as a nameless, faceless character on one of two islands - one named [i]Starter Island[/i] and the other named [i]Grimtale Island[/i]. I started off on the Starter Island to learn the core gameplay mechanics then moved onto Grimtale since that’s the title island. Once you’ve chosen your island, you’ll be spawned at a predetermined spawn location to start out your new life.

Since this is an open-world survival game, you’ll need to begin collecting materials to craft workspaces to progress through the tech tree. However, instead of punching trees and rocks to get resources, you’ll respectfully have to pick loose articles up off the ground, only getting the ability to farm rocks and trees with the appropriate tools later on. In addition to rock and wood you can expect to pick up other materials such as fiber and metal. There are some consumables, like food, found in bananas and apples; medicine, like med kits and rad pills; and ammunition, handgun magazines and single-rifle bullets.

Around the island there are three other lifeforms - bunnies and deer, which you can hunt and harvest for meat and fiber, and zombies - the only enemy that threatens your existence aside from the elements. In addition to zombies, you have to try to avoid the cold as well as keep yourself hydrated and fed using items you find around the island. If you explore enough, you may also find vehicles like LUVs, tanks that don’t fire ammo, and helicopters. Oddly enough, these vehicles are incapable of damaging wildlife and zombies -- you just bounce right off.

Lastly, there are several points of interest around Grimtale Island. There’s villages, small and large military outposts, a quarry, a destroyed city, and many other small locations that are lootable. There’s occasionally a robotic trader that you can find who will take rocks and wood [b]only[/b] in exchange for money, which you can use to buy ammo, weapon parts, and medicines. One thing you [b]won’t[/b] find on this island are tools or weapons, those are only obtainable through crafting.

Well, that’s about everything foundational to the game, so let’s move onto what I did like about Grimtale Island.
[h2]The Good[/h2]
The thing that I had liked most about Grimtale Island is the graphics -- regardless of whether or not they’re handcrafted or purchased assets. The environmental assets look great and nothing in the game reads like it’s a mish-mash of asset packs.

But unfortunately that’s about all I could enjoy, so let’s move into the ungood.
[h2]The Ungood[/h2]
So I typically start with smaller nuances and build up to what I think is the worst - so to start, I found the UI to be highly underdeveloped. It doesn’t convey limitations well and is pure text and numbers, which means you can’t visualize your inventory in any capacity. This also means that you can’t store multiple weapons or tools, with the latter being a real pain since your axe breaks after cutting down five trees or so. This led to me building a good dozen or so workbenches around the world just so I’d always have one with me.

Another item that chips away at the enjoyment is that there doesn’t seem to be any procedural generation, randomization, or regeneration. Now, my sample-size testing is limited to three plays, but I found the same items in the same locations in the same quantities. This isn’t the [i]worst[/i] thing, but this means your experience [b]will[/b] be the same every single time. This leads me to believe that loose materials have been put down by hand, which means you can only find rocks and wood near Points of Interest, which can test your patience if you have no tools to farm wood or rock and are in dire need.

Speaking of Points of Interest, we can segway into my third point which is the amount of underdeveloped Points of Interest. There’s several, but to call specific attention to three - the quarry, the military base, and the destroyed city -- these all are heavily lacking in lootable items, mobs, or decorative furniture. The quarry has no farmable rocks, which seems kinda [i]off[/i], the military base only really contains the helicopter yet spans like a couple hundred-thousand square feet, and the destroyed city, while looking busy and intimidating on the outside, has a dozen or so zombies and maybe two dozen items that are lootable out of the 20-odd something buildings. This is likely due to the development timeline, as these three locations are [i]really[/i] far away from the spawn, but it doesn’t take much to get there. While the closer locations are a little more fulfilling, this is also where I learned that you cannot interact with world-generated doors at all -- and with some doors [i]kinda open[/i] this leads to some interesting AI interaction.

The AI in this game is pretty basic - if a zombie sees you, it almost seems like they’ll follow you to the ends of the Earth. I’ve come across a conga line of zombies that likely followed me from one village and got stuck on terrain at some point and couldn’t break away, even though I hadn’t seen them for a half an hour. I’ve had some zombies follow me a good thousand feet or so away when I definitely broke line of sight. The zombies are also [b]very[/b] good at crowding around doors, but are without the ability of coming in if there are multiple coming in at an angle. If multiple zombies crowd around the door and you have no weapons and no means to make an axe, you’ll just have to die or restart your game. As an honorable mention, deer don’t run away when you shoot them. They just accept their death.

I try to keep it to six points, so to the short of my last point -- the game just isn’t finished. I don’t consider Grimtale Island to be in a finished state where it’s really enjoyable more-so than it being a memory of a passionate and hopeful developer that had an unfortunate hand dealt to them that paused development. If you haven’t read through the updates, the developer has unfortunately declared that Grimtale will no longer be able to be developed. This means that this state that it’s in [b]right now[/b] is its final state. There are some questions that arise from curiosity -- the developer posted the end of development news post in August of 2019 laying claim that it will end Early Access and be a free game. However, Early Access ended on November 27th [b]and[/b] the game currently costs 99 cents, and has for at least a whole year, save for sales which kicked it down to 89 cents, which happened twice in the last few months. While I can’t answer these questions, I think they’re important to consider if you’re thinking about purchasing this game.
[h2]The End[/h2]

[h1] TLDR: 6.5/10 It’s Crazy How a 10/10 Masterpiece Can Possess a Single Element That Drags It Down So Much. Hyper Light Drifter Is an Outstanding Art Piece of a Game…if You Can Look Past the Horrendous Controls [/h1]

[h3] Actual Review (No Spoilers) [/h3]
I really don't want to bitch about this game. It is such a work of art. It has a really heartfelt development history and a flawless aesthetic; from the pixel art, to the music, to the mysterious story and world. It could've be twice as long and still understayed it's welcome. It would've been extremely immersive with one of the easiest combat loops to get into a super fun flow state with. But this game suffers so incredibly hard from the controls, not even accounting for how annoying it makes 100%ing the game.

[h3] The Whiny “”””””Skill Issue”””””” Rant [/h3]
I have only two complaints about this game, and they really are just that massive. First, why are the controls so needlessly jank? I literally cannot describe in enough detail how much it ruins the fun of the game. I'm not even gonna talk about the keyboard controls cause that's honestly a lost cause. But even if you use a controller, this game will ask you to rigorously lab out timing and spacing - with no input buffer at a locked 60fps - as if HLD was a fucking fighting game. Dash is just annoying to deal with and you're better off literally never chain dashing. You will just slide off into the abyss or instantly smash into a wall cause your dash angle was half a degree off.

By all technicality this is a "skill issue" but saying that completely misses the point. Why would you make learning your controls frustrating, then EVENTUALLY start to become rewarding? They should be smooth and intuitive from the start and continue to feel better the better you get. And by the way, they never do become smooth, they will always be rigid without any fluidity. All you can do is just know the frame data better.

Secondly, HLD values being artsy over giving helpful in-game information. Like the map is basically useless outside of fast travel. "What do you mean you actually want to see what rooms connect to each other?" Did you know that each outfit isn't just cosmetic and actually have unique bonuses that you can mix and match? I didn't until my second playthrough with my eyes glued to the wiki because no where in the game does it say that. Not only does this make the first playthrough really confusing, but it also is a giant middle finger to anyone dumb enough to collect everything (like me).

[h3] Avoid the Achievement Grind Oh My God [/h3]
This game has a bit of asshole game design, and it comes out in full force when going for 100%. Why on earth is the chain dash challenge 800 dashes?? There is no reason to make it so long unless you actively want to give the player carpal tunnel.

My eyes were doing a full 360 degree roll the entire time I was attempting the one life achievement. This is where the terribleness of dashing comes out in full force. "Oh sorry you were 2 pixels too close to that tiny bit of wall during your chain dash, so now enjoy getting stunlocked and restarting"

It's not even worth talking about the boss rush, NG+, or collection achievements. Just avoid this game if you're a completionist.

[h3] HLD Will Either Be Your Favorite Game of All Time, or You’ll Have Serious Issues With It [/h3]
It seems like there's not really an in between with this game. You either look past it's issues, or have them ruin your experience. I definitely still recommend this game, honestly how can I not when the ideal first playthrough has THIS much potential? Just be aware that HLD has issues and you might not mind them, but still be mentally prepared. 6.5/10

『SaGa Scarlet Grace: Ambitions』は、オープン構造を基盤とした非線形型のロールプレイングゲームです。プレイヤーは複数の主人公から一人を選択し、それぞれ異なる物語のルートを体験します。物語は長時間のスクリプトではなく、短い会話シーンを軸に展開します。

探索はワールドマップ上のポイントを選択する形式で進行し、従来型のダンジョンは存在しません。アイコンを選択することでイベント、クエスト、戦闘が発生します。これにより移動時間が削減され、意思決定への集中が可能となります。

戦闘はターン制で、行動順が重要な要素となります。キャラクターは敵の行動を妨害し、コンボを形成し、タイミングを活用します。判断ミスは大きなダメージにつながるため、行動順の読みが核となります。

キャラクターの成長はスキル使用の頻度に依存します。スキルは反復使用によって進化し、固定的なレベルツリーは採用されていません。装備はパーティの役割を大きく変化させ、試行錯誤を促します。進行は線形ではなく、反応的な手応えが特徴です。

ビジュアルはスタイリッシュかつミニマルで、背景は簡素ながらキャラクターアートは鮮明です。音楽は重要な戦闘で躍動感のあるテーマを強調します。技術的なパフォーマンスは各プラットフォームで安定しています。

物語のテンポは断片的で、地域ごとの対立に紐づく短いシナリオが中心となります。会話は簡潔で、選択の自由度により旅路は個人差が生まれます。一方で、従来型のストーリー性による緊張感は薄いと感じられる可能性があります。

本作は戦術的な戦闘と戦略的な自由度を求めるプレイヤーを主な対象としています。初心者には簡素に感じられる場合がありますが、シリーズファンにとってはシステムの奥深さと高いリプレイ性が魅力となります。

과학 어드벤처 시리즈 세번째 작품의 이식판(카오스 헤드-슈타인즈 게이트-로보틱스 노츠). '슈타게 엘리트'처럼 애니메이션 장면을 곳곳에 사용해 엘리트라는 부제가 붙었습니다.
초중반이 지루하다, 포텐 터지기까지 오래 걸린다는 평이 많은데 생각보다 엄청 재미있었습니다.

로켓 발사장으로 유명한 타네가시마(한국으로 치면 나로우주센터가 있는 전남 고흥)가 배경입니다.
격투게임 폐인 주인공과 로봇부 부장 히로인, 그리고 로봇부 부원들과 섬 주민들이 힘을 합쳐 만든 거대로봇이 세계를 구하는 이야기.
느긋한 일상이 현실화된 음모론에 침식되어 가는 특유의 분위기, 충격적인 반전, SNS와 증강현실을 활용한 세계관 심화가 돋보입니다. 스토리상 다른 시리즈와의 연관성이 많은 편이고 중간중간 여러 캐릭터 시점으로 전개되는 것도 좋았습니다.

개성 넘치는 캐릭터들을 매력적으로 그려내며 좌절과 혼란 속에서 하나의 목표를 향해 나아가도록 케미를 빚는 솜씨가 여전히 훌륭하며, 애니메이션판에 기반한 성우들의 연기력도 출중합니다. 특히 중증 부녀자(腐女子)인 코지로 프라우의 매력이 상당하네요.
특이하게 캐릭터들이 3D 모델링으로 그려지는데, 이벤트CG와 갭이 있기도 했지만 움직임이 많아서 덜 지루해진 듯.

단점으로는 안타깝게도 PSV판만 공식 한국어라는 점이 가장 크겠습니다.
또 각 캐릭터 엔딩을 보고 메인 스토리가 진행되는데, SNS 답장에 따른 분기 조건을 알기 힘들어 공략이 필수라는 점입니다.

시리즈의 다른 작품들에 비해 슬로우 스타터는 맞지만, 취향에 따라서는 로봇 제작과 격투게임, 희미한 음모론이 떠도는 초중반이 전혀 지루하지 않을 수도 있습니다.
개인적으로는 후반부 엔딩까지의 불타오르는 전개가 너무 좋았습니다. 현실 속 거대로봇이라는 낭만을 대리만족한 느낌이었네요.

也许这个游戏让真正经历过世纪之交的人来写可能更好，我02年出生，其实并没有真正经历千禧年跨世纪的倒计时的感觉，但是却非常容易做到与游戏其中的年代感产生共情。
在我看来游戏里描述的1999年年末的年代记忆，却一直延续到了我记忆里的2010年。看着熟悉又遥远的富有年代感的物件，总能涌上一些关于童年细碎的回忆。

那时，未来对人们来说还充满着懵懂和朦胧。
那时，时代交替，街上到处是还未褪色的旧时代痕迹与新世界的影子。
那时，父母还很年轻。

小时候，父母在外面创业，我从出生到五六岁几乎没怎么见过他们。本着好奇心在爷爷奶奶家翻箱倒柜时，我翻到了很多相册。

那时相机还很一般，照片仿佛上了一层漂白的蜡色滤镜，里面有他们结婚前的照片，有叔叔伯伯姑姑婶婶的照片，也有和朋友们一起的合照。那些照片泛黄、颜色失真。照片里，是爸爸妈妈年轻的模样，穿着当年简单但干净的衣服，那时的他们脸上有笑，眼里有光，那时他们有梦，他们还很年轻。

后来，到了我五六岁，该上小学的年纪，父母终于来接我。
但在我的记忆里，那不是一个很温情的场面。
我把他们当成陌生人，甚至当成“要拐走小孩的坏人”。
我躲在奶奶家的橱柜里，拒绝出来。
爸爸把我抱上车时，我拼命挣扎，哭着闹着还咬了他一口。

即便到了父母的家，和他们相处的时间也并不多。
他们忙于工作，我从一年级开始就被送到老师家寄宿，只有周末才回家。

和我一起来到家里的，是一个大脑袋的 CRT 显示器。家里的书房专门折腾了出来一块地方来放它
我记得那年夏天，爸爸很兴奋，和他的朋友们在我家书房装大机箱、打印机、电脑桌。他们说这是电脑。

那年，书房的地上摆满了爸爸当年买的电脑书、光盘和硬件教材，其中不少还是盗版的。如今那些书现在还躺在我家书架上，封面早已褪色，抚摸时候却带着一种古早时代特有的震颤。
那个时代我能记起的词很少，仿佛像一个个零散零碎的化石一样，ghost装机、宽带拨号、Windows XP、自建 CSS 博客。还热衷于QQ空间DIY装扮。

这些字眼，当年我一句也看不懂，但它们曾驱动着最早的一代网民，凭着一种近乎原始的探索欲，摸索着一个尚未成形的世界。那时网络的万事万物都还没有被命名，所有操作都是试探，所有发现都带着原始的惊喜与渴望。

互联网就在这样的氛围里，开始了它的野蛮生长。

那时，妈妈唱歌很好听，钢琴也弹得很好
周末再忙，她也会陪我玩捉迷藏、摸瞎，或者讲童话故事。

小时候家里有一台机器，叫做DVD。我对爸爸的电脑兴趣不大，只喜欢妈妈陪我看动画片，现在还记得有小虎还乡，哪吒传奇，虹猫蓝兔。

那几年我仿佛感到以前都是理所应当的。
现在想想，她也许在努力给我一个家。

妈妈是个很有仪式感的人，她会在结婚纪念日带我们出去短途旅行、合照。我每一岁的照片她都有单独制作成影集，说要让长大的我看看我的成长变化。

她还是个虔诚的基督徒，至今也是如此。不过我小时候对它们没有什么兴趣。只会记得每年圣诞节，她都会让整个家变得亮亮的、暖暖的，把家里布置得像童话。

圣诞节妈妈会买许多气球、圣诞树和红色彩带把家里布置一番。晚上会举行圣诞晚餐。晚餐上总会有一个礼盒，礼物里总是毛绒玩具和裙子，我从小就喜欢这些东西，所以每年都期待圣诞节，比生日和过年还要期待。

除了圣诞节，妈妈还会陪我过万圣节。基督教是不过万圣节的，她也会陪我玩万圣节，陪我做南瓜灯，在市场里挑了一个巨大的南瓜，把南瓜掏空，点上蜡烛，和电脑里看到的一模一样。至今仍然记得那时的兴奋和成就感，以及不一会闻到了蜡烛把南瓜顶烤熟的悠悠南瓜香。

我戴着魔女帽和斗篷，在昏黄的灯光里转来转去，我以为我拥有许愿魔法，我以为我就是万能的魔女

原来万能的不是我，是妈妈。



有时候，她也会给我讲很多事情

听她讲起她小时候的事，她上学时候的故事。在姥姥家她是二女儿，我还有一个大姨和舅舅。姥爷家是有些重男轻女的，姥爷比较倾向于让舅舅读书。

姥姥家在那个年代就有电视机，算是那个时代少有的娱乐活动。全家人都在围着电视机时候，她主动在后厨房点蜡烛学习，然后大姨和舅舅学习也不好，特别是舅舅不爱学习。最终姥姥力排众议让妈妈继续读书。

我也听说起爸爸年轻时候多热爱游戏，他在没结婚之前就喜欢去街机厅，然后后面又花了好多钱买了一台游戏机（应该是红白机和ps2），不过他后面把游戏租给朋友玩，很快就回本了。。

我还听说，我本不是长女，我本应该还有一个哥哥。

那年，我憧憬着上小学。

那所小学很大，据说建于七八十年代，有一种苏联式的庄严、肃穆的巨构厚重感。

学校的道路两旁种满了巍峨的松树，时而有松果从上面坠下，有松鼠在斑驳的松树针叶间掠过。

学校深沉暗绿的墙壁上刷满了粗粝的砂砾，学校走廊里还挂满了中外名人画像和语录。桌子还是木工师傅手工制作的榫卯结构，桌子表面还是原生不规则的木剖面纹理，并不平滑，所以上面有一层滑滑的打蜡。散发着自然的木质清香。学校顶楼还是电脑微机房，每每进入微机房，还要戴上鞋套。

那时候我称呼它为大学校（对比我幼儿园的‘小学校’），我曾天真的以为这是世界上最好最大的学校。那是我第一次觉得世界很大、学校很大、未来也好像很大。

同学之间流传着，是学校白色大楼（一个平时不允许进入的大楼）里有女鬼、是据说教学楼五楼死过人、学校树林里有僵尸等奇闻怪谈。胆子大的男生还组织小分队带着木剑，十字架等等道具去探险。

校门口的小卖部，卖着那个时代最潮的玩具，赛车，溜溜球、各种各样的卡牌。同学们流传着折东西南北的纸猪爪。

上次偶然路过曾经的小学，发现那里被改造成了工厂，原来的教学楼被夷为平地。重新建起一栋办公大楼，记忆里的朗朗读书声被时间湮灭。只剩下松树被风吹过的猎猎作响。我是想去寻找点什么呢？

那个我以为永远不会变的地方，就这样消失了。

欲买桂花同载酒，终不似，少年游。



进入初中后，父母更忙，特别是爸爸变得沉默寡言。要求我独立生活。

然后我住在市郊的小楼独自生活，晚上高速公路的灯光从窗缝掠过。
其实小时候我和他的父女关系并不好，我很怕他，而且他也不善表达。但是高中的一些事情改变了我们许多。我不在这里赘述。

上半年，经历一些极度痛苦的事情。爸爸找到我后给我讲起了一些往事，讲起他年轻时候的创业失败，他当时最终找了他的父亲（也就是我的爷爷），爷爷专门开车去找他接他回家。他和我说，“我有爸爸，你也有。”



每次回家，丽姨总说我长得像我妈妈。但我总认为妈妈年轻时比我漂亮得多。

我把爷爷奶奶家那一叠老照片翻出来了。有两张照片格外印象深刻，一张是一个小女孩在花从中笑的照片，一张是一位女青年穿着白色衣服的照片。
眼角和嘴唇能看到淡淡的妆痕。但在我的印象里，从我认识她起就几乎没有化过妆。
我突然有点惊慌失措，妈妈的容貌已经被时间磨灭掉了。一想到她也曾年轻美貌过，为了漂亮化妆过，就不由的十分感伤。

忽然想起一句诗
 　“夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。”

但妈妈不是这样的。
她回忆年轻时的样子，只是很平静地和我说一句：“那时候啊。”
仿佛美貌、青春、那些被拍在照片里的日子，她从未紧紧抓住，也从未觉得失去。

妈妈也把陪伴她十多年的钢琴送给了我。
这些充满回忆的物件，我会感伤，在她来说断离舍却很轻松。

上个星期，我跟好朋友通电话时候，失声痛哭了一场。当时脑子里和脸上只有呜呜。
最后只剩下一句，我想爸爸妈妈了。



有时候，妈妈会给我唱歌。听丽姨说，她一直很爱唱歌。

[quote] 
 　小小的一片云呀
 　慢慢地走过来
 　请你们歇歇脚呀
 　暂时停下来
 　山上的山花儿开呀 我才到山上来
 　原来嘛你也是上山
 　看那山花开 [/quote]

不知为何，她特别喜欢给我唱《踏浪》。小时候的我并不喜欢这首歌，我更喜欢听爸爸车里那些“比较潮”的音乐。可现在，偶然再听到这首歌，我会控制不住地想掉眼泪。
我也说不清自己在怀念什么：也许是童年，也许是故乡，也许是那个还没学会真正长大、却一心想逃离的小小的自己。

那首歌不只是妈妈爱唱的一首歌。
山上不止有山花，还有被记忆蒙成一层梦核滤镜的幼时回忆。

This is a really cool matching game!  You are fighting/looting treasure chests, and if you beat it, you go further down the map and get a choice of rewards.  Then, you go to camp, pay the troll toll to save the boy's soul, equip inventory items, and distribute skill points.  Then on to the next fight.  There is an ending to the run when you beat the last boss and get the orb.

The dynamics of the game and skill point progression are really what make this.  Skill points add abilities to the tiles  (which are different characters, like paladin, druid, etc).  For example, a certain skill gives attacking next to a paladin an attack bonus.  After a match, the paladin next to each character becomes highlighted to let you know that it was adjacent.  Another example, the paladin and druid can be linked so that when one attacks, the other attacks.  The game shows a wavy line every so often between the two indicating that they are linked. 

So rather than a bunch of flashy effects when matching that don't really mean much, the match indicates special effects and the total damage done for every match, including cascades - on every tile/character matched.  So, nearing the end, matches look pretty awesome with all of the effects, but they also indicate what is happening (taking into account skills chosen).

This is a pretty awesome buy, and the price is good.  I would buy this again, even if it's not on sale.

I'm very close to completing [i]New Dawn Game Studio[/i]'s "Mewseum: Masterpieces". It's an incredibly simple Puzzle game with some very simple rules: in every puzzle, fill all squares, but the quadratic shapes you draw, can only incorporate one number inside of them, the number corresponding to the amount of colored squares meant to touch the numbered square and squares adjacent to it. Explaining it so verbosly makes it sound more complex than it is, but I assure you, it's fantastically simple.

The game is set to an array of classical pieces, which I turned off fairly swiftly, in favor of Youtube videos and my own, more energetic music, but the tracks chosen undoubtedly fit the game's theme of a classical art museum. The portraits that you'll be assembling, little puzzle region by little puzzle region, are rendered in passable, fairly flatly colored pixel art, which gets a pass, mostly for the paintings being cutely reimagined with any and all human(oid) subjects featured within being replaced with cats instead. After completing a given puzzle, you're given a summary screen, with a render of the full image, plus an info block, with the actual, original piece of art, telling you some pertinent info about the time period, the artist, the piece's creation and the relevance of the piece to classical art connoisieurs.

The only real objective flaws with the game are based on visual quality of life. Weird black squares will permanently cover up any wrongly demarcated regions, unless you click on it again to make it disappear. If a given region of a puzzle is either pure white or pure black/dark blue, the numbers are rendered invisible, leading to easy undoing of progress, due to a misunderstanding of how puzzle pieces intersect. A simple fix to this last issue would be the game detecting colors and always rendering numbers in a given color's opposite.

Overall, a cute, relaxing experience, that's not too difficult, but still gets your spacial awareness working. It's no masterpiece (unlike the titular paintings reimagined within), but it doesn't seem like it's trying to be. Just pleasant enough to get a recommendation from me, despite some obvious mediocrity.

I love mystery dungeons and there are so few these days. This one is not a bad game - I had fun with it and don't regret the time I spent, but I think there are a few too many issues to give it a thumbs up:

[*] An important thing that determines whether a mystery dungeon is fun is what happens if you die, and what mechanisms allow you to leave the dungeon before death. Imo, this game doesn't get the balance right. When you die, you lose everything, which makes the beginning of the game brutal because you basically can't get out alive unless you find a very rare herb. Mid-game you unlock a tagging system which lets you get back an item after death, but you have to go half way up the tower to get it back... Eventually I realised that there's actually a really easy way to get Undo Herbs back at town, which trigger upon death and let you either revive, or leave the dungeon with all your stuff. So I just filled my inventory with Undo Herbs and the game was trivial from then on.

[*] I love an old mystery dungeon called Azure Dreams. You also lost everything on death but your animal companion retained its level so while death was a big setback you still kept a lot of your progress. Tower of Fortune also has allies you can bring into the dungeon with you, who also retain their levels between runs, but my god they are stupid. The AI is so bad, you have to work really hard to get them in the right position to attack an enemy and they will die to every random danger. I pretty much just ignored them in the end.

[*] Inventory management is a nightmare. The game has a huge list of different items you can find, but cursed you with a tiny inventory. You can find pots as you play, which will hold 4-5 items for you, so you end up filling your bag with 10~ pots to hold everything. This turns the game into a menu simulator where you spend most of the time moving things into, out of, and between your pots.

[*] The boss of each 'level' is very difficult, so you need a bag full of powerful items to beat them. So I would pack my inventory full of powerful things, and play slow and steady up the tower so I didn't have to waste anything on weak enemies. This meant I couldn't pick up any of the loot I found on the way up, and played pretty boringly. But it was optimal - you don't want to spend hours on a run just to the die to the boss that's 10x harder than the other enemies

Gimmick! Special Edition is a lovingly restored and finely tuned revival of one of the most overlooked gems of the 8-bit era. Originally developed by Sunsoft and released in 1992 for the NES and Famicom, the game has been reintroduced to modern audiences through the efforts of CITY CONNECTION and publisher Clear River Games. What makes this release significant is not just that it revives a rare and technically impressive classic, but that it does so with a clear understanding of what made the original so distinctive. Gimmick! Special Edition preserves the challenge, artistry, and unique physics that set it apart, while adding thoughtful modern conveniences that make it accessible without compromising its integrity. It’s both a celebration of a cult classic and a lesson in how to respectfully modernize retro games for a new generation.

At its core, Gimmick! remains a deceptively simple platformer. You play as Yumetaro, a small green creature armed with the ability to summon a bouncing star—a power that doubles as both a weapon and a tool for traversal. The entire game revolves around mastering this one mechanic. The star moves with physics that feel surprisingly dynamic even by today’s standards—it ricochets, slides, and rebounds off surfaces in ways that can be both useful and unpredictable. You can use it to defeat enemies, break obstacles, or as a makeshift platform to reach higher areas. This single ability gives the game a depth of control that feels organic and rewarding once mastered. The level design complements this perfectly, constantly pushing you to think creatively about how to use the star to navigate each environment. The precision required to chain jumps and ride the star effectively makes the gameplay uniquely demanding, yet also deeply satisfying once the system clicks.

The Special Edition adds modern quality-of-life features that make the game more inviting without diluting its challenge. Players can now use rewind and quick-save functions, which allow for experimentation and practice without the frustration of restarting entire sections after failure. For purists, there’s a “Serious Mode” that strips these features away, recreating the raw, punishing experience of the original release. This dual approach makes the game accessible to newcomers while preserving its authenticity for veterans who crave that classic intensity. Additional features such as achievements, leaderboards, and a time attack mode inject new life into the game’s replayability, offering fresh incentives to refine your performance or compete with others. These additions strike a delicate balance—they modernize the experience, but they never intrude upon or overshadow the brilliance of the core design.

Visually, Gimmick! Special Edition stays true to the original’s vibrant 8-bit presentation, maintaining the crisp, colorful art style that made it stand out in its era. The game was one of the most technically advanced titles on the Famicom, using custom hardware to produce richer sound and more fluid animation than most of its contemporaries. That sense of craftsmanship remains apparent here—the backgrounds are full of subtle detail, and the sprite animation still has charm and character. The developers have wisely avoided overhauling the visuals or redrawing assets; instead, they’ve focused on high-quality emulation that retains the authenticity of the original pixel art. The audio has also been faithfully reproduced, preserving the exceptional chiptune soundtrack composed by Masashi Kageyama. The music’s complexity, made possible by the game’s expanded sound chip, still stands as one of the high points of 8-bit composition. Every track is both melodic and atmospheric, perfectly complementing the whimsical yet melancholic tone of the world.

While Gimmick! is a joy to play, it is also undeniably difficult. The physics-driven mechanics require precise timing, and enemies often punish even slight errors in movement or positioning. This challenge can be daunting, especially for those unaccustomed to the unforgiving design philosophies of early 1990s platformers. The game demands patience and repetition; learning each stage, memorizing patterns, and refining your control of the star is key to success. However, the difficulty is fair—each obstacle feels conquerable through practice and skill rather than luck. When you finally execute a perfect sequence of bounces or discover a hidden route, the sense of accomplishment is immense. This is the kind of game that rewards mastery rather than endurance, making every victory feel earned. The inclusion of the modern assists ensures that frustration never outweighs enjoyment, allowing players to learn and experiment at their own pace.

From a historical perspective, Gimmick! holds a special place in gaming history as one of the most ambitious and technically advanced NES titles ever made. Its combination of unique physics, challenging design, and outstanding sound pushed the limits of the hardware in ways few games did at the time. Unfortunately, due to its late release and limited distribution outside Japan and Scandinavia, it never reached the audience it deserved. This Special Edition serves as both preservation and revelation—a chance for modern players to experience a forgotten classic that feels remarkably fresh even three decades later. The gameplay, though rooted in old-school sensibilities, has aged gracefully because of how mechanically tight and consistent it is. It stands alongside the best platformers of its generation, offering a kind of creative precision that few games since have replicated.

While this re-release is an excellent tribute, it’s also modest in scope. Beyond the new modes and accessibility features, there isn’t a wealth of extra content or remixed material. Some fans may have hoped for a more expansive package with developer commentary, concept art, or a deeper retrospective on the original’s legacy. What’s here is a clean, faithful restoration, not an elaborate remaster. Yet that restraint may be to its credit—it keeps the spotlight squarely on what made Gimmick! special in the first place. The new visual filters, replay tools, and assist features all feel additive rather than intrusive. This kind of respectful curation is rare and refreshing, ensuring that the game remains true to its roots while being easy to enjoy on modern platforms.

Gimmick! Special Edition succeeds not because it transforms the original, but because it understands exactly what made it brilliant. The tight physics, inventive mechanics, and high skill ceiling remain intact, and the new features make them more approachable than ever. For fans of retro platformers, this is an essential addition—a window into a time when creativity and technical experimentation defined the medium. For newcomers, it’s an opportunity to experience a game that feels both nostalgic and surprisingly modern in its design philosophy. It’s not an easy journey, but it’s one worth taking, and the Special Edition ensures that it’s now accessible to anyone willing to give it a chance. In a market filled with remakes and reimaginings, Gimmick! stands out as a faithful resurrection of a lost classic, proving that great design never goes out of style.

在‘自动化与物流’游戏中，一直都存在着一个必须要去解决的问题，即：‘玩家生产的东西究竟要到哪里去’，只有成功解决这个问题，‘自动化与物流’游戏才会拥有‘自驱力’，令玩家不断自发的去解决一个又一个的生产难题，并从中获取到成就感与满足感。

而‘学习工厂’则是将‘玩家生产的是一种商品，并需要将它们提供给客户’这一概念，作为了上述问题的解决方案，并围绕着这一解决方案，设计并搭建了游戏的其他部分。

也正是因此，’学习工厂‘相较于’传统‘的’自动化与物流‘游戏而言，其不再拥有’明确‘与’可视化‘的’阶段性目标‘，也不再存在’准确‘与’完全固定‘的需求，从而以’随机性‘来增强趣味性。

然而，有趣的想法和设计并不能直接的代表一款游戏的好坏。

对’学习工厂‘来说，其基本的想法和设计固然是优秀的，但存在多个维度的各种小毛病却聚沙成塔，将游戏的优点掩盖了。

当然，如再仔细打磨的话，’学习工厂‘也将不失为一款好游戏，但截至目前的进度来说，我确实很难将它推荐给到我的朋友们。

[h1] 详评 [/h1]

[b] 优点 [/b]

·新颖的’直接供应式‘玩法，并增加了一部分的随机性，延长了游戏寿命。
·新颖的’研究‘机制，以一定的随机性，增强了趣味性。
·可自行规划的可重复采集资源点，降低了一定的生产流程难度。

[b] 缺点 [/b]

·极高的布局难度
存在多种类型的阻挡物，并包含’地上‘和’地下‘两种层级，可以’完全解决‘阻挡物的科技被安排的非常靠后，这直接使得玩家几乎不可能进行’物资的集中处理‘，显著增加了布局难度。

·极高的物流压力
没有相关的传送带升级，有关的研究项目效益差，从而使得’工厂‘的吞吐量被固定化，并显著的增加了物流压力与布局难度。

·可重复采集的资源点的获取与建造不合理
在研究后，可重复采集的资源点的获取，为’一次手动采集4%‘，这为想要自行布置可重复采集的资源点进行相关处理的做法，造成了极大的困扰；而另一方面，需要长时间成长的可重复采集的资源点，则导致游戏的垃圾时间陡然增加，即便在是使用了相关加成科技的情况下。
此外，不得不提的是，想要快速获取大量的可重复采集的资源点，则需要进行开图，但进行开图又会进一步导致更大的物流压力和布局难度。

·科技树与科研的设计不合理
在科技树中，有相当一部分的科技缺乏实际作用，且科研难度设定不够合理，而有关科学家的属性/特性设计，又进一步加重了进行科研的复杂性。

Crossroad OS is a uniquely atmospheric puzzle-adventure experience developed by Guy in collaboration with Daisy Games and published by Martin Games. It presents itself through the illusion of a digital interface, where the player explores a broken and decaying operating system as if navigating the corrupted remains of a forgotten computer. The game cleverly uses this familiar structure as a setting, transforming mundane digital environments into immersive spaces teeming with mystery. From the moment it begins, Crossroad OS blurs the line between user interface and game world, greeting the player with a simulated installation screen before plunging them into a surreal realm made up of folder mazes, glitched-out directories, and haunted applications that defy conventional logic.

The game draws on the nostalgic aesthetics of early computer systems—complete with CRT-style visual filters, pixelated icons, and the mechanical hums of an old machine booting up. However, beneath this retro charm lies a subtle undercurrent of unease. Every screen flicker, every corrupted file you attempt to access contributes to a growing sense of something not quite right. It's not overt horror, but a creeping atmosphere of digital decay and isolation that permeates every moment. As you delve deeper into the OS, you begin to realize you’re not alone. The system is populated by strange entities, decaying processes, and vestigial programs that seem aware of your presence. These encounters aren’t just aesthetic—they tie into the game’s puzzle design, requiring logic, observation, and often lateral thinking to progress.

Gameplay unfolds primarily through exploration and environmental puzzles. You’ll navigate digital corridors and system files that act as level maps, pushing blocks, solving color-coded maze puzzles, collecting keys, and unlocking further directories. Many puzzles revolve around spatial manipulation and pattern recognition, borrowing elements from classic tile-based games like Sokoban but presenting them with thematic twists. What makes Crossroad OS stand out is how it contextualizes each mechanic within the fiction of a broken operating system—file fragments become collectibles, hidden folders act as secret rooms, and corrupted executables hide both danger and reward. Despite its minimalist visuals, the game manages to build a convincing and memorable sense of place, aided in no small part by its haunting sound design that features distant echoes, ambient hums, and otherworldly glitches.

The progression system is straightforward, and the game doesn't rely heavily on traditional storytelling. Instead, it opts for environmental narrative, where players piece together the world’s history and context through exploration and observation. The absence of direct exposition gives the game a dreamlike quality, inviting speculation and interpretation. Each new layer of the OS reveals not just new challenges but new moods—shifting color palettes and soundscapes keep the experience fresh even in a relatively short runtime. The journey from screen to screen feels like traversing through a forgotten digital consciousness, one slowly unraveling, and perhaps resisting, your attempts to escape or repair it.

One of the few criticisms that can be leveled at Crossroad OS is its brevity. The entire game can be completed in under two hours, and while it offers a satisfying arc within that timeframe, some players may wish there was more depth to the narrative or additional layers of complexity to the puzzles. Certain late-game sections veer into trial-and-error, with a few solutions feeling less intuitive and more reliant on brute force or repeated experimentation. Nonetheless, the game’s pacing remains steady, and the puzzles, while occasionally obtuse, never feel unfair or unpolished. It’s clear that the developers prioritized mood, cohesion, and atmosphere over expansive content, resulting in a focused and tightly constructed experience.

Crossroad OS ultimately succeeds because it dares to turn something as mundane as a computer interface into a mysterious, engaging, and at times unsettling world. It’s a thoughtful and artfully restrained indie title that offers a refreshing departure from more conventional adventure games. By combining retro computer aesthetics with exploratory puzzle gameplay and a quietly compelling sense of unease, the game carves out a space that feels both familiar and alien. It doesn’t overstay its welcome, nor does it try to do more than it should. Instead, it commits to its concept with confidence and creativity, offering players a brief but memorable glimpse into a digital ghost story told entirely through code, corruption, and clever design. For those who appreciate atmospheric puzzles, unique settings, or meditative exploration, Crossroad OS is a standout that delivers more than its minimalist presentation might initially suggest.

Virtua Unlimited Project, developed by Virtua Ride System and published by Neverland Entertainment, is an energetic 2D action-platformer that blends retro sensibilities with modern digital culture. Set within a futuristic virtual society, the game follows Kana Aizawa, a VTuber pulled into a manufactured reality built atop the ruins of Earth. Humanity sleeps in suspended pods while artificial systems maintain the planet, and the civilization that thrives in cyberspace faces a mysterious threat that corrupts data, minds, and infrastructure. Kana’s mission becomes a journey not only to fight off the chaos infecting this world, but also to uncover the unsettling truth behind the “New World Plan.” The framing does enough to justify the adventure—its tone playful but dystopian, occasionally humorous, occasionally reflective—without overwhelming the action-focused experience.

The heart of the game lies in movement. Virtua Unlimited Project feels handcrafted for players who value responsiveness, rhythm, and momentum. Kana dashes across screens, wall-jumps up towering platforms, ground-pounds, air-kicks, and chains slides into slashes seamlessly. There’s a sense of joyful exaggeration in how she traverses environments—each ability linking into the next without friction. Mastery comes not from learning isolated inputs, but from developing a mental map of how motion flows. Stages are paced around this design philosophy, encouraging experimentation with air control, vertical movement, shortcuts, and stylish kills. Combat complements mobility, emphasizing aggression and combo chaining rather than careful spacing or cautious defense. When everything clicks, the gameplay resembles a fluid dance—swift, bold, and satisfying.

Combat depth grows as the game introduces Operators—boss characters whose defeated forms unlock new weapons and abilities for Kana. These loadouts change not only how she fights, but how she navigates levels, encouraging revisits and alternate approaches. Extensions further reinforce customization, offering passive enhancements like auto-charging, improved recovery, or terrain resistance. This light buildcraft system doesn’t turn the game into an RPG, but it gives players choice and personal expression. Boss fights themselves are often highlights, mixing patterns, platforming, and reaction-based challenge. They’re memorable not because they are punishingly difficult, but because their designs reward learning, adaptability, and movement awareness.

Visually, the game embraces pixel art with commitment and flair. Its sprites are clean, expressive, and animated with just enough detail to give personality without sacrificing the clarity needed in a fast-action platformer. Neon accents, circuit-patterned backdrops, and glitch effects reinforce the virtual world theming without overwhelming the eye. Kana and the supporting cast have distinctive silhouettes and attitudes that make them recognizable instantly. The soundtrack follows a similar philosophy—energetic, electronic, and upbeat, building tension without overwhelming the screen. The overall audiovisual presentation avoids nostalgia mimicry and instead presents a polished, contemporary interpretation of classic action-platformer aesthetics.

Virtua Unlimited Project isn’t free of rough edges, however. The story, while conceptually interesting, sometimes struggles with pacing and emotional punch. Dialogue can feel abrupt, translation phrasing occasionally distracts, and certain narrative revelations arrive too quickly or without enough buildup. For players invested primarily in storytelling, character arcs, or thematic depth, the narrative will likely feel functional rather than compelling. Some may also find the overall difficulty curve gentler than expected, especially if they are veterans of precision platformers. The game’s movement toolkit is powerful enough that standard levels rarely push back unless played on higher difficulties or under self-imposed challenge conditions.

Despite these criticisms, the game succeeds because it understands what makes 2D action-platformers enduring: brisk pacing, intuitive movement, satisfying feedback, creative enemy encounters, and short recovery time after failure. It respects the player’s time, never bogging the experience down with grinding, excessive exposition, or mechanical bloat. Stages are designed to encourage replay, whether to improve performance, uncover secrets, or experience newly unlocked abilities in different ways. It’s a game built to be revisited rather than simply consumed once and forgotten.

Virtua Unlimited Project ultimately feels like a love letter—to VTuber culture, to pixel-driven action games, and to the unpretentious thrill of mastering a moveset simply because it feels good. It may not revolutionize the genre, but it refines what it draws inspiration from and injects a playful digital identity all its own. For players who crave momentum-driven action, vibrant pixel art, and boss-focused platforming, it offers a fast, stylish, and engaging experience. For those seeking a narrative epic or significant mechanical complexity, it may feel too lightweight. But within its lane, it performs with confidence, personality, and infectious enthusiasm—qualities that make it easy to recommend and even easier to return to.

For the record, the game got like 40 to 1 positive reviews which I thought was strange considering that I ran into dozens of design or technical issues, so I started to compare the accounts that wrote them, and at least 9 of them had 1 review in total, for this game only (one dude didn't even use his account for years before writing it)... Also, nearly every review claiming that this game was amazing, was at 0 achievements at the time of me inspecting them, even if they had multiple hours into the game or claimed how good it was overall (there is a narrative achievement about 1 hour into the game). One of those 1 review users had the developer and other accounts with more reviews on the friend list. So maybe 20+ potentially related reviews? I mean, they could at least provide some negatives as well.

[b]To be clear:[/b] I have nothing against the devs, they helped me with the issues so far, but I feel I should provide an alternative view, considering how little criticism this game got from its "customers", and I seem to have a very different experience playing it.

To start with something positive, the first ~30 minutes or so I was somewhat impressed by the detail of the locations and the 3D modeling of the character, as well as a relatively smooth 3D animation, you can even control your flashlight independently which is a cool mechanic in this game for both puzzles and fighting enemies Alone In The Dark 4 style. For the most part, I think the locations look decent, although sometimes they can be a little too blurred because of all the filters and the frost effect which is also a game mechanic where you can slowly freeze.

Another complement I would give, the game has some* very good puzzles which incorporate interesting lore and world-building while solving them, granted, they are diluted with occasionally obtuse puzzles where I feel like humping every part of the game. That said, maybe with a little more help from the notes, I think it could be balanced into a decently paced puzzle experience.

It has a lot of content and optional collection, you can get 10+ hours out of it easily, but it's been a slog of random technical issues, mechanical frustration, and sometimes getting stuck on hard puzzles. The story during the game was not amazing, but I did like the endings. There is a decent game here below a couple design mistakes, if they can polish it more. I like that it has some different costumes, they seem to have different attributes like item capacity, speed or insulation (maybe).

Now, some of the big negatives. You can still get damaged in this game when being locked into a narrative segment, picking up items, or while you are locked in a puzzle animation. If you played any decent survival-horror game, usually the game pauses while you interacting. Some areas where the game chooses to give you narrative segments are also not safe, so you might lose the ability to interact with the environment talking on the radio while getting banged by 2 mini-bosses that are chain grabbing you back to back, you don't get an immunity after already loosing control of the character. 

- There is even a moment where interaction spawns enemies, but the animation recovery is slower than their attack, so you literally can take free damage, which is kind of a good analogy for the experience of playing it.

Another huge negative is the enemy design. Most of the game you fighting very dull and uninspired enemies, slugs or shadows, there is not that much variety. It also has 2 chasing type enemies, sorta like Nemesis but more boring, 2 of them actually, except one of the mostly patrols a few areas, and one of them can be almost anywhere. A big problem with these guys is that they rarely let you do puzzles, it feels like I get into a chase with the blob every 60 seconds, it gets very #### repetitive. 

The game is very big on "resource management", you can to track your temperature, your tools can break (even softlock your game if you not careful), as well as healing items and such. I do find it kinda odd that consumable items can lock you out of completing the game, although it seems sometimes you can find an extra item from a random event or the enemy drop, so it has some safety net for it. 

[h1] Pros: [/h1]

(+) I really like the character's movement & animation, the tank controls which I picked over the modern movement feels mostly good, not perfect, maybe the turning speed was a bit slower, but it's not bad.

You can also control your flashlight while moving which has some combat and puzzle purpose, honestly I have been swinging this thing for fun for most of the game.

(+) Maybe 60% of the puzzles have some interesting world-building and fair challenge, the other 40% probably could be a little more intuitive. 

(+) The story is hit and miss, but it has occasionally fun optional lore. Some locations look good

(+) Actually there is a lot of content, varies optional achievements and tasks. You can also find a few different costumes with different advantages. 

[h1] Feedback: [/h1]

[u] Maybe make the character immune during interactions with the environment or the narrative segments[/u] - unlike most survival-horror games, you can get damaged while picking up items, or even during some story segments, which is really stupid, I mean lets be honest, it's really bad.

[u] Too much Filter and excessive Darkness in some areas [/u] - look I get it's a horror game, but it does not mean my entire screen needs to be covered with foreground in some of these areas. Use these effects in moderation, the detail in the environment is what is important, not how much dirt I have over my screen. That game looks good, when you CAN SEE IT.

[u] Patrolling monsters have a bit too much presence [/u] - there will be a part of the game where you constantly getting into chase every like 30 seconds, they barely let you do puzzles. If it's not one guy it's the other, or both of them. They can also chain lock you into grabs, camp the save room, or just make it very odd to move around them in small areas. It's not hard, just very tilting and grindy. Like, there needs to be a more fair window to chill and do puzzles.

[u] Consumable Softlocks [/u] - I know it's very difficult to do it, and I know the game has many resources, but still, people assume consumables are not required for progression. That is logical. I think the girl can randomly drop you goodies, not sure if she can do it forever or if it's scripted. 

[u] Enemy Design [/u] - all the regular enemies are not all that interesting to run into. The shadows take a long time to vanish after the prison, and the slugs are just kinda there. It feels the game is missing that mid-tier enemy, you know what I mean, where is your licker or hunter type enemy so you actually get to fight something cool. 

Those things on the ground, honestly mostly immersion breaking, they feel like artificial obstacle. Maybe remove monster noises from safe room music.

On a side note, the game has some stutter issues in some areas of the game, I assume some light or particle effects. Could really use voice acting honestly.


[b] Overall Thoughts: 6.5/10 (after finishing) [/b]

What a fantastic horror game. I’m honestly surprised by how well it nails the classic survival-horror feel. As someone who grew up playing Resident Evil and Silent Hill, this game hit all the right nostalgic notes without feeling dated. It brings back that familiar tension and atmosphere, but with enough personality to stand on its own.

The art style is distinctive and genuinely interesting, and the audio work deserves real praise. Playing with headphones makes a huge difference — the sound effects and music add weight to every scene, and the sense of cold in the environment is almost tangible. The atmosphere is easily one of its strongest points.

The story also works really well. Anna’s narrative is clear, well-paced, and ties into the world in a way that kept me engaged throughout. It delivered exactly what I hoped for from a horror game like this.

So far, there’s really nothing I’d point to as a flaw… except the main menu. It’s functional, but it’s the one place that feels like it could use a little more polish to match the quality of the rest of the experience.

Overall, it’s a memorable and genuinely impressive horror title — nostalgic in the right ways, atmospheric, and absolutely worth playing.

I’d absolutely recommend this to anyone who loves the genre — and even to people who might be curious about exploring “new old” styles of horror that still hold up today. It’s a great reminder that some of the most timeless experiences continue to come from the roots of the genre.

I'm a turn-based JRPG fan. However, while I liked the SaGa games and owned them on the original Gameboy, I was never a huge fan of the series. The Secret of Varonis takes everything I love about the turn-based JRPG genre and wraps it in the aesthetic of the SaGa games while presenting a polished, modern feeling turn-based JRPG. It's everything I wanted the SaGa games to be while not actually being shackled by the hardware limitations of the time. I strongly recommend this game for turn-based JRPG fans. Random thoughts:

- My time played doesn't seem to be synching correctly between my steam deck and PC. I think I'm nearly finished with the game at the time of leaving this review, based on other reviewers' time spent.
- The story is surprisingly good and well-written. Usually indie RPGs really struggle to find the right tone, but I think this one nails it.
- I'm playing on the casual setting with random battles. I'm happy with that choice, but it makes the game a little easier than I'd like. I think doing "Casual" with FIXED enemy encounters could have presented a really interesting challenge, and I may go back and try that. I also think doing the "classic" setting with field-mode enemies could be fun too. I don't think a game's difficulty settings have ever made me want to replay it as much as TSoV's difficulty settings make me want to replay it.
- I did a 1 of each race party, and my monster is consistently underwhelming. This is probably related to the setting where items recharge at inns because of the "casual" setting. This will make mutant inherent abilities and monster inherent abilities both feel weaker. My mutant is strong though since I've probably fought more battles than I should have.

Final Fantasy Legend 1-3, but especially 1&2 are some of my favorite games of all time. Also known as SaGa 1-3 in Japan, and the series that would come after these games, they absolutely captivated me in a way that helped me get into JRPG's overall. 

Secret of Varonis is made by people who love them just as much, if not more, than I do. They fundamentally understand what made these games special, and build upon them. There's numerous quality of life features, ranging from expanded clarity of mechanics, to controlling how espers/mutants level up, etc. Truly, this dev team gets it. 

I would recommend this game to anyone who wants to experience a very unique set of mechanics where your party gains 0 exp or levels, yet everyone experiences growth and powers up in their own way. Even now, I can imagine different party comps to take care of certain things I didn't get to tap into too much. 

Also shout out to this being run at RPG Limit Break 2025 for making me aware of this game. I had never heard of it until it was run there, and I loved my time with this game. I cannot recommend this enough.

Guilty Gear X2 #Reload is one of the defining entries in Arc System Works’ legendary fighting franchise. It refines the mechanics of Guilty Gear X2, polishing balance and presentation while maintaining the series’ signature speed, style, and depth. Though later versions surpassed it, #Reload remains an important milestone in competitive 2D fighting history.

Combat is fast and aggressive, with a heavy focus on execution and momentum control. Every frame counts—attacks chain into explosive combos, and mistakes are punished instantly. Systems like Roman Cancels, Faultless Defense, and Tension Gauge management make each match a test of precision and awareness. The skill ceiling is high, rewarding mastery and creativity.

The roster is diverse, featuring 23 playable characters. Each fighter has a unique toolkit, from Sol Badguy’s close-range brawling to Zato-1’s shadow control. The asymmetrical design ensures variety while maintaining balance. No two matchups feel identical, which keeps both casual and tournament play engaging.

Visually, Guilty Gear X2 #Reload remains striking even by modern standards. Hand-drawn 2D sprites, fluid animation, and bold color contrast give every move personality. The metal-inspired aesthetic—chains, gears, and guitars—defines the series’ identity. Combined with fast pacing, the visuals deliver constant energy and spectacle.

The soundtrack, composed by Daisuke Ishiwatari, is iconic. Every track reinforces the intensity of combat with driving guitar riffs and melodic aggression. Sound effects are sharp and satisfying, making every hit feel impactful. The music and visuals together create one of the most distinctive atmospheres in the genre.

Single-player content includes arcade, survival, and mission modes. The story is eccentric and largely secondary to the action but adds charm through character-specific endings and dialogue. The AI can be challenging, though not as adaptive as later entries. Multiplayer still works locally, but online play depends on fan-supported setups, as official netcode is outdated.

Overall, Guilty Gear X2 #Reload stands as a classic of high-speed 2D fighting. It offers mechanical depth, visual flair, and musical power unmatched by most contemporaries. While newer entries like Accent Core Plus R and Strive refined the formula, #Reload remains a pure expression of what made Guilty Gear special—uncompromising style and technical mastery.

Frozenheim, developed by Paranoid Interactive and published by Untold Tales, Hyperstrange, and Gamersky Games, is a serene yet demanding blend of Norse-inspired city building and real-time strategy. Set within a harsh and beautiful landscape inspired by Viking mythology, it places the player in the role of a clan leader striving to establish a prosperous settlement amid unforgiving natural conditions and rival tribes. It’s a game that invites patience and reflection as much as it demands tactical awareness, offering an experience that values atmosphere, pacing, and immersion as much as conquest and efficiency. From its opening moments, it is clear that Frozenheim seeks to combine the meditative rhythm of settlement management with the tension of survival in a world where every season brings new challenges.

The first impression Frozenheim gives is one of tranquility. Its visual presentation is undeniably striking—lush forests, snow-covered valleys, shimmering lakes, and long shadows cast by a low northern sun. Seasons shift dynamically, and each brings both beauty and consequence. Summer’s green abundance allows the player to expand and harvest, while winter’s white silence demands preparation, rationing, and endurance. The attention to detail in its environmental design creates a sense of authenticity rarely found in the genre. Villagers move purposefully through the settlement, performing their daily tasks, and the changing weather affects everything from resource collection to morale. These small touches, coupled with a somber, Nordic-inspired soundtrack, ground the game in a rhythm that feels natural and immersive, even when the tasks themselves become routine.

At its core, Frozenheim is a hybrid of city-building and real-time strategy, though it leans more toward the former. The settlement-building mechanics are well realized, emphasizing careful planning and sustainability. The player constructs housing, hunting lodges, fisheries, farms, and fortifications, each of which plays a vital role in the settlement’s survival. The economy is simple but layered: wood, stone, and food form the basis of production, and the balance between consumption and storage becomes critical when the cold months arrive. The game captures the satisfaction of watching a small cluster of huts evolve into a thriving community, yet it also punishes carelessness. A poorly timed expansion or a winter without enough food reserves can doom an entire settlement. It is this balance between progress and peril that keeps the city-building portion engaging, especially in the early and mid-game.

When it comes to its strategic elements, Frozenheim introduces combat and exploration in a way that complements rather than overshadows the management systems. Players can train warriors, construct barracks, and form raiding parties that venture out to capture resources or defend the village from rivals. The combat is straightforward but functional, emphasizing positioning and preparation over micromanagement. Though the real-time battles lack the complexity of dedicated strategy titles, they add a necessary layer of dynamism to an otherwise contemplative experience. The ability to send out scouts or longboats creates a sense of expansion beyond the borders of one’s settlement, and this interplay between the security of home and the dangers beyond gives the game a satisfying ebb and flow. However, it’s worth noting that the artificial intelligence often behaves predictably, and once a player masters the basics of defense and raiding, encounters can become formulaic.

The campaign mode attempts to add narrative depth to this structure, with different sagas following the destinies of several Viking clans. Each scenario introduces unique objectives and environmental conditions, along with light storytelling that ties the missions together. While the storylines are serviceable, they often take a back seat to the gameplay itself. The missions tend to follow similar patterns—build a settlement, gather resources, prepare for winter, defeat an enemy—which can make the later chapters feel repetitive. The game’s pacing also leans heavily toward the deliberate, meaning that players seeking fast, high-intensity strategy may find its tempo too slow. Yet for those who appreciate methodical progress and measured challenges, the pacing reinforces the thematic tone of survival and endurance in an unforgiving land.

One of Frozenheim’s greatest strengths lies in its presentation. The lighting and environmental design are consistently impressive, capturing the austere beauty of the North in a way that feels both grounded and poetic. The sound design enhances this sense of immersion—crackling fires, the crunch of snow underfoot, and the distant howl of the wind all add texture to the experience. The game’s music, steeped in melancholy Nordic motifs, underscores the balance between peace and hardship. Even during moments of conflict, there is a calmness to the game’s atmosphere that sets it apart from more chaotic strategy titles. It invites the player to linger, to observe, to think before acting—a rare quality in a genre often defined by speed and aggression.

However, Frozenheim is not without flaws. While the mechanics are solid, they lack the depth needed to sustain long-term engagement. The resource management system, though functional, becomes predictable over time, and the combat, while serviceable, lacks tactical diversity. The user interface can feel clunky during large-scale battles, and unit pathfinding occasionally falters, leading to frustrating moments where soldiers take illogical routes or become stuck. The campaign’s narrative repetition and limited mission variety further diminish replay value. For many players, the greatest draw may be the sandbox mode, where the absence of rigid objectives allows for a more relaxed experience focused purely on building and surviving. Even here, though, the limited technology tree and simplified economy mean that the late game can feel more like maintenance than evolution.

Despite its shortcomings, Frozenheim succeeds in evoking a distinct mood and identity. It is a game that thrives on atmosphere and pacing, appealing to those who prefer quiet reflection over constant action. It captures the hardship and beauty of Viking life without romanticizing it, reminding the player that progress in such a world is slow, fragile, and hard-won. Its blend of settlement management and strategy may not reach the mechanical heights of genre titans, but its artistic direction and thematic coherence make it stand out as an evocative, meditative experience.

In the end, Frozenheim is less about conquest and domination and more about persistence and survival. It offers a vision of Viking life that feels grounded, deliberate, and reverent rather than sensationalized. It asks the player to find beauty in restraint—to take pleasure in the quiet growth of a village, the turn of the seasons, and the constant struggle against nature’s indifference. While it may not fully satisfy those seeking depth or variety in strategy, it succeeds as a beautiful and atmospheric journey through a world both harsh and hauntingly serene.

Rating: 7/10

Frozenhein é um RTS estilo Age of Empires, mas com foco na civilização e mitologia viking. [b]Captain of Industry[/b] is an in-depth industrial, logistics and survival game that balances complex economic management, advanced production chains and demanding resource planning. Where many city-builders focus on stylish urban planning or leisurely economic loops, this game places you in the role of an engineer-captain on a remote island, starting with a handful of survivors and a rusty naval factory. From there, you must build a self-sustaining industrial society from the ground up.

The game stand out by being a production and logistics game first , and a construction game second. The game offers one of the most detailed resource cycles in the genre. Earth is moved in huge quantities with trucks and dumpers, mines gradually sink, the terrain deforms dynamically, and you have to plan your excavation areas to avoid triggering disasters. In addition to classic raw materials such as iron, coal and oil, you will later gain access to refined chemicals, electronics, environmental components and even advanced fuels such as hydrogen.

Everything is integrated into logical, realistic production chains, where errors in one place can destabilize your entire economy. A dry tank of diesel or lack of cooling water can go from a minor problem to a complete production stop in a matter of minutes.

Transportation is a core component. Trucks move almost everything in the beginning, and their routes, fuel, and numbers are critical factors. Later, you can build huge belt networks , pipelines, and conveyor-based superfactories, but planning requires thought—especially when the terrain changes or you've dug up half the island.

The progression is heavily technology-driven. You start with simple mechanics and fuel production and end up, after many hours of play, with full automation, nuclear power, advanced chemical processes and global transport via container ships.

[b]Captain of Industry[/b] has a steep learning curve. The UI and tutorials help you along the way, but the complexity of production and logistics requires long-term planning, frequent restructuring, patience and desire to optimize. On the other hand, the reward becomes all the greater when you manage to transform a raw, unproductive island into a hyper-optimized industrial complex that feeds thousands of residents.

The graphics are functional, clear and uncluttered. It's not a visually flashy game like [i]Cities: Skylines[/i], but everything is easy to read, vehicles have good animations, and industrial complexes look impressive when running at full power. The sound effects support the industrial atmosphere well without becoming noisy.

[b]Captain of Industry[/b] excels as a deep, complex, and technically demanding industrial simulation that rewards players who love to delve into detail and build gigantic, interconnected production systems. It's one of the most ambitious and satisfying games in its niche - both because it challenges your planning skills and because it offers a rare feeling of building an entire industrialized civilization from scratch. A must for engineering game enthusiasts and logistics geeks.

Dragon Throne: Battle of Red Cliffs, developed by Object Software in collaboration with ZOOM Platform Media and Jordan Freeman Group, and published by Strategy First, is an ambitious real-time strategy title set against the turbulent backdrop of China’s Three Kingdoms period. It seeks to recreate one of the most iconic historical conflicts with a blend of city management, strategic warfare, and historical storytelling. Rather than merely focusing on base construction and unit production, the game strives to immerse players in the intricate political and economic systems that shaped the legendary battle for dominance between the kingdoms of Wei, Shu, and Wu. Its combination of myth, history, and military command gives it a distinctive flavor that sets it apart from many Western RTS titles, providing a rare Eastern perspective on empire-building and warfare.

The gameplay design reflects a deliberate attempt to merge micro-level tactical control with macro-level empire management. Players are tasked not only with training and commanding armies but also with developing cities, managing resources, and ensuring the prosperity of their territories. Each faction offers a unique campaign centered on a historical warlord—Cao Cao, Liu Bei, or Sun Quan—each representing different political ideals and strategic approaches. The player must manage professions within the population, training citizens as soldiers, artisans, or laborers, and then reallocating them depending on the kingdom’s needs. This flexible class system is one of the game’s most intriguing features, emphasizing the delicate balance between economic sustainability and military strength. It introduces a realistic tension that mirrors the actual challenges faced by ancient rulers during prolonged wars.

The military component operates on a separate battlefield map, emphasizing tactical positioning, morale management, and hero-driven engagements. The inclusion of historical heroes such as Zhao Yun, Zhou Yu, and Guan Yu adds a layer of depth to combat, as each character possesses specialized abilities and leadership bonuses that can sway the outcome of battles. These hero units not only serve as powerful commanders but also symbolize the legendary spirit of the era, tying the gameplay directly to the narrative’s historical context. The battles themselves can be expansive and demanding, requiring a strategic understanding of terrain, formation, and timing. Although the artificial intelligence can at times be inconsistent, and unit control may lack the refinement seen in more modern RTS games, the sense of scale and ambition is undeniable. Players who enjoy methodical, large-scale strategy rather than fast-paced skirmishes will find satisfaction in its slower but weightier rhythm.

Visually, Dragon Throne demonstrates the limitations of its era, relying on traditional 2D graphics and an isometric perspective. While functional, the presentation does not fully capture the grandeur or chaos of the historical conflicts it represents. The environments are somewhat repetitive, and the unit animations feel dated by contemporary standards. Yet, what the game lacks in graphical polish it compensates for in atmosphere and authenticity. The soundtrack and sound effects evoke the tone of epic warfare, and the period-appropriate music reinforces the historical immersion. The interface, though utilitarian, provides access to a complex array of statistics, production options, and diplomatic features that deepen the strategic layer of the experience. Patience is essential, as mastering its systems requires time and a genuine interest in the interplay between governance and warfare.

The single-player campaigns offer a long and demanding experience, with each scenario gradually escalating in complexity. The missions often revolve around securing resources, conquering rival territories, and defending key strongholds, but the interconnected economic and political systems give each campaign a sense of progression. Beyond single-player, the game includes a multiplayer mode that allows up to eight players to compete, offering a competitive challenge for those who wish to test their strategic mettle against others. This mode amplifies the depth of the system, as human opponents can exploit weaknesses and demand creative adaptation in ways the AI cannot. The economic micromanagement, while sometimes tedious, rewards long-term planning and strategic foresight rather than impulsive decision-making, making each victory feel earned through careful governance as much as battlefield prowess.

Despite its many strengths, Dragon Throne: Battle of Red Cliffs is not without flaws. Its pacing can be slow for players expecting quick combat resolutions, and the lack of visual dynamism may limit its appeal to those accustomed to flashier modern strategy titles. The game’s complexity, though impressive, may also intimidate newcomers unfamiliar with the genre’s older design philosophies. However, for enthusiasts of deep historical simulation and fans of Chinese history, these very qualities become part of its charm. The authenticity of its setting, the meticulous attention to economic and social systems, and the inclusion of legendary figures from the Romance of the Three Kingdoms lend it a sense of gravitas rarely found in Western-developed RTS games.

Ultimately, Dragon Throne: Battle of Red Cliffs stands as a testament to a time when strategy games dared to merge history, politics, and warfare into a unified experience. It does not simply retell the story of the Red Cliffs but invites the player to live through it—managing resources, leading armies, and navigating the fragile alliances that defined the age. While it may not rival the technical refinement of later titles, its ambition and authenticity make it a unique and rewarding journey for those willing to embrace its deliberate pace and complexity. It remains a memorable piece of strategy game history, capturing both the spirit of the Three Kingdoms and the strategic imagination of a developer unafraid to aim high.

Nonetheless, the developers had the right mindset making this game and I'm looking forward to them making similar albeit more intriguing puzzle games in the future.

Time Rifters, developed by Proton Studio Inc, is one of those rare indie shooters built around a single clever idea and confident enough to let that idea drive the entire experience. Rather than teaming you with AI companions or online players, the game turns your past performances into your future squadmates. You enter a combat arena, fight alone, and inevitably fail to destroy every target before time runs out. Then the timeline resets, you re-enter the same space, and the ghost of your previous run continues firing alongside you. After repeating this process several times, you’ve built a four-person strike team composed entirely of earlier versions of yourself. It’s an elegantly simple concept, but the consequences are profound—it transforms the traditionally solitary rhythm of a single-player shooter into something strategic, cooperative, and surprisingly introspective.

The arenas themselves are compact but thoughtfully arranged, essentially functioning as score-driven combat puzzles. Most enemies don’t attack—they exist to be destroyed efficiently. The challenge comes not from survival, but from optimization. Which weapon should your first run invest in? Should you sweep the outer perimeter before focusing on high-value targets? Will your future selves benefit from a setup shot made two resets earlier? Time Rifters rewards players who think several steps ahead, treating each loop like a chess move. The first life often feels exploratory, learning spawn layouts and vulnerabilities, while the final loop becomes a synchronized ballet of firepower, where each ghost-run contributes to a carefully choreographed takedown. That feeling—watching your former selves perfectly execute a plan you’ve spent minutes refining—remains uniquely satisfying.

Weapon customization supports this layered strategy without overwhelming it. Each gun offers distinct strengths—scattershot cannons for crowd clearing, precision rifles for weak points, plasma for sustained streams, rockets for burst destruction—and each can be upgraded mid-run. Because every life uses its own loadout, players effectively assemble a multi-role team, with each past self specializing in a particular task. Time Rifters doesn’t drown the player in unnecessary stats or complicated skill trees; instead, it asks them to understand cause and effect. The result is an accessible system with surprising depth, especially for those who enjoy min-maxing or experimenting with builds.

Visually, the game embraces a clean, minimalist arena aesthetic built from bright colors, geometric shapes, and glowing voxel enemies. The style isn't flashy, but it makes every battlefield readable and every target immediately identifiable—crucial in a game where seconds matter. The soundtrack leans into electronic rhythms that match the looping, time-bending structure, pushing the action forward without overwhelming it. Everything about Time Rifters’ presentation feels tuned toward clarity and momentum, ensuring focus remains on tactical execution rather than sensory overload.

Despite its strengths, the game’s limitations stem from its narrow focus. Time Rifters is not a sprawling campaign shooter, and players expecting narrative, world-building, character progression, or boss encounters may feel underwhelmed. Its 15 arenas offer several hours of experimentation, but once you’ve mastered their layouts and optimized your strategies, the experience naturally winds down. This isn’t a flaw in design—Time Rifters feels built for short but intense bursts of play rather than lengthy marathons—but it does mean longevity depends on how much you enjoy replaying for higher scores or perfect runs.

Its pacing can also feel unusual for players accustomed to shooters built around adrenaline and improvisation. Time Rifters encourages planning rather than spontaneity, deliberation rather than panic. It’s possible for new players to misunderstand the core appeal, treating the game like a standard arena shooter and missing the strategic dimension that makes it shine. But once that mental shift occurs, the game opens up into something much richer than its simple structure suggests.

What ultimately makes Time Rifters memorable is how personal it feels. Success is not granted through AI assistance or matchmaking luck—it’s earned by collaborating with your earlier decisions, strengths, and mistakes. Your ghosts don’t just help you win; they remind you that every run has value, even failures, because each contributes to the final outcome. In a genre built on forward motion, Time Rifters encourages players to look back—literally—and learn from themselves.

For fans of arcade shooters, clever mechanics, and score-based challenges, Time Rifters is an inventive, polished, and deeply satisfying experience. It’s short, focused, and proudly niche, delivering exactly what it promises without unnecessary padding. Those seeking narrative-driven campaigns or extensive content may move on quickly, but players who love mastering systems, refining strategies, and witnessing ideas pay off across timelines will find a standout gem. It’s a game built on the simple thrill of self-improvement—replayed, refracted, and made tangible through time.

Man… Eldest Souls is one of those games that makes you question your life choices. You know that feeling when you’ve been fighting the same boss for two hours straight, your hands are shaking, your eyes are burning, and every time you die at 2% HP, you just… stare at the screen in silence? Yeah. That’s this game.

This isn’t your usual “oh I’ll just grind and get stronger” kind of game  nah, this one locks you in an arena with a monster that feels like it personally hates you. Every fight is pure boss battle, no filler, no mercy. You die, respawn, and die again like 50 times per boss and somehow, it still convinces you to try one more time.

And when you finally win? When you land that last hit after hours of agony? You don’t even cheer  you just sit there, empty, maybe whisper a quiet “finally” while your soul leaves your body.

But here’s the thing… beneath all that frustration, there’s this weird satisfaction. The combat is fast, tight, and beautifully brutal. Every death teaches you something, even if it’s just “don’t get greedy.” The music hits, the visuals are gorgeous, and when you pull off a perfect dodge and strike back  for a second, you feel like a god.

Then you die again.

So yeah, Eldest Souls is not for the faint of heart. It will break you, test your patience, and probably make you cry once or twice. But if you survive it? You’ll remember every victory like a battle scar.

Sumire definitely falls into the "depressing coming of age story" indie subgenre, but it's just a really unique and well-done iteration of that. I bought it on a whim for the gorgeous art (and because it was 89 cents) and was surprised at how much I ended up liking it.

As is par for the course in these games, tween Sumire's life absolutely sucks. Her self-involved father is leaving her depressed mother, and her grandma, the only stable adult presence in her life, just died. Her childhood best friend has dumped her for a cooler crowd, and her crush is moving away. Just as things seem hopeless, Sumire is contacted by a flower spirit who promises to give her the best day ever in return for completing its tasks. Along with the spirit, Sumire is able to confront her problems and face her life with renewed hope.

I think part of the reason Sumire worked for me where a lot of these games don't is because it contextualizes Sumire's issues as just part of being human -- the conclusion isn't just the "everything sucks forever" of a lot of these games, but more, "Yeah, becoming an adult is hard and rough, but it's also a chance to decide for yourself who you are and how you want to live." Sumire's day is spent as much learning to appreciate the people in her village and the nature of her surroundings as it is confronting her bullies and her parents, and so it ends up a "this too will pass" coming-of-age story instead of something more doomerist.

It's also just really competently told. Sumire is easy to root for and believe in and the people around her feel real, the problems feel relatable, and the premise gives it a shot of originality these games often lack. The point-and-click elements are well-designed and the gameplay is smooth.

Part of it for me is definitely that I went in with no expectations, but if a short, bittersweet artsy game is your kind of thing, this is definitely worth checking out.
