Indiana Jones and the Infernal Machine, developed by LucasArts and published by Lucasfilm and Disney, marked a significant turning point for the adventurer’s transition into 3D gaming. Released in 1999, it was the first Indiana Jones title to embrace full three-dimensional environments, reflecting the influence of games like Tomb Raider while seeking to retain the personality and spirit of the beloved film series. Set in 1947, the game finds Dr. Jones drawn back into danger as Cold War tensions simmer. When Soviet agents begin excavating ancient sites in search of a mysterious device said to grant godlike power, Indy joins forces with a CIA operative to uncover the truth behind the so-called “Infernal Machine.” What begins as an archaeological expedition soon escalates into a globe-trotting quest involving myth, betrayal, and supernatural forces. The premise perfectly suits the tone of the franchise—equal parts pulp adventure and mystical thriller—and establishes a narrative that feels authentic to the Indiana Jones mythos even without a film to accompany it.

From the very beginning, the game’s ambition is evident. The design of Indiana Jones and the Infernal Machine emphasizes exploration and puzzle-solving over linear combat, creating a sense of discovery that recalls the best moments of the films. Each of the game’s seventeen chapters takes place in a distinct, sprawling location—from Babylonian ruins to Himalayan temples, from volcanic caverns to desert tombs—and each one is filled with elaborate puzzles, deadly traps, and environmental hazards. These levels are impressively large for their time, often requiring players to backtrack, experiment, and think spatially in order to progress. There is a satisfying rhythm to exploring these ruins: deciphering ancient mechanisms, swinging across chasms with Indy’s whip, or spotting a hidden lever that opens a new passage. The game rewards patience and curiosity, rewarding players with relics, upgrades, and secret areas for those who take their time. The design captures the essence of what makes Indiana Jones compelling—not simply fighting enemies, but unraveling the mysteries of lost civilizations through intellect and instinct.

Visually, the game was ambitious for the late 1990s. Built on a proprietary engine developed by LucasArts, it pushed the capabilities of consumer PCs of the time. While the polygon count is modest by modern standards, the environmental design and atmosphere carry the experience. Temples shimmer with eerie light, dusty ruins echo with the sound of wind, and subterranean chambers glow with the supernatural energy of the titular machine. The texture work and color palette successfully convey a sense of ancient mystery, and while the character models appear blocky today, the art direction remains strong enough to evoke the cinematic flair of the films. Clint Bajakian’s score channels John Williams’ spirit without direct imitation, delivering a sweeping orchestral sound that enhances the sense of scale. The voice acting, though serviceable, doesn’t feature Harrison Ford, and while the substitute actor captures Indy’s gruff charm reasonably well, the absence of Ford’s voice is still felt. Nonetheless, the game exudes the tone of an Indiana Jones adventure through its presentation and pacing, with in-engine cutscenes that were surprisingly cinematic for their era.

Where the game stumbles most noticeably is in its controls and camera system, both of which were typical growing pains of early 3D action-adventure titles. Movement feels stiff and deliberate, requiring players to line up jumps and time maneuvers with precision that the clunky mechanics don’t always accommodate. Combat is also awkward—Indy can wield pistols, shotguns, and his whip, but aiming and movement often feel imprecise, making fights more frustrating than exciting. The camera tends to shift unpredictably, especially during platforming segments, resulting in missed jumps or unseen hazards. These mechanical flaws are the most common criticisms of the game and remain its most significant barrier to accessibility today. However, with time and patience, players can acclimate to the game’s rhythm, and once the controls become second nature, the immersion begins to take hold. Despite its technical roughness, there is an undeniable sense of satisfaction in mastering its challenges and overcoming obstacles through persistence.

The narrative pacing of Infernal Machine does a fine job of maintaining interest throughout its lengthy runtime. Unlike many games of its time, which offered minimal storytelling, this title embraces dialogue and cutscenes to build intrigue. The interplay between Indy and the CIA agent Sophia Hapgood, a returning character from Indiana Jones and the Fate of Atlantis, adds both humor and tension to the plot. Their banter injects humanity into the story, balancing the darker tone of the Cold War backdrop. The fusion of mythology and science fiction—a recurring theme in Indiana Jones stories—is handled with creativity, culminating in a finale that feels suitably grand. While the game doesn’t have the wit or pacing of the original trilogy, it successfully channels the adventurous energy that defines the franchise. It gives players the sense of being part of a cinematic epic, moving from one exotic locale to another, piecing together ancient riddles, and facing impossible odds with nothing but courage and intellect.

For its time, Indiana Jones and the Infernal Machine was a remarkable undertaking. It offered a more complex and story-driven experience than most 3D adventure games on the market and stood as a rare example of a licensed game that aspired to more than simple fan service. The expansive level design and emphasis on exploration helped it stand apart from its contemporaries, even if comparisons to Tomb Raider were inevitable. The puzzles are often cleverly integrated into the environment, requiring a mixture of observation, experimentation, and lateral thinking. When everything clicks, the experience is deeply rewarding—solving an intricate temple mechanism or finally reaching a long-sought artifact after hours of peril gives the player a sense of accomplishment that few games replicate. However, the same ambition that makes the game engaging also exposes its flaws: repetitive platforming sequences, uneven combat, and the occasional pacing lull. Yet even in these moments, the atmosphere and sense of adventure carry it forward.

Looking back, Indiana Jones and the Infernal Machine represents both a product of its time and a precursor to the cinematic adventure games that would follow. Its clunky controls and early-3D limitations are undeniable, but beneath those flaws lies a game bursting with imagination and reverence for its source material. It captures the essence of Indiana Jones in a way few games have managed, combining danger, intellect, and the allure of the unknown into a cohesive journey. Even today, the game’s spirit endures—its ruins may be dated, its edges rough, but the sense of exploration remains timeless. For fans of the franchise, it offers a faithful and satisfying adventure that feels unmistakably Indiana Jones, and for enthusiasts of classic PC gaming, it stands as a fascinating artifact from an era when ambition often outpaced technology. Despite its imperfections, it remains a testament to LucasArts’ willingness to innovate and a reminder that true adventure is as much about persistence and discovery as it is about polish.

Rating: 8/10

I still remember the first time I played Indiana Jones and the Infernal Machine. I must have been around ten years old, sitting in front of a beige CRT monitor that hummed softly like a relic itself. The CD case had Indy on the cover — hat tilted, whip coiled — and just holding it felt like an invitation to adventure.

I didn’t care that the controls were stiff or that I kept falling into lava pits every few minutes. Back then, it all felt real. Every temple, every puzzle, every lost artifact sparked something in my imagination. I wasn’t just a kid at home — I was an archaeologist uncovering ancient secrets, racing against the Soviets, saving the world one dusty ruin at a time.

When that sweeping John Williams–style theme played, my heart would race. I’d scribble “maps” on scrap paper, pretending I was keeping notes in Indy’s journal. Even the frustrating parts — the jumps that never quite landed, the camera that betrayed me — are memories I cherish now.

Coming back to it today is like opening a time capsule. The textures are blocky, the animations stiff, but somehow, that only makes it more beautiful. It reminds me of when games didn’t need perfection — just imagination and heart.

Verdict:
For anyone who once dreamed of being Indiana Jones — this isn’t just a game. It’s a memory you can still play.

Sir Bedlam Productions really knew what he was doing when he made this game, and i think he did a great job on it.

The entire plug-in library is in Japanese. If you want to do anything other than just display still images and text, you need to read Japanese to use the tools available. Saying this software is available in English is legally true, but false in every way that matters.

Even displaying text is iffy. Just typing a few words is displayed easily through the beautiful interface for displaying text. If you want that text to contain a single variable, like the Player's name for example, all that text needs to instead happen in an awkward and slightly different interface for a different tool that uses some kind of proprietary twist on JavaScript. At which point, it becomes easier to just do all your text in that interface, instead. Saying you can use the software without any programming or scripting is again, entirely false in every way that matters.

This tool seems like it's super useful for Japanese people who have slightly more technical know-how than average. If you're an English speaker, it's basically a really expensive and hard to use PowerPoint clone.

It's a good starting tool for your first game dev project. It helps you think about what makes a good VN and enables it. If you want to do more customization than what this program allows, that's a sign that you need to graduate to a more in-depth language like Python, but again, this is a great place to start and focus on your visuals and story, not the code.

I’ll be honest, I’ve been avoiding this one. I picked it up around its original release because I’m a pretty big fan of the developer’s previous game, Spaceport Hope. The pitch is good, the game looks expansive, and so I had high hopes for digging deep into External Visions. But it didn’t take me long to start running into roadblocks to my enjoyment, more and more until I decided to put the game down for awhile. Maybe I wasn’t in the mood for an off-beat metroidvania, I thought. I’ve tried to get back into it several times since then, and each time has only solidified what I already knew… It’s not me, game, it’s you.

External Visions ostensibly takes place in the mind of a regular everyman struggling with depression. His battle has turned his mental landscape into an actual battlefield, rife with grotesque monsters and oppressive entities. If he is to have any chance of escaping his pain, you’ll need to guide him through the vast halls and labyrinths to do battle with the beasts that inhabit them. You’ll meet some helpful folks along the way, presumably positive parts of his psyche or memories of people that have survived the darkness. Ultimately you’ll be questing for a whole little society in here, which only makes the stakes higher.

Again, it’s a good pitch for a game, but the mind is forever a perilous place to place your game. Surrealism and symbolism aren’t as simple as putting cracks or mold on your floor tiles, after all. Every part of the game’s design needs to be informed by the decision to set it in an unreal place, making sure to consider the meaning of every enemy placement, color palette, and sidequest. To put it bluntly, External Visions doesn’t do that. You know this is all inside your character’s mind because people tell you, not because there’s any clear symbolism that reveals his traumas and coping mechanisms. There’s also no significant character development OUTSIDE your character’s mind, which gives less context and less reason to care about whatever happens INSIDE it.

That wasn’t even what hung me up on the game, though. External Visions plays like a solid enough metroidvania, giving you a vast map of interconnected rooms to explore and items to find among them. However, your primary means of overcoming obstacles is not in the items you collect, but in weapons you essentially borrow. There are terminals all over the game with numbers 1, 2, and 3 on them. Each is a ranged weapon with a special purpose, like 3 which fires yellow blasts that solidify into blocks you can jump on. You must find a terminal to use that weapon, and you can only use one at a time. I know what you’re thinking, and yes, those terminals are not terribly numerous. So to solve many of the puzzles in the game, you’re going to be backtracking just to pick up the weapon you’re supposed to have at the moment.

It’s an absolutely inexplicable design decision, and one that kills the pacing of the game. I’ve absolutely had moments where I had a choice between two weapons, picked one, and progressed for 5 or 10 minutes just to reach a roadblock I should have picked the other for. It’s hardly the only issue with the game, either. The difficulty is all over the place, starting out even enough for the first hour or two and then spiraling out of control from the library. Controller support is limited and may require manual bindings to get it working, and some of the choices for sound effects can seriously grate after awhile. These are mostly small complaints but the add to the big ones in a way that’s hard to ignore.

I know a lot of heart went into making this game, which is why I hate having to describe it in these terms. But there’s no getting around it, External Visions doesn’t come together in a satisfying way. The core themes are not as fleshed out as they need to be, and the core gameplay has serious deficiencies that make it hard to stick with. It makes it that much harder to see decent art direction and level design go into such a flawed game, but no matter how much I want to enjoy it, I can’t. I hope this title has been a learning experience for team BitClub, and that their next game is every bit the success I wanted this one to be.

Cubetory starts with a tiny island where you need to mine cubes, paint them, and send them to the mysterious pit. Upgrades are basically a series of increasingly complex spacial puzzles requiring automation and involving different cube types and patterns affected by how you manipulate your cubes and lay out your machines.

A few factors make this game very satisfying to play. All the little cubes move in sync but not only that, they move in sync with the original background music. I like that whenever I click a new upgrade it's because I've accomplished a goal, and that it sometimes leads to my island becoming bigger. As you continue playing, it gets satisfying to rearrange your island so that sections become symmetrical. A nicely laid out island generally leads to higher throughout, which we need anyway :3 If you like organizing and efficiency, the game is very addicting and very fun!

Cubetory is at the same time very chill and quite challenging, a hard balance to hit.

This puzzle factory game doesn't challenge you by making you race a clock or defend your factory from enemies but rather by forcing you to come up with a space efficient and performant design.

Having played the demo on it's initial release I can see and feel the amount of blood, sweat and tears that were poured into the game since then.

If what I described sounds interesting to you, give the game a shot! Recommended

G-Darius marks a passage of the series to 3D (or rather 2.5D), and also what was an occasional gimmick in Gaiden, capturing a few minibosses to use them like drones, ascending to a full-on game mechanic. The Capture Ball allows to catch almost any non-boss enemy and not just get additional firepower and a shield with the right positiong, as captured enemies can be either turned into bombs, or absorbed into a super-beam that becomes even more important against bosses, as they have their own beams which can be contained if not overwhelmed and absorbed by your own, causing massive damage to them. Add the captured minibosses having special attacks activated using fighting games control inputs (what?), and you can see how once again the Darius series was capable of innovating and improving itself.

The visuals, like a lot of 3D of the second half of the 1990s, haven't aged completely graciously. Of course, in that early era, seeing those 3D backgrounds move was impressive but nowadays they are just scarce in detail when not just empty. It's thankfully saved by not needing to be realistic, and once again the bosses steal the show, they still look fantastic in design, and the HD treatment makes them even more striking. So much that a special "Showcase" mode allows to confront a few of them simulating a dual screen setup, aka making full use of a widescreen monitor.
What has not aged at all is the soundtrack, which is very different from what you'd expect from a shmup, more often than not it is ominous and surreal (do I hear a voice saying "Meditation" when the end of level music starts?), another way Darius sets itself apart.

There are "only" 15 levels this time, as a run is made of only 5 levels, with 5 different final bosses and related endings. There are, however, mid-level points where depending on the position of the ship on the screen, you get to see variations on the levels and some differences in the bosses, so there is still quite a bit to play even within the same levels. And don't think a run is shorter than in Gaiden, because bosses take long to defeat. They are bigger and badder, with impressive arrays of attacks as they waltz from a side to another and attack even from the background at times, and lots of armor to whittle down unless you catch some minor enemies they release and go into a beam duel. If you play it right, it's exhilarating.

The biggest wall I've met is the difficulty. Really, even if it allows for unlimited credits and so to "cheese" a run, the enemy attacks are so overwhelming I often didn't find any fun even in that. It is that punishing, also showing how the balance of a game can be upset in the name of forcing to drop more credits in its original arcade incarnation. I wondered if my memories of G-Darius were skewed and turns out that the surprisingly decent PC port of the early 2000s, the first time I experienced the game, was based on the console version, which for obvious reasons was made more accessible to players. It is, in fact and thankfully, included in this Steam package, even if unfortunately it's the only one without an HD version, and the in-engine cutscenes are replaced by the badly aged CGI you can expect from the era.

Darius Gaiden stays my favourite due to better aged visuals and not having very long boss fights, but I can't be too harsh on G-Darius, even if I coudn't enjoy it fully I can appreciate a level of quality it hasn't lost almost three decades after it was made. It's clear it requires a level of skill and dedication I am not able to give.

M2 has done their usual good job, also adding a Training Mode that allows to at least have a few more advantages to start with and/or see later levels. The "gadgets" that fill the part of the screen not occupied by the game itself with info like next level branch, boss energy and special moves of the captured minibosses are always welcome. I just wish, once again, they put the ability to configure keyboard inputs at will.

My Girlfriend’s Special Place is a compact but polished romance visual novel developed by feng and published by Sekai Project, one that leans fully into the emotional rhythms and character-driven beats typical of Japanese romantic storytelling. It follows Youhei, an unassuming young man whose quiet life is abruptly disrupted when he crosses paths with his childhood friend Fuyuka Akiyoshi for the first time in years. What should be a nostalgic reunion instead becomes a fraught misunderstanding that leaves Youhei coerced into becoming Fuyuka’s personal butler. The premise is intentionally awkward, even provocative, but it sets the stage for a dynamic in which buried memories, unresolved feelings, and subtle class differences unravel over the course of a brief but focused narrative. The story wastes little time establishing the tension between them, and from there it allows small moments of gentleness and vulnerability to gradually soften the sharper elements of their relationship.

Visually, the game is polished and expressive in the way modern visual novels aspire to be. Character illustrations are attractive and detailed, with smooth shading, clean outlines, and outfits that shift naturally across different scenes. Fuyuka’s design, in particular, receives extra attention through multiple expressions, distinct poses, and outfit variations that reinforce her emotional range. The backgrounds support the tone well—quiet school halls, warm interiors, and nighttime streets offer a pleasing sense of place. Voice acting further elevates the presentation, giving Fuyuka’s lines warmth, impatience, or softness depending on the moment while maintaining the light, romantic tone the genre demands. Combined with a user interface that is crisp and easy to navigate, the game succeeds in delivering an aesthetically satisfying reading experience from start to finish.

Narratively, the visual novel blends romantic comedy, dramatic tension, and coming-of-age sentiment in a way that feels familiar but emotionally genuine. Beneath the contrived nature of the premise lies a surprisingly earnest exploration of how childhood bonds can distort or deepen over time. Youhei and Fuyuka’s relationship shifts quickly: moments of playful teasing give way to awkward hesitations, misunderstandings open the door to unexpected confessions, and the facade Fuyuka initially presents slowly cracks to reveal insecurities tied to her family history. The butler–mistress dynamic, while occasionally discomforting, becomes a narrative tool for exploring dependency, pride, and intimacy rather than remaining a simple comedic gimmick. The story’s pacing is brisk—players can complete the game in a handful of hours—but it remains emotionally grounded, giving its central relationship enough space to feel believable despite the short runtime.

Mechanically, My Girlfriend’s Special Place sticks closely to the established conventions of the visual novel genre. The bulk of the experience involves reading dialogue and narration, with occasional choices that lead to different endings and unlockable CG images. While the branching is limited and the overall structure linear, the game’s inclusion of scenes from Fuyuka’s perspective helps round out her character and adds emotional depth that complements Youhei’s viewpoint. Achievements and a gallery system provide small incentives for replaying choices, but this is primarily a narrative-driven work intended to be experienced rather than extensively gamed. For players seeking intricate branching paths or deep systems, the simplicity may be disappointing; for those who enjoy a concentrated romantic tale, the focus works in its favor.

Thematically, the visual novel touches on childhood nostalgia, class differences, vulnerability wrapped in pride, and the messy process of reconnecting with someone who once meant the world to you. While the story remains mostly lighthearted, it doesn’t shy away from exploring guilt, embarrassment, and insecurity in ways that feel relatable. Some moments—especially early scenes involving false accusations and coercion—may feel uncomfortable or questionable, even within a romantic-comedy framework. The game clearly expects players to accept these events as part of the setup rather than examine them too closely, but sensitivity to power dynamics varies from reader to reader. Those who are open to the premise will likely find the later emotional growth rewarding; those who are not may struggle to fully invest in the relationship.

As a complete package, My Girlfriend’s Special Place delivers exactly what it sets out to provide: a short, charming, visually pleasing romance with enough personality to stand out yet enough familiarity to feel comfortable. It doesn’t attempt to reinvent the visual novel format, nor does it aim for emotional grandiosity. Instead, it offers a focused story about two people rediscovering their connection, told with sincerity, humor, and polished presentation. For fans of romance visual novels—especially those drawn to childhood-friend narratives, soft drama, and expressive character art—it is an appealing and worthwhile experience. For players looking for a longer, more complex, or more interactive VN, it may feel like a brief interlude rather than a fully fleshed-out journey.

Neckbreak is an uncompromisingly stylish and aggressively fast first-person shooter that stands apart from both classic “boomer shooters” and modern cinematic FPS titles. Developed by MGP Studios in collaboration with Solid9 Studio and published by MGP Studios, it delivers a grimy, neon-drenched cyberpunk world where precision, reflexes and outright audacity matter more than armor values or military equipment. Set in the corporate-ruled city of Crimson Tide, the game follows an ordinary office worker by day who transforms into a vigilante by night—a duality that becomes the narrative and mechanical backbone of the experience. Through this structure, Neckbreak intertwines a looping daily routine with combat challenges, psychological strain and drug-enhanced abilities that create a world constantly teetering between clarity and chaos.

Combat is the game’s defining feature, and it wastes no time proving how punishing yet exhilarating it can be. Encounters are lightning fast—both you and your enemies can go down in a single mistake—which means the game rewards aggressive momentum rather than cautious peeking. You slide across floors, chain melee strikes, vault around corners and use a powerful superkick to send enemies or environmental objects flying. Guns feel deadly and direct, but they’re only part of a larger toolkit built around maintaining flow and maximizing style. A combo multiplier system encourages players to string together kills creatively, and well-timed kicks, environmental interactions and finishing blows all contribute to your end-of-level score. The level design supports this rhythm: tight corridors, sudden corners and explosive props ensure that battles feel intimate and unpredictable, forcing you to constantly adapt and reposition. This is a shooter where hesitation often equals death, and mastery of movement becomes just as important as aim.

Visually, Neckbreak’s cyberpunk aesthetic is bold, grimy and intentionally abrasive. Crimson Tide is a sickly neon metropolis where every streetlight hums with corporate indifference and every alley has the sense of something dangerous lurking just out of sight. The game blends low-fi textures with stylized effects, giving it a retro-inspired look without directly mimicking classic pixel art shooters. Psychedelic overlays, glitch-infused transitions and color distortions appear during high-stress or drug-influenced moments, reinforcing the protagonist’s fragile mental state. The sound design complements the visual grit, with industrial beats, sharp weapon reports and ambient city noise all contributing to the sense of a world that is both suffocating and alive.

Where Neckbreak distinguishes itself further is in its narrative ambition. Instead of a linear campaign, the game offers a branching structure with multiple paths and up to a dozen endings. Your choices—moral decisions, reliance on medication, combat behavior and how you navigate the protagonist’s daily routine—all subtly or dramatically affect outcomes. This encourages replayability not just for score-chasing, but for uncovering different story possibilities and gaining a deeper understanding of Crimson Tide’s social decay. The inclusion of a sanity system adds further nuance. As the protagonist’s psychological state shifts, visual and auditory distortions become more pronounced, altering not just the narrative tone but also the gameplay experience. It’s a bold choice, and though not every narrative thread is expanded as thoroughly as it could be, the overall sense of immersion is undeniable.

Despite its many strengths, Neckbreak is not without shortcomings. The same high-speed combat that exhilarates some players may overwhelm others, particularly during difficulty spikes where rooms full of enemies reduce reaction time to a split second. Some weapon animations and environmental interactions can feel rough around the edges, revealing the game’s indie limitations. A few players may find the shooting mechanics slightly clunky compared to more polished shooters, and the compact level design sometimes leads to encounters that feel repetitive. These issues, however, rarely overshadow the game’s commitment to its vision: a punishing, stylish cyberpunk shooter that prioritizes personality and flow.

As a whole, Neckbreak delivers a memorable and distinct experience for players who crave intensity, style and narrative experimentation. Its combination of breakneck firefights, branching storylines, psychological flair and gritty worldbuilding creates a shooter that feels both nostalgic and forward-thinking. While it may not appeal to those seeking long campaigns or AAA smoothness, it excels at offering a concentrated burst of adrenaline wrapped in neon shadows and moral ambiguity. For fans of indie FPS titles that dare to be unconventional, Neckbreak stands out as a bold and worthwhile adventure through the underbelly of a city that reflects its protagonist: unstable, violent, and undeniably compelling.

Baldur's Gate 2 is one of the best roleplaying games I have ever played and massively improves on the foundation that the first game laid out and expands on the Bhaalspawn story excellently. Only thing that pisses me off is they got rid of the "Toime for a bit of the old rough tumble" voice pack, which is really jarring as that was the voice of my character in the first game.

[h1]Baldur's Gate II: Enhanced Edition[/h1]

The past year or so I've been finding that I revisit old RPGs a lot. There's just some charm and magic that isn't there in newer titles. Obviously we still get a smash hit here and there, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 being a prime example, but there's a certain lack of Western-style RPGs that really nail it as of late.

I replayed Baldur's Gate: EE earlier this year and took my character through Baldur's Gate II: EE as well now. I've yet to do Throne of Bhaal, but I do look forward to it.

Baldur's Gate II is an absolute classic. It's the gold standard for what CRPGs have been over the past 25 years. The game all other CRPGs aspire to be like or to be as good as. Everything Baldur's Gate I did well is improved upon in II. Seeing as you continue your character from the first game, there's not a slog of going through low levels without much action economy. You start where you left off, in my case level 8, and build even further upon that foundation. More spells, more abilities, more amazing items — all of which is needed, because the game offers quite the challenge.

I played on core difficulty, and while it wasn't impossible for me by any means, having a decent amount of knowledge of the game's ruleset, Advanced D&D, there were quite a handful of fights where I had to reload multiple times. This didn't bother me at all, because it made me pause and rethink strategy. That's how these games are played. Combat-wise, there actually wasn't a dull moment in the roughly 55 hours it took for me to complete the Shadows of Amn campaign.

Continuing the same character also means a continuation of the story. Here, Baldur's Gate II also shines. Even the side quests offer interesting tales and are well worth doing due to the powerful rewards. Companions are much more fleshed out, most of them having long questlines that span the game, potential conflicts with one another, and even romances, if that's your thing.

Baldur's Gate II, and other gems of the past that I've replayed, just have "the sauce". Maybe it's nostalgia for a man in his 30s, but it honestly feels like they don't make 'em like they used to. They can be hard to get into, having dated graphics and systems that aren't well explained in-game, but they honestly just have depth. That's the secret "sauce" that's missing as of late, I think. Depth in the story, the systems, encounter design, and characters. Baldur's Gate II has it in spades.

A classic, [b]10/10 — must-play CRPG.[/b] The first one to do it best.

玩法较为简单。玩家排班、处理基础任务并做出对话选择。系统深度有限，但循环流程支持叙事推进。内容存在重复，但新场景解锁速度适中，进度感稳定。

呈现风格明亮且富表现力。角色立绘简洁且面部细节良好。背景简单但信息清晰。音乐轻快并循环频繁，符合轻松基调。性能稳定且加载时间短。

本地化质量可接受。存在少量语法问题但不影响理解。界面导航清晰，存档选项灵活。教程简短并足以解释基础系统。

总体而言，该作适合偏好角色驱动叙事的玩家。缺乏机制深度可能劝退追求挑战者。对于享受轻松恋爱构建与日常幽默的用户，本作在其目标范围内表现良好。

韩国galgame确实令我感到陌生，不过玩起来还是可以的。
没想到一周目一个都没有攻略，光顾着经营店铺了。还好可以直接看后日谈。

I'm borderline on refunding this after my first little look at it, but it's $9.99 and I've nothing to do this evening so I may fool around with it some more.  It's definitely something that I *should* totally love, but there are bugs since it's day-3 EA and more annoyingly literally nothing is explained.  I have no idea why I can't do certain things when I have the money, or why the agent person can't drive to the gas station so each day I just trade the lumber mill back and forth with the competitor (this isn't fun or engaging, just annoying).  I have no idea if there is a way to protect the lumber mill but maybe that's in the tech tree or something.  I had no idea why I couldn't research things when I had the cash, but figured that out I guess.  I have no idea why I can't test the cars.  It says you have to save it first, but I've saved it to a line and have been producing it, so... huh?  I had no idea why my factory stopped producing but figured out I need some wrench things, so I went to the assembly plant for that and it can't assemble them because I don't have the resources.  Where do I get the resources other than wood from the lumber mill?  No idea.  I went to the bank where it says you can order resources for $, and clicked to do so, but nothing happened.  Is this a bug?  Another thing that I just need to click around until I figure it out or don't figure it out?   If I can't get resources, the game just ends since I can't produce cars.

This feels more like what I'm used to as an alpha/pre-EA play-test on Steam rather than Early Access to be sold.  To be frank, the two pre-EA testers I'm fooling with now are more ready than this game, but I buy way too many games to be mad about something like that at this point so it's just a little annoying.  No click to move the map with mouse is a little annoying too, and no pause with space bar is always annoying in the rare games that don't have it like this one, but the bugs and the whole idea of just having to click around and try to figure things out yourself in a manufacturing game with logistics and competition for resources and such, is just really bad.  For some reason the camera stutters moving around the map too, which I've just never seen in a game like this, but I'd assume that's something that will get worked out if the game gets updates.

Car Manufacture was a total dud, Production Line is basically a buggy ancient mess, and I can't even remember the names of the dozen or so other car manufacturing games that have appeared and faded away, so I guess once I get too frustrated with this it's back to Gear City.  As I'm writing this I'm thinking I'll keep it and screw around some more, wait for updates, and see what happens because the options are few and terrible other than Gear City which is amazing but just spreadsheets, and this is pretty inexpensive so I think they know where they are with it right now.

起初看这部作为剧情作的评价不错才推的，这也是支撑我推完的动力。还特地等到了冬天去推。实际上是对我来说并不有趣甚至昏睡的充满荤段子的日常、谜语人叙事，每条线路最后透露一点似有似无的男主身份和早就猜到了的主线和结局。
玩到绫线时还是充满期待的，这条线也可以算是主线的前置剧情，把故事背景和人物联系都补充得更完善了。绫这个角色本身的塑造就很不错，不是传统刻板印象中的媚系学姐形象，而是给人一种介于帅气与可爱之间，更倾向于可靠、能令人安心的形象。我更希望没有End2，仅仅停留在TE中的绫就够了。先前有浏览到他人发表的对于End2的意难平评价，所以同样抱着期待先去打出这个End，感觉吃了一大口。我很难不怀疑这是强加上去的一种恶意。我不知道在这里初雪究竟是什么样的一种情感，在那个时间完成hs的KPI。在选项分歧的节点，初雪明明应该满溢着对樱和兰的思念想要完成他的复仇达到他自己的生存意义。与绫的关系止步于「同病相怜」，确实才应该是最合理的。如果选择进入End2线路，那么与绫的hs的发生就用“或许是出于孤独感”这一理由而展开，真的太悲伤了。绫在那一时刻就像处于湖中的初雪身旁出现的一块浮木，短暂地给予他依靠和安全感，最后还要落得被反复伤害的结局，真的除了恶意不知道怎么评价，像推进剧情用的工具人。但至少End2可以算是完成了复仇吧…
看到喷初雪这一角色塑造的也挺多的，个人在这一点上感觉没那么雷，樱和初雪说白了都是被强加上去的命运，复仇不该是初雪自己的义务。咲耶挺像守护甜心里的歌呗的，一直会幻视，其实对这个角色印象还挺好的……吾妻夜线里那个配角叫什么我已经忘了，但是太茶了反复恶心我，看的我无名怒火。其他地方对我来说没什么记忆点，甚至白熊线让我觉得很降智，直接把白熊塑造成纯纯的傻白甜，初雪无论干嘛都无脑追随，刺的哪怕是白熊自己估计都要写相信到最后，和TE里承受了这么多的痛苦最后还燃了一把但依旧选择原谅毕业如出一辙，甚至都没有感觉到生气而是真的觉得很蠢。除了记得fripside的OP以外真的和失忆了一样。水月陵的音乐在这部作品里面也没给我留下印象。总结，对不上新岛夕电波，没活硬整很膈应。

Asterix & Obelix Slap Them All! 2 is a colorful, boisterous beat ’em up that embraces the spirit of the classic French comic books with an enthusiasm that is hard to ignore. Developed by Mr. Nutz Studio and published by Microids, the game continues the hand-drawn, comic-authentic visual style of its predecessor while attempting to expand the scale and variety of its brawling adventure. From the opening frames, it’s clear that the developers once again prioritized capturing the charm of Goscinny and Uderzo’s world—every character animation, background painting, and punishing slap feels like it was lifted directly from the pages of the comic. This visual fidelity is not just surface-level polish; it creates a sense of stepping straight into an Asterix cartoon, and for fans of the series, that alone is a genuine delight.

The gameplay follows the traditional beat ’em up formula: moving from left to right, clearing waves of Roman soldiers, pirates, brigands, and an assortment of foes who all seem determined to stand between the Gauls and their objectives. You can choose to play as Asterix, who is quick and nimble, or Obelix, who moves more slowly but delivers massive blows. Local co-op remains one of the game’s biggest strengths—playing as the iconic duo side by side brings a lively, chaotic energy to the combat, echoing the camaraderie that defines the heroes’ relationship in the comics. Movement is smooth, the animations are packed with charm, and simply watching Romans go flying through the air after a well-timed slap often feels like a reward in itself.

The adventure spans a range of environments, from familiar Gallic forests to urban Roman settings, coastal villages, and underground lairs. Each level carries its own visual identity, and some stages introduce mild exploration elements, giving the game more depth than a pure corridor brawler. Boss encounters bring additional flavor, with exaggerated personalities and attack patterns that fit the humor and tone of the franchise. Collectibles, branching pathways, and small optional objectives add a layer of replay value, even if they don’t dramatically alter the core experience.

However, the game’s greatest weaknesses stem from repetition and limited mechanical depth. While the slap-heavy combat is satisfying in short bursts, the move sets are small, enemy types repeat often, and the encounters begin to blur together as the hours pass. Even with the attempt at variety across stages, the gameplay loop rarely evolves beyond defeating large groups of similar enemies using the same handful of combos. This repetition becomes especially apparent during longer play sessions, where the charm of the animations struggles to mask the formulaic structure underneath.

Difficulty balancing also fluctuates. Some stages feel breezy and approachable, while others suddenly spike with overwhelming enemy counts or projectiles that require precision the controls don’t always perfectly support. The knife-throwing enemies in particular break the otherwise casual rhythm of the game, introducing frustration in a title that generally aims for broad accessibility. The gap between Asterix and Obelix’s fighting styles also isn’t as wide as it appears at first glance. Despite their different animations and attributes, they share similar move structures, limiting the sense of experimentation or strategic switching between characters.

In terms of content, the campaign is moderately sized, offering a handful of hours of fun but not a great deal of long-term depth. While the game makes a good effort to keep things fresh with environmental storytelling and sharp visuals, it doesn’t introduce the kind of deeper progression systems, unlockable moves, or elaborate combos that modern beat ’em ups sometimes incorporate. The absence of online co-op also marginally restricts replayability, as the game’s strengths are most apparent when shared with another player.

Still, the presentation carries a lot of weight. The hand-drawn art is gorgeous, the animations are expressive, and the comedic tone is true to the original comics. Everything about the visual identity feels handcrafted with affection, from the detailed backgrounds to the exaggerated reactions of Roman soldiers sent flying off-screen. The soundtrack stays lively, leaning into energetic tunes that match the slapstick nature of the gameplay. For longtime fans of Asterix & Obelix, these elements will feel like a loving tribute, and younger players or newcomers will likely enjoy the cheerful, cartoonish style even without nostalgia.

Asterix & Obelix Slap Them All! 2 ultimately succeeds as a fun, visually stunning beat ’em up that knows exactly who it’s for. It excels at providing lighthearted brawling and cooperative entertainment wrapped in a lovingly crafted comic-book world. Its shortcomings—namely repetitive combat and shallow mechanical depth—keep it from standing alongside the genre’s more sophisticated entries, but it doesn’t really aim for that spot. Instead, it thrives as a spirited, humorous romp best enjoyed casually or with a friend in tow.

If you appreciate traditional beat ’em ups, adore the Asterix universe, or simply want a charming game filled with personality, this sequel delivers an enjoyable trip through Gaulish chaos. It may not reinvent the genre, but it offers a heartfelt and entertaining homage to two of Europe’s most beloved cartoon heroes.

Rating: 7/10

[h1] "Устранение терроризирующих болванчиков" [/h1]
От Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six Lockdown™ после прохождения я получил двоякое впечатление. 
С одной стороны имеются интересные задания с интересными локациями и с возможностью кастомизации и управления нашим отрядом. А с другой стороны имеем ужасную и кривую стрельбу и тупых противников. Разве что стрельба из пистолетов более приятная.
Перед началом каждого задания по своему вкусу выбираем снаряжение для нас и нашей команды. От огнестрельных пушек до специального оборудования и снаряжения. Поэтому буквально для каждого члена отряда можно специализировать свою роль в задании. Вроде бы круто, но в купе с тупыми противниками, эти подготовленные роли не имеют никакого смысла. Достаточно всего будет просто идти по заданию и по пути устранять противника. Тем не менее осторожность при прохождении задании все же не помешает, так как враг бьет достаточно сильно чтобы погибнуть за пару выстрелов
Стрельба из основного оружия в игре крайне не приятная. Все как будто очень криво и расхлябано. Не знаю как так получилось у разработчиков, но стрельба из пистолетов ощущается куда приятнее. Поэтому большую часть времени я проходил задания именно с пистолетом.
Пусть и локации линейные, но они сделаны крайне неплохо и разнообразно. Приятно было погулять по разным локациям во время прохождения задании, если конечно игра сама не принуждала продвигаться по сюжету.
И в целом я бы пропустил Lockdown™, так как она по мне не самая удачная часть серии и вряд ли заслуживает внимания.
4 из 10.

This game is a linear story that you will finish within two hours and probably be done with forever. It is also not a funny experience in the slightest, despite being made by the writer of The Stanley Parable. So know those things going in. 

With that said, I first played this game when I was 12. At the time, it had me in tears, and that doesn't happen to me often. But I really only processed it on a superficial level. In the decade since, I've thought back to this one numerous times. The layers have become apparent to me with time, and it's become one of the most prescient stories I think I've ever heard. Every year it seems more relevant to more people in my life, and I shout at more of them to play it. It becomes more relevant to my own dealings, and I find myself using it as a sort of blueprint when I'm trying to figure out if I'm crossing anyone's lines or making any ill-considered judgments.

If I were to write out on paper the lessons I took away from this game, they would sound shallow and obvious as hell. But it's clear to me that not enough people have processed them. Especially in our online-first world, this story is something I feel everyone should experience. Set aside two hours to play this, and set aside another two hours to just sit in it and think about it. And then ask other people in your life to do the same.
This game is so meaningful to me.  It finally got me to stop procrastinating and really get creative.

I just wanted to chase a white rabbit. Instead, I found a piece of my childhood.

The Night of the Rabbit is what happens when a fairy tale decides to get philosophical. You start off expecting a charming little adventure — a boy, a talking rabbit, a magical forest — and before you know it, you’re knee-deep in a story about time, memory, and the bittersweet ache of growing up.

Visually, it’s stunning. Every screen looks like it was painted on the edge of a dream. The world feels alive — not loud or busy, but softly breathing, like it’s waiting for you to notice its details. And the music? Pure magic. It’s the kind of soundtrack that could calm a thunderstorm.

Gameplay-wise, it’s that classic Daedalic balance: gentle puzzles, quirky humor, and moments where you accidentally combine a spoon with a frog and somehow progress the story. But the heart of it all is its tone — a quiet reminder that wonder isn’t just for kids, and that stories can be both kind and cruel in the same breath.

By the time the credits rolled, I felt that strange mix of joy and melancholy you only get from finishing something truly special. It’s not just a game — it’s a gentle goodbye to innocence, wrapped in a forest full of whispers.

Followed the rabbit, found myself instead...

Care Bears always seemed like a “budget” franchise to me, like something trying to be one of the cool toy and animation front runners for kids, but falls short in every way and ends up a bit like the last choice, and this game feels the same way.

Let’s start with the story, which is plain and uninteresting. Now I don’t know much about the Care Bears lore, but it didn’t take me long to start skipping the dialogue. There also is no voice acting, which is a big miss considering this game’s target audience likely is kids who can’t read yet, and just because the story blows, voice acting could have juiced it up a bit at least. So, if you ask me, just skip the cutscenes and go straight to the gameplay.

The gameplay is a straightforward platformer that again is made for kids, so not much of a challenge there. There are lots of levels though. The map has 5 worlds with 7 levels in each if I remember correctly. When playing you can collect stars and disintegrate enemies with your Care Bears love rays. Enemies drop health regen pickups when dead.

So why do I recommend this? I bought this on Steam for like 3 bucks on sale, which makes it way cheaper than most games for children sold here on Steam. It also runs well on the Steam Deck and even with its boring story, it was way more interesting than a game like e.g. Barbie Project Friendship, which is priced at 40 bucks. So I can totally recommend this at sale.

Barro GT is a compact, pick-up-and-play racing game that embraces a deliberately simple, toy-like spirit. Developed and published by SC Jogos, it joins the long-running “Barro” series as another entry aimed at players who enjoy lighthearted arcade kart racing rather than technical driving or realistic handling. From the moment you begin, it’s clear that the game’s focus is accessibility: brightly colored tracks, small stylized vehicles, intuitive controls, and a structure built to get you into races instantly without tutorials or complicated menus. That simplicity becomes the backbone of the experience, offering quick bursts of racing fun for players who aren’t looking for the depth or spectacle of higher-budget kart racers.

The gameplay is centered around short, fast races across 21 newly added tracks, each shaped with clean curves, sharp turns, and layouts designed for easy memorization. You can choose from a selection of 26 compact cars, all visually distinct but mechanically similar, reinforcing the idea that the game is built for casual enjoyment rather than competitive tuning. While the racing relies on straightforward acceleration and cornering, the handling is intentionally loose and exaggerated, giving the cars a toy-like floatiness that suits the lighthearted tone but may feel too simplistic for those accustomed to more robust physics systems. What carries the racing is the pace: races move quickly, AI opponents behave predictably, and the focus shifts toward the pure rhythm of finishing laps rather than strategic power-ups or advanced mechanics.

The game’s strongest feature is its time-trial mode, which forms the core of its long-term appeal. Here, the player is encouraged to refine their lap times, improve racing lines, and compete with leaderboard entries from other players. This mode helps compensate for the limited nature of the single-player races by offering a sense of progression rooted in mastery rather than rewards or unlocks. Additionally, Barro GT includes local split-screen multiplayer for up to four players, a welcome feature that adds life to the game. When played with friends, its simplicity becomes an asset—everyone can learn the controls immediately, races are short, and the chaotic, bouncy handling creates spontaneous moments of humor. It’s in this local setting that the game’s personality shines brightest.

Visually, Barro GT maintains the minimalist style that SC Jogos is known for: low-poly environments, bold primary colors, and tracks that almost resemble toy-box dioramas. The presentation has a clean charm, though it carries the unmistakable look of a low-budget indie project. The sound design follows the same ethos, offering straightforward engine noises, simple music loops, and effects that complement the game’s unpretentious nature. While none of these elements aim for realism or high polish, they suit the game’s identity as an accessible, budget-friendly arcade racer. If anything, the stripped-down presentation helps highlight the nostalgic feel of older racing games from early 3D eras, when simplicity and readability were often prioritized over detail.

As a whole, Barro GT succeeds by understanding exactly what it wants to be: a quick, inexpensive racing experience meant for short sessions, time-trial challenges, and couch multiplayer. It’s not a title built for depth, progression systems, or advanced mechanics, and players seeking a more complete kart racing package may find it too thin. But for those who appreciate lightweight arcade experiences, or who want a simple racing game to enjoy with friends without investment or learning curves, it offers honest and uncomplicated fun. Its value becomes especially clear considering its low price—this is a small game, but one that delivers exactly the kind of breezy entertainment it advertises.

Samurai Shodown: NeoGeo Collection, developed by Digital Eclipse and published by SNK Corporation, stands as both a celebration and a preservation of one of the most iconic weapons-based fighting game series in gaming history. This collection gathers together seven classic titles from the NeoGeo era—Samurai Shodown, Samurai Shodown II, Samurai Shodown III, Samurai Shodown IV: Amakusa’s Revenge, Samurai Shodown V, Samurai Shodown V Special, and the never-before-officially-released Samurai Shodown V Perfect. For fans of SNK’s legacy or newcomers curious about the lineage of precision-based fighters, this collection represents an exhaustive archive that captures not only the evolution of the franchise but also the broader artistry of 2D fighting during its golden age. Digital Eclipse, known for their work in retro game preservation, handles the technical emulation with impressive care, ensuring that the games look, sound, and feel true to their original arcade incarnations.

At its heart, Samurai Shodown has always been about deliberate combat—the contrast between stillness and sudden motion, patience and violence. This design philosophy remains intact throughout every game in the collection. Unlike other fighters that emphasize rapid combos or flashy chains, Samurai Shodown thrives on the intensity of timing and positioning. A single well-placed strike can decide the outcome of a duel, reflecting a philosophy that blends game design with the samurai ethos itself. Each installment refines these ideas differently: the first two titles prioritize fundamental dueling mechanics, while the later games introduce deeper move lists, defensive techniques, and more cinematic flourishes. Playing them back to back reveals a fascinating historical progression, from the raw but charming early entries to the more complex and polished Samurai Shodown V Special. The inclusion of Samurai Shodown V Perfect—previously unreleased—serves as the crown jewel of this collection, completing the historical record for enthusiasts who have followed the series for decades.

The authenticity of the emulation work cannot be overstated. Digital Eclipse’s approach to recreating the arcade experience is meticulous, capturing the sound, pacing, and even the visual grain of the original NeoGeo hardware. The games run smoothly, and input response feels natural whether you play on a controller, keyboard, or arcade stick. Various display options allow for scaling, scanlines, and bezel customization, ensuring both nostalgic and modern players can enjoy the visuals in their preferred format. The attention to detail continues in the sound design; every sword clash, shout, and background melody evokes the fierce atmosphere of feudal duels. While the games themselves have not been visually remastered, their preserved pixel art remains striking, demonstrating how effective 2D animation can be when it’s built on strong aesthetic foundations.

One of the most outstanding aspects of the collection is the Museum mode, a vast gallery of archival content that showcases the series’ development history. It includes concept art, design sketches, character bios, promotional materials, and in-depth interviews with the original development team. For long-time fans, this feature is almost as valuable as the games themselves, offering a rare glimpse into SNK’s creative process and the design philosophy that shaped one of the most distinctive fighting franchises ever made. Coupled with the complete soundtrack library—featuring hundreds of tracks spanning every title—the Museum mode transforms the collection from a bundle of old games into a cultural record of Japanese arcade history.

While the offline experience is excellent, the online component is one of the few shortcomings. Although the collection includes online play with rollback netcode, the player base is unfortunately small, making it difficult to find consistent matches. The netcode works well when connections are stable, but the limited community diminishes its long-term value as a multiplayer experience. Additionally, newcomers might find the lack of a comprehensive training mode disappointing. The original games were designed for arcades and expect players to learn through repetition and observation, but in a modern context, the absence of tutorials or practice tools makes mastering each title a slower process. These omissions do not detract from the collection’s overall quality but do place it more in the realm of historical preservation than a fully contemporary fighting game platform.

Despite these caveats, Samurai Shodown: NeoGeo Collection is a masterful anthology that honors SNK’s legacy and Digital Eclipse’s commitment to authenticity. It captures the spirit of a series that defined the concept of tension and restraint in fighting games, proving that measured combat can be as thrilling as fast-paced brawls. Whether you are reliving arcade memories or discovering these games for the first time, the compilation offers an insightful look into how design philosophies matured across successive generations. Each duel feels deliberate and intense, each victory earned through precision rather than brute force. In a time when fighting games often chase spectacle and accessibility, returning to the purity of Samurai Shodown’s sword-based combat feels refreshing.

In conclusion, this collection is both a time capsule and a celebration. It preserves the artistry of hand-drawn sprites, the weight of every swing, and the atmosphere of classic SNK craftsmanship. While its lack of modern features may limit its appeal to casual players, for purists, historians, and fans of traditional fighting design, Samurai Shodown: NeoGeo Collection is essential. It stands as one of the finest examples of how video game preservation can be done right—respecting the past while making it accessible to the present. Through its careful restoration and inclusion of never-before-seen content, it ensures that the legacy of Samurai Shodown continues to inspire admiration for the art of the duel.

Originally released in 2001 and then remastered in 2019 for modern platforms, Onimusha: Warlords is an utter thrill of a game where you get to fight against demons in Sengoku period Japan with gameplay and design inspired by Capcom’s early Resident Evil games.  

The story is about Samanosuke Akechi, a samurai who received a letter from his cousin, Princess Yuki, requesting to get rescued after suspecting monsters are killing off maids and servants at her castle. Samanosuke, along with his kunoichi partner, Kaede, makes their way to the castle Yuki is held captive in. After splitting up from Kaede, he gets defeated by one of the demons residing near the castle, but suddenly, Samanosuke gets given a mysterious gauntlet by a group of Oni. With the gauntlet’s power, Samanosuke is able to fight against the demonic forces that stand in his way and goes on a journey to rescue the princess.

Given the game’s very short length, the story isn’t particularly too detailed, but it’s fine enough for what it is. It helps that I really liked what I heard from the Japanese voice acting (which is actually redone with brand new recordings for this remaster), as I feel it made me more invested in the cutscenes. In particular, Takeshi Kaneshiro’s voice acting as Samanosuke is absolutely fantastic to listen to, and I think his voice alone makes the game worth playing with the Japanese voice cast any day over the bland English dub. I also find myself interested in the game's historical setting mixed with a supernatural theme. Despite not being able to skip the in-game cutscenes, the game itself is surprisingly short, even for a blind first playthrough.

The gameplay is fun, albeit a little janky given its age. Onimusha essentially plays like it’s a faster-paced, classic Resident Evil game, with it even having the exact same style of presentation with fixed camera angles and use of pre-rendered backgrounds. I’ve previously struggled to get into similar Capcom games with the fixed camera and tank controls, but thankfully, there is the option for free analogue movement newly added to this release of the game, which genuinely makes it feel more comfortable to play. Once I got adjusted to how the game works, Samanosuke felt satisfying to play as, and I really liked his variety of weapons that you could use to slash away the demons. Killing enemies with Samanosuke grants you different coloured souls that you can absorb with his gauntlet. Yellow souls recover your health, blue souls recover magic that is used for hard-hitting elemental attacks, and red souls function as a currency which allows you to upgrade Samanosuke's arsenal of weapons. If you time it correctly, you can also parry enemies with your weapon, and you get rewarded with extra souls, especially with more yellow souls, so you're encouraged to be more patient when dealing with enemies.

Additionally, there are various puzzles, such as decoder boxes that require you to find items that list out the text that you need to answer encrypted questions and boxes where you have to match the numbers in order under a limited number of turns. The majority of these are optional; I personally thought they were designed well and not overly frustrating. When you solve those puzzles, you are rewarded with items that can really aid you on your playthrough, so it’s recommended to try to finish as many of them as you can. 

You also get to play as Kaede during specific portions of the game, but unfortunately, I find those moments to be rather half-baked considering the short amount of time you’ll be using her for, and there’s less depth to her gameplay. You certainly feel weaker using her compared to using Samanosuke, who has all these extra tools at his disposal to help him take down the demons, whereas Kaede only has a knife, kunai and a smaller health bar that you can’t even upgrade. I think her segments could have genuinely benefitted from having additional gameplay mechanics and making those playable parts with her last longer to increase the overall game’s very small length.

Due to controversy surrounding the original release’s credited composer, Capcom decided to completely replace the soundtrack with an entirely new score composed by Rei Kondoh, known for his work on Okami and various Nintendo games. From what I’ve heard while playing the game, I thought the new music fits the game’s overall setting really well, and you truly feel like you’re part of an epic demon-slaying adventure while listening to the background music. Whether it’s better than the original soundtrack or not is purely down to personal opinion, but as a new player, I really enjoyed listening to the newer music for what it is.

The PC version works perfectly fine. It ran out of the box for me with no technical issues at all. The new accessibility additions to the game, such as the free analogue movement and being able to swap weapons without having to use the menu, are super helpful and will definitely help a lot of players get hooked on the gameplay. Despite that, content-wise, this remaster does not include the additions and alterations that came from the original Xbox version of the game titled Genma Onimusha, which I find their lack of inclusion to be particularly odd given the extra effort Capcom has invested in regards to the new voice acting and music. As mentioned above, there’s no original soundtrack available, but you have the option to mod it back in, so it’s not much of a problem, at least on PC.

Onimusha: Warlords is a blast to play and definitely a classic worth checking out if you don’t mind the older Resident Evil-based gameplay. It has a few shortcomings, but I do not feel that they’re bad enough to detract from the overall enjoyment you gain from playing the game. Given the game’s age and how it was originally designed, I was pleasantly surprised by my time playing it, and I will be looking forward to trying out the other games in the future.

就感官而言，《Lakeview cabin》真正做到了让玩家恐惧，游戏用了像素画和VHS录像带的手法弱化游戏的残酷感，但浓重的血腥气息和邪典风仍然在游玩过程中扑面而来，同时让喜欢砍杀片的玩家笑出声——第三章是《十三号星期五》、第四章是《德州电锯杀人狂》、第五章是《月光光心慌慌》、第六章是《异形》，Roope Tamminen完美地把握到了上世纪恐怖片的恐怖哲学，用最低的成本做出最恐怖的效果以及那么一丝黑色幽默。这是许多当代恐怖游戏抓破头也做不到的。

虽然整个系列讲述的是一系列发生在电影里的虚构内容，度假四人组、少女乐队、小镇居民和飞船乘客并没有真正遇害，反而在2里成为了家喻户晓的大明星，但Red大叔杀妻杀子女的事却是真实发生的，许多不相干的人都死在他手里，而罪魁祸首“邪教”也是真实存在于游戏世界的，他们囚禁迫害金发女妖，并在之后毁了她和她的家人——即Lakeview的起源。每当我意识到这一点，我就觉得不寒而栗。巨婴、面具杀手的原型已经遇害，被父亲亲手杀死，而邪教可能真的会继续像电影里那样对无辜者下手（这一点在2里得到确认，导演一家和演员们遭到邪教暗杀），惨剧仍在延续。这系列表面上是恶趣味、乱杀乱死、像素血浆，但它最深的结构是反杀戮、反神化暴力的：游戏里的胜利目标是阻止杀手害人，让四人能有机会全部存活；让玩家亲眼见证变态邪教的手段（杀婴、火刑、洗脑）。我相信每个玩家玩完之后，反而会对生命、善良与正义有更深刻的理解。

DEATHWATCHERS is an atmospheric and tension-driven cooperative horror experience that takes the familiar framework of ghost-hunting and transforms it into something more methodical, investigative, and deeply unsettling. Developed and published by Swain Games, it places players in the role of paranormal investigators dropped into hostile, haunted environments where the goal isn’t simply to survive—it's to observe, document, and ultimately banish whatever entity occupies the space. From its earliest moments, the game establishes a suffocating sense of dread through its dimly lit interiors, unpredictable phenomena, and a constant feeling that something unseen is watching your every move. While playable alone, DEATHWATCHERS is crafted with co-op at its core, and its tension is magnified tenfold when shared with friends.

At the heart of the experience is a careful blend of observation and deduction. Each investigation involves combing through rooms looking for anomalies—flickering lights, moving objects, unusual sound cues, temperature shifts, electromagnetic spikes, or more grotesque manifestations. The game rewards methodical play: setting up equipment, reviewing footage, logging anomalies, and piecing together clues to determine the components of the ritual needed to banish the haunting. Every run becomes a puzzle, and the way clues emerge naturally in the environment gives the game a grounded feel. Rather than relying heavily on jump scares, DEATHWATCHERS builds fear through silence, anticipation, and a steady escalation of paranormal activity as the entity grows more aggressive.

Equipment management adds another strategic layer. Before entering a location, you choose what tools to bring—cameras, UV lights, scanners, audio recorders, and various forms of detection gear. Limited inventory forces you to coordinate with your partners, dividing responsibilities and deciding who carries what. As the investigation unfolds, you will frequently need to relocate equipment, re-check earlier rooms, and keep track of which clues correspond to which ritual components. The result is a constant back-and-forth between reconnaissance and risk, because the longer you stay inside, the more the haunting intensifies. A well-timed discovery can feel exhilarating, but staying too long invites danger that can abruptly spiral out of control.

Cooperative play is where the game truly shines. DEATHWATCHERS encourages communication and teamwork at all times, requiring players to share findings, debate interpretations, and coordinate safe routes based on the entity’s movements. Some of the most memorable moments arise organically—one player panicking while scanning a hallway, another shouting warnings over the radio, a third sprinting to regroup after hearing something stalk them down a corridor. The unpredictability of the entity’s behavior keeps every moment tense; some spirits lurk quietly and ambush without warning, while others stalk openly and force constant repositioning. The AI feels reactive and genuinely threatening, adding to the game’s oppressive atmosphere.

However, DEATHWATCHERS does have rough edges, some tied to its ongoing development and others inherent to its design. The learning curve is steep, and the game does little hand-holding beyond its lengthy tutorial. Understanding how events are categorized, how to interpret logs, and how to deduce the correct ritual components can feel overwhelming for newcomers. The interface, while functional, sometimes lacks clarity, and minor mechanical quirks—unintuitive controls, missing prompts, or unclear tool interactions—can lead to confusion. Content variety is another limitation: with only a handful of maps and a finite number of event types, some players may feel the investigations become repetitive over time, especially when playing solo.

Despite these shortcomings, the core atmosphere and tension remain compelling. Every investigation feels like entering a puzzle-box filled with danger, and every success—whether identifying the haunting, completing the ritual, or simply surviving—hits with a satisfying sense of accomplishment. The game’s sound design, from distant creaks to unnatural whispers, is particularly effective at maintaining a constant undercurrent of fear. The dim lighting, cramped environments, and unpredictable event triggers ensure that even familiar rooms never feel entirely safe.

Ultimately, DEATHWATCHERS succeeds as a smart and unnervingly immersive cooperative horror game that blends strategy, deduction, and nerve-wracking encounters into a uniquely captivating experience. It is best suited to players who enjoy slower-paced, cerebral horror rather than action-heavy experiences. While it may lack polish in places and has room to grow in terms of variety, its foundation is strong, and its atmosphere is gripping. For groups of friends seeking a fresh take on paranormal investigation—with more emphasis on puzzle-solving and creeping dread than loud scares—DEATHWATCHERS offers a richly tense and memorable journey into the unknown.

If you're coming from A Legionary's Life and enjoyed that game, you'll like this one too. But be warned: RNG kicks harder than in the predecessor, but as a veteran you should be able to handle it. Definitely recommended. If you want the full experience right from the start, it's better to wait until the full release (the last chapters are still in progress).
Important note: There is now a proper save system – game over is not final this time – save scumming is possible.

For everyone else:
The most important thing first: you need a high frustration threshold for this game. Everything in the game is rolled with a D100 – you'll see a lot of failed rolls and a lot of bullshit successes from your opponents. If you don't have the patience for that, I advise against this game, as it's more likely to cause frustration than fun. But remember, it is Early Access, so it may be a subject of change.

Anyway: Have you always wanted to accompany Caesar on his campaigns, experience the conquest of Gaul, and fight in the civil war of the first triumvirate? Then there's no better game than Never Second in Rome.
You take on the role of a centurion leading a century. Under your command are 80 legionnaires to train and lead.

Follow Caesar on his campaign:
Never Second in Rome is a text adventure, the plot and dialogues are presented exclusively in text – but it is very well written and as historically accurate as it can be.
The story is written from the narrator's perspective as well as from the perspective of your character and, in part, that of your soldiers. It takes you on Caesar's campaigns and shows you the impact the wars had on the people and soldiers on both sides. I don't want to say too much about it—because the story is a big part of the game that is best simply immersed in.
Nevertheless, you can exert a certain amount of influence through decisions you make in the story—whether these are successful or not is determined by rolling dice based on your abilities. This can influence small story elements, unlock additional story events and possibilities, and bring advantages and disadvantages for you, your soldiers, or your opponents. Values such as humanity (you can play good or evil) or valor are also part of it. This is supported by some artwork – although I think the game could use a lot more of it.

Develop your skills and train your legionnaires:
Your character, your “officers” (partially playable charakters), and your regular soldiers all have skills that need to be developed strategically. This is the game's management system, where you create a training plan and prepare your men as best you can for the upcoming campaigns.
It's up to you to decide how you train your soldiers and yourself. Whether you want to specialize in sword fighting or javelin throwing, lead a very resilient century with a focus on defense, or simply maintain a balance. You can develop your people in many different directions.
Morale and fatigue play a role here too, as do the administration of the camp and the supervision of your subordinates.

Fight for your survival:
There are two types of combat: individual combat (man-to-man) and century combat.
The two are quite different, with individual combat influencing century combat.
The combat system is more of a simulation than a “game” – quite similar to the combat systems of classic pen-and-paper games. Each character has their own attributes, developed to varying degrees, and your actions are rolled against each other. The aim is to break your opponent's stance while maintain your own. Body parts can be targeted to either bypass the opponent's armor or achieve certain effects in addition to damage (a blow to the arm or leg, for example, increases the opponent's exhaustion, while a blow to the groin reduces morale more). There are different fighting stances and other skills that can make the fights extremely dynamic.
However, the same rules also apply to your character. If you don't pay attention to your stance or exhaustion, you may find yourself dead very quickly. You are not a superhero—just a soldier like any other.
Combat with the century works differently, however. Here, you lead your men in formation and try to break the cohesion of your opponents, which can lead to individual combats and influences the battle. 

A Centurion's Life:
That's the game. You play a Roman citizen who has joined the military and is trying to survive the war and bring his soldiers home safely (or just thinking about saving his own skin). You're not the main character, nor are you a supporting character; you're just one of thousands on Caesar's stage.

By the way, there are other elements in the game that I haven't covered, such as skill-based construction mini-games or searching for supplies, but that would go beyond the scope of this review.

So if you have a reasonably high tolerance for failure (and you will fail) or find ancient Roman times interesting (especially the story of Caesar): go for it!

If you're simply looking for an interesting text adventure with historical accuracy: go for it!

If you're bored and want something new or are looking for a niche product: go for it!

There is also a demo available for this game if you want to try it out before buying it—which I highly recommend so you can see if this game is right for you.

The price is absolutely justified, even for early access. If you want to wait to play through the story in one go, check out A Legionary's Life – it will give you a good insight into how the game works.

Otherwise, here are a few tips for you if you decide to buy it:
- Try one or two rounds and see how it goes. You'll probably die and have no idea why (partly because of the RNG). Just check out a guide and let it walk you through the first 5 chapters or so (SkyTurtle has written a good one). That'll give you an idea of how the game works, and from there, try to make it to the end.
- Don't set your goals too high at first. Just try to survive the war – you can be a hero later.
- Again: the game has ridiculous RNG. It's EA, so maybe that will change, but don't be surprised when your >+25 throws fail and your opponent's <-40 throws succeed three times in a row. That's normal.
- Remember that there is a save system.
- If you still don't understand how the game works after that, don't be ashamed to cheat. Just use CheatEngine, pump up your character a bit, and try again to the point of your failure. This will eliminate the RNG factor (well, at least a little) and make the game much easier to understand. Then try again the normal way—and suddenly the game will open up like a flower! (but be warned, achievements may also be unlocked this way.)

The music soundtracks for each zone is very well composed and I really loved it, the retro 8-bit classic music that is known since the childhood days, the devs really didn't disappoint with this one.

The boss fights can be tough if you're not timing your jumps / slides correctly and you can get killed very quick if you're not careful. The designs were super nice and has really some unique ideas!!

It's a very recommended 2D Retro Action Platformer for the fans of the genre or if you love retro action in general.

Hay remakes innecesarios… y luego está Gabriel Knight: Sins of the Fathers – 20th Anniversary Edition, que llega, se sienta en tu disco duro y te recuerda cómo se hacía una aventura gráfica con cara y ojos.

El juego recupera el clásico de los 90: un escritor de novela negra en horas bajas, Gabriel Knight, que regenta una librería medio muerta en Nueva Orleans junto a la mucho-más-competente-que-él Grace Nakimura. Mientras él intenta escribir su próximo éxito (spoiler: no lo hace), la ciudad se llena de asesinatos relacionados con el vudú, y, como no podía ser de otra manera, Gabriel se mete hasta el cuello en el caso… y en los secretos bastante turbios de su propia familia Schattenjägger.

La edición 20 aniversario actualiza los gráficos, las animaciones y parte de la interfaz, haciéndolo más digerible para ojos que ya se han acostumbrado al HD y al 4K. El resultado visual no es perfecto, pero cumple y mantiene el encanto raro y ligeramente kitsch de la saga.

Uno de sus puntos fuertes es el sistema de pistas integrado: no te suelta la solución a la cara, sino que te va lanzando miguitas cuando te atascas, algo muy de agradecer en un juego donde, sí, puedes morir. Y a nadie le apetece repetir media hora por no examinar un píxel sospechoso.

Guion sólido, atmósfera densa de novela gótica sureña, personajes carismáticos y puzles que (la mayoría de las veces) tienen sentido: esta versión es una puerta de entrada muy digna al universo Gabriel Knight.

¿Veredicto?
Para fans de las aventuras clásicas y del misterio con olor a incienso vudú y café de Nueva Orleans, sigue siendo un muy buen juego y un regreso más que recomendable.

한때 전국적인 명성을 자랑하던 새벽일보는, 현재 낮은 신뢰도와 판매 부수로 폐간 위기에 처해 있다. 상황을 반전시킬 마지막 희망은, 이제 막 새로 부임한 편집장의 능력에 달려 있다. 플레이어는 첫 출근 날, 누구보다 무거운 책임감을 안고 새벽일보 편집장실로 향한다.

간단한 인사 후 이어진 대표와의 짧은 면담. 대표는 곧장 현재 1면을 장식한 기사에 대해 언급하며 본론으로 들어간다. 1996년, 어느 날. 국민적 지지를 받으며 차기 대선 후보로 거론되던 ‘창발당’ 소속 지광현 의원이 자택 인근 산에서 시신으로 발견된다. 전 국민이 충격에 빠졌고, 언론들은 앞다투어 이 사건을 다뤘다. 하지만 여전히 많은 의문이 남아 있다.

대표는 새벽일보가 그 누구보다 앞서 진실에 다가갈 수 있다면, 과거의 영광을 되찾는 건 꿈이 아니라고 말한다. 플레이어는 잠시 생각에 잠긴 뒤, 조용히 고개를 끄덕인다. 그는 지광현 의원 피살 사건의 범인을 찾는 것을 최우선 목표로 삼기로 결심한다.

그 순간, 대표는 조심스럽게 사진 한 장을 꺼내 책상 위에 내려놓는다. "중앙수사국이 유력한 용의자를 특정했다"는 말과 함께. 사진 속에는 숨진 지광현 의원, 그리고 그 곁에는 그의 최측근 보좌관, 진선명이 담겨있었는데...
