It's functioning. That's the best I can say about it. for 20 EUR is overpriced as hell.

Story 
The story is trash, both endings feel like bad endings and they're both trash and lazily written. My 10 YO can think up a better story than this. Yuck.

Movement 
- it's not fluid, let me tell you that. Your characters moves slowly and there is no option to run but if you spam dodge-roll you move twice as fast thus you're incentivised to roll all the time which looks ridiculous and no fun at all.
- jumping is janky and the hitboxes of platforms are messed up, making you miss the landing. Most of the platforming becomes obsolete with the double jump that spans the whole height of the screen so there goes any need for problem solving.
- there is no option to fast travel so most of the game you just backtrack the same rooms you already visited. 

Map
- map is barebones, denoting only explored squares and savepoints. No markers for locked doors or points of interest, no way to drop a marker of your own, not even a name or color for different parts of the map.

Level design
- bland and same-ish rooms incoherently strewn together, biomes or sections almost indistinguishable from each other
- Doors are all same looking and if you interact with them "locked" pops out with no way of telling whether you need a prison key, thief key, rusty key or to find a lever that opens it. So with every new acquired key you backtrack like a fool and try bumping every door to see if it opens. Also remember none of the doors are marked so good luck finding them.
- some parts of the map are sectioned off by roots blocking two conjoined corridors that look like you should be able to burn or punch through but no, they're only there to make you go around like an idiot while backtracking for the umpth time.

Combat
- very basic and janky at the same time. Every attack you connect with locks your character for a milisecond to produce "HIT" flash so if you strike multiple foes you get hit back before all those "HIT" animations happen. It's like stun-locking yourself every time you swing and boy oh boy is it annoying.
- there is zero tactics required to kill any of the bosses in this game. Just press forward and spam attack and heal. No need to dodge, parry, jump away or anything. Just mash buttons till it's dead. Trying to fight strategically gets you killed more often than if you just lay it on. Final boss takes like 30 seconds to kill that way.
- at the very end you get "dash attack" that is only ever used to bridge few artifical gaps on the final stretch of the map. It's useless in combat btw.

Everything about this game screams cashgrab. Not worth for free, not worth the 10 hours to finish it.

I've been wanting to recommend BTTH since it released because I truly do believe it deserves all the support it can get, but I kept telling myself I'd wait to do it until I had finished it. I still haven't finished it because other things took my attention and I may also be a little bad at it and got stuck like 4 or 5 checkpoints before the end. Might be the hardest game I have ever played that I can actually see myself finishing someday tbh. At this point it's been so long I'll just do a new playthrough from the start whenever I get back to it, but who knows when that'll be.

That said, I do still wanna put this out there because despite my big break from it, I kept thinking about it constantly and not ONLY  because I have brainworms about anything I don't finish. It's easily one of my favorite games in recent memory and has me very excited to keep following ceroro to see what else she'll come up with in the future. It really feels like she had a, on paper, relatively simple idea in mind and attempted to push that idea as far as possible and it shows. If the concept appeals to you at all and you're up for a journey that'll really test you, it's absolutely worth trying.

Vibes-wise the game stands up there with how the likes of Celeste make me feel (this is extremely high praise in my book), it's so cute and the music is really comfy and nice too. There were many, many times where I got stuck at the same spot for hours but I kept pushing because I wanted to see what's beyond. I'm also still not sure if I got through some parts the "intended" way, but there's a lot of tech to the mechanics that you can use to make your life easier, if you're willing to delve into it. It's just really good. I just really enjoyed my time batting to the heavens, even if I may or may not ever be good enough at it to finish it.

[h1]Red Faction II. A Rebelião Perde o Fôlego[/h1]

[h2]1. Da revolta marciana à guerra sem rosto[/h2]

Lançado em 2002, Red Faction II tentou expandir o universo da franquia com mais ação, personagens e um enredo “épico”, mas o que nasceu como uma história sobre opressão e resistência, em Marte, virou um shooter militar genérico na Terra, agora, o jogador encarna Alias, um supersoldado bio-modificado a serviço de um governo corrupto que logo se volta contra ele, o tema da rebelião ainda existe, mas sem o peso simbólico do primeiro, não há mais o mineiro comum lutando contra a corporação, e sim um exército de clones lutando contra outro.

A Volition tentou dar um ar cinematográfico à série, mas acabou apagando o que tornava o primeiro especial, o senso de isolamento, a ficção científica suja e o tom político que ecoava Total Recall e Outland, aqui, sobra barulho, mas falta propósito.

[b]“Em Marte, Parker lutava por liberdade, na Terra, Alias luta por roteiro.”[/b]

[h2]2. Geo-Mod 2.0. O mito que se perdeu[/h2]

O Geo-Mod Engine, orgulho do primeiro jogo, retorna, mas como uma sombra do que foi, a destruição ainda existe, mas agora é limitada, contida e previsível, o jogador só pode destruir certas paredes e objetos pré-definidos, uma ironia cruel para uma franquia que nasceu da ideia de liberdade.

O impacto emocional do Geo-Mod sumiu, antes, explodir uma parede era um ato de rebeldia, uma declaração contra o sistema, agora, é apenas parte de uma sequência de ação roteirizada, sem qualquer significado narrativo, a Volition parecia tentar seguir o padrão de FPS do início dos anos 2000, mais lineares, mais “cinematográficos” e, com isso, abriu mão do que fazia Red Faction ser Red Faction.

[b]“Quando a destruição vira decoração, o mundo para de reagir.”[/b]

[h2]3. O caos sem contexto[/h2]

Os combates são mais intensos e variados, com veículos e explosões maiores, mas perdem em identidade, Red Faction II tenta compensar a falta de profundidade com pirotecnia, você controla tanques, torres e lança-granadas, mas tudo parece passageiro, sem impacto real.

Os inimigos são genéricos, os companheiros são caricaturas, e o ritmo apressado não deixa o jogador respirar, a narrativa pula de missão em missão sem estrutura, como se quisesse apenas gritar mais alto que o anterior e quanto mais grita, menos ouvimos.

A ironia é que o jogo busca ser mais humano, com diálogos e personagens dublados por nomes famosos como Lance Henriksen e Jason Statham, mas nenhum deles tem tempo de existir.
É ação sem alma, ruído sem emoção.

[b]“Red Faction II fala alto, mas não tem nada a dizer.”[/b]

[h2]4. Entre Marte e Terra. O que se perdeu no caminho[/h2]

Comparar Red Faction com Red Faction II é quase comparar ideologia com espetáculo, o primeiro era político, sujo, claustrofóbico, o segundo é patriótico, polido e superficial.

A troca de Marte pela Terra é mais simbólica do que parece, sai o cenário inóspito e alienante, entra a cidade genérica de uma distopia militar qualquer, sai o mineiro que luta por sobrevivência, entra o supersoldado que luta por comando e sai a revolução, entra a guerra.

A Volition parecia querer alcançar o público de Halo e Medal of Honor, mas no processo, sacrificou o DNA narrativo da série, o Geo-Mod virou truque, a crítica virou patriotismo, e o jogador deixou de ser o rebelde para virar apenas mais um soldado.

[b]“A chama da rebelião não se apaga com balas, mas com a perda de propósito.”[/b]

5. O visual sem identidade

Tecnicamente, o jogo é sólido, texturas nítidas, modelos detalhados e cenários urbanos mais amplos que o original, mas artisticamente, é vazio, as minas vermelhas e corredores industriais do primeiro jogo transmitiam opressão e atmosfera, aqui, tudo é metálico, repetitivo e sem alma, os ambientes da cidade de EDF parecem genéricos, intercambiáveis, sem o menor senso de lugar, nada lembra Marte, nada ecoa o isolamento, e o design de fases é linear até o limite, você segue por corredores que explodem e fecham atrás de você, o oposto do que o Geo-Mod prometia um ano antes.

[b]“Red Faction II é bonito por fora, mas oco por dentro, uma concha metálica sem coração.”[/b]

[h2]6. A crítica e o público: o silêncio após o estrondo[/h2]

Na época, Red Faction II recebeu avaliações mornas, a crítica reconheceu a boa ação e os gráficos competentes, mas lamentou a perda da destruição livre e da atmosfera política do original, os fãs, então, dividiram-se, alguns gostaram da velocidade e das armas, mas muitos sentiram que o jogo havia traído suas próprias origens.

O tempo foi impiedoso, hoje, o segundo jogo é lembrado como o elo mais fraco da sériem um experimento que tentou ser blockbuster e perdeu o espírito cult do original, enquanto Red Faction é estudado como marco técnico, Red Faction II é uma nota de rodapé, a sequência que esqueceu o manifesto que a inspirou.

[h2]7. Um legado enfraquecido e a perda do impacto[/h2]

Enquanto o primeiro Red Faction foi lembrado por sua ambição e por tentar mudar as regras do gênero FPS com a destruição geomod, Red Faction II parece ter perdido o rumo e, junto dele, boa parte da relevância conquistada, o jogo soa como uma sequência feita às pressas, sem confiança em seu próprio potencial, a ausência de um enredo envolvente e a superficialidade dos personagens demonstram um afastamento do que tornava o original tão intrigante, a tecnologia de destruição, que antes era o coração do projeto, aqui é tratada quase como um detalhe, um recurso secundário que raramente serve a algo além de breves momentos de espetáculo vazio.

A sensação é a de que a franquia trocou inovação por conveniência, e identidade por clichês, o peso político e a tensão social do primeiro título, com sua luta de mineiros contra corporações opressoras, foram substituídos por um patriotismo artificial e genérico, mais próximo de um jogo de ação descartável do início dos anos 2000 do que de uma continuação legítima, Red Faction II não apenas falha em evoluir a série, como parece retroceder, apagando o que havia de mais único em seu antecessor.

No fim, o legado do jogo é o de uma oportunidade desperdiçada, uma continuação que teve todos os recursos técnicos para se destacar, mas nenhuma visão criativa para realmente marcar seu tempo.

[h2]8. Conclusão. A revolução domesticada[/h2]

Red Faction II não é um jogo ruim, é um jogo sem alma, ele troca liberdade por controle, ideologia por espetáculo e coragem por conveniência, no processo, transforma uma franquia promissora em mais um produto da era dos FPS genéricos.

O que era grito virou eco.
O que era manifesto virou manual.
O que era revolução virou rotina.

E quando a destruição deixa de libertar, resta apenas o silêncio metálico de uma rebelião esquecida.

Gripper, developed and published by Heart Core, is a visually striking and emotionally charged action game that attempts to merge high-speed motorcycle combat with a deeply personal story about loss, guilt, and self-discovery. It tells the tale of a young man named None, who embarks on a desperate journey through a desolate, cyberpunk-inspired world to save his family and uncover the mysteries of his past. Guided and taunted by an artificial intelligence named Zero, he must confront massive biomechanical bosses, each representing an aspect of his emotional turmoil. The game blends kinetic vehicle combat with symbolic storytelling, striving to create something as introspective as it is intense. While its ambition is undeniable and its presentation captivating, the experience is uneven—bold in concept but inconsistent in execution.

At its core, Gripper is built around a unique combination of racing and boss-fighting mechanics. Instead of traditional on-foot combat, the player controls None’s futuristic motorcycle, using a grappling hook as the main offensive and defensive tool. The hook can latch onto objects, tear apart enemy components, or hurl debris to expose weak points. Each boss encounter plays like a dance of movement and precision, where timing, positioning, and spatial awareness are crucial. The grappling mechanic is the game’s central innovation, providing a satisfying sense of impact when it works as intended. The feeling of yanking a mechanical limb off a towering enemy or pulling explosive cores free from a vulnerable point can be exhilarating. However, the system’s precision is inconsistent—auto-targeting occasionally locks onto the wrong object or fails to register an input at key moments, breaking immersion during otherwise thrilling battles. These inconsistencies can turn moments of triumph into frustration, as what should be a smooth ballet of destruction becomes a struggle against the controls.

The pacing alternates between boss arenas and fast-paced tunnel sequences. The latter serve as transitions between major fights, functioning like high-speed obstacle courses filled with hazards and quick-time events. These moments are visually impressive, drenched in neon light and pulsing with energy, but they often rely on trial and error. The sudden appearance of traps or narrow corridors can feel punishing rather than challenging, forcing repeated retries until patterns are memorized. While this structure gives the game rhythm and variety, it occasionally interrupts narrative momentum and contributes to fatigue during longer play sessions. Still, when everything clicks—the racing, the music, the perfectly timed grapple—it’s hard not to appreciate how ambitious the design truly is.

Gripper’s story strives to balance emotional intimacy with apocalyptic spectacle. Through fragmented memories and cryptic dialogue, players learn about None’s childhood, his parents’ disappearance, and the emotional trauma that drives his quest. Each boss represents a stage of grief—anger, denial, acceptance—and confronting them is both a literal and psychological act. The concept has strong potential, but the writing doesn’t always deliver the depth it promises. Dialogue often leans on clichés and lacks the subtlety needed to make its emotional beats resonate. The narrative themes are spelled out too bluntly, leaving little room for interpretation. That said, the sincerity of the story still carries weight. There is an earnestness in the way Gripper deals with grief, memory, and human imperfection. Even when the script falters, the music, atmosphere, and visuals do much of the emotional lifting, helping to evoke the introspective tone the story strives for.

Visually, the game is a standout. Its cyberpunk-inspired world is rendered with strong color contrasts, neon lighting, and bold geometry that gives every location a sense of purpose and weight. The art direction recalls classic anime influences like Akira, combining a sense of speed and danger with emotional melancholy. The environments feel both mechanical and organic, mirroring the hybrid nature of the world’s creatures and the protagonist’s own conflicted identity. The soundtrack enhances this atmosphere, blending pulsing synths with emotional melodies that mirror the game’s tonal shifts—from the intensity of boss fights to the quiet moments between them. The result is a cohesive audiovisual identity that remains one of Gripper’s most impressive achievements.

From a gameplay perspective, however, the game’s difficulty curve and control design can be divisive. The boss fights, while creative, often overstay their welcome due to repetitive attack cycles and lengthy invulnerability phases. Many encounters demand perfect execution with little margin for error, which can be frustrating given the unpredictable nature of the grapple mechanics. Checkpoints are sometimes placed far apart, meaning that a small mistake late in a fight can send the player back to the start. These moments can sap momentum and diminish the sense of accomplishment that comes from overcoming a difficult encounter. The lack of fine-tuned responsiveness in the controls further compounds this issue, occasionally making it feel as though victory depends more on luck than skill.

Despite its flaws, Gripper’s passion and ambition shine through. It’s clear that Heart Core poured genuine care into its world-building and emotional themes, attempting to craft something distinct within the indie action space. The fusion of motorcycle combat, boss-rush intensity, and narrative introspection is rare, and while not all elements succeed, the effort itself is commendable. There are flashes of brilliance—moments when the combat, music, and story converge into a rush of cinematic energy that feels unlike anything else. It’s in these flashes that Gripper reveals its true potential, even if it never fully realizes it.

Ultimately, Gripper is a game defined by its contrasts: mechanical frustration offset by visual splendor, narrative sincerity hampered by clumsy dialogue, and exhilarating moments tempered by uneven design. It’s not a flawless experience, but it’s one that lingers because of its creativity and heart. For players drawn to emotionally charged indie games that take risks with form and style, Gripper offers an experience that is flawed yet memorable—a rough, roaring journey through grief, love, and the mechanical chaos of a world that mirrors the turbulence of the human soul.

This was made with the Unity engine, and by two people. The animations and gameplay can be jank, and the price is a little high for what it offers, but not egregiously so. Still within tolerable levels especially for the story and the designs of the imaginary friends and the work put within them.

There's some awkwardness to the story, like what the 'secret' imaginary friend discovered and whatever the 'Void' was, but the friends otherwise work well within the story. It's also telling that they're the only true source of color and outward personality in the asylum, especially from the perspective of the children. The developers claim to have done a lot of research to make this seem as realistic as possible in terms of asylum depictions for the 40s, and from the little I know, they did a pretty good job.

The children all have their own quirks and personalities, as small as it might be (Trust me when I say it's REALLY hard to juggle with more than four characters at once when you're writing a story). As such, only a select group of characters are able to get a more developed background and personality, helping focus the content. 

I also enjoyed how all the characters only have outlines and you can't see beyond that. It's a very creative way of making characters without having to go into precise detail for all of them. You already know who is who when they're important. The imaginary friends also have fantastic designs that really grab your attention, though I'm unsure why the painter is shown without his mask in the Steam Store.

This is a clear recommendation from me. It's, unfortunately, underrated and ignored for the likes of more well-established horror series, but if these developpers got proper backing and more experience, I'm certain that they could make something far more developped graphically and, more importantly than graphics, functional. Despite the inexperience in developing (or perhaps limitations brought about by Unity), the playthrough was very smooth. I only encountered one bug with the patient sheets and an automatic scene trigger opening at the same time, getting the sheet stuck and forcing me to restart the game.

The game is quite short, taking only a few hours, but the experience of the story and seeing what the developers are capable of was a very enjoyable experience.

The Final Hours of Tomb Raider, developed and published by Geoff Keighley, is an interactive digital book that takes readers deep behind the scenes of Crystal Dynamics’ ambitious 2013 reboot of the iconic Tomb Raider franchise. It is part documentary, part written feature, and part multimedia exploration—a hybrid experience that merges text, photography, video, and interactivity to document how one of gaming’s most beloved heroines was reinvented for a new generation. Rather than being a simple collection of interviews or concept art, it acts as an immersive chronicle of the creative process, examining how a modern development team revived a classic property while facing both creative and technical obstacles. The project benefits greatly from Keighley’s experience as a veteran games journalist and storyteller, delivering a polished, cohesive narrative that captures the highs and lows of game production with genuine insight.

From the outset, The Final Hours of Tomb Raider distinguishes itself through presentation. The experience unfolds like a digital magazine—readers navigate through sections filled with richly illustrated concept art, embedded video interviews, and panoramic images of Crystal Dynamics’ studio. The design encourages exploration, allowing readers to see environments evolve from sketches to playable stages and to hear developers discuss the creative decisions that shaped Lara Croft’s rebirth. The multimedia elements work seamlessly with the narrative text, offering a cinematic form of storytelling that traditional written retrospectives often lack. This blending of formats creates a sense of immediacy: the reader doesn’t just learn about the development process—they feel embedded in it, almost as if standing among the developers as they debate design ideas or refine character animations.

The story that unfolds through this interactive chronicle is as much about human ambition as it is about technology or design. Keighley follows the evolution of the project from its early concept phase, when the studio sought to redefine Lara Croft not as a flawless adventurer but as a vulnerable, human protagonist thrust into survival against overwhelming odds. Through candid developer commentary, the digital book reveals the internal discussions that guided this transformation—how the team balanced honoring the franchise’s adventurous spirit with modern storytelling sensibilities. Readers learn about the long production cycle, the challenges of adapting the project to a new generation of consoles, and the immense pressure the team faced to meet both fan expectations and the publisher’s ambitions. In these sections, Keighley’s writing shines, blending factual detail with a clear narrative arc that builds tension and empathy for the developers behind the scenes.

The Final Hours also serves as a valuable historical snapshot of game development at a transitional time for the industry. It captures the moment when major studios began embracing cinematic storytelling, performance capture, and narrative-driven design, moving away from purely mechanical experiences. The inclusion of interviews with key figures at Crystal Dynamics adds depth to the account, providing a clear view of how creative direction evolves within a large studio. Concept art and early prototypes reveal how drastically the project changed during development—mechanics were added, removed, or reshaped as the team pursued a unified vision of realism and emotional depth. For those interested in game design or production, these details are illuminating, offering rare transparency about the iterative, often chaotic process that defines AAA development.

While the digital book excels in accessibility and presentation, it does have limitations in scope. Readers seeking an exhaustive, analytical study of the game’s creation may find it somewhat surface-level, as the tone leans more celebratory than critical. Keighley focuses on the passion and perseverance of the developers rather than industry politics or corporate influence. This approach makes the experience more approachable for fans but less academic or investigative than some might expect. Still, what the book lacks in depth, it compensates for with authenticity—its emotional honesty and detailed production insights make it an engaging, approachable account of one studio’s creative journey.

From a technical standpoint, The Final Hours of Tomb Raider is remarkably well-executed. The interface is intuitive, with smooth navigation between interactive segments, and the embedded videos load seamlessly even on modest hardware. The audio-visual balance is carefully calibrated, enhancing immersion without overwhelming the reader. It’s a testament to Keighley’s production standards that the experience feels timeless despite its 2013 release. However, the interactive format also means it exists in a somewhat niche space—more substantial than a trailer, less academic than a book, and dependent on hardware compatibility that may age with time. Even so, its blend of journalism and technology makes it one of the most innovative digital publications tied to a major game release.

Ultimately, The Final Hours of Tomb Raider stands as both a love letter to the franchise and a thoughtful reflection on modern game creation. It humanizes the process behind blockbuster entertainment, reminding readers that even massive projects are built on passion, creativity, and collaboration. By combining vivid writing with interactive storytelling, it transforms what could have been a static making-of feature into a living, breathing document of artistic reinvention. O jogo apresenta uma boa história, centrada em dívidas financeiras e no relacionamento do protagonista com sua mulher. Buscando uma solução rápida para sair do "vermelho", ele recorre ao “jogo do tigrinho” (Treasure Tiger) na esperança de levantar dinheiro para o casal. O problema é que o jogo aparentemente é amaldiçoado, e o monstro/tigre sequestra a mulher do protagonista, dizendo que só vai devolvê-la em troca de 100k reais, o que o obriga a continuar apostando para conseguir esse dinheiro. 

A narrativa, apesar de não ser o foco, é bem interessante e convincente, ela sugere que o personagem está emocionalmente esgotado, o que o torna presa fácil do sistema de apostas. A progressão ocorre ao longo de cinco dias, com novas mecânicas sendo introduzidas conforme o avanço do jogador.

Há uma tensão crescente ao longo da experiência, apoiada por jumpscares bem executados, e ótima atmosfera. A gameplay se baseia em sobreviver enquanto aposta e o Treasure Tiger tenta invadir a casa. 

Grande parte da lore é apresentada por meio de páginas dispersas pelo cenário, incentivando exploração. O jogo também inclui referências culturais brasileiras, como o tradicional filtro de barro, além de menções a criadores de conteúdo como Felca e Orochinho. A duração é curta e a dificuldade é moderada, com o último dia sendo o ponto mais desafiador. 

É um jogo muito divertido e criativo. Ótimo jogo de terror nacional, além de ter um preço bem em conta.

Отличный представитель жанра, но если сравнивать Ван Хельсинга с остальными подобными играми, то можно с уверенностью сказать, что он — их младший брат. Увы, не слишком удачный. Зато имеющий в себе неповторимый антураж тёмного фэнтези. С небольшими нотками техно.

В игре вас ожидает типичная для жанра резня монстров, собрание билдов посредством прокачки персонажа, и какой-никакой сюжет в духе классического Ван Хельсинга.

Отдельно хочется отметить Катарину — спутницу главного героя. В игре, она заменяет питомца, выполняя роли гонца (отправка в магазин) и лутателя (сбор предметов). Разработчикам удалось сделать не просто товарища для главного героя, но и наделить его узнаваемым темпераментным характером.
То, как Катарина рушит четвёртую стену, своим вечным недовольством — пожалуй, только ради этого и стоит играть в игру.

А правда, стоит ли в 2025 году тратить время на Ван Хельсинга?

Вопрос неоднозначный.

Кроме прочего, нельзя не затронуть тему сюжета. Он здесь посредственный по сценарию, короткий и забывается, едва ли не сразу после окончания. Резюмируя, скажу, что цена игры полностью соответствует её содержанию. Это не что-то инновационное, даже по старым меркам, но в то же время, способное подарить свежие эмоции и скрасить несколько вечеров. Советую любителям жанра. Остальным — нет.

看似制作粗糙实则意外好用的NTR佳作。是在NTR爱好者圈子里小有名气的“毛ガニ研究室（kegani lab）”社团推出的作品中人气较高的一部。

了解这个社团的机长都知道，这个社团的游戏几乎都是这类简陋但好用的3d画风+NTR故事内核的风格，玩法上也都是比较简单粗暴的小游戏设计，主要卖点还是NTR部分。不过，虽然主打卖点是NTR，但实际上是有可达成的纯爱乃至后宫路线，只不过相比于NTR路线来说的内容会少很多（大概少个70％罢）。因此，只能说对于纯爱战士来说，该作是可以食用的，但作为一款黄油来说不是很适合（确信）。

如果玩家一味地推进剧情和努力去达成纯爱结局的话，游戏的流程不算长，大概两个小时以内就能玩到结局，而且全程cg可以说只有几个寥寥无几的重复动作。想要完整体验该作品的话，无论是将青梅竹马们拱手相让，还是故意败北让蛮族将其抓走调教都是不得不品鉴的一环。
如果你恰好是一位牛战士的话，那么这部作品一定能够满足你最基本的喜好（确信）。游戏虽然没有特别激进的内容，但是作为一款NTR主题作品来说，对NTR的刻画与描写都没什么槽点，属于基本功很扎实的NTR。并且虽然画风简陋，但很多时候这种低模甚至带点劣质的3d风格却意外的涩，即使不是牛战士，对于非纯爱战士外的·一般向黄油爱好的来说，可食用程度方面还是可以放心的。

总之，作为一款游戏比较简陋，但作为一款黄油还不错（美中不足是打了补丁后还是骑兵）。纯爱战士酌情折扣入手，黄油爱好者可折扣入，牛战士可无脑入。
bug不少，流程来说很重复，虽然很有创意但是画风确实是减分项目。我是真的遇见了几个因为快速刷数据导致的，无法正常触发数据和更新人物状态的bug，整体有点影响游戏体验。玩法来说重复度过高也是一大问题，总体上体验中游偏下，无论是画质上的粗糙还是bug的影响，或者说流程的乏味都让我对这款游戏的评价降低比较多。考虑再三认为并不能推荐这款游戏。

Concept prometteur, réalisation décevante (pour l'instant)

Fargone a du potentiel, mais il est plombé par des choix de conception agaçants. L’économie du jeu est totalement déséquilibrée : les ressources clés comme les médicaments et les munitions coûtent une fortune, alors que les missions rapportent presque rien. Du coup, avancer devient une vraie corvée, sans aucune satisfaction.

Les réglages de sensibilité posent aussi problème : limités aux nombres entiers, ils ne permettent aucun ajustement précis. On se retrouve à devoir choisir entre une visée lente ou ultra-rapide, sans option intermédiaire. Le monde et la disposition des points d’intérêt respirent l’amateurisme, avec un manque de cohérence, des bâtiments placés au hasard et peu d’originalité. Quant aux mécaniques de survie comme la faim et la soif, elles se vident bien trop vite, rendant l’expérience lourde et frustrante.

Cela dit, il y a quelques lueurs d'espoir. Les factions, bien que basiques, ajoutent un peu de saveur, et l'IA, malgré sa simplicité, fait son travail. Le système de météo dynamique est aussi un ajout sympa.

Je suivrai les mises à jour, mais pour l'instant, il est difficile de le recommander.

I've played a fair amount of puzzle games and I'm no genius but I'm no stranger to challenging my pattern-seeking brain. Too many of the puzzles in this game lacked sufficient clues or internal logic . Each room has an "order" it expects you to go in , but doesn't communicate this. 

Looking at item/clues is also clunky , I could forgive this if the puzzles themselves were better.

This game ran well technically; I did not encounter any bugs. I rather enjoy the art design and style. But its the story and the puzzles that make me not recommend this game. 

I love escape rooms and puzzle games (think Escape Simulator, or escape rooms in real life). Quite a number of puzzles did not make sense. Some were overcomplicated/altered to intentionally confuse ([spoiler]thinking of the rings and line math and the bar chart in Augustus's office, the number rings in the game room[/spoiler]), and others just flat out did not need to be completed ([spoiler]telescope in Amelia's bedroom[/spoiler]). There was one puzzle I could not figure out how the right answer was right ([spoiler]Amelia's 3 digit number lock, we are using the corners of 2d shape but a 2d pyramid is a triangle which should be 3, no?[/spoiler])

These puzzles are not fun, and hardly connected to story or logic. I see there is a second game coming out. I hope the problems listed in the negative reviews are noted so as to avoid the same issues with the new game. I wish for the best for the second game, as I believe this game/series has real potential. But for Secrets of Blackrock Manor, I cannot recommend.

Conan the Mighty Pig is a small but surprisingly delightful indie platformer that combines classic exploration-driven gameplay with a lighthearted sense of humor and simplicity. Developed and published by Mihai Morosanu, it tells the story of an unlikely hero—a pig named Conan—who embarks on a journey to recover his lost truffles scattered across a series of interconnected environments. What seems at first like a playful concept quickly reveals itself as a surprisingly polished and charming experience, especially for a game of such humble origins. It’s not an expansive adventure or a punishing test of skill, but rather a compact, well-crafted slice of classic 2D exploration that focuses on accessibility, atmosphere, and steady progression.

At its core, Conan the Mighty Pig is a side-scrolling platformer with mild puzzle and exploration elements. You guide Conan through forests, caves, and mountainous regions in search of truffles while avoiding obstacles and enemies that stand in your way. The game’s world isn’t just a collection of levels to be beaten in sequence but a network of interconnected areas that encourage revisiting and curiosity. As you explore, you’ll come across special plants that grant temporary powers—abilities that open up new sections of the map or make traversal easier. This mechanic gives the game a subtle “metroidvania” flavor, rewarding players for paying attention to their surroundings and experimenting with what they’ve learned. The design keeps things simple and intuitive, ensuring that exploration feels inviting rather than overwhelming, and each new discovery feels earned.

The gameplay loop is intentionally straightforward but satisfying. Movement is responsive and precise, allowing Conan to jump, dodge, and maneuver through hazards with ease. The level design makes excellent use of verticality and hidden paths, rewarding players who take the time to look beyond the obvious. While combat is minimal, the challenge comes from timing jumps, avoiding environmental dangers, and navigating terrain that gradually becomes more complex. Collecting truffles serves as the game’s primary objective, but it’s the journey itself—the exploration and discovery—that provides most of the enjoyment. There’s a gentle rhythm to the pacing that makes the experience feel relaxing rather than stressful. The difficulty curve is forgiving, which may disappoint those seeking an intense platforming challenge but makes the game approachable for a wider audience, including younger or casual players.

Visually, the game embraces a colorful and slightly rustic aesthetic that fits perfectly with its rural adventure theme. The environments are hand-crafted with care, featuring lush forests, dimly lit caves, and sweeping mountain passes that create a sense of place despite the game’s minimalist style. Each region has its own atmosphere, enhanced by simple but effective use of lighting and color. The visuals strike a balance between charm and functionality—clear enough to navigate easily, yet textured enough to feel alive. The soundtrack complements this with ambient melodies and soft background tunes that help immerse players in Conan’s journey. It’s a peaceful, almost meditative experience at times, enhanced by the subtle audio cues of nature and exploration rather than bombastic sound effects or constant tension.

One of Conan the Mighty Pig’s strongest qualities is how it embraces its limitations and turns them into strengths. There’s no pretense of grandeur here—no sprawling narrative or elaborate cutscenes—just a focused, cohesive adventure that knows exactly what it wants to be. The controls are simple, the interface clean, and the mechanics easy to grasp within minutes. Yet despite its simplicity, there’s a genuine sense of care in how everything is put together. The interconnected map structure encourages exploration and replaying, and the plant-based ability system adds a layer of variety that keeps the experience fresh throughout its short runtime. Even though the story is almost nonexistent beyond the setup, the world feels cohesive and inviting enough to carry the experience on atmosphere and curiosity alone.

That said, the game’s simplicity also comes with its drawbacks. Conan the Mighty Pig is short—most players can finish it in a single sitting—and while its world is charming, the lack of deeper progression systems or significant difficulty spikes may leave more experienced players wanting more. Once you’ve unlocked the key powers and explored the major areas, there’s little left to discover beyond completionist runs. The lack of narrative depth or character development also limits emotional engagement; Conan is a cute protagonist, but his motivations and world remain lightly sketched. Still, given the game’s price point and scope, these limitations feel appropriate rather than disappointing. It’s clear that the developer’s focus was on creating a small, self-contained experience rather than a sprawling platforming epic, and in that regard, it succeeds admirably.

Where Conan the Mighty Pig truly shines is in its sense of charm and personality. There’s something endearing about a game that doesn’t try to be more than it is—a relaxing, cheerful, and slightly whimsical platformer that invites players to explore for the sheer joy of it. It evokes the feel of classic 16-bit adventures without mimicking them directly, relying instead on its own unique flavor of exploration and humor. The pacing is calm, the difficulty fair, and the tone consistently upbeat. For players looking for a break from the intensity of larger games, it offers the perfect balance of simplicity and satisfaction. The positive reception from players on Steam reflects this; many have praised it as a hidden gem—short, sweet, and surprisingly enjoyable despite its humble presentation.

In the end, Conan the Mighty Pig stands as a reminder of what makes indie games special: creativity, heart, and a clear sense of purpose. It may not boast complex mechanics or a sweeping story, but it delivers an experience that feels genuine and thoughtfully crafted. Its colorful visuals, easy-to-learn controls, and accessible design make it suitable for anyone looking for a short, relaxing adventure. It’s the kind of game that invites you to slow down, explore at your own pace, and enjoy the simple pleasures of discovery. Mihai Morosanu’s little porcine hero may not wield a sword or save the world, but in his own quiet way, Conan leaves a lasting impression—proof that sometimes, the most modest adventures can be the most memorable.

Little Problems: A Cozy Detective Game is exactly what it says on the tin. If you've ever played The Case of the Golden Idol (or the sequel), this is the exact same game, but in a cozy, low stakes setting. And I'll be honest, that really does it for me.

The game and its artstyle are very charming, the vignettes which you have to solve are cute and paint a lovely picture. No, the overarching story isn't as complex or as compelling as The Case of the Golden Idol, but then again, that game is a masterpiece, and an interwoven story playing out in the background just wouldn't fit the vibe of this game as well. Rather, it's just a cute game with cute characters doing cute things.

The actual puzzle/mystery solving elements are also simpler than TCGI, but that's appropriate for what it is going for. I was never stumped on a level, they all went by painlessly, and except for one singular cupcake collectible, I did everything without too much of a fuss. This isn't the type of game to frustrate you, unless mystery games are just totally not your forte. And just like TCGI, there's a certain amount of bruteforcing of the solution possible, which I think tends up being a good thing in these games, since sometimes you're 99% of the way to the solution, but just missing that one piece of the puzzle that could end up taking you hours.

So, were the levels satisfying enough then? I would say so. They were excellently paced, had enough hints to their solutions, while allowing you to work towards the solution from multiple angles, and also not [i]so[/i] easy as to not engage my brain at all. It was in that sweet spot of hard enough to make me think about the solution, but not so hard as to be tediously difficult and/or long. Perhaps a bit on the lower end of the "hard enough" thing. If there was ever a follow-up (which I felt like was teased), I think I would prefer if the puzzles were roughly 10% harder, but I think if they were 20% harder, that might interrupt the flow of things, so ultimately, the game strikes a good balance.

Regarding the length of the game, I do admit that it's on the shorter side. I think I would've preferred perhaps one more extra level - though I think the final level is an excellent and fun send-off for the vibe of this game, ending on a murder mystery party - but I also don't find that it was too short.

However, I can imagine that paying €10 for a ~3 hour game isn't justifiable to everyone. Personally, I got the game for €9 due to a bundle discount - with The Roottrees Are Dead, an amazing game, definitely check that one out - and I felt that to be a reasonable price for the experience. I don't regret spending that amount of money on it, and I'm someone who tends to be on the more frugal side when it comes to my purchases. However, I am also a fiend for mystery games, so I am also biased in that regard.

Personally, I would say that this experience was worth ~€10,75 to me, which is to say that I actually think this game is underpriced for what it gives you. However, if you're on the fence, I wouldn't blame you for waiting for a 50% sale at some point. And at that point, I would say that the game is well worth €5, so definitely pick it up if that happens.

Review After Launch
-----------------------------
This review is being made after a day-one patch that seems to have fixed issues launching the PCVR/Steam port of the game.

PE1 & PE2 mean Pro Era 1 and 2.


TLDR: This is a decent upgrade from PE1, however you could argue a good chunk of the game could've been updates. I would recommend you to buy if you fit into one or more of the following:

- If you don't own PE1 and are interested in a Quarterback Simulator
- If you're a die-hard football fan and enjoyed PE1
- If you like PE1 and want multiplayer.

This is going to be a bit of a wordy review, but I really want to get all my points across on the game as it stands right now so bear with me, and please do take the time to read my review fully.

On launch as it's been discussed, the PCVR/Steam version of the game was legitimately unplayable. The .exe wouldn't launch and you couldn't boot up the game. This could obviously leave you with a bitter taste in your mouth, but I wouldn't try to judge a game too much on release. The issue has been now fixed.

When actually getting into the game itself, I would like to preface my review with the following:

I have played a lot of PE1 (Pro Era 1) ALL OF WHICH I played the Quest Version of. I also did just get the Meta Quest 3 and I have not played PE1 on the Meta Quest 3. So some comparisons I will draw between PE1 and PE2 may be partially due to the upgraded hardware, and the fact that I am this time playing on PCVR.



VISUALS:

Visually speaking, the game  is pretty darn similar to PE1. I got a chance to play the Quest Version of this game, and it looks damn near identical to it's predecessor. The Steam version I am reviewing here, does have some nicer visuals to it. Helmets shine more, the grass isn't just a flat texture, uniforms seem a bit better, and meshes seem higher poly. In particular this game has nice looking speedflex helmets on a lot of the players. Aside from that there are actually some instances I've seen what appear to be downgrades, like distant trees and foliage. However given this games pace, it's not the most noticable.



SOUND:

The audio in this is pretty similar to PE1. There are more voice lines, new sound effects, but you'll hear a lot of what you heard if you played the previous game. I myself have not heard any actual songs play in the game yet. I don't know if this is a bug, but if not it's a disappointment in that regard. Some of the songs in PE1 like Desperado were really good and would get you hyped up.

GAMEPLAY:

Ok here's the meat and potatoes and what actually matters. Given that the graphical upgrade isn't the largest, the game-play really needs to shine through. And it kinda does? If you've played PE1, you're getting a smoother version of that, there's more plays, better scrambling, etc. The game seems to be a good bit more difficult which I like given that you're supposed to be a rookie QB. I've been messing up much more here then when I first tried PE1 which is strange considering I've played the predecessor to this. But your bad throws really end up being bad, and you have to learn from it. You also have to earn your coaches trust this time before being able to do certain things like call audibles.

IMMERSION:

The immersion in PE2 is one area I think it does take a good step forward when compared to PE1. The locker room is a bit nicer, you can customize yourself a bit more extensively here. You now run out of the tunnel with your team which is really a cool feeling being a huge football fan. On the sideline you can regain some stamina by drinking some unbranded gatorade & fist bump your teammates. You'll also hear them talk a little bit now too which is kinda cool but the Voice Acting on them isn't the greatest. You can now also highfive teammates on the field after a play which is nice. When you get sacked or tackled you'll now actually be on the ground for a second as well which is pretty neat but can be jarring for some. The BIGGEST issue with immersion in this game is the Player Likenes. Aside from Quarterbacks it seems pretty damn random how other players look. I know we're not getting facescans for this but the likeness is pretty damn atrocious. For example, in my game I've chosen to play as the Patriots. Cole Strange the Right Guard is black which he is not in real life. I saw players on opposing teams with this as well like black players been white. Please do not take this the wrong way, it's just in a game about immersion they should at least get the right ethnicity or skin tone for players. Some players also wear the wrong numbers. Again in my instance on the Patriots, Devante Parker (#1) is #29. Ezekiel Elliot (#15) is listed at 48.

I'd really like to see some content updates for this game as we didn't get any for PE1. Given that we didn't with PE1 my hopes are low, but a roster update or two would be nice, and maybe adding some features would be really nice. Given how this seems like it'll probably be a yearly release I doubt that, but the amount of new/updated content for the game can make it difficult to justify the pricetag for many.

I personally recommend it as I'm a huge Football fan and I really do enjoy playing.

I might come back to add more to this, but I have to say, I'm not sure why it's got so many negative reviews.

The game is pretty straight forward with what it is giving you from the jump. Killing enemies to increase the Hatred Level makes it more challenging (obviously) and that's good. I've seen people saying "it punishes exploration." No, it doesn't, it gives you something to do to make each play a little different. The "Hatred Corruption" mechanic is good for game hoarders like me. It really makes you think about what you may or may not want to sacrifice, or if you want to punish yourself for getting too greedy or distracted from what you need to do.

Yes, the story is pretty light, but that's okay. I picked it up the first time after work tonight, and honestly, it fits perfectly into the "I need to turn off my brain for a bit" niche.

Yes, there are a few things that could potentially be built out, but it's not totally necessary. It's a 3D Open-World "Beat-em-up" type with a fun transformation/fast travel mechanic. I haven't beaten it yet, but I'm already hoping for a sequel at some point. Everspace was like this, and then Everspace 2 came out and WOW did they build their world and lore out. I'd love to see the same done here. Keep this one out there, and let us have a continuation so we can learn more about what we've been given here. Or maybe give us a LITTLE expansion for some story and to whet our appetites for more of this world, but I would save a "Deep Dive" for lore and the myth for a larger title in the future.

Overall, I'd recommend it for anyone looking for a quick sprint for late nights before bed, or any other limited sessions. It works like Black Desert. Pick it up and put it down easily without worrying about trying to remember "what was I doing?"

[h1]Experienced on the Meta Quest 3[/h1]

You can view my gameplay & early impressions here: https://youtu.be/sk8rxwQoIjk

Quite simply, I had fun. This is a budget-priced arcade kart racer where you push yourself forward like you're on a wheelchair in this open-world obstacle course. You can boost, double-jump, or glide in the air as you try to get to your location to complete quests. It's closer to a platforming game than an actual racing game, but you can definitely race against your friends online.

The controls are quite easy to learn, but can be challenging to master, especially when you try to go up an incline with the wind trying to blow you off. I do think the game can use a better tutorial, especially for the more advanced tricks you have to learn to get around some obstacles. There is usually a ghost (AI player) you can sort of follow to learn how to do it though.

Pushing yourself around is actually pretty easy so it's not an intense workout. The challenge is mostly trying to figure out the obstacle course. I wasn't sure about the content, but after about an hour, I'm still no where close to finishing the race just due to the challenge. It's a really huge map.

Game is running on the Unity Engine. On my RTX 3080, I was getting a steady 72 fps (Q3 default). I did not experience any serious issues or bugs. You can play comfortable seated, as long as you can move your hands backwards to forward from your side. You can easily re-center as well in-game. The game uses an automatic tunnel (vignette) and helmet, you can turn those off in the settings to get a clearer view.

My biggest complaint is that the scales are a bit off. It just feels like the world is big and you are small. Also, it seems like the game automatically shows your IP address in the main hub area. There is no off-line mode. The game could use some graphical settings as well. It does need a better tutorial for the more advanced techniques. However, all in all, the game is fun and is off to a good start in Early Access. It just needs more people (and possibly a more secure connection).

I don't normally bother posting reviews, would rather spend the time actually gaming. This is the first one I'm posting, as I don't think the game deserves less than a "positive" overall opinion.

My perspective comes from having always enjoyed CCGs and TBS, since earlier days of e.g. Magic: The Gathering and Final Fantasy Tactics/Fire Emblem. Naturally, I was excited to see a game marrying both elements (not that it's the first out there), and I've been playing C&C for months now on mobile. So what's kept me playing, and why should you play, or not play it?

ART:
YMMV. The game goes for a particular cartoonish art style, which you'll like or dislike instantly - just see the screenshots. Clear differences between the 5 factions. If you appreciate the style, the art and animation are excellent. If not, perhaps the game isn't for you. However, there's no reason to diss the graphics as terrible; contemporaneous CCG-type games such as Hearthstone or Card Hunter have totally different art styles which are equally attractive. In comparison, I don't like how March of War looks - it's all personal taste.

MUSIC:
...adequate for the genre - i.e. turn off in favour of your own music after 1 hour.

GAMEPLAY:
5 factions, which you may choose to play solo, or combine with another faction (e.g. crusader/warlock or warlock/pirate) for a total of 15 different combinations. Playing solo factions gains you access to powerful faction-specific "hero" cards, while including a 2nd faction obviously provides versatility. Factions are distinct with their own playstyle, and quite well-balanced (especially after recent changes to pirates). Also, all deck types are viable - aggro, midrange, control, ramp, whatever type your fevered mind can dream up.

P2WIN-NESS:
The obvious bugbear for some. If you're looking to gain a significant collection without putting in any effort, I would suggest against playing any digital CCG-based game.

What some people may be sore about is facing players with many epics/legendaries and getting stomped. Do realise - the game has been out on mobile for > 1 year, and many players have near-complete collections. However, many of them haven't paid significant amounts of real $$, and you're getting stomped as they know the game better than you do, not because their cards are significantly better than yours.

The question is, can you compete as a new player? It's entirely possible with mostly common/uncommon cards, with a smattering of rares. Legendaries are limited to 1 copy each/deck (used to be up to the normal 2 copies/deck until a couple of months ago), which helps to limit their use. Overall, no better or worse than Hearthstone (which seems to be the benchmark, after all) in this aspect.

Finally, no gameplay element is locked behind a real $$ paywall, only cosmetic stuff (e.g. different castle looks) or more deck slots (>9).

ACCESSIBILITY:
Big one for me - the ability to play asynchronous games, which is what I wish Hearthstone had. Not as relevant to the desktop gamer, but hey - you can play on your desktop, and continue to play in short bursts on the go on mobile.


CAVEATS:
I decided against putting in a "Pros" section - I've covered most of the points above. Let the game speak for itself, it's free to try now anyway. However, some caveats are as follows, especially if you're considering putting in real $$.

- As some have pointed out, it's harder to craft epics/legendaries in C&C compared to e.g. Hearthstone. The cost for those was increased a couple of months ago, ostensibly so that crafting them would be harder and actually getting one would be more exciting. ...Whatever the reason, do note that it won't be easy to obtain epics/legendaries without spending at least a little $$.
- Smaller card pool. Currently, the card pool is in no way comparable to e.g. Hearthstone, even vanilla Hearthstone from way back. I don't feel like there's a lack of variety even after 4-5 months or so of playing, but it's just something to keep in mind. There's an expansion (Age of Dragons) coming up Jan 2016, which will help shake things up.
- Grindiness. The gold (non-premium currency) earning rate was nerfed, and coupled with the high cost of crafting epics/legendaries, you may feel pushed to spend just to get the juicy looking epics/legendaries. That said, as mentioned above - you can compete (in a fair fashion) using common/uncommon/rare cards. Some figures for the current state of the game - 1 quest per day (generally 800-1200 gold), average of 15-50 gold/win, 1 booster costs 2000 gold ---> 1 booster every 2 days (or slightly less, depending on how much you play). Whether or not you think it's worth your time, you decide.
- Fluidity. The game has had more significant card/balance changes since its mobile launch days than e.g. Hearthstone, including some changes (e.g. to ranged units, or to many pirates cards) which happened even after the devs posted that they were done with significant changes to gameplay (after the 2.0 update on mobile). While the changes have been beneficial for game balance and shows that the devs are responsive, C&C does not (and may never have) have the stability/polish that the big players (e.g. Hearthstone or MTG) exhibit. To their credit, it's rather hard to match the big boys when you're a small developer with a small team. Anyway, be prepared that what you like/don't like about certain cards/factions can change (sometimes suddenly).
- Fluctuating business model. Let's just say that changes in costs (both upwards/downwards) for many things (crafting, boosters, the recent "wing-based" expansion, draft tournaments) have made some unhappy. While I would not call out the developers for greed/making the game P2W, they're experimenting as they go, so prices may not be as stable as some would like (definitely not as stable as e.g. Hearthstone). Be prepared before you spend any $$ (although, the premium currency prices have not changed at all since I started playing - what's changed is the costs of what you can buy with it).

TL;DR:
- All things considered, C&C has lots of charm, and a good degree of game balance/variation. It scratches my itch for a TBS/CCG mashup and isn't overly complex. Furthermore, there are many potential mechanics yet to be explored, so the game has lots of room to grow.
- The best testament: I stopped playing Hearthstone. I still play C&C.
- Don't want to get stomped by the pros? Join now! Since it's recently out of early access, more new players will be flooding in. This is the best time to fumble around together :)

Jogo muito bom! É um dos poucos soulslikes isométricos que joguei, e adorei a lore de piratas presente nele. Até recentemente, fiquei sabendo do jogo que serviu de inspiração para este: Death's Door. Pretendo dar uma chance a ele futuramente, e, se for tão bom quanto este, com certeza vou curtir também.
Quero apontar duas frustrações que mais me irritaram durante a jogatina:
1. A falta de um mapa decente. Até existe um no menu do jogo, mas é impreciso e vago, não ajuda em nada na localização exata do jogador ou na orientação dos caminhos. Também não há indicador de objetivo ou missão. Muitas vezes, você se vê completamente perdido, sem saber para onde ir ou qual caminho seguir, particularmente, isso é bem revoltante.
2. A dificuldade sem sentido. Inimigos comuns ao longo do jogo são mais fortes que os próprios chefes (bosses), o que atrapalha demais na busca pela platina. E falando nela: por conta da falta de informações dentro do jogo e da escassez de guias na comunidade, deixei de conquistar três troféus que faltavam para a platina, tudo por causa de uma decisão errada em uma side quest. QUE ÓDIO!
O jogo é legal, mas tem um ritmo lento, o que não me motiva a jogá-lo novamente só para pegar essas conquistas.
Apesar disso, gostei bastante. Está recomendadíssimo! Não vou negativar um jogo por conta de uma ou duas coisas que desaprovei nele.
Aos meus conterrâneos brazucas que desenvolveram esse jogo: PARABÉNS! Vocês demonstraram o carinho que tiveram na produção desse game. Alguns jogos feitos no Brasil merecem mais destaque e reconhecimento, como é o caso de Mark of the Deep.

This takes two of my favourite games - Slay the Spire and Into the Breach - and creates a delicious chimaera of them. So far I'm enjoying it.

Hard to shake some of the similarities to STS (you might pick up a card and think "oh it's a Blade Dance", "oh it's a Catalyst"), but there's enough interesting and unique stuff that it feels like its own thing.

The similarity to Into the Breach is more in terms of the battle mechanic, but the comparatively generous health bar leads to less pure puzzle-solving.

The art direction is great, particularly the background environments. Bosses and elites are cool.

The music SLAPS. I find myself jamming out to it the entire time I'm playing.

The game itself is ok. I definitely enjoy playing it and I definitely recommend the game even if you were to play without sound.

...but seriously....the music is rad as hell

If I could, I would elect to give this a neutral rating. I came to the conclusion that I just don't like the genre of action-isometric games. Played a few of them now and it just doesn't work for me so bear that in mind for the review. 

This game has a lot of content, tons of lore, and a decent amount of replay-ability. Some aspects of the game are very obscure and it doesn't help that there isn't much discussion around to help you when you get stuck. There is a wiki now but there wasn't when I played. For example, there was a quest about finding statues that I could never finish even after visiting every poi and doing all the combat zones. Most quests have markers though and I don't think you are intended to do everything in one playthrough. I made manual backups of my saves which is not an intended game mechanic, but it can be done.

I got burned out on the game when I accidently sold, at least I think I did, a quest item that I wanted to finish. Decided to rush the final boss and end the game forgetting the advice I read about the final boss not allowing companions which I had grown far too accustomed to having as fodder. The final boss is very challenging by comparison and you cannot back out after starting it. You can respec and respawn but that's it. 

Combat is a mixture of weak mobs and strong enemies that have to be carefully fought. Not always together but many of the tougher challenges have both. I got used to using cc and spells to deal with weaker enemies while also having some methods of killing stronger ones. I didn't spend as much time learning the melee move set but I imagine the final boss would have been significantly easier had I done so. The economy of the game isn't that hard to handle if you take the skills that let you repair your own gear. I didn't have any trouble stockpiling gear and materials by running repeats of defeated dungeons. 

Since I don't really like the genre I'm not really sure how to recommend this to other people. I had heard it characterized as a souls like in third person but I wouldn't agree with that. If you like the idea of doing a series of dungeons, possibly multiple times, while managing resources then maybe give it a go. While there are quests and levels in the game it doesn't work like a traditional rpg so don't go in expecting that. It's more of a hybrid that I think people who like the combat style will enjoy a lot more.

Alaloth is really nice action RPG with soulslike fights.

Leveling is different than in all RPGs - you get XP when you conquer fighting arena. No XP for finishing quests, killing enemies etc.

Itemization is really good - there are no godly options for your build of choice - your skill matters. Ofcourse there are tiers of items and usually legendary is better than epic but with my orc playthrough I switched from legendary 2H sword to epic one because of higher crit chance and crit damage.

No voiceover! :( that's really shame, all dialogues you have to read by yourself.

No obvious class (you choose your race in the beginning) - you can use all skills available on any character. For instance my orc really liked to summon imps for distraction and use some shaman buffs with arcane teleport to leave decoy :)

Only one main quest - rest are side quests which can be done in any order - that gives strong roguelike/roguelite vibe with rewards being gold/items/crafting materials. Remember - no XP for those, only for conquering fighting areas.

Beautiful sceneries (Bloody Lake, The One Tree, Sea of Stars) - breathtaking and really well crafted images to watch.

Music is just fine but nothing really stands out for me.

Evil/Neutral/Good alignment - sadly you don't get such freedom with this choice like in typical RPG game (Baldur's Gate/Neverwinter) - it mainly affects companions which you can hire.

Companions - your "party" members to choose from, every alignment get 4 of them with different skills and different rewards for completing their quests.

DRAGONS! they are extremely well crafted, presented and fights are very intense, hard and fun.

Overall Alaloth is solid action RPG game with some innovative systems and quite deep lore behind. If you are looking for challenging game to play - get it.

Important! game is best played on controller and I really recommend to use one.

《溯光行》：8.4 / 10 （优秀）

单周目流程时长： 8 - 14 小时
类型：俯视角，动作解谜，类塞尔达

——————
吐槽时间
——————

空间回溯，一个既新颖、又难以驾驭的机制。它理论上的可拓展性实在太大，很难用单一的框架就将其完全束缚。而以这个机制为核心的作品，按理来说，怎么也应该是那种天马行空，剑走偏锋的类型。

但是，《溯光行》给我的感受却完全相反，这是一部极其循规蹈矩的作品。你在它身上看不到明显的短板，但它的所有长处，也都能在其他游戏中找到对照。

若你对它抱有极高期待，它可能会让你失望；但若你对它毫无预期，它又可能会带来一段相当顺滑流畅的优秀体验。

怎么说呢，这就是一部把“中庸”诠释到极致的作品。它的流程融入了极多的创意，但最终还是局限于固有的框架之内。

——————
视听演出
——————
先说说本作最为突出的部分。

游戏的画面虽然称不上豪华，但美术风格极为亮眼。尤其是几场 Boss 战，大量素材堆叠出的场景美感十足，特效与演出也是一场比一场华丽。

而它的音乐表现同样出色，气氛营造得非常到位。尤其是序章的那一段背景音乐，好听到直接坚定了我通关本作的决心。

（可惜这首曲子貌似就只在序章出现过）

——————
游戏性
——————

游戏性方面，无论是关卡模式还是流程设计，本作都很像是《死亡门扉》。主角会在不停的关卡之间穿梭，每完成一个关卡，都会回到大本营进行一段剧情，然后继续下一个关卡，以此循环。

而在解谜方面，本作又和大部分同类俯视角游戏一样（比如《Tunic》），非常喜欢利用视觉差、视角变化以及独特的机制来指引道路、隐藏秘密、又或者是揭示宝物。

至于它的成长以及战斗方面，也是相当常规。游戏提供了多种主动以及被动技能，玩家可以选择3种主动攻击手段，以及根据槽位选择多种被动。除此之外，还有天赋加点的设计，通过加点可以让数值或机制得到一定的成长。这就是很常见的那一套玩法，做的也不算出彩，因此就不多赘述了。

那么，本作有没有独属于自己的特色呢？

当然有了，那就是本作主打的玩法——空间回溯。

回溯，可以简单拆分成两个机制。一个是“记录”，另一个则是“传送”。

记录，融合了闪避和奔跑，主角会在闪避或奔跑的同时，在身后留下一道记录行踪的轨迹。传送，则是可以将主角传送到这条轨迹的任意节点。

简单来说，就是主角通过闪避或者奔跑，消耗“体力”，来记录自己的行踪轨迹，然后可以随时回到过去记录过的位置。

值得一提的是，这个机制虽然也结合了其他游戏里的闪避和奔跑。不过战斗中的基本逻辑却与闪避有很大不同——它并不是依赖于即时反应，而是需要提前规划好位置的预判能力。

另外，如果回溯到敌人的视野盲区，还能获得强化攻击。不过这个功能相当鸡肋，不仅难触发还相当繁琐，打boss也无法用。所以基本可以当这个机制不存在。

讲到这，想必有个问题很多人都能意识到了，这个回溯，在战斗中能够取代闪避吗？

答案是完全不行的。其一，是因为回溯机制实在是太拖沓了，想要流畅战斗肯定还是闪避更加适合。其二，则是这个机制的逻辑比较独特，因此想要熟悉还是需要一定的适应时间的。

所以，回溯在战斗中的定位，更像是一个在危机环节快速换位的保底手段。主体部分还是闪避。

但你要说，回溯没啥用吗？大错特错，回溯恰恰是本作最为强大的战斗手段。因为游戏里最为轮椅的一个战斗技能，就是强烈依靠回溯的——回指旋斩

这个技能听着描述平平无奇，但实际用了你就知道有多轮椅了。攻击可以增加技能段数 - 释放途中保持无敌 - 技能本身的攻击也能增加段数 - 无cd。

这么一套循环下，只要boss不是那种喜欢四处乱动的类型，主角就可以靠着这个技能，全程无敌并保持高伤害，一路乱杀。玩着能不笑的，鉴定为有抑郁症。

战斗讲完了，那么回溯在解谜中的表现又是如何呢？

本作在每一关都会解锁新的能力，而这些能力往往都和空间回溯有关系。序章是利用回溯的换位特性快速通过限时机关；第一关则是让回溯结合吸取能力移动物品；第二关是让回溯结合照明能力通过黑暗；第三关则是让回溯轨迹充当电路，同时可以瞬移到电源处；第四关则是对于回溯机制的究极考验。

这些谜题的设计相当成熟，不仅对各种能力机制利用到极致，难度也是控制的极佳，不至于让人卡关。唯一比较遗憾的就是，我觉得“空间回溯”这个设定应该能够创造出更多出彩的设计，但本作对其的运用就略微有点保守了。

此外，在每个大关卡中，还有一些有趣的子关卡。这些子关卡的设计可以参考《塞尔达：荒野之息》，基本都是一个又一个的创意解谜。不过可惜的是，这些部分也就仅限于“有趣”了。实际体验下来，除了“3d弹球”以及“跳跃记录”之外，都是极为普通的益智谜题，无法给人留下太深的印象。

最后，还有一个非常需要提及的部分，就是本作目前的Bug数量极.其.夸.张。

对话结束页面还在；速频穿刺攻击无法摧毁物品；莫名被困在修理站里；冲刺键失效；怪物飞到地图外导致战斗结束不了；背刺卡进墙里；打完boss不结算等等等等，多到我压根举不完，一个比一个奇葩，套路基本不重样。

而在细节方面，游戏的漏洞也是非常多。没完全封死的解谜道路；能直接靠传送抵达的未接触裂隙；物品数量标识错误（部分章节收集物和次要芯片数量比地图收集显示的要多）等等等等，同样是多到吐槽不完。

不幸中的万幸是，本作的自动保存非常频繁，当遇到卡关bug时可以随时回档，不至于产生太大的负面影响。不过一步一个bug的感受多少还是让人有些心惊胆颤的。

——————
剧情
——————

本作的剧情含量中规中矩，因此不用剧透也能谈几句。

在讲述设定之前，先说说剧情一个比较大的问题——专有名词过多。本作几乎所有常见的词语包括招数技能，都特地造了个新词，或者特地用那种不常用的词语组合。甚至是人名，也都替换成了很难记住的代码。我理解这是为了构建世界观，但一个好的世界观，往往也不需要替换这么多词语啊。

最后整体剧情看下来，这套设计除了把容易理解的东西变得复杂，影响阅读流畅性之外，也没有给世界带来多少增色，或者提供多少信息。

上次我看到这么一套繁琐的设计还是在《逆向坍塌：面包房行动》里，但那个游戏是有二游的世界观支撑的，而本作则是啥铺垫都没有的独立游戏。不过，联想本作以前的一些宣发，貌似也不是不能理解。

这边搬下游戏的页面开场，可以来感受下。

“3323年，为及时排除极端心态可能带来的社会隐患，元与人类共同发起了元镜计划，创造了元镜领域与执行者。当偏执个体报名参加元镜计划后，他们的思想世界会被投射到元镜领域，转化为各种光怪陆离的镜魇。执行者的任务是进入镜魇，消除其中的镜念，从而引导偏执个体回归正轨，维护社会的稳定与安全”

仔细思索，可以理解大概。但要想一口气理解，似乎不太可能。为了之后方便理解，这边我就用更加直白的词语概括下本作的设定。

简单来说，人类之所以会伤害他人或者伤害自己，是因为过往的经历造就了这些。那么如果可以把这些经历给消除，人类就能够走向正轨，回归社会。而本作的计划，则是将这些过往的记忆具象化为“梦魇”，从而创造出消除的手段。

本作的主角“拾”，则是一个智能战斗程序机器人（简称：执行者）。他的任务，就是进入一个个人类的梦境，消除这些被具象化的记忆，从而让人类恢复“正常”。

游戏的叙事主要依靠两种手段。一个是主角和其他角色的直白对话，比如闲暇时间的通信，主线时的相处。另一个则是充满碎片故事的“数据库”，这里记录着主角与朋友们的关系、关卡中的信息、各种世界观设定、以及过往的经历。这个数据库同时也是剧情重要的一部分，因此里面时不时能够获取一些剧情上的关键信息，或者是角色之间的彩蛋小吐槽。

就这个类型来说，剧情还是相当不错的。虽然比较庸俗，但好歹也是探讨了一个不错的主题，最后一刻的伏笔揭露也是让人惊喜（不过这个设计如今也不太新鲜了）。每个关卡对其故事本身的阐述比较简陋，但立意也都相当不错，并且时刻围绕着那个核心——

如果可以删去脑海中那些带来过苦痛的记忆，你会这么做吗？这么做是对的吗？当一个人的情感和意志被剔除后，还会是原来的自己吗？

要说有啥明显的问题，就是结局过于草率了。说好听点是为玩家留下了很多遐想的空间，为续作留下了很好的铺垫。说难听点，直接走流程，断章+1。

聊聊一个核心问题吧——本作，有意思吗？

《溯光行》是一款非常典型的学院派作品。它的设计、剧情、主旨、解谜，乃至最为核心的回溯机制，你几乎都能在《死亡门扉》、《晶体管》、《Tunic》、《波斯王子》、《去月球》等作品中找到影子。这让它在各方面都显得稳健、成熟，尤其是在关卡设计与解谜节奏上，几乎挑不出太大的毛病。

但同时，本作也是相当的“无趣”。至少就我看来，它的流程，除了几场观感极佳的 Boss 战之外，并没有太多能够给我留下深刻印象的段落——大部分体验我都已经在其他作品里经历过了。

以一部独立游戏的标准来看，四名应届生为主体的阵容能够选择这么一个冷门的题材，做出如此完整的作品，确实是没法苛责太多。而以一款商业化作品的标准来说，本作也是提供了相当不错的游玩体验。

所以这种异样感究竟是哪里来的呢？终于在本文的最后，我意识到了。

独立游戏的迷人之处，从来不在于“做得像样”，而是那种明知资源有限，却仍然“敢做只有自己才会做的”那种疯狂。《溯光行》并非没有创意，但是，这些创意更像是被简单的拿来装饰和打磨一套已经成熟的框架，而不是让整套框架去为那一个点子服务，从而牵动整个游戏。

它的骨架、设计、节奏，都更接近于一款稳健的商业化作品；而真正像独立游戏的，反而只有题材、体量以及不足的打磨。而当一部独立作品的“灵气”和“任性”都被精心收束在安全的范围内时，就会变成一种微妙的违和感——

我知道它很好，但我总觉得，它本可以更“不像话”一点。

“Mitsurugi Kamui Hikae” is a compact third-person action game built around fast sword combat, mobility, and parry timing. The core loop resembles a simplified character action system. You strike, dodge, and cancel attacks while maintaining pressure. Inputs are clean and readable. The result is a focus on execution rather than combo memorization.

Enemy waves escalate across short stages. New foes add armor, ranged pressure, or burst damage. These additions force you to learn priorities and spacing. The parry window is generous. Successful counters create momentum and reward aggression. Difficulty spikes appear when multiple enemy types overlap, but patterns remain learnable.

Upgrades expand your toolkit. You invest points into new moves, improved counters, and defensive options. The progression is linear but meaningful. Unlocks reduce repetition by adding combo variety. However, few moves become mandatory, which can flatten the curve for high-skill players. Depth exists, but it is compact.

Boss encounters highlight the combat system. Attacks are telegraphed, and reactions matter. Watching wind-ups and punishing whiffs feels satisfying. Some bosses push damage checks instead of pattern mastery. These fights are short but intense. They reinforce fundamentals rather than spectacle.

Presentation is modest. Character models are stylized with limited detail. Animations are clean and functional. Stage designs are minimal and repeat asset themes. Visual clarity supports combat readability but lacks environmental identity. Technical performance is stable. Frame consistency helps precision.

Audio support relies on sharp hit sounds and looping music. Effects confirm timing and punish states. Voice delivery is sparse. Music repetition becomes noticeable in longer sessions. Sound operates as feedback rather than atmosphere building.

Overall, “Mitsurugi Kamui Hikae” delivers a concise action experience centered on timing, counters, and mobility. It offers short bursts of satisfying combat with lean systems. Limited stage variety and modest presentation reduce long-term retention. Players who enjoy focused execution challenges will find value in its tight loop.

Gish is one of those oddball indie titles from the early 2000s that stuck in people’s memory precisely because it was so different. Instead of a standard platforming hero, you control a living ball of tar with the ability to stick to walls, flatten to squeeze through gaps or harden to crush enemies. It’s a physics-driven platformer before “physics platformers” were really a thing and the mechanics are still clever today.

When the game works, it’s genuinely fun. Using momentum to slingshot yourself across gaps, climbing walls by clinging like tar or smashing enemies with a well timed slam all feel satisfying. There’s creativity in how each level demands you experiment with Gish’s malleable body.

But here’s the rub: physics-based controls can be as frustrating as they are innovative. Movement is slippery and imprecise, and some levels feel designed more to test your patience than your skill. It’s not uncommon to fail a section simply because the blob didn’t bounce or grip the way you expected. Add in occasional camera issues and a difficulty curve that spikes hard, and the fun can quickly sour into annoyance.

Despite its flaws, Gish remains an important piece of indie history. It’s rough, quirky and often awkward, but also inventive in ways most platformers of its era never dared to be. If you have patience for clumsy physics and want to experience a pioneer of the indie scene, it’s worth a look. Otherwise, it’s probably more fun to remember than to actually play today.

Hideko is a small but enchanting sandbox game that embodies the spirit of quiet discovery. Rather than guiding the player through quests or structured objectives, it hands you a pocket-sized world filled with natural elements, tiny creatures, and simple objects, and encourages you to tinker until its underlying logic reveals itself. You begin with only a few items and a small play area, but even in those early moments the charm is unmistakable. The world reacts to your actions with gentle animations, soft sounds, and a sense of life that feels surprisingly warm for such minimalistic design. Hideko never rushes you. Instead, it invites you to slow down, experiment, and enjoy the soothing rhythm of observing how things interact.

The heart of the game lies in its combination-based experimentation. Every object can be dropped, merged, fed, or otherwise placed into contact with another to see what emerges. Maybe two seeds produce a different plant, or a creature’s reaction to an object becomes the key to discovering a new resource. Sometimes the results feel intuitive, other times surprising, but in both cases the satisfaction comes from the simple joy of figuring things out on your own. As you uncover new combinations, the game rewards you with stars, which gradually expand your inventory capacity and unlock new areas of the small world. The pace of progression feels natural—just enough to encourage further play, yet calm enough to preserve the game’s meditative tone.

Hideko’s atmosphere is one of its strongest qualities. The art style uses soft palettes and clean pixel visuals to create an inviting sense of space, and the animations are subtle but expressive. Tiny creatures wiggle, plants sway, and the sandbox feels alive in a way that encourages you to linger between interactions just to observe the world breathe. Sound design plays an equally important role. Rather than relying on a heavy soundtrack, the game allows ambient noises and small audio cues to take center stage. These sounds—rustling leaves, bubbling water, faint chirps—give the experience a natural warmth that complements its theme of gentle experimentation.

The experience is intentionally short, often lasting only a couple of hours, but this brevity works in its favor. Hideko is designed to be a compact burst of curiosity, a relaxing break rather than a long-term commitment. Some players may wish the game were longer or offered more combinations to discover, but the limited scope prevents it from overstaying its welcome. The world feels complete within its boundaries, offering just enough depth to feel rewarding without overwhelming the player with complexity. There may be moments where certain interactions feel a little finicky or unclear, and a few usability quirks can appear, yet these small issues rarely interrupt the sense of flow.

Because of its structure, Hideko appeals most to players who enjoy discovering systems organically and who find pleasure in quiet, unpressured creativity. Those seeking a narrative arc, strategic depth, or intensive gameplay loops may find it too light, but for players drawn to games that evoke curiosity and calm, Hideko delivers a refreshing and memorable experience. It feels like a digital terrarium—small, self-contained, and full of subtle wonders for those willing to observe and experiment. Ultimately, Hideko succeeds not by grand ambition, but by offering a peaceful, imaginative playground that invites you to explore at your own pace and enjoy the simple joy of making new things grow.

Crawling Lab is an adult-themed horror puzzle game that combines light erotic content with dark, laboratory-based exploration.

Gameplay focuses on solving simple puzzles, finding keys, and avoiding hostile creatures within a confined lab environment. Players move through dimly lit corridors, collecting items and unlocking scenes that mix tension and fanservice. The structure is linear and short, emphasizing atmosphere over mechanical depth.

Visually, the game blends anime-inspired character art with 3D horror environments. The contrast between stylized characters and grim settings creates a distinct but uneven tone. Animation is limited, but static artwork is detailed and polished for its niche audience.

Sound design relies on ambient noise, low background hums, and occasional jump-scare cues. Voice acting is minimal or absent. The music is sparse, serving mainly to maintain suspense.

Performance is stable, with fast load times and smooth framerates even on modest systems. Controls are basic—movement, interaction, and inventory use—suitable for a short indie project.

Content is brief. The entire game can be finished in under an hour, with limited replay value aside from revisiting unlocked artwork or alternative endings. It functions more as a visual experience than a traditional horror title.

Overall, Crawling Lab delivers a compact blend of horror and eroticism built on simple exploration and puzzle mechanics. It succeeds as a short, atmospheric curiosity but lacks depth, challenge, or narrative strength to appeal beyond its niche audience.
