Garden In! is a warm, contemplative sandbox about nurturing plants and creating cozy indoor spaces, and its greatest triumph is how effortlessly it invites players into a slower rhythm. Developed and published by Dramatic Iceberg, the game leans entirely into gentleness—soft colors, delicate animations, and a quiet sense of progress that unfolds at its own pace. Rather than pushing the player toward efficiency or competition, it instead encourages presence. You begin in a small, sunlit room with only a few pots and seeds, and from there the game steadily opens into a soothing loop of planting, watering, decorating, and discovering new flora. It’s an experience built less on challenge and more on the simple pleasure of tending something beautiful over time.

The core mechanics revolve around selecting pots, choosing soil types, planting seeds, and watching your plants grow gradually in real time. Garden In! doesn’t hide behind complex systems or heavy simulation; instead, it embraces simplicity as an aesthetic choice. Growth takes hours rather than minutes, and plants continue developing even when the game is inactive. This design invites a check-in style of play—watering your seedlings, rearranging a shelf, or experimenting with hybridization before stepping away again. It echoes the cadence of caring for real plants, where patience is part of the reward. Unlocking new plant species through combinations or achievements adds a sense of discovery that motivates you to keep experimenting without the pressure of deadlines or failure.

Visually, the game is charming without being overstated. Gentle lighting, pastel hues, and clean lines create interior spaces that feel inviting and personal. Each room you unlock becomes a canvas for expression, allowing you to customize layouts, place furniture, change décor, and arrange plants in ways that reflect your own aesthetic sensibilities. This freedom is amplified by the fact that nothing in the game costs currency—every pot, furniture piece, and decorative item is instantly available once unlocked. It makes experimentation frictionless, allowing you to redesign rooms on a whim without worrying about resource management. This openness transforms Garden In! into as much a decoration game as a plant-growing one, giving it appeal that stretches beyond fans of gardening themes.

As calming as the experience is, the game does carry some limitations that stem from its design philosophy. Because the growth cycle is slow and depends on real time, players expecting active engagement may find the pace too passive. For those accustomed to quick gratification in simulation titles, Garden In! can initially feel like a string of small chores—water here, spray there, wait a few hours, then repeat. When managing numerous plants, these actions can become repetitive. Likewise, while hybridization adds depth, the interface is not always clear, and it can be difficult to remember which seed combinations yield which new plants. The late-game progression, where tasks require high quantities of plants or repetitive actions, can turn meditative calm into mild grind if approached too mechanically.

Despite these drawbacks, Garden In! succeeds at the experience it aims to deliver. It is a gentle, aesthetically grounded retreat that asks the player to slow down and enjoy small moments rather than chase constant stimulation. In a landscape of fast-paced, high-pressure games, its quietness feels intentional and refreshing. It works best not as a game to binge for hours, but as a companion you revisit periodically—watering some vines, adding a new shelf, planting a fresh seed, then stepping away to let time do its work. When framed this way, the game becomes a soothing ritual rather than a task list.

Ultimately, Garden In! is a lovingly crafted ode to growth, creativity, and calm. It won’t appeal to players looking for complexity, but for those who appreciate gentle pacing, soft aesthetics, and relaxed sandbox play, it offers a cozy and restorative experience. Whether you’re tending a digital terrarium to unwind after a long day or crafting the perfect virtual plant-filled nook, Garden In! provides a charming little sanctuary where patience blossoms into beauty.

Rating: 8/10

Fell for the positive reviews (+ a very good Steam sale at the time) and, honestly, some of them are kinda disingenuous. Basically, it's a more polished take on the board game from V3, but still nothing special. All characters play the same, with 95% of the cast locked away behind a gacha system whose only purpose is to have an excuse for high rarity units and to artificially extend the grind for a successful run. I think it would be easier to just tell you what you get and what you don't when you buy this shii.

[h3]What you get:[/h3]
A mild board game which rewards the same strategies every single time.
A pointless battle tower where you get to fight generic enemies forever with no end in sight.
A battle system that makes the average RPGMaker game look complex.
A tedious gacha which takes countless runs to even have enough currency for a 10 consecutive pull.
Redrawn sprites, some of which are very uninspired or just weird looking.
Two new boring tracks that you will get tired of really fast.

[h3]What you don't get:[/h3]
Unique moves or strategies for each unit.
Actually interesting dialogue events that don't feel forced or out of character.
No CG / Concept Art gallery (Really?)
New voicelines.

It's not like you will hate it or anything, but it will  grow old fast. It certainly did for me. I payed around 5 bucks and still feel cheated lol. Just don't buy it, even for "Completionist" purposes, especially if you already own V3.

Cute Honey: Bunny Girl is a casual puzzle game developed by Lovely Games that mixes simple mechanics with anime-style adult visuals.

The gameplay focuses on rotating and aligning pieces to complete pictures of the main character, a cute bunny girl. The puzzles become slightly more complex as you progress, but the overall challenge remains low, making it easy for anyone to play.

The main attraction is the art. The character is drawn in a colorful anime style, and short animations play once you finish each stage. There isn’t much of a story, but the light, playful tone fits the theme well.

The sound design is simple, with short looping background music and a few basic sound effects. They do their job but don’t stand out.

Technically, the game runs smoothly and loads quickly, even on low-end systems. However, it lacks extra features like a gallery or difficulty settings, which limits replayability.

The entire game can be completed in less than an hour. After that, there isn’t much reason to return unless you really enjoy the artwork.

Overall, Cute Honey: Bunny Girl offers a short, polished experience focused on visuals rather than gameplay. It’s best suited for fans of anime-style adult art who want something simple and relaxing.

何に重きを置くかで評価が変わる作品かなと思います。わたしはこの手のゲームでいうと「爽快感」とか、どんどん「強くなる」実感とかを重視しているので、今回はおすすめしません。
少しずつガチャ石のようなものをダンジョンクリアで獲得し、操作するプレイヤーが使えるジェム（攻撃魔法や補助魔法、または補助行動）や新キャラクターを開放し、ダンジョン内で出現するようにできます（図鑑の開放）。ここまでは良いのですが、これが嬉しい反面イライラする原因になりました。

キャラは3体で☆を１上げることができ、同☆キャラを３体あつめると最高レアになります。単純にステータスやスキルがアップします。このキャラ達はダンジョン内で拾えたり購入できたりすることで揃えていくのですが、図鑑を開放していけばそれだけキャラやジェムが増えるので、必然的に揃えにくくなります。ただ、そこらへんも一応考えられていて、揃いやすいショップがあったりと工夫はあるのですが、揃わないときはそろわないのでかえってイライラ度が増すというかなんというか・・。

結局使いやすいキャラに落ち着いていくので、プレイの幅も広がるかといえば難しい所です。せめてダンジョン毎に今回は何十種のうちのこの６属性だけでます！とかならキャラも使いこなせたのかもですが、それをしてしまうと☆を一つ上げたキャラの持っている属性はキャラを売っても残るという特性があり、簡単に属性が揃えられてしまうと今度は攻略が簡単になってしまうというジレンマに襲われてしまうのでしょうね。属性の説明はうまくできませんが、要は炎属性を規定数集めると毎ターン敵に20の炎上ダメージを与えられる！みたいな感じです。

上手くはまれば敵の攻撃を０ダメージにしつつ、こちらは連撃の嵐で一網打尽！を味わえますが、普通にそんなこともなく、進めば進むほど爽快感が失われていく・・という感じの印象が強かったです。ゲームは楽しいんです。キャラも可愛いし音楽だっていい。ただ爽快感ややりこみとこれは違うかなぁと。やり込みってクリアしていった先にある、ある種の自己満の領域だとおもうのですが、これはクリアする前からそれを強要する感じになってしまっていてなんだかなぁと。ローグライクなんだろうけど敵の出方は同じだし、ハクスラかといえば先に指摘した通り、やればやるほど揃いにくくなるというジレンマ。ダンジョン自体を何度もやり直すのは構わないのだが、またキャラを揃えて☆をあげて・・あ～・・あのキャラが先に出たか・・キープしておきたいけど手持ちが多すぎると重量オーバーが・・と、いつまでたってもすっきりしないゲームでした。

可愛い見た目だが難易度は可愛くない。
戦闘は自分が組んだパーティがオートで戦う。
自分が戦闘介入する手段はターン最初に使うジェムのみ。
主人公が強いのはダンジョン序盤だけで、終盤はサポート役に立ち位置が変わっていく。
キャラ集めや主人公が使用するジェム集めはガチャなので手に入ったもので立ち回りが変わることがある。

同じキャラを３体集めるとキャラがパワーアップし、そのキャラが所有するシンボルを獲得出来る。
そして「獲得したシンボルはそのキャラがパーティに入っていなくても、売却しても効果が残る」
これがこのゲームで一番重要なシステム。
このシステムを活用してクリアに必要なシンボルを集めて強いパーティをつくっていく。

難点は強いシンボルと弱いシンボル、強いキャラと弱いキャラの差が大きく、勝ちパターンは割とかぎられていること。
勝ちパターンがわかってくると面白い。

Лисичка (лат. Cantharellus) — род шляпочных грибов порядка лисичковых. Русское название связано с внешним сходством окраски с цветом лисьего меха. Среди народных названий — «петушок» или «петушки».

Описание:
Воронкообразная шляпка диаметром от 3 до 7 сантиметров, края часто закручены вниз.
Мякоть белая или желтоватая, плотная, с приятным ароматом, напоминающим абрикос.
Ножка длинная — до 6–7 сантиметров, толщина — примерно в два пальца, внизу сужается.

Виды
Некоторые виды лисичек:
Обыкновенная (Cantharellus cibarius) — ярко-жёлтая или оранжевая окраска, ножка плотная, мясистая.
Трубчатая (Craterellus tubaeformis) — коричневатая шляпка с мелкими чешуйками и ярко-жёлтая, полоя внутри ножка.
Серая (Cantharellus cinereus) — серая или серо-коричневая окраска, с более светлой нижней стороной шляпки.

Места произрастания
Лисички растут в лиственных и смешанных лесах, особенно в сосновых и еловых. Образуют симбиотические отношения с корнями деревьев. Лисички можно найти на земле, среди мха, в траве и под опавшими листьями. 
Сезон сбора — с конца мая и продолжается до сентября, в зависимости от климатических условий региона. 

Сбор
Некоторые рекомендации по сбору лисичек:
Лучше собирать после дождя, когда грибы особенно сочные и ароматные.
Лучше всего собирать утром, когда свежий воздух и влажная почва.
Использовать нож для срезания грибов, не вырывать их с корнями — это поможет сохранить сеть мицелия для будущего роста.
Не собирать грибы вблизи дорог или промышленных зон, так как они могут накапливать опасные вещества.

Приготовление
Лисички можно готовить разными способами: жарить, тушить, варить, мариновать, солить и замораживать. 
Перед заморозкой лисички желательно отварить около 15 минут, чтобы снизить риск появления горечи после разморозки.

«Dragon Conqueror» - игра 2024 года, выпущенная студией «BanameiR». Простая JRPG с большим количеством H-контента и не самым плохим сюжетом.

[b]Стоит ли покупать/проходить данный H-проект?[/b]

[b]Если вы пришли сюда за геймплеем, то получите простую JRPG[/b]

Хоть подход к битвам тут и не самый обычный, но чего-то интересного, лично я, здесь не нашел. Все бои идут примерно по одному сценарию - наложить «понижение брони» через «Sky Slash», после чего спамить умениями из «Agile Slash». 

Особой вариативности в билдах нет. Фармить что-нибудь для заданий вы вряд ли будете, так как шанс получения дропа тут не 100%, а сам гринд не оптимизирован. Поэтому, все необходимые части монстров будете покупать в «Underground Slums». 

[b]Если вы пришли сюда за H-контентом, то, наверное, останетесь довольны[/b]

H-контент представлен как в виде слайд-шоу из CG, так и небольшими анимациями (совсем небольшими). Сцен, для игры такой продолжительности, довольно много. Единственное, рисовка здесь своеобразная, т.ч. рекомендую её оценить заранее. Также, здесь весь контент с ББ, так что лично мне здесь ничего особо не зашло…

[b]Если вы пришли сюда за сюжетом, то получите типичный сэнен с хорошо реализованной «завязкой»[/b]

Честно, здесь хорошо реализована «завязка» через «ненадежного рассказчика». Лично я до самой «развязки» гадал, что именно произошло. И, что самое главное, не угадал… Мне эта часть сюжета очень зашла.

В остальном же - обычный сэнен. С «добрым добром» и «злым злом», приправленными кучей штампов, характерных для данного жанра.

[b]Итог[/b]

Если вы пришли поиграть в простую JRPG, то покупайте и приступайте к прохождению. Пришли «посмотреть на картинки» - сначала оцените рисовку, так как она здесь специфична. Захотелось прочитать что-то интересное - можно приобрести и прочитать.

Next Run is an interesting take on the open world roguelike RPG genre.  Basically, you pick a class that matches how you want to play the game and then focus on leveling up, finding or crafting gear or improving your magic to survive stronger waves of enemies.  You have X number of turns until the next wave (unless you turn on sandbox mode, which disables waves entirely), and you spend turns doing the aforementioned activities, with your stats determining how many turns an action takes to finish.  There are multiple paths to victory, from amassing resources to build a good portal to combat the evil one, destroying the evil portal yourself, performing a ritual to seal the evil portal or just winning against the last boss when it spawns.  

My biggest complaint is that each class is very strongly locked into playing only one way, with doubled benefits from increasing the stats associated with their class (ie most classes get 10% more attack from each point of strength, but the warrior gets 20% more instead).  If you play as a warrior, it will be very difficult to use magic or do a lot of crafting beyond some basic upgrades.  Or if you play as a mage, you probably won't be able to lead an army of followers or build up a city's industry very effectively.

I'd love it if the game gave more options to us when playing as each class.  Right now, if I choose warrior and then there's no good weapons to be found or bought from stores because of RNG, then I'm basically screwed.  I "can" craft my own weapons if I find a blueprint, but it will take a very long time compared to the artisan, who specializes in gathering and crafting.

Overall, I think Next Run is worth the asking price of $10.  It's very challenging though, and it sometimes boils down to getting lucky enough to find the right things we need for our class along our path towards the evil portal.

Pro's: Become Superman/Supergirl and go where you like; visit your own house; go to that place you always wanted to; sit on cliffs and scare yourself to death; "Leap" from tall buildings; Take off and go into space then land on the other side of the planet; go to that holiday place again (without the traffic jams); play a game of "can I find it again from space without getting lost on the way down"; save your own favourites and jump straight there next time. Change the time of day or night by dragging the Sun across the sky. All for FREE !!!!

IN MY OPINION - the best and most enduring VR experience ever, and probably for a long time to come.

Cons:

Well, not really any, but I would like to see the following features added as this gem is polished:

To be able to leave human scale on ALL THE TIME. I know it is great to feel like Gulliver, walking between the mountains or skyscrapers, but for immersion I'd like to be able to leave my eyes 70mm apart and view the Earth in normal scale (at least have the option).

Ability to reverse the "BRAKE" option so that you are slow by default and you pull the trigger to accellerate; I, personally, want to take it all in, not rush off.

I am not bothered about the comfort mode and prefer not to use it, but for those that get motion sickness, an option to change the size of the "tunnel" view to suit.

I for one, don't mind that you can't text-search for places to "teleport" to; searching adds to the enjoyment, but I'll expect a lot of people would prefer the option.

I know there's mirror mode, which you can modify to show just left/right eye as a circle on the screen, but for your friends to be able to view the experience full screen. I appreciate this could affect FPS etc, so just the option would be nice. 

Graphics settings, perhaps.

Oh, I don't know, fly to and around the Moon next maybe?  ;-D

These are not complaints, just hopes for the future. This App is nothing short of incredible!

Yokai’s Secret is a side-scrolling action game that mixes traditional Japanese mythology with light adult themes. The art style is colorful and detailed, with strong anime influences and polished character designs. Backgrounds and music help create a distinct atmosphere that fits the mythological setting.

Gameplay focuses on platforming and simple combat. Controls are responsive, but the overall design is straightforward. Enemies and bosses follow predictable patterns, making the game more about timing than strategy. Some stages feel repetitive, though occasional mini-events add variety.

The story is minimal but serviceable. It relies on mythic creatures and brief dialogue scenes to move things forward. Players seeking deep narrative or complex character development will not find it here, but the tone remains consistent and lighthearted.

Performance is stable, and load times are short. The game runs smoothly even on modest hardware. The biggest appeal lies in its visuals and fanservice rather than mechanics or story depth.

Yokai’s Secret delivers a short, polished experience aimed at a niche audience. It’s not groundbreaking, but it does exactly what it intends to: provide simple gameplay and vibrant art for those who enjoy this style.

This is a simple roguelike game. It's a good game to play for a few minutes, assuming of course you can force yourself to shut it down; it's rather addictive.

You can only carry two items at a time, which means you will sometimes have to go back for items. You need a key to get to the next level, but be careful when you pick a key up, as it takes up one of the two valuable item slots.

There's no option to change the graphics or sound. The graphics is in a vertical column, as you see on the screenshots above. The sound is always on and at full volume, which is a pain if you want to watch TV at the same time.

I would recommend this game to anyone who wants a fun and simple roguelike game.

I would not recommend this game to anyone who wants a highly detailed game full of roleplaying and complexity.

I got the game for $2.49, and I was fine paying that for this. I think I played for about 30 minutes, and it was probably worth the $2.49. My biggest issue with it would probably be the addition of the bottom graphics caused a little bit of confusion as I kept trying to navigate with it rather than use the pixel map as you normally would with a rogue-like. 

Plus, I think I picked the hardest class to start with (mage), and since you can only hold two spells at the beginning (one if you have a key on you), I was getting pretty rocked. 

Still, it was entertaining for the little while I played, and I found it pretty cute.

One of my favourite roguelike games, with great music, a great atmosphere, and a lot of replay value. Combat with a controller can feel a bit iffy, but you get used to it after a while. I like that the game rewards you for getting perfect rooms by allowing you to use the souls you gather throughout the run (basically your health potion like in Hollow Knight) to convert them into permanent health, and later on use that permanent health to buy upgrades. The lore of the game is quite cryptic but very interesting nonetheless. I do not want to talk too much about it for spoiler reasons, but it kept me hooked throughout all of my runs until I got the true ending.

Если Reignbreaker — сын, то Hades — сын маминой подруги. И, наверное, это самое важное, что вам нужно знать. В целом она весьма неплоха и старается изо всех сил быть достойной, но всё же остается лишь тенью Hades.

Тем не менее, у неё есть свои неоспоримые плюсы: шикарная музыка и визуал. Особенно порадовал трек в главном меню. Дизайн персонажей весьма и весьма хорош. С геймплейной частью всё обстоит хуже.

Локации однообразны и похожи друг на друга. Буквально 6-7 разновидностей врагов, которые отличаются только бафами, появляющимися на них. Оружия, хоть и заявлено 55 единиц, но основных типов всего 5: пулемёт, дробовик, бомбы, аналог лазера и ветер. Всё остальное — десятки различных вариаций с небольшими изменениями модификаторов.

Тем не менее, боёвка весьма динамичная, и игра неплохо держит в напряжении. Боссы достаточно интересные и заставляют попотеть. А уж сочетания врагов и расположение ловушек в комнате… Но, как и в большинстве рогаликов, успех вашего забега очень часто зависит от рандома. Если нападает много крутых и полезных усилений и навыков — вы в шоколаде. А если падают низкоуровневые умения из разных веток прокачки — скорее всего, вы проиграете, несмотря на прямоту ваших рук.

Сюжет тут весьма прямолинейный, но всё же он есть и развивается по ходу игры. Взаимодействия между героем и различными персонажами прописаны неплохо и пару раз даже заставят улыбнуться. Но стоит понимать, что не стоит ждать от экшн-рогалика сюжета на уровне "Игры престолов".

В целом, могу смело рекомендовать, но, вероятно, лучше приобретать по скидке — так вы точно не обломаетесь.

[H1]Это мой надел, вообще-то[/h1]

Кем вы хотите быть в фентезийном мире, если нет определённой цели? Не нужно спасать мир, нести макгаффин на другой конец мира, получить убер-саблю или сбежать от апокалипсиса. Вам не нужно мстить или спасаться от мести, просто жить в своём поместье и верно служить королю, отвоёвывая место под солнцем у всякой нечисти в округе, привлекая население к полезной работе и застраивая свой небольшой городок. При этих условиях – кем бы вы хотели быть?

От орка до куртизанки, от гнома до рыцаря – выбор ролей большой, но каждый имеет свои плюсы и минусы, даже в ролевом отыгрыше, пусть его тут почти нет. В Хинтерлэнд как хэк'н'слэш/стратегии/РПГ этот момент работает только на базовое восприятие своего альтер эго, его внешний вид и немного на игровые условия: от дохода до боевых качеств и т.п.

Игровая сессия заключается в полном отвоевании жизненного пространства в сгенерированной рандомно местности, попутном застраивании своего городка и собственной прокачке. Можно брать поселенцев в рейды, снаряжать их лутом или не тревожить, позволяя им создавать для поселения ништяки, торговать и производить пищу. А уж микроменеджмент в случае производства и обороны решает очень многое. Например, хороший молот для ремесленника ускоряет производство оружия и брони, а пика вместо лопаты и кольцо защиты вместо мешка овса может спасти поселенцу жизнь.

Это хорошая маленькая игра с репетативным геймплеем и некоторым вызовом вашему внутреннему менеджеру, в которой не так уж и нужно спасти мир, зато можно лучше понять фентези-повседневность и сполна ею насладиться, если некуда спешить.

И ничего, что после первой победы на хардкоре вам больше ничего нового в игре не увидеть, можно же просто заново пройти этот путь. А вообще, запомните: повторение – мать заикания.

Well dang... It's not just a chip fabricator game, but it's a really good, well made chip fabricator game. You have two MOSFETs, and get to make all the gates and logic units based upon those. It has blueprinting, a neat chip editor, scoreboards, a basic plot, and it runs fine on my Ryzen integrated graphics. 

Documentation feels a bit light in parts. For example, I've unlocked probes but haven't yet been given any info on how to use them, so that's very much been trial-and-error. However there are regular updates and a responsive developer, so I'm sure the UX will improve even more over time. It also runs just fine under Proton.

This will either be *very much* your thing, or not at all your thing. [b]Play the demo[/b] and you will definitely know for sure.

The issue is how you counter moves with a freeze, the enemy should be staggered not free to start moving at a random time when they unfreeze. There is also mission length, each mission is to long, quick challenges finished by boss fights is more or less the correct format for this game style. Missions should take about 20 minutes. The game isn't bad, art direction and story are interesting, but the actual gameplay needs polish.

Excellent tactical TBS. I've been playing with the DLC so I got no idea exactly how much it adds but there's a lot of ways for a particular playthrough to go depending on your starting agents and what you can get going once everything is left to fate depending on the missions you go on and what you find once inside.

Definitely you need to start to play in beginner mode with all the failsafes in place because its very easy to commit mistakes while you learn your agents strengths and weaknesses not to mention all the enemies and the level's defenses.

Seems like you can go in full stealth, nonlethal or go full homicidal and clear everyone out depending on playstyle its all viable but you need to unlock agents through playthroughs to get a good combination going with at least your starting pair (the DLC gives you four more choices from the get go to go along with the two starters). But that's part of the the old school fun vs what is standard now and paying to 'unlock' new characters instead of through actually playing the game itself.

The game basically remained invisible in my game library for a decade but no more. If you're a genre fan and you haven't tried it yet... get around to it when you can.

Great game, can be customized for very different audience, from complete amauteurs of TBS strategy games to veterans. What I personally like the most, is the tension during the missions, hard choices the gameplay presents, high stakes (especially on Expert difficulty, which I am about to beat someday), objective-oriented stealth missions instead of "kill-them-all". Also, you have good variety of characters, augments, hacking programms, devices and weapons to deal with threats the way it suits your playstyle. Apart from that, you can manipulate your enemies by abusing their periferal vision and hearing to place them where you need them to be or to lure them out of crucial location. 

The beauty of this game is that your tiny inattention or mistake can lead to a cascade of negative events which can turn your strategy upside down and turn your squad of elite spies in bloodthirsty chickens running for their lifes to the exit. 

It is really action-packed with minimum "meta-gameplay" where you should manage your base, so the 90% of time you spend in the game, you are engaged in tactical simulations, not the high-level management. One campaign can take about 5 hours probably, so it is pretty short and not so tedious like some Xcom / Xenonauts games, for example. 

Every choice, be it on a tactical level (AP or Power spending), economical (Credits and XP spending), or mission selection (rewards and enemy defences choosing) - is crucial. But as I said, you are not spending dozens of minutes by meta progressing your squad or base. The decisions are pretty quick on a strategic level.

The title has roguelite elements, cause no matter the campaign results, you always progress and unlock new starting hacking programms and characters, so even if you fail, you get some kind of reward for your tries which can enrich your experience, let you try other playstyles. Given how many modificators influence procedurally generated missions, campaign walkthrough is never the same. 

I also like the artstyle. Given that the Invisible, Inc. takes place in dystopian cyberpunk universe, its artstyle is cartoonish and not grim and dark. I kinda like that for a change as well.

All in all, I like it and will probably try myself with Expert difficulty.

JumpJet Rex is a vibrant and fast-paced 2D platformer developed and published by TreeFortress Games, paying homage to the golden age of arcade precision games while injecting its own unique sense of humor and energy. The concept alone sets the tone for what’s to come—you play as Rex, a jet-boot-wearing tyrannosaurus tasked with saving the galaxy’s dinosaurs from annihilation. It’s an absurd premise delivered with charm and style, but beneath the cartoonish humor lies a tightly crafted experience built around reflexes, timing, and mastery of movement. The game feels like a blend of old-school simplicity and modern finesse, presenting itself as easy to pick up but challenging to truly conquer.

The gameplay structure revolves around short, time-focused levels where every movement counts. Rex can jump, hover, dash, and stomp using his rocket boots, and the control scheme is designed to make these actions feel instinctive and responsive. The levels themselves are filled with hazards, spikes, lasers, and narrow corridors that demand precise maneuvering. What makes JumpJet Rex stand out from typical platformers is the sense of weight and fluidity in its movement—every boost and dash feels deliberate, and learning how to chain them efficiently is the core of its challenge. Success depends not just on surviving but on optimizing your route, minimizing wasted motion, and beating the clock. It’s a design philosophy that rewards repetition and skill improvement in the same way as classic arcade titles.

Visually, the game embraces a 16-bit art style that is both nostalgic and full of personality. The environments range from alien planets and asteroid fields to neon-lit space stations, each offering unique layouts and visual cues to keep the experience fresh. The pixel art is crisp and colorful, and the animations are smooth enough to make the action easy to follow even at high speeds. Complementing this is a wonderfully catchy chiptune soundtrack that perfectly matches the game’s rhythm. The music shifts between energetic beats and tense melodies that drive the player forward, reinforcing the sensation that you’re always racing against time. The combination of retro visuals and sound creates a distinct atmosphere that feels both familiar and fresh.

As the player progresses, the levels become more intricate and the margin for error narrows considerably. The difficulty curve ramps up quickly, transforming early casual runs into tests of precision and patience. To unlock new areas, players must earn stars by completing levels under specific conditions, such as finishing within a time limit or without dying. This star system introduces a layer of replayability that pushes players to refine their technique and master every stage. However, it can also become a source of frustration, as later stages require near-perfect execution to continue advancing. The game’s checkpoint system alleviates some of the tension, but the pursuit of perfection remains its driving force, which may alienate more casual players.

Despite the challenge, JumpJet Rex offers enough variety to keep its core loop engaging. Each level introduces subtle changes in design that test new aspects of movement, and the inclusion of boss fights adds brief bursts of intensity that break up the flow. There’s also a local co-op mode that allows players to tackle the campaign together, adding a chaotic but fun dynamic as both try to navigate the tight spaces without crashing into each other. On top of that, the game includes cosmetic customization options, letting players dress Rex in silly hats and accessories. It’s a small touch, but it contributes to the game’s lighthearted tone and gives players an incentive to collect coins scattered throughout levels.

What truly defines JumpJet Rex is its focus on mastery. Every level feels like a playground for speedrunners, with its short length encouraging experimentation and optimization. The design invites replay after replay until you nail the perfect route. It’s the kind of game that thrives on player determination—one where every failure feels like a learning experience rather than a punishment. The joy comes from the gradual improvement, the feeling of shaving seconds off a time trial, and the moment when muscle memory finally clicks into place. That sense of progress is what makes the game addictively satisfying despite its occasional spikes in difficulty.

Overall, JumpJet Rex is a love letter to precision platformers of the past, wrapped in a quirky and modern presentation. Its simple premise, tight mechanics, and high skill ceiling make it both approachable and deeply rewarding for players who enjoy the process of mastery. While its brevity and steep challenge may limit its appeal to certain audiences, those who stick with it will find a polished, well-crafted experience that captures the exhilaration of perfect movement and fast-paced gameplay. It’s a game that doesn’t overcomplicate its formula—just a jet-powered dinosaur, some creative level design, and the timeless thrill of chasing perfection.

Carly and the Reaperman is a cooperative puzzle-platformer developed and published by Odd Raven Studios that stands out for its imaginative concept and inventive use of asymmetrical gameplay. Set in a whimsical version of the underworld, the game follows Carly, a daring young girl who seeks to ascend from the realm of lost souls, and her unlikely companion, the Reaperman—a towering skeletal figure who guides her path. Together, the two must work in harmony to overcome obstacles, solve puzzles, and navigate intricate levels that rely on communication, coordination, and trust. The premise sounds simple, but what makes the game so engaging is how it blends two very different perspectives and play styles into one cohesive experience that feels both intuitive and deeply cooperative.

The design of Carly and the Reaperman thrives on its core mechanic of asymmetrical teamwork. Carly, controlled in third person, embodies the agile, hands-on platforming half of the duo, jumping between ledges, collecting items, and avoiding traps. The Reaperman, in contrast, controls the environment from a higher, almost omniscient perspective, manipulating platforms, moving objects, and creating pathways for Carly to traverse. This duality creates a natural dependency between the two characters—Carly cannot progress without the Reaperman’s aid, and the Reaperman’s efforts are meaningless without Carly’s daring navigation. The result is a cooperative experience that feels organic rather than forced. Each role demands focus and awareness, but it’s the synchronization between players that gives the game its charm. When the coordination clicks, it feels magical; when it falters, it produces hilarious moments of chaos that strengthen the bond between players.

The game features over fifty levels, each with its own distinct challenges and environmental themes, ranging from eerie crypts to mysterious caverns illuminated by spectral light. The pacing is well-crafted, introducing new mechanics and obstacles gradually so that both players can adapt naturally. Early levels teach the fundamentals—timing jumps, moving platforms, and avoiding pitfalls—but later stages introduce new wrinkles such as darkness, shifting hazards, and time-sensitive puzzles that demand faster communication. There are also collectibles and hidden fireflies scattered throughout the levels, offering additional challenges for completionists and giving players incentive to revisit earlier stages. The learning curve feels fair, and while difficulty occasionally spikes, it never feels punitive. The variety of puzzles and the interplay between dexterity and logic keep the experience engaging from start to finish.

Visually, the game adopts a stylized, atmospheric approach rather than striving for realism. The underworld is rendered not as a grim and terrifying place but as a fantastical realm filled with color, contrast, and personality. The environments are built like dioramas—small, self-contained worlds that the Reaperman views from above, while Carly moves through them at ground level. This layered perspective enhances the sense of scale and connection between the two players. The character designs are simple but expressive: Carly’s youthful energy and the Reaperman’s looming yet gentle presence create a memorable visual contrast. The game’s soundtrack complements the tone perfectly, with gentle melodies and ambient soundscapes that alternate between mysterious, melancholic, and hopeful, giving the underworld an emotional warmth rarely found in platformers.

Although Carly and the Reaperman can be played solo, it is clearly designed with co-op play in mind. In single-player mode, the player switches between controlling Carly and the Reaperman, which introduces additional challenge but also removes the spontaneity and emotional rhythm that comes from working with another person. The cooperative mode, on the other hand, shines brightest when played locally, as verbal communication becomes an essential part of the gameplay. Timing, coordination, and trust transform each puzzle into a shared accomplishment. When Carly leaps onto a moving platform that the Reaperman just positioned in time, or when a last-second maneuver saves her from falling, the resulting sense of teamwork feels immensely satisfying. This design makes the game ideal for friends, couples, or families looking for a shared gaming experience that relies on communication rather than competition.

Technically, the game is well-optimized and performs smoothly, though its origins as a VR title are occasionally evident in the camera perspectives and environmental interactions. On standard PC setups, the controls are intuitive and responsive, though the Reaperman’s perspective can occasionally feel unwieldy in tight spaces. Despite this, the game remains stable and reliable, with charming polish in its animations and level transitions. The art direction and lighting create an appealing visual rhythm that keeps the player invested even when the mechanics become demanding. The game’s overall presentation radiates warmth and creativity, clearly built by a small team with a passion for cooperative play and clever puzzle design.

While Carly and the Reaperman is not without minor flaws—occasional control awkwardness, uneven camera angles, and a story that serves more as backdrop than narrative centerpiece—it compensates with sheer originality and heart. It’s rare to find a cooperative game that so effectively requires genuine teamwork while remaining accessible and inviting to all kinds of players. Its world is inviting, its puzzles are thoughtful, and its atmosphere is equal parts eerie and comforting. Whether you’re playing it as a lighthearted couch co-op game or as a mental exercise in spatial coordination, it offers an experience that feels distinct from most modern platformers.

Ultimately, Carly and the Reaperman stands as one of the most creative cooperative puzzle games in recent memory. It is a testament to how strong game design can make simple mechanics feel fresh when executed with imagination and care. The connection between the two characters mirrors the connection between players, turning every success and failure into a shared story. For those seeking a game that balances challenge, creativity, and emotional warmth, this journey through the underworld is a deeply rewarding adventure that lingers long after the credits roll.

Put this one back in the oven boys, it ain't done yet. The core concept is appealing, and the moment-to-moment gunplay feels OK, but everything from UI to the primary gameplay loop feels half-baked in the game's current state. This isn't the Hunt roguelike I was hoping for, but one day it might be. Refunding for now, will revisit the game down the line if it gets some refinement.

Gripes for the devs:

The world/story appealed to me, but everything from the tutorial text to the lore entries in the journal was spotted with spelling and grammar errors. I saw 'hunters' spelled "hunters", "hunter's", and "Hunter's" in three different places in the first few minutes. I love lore, but find it hard to enjoy when the language is off.

There are no graphics options, and my framerate tanked in certain spots, usually when fog was around. My CPU/GPU weren't working too hard at the time, so this is probably just something that will be optimised in future, but having no options to change graphics settings to mitigate this was a bit of a slap in the face. How can there be no options at all? Even to change resolution?

On first play, the primary gameplay loop appears to be try, die, repeat, but there is almost no progress made between hunters. The optimal play style I discovered involved entering the hunt, shooting some critters, then using the 'Main Menu' button to return yourself to the town, silver in hand, to upgrade gear and increase the chances of keeping your current hunter alive. (I was quite surprised when I clicked 'Main Menu' while looking for the aforementioned graphics options, and discovered this improvised town portal system.) The gameplay says "push forward to the boss!" then punishes you if you attempt this with basic equipment. I like the idea of doing some little hunts prior to taking on the big bad, but the way this executed (at least in the part of the game I played) was pretty unintuitive.

I'll keep the dream alive and monitor the game for updates, as I think there's something worthwhile at the heart of this project. But for now, I'm stepping out. Cheers team.

➊黎轨2的评价我从间章开始就一直在纠结了，通关后想想还是暂时给个好评吧。评价可能涉及部分剧透，明显的我会码掉，但也有可能无意间透一些我没察觉到的信息。

➋轨迹系列每个双数版本都让我玩的会有点痛苦...其实从SC开始就是，每双数的一代都出现大量的地图美术素材复用，反复跑图。奇数代都是新代，让玩家认识新的国家、新的城市，结识新的伙伴，双数代就开始在奇数代的基础上加点内容，本质就是个大型DLC。只不过sc、碧轨剧情尚可，算上闪轨4就都是一个国家的终章，所以还能玩的稍愉快。但是闪2和黎2玩到中间部分后真的会比较乏味，这两代都是让我玩到一半要缓好久才愿意继续的游戏。

➌这个游戏从序章到间章部分其实没有特别的差，虽然有些回溯也是比较强行但至少能说得过去。从间章开始整个战力就崩坏了，反派之一的[spoiler] 结社成员破戒在岛上[/spoiler]设计了数个毒气弹，然后直接把该章节聚集的[spoiler] 全部黎轨里最强战力的角色全体秒杀，强行回溯 [/spoiler] 。

➍第三章开始更是又臭又长，很多回溯非常的强行，完全不符合以往的人物设计，和间章一样，属于典型的战力崩坏。很多回溯的死因不是[spoiler]被炸弹炸死[/spoiler]、就是[spoiler]被埋伏干掉，还有飞船撞屋顶团灭的[/spoiler]。而且死的人还经常包括那些B格被吹上天的角色，你要按照没有创世那会的剧情，这些大神角色遇到这种危机不是直接瞬移传送走就是一个跟头翻几十里远，或者根本就不会进这个局。为了回溯强行拉低角色智商、经验和战斗力，没活就别硬编，比吃书都尬。

➎到了终章节奏倒是正常一些了，可以说黎轨2为数不多的加分点就是终章的十几个羁绊剧情，虽然听着多且没配音，但是体验其实远超前面的主线了。这是轨迹这么多代下来的通病，这游戏从闪轨开始就是，刻画主角和另外一两个角色的小短片是很会写的，人一多就完蛋，经典的一人一句话说完了才能开打。尤其是玲的羁绊剧情，老玩家看了绝对相当有感触。最后的尾声还可以，告别了过去的一些执念，迎接新的未来，但也要面对新的难题，留给后面一作继续讲述。

➏其实我一开始是想给个差评的，但是怎么说呢，你都玩到黎轨2了，怎么也是个轨迹系列的老玩家了吧？硬要说跳过黎2直接界轨我觉得应该也不会有太大影响，但这代多少也填了一些角色的坑，如果在史低的情况下入手我觉得还算ok。steam的评价比竟不只是对游戏本身的评价，还有“是否推荐该游戏”一说，所以你说面对一个轨迹粉，推不推荐？都到吃到这了只要价格合适怎么也要玩下看看吧。这一作的另一个优点是因为素材复用省一部分美术成本了，所以在动作优化上反而上了些成本，动捕场合变多，终章的舞蹈部分明显比闪轨创轨好太多，至少不尬了，其实比黎轨1也好，1代那二人转重复播也蛮尬。因此如果你对黎轨的角色比较有爱，我还是推荐你玩玩看的。大不了就放弃白金，全程VE难度嘛。

[b]剧情[/b]

这部让我感觉最弱智的部分是第三章b线和bc线结束之后那段。
b线连着两次回溯真的蚌埠住了，过于随便。都说这部因为有时间回溯所以过于随便什么的其实我觉得也就这个特别的难以接受。
然后基于bc线结尾发生了一样的事，可以知道第一次发生的时候那俩人就已经被侵蚀了，回退之后似乎他们的侵蚀状态也解除了？那么他们竟然没有一点被侵蚀的记忆？哪怕他们没有，明明师姐和茱蒂丝当时就应该受到了攻击，回溯之后他们没有记忆？

就不说为什么回溯之后被回溯掉的进程中拿到的创世凭什么的就算拿到了这种bug了。
如果说上边两段剧情是本游戏弱智的极点，本游戏最致命的还是第三章的boss太逊，第三章后期看他说什么要纠正错误的历史还以为他要爆个大料，比如说女神是个骗子什么的，甚至有点期待，结果就这？

除此之外玩起来倒是挺好玩的 😂 不过弱智归弱智，黎轨1第四五章的弱智让我更生气 😂 难道黎1时候一帮人傻乎乎的玩死亡游戏，然后打过的boss死了活活了死就不弱智吗？反正对我来说是更难忍受。

而且这部的剧情推进也没有黎1那么套路，黎1前四章的剧情结构完全一模一样，玩到后边真的感觉很无语，而这部始终都能保持新鲜感。而且不知道是不是因为魔装鬼很少出现不会傻乎乎的跟boss对吼，这代的演出观感提升很多，没有了一代每一章高潮就尬演的毛病，一代真的每到剧情高潮就是出戏之时……

可能因为从闪轨开始就没玩过轨迹吧，空零碧也都忘得差不多了，所以我对主线发展什么的完全没有那个执念。也可能因为我黎1和黎2连着玩的，没有了酝酿很长时间的期待，就没有随之而来的失望。

[b]其他系统[/b]

这代加了一大堆乱七八糟的系统和小游戏，我觉得倒是还挺有调节作用的。
- 钓鱼：因为我这个人有那么一丁点收集癖但是不多，钓鱼我还蛮喜欢的，沿路看到钓点我都会钓一钓，至于A级的鱼在有big hit chance的钓点都很容易就能钓上来，最后也很容易就全收集了，所以这个钓鱼系统还是给个好评。
- 打牌和打篮球：完全没有兴趣。好在成就要求的次数也不多，虽然那个篮球三次的成就我甚至没有达成 😂 
- 童话庭园：还行。满城对话烦了的时候去打一下本章的庭园起到一个调剂作用感觉还可以。附带的抽卡系统最开始引入的时候感觉很无语，不过实际体验还行，每次刷完之后顺手随便抽一抽。
我完全没有每层刷三星的执念，低级的几层我都是在后期给板凳队员刷mvp的时候快速通过轻松三星，高级的几层就无缘再也不见。至于这个刷mvp因为给15点技能升级点还是挺有吸引力，但是刷到剩最后三个人的时候突然懒得刷了，那就算了。

[h2]365 days... and for what?[/h2]

[i]Idle Biceps[/i] is a simple idle game where you well, build your biceps. Basically, you lift the weight to gain mass and reps, which then goes towards your growth bar, once the bar is full, you reach a new growth level, and the threshold increases. You then do that over and over, till you can't no more.

After you gain growth levels, you are then able to ascend, and are granted ascension points based on your growth level, which can be invested into permanent upgrades to make starting over a lot quicker.

There are also supplements you can take, which instantly increase your growth bar based on which you take.

You can upgrade how much you lift, and how many reps you do per second, but after a certain point in the game, none of the upgrades matter, as the growth level up threshold stops increasing, so you basically gain levels at a fixed rate. The global leaderboards are basically a showcase of who has left their game open the longest.

As much as I love the music and the animation, I just cannot justify recommending this game for the price it is. Full disclosure, I got it on sale for 20 dollars, but I'm really not satisfied even at that price after 100%ing the game.
Pros:
- Beautiful stop-motion animation. Really, the team did a wonderful job here.
- Amazing soundtrack. I love Will Wood, his work is always amazing.
- Good story and lore. The main story was adorable, and the Éadóchas achievement's ending was fantastic. There's wonderful moments of tension throughout the game that had originally hooked me.
Cons:
- Tedious gameplay. Dying completely resets the progress on the puzzles you've already completed. Considering the length of the game (which is not necessarily a problem, mind you), replaying sections you've already completed is going to take up a majority of your playthrough.
- Slow traversal. Part of the game is to explore, which is all fine and dandy! But because of the animation (lovely as it is) and mazelike map, it becomes frustrating when you want to quickly backtrack to a previous room. (This also applies for puzzle inputs, particularly the grid puzzle.)
- Repetitive goals. For those wanting to fully complete the game, you will have to grind out two things. One are cheeses, which luckily replenish instantly, making it only a minor annoyance. The second are deaths, which as previously stated, completely reset your puzzle progress. Had there been more unique deaths, more dangers throughout the maze, the requirement for 24 deaths would not be as frustrating as it is. But there's only six unique deaths (not including the Éadóchas ending), meaning you have to go out of your way to farm the other 18, and throwing your progress entirely away while you're at it! Again, had I not had to replay so much of this game over and over again, this really wouldn't have been as frustrating as it is.
It's really disappointing, as I had been looking forward to this game since it was announced, and I really wanted to like it! But the fundamental gameplay is just something I can't overlook. If you're a Will Wood or Tomcat Disposables superfan, it might still be worth it to purchase this game. I for one don't really regret buying it completely, but I can't really recommend it either. I hope this team takes what they learned from Éalú and makes something even better in the future!

Shut in is a game with multiple endings, a funny narrator, lots of different ways to get killed and different paths to explore in a cramped environment. I've never suffered from depression so it was interesting to get a look into somebody with what I refer to as 'the victim's mindset'.

Life is sh*t and then you die, but a lot of small things can go a long way to imrpove things at least a bit?

The game is about depression and isolating oneself and sometimes way too relatable. It also keeps insulting you about it, like the little mean "voice" in your head - what if people judge me, what if sorting through my stuff takes forever? It doesn't do so in a nice way either.

I liked the atmosphere and apparently there's different endings and ways to solve it. 
I definitely won't recommend it to anyone. Definitely not a recommendation if a game insulting you about the same things your depression does might be triggering. Deathwatch is a combination of "I'm on Observation Duty" and a game like "Five Nights at Freddy's". That is to say, you watch camera feeds of a location looking for any changes but also contend with a monster stalking you in your room that you need to be aware of.

All the positive reviews seem to mention VR, so that may add a lot to the experience, but for me playing this without VR the onboarding process was bad enough that I just didn't want to get far into it. The problem is that locations are pretty cluttered and you search your own room with a small flashlight, which makes it very, very hard to notice changes at the beginning. You also have to go to a separate screen to report anomalies, And when you do report anomalies, they don't go away, they just... stay. And the anomalies seem to be pretty subtle to boot. And the anomaly descriptions and types seem to be taken largely from the Observation Duty games, which honestly were not the best to begin with. 

What it all ends up with it, it will take quite some time to practice and get good at not just the game and its quirks, but also the individual levels. And when I see this game as basically Observation Duty with more stuff added but not well integrated, I don't have enough patience for it.

But credit were credit is due. The game can be scary. There is so much to do and its so overwhelming at first, that it does heighten the tension. It doesn't feel good to play, but that can make for effective horror. I lost interest when I stumbled upon a goofy looking version of slenderman, which felt like a pretty lame addition, but when its not kneecapping itself with a stupid add on, its pretty scary. The levels have great atmosphere and the whole concept has you worrying about an inevitable jumpscare. 

For me the bottomline, and why I wrote this long review, is that I love what this game is trying to do. Observation Duty with an exorcism/ghost hunting aspect is SUCH a good idea. If its something that series needs is a better integrated fail state. But this current incarnation of this game feels clumsy and too difficult to get into. It might be great after a few hours, but for most the game will only last a few hours. I see the devs working on a sort of sequel so I am hopefully we will be seeing a better version. But for now, I can't really recommend Deathwatch.

Island Cities, developed and published by Mens Sana Interactive, is a relaxing puzzle experience that transforms the familiar concept of city building into a meditative exercise in spatial logic and visual harmony. The game invites players to restore beautiful floating islands made of blocky, modular cities that have been scrambled, turning urban architecture into a soothing jigsaw puzzle. It’s a premise that captures the developer’s signature philosophy—games designed to calm, focus, and relax rather than challenge or frustrate. Island Cities is not about efficiency, speed, or competition. Instead, it’s about slow and deliberate interaction, where every click restores order to a small, tranquil world and rewards you with the quiet satisfaction of seeing life return to motion.

Visually, Island Cities is a delightful blend of minimalism and warmth. Each puzzle takes the form of a small island floating in an endless sea, built from bright, colorful blocks that depict roads, houses, trees, and miniature details that give the world a sense of charm. The art style is clean and low-poly, but its simplicity is part of the appeal—it creates a gentle and clutter-free space where the player can focus on the act of reconstruction without distraction. Once a puzzle is solved, the islands come alive with subtle animations: water ripples around the shores, smoke rises from chimneys, and little cars begin to move through the streets. These touches make the completion of each puzzle feel like more than just a logical achievement; it’s a moment of quiet reward, a brief transformation from stillness to life that reinforces the game’s tranquil rhythm. The soundtrack complements this aesthetic perfectly, using soft ambient melodies that blend seamlessly with the natural sounds of the world. There’s no urgency in the music—just a calm flow that matches the game’s peaceful tone.

The gameplay structure is wonderfully straightforward yet satisfying. Each level begins with a complete view of the island, giving players a chance to memorize its layout before the tiles are scrambled. The goal is to swap pieces back into their correct positions, reassembling the city so that every block fits neatly into place. Unlike traditional jigsaw puzzles, where pieces must be manually rotated or dragged into alignment, Island Cities relies on simple two-block swapping, which makes the experience smooth and unintimidating. It’s a mechanic that anyone can understand in seconds, but one that retains just enough depth to remain engaging as the puzzles grow larger and more complex. Early levels consist of small islands with only a handful of tiles, ideal for beginners or short play sessions, while later stages introduce sprawling cities that take more time and attention to restore. Despite the growing scale, there’s never any time pressure—no countdowns, no penalties for mistakes, and no competition. This lack of stress is what gives Island Cities its unique charm. It’s not about beating the puzzle; it’s about enjoying the process of rebuilding.

One of the game’s clever touches is how it layers visual feedback into its puzzles. As you progress and complete sections of the city, the landscape subtly shifts to reflect your progress. Seeing a bridge reconnect or a coastline line up correctly provides a small but satisfying burst of recognition. Each finished puzzle culminates in a charming reveal as the island springs back to life, rewarding the player with movement, color, and a sense of completion. These visual payoffs make the experience surprisingly rewarding, even without a traditional scoring or achievement system. It’s a form of intrinsic motivation—the joy of seeing your careful effort literally reconstruct a world. The gradual increase in complexity keeps things engaging, while the overall tone remains unhurried and contemplative.

Island Cities’ greatest strength is its accessibility. It’s a game anyone can pick up and enjoy without the need for instructions, reflexes, or gaming experience. The interface is clean and intuitive, making it suitable for both younger players and adults looking to unwind. Because there’s no failure state or high difficulty curve, it’s an ideal title for people seeking a relaxing break from more demanding games or for those who simply want to focus their mind on something calm and beautiful. It also runs smoothly on almost any computer, reflecting the developer’s commitment to keeping their games inclusive and easy to access. Like other titles from Mens Sana Interactive, it fits perfectly into the “wellness gaming” niche—simple, positive, and restorative experiences meant to soothe rather than stress.

However, this simplicity can also be a double-edged sword. For players accustomed to deep puzzle mechanics or complex systems, Island Cities may feel too lightweight after a few hours. The core loop—memorize, swap, and complete—remains largely unchanged from one puzzle to the next, which can make the gameplay feel repetitive over time. While the visuals and environments vary, the underlying structure doesn’t evolve much beyond scale. There’s also no overarching narrative or progression system beyond the satisfaction of completing each island. But these limitations are largely intentional. The game isn’t designed to provide long-term challenge or narrative depth; it’s designed to offer a peaceful, self-contained experience that encourages relaxation through simplicity. It’s the kind of game that rewards patience and mindfulness rather than strategy or mastery.

For what it sets out to do, Island Cities succeeds beautifully. It’s an elegant, meditative puzzle game that combines pleasing visuals, gentle audio, and intuitive mechanics to create an atmosphere of calm reflection. The act of rebuilding the islands feels both creative and restorative, as if each click brings the world a little closer to harmony. It’s the perfect game to play when you need to unwind, focus your thoughts, or simply take a break from the noise of daily life. While it may not challenge your intellect in the way more complex puzzle games do, it offers something equally valuable: a sense of peace and satisfaction that comes from quiet, deliberate interaction.

In the end, Island Cities is less about problem-solving and more about balance—about restoring order to small, colorful worlds and finding comfort in their completion. It embodies the meditative side of gaming, where progress is measured not in points or achievements, but in moments of calm and clarity. Its charm lies in its restraint, in its ability to create joy from something as simple as rearranging blocks until everything falls into place. For players seeking a gentle escape or a mindful way to relax, Island Cities offers exactly that—a small oasis of tranquility floating in a sea of noise.

Tactical party-based roguelites are pretty rare compared to the collection of action roguelites out there. This game is pretty fun once you get used to its combat system.

一、游戏性，战斗表现力优秀，构筑内容丰富，玩法框架是有深度的，可惜设计缺少深度，少了rogue游戏的一大精髓——敌我互动。这倒不是因为技能、道具之类的构筑不有趣，而是敌我的交互设计欠考虑，攻杀构筑优势无限大，所有不提供运转和伤害的部件全变成干扰项，可玩性大大降低。
以我玩得最多的rogue卡牌游戏为例，dreamquest、杀戮尖塔，攻杀的上限虽能碾压，但其他策略也有通关的办法，比如防杀、局内成长，甚至借助各种状态和控制抹消敌人的行动，当然，更多时候是进攻和防守都及格从而通关。本游戏则失衡了，原因一是每场战斗都有随回合数不断累积的惩罚机制，伤害、增援、变数，全都是回合越多损失越多，不能快速消灭敌人则很难避免战损；二是玩家的进攻构筑太畅通无阻，进攻能百分百替代防御的功能，没有类似每次行动都要承受战损，或者一定行动次数后强制结束回合这样考验防御的机制。结果就是，敌我基本没有互动，游玩过程从应对各种各样的战斗，变成了堆进攻数值打木桩，困难难度刚通关一两次的时候很有成就感，但是重复游玩就没什么乐趣了。
二、人物与剧情。Furry游戏人物是很大的卖点，我对里头每一个角色的形象都很喜欢，可惜本游戏在角色塑造上几乎是失败的。从故事基调上来看，想讲异常灾害下的群像故事，生存斗争、探寻身世、揭露黑手，他们似乎做了很多事，但结果大部分人都一无所获，都缺少弧光，我们不知道他们如何与人相处，因何而喜怒哀乐，能令玩家产生共情的点一个也没有。人是社会关系的总和，游玩过程中三名角色齐心协力，时而探讨事态，时而并肩作战，但最终这些文字几乎没有呈现他们的社会关系，他们似乎都成为了世界观的齿轮无情碾过的痕迹，变成世界观塑造的垫脚石，而唯一的破局者似乎选择了继续同流合污——太令人失望了，这是一个找不到人性闪光的黑深残故事。剧本没有重点塑造角色，反而去塑造老掉牙的类SCP世界观，这和你们的营销策略并不吻合，也让我可惜游戏里精美的人物设定基本成为了一具具空壳。

A minimalistic Roguelike with a wonderful aesthetic and unique core gameplay mechanic.

Keep in mind that this game is very lean in its design, especially compared to most Roguelikes/lites. Specific heroes and bosses have unique mechanics that add some little twists, but otherwise the gameplay doesn't change up much.

Still, the puzzle system is quite engaging at base, enough to last for the game's intended length, either for a few hours to get a couple wins, or ~10 hours to win with each hero if you're dedicated. There's a nice interplay between the four tile types and a flow to combat where smart choices can be about which tiles are most valuable in a given turn, not just finding the biggest tile combo.

It is a shame though that the idea isn't pushed further, it definitely feels like there is room to layer on some more interactions/mechanics without making the experience feel bloated.

The TL;DR version: If this looks like your thing, you will enjoy it. It has a simple set of mechanics and only really one system, everything is on display, and you can run the numbers on paper they're that simple.

the long version: It doesn't outstay its welcome. It does not distract you with flashy tricks or multipliers, nor huge combo chains, nor splashy effects you hope to pick up and carry your run with. The numbers are not huge. The grid is only 5x5. You only slide one row or column on your turn. There is one single "power" for each class, and you have it all game long.

To those expecting some surprise masterwork of psychological writing, or a whole extra layer of new game, or some fourth-wall stuff - no, that is not here. Here, there is only the long night.

You can feel a rhythm to everything. You can see the way things are going before the conclusion arrives, barring unexpected twists or streaks of ill fortune. You walk slowly into an unfriendly night, and you will often die a slow death, but you will go down fighting with your last breath.

Following the trend of gimmick-based horror games that challenge the norm, Egg Squeeze is like Ratshaker's cute little brother that probably hurls eggs at you if you look at him the wrong way. Egg Squeeze feels like an experiment in self-control and gambling; you play as a test subject who's been ordered to squeeze eggs to test a "psychic" ability that allows them to do interesting things with eggs. Though, admittedly, the main point of the game is you squeezing eggs and trying not to crack/break them. 

It's a pretty simple premise, all things considered, but it's a surprisingly addictive little game, with its own secrets and even little brainrot features as you get further into the game. The game isn't particularly frightening, if scary at all - but there are moments where if you've gotten hold of the "spirit box" add-on, you start seeing unsettling things. Not to mention that losing sanity by cracking eggs has the potential to be spooky. 

Sound design is important here; if only because it's obviously an indie game - the beauty of the score and soundtrack are that they're composed by indie vets, and it can range from catchy, jaunty little tunes to atmospheric and eerie sound work. 
It's another retro-looking game, but that actually works somewhat in its favour as the visuals play towards the eeriness of the game, and the way it illustrates the simplicity of the core gameplay while the darkness creeps around you. 

I think what I like most about this is just that you're not really sure what to expect from this game. A lot of horror games build a cryptic mystery, something that is ultimately answered by the grand payoff, but something that can - for the most part - usually be predicted as you go through the game. This one plays with its cards close to its chest, and only breadcrumbs you, which I enjoy. 

If you're looking for something scary, or something in-depth, you might be looking in the wrong place, but there is a considerable amount of love placed into this little title, and I can't help but feel like it was a fun time, albeit short. 7.5/10

Также в игре присутствует большой арсенал оружия с разными особенностями, в сочетаниями с 3 классами персов(Инженер, мародёр, наёмник), создаёт большую вариативность геймплея.

Визуал приятный, слава богу разрабы не насрали огромной кучей спецэффектов, спасибо.
В итоге получился приятный рогалик, не особо сложный, отзывчивый в плане управления, рекомендую.

Blazing Chrome is the spiritual successor to Contra III and Contra: Hard Corps. I have had an absolute blast playing this game. The game is non stop action. There are no puzzles to solve, no branching paths to explore, no story arc to follow. In my opinion this game perfects the 16 bit Contra gameplay. I always felt that Contra III and Contra HC lost their way and felt too much like boss rushes. Yes Blazing Chrome has some very big, beautiful, and creative bosses like those originals but it also has plenty of cannon fodder and platforming more similar to the original NES Contra and Super C. It really is the perfect blend of the 8bit and 16bit eras of Contra.

Several reviewers have noted that it is too difficult. I can see how newer gamers may feel this way. This game does not provide any hand holding. As someone who grew up in the “git good” era of gaming I feel like the difficulty level is appropriate. It's all about memorizing patterns and learning from mistakes. That's part of the fun. If you don't like a challenge you may want to pass on this one. But when you've finally beat a level after several failed tries you'll be pumping your fist with excitement and that feeling is so hard to find in modern gaming.

Was looking forward to this game for 2 years after playing the demo they released a long time ago. Loved it back then, but do not anymore. 

Large fleets and being able to send out ships to do tasks in a system was a thing back then, but now we have not only command point limits (which would be alright), we also have a ship limit that is way less than that, meaning you are limited in your ship deployment options. Deploy all the biggest ships you can, because anything smaller and you are wasting your ship limit capacity.

The upgrade system is similar to the world of games, like tanks or warships, but it extremely dismal in size and only encompasses 18 ships total, along with 4 weapon types of 3 different sizes, but many types and sizes either don't exist or have very few or only a single option.

The cherry on the cake is the horrible command system, where ships will ignore your command once they see an enemy. Once they engage, it's kill or die, there is no withdrawing no matter how you give the orders, they refuse to leave until they get destroyed, which costs you even more money and time.

The mission varient is extremely small, having you rinse and repeat the same 4~ tasks over and over again until you've leveled up enough to move to another system, where the process repeats.

Overall, this game may be somethings someday, but it's been 2 years now and while i know things have gone forward, it just doesn't feel as promising as it did back then.

非常有趣的独立像素动作游戏，你操纵一位使用鱼叉的主角，协同4件副武器（刺剑、巨剑、弓弩、霰弹枪），征战不同的区域。剧情也不复杂，收集3枚打开封印门的钥匙，从而回家。
游戏的特色是像素平台风，利用鱼叉和巨剑的瞬移功能进行解谜。大部分谜题较为简单，只有一处谜题需要你先将鱼叉导电后掷出，再跳到对面平台捡起带电鱼叉去打开电流门。之所以要先掷鱼叉是因为地面积水，如果带着带电鱼叉沾水会流失电能，导致无法打开电门。
游戏设计了几个boss，其中3人组boss要优先击杀术士、而最终boss魔鬼船则需要利用刺剑灵活走位，先击杀触手后集火头部弱点。游戏的战斗难度不低，特别是最终boss，建议升满血量后再去挑战。
游戏流程不长，5~10个小时可通关，但是收集要素因为涉及到很多高难度的平台跳跃，就不适合手残玩家挑战了。
一下午就玩完了，挺简单的，故事有趣，就是渔叉定位的手感很烂，但这不影响它成为一款值得一玩的游戏

I don't know when I'll finish Dustforce but I don't think my opinions will change by then, so I'll get this out now. It's a really unique and fun game, but it takes some work to get into. 

I think a lot of platformers try take aspects from other games in the same genre to feel familiar, which is not a negative thing per se, while Dustforce is trying to be the most singular it can be. There's a lot of movement tech that I haven't seen implemented like this anywhere else and playing with the physics and discovering new ways to dash around feels very fun. Moves as simple as wall jumping and wall running feel different in Dustforce and I believe that's great.

My main issue with this is sometimes having to approach the game with a focus on "how do I do this" instead of "executing this is hard", when the latter is what scratches my precision platforming itch the most. Playing it while streaming and getting some tips from friends and better players did tip the experience more towards the former, which was fun.

Overall I think Dustforce plays in a very interesting and distinct way, complemented by great visuals, soundtrack and usability. It's a very hard but weirdly chill game.

I really enjoyed it, it's more Wing Commander 1 than TIE Fighter or Freespace so the scope is limited but they did manage to cram more variation than I expected in the campaign.
Dogfighting is classic Wing Commander with some momentum to allow some moves, but they added lateral thrust, reverse thrust and drift as well as energy and shield quadrant management so the dogfights are involved enough.
It also has HOTAS support (I played it with a VKB hotas, a STECS Max throttle and a Gladiator NXT joystick to be specific) as well as gamepad. I don't have VR so I can say it plays well on a normal monitor, I did use headtracking though.
This being from a small indie studio there is no voice acting and the dialogues are conveyed through JRPGS-style dialogue boxes and the developers have been thoughtful enough to allow binding HOTAS controls to the full interface to allow among other things to scroll through them without having to reach for the mouse.
The story could have fit easily as an early Wing Commander title, a simple story of pirates, war, etc with a few nice twist and turns, sometimes conveyed during the missions.
Personally I liked the Star Fox vibes the characters give, it surely is something different and makes me sort of wish for a Star Fox spacesim.

Okay, first things first. This is a fandisk. So don't go in expecting a full sequel or some brand new story. It's more like extra content that builds on the individual routes from the original game. Basically, extended endings and "what happened next" scenes. If you loved the main game, this is a nice little bonus. If not, you can probably skip it. 
I was actually surprised because the romance isn't the main focus here, which is unusual for a fandisk. Instead, it's more about hanging out with the characters and seeing different sides of them. Each route has its own unique moments and isn't just a copy paste of others, which was refreshing. it's a lot more chill and sweet than dramatic and intense. 
The art and music are exactly the same quality as the main game, which is great because both were really solid. Plus, they added animated character sprites, so the visuals feel more alive. That was a nice touch. Unfortunately, there's still no voice acting, which is disappointing but also kind of expected given the price and scope.
It kinda felt like I was diving back into my childhood when I played this game. Of course my first route was Klaude, who was my favorite (and still is) from the original, and it was nice to see how his story continued. The game really leans into nostalgia, revisiting those characters and their stories in a relaxed way. But let's be honest. The story itself isn't anything new or groundbreaking. It's fluff and filler at times. No big plot twists or major story arcs, just sweet little moments after the fact.
So if you want something relaxing, sweet, this is for you. But if you're looking for a deep story or exciting new content, it's probably not worth your time.
I would 100% recommend it if you liked the original game. It's solid way to get some more info and spend time with the characters you love. Supporting the developers is also always a plus. But if the original wasn't your thing, you can safely pass this one.

Hidden Object Bundle 4 in 1, developed and published by Alawar Casual, is a compilation designed to deliver maximum value to fans of hidden object and casual adventure games. It collects four full-length titles—Stray Souls: A Dollhouse Story, House of 1,000 Doors: The Palm of Zoroaster, Dark Strokes: Sins of the Fathers, and Eternal Journey: New Atlantis—into one accessible package. Each game has its own narrative tone and setting, ensuring that the collection doesn’t feel like a repetitive assortment of the same formula, but rather a tour through the most defining traits of the genre: mystery, atmosphere, and a balance of storytelling and puzzle-solving. While all four titles share the same core gameplay of exploring scenes and uncovering cleverly hidden objects, the variations in theme—from gothic horror to spiritual fantasy to sci-fi adventure—give the bundle an appealing sense of variety that extends its longevity and appeal.

The first title, Stray Souls: A Dollhouse Story, opens the collection on a dark and emotional note. It tells the story of a woman searching for her missing husband, leading her into a cursed town filled with haunting imagery, eerie dolls, and supernatural presences. The atmosphere is rich and unsettling, using muted color palettes, haunting music, and evocative background art to immerse the player in its tragic tale. The hidden object scenes are well-composed, featuring detailed artwork that rewards careful observation, while the puzzles complement the exploration without becoming overly difficult or tedious. This title sets the tone for the collection as a whole—it is story-driven, visually detailed, and designed to be engaging without demanding too much from the player, making it ideal for casual gamers looking for something immersive yet approachable.

House of 1,000 Doors: The Palm of Zoroaster continues the mysterious momentum with a more spiritual and exotic theme. Players step into the role of a writer who must travel through portals to different parts of the world, encountering ghosts, curses, and ancient relics. This installment leans more heavily into narrative and world-building, blending hidden object gameplay with light adventure elements such as puzzle-solving and item combination. Each environment—from the mystical temples of Tibet to the desolate ruins of Jerusalem—is meticulously illustrated, making exploration a pleasure in itself. The voice acting and soundtrack add a sense of cinematic quality, elevating the experience above many games in the genre. While the gameplay remains familiar, the story’s scope and imaginative setting make it one of the more memorable entries in the bundle.

Dark Strokes: Sins of the Fathers shifts back into a gothic atmosphere reminiscent of classic literature, weaving a tale of love, loss, and the supernatural. You play as Ethan, a man whose fiancée has been kidnapped by faceless entities, forcing him to journey through cursed towns and eerie manors to uncover the truth. The emotional weight of the story and the consistently high-quality artwork make this one of the standout titles in the set. Its hidden object scenes are tighter and more inventive, occasionally blending object searches with environmental puzzles. The pacing is excellent—never too fast or slow—and the gradual revelation of the game’s mystery keeps players invested. Though it follows familiar tropes of the genre, it executes them with enough polish and atmosphere to feel satisfying rather than derivative.

Eternal Journey: New Atlantis concludes the bundle with a surprising change in tone, taking the player into a futuristic sci-fi setting while maintaining the core mechanics of hidden object discovery. This title follows an archaeologist uncovering the secrets of Atlantis before transitioning to a story set in outer space, making it one of the most conceptually ambitious games in the collection. The juxtaposition of ancient history and futuristic technology gives it a unique visual flair compared to the more traditionally gothic settings of the other entries. The puzzles are a little more complex here, involving mechanical interactions and spatial reasoning rather than simple item collection. Despite the genre shift, the transition works, demonstrating that the hidden object formula can adapt to different narratives and still feel cohesive. The strong atmosphere and imaginative environments make it a fitting finale to the compilation.

Taken together, Hidden Object Bundle 4 in 1 represents a curated showcase of what made Alawar Casual a staple name in the genre. Each game shares the studio’s hallmark design traits—clear object placement, intuitive puzzle progression, and smooth pacing—ensuring accessibility without sacrificing engagement. The art direction across all four titles is consistently high quality, relying on beautifully painted backgrounds and ambient effects that keep each setting immersive. While none of the games push the boundaries of the genre mechanically, the combined collection offers a wide range of themes and moods that keep it from growing monotonous. It is a comfortable, familiar experience for players who enjoy methodical exploration, gentle challenge, and richly illustrated worlds.

The bundle’s main appeal lies in its value and accessibility. For a low price, it provides hours of content across four distinct stories, making it an excellent entry point for newcomers to the hidden object genre or a convenient compilation for longtime fans. However, it also bears the genre’s limitations: linear storytelling, relatively low replay value once puzzles are solved, and predictable pacing that prioritizes relaxation over challenge. Yet these qualities are also part of its charm. The absence of time limits or complex systems allows for an experience that is soothing rather than stressful—a chance to engage with stories at a slow, reflective pace. The result is a compilation that captures the enduring appeal of hidden object games: immersive worlds, gentle puzzles, and a sense of quiet discovery.

In the end, Hidden Object Bundle 4 in 1 is not about innovation but about comfort and consistency. It offers four polished, atmospheric adventures that exemplify the genre’s best qualities without overcomplicating the formula. Players who approach it with the right expectations—seeking mood, story, and simple yet rewarding gameplay—will find a great deal to enjoy. Alawar Casual’s attention to pacing, art direction, and thematic diversity makes this collection a pleasant, worthwhile addition to any casual gamer’s library. It’s a gentle reminder that games don’t always need spectacle or innovation to be engaging—sometimes, all they need is a good mystery, a haunting setting, and the quiet satisfaction of finding what was hidden.
