🎮 Gameplay
Orbt XL è il classico esempio di come un’idea semplice possa diventare una droga digitale. Un solo pulsante: tieni premuto e il tuo pianeta si allontana dal buco nero, lascia andare e vieni risucchiato. Sembra facile, vero? Certo, come dire che “camminare su una corda sopra un vulcano” è una passeggiata.

Il gioco ti premia se ti avvicini al buco nero, ma più ti avvicini più rischi di finire risucchiato. È come flirtare con il pericolo: divertente, ma sai già che finirà male.

🤯 Difficoltà
Non lasciarti ingannare dal look minimalista: Orbt XL è un maestro zen del sadismo.

Partite brevissime: duri 10 secondi? Complimenti, sei già un campione.

Ostacoli casuali: asteroidi e sfere che sembrano avere un radar puntato su di te.

Punteggio: ogni volta pensi “stavolta batto il record”… e invece il buco nero ti ricorda chi comanda.

✨ Grafica
Minimal, pulito, quasi ipnotico. È il tipo di gioco che potresti mostrare a un amico dicendo: “Guarda, è semplice!” e poi ridere mentre lui mentre bestemmia dopo essere crepato dopo 5 secondi

😂 Ironia della sorte
Orbt XL è il gioco perfetto per chi ama soffrire con stile.

Vuoi rilassarti? Non farlo: il buco nero ti aspetta.

Vuoi dimostrare riflessi pronti? Preparati a scoprire che hai la prontezza di un bradipo.

Vuoi solo “una partita veloce”? Tre ore dopo sei ancora lì, convinto che “stavolta ce la faccio”.

🏆 Conclusione
Orbt XL è un piccolo capolavoro arcade: semplice da capire, impossibile da dominare, e tremendamente divertente. È il tipo di gioco che ti fa ridere, imprecare e dire “ancora una volta” fino a quando ti rendi conto che il buco nero ha già divorato la tua serata.

Voto ironico: 10/10, perché il buco nero non accetta mezze misure.





🎮 Gameplay
Orbt XL is a classic example of how a simple idea can become a digital drug. Just one button: hold down and your planet moves away from the black hole, let go and you get sucked in. Sounds easy, right? Of course, like saying that “walking on a rope over a volcano” is a walk in the park.

The game rewards you if you get close to the black hole, but the closer you get, the more you risk getting sucked in. It's like flirting with danger: fun, but you already know it's going to end badly.

🤯 Difficulty
Don't be fooled by the minimalist look: Orbt XL is a Zen master of sadism.

Very short games: 10 seconds long? Well done, you're already a champion.

Random Obstacles: Asteroids and spheres that appear to have radar trained on you.

Score: Every time you think “this time I break the record”… and instead the black hole reminds you who's in charge.

✨ GRAPHICS
Minimal, clean, almost hypnotic. It's the kind of game you might show a friend by saying, “Look, it's simple!” and then laugh as he gets sucked in in 3 seconds flat.

😂 Irony of fate
Orbt XL is the perfect game for those who like to suffer with style.

Do you want to relax? Don't do it: the black hole awaits you.

Want to demonstrate ready reflexes? Get ready to find out you have the readiness of a sloth.

You just want “a quick game”? Three hours later you're still there, convinced that “this time I can do it”.

🏆 Conclusion
Orbt XL is a little arcade masterpiece: simple to understand, impossible to master, and tremendously fun. It's the kind of game that makes you laugh, curse, and say “again” until you realize the black hole has already devoured your evening.

Ironic rating: 10/10, because the black hole doesn't accept half measures.

To note, this is a collection game of the Evoland 1 & 2, so is strictly better than buying them individually. I will split this review into two parts, one for each game.
Evoland 1:
Super short game, only took 3 hours, but has one of the coolest concepts I have seen in a game where you continuously progress through the different eras of gaming. This game main revolves around either JRPG or top down Legend of Zelda game play, with occasionally some other game types thrown in. This definitely has a lot of promise, but the game play i found clunky. Additionally the story is boring and filled with lots of bad stereotypes. One thing I really wish was that there was actually more often switching between the two main styles instead of areas being pretty much compartmentalized into the different types of game play.
Evoland 2:
This is actually a complete and polished game taking me 30 hours to 100% (collectibles wise). The game is reduced to be legend of Zelda game play for 50% of the time, 30% 2D platformer, with the rest being occasional story driven game play style changes. These span, bullet hells, fighting games, beat-em-ups, bejeweled, JRPGs, among others. The evolving through the ages of gaming has been entirely replaced in this game and is replaced with each era of gaming representing a different time in the time line. That is right, this is a time traveling game. The story is actually quite good in this game and has quite a bit of depth if you are one to try and figure out the lore. All and all I would recommend this game for people to play if you are a fan of more exploration and puzzle based games.
Final thoughts:
I would say that I much more enjoyed my time playing Evoland 2 than 1, but that Evoland 1 has the better potential game concept.

[h1]Qué recuerdos del juego de Jurassic Park de PS2[/h1]
Me encanta, aunque tiene sus matices.

Este juego es, en esencia, una extensión de las películas —sobre todo de las de Jurassic World. Tendremos la oportunidad de gestionar las cinco islas que rodean a Isla Nublar (la isla principal de las películas), donde deberemos superar diferentes desafíos en una campaña basada en objetivos y gestión. Al completar ciertas misiones, avanzaremos a la siguiente isla, desbloqueando nuevos edificios, atracciones y, obviamente, nuevos fósiles de dinosaurios.

A lo largo del juego aparecen varios personajes de las películas, además de distintos eventos, como fenómenos climáticos o desastres provocados por los propios dinosaurios.

Y poco más: para ser un juego de gestión de recursos, es bastante sencillo y no tiene una dificultad demasiado alta. El mayor reto suele estar relacionado con el dinero; si no sabés administrarlo bien, podés quedar acorralado más de una vez. Pero por lo demás, si gestionás bien la electricidad y los recintos de los dinosaurios, una buena tienda con precios ajustados hará su magia para mantener un flujo constante de ingresos.

Obviamente, los dinosaurios son los protagonistas de la saga, y en esta ocasión tendremos la oportunidad de criarlos y convertir su “reexistencia” en una atracción. Ahí entra un poco el dilema del juego (y de las películas): hasta dónde ceder ante la experimentación científica, la explotación del entretenimiento o la seguridad de los visitantes.

Mecánicamente, es un juego sencillo, donde todo gira en torno a mejorar el genoma de los dinosaurios, incubarlos y liberarlos. En el medio tendremos que gestionar los recursos y lograr la autosuficiencia económica de las islas, manteniendo todo bajo control.

El juego es curioso y entretenido. Sé, por el meme, que el 2 es prácticamente lo mismo y que el 3 es como el 1 y el 2 combinados, así que capaz me tire más por esos.

Un de plus....fais chier...
Un jeu qui peut plaire, qui a des atouts, qui pourrait percer...si la RNG ne venez pas tout foutre en l'air !

Bon allons-y pour les explications.
Vous commencez par diriger une "escouade" de 3 recrues, faible en stats et avec un trait négatif chacune.
Ce trait (il y en a plusieurs différent et chacun avec un malus différent, entraînant un effet négatif différent) peut être enlevé si vous faites l'action qu'il faut : soit un entrainement, soit une corvée (cuisine, chiottes...).

Si les conditions sont respectées, le trait est enlevé, vous gagnez de la renommée et vous êtes peinard.
Si non respectées, la recrue peut risque une blessure pendant l'entrainement (elle part à l'hôpital et ne reviendra plus), ou elle peut s'enfuir pendant une mission (pour différentes raisons : peur de l'eau, timide..).

Les Stats sont les suivantes :

- Force - Permet de porter plus de provisions en mission
- CàC/Mêlée - Quand les munitions viennent à manquer... (augmente les chances de victoire en combat rapproché)
- Agilité - Pour les opérations discrètes (augmente les chances de victoires lors d'opérations et d'actions qui requièrent de la discrétion / de la furtivité)
- Tir - Augmente les chances de toucher lors des combats à distance
- Intelligence - Affecte la rapidité du rechargement de l'arme lors du combat
- Discipline - Affecte les chances de fuite en combat (???)

Autant le dire clairement : 2 des stats ici seront clairement inutiles.
Le CàC (Corps à Corps ou Mêlée) -> Vous aurez rarement des combats de ce type. La presque totalité se fera à distance (principe d'une guerre...)
La Discipline ne servira que lors de la phase d'entrainement des recrues, pour UN événement qui survient toujours le même jour.
En combat, s'enfuir revient à la recrue d'être considérée comme tuée. Elle ne reviendra pas au combat et ne réapparaîtra plus.
L'utilité ? Aucune idée. On diminue juste nos chances de fuite d'une recrue donc.
Sachant que la fuite ne se fera surtout que lorsque la recrue à un trait négatif encore actif.
Statistiques complètement inutiles, pour l'une comme pour l'autre.

Note à ce sujet : les autres stats serviront autant pour les entrainement, les compétitions surtout, pouvant rapporter de la renommée lorsque vous êtes premier, que pour la phase de combat.
Les stats de Force, de CàC et d'Agilité pour certaines épreuves (piscine, boxe, sprint...) et les stats de Tir et d'Intelligence pour l'épreuve de Sniper (les épreuves sont variables et les stats des concurrents augmenteront à chaque fois après une phase de guerre).

La Renommée servira à acheter de l'équipement plus pointu pour se spécialiser plus vite et plus efficacement.
Il faudra aussi gérer la fatigue, l'Endurance qui baissera et le Stress qui augmentera à chaque action.
L'un comme l'autre peuvent être augmenté ou diminué selon l'action adéquat faite sur une recrue.
Une Endurance trop faible augmente les chances de rater un entrainement ou une épreuve (0 points, disqualification) et un Stress trop élevé peut entraîner un départ de la recrue et une impossibilité de certaines action.

La RNG vient ici foutre le bordel parce que, en situation de combat, même avec 2 ou 3 recrues très bien entraînées et une chance de protection de plus de 50%, elle peut mourir en 1 coup...par UN sniper ennemi. UN seul.
En 3 batailles successives, j'ai par exemple perdu 3 soldats surentraînés (80+ stats) sur une escouade de 4.

50% de chance, dit le jeu ? Bizarre mais je n'y crois pas trop.
Etrangement, mon dernier soldat à réussi à faire 3 combats, tout seul, contre 1 voir 3 soldats, dont 1 sniper ennemi sur 2 batailles successives, sans mourir ou être touché.

Je ne donne sans doute pas sa chance au jeu, je le conçois.
Mais le jeu ne m'en donne pas tellement non plus.
Cela sent le script au début et la RNG sur la suite et je n'aime pas ça du tout.

Ah oui : Et les succès sont buggés aussi !
Je devrais en avoir bien plus de la moitié et rien ne s'est activé.

Dommage, je trouve que le jeu est sympa et relaxant...pendant la phase d'entrainement.
Puis c'est toi qui subit le stress du combat, puisque tu peux tout perdre en très peu de temps....
Si vous êtes fan des coups de chance, vous apprécierez.
Ce n'est pas mon cas. Regrettable.

Like MG, MG2 is a turn-based gladiator style of game. You may eventually have a team of up to four toons, each equipped with skills and equipment granted at level-up or gained through battle. The big change from MG seems to be the addition of a StS node-based system of progression through three areas. After each battle, you are awarded some loot (more if you took the harder version of the fight) and some experience. At level-up you have the choice to add a skill or increase a variety of stats. The run ends after you lose twice in a given area or after you beat the third boss.

Pros:

+++ Event-based dialogues contains no randomness and show you the consequences of your choices, as my personal preference is not to layer random outcomes on top of a random event.

+++ The option to take a harder fight for better loot is appreciated and does add to the strategic aspect of the run.

++ Level-ups are fun and meaningful.

++ Game mechanics (buffs/de-buffs) are unspectacular, but solid.

++ Tactical play is still strong (as it was in MG).

+ Equipment is fair.

Cons: 

-- Game is way too hard at highest difficulty levels. It took me ~10-15 tries to beat "10", and then I realized that there is  an 11.

-- As with many games where you gain characters as you go, the toons you buy later are almost always better than the ones caringly leveled-up from scratch. This makes me feel like I am not so much progressing as just buying a team.

-- Replayability is limited as the artifact pool isn't so deep and doesn't have near the passive effects of relics in StS.

Summary: While I haven't done a deep-dive comparison, my impressions of MG2 aren't much different than those of MG. The added node-system is appreciated, but much like MG, ultimately I don't really have any reason to keep playing, despite the fact that I am not really bored with the game (as such). The difficulty is crushing at level 11, past the point of fun, and there is no real run-to-run diversity in terms of gameplay.

Still, I got some good time out of MG2 (not quite my time shown as I often leave my games open and unattended for hours on end) and is pretty cheap. I guess if you liked the first one, you will like this one (just wait for a sale, of course).

Overall: 7.0/10

The Testament of Sherlock Holmes is a masterclass in detective storytelling. From the moment I stepped into 19th-century London, I was hooked by the dark, atmospheric setting and the morally complex narrative. This isn't your typical Holmes tale—it's grittier, more personal, and full of twists that kept me guessing until the very end.

The puzzles are clever and varied, striking a great balance between challenge and satisfaction. I especially appreciated the ability to switch between first-person, third-person, and even a top-down view—it made exploration feel fluid and immersive. The voice acting is top-notch, with Holmes and Watson delivering performances that feel true to their literary roots while adding a fresh edge.

If you're a fan of detective games, rich narratives, or just love a good mystery, this game is a must-play. It's not perfect—some animations feel a bit dated—but the story and atmosphere more than make up for it.

🧩 Come for the puzzles, stay for the plot twists. Holmes has never been darker—or more compelling.

The Testament of Sherlock Holmes is the moment Frogwares truly sharpened their vision for a modern detective adventure. It may not be the most polished entry in the series, but it remains one of the boldes, dark, morally tangled and refreshingly committed to portraying the great detective as something more complicated than a brilliant Victorian puzzle machine.

Set in 1898, the story plunges Holmes and Watson into one of their most fraught investigations: a trail of stolen jewels, missing children and mounting evidence that seems to implicate Holmes himself. It’s a clever subversion, watching London’s trust erode while Holmes becomes increasingly secretive lends the entire tale a simmering tension. For once, the question isn’t just who did it, but who Holmes truly is beneath the legend.

Gameplay is a mix of environmental puzzles, deduction boards, lock mechanisms and clue hunting. Frogwares experiments heavily here, and while not every puzzle lands, many are inventive and satisfyingly tactile. There’s an admirable willingness to let players solve things without handholding, and the deduction sequences in particular offer a gratifying sense of agency.

Visually, the game shows its age, but the atmosphere remains potent. London’s gaslit streets, cramped tenements and stately drawing rooms are rendered with enough texture to feel lived-in. The voice acting - especially Holmes’ clipped arrogance and Watson’s simmering concern- grounds the story emotionally even when the production values wobble.

Where The Testament of Sherlock Holmes truly excels is its tone: grim, brooding and unafraid to push Holmes into morally ambiguous territory. It’s a detective story that respects its audience, trusting players to navigate shades of gray rather than the clean resolutions of classic whodunits.

Despite some dated design and uneven pacing, The Testament of Sherlock Holmes stands as one of the series’ most intriguing chapters, a daring portrait of a legend at his most vulnerable and dangerous.

Netherspace is a beautifully crafted retro-looking shooter game with quite a funny twist in most of the interactions that take place between the two starring heroes.
There is great variety in terms of what the player can choose to invest in per playthrough, as the many ship's stats prove to be a major factor in choosing a personal gameplay style.
The teleportation and shield mechanisms are both vital for survival and the ability to move at double speed when not firing gave me a good choice of defenses without which it would be impossible to reach the game's ending, so kudos for nice variety in that area.
The ship's weapons have separate ammo each and up to four can be equipped. They each have their strengths and weaknesses, whether it is in terms of ammo, ammo recharge rate, fire rate, hitbox size, damage and certain special weapons even have spread and their bolts teleport along with the ship.
What I enjoyed most, other than the direct gameplay, was the beautifully written script.
Both heroes are interesting and the presentation of the plot after each defeated boss and upgrade screen, exclusively through the dialogue of the protagonists, worked perfectly for me.
In the end, I've had fun with this little game and see no reason not to recommend it to shoot'em'up and retro-looking games lovers.

Wow! What a trip down memory lane! My story with this game might differ somewhat from others, as it was a part of my childhood but I didn't actually play it. No, my cousin did. Neither of us spoke English nor were we especially bright with this type of game, as we were quite young. For that reason, we didn't go very far. I distinctively recall he restarted the game a lot for whatever reason, so quite a considerable amount of time was spent at Citadel Island specifically.

Fast forward nearly 30 years and I *finally* get to play it for myself after eyeing it here on Steam for a few years now and after refunding the first game for not being particularly impressed by it. I'm just a few minutes in, feeling like a child again running around Citadel Island not really knowing what to do (except I now speak English fluently, so I'm learning how to progress) and good God, they really don't make games like this anymore. There's something really special about LBA2 and it clicked for me immediately. It's not just nostalgia either as I didn't personally play it.

I'm also quite surprised by how well it plays on the Steam Deck. Not because I expected it to perform poorly, but because the controls are phenomenal. I made no changes to the default control scheme and despite being unorthodox even by 1997 standards, it just makes sense. In fact, I think having RT as forwards and LT as backwards makes perfect sense with tank controls. I don't recall actually playing this game much if at all (besides watching my cousin explore Citadel Island), let alone with a controller, and it feels like riding a bike... if I hadn't learned how to ride one.

I'd definitely recommend getting this whether you played it or was exposed to it as a child, or if you heard of it just recently. It actually aged surprisingly well, although parts of it do look and feel dated. It's a very unique game, the likes of which you'll struggle to find nowadays.

Shift 87, developed by Pixelsplit and published by Daedalic Entertainment, is a psychological observation horror game that focuses on attention, perception, and the discomfort of repetition. It takes the familiar framework of “spot the difference” and transforms it into an eerie descent into unease. The player assumes the role of a nameless anomaly detector, stationed in an isolated, sterile facility where strange occurrences disrupt the mundane. The job is simple on paper—patrol the floors, memorize your surroundings, and report anything that looks out of place—but in execution, it becomes a tense exercise in paranoia. Every flickering light, missing chair, or subtly altered shadow might be the sign of something wrong. It’s a minimalist setup that relies entirely on atmosphere and the player’s sense of observation rather than scripted scares.

From the very beginning, Shift 87 excels at creating an oppressive atmosphere. The environments are mundane—an empty office, a lifeless factory, a lonely gas station—but that ordinariness becomes its greatest weapon. The lighting is deliberately dim, casting long shadows that distort familiar spaces. The hum of machinery, the buzz of fluorescent lights, and the occasional distant creak form an ambient soundscape that amplifies tension without ever needing loud or sudden noises. Every element of design seems built to erode the player’s sense of comfort. You walk through the same hallways again and again, studying every object, every flicker of light, every corner of the room, until something feels wrong—but you can’t quite pinpoint what. That creeping uncertainty is the essence of the game’s fear.

The gameplay loop is deceptively simple yet psychologically taxing. Each level begins with a baseline tour, giving you a chance to memorize the layout. After that, you repeat the same path, scanning for anomalies—changes that range from subtle shifts in lighting to more overt distortions. When you find something, you report it through your scanner; too many mistakes, and you’ll have to start over. There’s no combat, no monsters to fight—just your own perception as your tool and your greatest enemy. The challenge lies in how the game forces you to question your memory. Did that painting always face that way? Was that door open before? The more you play, the more you begin to doubt your own recollection, blurring the line between reality and imagination. It’s a gameplay mechanic that trades traditional horror for cognitive unease, relying on tension that builds slowly but steadily.

Shift 87’s progression system divides its horror across three main environments, each containing a series of randomized anomalies. This randomization adds replayability, ensuring that each new run feels unpredictable, but it also contributes to the feeling of disorientation. You never quite know what form the next anomaly will take or when it will appear. The repetition of environments could have easily grown stale, yet the randomness and ambient sound design maintain a constant state of anxiety. Each discovery—whether it’s a missing object or a distorted figure in the distance—hits harder because of the monotony leading up to it. The player is lulled into a false sense of routine before the game subtly violates it, creating that quintessential horror of the familiar made strange.

While the concept is strong, Shift 87’s structure has limitations. The game’s short runtime—typically two to three hours for a full playthrough—suits its minimalist design but may leave players wanting more depth. The lack of narrative context, while intentional to preserve mystery, means the experience is more mechanical than emotional. You are not given much reason to care about who you are or why the anomalies exist; you simply observe and report, an anonymous cog in a surreal system. For some, that detachment enhances the sense of alienation, but for others it might come off as hollow. Additionally, the core loop can become repetitive after prolonged play. Once you’ve acclimated to the rhythm of observation and reporting, the novelty of the concept begins to wane, especially when environments start to feel too similar.

Despite its simplicity, Shift 87’s craftsmanship is commendable. The visuals are crisp, and the use of lighting and texture gives each location a distinct mood. The performance is smooth and optimized for lower-end machines, making it accessible to a broad audience. The sound design deserves particular praise—it’s subtle yet vital, using silence and ambient noise as tools of psychological manipulation. The absence of jump scares or traditional enemies allows the tension to breathe naturally, rewarding patience and attentiveness rather than reflexes. The minimalist interface and lack of unnecessary HUD elements keep immersion intact, ensuring the player’s focus remains squarely on the environment and their own creeping uncertainty.

Ultimately, Shift 87 is a quiet but effective exercise in observational horror. It takes the mundane and twists it just enough to provoke discomfort, creating a slow-burn tension that lingers long after you’ve stopped playing. It’s not a game of action or narrative spectacle but of quiet anxiety, built on the fear of noticing too much—or not enough. Its repetition and lack of deeper story might limit its appeal to players seeking a traditional horror experience, but for those who appreciate subtle psychological tension and atmospheric design, it offers something genuinely unique. Shift 87 is a testament to how horror can emerge from silence, stillness, and the smallest deviations in the world around us. It’s a short, unsettling experiment in perception that proves sometimes the scariest thing isn’t what’s lurking in the dark—but the nagging feeling that something has changed, and you can’t remember what.

本作是一款建造运营类的模拟游戏，背景设定是在第一次世界大战的末期，玩家将扮演英国的亨利威尔斯上校，在一战末期的战场上负责一家资源不足、岌岌可危的野战医院，想尽一切办法拯救更多的伤员。相比其他经营类的游戏，本作的题材是比较新颖的，之前在市面上很少见到野战医院的模拟游戏。但本作依旧没有脱离和传统的经营模拟范畴，仍是通过资源控制、指标管理来达成每局的游戏目标。游戏发生的背景大约是距离一战结束的倒数几个月，主线内容共有三章，每章的内容大同小异，玩家需要从前线接下一波又一波的伤员，保证部队的战斗力，确保战线不会被击垮。玩法上，本作和知名的经营游戏冰汽时代简直太像了。尤其是支线探索的玩法，玩家需要派出侦查和运输部队来完成各类事件，和冰汽时代的大地图探索极其相似。在每一章，玩家都需要进行周期性的工作，首先从前线战壕里接下伤员，然后依据他们的伤情轻重、类型，分配到不同的手术室进行救治，之后再分配到各个病房进行后期康复，最后再决定士兵们的最终归宿。如果让士兵重归战场，则可以增加前线战力，防止被击溃；让士兵前往后方，则可以获取军票，用来申请更多的物资；让士兵退役，则可以获取士气，提升医院的工作效率。总的来说，游戏的玩法刚开始玩会感到比较新颖，但多玩一会就会觉得很枯燥。一方面是因为重复程度太琐碎了，玩家需要不断点开医生和患者的属性进行分配，在中期资源不足，病人暴增的时候，更是手忙脚乱。而且难度也极其不平衡。每关的难度曲线很不平滑，前期无所事事，中期会有一段很难的时期，而后期资源溢出又会特别简单。游戏屏幕上的那个善恶值系统，说实话并没有体会到有什么用，除了成就以外好像没什么别的影响？不得不提的还有，游戏的bug好多，翻译也很多乱码，很容易烂档，优化也极其烂。满分十分的话我只能给6分，可以肯定的是这是一个完全的半成品游戏，除了题材新颖，意义较深以外毫无可玩之处，如果后续制作组还没有补救的话，即使是史低的20块也不值得购买。

Freedom Planet is often described as a "Sonic fangame," which is what it originally started out as before Galaxy Trail went off in their own direction and crowdfunded, but it's really a huge shoutout to Studio Treasure and an ode to 2D games in the 32-bit era. 

This is one of the few retro-style games that I could honestly see being made almost exactly as is in the era that it's trying to emulate. Everything about this game screams 'lost Sega Saturn exclusive' from the graphical and animation style to the voice acting and cutscenes to the general game design and even the bugs and incomplete features. Ir all feels really true to the late 90s in the way everything in the game is designed and put together.

General stage design will immediately remind you of Sonic, especially early on, but there are a heap load of influences from all over the place. Graphics feel akin to Astal on the Saturn, and there are bits of Megaman X all over the place. There's even what feels like a shoutout to Dragonbreed towards the end of Lilac's campaign. However, the biggest influence is very clearly Gunstar Heroes, Alien Soldier, and even a little Dynamite Heady and Mischief Makers mixed in from Studio Treasure. If you are familiar with Treasure's games at all this will especially become apparent in many bossfights where there is a similar level of creativity and frenetic energy on display. As a Treasure fan, it was absolutely delightful to see the many overt and subtle references to them across the game.

As for what Freedom Planet's gameplay actually boils down to: it's a 2D High-Speed Action Platformer with three playable characters. There were supposed to be five, according to the Kickstarter, but I don't think the other two are ever being added in at this point considering the second game is done and Galaxy Trail have indicated they are working on a third game. If you're used to Sonic, this game will immediately throw you off in many ways. First of all, there is an actual functional combat system and no contact damage. You have to attack enemies to hit them and you'll only be hit when attacked. Like I said with Spark the Electric Jester, I think this is both an extremely good change and a direct improvement over Sonic's current 2D outings (not to put them down; I just prefer systems like this).

The other thing that will throw you off if you're used to Sonic is the length and structure of levels. Levels in this game can go on for twenty five minutes if you're looking for collectibles, and many of them contain multiple sections with their own gimmicks. Plus, stages are not always a race to the end. Pretty early on, you'll run into sections where you have to take multiple detours to hit switches so you can open a door to the way forward. Personally, I was a fan of the level design throughout, though I will say I had to split up play sessions because of hos long they were. It just got tiring, especially since I was looking for all the stuff. I recommend saving that for a second run if you play it yourself.

Graphically, the game looks gorgeous with load of details in the backgrounds and really impressive sprite layering. The real standout is the bosses, however, which not only use the same sprite layering to display massive monsters and machines with multiple simultaneous moving parts, but some even feature other members of your team coming in to help you out as well. Not only do they manage to maintain clarity among all the visual noise, but the scenarios themselves are just a spectacle to behold. Actually fighting them is a mixed bag. I enjoyed most of them for both the visuals and genuine challenge, but a few leaned a little too hard into arcade trial and error design.

I feel the need to shoutout the alternate characters. Lilac, Carol, and Milla all play very differently from each other. It's not like Sonic where Knuckles and Tails are basically Sonic with an extra ability. No, Carol's motorcycles and Milla's gooey block powers will significantly change how you play the game compared to Lilac's Dragon Dash. and it's an accomplishment that all of them are fun.

Also, the soundtrack is amazing, and you should buy it.

So yeah, I absolutely recommend Freedom Planet if you're a fan of Action Platformers. Just be aware that if you go in expecting a Sonic game, you won't be getting that.

As you can see from some reviews some people will just cry that a game is a copy of a game that came before it. Yes Anno is still Anno...obviously. Somehow this surprises people. It's also about a 20 second wait for the Ubi launcher the first time you launch the game so these complaints not recommending the game are a bit nonsensical to me. Heres a list of good changes imo. There's a surprising amount

-This is a step up graphically. Anno 1800 looked great, this just adds a bit more weather and atmosphere. The building models and maps are more detailed but things like character models are a significant upgrade. 

-Performance has mostly been a locked 60 with high/very high, raytraced shadows, and DLSS on balanced/quality. I run a 4080 with a R7 9700x and 32gb DDR5 @ stock speeds. I have a 35 inch 3440x1440p monitor so I was very happy with this. When I turned raytracing off and unlocked the frame rate I was getting 100fps in my small town. There was way too much screen tearing without it locked though so I went back. 

-They introduce the game mechanics quite a bit better this time around. New players will have an easier time with this. Small things like game tips popping up in a silent visible notification on the top left of the screen instead of most games where tutorial tips are literally forced on you and often pause the game. This allows some learning at your own pace if you're new.

-This has a much more fleshed out combat and military system which was needed. Actual ground combat was a welcome surprise. I'm excited to be able to play a military RTS, city builder, and logistics simulator all in one game. There's actual varied mechanics to the individual ships and units which is cool to see. 

- You can now build more unique cities. The ability to build curved roads and rotate buildings at a 45 degree angle adds quite a bit to the variety surprisingly. 

- I didn't think I would care for yet another historical  setting but thay manage to make their take on the roman era interesting. I do hope the next title is something completely different though. I'm salavating at the idea of a 1950's Soviet/US era or something that's a fresh take for the series. 

-This launched with more standalone items compared to 1800 if I'm remembering correctly. Decently cool statues and ornaments. 

-This developer is great with UI and this game improved on the already good UI in the previous game

-Added a religion mechanic with varied interesting options

-The story is halfway intriguing so far, which was not expected. I saw some negative reviews that called it "woke" which is just hysterical/sad to me. 

-They've kept some quality of life stuff introduced as dlc in the previous game.  

-Added a research progression tree with three main varied subcategories that will allow rushing certain builds/playstyles which gives you a much more varied playthrough if you want to start fresh. This tree impressed me because it determines pretty impactful changes that can alter a playthrough.

-They added a brush tool that allows you to brush over buildings to change the look of them which adds to the city building element even more. 

Overall, I think this is in an excellent spot. It adds meaningful and welcome changes to the formula without removing core elements that make Anno the series it is. They're doing a lot with this game and I'm looking forward to seeing what they can do with it in the coming years.
Initial thoughts are this game is exactly what most Anno fans will want, same gameplay as before but with tones of new and additional features that still keep it feeling fresh.

这种心累体现在几个方面：一号罪魁祸首就是八个碎片才能攒一个残机的设计。说真的这根本没什么道理，你道中给的残碎片本来就不多，又不是绀珠传那种擦弹就能拿残碎片的机制，人家还是三个碎片就能拿到一个残机呢。虽然开灵界能拿更多的碎片，可攒满一次花的功夫又需要很久，碎片还给的很分散不能一口气在灵界时间内把这一整面的全拿到，拿不到的就只能亏了——虽然zun降低了弹幕难度来让这个低容错率没有那么折磨，但四五面但凡不小心撞一下那挫败感还是能直接让我想幻想入。
其二就是这个神灵了。说真的，本身东方这个把p和点分散成很多小份的设计并不算坏，因为有上线收点这个机制让你找到一次往上顶的空隙就能把全屏的p点收掉；但是这个机制到了神灵这块就没有了！又不会下落，又不能用特定的操作一口气收掉，只能硬生生往弹幕里一遍一遍钻，而且需要收集超多才能开一次灵界，这玩的不累才怪吧。这一作很多弹幕是不难，但是我会在其他作都不会死的地方死，就因为其他作我看到密的弹幕就躲到版底老老实实扭去了，而这作还得往上硬钻。是，有些时候只要老老实实待在板底就会相当安全，但看着那么多神灵就这样消失，那憋得也很难受啊）
就这两点，让神灵庙的资源收集变得非常不爽但又很有必要，也让这游戏撞一下受到的惩罚非常高。说真的，大往生的hyper攒的都比这快而且舒服多了。还是之前提过的，zun降低难度让这个过程没有那么折磨，但不代表玩家就会觉得这很好玩了（而且降低难度的同时弹幕设计也下去了，还加了很多相当意义不明的操作。你是说玩家会觉得，宫古芳香吸神灵回血怎么都打不死很开心？还是说青娥拿芳香当盾牌还放一堆追踪球扭起来很舒服？）
明明没必要的，但强行用又慢又不舒服的资源获取让玩家有背板需求，这作玩起来的感觉就是很心累啊。
但这也就是几句牢骚。说到底游戏本身没有那么难，所以这些问题也没有那么不能接受。在星莲船的一个极端之后体验一下截然不同的风格，也算是有点意义吧。（仅从游戏体验层面，剧情上这作引入的角色可太重要了）
能不能让一下秒的妖精回归啊）

Sagrada’s digital adaptation by Dire Wolf transforms the acclaimed dice-drafting board game into a polished, visually rich puzzle experience that plays beautifully on PC. What immediately stands out is the strong commitment to preserving the tactile charm of the tabletop original. The game’s stained-glass theme translates naturally into its digital form: vividly colored dice shimmer as you place them into intricate window patterns, and the interface glows with a subtle warmth that mimics the feel of assembling an ornate mosaic. Even before you internalize the rules, the aesthetic clarity and charm make the game welcoming. The digital version effectively captures the meditative flow of drafting dice and watching your window slowly come together piece by piece, each placement locking you further into a long-term strategy that must remain flexible as the available dice shift.

At its core, Sagrada revolves around deceptively simple mechanics. Each round, dice are rolled into a shared pool, and players draft them one by one. Each die has a color and value, and these characteristics must comply with the specific constraints on your window board—some squares demand a particular color, others a specific number, and no adjacent dice may share either. These rules force you to think several turns ahead, weighing the importance of blocking a future spot against the temptation of scoring objectives early. Public objectives encourage building patterns or sequences across the entire board, while your private objective nudges you into a more personal strategy. Tool cards, which allow one-use rule-bending abilities, add an additional layer of decision-making: you must choose the right moment to spend your limited tokens, ideally rescuing yourself from a looming placement disaster or capitalizing on a high-value opportunity.

The digital edition enhances the experience through thoughtful quality-of-life features. Automated scoring eliminates the arithmetic burden of the physical game, allowing you to focus entirely on planning rather than bookkeeping. Drag-and-drop placement, instant rule validation, and an optional undo function make experimentation frictionless, especially for new players learning the constraints. The single-player mode includes AI opponents with varied difficulty levels, while multiplayer supports both real-time and asynchronous matches. This flexibility makes it easy to fit a game into your schedule regardless of your preferred pace, and the interface remains clean even when multiple abilities and objectives are in play. Dire Wolf’s attention to presentation ensures that the game remains readable and inviting, even as the board fills with dice of every color.

Despite its strengths, the digital version retains the same structural vulnerabilities as the board game. Dice randomness is always part of the equation, and while strong players can mitigate luck with good planning, sometimes rolls simply do not cooperate. This can lead to moments where your carefully planned window collapses because no suitable die appeared in the draft. For some, this unpredictability adds tension; for others, it may feel like an unavoidable frustration. The digital multiplayer scene can also vary in activity depending on the time of day and community size, which means players who primarily want online opponents may encounter occasional matchmaking gaps. From a content perspective, the game remains focused on the base mechanics without extensive expansion modules, so those looking for long campaigns or evolving progression systems may find it more compact than other digital board-game adaptations.

Still, Sagrada excels in what it sets out to do. It is elegant, strategic, easy to learn, and endlessly replayable within its streamlined framework. Each match delivers a blend of puzzle-solving and opportunistic drafting that feels satisfying whether you win or simply craft a window you’re proud of. The digital version amplifies its strengths with smooth controls, charming visuals, and a calm, polished presentation that makes every match feel like assembling a work of art. It is a game that rewards foresight, adaptability, and aesthetic appreciation, all while remaining accessible enough to enjoy casually. For fans of clever abstract puzzles or those who cherish the board-game experience translated to digital form with care and respect, Sagrada is a superb and enduring choice.

【概要】
かつて「リョナゲーム製作所スレ」にて投下されてその容赦ない女の子へのグロリョナ描写でカルト的人気を誇ったDemonophobia(デモノフォビア)の作者の新作。
通常起動のままなら可愛い女の子がホラーな目に合う全年齢版ゲーム。
外部パッチを当てれば可愛い女の子がグロリョナな目に合うR-18Gゲーム。
以降、基本的に言及がない限りは外部パッチを当てた1R-18Gゲームとしての前提で語る。
今作でも３D表現という新たな表現方法に移りつつも、その容赦のないグロリョナは健在で、Demonophobia(デモノフォビア)ファンの人は満足できるだろう。
一方で遥かにマシになったが操作性の悪さと難易度の高さも継承している

【良かった点】
・徹底的なグロリョナ表現。
流石は知る人ぞ知るリョナゲを作った人で３Dになってもそれは一切衰えておらず、それどころか３Dである事により更に磨きがかかっている。
単純な死亡だけでなく、サイコロ切断、圧死、食われるといった演出も単純にモデルが破損して終わるだけじゃなく、肉がちぎれて骨が見えて内臓が見えるところまでしっかり作りこまれいてる。
縦に一刀両断のシーンは断面図で特定臓器が動き続けているのが見えるというこだわりっぷりだ。
これはとてもじゃないがアセットだけ流用して作った作品では絶対にできないことだろう。
そういった猟奇的グロリョナを求めている人ならば後述する不満点をすべて飲み込んでも購入する価値が間違いなくある

・ホラー"雰囲気"が素晴らしい
目覚めた謎の施設から謎の異空間から肉や臓器で浸食された異界とおどろおどろしい不気味な世界観が実に巧妙に表現されている。
特に素晴らしい点はプレイヤー的にはそこまで怖くなく、怪物が出てくるところに少し驚く程度でホラーが苦手な人でもできそうな点である。
あくまでそういったホラーな"雰囲気"はプレイヤーを怖がらせることよりも「主人公である女の子はとても恐怖を感じているだろう」とプレイヤーに感じさせる舞台装置となっている。
プレイヤー本人は特に怖くないが、主人公の女の子にとっては非常に恐怖だろうと思わせてくれる絶妙な塩梅だった。

・巧妙かつ素朴なホラー演出とストーリーの匂わせ
直接的に怪物が出てくる以外にも想像を掻き立ててくれる要素がちりばめられている。
ネタバレになるので詳しくは避けるが、先ほどまで普通の部屋だった部分が"ある事"知った後に戻るとハッっとなる変化をしてたり、そういったステージの変化も巧みに演出されている。
また要所要所に手記やメモがあるのだがこれがストーリーの伏線や真実を巧みに露わにしてくれる他に、その傍にあった"残骸"やその後に出会う"異形"などからこれを書いた人物がどうなったのか、あるいは書いてあった内容の末路について想像を掻き立ててくれる。
上記のホラーの雰囲気の良さと合わせて、グロが苦手ならR-18Gパッチを当てずに全年齢版でプレイする価値はあるだろう。

・声優さんの演技が素晴らしい
私はこういった同人またはインディーズにおける声優事情についてあまり詳しくないが、アマチュアの方を雇っているのだとしたら驚くほど演技が素晴らしい。
怪物に出会った時の「い、いやだ！こ、こないで！」や「し、死にたくない！」「やだやだやだぁ！」といった恐怖を感じるセリフ。
文字で起こすとありきたりではあるが、実際に聞くと恐怖におびえる少女の声が実によく表現されており、リョナラーの心の琴線に触れること間違いなしだろう。
前述したホラーの雰囲気の表現の立役者であること間違いなしだろう。
ちなみに自分が一番好きなのは全裸の状態で監視カメラの前に立った時の「…えっち」です！

【悪かった点】
・操作性が悪すぎる
主人公の回転半径が広すぎてプレイヤー意図する曲がり方を全然してくれない。
リョナゲのか弱い女の子なのだから長く走れない、走っても移動速度が遅いなどは解るがコーナーを曲がるだけでも外に膨らむのは違う気はする。
通常移動でも少しストレスだが唐突に表れた怪物から逃げるというシーンでは素早い移動が必要となり、単純な旋回だけではなく即座の180度回転も要求される。
一応、クイックターンもあるのだがW＋スペースキーなので焦ってしようとすると操作をミスってゆっくりと後ずさりをするなどが暴発する。
別にスペースキーに他の役割はないのだからスペースキー単体押しで発動させてもいいのではないだろうか。
特にこの辺りは後述するカメラワークのヤバさによって更にイライラが加速する。
ちなみに最初のデモ版では今とは比較にならないほど回転半径とマウス感度が悪く、90度の廊下の曲がり角を曲がるためにマウスを机の端から端まで動かして、さらに持ち上げて元に戻してまた動かしてようやく曲がれるというほどであった。
流石にご不満が殺到したので徐々に緩和されてやっと今の形に落ち着いているが、逆に言うとそれでも今の状態にしかなっていない。

・カメラワークが酷い
壁に近いところでカメラを動かそうとすると壁にめり込んで接写になったり、ずるっと滑って一気に予想しない方向に行ったりする。
狭い箇所が多いので頻繁に発生し、位置を見失うことも多く酔いやすい。
３Dアクションゲームを数多くプレイしてきており、３D酔いというのとは基本的に無縁だった自分だが、これが発生するとわずかに酔ったので耐性がない人はかなり厳しいだろう。
また唐突な怪物が出てからの逃走などでも急にカメラを動かそうとするので発生しやすく、どこを向いているのかわからなくなりそのまま死亡ということも多いのでストレスが溜まりやすい。

・難易度が高い。しかも理不尽・イライラする方向で
簡単にクリアされたら悔しいじゃないですか。
上記の操作性の悪さとカメラワークの悪さも相成って難易度が高い。
Demonophobia(デモノフォビア)では非常に粗悪な操作性とステージの難易度の高さもあったが、これは当時のスレで公開されていた時にフリー公開のリョナゲは、まるでFCのドラクエ２の頃の様に『難易度は理不尽に高くてもよい。むしろ高い方がよい』という傾向がいくらかは存在していたので、作者が悪い訳では無くむしろ需要に合わせた結果ともいえるだろう。
だが、令和のこの時代においては『高難易度を売りにしたのが明確なゲーム』でなければ有料販売のゲームで難易度が高すぎるのは正直マイナス点だろう。
これを読んで「難易度が選べて歯ごたえを求める人は高難易度を、ストーリーを追ってシコりたいだけの人は低難易度を選べればいいんじゃね？」と思われるだろう。
実際にこのゲームにも3段階難易度はあるのだが……一番簡単なアシステッドでもなかなかの難しさ（と理不尽さ）を誇っている。
それもステージが難しいが歯ごたえを感じるわけではなく、操作性とカメラワークの悪さと相まって理不尽さとイライラさを感じさせる方向なのでかなり辛い。
３D酔いがしやすい人やアクションゲームが苦手な人はクリアできるか微妙である。
特に最終ステージは薄暗い中で目印がない入り組んだ迷路、しかも一部ループ構造すらある中を捕まったら即死の怪物が突然近くにポップする中でカギを拾って出口に向かうというもの。
目印になりそうな構造体もなくループ構造なので地形を記憶したりマッピングしたりするのも困難である。
cienのコメントや某所のスレでもここでギブアップしたという報告が続出した。
しかも、ここには人形（マップの各所に配置されているコンプでボーナスのある隠しアイテム）もあるのでそれを探そうとするとさらに酷くなる。
自分は仕方がないので、ひたすら当てもなくうろうろしながら探し、運よくたどり着いて獲得した。
せめてアシステッドという難易度を用意してるなら『ストーリーや雰囲気を楽しみたい』『もっと言えばシコるためにやってるのでゲームとしてのやりがいは求めていない』という人に振り切った難易度にしてもいいのではないだろうか

・回想シーンの回収がとんでもなく面倒
簡単に回想シーンが埋まったら悔しいじゃないですか。
このゲームでは一度見た死亡シーンは回想シーンに登録されるのだが、それぞれの死亡シーンにクリーチャーごとの条件があり

①全裸かどうか
②攻撃を受ける方向
③特定の場所で死ぬ事

といったような条件がある。
これらはノーヒント。
一応、クリア後には未開放のシーンを選択すると解放できる場所が表示されるがそれだけ。
ロードしてそのクリーチャーがいる所まで移動して、いろんなパターンの死亡を手あたり次第試すしかない。
しかも、『条件を満たしているとその攻撃を"ランダム"でしてくるようになる』というだけなので、『全裸・背面から攻撃を受ける』でやられて新規シーンにならなかったとしても、運悪く未開放シーンにつながる攻撃をしてこなかっただけという可能性がある。なので何度も何度もそのパターンで死ないと『このパターンでの未開放シーンはない』と判断できない。それですら更に引きが悪いだけかもしれないので『多分無い』と不安が残る判断にしかならない。
ちなみに条件に③の「特定の場所で死ぬ事」が必要だった場合はそれらの作業はすべて無駄となる。しかし、事前にそれを判別する手段はない。
よしんば攻略情報が出回り、条件がすべてわかってもその死亡シーンにつながる攻撃モーションをしてくるかはランダムなので、結局はある程度はセーブポイントから移動してそのくだらないうえに面白くもないリタマラをする羽目になる。
はっきり言って意味不明の仕様である。
確か前にcienの記事で全開放機能があるとは言っていた気がするのだが、発売前になって『簡単に回想シーンが埋まったら悔しいじゃないですか。』となってしまったのだろうか？
クリア後にひたすらセーブポイントから敵まで移動して目的のシーンになるまで殺され続けるためにリタマラする作業のどこに面白さを感じろというのだろうか？
せめてクリア後は全開放してくれてもいいのではないだろうか？
ちなみにセーブポイントから～と言っているようにチャプターごとの開始といった機能はない。
セーブデータを細かく分けていないと、クリア後に解放しようと思ったらそのクリーチャーにたどり着くまでまた1から開始してそこまでたどり着く必要がある。
もし自分がセーブデータを上書きする形で進めていたらもうコンプセーブデータが流れるまで触らないだろう。

・エロ要素はかなり希薄
元がリョナグロ全振りでエロはほとんどなかったDemonophobia(デモノフォビア)の人なので、元からファンの人は知ってた速報だろう。
とはいえcienでも今作ではエロ要素もあるといい、実際にDLsiteで登録されていた画像等はエロ要素をアピールしていたのでリョナエロを期待していた人も多いかもしれない。
だがエロにつながるシーンは全体の割合でも少なく、それらもかなりアッサリ終わる。
ペニスを挿入する系統のシーンはあるが、かなり単純に腰を動かしてチンポの部分のモデルが主人公の女の子の股の中に埋まっていくだけ。
そもそも女の子の股にはモザイクすらなくツルツルの何もないテクスチャがあるだけである。
（ちなみにデモ版ではしっかりと性器があったのでcienで中国人がキレまくってる）
触手に絡まれて侵されるというホラーリョナエロ好きからすると「おお！これだよこれ！」というようなシチュもあるが、{挿入　→　ピストンして女の子が感じる　→絶頂＋射精　→その後にリョナ}　というような段階は一切存在せず　{挿入　→　即座に口まで貫通して死亡}というある意味実に男らしいシーンとなっている。
クリーチャーから指マン・クンニというシチュもあるがこちらも全体として特に動きに変化もなく穴も何もない部分を弄るだけなのでエロさは微妙。
もうちょっとこうおっぱいを揉むシーンに変化付けたり、乳首をつまんだり、精液をかけたりといった変化が欲しかった。
またせっかくの３Ｄエロシーンなのにカメラが動かせる範囲が狭すぎるため、良い感じの視点で見れないのもかなりの減点対象。
たぶん、粗が目立つので結合部分をはっきり見せたくないのだろう。
幸い、女の子の反応モーションと表情、そして声優さんの素晴らしい演技によってそこはエロい。

【人によって変わりそうなところ】
・エンディングがアッサリ気味
そこまでかなり丁寧かつ興味をそそられれる形で手記やメモによってストーリーが明かされていくのでエンディングですべてが判明するのか！？と思ったら特に何も語られることもなくかなりアッサリ終わって肩透かしだった。
ただし、これは人によっては多くを語らない事で想像が掻き立てられると評価につながるかも。

【総評】
リョナグロ演出に関しては間違いなく図一なので、女の子が猟奇的にグロい目に合うのが見たい人なら間違いなく買い。
ただ、全体のユーザー傾向からするとそういった需要は同人エロゲーを求めるというそれだけでもニッチな層の中でもかなり限られた層だろう。
それよりはもっと多い、『ホラーゲーとして楽しみたい』『女の子がかわいそうな目に合うエロゲーとしてやりたい』という層に対しては『ゲーム性の悪さ』、『難易度の高さ』、『回想シーンの解放の劣悪な仕様』、『ぶっちゃけあまりエロくない』といった点からどちらかといえば『お勧めしない』という評価に。
ただし、『ゲーム性の悪さ』、『難易度の高さ』、『回想シーンの解放の劣悪な仕様』に関しては後付けパッチでどうとでもなりそうなのでそれが改善されたらお勧めできると思う。

The best part of this is the gameplay. In spite of the non-tactile controls, you feel like you're in command of the mech. 

Things I would ask devs to improve with the game:
1. Dumbfire weapons don't have informative reticles, it's kind of trial and error there. This advanced mech would be able to project trajectories by drawing lines on your hud, but this HUD is extremely simplistic. You just have to judge your range and arc manually by firing, watching where the thing goes, and then firing again.

2. You can't see your mech's clearance when jumping obstacles. If it threw a visual foot plane down while jumping, I could tell if I cleared the thing or not.

3. The story isn't bad but it's nothing to write home about. It's a heavy-handed narrative about what it means to be a machine and have consciousness. It doesn't break any new ground in that area or put any spin on the topic. About 1/3 into the story you pretty much know where it's going. Downtime activities between missions are filled with nuisance fetch quests.

4. Some voice actors have thick accents which make it difficult to follow what's being said. Dialog is clunky at times, and the VAs needed stronger direction as to where to place the emphasis in their sentences. Some VAs like 'Jess' are overall better than others, but the overall exchange and interplay between VAs just doesn't feel right. The audio quality between voices heard on the radio and those heard in person is just not different enough. The TTS or modulated AI voices in the game (Can't tell which) are just bleh... Part of it is what they're saying is not interesting, but the fact they do it in such garbled mumbly voices is also annoying as well. Voices in an internal ship space need some light reverb to make it sound as if they aren't speaking right into your ear.

5. I recognize they needed this game to be able to run on 2018 hardware, but they should revisit the visuals and refresh them for 2025. Polygons are sometimes very flat and uninteresting. The animations are fluid and decently paced, but the flatness of the textures and the lighting/shading simplicity doesn't quite meet expectations on modern hardware. Also the character models themselves just look weird. They aren't heavily stylized like a cartoon, but they also look very thin and wiry as if no one in this world has musculature or anatomy. I don't know why this is, but it is very jarring.

Overall a solid 7/10. The biggest drawbacks being the visuals and the voice acting, but the gameplay pretty much makes up for it.

Primal Light, developed and published by Fat Gem, is a side-scrolling action platformer that pays homage to the pixelated era of the 16-bit classics. The game’s world is one of desolation and myth, where players control Krog, a lone blue-skinned warrior clad in a red loincloth, on a journey through a world of ruin, haunted temples, and monstrous creatures. The premise is simple but evocative — Krog seeks to avenge his fallen tribe and restore what was lost, traversing a series of deadly stages filled with traps, enemies, and formidable bosses. Its story is told largely through atmosphere and visuals rather than dialogue, evoking a timeless feeling reminiscent of early console adventures. Primal Light embraces minimalism not as a limitation, but as a stylistic choice that reinforces its identity as a love letter to the action platformers of the early ’90s.

The visual design of Primal Light is one of its defining strengths. Each level is crafted with meticulous attention to detail, blending gothic architecture, ancient ruins, and eerie caverns into a coherent world that feels both alien and ancient. The pixel art style is vibrant yet somber, capturing a haunting beauty that feels both nostalgic and fresh. The animation work, particularly during boss encounters, showcases a clear passion for classic sprite design. Massive, grotesque creatures move with surprising fluidity and menace, giving each battle a sense of spectacle that defies the game’s modest production scale. The environments, though constructed with a limited color palette, make excellent use of lighting and contrast to set the mood, while the soundtrack enhances the experience with ambient, rhythmic compositions that feel primitive and mystical at the same time. The music never overwhelms the player; instead, it builds tension and complements the sense of solitude that defines Krog’s journey.

The gameplay mechanics are deliberately old-fashioned yet satisfying when mastered. Krog moves, climbs, rolls, and attacks with deliberate weight, demanding precision and timing from the player. As the adventure progresses, new abilities are unlocked that subtly expand the gameplay possibilities, allowing access to previously unreachable areas or improving combat flow. Every level introduces unique environmental hazards, from swinging blades to collapsing floors and flame traps, demanding players to adapt quickly. The inclusion of collectible charms and hidden upgrades gives exploration a meaningful purpose, rewarding players who take time to look beyond the linear path. Fat Gem’s design philosophy clearly emphasizes mastery and repetition: each failure teaches a lesson, each success feels earned. The level structure and checkpoint system maintain a fine balance between challenge and frustration, though this balance can feel unforgiving to those unaccustomed to the punishing precision of retro platformers.

Combat in Primal Light is simple but tense, relying on sharp reflexes and observation rather than button mashing. Enemies vary in behavior and attack patterns, often forcing players to engage with a mix of patience and aggression. Boss fights stand as the highlight of the experience, each one distinct in design and mechanics. These encounters range from enormous beasts that dominate the screen to agile foes that test timing and movement skills. Defeating these creatures provides an immense sense of satisfaction, and the pixel animations that accompany their defeat serve as fitting rewards. While some players may find the difficulty curve steep, particularly during the later stages, it is clear that the developers intended this game to be a test of endurance and skill. Even on the lower difficulty settings, Primal Light remains challenging, occasionally to a fault, but this consistency reinforces its identity as a pure retro experience rather than a modernized reinterpretation.

Despite its many strengths, Primal Light is not without its flaws. The rigid movement and deliberate combat pacing, while authentic to its inspirations, may feel clunky by modern standards. The jump arcs can be unforgiving, and the hit detection occasionally demands near-perfect precision. Some levels lean too heavily on repetition, with certain enemy types and traps appearing across multiple stages with minimal variation. The game’s brevity also stands out — a skilled player could complete it in roughly three to five hours, and while that fits its retro design ethos, it leaves some wishing for a bit more depth or additional side content. Still, the charm of Primal Light lies not in its length but in the quality of its moment-to-moment gameplay and atmosphere. Each stage feels crafted with care, and the difficulty, though punishing, rarely feels cheap. Players who persevere through its hardships are rewarded with a sense of triumph that few modern games manage to replicate.

Ultimately, Primal Light succeeds as a concentrated burst of nostalgic energy and craftsmanship. Fat Gem has delivered a game that, while small in scope, embodies the dedication and artistry that defined the golden age of platformers. It is brutal, beautiful, and unwavering in its vision — a game made for those who relish challenge and appreciate pixel art done with purpose. For players who grew up on classics like Castlevania, ActRaiser, or even the early Souls-inspired 2D indies, Primal Light offers a refreshing, authentic experience that demands precision and rewards persistence. It may not appeal to everyone, especially those looking for a more forgiving or cinematic journey, but for those who crave the raw, skill-based thrill of old-school action, Primal Light stands as a worthy modern heir to a long-forgotten tradition.

Bigger, bolder, and packed with action, Tomb Raider II takes everything from the first game and dials it up. The Venice and Great Wall levels are memorable, and new features like vehicles add excitement. Some levels drag on a bit, but it’s a fan favorite for good reason.

Tomb Raider II, developed by Core Design and published by Eidos Interactive, stands as one of the defining sequels of the late 1990s—a game that expanded the vision of its groundbreaking predecessor and transformed Lara Croft from a promising video game character into a cultural icon. Released in 1997, the sequel built upon the solid foundation of the original Tomb Raider, enhancing nearly every aspect while shifting its tone from isolation and mystery toward something more cinematic and action-oriented. Where the first game felt like a lonely expedition into forgotten tombs, Tomb Raider II felt like an adventure film come to life, filled with new enemies, sprawling environments, and an even greater sense of danger.

The story follows Lara Croft in her relentless pursuit of the mythical Dagger of Xian, an ancient artifact said to grant its bearer the power of a dragon when plunged into the heart. The chase takes her across an extraordinary variety of locations, beginning with the iconic Great Wall of China and continuing through the canals of Venice, the wreckage of a sunken ship in the South China Sea, and the frozen peaks of Tibet. This globe-trotting narrative gave the game a sense of scale and diversity rarely seen at the time. Each location was filled with detail and atmosphere, with secrets tucked away behind treacherous climbs and deadly traps. The shift from ancient tombs to modern or man-made settings such as Venetian rooftops or oil platforms also marked a significant evolution in the series’ design philosophy, blending archaeology with espionage and adventure.

Gameplay-wise, Tomb Raider II refined and expanded the mechanics that defined the original. Lara’s movements remained governed by the same precise, grid-based system, but the addition of new maneuvers such as climbing, rolling, and mid-air direction changes made her feel more agile and versatile. Combat also took a more prominent role, introducing a wider range of weapons—from Uzis and shotguns to harpoon guns and grenades—and a greater variety of enemies, including human adversaries. This heavier focus on combat gave the sequel a faster pace and more intensity but also altered the tone; the sense of solitude that made the first game haunting was replaced by the tension of firefights and ambushes. The inclusion of vehicles, like the speedboat in Venice and the snowmobile in Tibet, added thrilling moments of variety and showcased Core Design’s ambition to make every level feel distinct.

The level design remains one of Tomb Raider II’s most remarkable achievements. The environments are vast and intricately constructed, requiring players to think spatially and explore vertically as much as horizontally. Every area feels like a puzzle box—interconnected rooms, levers, traps, and secrets creating a sense of accomplishment with each discovery. Some of the levels, such as the underwater wreck of the Maria Doria or the sprawling Tibetan monastery, are legendary for their atmosphere and complexity. Yet with that ambition came a notable increase in difficulty. The game demands precise movement, keen observation, and a willingness to backtrack through labyrinthine structures. Mistimed jumps, hidden traps, and limited save points could easily punish carelessness. For some players, this uncompromising design was frustrating; for others, it was part of the appeal, giving every success a genuine sense of triumph.

Visually, Tomb Raider II was an impressive step forward for its time. Lara’s character model was more detailed, with smoother animations and a sleeker appearance, while the environments benefited from richer textures and lighting effects that made caves, temples, and cityscapes more immersive. The shift in settings allowed for greater visual variety—the golden light of Venice, the eerie glow of underwater ruins, and the cold blues of snow-covered mountains all gave the game a vibrant, globe-spanning aesthetic. The atmospheric music and environmental sounds complemented this beautifully. The silence of ancient ruins, the echoing splash of water, and the sudden swell of orchestral stingers when danger struck all reinforced the cinematic mood the developers were striving for. Despite its technical limitations, the world of Tomb Raider II still feels alive and adventurous even decades later.

However, for all its improvements, the sequel also exposed some of the series’ underlying issues. The tank-like controls, while functional and precise, could feel stiff during intense combat or delicate platforming. The camera occasionally fought against the player in tight spaces, leading to awkward angles or sudden deaths from unseen threats. The emphasis on gunfights and human enemies was divisive among fans who preferred the eerie solitude of the original’s tomb exploration. Some of the later levels, packed with traps and enemies, felt more exhausting than exhilarating. Yet these flaws are a reflection of its ambition—Tomb Raider II pushed the boundaries of what the hardware and design conventions of the time could achieve, and in doing so, it defined the challenge and spirit of the 3D adventure genre for years to come.

What makes Tomb Raider II enduring is how it captures the essence of adventure. There’s a tangible sense of wonder in uncovering hidden relics, a rush of adrenaline in escaping collapsing ruins, and a thrill in facing off against impossible odds. Lara Croft’s personality shines more confidently here—witty, composed, and unshakable in the face of danger. The narrative may be minimal compared to modern standards, but the sense of purpose behind every level gives the game a strong momentum. It embodies the spirit of exploration that made the series iconic, while also laying the groundwork for the cinematic storytelling that would later define the franchise’s reboots.

Even decades later, Tomb Raider II remains a landmark in gaming history—a time capsule of late-90s design philosophy and ambition. Its influence can be seen in countless adventure titles that followed, from Uncharted to the modern Tomb Raider reboots. It’s a game that rewards patience, precision, and perseverance, reminding players that true adventure is never easy but always worth the effort. Though its mechanics may feel dated by today’s standards, its sense of scale, atmosphere, and discovery remains timeless. Tomb Raider II is more than just a sequel—it’s a statement of confidence from a series finding its identity, one that solidified Lara Croft’s place as one of gaming’s greatest and most enduring heroes.

Schism, developed by Fami and published by 2 Left Thumbs, is a frenetic, system-rich action roguelike that thrives on complexity, experimentation, and high-intensity combat. From the opening moments—your character tumbling into a vast mountain of scrap in a dying world—it becomes clear that Schism is not merely another top-down shooter. It is a layered ecosystem of intertwined mechanics where buildcrafting, reflex-driven bullet-hell dodging, and long-term strategic planning constantly feed into one another. Rather than relying on heavy storytelling, the game frames its world through atmosphere and gameplay: you search for the broken Schismatic Engine while navigating ruins, bizarre enemy factions, and divine entities whose powers you can invoke. The narrative mostly stays out of the way, but the stark mood and environmental touches do enough to establish tone without slowing down the relentless flow of action.

Where Schism excels is in its breadth of customization and its willingness to let players break the game in creative ways. Each run begins with a modest weapon, but the arsenal quickly spirals into an elaborate workshop of upgrades, attachments, frequency conversions, and relic-based enhancements. The game features an unusually large number of interacting systems—over two hundred relics, dozens of weapons, and a philosophy-driven deity alignment system that reshapes how your character behaves. Weapons aren’t just found; they’re tuned and modified, gaining new firing patterns, elemental effects, or utility functions as you stack upgrades. Relics further alter the rules, introducing synergies that can shift a mediocre build into a devastating one. The gods add another strategic layer: aligning yourself with specific deities grants blessings, demands sacrifices, or alters the trajectory of your run depending on how you appease them. These overlapping systems give each attempt its own flavor and encourage players to experiment relentlessly.

The game’s bullet-hell inspiration adds another defining layer of depth. Schism adopts a color-frequency mechanic reminiscent of titles like Ikaruga: matching your character’s frequency to incoming projectiles allows you to pass through them unharmed. This transforms combat into a dynamic dance of switching frequencies on the fly, dodging contrasting shots, and weaving through kaleidoscopic barrages. The mechanic is not a gimmick—it is central to survival, and mastering it becomes just as important as perfecting your build. Because the game demands constant attention to both positioning and color, even experienced roguelike players will find themselves tested in new ways. Boss fights, in particular, showcase the game’s commitment to fast-paced spectacle, with arenas lighting up in patterns that challenge both reflexes and mental focus.

Visually, Schism embraces a gritty sci-fi aesthetic infused with neon accents and industrial decay. The graphics lean toward stylized pixel art, but the clarity of effects, projectile patterns, and UI elements ensures the chaos remains readable. This is important given how dense the screen can become during high-level combat. While the environments repeat in structure due to procedural generation, their thematic identity—a blend of techno-ruins, scrapyards, and arcane machinery—supports the atmosphere well. The soundtrack complements the intensity, offering pulsing electronic beats and dark synth backgrounds that push the pace forward without overwhelming the senses.

Of course, with depth and complexity come barriers. Schism’s learning curve is unapologetically steep. New players may feel overwhelmed by the volume of stats, relics, weapon mods, and deity effects, especially before learning the nuances of the frequency system. While this complexity is a selling point for enthusiasts, it may alienate those seeking a more approachable or narrative-driven experience. Additionally, though performance is solid for many, certain players have reported minor UI quirks, scaling issues on handheld devices, or rough edges from its indie development roots. The storytelling is also minimal, which may disappoint players who expect a more substantial narrative arc.

However, for those who enjoy games where mastery emerges through repeated experimentation, Schism is immensely rewarding. Each run introduces new synergies, new relic combinations, and unexpected weapon setups that can dramatically alter how you play. The game encourages creative problem-solving and rewards players who think beyond traditional builds, pushing its systems to their limits. Even failed runs contribute to long-term growth, making progress feel steady and meaningful. With its exceptionally positive community reception and high build diversity, it’s clear that Schism resonates strongly with players who appreciate complex, replayable roguelikes.

In the end, Schism stands as a bold and meticulously designed entry in the action-roguelike genre. It combines intense bullet-hell mechanics, deep customization, and a flexible progression structure into a cohesive, exhilarating experience. It is not designed for everyone—its difficulty, density, and lack of narrative focus demand a particular kind of player—but for those who enjoy digging into mechanical depth, pushing the limits of a system, and refining reflex-driven skills, Schism is a standout achievement. It offers a world where every run is an experiment, every build a possibility, and every chaotic battle a new chance to reshape the rules of the game.

The Maw, developed and published by Twisted Pixel Games, is a charming and imaginative action-adventure title that captures the essence of what made early digital download games so memorable. It tells the story of Frank, a small, horned alien who finds himself stranded on a strange planet after a spacecraft crash. His only companion is the Maw, an amorphous purple creature with an insatiable appetite and an oddly endearing personality. What unfolds over the course of several levels is a blend of platforming, puzzle-solving, and light exploration, all centered on the unique relationship between Frank and his gluttonous sidekick. The game’s premise is refreshingly straightforward, yet it manages to build a surprisingly emotional connection between the two protagonists while maintaining a playful tone throughout.

At its core, The Maw is driven by a single mechanic: consumption. The Maw eats almost everything in its path, from small critters to large structures, and each meal helps it grow in size and power. As it devours the local fauna, it sometimes gains new abilities that temporarily alter how you interact with the environment—breathing fire, floating through the air, or shocking enemies with bursts of electricity. These powers are used to solve environmental puzzles and open up new areas, creating a steady rhythm of discovery and experimentation. Guiding the Maw is Frank, who uses a leash-like energy tether to direct the creature and keep it from wandering too far. This partnership gives the gameplay a sense of cooperation and dependency: Frank provides direction, while the Maw provides muscle. Watching the creature evolve from a small, docile blob into a planet-sized force of nature is both amusing and oddly satisfying, a visual metaphor for the escalating chaos of the adventure.

What sets The Maw apart from other small-scale indie titles of its era is its presentation. Twisted Pixel imbues the game with a high level of polish and personality, rare for a studio working on a relatively modest budget at the time. The environments are vibrant and colorful, evoking the charm of animated sci-fi worlds like those of Pixar or classic platformers from the early 2000s. The animation is fluid, particularly for the Maw itself, whose expressions and movements convey a surprising amount of emotion for what is essentially a blob with teeth. The sound design complements the visuals beautifully, with upbeat and atmospheric music that mirrors the tone of each level. The playful melodies shift effortlessly between lighthearted exploration and moments of mild tension, maintaining the game’s whimsical atmosphere even when the action intensifies. The overall mood is one of wonder and humor rather than menace, making it approachable for players of all ages.

The simplicity of the gameplay works both in its favor and against it. On one hand, the controls are intuitive, and the puzzles are designed to flow naturally, rarely requiring more than observation and timing to solve. The game’s pacing is smooth and forgiving, encouraging players to experiment with the Maw’s growing powers without fear of failure. On the other hand, this same accessibility can leave more experienced players wanting greater depth. There are few real consequences for mistakes, and the challenge level never escalates beyond mild problem-solving and light exploration. Once you understand the pattern—eat, grow, gain ability, move forward—the game unfolds predictably. It’s a structure that works perfectly for a relaxed, story-driven experience but may disappoint those expecting more complex systems or combat mechanics. Still, the restraint in design feels intentional. Twisted Pixel clearly aimed for a concise, focused experience rather than an overextended one, and in that regard, The Maw succeeds admirably.

Narratively, the game keeps things minimalistic, telling its story through actions, animations, and expressions rather than dialogue. Frank and the Maw communicate through gestures and sounds, building a wordless rapport that becomes the emotional center of the experience. The Maw’s childlike curiosity and bottomless hunger lend it both innocence and danger, and the bond between it and Frank grows more nuanced as the levels progress. The game subtly touches on themes of companionship, survival, and the uncontrollable nature of growth. There’s a sense of bittersweet progression as you realize that the Maw’s appetite, while useful, could become its undoing—or yours. Without ever spelling it out, the story evokes a kind of friendship forged through necessity, one that teeters between comedy and melancholy by the end. The result is a narrative that feels complete despite its simplicity, relying on charm and visual storytelling rather than exposition.

Despite its many strengths, The Maw’s biggest limitation is its length. The entire adventure can be completed in just a few hours, and once the story concludes, there is little incentive to return. Optional achievements and collectible creatures provide some replay value, but they don’t significantly extend the experience. The brief runtime, however, feels in line with the game’s design philosophy—it was never intended to be an expansive odyssey, but rather a concise, well-paced story about two unlikely friends. The tight focus ensures that the game doesn’t overstay its welcome, though it also leaves players wishing there were a few more levels to explore or additional powers to experiment with. Twisted Pixel would later expand upon the universe in other projects, but The Maw remains the purest expression of the studio’s knack for humor, personality, and straightforward fun.

What makes The Maw endure is its sincerity. It’s a game unburdened by cynicism or unnecessary complexity, content to offer a few hours of imaginative escapism grounded in solid design and heartfelt presentation. The relationship between Frank and the Maw carries more emotional weight than expected, and the journey from crash site to freedom unfolds with warmth and humor. While it doesn’t challenge the genre’s boundaries, it refines a simple concept into a polished and memorable adventure. Twisted Pixel’s craftsmanship and affection for its characters shine through in every detail, from the expressive animation to the gentle pacing. The Maw may be short, but it’s also sweet—an example of how creativity and charm can make a small-scale game feel big in spirit. For anyone who appreciates clever mechanics, bright aesthetics, and the kind of storytelling that relies on emotion rather than exposition, The Maw remains a delightful gem worth revisiting.

Gomoku Let’s Go, developed by Studio Amateur and published by indienova, takes one of the oldest and simplest strategy games in existence and translates it into a sleek, modern digital format. Gomoku, often called “Five in a Row,” has long been a favorite for those who enjoy elegant simplicity hiding deep tactical complexity. Studio Amateur’s version aims to honor that heritage while updating it with quality-of-life features, modern aesthetics, and several new modes designed to make the experience accessible to everyone—from casual players learning the basics to seasoned strategists honing their pattern recognition skills. The result is a quiet yet thoughtful puzzle experience that retains the timeless tension of placing stones on a board while adding the conveniences and polish expected from a contemporary release.
At its core, Gomoku Let’s Go remains faithful to the original formula. Two players take turns placing black and white stones on a grid, and the first to create an unbroken line of five wins. What sets this digital adaptation apart is the range of options and refinements it offers. Players can choose between classic Gomoku rules and the Renju variant, a more competitive version that introduces restrictions for the first player to counterbalance their inherent advantage. This inclusion alone demonstrates an attention to balance and authenticity often missing in minimalist board game adaptations. Beyond standard play, the game also includes over fifty predesigned endgame puzzles—clever tactical challenges that test a player’s ability to think several moves ahead and anticipate both offensive and defensive outcomes. These puzzles add variety and educational value, helping newer players internalize patterns that expert players often recognize instinctively.
The single-player experience is built around a capable AI system that features eight difficulty levels. This allows the game to scale smoothly from a beginner-friendly introduction to a legitimate test of strategic foresight. The AI behaves thoughtfully, adapting its play style and gradually teaching players the importance of foresight, spacing, and psychological misdirection—all of which are essential to mastering Gomoku. For those who prefer competition against real opponents, the game supports both local multiplayer and online play, complete with leaderboards and an Elo ranking system. The online structure is a welcome inclusion, though it does depend heavily on the player community’s activity. When matches are easy to find, the system functions beautifully; when they aren’t, the experience becomes limited to AI play and puzzle-solving.
Presentation-wise, Gomoku Let’s Go embraces a minimalist “Zen” aesthetic that perfectly suits its contemplative tone. The clean, polished interface and softly colored backgrounds create an atmosphere of calm focus rather than intensity. Every move feels deliberate, with the gentle placement sounds and subtle animations reinforcing the meditative rhythm of play. The visual design manages to strike a delicate balance—it’s elegant without being sterile, modern without losing the tactile charm that defines traditional board games. The game’s multilingual support also deserves recognition, as it includes English, Japanese, Chinese, Korean, German, and Russian, which broadens its accessibility to international players. This cultural inclusivity fits perfectly with the timeless and universal appeal of Gomoku itself.
Despite these strengths, the game does face a few limitations. The biggest issue is its online ecosystem, which suffers from a relatively small player base. Because the game focuses on a specific and traditional format rather than flashy new mechanics, it tends to attract a niche audience. As a result, finding live opponents for ranked matches can be inconsistent, particularly outside peak hours. This diminishes the competitive longevity of a title that clearly aspires to foster a community of dedicated players. Similarly, while the AI offers solid variety, the overall gameplay loop can start to feel repetitive after extended play, especially for players who quickly master basic patterns. Gomoku, by its nature, is a minimalist experience—there are no surprises once the player understands the core strategies, and that lack of progression can make long-term engagement difficult without a lively multiplayer scene.
However, these drawbacks don’t undermine the quality of the adaptation itself. As a digital rendition of Gomoku, this is one of the most refined and user-friendly versions available. It stays true to the simplicity of the original board game while adding just enough modern polish to feel fresh. For newcomers, it serves as an excellent introduction to a classic logic game that rewards foresight and patience. For veterans, it offers a clean and efficient way to practice, whether alone or against others. The Zen-inspired presentation and flexible rule options make it equally suited to a few minutes of casual relaxation or longer sessions of competitive focus.
In the end, Gomoku Let’s Go succeeds because it understands exactly what it needs to be. It doesn’t overcomplicate its source material or clutter the experience with unnecessary features. Instead, it refines, modernizes, and respects the core idea that has made Gomoku endure for centuries. It may not have the vast depth of Go or the excitement of modern esports strategy titles, but it offers a quiet satisfaction that few games capture—a battle of minds fought one stone at a time. For players who appreciate intelligent simplicity, calm competition, and minimalist design, Gomoku Let’s Go is both a relaxing pastime and a subtle test of skill that stands gracefully between tradition and technology.
