The Abandoned Planet, developed by Dexter Team Games and published by Snapbreak, is an atmospheric point-and-click adventure that captures the essence of classic science fiction exploration while combining modern storytelling and design sensibilities. The game begins with a simple but intriguing premise: a lone astronaut awakens on a desolate world, stranded after an accident that leaves them cut off from civilization. What unfolds is a slow-burning narrative of discovery, survival, and mystery as players explore the ruins of an alien civilization, decipher its remnants, and uncover the secrets that caused its downfall. It is a meditative experience more concerned with atmosphere, logic, and immersion than with fast-paced action or spectacle.

Visually, The Abandoned Planet embraces a meticulously crafted pixel-art style that evokes the charm of retro adventure games while incorporating modern lighting, animation, and texture effects. Every frame feels hand-painted, from the alien landscapes and subterranean caverns to the crumbling towers and strange machinery that dot the world. The color palette shifts fluidly to mirror the tone of each area—cool blues and greys in quiet ruins, harsh reds in active volcanic zones, and warm golds in moments of revelation. These details, combined with subtle environmental effects such as dust, fog, and rainfall, lend the game an uncanny sense of depth and life. The presentation is further elevated by a hauntingly ambient soundtrack that hums quietly in the background, emphasizing solitude and reflection. Occasional voiceover work adds just enough humanity to ground the otherwise otherworldly tone.

The gameplay adheres to the traditions of classic first-person puzzle adventures like Myst and Riven, relying on exploration, careful observation, and logical problem-solving. Players navigate through interconnected screens, examining objects, gathering clues, and using inventory items to unlock new paths or decipher alien technology. What distinguishes The Abandoned Planet from its predecessors is its streamlined interface and intuitive controls, which make puzzle-solving more fluid without sacrificing complexity. The puzzles themselves range from mechanical challenges that require manipulating ancient devices to symbolic riddles involving alien scripts and environmental patterns. None are unfairly obscure, but they do demand patience and attention to detail, rewarding those who take time to study the world’s intricate design. The absence of explicit hand-holding contributes to the game’s immersive quality, allowing players to feel like genuine explorers uncovering lost knowledge rather than simply following a set of instructions.

Narratively, The Abandoned Planet takes a minimalist approach, revealing its story through environmental clues, recordings, and fragmented messages rather than direct exposition. As players progress, they piece together the history of a civilization that once thrived and vanished, leaving behind echoes of its brilliance and tragedy. Themes of isolation, loss, and human curiosity run throughout the experience, often reflected in the astronaut’s internal monologues and the silent grandeur of the planet’s ruins. The storytelling avoids melodrama, relying instead on mood and implication. This subtlety gives the world a sense of depth that encourages contemplation long after the credits roll. While the lack of explicit dialogue or branching choices may leave some players desiring more narrative interaction, the ambiguity serves the atmosphere perfectly, maintaining the mysterious tone that defines the experience.

One of the game’s greatest strengths lies in its pacing. The Abandoned Planet understands the rhythm of discovery—it alternates between moments of quiet exploration and sudden bursts of realization, where a previously unsolvable riddle finally clicks or a hidden passage reveals a breathtaking vista. Each of the game’s distinct regions introduces new environmental mechanics and aesthetic moods, ensuring that the sense of wonder never fades. The design subtly guides players without overt markers, using lighting, sound, and architectural framing to draw attention to points of interest. Even moments of backtracking feel purposeful, as revisiting old areas often reveals new details once new knowledge or tools have been acquired. It’s a deliberate and confident design philosophy that values immersion over convenience.

Despite its many accomplishments, The Abandoned Planet is not without shortcomings. The minimal storytelling, while artistically fitting, can feel underdeveloped to players who prefer strong character arcs or emotional stakes. Some puzzles, though well-constructed, may lean too heavily on pattern recognition, creating brief lulls in pacing. There are also occasional instances where the interface feels slightly unresponsive, particularly when trying to interact with small or distant objects. Yet these flaws are minor in the larger context of the experience. The game’s coherence of vision, its dedication to exploration as an act of curiosity rather than conquest, and its consistent tone make it an absorbing adventure from start to finish.

In the end, The Abandoned Planet is a beautiful and contemplative homage to the golden age of point-and-click adventures, refined through the lens of modern indie craftsmanship. It is both nostalgic and fresh—familiar in structure but elevated by its emotional restraint, visual artistry, and subtle world-building. Rather than overwhelming players with action or exposition, it invites them to slow down, observe, and connect the fragments of a lost world piece by piece. For those who appreciate puzzle-driven storytelling, atmospheric sci-fi, and games that value introspection over spectacle, The Abandoned Planet stands out as a remarkable journey. It is a quiet masterpiece of design and tone—an elegant reminder that sometimes the most profound adventures are the ones that unfold in silence, far from home, on a world that has long since been forgotten.

I'm happy to give Anuchard a recommendation because it's a fun and rewarding game with a lot of cool ideas. The art style stands out for me as being the main draw because it's so unique. It's an consistently brilliant looking game from start to end. The only minor issue I have with the art style is that the lack of facial features of the characters made them a little bit difficult to distinguish from one another.

The music and sound design is really excellent too. I found that the sound design really complimented the aethetics of the game perfectly, and combined to make Anuchard sound unique in a way that very few other games achieve. The rhythmic, plinky plonky sounds that feature in every audio element of the game in addition to the soundtrack create a sensory offering that I found very compelling.

The writing is light hearted, funny, and definitely adds a lot of charm to the character of the game. I played in English, and found that some jokes and phrases were a little difficult to understand or didn't land. Beyond that, there's so much dialogue throughout the game, but sometimes I felt that many of the conversations could have been cut down for the sake of brevity. But it's not a big problem for me, I still enjoyed the story on the whole.

The dungeons aren't too challenging, but felt engaging. There were a few times when the level design or certain puzzles didn't make sense, and I encountered several major bugs along the way. Nothing game breaking. I found the combat to be slightly simplistic, and might have benefitted from the introduction of some light RPG upgrade mechanics, but that's just personal preference.

So, Anuchard is an indie game with big ambitions, a lot of character, and which maybe goes on a little too long. I really enjoyed my time with it, and look forward to whatever comes next.

if the first loren game was akin to dragon age origins, then an elven marriage is more akin to dragon age two, for better or for worse. perhaps playing LTAP right before jumping into this one set my expectations too high, as i expected the same sort of quality from this one. i liked the concept; a VN with rpg elements, holy shit what a good concept, what a great way to move the medium forward! but AEM didnt really do that, and id argue it sort of went backwards in execution.

the UI is somehow...slightly worse than LTAP. it was clunky, big, messy-- but it still worked. everything i need was great and easily visible. resistances made sense and easily legible. "critical", "weak", simple words that instantly told you how to tackle enemies. in AEM, it's percentages, which even after reading the tooltip, made it near impossible to know what was effective against an enemy and what wasnt. i liked the tactical thinking i did in the first game, where here i was pretty much choosing which skill did the biggest number. the UI itself is slightly uglier and chunkier than previous games, and i dont know if its due to the constraint of the engine theyre using or what, but nothing looks particularly sharp, it's all got a slight blur to it (im playing on a 24in monitor), which is also annoying in combat. LTAP had this too, to a lesser extent i feel.

the ui being a mess is more obvious in the inventory and shopping screen. important buttons like purchasing, selling, unequipping are small as hell, and navigating it is a pain. maybe if i could make the UI smaller instead of having it scream in my face it would be better? i dunno, overall it's just very loud and in your face. it's not as busy or ornate as LTAP, which i appreciate, but it's still very difficult to navigate. 

on that note, there's also a wild level of art inconsistencies that personally take me out of the game at times. gruff's sprite not being as detailed as the rest of the team, apolimesho using his old sprite despite how critical he is to the story, NPCs with sprites that are just plain sloppy looking and not as detailed as everyone else, myrth's sprites not being cleaned or properly finished...the list goes on, but it just doesn't look good all together. i liked the old style that looked almost comic booky and the stark, black shadows were really unique. it's really obvious when certain npcs stand next to each other in a scene. did the devs just run out of money, did they use two different sprite artists, or what? it just makes the game look incomplete; i understand you dont want to put time into trash mobs or one off npcs, but even LTAP gave all the sprites the same work, even if they did color palette swaps or w/e. it made everything whole, and consistent. i know art is subjective to the viewer, but at the price (though slightly lower than LTAP at full price), i would expect a certain degree more "consistency". hell [spoiler] ashtran shows up and his sprite is just his head from LTAP slapped onto the body of a sprite that gets reused for the ugliest motherfucker of a boss ive ever seen. bruh. [/spoiler]

my last VN before LTAP was hatoful boyfriend, so maybe art inconsistencies are to be expected, but lord it was distracting, and i couldnt help notice it once it kept coming up.

anyway, the story itself was...okay. just okay. i appreciate it being far more grounded than LTAP, it felt more like a set up for the Big Bad Evil in a future installment than of a direct sequel, and that's probably their intention. i found myself laughing and going "what the fuck thats so stupid" or just going "WHAT??" often near the end, like if they just ran out of ideas and were just pulling drama out of nowhere. there wasn't any set up to (MAJOR SPOILER) [spoiler] nathir summoning his deus ex machina of a god to help revive elenor after she gets her soul sucked by jul. HUH? and then ANOTHER GOD shows up to claim elenors soul, and then nathir has to do a challenge to get it back. i know nathirs faith is strong but there was NO lead up to this; nothing that said his faith was so otherworldly it would summon a literal god to his help. [/spoiler] 

and i think that's really my biggest issue with the overall narrative: a lot of character actions are so inconsistent. this felt immediately obvious playing as an elenor who was continuing a romance with rei; the way elenor acted with him, to others, and in the story felt like it was written by varying writers. the way an elenor would flirt and act interested to lydia and nadir despite being in a supposed romance with rei, to the way she would be weirdly callous in dialogue...it didnt feel like the elenor from the previous game. if the game was trying to show that elenor came out of her shell after being a slave to loren, it was doing a poor job at it. elenor in LTAP felt more humble and helpful, the friendly disposition i chose for her made her incredibly more sensible and kind to those around her. this elenor felt...rude, callous. again, maybe this is how she truly is as she's no longer a slave who feels indebted to the amazons, but the discrepancy is wild. there were really some words that elenor was saying that i felt like i was playing like a violently different character. and ultimately, as she was my vehicle during this whole story, i didnt feel like she was getting the kind of character development she deserved.

side note: the quest log still sucks. again, im guessing this cause of engine restraints, but we couldnt have a better quest tracker? something to let me know what i have to do and where to go, instead of just saying the text of the initial quest screen? it sounds dumb to complain, but with how much text is vomited at you i feel like i just forgot what i was doing, and the lack of summary of what i did is not helping, and i had to reload a few times to redo what i did.

anyway, the romance itself was a wild ride. like i mentioned before, this elenor didn't feel like the same in LTAP, and really, so did rei. he wasn't as "gentlemanly" as i would expect, but at the very least it was obvious that he cared for elenor. i didn't feel like the progression for this romance was as fun as previous, and again, a lot of the conversations they had together made me go fucking insane with how out of left field it was. (spoiler for tail end of the romance) [spoiler] elenor suddenly blowing up on rei for mentioning he used to be a better shot before he met her? girl, let him SPEAK instead of getting mad for no reason. why are you so weirdly petty? [/spoiler]. it didn't feel fulfilling, and i imagine the new romances are probably more developed cause they're brand new, but still...i did like at least that their romance was mentioned throughout the game and others would comment on it, but good lord they needed to get a room at times and not be horny freaks..

so, based on this review it sounds like i hated my time with the game, but honestly, i didn't it. again, it was a passable game at the very least, but there were so many small things that make me hesitant to recommend it unless you really, really like the series. there was a game breaking bug i ran into where one of rei's skills would completely crash the game and there was a 50/50 shot i could ignore the message, or just have the game crash and id have to leave rei out of a fight as a result. the over all lack of polish on sprites, the occasional misspelling, or just wild mis-characterization of a character in a scene that would make me wonder what the hell they were on about. but i did like things.

but the overall package, as it stands, needs significant polish. if youre a huge fan of LTAP, it might be worth going through. if you're new, i recommend picking up LTAP on sale and wait for a few more spit shines to this game; i think it can be something good, but maybe i just had high hopes, and a too critical lens to overlook the things i hated. it had its good moments i assure you, but i think it needed more time to bake.

[h1]ひとりきりの深夜のお散歩[/h1]	
かわいらしいキャラデザと暗めの雰囲気の組み合わせに惹かれて購入。行方不明の飼い犬を探す少女を操作し、町をさまよう様々な「何か」から逃げつつ深夜の町を巡り歩くゲームです。
往年のツクールを思い出しました。

[h1]良かったところ[/h1]	
[list]
    [*]夜の空気感
基本的にゲーム内に音楽は流れず、静まりかえった夜闇に僅かに交じる虫の声などをBGMにプレイすることになる。これが暖かみのある背景と相まって、怖いだけではなく、生ぬるいような、優しいような独特の夜の空気感が出ていてとても好きだった。
    [*]リトライ性の良さ
主人公の少女は普通の少女なので、いわゆる敵キャラに接触したら即死する。ただ、復活のロードが早いこと、セーブポイントがあちこちにふんだんに配置されていることから死んでもあまりストレスにはならなかった。
また、マップ画面から主拠点である自宅にファストトラベルできるのもプレイのサクサク感に一役買っていた。
[/list]

[h1]気になったところ[/h1]
[list]
    [*]死亡の軽さ
初見のエリアの探索時に敵キャラと接敵した際、逃げた先の道に別の敵キャラがいて挟み討ちで死亡確定、のようなシチュエーションが割とあり、死んで覚えることを前提とした初見殺しに感じてしまった。死に覚えは嫌いではないが、その頻度が高いせいで死を軽く感じ、恐怖が薄れてしまったように思った。
[/list]

[h1]まとめ[/h1]
子どもの頃に感じていた夜の空気。今にも何かが出てきそうなその暗闇をあちらこちらへ迷い歩く。そんな雰囲気を浴びたい方にお勧め。
おそらく10-15時間前後もあればクリアから全要素回収までできると思うので、気軽にプレイしてみてください。

Yomawari Night Alone is a decent little game with a great artstyle. I've bought it multiple times, and every single time I've had a great time with it. You can complete it in about 5-7 hours depending on your skill level with games like this.

The story is nothing to write home about. You're mostly looking for your dog and sister while what lurks in the shadows (literally, you can only see most monsters in the light of street lamps or your flashlight) hunt you down.

The gameplay loop is doing a set bit of story each night, wandering about the town and dodging lots of genuinely cool monsters. Monsters that aren't boss monsters you can kinda just end up running past with reckless abandon eventually, but boss monsters demand you respect their mechanics. At points the game does feel cheap with its deaths though, as the hitboxes of various enemies are genuinely atrocious, and some enemies either teleport or are very fast.

Post game content is there, but it's nothing to write home about. You're mostly looking for items, some of which are behind rare monster events that will require you to keep resetting to your house to get. Tip though, once you do, save at a Jizo Statue as it keeps the event working in case you get killed. Also amass the maximum amount of salt, you'll thank me later for recommending this.

Why do I not recommend this game then? It has two sets of critical bugs that can literally make it unplayable. 

The first bug is that it can just not open. It'll get to the loading screen before the title and then just simply close with no error put on the screen. The other one is that even if you don't resize the window, the game will freak out and think you did, giving an error then closing the game once you get to the same loading screen error. All suggested fixes I've seen on the Steam forums and beyond have not worked for me. What makes it weird is that the game did work fine once or twice, so the issue can appear at complete random.

However, this game does work totally fine on my Steam Deck 512 GB LCD unit. I was able to play the game from start to end with zero issues. I've even been doing the play for fifty hours achievement on it, which admittedly is me just sitting in the protagonist's room, ha ha. That achievement counts ingame time by the way, not Steam hours time. It runs at 60 fps with no issues with sound, graphics, or the before mentioned crashing while maintaining at least three hours thirty minutes of battery life. I did not need to mess with my version of Proton to make it work.

If you do wanna get this game, get it on sale and don't be afraid to refund it. I'd honestly recommend getting it on another platform if you can, as it is a decent little adventure. The chance is very minimal, but I do hope one day this game gets fixes.

游戏的剧情整合的非常顺畅，按照时间线完整的表述了三国那段历史的推进，由于故事的内容是采取历史和演义结合的方式，所以会有不一样的剧情体验，好评。而且作为第一人称战旗游戏，随着刘备的视角，可以有很深入的沉浸感，能感受到乱世人命如草的残酷和悲壮。故事推进中的每一个出场的人物，都是有血有肉的，能感受到不一样的历史体验，和知名大作《三国志系列》比起来，你能明显感觉到，每一个出场的人物都有他们对国家的态度，对乱世的看法，和对天下大势的影响，不再是冰冷的数字和符号，这里的吕布和诸葛亮，也不仅仅是两个文武巅峰的符号，他们有自己的故事和性格，能让玩家切实的感知到一个活生生的人物形象，这是我对这个游戏最直观也是最满意的一点。

好了，优点说完了，现在来说缺点。作为一个战旗游戏，游戏推进过程中，能提升队伍实力的手段非常单一，而且还会根据剧情进度锁等级和兵种进阶。每一个战场的全收集，对于很多战场获胜条件来说都很苛刻，换句话说，你大多数时候都没什么时间或者机会去完成战场上的所有任务。而完成战场的所有任务达到进度100%，给的奖励也只是1-3本能提升人物基础属性的书，收益和付出不成比例，玩的很难受。尤其是有些关卡的获胜条件，简直是折磨人，甚至有些战场的任务还是分阶段的，你不完成第一阶段，就不知道第二阶段的获胜目标是什么，然后就会出现第一阶段让你去击退某个敌将，然后第二阶段就让你成功撤退，然后你会发现，你已经被敌军包围了，只能重新开始然后重头规划，这种就是纯纯的浪费时间。

如果只是喜欢战旗的玩法，不建议你买。如果你是想体验不一样的三国故事，那我非常建议你买，但是在你玩的时候，建议你直接开修改器，把能加属性的几个道具全部刷满，还有一个直接满蓝满血的药，也直接刷满，放心刷，这些并不会破坏游戏平衡。这也是这个游戏设计的最奇葩的一点，或者也能称之为另一种平衡？

アニメ調のキャラによる会話シーンが目を引く料理をクラフトしてパワーアップする2Dアクションゲーム。
脇道が所々あるだけのほぼ1本道で探索要素が薄いためメトロイドヴァニアではないと思う。
メイン登場人物達が幽霊である事を存分に生かした顔？芸や荒いものの場面に合わせてしっかり描かれたドット絵が印象に残る。

いきなりだがこのゲームはセーブデータ消失バグといっていいのか分からないが、とにかくセーブデータが消える事がある。
私はある日2番目のボス戦で負けたのでそこでゲームを中断し、後日セーブデータを読み込んでゲームを再開したら黒い画面が表示されて何もできなくなったため、ゲームを再起動したら何のメッセージもなくセーブデータがあっさり消えていたのだ。
このゲームはオートセーブのみなのだがどのタイミングでセーブされているかはゲーム中に何の説明もなく、特にアイコン表示もされないため全く不明である。
そして私はボスに負けてリスポーンポイントで復活した直後にゲームを終了したため、恐らくはその時がセーブ中でいきなり終了させたためセーブデータが破壊されたのではないだろうか。
このゲームはセーブデータのコピーもできないので消失を避けるには[b] 必ず [/b]メニューから「メインメニューに戻る」または「デスクトップに戻る」を選択してからゲームを終了させる必要があると思われる。
今まではいはいと流していたセーブ中アイコンの表示がこれほど大事なものだとは思わなかった。

この問題の他にも通常表示用のフォント以外が中華フォントだったり、メインメニューが表示されるたびに言語などのオプションが初期化されたり、ロード後に真っ暗な画面のままになる現象が頻繁に発生したりと作りが甘いの一言に尽きる。
インタラクトできるオブジェクトに近づくとボタンの表示が化けて「< ■ >」が画面下に表示される現象が高確率で起きるのも気になる。
また以下の事に説明がないのも不満である。
調べれば分かるのものあるがユーザーフレンドリーが基本の現代のゲームなら説明すべきだろう。

[list]
    [*]オートセーブのタイミングと条件。
       これが分からないので下手にゲームを終了できない。
    [*]電球の横の数値の意味。
       どうやら素材を取得する事で獲得し、クラフト画面で消費するポイントらしい。
    [*]料理の装備枠。
       このゲームは料理によって特殊能力を得たりステータスが強化されたりするが、料理は作成するだけでは効果を発揮せず作成後に選択して料理手帳画面の下の灰縁の枠に対象の料理のアイコンが表示されるようにしないと効果を発揮しない。
    [*]盾の仕様。
       盾を構えると白いゲージがHPゲージの右端に現れ、攻撃を盾でガードするとHPの代わりにこのゲージを消費する。
       これが0になると盾が割れるエフェクトが表示され、HPにダメージが入るようになる。
       なお盾ゲージは使用していないと時間で回復する。
       この説明は後半に作れる物にはざっくり書いてあるのだが何故序盤の盾には書いてないのか謎である。
       普通は逆だろう。
    [*]魔力ゲージ。
       魔法杖やレーザーなど一部の武器はHPゲージの下に青いゲージが表示される。
       これは対象武器を使用すると消費され、0になると対象武器が使用できなくなる。
       なおこのゲージは対象武器を使用していないと時間で回復する。
[/list]

このように不満点が多いゲームではあるが豊富な料理や武器を組み合わせて主人公をカスタマイズするのは楽しかった。
しかし装備セットを切り替える機能が最終盤にならないと開放されないのは何考えてるんだと思わざるを得ない。
また攻撃が敵に当たった時のヒットストップやノックバックがないため爽快感が無くてカスタマイズの楽しさも台無し気味ではある。

以上の通りアクションゲームとしては雑の一言ではあるが、キャラクターやストーリーは素晴らしかった。
最初はファンタジーコメディといった感じで始まるが、だんだんと不穏な描写が目立ち始め1章の終わりには完全に違うジャンルになる。

Dex, developed by Dreadlocks Ltd. and published alongside Techland and WhisperGames, is an ambitious cyberpunk action RPG that dares to merge classic side-scrolling gameplay with the freedom and complexity of open-world design. Set in the sprawling neon slums of Harbor Prime, the game follows the story of a young woman named Dex, who suddenly finds herself hunted by corporate assassins for reasons she doesn’t yet understand. Her journey of survival soon becomes one of self-discovery as she uncovers a conspiracy involving artificial intelligence, human augmentation, and the growing disconnect between the digital and physical worlds. From the outset, Dex captures the essence of classic cyberpunk storytelling—its atmosphere is oppressive yet electric, its themes are rich with questions about identity, technology, and rebellion, and its visual world pulses with both decay and vitality.

The first thing that strikes you about Dex is its presentation. The hand-drawn 2D art and pixel-inspired visuals are immediately evocative of 1990s PC classics, yet they are elevated by detailed animations, expressive lighting, and richly layered environments. Harbor Prime feels alive, with flickering neon signs, grimy streets, and shadowy figures lurking in every corner. The game’s art direction and environmental design manage to create a sense of immersion rare for a side-scrolling perspective. Each district has its own mood—from seedy undercity bars and back-alley clinics to sterile corporate towers and black-market tech dens. This diversity gives the city a tangible weight, and wandering through its alleys often feels as compelling as completing the main missions. The soundtrack, composed of ambient electronic beats and moody synth rhythms, perfectly complements the visual tone, immersing players in the melancholic hum of a society ruled by technology and greed. Even without dialogue, Dex’s world tells its story through every glowing sign, rain-slicked surface, and mechanical hum.

The gameplay blends exploration, combat, and hacking in a manner that invites experimentation. Dex’s defining feature is its open-ended progression system—players can customize her abilities to favor stealth, persuasion, combat, or hacking, allowing for varied approaches to nearly every encounter. Those who prefer subtlety can sneak through enemy strongholds, disable security systems, and use dialogue choices to manipulate outcomes, while more aggressive players can engage in hand-to-hand combat or gunfights. The hacking system, which plunges you into a virtual network filled with hostile programs and firewalls, acts as a mini-game that reinforces the game’s thematic focus on digital warfare. While this system is conceptually brilliant, its execution can sometimes feel uneven, with abrupt difficulty spikes that interrupt pacing. Likewise, the melee combat, though functional, often feels clunky and lacks the fluid precision of more refined action titles. Still, when taken as part of a broader experience, these mechanics contribute to the feeling of agency and versatility that defines Dex’s journey.

Narratively, Dex excels in creating a believable world filled with morally gray characters and layered stories. Harbor Prime is populated with hackers, mercenaries, corrupt executives, and rebels—each with their own agendas and secrets. The writing balances noir-like cynicism with moments of humanity, offering side quests that feel meaningful rather than filler. From helping an underground journalist expose a corporate crime to deciding the fate of a rogue AI, the choices you make subtly affect your reputation and the world’s perception of Dex. The main story weaves familiar cyberpunk themes—corporate oppression, transhumanism, artificial intelligence—into a personal narrative about identity and autonomy. What sets Dex apart is that it doesn’t romanticize rebellion; it depicts it as messy, dangerous, and uncertain. The protagonist herself is not a superhuman savior but a vulnerable, evolving figure trying to find her place in a world designed to erase individuality. This grounded approach lends weight to the story’s emotional beats and keeps players invested beyond the surface-level intrigue.

Despite its many strengths, Dex is not without flaws. Its ambition occasionally outpaces its technical execution. The combat, particularly melee encounters, can feel stiff and repetitive, while some animations lack responsiveness. There are moments where mission pacing falters due to unclear objectives or uneven difficulty spikes. Yet these issues, while noticeable, never fully detract from the experience because of how cohesive the world feels. The hand-crafted design, meaningful side content, and consistent thematic tone make it easy to forgive the game’s rough edges. The developers’ passion is evident throughout, and the sheer depth of lore packed into its dialogue and environments gives it a sense of authenticity that many higher-budget games lack. Dex’s imperfections, much like those of its protagonist, feel like part of its identity—a reminder that raw ambition and creative vision often come with jagged edges.

In the end, Dex stands as a testament to what small studios can achieve when they approach worldbuilding with heart and conviction. It may not rival the polish of mainstream cyberpunk titles, but it captures the genre’s spirit in a way that feels intimate and sincere. Its hand-drawn art, branching narrative, and immersive atmosphere create a memorable experience that blends nostalgia with originality. For players who appreciate narrative-driven adventures, complex moral choices, and the gritty allure of dystopian futures, Dex offers a journey worth taking. It’s a flawed but fascinating gem—an indie cyberpunk tale that proves that sometimes, even in a world dominated by corporations and machines, a little humanity still shines through the neon haze.

I've thought of many things to say about this gem, but I'll try to keep it simple: this is the most underrated game I've ever played.

If you're the type of player that likes to challenge yourself and hone your skills, and you like retro graphics, then you will absolutely love this game.

In TowerClimb, you can have an exciting 2-3 hour session where you're really focused, but it's also great for casually playing for 5-10 minutes just to pass time. 

The gameplay is really deep and well-planned. There are many ways you can creatively overcome obstacles, but at the same time the game feels simple. Few games manage to pull this off. The charming graphics, sounds and music create a cozy, yet scary atmosphere that draws you in while fitting the challenging nature of the game.

The tower has many intriguing mysteries, guaranteed to sparkle your curiosity. But you can't just go ahead and explore them, because it's extremely dangerous. One mistake, and you could end up in floor 1 again. Which makes the mysteries so exciting! You have moments of tension where you think "should I go in there? seems dangerous... but I wonder what's inside that door!" And the game rewards you properly for your trouble. It's not just silly easter eggs or useless items. The secret areas reward you with a lot of great stuff, new content, new music, game modes, etc.

One last thing: this game even has a great, wholesome community, where people share their experiences and motivate each other to beat the game.

TowerClimb was made with a lot of passion. I hope you give it a try!

Pocket Stables, developed and published by Kairosoft Co., Ltd, is a charming management simulation that captures the cozy satisfaction of running your own horse ranch while blending it with the studio’s familiar formula of incremental growth and pixelated charm. Known for crafting addictive simulation games with deceptively simple mechanics, Kairosoft once again delivers an experience that’s both relaxing and rewarding in its rhythm. Originally a mobile title, the Steam version of Pocket Stables gives the game a second life on PC, where its mechanics and visual charm translate seamlessly to a larger screen. It’s not a dramatic departure from other Kairosoft classics like Game Dev Story or Hot Springs Story, but its equestrian theme and gentle pace make it one of the developer’s more endearing experiments.

At its core, Pocket Stables is all about turning a small ranch into a prestigious horse-racing empire. You begin with humble facilities and a couple of staff members, gradually building out your ranch with training areas, tracks, stables, and leisure attractions to draw in visitors. The gameplay loop is simple but effective—train your horses, enter them in races, win prize money, and reinvest in better infrastructure. Each horse has unique stats like stamina, speed, and temperament, and balancing their training regimen to prepare for the next competition is one of the most engaging aspects of the game. You also have to manage your staff and facilities, ensuring your ranch remains efficient and profitable. Over time, your ranch becomes a bustling complex filled with activity, from cheering crowds to galloping horses, giving you a tangible sense of progress that fuels the game’s addictive momentum.

One of Pocket Stables’ most enjoyable features is the breeding system, which allows you to pair horses to produce offspring with potentially superior traits. This mechanic adds a satisfying layer of long-term strategy as you try to create the perfect lineage of champions. Breeding decisions can lead to exciting surprises—sometimes producing unexpected prodigies and sometimes less promising results. The system encourages experimentation and patience, rewarding players who pay attention to bloodlines and training synergies. As with most Kairosoft titles, success isn’t just about efficiency but also about learning the subtle cause-and-effect relationships that govern your ranch’s growth. Watching a horse you’ve trained and bred rise through the ranks of competition is deeply gratifying, turning what begins as a casual sim into a personal story of triumph.

Visually, Pocket Stables radiates the warmth and whimsy that have become hallmarks of Kairosoft’s design. The pixel art is colorful, detailed, and full of personality—tiny jockeys, playful horses, and bustling crowds create a miniature world that’s lively and inviting. The game’s animations are simple but expressive, and each new facility you build adds visual variety to your ranch. The upbeat soundtrack complements the experience perfectly, looping gentle, cheerful tunes that reinforce the game’s lighthearted tone. It’s easy to lose track of time as you expand your ranch, tweak your training routines, and watch the seasons pass, all while accompanied by the comforting chime of Kairosoft’s familiar sound effects. The presentation may not push any technical boundaries, but it captures the nostalgic appeal of classic pixel-based management games with impeccable polish.

While Pocket Stables excels in accessibility and charm, it doesn’t completely escape the limitations common to Kairosoft titles. The gameplay, while pleasant, can become repetitive over long sessions. The progression follows a familiar curve—early challenges give way to comfortable efficiency, and once your ranch is thriving, the sense of discovery fades. The races themselves, though entertaining to watch, rely more on preparation than active participation, which may leave some players wishing for a more interactive system. Additionally, the game’s pacing can feel slow in the beginning, as you must grind through smaller races to unlock higher-stakes competitions and better facilities. Yet, even with its repetition, the gameplay maintains a soothing rhythm that makes it ideal for short, meditative sessions rather than marathon playthroughs.

What sets Pocket Stables apart from other Kairosoft titles is its serene theme and emphasis on balance rather than speed. There’s something inherently relaxing about nurturing horses, planning breeding cycles, and carefully preparing for the next race. Unlike games that pressure you to optimize every second, Pocket Stables invites you to play at your own pace, experimenting, observing, and taking pleasure in the slow, steady progress of your ranch. It’s this unhurried approach that gives the game its charm—it’s less about racing against the clock and more about enjoying the process of growth and improvement. The satisfaction of seeing your horses win races or your ranch attract more visitors comes not from grinding, but from the steady accumulation of small victories.

Despite its simplicity, Pocket Stables possesses a certain magic that Kairosoft fans will recognize immediately. It’s not a groundbreaking simulation or an intense strategic challenge, but rather a relaxing retreat into a world of routine, progress, and pixelated joy. The game captures the essence of what makes management sims so satisfying: the steady expansion of your little world, the gradual improvement of your operations, and the quiet pride that comes with watching your hard work pay off. For those familiar with Kairosoft’s portfolio, it’s a comfortable continuation of their signature style. For newcomers, it’s an inviting entry point into a universe of wholesome, bite-sized simulations that value charm and clarity over complexity.

In the end, Pocket Stables is a cozy and rewarding experience that proves simplicity can be its own form of sophistication. It doesn’t aim to reinvent the genre, but it perfects the Kairosoft formula of slow-burn satisfaction, cheerful presentation, and endless replayability. Managing your ranch, nurturing your horses, and watching them cross the finish line evokes a quiet sense of pride that keeps you coming back for more. It’s the kind of game that grows on you, not because of dramatic moments or high-stakes decisions, but because it captures the gentle joy of progress at your own pace. For anyone looking for a laid-back yet engaging management sim, Pocket Stables offers a delightful escape into a world where hard work, patience, and a little luck lead to pure pixelated happiness.

最后本作唯一一条bl线，3代正作里实在无力吐槽，被攻略者最开始冷冰傲娇、不容靠近，把自己家庭私事像捂底裤一样捂着不告诉主角，突然某天酒吧里面搂着主角说兄弟猜猜看我喜欢的是谁。感受不到爱只感受到为腐而腐，后作甜蜜乐章里的同妻剧情才是真的让我感到反胃和恶心的。同妻这件事本就值得打二十大板了不多说了，最让我感到不舒服的是在甜蜜乐章里这俩男同的感情线始因永远都是“主角和萧依莉在恋爱，纪翔吃醋、落寞退出”，在这样的故事结尾总是主角追回纪翔达成结局，但最开始的“和萧依莉在恋爱”的这个桥段呢？合着上一部里面的轮回恋人女主到这里就是男同的垫脚石呗？这家游戏的剧情策划对角色简直是哪里需要哪里搬，上一部还是用心刻画的重要角色，下一步就是引发男同吃醋情更浓play的一环，这种对角色的轻视态度使我感到非常不舒服。在甜蜜乐章中不论是金皓薰和杜云芊、杜云芊和纪翔、还是金皓薰和纪翔的感情线都干巴快速，食之无味，每当回味起来只为自己吃到了这样劣质的东西而感到愤怒。

编剧杨女士作为一个女人，能够写出3代里那么多恶俗的带有凝视意味的剧情，写bl也非常的混乱轻浮，让我感到非常不解！非常痛苦！

诚然，这个游戏的确让我快乐过。动人的音乐制作、耐玩性极强的游戏玩法、充满趣味的人物设定和迥异的性格、模拟经营的成就感，但即便是这么多美好的部分仍然无法覆盖我心中对于这些感情刻画的深恶至极。这些感情线剧情带给我的痛苦和不适已经严重超过了游戏带给我的快乐，所以我在这里给出我的差评！

[H1]For players who love games with cats, soul(s), and finding tiny things[/H1]

Whisker Wanderlust: The Mosaic of Souls is easily one of the quirkiest hidden-cat games I’ve played, and that’s saying something in a genre where cats regularly hide inside teacups, flower pots, and spaceships. This time, though, you’re searching for souls, sweet little afterlife-bound kitties that somehow wandered back to Earth in pursuit of canned fish. The game offers two modes: a “story” mode where you gather souls and help the living with assorted tasks (story-lite, but still charming), and a much trickier Hide & Seek mode where you illuminate each map with your cursor to find cans of fish in the same environments.

The art style is wonderfully unique for a HOG and brings a surreal, cozy vibe that fits surprisingly well. Each map is packed with varied items to find, tons of content for the price, and a zoom range so powerful you can practically examine particles of dust on a cat’s whiskers. Hints are infinite and rechargeable (slow, yes, but you can skip the timer by hopping out of a level and back in during Hide & Seek, which feels sooo sneaky). There’s also a handy option to reposition your task bar (bottom or right), and the split between forgiving story maps and tough Hide & Seek maps makes the whole experience surprisingly accessible for all skill levels.

There are a few oddities, though. Some maps seem to behave differently zoom-wise, which took me a moment to adapt to while completing Hide and Seek levels. Some background elements look exactly like things you’re supposed to find, but are not, which can throw you off just enough to stare at your screen in polite confusion. And while the “story” isn’t exactly gripping, it’s short enough that the mild boredom never becomes a burden.

Still, the gorgeous art, cozy challenge, and clever twist on the classic hidden-cat formula make for a delightful experience. Yes, a few items are the size of a pixel, but the zoom is strong enough to compensate and finding every last one of the little wanderers is genuinely satisfying. A great pick for HOG fans who want something visually fresh with a perfect dash of afterlife whimsy.

10 minutes was all I needed to know this game is exactly like the Urban/Desert/Jungle/Nuclear/Soviet Strike games of the past and that's exactly what I wanted!

30 years ago, I was a kid following my parents on an evening stroll around the town in China. We walked past a computer shop and I was attracted by the sound of video game inside. I stopped and watched them playing a game, where a helicopter was flying over enemy bases in the desert, shooting and firing missiles, and picking up barrels of fuel. I was instantly hooked, but my PC at the time was too old to run any games like that. So it remained a childhood dream of mine... until NOW!

Clear Hot lets me relive this childhood dream! Inspired by the classic Desert Strike (the game I saw as a kid), everything felt just like what I remembered, with modern controls and 3D graphics. The music was lit and combat was intense, and it even expanded the original concept with your own base. Being a fellow indie developer, I can feel the love and excitement of the devs!

There are some opportunities for improvement, especially with combat:

- Aiming the crosshair onto enemy targets feels difficult due to the camera movements. 
- The minigun "heat level" is shown on the player helo but my eyes are not there during combat. It should be near the crosshair
- There are lots of objects that you can pick up but most are color-coded red, making me wonder if they are supposed to be destructible. Probably need more color coding
- The process of picking up objects feels OK enough, but I still struggles at times 

Camera work is going to be the most challenging part to develop, I went through the same troubles working on Tunguska: The Visitation. It's a constant battle between motion sickness and not able to see far enough and getting shot by enemies outside the screen - a signature problem for top-down view shooters. I had to implement a lot of nuanced camera movements to reduce discomfort.

Everything about this is worthwhile. The music, voice acting, visuals and writing are very well done and memorable. I enjoyed pretty much all of the puzzles (especially the kiosk one), and it's nice to see that some of them can be solved in multiple ways.

I'd also recommend turning on the developer's commentary on a second run - it's very interesting to get a look behind the scenes, but there are some spoilers in there.

Completionist's note: Some achievements are very easy to miss, but a second playthrough to get them doesn't take very long.

I don't think this is a bad game overall, but for every good thing about it there are also some of the worst traits in the point-and-click genre bringing it down. Beyond that: Whilst this has an interesting story, it doesn't deliver on one of the more intriguing aspects and has a cheesy "comedy" style to its characters that was more often eye-rolling goofy slap-stick rather than being drily or darkly funny.

The latter aspect will be one of personal taste. It didn't have to be deadly serious, and some humour is welcome, but it undermines the drama somewhat with its twee "buddy buddy cop movie" tone. Here's the dry humourless straight guy bickering with his buffoonish "comedy" side-kick....ha....ha....huhhhhhh....

Given that the voice-work is pretty solid I would have to say that it's not the delivery that's the issue, but that it's pretty lame to begin with. Thematically there's some "ship of theseus" vibes to who your character is, given that they are a robot who has been rebuilt and reprogrammed time and time again, and it eludes to a dark past but doesn't go into detail.

They aren't a blank slate  and do have some personality, it's just more interesting about what they supposedly used to be. Yet it doesn't matter much in the context of the narrative and is only a slightly different take on the trope of amnesia. Albeit one that this is more justifiable given how "memory" and "identity" is just a certain arrangement of zero's and ones in this machine world.

On the game-play front it depends on how much attention you are paying to seemingly insignificant details, or whether you mind pixel-hunting and inconsistent puzzles. I personally don't like games where you can get to a puzzle before you need to use it, and they will indicate there's nothing of interest.....at that point in time. Nor will there be any reaction until much, muuuuuch later.

Then you come back after an hour (or two) and you're going to poke it again for a badly sign-posted solution.....why? An example of this would be: You come across a robot killing other corrupted robots and they put their heads on a spike. At this point you get  a standard response if you look at the heads, "head on a spike" for this one, "head on a spike" for that one, and so and so on. None of them are different.

Then after however long it takes you to figure out umpteen puzzles later, you come back to there and suddenly one of the heads is different....for reasons, and you recognise it as being a certain robot...even though you've never seen them before to now suddenly identify it as being of interest. Makes sense.....not! 

There's other examples where they give you a clue but it's loooong before the puzzle become active, and it's easy to forget these details. One instance is a whole chapter earlier, and not only is it way, way, waaaaaay before you encounter the need for it, but it's also irrelevant at the time you experience it. 

It's only the fact that it's an optional solution that makes this less irritating, Some "clues" are logged for you and some "hints" are provided, but they are either incomplete in the case of the former or quite vague for the latter. I had to look up some of the solutions in a guide and even then I wouldn't say they worked as explanations, though eventually it twigged with me. 

Albeit from the position of being able to work backwards, rather than feeling the problem provided enough detail to figure it out. Maybe I'm stupid, or maybe some of the positive reviews didn't take into account whether they used a guide, and if so: perhaps the game needed better logic? And if it needed better logic, then maybe it's not a good game?

Because that's somewhat of a failing when the puzzles are too smarty-pants for their own good, or are structured in such a way that back-tracking and clicking everything over and over again just in case it's now active. It isn't great design and feels a bit old-school compared to other titles that felt "smart" but didn't have to pull this crap.

I guess I'm just used to point-and-clicks that have cut away this flabby excess and offer a more focused experience, with a better indication of where and when you might need the information or items you have been given. For the price it isn't awful, but I'd be lying if I said that I'd enjoyed this as much as other titles in the genre.

[h1]Power Network Tycoon – Review From an Electrical Engineer[/h1]

[i]First of all, I should mention that I’m not playing on Hard Mode. 
Some of the features I point out might exist there, but I will still share my thoughts.[/i]

Before anything else, I want to say this:
[b]As an electrical engineer, I was genuinely excited when I discovered this game.[/b]
I’ve been waiting for something like this for years, so finding it unexpectedly 
made me really happy. Please take my criticism as constructive feedback from someone
who truly wants this game to grow.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Major Technical Issues[/h2]

[b]- Unrealistic power factor values shown for residential customers[/b]  
This is not realistic. There are no reactive power penalties, but residential buildings still display power factor values like 0.6, which is unrealistic because household PF is not individually measured or monitored in real networks..

[b]- Compensation done with capacitor banks placed in open fields[/b]  
In reality, utilities do NOT install capacitor banks for customers. Compensation is always the responsibility of the facility owner.

[b]- Capacitor banks emitting EMF[/b]  
This is incorrect from a basic circuit theory standpoint. Capacitors do not produce EMF “fields” like the game suggests.

[b]- EMF events inside substations[/b]  
Distribution utilities do not monitor EMF levels as part of their operations. This mechanic feels unnecessary.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Unrealistic Elements[/h2]

[b]- A thief stealing copper inside an energized substation[/b]  
This is practically impossible due to immediate electrocution risk. Copper theft usually happens on de-energized low-voltage lines, not inside substations.

[b]- No SCADA system[/b]  
Even the simplest real-world network has basic SCADA:  
• breaker status,  
• fault alarms,  
• remote open/close.  
A lightweight version would greatly improve realism.

[b]- No protection relays[/b]  
Substations should have at least overcurrent and earth-fault protection. Even a simple “Healthy / Tripped” indicator would be enough.

[b]- No low-voltage cabling[/b]  
The game shows phase imbalance, but we never see:  
• neutral current,  
• neutral heating,  
• LV cable loading,  
• transformer stress from imbalance.  
Adding simplified LV cabling would make phase balancing much more meaningful.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Things I Liked[/h2]

[b]- Grid inertia mechanic[/b]  
This is incredibly well done. Inverter-heavy systems making the grid more fragile is a very realistic behavior.

[b]- Earth Potential Rise (EPR)[/b]  
Accurately implemented, which honestly impressed me.

[b]- Lightning protection[/b]  
Solid implementation.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Suggestions[/h2]

[b]- A realistic reactive power penalty system for industrial facilities[/b]  
Instead of applying PF penalties to homes, apply them properly to industrial zones.  
The utility could:  
• collect penalty revenue,  
• send warnings,  
• impose harsher penalties,  
• disconnect extreme violators.

Poor power factor could also cause realistic technical impacts:  
• higher transformer temperature,  
• overheated cables,  
• voltage drops,  
• increased losses.

These could generate interesting events:  
• “Cable failure due to excessive reactive current.”  
• “Transformer overload caused by inductive load.”  
• “Customers complaining about low voltage due to factory PF issues.”

[b]- Add simplified low-voltage cabling[/b]  
Automatic sizing is fine, but player-controlled routing would add strategy.  
Improper balancing could overheat the neutral conductor or stress the transformer.

[b]- Make the EMF system optional[/b]  
EMF is not something utilities normally deal with.  
It could remain only for specific buildings (hospitals, data centers, etc.).

[b]- Add a solar irradiance map[/b]  
Even a simple “Good / Medium / Poor” sunlight map would improve solar planning.

[b]- Vegetation and fire/fault events[/b]  
Trees contacting lines can cause:  
• flashovers,  
• outages,  
• fires.  
This would be both realistic and engaging.

[b]- Add a lightweight SCADA interface[/b]  
No need for complexity. Just:  
• breaker open/close status,  
• fault alarms,  
• remote reset,  
• simple relay indicators.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]

Despite the issues, I want to emphasize again:  
[b]I’m truly happy this game exists.[/b]  
Seeing concepts like grid inertia, grounding behavior, and EPR in a tycoon game is something 
I genuinely didn’t expect.

With a few improvements—especially in reactive power logic, LV behavior, and basic SCADA—
this game could easily become the most realistic and enjoyable power network simulation .

I’m excited to see where it goes next. As I continue playing the game, I’ll keep writing more feedback whenever new ideas come to mind.

Megadimension Neptunia VII is one of the most ambitious entries in the series, presenting a larger narrative scope, expanded mechanics, and a more polished structure compared to previous games. The story is divided into three major arcs—Zero Dimension, Hyper Dimension, and Heart Dimension—each offering a different tone and set of challenges. This segmented approach creates a stronger sense of progression and variety throughout the adventure.

The Zero Dimension arc sets a darker tone than typical Neptunia titles, introducing Uzume and exploring themes of loss, resilience, and desperation. The shift in atmosphere gives the narrative emotional weight while still leaving room for the franchise’s trademark humor. Later arcs return to more familiar comedic territory, but the combination of tones helps keep the storyline engaging.

Combat uses a turn-based system with a focus on positioning and customizable combos. Players can adjust attack strings, manage SP usage, and take advantage of formation skills to maximize damage. The introduction of the NEXT forms for the Goddesses adds powerful transformations that enrich late-game strategy. The system is accessible yet layered enough to support deeper experimentation.

The cast is a highlight, with returning favorites and new characters contributing memorable moments. Uzume in particular stands out, offering a compelling mix of determination and vulnerability that anchors key parts of the story. Character interactions remain lively and self-aware, blending parody, emotion, and lighthearted banter in a way that defines the franchise’s charm.

Visually, the game marks a noticeable improvement for the series. Environments are more detailed, character models are cleaner, and special effects add flair to combat scenes. While some dungeon layouts remain straightforward, the overall presentation feels more cohesive and polished than earlier titles. The soundtrack reinforces each arc’s atmosphere with strong thematic tracks.

Side content includes optional quests, crafting, scouting, and dungeon exploration, providing additional activities between major story beats. Although some tasks follow familiar patterns, they contribute useful rewards and help maintain steady progression. The pacing balances story, combat, and exploration effectively across the game’s lengthy runtime.

Megadimension Neptunia VII succeeds as a standout mainline entry that elevates the series’ formula with a stronger narrative structure, refined combat, and improved presentation. Its blend of humor, character-driven storytelling, and RPG mechanics makes it appealing to both longtime fans and newcomers. Despite some familiar quirks and repetitive elements, it delivers one of the franchise’s most complete and engaging adventures.

Игра мне понравилась, да настолько что я провёл в этой, довольно-таки простой (по структуре), игре почти 20 часов. Хотя это можно объяснить моей любовью к FPS жанру, но рельсовый шутер очень условно можно отнести к FPS жанру. Формально он входит в этот жанр, но я бы сказал, что только формально. Как можно понять из названия этого жанра, в игре мы не можем самостоятельно передвигаться и вместо этого мы катимся как будто по железнодорожному полотну, т.е. сам компьютер руководит нашим взглядом и скоростью передвижения. Поэтому всё, что от нас зависит, это выбор цели, т.е. куда направить прицел и когда выстрелить (и, главное, в кого) из нашего револьвера (это единственное оружие в нашем распоряжении). Так как у нас классический Дикий, Дикий Запад, то весь дизайн подчинён этой стилистике начиная с фона (место действия) и заканчивая врагами. В дополнении к этому весь этот дикий запад реализован как бы в карикатурной манере или манере комикса (самым близким примером будет серия Guns, Gore & Cannoli). Достаточно одного взгляда на основное меню чтобы стало понятно, что речь идёт о комедийном боевике, где всё подчинено юмору и, в некотором роде, сатире и где нет ни капли серьёзности. Но как же те сотни трупов, что остаются после каждого боя? Так это фанера! В игре, и игра этого совершенно не скрывает, мы стреляем по фанерным целям. Да, это сделано очень качественно и красиво и сначала даже думаешь что это просто такой стиль, но в нескольких моментах, когда цель только появляется, мы видим что это типичные цели из фанеры и картона. Да, сделано это очень красиво и очень круто, особенно когда они разлетаются на мелкие кусочки, но, тем не менее, разработчики прямо говорят – это тир.

Плохо ли это? Нет, конечно, ведь игра действительно очень весёлая. Во-первых, она в целом красивая. Во-вторых, стрелять по врагам и по другим мишеням тут очень и очень весело. В третьих, эта игра, подобно серии «Sky Force», делает очень сложную вещь – постепенно и очень плавно увеличивает сложность, благодаря чему интерес сохраняется на протяжении многих часов. Фишка в том, что на карте враги появляются в разных количествах, но не все они стреляют в нас (если бы каждый враг стрелял в нас, мы бы не продержались и одного круга). В итоге, игроку кажется, что всё просто, но один (или даже два-три) из этих врагов, всё же выстреливает из-за чего, с одной стороны, наше сознание убеждает нас, что тут всё просто, но вот реальность говорит чуточку об ином. Да, враги не появляются моментально и одновременно по 6 штук, но на каждом этапе мы видим разное количество объектов, в которые нужно попасть и попасть либо в голову, либо в любую точку тела, либо вообще стрелять не по врагам, а по предметам, которые могут дать либо бонусы, либо просто очки. Поэтому либо мы должны очень быстро менять цель, а так же уничтожать эти цели, либо ставить приоритет – уничтожить противника, который может выстрелить в нас либо рискнуть и получить бонус, а если есть время, то уничтожить предмет, который нужен для достижения цели (задания, к примеру, уничтожить 25 кактусов или тыкв или бутылок) или просто для получения дополнительных очков. Локация, по которой мы передвигаемся, не состоит из одних лишь врагов, особенно тех врагов, которые нас непременно будут атаковать, а она состоит из множества других уничтожаемых объектов и часть этих предметов приносит иной бонус, нежели простое уничтожение врага. Вот это и создаёт интерес. Мы не просто тупо стреляем во всё, что движется, а выбираем цель, хотя времени у нас на такой выбор не так и много. 

Приведу пример. По ходу движения мы попадаем в каньон, где расположены бочки и ящики, уничтожая которые мы можем получить либо бонус, как например временная неуязвимость, дополнительные жизни либо бомбу, которая нанесёт нам урон, если мы по невнимательности выстрелим в неё. По ходу движения по каньону появляются враги в разных количествах, а так же гражданские либо гражданские которых можно освободить, выстрели в определённую часть их тела (вернее в замок, который сковывает их). Так же на локации присутствуют разнообразные уничтожаемые предметы, которые приносят лишь очки, плюс различные животные, которые не опасны для нас, но которые могут быть частью задания либо просто использоваться в качестве источника очков. Вот и получается, что у нас есть несколько секунд чтобы решить, на чём сосредоточить внимание – на коробках и бочках, которые могут дать бонусы либо ждать появляющихся врагов/гражданских (плюс не забываем, что выстрелы врагов можно отбить, что опять же проверяет нашу реакцию). В итоге, 80% всего времени мы во что-то стреляем. Вариативность целей на «поле боя» – главный или одни из главных плюсов.

Конечно, минусов у игры тоже много, как например всего лишь три локации в игре, что означает, что за полчаса можно увидеть все локации игры. Около 10 типов врагов, около 5 гражданских, которые выскакивают подобно врагам, но за уничтожение которых с нас снимают одну жизнь (т.е. это как если вражеская пуля попала в нас). И плюс около 5-6 различных животных, которые обозначаются как враги, но которые не опасны для нас и нужны либо для выполнения задачи, либо просто в качестве дополнительного источника очков. Действительно, в этом смысле игра ну очень простая, настолько простая, что Sky Force будет считаться верхом разнообразия. Но вот, несмотря на это, игра меня очень сильно увлекла, примерно так же как другая простенькая миниатюрная игра ARMORED HEAD.

Так что насчёт сюжета? Его тут нет. Я не зря привёл пример с ARMORED HEAD, так как в этом они больше всего походя друг на друга именно по духу. Хотя тут нет никакого набора уровней или волн противников, но именно с этой игрой мне хочется привести параллель. В Mad Bullets мы просто каждый раз начинаем наше движение по кругу, по трём локациям с одной целью – как можно дольше продержаться, попутно выполняя одно каждодневное задание и три постоянных, за выполнение которых дают звезды, которые нужны для увеличения нашего уровня. Вот и все, что есть в этой незамысловатой игре. Ах да, деньги. Они нужны для покупки улучшений. Но этим сюжетная сторона игры и ограничивается (т.е. как такового сюжета тут нет от слова совсем, как нет его в любом тире). Изначально может показаться всё это скучным и не интересным, но это миниатюрная игра, которая призвана развлекать игрока своим тиром, проверяя его реакцию, скорость стрельбы и умением быстро выбрать приоритет.

This game is a very cute story about a fox girl trying to save her mother and get them both out of the depths of a dungeon. The gameplay consists of an auto-battle mode followed by skill tree progression and a prestige system to get permanent upgrades. The game itself is not very long but remains fun throughout the whole experience. This is helped by the fact that the skill tree progression doesn't feel all that grindy and a couple of minutes in battle will get you all the gems you'll need for a while. 

The art for the cutscenes and the menu scene are well done and nice to look at. The pixel art is fluid and nice as well. Plus, there are enough elements in the world and plot to potentially launch a sequel game, prequel game, or another game in the same world. Along with the heartwarming plot and our cute protagonist, these elements make the game fun and appealing for the entire length of your time playing it.

All that being said, the best part of this game is getting to headpat a cute fox girl and say "That's my good girl!" when she clutches a boss fight.

For a first time (I believe) indie game, Escape the Cradle is very polished though it is not without some small bugs. The first one i encountered was that if you defeated a boss with poison damage but died at the same time, you would get the reward for defeating the boss but not the gems and would have to replay the level. The second is that navigating through the skill tree is quite "jumpy" when trying to drag it around with out mouse to look at different areas. These small issues in no way detract from the game as a whole and I wholeheartedly recommend this game to those who enjoy cute stories and simple, cozy gameplay.

From the series, I have played WWI and American Civil War in addition to this. While this is probably the weakest of Strategic Command games, World at War is still fun and very much recommended. 

Pros:
+ Easy to learn, harder to master. Moving units and fighting with them is simple. Hard part is to decide where to fight and when, what to researrch and when, what to build and when.
+ Clear and pleasing visuals. Some mods are even included to improve on this.
+ Some historical flavor events, which don't affect gameplay but are nice addition
+ Map covers the whole world which is somewhat unique to turn based games
+ Option to leave some countries under AI control
+ Supply system is simple but effective

Neutral:
* Scale limits making breakthroughs and encirclements, although one could argue that this is intentional for more grand strategy focus instead of operational
* Game might radically break away from historical outcome, but this allows for "what if" situations
* Repetetive music, but not really important in a game like this

Cons:
- Turn resolution takes quite some time even with fast animations on
- Some absurd turns of events can happen like in my game Italy occupying France as Italian unit took Paris instead of a German. This lead to France being liberated when Italy surrendered to invasion from Sicily, which in turn left an empty France behind German Atlantic Wall. Needles to say, Landing in Normandy was then a piece of cake.
- AI controlled countries do questionable actions. For example in my game playing only as UK, USA moves it's fleets seemingly at random without any plan and also is super passive against Japan.
- Map is too small for covering whole world, making some places too cramped
- Some unit types do not belong in a game of this scale like anti-tank and anti-air. They should instead be upgrades to other units.
- Naval system really should have fleets instead of individual units making naval battles cover half the Mediterranean Sea
- Other scenarios than full war are uninteresting for me

While I have not played War in Europe nor War in Pacific, I would bet both of those are better if you are only interested in those fronts separately. This one offers global war but brings with it some downsides mentioned above.

Super Sami Roll, developed and published by Sonzai Games, is a vibrant 3D platformer that draws inspiration from classics like Super Mario 3D World and Chameleon Twist. Released on July 21, 2021, the game introduces players to Sami, a charismatic chameleon on a mission to rescue his friend Vera from the clutches of the villainous Albert VII. Set against a backdrop of colorful environments, players embark on a journey filled with rolling physics, hidden secrets, and challenging platforming sequences.

The gameplay mechanics center around Sami's ability to roll, jump, and utilize his tongue to grapple onto ledges, creating a dynamic movement system that encourages exploration and precision. Each level is meticulously designed, offering a blend of traditional platforming elements and innovative mechanics that keep the gameplay fresh and engaging. The inclusion of collectible raspberries and unlockable secrets adds depth to the experience, rewarding players for their curiosity and skillful play.

Visually, Super Sami Roll boasts a charming art style that combines hand-crafted pixel art with modern 3D graphics. The environments are diverse, ranging from lush green fields to arid deserts and icy landscapes, each meticulously crafted to provide a unique aesthetic experience. The character design is equally appealing, with Sami's expressive animations bringing the character to life and adding personality to the adventure.

The soundtrack complements the game's tone, featuring upbeat and catchy tunes that enhance the overall atmosphere. The music adapts to the different environments, immersing players further into the world of Super Sami Roll. Sound effects are crisp and responsive, providing satisfying feedback during gameplay and contributing to the game's polished presentation.

One of the standout features of Super Sami Roll is its accessibility and replayability. The game offers a "Relaxed" difficulty mode, introduced post-launch, which removes time constraints on levels, allowing players to enjoy the experience at their own pace. Additionally, the multiplayer mode, unlocked through in-game progression, provides a fun and competitive aspect, reminiscent of classic party games, where players race through obstacle courses to reach the finish line first.

However, the game is not without its challenges. Some players have reported issues with camera controls and occasional awkwardness in movement mechanics, which can impact the overall experience. Despite these minor drawbacks, the core gameplay remains enjoyable and rewarding, with the game's charm and creativity shining through.

In conclusion, Super Sami Roll is a delightful 3D platformer that successfully combines nostalgic elements with fresh ideas. Its engaging gameplay, charming visuals, and accessible design make it a standout title in the indie game scene. Whether you're a fan of classic platformers or new to the genre, Super Sami Roll offers an entertaining and memorable adventure that is well worth experiencing.

整体剧情中规中矩，如果不太喜欢那种以白男回忆为视角的异性恋叙事电影，建议不玩。不过本作的画面与分镜设计无与伦比，尤其场景过渡自然，堪称教科书级的运用（但是偶尔穿模有点出戏）, 个人欣赏的点是讲故事的方式。设定在冷战时期的南极，男主彼得飞机失事后，一边找出路，一边回忆与女主克拉拉的过往。[b] 本作探讨的是，冷战互相猜疑的时代背景下，个体如何被裹挟，又被父权制和大男子主义气概规训所影响。[/b]
前期彼得不管选择哪个选项，他都尽可能表现出善解人意的形象，不过面对教授和朋友们的暗示，会回避尖锐的话题和权益斗争。他始终唯唯诺诺，不敢真正反对以及表态，又会浑噩地想起父亲对他缺乏传统男性气质的失望。本故事通过不断闪回，最终拼凑出他和克拉拉相识到分手全过程。
再来讲画面和分镜。一直很喜欢lowpoly游戏，只要开发者审美好，游戏美术会十分惊艳。本作是典型，采用简化几何块面和大块明度分区，因此画面十分耐看。一般回忆时，本作会利用一个视觉锚点让两个时间互相衔接，切换流畅。以及有心理蒙太奇剪辑，男主做现实的动作时会映射创伤和记忆，其心理状态决定下一个匹配情绪的回忆场景。此外，本作也采用并置时间剪辑，现实空间不变，但叙镜头调度与人物关系转入过去，过去的人物直接出现在当前场景中形成。
个人喜欢克拉拉的好友莫莉：一位目标明确、能说会道、敢于为不公抗争的职业女性。游戏到最后，挑明事情的真相。[spoiler] 当彼得和克拉拉争吵的时候，他们以前许下诺言一个个浮现，后面争执发现，在克拉拉口中那些诺言完全对不上号。她质问彼得为何忘记承诺以及相处的细节？随着吵架越发激烈，系统上方代表诺言的选项逐渐消失，过去的记忆完全混乱。由此看出，彼得并没有像之前表现得那么尊重女性，回忆他会自我美化与修饰。他之前看似一直捍卫克拉拉的署名权，可最后依旧决定将克拉拉除名，共同合作的论文独占其成果。[/spoiler]  结局应该是开放式，彼得有没有活下来，我们不得而知。

There's some stories for which a game is a perfect device. I'm afraid to say, this title isn't the case.
It might just not be for me personally, but I really don't think I could recommend this game, which is a shame, because the voice acting is great and the art style - while not my thing - is enjoyable.
The problem with this game is that it's not really a game. It's a visual novel through and through. Which would be great if there was either some kind of choice from the player, or little input from the latter to progress the story.
The "game" gives you the illusion of choice on what to say and decide, but it's all for naught. No choice in this game really matters in the long run, and conversations don't really change if you choose not to answer. There are times where you are only given one choice of response, and if you don't agree with the general sentiment of the response, you can't choose to avoid saying it: the game automatically chooses that choice for you. It's a travesty, to be honest. Moreover, there are scenes in this game in which you can't progress if you don't walk, which would be fine if this was a walking simulator, or if it gave you even the slightest choice on where to go, or even if it was in first person, but no: the game is on a rail. And what does the game expect you to do to progress?
Hold your mouse button.
That's it. You hold your mouse button and the character moves, painfully slowly no less.

[contains spoilers] As a longtime fan of the MCF series, this game was.... kind of a letdown from all angles. While I've enjoyed the plots of some of the more recent games, the gameplay has been dropping in quality for awhile and this one is one of the worst examples thus far.
Many of the HOPs were boring and lackluster, if not an absolute mess (I've always disliked HOPs that require you to find dialogue cues, and this one had far too many of those). The puzzles were often just sequential fetchquests with a slight rearranging of the pieces, and many of them dropped multiple items (sometimes in completely different spots), which means that if the player doesn't notice at first, the gameplay stumbles to a halt until they figure out what they missed. There's even a glitch because of this that locks players in an inescapable room if they missed one crucial item.
The plot wasn't even close to enjoyable; I'd really hoped after the conclusion of the Ravenhearst arc that we would stop getting villains whose main trait is mentally ill, but this game seemed to latch onto that and forget that the main appeal of the series has always been supernatural elements. While I did enjoy the throwback to older games, and learning more about the background operation of the MCF organization, the villain was cartoonishly out of touch and spent the entire game mocking the master detective for imagined failings, which made absolutely no sense and really ruined the gameplay. The finale of the game wasn't even close to satisfying after all of the grief he put the characters through. The bonus story wasn't much better; I had hoped it would be from one of the captured agents' perspectives, as most bonus stories take place before the events of the game, but it was set after and was just a continuation of the villain harassing the master detective postmortem.
Overall, 3/10, would not recommend unless you need to kill 5 hours in as frustrating a way as possible.

100% achievements in ~2.5h

tl;dr = Digseum clone but inferior

Pros
+ items
+ badges telling a story of human history and civilization as we move through the ages

Neutral
= active gold gain: passive gold gain is relatively low, your game is split into rock breaking in caves phase and gold farming in hometown phase. It's different and has a strategic aspect (e.g. speedrun) but some people will hate the clicker part of the game.

Cons
- all the badges are the same: you break rocks and get badges, all badges are the same unlike Digseum that at least had different shapes on the map
- all the maps (= caves ~= rocks, I'm just going to call them maps) are the same: just different durability and count/layout which is not a meaningful difference at all
- boring gameplay: spam click rocks, no brain used
- boring tool upgrades: due to overly simplistic rock breaking gameplay, tool upgrades are also incredibly vanilla and boring
- boring tree upgrades: no new mechanic unlocked, just increases numbers of basic stats
- too many maps and badges: this could have been a strong point but because all the maps are the same and all the badges are the same, unlocking a new map or obtaining a new badge is unexciting and gets too mundane. Having so many maps and badges makes each less remarkable as it's just another one out of hundreds. Like you go through 100+ badges in half hour period and 94+ of them get obsolete in the same time window so of course each badge is unmemorable. Literally only 1 memorable badge (spoilers, but might be obvious).
- low playtime for price: this game is ~2.5h for $4 which better than Click and Conquers' 100 minutes for $4 but too many incremental games offer 1h+ / $ without being grindy as they have interesting tree and thought out pacing

Minor gripe
- arrows in skill tree makes no sense. The direction doesn't affect anything but doesn't convey anything either.
- items auto used: there is no way to disable or save an item for later, so the item dictates what you should do for optimal usage. Normally you decide when to use an item. This makes it so you have to grind for an item again when you need it.

Anyone who is making a game inspired by Digseum should study Far Fishing and Pinata Go Boom to learn how interesting maps, objects, mechanics that change gameplay and thought out pacing are in incremental games in 2025 as the genre has evolved a lot this year.

THE KING OF FIGHTERS ’98 ULTIMATE MATCH FINAL EDITION on Steam represents a rare example of a fighting game that has not only endured but continued to thrive decades after its original release. Developed by SNK CORPORATION with modernization support from Code Mystics and published by SNK CORPORATION, this edition proudly honors the legacy of the franchise while updating it just enough to meet contemporary expectations. KOF ’98 has long been regarded as the series’ most refined and beloved entry, often referred to as “The Dream Match” thanks to its roster and absence of strict narrative continuity, and this definitive version ensures that legacy remains accessible to both longtime fans and new players discovering it for the first time. Instead of overhauling mechanics or presentation, the developers wisely chose to preserve the original’s pacing, structure, and competitive identity, creating a version that feels authentic rather than reconstructed.

At its core, the game remains a pure expression of traditional 2D fighting design—fast, technical, and deeply strategic without sacrificing personality or approachability. The four-button control scheme is deceptively simple, enabling players to ease into the fundamentals without feeling overwhelmed, yet beneath that lies a vast layer of nuance defined by hops, rolls, cancels, blowback attacks, guard mechanics, conditioning, and spacing battles. Movement is central to the experience, and mastering the timing of short hops and hyper hops becomes just as important as executing special moves or combos. Unlike many modern fighters that lean into long strings and cinematic execution, KOF ’98 prioritizes neutral footsies, reads, and momentum shifts. The three-character team system deepens this even further, encouraging players to think about order selection, matchup advantages, and meter distribution across the full duration of a fight.

The roster remains one of the game’s greatest strengths and a major reason it continues to be played competitively. With more than 60 playable characters, the selection spans multiple SNK franchises and eras, offering everything from established tournament staples like Kyo, Terry, Iori, and Chizuru to more experimental fighters with unusual toolkits. Each character feels handcrafted, with distinctive normals, movement speeds, specials, mix-up options, and combo opportunities that reflect a specific fighting philosophy. What stands out, especially compared to other retro fighters, is the surprising level of balance. While tiers exist, the majority of the cast remains viable, and skilled players can succeed with personal favorites rather than being forced into a narrow meta. The choice between Advanced and Extra playstyles allows players to tailor their strategy further, providing different approaches to meter building, defensive options, and offensive pressure.

Code Mystics’ enhancements elevate this edition beyond a simple port, ensuring its longevity in an online-driven era. The implementation of rollback netcode is transformative, allowing smooth online matches across long distances, something essential for a competitive fighter built on precise timing and tight neutral engagements. Online lobbies, ranked matchmaking, spectator functionality, and multiple connection customization options show a clear dedication to community-driven play. The training mode has also been expanded to facilitate lab work, testing combos, punishes, setups, and defensive responses. Importantly, none of these improvements interfere with the original mechanics, animations, game speed, or timing windows—elements competitive players depend on remaining consistent.

Visually, the game exudes retro charm without feeling dated. SNK’s sprite work remains expressive, kinetic, and full of personality, achieving clarity and animation quality that many modern pixel-art games still struggle to match. Character animations convey weight, intent, and emotional flair, making every punch, throw, fireball, and anti-air feel distinct. Stages showcase a variety of international settings, each filled with colorful crowds, atmospheric details, and memorable musical themes. The soundtrack is equally timeless, mixing rock, jazz, synth, and orchestral influences into energetic battle themes that still resonate with players decades later. Together, the visuals and music create a competitive atmosphere that feels energetic without overwhelming the senses, allowing concentration while still delivering excitement.

As polished and feature-rich as this edition is, it remains a product of its era, and those qualities may not resonate with every player. The game offers little in the way of narrative presentation, cinematic flair, or single-player depth—its arcade mode serves as a traditional endurance ladder rather than a story-driven campaign. Tutorials remain minimal, requiring newcomers to research techniques such as option-selects, safe jumps, hop pressure, buffering, and character-specific combos. Some older roster quirks and matchup imbalances persist, especially at the highest level of play. Yet for many fans, these elements contribute to its authenticity rather than diminishing it, reinforcing the game’s identity as a competitive-focused fighter grounded in skill development and long-term mastery.

Ultimately, THE KING OF FIGHTERS ’98 ULTIMATE MATCH FINAL EDITION is more than a historical re-release—it is an active competitive platform, a celebration of SNK’s fighting legacy, and a testament to how well-crafted mechanics can outlast technological trends. Its fluid combat, massive roster, balanced systems, and intense neutral game continue to draw players who appreciate depth earned through practice rather than shortcuts. For returning veterans, it serves as the definitive way to revisit a foundational classic. For genre newcomers, it offers an opportunity to experience one of the most influential and enduring fighting games ever made. Few titles maintain relevance for over 25 years, yet this one not only survives—it continues to thrive, proving why many still regard it as the pinnacle of 2D team-based fighting design.
