"September 7th” es un juego de terror psicológico corto, de esos que te atrapan con lo simple y te dejan con esa sensación de “a qué carajo acabo de jugar?”. 
Te pones en el papel de Dima, un chico que se muda con sus viejos y recibe un muñeco de elfo navideño que, obvio, no tiene nada de tierno. A partir de ahí, todo se pone raro: ruidos, luces que parpadean, y una atmósfera que te aprieta el pecho sin necesidad de monstruos gigantes. 

El juego dura unos 40 minutos, lo justo para pasarlo de una sentada con auriculares puestos y las luces apagadas (si te animás). Visualmente cumple, los efectos de sonido están bien logrados y el ambiente soviético tiene ese encanto inquietante que te mete de lleno en la historia. 
Es un walking simulator, o sea, explorás, observás y te comés los sustos sin mucho más que eso. No vas a tener batallas, ni puzzles complejos, ni decisiones que cambien el rumbo del universo. Pero lo compensa con una tensión constante que no decae hasta el final. Ideal para una noche de lluvia o para hacerte el valiente frente a tus amigos. 
Lo malo: es corto y la trama no se va por las ramas, así que si esperás una historia profunda o giros locos, vas a quedarte con gusto a poco. Pero si lo tomás por lo que es —una experiencia de terror condensada, directa al hueso— vas a pasar un muy buen mal rato. 

En resumen: un indie chiquito, efectivo, con alma, que cumple lo que promete. Si te gusta el terror psicológico, jugalo, recomendalo y después pasate por acá a dejarme un premio de Steam, que te lo conté con el corazón gamer en la mano. 

Nota final: 7,5/10, y un premio extra al elfo por arruinarme el sueño con estilo. Es ideal para asustarte sin perder el sueño (bueno, casi).

> The most beautiful thing to make me want to throw my Steam Deck across the room

## Why

- Distinctive art-style
- Nice music
- Some interesting puzzles/really beautiful areas

## Why Not

- Platforming can be painful at times

## Impressions

A beautiful little puzzle game aiming for a cozy, relaxing experience that lets itself down a bit with rage-inducing platforming.

You're a little girl minding her own business when a scary looking bug dude called the Oscuro comes along and steals the light that seems to make everything in this universe function. Since you and the bug are the only two sentient beings in existence, it's up to you to get the light back in plants where it belongs. You do this by travelling through a series of puzzles confined to rooms which (thankfully) spawn you back at the start of the room if you die. None of the puzzles are especially hard; they mostly make you think just enough to stay engaged though some are trickier.

The reason to be thankful for Celeste-style respawns is the decidedly not Celeste-style platforming. I can't quite put my finger on _what_ makes it so objectionable, but there's definitely something. It feels kinda laggy, and I swear inputs just don't register occasionally. Maybe I'm used to games giving me a bit of leeway when jumping a little late off a ledge or something, but if this is what it feels like without that leeway I can see why everything else has it.

Instant respawns mostly mitigate this and allow you to enjoy the beautiful soundtrack and art without too much stress, though there are a few too many times where the solution is 'just wait', as well as some respawns which re-trigger overlong pans around the room where you can't move. It's also possible to soft-lock yourself in a few cases by not having an absorbed light handy, so try to ensure you do whenever possible.

I probably seem like I don't like the game given that I'm focusing so much on negatives, but I actually enjoyed it overall. It definitely has a distinct look, the soundtrack is nice and it's generally a relaxing, rewarding experience with the background of a show-don't-tell story. There are a lot of cool things to experience here despite the drawbacks, and I'm interested to see what else these devs can come up with (as long as they fix platforming -\_\_-).

So, let me list the Cons first and THEN the Pros.  You'll see why.

Cons -
- The AI isn't very smart.  After about two hours it starts to forget things and the story will become derailed.
- The Narrator is designed to believe the best stories have tension and conflict.  And will try to kill you in many cases.

Pros
-  There is a Database and you can add history, pre-made characters and lore to help shape the setting.  And help the AI remember stuff.  And yes the AI can add terms and characters all by itself.  Sometimes.
-  The Narrator can be edited.  In other words you can change the rules - make a cozy game for example.  Tell it NOT to create conflict and so on.  You can make a cozy murder mystery if you edit it properly.  And start off with a well worded Prompt.
-   The Prompt is the starting point of the game.  The Database and editing the Narrators help keep it going in the direction you want.
-  Instead of saying "I have the crew shoot their fire arrows at the giant flying Roc"  say "My crew shoots their flaming arrows at the flying giant Roc.  Its feather catch fire and it falls into the sea, dead and roasted."   Yeah, you can lead the Narrator or even tell the results of your actions.  You can talk to the Narrator OOC and ask it to redo a scene or change something.  Or just chat to it about what type of game you want.  It might not remember after two hours or so but you can keep reminding it of stuff.
-  Check out the Reasoning function.  It sometimes work.
-  You CAN be the Game Master and make the Narrator be the players.  No really, there are Prompts for that.  And yes, there is a dice function.
-  The game is cheap when you take into account the Workshop, at this time, had over 400 pre-made prompts.  In other words over 400 games.  It will grow larger over time.  And you can sub to them to play them.  OR study them on how to make your own prompts.  It is almost as fun as playing them.  And not all have to be fantasy or sci-fi.  They can be Sims or even educational.  The horror!
IT is cheap, you will enjoy playing with it, even when the AI goes crazy.

Let me make this clear - while I did enjoy this game enough to roll credits on Hard difficulty, it didn't quite scratch the itch of what I was expecting for an arcade-style game such as this.

The overall design of the game feels overtuned difficulty-wise. I see people on the forum complaining that even Novice mode is too hard. Personally I think the checkpoints + healthbar are reasonable enough on the lower difficulties, but the perfection required in "Arcade" mode seems a little overboard, not automatically receiving any health refills and only being allowed to purchase 1 HP at each stage's shop.

The game feels very cruel with its stage tallies removing money from your clear bonus if you take too many hits or take too long in a stage. The former is to be expected from the game's "play perfect or ELSE" design philosophy, but the latter had me scratching my head. I'm being punished for taking too long, when there is no timer on-screen to tell me how long I've taken? How is the player to know that they've done something wrong here? I took things a little slow on my first playthrough because I wanted to be careful (and enjoy the gorgeous backgrounds), but apparently this is a bad thing. Maybe consider removing the demerits and just leave the bonus blank at 0. Shooting civilians I understand being a demerit but I also feel the amount of money you lose ($6000??) is a tad too high.

I noticed that mashing the regular shot button produces faster bullets than holding it down. I don't mind this, but most people in 2025 hate the concept of having to mash a button, so it's kinda weird the game's built-in autofire isn't fast enough.

The toggle for crosshair cursor speed starting on Slow on every stage/attempt is maddening. Please give us an option to start with Fast crosshair.

The flying robot enemies are such a hassle to deal with. They take multiple hits and are hard to kill in one jump, you can't jump past them because they're one of the rare enemies that do contact damage, if you destroy one of the ones that shoots at you then you can still get damaged when it crashes into the ground... I hate these things and they're everywhere.

Perhaps my biggest complaint though... why is there no scoring system? It's an arcade-style game, you have a difficulty called Arcade. And yet no scoring system outside of the 5-star rating. Maybe it was hard to balance around the checkpoints, but some sort of basic scoring system could have been implemented on Arcade difficulty at least. Heck, failing an Arcade mode run basically gives you NOTHING to denote how far you got. Wouldn't it add more replayability to be able to track your progress in getting farther and farther against a leaderboard? Or heck, even a speedrun leaderboard for those that want to go quick? I feel like the game's long-term replay value is not being considered that well.

It's a shame because the game's pixel art visuals are GORGEOUS, it controls great, the melee attack is really fun to use (diverting bullets with it is interesting too), there are lots of fun setpieces that make you want to keep playing... but now that I've finished it, it's hard to find the motivation to want to keep playing it to master it in Arcade mode because of the reasons listed above.

EDIT: I had some more space to mention something I forgot. I REALLY don't like the implementation of the special weapons. They're prohibitively expensive in the shop and have very limited ammo, and there's no way to switch back to your regular weapon once you equip one (too many buttons being used on the controller, lol). It's already hard for players to get the money on their first playthroughs because of the aforementioned nasty demerits. A basic powerup or two in the stages would have added some nice variety...

《林葬屋前传：冥声》是一部典型的劣质恐怖故事作品，故弄玄虚，弄拙成更拙，他或许有一些新意但不值得购买。
坦白的说，他还是有一些优点的，那就是他确实试图吓人，最起码没有像很多劣质网剧一样，将一切归类在精神病患者身上，乃至于创作者甚至刻意卖了个破绽，让你最开始以为没有鬼，这点还是蛮有意思的，而且它的这种模式也挺有新意的，用更多的推理出来的真相剧情去填补主线，这也算是一个很有意思的创新了。
而且女鬼的跳脸杀做的很不错，真的吓人，这种游戏要是不吓人那就太讽刺了，别管是不是跳脸杀能达到震你一下的目的就不错了。
但除此之外，游戏的问题可太大了，首先是剧本，剧本极大地限制了演员演技，女主角从头到尾闷着一张脸，我倒不是对这个女主角有什么不满，说白了这个剧情换谁来都得这么演，因为整个游戏里，女主角都是旁观者——字面意义上的旁观者，她根本没有参与到其中，她跟这个屋子的联系甚至没有那个搞自媒体的大哥深，但就是这么一个女主角，一开始还要安排一幕——重男轻女的戏份，说白了这就是反向契科夫的枪，纯粹的废笔，除了暗示暗示映射映射女鬼的故事真的没什么营养，说白了，女主角的戏份跟女配角没什么区别，事实上后面确实也没什么她的戏份。
故事里存在感最高的估计就是那个沈绵绵了，事实上，我觉得这个女演员演的很努力，特别是隐藏剧情中，她笑的特别吓人，只不过碍于剧本本身的问题，这东西逻辑不通顺你知道吧，编剧似乎想要刻画一个既有女鬼又有现实凶杀案的故事，但很抱歉，架构不算成功，沈绵绵的整个剧情都有点神经质，虽然沈绵绵本身精神不正常，但我觉得这种解释太牵强了，尤其是隐藏剧情沈绵绵杀了其他人之后买花祭奠女鬼，怎么看怎么奇怪，狼狈为奸这一块。
至于自媒体和记者，这两个人说实话，也是很游离于剧情之外，整体给我的感觉类似于剧本上抽到了什么角色就在那楞扮演，楞参与没有合理性。

I just couldn’t get into this game for some reason. I liked the demo, but the full game lost me just when it seemed to be picking up. The game claims it’s inspired by Paper Mario, but it doesn’t play much like it at all; every attack is based around one of a small set of timing minigames that rarely match up with the animations themselves, which makes the combat feel very repetitive and unengaging. Part of the reason for this is that the game drowns you in alternate equipment and weapons, each of which give you a different ability. I’m sure this is appealing to some gamers, but I just felt overwhelmed, especially since most of them were so similar. I never changed my loadout very much throughout the game, even as the game kept throwing more and more items at me.

The story is pretty impenetrable. It tries to be in medias res, but it never does the part where it catches you up afterwards. The world used to be ruled by gods (named after planets), but their children (the Zodiacs) rebelled, overthrew them, and divided their territory among themselves. The protagonist, Virgo, is some sort of tradcath monarchist who wants to bring back the good old days when the gods were in charge, so she’s taken it upon herself to fight the other Zodiacs and take their crowns, which will accomplish this… somehow.

I initially thought the gods had been killed, but then in the third area Virgo’s parents just show up out of nowhere, so apparently they’re just in exile somewhere, in which case I don’t understand why they haven’t reclaimed their own territory and why Virgo needs to do this? We’re also told there’s a lot of history between Virgo and the other Zodiacs, but they only reference this obliquely. The game lets you make choices about how to deal with them that change the course of the plot, but because I don’t have Virgo’s knowledge or share her emotional attachments, I felt completely disconnected from Virgo’s actions and had no idea what the consequences of my choices would actually be. Like, Virgo says the other Zodiacs are evil and deserve to die, but are they? The game claims she’s an unreliable narrator, but doesn’t provide much in the way of alternate viewpoints. I just ended up feeling incredibly lost and confused. The gameplay still could have carried that if it wasn’t horribly boring and repetitive, but alas.

I loved Studio Elan's Heart of the Woods, it was a wonderful modern fairy tale and an instant favorite, so I grabbed this hoping it would also be great but it was a significant step down. It was apparent right from the start that the writer(s) was different and a lot less skilled. Even putting aside the edginess of blood magic, the characters and their relationships are rather shallow, the motivations are questionable and it just feels like it was written by someone rather young who had specific ideas they wanted to build a story around but wasn't yet skilled enough to develop them into a cohesive, fleshed out and logical story. 

Overall, it's not bad but I would only describe it as "alright", not great or even particularly good. It's alright enough for a positive rec but just barely. If you are *really* hyped to read this, I won't discourage you but I would recommend Heart of the Woods WAY more than this. I'll go into my criticisms in a bit more detail here so stop reading if you don't want any spoilers...

**SPOILERS**

One of the biggest issues was Honoka and Yasue's relationship... It just wasn't built on a solid foundation. One girl is young and mentally isolated to the point of needing therapy and the other is very old and physically isolated to the point of needing therapy. Seeing these two kick it off basically instantly, with no build up set off massive red flags. At one point the story did make the teeniest tiniest acknowledgement that this might not be a healthy relationship but it was quickly brushed aside. This was not a relationship that I could feel happy about. 

The ending also has a lot of character interactions that I won't explicitly spoil but I'll just say there were a lot of interactions that didn't feel earned or make sense given the events these characters had just gone through. It all felt kind of sloppy and railroaded based on what the writer wanted rather than what made sense for the characters.

Cute little visual novel that has completely won my heart. Granted, it may not be perfect, but the quality is exceptional here. So many small things that really compound together to make this visual novel a cut above the rest. Before going in, very big content warning for self-harm and suicidal ideation. If you are someone who struggles with suicidal thoughts or is uncomfortable with that sort of content, I would recommend giving this game a pass. (There is always someone willing to listen and help, please do not give up)

[b]Presentation.[/b] Amazing!! I love the art for one, the characters all have very distinct, standout looks to them. And the vibes set up by the mix of snowy countryside and dark cityscapes makes me feel so cozy and warm. There is an extra layer of pizazz thrown in that really stood out to me when I played the demo forever ago. The intricate designs of the nameplates for each character, with both their English and native language names present, with a unique colour for each... it's so cool. The extra cinematic effects during scenes, such as cut-ins to characters or cool perspective tricks or transitions from scene to scene are just the cherry on top. The visual aspect of this visual novel was top-notch.

[b]Audio.[/b] Another win for this visual novel. Diegetic sound effects are the king here, from the harsh winds of winter to the hustle and bustle of city life. Even something mundane, like placing drinks on a table, gets an accompanying sound effect. Music is also very well composed, with plenty of soft, soothing melodies mixed in with haunting, tense droning. It's all very well crafted, which was something I was not expecting from a visual novel. Not gonna complain tho

[b]Characters.[/b] Admittedly, a bit of a mixed bag, even though I like them all? 
Our main character, Honoka, is easily my favourite. Not only do we get to spend the most amount of time with her, but her internal dialogue is very strong at characterizing her. And it makes me both viscerally uncomfortable and scared. It may not hit the same for everyone, but I have known many people who speak the way she does. Disturbed. Hurt. It pains me to watch, but at the same time her mind is so fascinating I can't help but watch. 
Yasue is another one of the characters who stands out about the rest. Her screen time may be limited in comparison to Honoka, but she felt good to me. Her bubbly, jovial personality was always a good refreshing from the depressing subject matter around her. 
Final standout is Shino, who I didn't think much of during the demo, but I really came to love. Her perspective on everything is so unique, and her voice is quite soothing. 
Unfortunately, the rest of the main cast is not as compelling to me. Not to say I hate them, I like them and I think they all have their moments, but they do not get the screentime necessary to make me enjoy them as much. 
Tatiana is the straight woman, keeping everything by the book. 
Kaoru is the comic relief, boisterous and loud and silly.
Yonehara is quite cold and aloof. [spoiler] And also very evil. Every good story needs a good villain, and she does an alright job filling that role, but I feel like... she needed a little more time to hit even harder. [/spoiler]
Overall, the cast works in my eyes, even if some of them are more developed than others

[b]Story.[/b] A phenomenal Act 1, that builds up a lot of interesting stories beats and ideas. Sadly, even here I feel like the yuri sits on the backburner a lot of the time, and the moments it does exist feel a little... wrong? The game definitely would have benefited from a little longer runtime, perhaps to develop that aspect of the story more. After Act 1, the story seems to pick up, which unfortunately can leave things feeling a bit rushed. Act 2 is a bit of an outlier, as [spoiler] it's a retelling of Act 1 from the perspective of Shino, giving context as to the background story that you couldn't get while with Honoka [/spoiler], but everything else is a lot shorter in length and faster in pace. I feel like the game would benefit from a longer run-time, just in order to not make the latter half of the story feel uber fast, and also to flesh out the characters who need it and develop the romance more (if that was the plan). Still a decent dark fantasy story tho <3

Overall, I really enjoyed it and was eager to keep jumping back into it, despite its flaws. I kinda miss it actually

I started playing this thinking it sounded nifty. Strange. And I worked on advancing through the dungeons, strategizing, all of that. It was okay.

Then I got the point of it all.

When you rob a random house blind and then take the house and put it up for sale in your shop, maybe the inhabitants too, then move on to the next. When you start having fun with the idea of whacking monsters with random objects and seeing what they do. Enjoying all the jokes that are everywhere.

And guess what, the to-do list more or less finished itself when you weren't thinking about it.

I know it's a given that a game like this was never meant to be taken seriously but my advice is to take it even less seriously than you're thinking. If you like parody RPGs you will enjoy yourself.

Fatty Bear’s Birthday Surprise, developed and published by Humongous Entertainment and re-released by Nightdive Studios, is one of those early point-and-click adventure titles that perfectly captures the charm and innocence of 1990s children’s computer games. It was originally released in 1993 as part of Humongous Entertainment’s “Junior Adventure” line, using the same SCUMM engine technology that powered many of LucasArts’ classic adventures. What makes Fatty Bear’s Birthday Surprise memorable is its gentle sense of discovery and its whimsical approach to storytelling. The game follows Fatty Bear, a stuffed toy who springs to life one night to prepare a surprise birthday party for his owner, Kayla. Along with the help of Matilda Rabbit and Gretchen the Doll, Fatty Bear must bake a cake, decorate the house, and keep mischievous obstacles—like a puppy running loose—under control before morning. The setup is simple, yet it captures the imaginative wonder of a child’s world where toys come alive when no one is watching.

At its core, the game functions as a light, exploratory adventure designed to encourage curiosity rather than challenge. Players guide Fatty Bear through Kayla’s house using an intuitive point-and-click interface, collecting items, combining them to solve small puzzles, and uncovering countless interactive details hidden in each room. The gameplay is purposefully slow-paced and forgiving, allowing children to experiment freely without fear of failure. There are no time limits, health bars, or game-over screens—just a cozy environment where the joy comes from discovery. The game rewards curiosity with hundreds of “clickable” animations: furniture springs to life, kitchen utensils dance, and strange, playful noises burst from everyday objects. This abundance of interactive detail was one of Humongous Entertainment’s defining trademarks, turning every scene into a tiny playground of visual humor. Even simple actions like opening cupboards or playing the piano feel magical because everything in the house seems to respond in its own charming way.

The puzzles themselves are designed to be approachable but still satisfying. Players must gather ingredients to bake a cake, find decorations for the party, and recover lost items such as missing letters from a birthday sign that a curious puppy has scattered around the house. These objectives are straightforward enough for young players to follow, but they introduce fundamental adventure game logic—fetch quests, object combinations, and environmental clues—without overwhelming them. Some tasks change slightly from one playthrough to another, such as item locations, which gives the game a small degree of replay value. The pacing is gentle and unhurried, which was typical of early Humongous titles but remains one of their most enduring qualities. Fatty Bear’s Birthday Surprise never rushes the player; instead, it invites them to enjoy the process of helping others and seeing the results of their efforts unfold naturally.

Visually, the game’s art direction captures the warmth and innocence of its setting. The environments are rendered in bright, hand-drawn colors, filled with the comforting clutter of a lived-in home. Despite being confined to a single house, each room feels distinct, from the kitchen’s glowing oven to Kayla’s cozy bedroom filled with toys. What gives the game its distinctive atmosphere, however, is the nighttime backdrop. The entire adventure takes place under the soft glow of moonlight, giving everything a slightly dreamlike tone. This setting, combined with the toy characters’ lively animation, creates a whimsical but subtly uncanny effect—as though the player has stepped into a child’s dream where everyday objects awaken with secret personalities. The soundtrack and voice acting reinforce this tone with gentle music and expressive, enthusiastic performances. The MIDI-based score may sound simple by modern standards, but it carries a nostalgic charm that suits the game’s tone perfectly.

Because Fatty Bear’s Birthday Surprise was one of Humongous Entertainment’s earliest titles, it also stands as a fascinating precursor to the studio’s later, more famous series like Putt-Putt, Freddi Fish, and Pajama Sam. In many ways, it feels like a prototype of the formula they would refine over the next decade: a kind-hearted protagonist, a world full of interactive objects, and puzzles designed to teach basic logic through play. What sets Fatty Bear apart, however, is its tone. While later Humongous games are brighter and more overtly cheerful, Fatty Bear’s story unfolds in the quiet hours of the night, giving it a slightly more subdued and mysterious atmosphere. It’s not dark or frightening, but there’s an underlying sense of calm anticipation that makes it feel unique among its peers. This moodiness, combined with the cozy domestic setting, gives the game a nostalgic, almost timeless quality that appeals to players revisiting it decades later.

The re-release by Nightdive Studios ensures that modern audiences can experience the game on contemporary hardware without losing its original charm. The Steam version preserves the full voice acting, visuals, and interactivity of the original, while offering smoother compatibility through ScummVM support. Despite its age, the game remains surprisingly functional and easy to navigate, with clear visual cues and responsive controls. Reviews from modern players on Steam have been overwhelmingly positive, reflecting both nostalgia and appreciation for its simplicity. Many adults who played Fatty Bear as children now revisit it with their own kids, finding that its core appeal—the joy of exploration, the kindness of its characters, and the sense of accomplishment from completing small tasks—remains intact even in an era of complex games.

As a whole, Fatty Bear’s Birthday Surprise is a snapshot of an era when educational and family-friendly games balanced creativity with warmth. It’s not long or difficult, and it doesn’t aim to be more than what it is: a gentle adventure about preparing a surprise for someone you love. Yet that simplicity is exactly what makes it special. It’s a story about care, friendship, and quiet determination, told through the lens of a teddy bear who just wants to make someone happy. Its charm lies not in challenge but in atmosphere, the way it transforms a normal household into a world of imagination. For those who grew up with Humongous Entertainment’s library, it remains a nostalgic treasure; for newcomers, it’s a charming piece of gaming history that still radiates the same cozy magic it did over three decades ago.

3. Беготня туда-сюда за пополнением армии тратит время (если нужный магазин с нужными юнитами находится на другом континенте в другом конце карты в пещере в которую можно попасть пройдя через другую пещеру, то удачи запомнить куда надо бежать). Квесты с беготней тоже не делают погоды.

First of all, most of the negative reviews for this game appear to be 12-year-olds who just can't wrap their brains around the concept of a world without cell phones and GPS devices to tell you where to go.  The game is set in the 90s and the point is to learn to navigate the old school way and drive old-school cars (stick shift).  Stop crying about mini-maps and take the extra 30 seconds to look at the map, figure out your location (you can even buy a compass if you're too lazy to figure it out on your own), and plot a route.  This is how navigating used to be done and I, for one, appreciate the dev for trying to make this a unique part of the game.

The game itself isn't perfect.  The driving physics are so-so but tolerable.  I like the idea of having to sit by your phone waiting for jobs, this is how life used to be.  They give you the option of speeding up time by watching TV, so it's usually just a minute or two before you get the call if you've opened up a few jobs.  But, the progress has been satisfying so far and I'm looking forward to coming back to this title for a relaxing experience.

Siegebreaker is a focused and confidently crafted tower-defense experience that places strategic depth and thoughtful level design at the center of its identity. Developed by Immortal Forge and published by indie.io, the game embraces the classic fundamentals of the genre—waves of enemies following defined paths, towers with upgrade branches, resource-driven decision-making—while adding its own flavor through a rich fantasy aesthetic and a strong emphasis on build variety. The result is a compact but satisfying title that knows exactly what it wants to be: a tactical challenge built around experimentation, clever problem-solving and repeated refinement of your defensive layouts.

From the outset, Siegebreaker communicates the importance of constructing well-synergized defenses rather than relying on raw tower spam. Each tower has upgrade branches that dramatically change how it behaves, encouraging players to specialize rather than spread resources thin. Over time, you begin to appreciate the game’s design philosophy: every map introduces new pressures, and every wave forces you to adapt your strategy. There is a gratifying rhythm to this process—early waves allow you to establish your foundation, mid-game waves test your resource allocation choices, and late waves demand both precision and foresight. The sense of incremental mastery is strong, especially when you discover powerful combinations that cut through enemy lines with satisfying efficiency.

The game’s handcrafted levels contribute significantly to its appeal. Rather than relying on procedurally generated layouts, Siegebreaker offers a curated campaign of more than two dozen maps spread across distinct fantasy regions, each with its own look, mood and structural challenges. Forest paths twist through natural terrain, desert routes emphasize long sightlines, icy slopes create choke points, and volcanic corridors teem with aggressive enemy behaviors. This variety helps keep the experience fresh, and the visual clarity ensures that even chaotic waves remain readable. The environments also serve as subtle teachers—encouraging you to learn where bottlenecks naturally form, when to prioritize range over damage, and how to manipulate upgrade choices depending on map geometry.

A major strength of Siegebreaker is the polish applied to user experience. The interface is clean, upgrade trees are easy to read, tower stats are transparent, and progress through the campaign feels smooth and rewarding. Visual feedback for tower upgrades and enemy effects is crisp without cluttering the screen. Quality-of-life touches—such as fast-forward options, clear enemy previews, and responsive controls—help keep the pacing tight and the strategy front-and-center. It’s evident that the developers studied well-established modern tower-defense systems and implemented the elements that enhance flow without overwhelming players with unnecessary complexity.

As with many titles in this genre, the later stages can introduce difficulty spikes that test even well-prepared tower networks. Boss encounters, in particular, can be punishing, requiring very specific upgrade planning or perfectly executed tower placements. While these spikes create tension and force creativity, they can occasionally feel abrupt, especially for players who prefer a more relaxed or steady challenge curve. Likewise, the game’s scope is clearly designed for single-player enjoyment; players seeking endless survival modes, roguelite meta-progression, or extensive multiplayer components may find the content focused but limited.

Still, Siegebreaker’s strengths outweigh its constraints. The game succeeds by presenting a polished, replayable strategy experience where every decision feels meaningful. Its upgrade variety encourages experimentation, its handcrafted levels provide structure and pacing, and its presentation strikes a satisfying balance between clarity and fantasy ambience. It is a game well suited to players who appreciate deliberate, skill-based tower defense—those who enjoy perfecting builds, replaying maps for improved outcomes, and exploring different upgrade combinations to tackle progressively harder scenarios.

In the end, Siegebreaker stands as a confident and well-executed entry in the tower-defense genre. It may not push the boundaries of what tower defense can be, but it offers a tight, rewarding campaign filled with thoughtful encounters and strong mechanical cohesion. For players who value strategic experimentation and polished level design, it is a worthwhile and absorbing addition to any tower-defense library.

This game honestly surprised me with how good it was. The only real flaw I noticed is the puzzle design. No matter where you are at in the game, they’re either way too easy and straightforward or completely obtuse and clunky.

Usually I think a game is “good” if it has at least one thing that really stands out and makes me think back to it months later. And Pocket Mirror actually has two of those.

First, the atmosphere. Despite the limitations of the RPG Maker engine, this game is absolutely gorgeous with it's stunnig art and music. The environments are incredibly creative and varied, from whimsical gardens to dark, haunted mansions.

The second thing is the mystery. The way the game slowly drip feeds you bits of information and lets you piece things together yourself was really captivating. For some people, that approach will feel too vague and frustrating. Every character you meet dodges your questions, and it’s completely possible to finish the whole game without understanding the story at all. But I loved that about it. The cryptic stage play scenes, the items and the little secrets you find. All of it felt like this beautiful puzzle you need to figure out yourself.

Just wandering through those hauntingly beautiful areas and stumbling across new secrets was enough to keep me completely hooked.

One small caveat, though: the dialogue can get very anime at times, which might not be for everyone. But if you’re into atmospheric, horror-ish RPG Maker games, Pocket Mirror is absolutely worth playing.

For The Warp is an absolute gem of an indie title, a fast-paced, turn-based roguelike that masterfully blends strategic deck-building with thrilling space combat. The game shines with its "just one more run" addictive quality, making it easy to sink hours into exploring its vibrant, retro-styled galaxy.

The core gameplay loop is incredibly satisfying. You build a unique, powerful deck of cards to manage your ship's resources, weapons, and defenses, and every encounter feels tactical and meaningful. The combat system is easy to learn but offers plenty of depth for those looking to optimize their strategy and synergy.

Visually, the game is a treat. The pixel art style is charming and full of character, perfectly capturing a classic sci-fi aesthetic. The dynamic environments and enemy designs keep things fresh, and the soundtrack perfectly complements the adventurous atmosphere.

What makes For The Warp truly stand out is its engaging progression system and high replay value. With a variety of playable ships, numerous random events, and different paths to take, no two runs are the same. You are always discovering new card combinations and strategies, which keeps the experience exciting and rewarding.

Overall, For The Warp is a fantastic, well-executed game that delivers an engaging and delightful experience. It's a must-play for fans of deck-builders and roguelikes alike.

No One Lives Under the Lighthouse: Director’s Cut is a horror-adventure “mental unraveling” simulator developed by Marevo Collective, a Ukrainian group of developers who were formerly named “Sowoke Entertainment Bureau” before the group went from 3 to 6. With the Ukraine Invasion by Russia going about, I’m sure that the development was strenuous and stressful and it probably took a lot of inspiration from the 2019 Robert Eggers hit “The Lighthouse” featuring Willem Dafoe and Robert Pattinson. What else I know is that it was originally just released as its original game before the Director’s Cut would come out later, and that they had worked on “You Can’t Do it Alone” and “Cha.in”, the links of which will be down in the links below. My introduction to this game however, I feel takes place at the same time a lot of people’s introduction to the game took place: April 2020, the COVID era when a lot of people could sit home and watch Youtube Letsplays. Now I don’t remember where I first heard this, though considering the PSX graphical style I could’ve encountered it from the likes of Bloody Disgusting, or through the likes of a Discord server here and there that I could find like the Goth Gamer Nation. However I remember seeing it around regardless, fascinated by how it looked and would eventually purchase it in May 2021 (alongside Duck Season PC and Far Cry 3 apparently)…where I wouldn’t touch it for around four more years or so. A lot of people would watch it through Mandalore’s channel, but I first got my true deep dive into it through my buddy Bad Ghosts’s excellent videos on it (links below) that would get me truly interested in the game. That being said I have a huge backlog, but I was soon able to knock it out after my playthrough of The Flayed Man over a period of two Wednesdays where I was streaming it for a buddy of mine. Now that I finally finished it as one of my last two “Halloween Indie/Free Horror Gameathon” playthroughs, how does it hold up compared to the others? Is it great? Lets start with the plot.

Here’s the plot setup for the game alongside gameplay: the first chapter has you play as a Lighthouse Keeper working to maintain the aforementioned lighthouse, but paranormal things start to happen and they disappear. Afterwards a new keeper arrives, with the man in charge telling him about how they disappeared alongside how to actually do your job and letting you know that you’ll have a week until he gets back where he’ll bring an assistant. Here’s what I’ll tell you from here: for the next couple of days, you’ll be maintaining the lighthouse, settling on repetitiveness with a first person point of view. From there the horror starts to get increasingly spooky, ranging from a chase sequence or two involving a very strange creature.

For Rest of Plot/Gameplay and everything else (Spoilers intertwined but my thoughts were, solid horror game but confusing to follow plot in a good way?)

I came out of No One Lives Under the Lighthouse: Director’s Cut feeling that it’s genuinely one of the best Playstation 1-esque retro horror games to come out in recent memory, and for me that’s a lot considering I’m a HUGE sucker for these games. Whereas I don’t necessarily feel like the game “turns the wheel” a bit like The Heilwald Loophole, I felt like the narrative of the game became one of the most interesting narratives I think I’ve gone through this year. Is it truly a Lovecraftian tale? Is it madness disguised as grief? I have no clue, but the director cut warps it in a way that makes the story feel both confusing as hell but in a way that makes you think about it. The gameplay may not be the most engaging considering it tasks you with doing repetitive chores for the first part but once you delve further into the madness within it starts to expand in interesting ways, filled to the brim with surprisingly tense moments and cool details I didn’t notice before. The art style? Fugghedaboutit, you already know what I’m going to say: beautiful, dark, dreary and the actual soundtrack and sound design only seek to enhance this atmosphere further. Is it to say that it’s perfect? Not always, there’s some parts of it that had me confused and kind of glitchy, but whereas I believe the game itself might be a four out of five, personally it reaches at the top with a 4.5 just due to the sheer gravitas of it all. Clearly a lot of people felt similar ways with the amount of reviews that basically said the same things, the amount of letsplays and lore deep dives and the memory of it all entrenched within the horror indie gaming scene. Hell it was popular enough for Torture Star (a production company created by Puppet Combo) to publish it on consoles for people to play as well so if you don’t want to play it on PC, you can always play it on the big screen (or little CRTV) of your wishes. As for my Halloween cheap/free game marathon, I’ll say that I’m happy that this game was one of the last ones (alongside The Shore) that I’ve completed and one that I would recommend to basically everyone who wants a short and spooky mystery for All Hallow’s Eve. As for what’s going on with Marevo Collective? They still seem to be working on three games coming up: one’s “Hollowsk 1999 3D”, an early PC/PS2 styled first person survival horror that looks like it could take place in an abandoned Eastern European city; the next one is “Kargo - A neo-noir adventure”, which looks right up my alley as a minimalistic top-down open world crime game! The last one however is the closest it might be to release and feels VERY personal: Zero Losses, aka Ukranian War horror, which makes sense considering the terror the developers must feel on a constant basis. Whichever comes out first, I’m very much interested in seeing how these guys continue because they proved they could make something magnificent here. For those who want to know what’s going on now though, the price for the game currently is $1.74 U.S. dollars so it’s REAL cheap.

This game hits a certain memory cluster in your brain if you were on the internet without any money in the late 2000s, early 2010s, when you were on itch.io or ModDB downloading whatever free crap you could find to pass the time. Games like Amnesia The Dark Descent and Slender were basically creating YouTube culture as we know it, and everyone with a free Unity license was churning out "find 8 pages and run from the instadeath monster" like there was no tomorrow. This game is like a slightly spruced up version of your memory of those kinds of games, with everything that brings with it.

The main gameplay loop, once you understand it, gets a rating of "oh that's interesting, I see where you were going with this." The 10 floors do start to drag on, it could have done with maybe one extra game mechanic to complicate things.

Of particular note to me is the general art direction. You see enough games in the Steam Discovery Queue, you start to see all the marks of people that barely care or don't care at all and are just churning something out. That's not here in this game. An actual cohesive art style with assets that were either made by hand or picked an actual sense towards an art style. An actual sense of decent lighting. A soundscape that mostly stays out of the way until it's needed. The story animation is pretty nice, reminds me of flash games.

[h1][url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/34294631/] Follow Far2close - Visual Novel Playthroughs Curator Page [/url][/h1]
[b]Crimson Gray: Dusk and Dawn[/b]
Developer: Sierra Lee
Publisher: Sierra Lee

[h1]Intro:[/h1]
Sequel to [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/655770/Crimson_Gray/?curator_clanid=34294631]Crimson Gray[/url], you look through the eyes of Lizzie this time. Experience her homicidal urges in order to protect John, while also trying to get through college. Depending on your choices, you can make or break your relationship.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[b]1.[/b]
I appreciate that the story goes into their college years with some aftermath from KoiTec's controversy. It's a fine closing for John and Lizzie's relationship, especially with how this situation can stress John out to where [spoiler]it can interfere with your wedding.[/spoiler]
[b]2.[/b]
Small amount of new characters: Aaron, Rose, and Francesca Kelsey. They're minor characters, but they do help bring the story forward. I also like how Lizzie interacts with them. Lizzie sees the problematic women as seductive and threats to John. If she deems them safe, they look normal to her. [spoiler]This changes when she finds out Aaron is gay and her view of him changes to where she sees him as a threat.[/spoiler] I do enjoy how we play as Lizzie so we get to see her thoughts. 
[b]3.[/b]
The first game we played as John, his depression made the visuals gray and dull. Here we see how Lizzie's rage affects her to where she sees red. It also makes her sets of choices destructive where some choices transition words with their true meanings such as [b]Talk to Aaron = Interrogate Aaron[/b]. I also like how she refers to John as "Him" than his name. [spoiler] The wedding part where there's the same choices but the capitalization is different is neat. Capital H is obsessive and dangerous Lizzie, while lowercase H is docile Lizzie. I find that neat![/spoiler]
[b]4.[/b]
The art by Redd Art (Reddverse) returns and is great to see again! Soft and wonderful art, sex scenes are intimate and works great in showing their relationship.

[h1]Neutrals:[/h1]
[b]1.[/b]
The music is royalty free [url=https://incompetech.com/]Kevin Macleod[/url]. It fits in, but no other comments to make again.

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[b]1.[/b]
The story does feel milquetoast. While that's not entirely bad, it was quite the jump from the first game. KoiTec is still a dominating force, but not to the extent of the previous one. Aside from putting pressure on John and Lizzie indirectly, they don't have much presence, even after a massacre. The conflict is very light in this title, the main one is just not succumbing to Lizzie's murderous tendencies.
[b]2.[/b]
Unsure if it's intentional because it's Lizzie or due not enough funds, I wish there were more character sprites. Seeing clones of the same girl and no sprite for Francesca Kelsey is a bit disappointing.

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
I enjoyed how it wraps up John and Lizzie's love for each other, along with a well done POV of Lizzie. It does lack the tension from the first [i]Crimson Gray[/i], making the experience extremely tame.

Crtl Alt Ego es de esos juegos que “no conoce” nadie y que hay que poner remedio cuanto antes. Desarrollado por tan solo 5 personas (según los créditos) han creado uno de los mejores “Inmersive Sim” que he jugado en cuanto a libertad de acción. 
Aquí realmente no controlamos a un único personaje, ya que somos una especie de “ente consciente” con el cual podremos hackear todo tipo de máquinas. Cada máquina tiene una función, y se nos darán muchísimas situaciones donde podremos ser bastante creativos para solventar los problemas. A veces será necesario el sigilo, otras la fuerza bruta y muchas veces bastará con la observación.
En mecánicas me ha recordado un poco (salvando las distancias) a una versión superelaborada de Scrapland de Mercury Steam, ya que iremos cambiando de robots para según que situación. Otras veces directamente iremos saltando de cámara en cámara, (algo similar a los Watch Dogs) para llegar a los sitios incorpóreamente para luego imprimirnos un cuerpo en otra estancia y seguir desde ahí.

Los desarrolladores te avisan desde bien pronto, que en el juego no hay manera de jugar correcta o incorrecta, depende de ti. Pero lo cierto es que el juego es muy orgánico en la manera en que te van dirigiendo en tus objetivos. Eso sí, como en todo buen Simulador inmersivo que se precie, aquí la observación es clave, y más si lo juegas sin ayudas, ya que tendrás que usar tus ojos para encontrar las cosas importantes. En este sentido me ha recordado mucho a System Shock Remake. Y es que la sensación de ser tú el que descubre las cosas está muy bien conseguido.
Lo he jugado en dificultad Estricta (hay aun una más por encima) y con las ayudas desactivadas. No he necesitado del uso de ninguna guía a pensar de que pensé que igual me había columpiado un poco al seleccionar dicho modo de juego, y sí que es cierto que jugándolo así exige bastante atención por parte del jugador, pero al menos para mí es parte de la gracia del juego, no te lleva mucho de la mano.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3606944402

Globalmente, no me parece mejor que otros exponentes del género, ya que aquí la historia sin ser mala, no está tan elaborada como en otros juegos como Prey 2016, Dishonored o Deus Ex por ejemplo, pero en general tiene calidad y merito para estar entre los grandes. Por ejemplo a nivel de diseño de escenarios y posibilidades es que está MUY currado, sobre todo los 2 últimos capítulos que son bastante grandes, (lástima que estén cortados mediante tiempos de carga). Nuevamente, en esto igual no llega a la salvajada que es el mapa de System Shock Remake, o de Prey 2016, pero es que es un juego debut de un equipo indie de 5 personas, y que hayan creado tan bien el escenario y todas sus mecánicas jugables funcionen tan bien, tiene un mérito del copón.

Pese a que antes he dicho que no hay un personaje propiamente dicho, es una mentira a medias. Llevaremos en todo momento un robot (llamado 22), que este sí que iremos mejorando mediante disquetes de ampliación de programas, que nosotros decidiremos como invertir según el estilo de juego que queramos. En la dificultad que he jugado, al menos la faceta de combate no la veo muy útil, pues la escopeta parece de juguete y los enemigos no hacen más que recargarse la vida. En dificultad normal creo que esto no ocurre e igual ahí enfrentamiento directo es algo más útil. Además, dichas habilidades tienen muchos niveles de mejora.
Al ir hackeando elementos del escenario nos van dando "Ego" que podríamos decir que es la “munición” del juego, con ello haremos casi todo, ya que para hackear enemigos y algunos elementos necesitamos Ego, que recuperamos hackeando otros componentes.

Mención especial a la localización al español, con textos de pantallas, cartelería y pintadas en las paredes traducido al español físicamente, es decir, no mediante subtítulos al mirar una palabra en inglés como ocurre en otros juegos.
Los gráficos en general no son nada del otro mundo, pero tampoco me han parecido malos, son simplemente “básicos”, pero desde luego que tiene unos gráficos y estilo bastante particulares.

La banda sonora tampoco destaca demasiado, pero la verdad es que los efectos de sonido sí que me han gustado en general, y casa muy bien con el tono tan desenfadado que tiene todo el juego en sí.

En definitiva, es el primer juego de este estudio llamado Mind Thunk y espero que no sea el último, porque es una carta de presentación brutal y se me hace raro que esté causando tan poco revuelo. No es una obra maestra, y para alguien que se adentre en el género por primera vez recomendaría antes juegos más “normales”, pero desde luego que es un juego que hay que tener MUY en cuenta y debería de tener mucho más calado del que tiene.

Veja, bem, eu tenho sentimentos contraditórios em relação a esse jogo. Eu acredito que de um ponto de vista artístico, é um dos melhores RPG Makers que eu já vi abordando temas pesados como depressão na adolescência e sua direção de arte é extremamente agradável e fofa, além da escrita ser interessante.
Porém, olhando para essa obra como um jogo em si, ela acaba falhando em muitos aspectos. O nível de precisão que o jogo exige do jogador em alguns puzzles e boss fights para adquirir um final bom é absurdo, considerando que a gameplay do jogo em si é bugada. O sistema de save é abismal também.

Me explica como o jogo espera você sofrer NO MÁXIMO, 10 anos em uma área inteira, enquanto o mesmo não te dá uma maneira rápida de dar load em um save anterior durante a gameplay. Não, você tem que apertar "r", ir até a tela de título, para aí vc conseguir dar load em um save anterior. Isso quebra a imersão e a continuidade do jogo. Criando um nível de frustração além do normal, fazendo com que a maioria das pessoas desista de fazer um final bom ou até do jogo inteiro em si. É possivel perceber isso pela porcentagem de pessoas que conseguem as conquistas de "remembrances" (básicamente os finais bons de cada área), que vai diminuindo exponencialmente ao longo das áreas.

Eu recomendo o jogo apenas para quem está curioso o bastante para ver a história e seus temas se desenrolarem, que eu acho que valem a pena. E está disposto a sofrer um nível de frustração que não complementa a qualidade do jogo em si, principalmente nas área 3 e 4. Como eu disse, sentimentos contraditórios. Deixar claro que eu aprecio bastante o jogo.

雖然以前看過不少 NTR 類題材的漫畫，但這是我第一次真正玩到這種類型的遊戲。
之前一直都是玩純愛系 galgame，沒想到這款會讓我整個改觀。

這款的日文原名是「エガオノリユウ」（中文譯名是「微笑的理由」），當初會入坑完全是因為畫風對味，加上沒玩過這種類型，就想說試試看。
結果一玩下去不得了，第一次真正體會到 NTR 的獨特魅力 XD。

這款真的可以說是「NTR 入門教科書級」的作品，該有的要素全都到位。
最讓我驚訝的是，原本在 DLsite 上賣的價格就很便宜（大約 2000 羊左右），但不論是插畫品質還是聲優表現，都完全不輸給高價位的商業作品。
現在登上 Steam，價格又更親民，CP 值超高。

劇情的鋪陳也很用心，從男女主角的相遇、互動、感情升溫，到正式交往、再到與間男介入，整段都有相當長的劇情篇幅，大概能玩上 2～3 小時。
也正因為前期的情感鋪陳夠深，之後進入壞結局時，那種撕心裂肺的感覺才會特別強烈。

劇情不只是固定套路的壞結局，裡面也有溫馨、完整的好結局。
好結局共有兩個，兩種都值得先跑一遍；
壞結局則分為兩種版本──一個是理性還在但身心崩潰，另一個是理性和情感都徹底崩壞。
建議先跑完好結局再去體驗壞結局，心理衝擊真的超強烈。
我非常推薦一定要照這個順序玩。

最後，還有一個重點，這款根本「好用到炸裂」，衛生紙要多準備一點。

後來我也試過其他同類型的作品，但無論是劇本還是情感張力，都沒這款來得深刻。
如果你想第一次嘗試這類題材，這款真的非常值得入坑。

As a brief warning, this game will pop a content warning the first time you open it, and I suggest reading it if you have sensitivity to difficult content. If you skip that warning, you will end up head-first in some shockingly dark content. There is little warning of the harsh tone shift in the moment. 

Firstly, this is not a light flighty romance story; this is a character study. Those seeking straightforward [i]fuwa fuwa[/i] sparkly sunshine yuri should look elsewhere. Romance is a factor, but the relationships between the characters and their capacity to grow as individuals is the lynchpin of the narrative. 

Briefly; the main character is Eve, a ranger in the National Park Service with a love for nature, disdain for humanity, and a hot, often violent, temperament. The story is about her growth alongside three personifications of National Parks; Yosemite, Yellowstone, and Zion. 

While there are episodes dedicated to exploring each of the titular National Park Girls, the overarching story is focused on the relationship between Yosemite and Eve. Yosemite shares Eve's prickly personality, and the heart of the story is finding their emotional well-being. I found the dynamic between Yosemite and Eve infinitely appealing, no matter the context. Their lightly combative dialogue is always fun, and keeps the story from getting too sappy. The voice acting in this is also quite lovely, for all the characters, but particularly in Yosemite and Eve's escapades in Episode 4, which was the highlight of the game for me. 

I don't review the majority of visual novels I play, but there is something very strange about this that is inspiring me to write. This story was released episodically, and even with a bumpy release schedule, the first three episodes seemed to maintain a consistent tone: overall light stories with emotionally resonant elements. The two part Eternal Evergreen is where a serious issue emerges.

National Park Girls' flaw is that it keeps trying to claw back a lighter tone, even once the characters start shattering against the realities of the world.  If you want my pure speculation: the story of "Eternal Evergreen" underwent some serious rewrites halfway through when the team wisely decided to not try and tackle the trauma of Native American genocide in a game about anime women cosplaying as National Parks. I have [b]no[/b] proof of that, beyond some references in Part I that are not followed up on, but that's my only real explanation for the messy state of Episode 5 "Eternal Evergreen Part II."

Serious Spoilers;
[spoiler]Episode 5 is insane. What began as a Meet Cute™ in the woods ends in shooting a dog at the conclusion of Episode 4. This leads to a split narrative in Episode 5. The weak strand is brokering peace between a Samurai Cowgirl and talking rocks via a rap battle (this is not a joke), meanwhile Best Girls™ are in the middle of confronting a suicidal fugue state. The story leaves Yosemite National Park, and takes all of our characters to Death Valley National Park. Eve has imploded on herself in guilt-ridden anguish and is actively seeking to drink herself to death in isolation. Eve starts imparting to other characters her new found suicidal ideation, and it gets really uncomfortable. The discomfort is intentional, and effective, this wild tone shift is not the problem. We also get a new addition to the cast, Death Valley, who is an angry Samurai Cowgirl in the grand tradition of Gemini Sunrise's alter ego in Sakura Wars: So Long My Love. Maybe not a grand tradition, but I will take any chance I can get to mention that Gemini Sunrise exists. While I am not the biggest fan of her character, she is not the issue in Episode 5.[/spoiler]

I think the source of the conclusion's issues is a need to keep all our characters busy. While Eve and Yosemite go out to discover what they mean to one another and try to piece together their relationship, the remainder of the cast is left to fight it out in an action comedy about anthropomorphic rocks. While Eve and Yosemite's story highlights important moments of character development and growth, combined with a long-awaited resolution to their relationship, the other plot with Zion and Yellowstone story about rocks is frankly worthless. Intercutting between raw emotional scenes of pure despair and a mad cap comedy was not the solution to a shifting tone.

The choice for a split narrative is near incomprehensible to me; Episode 5 begins with those two tones hitting each other like two speeding semis on a freeway. The ensuing crash is the transition, it is messy, it is surprising, and most of all it is effective. It is only after that initial shift that the story splits the group in two, and begins muddying the tone with ill-advised and not terribly funny comedy. Why there was a perceived need to drag a comedy plot line throughout the entire episode is baffling to me; the plot line is meaningless, takes up space, and it leaves a terrible impression. If the goal was to offset the darkening tone, then that was entirely misguided. The shifting tone is the story, pumping the brakes on it is just a creative hedge that gives the reader whiplash.

Despite that, I really enjoyed my time with this. No amount of questionable comedic road bumps will be enough to make me forget the emotional core of this story. Eve's journey is worth reading, and it gets the attention it deserves. The pay-off here is not two cuties kissing, it is leaving a relationship to blossom on its own terms; marching forward arm-in-arm into the infuriating inanities of the everyday with the newfound emotional maturity to meet the world head on, without smashing oneself to pieces against it. Even with its faults, this story is worth your time.

В свое время мне пришлась очень по нраву игра Highway Blossoms, так что я полез смотреть, есть ли у разработчиков еще что-нибудь подобное. Есть, и немало, в том числе эта игра. Сразу важно отметить, что новелла кинетическая - выборов вы не делаете, просто следуете сюжету с картинками и озвучкой.

Удивительное.
Сравнения с Highway Blossoms напрашиваются. Действие происходит точно так же в западной части США от пустынь и скал до Калифорнии. Даже тот самый огромный термометр завезли. Но на этот раз история мистическая в духе каких-нибудь "Американских богов" Нила Геймана. И с более сложным сюжетом - настолько сложным, что на нем как будто надорвались сами сценаристы. В Highway Blossoms был очень простой посыл: герои отправляются за сокровищем, только чтобы понять, что истинное сокровище все это время было рядом с ними. А в этой игре есть и поиск себя, и рассуждения о солипсизме и бесконечном творении, и загадочная тайна, требующая раскрытия. Но все эти ростки разом обрезают - по сути это просто объемное наполнение сюжета, чтобы не сразу выстрелило чеховское ружье, заряженное в начале первой главы. И у нас получается эдакий ситком. В первой главе четыре героини сходятся, а потом по главе на раскрытие каждой, и почти всегда действие изолировано и откатывается к статус кво. Кроме последней пары глав с тем самым ружьем, которое выстрелило не только метафорически, но и реально. У меня при прохождении было впечатление, что авторы спохватились, заметив сериальный подход бесконечной разработки или устали от самой истории, захотев резко ее завершить. Но с длиной и насыщенностью последней главы это не очень вяжется. Можно сказать, что в ней авторы пересели с легких на тяжелые.

Плюсы.
- Визуальное оформление отличное - яркое и запоминающееся.
- Саундтрек сильно уступает Highway Blossoms, но в целом неплох. А озвучка сделано на крутом уровне опытными актерами.
- Лучшее, что есть в мутной и перегруженной пятой главе, - это новая героиня Долины Смерти. У нее шикарный мексиканский акцент, а в речь есть вкрапления не только испанских слов, но и знаков препинания!
- Вообще диалоги и повествование на уровне отдельных сцен сделаны очень вдумчиво и с душой, а еще с большим словарным запасом, бросающим вызов моему знанию английского. Эта история вполне заслуживает экранизации и даже наверное франшизы.
- Тема крепкой женской дружбы на этот раз вполне может трактоваться именно в направлении этой самой дружбы, так что ничьи чувства не должны быть уязвлены.
- Атмосфера веселого безумия, создаваемая одной из героинь, перекочевывает в приложение к игре, где для открытия бонусных артов нам нужно натурально зарабатывать монеты и спускать их в азартном автомате.

Минусы.
- Главный и самый тяжелый сюжетный поворот высосан из пальца. Главная героиня просто по должности не может себя так вести, не может совершить ту ошибку, что приведет к трагедии. Я тоже ходил в поход по заповеднику (в РФ, само собой) и видел нашу версию рейнджеров. Они были максимально рассудительны в таких вопросах, знали свое хозяйство и всех его опасных обитателей наперечет, жестко инструктировали насчет поведения в дикой природе. И ведь в моем случае это был не жалкий [spoiler]детеныш койота[/spoiler], а молодой [spoiler]кавказский медведь[/spoiler].

Притчи о бессмертии и перерождении не вышло, но как минимум игроки вынесут урок о том, что дикая природа остается дикой и может навредить при неосторожном обращении. И по пути к этому тривиальному выводу игроков ждет множество смешных, милых, философских сцен, остроумных диалогов и красивых пейзажей.

Balrum, developed and published by Balcony Softworks, is a quietly ambitious indie RPG that combines the sensibilities of classic isometric adventures with modern survival mechanics and deep player freedom. Set in a hand-crafted fantasy world filled with forests, villages, and ruins, it invites players into a slow-burning journey of exploration, discovery, and self-sufficiency. You begin as a young villager living a secluded life with your grandfather, but the calm routine quickly gives way to a greater mystery that forces you to venture beyond your home and into a world both dangerous and wondrous. From its opening moments, Balrum establishes itself not as a streamlined, cinematic RPG but as a thoughtful and deliberate experience that values patience and immersion over spectacle.

The narrative framework of Balrum is simple yet effective. Rather than relying on heavy exposition or lengthy cutscenes, the story unfolds naturally through exploration, journals, and small interactions with villagers and travelers. There are hints of dark magic, old kingdoms, and forgotten lands, but the world’s history is largely left for the player to uncover. This open-ended approach allows you to shape your own pace and priorities—some may chase down quests and uncover the central mystery, while others might spend hours building farms, crafting items, and preparing for survival. While the storytelling lacks the emotional drama and complex character arcs found in narrative-heavy RPGs, it succeeds in creating a believable sense of place. Every ruin, dungeon, and patch of wilderness feels like it has a story behind it, even if it’s one you piece together yourself.

Gameplay in Balrum blends traditional turn-based RPG mechanics with systems more often found in survival and simulation games. Combat unfolds on a grid where positioning and timing matter, and each battle rewards caution and resource management over brute force. At the same time, the game constantly demands that you care for your own survival. Hunger, thirst, fatigue, and even pests in your backpack all affect how efficiently you can explore and fight. Crafting plays a central role—you’ll hunt for ingredients, mine ore, cook food, and craft tools and weapons. The freedom of this system is one of Balrum’s greatest strengths. You can focus on combat mastery, turn your home into a self-sustaining farm, or specialize in alchemy and crafting to gain an advantage through preparation rather than strength. It’s a level of freedom rarely seen in indie RPGs, and while it can feel overwhelming at first, it offers a uniquely personal rhythm once you adapt.

One of Balrum’s most rewarding features is its sense of world-building through exploration. The map is vast and segmented into large regions, each with distinct biomes, secrets, and dangers. There are caves to delve into, hidden caches of treasure, ancient ruins, and side quests tucked away in remote corners. The game encourages curiosity and rewards observation—paths often lead to unexpected discoveries, and the progression feels organic rather than guided by strict objectives. The ability to build and maintain your own base adds another dimension to exploration. You can construct a home, plant crops, raise animals, and even set traps for intruders. Having a place to return to after long journeys gives the experience a comforting loop of adventure and retreat, a structure that mirrors the life of a wandering survivalist in a fantasy world.

The combat, while functional, tends to divide players. It follows a turn-based format that emphasizes careful planning and positioning, but its pacing can feel slow and occasionally punishing. Early battles, especially against multiple enemies, demand precise resource use and good preparation, and magic users in particular face a steep learning curve. Those expecting fast, dynamic fights may find the system tedious, yet players who enjoy methodical strategy and risk management will appreciate its depth. The same could be said for the game’s overall design philosophy—it requires time and patience to appreciate. Balrum does not hold the player’s hand, and the lack of detailed tutorials or quest markers can be intimidating at first. However, once the systems click, the experience becomes deeply satisfying in a quiet, measured way.

Visually, Balrum embraces a clean, retro-inspired aesthetic that suits its tone. The environments are isometric and richly detailed despite their simplicity, with forests, lakes, and villages rendered in a way that recalls late-90s CRPGs. The muted color palette and hand-drawn textures lend it a rustic atmosphere that complements the sense of isolation and discovery. The interface, though utilitarian, conveys a sense of authenticity to the world’s handmade charm. The soundtrack is subtle but effective, using gentle melodies and ambient soundscapes to heighten immersion without distracting from the experience. Everything about Balrum’s presentation reinforces its slow-paced, immersive identity.

In the end, Balrum is a game that rewards patience and curiosity. It’s not built for players who want instant gratification or cinematic storytelling; instead, it appeals to those who enjoy systems-driven worlds and the satisfaction of gradual mastery. It can be rough around the edges, with occasional pacing issues, dated visuals, and uneven combat balance, but its heart is unmistakably genuine. The combination of exploration, crafting, base-building, and survival gives it a distinctive identity that sets it apart from both mainstream RPGs and smaller indie experiments. Balrum feels like a love letter to a bygone era of role-playing—one where discovery, hardship, and imagination were the true measures of adventure. For players who value depth over gloss and autonomy over direction, it remains one of the most quietly captivating RPG experiences in the indie space.

Sniper Elite V2 is a solid arcade shooter. These days everyone expects ultra realistic sims which, honestly, barely exist even from big AAA studios but this game never pretends to be one. Yes, some moments are noticeably scripted, but it’s still a fun, satisfying shoot ’em-up. It’s not all sniping, either. Movement can feel a bit clunky at times, and the machine gun takes some getting used to, but the levels are interesting, the visuals are good, and the kill cam is always entertaining. The game is surprisingly addictive, blending sneaking, fast action, and some light planning. On Normal and higher difficulties it can put up a fight, but it’s definitely manageable. One odd design choice is that levels must be completed in one sitting if you make it through several checkpoints and quit, you’ll be starting over from the beginning next time. Not sure why they went with that, especially since most people don’t have unlimited free time. Still, I can see myself replaying levels just for fun. Sniper Elite V2 might not be everyone’s cup of tea, but if you enjoy shooters third person movement with first person aiming you’ll likely have a good time. Just don’t expect it to be something it isn’t. If you just want a fun, well-made arcade sniping experience, this is worth a try.

Wow, the art style just pops out at ya and the music was somethin' I didn't know I would be nostalgic for. The creator really nailed that 90s feel from the n64 era and would really fit right in.  On to the gameplay, where I had some issues. It's fun, though I'm a little disappointed that there's no multi-player although its definitely worth passing the controller around with friends. The problem starts at the practice levels or the lack of them. You get two short practice stages and then your pretty much thrown to the fire. While most games would start you off with some easy levels to get used to the mechanics, in candy ranger it wont be long before you get overwhelmed at the 3rd stage. Enemies spawning above ya and behind while tryin' to juggle 4 different color specific mobs feel like a lot on your plate. And when that wasn't enough they introduce 4 more mechanics. I could feel my eyes glaze over a bit as I was still tryin' to process what I learned two levels ago but still I grit through.
Onto the biggest problem I have with the game, progression. Through out the overworld there are sections that are gated off with coin barriers. They kind of work like stars in super Mario or jiggies in banjo but the reason they work in those games is that they encourage exploration. The game is on rails and because of that you have chances to miss coins on different paths that you weren't even aware. But the biggest sin was that your were never told this until you get to the the coin barriers. So this whole time I'm thinking these are just collectibles like yoshi coins not the goal of the level. By the time I realized this, I had missed a number of coins and rather than going back and playing the levels again. It just took the air out of my sail and I quit. I'll probably go back and try again because the game just oozes charm but it left a sour after taste. I think if an update fixed the inconsistent difficulty at least at the beginning area I may change my review. While the game feels very polished the corse parts make it hard recommend.

[h2]Sinopsis[/h2]
Mi Gran Comisión de Conejitos (I Commisioned Some Bunnies) es un título de buscar pequeños conejos y sus zanahorias, escondidos a través de una serie de escenarios pintorescos, dibujados a mano y con un diseño diferente según el artista que lo ha realizado.

[h2]Jugabilidad / Apartado técnico[/h2]
En cada escenario tendremos que observar y encontrar un total de 50 conejos y 50 zanahorias. Las características del juego podrían resumirse en las siguientes: [list]
[*][b]Apartado gráfico[/b]: Diseños elaborados, con muchos detalles y color. 
[*][b]Banda sonora[/b]: Música entretenida que acompaña a cada escena.
[*][b]Número de niveles[/b]: 15.
[*][b]Número de elementos ocultos[/b]: 100 (50 conejos / 50 zanahorias).
[*][b]Sistema de pistas[/b]: Sí. Pistas ilimitadas y sin esperas pulsando la tecla “H” del teclado. Una flecha nos mostrará la dirección en la que se encuentran los elementos restantes.
[*][b]Dificultad[/b]: Muy Fácil.
[*][b]Elemento diferenciador[/b]: Ninguna mecánica innovadora. Buen diseño gráfico.
[*][b]Logros[/b]: 16.
[*][b]Otros[/b]: Varias ranuras de guardado y cronómetro. [/list]

[h2]Valoración[/h2]
“Mi Gran Comisión” son una saga creciente de juegos de encontrar objetos ocultos que se ha granjeado una fama a través de su bello arte y diseño. Son juegos, por lo general, mucho más sencillos que la media dentro del género, pero cuenta con varios niveles para poder sacarle partido. Mi Gran Comisión de Conejitos me ha parecido un poco más soso que el resto de los que he probado, ya que los diseños son menos variados y alguno presenta una resolución algo baja. A pesar de ello, se puede disfrutar al 100% y la calidad está asegurada.

Lo salvaría de un incendio! 👨‍🚒👍🔥

Such a good game and such an unexpected gem! Games don't need to be overly complex to be good, and Xenopurge is proof of that. 

Core gameplay is simple: assemble your squad, drop them into the fray, watch as your units explore and enter battles with enemy units, input commands in real time, survive and escape. 

But there there are more layers of strategy, which is the best path to take to make it to the end, unit synergies, upgrades (or downgrades), positioning choices and much more.

The sci-fi theme is great, music fits perfectly and gives an overall eerie feeling with a sense of urgency. And there is another hidden layer of things to explore that I don't wish to spoil during my review.

This game might be a little too clever with its visual subversion, like I am an open minded gamer and all, and I still had to scratch my head trying to understand the direction here. I honestly took one look at the trailer and like, clearly this is garbage, there is no way it's some kind of experimental melancholy narrative with the vibes from an unfinished map asset. And well $$$$, that seems to be exactly what it is. Although I am still not sure if the developer knows exactly what he is doing, or maybe he does and not doing amazing job with it, the game is just so oddly paced with the narrative and psychological effects, sometimes it still feels like some asset flip, and sometimes I am like yea, I am vibing, yea.

Strangely it has way too much narrative content, 7+ hours and still not done (make sure you play past the prologue credits). About half of it is FPS, it plays okay, but usually the areas have between 1 and 3 enemy types so it will get stale. It's like, the dev is trying to make the most epic story, but simultaneously not having nearly enough game design experience to even come close, it's actually charming. It's like, the game is flying an air balloon by farting into it, it's truly a work of pure artistry. 

Your opinion of the game probably will change a lot, up or down, the deeper you go. Like it has fun parts don't get me wrong, it's just a little weird the way it's presented overall, I actually think it kinda gets better after the first 90 minutes. So now I am in a weird place where I am trying to advocate for this rather odd game, that frankly does not even feel that great at first. The care that developer puts into the level design also feels very sporadic, sometimes it's dull with no textures, and sometimes it actually has some neat aesthetic going for it, even with a sense of escapism depending on the level.

Another odd thing. After the dream section, it shows the credits, but I think it's like "introduction credits", the game keeps going after you interact with the computer, and frankly it will get even stranger, almost like some odd arthouse game. The game kinda alternates between narrative and FPS sections, sometimes with odd horror/psychological moments. It's pretty basic overall, but I guess that is what it's going for, charm in simplicity and the overall trashy feel of the game.

[h1] Pros: [/h1]

(+) There is no logical or objective way to describe why this game feels somewhat enjoyable, but I think depending on the level, it has some cool vibes and escapism in simplicity or just how odd it is, more so later in the game after the lengthy introduction chapter.

(+) Well, I did like the music, not sure if it was composed for the game or not, but usually had that ambient/melancholy tone which helps with the atmosphere 

(+) Some area later in the game don't look as bad as those in the early game, I think the texture in the swamp looked okay, the graffiti walls looked okay. It's a bit sporadic though

[h1] Feedback: [/h1]

- a few more guns or enemy types would help (ideally early in the game), it's like 1 to 3 enemies most of the game. It's also a bit weird that you seem to take damage even if you shoot first, like it's very hard not to trade health even if you get the first attack

- I wonder how many people will assume the credits is the end of the game (instead of it being more like a beginning of the game lol), maybe not the best idea

- even if I accept this game as some odd arthouse feeling melancholy experience, which seems to be what it's going for, I still feel like there is a lot of design fluff in the game, oddly paced, and I usually have to complete some boring levels to find something interesting. Like you doing some cool aesthetic and weird **** in some levels which I like, I just feel like that should be most of the game, and not me running into interesting moments here and there.

I guess what I am trying to say, if you doing levels with a lot of walking, make sure there are enough things that can catch your attention, sometimes you do that, and sometimes it feels like there are huge empty section with nothing to look at. Players like to explore and look at things, and you’ll be a much better developer if you can reward that line of thinking. 

- I think the area with the skater boss had good use of texture, graffiti in that case, which is somewhat of a rare aesthetic in this game where you actually adding some colors and detail on walls. It would be easier for people to purchase your game if they saw that level design more consistently, otherwise I feel the game kinda gives odd asset flip arena vibes, it’s not, but just based on the trailer, I can’t tell if it’s a legit project, and I think it comes down to making sure you are putting more love into level design, even if they are meant to be a bit simple.

With Evolution, this moment comes very early, sometimes even before the 10th generation.
While there is some complexity in the bots behaviour, the game lacks in any other regard.

You can't even save creatures in your pond to lett the "winners" compete against each other.
There is absolutely no environmental diversity.
Important evolutionary features like mating for example are missing as well.

Also, other than in the laboratory, you don't have a quick way to play intelligent designer and tweak a creature on the go.
