3dSen, developed and published by Geod Studio, is one of those rare gaming projects that immediately communicates its purpose through a single glance. It’s not a game in the traditional sense, nor is it just another NES emulator—it's a reinterpretation of retro gaming itself. Its core function is deceptively simple: take classic 2D NES titles and convert them into fully navigable, three-dimensional diorama-like spaces. Yet the impact of that transformation is profound. For anyone who grew up on 8-bit platformers, shooters, and action adventures, seeing those familiar sprites suddenly become layered environments is almost surreal, as though lost childhood memories have been rebuilt in physical space.

The real magic of 3dSen lies in how effortlessly it bridges nostalgia and novelty. Instead of replacing original gameplay, it preserves every mechanic, layout, hitbox, glitch, and movement pattern—only now they unfold inside a voxel-styled reconstruction that feels like a pop-up book or miniature stage. The first time you rotate the camera around Mario, Samus, Simon Belmont, or any other retro protagonist, your brain pauses, almost confused, as if experiencing a dream that makes perfect sense despite breaking every rule of reality. Enemies become puppets suspended in space, backgrounds become sculpted scenery, vertical shafts become towering chambers. It reframes familiar levels not through alteration, but through dimensional perspective, inviting players to rediscover games they thought they knew completely.

Beyond its visual reinterpretation, 3dSen functions as a surprisingly robust platform. Its list of supported titles continues to expand, and compatibility includes both commercial classics and modern homebrew creations, giving developers and modders new possibilities to showcase their work. The emulator features expected conveniences—save states, controller support, performance adjustments—but also more experimental tools, such as exporting scenes or manually adjusting the camera to capture screenshots and videos. In its VR version, the experience becomes even more theatrical, letting players physically lean into environments and observe their favorite games as floating miniature worlds. That alone makes 3dSen feel like a museum exhibit for interactive history.

Because of its nature, however, the software’s appeal comes with certain conditions. It does not provide NES ROMs, so players must supply legally obtained titles, which means the experience relies heavily on personal game libraries. The novelty also depends on emotional connection—someone with no history of NES gaming may see it as a technical curiosity rather than a revelatory reinterpretation. Some games convert more gracefully than others, and certain fast-paced or visually dense titles can feel visually cluttered in 3D space. The tool never claims perfection, and part of its appeal comes from experimenting, adjusting views, and finding the most flattering angles rather than expecting uniform output.

Still, the strength of 3dSen is not just technological—it’s emotional. It understands that retro gaming is not merely about playing old titles, but about how the mind remembers them. Childhood imagination often filled in visual gaps, invented depth, and built worlds larger than the pixels on screen. 3dSen reconstructs that imagined dimension and brings it forward into adulthood. Instead of flattening nostalgia into static memory, it gives it physicality, weight, and renewed wonder. It allows players to experience retrospection as active play rather than passive recollection.

Ultimately, 3dSen feels like a love letter to the foundational years of video games. It doesn’t rewrite history or modernize classics, but reframes them in a way that encourages appreciation, curiosity, preservation, and creative re-exploration. For longtime retro fans, collectors, streamers, digital artists, and VR enthusiasts, it offers something genuinely special—the chance to revisit the past not as it was, but as it once felt. It is niche by nature, but delightfully, unapologetically so, and it fills that niche with remarkable care and imagination.

Taisho x Alice Episode 3, developed by Primula and published by Pencil, is the third installment in a uniquely structured visual novel series that combines fairy-tale motifs, romantic storytelling, and psychological depth. Continuing the overarching narrative that began in the first two episodes, this chapter further unravels the mysteries of the mirror world while offering two new routes centered on the reimagined characters of Snow White and the Wizard. As in the previous episodes, the story begins with the heroine awakening in a dark void devoid of memory, encountering the mysterious Alice, and entering the mirror world where familiar fairy-tale characters have been inverted into fresh and sometimes surprising forms. What sets this episode apart is its more mature tone and emotional complexity. While earlier entries leaned heavily into whimsical romance, Episode 3 begins to reveal the darker foundations of the series’ world, transforming what seemed like a simple fairy-tale setting into a layered narrative about trauma, identity, and redemption.

The game’s writing and structure reflect a growing sense of cohesion and ambition. Each route feels more purposeful and intricately woven into the overarching mystery that connects all the previous chapters. The Snow White route, in particular, delves into themes of self-perception and personal worth. It transforms the traditional image of Snow White’s purity and passivity into something far more introspective, portraying a character struggling with internalized guilt and emotional vulnerability. The Wizard’s route, by contrast, leans into suspense and mystery, exploring the blurred lines between reality and illusion. These two paths complement each other beautifully, balancing emotional introspection with narrative intrigue. Both routes maintain the series’ trademark charm—romantic storytelling told from a female perspective—but they also expand it, inviting the player to question what lies beneath the surface of these fairy-tale archetypes. The writing strikes a delicate balance between sweetness and melancholy, crafting a narrative that feels both fantastical and grounded in human emotion.

Visually, Taisho x Alice Episode 3 continues to impress with its delicate art direction and elegant character designs. The sprites are detailed and expressive, with every subtle movement or change in expression capturing the characters’ emotional states. The backgrounds, inspired by early 20th-century aesthetics, create an atmosphere that fuses the elegance of the Taisho era with the surreal dreamscape of the mirror world. This combination of period style and fantasy gives the game a distinct visual identity that sets it apart from other otome titles. The CG illustrations are particularly beautiful, showcasing moments of intimacy or tension with painterly grace. The soundtrack complements this aesthetic perfectly—it ranges from ethereal melodies to haunting piano themes, enhancing both the romantic and mysterious tones of the story. The Japanese voice acting is top-tier, adding nuance and emotional resonance to every scene, while the localization captures the whimsical humor and dramatic flair of the dialogue, though some players might find certain lines slightly over-stylized or modernized compared to the original tone.

In terms of gameplay, the experience remains faithful to the visual novel format. The player primarily reads through text and makes key decisions that influence the branching paths of the story. Each route offers multiple endings, from happy to bittersweet, rewarding players who explore every dialogue choice and replay to discover the full narrative scope. The pacing is measured, taking its time to build atmosphere and character relationships. For players accustomed to more dynamic or interactive visual novels, the deliberate pacing may feel slow, but this approach allows the story’s emotional beats to unfold naturally. The game’s interface is simple and user-friendly, with convenient save and skip options that make route exploration smooth and accessible. It’s not a mechanically complex experience, but like most otome titles, the emphasis lies in immersion and storytelling rather than challenge or interactivity.

Where Episode 3 truly excels is in its emotional depth. The relationships between the heroine and her romantic leads feel more developed and genuine than before, moving beyond simple affection into explorations of healing, understanding, and trust. Each route tackles emotional obstacles that resonate with the overarching theme of self-acceptance. The heroine’s role as an active participant in these relationships also feels stronger than in previous episodes; she is not a passive bystander but a character with agency, empathy, and growing awareness. The storytelling interweaves personal growth with romance, resulting in moments that are both touching and thought-provoking. What begins as a fairy-tale rescue story ultimately evolves into something introspective and meaningful, reminding players that the series’ true heart lies not in saving others, but in rediscovering oneself.

Despite its many strengths, Taisho x Alice Episode 3 is not without its minor shortcomings. Some players may find the pacing slow or the routes shorter than expected, particularly if they are used to longer visual novels with extensive branching. The dialogue occasionally indulges in melodrama, and while this suits the fairy-tale tone, it might feel exaggerated to those seeking subtlety. Nonetheless, these are small criticisms in a game that otherwise succeeds in its ambition. What makes this episode stand out is how it bridges the lighter, romantic tone of the earlier entries with the deeper, more philosophical revelations that prepare players for the series’ conclusion. It’s a careful balance between closure and anticipation, giving fans both emotional satisfaction and curiosity for what comes next.

Taisho x Alice Episode 3 is one of the most polished and emotionally fulfilling chapters in the series. It builds upon everything that came before it—expanding the lore, deepening the character development, and refining the storytelling style. For players who have followed the series from the beginning, this episode serves as a pivotal moment where the pieces begin to fit together and the true scope of the mirror world becomes clear. For newcomers, it remains an accessible entry point that can stand on its own, though the experience is richer when played in sequence. Through its evocative art, enchanting music, and heartfelt writing, the game captures the timeless appeal of fairy tales while grounding them in the complexities of human emotion. It’s a delicate blend of fantasy and introspection, one that reaffirms Taisho x Alice’s reputation as one of the more distinctive and emotionally intelligent series in the otome genre.

Sprawl was a game I was mega hyped to play and overall it was worth the money I paid for it, but that doesn't mean I couldn't have expected more. 

My quick breakdown: Sprawl is an absolutely gorgeous and stunning love letter to Titanfall fans, Quake fans, and Blade Runner fans. It has gorgeous artwork, with a stunning soundtrack, and is a visual masterpiece. The gameplay falls a little short, but is mostly enjoyable, with the game's story falling a little on the flat side of things.

The Story: The story is unfortunately, in my opinion, the worst part about the game. I was super intrigued to learn about the universe of Sprawl and its characters, but unfortunately I felt like I didn't learn much. Anytime the story seemed to be going anywhere good, it just didn't follow through. I was left at the end of the game with me searching up "Sprawl Game Ending Explained". The basic idea of the ending is super understandable, but the overall conclusion is lacking a satisfying feeling. I was left not knowing who characters were, what their purpose was, and just anything about them. 

The Artwork: Like I said above, this game is absolutely stunning. It is so gorgeous and masterfully directed in what it presents. The soundtrack is top notch and the environments are superb! My biggest complaint with the art direction is that the levels end up feeling very samey. They're gorgeous, but variety is lacking. I would love to see a Sprawl with more unique areas spread out through each of the 3 Episodes, other than that, 10/10 on what WAS executed!

The Gameplay: Sprawl was a fun game, but there were many frustrating things about it. First off, the weapon progression feels inconsequential. None of the weapons build up hype. You get them too fast and they don't hit as hard as you're hoping. The balancing is a huge thing that is off with this game. Once you get the chain gun there is little reason to use any other weapon. You can bunny hop and just use the chain gun to mow down everything. The shotgun also seems odd with the tight spread, and the smgs feel like peashooters. The rocket is dissapointing (very cool idea with the shotgun rocket, but poor execution) and the railgun feels way too weak for the charge up period. There isn't much feedback for most of the guns, and this leads to a experience where you don't always know if you're hitting shots (without looking at enemy health bars). The headshot mechanic with the bullet time is cool, especially when paired with the movement, but many of the arenas and the restrictions to movement felt like I got punished for trying to be creative. I did the best by just bunny hopping with the chaingun instead of using freeflow movement and swapping weapons with using adrenaline for headshots. The foundation/bones are there for a really solid gameplay loop, but the supporting structure (level design, enemy design and balancing) doesn't entirely support that theoretical solid gameplay loop. 

The Bosses: BY FAR THE MOST DISSAPOINTING THING IN SPRAWL! I love a really good boss, and the Sprawl bosses were such a let down. The first boss had insanely good build up, and the arena was a cool arena, but the mechanics just sucked. It was way too easy and repetitive. The bosses never felt like a real threat or a challenge to overcome. The other two bosses didn't have any of the build up the first one had, and were even more of a joke. The big flying mech boss was frustrating to figure out, but a joke once I figured it out (SPOILERS: You drop in an arena with toxic coolant and he has a shield, you have to disable his shield to damage him. There are beams aiming at him that project the shield, so you would think to shoot the "eye" of the beam, but it's not that. You have to aim much farther down to destroy the foundation of the pillar the beam comes from. It does have a health bar, but is unfortunately not named so it can be easily lost), The third and final boss was also a complete cake walk. I used the chain gun and rocket spammed the turrets and didnt find any challenge or threat to this boss. I was not invested in the boss either and didn't know who i truly defeated after killing the final boss. That is a big mistake. The final boss of a game should be mega impactful, not some random flying drone with a voice of a character i dont even know. 

Overall, I was glad I bought Sprawl and it genuinely was a good use of my time. I don't think I'll ever replay it after beating it all the way through, but I would happily check out a sequel or any DLC that could come out. There is alot of potential with Sprawl and its universe, but it felt weakly executed on. I would have to give it a 7/10 on overall quality. Its a good game, but not a great game. The saddest part is the potential for greatness is there. But I have hope!

Even in demo stage, which I had the privilege to play-test, ODev's highly anticipated release "Fitting-In" proves itself as a refreshing and ever-joyous puzzle game. Delighting in the minutiae of game design, "Fitting-In" provides a touching metaphor for social interaction as the protagonist, at first cautious and childlike, learns new patterns and becomes familiar with new situations. Simple, boxy levels give way to serpentine labyrinths - but the player has learned how to cope with novel problems, solving every puzzle with different plays on the same rhythm-based jumping mechanic. Despite the simplicity of the basic rules, ODev continues to deliver in every level, introducing additional environmental mechanics just as we begin to understand the world we inhabit. However, the overarching emotional theme of the game is one of satisfaction and serenity - no matter how chaotic the playing field seems at times, the player always finds where they fit.

The Longest Journey: A Modern Retrospective

Summary:
While appreciated for its overall puzzle quality and the time spent in its world, The Longest Journey (played in 2025) ultimately does not warrant its classic status as a point-and-click adventure game. The narrative shows its age, feeling clunky and cliché by contemporary standards. Although the puzzles were generally satisfying, the finale was pedestrian and lacked the dramatic payoff expected of an epic adventure, resulting in a somewhat anticlimactic conclusion.

Key Takeaway:
A decent experience for its genre history, but time has exposed weaknesses in pacing and writing that prevent it from standing up against modern narrative games.

One of my favourite adventure games of all time. It's considered a classic for good reason. But be warned, this is a game in desperate need of a remaster, and it will certainly feel its age in terms of graphics and a handful of obtuse puzzles.

It's something of a miracle that this game runs at all on modern systems. Tip: if the yes/no confirmation dialog when overwriting saves/quitting the game renders as a white box, you can just press Y/N.

Julian & Friends presents itself at first glance as a cheerful, pastel-colored adventure, but beneath its friendly exterior lies a cleverly orchestrated psychological horror experience. Developed by JacksonG13 and published by JacksonGameStudios, the game opens with a simple and wholesome premise—Julian wants to prepare the perfect birthday surprise for his close friend Julia. With bright visuals, upbeat music, and a town full of eccentric characters, the early moments feel like a charming throwback to early 2000s point-and-click titles. But the longer you play, the easier it becomes to notice the cracks: awkward pauses in dialogue, visual distortions, sudden tonal shifts, and characters whose behavior doesn’t quite fit their cheerful facades. The game delights in slowly peeling those layers away until what began as a lighthearted celebration becomes something far more disturbing.

At its core, the game mixes narrative-focused exploration with a series of ten minigames that punctuate Julian’s journey around town. These minigames range from rhythm challenges to simple tasks that seem straightforward but gradually grow stranger and more difficult. The branching structure allows for multiple endings, some of which can only be accessed by entering specific codes at the start of the game. This design encourages replaying and experimenting, and many of the game’s most unsettling or surprising moments are hidden behind these alternate routes. While some minigames can feel unforgiving or mechanically clunky, they serve a larger purpose: they destabilize the player’s sense of comfort, echoing the game’s overall shift from innocent fun to uncanny horror. Even small failures often lead to odd visual glitches or unexpected dialogue that subtly hints at a deeper narrative thread.

The presentation plays a significant role in shaping the experience. The bright, cartoonish art creates a friendly, welcoming atmosphere that perfectly masks the darkness beneath. Characters like Gerald, Darcy, and Mr. Write appear harmless and whimsical on the surface, yet the longer you interact with them, the more unsettling they become. The game corrupts its own aesthetic in clever ways—backgrounds flicker, characters briefly distort, and audio clips warp into dissonant noise. These glitches do not feel accidental; they reinforce the sense that the world itself is unstable or hiding something. The contrast between the childish visuals and the darker discoveries gives the game a unique tone, one that fans of glitch horror and ARG-inspired storytelling will appreciate.

The narrative is intentionally fragmented, inviting players to dig deeper to fully understand what Julian’s world really is. Each playthrough offers pieces of a larger puzzle, and discovering all endings reveals how much emotional weight is hidden behind the birthday-party framework. Themes of memory, trauma, denial, and masked emotion weave subtly through conversations and visual details. Dedicated players have gone so far as to analyze audio spectrograms, hidden files, and cryptic in-game codes to uncover secrets, and this meta-layer of storytelling adds a sense of mystery and community-driven discovery. The game rewards curiosity, not just in unlocking new endings but in understanding why certain characters act the way they do and what lies beneath their cheerful exterior.

Overall, Julian & Friends succeeds as a compact yet deeply atmospheric psychological horror experience disguised as a harmless adventure game. It blends humor, nostalgia, and colorful design with an underlying darkness that gradually consumes the narrative. While some of its mechanics may feel unpolished and certain minigames can be frustrating, the emotional payoff and thematic depth outweigh those bumps. It is particularly appealing to players who enjoy unraveling secrets, diving into hidden content, and piecing together story fragments across multiple runs. By the time the truth begins to surface, the earlier charm of the game takes on a haunting new meaning. For fans of indie horror with an experimental twist, Julian & Friends is an unsettling and memorable journey well worth experiencing.

Петька и ВИЧ — культовый юмористический квест, который даже спустя десятки лет отлично воспринимается. Я не застал оригинал, не являюсь частью той культуры, но чисто исследовательски мне было любопытно, что собой представляет эта СНГ-шная классика.

Над переизданием потрудились на славу, и речь не столько о стабильности игры на новых системах и поддержке геймпада, сколько об изменении схемы управления. Теперь в настройках, помимо сильно перегруженного классического режима, можно выбрать упрощённое управление, в котором привычная point-and-click схема работает по принципу: нажал на предмет — увидел все возможные опции взаимодействия. Это ключевой момент, поскольку игрок может не знать, что нужно использовать надувную куклу на вороне, но при исследовании мира, «прощупывая» предмет за предметом, он увидит  эту опцию без малейших догадок. Такое серьёзное упрощение геймплея позволило мне с огромным удовольствием залпом пройти игру без особых «мук роженицы», присущих подобным квестам, когда ты кликаешь вообще всё на всё в надежде найти нужную комбинацию. Логика во взаимодействиях чаще всего присутствует, так что с упрощённым управлением затупов поймать сложно, но даже так в игре есть система подсказки по клику, которая предельно чётко направляет игрока к следующему сюжетному триггеру.

Рисованные задники до сих пор радуют глаз, нарисованные в пейнт модельки персонажей и их редкая анимация хоть и выглядят вычурно, но в общую картину вписываются. Но самое главное — это словесные каламбуры наших карикатурных героев и тупейшие ситуации, в которых они проявляют свою смекалку и богатый жизненный опыт. Да, местами — плоская шутка на шутке или даже детское кривляние, но это настолько плохо, что уже через час ты хохочешь над очередным пошлым оборотом. По сути, это сборник бородатых анекдотов в карикатурном мире с такими же претенциозными персонажами и смыслами, которые с полуслова понятны нашей ментальности, ведь это концентрированное отражение нашего прошлого и настоящего с намеренным преувеличением и сатирой. Широкий набор тем — от противостояния красных и белых времён революции до спасения мира от пробудившихся на Луне инопланетян. Фоном постоянно проходит упоминание современных терминов и идей, что превращает происходящее в фарс, где всё построено на абсурдных ситуациях, нелепости и внешней комичности.

В игре три акта, каждый из которых выделяется своим набором персонажей и антуражем. В начале мы ковыряемся в посёлке Гадюкино и среди алкашей красной армии пытаемся найти хотя бы одного трезвенника; второй акт почти весь играется за Анку (комсомолку, двойного агента и по совместительству проститутку) — в лучшей локации игры, борделе, где на каждом углу расставлены красивые декорации, и что ни персонаж — то кладезь. Третий акт и вовсе не похож на всё ранее увиденное. В общем, добротный квест на пару вечеров с олдовой атмосферой, которая понятна даже тем, кто ранее с ней не был знаком.

Есть технические огрехи — например, Петька говорит устами Чапаева, или персонажи загораживают собой квестовый предмет, точку перемещения из локации, — но самой большой проблемой для меня была их медленная ходьба. Хоть убейте, не понимаю, зачем мне смотреть, как они неспешно топают. Хотелось бы видеть облачные сохранения, чтобы играть с разных устройств, но уже за достижения в стиме спасибо — для некоторых это прям отдельное удовольствие.

Sacred Citadel is a colorful, side-scrolling beat ’em up set in the Sacred universe; a franchise that's known more for its groundbreaking RPG games that shook the world at some point in the past. Does Sacred work well as a beat 'em up? Let's find out!

At its core, Sacred Citadel is straightforward: pick a class, smack hordes of monsters, collect loot, and unleash flashy combos. It’s simple, sometimes too simple, but undeniably satisfying in short bursts. The four character classes (ranger, warrior, mage, shaman) each feel distinct enough, and their moves evolve as you level up... But all of them just stick to the same formula; combos, finishers and Orc-smacking! 

However, the combat can become repetitive during longer sessions. Enemy variety is serviceable but not particularly inventive and missions often feel like pallette swaps of each other, and so do the limited number of creatures you fight along the way. Moreover, while there is a sense of progression, you'd essentially be doing the same thing over and over again... Grinding gear, leveling up, fighting repetitive pallette swap bosses... Nothing feels inventive enough to have you go like "oh, now I'll play as the other class, this game feels so much alive and replayable!"

Finally, the most creative thing about the game is its graphics. The cartoonish art direction feels like a step in the right direction and the soundtracks really set the tone of each level... It's epic, in a sense. I wish it made the game any less repetitive though. For me, this gets a [b]6/10[/b]. Will I touch it ever again after finishing it? Nope! Hard pass. It does however build on some of the lore from the Sacred Universe, so you should probably play it just for the sake of that, plus the amazing visuals.

[b]Galimulator[/b] is what it says on the tin: a galaxy simulator. You [i]can[/i] interact with the galaxy by taking control of emergent factions; through editing or adjusting various names, traits, etc; and/or by unleashing cosmic horrors and other crises upon your cosmic subjects. Ultimately, though, you are merely an observer.

This game is, essentially, a simplified and accessible version of those AI battle royales for games like 'Stellaris' where most of the fun comes from watching the history unfold before your eyes, and logging the procedural lore that creates. The only issue with this is that sometimes it is hard to actually tell what all is happening. Sure, I can see the red guys are taking over the green guys, but what is [i]actually[/i] happening? Well, there are a lot of menus and other detail panels to explain things, but its up to you to actually go down and look at it. Further, while there are ships and things flying around, zapping each other and the like, the design of the game remains fairly simple and while, logically, there would be millions of vessels zipping around your galaxy, you will only see maybe a few hundred or some thousands on screen at any time and it is hard to say what some of them are doing at any given moment.

Ultimately, while elements of this [i]can[/i] be hard to read at times and [i][can[/i] be overwhelming, I think it ultimately just comes down to familiarity. If nothing else, you can just watch blobs of color take over other blobs of color on your desktop as a sort of living screensaver, and even earn a few achievements as you do so.

Value will vary from user to user, but if you are a fan of these sorts of idle games, you can certainly do worse for the price, and if you see it on sale perhaps you should give it a shot. I think this is well worth checking out!

レジストリは余計なところを触ったり、間違った値を設定するとPCの動作に支障を来す可能性が大きいです
全てを自己責任で行ってください
まず全ての作業を行う前に信長の野望 革新の起動ランチャーを開き、設定の初期化ボタンより、環境をクリーンな状態にしておきます
初期化→決定で閉じる ※これはすでに1980×1080に設定済みの状態で撮影したので画面モードが空白になっています(詳細は後述)
初期化が済んだらランチャーを閉じ、信長の野望 革新が起動していない状態にします
次にWin10の「プログラムとファイルの検索」の検索窓にregeditと入力してレジストリエディタを起動します
コンピューター\HKEY_CURRENT_USER\SOFTWARE\KoeiTecmo\Nobunaga12PK\Configs
を開き、そこにある
WIDTHの数値を「10進数」で1920と入力→OK
HEIGHTの数値を「10進数」で1080と入力→OK
とします。これでレジストリエディタの作業は終了です
次にSteamから信長の野望 革新を起動し、起動ランチャー画面を呼び出します
起動環境設定を開きましょう
通常の設定タブで「画面モード」のところが空白になっていればうまくいってます
※この画面モードのところは空欄を確認した後は選択ボックス内を触らないほうが良いでしょう
CG品質は初期化で中になっていると思いますが、高設定に変更してOKです
また高度な設定タブに移動すると、フルスクリーンかウインドウモードかの選択がありますのでフルスクリーンにしておきます
この状態で信長の野望 革新を起動すると1920×1080のフルHDで表示されます
なお1920×1080の解像度にしても、OPのムービーやタイトル画面は横に黒帯が出る懐かしの4:3比仕様のようです

Bought the game because I was interested in the concept of card games that play like arcade fighters. Took about a dozen matches to acclimate to the game, for it to stop feeling arbitrary and start feeling like a real fighting game.

The only other game in the genre I've played is Combo Fighter. While an approachable and well-made game, Yomi 2 exceeds Combo Fighter in every respect except, imo, art. Yomi 2's art is not quite distracting (with the exception of my current main, Persephone), but it isn't why I'm playing.

Gameplay is wonderful, with enough decisions to make and variables to weigh so as to be engaging but not overwhelming. I especially love the swap feature, where you can swap a basic card from your hand for one in your discard, in full view of the opponent, for better or worse. I've only scratched the surface, but all the characters feel very different to play and are interesting. While the gem system (customizing feature that adds one of many sets of five extra cards to your character's deck) was a little overwhelming at first, it's grown on me and I now find it to be the perfect amount of customization.

I've been mostly playing against robots and I find even this fun and satisfying, trying to figure out both the character and the robot's programming. I've played once so far with an irl friend using the play and pass feature. She found the tutorial tedious and too restrictive (I agree, I probably should have taught her myself by talking through matches with robots), but she really took to the game after finishing it and enjoyed playing against me.

My friend is not a videogamer and does not have steam, and so I am a little sad, especially for how well suited Yomi 2 is to correspondence play, that it is not available on mobile or browser, but I understand resources are limited.

All in all, very fun and engaging game; scratches my itch for card and(!) fighting games. I look forward to introducing it to more of my friends and I will probably be getting the physical version when it releases, if I can get enough people hooked.

Astrodle, developed and published by Robin Nicolet, is a vibrant and relaxing indie game that blends idle progression with space-shooter mechanics in a colorful, cosmic setting. The game takes a simple premise—shooting, collecting, and upgrading—and transforms it into an endlessly satisfying feedback loop built around numbers, growth, and rhythm. You pilot a small ship in a universe inspired by the constellations of the zodiac, battling waves of floating, blob-like enemies while gathering their essences to strengthen your vessel. It’s a concept that doesn’t rely on narrative or complexity to engage the player; instead, it thrives on the hypnotic pleasure of watching your ship become more powerful, your stats climb higher, and your screen fill with a cascade of glowing projectiles and rewards.

At its core, Astrodle is about progression and momentum. The gameplay loop is simple: destroy enemies, collect their drops, invest resources in upgrades, and watch the results compound. Over time, your weapons become stronger, your firing rate faster, and your capacity to collect essences greater. What sets the game apart from standard idle experiences is the inclusion of real-time shooting mechanics—while your ship can automate its attacks, manual play offers more engagement for players who prefer an active experience. The balance between idle automation and hands-on control gives Astrodle an approachable versatility; it’s equally enjoyable as a background game running while you multitask or as a short, focused session where you actively manage upgrades and positioning. This dual design allows the game to appeal to both casual players and those who enjoy min-maxing numbers for efficiency.

Visually, Astrodle adopts a clean and cheerful aesthetic that complements its casual tone. The action unfolds in a dark, star-speckled void filled with glowing projectiles, softly pulsating enemies, and streams of colored energy. The color palette is vibrant without being overwhelming, and the minimalistic design makes the interface easy to read even when the screen fills with dozens of objects. Each upgrade subtly enhances the spectacle—bullets become faster, explosions larger, and numbers more extravagant. The presentation captures the simple joy of watching chaos unfold in a controlled, almost meditative pattern. The soundtrack, meanwhile, mirrors this atmosphere perfectly: calm electronic rhythms and ambient tones that make the experience soothing rather than stressful. Together, the visuals and audio create a feedback loop that encourages flow-state play, where time disappears and the player becomes absorbed in the cycle of action and reward.

Thematically, the game draws inspiration from astrological symbolism. Players interact with celestial beings representing the zodiac, each embodying a distinct aspect of power and progression. Collecting their essences becomes both a literal and metaphorical act of ascension as you move closer to “godhood.” While the narrative element is thin, this zodiac framework gives the gameplay a gentle sense of identity that elevates it beyond a purely mechanical idle shooter. It’s more of a stylistic flourish than a storytelling device, but it fits nicely with the cosmic tone and serves as a loose goalpost for completion. The result is a game that doesn’t need a deep plot to feel purposeful—it’s the satisfaction of continual growth that provides motivation.

In terms of structure, Astrodle offers two main play modes: an active shooting mode where players control the ship directly and an idle progression system where upgrades accumulate over time. The design encourages experimentation with builds and efficiency. Players can focus on maximizing firepower, optimizing resource gain, or balancing upgrades for steady progress. The mechanics are easy to understand, and the interface makes it clear how each choice contributes to long-term growth. This accessibility ensures that the game never feels intimidating, even for newcomers to the idle or incremental genre. However, it also means that the depth of the systems plateaus quickly. Once you’ve explored most of the upgrade tree and collected a few constellations’ worth of essences, the gameplay becomes more about repetition and spectacle than new discovery. For many players, this simplicity is part of the charm; for others, it might lead to fatigue once the novelty wears off.

Despite its minimal scope, Astrodle achieves a sense of progression that feels rewarding. Every few minutes brings a tangible improvement—stronger weapons, faster collection speeds, and more visually explosive attacks. Watching your ship evolve into a powerhouse is inherently satisfying, especially when accompanied by the rhythmic pulse of background music and the cascade of numbers filling the screen. It’s a sensory experience as much as a mechanical one, built to deliver a consistent dopamine hit through growth and feedback. The game doesn’t pretend to offer complex systems or narrative twists; instead, it focuses on being pure, distilled relaxation—a playground for incremental advancement.

The game’s simplicity also extends to its technical design. It runs smoothly on nearly any system, with minimal requirements and stable performance. Load times are instant, crashes are virtually nonexistent, and the interface is intuitive enough to be grasped within minutes. This level of polish helps it achieve exactly what it aims for: a game that is lightweight, accessible, and immediately gratifying. There’s no friction between the player and the experience, no unnecessary complications or steep learning curves. That clarity of purpose is one of the reasons why Astrodle succeeds where many indie idle titles stumble—it knows exactly what kind of experience it wants to deliver and doesn’t overreach.

Astrodle’s biggest limitation lies in its longevity. With its core systems easily mastered and its end goals attainable within a relatively short span, it lacks the extended progression curve that keeps some idle games engaging for weeks or months. Once you’ve maxed out your upgrades and ascended through the zodiac, there’s little incentive to continue beyond the pleasure of watching numbers rise. That said, the game’s short and self-contained structure also works in its favor—it’s the kind of title meant to be enjoyed in bursts rather than marathons. It doesn’t demand a long-term commitment but instead offers a compact, feel-good experience that’s satisfying from the moment you start.

Astrodle ultimately succeeds as a light, colorful, and relaxing blend of shooter and idle mechanics that understands the appeal of simplicity. It doesn’t strive for depth or complexity, but it delivers exactly what it promises: a visually pleasing, numerically addictive, and endlessly watchable loop of progress and reward. It’s the sort of game that can be both background noise and a brief obsession, offering bursts of enjoyment that don’t overstay their welcome. For players who enjoy incremental design, satisfying feedback loops, and games that celebrate growth for its own sake, Astrodle is a delightful and polished example of how less can often be more.

Carrier Battles 4 Guadalcanal, developed by Avalon Digital and Cyril Jarnot and published by Avalon Digital, is a deeply immersive and detailed wargame that places players in command of naval and air forces during some of the most pivotal battles of the Pacific Theater in World War II. The game focuses on the intense naval-air combat between the United States and Imperial Japan, specifically from 1942 to 1943, a period marked by high-stakes engagements such as the Battle of the Coral Sea, Midway, and the prolonged Guadalcanal campaign. With a strong emphasis on historical accuracy and strategic depth, this title appeals especially to enthusiasts of classic hex-and-counter wargames and those who appreciate methodical, turn-based planning over fast-paced action.

The gameplay centers around commanding fleets consisting of aircraft carriers, battleships, cruisers, destroyers, and squadrons of reconnaissance and strike aircraft. Each turn presents players with decisions that simulate the real challenges of naval command: launching reconnaissance flights to scout enemy positions, coordinating airstrikes on hostile ships, managing fleet formations, and anticipating enemy moves under the fog of war. The game's intelligence system is particularly noteworthy—it realistically limits the player’s knowledge of enemy fleet composition and location until reconnaissance aircraft have scouted the area, reflecting the uncertainty commanders faced in actual combat. This fog of war mechanic adds a thrilling layer of tension, forcing players to make critical decisions with incomplete information, much like the historic commanders did.

Carrier Battles 4 Guadalcanal shines in its detailed damage and combat resolution system. Ships and aircraft units can suffer partial damage that affects their operational capabilities rather than just being instantly destroyed. This means that damaged vessels might limp back to port, require repairs, or operate at reduced effectiveness, adding nuance to strategic considerations. Players must decide whether to risk pushing forward damaged forces or pull back to preserve their fleet. The careful balancing of aggression and caution makes the game deeply engaging, rewarding patient, well-considered strategies while punishing reckless decisions.

The variety of scenarios offered in the game enhances its replayability and historical depth. Each scenario places players in different tactical and strategic situations, from protecting supply lines to launching surprise attacks on enemy fleets. These scenarios allow players to explore alternative outcomes of well-known battles, testing their command skills against both AI and human opponents. The inclusion of multiplayer functionality, featuring cross-platform play, broadens the appeal by enabling competitive and cooperative engagements with friends or strangers worldwide. Meanwhile, the AI offers a competent challenge for solo players, adjusting to different skill levels and playstyles.

Despite its many strengths, Carrier Battles 4 Guadalcanal does have areas that could be improved. Some players find that extended sessions may lead to a sense of repetition since the core gameplay loop—reconnaissance, fleet positioning, and strike execution—remains consistent across scenarios. Additionally, the absence of submarines, a key element of Pacific naval warfare, has been a point of criticism. Submarines could add an extra strategic dimension, such as stealth attacks and supply interdiction, which are currently not represented. However, the developers have been responsive to player feedback and have indicated plans to include submarines in future updates, which should enrich the gameplay experience further.

In terms of presentation, the game opts for a functional and clear visual style. The hex-based maps are detailed yet uncluttered, allowing players to easily interpret tactical information such as unit positions, damage status, and range of aircraft. While the graphics are not flashy or modern in the conventional sense, they effectively communicate all necessary information and support the gameplay’s emphasis on strategy over spectacle. The sound design and musical score complement the setting without distracting, enhancing immersion subtly.

Overall, Carrier Battles 4 Guadalcanal offers a rewarding and authentic wargaming experience for players fascinated by naval warfare and World War II history. Its careful balance of historical fidelity, strategic complexity, and accessible interface makes it a standout title within its niche. While it may demand patience and thoughtful play, the game’s depth and challenge provide a rich sense of accomplishment for those who invest the time. For fans of methodical, realistic military simulations, it is an essential addition to their collection and a compelling window into one of the most dramatic theaters of naval combat in history.

I bought it expecting maybe a run-of-the-mill beat'em up with a fun Tokusatsu theme. I love King of the Monsters for the SNES so I was generally excited for this even if it was just ok. My only issue with the augments is that it was generally always beneficial to stick with the higher tier augments, so we didn't often have too many to choose from at any given time as we were often getting newer higher tier augments. Still it was a nice addition that helped the gameplay evolve as we went through the story mode.

From the fandom side, we really loved unlocking all the different skins for the characters and trying to figure out what they were references too. Some are definitely more obvious than others. Clearly the developers of this game absolutely love the genre as the whole thing was a big love letter to it.

Space Pilgrim Episode III: Delta Pavonis — это третья часть серии интерактивных приключенческих квестов в жанре визуальных новелл, разработанных компанией Apocalypse Games. Продолжая космическое путешествие, игра предлагает игрокам погрузиться в новую историю, полную загадок, моральных дилемм и интересных персонажей, с сохранением стилистики и духа серии.

Основные особенности
Сюжет и атмосферa
Действия происходят на планете Дельта Павонис — новой таинственной локации, где главный герой сталкивается с неожиданными опасностями и неожиданными открытиями. Сюжет включает исследование заброшенных построек, взаимодействие с местными обитателями и разрешение загадок, связанных с прошлым и тайнами планеты.

Атмосфера сочетает научную фантастику с элементами мистики и психологической драмы. Визуальный стиль — мультяшный, яркий и стилизованный, что создает уютную и одновременно загадочную атмосферу многогранного космического приключения.

Геймплей
Интерактивный квест: перемещение между локациями, сбор предметов, взаимодействие с объектами и персонажами.
Диалоги и выборы: решение моральных дилемм и выбор реплик, которые влияют на развитие сюжета и финал игры.
Исследование и разгадывание загадок: поиск улик, разгадывание головоломок, анализ окружающего мира.
Многообразие финалов: разные решения приводят к различным концовкам, повышая реиграбельность.
Графика и звук
Игра выполнена в ярком мультяшном стиле с аккуратными иллюстрациями персонажей и локаций. Музыкальное сопровождение и звуковые эффекты создают глубокую атмосферу, дополняя сюжетные повороты.

Что выделяет Space Pilgrim Episode III: Delta Pavonis:
Более зрелый и эмоциональный сюжет с глубокими моральными дилеммами.
Несколько концовок, дающих возможность переиграть и исследовать все возможные исходы.
Интуитивный интерфейс и дружелюбный геймплей.
Хорошая балансировка между исследованием, диалогами и загадками.
Недостатки:
Мультяшный стиль не подходит всем; кому-то может показаться слишком простым или стилизованным.
Некоторые головоломки не очень сложные, что может снизить интерес у любителей высокой сложности.
Сюжетные повороты предсказуемы для опытных игроков.
Итог
Space Pilgrim Episode III: Delta Pavonis — это увлекательный и атмосферный интерактивный квест, продолжающий серию с хорошим балансом сюжетных элементов, выбора и исследования. Игра отлично подходит для любителей научной фантастики, моральных дилемм и сюжетных приключений. Если вы цените возможность влиять на развитие истории и получать разные финалы, эта часть станет достойным дополнением к серии.

Humongous Entertainment has wrapped up the trilogy with the vulpid’s most ambitious sequel yet, and while it is nothing revolutionary, it is a good last step for the series.

The antagonist in [i]“Operation Ozone”[/i] is the most outrageous one that I have seen in [i]SPY Fox[/i]: a businessowner so immensely arrogant that she is willing to destroy the earth’s ozone layer just so that she can market more sunscreen. It is all too tempting to suggest that there is some politico-economic commentary underneath this awfully prescient plot, but whether that was intentional or not is another matter. Either way, it fits the stereotypical Saturday morning cartoon mould well.

Most of the characters that SPY Fox meets are new, and if you never tried any of the previous entries, you’ll have no trouble making sense of the story here. New characters include an almost lifeless bowling alley manager, a timid scientist critical to the mission, a bizarre owner of an antiques store, an ambitious worker for a doughnut/pizza shop, and so on. None of the characters is deep, but they are distinguishable and fine for what they are. Many of the jokes are cringeworthy puns unlikely to amuse an ordinary adult, but there were a few other jokes that made me laugh.

Unlike earlier adventures, this sequel has the most locations of the trilogy: North America, South America, Africa, and Eurasia. Although this sounds impressive, in actuality you only get to explore tiny segments of each continent. Even so, it makes for a relatively diverse environment, showing us that Humongous wanted to do something special for this sequel.

As with the earlier adventures, this sequel is easy — maybe even the easiest [i]SPY Fox[/i] to date. There are no mindnumbingly cryptic challenges, but there are a few weird ones, like the one where the protagonist has to sneak a prickly pear past a guard. While it did stump me for several minutes, it did not take ridiculously long for me to put two and two together as I reexamined the backgrounds. In another case where I was stuck, all that I had to do was explore another continent before I figured out what I was supposed to try. Almost everything else is smooth sailing.

I remember feeling a little overwhelmed at the beginning of the adventure, but it only took me two hours to finish it, and I could recomplete it in less than a quarter of that time. As always, Humongous programmed different challenges to appear in the adventure every time that you replay it, which greatly adds to the replayability, so do not let the brief running time discourage you.

Most of the sequel’s problems are the usual suspects, though: [url=https://tcrf.net/Spy_Fox:_Operation_Ozone]content that goes unused partly due to erroneous programming[/url], and subtitles are once again English-only. The only new issue is how slow the interface feels: if SPY Fox has a lot of stuff in his inventory, it can take a few seconds for his Super deep SPY pocket to unfold them all, which can grow tedious when you misclick or apply the wrong item. These are all minor issues, but it is unlikely that anybody is going to officially update this software to address them, which is a bummer.

The sound effects are the same cartoon clichés that we know from previous entries, but they are fine. The voice actors, likewise, all performed adequately (if unremarkably), though some may be disappointed to hear that Gina Nagy (who voiced Monkey Penny) is absent from this sequel. The music is more impressive: there is a diverse plenitude of tracks in this and they are all competent, though I would hesitate to call any of them catchy.

The graphics likewise get the job done: the characters all look fine, but they still suffer from the edgy pixels and want of detail that I mentioned in my other reviews. The backgrounds fare much better, and as always there are plenty of clickpoints that you can activate if you mistake something for a relevant object or merely want to watch the little spectacles unfold. Visual glitches are rare: I noticed that half of SPY Fox’s body repeatedly disappeared as he stared at the small body of water in North America, but other than that the visuals work like they should.

[i]“Operation Ozone”[/i] is another good children’s adventure game and worth getting alone for $7, but even so I strongly advise you to get this as part of the Spy Fox Complete Pack instead as most of the games therein are also worth trying. Knowing that this may well end up being the last official [i]SPY Fox[/i] title that we’ll get can make the experience a little saddening, but I don’t regret a single minute that I spent on this adventure.

Beat Hazard 2 is a music-driven twin-stick shooter that turns your personal soundtrack into explosive gameplay. Developed by Cold Beam Games, it continues the concept of the first Beat Hazard—every song you play dynamically shapes enemy behavior, weapon strength, and visual intensity. It’s a seamless fusion of rhythm and arcade shooting, making your music collection the core of the experience.

The gameplay is simple but hypnotic. You pilot a small ship, blasting enemies and collecting power-ups while your firepower rises and falls with the beat. Fast songs create chaotic waves of enemies and blinding particle storms, while slower tracks offer calmer, more deliberate pacing. The system rewards timing and situational awareness rather than memorization, keeping every session unpredictable.

Visually, the game is a light show. Bright colors, lens flares, and pulsing effects dominate the screen, perfectly synced to the rhythm. The visual overload is part of its identity—beautiful but almost too much at times. The developers added more control over the intensity of the effects, allowing players to reduce visual noise if it becomes overwhelming.

Compared to the original, Beat Hazard 2 improves both technically and mechanically. The new rendering engine delivers sharper visuals, smoother framerates, and deeper color contrast. The beat detection algorithm is also more accurate, syncing player firepower and enemy patterns more tightly with the music. It feels faster and cleaner overall.

Music integration is versatile. You can play songs from your local files or from streaming platforms like Spotify, which greatly expands the variety of experiences. Each track becomes a level, and the game’s algorithm translates volume, tempo, and rhythm data into procedural gameplay that feels handcrafted for each song.

The progression system offers unlockable ships, upgrades, and perks that give the player meaningful goals beyond just scoring high. These additions make the game feel more structured without losing the freeform creativity of its music-driven design.

Overall, Beat Hazard 2 is an intense and innovative shooter that perfectly captures the energy of your music. It doesn’t reinvent the series but refines it into a smoother, more polished experience. For players who enjoy rhythm-based games and pure visual chaos, it remains one of the most satisfying ways to play your music rather than just listen to it.

Zipp’s Café короткая, но уютная визуальная новелла с элементами кафе-симулятора от авторов Chicken Police. За пару часов ты проживаешь историю енота Зиппа, бывшего бандюги, который теперь заваривает кофе вместо махинаций. Атмосфера сплошной нуар и самоирония, а для тех, кто играл в Chicken Police, тут куча отсылок: упоминается Улей, появляются знакомые морды вроде лиса Моисея. Даже я, проходившая только демку второй части, ловила кайф от этих мелочей. 

Геймплей простенький: болтаешь с клиентами, готовишь им кофе, яичницу и хот-доги через мини-игры. Всё приятно оформлено, но со временем немного однообразно. Особенно раздражает интерфейс рецепты напитков спрятаны в меню, а на экране полно свободного места, где их можно было бы вывести. Один раз запуталась с комбинированными напитками, но быстро разобралась. Зато можно переигрывать неудачные попытки, что приятно. 

Сюжет есть, но больше как предлог побыть в мире Chicken Police: немного меланхолии, немного романтики и разговоров о прошлом. В целом лёгкий, короткий вечерний релакс. Графика красивая, саундтрек уютный, герои с характером. За цену в 165 рублей вообще отличная покупка. Если бы стоила дороже, уже можно было бы покритиковать, но за эти деньги маст-хэв. 

Итог: классная, атмосферная, но короткая история. Не ради геймплея, а ради настроения. Для фанатов мира Chicken Police must play. Остальным просто приятная чашка кофе на вечер.

For full context, play time is around an hour and I got to the end of stage four. Big Fightn'Rage and Streets of Rage 4 fan, along with older beat'em ups. Played on Normal mode, didn't even go to the options menu until after I stopped. Double Dragon Neon and River City Girls also come to mind on what I'm used to.

I dig the music, it's pretty rocking. Sadly, I don't care for the rest of the game. The move sets are pretty basic which isn't a bad thing in of itself, The gun doesn't really do much for me because it doesn't deal more damage than a standard hit. The enemy variety is there but outside of how their attacks look I can't understand what makes them different. In the two above mentioned games, enemy variety is upfront and center to the point you really need to focus on dynamics when facing a crowd. In this, you have different models and names but almost nothing stands out except for when they feel like attacking.

On the topic of enemies attacking, I've left my back open plenty of times and I'll see foes meander around without going in to attack. Maybe it's because it was on normal mode but that felt really weird to me. Enemies are durable but they really don't do a lot about it. The Breaker guys especially will block your entire combo except the last hit and that's... kinda it. The quickest option is to just grab and knee him four times per grab. Will take you maybe three or four grabs.

I really am not the sort to rag on graphics because I grew up playing ASCII roguelikes. I'm not a shallow man. That said, the animations and graphics just look odd to me. Maybe its the frame rate they're at or that they seem stiff but something about it is off to me.

When it came to the two bosses I fought, I used the game's Rage Mode to basically erase them without really learning any movesets. The first boss had grenades blowing up all at once which blasted through my speakers, that wasn't fun. Second boss... he was there. He shot me a few times because the super mode took off around 90% of his HP except for his i-frame stances that made him immune to damage.

You can argue it's not much of a gripe but I also don't care for how, when you pause, your only option is to quit or continue. When you realize how common grenades are and how badly they'll assault you through sound, you're going to have to alt-tab out or lower your speaker volume a ton. There are many grenades. As well as grenades, items are dropping all the time but they're random baubles that increase your score or give you ammo for your sidearm. I didn't die though I came close in the fourth level, just for a burger to pop out for a full refresh. I don't know if they're randomized or come out at specific points but healing items aren't so rare.

Again, I dig some of the ideas and got to touch on the driving game mode. I dig that a lot. The rest of it... I just don't. It feels too weird. It feels very stiff for what it is and the enemies aren't really taking it seriously. It could be because I was on normal and am used to other games going hard. If you want something that is a side-scroller and really gets you going beyond just music, go with any of the above mentioned titles.

Engaging co-op experience

I went into The Cult of the Child Eater with curiosity, and I've been pleasantly surprised by how much fun this game delivers even in it's early access state, especially when playing with friends.

The teamwork mechanics are where this game really shines. Each character has distinct abilities that complement each other, and you genuinely need to coordinate to overcome the tougher challenges. Whether it's one person distracting enemies while another solves puzzles, timing your attacks perfectly during enemy encounters, or telling the puzzle clues you've just found over a walkie-talkie to you mates, the game rewards good communication and planning. Playing with randoms can be hit-or-miss, but get a solid group together and you'll have a blast.

The atmosphere is appropriately creepy without being overwhelming, and the progression system keeps you coming back for more. The difficulty curve is well-balanced: challenging enough to feel rewarding when you succeed, but not so punishing that you want to quit.

Sure, it has some rough edges here and there (remember, it's early access), but nothing to write home about. It's fresh, it's creative, sometimes even funny, and for the price point, it's a solid co-op experience that delivers on its core promise. If you've got a group looking for something different to play together, this is definetely worth picking up.

Recommended for co-op enthusiasts looking for a sufficiently spooky team-based adventure.

Later, I switched to Xbox and couldn’t play it for years until I found out it was available on Steam. I bought it right away and have been playing it a lot since. The only issue I have with this game is that the missions aren’t very friendly for people with learning disorders or autism. For me personally, the missions often don’t make much sense and require extra, complicated steps to complete. That’s one of the reasons I’ve slowly started to stop playing. Still, it’s such a beautiful and nostalgic game for me. It’s one I’ll remember for the rest of my life because it genuinely helped shape my childhood. I love all of its mechanics. you can fish, feed animals, decorate areas, clear murk, and explore freely. It even reminds me a little of Genshin Impact. It’s a great game for kids and also perfect for relaxing after a long day. I love the sunsets and the scenery, which are absolutely stunning, and there are so many places to explore. You can customize your character, collect items and plants, mine stone, cut trees, and grow things. It’s amazing, and I highly recommend it. I just wish it had a multiplayer option.

Лиги, Гильдии, битвы между гильдиями, глобальный рейтинг, ежедневные задания, тщательная группировка и изменение колоды карт, огромное количество карт персонажей. Все это доступно бесплатно и сбалансировано. Премиум покупки не дают перевеса, но дают взглянуть на игру по новому.

Simple yet surprsingly fun, Astral Heroes brings all of the enjoyment of an online CCG without all the bells and whistles of more popular games like TES Legends, Hearthstone or Eternal. If you have a slower PC or you just find games like Hex and MtG too complex, this is the game for you. The fast paced gameplay and non-ptw style will provide you with hours of fun.

When you start off the game progression moves at a proper rate.  However, I have noticed a bottleneck once you hit 8 or so hours in. Makes it a little less exciting to keep playing, considering all the really good CCGs/TCGs that have recently been released.

This game has its place in the card game genere, but it's in a very narrow niche. For my time/money I choose to play the other games listed above, but you should definitly givee this one a shot and see if it's a good match.  

Rate:: 6.5/10

Otro gran producto de Terarin, que una vez más ha estudiado a fondo cómo trasladar las antiguas mecánicas de puntuación del mundo Caravan de Hudson, a un horizontal con la velocidad característica de Thunder Force III (y toda aquella hornada de shmups horizontales que imitaron a dicha saga). Podríamos hablar de una simplificación, muestra o disección de segmentos característicos de TF III con un poco de inventiva propia. Por cierto, admirable la velocidad de hacer juegos que tiene este hombre y sin hacer nunca juegos mediocres.

El resultado es una aventura repleta de posibilidades para lucirse a puntos, pero que no es tan llamativa o tan redonda en la ejecución de las rutinas o diseño de niveles, que es bastante más que correcto pero sin llegar a la excelencia. En ese sentido creo que Moon Dancer es su techo (por ahora), y diría que es mejor haciendo verticales que horizontales, incidiendo en que esto que ha hecho aquí sigue siendo notable. De hecho el caravan está bien, pero no tan bien como otros de sus juegos. 

Tenemos tres armas que pueden mejorar globalmente hasta nivel 3 (arma teledirigida, arma delantera y trasera), además del sistema de Charge o Carga, que me ha llamado mucho la atención: consiste en dejar de disparar para que nuestro poder aumente, siempre y cuando llevemos con nosotros los options o ayudantes. Un sistema que te obliga a estudiar las oleadas y a dejar de disparar durante ciertos momentos de los jefes. 

Buena música y un buen aspecto; quizá demasiado rápido en scrolls, y creo que tampoco era necesario mostrar esa velocidad (sabemos a quién quiere homenajear, pero considero que puede entorpecer a nuevos jugadores). Beat Hazard is a twin-stick shooter that merges your music library with arcade-style combat. Developed by Cold Beam Games, it introduced a fresh concept where every song becomes a unique level. The gameplay, enemy patterns, and weapon intensity all react to the rhythm, volume, and tempo of the track playing, turning music into an unpredictable and personal challenge.

The core mechanic is simple: you control a small ship, shoot enemies, collect power-ups, and survive waves of attacks. What sets Beat Hazard apart is how your firepower and the behavior of enemies synchronize with your music. When the track intensifies, so does the action; when it slows down, combat eases. The result is a seamless mix of rhythm and reflex-based gameplay.

Visually, the game is a sensory overload. Explosions, flashes, and particle effects pulse in time with the music, creating a hypnotic but chaotic light show. It can be dazzling or disorienting depending on your tolerance for constant visual noise. Despite being a small indie project, the presentation is bold and memorable, standing out for its energy and atmosphere.

The soundtrack system is the real innovation. You can import your own MP3 files, meaning every song you own becomes potential gameplay. The procedural generation system interprets each track differently, translating beats into enemy waves and drops into bursts of power. This personalization gives the game limitless replayability.

The controls are responsive and intuitive, following the standard twin-stick format. Movement is smooth, aiming feels precise, and difficulty scales naturally with the music’s intensity. While enemy design is fairly simple, the music-reactive system keeps encounters engaging.

Technically, Beat Hazard runs efficiently even on modest systems. It’s lightweight but visually rich, and the performance rarely dips despite the heavy effects. The biggest limitation is that its gameplay depth relies entirely on your song selection—long tracks and diverse genres create more interesting experiences than repetitive or quiet music.

In summary, Beat Hazard is a creative blend of rhythm and shooting that laid the foundation for its sequels. It’s simple in structure but endlessly replayable thanks to its music-driven design. For players who enjoy high-energy visuals and personalized challenges, it remains one of the most original indie shooters of its generation.

There is some silly fun to be had here, and especially with Steam Remote play you might get a couple of hours of fun just goofing around with friends, but there is no reason to return to the game after that.
I doubt it will happen, but I'd love to see the devs return to the game and actually finish it, as I think the core concept is surprisingly solid. However, I can't recommend it in it's current state.

这个CEO我当定了！developed by 叁石肆两 and published in collaboration with Liquid Meow, is an interactive full-motion video game that immerses players in the turbulent world of corporate ambition, power struggles, and personal choice. The story follows Lin Ran, a recent graduate who steps into the dazzling yet perilous environment of a major corporation, determined to climb the ladder and make a name for himself. From the moment the game begins, it establishes a tone that is both sleek and dramatic, drawing inspiration from workplace dramas while blending it with the tension and branching decision-making typical of interactive visual novels. It’s a game that places the player not in a fantasy realm of magic or warfare, but in the all-too-familiar battlefield of office politics, where every smile hides a motive and every decision can make or break a career.

What immediately distinguishes 这个CEO我当定了！from most indie visual novels is its use of full-motion video to tell the story. Every scene unfolds through live-action footage, with real actors performing in vividly shot corporate settings—from meeting rooms and lavish offices to smoky bars where secret deals take place. The production values are surprisingly high, with professional cinematography and a cast that delivers convincing performances. Each character embodies a distinct archetype: the charismatic yet manipulative CEO, the ambitious rival, the charming but dangerous HR manager, and the well-meaning colleagues who may or may not be what they seem. The game’s visual direction and acting are confident enough to carry its narrative, making it feel less like a traditional game and more like an interactive drama where your choices subtly shape the outcome. The feeling of immersion is strong; you don’t just watch Lin Ran’s story—you influence it.

Gameplay focuses almost entirely on player choice. The interface is minimalist, presenting dialogue options and moral decisions that steer the narrative in different directions. At key points, the player decides whether Lin Ran plays it safe, challenges authority, or risks everything to advance his position. Some choices concern career ambitions—whether to support a superior’s questionable proposal or expose it—while others delve into interpersonal relationships, including moments of trust, betrayal, or emotional entanglement. The consequences of each decision unfold through branching storylines that lead to multiple endings. While some paths feel more rewarding than others, the cumulative experience highlights the complexity of navigating ambition in a world where loyalty and self-preservation constantly clash. The game doesn’t rely on traditional mechanics or puzzles; instead, its power lies in the moral weight of its choices and the realism of its corporate scenarios.

Visually, the game’s attention to presentation is one of its most striking aspects. The camera work is cinematic, using close-ups, soft lighting, and measured pacing to convey tension and intimacy. Boardroom meetings are framed like battles, with subtle shifts in body language and tone replacing sword clashes. The color palette mirrors the story’s shifting emotional temperature—warm, inviting hues in the beginning, gradually replaced by cooler tones as deception and ambition take hold. The sound design complements this, with a subdued score that punctuates key moments without overwhelming them. Voice performances are strong across the board, particularly the portrayal of the HR director, whose layered expressions and carefully modulated tone have been singled out by many players as a highlight. Together, these elements give the game an authenticity that elevates it beyond the typical FMV experience.

Narratively, the game’s themes of power, integrity, and ambition are its backbone. It explores the moral compromises people make when pursuing success and the personal costs of playing the corporate game. Lin Ran’s journey mirrors that of countless young professionals who enter the workforce full of hope, only to be tested by manipulation, inequality, and the unspoken rules of hierarchy. The writing captures the nuances of modern office life with sharp dialogue and realistic conflict. Beneath the polished veneer of professionalism lies a study of human behavior—how ambition can corrupt, how kindness can be exploited, and how the façade of teamwork often conceals personal agendas. It’s a story that resonates because it’s grounded in truth. There’s no supernatural twist or fantasy escape here; the tension comes from human interaction and the ever-present pressure to succeed.

Despite its strengths, 这个CEO我当定了！is not without its flaws. Its biggest limitation is its brevity—most players can reach one of the endings within two hours, and while there are multiple routes, the overall structure remains linear. The choices, though engaging, sometimes lead to outcomes that feel more cosmetic than transformative. Some reviewers have noted minor technical inconsistencies, such as subtitle timing and limited menu options, which slightly detract from the otherwise smooth presentation. The game’s format also makes it more of a cinematic experience than a traditional game, meaning those seeking complex systems or extended replayability might find it lacking in depth. Yet for what it aims to be—a polished, story-driven experience about moral choices in a high-stakes corporate setting—it accomplishes its goals with confidence.

Ultimately, 这个CEO我当定了！stands out as an ambitious and stylish entry in the growing field of Chinese FMV storytelling. It succeeds in capturing the allure and toxicity of corporate culture with both flair and empathy. Its performances, cinematography, and branching choices create an immersive and emotionally charged experience that bridges the gap between television drama and interactive fiction. Though short, it leaves a lasting impression, encouraging players to reflect on what it truly means to chase power—and what must be sacrificed along the way. For fans of narrative-driven games or anyone intrigued by the concept of interactive cinema, this title offers a refreshing and mature exploration of ambition, morality, and survival in the modern workplace.

I really wanted to give this game a chance and like it but alas I don't think I can recommend this game.

First off the lack of custom controls was frustrating and I ended up using reWasd to rebind my controls. For future reference, default keyboard controls for platformers are generally z jump x attack. Never never use space bar for jump.

The music frequently glitched in areas that used to have music but then no music. According to sound/music guy it's not a bug but it seems like one to me.

What you see in the demo contains pretty much ALL of the enemies in the game. Which is a huge turn off. Maybe 1 or 2 is missing max. There are 0 bosses in the game. Zero. Not even a last boss.

The way the game challenges you generally is to mash a bunch of trash mobs in the same room and make you kill them. But if you are also hit on the edge of the door, the knockback makes you teleport across the door. This happened to me two times. At the end of the game it introduces some slight additional mechanics to the trash mob fights but not really that much different except one room is almost impossible not to get hit and is a matter of face tanking and killing the mob.

The only soul like thing about the game is the healing pots take like 3 seconds to use and just the existence of a roll/dodge button which pretty much if that's the defining feature of a souls like game then most platformers could be considered souls like. Each enemy only has like one or two attacks which makes them very easy to kill once you know what those are. Seems like the users who tagged the game as souls like and the other reviewers claiming this is playing this type of game for the first time. Combat challenging? Not really because aforementioned each enemy is linear with 1 or 2 attacks with basically the same timing. The reason why the Dark Souls series is hard to most people is because you have to dodge attacks which require observation. There are slow and fast attacks mixed in so there are a lot of animations to keep track of. You don't have to do that in this game because the moment you see an animation you dodge because they instantly attack. It's really simple.

I did like that you don't really button mash to kill mobs because that gets you killed. But due to the lack of variation the combat is pretty lacking. I liked how every mob in the game had a different strategy to kill them.  Non-button mashing combat should be a given in any decent game though.

The exploration was fun briefly but since there is a lack of interesting upgrades, lack of any real danger, any real bosses or exploration value there wasn't much incentive and fun after a while. 

The game does not have any replay value. At the very least the way some games achieve replay value is through the achievements but it doesn't seem like there are any additional challenges either. No reward for finding all the optional exploration tokens other than the achievement which is lame.

Also, the credits was super awkward - developer should just delete the last section of it and not thank the player for playing 100 times and repeat the email over and over again with slowly disappearing and reappearing text.

If there were more enemy types or boss fights I might have been able to recommend this, but nope. Overall can't recommend this.

I'm not completely done with this game (I just unlocked the funal area), but what so far I had a pretty good time with it. What really appreciate about this game is how well it manages to differentiate its enemies. The game also feels really nice to control and offers a bunch of different movement and combat options that help you not only to deal with the various encounters, but also make moving through the space interesting and varied.

A last thing i really appreciate is how well Frauki's Adventure manages to create an interconnected space that rarely forces you to backtrack for a long time. It's a bit unfortunate, that there's only one checkpoint so to speak, but you quickly get anywhere you need to be and it's to discover how areas of the game loop into one another.

As I said, I really enjoyed my time with it and if you're into combat-focused exploration games, i think you savely pick this one up.

The game is a hidden gem and quite innovative in its sub-genre that combines deck-building with tactical combat.

+ Setting, atmosphere and world-building are great, the mix sci-fi / horror is quite a rare combo and it is excellently executed here
+ The pixel-art graphics for units, cards, transitions and boss intro animations are superb, an obvious labour of talent and love
+ The combat is extremely satisfying combining tactical placement / movement of your ships and card combos from a wide variety of types
+ There is meta progression done very well with well-paced unlocking of new characters, ships, cards and lore

= The game has decent replayability value; could do with a couple more enemy types and at least one more boss per act
= With a couple of exceptions, chaos relics are very weak (i.e. their effects are negligible)

Cons:
- Not every game mechanic is perfectly explained, some will have to be learned via trial & error (e.g. rifts and keys, faction upgrades & card unlocks)
- Music, while well suited and atmospheric, could be a bit more present, more varied and dynamic
- Difficulty curve raises sharply after the first act. Expect serious balancing issues through acts 2, 3 and 4
- No cloud saving
