No Way Home is a vibrant and energetic twin-stick shooter that blends exploration, fast-paced combat, and lighthearted storytelling into an accessible space adventure. Developed and published by SMG Studio, the game opens with a simple but charming premise: your character, Cho, crash-lands in an unknown star system far from Earth, armed with nothing but determination and the help of a quirky robotic companion named Matey. This setup frames a journey through a bright, comic-styled universe full of strange planets, oddball alien species, and a surprising mix of handcrafted and procedurally generated encounters. While the narrative doesn’t aim for dramatic emotional stakes, the tone is consistently playful, giving the game a personality that helps it stand apart from more serious sci-fi shooters.

Moment-to-moment gameplay is where No Way Home shines most. The twin-stick controls feel intuitive and responsive, letting you dodge enemy fire while unloading a barrage of shots in any direction. A notable feature is the grappling hook, which adds an unusual layer of movement and environmental manipulation—you can tug objects, reposition hazards, or pull yourself into safer spots mid-battle. Combat is deliberately chaotic but never unreadable, thanks to clean visual design and well-defined enemy silhouettes. Over time, you collect more than fifty weapons ranging from traditional blasters to stranger, more experimental tools, and your ship can be upgraded across multiple systems. This variety gives each run a satisfying sense of growth as you refine your loadout and adapt your tactics to the escalating threats scattered across the starmap.

Exploration complements the combat without overwhelming it. The galaxy is divided into sectors that blend procedural layouts with scripted story missions, optional contracts, and surprise encounters. Each sector offers new loot, new enemies, and different environmental hazards that encourage you to experiment with your equipment. The game balances freedom and structure effectively: you can pursue the main storyline, take on side missions for extra rewards, or simply drift through space to see what unusual characters or secrets you uncover. It’s not a fully open-world experience, but the sense of discovery is strong enough to keep you moving from system to system, gathering materials, crafting upgrades, and improving both Cho’s ship and Matey’s support functions.

Visually, No Way Home embraces a colorful comic-book style that pairs sharp outlines with vivid palettes. This helps maintain clarity during busy battles, but it also contributes to the game’s light comedic tone. Aliens are expressive, environments are lively, and even the UI carries a sense of personality. Sound design supports the action with punchy effects and an upbeat soundtrack that keeps the momentum going without overpowering the experience. Together, these elements create an inviting atmosphere that makes even the more frantic battles feel fun rather than exhausting. It’s a world designed to be enjoyed rather than brooded over, and the presentation plays a major role in that appeal.

For all its charm, No Way Home does have limitations. The progression, while satisfying in the early and mid-game, begins to feel familiar as the hours pass. Many mission types repeat, and some procedural sectors echo each other in structure. The combat remains enjoyable, but players who prefer systems that continually evolve may notice that the core mechanics change more in intensity than in complexity. The story, though humorous and engaging, doesn’t escalate into anything deeper than a light adventure, which may leave narrative-focused players wanting more. Yet none of these issues undermine the game’s core strengths—they simply reflect the scope of a title designed around immediacy and fun rather than expansive RPG depth.

Ultimately, No Way Home succeeds by knowing exactly what it wants to be: an upbeat, fast-paced shooter filled with personality, satisfying combat, and enough exploration to keep the experience fresh without weighing it down. It’s a game for players who enjoy responsive twin-stick action, colorful sci-fi worlds, and a steady supply of new weapons and upgrades to experiment with. Its charm, humor, and strong sense of style make it easy to enjoy in short bursts or longer sessions, and its accessible controls make it welcoming for newcomers to the genre. While it may not offer the complexity or narrative weight of larger space adventures, it delivers a polished and consistently entertaining journey through a universe that never takes itself too seriously.

PaperKlay est un jeu correct, qui plaira sans doute davantage à un jeune public qu'aux mordus de collectathons ayant écumés les Banjo-Kazooie et consorts. C'est aussi un jeu qui m'a fait penser aux nombreux jeux de plateformes corrects du début des années 2000.

En bons points, le gameplay de base reprend les classiques du genre et s'en sort globalement bien, j'aime le design de certains personnages et quelques idées de gameplay (les vis à tourner pour révéler la suite du niveau, l'aspect carton des décors, les bouts de niveau que l'on fait tourner) et le jeu se révèle être plaisant à parcourir de part sa difficulté assez basse et le fait qu'on alterne entre hub à explorer, niveaux linéaires et petits niveaux bonus à la Capitaine Toad.

En revanche, je trouve les niveaux trop longs, ils auraient mérités d'être découpé en deux actes, surtout lorsqu'on fait la chasse au 100% et qu'on parcourt à nouveau un niveau pendant 15-20 minutes pour trouver les deux boutons (sur 200 voire 350) qui nous manquait. Le jeu manque aussi de renouvellement, car l'essentiel des idées se trouvent dans le 1er hub et les premiers niveaux malheureusement, et le système de badge ne nous fait pas vraiment apprendre de nouveaux mouvements comme pouvait le faire un Banjo. La bande-son est parfois aussi un peu énervante, à vouloir singer Banjo (encore lui) et ses instruments parfois étranges. Enfin, comme beaucoup de jeux indés, il se fait trop bavard avec des doublages de qualité variable.

Néanmoins j'ai passé un bon moment sur ce jeu, qui ne révolutionne rien et qui peut tout à fait occuper un week-end tranquillement, si tant est que l'on sait dans quoi on s'aventure.

果然还得是十年前的日式RPG啊，一边走在那条无人的山路上，一边听着蝉鸣和风声，简直梦回雏见泽。

这个故事给我最强的感受不是恐怖本身，而是一种奇妙的、说不清楚的懐かしさ。比起什么猎奇解谜，我反而更像是在体验某种消失的乡村日常：钓鱼、盖章、在暮色下的小路奔跑。说实话，与其说这是个恐怖RPG，我更愿意称它是个夏日记忆模拟器，虽然我明明是在城市的夜里对着电子屏幕玩的（笑）。

然后是子狩鬼的设定。设定本身是真的好，有种深藏于地方传说中的沉重与哀伤，那种“原本可以成为一段悲歌”的感觉，但最终却只是作为一个机制意义上的Boss被推进剧情。她的过去，她的痛苦，都只是被淡淡带过，好像不值得更多停留似的。明明是可以写得更深的，真的可惜了。

最后必须要提一下本作阳光治愈担当：诗织。那种从她身上流淌出来的温暖和纯粹，真的像一团小太阳（不禁让人想起小艾，一样的笑容，一样的坚定）。她是这个压抑的村庄中为数不多让人真正感到安心的存在。虽然有5个BE，至少唯一的一个HE是让人真正释怀的。めでたしめでたし～

If you can get the game on a sale go for it. There's a lot to love in this game, and I won't say I hated playing it. However there are some glaring issues with it that can't be overlooked. If there was a "meh" option for recommendations I'd have chosen that.

Moving around the maps can be kinda difficult. Everything about this game is slow, and while that works well to get the feel of Hellboy, it just doesn't work for moving long distances, There is no map so trying to remember where the exit is can be a pain in the ass when going back for unopened rooms. It's like you're moving through mud blind, and that just takes you out of the experience. 

You have to play through every map 3 different times fully to beat the game. I'm not talking about three runs in a row. You have to beat all the of the maps once, then after that beat them all again(this time 2x as there's an added 2nd level to each one), then finally beat them all again. This gets old fast as there really isn't much of a change between the runs aside from each Zone has it's own enemies. This is honestly the main reason I can't recommend it I got so tired of doing the same levels over and over again and progression wasn't felt. I just got tired of it and quit.

Also, and this is minor, the tutorials will always re-enable when you open the game. I don't know why, but it got me killed a few times cause the button to clear the text box is a combat button. It was kind of irritating.

With all that said, there is some good here. 
- Lance Reddick as Hellboy? Perfect. The other actors? honestly also kinda perfect, no one felt out of place.
- The art design was perfect. It felt like playing a comic. 100% would play more games this style.
- Fighting felt good. I felt like I was swinging big every time. It very much matched Hellboy's style and feel in the game, and that feeling is always a win.
-Punching Nazis!!! Always fun.
- The story was pretty good also. It really did feel like a comic story line.

This felt like a ok first roguelike. While I don't fully recommend it, I will still be looking out for more games by the devs to see how they evolve.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
This is a story-based game, generally in the vein of a Maniac Mansion/Monkey Island/Telltale Games story, but placed on repeat, befitting the Groundhog Day premise. The single day has seven possible scenes, of which you typically explore up to six on any given day, depending on your choices.

The primary gameplay mechanic is selecting floating bubbles that determine Phil Jr's general intent of what to say. Mostly it aligns, though sometimes the actual script is slightly unexpected. As you play through the day again, new bubbles become available, opening different actions for the scenes.

Six minigames pepper the story on occasion: a cooking minigame (think Job Simulator), a shooting minigame, a spray painting minigame, a dancing minigame, a stone chopping minigame, and a guitar playing minigame. A seventh, apparently cut, drawing minigame still has its mechanics in the game, as well as a lampshade about how they spent the effort implementing it.

Each minigame is basic, generally works, but is not fleshed out enough to warrant any kind of replay value. The main story requires "passing" each minigame challenge, which typically boils down to replaying the game with slightly increasing levels of difficulty until you succeed. This is supposed to represent Phil Jr achieving mastery over the given skill.

An additional control is opened up after the first day, allowing you to select whether to replay the entire day, or just a specific scene. The scene restart in particular is an excellent addition and essentially works as if you restarted the day and made the same choices leading up to the start of the scene. New dialog options may be available, allowing a quick exploration of a particular character's storyline.

Controls are similar to Vacation Simulator. You can teleport around the scenes (albeit to very limited areas), and interact with objects to a varying degree. Object controls are workable but not excellent, and especially throwing items or releasing items results in unpredictable behaviour, sometimes requiring restarting the scene.

I used the Valve Index headset, and Index controllers to play the game. Headset support was excellent. The controllers had basic functionality (no finger tracking). Crucially, however, the virtual hands did not align with my actual hands, leading to awkward hand bending.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The storyline is pretty much as expected. Our unlikeable protagonist, Phil Jr, for some reason has a following and is working his way up a career in broadcasting. He hates Punxsutawney, would nothing rather than leave, is rude and dismissive of everyone he meets, and is stuck in the town because of a snowstorm. 

As the single day repeats, Phil Jr slowly learns to listen to other people and their concerns, becomes less snarky and rude, and tries to make the best of every day. Unfortunately, that means he goes from incessantly snarky to incessantly optimistic by the end.

Overall, the story is enjoyable, although it sometimes feels cut short. Phil Jr goes from grumpy to "I have to better myself" in just a couple of time loops, and the game completely misses the ability to wreak havoc on the town. Towards the end though I couldn't help but care a little bit about the characters, especially how they progressed in their own little stories.

As you go through major story beats, you're further rewarded with an additional between-day cutscene of memories with Phil Sr, showing the father-son relationship in three disjoint points in time. It is a nice touch, although it is not too substantive.

One major unexplored part of the story itself is the time skipping itself. [spoiler]Phil Jr seems more grumpy than amazed or depressed at the reliving of the day part. His mother is aware of the time loops and prods him to become a better person, and, surprisingly, he just ups and does it. There is no moral concern over whether it's okay to use the time loops to pry people's secrets out. Equally unrealistic is the characters' reaction to hearing this story -- which Phil Jr happily shares. Nobody seems to mind that he has seen all their secrets and done things they don't know about to them.

This omission takes some depth out of the story. One of the strengths of the movie was that it allowed its protagonist to sink into the darkest depths of his psyche, see the emptiness and loneliness therein, and therefore change and become better. To me this is the primary reason why Phil Jr's change seems more that it's "because the plot demands it" rather than "he realised".[/spoiler]

[h1]Sound & Visuals[/h1]
Audio design of the game is reasonably good. There are plenty of background sounds, and even background coversations to eavesdrop on, making each scene appear reasonably lively. There are various radios throughout, which thankfully can be shut off as the repetition of any one scene has a tendency to become nerve-grating. 

The visuals are a bit of a letdown. The characters themselves are unique, but exhibit a bobblehead effect when talking. The characters didn't really capture my attention too much when speaking, which is a bit awkward. Thankfully they don't care that I fiddled with my phone while they're talking. The environment visuals are decent, however, and the environments -- when interactible -- reacted okay enough to it.

Mystery Case Files: Black Crown is the newest game of the series to hit Steam, and once more you step into the shoes of the Master Detective.  This time, you are called to an isolated asylum to unravel the mystery of a mute girl and the obsession she has with the so called Black Crown.  Of course, as soon as you arrive, you find yourself embroiled in more supernatural shennanigans.

Plot/Story:
As with a lot of the newer Mystery Case Files games, the story is definitely serviceable, but nothing really outstanding.  

This is a shame because I appreciate the fact that it wasn't tied into the Delimar/Ravenhearst storylines.  For the curious, it actually has ties to [spoiler] Mystery Case Files: 13th Skull[/spoiler]

Unfortunately, the game doesn't really explore these connections than other on a superficial level.  For one thing, the ending of [spoiler]13 Skulls[/spoiler] was rather...final...so in a sense this game causes yet another retcon to the series as a whole.  Mind you, this is one detail that could be easily addressed, but really isn't.

Visuals:
Once again, the visuals are serviceable, but nothing really stands out.  In fact, many HoGs often have a map for quick travel, but I didn't need it for this.  

However, I personally give this game a slight thumbs down on visuals.  The reason?  As I mentioned, this game ties into an earlier Mystery Case File...and there, the people were actually living actors, and it gave an FMV feel to the game (many of the case files of the time did it).  So when they showed snippets from that game...and then stuck to just the drawings in this game, I found it jarring, and actually struck me as them being to cheap to put in some extra effort.


Gameplay:
As a Hidden Object Game, it naturally has Hidden Object Screens.  At least some of the screens mix it up a little such as some items requiring a step or two to reveal, and other such small variations.  

There are also the usual assortment of logic puzzles ranging from easy to difficult, but pretty much old hat for any seasoned player of a Hidden Object Game.  Lately, the current developers of the series have tried to bring back larger, more involved puzzles.  In previous games they can be obtuse, but in this game they felt about right.  

As with recent HoGs, it also has two 'hidden' things on each screen; a morphing object and a crab.  Finding all of them can unlock a few things in the extras section.

If you run into problems, you can always use the Hint button to find what you should do next, or to skip a puzzle entirely.

Sound/Music:
The game has some limited voice acting which fit the game for the most part.  I'm just glad the voice actors didn't sound like they were bored and gave a wooden reading from the script.

The music also works for the game, and since this is the collector's edition, you can listen to it separately.  However, nothing really stood out so this feature would be wasted on me.

Difficulty:
This game has 4 difficulty settings, with three being Casual, Normal and Hard.  The fourth setting actually allows for personal customization such as how fast it takes to recharge the hint system or to skip a puzzle that is too difficult.

Extras/Achievements:
This game has a bonus chapter when you complete the base game.  It doesn't take long to finish, and unfortunately, it also showed that FMV/current art dissonance I mentioned above.

The game also has Achievements for those who care about it, but none of them are linked to Steam.  


Miscellaneous:
This game managed to avoid two of the biggest pet peeves a lot of recent entries in the series often display.  

The first is the Mystery Detective themselves.  This game essentially had a genderless Master Detective.  This may not seem like a big deal, but some earlier games they let you choose gender, the Madame Fate game showed the detective as female (and what I tend to think of 'my detective being', and yet another went with a male.  The previous game actually mixed the two together (one NPC calling the detective him...and yet falling had a female scream).

The other thing is this game didn't go to far for on the 'we need to find a knife/dagger/broken glass/metal shard/etc.' trope to cut stuff up.  Eipix can occasionally get ridiculous with this; one game they worked on had 10 tasks which were essentially the same thing.  Obviously playing an HoG requires a bit of suspension of disbelief, but when it goes to that extreme, I can't help but think 'damn it, just start carrying a knife with you on future cases.'

The game can also be a little heavy-handed on backtracking.  Once again, it is a hallmark of the genre, but sometimes it feels like to much of a time sink.  

Recommendation:
So would I recommend this game?  Actually, yes.  I know I've seen the highs and lows of the Mystery Detective series (even wrote some reviews of them), but this seems to be a middling of the road entry to the series.

However, if you decide to get it, I would wait for it to go on sale.  What is presented here is hard to recommend at full price except for the most die hard fan of the series.

This is a solid logic puzzle game. There's no point where you're forced to guess what the answer might be, the hints will all point to the answer if you can figure it out. There is a little campaign mode. I blew through that quickly. What I spend most of my time playing is the free play mode-endless puzzles and replayability. The puzzles are randomly generated and all of them are solvable. Some puzzles are harder than others, and I don't mind the challenge. I played the demo of this game and got hooked. If you're on the fence about this game, grab the demo and try out the free play mode. If you enjoy the free play mode a lot, then the full game will keep you hooked.

As much as I like this game, I do find a few things frustrating. The groups of icons can look all too similar, which leads me to clicking the wrong one from time to time. Also, even on mouse and keyboard, the game can struggle when you click on an icon. You might have to click 2-3 times before it registers. It seems to be random when it doesn't work and it's not very common.

On the positive side, this runs beautifully on Linux with Proton, with no issues. The vibe is very chill and relaxing. The campaign mode is cozy with cute characters and short simple plots. The different icon themes are all very fun and nicely made. I like them all, but the food based ones are my favorite. The music is pleasant, but can get repetitive if you play the game frequently. The daily challenge mode is fun to play and see how you score up against others and keeps me coming back daily.

I got this on sale and it's well worth more with how many hours I have put into it. I'll probably get the DLC for this eventually because the new campaign levels and icon themes seem like a lot of fun. I definitely recommend this if you enjoy solid logic puzzles, well worth the purchase.

Экономическая модель своей простотой и лаконичностью очень похожа на Stronghold, однако у нее нюанс: у всех (!) зданий ограниченный радиус действия. Другими словами если в Stronghold вы могли поставить пару лесопилок на другом конце карты и забыть о них, то в Imperium Romanum близ удаленных месторождений ископаемых придется основывать дополнительные деревни с главным зданием в центре и полноценной городской инфраструктурой вокруг: начиная с домов, акведуков, школ и рынков в начале, и заканчивая храмами, академиями и театрами на поздних этапах развития.

Из интересного: в Imperium Romanum есть гендерное разделение труда. Мужчины здесь как правило работают в мастерских и занимаются тяжелым производством: это лесопилки, шахты и разнообразные мастерские (пекари, мясники и кузницы, охрана правопорядка и пр.). Тогда как женщины работают преимущественно на фермах, прядильнях, рынках и изредка на торговых аванпостах.

Ну и конечно еще есть рабы, которые обязательно поднимут бунт, стоит только их немного перегрузить работой. Поэтому важно не раскидывать здания одной производственной цепочки далеко друг от друга.

На удивление - вся эта тема неплохо сбалансирована, и после того как вы разберетесь в CORE-механике головной боли при отстройке города не создает.

Боевая часть по сравнению со Stronghold очень сильно упрощена, и скорее является очередным экономическим вызовом игроку типа "построй достаточно стабильную экономику что бы содержать армию прежде чем твой город сожгут", чем чем-то самостоятельным (за исключением дополнительной кампании "Гражданская война Цезаря", где нужно выживать и побеждать против численно превосходящего противника, вот это занятно).

I have played a lot of Survivors-like games. The core mechanics are simple and they may be cheap-looking games, but I find them fun.
This game, on the other hand, is NOT fun. I am going to explain why I didn't enjoy this game.
I am not going to talk about graphics and sound, since I have played games with worse quality in those areas, but they ended up being enjoyable. You can just watch the trailer, that is all you need to know about the game.

First, a lot of survivors-like games feature some kind of progression. You start a run, get some resources (maybe materials or some kind of money), die, use those resources to make you stronger (like increasing stats, getting new skills/items), repeat the process.
This game doesn't have any kind of progression/way to get stronger. You unlock characters and items by getting achievements. While some items are pretty good (like the Voodoo Doll and Elegy of Metamorphosis), there is no way to make your characters get stronger. Every new run is from the beginning. How strong a character is is how "lucky" you are with the stats and items you get in your run. And that wouldn't be that much of a problem if the game were balanced.

I have completed the game (getting all the achievements). To do that, you have to beat the game with all the characters in Standard difficulty. One (minor) problem is that you need to beat the game on Easy difficulty with each character (15) to unlock their Standard difficulty. So you have to beat the game at least 30 times, a thing that wouldn't be that bad if the game was enjoyable.
While Easy is quite an enjoyable difficulty (and it isn't too easy, I think it should have been the Standard difficulty), Standard is the problem. It is supposed to be the intended difficulty for the game. While you can beat it without much of a problem with a few characters, most of them will have trouble... if you play honestly.
Here comes the biggest problem with this game: lack of balancing and infinite retries.

First, I am going to talk about the infinite retries. If you Pause the game and return to the Title, an option to Continue the game will appear. This will let you restart from the beginning of a Wave (also called Round sometimes). You have to beat 20 waves to complete a run (you can later select Endless mode if you want to keep playing). At first, I thought this was some kind of bug and was something that was going to be fixed. But the more I played, it seemed like it was the intended way to play the game.
The two main reasons to keep trying the same wave over and over are to select good stats, items and weapons, and to get a "no-hit" round.
About the stats and items, when you kill enemies, they drop experience you have to grab (like most survivor-likes). At the end of the wave, you can select a stat to increase (of 4 chosen randomly) for each level up you got. Killing a mid-boss drops a chest. Generally, you can only get one chest per wave, unless you picked an item that can change the number of chests you can get. At the end of a wave, you can select an item (of 3 chosen randomly) for each chest you got.
With weapons, you can select a new weapon at the end of every four waves. It works similarly to items; you can select 1 of 3 random ones. You can have two weapons equipped (some characters can only equip one, and another character can equip six). There is a special item that lets you use the two weapons at the same time, with a minor damage penalty.
Getting "no-hit" for three waves in a row lets you select some strong level 4 items (you have 3 random choices like the chest items), but if you decide not to select an item and get a "no-hit" wave again, you can select level 5 items (most of them are the same as level 4 but with no penalties).

Contrary to some reviews saying this game is easy, I can say that this game (on Standard difficulty) is hard, or a more properly word would be unjust.
This game has bosses that serve as DPS checks. If you aren't strong enough to kill them, then it is better to start the run again. You may think that it would be easier to just run away from the bosses and let the timer run out, but good luck trying to do that with the last two bosses. If you don't have shields or any other way to protect yourself, they may kill you in one/two hits (once your HP drops to zero, even if you pause the game and return to the title, the Continue option won't appear).
That means you have to restart a wave over and over to get the stats and items you need to get stronger. This is tedious and not fun at all. Good luck if you don't want to "cheat" and just play with what the game decides to give you in each run.
This is like when people tell you to reroll in gacha games because a character makes the game easier, more enjoyable. If a game isn't fun with the characters and resources it gives you and you need specific characters to make the game "playable", then it is a bad game design (this is why I never reroll in gacha games).
With a properly balanced game, unless you have horrible luck, you should be able to beat the game with the random things they give you. The only thing you have to do is adjust your gameplay style and plan ahead. Not Survivors isn't balanced at all. 
Most builds have to focus on high Power (Attack or Magic), Attack speed (the game is confusing, because Attack Power is just for Physical attacks, but other mentions of "Attack" are used for both types) and critical. Your goal is to quickly kill any enemy, especially bosses. Any other stat doesn't matter too much (you need some extra Speed to move aroung and evade things), since you can retry any number of times. You don't have enough levels to get a more tanky build (some characters can, like the Tree).
Ranged weapons are a lot better than melee ones. Getting into close combat is just a way to get hit easier (meaning, more resets). The basic weapon like the AK-47 is too strong with a 2000% critical effect (I think it should only be 200% like most weapons, since the rare version of the AK-47, the M4A1, has the second highest Critical at 400%).

I think I mentioned all the reasons why I think this game isn't fun and I wouldn't recommend it. As mentioned previously, Easy difficulty is actually enjoyable; you have the chance to experiment with more builds, there is no need to "reroll".
If you like survivors-like games, there are a lot of other options. But if you like rerolling, a cast of "parody" characters (borderline copyright infringement), and pop culture references, then it may be your game. It is kinda cheap, so it isn't all that bad.

Gra miała być realną konkurencją dla Cities Skylines i w pewnym sensie nią została. Pomysł na połączenie mechaniki tworzenia metropolii znaną ze wspomnianego wyżej Cities Skylines z mechaniką surowców znaną z Anno był strzałem w dziesiątkę. Jednakże wraz z czasem spędzonym na grze i rozrostem wirtualnego miasta wychodzić zaczyna wiele problemów jakie dźwiga na sobie Highrise City.

1. Optymalizacja - gra kuleje strasznie w tej kwestii. Już miasto posiadające 100.000 mieszkańców potrafi mocny sprzęt wystawić na ciężką próbę. Zapisywanie stanu gry potrafi trwać kilkadziesiąt sekund i w tym czasie nie można korzystać z komputera, gdyż ten dosłownie się zawiesza (a przynajmniej takie wrażenie sprawia). Wywalanie gry do pulpitu, gubienie klatek i pojawiające się znikąd w losowych momentach FPS-dropy to absolutna norma.
2. Gra na ten moment wydaje się być porzucona. Twórcy nie robią absolutnie nic w kwestii wydawania łatek (a jest co łatać). Od ostatniej łatki, która zmieniała dosłownie pierdoły minął rok.
3. DLC, które wprowadzało system metra jest popsute. Gra potrafi często stwierdzić, że tunele podziemne/podwodne nie są możliwe do połączenia...BO NIE. Nawet jak tunele uda się połączyć to gra i tak nie będzie potrafiła odnaleźć ścieżki dla pojazdu.
4. Gra wyszła trochę za późno do fazy wersji pełnej, gdyż chwilę później pojawiło się Cities Skylines 2 (które, o zgrozo, posiada równie fatalną optymalizację co Highrise City).

Z ciekawostek można wymienić system mini-zadań, które najczęściej polegają na dostarczeniu przy pomocy furgonetki towaru z punktu A do punktu B w określonym czasie przejeżdżając przez wyznaczone bramki. Zdobywamy przez to gotówkę oraz surowce na dalszy rozwój. Jednak biorąc pod uwagę wspomnianą optymalizację (a raczej jej kompletny brak) z czasem jazda po naszym mieście staje się utrapieniem tym bardziej, że silnik Unity na którym gra funkcjonuje ma tak bardzo upośledzoną fizykę, że nasz pojazd zaczyna samoczynnie skręcać a nawet przewracać się przy większych prędkościach. Sam system przemysłu jest bardzo rozbudowany i nieraz (szczególnie przy większych miastach) możemy zostać postawieni przed dylematem czy nie postawić jakiejś fabryki w miejscu wieżowca, bo logistycznie będzie większy porządek itd. Generalnie jest to gra w pewnym stopniu do polecenia dla osób, które chcą budować miasto ale nie chcą być ograniczani toną dodatków płatnych (tak, to do was Paradox). Tutaj są dwa dodatki i będę mocno zdziwiony, jak będzie ich więcej. Przynajmniej ścieżka radiowa jest wliczona w cenę gry i nie ma konieczności wykupowania oddzielnych DLC ze stacjami radiowymi (tak, to też do was Paradox). W kwestii samego silnika gry i jego zdolności kreowania obrazu nie ma co się rozpisywać - potrafi on mimo swoich ograniczeń wygenerować ładne widoki.

El primer título de Gabriel Knight me conquistó al instante en su día y lo colocaría sin dudarlo en lo más alto junto a obras maestras del género de la aventura gráfica como Broken Sword. Ese entusiasmo me llevó a probar rápidamente esta secuela hace tiempo, también muy elogiada por la crítica experta. Sin embargo, el cambio a FMV me disgustó bastante, la dificultad del juego acompañada a las cinemáticas sin subtítulos tampoco ayudaron y las señalizaciones, los diálogos y los nombres en alemán terminaron definitivamente con mi paciencia, fue una experiencia amarga y no pasé del primer capítulo en ese intento. 

Hace poco decidí darle una nueva oportunidad con un parche al español y aunque el principio se me ha vuelto a hacer un poco coñazo y desesperante, una vez superado ese primer capítulo la historia va ganando muchísimo porque se enriquece con un contexto histórico interesante, el cual está elaborado a la perfección en las fases de investigación y de documentación bibliotecaria, cuando manejamos al personaje de Grace. Esa decisión de intercalar las aventuras de Gabriel en Munich con las de su ayudante en las zonas más rurales sí que me ha aparecido un acierto que le da una ventaja al videojuego con respecto a su predecesor. Los encuentros con la policía y con los miembros del club también van ganando en intensidad volviendo el caso más interesante y los puzzles se resuelven con una mayor fluidez ¡Gracias a Dios! Al descubrir todo esto entiendo su fama, pero sigo sintiendo que ha envejecido un poco mal.

ENGLISH
Gabriel Knight's first title instantly captivated me, and I would undoubtedly place it alongside masterpieces of the graphic adventure genre like Broken Sword. That enthusiasm led me to quickly try this sequel some time ago, which was also highly praised by critics. However, the switch to FMV gameplay was quite disappointing. The game's difficulty, coupled with the lack of subtitles in the cutscenes, didn't help matters, and the German signage, dialogue, and names finally exhausted my patience. It was a bitter experience, and I didn't get past the first chapter on that attempt.

I recently decided to give it another try with a Spanish patch, and although the beginning was once again a bit of a drag and frustrating, once I got past that first chapter the story improved considerably. It was enriched by an interesting historical context, which is perfectly crafted in the investigation and library research phases when we control Grace. The decision to alternate Gabriel's adventures in Munich with those of his assistant in the more rural areas was definitely a success, giving the game an edge over its predecessor. The encounters with the police and the club members also become more intense, making the case more interesting, and the puzzles are solved much more smoothly—thank goodness! After discovering all this, I understand its fame, but I still feel it hasn't aged well.

Oyunu tavsiye ediyorum.

Yapım tarz olarak Kingdom: New Lands’i andırıyor, ancak oynanış ve amacı farklı. Genel olarak gayet güzel olmuş. Fakat her yeni bölüme geçtiğinizde yaptığınız yükseltmeler sıfırlanıyor, bu da biraz saçma olmuş. Bazı bölümlerde sinir bozucu olabiliyor. Tavsiyem, bir bölümü bitirdikten sonra oyunu kapatıp ertesi gün yeni bölüme başlamanız. Aksi halde üst üste oynayınca fena bayıyor ve sinir edebiliyor.

Bazı eksikler de dikkat çekiyor. Örneğin düşman bölgesini işgal etmek için asker eğitip saldırıyorsunuz, ama düşman okçular yüzünden askerlerin çoğu ölüyor. Duvarlar da aşırı dayanıklı, kırmak oldukça zor. Benim tavsiyem, tam kadro okçu eğitmeniz. Hatta yükseltmeleri yapıp yanınıza okçular alırsanız düşmanlar yaklaşamıyor ve bölgeyi rahat işgal edebiliyorsunuz. Ancak bu taktik son bölümlere doğru işe yaramamaya başlıyor; mancınık gibi farklı birimlere ihtiyaç duyuyorsunuz.

Bazı özellikler eksik kalmış gibi. Oyunun çıkışından önce biraz daha geri bildirim alınsaymış, denge açısından çok daha iyi olabilirmiş. Fragmanda gösterilen bazı sahneler de oyunda yer almıyor, muhtemelen sonradan kaldırılmışlar.

Genel olarak kafa dağıtmalık, zaman geçirmelik bir yapım. Resmi Türkçe dil desteği mevcut.

Worms Clan Wars, developed and published by Team17 Digital Ltd, represents one of the studio’s most polished iterations of its long-running turn-based artillery series. Released in 2013, the game refines many of the ideas that had been introduced in earlier entries such as Worms Revolution while attempting to reestablish the franchise’s multiplayer identity through deeper customization, improved visuals, and dedicated clan-based online play. At its core, it remains quintessential Worms—a chaotic and strategic competition where teams of tiny, wisecracking worms blast each other to pieces using bazookas, exploding sheep, banana bombs, and a vast arsenal of comedic weaponry. What distinguishes Clan Wars is its focus on community and shared play, both locally and online, expanding the classic formula without losing the humor and unpredictability that have made Worms a staple of multiplayer gaming for decades.

Visually, Worms Clan Wars delivers the most refined presentation the series had seen at the time. The game uses a 2.5D perspective, combining traditional 2D gameplay with fully 3D environments and lighting effects that lend each map a sense of depth and dynamism. The destructible terrain remains the centerpiece of the experience—each explosion reshapes the battlefield, creating new strategies and hazards as the match progresses. Dynamic water mechanics add an extra layer of chaos: floods can drown worms, erode terrain, or shift the balance of power mid-match. The thematic diversity of the levels also keeps the action fresh, ranging from ancient ruins and Viking battlegrounds to steampunk industrial zones. While not revolutionary, the art design and animation retain the series’ whimsical personality, with expressive worms, exaggerated destruction, and a lively color palette that fits the tongue-in-cheek tone perfectly.

Gameplay in Clan Wars follows the familiar Worms rhythm: each team takes turns moving a single worm, using weapons, or positioning themselves strategically before ending the turn. Victory is earned through a combination of tactical precision, environmental awareness, and a bit of luck. Clan Wars introduces refinements rather than major changes, building on the class system from Worms Revolution. The four worm classes—Soldier, Scout, Scientist, and Heavy—each offer unique advantages that subtly influence team composition and tactics. The Scientist, for example, passively heals allies and excels with utility weapons, while the Heavy deals greater damage but moves sluggishly. These differences create more depth in planning, though the balance remains gentle enough that players can still succeed with any combination of worms. The weapon selection, featuring more than sixty tools of destruction, offers both returning favorites and a handful of new additions that keep the carnage unpredictable. From jetpacks and teleporters to airstrikes and explosive animals, every match maintains the playful sense of absurdity that defines the franchise.

The single-player campaign provides a structured experience with a light narrative featuring the eccentric inventor Tara Pinkleton, voiced with delightful eccentricity by Katherine Parkinson. Spread across twenty-five missions, the campaign mixes standard combat encounters with puzzle-style levels that require creative use of weapons and movement tools. While the humor and charm of the dialogue are consistent with Team17’s style, the campaign itself serves more as a tutorial and light diversion than a core attraction. The true heart of the game lies in its multiplayer, which has been significantly expanded and modernized in Clan Wars. Players can create or join clans, design emblems, climb ranked leaderboards, and compete in cooperative or competitive matches. The integration of the Steam Workshop allows for user-generated content—new maps, landscapes, and custom items—which gives the game an impressive level of longevity. These community tools, combined with the series’ timeless mechanics, make the multiplayer experience both endlessly replayable and deeply social.

In motion, Worms Clan Wars captures the essence of what makes the franchise so enduring: its ability to balance tactical thinking with spontaneous hilarity. Matches often unfold as a mixture of skillful shots and spectacular blunders. A perfectly timed bazooka strike can demolish an entire enemy squad, while a mistimed grenade or overpowered jetpack can send your own worms tumbling into the sea. It’s this combination of precision and unpredictability that continues to make the game such a joy, especially with friends. Few multiplayer games are as capable of producing laughter and frustration in equal measure. Clan Wars excels at fostering this atmosphere, and the introduction of clan competition amplifies it by giving groups of players a reason to keep improving and returning.

Despite its strengths, the game is not without flaws. Many players and critics have noted that while Clan Wars polishes the existing Worms formula, it does not dramatically evolve it. The series’ mechanics remain largely unchanged, and for long-time fans, the differences between this and earlier versions can feel incremental. The campaign, though charming, lacks compelling challenge or narrative depth, and the artificial intelligence remains inconsistent—oscillating between laughably poor and supernaturally precise. Furthermore, while the number of weapons and customization options is impressive, the limited set of environment themes and the absence of groundbreaking new mechanics mean the game occasionally feels like a refined update rather than a bold new entry. Still, for a series as time-tested as Worms, refinement may be exactly what long-time fans want.

Ultimately, Worms Clan Wars succeeds as a love letter to the franchise’s core strengths: clever tactics, explosive chaos, and humor born from disaster. It offers a more modern and accessible platform for both casual and competitive play, bolstered by its focus on clans, online integration, and player-created content. While it may not win over those seeking something entirely new, it stands as one of the most complete and feature-rich Worms experiences ever released. The balance between classic gameplay and contemporary presentation makes it an ideal entry point for newcomers and a satisfying continuation for veterans. Worms Clan Wars reminds players why the series remains relevant decades after its debut—it’s endlessly entertaining, deceptively strategic, and always capable of turning even the most serious match into a moment of laughter-filled chaos.

Power of Ten is a space-faring roguelite that builds its entire identity on the feeling of being outnumbered, outgunned, and constantly on the move. Pew Times Three frames the experience around a lone starfighter trying to save civilian planets from a steadily advancing enemy armada. Instead of relying on scripted levels or linear missions, the game throws you into procedurally generated sectors where every decision carries weight—when to fight, when to flee, when to gather resources, and when to risk approaching a planet under siege. This structure creates a loop that feels tense even in its quietest moments, because the threat is always closing in and your ship is always only a few mistakes away from destruction.

Moment-to-moment gameplay mixes fast-paced shooting with a surprising amount of resource and time management. You aren’t simply blasting waves of enemies; you’re mining asteroid fields for materials, trading with neutral ships, activating planetary shields, rescuing civilians, and navigating the map to keep pace with the encroaching fleet. Each run becomes a balancing act of survival and heroism. The upgrade paths add an extra layer of strategy, allowing you to equip weapons, combine them into hybrid forms, and gradually alter the capabilities of your ship. The differences between the unlockable ships meaningfully change how a run unfolds, turning each new vessel into a fresh challenge to master rather than a simple cosmetic change.

The game’s atmosphere is one of its greatest strengths. The pixel-art presentation strikes a balance between minimalism and detail, creating star systems that feel vast but never empty. Nebulae glow softly in the distance, planets spin with subtle shading, and debris drifts through the void, giving each sector a clear identity. The sound design reinforces that sense of isolation—low, ambient tones accompany long stretches of exploration, while laser bursts, explosions, and warning signals cut through the stillness when a battle erupts. Power of Ten often feels contemplative, even serene, especially during mining or scouting phases. Yet that calm is always temporary, because danger remains only one hyperspace jump away.

At the same time, the game’s pacing may not appeal to everyone. The early parts of a run can feel slow, especially when you’re gathering the resources needed to gear up for tougher encounters. Some players will appreciate the quiet buildup, but others might find that the mining-focused segments drag before the action escalates. The controls, while responsive once mastered, can feel unconventional at the start due to the strafing and movement model that demands deliberate positioning. Not all upgrades feel equally impactful, and a few weapons take time to show their usefulness, which can make early encounters feel repetitive until you unlock more options.

Despite these imperfections, Power of Ten succeeds in creating a distinct rhythm that blends strategic planning with intense bursts of combat. Each failed run feels like a lesson rather than a frustration, and the procedural nature of the universe ensures that no two attempts unfold in quite the same way. The game rewards patience and thoughtful play, and its slower, more atmospheric approach sets it apart from the many arcade-leaning shooters in the roguelite space. For players who enjoy the gradual tension of building up a fragile ship, making tough choices, and attempting one more heroic stand against overwhelming odds, the experience becomes genuinely addictive.

In the end, Power of Ten stands out as a carefully crafted indie roguelite that prioritizes tension, atmosphere, and decision-making over pure reflex challenges. It may not deliver immediate spectacle, but it offers a satisfying arc of progression and a sense of star-spanning adventure that grows stronger with each ship you unlock and each sector you survive. With its blend of exploration, combat, and strategy, it provides a rich and meditative space-shooting experience that rewards those willing to invest the time to understand its rhythms.

Yet another collection of flash point & click horror games I played when I was younger. While I don't remember these as much as Don't Escape, I find them to be far better at the horror side of things. 

Deep Sleep, Deeper Sleep, and Deepest Sleep all do an excellent job at getting you anxious while playing. The darker segments where you have to reveal the scare work so much better than any jumpscare you'll find in a traditional horror game. The puzzles aren't too hard and there are a fair few secrets to find. I love the story behind a lucid dreaming state that takes you so deep into the realm of dreams that you end up in a whole new reality. One where shadows and monsters live, far beyond the comprehension of normality. These games are bit of their time, but in a charming way that lets you relive some nostalgia if you played back in the day. I love these games, they helped pave the way for a lot of point & click horror titles. They terrified me as a kid which I wholeheartedly thank them for. The vibe they put off and their designs all stick out in my mind as signature features of the scriptwelder style. I'm so glad this series got a new entry!

Definitely check this collection out! If you love point & click horror or just want a short jaunt through hell, then pick this one up! 100% recommended for returning fans of this series and other scriptwelder works.

Hello Lady! is a visual novel that embraces ambition rather than playing it safe, and that ambition is immediately visible in its tone, structure, and thematic scope. Developed by AKATSUKI-WORKS and published on Steam by HIKARI FIELD, it presents itself not merely as a romance VN, but as a character-driven mystery wrapped in philosophical conflict and superpowered intrigue. The story centers on Shinri Narita, a transfer student who arrives at the prestigious Amakawa Noble Academy—an institution reserved for society’s elite and those with extraordinary abilities. Instead of quietly assimilating into the hierarchy already ruled by five revered young women, Shinri challenges it, forcing the school and its inhabitants to confront the ideals they claim to uphold. That premise immediately sets the narrative apart from typical academy settings, establishing an environment where arrogance, privilege, trauma, and justice collide.

One of the most striking aspects of the game is its protagonist. Shinri is not the blank slate or passive observer common in many visual novels—he has defined convictions, strategic intelligence, a sharp tongue, and a past that informs his worldview. He pushes the story forward rather than being pulled along by external forces, and his dynamic with the heroines feels earned instead of preordained. Each route expands on his complexity, revealing conflicting motivations and vulnerabilities that prevent him from becoming a simple power fantasy. The heroines themselves are not treated as interchangeable romantic goals; they possess agency, ideological friction, and deeply rooted emotional wounds. Their relationships with Shinri evolve not through superficial affection, but through confrontation, revelation, and mutual challenge. As a result, the romantic payoffs feel meaningful because the narrative takes its time exploring the cost of intimacy—social, psychological, and existential.

Visually, Hello Lady! is polished and expressive. AKATSUKI-WORKS is known for dramatic character design, and the game delivers detailed sprites, stylish uniforms, intense facial expressions, and CGs that enhance emotional peaks rather than simply decorate them. Environments, though less visually elaborate than the characters, reinforce the elite, insulated atmosphere of the academy. The soundtrack further elevates the experience, balancing dramatic orchestral themes with quieter, contemplative pieces, ensuring the story’s tonal shifts—slice-of-life levity, philosophical debate, romantic tension, or explosive combat—feel seamless. Voice acting contributes significantly to immersion, adding personality, vulnerability, and gravitas to both protagonists and supporting characters.

Structurally, the VN follows the traditional common-route-to-branching-path model, but execution matters more than format. Each heroine route is designed not only to deepen personal relationships but to uncover new layers of the overarching narrative, meaning multiple playthroughs are essential to fully understand the world and the motivations of its cast. The story explores themes such as elitism, institutional corruption, trauma, morality, and the weight of societal expectations, often through morally ambiguous choices and uncomfortable truths. The true route reframes earlier events, connecting scattered narrative threads into a broader, more existential conflict. Though this structure creates satisfying narrative payoff, it also means the pacing can feel heavy or overwhelming, especially when the story accelerates toward its climax and introduces new information rapidly.

Hello Lady! is not without rough edges. Its tonal shifts—from comedic banter to psychological introspection to explosive supernatural conflict—can occasionally feel abrupt. Some players may find the later sections overly dramatic or dense with exposition. Certain character arcs resolve more elegantly than others, and the true route in particular risks narrative overload, trying to tie together every thematic and emotional thread at once. Additionally, because routes interlock narratively, the game demands patience and rereads of familiar scenes, which may diminish momentum for players seeking a shorter or more streamlined experience. Its mature themes and erotic content also place it firmly within a specific audience—one that appreciates romance as an extension of character development rather than a standalone attraction.

Despite these imperfections, Hello Lady! stands out among visual novels for its confidence, thematic ambition, and emotional sincerity. It is a story unafraid to wrestle with difficult questions about human worth, justice, privilege, and the tension between personal desire and societal responsibility. It offers memorable characters, sharp writing, well-orchestrated dramatic peaks, and a protagonist capable of carrying a full-length narrative without fading into the background. For readers who enjoy layered storytelling, flawed but compelling characters, and narratives that mix romance with ideological conflict and cinematic set pieces, the game delivers a deeply engaging experience. It may not be the most accessible or universally lighthearted VN, but for those willing to invest time, reflection, and emotional energy, Hello Lady! becomes not just entertaining, but genuinely resonant.

It’s a Turn-based, Strategy, Card game featuring a unique setting and a quirky art style. But what really makes the game awesome, is the racing meter at the top of the screen. During combat you and your opponent race to checkpoints where you play your attack or defense cards. Every card you play speeds you up or slows you down. This game mechanic adds an extra layer of strategy when deciding what card to play next. Very original, very fun! The game is a little short, with limited enemies to battle. But the main problem with the game is it’s title. Vegangsters? Really? I guess that’s supposed to be a portmanteau of vegan gangsters? Which doesn’t make sense, because there are no vegans in this game. There’s personified vegetables, but they aren’t eating each other. Now that I think about it, gangsters is a misnomer as well. The enemies you battle are thugs and street toughs but they don’t seem to be affiliated with each other or any “gang” as far as I could tell. So why call it Vegangsters? I don't understand. Don’t people make fun of vegans? All I'm saying is, if I made a game, I wouldn’t give it a confusing name that makes you sounds stupid when you say it out loud. But that’s just me. Anyway, would I recommend this game? Definitely! Check it out.

Игра значительно слабее Long Live The Queen. Наша задача такая же как и LLTQ, прокачать за год своего персонажа чтобы он мог противостоять всем невзгодам. Всего есть около 20 характеристик на прокачку, но вот в чем проблема: Они минимально влияют на события (возможно это отсылка на великую игру Underground man). У вас не будет событий где нужно взламывать компьютеры, сражаться с врагами, танцевать или убеждать других. Цикл недели проходит следующим образом: Вы выбираете занятие на день (учеба/работа/отдых), затем ночью (охота/отдых/торговля/алхимия/и тд). И так на каждую неделю. У вас не будут появляться каждую неделю сюжетные события, типа вторжения охотников, появления нового персонажа, переговоров с другими вампирами или еще чем-то. Недели просто будут проходить почти на автомате, иногда останавливаясь на атмосферные события, вроде нового года или пасхи, когда наш персонаж просто будет обсуждать этот праздник со своей прислугой.

Все ваши характеристики влияют лишь на доступную вам работу и на концовку. Но концовки сделаны плохо. Всего их 21 и 18 из них привязаны к максимальным характеристикам в конце игры. У вас максимальный уровень экономики и науки? Концовка где вы разовъете медицину. Прокачали искусство и поп культуру? В конце будете художником. В самоей же игре, эти статы вам понадобятся лишь как заработок денег. Здесь нет скрытых проверок характеристик или появления новых вариантов в  диалогах при развитии какого-то навыка. Более того, здесь нет активных персонажей кроме ГГ и ее прислуги. 90% диалогов будут лишь между ними, и в них практически не будет выбора вариантов ответа. Игра проходится за полтора часа и у меня абсолютно нет желания перепроходить ее.

По скринам игра очень похожа на LLTQ, однако не стоит обманываться. Это совсем не она. Для сравнения, я оставлю ссылку на статью из вики, на одну неделю из LLTQ и на то, как сильно в той влияли навыки и ваши решения на последствия в игре. https://longlivethequeen.fandom.com/wiki/Week_17

For some background, I initially found out about this game from the Developer posting about it in a Discord Server I'm in. After some initial ribbing (because of course) I got the demo and played it, from then on [i]I was hooked...[/i]

To summarise the game as simply as I can, it is a 2D Collectathon Platformer that, quoting the developer, [i]"is meant to be a spiritual successor to Super Mario 63"[/i], and while it may not look like that from the outset, it wears it's inspirations on it's sleeve proudly. The general gameplay loop of going between a selection of levels in a Hub World, and searching for Primary Collectibles to achieve a grander goal very much takes it's roots from the Classic 3D Mario Formula. But the game makes it's own flavour with it, and it's a blast to play through.

To get the elephant of the room adressed, I will acknowledge that the game may not look the most appealing (especially in the modern landscape of Raytraced Photo-Realistic Graphics and/or Super Stylized Art Pieces), but the "simpler" art style this game has works in it's favour if you ask me. It makes things very easy to understand with a quick glance, and gives the whole game an Authentically Earnest vibe that is a joy to look at.

Beyond that, the gameplay is a joy to pick up and rewarding to master. Clifford's signature Cone Rush ability is well utilised throughout the game for some challenging platforming. But by far my favourite move to use is the Air Dash, on it's own it may seem like yet another horizontal movement option, but with the added feature of Star Guard allowing you to "parry" enemy attacks and obstacles makes it thrilling to try and use it to speed through obstacles. And while there are [i]some[/i] issues I have with the movement (such as jumping being one of two fixed heights, something one should be wary of when precisely manoeuvring a level) they aren't too impactful to the experience overall, and are easily counteracted by smarter play.

The Story is also a real treat to watch unfold. The overall quest of the game involves the player as Clifford, guided by his friend Boxer, to find and collect A large amount of missing Flash Drives scattered around the world to repair Boxer's home: the Star Prism. It makes for a simple enough plot to get you motivated on the adventure, but leads into a fun and engaging story as the opposing force gets developed, and provides intriguing concepts for worldbuilding when you learn about the Star Prism's origins. I won't spoil too much of the story however, as I want to leave that as something prospecting players can enjoy :]

The characters are also a treat to see. The main characters of Clifford and Boxer bounce off of eachother impeccably, with Boxer being more Analytical and Clifford being a Wide-Eyed adventurer looking forward to the next thing to do. And beyond our two leads, the side characters and NPCs have some great interactions with the Duo as well. The bosses all have great personalities that really sell them as characters beyond differing attack patterns, and they have some wholesome and funny interactions with the Main Duo.

[hr][/hr]

Overall, this game truly is a Hidden Gem, if you haven't played it yet then you should. It is definitely worth much more attention than it currently has (as of writing this is the [i]only review on the Steam Page[/i], which is rather unfortunate.) It's only 13 dollars, and well worth the money! >:]

I like this game a lot for reasons many game critics probably won't, and that can be summarised to how far off the checkpoints are from one another (even bosses not having checkpoints), and the lacking mitigation of challenge, like gaining the invincibility leaf in super mario world 3d by dying repeatedly. 

Instead it apts for the service of encouraging players by rewarding players for utilising mechanics in levels that include air dodging through obstacles at the right time to gain a moment of I frames WITH additional dash attacks, and having the little triangles you collect not only (albeit slowly) recover your health but also (once you collect enough) give you an instant revival just when you think your down for the count.

The aforementioned challenges steadily but surely amount to hectic ordeals with lots of platforming requiring you to be nimble but also be quick to get on again, (hopefully at the right time and platform), while taking count of the dashes and jumps you have. 

The collectathon part to this game however, is more a series of obstacles that are between you and the collectibles, the game likes to call flash drives, rather than a token hidden in the level somewhere you'll have to find (Not a punt on the game design just something I realised) 

The bosses are also all very good, requiring you to use the  gimmicks you've learnt during levels to evade the bosses attacks while still giving them what for. 

A lot of games nowadays feel like they'd regulate this kind of stuff to a harder mode or a checklist of things you have to do in level; this isn't an issue per se, yet it feels like they're hiding it from an audience of players who want to experience an avenue of challenges that'll test their mettle and raise their adrenaline.

But this game doesn't feel like it shys away from that audience at all, and obliges players to levels that require a good amount of attention and execution while still being fair. 

This game may intimidate players who wish for a casual and easygoing game, but I think it's great that this game feels like it focuses more on the demand for challenge filled platformers, rather than the inbetween that feels too hazardous in its approach to be ambitious with itself.

So this coming from a guy who's done 80% of it all (sadly couldn't find the rest of the 12 flash drives...), I say try the demo out first, because that's pretty much how I knew the game was for me just from that... 

Also midi music for the win. peace.

## 🔥 **Análise Rápida: Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway**

**(Nota Pessoal: 8/10)**

Se liga, esse jogo é um clássico que envelheceu bem em uma coisa e mal em outra. Na minha opinião, ele merece um **8/10** fácil, principalmente pela jogabilidade.

### 👍 **O que Brilha (Pontos Fortes)**

* **A Fórmula Perfeita:** A grande sacada do *Hell's Highway* é a mistura de **estratégia pura** com o **tiroteno da Segunda Guerra**. Você não só atira, você *comanda* o esquadrão, flanqueia e usa a cobertura. É isso que faz o jogo ser único.
* **Melhor da Série:** De todos os *Brothers in Arms*, esse aqui é o que mais acertou na mão. Se a Gearbox resolvesse fazer um *remake* (sonho!), valeria muito a pena **começar por ele**.
* **História Imersiva (10/10):** A narrativa é fod*! É muito fácil se envolver com os personagens e o drama da guerra. A história é, sem dúvida, o ponto alto do jogo.
* **Variedade:** Gosto muito das partes onde você **pilota tanques dos Aliados**. Adiciona uma quebra na jogabilidade de infantaria e é sempre divertido.

### 👎 **Onde a Idade Pesou (Pontos Fracos)**

* **Gráficos (7/10):** Não tem como negar, os gráficos gritam **"geração PS3"**. A parte visual envelheceu, e quem é muito exigente vai notar.
* **Preço Atual (Atenção!):** O jogo **não vale mais o preço cheio** (caso você encontre por aí), e isso porque o **modo *online* não existe mais**. Hoje, ele é puramente uma experiência *single-player*.
* **Faltou o *Stealth*:** Fico P da vida que não liberaram mais **armas com luneta**. Se tivessem investido mais nisso, o jogo ficaria mais *stealth* e tático, e a imersão seria ainda melhor.

### 🎯 **Veredito:**

Só recomendo se você for um jogador que **não liga tanto para gráficos de última geração** e **busca uma jogabilidade mais pensada, lenta e tática** do que os *shooters* rápidos de hoje. É um ótimo resgate da $\text{2ª Guerra}$ com uma dose de estratégia.

The Smurfs – Village Party is a cheerful, family-oriented party game that blends light adventure exploration with a large collection of accessible mini-games. Balio Studio’s interpretation of the Smurfs universe leans heavily into its colorful, inviting charm, offering a game that is clearly designed to bring players of all ages together. From the moment you start, the tone is upbeat and friendly: Papa Smurf is preparing a grand celebration and tasks you, as a customizable young Smurf, with traveling across various regions to invite the entire village while keeping Gargamel’s mischief at bay. This narrative wrapper provides just enough structure to frame the experience without overshadowing the simple joy of playing through its activities.

Adventure Mode serves as the backbone of the single-player experience. Here, you wander through different themed environments—lush forests, icy mountains, Gargamel’s murky territory, and the heart of the Smurf Village—collecting items, helping various Smurfs with small quests, and progressing toward the grand party. The environments are bright and visually faithful to the franchise, and character animations retain the expressive charm associated with Smurf media. While the adventure maps are generous in size and variety, their design can feel uneven at times. Some areas are vibrant and bustling with activity, while others appear sparse or underdeveloped, giving the exploration an inconsistent sense of life. Still, the mode succeeds in providing a playful, low-pressure context for discovering characters and unlocking costumes, collectibles, and new mini-games.

The heart of the game lies in its Party Mode, which boasts 50 mini-games spanning a wide range of activities—racing, reflex challenges, memory games, accuracy tests, athletic contests, and more. Most mini-games are short, easy to understand, and designed to be picked up immediately by newcomers. Their visual humor and simplicity make them especially enjoyable for younger players or mixed groups who want a casual, lighthearted competition. While not all mini-games are equally memorable, the sheer variety ensures that each session feels fresh, and the fast pace encourages repeated play. With local multiplayer support for up to four players, the game shines brightest as a couch-co-op centerpiece, ideal for family gatherings or casual social play.

However, The Smurfs – Village Party is not without limitations. Experienced gamers may find that many mini-games lack mechanical depth or long-term challenge, making the experience feel more like a compilation of short distractions than a competitive party title built for mastery. The absence of online multiplayer is a notable drawback, especially for players who hoped to enjoy party sessions with friends remotely. Additionally, the adventure mode’s ambition sometimes exceeds its polish—minor camera quirks, inconsistent texture quality, and occasionally repetitive side quests can interrupt the flow. None of these issues are severe enough to break the game, but they do highlight that the title is best enjoyed with modest expectations.

Ultimately, The Smurfs – Village Party succeeds as a warm, approachable, and family-friendly party game. Its upbeat tone, colorful presentation, and wide range of mini-games make it a delightful choice for younger players or for families wanting a shared gaming experience without steep learning curves. Those seeking deep mechanics or long-term progression will likely find it too simple, but players looking for a light, joyful romp through the Smurf universe will appreciate the charm and accessibility it offers. As a casual multiplayer experience, it provides exactly what it promises: a lively village party where everyone can join in the fun.

Não é apenas um jogo de tiro em primeira pessoa ambientado no Velho Oeste — é, sinceramente, o melhor jogo que já joguei. Poucos jogos conseguem unir carisma, estilo, desafio e atmosfera de um jeito tão marcante quanto Outlaws faz. Mesmo usando a engine aprimorada do Dark Forces, ele entrega combates rápidos, armas poderosas e inimigos que realmente te fazem pensar. Cada fase tem aquele toque LucasArts: cenários criativos, segredos escondidos e missões que parecem cenas de um filme de faroeste. O clima de Velho Oeste é autêntico, com vilas empoeiradas, fortes abandonados, cavernas úmidas e trens em movimento, criando uma experiência cinematográfica que até hoje parece única. A trilha sonora, composta por Clint Bajakian, é simplesmente a melhor que já ouvi em um jogo. Ela combina orquestra com temas de faroeste dignos de Ennio Morricone, fazendo você se sentir dentro de um clássico bangue-bangue. Cada música encaixa perfeitamente no momento: dos duelos tensos aos trechos de exploração silenciosa. A história, seguindo James Anderson em busca de vingança após perder sua família, é simples, mas muito bem contada, com cutscenes em estilo animação que dão um charme especial e vilões com personalidade e presença. Outlaws tem algo que muitos jogos modernos perderam: alma. É direto, criativo, emocionante e totalmente envolvente. A mistura de ação, ambientação, narrativa e aquela trilha sonora inesquecível faz dele uma experiência completa — daquelas que você termina e pensa: “Isso foi incrível.”

(ストリーミング起動はできますが、もちろんゲーム側 PC の操作を奪われます。)

あらかじめこの制約を理解して、別のアカウントで購入しておけば起動できると思います。
もしくはゲーム側をファミリーシェアリングで起動するとか。セーブデータなどの管理も考えると、そこまでする気は起きないですね。

ただし本ツールは、古いゲーム (DOSBOX など) で対応一覧にある物はリアルタイムで同期してマッピング表示させる機能があるっぽいです。これは面白い機能だと思います。

Does this make any more sense to you? Is this who you wish to be at the end of the day? Is this how you want to live your life? Is it your fault that this is how you are living it? A leg that is just bone and dancing clown and a city in a bottle and a fetus made of stolen imagination. A gig economy and endless marketing and renting the right to life from those who get to choose. Every once and a while, I have a thought pass through my mind, for just a moment. It would be nice to be wrong. To be crazy. To learn that the horrors I perceive around me are not the evils I see them as. 「Sakura Dungeon」は、ビジュアルノベル要素を併せ持つダンジョン探索型RPGです。読解と探索が主要なアクティビティであり、主人公は仲間を率いて階層を進み、敵や宝物に対処します。

物語は軽度のファンタジー的対立を提示します。多くの展開は戦闘間の対話で提示されます。物語の深度は限定的ですが、章ごとの進行テンポは安定しています。

アートは明瞭かつ表情豊かなキャラクターポートレートと敵デザインが特徴です。背景はダンジョン通路やキャンプシーンを描写します。アセットの反復は確認できますが、探索前提の構造として機能的です。

音楽は探索中に控えめなループを形成します。戦闘時は単純な緊張感を付与します。効果音は基礎的で、全体として音響演出は最小限です。

ゲームプレイはターン制戦闘です。プレイヤーはタイル状マップを探索し、モンスターと交戦し、仲間を捕獲し、装備を管理します。進行は段階的であり、装備を適切に更新すれば難度は穏当です。

作品のトーンは軽快で、ややフレンドリーな要素を含みます。ドラマ性は限定的です。探索の性質上、プレイ時間は長くなりがちです。

総括として「Sakura Dungeon」は、ビジュアルノベル的な枠組みを備えた素直なダンジョンクロウル体験を求めるユーザーに適しています。予測可能な進行、馴染みあるアート、簡易なパーティマネジメントを提供します。

В зависимости от уровня сложности время, отведенное на принятие решения, будет отличаться.

[code] О б    у р о в н я х    с л о ж н о с т и[/code]

Кстати о сложности. Легкий режим максимально приветлив и быстро обучает основам, помогая избежать долгого периода "а что вообще делать?". Особенности будут сразу указаны на доске, а визитки кукол сопровождаются их фото - вы без труда определите, кто выбрался из коробки.

Дальше игра постепенно начнет отбирать у вас подсказки, время и даже скрывать данные с визиток кукол. В некоторых режимах действительно не хватает ориентиров, и поначалу можно растеряться, но если внимательно изучать предметы и их описания, понимание придет само.

Каждое успешное прохождение сложности открывает следующую, а затем - экстра-режимы с новыми подходами к поиску самозванца.

Для эффективного расследования вы сможете использовать особенности каждой локации, превращая их в ловушки для кукол. Но будьте внимательны: некоторые куклы применяют приемы, чтобы запутать вас и сбить со следа - сверяйте данные внимательно!

[code] Н а с т р о й к и [/code]

Радуют гибкостью. Хотите спокойное исследование без внезапных скримеров? Прямо во время расследования можно нажать соответствующую кнопку и выключить их. То же самое касается и робота, который вас преследует. Единственное исключение - особые контракты, где отключение ограничено.

[code] М и н у с ы   и   п л ю с ы [/code]

[i][b]Оптимизация[/b][/i] слабовата: при поворотах камера подергивается, а минут через десять игра может сообщить, что обнаружила сложности у вашего компьютера и любезно предложит снизить настройки.

[i][b]Перевод[/b][/i] тоже подкачал. Советую играть на английском: интерфейс интуитивный, а на русском это превращается в дополнительный челлендж. Некоторые профессии переведены неверно и способны запутать вас похлеще самого импостера, да и информация на карточках переведена так, что вам придется по звездам гадать, что такое они там имеют ввиду.

Зато [i][b]контента[/b][/i] стало значительно больше, чем на релизе: появились новые режимы, контракты, внутриигровая валюта, коллекции и онлайн. Кстати, кооператив работает отлично, хотя у некоторых игроков бывают вылеты при создании лобби, мы ни разу не столкнулись с подобной проблемой.

[h1]良かったところ[/h1] 
[list]

このゲームではステージクリアのたびにふんだんな給与が支給され、そこから能力強化・武器購入・サブウェポン購入などに資金を当てていく。もっとも、給与の9割以上は重税…もとい偉大な祖国を支える各種社会保険料や年金などで持っていかれるので、リソース割り振りに非常に悩むことになる。特に、武器は使用回数に耐久値があり、壊れると貧弱なハンドガンで無数の敵に立ち向かう羽目になるが、武器も安くない。しかし、少ない手取りをやりくりしてステージを進めていくのは意外と楽しく、このゲームの醍醐味とも思えた。

ゲームの大半を占めるアクションパートは、ステージ左端の防衛対象に敵が到達しないよう右端から出現する敵を撃つだけの展開。主人公は攻撃されないため、開幕から画面右でひたすら敵にカーソルをあわせるだけの単調な展開になりがち。マルチエンドを見るには周回が必要なのだが、一周約40分これを繰り返すのはやや退屈に感じた。

偉大な祖国を讃えるテレビ・ラジオの流れる中、緑のゲル状の配給食を食べる。そんな中でも、前に進もうとする少女たちの明るさに少しだけ救われるゲーム。お値段も手頃で、10時間もあれば実績コンプできるので是非プレイしてほしい。
