Dream House Days DX, developed and published by Kairosoft Co., Ltd, is a charming and quietly addictive simulation that places you in charge of both designing and managing a residential apartment complex. In typical Kairosoft fashion, the game embraces simplicity in presentation while layering its systems with surprising depth and satisfying progression. It’s a familiar formula for anyone who has played the developer’s earlier titles like Game Dev Story or Pocket Academy: accessible mechanics, steady growth, and a sense of cozy accomplishment that comes from watching your tiny empire evolve over time. In this case, your empire isn’t a corporation or a school—it’s a building full of tenants whose happiness, relationships, and livelihoods depend entirely on your design sensibilities and management skills.

The premise is immediately inviting. As the architect and landlord, you build apartments, furnish them, and welcome tenants who each have distinct personalities, jobs, and aspirations. What begins as a simple one-floor building quickly blossoms into a bustling residential complex teeming with life. Every decision—from what furniture to buy to where to place it—matters, because layout and comfort directly affect rent, tenant satisfaction, and progression. The game gives you an array of furnishings to choose from, ranging from the practical (beds, kitchens, and closets) to the luxurious (game consoles, hot tubs, and rare décor items). Combining certain pieces can create themed rooms that boost stats or attract wealthier residents, which adds a subtle layer of puzzle-solving to what might otherwise be a passive experience. It’s a balancing act between aesthetics, efficiency, and profit, all wrapped in the charming pixel art style that Kairosoft has made its signature.

What sets Dream House Days DX apart from other simulation titles is the way it intertwines personal stories with management gameplay. Your tenants aren’t just faceless numbers—they’re characters with goals and quirks. They form friendships, fall in love, get married, have children, and even move out when the time feels right. Watching generations of families grow within your complex creates an oddly emotional rhythm that transforms your building into more than just a series of rooms—it becomes a small community. You’ll find yourself invested in their success, guiding them toward new careers, furnishing their homes to suit their ambitions, and celebrating milestones like weddings or promotions. This touch of humanity gives the game its soul and helps break up the monotony that often plagues long-running management sims.

The progression system is gradual but rewarding. The in-game calendar advances in seasons and years, unlocking new furniture, expansion options, and customization opportunities. You start small, but as profits rise, you can renovate, expand to new buildings, and attract higher-paying tenants. The DX version, which debuted on Steam after the original mobile release, streamlines the experience by removing microtransactions and mobile-based limitations. Instead, progression flows naturally, powered by in-game achievements and player choices rather than time-gated purchases. The pacing remains relaxed, encouraging you to take your time rather than rush through objectives. Dream House Days DX is designed for long sessions of slow, steady growth—it’s the kind of game that rewards patience, strategy, and experimentation over quick reactions or competitive play.

Visually and tonally, the game radiates charm. The pixel art is crisp, colorful, and full of personality, with expressive character sprites that make the residents feel alive. The soundtrack, a collection of upbeat chiptune-style loops, contributes to the cozy atmosphere even if it can become repetitive after hours of play. The interface is simple and easy to navigate, though it occasionally reveals its mobile roots through menus designed for touch controls. On PC, however, these quirks are minor inconveniences, as the mouse interface translates well enough to maintain the same relaxed feel. The presentation captures that nostalgic Kairosoft identity—a world that feels simultaneously small-scale and infinitely replayable.

The game’s weaknesses lie primarily in its predictability and repetition. Once you’ve mastered the core systems, the challenges become routine. The early sense of discovery—experimenting with furniture combinations, unlocking new upgrades, and guiding tenants toward success—gradually gives way to a comfortable but repetitive loop. The AI behaviors are charming but limited, and veteran players of Kairosoft’s catalog may notice familiar mechanics recycled from previous titles. Still, these drawbacks feel less like flaws and more like features of the Kairosoft formula: consistency and accessibility are part of their appeal. For players seeking relaxation over intensity, the unhurried pace and simplicity are strengths rather than shortcomings.

Ultimately, Dream House Days DX embodies what makes Kairosoft games beloved among fans of casual management sims. It offers the satisfaction of creation without overwhelming the player with complexity, and the joy of watching small stories unfold within a system that’s easy to learn but difficult to exhaust. Its blend of community-building, strategic furnishing, and life simulation makes it a gentle but compelling experience that can quietly consume hours. Whether you’re optimizing rent values, designing the perfect living space, or simply watching your tenants grow old together, there’s a quiet magic in the game’s rhythm. Dream House Days DX is not about speed or spectacle—it’s about nurturing a world where comfort and progress coexist, one tiny apartment at a time.

[h3]●結論[/h3]
かなり面白いです。定価７００円で遊べていいレベルは優に超えています。
そもそもが安いので、セールなど待たずとも定価で買って損はしませんとだけお伝えしたいです。


[h3]●どんなゲームなの？[/h3]
一言で説明するとSlay the Spire（以下スレスパ）の派生ゲームです。
加えて本作独自の要素が綺麗に噛みあっており、序盤～中盤における１プレイの緊張感は特筆すべきものがありました。

スレスパとの大きな違いは、周回要素が前提のゲームバランスになっているため、最初のプレイでラスボス撃破まで進められるのはほぼ不可能ということです。
システムを理解し、資産がたまってきた段階でようやく「そろそろ１層のボスを殺しにいくか」と決意を固める感じです。

「こういうゲームって初見でも運さえ良ければクリアできるんじゃないの？」というスタンスのかたは肌にあわないかもしれないので、まずは一度デモ版を遊んでみることをおススメします。


[h3]●ゲームタイトルが酷い件について[/h3]
ゴールドと墓

こんなに面白いゲームなのに、このタイトルのせいでストアページまできた８０％くらいの人が引き返しているような気がするのは自分だけでしょうか。
英語ならまだいいのかもしれません。

日本語のタイトルをみてください。

ゴールドと墓

あってます。あってますけど……そこまで直訳にしなくてもいいのでは……。
もし自分がこのゲームのプロモーション担当だったら、開発の家族を人質に取ってでも日本でのタイトルは一考してもらうか、日本語訳はせず英語のまま発売してくれとお願いしていたと思います。

一応擁護しますが、このタイトル……Gold and Gravesという言葉はゲームの肝にもなっている部分で、本編内でもちょくちょくと登場します。
先に進むか、戻るか。黄金か、墓場か。覚悟を決めろ。
みたいなニュアンスです。

この『押すか引くか』といった駆け引きが一番面白いところではあるので、そこをタイトルに持ってきたのかなと。
しかしそうした意味合いがわかるのは自分がこのゲームをそこそこ遊んだからであって、初見の人は「ゴールドと墓」というタイトルでだいぶ身構えてしまう気がしなくもないです。

本質を伝えるという意味で、「I love you」を「月が綺麗ですね」と訳すくらいのアクロバティックな表現をみれたら最高でした。

It is a great city building game. The progression of the game is very satisfying, The difficulty have been optimized pretty nicely.

En general, es un muy buen juego, con mucho potencial para ser de los mejores del género. La verdad es que disfruto jugándolo y suelo volver cada cierto tiempo, cuando necesito algo libre de estrés. Pero para que lo disfrutes, debes ser muy fan de los city builders o te vas a aburrir, ya que tiene un paso bastante lento.

En general está bastante completo como está, aunque le faltan algunas cosas básicas de otros city builders, como un transporte entre almacenes o más variedad de cultivos. Tampoco me termina de gustar el sistema de combate, que es básicamente un juego de "cartas con porcentajes" donde el mejor ejército tiene mayor probabilidad de ganar. En resumen, como tirar un D20 jugando DnD. Es original, simple, fácil de entender, pero... 

El sistema de eventos aleatorios es una excelente idea pero está muy, muy incompleto. Hay muy pocos y son predecibles, lo cual lo vuelve solo un aviso molesto. Con un poco más de trabajo, haciéndolos más variados y complejos, sería una de las mejores características del juego.

Tiene varios bugs que no son muy frecuentes pero son bastante graciosos, como que la gente se suba inexplicablemente a los techos o camine bajo el agua, y otros no tan graciosos, como que ciertos edificios se paralicen y no cumplan su función (como el astillero, que se traba luego de un rato con la reparación automática activada), edificios que desaparecen sin explicación, expediciones que se traban esperando un aldeano que nunca llega...

También tiene un problema con los saves, ya que al cargar una partida los aldeanos dejan lo que estaban haciendo, tiran al suelo cualquier objeto que lleven y se van a hacer otra cosa; los puentes tienen un glitch que hace aparecer un minipuente en medio que bloquea el paso; la misión "Las necesidades de los adalides" se bloquea si cargas la partida mientras está activa y se hace imposible de finalizar.

En fin, para mí es un excelente juego y vale la pena darle una oportunidad. Pero si lo compras ve sabiendo que no es para todo el mundo y tiene bastante por arreglar.

Não sou nenhum entusiasta de jogos de avião, nem sou amante de tais veículos. Dogfight 1942 é o primeiro jogo de avião que eu jogo na minha vida (batalha de avião no BF1 conta? kkkk). O preço de R$ 32,99 está salgado, levando em consideração toda a simplicidade do jogo e o fato de que ele vende duas DLCs de história separadamente, cada uma custando R$ 10,49. Em promoção, Dogfight 1942 fica por menos de 5 reais — aí sim vale a pena, principalmente caso esteja buscando um game de avião com mecânicas acessíveis para quem não é entusiasta do gênero.

Hesitant Recommendation. But If you ever wanted to play a giant robot turned based role playing game with customizable robot parts this is the game for you. I kinda just poured out my feelings of this game so be advised there might be potential spoilers but no plot points spelled out.


The major problem is the story although it's gameplay has some rough patches itself, it feels like it needs a sequel to explain everything that happened. You play two characters, Dominic Shade a man running away from his past with a dreary perspective on life and Knife Leopard, the Mecha pilot who has this unyielding optimism looking on the bright side of things. Together they are giving a mysterious robot from their deceased friend. Their Goal? Make it to Number 1 in the Robot Fighting Ranking system and get a big payout. 
Shade is our prominent protagonist he's the one who we see the most of however he works kinda like a manager setting up matches and doing menial tasks. Throughout the game you are giving a couple of mini games you can do that get you money, for repairing your Mecha after a fight, parts for your Mecha, and Pineapples, gift you gift to specific people who then reward you by gifting parts and tools making most parts you get in mini games obsolete. Tools are either used to make mini games easier, giving you more prizes at once, or makes the prices of repairs go down but because all the stuff you get in minigames are randomized you could just keep on rerolling until you get every pineapple you need and you have almost all the parts your Mecha will need till end of the game as early as the third fight of the game. 
Shade is the main focus of the story we see a lot of stuff from his point of view but he ultimately struggles by being a character who either monologues or lectures someone into a monologue about how hard life is and that he is not suited to live a happy life. However the gameplay he gets to do actually ties into his themes because he's basically tasked with running errands that bring him everywhere in the over world forcing him to create bonds with people showing that even if he wants to he can't escape being involved with people's live. Shade also gets involved helping a dying business by investing money and then he can get daily profits, however just because doing the mini games has no cap per day there's not a real reason to invest. 
Knife Leopard is your other playable character, you only play him during the mecha fights but his gameplay is super customizable. After the third fight I believe you are given all these options for customizable stuff that make it hard to try out everything in one play through. Active skills, Passive Skills, Underlying ability traits, and even Support Skills this game give you a load out and then some that's completely customizable. You can make your Mecha a full Melee unit, A long ranged gun user or a mid ranged all rounder. I went with Melee unit and it was a fun time, Guns are fine however you'll need to equip mecha parts that give you more ammo slots and you will constantly need to have one of your passive skill slots to be reloading ammo. The ability traits you are given are stuff that help increase your support meter quickly so you can use support skills that buff your mecha. The traits are correlated to stuff you can do on the battlefield which can be something as simple as getting hit a lot, making your support meter go up. The battle field is a straight line of boxes, using your robot's movement point you can position yourself where you want so you can deal optimal damage. There's a couple of squares in combat boosting or debuffing your attack, push someone to the edge and you've deadlocked them, making you deal exponentially more damage. The biggest problem I had is sometimes the battles went on for a bit and it seemed more chore then challenge most of the time. Overall fun Combat.
Knife Leopard as a character is told much from Shade's story. You more or less only use Knife Leopard for the robot fights otherwise he's at the base of operations majority of the time. It's implied that he's supposed to be very handsome which is I guess it's just not fully verbalized people think he's super hot and more you'll have to go through at least two people in the main cast of characters hit on him exactly once. For the most part his overlaying optimism and naivete should be a good parallel to Shade ultimately they kind of don't even feel connected. Biggest problem is Shade's struggles feel out of place with the big Robot tournament going on. It honestly feels more like both sides clash with eachother instead of helping making the game better and that is unfortunate. 
The rest of the cast of characters are fun and quirky the type of supporting cast that each character has hints sprinkled throughout the story about what they were before meeting them but still enough that isn't shown to us that you can make your own conclusions. 



*Major Spoiler*
There are two major points in the story that make next to no sense to me. There's a point where cultist are slowly showing up and finally one day they enact a plan, however that day is so weird and different to every day before hand where it starts eerie and has the cast be put in the middle of the ritual with no context how they got there. This was the weirdest moment but the worst part about all this is that the main characters AGREE TO NEVER MENTION THIS AGAIN AND FOLLOW THROUGH WITH THIS. Technically it gets referenced again but they don't really acknowledge the event and more of the mech you encountered in that event. 
Then the other thing is at the right end of the tournament for the strongest robots it's revealed that one of the benefactors for this tournament was secretly using this to create ultimate robot and goes on a speil about government and the United States that just feels so out of place because this game never really made an effort to put in politics as an issue, it shows up sparingly kinda but it's only ever made by a couple news stories never by actual characters that matter. So the entire plot point feels more like a hamfisted attempt at being political like they just remembered they were a mecha game and they had to put in politics at the near end so they did. It doesn't even matter because the game's ending doesn't focus on the poltic spiel at all, they could remove it and the game doesn't change at all. 
*end of spoilers*

Узнал об этой серии игр совершенно случайно в прошлом году.

DROD (Deadly Rooms of Death) — это игры-головоломки с довольно приятными и не вполне обычными механиками. По сути своей, это пошаговые игры, состоящие из "Уровней", разделённых на комнаты-экраны. Цель практически каждого экрана — ликвидировать всех противников (либо решить какую-либо головоломку). Уровень завершается (и открывается переход на следующий) обычно в тот момент, когда игрок зачищает все экраны уровня и/или проходит все головоломки. Помимо этого в играх также присутствуют секретные комнаты, не обязательные для прохождения.

Под контролем игрока персонаж, вооружённый мечом (в некоторых частях на определённых уровнях меч заменяется на копьё, кирку, палку и т.п.) — и каждый ход может либо переместиться на одну клетку (ортагонально: по вертикали, по горизонтали или по диагонали), либо повернуться на 45 градусов, либо ничего не делать. Tokyo School Life, developed by M2 Co., Ltd and published by Dogenzaka Lab, is a charming romantic visual novel that captures the essence of Japanese high school life through the lens of an idealized exchange student experience. The game follows the story of a foreign student spending a semester in Japan, offering a narrative that blends everyday school life, lighthearted comedy, and youthful romance. It is a title designed to appeal to fans of slice-of-life anime and dating sims, combining a relaxed atmosphere with an affectionate portrayal of Japanese culture. Rather than telling a dramatic or complex story, Tokyo School Life focuses on warmth, familiarity, and the gentle rhythms of daily routine, making it an inviting experience for both newcomers to the genre and long-time visual novel enthusiasts.

From the very beginning, Tokyo School Life establishes a strong sense of place and tone. The player arrives in Tokyo, wide-eyed and eager to experience the customs, language, and pace of life in a new country. The story unfolds largely from the protagonist’s perspective as he navigates dorm life, club activities, and the joys and awkwardness of building relationships with his new classmates. The game’s three central heroines—Aoi, Karin, and Sakura—represent distinct archetypes common to the genre but are fleshed out through their unique personalities and subtle emotional growth. Aoi embodies the dependable and nurturing type, Karin carries the fiery energy of a tsundere, and Sakura expresses a quiet, artistic kindness. While these character types are familiar to anyone who has played romance visual novels before, Tokyo School Life gives them enough individuality and heart to make their routes enjoyable and distinct.

One of the game’s most impressive qualities is its presentation. Unlike many static visual novels, Tokyo School Life uses the E-mote animation system, which gives its 2D character sprites fluid, natural motion. Characters blink, shift posture, and express emotion dynamically, which enhances their sense of presence and makes interactions feel livelier. Combined with the colorful backgrounds and clean interface, the game exudes the look and feel of a high-quality anime production. The Japanese voice acting is another highlight—the cast brings genuine warmth and personality to each heroine, helping to make conversations and emotional moments feel authentic. The soundtrack complements this tone perfectly, mixing gentle melodies for slice-of-life moments with cheerful themes for comedic scenes and sentimental pieces for more intimate ones. The opening song, fully voiced in Japanese, captures the energy and innocence of youth that defines the experience.

Narratively, Tokyo School Life keeps things grounded and relatable. The story is not about dramatic twists, fantasy elements, or tragic revelations—it’s about connection and discovery. Each route follows a natural progression as the protagonist grows closer to one of the girls, learning more about her background and personality while also coming to understand his own feelings about his time in Japan. The writing balances humor and sincerity, often leaning into playful banter and comedic misunderstandings before transitioning into more tender or reflective moments. The pacing is measured and comfortable, which suits the tone but can occasionally feel slow for players expecting deeper plot developments. Yet this simplicity is part of the game’s charm—it’s a soothing narrative that evokes nostalgia for the innocence of student life and the excitement of cultural exploration.

Beyond its story and presentation, Tokyo School Life offers a few touches that set it apart within the genre. Its bilingual text feature allows players to switch between Japanese and English, making it not only entertaining but also valuable as a learning tool for language enthusiasts. Players can display romaji, hiragana, or kanji alongside English subtitles, which is especially useful for those studying Japanese. This small but thoughtful inclusion broadens the game’s appeal beyond visual novel fans to learners of Japanese culture and language. The interface itself is intuitive, offering an easy-to-navigate menu system, clear save options, and customization for text display and voice volume. It’s designed to be accessible and user-friendly, ensuring that nothing disrupts the immersive flow of the story.

Despite its strengths, Tokyo School Life has some limitations. The narrative, while pleasant, rarely pushes beyond the conventions of the genre. It relies heavily on familiar tropes—school festivals, hot springs, shy confessions—and the protagonist, though likable, is deliberately plain so players can project themselves onto him. The brevity of the game also leaves some emotional beats feeling underdeveloped; each heroine’s route concludes just as the romance reaches its most engaging point. The overall experience can be completed in a few hours, which might leave players wishing for more depth or expanded endings. However, these constraints don’t detract from its overall appeal—they simply position the game as a light, approachable story rather than a sprawling epic.

What truly makes Tokyo School Life memorable is the sincerity of its tone. It is not a cynical or subversive work; it doesn’t seek to challenge the norms of its genre but instead embraces them with affection and polish. It invites players to experience the warmth of friendship, the awkwardness of first love, and the small joys of daily life in a foreign country. Its optimism and respect for cultural exchange give it a universal appeal, allowing players to appreciate Japanese traditions while empathizing with the feelings of curiosity and belonging that come with new experiences. The game’s heartfelt simplicity, supported by its strong voice acting, expressive visuals, and comforting soundtrack, makes it an ideal choice for anyone seeking an uplifting and aesthetically pleasing story.

In the end, Tokyo School Life succeeds not by breaking boundaries but by perfecting the fundamentals of a classic romantic visual novel. It offers an engaging cast, beautiful animation, and a story that feels genuine in its portrayal of youthful emotions and cross-cultural connection. While short and modest in ambition, it delivers exactly what it promises—a heartwarming, slice-of-life romance full of charm, humor, and gentle sentimentality. For players who enjoy relaxing, character-driven stories or wish to experience an idealized version of student life in Tokyo, it stands as a delightful and lovingly crafted experience that captures the joy of discovery and the sweetness of first love.

GalGun: Double Peace* is an on-rails shooter developed by Inti Creates, continuing the arcade-style structure of its predecessor. The game adapts traditional shooting mechanics to a linear, stage-based progression system, focusing on fast reactions, target prioritization, and scoring accuracy. It functions as a compact, timing-based action title rather than a full exploration game.

Gameplay follows a predictable rail-shooter formula: the player’s movement is automated while aiming and shooting manually. Each level presents waves of incoming targets and occasional mini-boss encounters. Scoring depends on accuracy, hit timing, and identifying weak points. The design rewards memorization and consistent precision.

The control system is responsive across both controller and mouse inputs. Calibration options allow fine-tuning of aiming sensitivity, improving consistency compared to earlier entries. The difficulty curve is gentle, making it accessible to casual players while still providing challenge in higher modes.

Visually, GalGun: Double Peace* uses a bright, stylized 3D anime aesthetic. Environments are colorful, simple, and designed for quick readability during fast-paced sequences. The framerate is stable, and load times are short. Performance across platforms remains smooth even during dense action.

Audio complements the visual tone with light, upbeat music and short sound cues. The mix emphasizes clarity over realism, and the sound design serves a primarily functional purpose—tracking hits and giving quick feedback to the player.

The structure includes multiple routes and endings, giving moderate replay value. While narrative depth is minimal, route selection and performance rankings add incentive for repeated runs. Between missions, brief dialogue scenes provide context and pacing without extending playtime unnecessarily.

Overall, GalGun: Double Peace* is a competent and polished rail shooter. It offers fast reaction-based gameplay, accessible controls, and smooth technical execution. For players who enjoy short, arcade-style shooters with branching routes and light narrative framing, it performs its function effectively within its limited scope.

OPG: Clan Wars, developed by Anarchy Games and published by Street’s Game, is an ambitious indie project that attempts to merge open-world survival mechanics with fast-paced multiplayer combat in a setting that blends post-apocalyptic grit with clan-based warfare. It aims to offer an experience where players can gather resources, craft equipment, build bunkers, and engage in dynamic PvP and PvE battles across a vast, hostile landscape. On paper, the idea sounds promising—a hybrid of shooter, survival, and strategy—but in practice, it’s a game that shows both the reach of its ambition and the limitations of its indie roots. What emerges is an experimental but uneven experience that feels as much like a prototype of something bigger as it does a fully realized game.

At its core, OPG: Clan Wars gives players a sandbox where survival is tied to both resource management and combat prowess. The world is an open zone filled with bunkers, fortifications, and scattered remnants of civilization, encouraging exploration and looting. You can move between regions, collect materials, construct shelters, and prepare for the ever-present threat of both AI-controlled enemies and rival players. The inclusion of vehicles adds mobility and tactical variety, letting you traverse long stretches of land or storm enemy bases more efficiently. The clan system ties everything together, promoting teamwork as players group up to defend territories, raid others, and compete for dominance in the global “Clan War” mode. It’s a concept with real potential—one that aims to deliver a persistent sense of community warfare—but the lack of player population and technical refinement makes it difficult to fully experience as intended.

Visually, the game leans into a rough, utilitarian aesthetic that suits its grim tone. The environments—dusty plains, crumbling fortresses, and industrial ruins—establish a convincing atmosphere of decay. However, the graphics themselves feel dated, with low-resolution textures, stiff animations, and limited environmental detail. While the game’s visual ambition is admirable, the execution often falls short, giving the impression of an early-access title rather than a complete release. The lighting and particle effects occasionally add flair during firefights or explosions, but overall the world can feel empty and static. The user interface, too, lacks polish, with clunky menus and inconsistent visual cues that occasionally interfere with immersion. Despite this, the aesthetic direction—the feeling of desolation and danger—remains one of the game’s more effective qualities, and it does a decent job of setting the tone for its survival-based gameplay.

The gameplay loop revolves around a mix of exploration, crafting, combat, and base-building. Players start off scavenging for weapons and materials, gradually improving their arsenal and fortifications as they progress. The crafting system allows for creating basic gear, ammunition, and tools, adding a layer of preparation to the constant tension of open-world encounters. The inclusion of multiple modes—such as solo missions, team battles, raids, and global clan warfare—gives the game a sense of variety. Unfortunately, this variety doesn’t always translate to depth. Many of the mechanics feel underdeveloped or imbalanced; combat can be chaotic and unresponsive, AI enemies behave erratically, and the balance between survival and shooting mechanics is inconsistent. The lack of detailed tutorials means players often learn systems through trial and error, which might appeal to some but can frustrate newcomers who expect a smoother introduction to the game’s many moving parts.

One of OPG: Clan Wars’ biggest challenges is its online component. For a game that leans heavily on multiplayer interaction, its small player base severely limits its potential. Without active players, the clan warfare and raid systems lose much of their intended impact. Matches can feel empty, and the sense of large-scale conflict is diminished when you’re wandering the wasteland alone. Those who manage to play with friends or coordinate in small groups will find more enjoyment, as the cooperative elements—such as raiding bunkers or defending territories—become far more engaging with teamwork. Still, even in multiplayer settings, issues like server instability, lag, and occasional crashes can interrupt the experience, making it difficult to maintain consistent momentum.

Performance and optimization are ongoing concerns as well. The game’s engine struggles with frame rate drops and visual pop-in, especially in larger maps or during intense firefights. These technical shortcomings, while not uncommon for small-scale indie projects, contribute to the sense that OPG: Clan Wars was released before it had time to fully mature. There are moments when the gameplay clicks—when you’re driving across the barren landscape under a glowing sunset, scavenging for resources, or fending off a rival clan—but these flashes of excitement are often undermined by technical roughness or lack of long-term progression systems. The potential is undeniable, but the execution feels inconsistent and unfinished, leaving the player with the impression of a game that could have been more with additional development time and community support.

Despite its flaws, OPG: Clan Wars isn’t without charm. It’s the kind of game that appeals to a specific audience—players who enjoy experimental, rough-edged indie titles that push big ideas with limited means. For those willing to overlook its imperfections, it offers a glimpse of what could be a unique hybrid of survival and competitive gameplay. The low price point also makes it an accessible experiment, inviting players to try something different without much investment. But for those seeking a polished, content-rich experience or a vibrant online community, it may prove disappointing. The game feels like a bold but unfinished project, one that captures ambition more than achievement.

In the end, OPG: Clan Wars stands as a fascinating example of indie ambition—an attempt to blend multiple genres into one cohesive experience. It reaches for the scale of a large multiplayer survival world while constrained by the realities of limited development resources. The result is a game full of ideas, but lacking the refinement and player base to bring them fully to life. It’s not without merit, and for those who appreciate raw experimentation in game design, it offers some fleeting moments of tension and excitement. Yet it also serves as a reminder of how difficult it is to balance scope with execution. OPG: Clan Wars is a world that feels alive in concept but quiet in practice—an intriguing, imperfect experiment in survival and warfare that could someday evolve into something truly special if given the support and polish it deserves.

The decisions you make during the game not only have an emmence effect on your current chapter, but also determine how the following chapters play out. This creates a massively branching story tree, with a huge number of possible end-game scenarios.
The game plays in seven chapters, each having a different protagonist. The time lines of the chapters patieally overlap, which sometimes allows vieweign the same events from different perspectives. This also means that high-pace events ending each of the chapters are switched to slow-paced beginning of the next chapter. This might make the game feel slow at times. 
Each chapter has a "good" and a "bad" ending, creating 7! (seven factorial) different end-game combinations. In addition to the "horror" aspect of the game, there is a "romance" aspect. Certain in-game decisions increase/decrease you current character's standing with other characters, which could lead to end-game romance. There are a total of seven different romance options in the game.
Regarding the story itself, given the amount of branching in the game, it is very difficult to get all questions answered in a single play-through. Of all the different end-game combinations, there is only one that is considered "true ending". To achieve it, some of the characters must die in the course of the game. The decisions that lead to each chapter's outcome are not always obvious. THis might make it a surprise how your current character ends up at the end of the chapter.
To summarize, this is another example of a superb game from this studio. The main highligh if of course the story. I am looking forward to playing the next game they release!

Your Sisters is an unconventional little experience that blurs the line between game and desktop companion. Developed by Team 35 and published by waifuGames, it is less about progression, challenges, or story and more about providing a small dose of charm and comfort in digital form. The premise is simple yet endearing—you invite a group of animated “sisters” to live on your computer screen, moving around, reacting to your actions, and brightening up the dull spaces between your daily routines. It is designed as a playful overlay that doesn’t demand your full attention but instead quietly accompanies you as you browse, work, or play other games. There’s something inherently nostalgic in its simplicity, reminiscent of the old days of virtual pets or desktop mascots, where the act of having a small, animated presence on your screen was its own kind of delight.

The characters are the heart of the experience. Each sister comes with her own appearance, expressions, and idle behaviors, giving a sense of personality even without dialogue or elaborate backstories. They can walk, wave, sit, follow your mouse, or react when you interact with them directly. The game allows you to position them anywhere on your screen, resize them, and unlock cosmetic variations as you accumulate points through interaction. These points, dubbed “Love Points,” act as the game’s light progression system—earned by simply spending time with your sisters or engaging with their animations. It’s a small but effective system that encourages casual engagement without ever feeling demanding. The result is something that feels more like a companion than a game, creating a soft sense of routine as the sisters quietly move about your screen while you go about your day.

Visually, Your Sisters is bright, colorful, and intentionally simple. The character models are drawn in a stylized anime aesthetic, with smooth animation loops and subtle details that make them feel alive without being distracting. The art direction leans heavily into cuteness, but it’s done with care and consistency rather than excess. The interface is minimal, easy to understand, and free of clutter, making it accessible even for those unfamiliar with desktop companion software. The ability to choose between different visual styles, adjust transparency, and customize how many sisters appear on screen adds an appreciated level of control. For users who prefer a single character quietly keeping them company or others who enjoy a full ensemble decorating their workspace, the flexibility ensures that the experience can be as subtle or as lively as you like.

Beyond its visuals, what gives the program its appeal is its tone. There’s a distinct warmth in how Your Sisters approaches digital companionship. It doesn’t try to simulate complex emotional relationships or bombard you with dialogue—it simply creates an ambient sense of comfort. The sisters exist in that strange in-between space of being interactive but not demanding, familiar yet artificial. Watching them move about your screen while music or background noise plays can be unexpectedly calming, almost meditative. It’s the kind of quiet digital intimacy that offers small moments of joy throughout the day. For some players, it might even become a ritual—launching the program not to play, but to have a little presence sharing the screen as they work or unwind.

Of course, its simplicity is also its main limitation. Once you’ve explored the available characters, unlocked a few outfits, and spent some time observing their animations, there’s not much left to do. The lack of deeper systems or evolving behavior means that the novelty can wear off after a few hours unless you genuinely enjoy the passive company it provides. The developers clearly intended it as a minimalist experience, but players looking for something with narrative progression, more meaningful interaction, or emotional depth might find it too light. Still, that minimalism can also be a strength—there’s no pressure, no objectives, just the quiet companionship of a few charming sprites keeping you company on an otherwise empty desktop.

From a technical standpoint, Your Sisters performs well. It’s lightweight, with minimal CPU or memory usage, and runs smoothly even alongside demanding applications or games. The installation is quick, and the controls are intuitive—dragging, resizing, or repositioning characters is effortless. It’s designed to coexist with your workflow rather than interrupt it, which is a rare and appreciated quality. The program’s stability makes it feel polished despite its humble concept, and the price point is low enough to justify it as an impulse purchase for anyone curious about adding a bit of personality to their computer environment.

What ultimately makes Your Sisters stand out is its sincerity. It doesn’t pretend to be more than it is, and in doing so, it manages to fill a niche that many people didn’t know they wanted. It’s a gentle reminder that not every digital experience needs to be grand or competitive—sometimes it’s enough for it to be kind, pretty, and present. Whether you’re someone who spends long hours on the computer and wants a bit of visual companionship, or simply someone who appreciates small, comforting distractions, Your Sisters delivers exactly that. It may not be a game in the traditional sense, but it succeeds as a digital comfort—a quiet, smiling presence on your desktop that reminds you that even in the endless space of a computer screen, there’s room for a little warmth.

Having just beaten Ori, it's easy to see why this game is so beloved. It is an incredibly beautiful and well-paced game that does most things right, but I think it suffers a bit when put under the microscope in a few aspects. Not enough to make it bad, not enough to warranting a thumbs down or not recommending it, but enough to prevent it from being a masterpiece.

First, praise where praise is due. Let's start with the visuals, which, for the most part, are absolutely top-notch. It's been a while since I've seen a 2D game look that good. The parallax and depth of field is insane, always gorgeous and making you feel you're actually inhabiting a real world, not a 2D slice of one. The environments are varied, and the animation for all characters (but in particular for Ori) is mindblowing. The gracefulness of its movements is something you don't see every day. Effects overall are also really well done. My only criticism in regards to visuals is also a criticism I'll come back to when talking about combat - there's a bit too much visual noise at times to allow for effective combat/platforming. This was mostly an issue when enemies shot projectiles at me, and I either couldn't see them against the background or against all the visual effects already on the screen. While this is not game-breaking in regular gameplay, I can see that being a MAJOR issue if you're going for the no-kill achievement.

When it comes to sounds, there's nothing groundbreaking here, but what's on display absolutely delivers. Ori mostly features an orchestral score that dictates the mood of each scene and action sequence without being too intrusive. It's beautiful, it's haunting, it can get your heart pumping in the right moments, and in summary, works. It does what it has to, but is not a soundtrack you'll be remembering for ages, I guess. Could be good background music for studying or meditation, but hardly rises above that.

The lore is partially delivered via short sentences and long visual storytelling. The devs excel at 'show, don't tell', and it's pretty easy to follow what's happening and get invested in the world and its characters. I was still a bit confused about what really set all the events in the game in motion and I'm not sure I know the answer to that, having beaten the game, but that never prevented me from enjoying the story or getting excited about its developments. Personally I don't think Kuro works as a great villain / antagonist, but that's probably more a matter of personal preference. Last but not least, I thought the endign was a bit abrupt - I was sure there would be a final dungeon after you beat the three legacy ones, but no, credits rolled when I was still craving for more. The pacing towards the end is a bit unclear and I think the tension doesn't build as high as it could if you're expecting that kind of final challenge gauntlet, so the whole endgame experience was a bit jarring for me, but I can also see that being an issue for how conditioned I am with Metroidvanias pulling the `point-of-no-return-last-dungeon` trick over and over.

And finally, the area where I reserved most of my criticism - gameplay. I always review Metroidvanias saying they have three jobs that MUST be done right - combat, movement, and exploration. Exploration is the easiest so I'll start there - Ori is fine. There is a lot to find around the world, and most of it is not super hidden, so you immediately know there'll be backtracking. The map is really useful in keeping track of it for you, but the abilities that you get to unlock further exploration feel a bit tacked on - it's like, you know there's a breakable wall as soon as you start the game, and eventually you get the breakable wall ability, so it's a key fitting a hole and not an eureka moment. It works, but is not incredible.

Movement is 8 or 80: moving around with Ori is a blast for most of the time, in particular as you start to combo abilities. Bash is one of the most incredible moves ever created, and combined with double jump and hovering, it's a lot of fun. What brings movement down for me is that some areas (in particular chase sequences) don't communicate really well what they want from you, requiring prior knowledge of the obstacles in order to avoid them. I hate when you get to a point and die to an unfair obstacle without any chance to avoiding it, and I hate when the game uses that as a way to teach you what to do in the next attempt. A fair game will always let a skilled player clear a challenge like that in the first go, and Ori refuses to do that in pretty much all escape sequences. It's a bit frustrating that such a good moveset is hampered by somewhat obtuse level design, but it's not enough to abandon the game.

And finally, combat. Which is the weakest link. Combat is just not satisfying here, and I'm glad it's not a bigger part of the game. What you do is spam the attack button, since enemies are spongy from the beginning to the end of the journey and you don't get significant improvement on your combat options outside of Bash. To make matters worse, there's not a huge variety of enemies. There's the guy that jumps and you run under, the armored guys that rush you, the guys that rush you and explode, the slugs that don't move and shoot bullets you can bash, and the slugs that move but which bullets you cannot bash, the frogs and the owls. And they just keep repeating over and over and over with different palettes but the same strategies. To make things worse, some projectiles are bashable and others aren't, so even bash is not dependable throughout the game. Combat is at its best when you're taking full advantage of your moveset to avoid enemies mid-air and hitting them with their own projectiles, but very often you'll be on ground having to hold on to ledges to take poke shots at enemies while barely seeing their attacks. Again, it works fine for a regular gameplay, but I can see that being infuriating in a one-kill playthrough.

Overall, Ori does many things right and while hard, can be a good first Metroidvania for people getting into the genre. It's beautiful to look at and to listen to, there's an engaging and well told story, exploration is fine, movement is quite expressive although level design frequently plays against it, and if you can endure combat here, it mostly only gets better in other games of the genre. It's a great game that stops a few steps away from being a timeless classic.

L'histoire fait le boulot (amener les persos d'une bataille à l'autre), mais comme pour toute histoire de voyage dans le temps, il vaut mieux éviter de trop y réfléchir. On a joué en mode "histoire étendue" (plus sûr du nom) qui rajoute des dialogues, et c'était plaisant à suivre, sans être extraordinaire.

2/5 stars, an honest attempt was made to simulate trench warfare but there are just so many issues here that I just can not recomend this game at all

First the campaign progresses incredibly slow, territories need multiple assaults that have to end in total vicory to be taken, which leads to you conquering the same map over and over again. Infantry squads are predeployed on the map and can not be purchased exept with a few techs and events, the only things you can actualy purchase are tanks, planes and off-map siege artillery

Manpower is, for some reason, endless and units on the campaign map can never be compleatly destroyed, therefore removing any strategical layer that could have been added by making menpower an actualy recource. 

The only resources are money, which is the currency on the strategical map, and supplies, which is the currency on the tactical map, both are used for replenishing units at the end of a battle but that is just cosmetic, they will always be full strenght at the end. 
Supplies can be bought with money on the campaign map and used in battles limited by your regions supply capacity, which is dependant on the number of troops you have and its supply building level. That limits your ability to bring troops on the field, limits artillery fire and limits how many trenches and entrenchments you can build until you upgraded your supply hub which slows the campaign down even more. 
Btw, your enemy doesn't need to worry about global supply, he has endless amounts and while his regional supplies are limited, it will always have more than you even on normal difficulty. Most of your arsenal is also gated by tech, which unlocks very slowly and again, the AI cheats and will always outtech you.

The result is a campaign that progresses incredibly slow, limits you greatly in what you can actualy do and where your victories don't actualy matter. Both factions have a national will level that gets depleated by losses or high casualties, if your rivals will reaches zero, you win. Since the national will level is incredible arbitrary(it doesn't even took account of me taking Versailles due encircling it because there was no battle) and resources are technicaly endless, the most effective way to progress is attacking weak enemy regions but never taking them, battling the same map over and over again while you bait your enemy into high supply territories with small garrisons where you can just spam motars and MGs to decimate them and deprive him of will even if he gains ground.

This game makes chess fun. You play a variety of openings, puzzles, end-games, goofy positions, alternate board setups, and traditional games -- with a few extra tools to take the edge off the AI when it decides to play like Stockfish for 20 turns straight.

The game gives you limited, consumable items that you can use (totally optional) to see what the engine thinks is the best move; or to encourage the AI to blunder; or to just take back a bad move and try the turn again.

I'm not sure these mechanics completely solve the issue of how much your opponents' elos swing from the beginning of the game to the end... but its a fun and useful band-aid for it.

Some complaints: Opponents are way harder by the last 2/3rds of the game than they started at, and it feels like the elo progression is plainly unrealistic. Chess is a life-long game. No one is going to start at 700 and end at 1600 in the course of playing a title like Chess, Texas. But that's what it feels like the difficulty curve is asking of you.

And there are some bugs creeping around in here. In the non-standard board setups, I've seen the AI castle THROUGH its own pieces. And I just had the experience of playing a move, using a Hint, then taking a Mulligan... which froze my side of the board completely. I simply couldn't make another move after that and had to reset.

But the bugs are few and the unrealistic difficulty curve isn't unique to Chess, Texas. It's endemic throughout the sport of chess. So its hard to be angry at a solo dev who didn't manage to crack the code that Chess.com still hasn't come to understand. Which is this: 90% of the players of this game have a 3-digit elo. But you all keep making Chess activities aimed at the upper 10%. ignoring the majority of the player base. The high-elo players acting as the keepers of the sport of Chess have an irrational (and elitist) bias telling them that 1200 is the "middle." It's not. The middle is 600. That's a statistical fact. Start serving the broader audience and more players will stick around long enough to get better.

But I digress. Chess, Texas is the most fun I've had playing Chess... maybe ever. It's a challenge. It's an ego-boost. It's a good way to learn. And it's frequently funny in places you don't expect.

I give it my full recommendation, especially at this price. And I hope the developer makes more like it - improving on the formula and smoothing out the rougher edges - as they go.

我原先以為這款要價NT380的類銀河城遊戲有一點貴得太離譜，因為光是看宣傳片我都感受不到這款遊戲是否值得這個價位，於是我在折扣40%入手之後遊玩並發現「這款遊戲完全值得」，因為它的遊戲內容比我想像中還要更加豐富，我玩得很開心。
不過我還是建議折扣40%入手，因為他並不是一款值得讓人一再回味的類銀河城，它只是在「可以玩玩看」的程度而已。

[h3]▼優點[/h3]
+金幣賺取容易
+優秀的跳躍操作手感
+每個區域都有充足的傳送點，探索較為省時
+豐富的魔法招式作為搭配，並且還附有魔法欄位可供切換

[h3]▼缺點[/h3]
-受到攻擊時沒有無敵，時常吃下離譜的連擊傷害直接死亡
-後期怪物攻擊傷害爆棚，容錯率極低 (雖然聽過已經修改了但遇到一大群怪物仍然是要你的命的)
-DeBuff產生機率極高，且沒有任何抵抗手段，遇上冰屬性攻擊很大概率會直接被冰凍
-劇情引導不明確
-有些謎題考驗投擲桶子的物理碰撞，這很讓人詬病 (如果有投擲拋物線那就理想多了)
-空中施展詠唱技能居然要個別練到Lv.8，門檻太過於嚴苛 (空中詠唱其實也沒多強)
-很多地方都得要「衝刺+極限跳躍」才能通過，不免讓人有些厭煩

[h3]■總結[/h3]
我撰寫評論到這裡...沒想到缺點比想像中還要更多，雖然這些缺陷對我而言都不是很致命，至少它沒有浮誇的跳跳樂以及多到數不清的解謎把我勸退，他就是一款「老老實實讓你與怪物戰鬥、探索地圖直到破關」的類銀河城遊戲。
雖然我最後玩得有點不太開心，因為Boss戰難度太誇張，我甚至連自己怎麼被打死的都不曉得，但是熬過來後我認為這一切都很值得，是一款好遊戲。

游戏中最戳我的点是其碎片式叙事及其剧情，不断收集照片并将其拼成一个反战的故事，配合场景去理解深思令人潸然泪下，二周目帮助战后人民（or退伍老兵）摆脱战争的阴影从而升华主题，反对战争并在战后让我们去拥抱更广阔的世界（即打破笼的束缚）

[h1]《笼中窥梦》本质上是制作组对于“高雅”艺术形式的探索和追求，至于大众玩家的体验，他们并不在乎。本作制作的目的是以能够获得西方奖项为前提以自我实现而制作的一个文艺的、小众的互动装置艺术。[/h1]

——解谜的部分足够糟糕，对于解谜缺乏打磨，脑洞过大，缺乏引导，谜题设计毫无逻辑的解决办法是粗暴地全部放到提示里，再不行就直接放演示画面。（确实花了心思，但本质问题是谜题本身的设置缺乏逻辑和引导）
——不在乎玩家是否能够理解剧情，只强调自我表达，所以把关键故事剧情的照片隐藏在了各个角落。
——割裂了玩家的游玩和“听”故事的体验，并且强迫玩家反复重复游玩。本作的游戏设计完完全全就是失败的，只能将视错觉核心玩法和所要讲述的剧情割裂开来。

[b]只关注艺术上的自我表达，而忽略了一般人对于游玩和听故事的需求，那是肯定不能引起大众的共鸣的，起码《笼中窥梦》没有在我心中点起一丝波澜，当然他们确实也不在乎，正如本评测的第一段所言。[/b]

Знаете, иногда так хочется вернуться в какую-нибудь старую, проверенную игру — не для острых ощущений, а как в уютное, хоть и жутковатое, воспоминание. Для меня Fran Bow — именно такая классика.
Впервые проходил её годы назад, и сейчас, переигрывая, снова испытал эту странную смесь грусти и нежности. Да, это история о девочке в психиатрической больнице, о её травмах и страхах, но подано это так... по-детски прямо и в то же время пронзительно. Ты не просто наблюдаешь за кошмарами Фран — ты смотришь на мир её глазами. А её мир, стоит принять волшебную таблетку, мгновенно превращается из грустного и несправедливого в пугающий, сюрреалистичный и населённый самыми причудливыми существами.
Мне кажется, главная магия игры не в пугающих образах (хотя и их хватает!), а в этой двойственности. Головоломки заставляют думать, но не слишком сложные — идеально, чтобы расслабиться вечером. Рисованная графика стареет как хорошее вино, с каждым годом приобретая ещё больше шарма. И конечно, мистер Полночь — тот самый чёрный кот, который скрашивает любое, даже самое мрачное приключение.
Это одна из тех игр, после которой не хочется сразу переключаться на что-то другое. Хочется немного посидеть в тишине, обдумать всё увиденное и просто поблагодарить разработчиков за то, что они подарили нам такую нежную, странную и запоминающуюся историю. Если вы ещё не играли — очень рекомендую выделить на неё несколько вечеров. Это тот самый случай, когда игра становится не просто развлечением, а настоящим переживанием.

Vigil: The Longest Night is a haunting, meticulously crafted action RPG developed and published by Glass Heart Games that merges the precision of a Metroidvania with the punishing sensibilities of a Souls-like adventure. Set in a world swallowed by endless darkness, the game follows Leila, a member of the Vigilant Order, who returns to her hometown only to find it consumed by shadow and decay. Her mission to uncover the truth behind the eternal night quickly transforms into a descent through a realm of cosmic horror, grotesque creatures, and shattered faith. What defines Vigil is not just its mechanics, but its atmosphere—an oppressive fusion of beauty and dread that feels both mythic and personal, like a nightmare you can’t wake from but don’t want to leave.

The gameplay draws heavily from both classic and modern inspirations, borrowing the exploratory freedom of Castlevania: Symphony of the Night and the unforgiving combat rhythm of Dark Souls. Each area of the world is interconnected, full of secrets, hidden paths, and shortcuts that reward curiosity and persistence. Leila’s movements are fluid yet deliberate, forcing the player to consider timing and positioning during every encounter. The combat system relies on stamina management, precise dodges, and calculated strikes. Every weapon—sword, axe, bow, or dagger—has its own unique feel and rhythm, and while experimentation is encouraged, mastery of timing is the real key to survival. The game’s boss fights, numbering around twenty, are a highlight: each one is a brutal test of reflexes and patience, combining pattern recognition with raw adaptability. The difficulty is never arbitrary; it is earned, and overcoming these foes gives the sense of triumph that only games in this lineage can provide.

What separates Vigil from its inspirations is its gothic-horror aesthetic, which permeates every facet of the experience. The world is one of perpetual twilight, painted in layers of despair and decay. The environments—crumbling villages, mist-choked forests, underground cathedrals, and grotesque dreamscapes—are designed to feel at once familiar and alien. The art direction is striking, rendered in hand-drawn 2D visuals with a painterly depth that gives the illusion of three-dimensional space. The result is a visual tone that evokes dread and melancholy in equal measure. Each creature you encounter looks like it has crawled out of some fevered myth, all twisted limbs and haunted eyes. The game’s use of lighting and color enhances this sense of unease; bright areas are few and fleeting, and even in moments of respite, the world feels wounded. The music, composed by Jouni Valjakka, mirrors this tension with somber melodies that swell into dark crescendos during combat, reinforcing the emotional weight of Leila’s journey.

The narrative unfolds gradually, relying on implication rather than exposition. Instead of spelling out the lore, the game allows the player to piece together its mythology through fragmented dialogue, cryptic notes, and environmental storytelling. The story touches on themes of loss, faith, and the cyclical nature of corruption, with each discovery adding another layer to the tragic tapestry of the world. Leila’s quest is as much about self-discovery as it is about banishing the darkness, and the game’s multiple endings reflect the choices and interpretations players bring to the story. This ambiguity gives Vigil a literary quality, rewarding players who take time to read between the lines. Yet this approach can also alienate those seeking a more straightforward narrative; its restraint means that some moments feel opaque, leaving interpretation up to the imagination rather than delivering direct emotional closure.

From a technical and mechanical standpoint, Vigil is an impressive feat for an indie production, though it bears the hallmarks of a small team’s ambition. The game runs smoothly on most systems, and the controls are generally tight, though occasional hit detection issues and platforming quirks can break the immersion. The map system, while functional, can feel cumbersome during heavy exploration, particularly when backtracking through multiple layers of terrain. Some players may also find the difficulty curve uneven; certain bosses and areas spike in challenge unexpectedly, while others fall short of the tension built by their design. The weapon and skill upgrade systems are robust, though some choices feel less impactful over time. These imperfections, while noticeable, rarely overshadow the experience as a whole—they serve more as reminders of the game’s independent roots than as serious detriments.

Where Vigil excels most is in its atmosphere and tone. The developers understand how to make silence as powerful as sound. Every ruined village and forgotten temple carries an echo of tragedy, and the small details—candles flickering in abandoned homes, distant screams in the fog, the sound of blood dripping in caverns—create an unshakable sense of presence. The game doesn’t rely on cheap scares; its horror is existential, built from loneliness and decay. It’s a world that feels like it’s dying slowly, dragging the player along with it. This somber beauty makes exploration inherently rewarding even when the rewards are intangible. The sense of melancholy, reinforced by subdued writing and mournful visuals, makes Vigil one of the few modern Metroidvania games that captures true horror through atmosphere rather than spectacle.

In terms of content, Vigil offers substantial value for its scope. A single playthrough can take between twenty and thirty hours depending on how thoroughly you explore. The world is dense with secrets, optional bosses, and hidden story fragments that encourage revisits. The inclusion of multiple endings adds replayability, as does the variety of weapon types and combat approaches. The pacing alternates between intense combat sequences and slower, reflective exploration, giving players time to absorb the world’s mood. This rhythm of violence and silence forms the emotional backbone of the game, and it’s what keeps the experience from feeling repetitive even after long sessions. For players who crave the satisfaction of steady growth and mastery, Vigil provides that in abundance.

Ultimately, Vigil: The Longest Night is a dark gem in the modern indie landscape—a game that pays homage to its inspirations while forging its own identity through atmosphere, tone, and artistry. It’s not perfect; its rough edges, occasional pacing issues, and opaque storytelling can test a player’s patience. Yet its strengths far outweigh its flaws. Few games manage to blend challenging combat, evocative world-building, and genuine emotional weight with such confidence. It stands as a reminder that games can be both brutal and beautiful, terrifying and tender, mechanical and meaningful. For fans of gothic horror, Souls-like difficulty, and atmospheric exploration, Vigil: The Longest Night is not just worth playing—it’s worth getting lost in.

[b]③提示された謎や伏線を丁寧に回収し、かつ文章や展開が冗長にならないよう工夫されている。[/b]
推理パートに関しても丁寧に作られているのを感じました。
推理中に新たに出てくる疑問点に関してもすぐ拾ってくれるため、特にモヤモヤすることなく読み進めることが出来ました。
それだけ丁寧に進行するため文章量が多くなりがちですが、ロールバック機能の活用により展開が冗長にならないよう纏められているのもよくできているな～と感心しました。

[b]④ストーリー展開[/b]
ひたすら構成がうまいなと唸らされました。
メリハリのつけ方がよく、飽きさせない展開になっており作者の手腕を感じました。
もちろん登場するキャラクターたちもそれぞれ魅力的でした。

[h3]・微妙に感じた点[/h3]
[b]①少々ギャグのノリがきつい[/b]

推理ゲームとしてユーザーが遊びやすく高い水準で作られておりストーリーやエンディングに関しても納得感がありタイトルのインパクトに負けない出来でした。

El Paso Elsewhere is a game that wears it's inspirations on it's sleeves-- Max Payne being the obvious one. I was sold on the idea of a Max Payne game with supernatural elements alongside some non-euclidean levels to go along with it. The voice direction and music are all PHENOMENAL as they are done by RJ Lake and he is quickly becoming one of my favorite artists. As a result, the plot was really engaging and it made me really want to see what would happen to James Savage at the end of his journey. While the story itself is extremely good, the gameplay itself overstays it's welcome a little bit. You have 50 levels of running and gunning where as Max Payne you had way less than that and is generally a shorter but overall better experience. You get enemy types sprinkled here and there but you see the full cast of baddies pretty quick. The guns are also good to use, but it was really disappointing that we couldn't dual wield anything besides the starting handguns. As a comparison, you had dual handguns in Max Payne but you could also get dual magnums, uzis, etc. There are some boss fights but they are just okay and basically demand that you get really used to the dodge roll if you hadn't been using it up until this point. 

Overall though, I recommend giving this game a try if you don't mind a longer Max Payne game and are okay with a lack of variety. If they ever decided to go back and redo this game, I would maybe cut some levels just to make it a tad shorter (and they might have done this to emphasize how tired James is at the very end) and add in more enemy types and definitely more guns-- it would've helped blasting through those levels and make an alright experience into a better one. :)

Burger Shop is one of those games that surprised me in a simple way. It is not life changing and it is definitely similar to a lot of other cooking or serving style games, but it still manages to be fun and satisfying when you just want something fast and easy to focus on.

There is no actual cooking in it, but the game still brings the same pressure as a cooking game. You are juggling orders, bouncing between stations and trying to keep up as things speed up. It pushes your hand eye coordination and short term memory without feeling overwhelming.

The variety is probably the best part. You get burgers, breakfast items, drinks, ice cream, dinner foods, and each thing only takes a couple steps to build. It moves fast, which is the whole point. It never feels slow or dragged out, but it also never becomes so complicated that it turns stressful.

I like that every customer is a little character with their own habits and preferences. You start to recognize them after a while which helps you move a bit quicker, but not enough to make everything predictable. There is still that little rush when someone walks in and you already know they are about to order half the menu.

The auto serve robot is a nice touch. You save it for the annoying order, drop it at the right moment and keep going. It adds a small layer of planning without turning the game into something it is not.

One thing I noticed is how smooth the ingredient system is. When you need something, the machine just pops it out at the right moment. You almost never miss ingredients because the game makes it easy to stay in the flow.

The little comic style story cutscenes in between levels are cute. Nothing deep, but a fun extra.

Overall, Burger Shop is a simple, fast paced game that scratches the same itch as other food building games. It is easy to get into, it moves quickly, and it is something you can pick up when you want a light, quick game to keep your brain moving.

Leveling and accumulating points and experience for various things is one of the most gratifying aspects of this game.  For example:
+ Successful quests give you more approval at 5 cities and 3 vendors
+ Each individual talent levels up quickly at 10-30-75-150 experience
+ Experience gives attributes and skill points
+ Armor and weapons can be leveled with money and materials

None of this is unique, but it is well integrated into the progression of the game without being too linear.  Eventually you'll have to level everything, but the order is completely up to you.
+ The approval quests give make everything more profitable and help you accomplish the final goal, but there are many other ways to get money and still have fun with the game -- so there is no super rush (although it's certainly the most efficient way to play.)
+ Strength paired with the skills Athletics and Meditation are the best way to start out, but my characters were still very viable before I figured this out.

What I didn't realize right away is that talents are essential at the games most difficult settings, and to level them you need stamina which is expensive unless you generate for free by passing time with the space bar.  You don't have to do this forever, because money starts pouring in around level 15, but in the early game it's a bit of a pain.

I also think the game get significantly easier after level 15 and the spread between your abilities and the mobs seem to widen as the game progresses.

[h1] DARK WISH [/h1]

This game is a typical cheap product that focuses on specific content.

The essence is extremely simple: there are only 75 levels, five for each of the presented anime girls.

Depending on whether you have an NSFW patch installed, you alternately assemble puzzles from different numbers of pieces. The first four levels can either show stock pictures (people or some harmless inscriptions), or, if there is a patch, gradually reveal certain parts of the characters' bodies.

Frankly speaking, there are no positive aspects to this game.

Honestly, this game doesn’t have any redeeming qualities.  

The main issues are with the sound design. Not all the sounds are terrible, but there’s one thing that’s really annoying: in the NSFW mode, while putting together a puzzle, the character starts making these characteristic moans. The worst part is that the moan loops continuously and you can’t turn it off until you leave the current level. If the NSFW patch isn’t installed, every misplaced puzzle piece is accompanied by the same character giggling, which gets super annoying really fast. And all of this sound is supposed to be a hint: placing a piece correctly comes with a certain signal.  

As for the content itself: with all due respect to different player tastes, the very fact that something like this is being sold and bought on Steam seems, to put it mildly, a questionable idea.

If you value your money, have any sense of taste, and aren’t after easy achievements or collectible cards, then just send this game far away on a bedtime journey.

That said, I’ll state my position on these kinds of games separately. Yes – I’m asexual, I despise NSFW content and porn in general. Personally, I find it disgusting. But that doesn’t give anyone the right to insult me or others who share this opinion, or poke around in other people’s wallets to see what we buy.

The point is, I’m a collector – and even if I spend my money on this kind of trash, I try to judge it fairly and objectively. Saying that I’m a “gay furry boy” is just plain stupid.

[h1] ЖЕЛАНИЕ ДЖЕЙМСА САНДЕРЛЕНДА [/h1]

Эта игра представляет собой типичный дешевый порно-продукт, ориентированный на специфический контент.

Суть предельно проста: здесь всего 75 уровней, по пять на каждую из представленных аниме-девушек.

В зависимости от того, установлен ли у вас NSFW-патч, вы поочередно собираете пазлы из разного количества кусочков. Первые четыре уровня могут показывать либо стоковые картинки (человечков или какие нибудь безобидные надписи), либо, при наличии патча, постепенно раскрывать определенные части тела персонажей.

Положительных сторон у этой игры, откровенно говоря, нет.

Основные проблемы заключаются в звуковом оформлении. Не все звуки абсолютно отвратительны, но есть один момент, который по-настоящему бесит: в NSFW-формате, во время сбора пазла, персонаж начинает издавать характерные стоны. Хуже всего то, что этот стон зацикливается и его невозможно отключить, пока вы не выйдете из текущего уровня. Если же NSFW-патч не установлен, каждый неверно размещенный кусочек пазла сопровождается хихиканьем того же персонажа, что очень быстро начинает раздражать до чертиков. При этом звук тут должен служить подсказкой: правильное размещение кусочка сопровождается определенным сигналом.

Что касается наполнения: при всем уважении к разнообразным вкусам игроков, сам факт продажи и приобретения подобного контента в Steam выглядит, мягко говоря, сомнительной затеей.

Если вы цените свои деньги, обладаете хоть каким-то чувством вкуса и не гонитесь за легкими достижениями или коллекционными карточками, то шлите эту игру в далекое постельное путешествие.

Хотя все же, отдельно обозначать буду касаемо данных игр свою позицию. Да - я асексуал, я презираю NSFW и порно само по себе. Лично для меня это отвратительно. Но это не дает никому никакого права осокорблять меня и других с данным мнением, а также совать нос в чужие кошельки чтобы смотреть, что мы покупаем.

Я это все к тому, что я коллекционер - и даже если я трачу на подобный шлак свои деньги - я стараюсь честно и обьективно оценивать его, и говорить о том, что я "гей фурри мальчик" просто тупо.

Love Wish is a romance-focused visual novel that blends light fantasy elements with a branching relationship structure built around player choice. The story centers on a group of heroines connected by fate, with the protagonist drawn into their intersecting lives through a series of emotional events. The narrative emphasizes intimacy, personal growth, and the dynamics of forming meaningful bonds. Its tone is warm and sentimental, leaning toward idealized romance rather than dramatic tension.

Gameplay is built on standard visual novel conventions: reading dialogue, selecting choices, and following character routes that diverge based on your decisions. Most choices carry clear emotional weight and guide you toward different endings, giving the game a sense of agency despite its linear storytelling framework. The pacing is gentle, focusing more on character development and small moments than on plot twists or high-stakes drama.

Character writing is one of the game’s strongest aspects. Each heroine has a distinct personality and arc, providing a mix of upbeat, shy, confident, and quietly complex characters. Their interactions feel sincere, and the game often highlights vulnerability and trust as core themes. While some tropes are familiar to fans of the genre, the execution keeps them engaging, with enough nuance to avoid feeling purely formulaic.

The art direction supports the emotional tone. Character designs are polished and expressive, with detailed portraits and subtle variations that add personality to each scene. Backgrounds are soft and atmospheric, enhancing the romantic mood. The soundtrack leans into calm, melodic tracks that complement both tender and reflective moments, contributing to the overall sense of warmth.

The game’s structure encourages replays. Each route reveals new facets of the story and different emotional beats, and the game rewards exploring multiple endings. While the overarching narrative remains relatively simple, the varied perspectives across routes add dimension to the world and deepen your understanding of the cast’s relationships.

Some weaknesses stem from predictability. Players familiar with romance visual novels may find certain story beats expected, and a few routes follow similar emotional rhythms. Additionally, the pacing can feel slow in the early chapters, especially before the romantic focus becomes clear. However, once character routes begin to unfold, the emotional engagement noticeably increases.

Overall, Love Wish is a heartfelt and gentle visual novel that prioritizes warm character interactions, attractive presentation, and branching romance. It may not break new ground in narrative design, but it delivers a satisfying, emotionally sincere experience for players who enjoy character-driven storytelling and multiple relationship paths.

Banners of Ruin to gra typu rouglikeowy deckbuilder. Rozgrywka podzielona jest na 3 akty (po pierwszym ukończeniu gry dochodzi akt 4), te znowu podzielone są na piętra- każde z nich to event typu walka, sklep, lub fabularne wyzwanie. Po rozwiązaniu go otrzymujemy różnego rodzaju nagrody związane z modyfikacją Naszej talii kart. Zaczynami więc z podstawowymi atakami i obronami, a Naszym celem jest skonstruowanie działającej kompozycji, która poradzi sobie z ostatecznym wyzwaniem jakim jest książę, a później wilczy władca. To co jest niestandardowe dla tego gatunku gier- karty są w większości przypisane do konkretnej postaci. W czasie każdej rozgrywki możemy posiadać aż 6-ściu bohaterów! Przy pierwszym uruchomieniu dostępne są tylko dwie rasy- myszy i misie, wraz z kolejnymi przejściami- łasice, bobry, wilki i króliki. Umiejętności są ściśle związane z stareotypami, które przypisujemy futrzakom- wilk dba o stado, króli skacze pomiędzy pozycjami na polu walki, miś będzie odporny na negatywne efekty, mysz jest zwinna i szybka. 

Mając już zarys stwórzmy więc bardziej konkretny opis gry: Banners of Ruin polega na stworzeniu drużyny sześciorga zwierzątek, które dopełniając się swoimi umiejętnościami w walce dokonają rewolucji i obalą w zbrojnym powstaniu wilczego władcę. Ich arsenał i zdolności przedstawione są za pomocą kart, każda z nich posiada wartość punktów wytrzymałości lub ducha, a te znowu zdobywamy wraz z poziomowaniem Naszych podopiecznych. Poziomowanie! Rozwój odbywa się na dwóch płaszczyznach- pierwszy związany z dostępnym dla Naszego konta postępem, drugi związany z konkretną rozgrywką. W swoim podstawach produkcja przewiduje więc repetytywność- im więcej razy przejdziemy przygodę tym większa pula zwierząt i umiejętności będzie dostępna,  i wreszcie- tym bardziej skomplikowane będzie wyzwanie. 

Brzmi jak świetny pomysł i recepta na długie godziny przy doskonałej i zróżnicowanej zabawie? W praktyce jest tylko jedna gra, która moim zdaniem powtarza tę recepturę z sukcesem i jest to oczywiście Slay The Spire. W porównaniu do króla gatunku Banners of Ruin wypada niestety dość blado. Podsumowując:

+ Dobrze znany i sprawdzony system aktów i pięter- proces progresji jest doskonale odczuwalny
+ Historia zwierzątek jest ciekawie opowiedziana. Mechaniki kart świetnie odzwierciedlają to co znamy z rzeczywistości
+ W związku z ilością bohaterów walka podzielona jest na 2 szeregi i 3 linie- poza zagrywaniem standardowym kart dochodzi jeszcze element taktyki
+ W czasie jednej rozgrywki wyzwanie jest bardzo zróżnicowane- budowa talii jest satysfakcjonująca i daje radość z pokonania wszystkich bossów
+ Karty i przeciwnicy są zbalansowani- gra karze i nagradza za dokładne czytanie zasad specjalnych i wykonywanie czynności w odpowiedniej kolejności. Szczegóły mają znaczenie- każda umiejętność oponentów jest na swój sposób zdradziecka.

- Dla weteranów gatunku przejście gry nie powinno zająć więcej niż 1-3 prób. 
- Bossów kończących kolejne akty jest bardzo mało- praktycznie każde podejście ma dokładnie ten sam scenariusz. 
- Talie przy kolejnych przejściach są do siebie bliźniaczo podobne. Archetypów owszem- jest sześć, ale wybierając jeden z nich zamykamy się w puli bardzo ograniczonych opcji.
- Szybko poznajesz wszystkie dostępne mechaniki, karty nie posiadają poziomu unikalności. 
- Kolejne przejścia nie zwiększają trudności, tak jak kolejne poziomy ascendencji w StS. Gra szybko się nudzi (w większości przypadków po 10-15 godzinach)

Daję ostateczną ocenę: mocne 6,5 / 10. Dla amatorów Banners of Ruin to świetne wprowadzenie do gatunku gier karcianych. Poprzez poziom trudności i świat przedstawiony gra jest przystępna, czytelna i satysfakcjonująca. Dla weteranów do kupienia raczej tylko w promocji i jako ciekawostka. Nie jest to w żadnym wypadku strata pieniędzy, ale nie spodziewam się, że wprowadzi rewolucje w postrzeganie tego typu gier. Osobiście spędziłem w grze `20h i zdobyłem wszystkie achivmenty. Wydaje mi się, że poznałem w tym czasie wszystkie mechaniki, ukończyłem grę 3-krotnie. Odblokowałem większość umiejętności, ale nie dokonywałem żadnych utrudnień w poziomie trudności. Może wprowadziłoby to trochę pikanterii, ale czuję, że formuła już się przejadła i czas na inny tytuł.
