Once you literally beat it once, there's no real point in playing it again. Game play is... extremely repetitive. Sure, you have a few different tower types to pick from but some towers are significantly better than the rest. You get one 'build' that works for you through trial and error, like I did, and... that's it. Because other combinations just aren't as good as certain ones. And it's not always good to diversify your towers in this game. In fact, I had my best runs specializing in 2-3 tower types instead of going for more of the available options. And this falls back to some tower types being superior to others, too.

After 10 hours of gameplay, I was getting bored by the same gameplay loop. I tried different tower combinations. Different spells. But nothing really changed. I try to live by a standard of '1 hour to 1 dollar' gameplay value. I had to force myself to get to almost 26 hours of gameplay because there's not enough interesting gameplay or combinations involved.

They have a system of currency, Honor, that you can spend on buffs and whatnot but its tragically easy to get it. And then after that... cosmetics! Woo. And... there's not much of that either. I did spend a few extra hours in that 26 hours just getting a few cosmetics but... yeah...

And part of it was like an abusive relationship. I kept coming back because, in the beginning, the game was fun. It was interesting. But, again, after about 10 hours, the game got stale and I'd already seen and done everything.

Is it worth playing? Sure. But wait for a sale. 20 bucks might not be a lot for many people but it is, in my opinion, too much for this.

First 20 waves are fun, but numbers get very high very quickly and it's not fun to figure out anymore. Way too much calculation when you gain thousands of resources, manage hundreds of towers, millions of hitpoints... it becomes a slog and a nightmare to do any sort of calculation. If the game was balanced towards 30 waves and played more like a rogue-like, it would be way better.

徘徊者は様々な特徴があるが、共通して能面を被っているやつがやばいので要注意。捕まったらアウト。
ただし、回廊内に落ちているアイテムを上手いこと利用することで、襲撃を回避することもできる。
上手く徘徊者をよけながら、勾玉を回収して脱出することが目的となる。

[h2]・操作性について[/h2]

慣れるまで、ちょっと大変かもしれない。
基本的にアイテムは、棚に置いてあったり箪笥にしまってあったりする。
前者の場合はまだいいのだが、後者の場合は箪笥を開ける動作でもたもたしてしまうことが多い。
また、アイテムの回収もしっかりポインターに合わせてボタンを押さないといけないため、走りながらだったりとかするとうっかり取り損ねたりすることも多々ある。

あと、視界が一人称（操作キャラ視点）なのもあるのと、結構視点をぐりんぐりん動かせるので、慣れないと酔う可能性あり。
とりあえず慣れないうちは一番難度の低い「初心者」を選ぶだけでも十分楽しめる。
ただし隠し要素は基本的に「挑戦者」以上の攻略が必須となる。覚悟すべし。

[h2]・困ったときのアドバイス[/h2]

困ったらこけしを探そう。もしかしたらあなたの助けになるかもしれない。
なお、有料DLCの回廊「外縁」の購入に関しては保証しないものとする。
クリア特典でこけしを探しやすくなるものが使えるようになるとはいえ、内容は「本編クリア相当の難度を誇る回廊」ですので。

[h2]A lenda de Tim[/h2]
Reventure é um jogo [b]2D em pixel art retrô, não linear, com 100 (+1) finais diferentes, desenvolvido pela Pixelatto e lançado em 2019 utilizando o Unity.[/b] Com uma clara inspiração paródica em The Legend of Zelda, controlamos Tim, um jovem que procura aventura e tenta salvar a princesa feita refém pelo terrível Lorde das Trevas em seu castelo.

Como iremos fazer isso depende de nós: o jogo oferece diversos itens e interações que podem levar a finais diferentes. Cada final desbloqueado é registrado em uma espécie de galeria, acompanhado de uma cutscene. O detalhe mais interessante é que todos os finais são canônicos, não importa a ordem em que o jogador os descobre.

À medida que avançamos, [b]o mundo e o próprio personagem mudam:[/b] passagens secretas aparecem, itens surgem em locais diferentes, e novas possibilidades se abrem.

Entre os itens, temos a pá, a espada, [b]a feijoada (nham!)[/b] e muitos outros que podem ser usados para interagir com o mundo e alcançar finais variados. Além disso, o jogo guarda segredos e até um final extra.

Os cenários são bem construídos e cheios de detalhes. Confesso que me vi apreciando cada efeito e trecho do mundo. A trilha sonora é igualmente marcante: chiclete, divertida, daquelas que eu acabei cantarolando no início de cada jogatina sem perceber.

[h2]A aventura está lá fora[/h2]
Por isso, tem um excelente senso de humor, brincando com RPGs, obras medievais e, claro, com The Legend of Zelda. Ele respeita suas inspirações, mas também ri de si mesmo em cada referência, diálogo e final.

Ele valoriza o pensamento do tipo "e se eu pegar item X e for para o lugar Y". Qualquer ação, do erro mais absurdo ao acerto perfeito, pode gerar uma história cômica e, de certo modo, ser uma vitória.

Assim, é um jogo que recomendo fortemente seja para platinar ou simplesmente aproveitar em uma promoção.

Obrigado mais uma vez por lerem a análise. Sempre é um prazer e uma honra tentar dar um pouco do que penso sobre os jogos, abordando algo cômico, filosófico ou até mesmo icônico ao meu ver.

Qualquer dúvida ou elogio é mais do que bem-vindo nos comentários. Terei prazer em conversar com vocês.

Se cuidem, um abraço, uma ótima semana a todos, tudo de melhor sempre e excelentes festas de fim de ano. (-u-)b

[b]Wars Across The World [/b] — это уникальная пошаговая стратегическая игра, созданная для моделирования различных исторических конфликтов от доисторических времен до современности. Игра представляет собой цифровую адаптацию настольного варгейма с глубоким тактическим геймплеем.

[b]Основные достоинства[/b]
[list]
    [*]Универсальная система правил: игрокам достаточно выучить базовые механики один раз, чтобы играть в различные исторические сценарии
    [*]Качественный геймплей: игра предлагает продуманную механику с картами событий, лидерами и разнообразными юнитами
    [*]Визуальное оформление: приятные модели солдат, генералов и карт боевых действий
    [*]Разнообразие сценариев: возможность играть в различные исторические конфликты
    [*]Достойный ИИ: компьютер предоставляет достойное сопротивление, победа над ним приносит удовлетворение
[/list]

[b]Игровые особенности [/b]
[list]
    [*]Пошаговая система с очередями ходов
    [*]Разнообразные типы юнитов (сухопутные, морские, воздушные)
    [*]Система лидеров с уникальными бонусами
    [*]Карты событий, влияющие на ход игры
    [*]Простая финансовая система
    [*]Возможность создания собственных сценариев
[/list]

[b]Недостатки [/b]
[list]
    [*]Проблемы оптимизации: некоторые пользователи отмечают баги с интерфейсом на мобильных устройствах
    [*]Модель монетизации: базовая версия содержит только один сценарий, остальные нужно покупать отдельно
    [*]Высокая стоимость DLC: цены на дополнительные сценарии могут показаться завышенными
    [*]Отсутствие обновлений: длительное время без значимых обновлений
[/list]

[h2]Заключение[/h2]
Wars Across The World — это качественный стратегический варгейм для любителей исторического контента и настольных игр. Несмотря на некоторые технические недочеты и спорную модель монетизации, игра предлагает глубокий и увлекательный геймплей. Edna & Harvey: Harvey’s New Eyes is one of those rare games that makes you laugh, feel weirdly guilty, and question your sanity — often all in the same puzzle. On the surface, it’s a bright, cartoonish point-and-click adventure about a quiet little girl named Lilli. But give it five minutes, and you’ll realize this isn’t a children’s story. It’s a beautifully twisted fairytale wrapped in pastel colors and passive-aggressive nuns.

The humor is dark, but never mean-spirited. It’s that kind of satire that makes you grin while muttering “...wait, should I be laughing at this?” And somehow, it balances that tone perfectly — between absurd comedy and uncomfortable truth.

Gameplay-wise, it’s classic Daedalic chaos: clever, slightly illogical puzzles that make you feel like a genius and an idiot in equal measure. The world is bizarrely alive, full of characters who feel both hilarious and deeply broken — like everyone’s hiding a trauma under a smiley sticker.

By the end, you realize the game isn’t just telling a story — it’s dissecting innocence, obedience, and denial, all while keeping you entertained enough to forget you’re being emotionally ambushed. It’s short, punchy, and unlike anything else out there.

If you like your adventures with equal doses of laughter and existential dread, play this one. Just... don’t trust the bunny.

Fading Serenades is one of those rare games that proves you don’t need 3D graphics or complex gameplay loops to create something truly special. What you need is inspiration, intent, and a meaningful story.. And this game delivers all of that really beautifully.

From the moment I started playing, I was amazed by both the sound design and nostalgic visuals. The calming atmosphere just made me take a deep breath and fully drew me in. Each area feels different and alive, through little visual and sound cues, which made it really easy to navigate even without a map. The island is filled with small details that make the world feel real and calming... but in no way boring.

You play as Callum, someone new to the island looking to escape the stress of daily life by delivering parcels. At first, the gameplay seemed simple, but the mix of a limited backpack, a ticking clock, and stamina adds a surprising amount of strategy. “Can I reach one more person before the day ends?”.

The characters were an absolute highlight for me. Each one is thoughtfully written, full of nuance, quirks, and personality. They all feel real in their own strange and fun ways. What really amazed me was how well I got to know each character through the parcels they sent and received. Every delivery revealed a little more about the characters and their connections. As the days went by I felt more and more like I was a part of this island and really got to know each character.

The story was a really fun mystery to unravel as the days went by. I loved being able to choose between pushing the story forward or taking time to finish deliveries, as it gave me full control over the pacing. My only wish is that the relationship between Callum and Par had been explored just a bit more, especially toward the end. I would have really wanted to know more about Par.

If you’re looking for a heartfelt, relaxing game that lets you escape into a meaningful world, Fading Serenades is absolutely worth your time. With its beautiful sound design, thoughtful storytelling, and nostalgic art style, it’s a game that stays with you long after.

[hr][/hr]
Aunque la idea inicial, los tráilers y las capturas de pantalla lucen geniales, en realidad se trata más de una estrategia de marketing ingeniosa que de un juego sólido. Attack of the Earthlings ofrece una experiencia superficial, repetitiva y, en muchos momentos, desesperante.

El juego dura entre 6 y 8 horas y consta de solo 7 misiones sin posibilidad real de rejugarlas. Todos los enemigos y eventos están completamente predefinidos y siguen exactamente el mismo patrón cada vez, lo que elimina cualquier tipo de sorpresa o variación táctica. No se pueden repetir niveles ya completados, y si quieres volver atrás tendrás que empezar una partida desde cero. Los enemigos emiten sonidos ridículos, el humor rara vez funciona y la música se vuelve repetitiva muy pronto.

[hr][/hr]
[h2]Pros[/h2]
[list]
[*] Concepto original: jugar como el alienígena.
[/list]
[h2]Contras[/h2]
[list]
[*] Muy poca rejugabilidad.
[*] Árbol de progresión lineal y poco interesante.
[*] Interfaz molesta: clic derecho falla con frecuencia.
[*] Apartado visual mediocre y sin personalidad.
[*] Humor forzado y diálogos pesados.
[/list]

[hr][/hr]
[h2]Conclusión[/h2]
[i]Attack of the Earthlings intenta ser un “Invisible Inc. al revés”, pero se queda muy lejos de lograrlo. La falta de ritmo, la interfaz torpe y la ausencia de rejugabilidad lo hacen sentir como un juego en acceso anticipado más que un producto terminado. Original review follows:

This is a sole developers first time project, from a developer who, at the time, was apparently unable to secure work as a professional game developer.  Now, I'm not one to overuse analogies, but if you had to go on a plane flight, would you choose the plane designed and built by hundreds of engineers at Airbus, or the plane designed by the guy who never made a plane before, couldn't get a job at Airbus, and made the thing in his backyard in his spare time?  Yeah.  So why are you even reading reviews for this game?  Move along, nothing to see here.

The game is very simplistic, small and limited in scope and ambition.  This feels more like a tech demo, proof of concept or student homework assignment rather than a fully fledged product designed for PC gamers.  As such it doesn't offer any real value as a serious PC game.

As always reviews are all about the game, and this one is a rather poor one, even if it was a genuine attempt by someone unqualified to do the thing they're not qualified to do.  It's a first person adventure/puzzle game of somewhat inferior quality to the average Russian haunted house Unity asset flip.  There's an egyptian kind of theme (I guess?) but for some reason the title screen has some American mesas in it... and really the quality is just so low none of that matters.

You don't have to take my word about how bad the game is, we can measure the interest in a game by how much people bothered to play it.  Derision has achievements, and they show us a very clear picture that the game absolutely failed to capture any interest from gamers.  The most commonly and easily attained achievement is for finish the (short) game, trivial to achieve, but less than 8 percent of players bothered to get that far before uninstalling the game.  That's a tiny, tiny proportion of gamers who even bothered with this.  Ouch.

The poor quality of this game is also reflected by how many people spent time with it.  At the time of this review, SteamDB shows the game all-time peak player count was only ONE player.  That's right, only one person ever played this at a time.  When I played this for the purposes of reviewing it, I equalled the peak player count for the game.  OUCH.  The only player activity occurs once or twice a month, presumably someone loading it up to see what it is then quickly uninstalling it.  Considering there's over 120 million gamers on Steam and well over 100,000 games for gamers to choose from, the overwhelming lack of interest in this low quality game is to be expected.

So, should you buy this game?  Is this one of the best of the 100,000+ games on Steam?

Derision is relatively cheap at $1 USD, but it's not worth it. Given the defects and quality issues with the game, coupled with the unrealistic price, this is impossible to recommend.  This is also competing with over 11,000 free games available on Steam, many of them far better than this paid product.

A soft RPG brawler with more ambitions than it's willing to flesh out. Combat is rewarding, with good physics based environmental fighting, The stealth is present, but most stealth paths are high above or out of view for guards, making the skill itself mostly impactful for stealth take downs which become unimportant. All other systems serve to grant rewards that are mostly useless, as money has no real functional purpose in the game. Both speech skills save you money on bribes or avoiding fights. Hacking mostly gets you codes to storage units with money in them. Lock picking does the same at the extra bonus of being unneeded to pick any lock in the game. Grit defines your tank capability but holding block denies all damage in the game.

The result is a melee brawler claiming to be an RPG despite the only important stats being: Nerd (hard locks pulses used for hacking) and Strength (controls combat) while dumping everything into combat and stealth to get the relevant perks. 

I will say the melee is fun, but if you are looking for the expressive immersive RPG the game markets itself as, you will be sorely disappointed. It took me about nine hours to complete 100%.

Christmas Night is a compact first-person horror experience that takes the warmth and familiarity of a holiday setting and slowly twists it into something unnerving. Developed by CROSSRED and published by SKYFOSTER, the game places you in the role of Vanessa, a twelve-year-old girl spending Christmas Eve with her mother in their quiet Alaskan home. What begins as a typical night filled with decorations, gifts, and cozy domestic details gradually shifts as the house’s comforting glow starts to feel heavier, colder, and more oppressive. The premise hinges on a simple question—whether good behavior earns reward or punishment—but the way the game explores that idea is what gives it its unsettling tone.

The gameplay structure centers on exploration and tension rather than complex mechanics. You move through dim hallways, peek into rooms, and interact with household objects while the environment steadily grows more hostile. Doors that once opened easily now resist you, shadows seem thicker than before, and everyday noises take on a threatening edge. The house itself becomes a maze of dread, and the game’s pacing does a strong job of letting the unease build slowly before delivering sharper, more frantic moments. Occasional light puzzle elements break up the navigation, but these are deliberately minimal so as not to distract from the atmosphere. The game is short, meant to be played in a single session, and this tight scope works to its advantage by keeping the tension concentrated.

Christmas Night relies heavily on audiovisual design to create fear. The graphics are modest but effective: decorations are scattered around the house in ways that feel lived-in, and the holiday elements—twinkling lights, wrapped presents, the Christmas tree—are presented with an almost sentimental charm at first. As things escalate, this cheerfulness becomes eerie in contrast with the darker events unfolding. Flickering lights, abrupt sound spikes, and sudden environmental shifts do much of the heavy lifting, allowing the game to produce panic without resorting to excessive jump scares. Sound design in particular stands out; the creaks, muffled thumps, and distorted holiday ambiance give the impression that something unseen is always nearby.

The storytelling is subtle, leaving most of the interpretation to the player. Through hints in the environment and Vanessa’s reactions, you begin to piece together a picture of a family under strain and a child caught in forces she doesn’t fully understand. The game doesn’t push its themes overtly, but they linger in the background, adding emotional weight to the events. Because it is told entirely from a child’s perspective, ordinary fears feel amplified—dark rooms loom larger, footsteps echo louder, and the unknown presence stalking the house feels overwhelming. This perspective helps the narrative maintain its tension without needing elaborate plot twists.

Christmas Night’s strengths are tied closely to its scope. It is short, atmospheric, and focused, offering a brief but effective dose of holiday-themed horror. However, this also means the experience may feel limited for players who prefer longer campaigns or deeper mechanics. Once you understand the core loop—explore, escalate tension, survive the reveal—there are few surprises left. Those accustomed to complex puzzles, branching storylines, or intricate worldbuilding will find this game more of a mood piece than a substantial adventure. Yet, its simplicity is intentional, and it excels at what it chooses to prioritize: mood, pacing, and an escalating sense of dread.

Ultimately, Christmas Night works best as a bite-sized horror story wrapped in festive trimmings. It delivers a well-crafted atmosphere, strong sound design, and a creeping tension that turns a comforting holiday setting into a claustrophobic nightmare. For fans of short indie horror titles that rely more on tone than complexity, it offers an engaging, chilling experience. For others, it may feel like a brief interlude rather than a full meal—but as a dark holiday tale told in one evening, it hits exactly the notes it aims for.

Ocean’s Heart is a heartfelt indie action-adventure created by Max Mraz and published by Nordcurrent Labs, and it immediately signals its devotion to classic top-down exploration games. Rather than leaning on spectacle or overwrought drama, it opens with a simple but compelling emotional hook: Tilia, a young woman living in a quiet seaside town, sets out to search for her missing father after a pirate raid changes her life. The premise is familiar, but it functions as a catalyst rather than the focus—the real story unfolds as you travel across a vast island chain filled with secret alcoves, abandoned ruins, remote villages, eccentric characters, and buried histories. From the very beginning, the game emphasizes curiosity, encouraging players to drift off the main path in pursuit of something unexpected.

The moment-to-moment gameplay balances combat, exploration, light puzzle solving, and resource collection. Tilia begins with only a basic sword and bow, but as the journey progresses she gains new tools—bombs, magic abilities, special potions, environmental gadgets—that gradually expand what the world allows her to access. Many areas initially appear unreachable or incomplete, but returning later with better abilities reveals shortcuts, treasure, and hidden quests. This gentle form of progression makes exploration rewarding without forcing constant backtracking. Combat itself is simple and accessible, relying on timing, spacing, and item usage rather than elaborate combos or skill trees. Enemies vary just enough to keep encounters engaging, and boss battles, while not particularly complex, serve as satisfying punctuation marks scattered throughout the world.

Ocean’s Heart places heavy emphasis on optional content. Nearly every town, island hut, or ocean cliffside contains someone in need of help, whether it’s retrieving heirlooms, solving small mysteries, clearing dungeons, or simply offering a moment of narrative humor. These side quests give the archipelago personality and prevent the world from feeling like a set of decorative backdrops. Some quests reward meaningful upgrades or rare items, while others simply enrich the setting or offer playful jokes, reinforcing the game’s lighthearted tone. The main story operates comfortably in the background, allowing players to progress at their own pace rather than funneling them through a linear sequence of objectives.

The presentation is one of Ocean’s Heart’s greatest strengths. The pixel art is thoughtfully composed, with vibrant biomes, expressive character sprites, cozy interiors, and environmental details that invite slow observation. Coastlines shimmer, forests feel lush, and old stone structures seem worn down by salty winds. The soundtrack complements this visual storytelling with gently adventurous melodies that shift between melancholic, whimsical, and mysterious depending on location. Both art and music evoke nostalgia without feeling derivative—they capture a sense of youthful wonder often missing from modern action games. Combined with clean menus and intuitive interface design, the result is a world that feels familiar, inviting, and alive.

While Ocean’s Heart succeeds in creating a charming and exploration-driven experience, it does have limitations. The combat, though functional, never grows substantially more complex, which may disappoint players seeking systems to master. Difficulty remains forgiving throughout, and aside from occasional damage spikes, most encounters can be handled with basic movement and item usage. Navigation can also be occasionally imprecise—though the world is well designed, the map lacks detailed markers, and players may temporarily forget where certain quest locations are. Some side quests end abruptly or offer modest rewards, and not every narrative thread reaches a meaningful resolution. These shortcomings don’t derail the experience, but they may mildly temper expectations for those seeking deep tactical or emotional payoff.

Despite its smaller scope, Ocean’s Heart thrives because it understands what makes exploration satisfying—secrets tucked behind waterfalls, caves hidden beneath foliage, a locked door remembered hours later, or a quiet village with a personal story to uncover. It is not concerned with revolutionizing the action-adventure genre but instead aims to recreate the joy of wandering through a handcrafted fantasy world without pressure, frustration, or excessive complexity. It respects the player’s time and intelligence, offering consistent discovery without overwhelming them with systems, markers, or directives.

For players who grew up loving 2D adventures or for those who simply want a gentle, well-built indie game rooted in exploration, Ocean’s Heart is a rewarding journey. It offers warmth instead of intensity, curiosity instead of urgency, and sincerity instead of spectacle. It may not strive to be the biggest or boldest action-adventure on Steam, but it excels at capturing the feeling of setting sail toward the unknown—guided not by destiny, but by the simple desire to see what’s waiting beyond the next island.

[b]The Lightkeeper[/b] - [b]отличная атмосферная бродилка[/b], если вы ищете короткий психологический хоррор на вечер. Среди множества проектов на Unreal Engine 5 эта игра дарит [u]неплохую историю[/u], пару скейров и [i]очень мрачную, вязкую атмосферу[/i].

Сюжет повествует о мужчине, который после войны получает работу смотрителя маяка на небольшом острове. С первых минут ясно: герой откровенно от чего-то бежит, а на самом маяке произошло нечто ужасное - три предыдущих смотрителя пропали без вести. Очень быстро становится понятно, что место хранит чудовищные тайны, и вам предстоит не только пережить ужасы, но и докопаться до истины.

История интересная и подана достойно: есть записки, кат-сцены (хоть и сделаны слабовато), [b]хороший темп[/b]. Следить за происходящим увлекательно, но есть нюанс: уже одна из первых записок довольно прямо намекает, что всё случившееся тесно связано с самим протагонистом. Изначально игра флиртует с мистикой, но быстро считывается, что это именно психологический хоррор про тёмные секреты героя - догадаться о направлении несложно. Тем не менее ритм выдержан, и [u]сюжет тащит[/u].

Геймплей - классический "ходячий симулятор": изучаете локации, читаете записки, впитываете атмосферу, иногда решаете простые задачи на поиск ключей или примитивные головоломки. Погонь и стелса нет. Начало развивается медленно - первые 20 минут вы повторяете однообразные действия и много ходите, почти без событий, - но затем игра вываливает череду более увлекательных эпизодов и мгновенно приковывает внимание.

С атмосферой порядок, особенно в середине. Она мрачная, местами грустная; есть пара неплохих скейров, но в целом напряжение строится на картинке и звуке. [i]Графика приятная[/i] - Unreal делает своё дело. Отдельный плюс - освещение: в тёмных местах вы не идёте "в угольной пещере", глаза не устают.

[quote]Если ищете атмосферную, мрачную бродилку на час с увлекательной историей и простым геймплеем без постоянной опасности, да ещё и с парой скейров, - [b]The Lightkeeper отличный выбор[/b]. Игра стоит недорого и делает многое правильно: крепкая атмосфера, сюжет держит внимание. Любителям психологических хорроров - смело брать.[/quote]

So I have to be a little strict here.
It's an okay game that plays on your nostalgia. I am about halfway through and will bring myself to finish it.

BUT I can't recommend it. Why? There is literally ONE mechanic in the game, which is dragging items in the inventory and sorting them. One action.. and it doesn't work properly. Items you drop don't go to where you want them and you have to drag them slightly out of the blocks you want to place them in, which is just.. bad. It seems like the developers didn't want to bother patching it either.

Tbh, part of my dissatisfaction with the game is me going into it expecting it to effectively be Save Room 3, which was my own fault, especially since I played this immediately after both of the Save Room games, but I kept thinking about them a lot while playing The Auto Sort Is Broken because it gets wrong a lot of what they got right.

First off, the controls. I'm personally not a fan of how you have to drag the items rather than clicking once to pick up and then clicking again to put down, but that's just personal preference and I can look past it. What I can look past considerably less is how the game's detection of where you're placing the items is MUCH worse than the Save Room games. In both SR game, placing items down felt perfect, I'd always place something down where I meant to without fail (whether or not placing it down there was a good idea is a different story). In Auto Sort however, I'd frequently find that the items get dropped one tile off in one or both axes and it would take a lot of fiddling in order to get the items to go where I wanted them to. This is something these devs had down to a science, I don't understand what happened.

Secondly, the puzzles themselves. I like the changed focus towards grouping items next to each other, but the puzzles overall never get all that complicated. The game does try to make them harder sometimes by putting you on a time limit, but I honestly do not enjoy that mechanic as I often found that it was a complete crapshoot as to whether I'd solve them in time depending on if I happened to put everything in the grid in an optimal way on my first try. It did make them harder I guess, but in a way that made them frustrating instead. I did like the puzzles where you have to have to fit the players items in while avoiding the junk they picked up along the way, but sometimes it was too difficult to figure out what was trash and what was treasure, so to speak.

Lastly, I'm not a fan of the achievements system. You just do puzzles until you get them seemingly at random, and then you buy them with the gold you earn also from doing puzzles. There's no skill or intricacy to them beyond progressing through the game, they just happen, so they ended up not feeling like much of an achievement to me. It also doesn't help that with the exception of the final achievement I already had all the gold needed to buy them the moment they popped up, and that when playing in a narrower than 16:9 resolution (my monitor is 16:10), the "You have new achievements" popup softlocks the achievements button as well as every other button. I had to alt+F4 every time this happened in order to actually buy the achievements I'd "earned".

All in all, massive downgrade from the prior games these developers have made like this. Go buy the Save Room games instead. They're much more substantial for literally the same price individually.

TLDR: Don't accept defense missions at your current base location.

I wanted to like this game. I loved Wing Commander. I loved Privateer. I loved Freelancer. I like Rebel Galaxy, but it wasn't like those other games. This one had so much promise. It had all the little touches: good soundtrack, good plot and characters, the freedom to pick and choose what missions to do next. They even did the cockpit layout change with different ships like WC. But as much as I hate to say it, I can't recommend the game for two reasons.
1. The difficulty scaling is all over the place. For whatever reason, Rebel Galaxy didn't have this problem. If the mission difficulty said high, you knew it was risky. If it said low, you could be reasonably sure you could complete it. But I can't trust what this game says. Orzu asks me to stun some police ships; the banner says mild but I get blown to dust. The enemy missile spam is relentless, even on "easy" missions. Running for your life just delays the inevitable.
2. You can soft-lock yourself. I'm not just talking about game bugs, but I'm talking about getting into a situation where you are just stuck. The game saves when you leave a base. If you run into enemies when you leave that you can't defeat or escape, you are screwed. You'll die, then respawn at the same base. With the same enemies. Who will kill you again. And you can't run back inside the base to hide or cancel the mission because it won't let you dock when hostiles are present.
Of course, if you could have multiple saves in a playthrough, this wouldn't be a problem. Not sure if a mission is possible? Just make a save in the base before you accept and try it. If it's too hard, just reload and try something else. We had this figured out in the 1990s, but apparently we lost that ability in the intervening 30 years. Now you get one save and you can't control when that save happens, so the game forces you to play conservatively.
I got this on sale so I'm not too salty, but I want to warn others of my experience.

It is clear to me that the perception of this game is going to be very different depending on whether you are an old school player of Wing Commander Privateer or anyone else. Calling Rebel Galaxy Outlaw a spiritual successor or a tribute to Privateer does not cut it, the similarities are stronger. This game does everything to make a fan of Privateer feel right at home.

Having played Privateer several times over the decades I developed small routines, like starting a new game by immediately selling the laser and missile launcher to buy mass driver and torpedoes. I was amazed to discover that I could do exactly the same here, and even the layout of each screen was similar. The static camera angles of various locations are just like they were in Privateer, the merchant and mercenary guilds are so close to a replica that it feels funny, and many of the phrases and sound effects are nearly identical.

It also does not fail to reproduce one thing that I loved about the Privateer the most: every ship you purchase has a unique cockpit. Buying a new one becomes exciting, like moving to a new home. This makes it possible to love or hate specific ships based on the layout and the field of view alone. And when the damage to the ship is reflected by instruments blowing up, it can feel personal.

The controls may feel just as clunky as in the old game but the assist is really good at smoothing them out. Playing with a controller, I found myself using the assist but constantly correcting it manually, and it is really satisfying this way. I maneuver fast to land a good hit, but with the assist active, which helps to not overshoot or lose track of the target.

All this makes Rebel Galaxy Outlaw a better sequel to Privateer than the Darkening was. Well, except for the story. The first game had an interesting atmosphere, being set behind the lines of a larger conflict, a war with aliens, and the second one was pretty much a movie in disguise. Here the setting feels more like a western, perhaps a nod to Firefly fans, but a bit shallow. There is no flying to unexplored systems with barely enough fuel to discover ancient mysteries, neither is there a great acting. This is where I feel the game lacks something. But, hey, at least I can buy and build up my own station!

I enjoy playing games that require in-depth analysis and reflection. For me, Bombe stands out as the best logic puzzle I've ever encountered. The basic play involves creating rules that can be applied to Minesweeper-like puzzles using truth tables, which can then be automatically applied to a database of various puzzles by the computer. The most effective rules are those that are versatile enough to be used in a variety of scenarios, and clear enough to solve as many puzzle cells as possible. This versatility and clarity are what make Bombe so intriguing and worth exploring.

I find that I often get "stuck" in Bombe, but that's a good thing. It means that the puzzle is challenging and requires thought. When the answers come, you sometimes wonder why it was so hard to find.

This isn't a game you will complete in a few weeks of play. Even if you possess Mensa-level abilities, this game may take months or years to complete.

​Second time's the charm! I had played some of this game when it came out, but I became frustrated and gave up. I couldn't let go of the idea, though, so I had it sit on my backlog until the time felt right. And it did, and it was! There is so much to do in this game, even if you're interested in only the JRPG stuff. It's got only a few puzzles scattered around, but you can make the combat as simple or as complex as you like, and there is a ​lot ​of optional stuff. So much that you're liable to find some of it accidentally!

Oh, and it's beautiful! The art is gorgeous, cleanly shifting between pacific and horrifying, or even downgrading the graphics to 8-bit for a story beat. The music that accompanies all of it is fitting. I don't think I had any songs or sound effects that stuck with me, but I felt compelled to keep my headphones on because it adds so much to the ambiance.


For better or worse, all of the above sits on a more complex story. Jimmy is an 8-year-old boy and this is explicitly a dream that he's having. However, the dream becomes corrupted over time. Maybe someone could dismiss the early signs as either being off-tone or superficial random weirdness showing up in a kid's dreams. But sooner or later, it becomes clear that Jimmy is struggling with something that nobody should have to go through, and a lot of the game is about him trying to make sense of it all. I'd love to say more, but I'll stop there out of concern that I'm teetering on the edge of what I can share without outright spoiling it.

The game's final moments didn't do as much for me as I'd hoped. I expected some difficult emotional beats. We do get one of those if you do a certain action that becomes available in the end-game, and I've heard it's likewise if you fully explore one special dungeon, but all of this is after the credit roll and has to be initiated after the emotional beat of the climax has waned. I would've been happier if we got just a little more. To hear the final thoughts Jimmy has on the whole situation.

In any case, fantastic game and worth picking it up. I spent almost 27 hours on it and that's with leaving the post-game content untouched. You'll get your money's worth.

Cats Around Us: Giant Cat, developed and published by Noobzilla, is a soothing and delightfully whimsical hidden-object experience that captures the simple pleasure of observation. It takes a minimalist approach to gaming, trading action and complexity for the calm satisfaction of discovery. The premise is both amusing and imaginative: a gigantic cat has descended upon a small, hand-drawn village, and among the chaos are over two hundred smaller cats scattered throughout the environment, waiting to be found. The game transforms this quiet premise into an experience that feels more like meditative art than traditional gameplay. Every click becomes an act of curiosity, and every discovery a small reward for patient observation.

At its core, Cats Around Us: Giant Cat is about exploration and attention to detail. Each of the four large illustrated pages functions as a self-contained scene, inviting players to zoom in, scan, and uncover cleverly hidden felines tucked into rooftops, windows, alleyways, and foliage. The game blends the satisfaction of puzzle-solving with the relaxed pace of a visual storybook. It never rushes the player; there are no timers, penalties, or fail states, just a peaceful flow of interaction. The jigsaw puzzles integrated between stages add another layer of variety, encouraging a shift in focus while maintaining the same spirit of quiet engagement. These interludes complement the hidden-object sequences nicely, keeping the experience from feeling monotonous. Each puzzle solved unlocks new areas to explore, creating a gentle rhythm of progression that feels natural and rewarding.

Visually, the game’s strength lies in its art direction. The hand-drawn illustrations by Kathrinna Rakhmavika are brimming with warmth and detail, filled with cozy textures and charming scenes that radiate personality. The village is alive with small visual stories—a cat lounging by a window, villagers reacting to the enormous feline, tiny kittens peeking from barrels—and each discovery adds a layer of personality to the world. The palette is soft and inviting, with carefully balanced colors that enhance the sense of tranquility. Every screen feels crafted with care, and the composition of each panel draws the player’s eye naturally from one corner to another, ensuring that exploration remains intuitive rather than frustrating. The presentation is minimalist, yet full of charm, allowing the player’s focus to remain on the act of finding rather than being distracted by excessive interface clutter.

The game’s audio design supports this visual serenity beautifully. Soft ambient sounds and gentle background melodies create a peaceful atmosphere that enhances immersion without ever becoming intrusive. It’s the kind of soundscape that fades into the background, allowing the player to relax fully while still maintaining focus. The interface is equally considerate: adjustable brightness, cursor color options, and a photo mode make the game accessible and customizable for a wide range of players. It’s clear that Noobzilla approached the project with accessibility and user comfort in mind, understanding that the appeal of hidden-object games often lies in their calming, inclusive design rather than their difficulty.

While Cats Around Us: Giant Cat excels as a cozy visual experience, its simplicity also defines its limitations. With only four pages to explore, the game can be completed in a few hours, and players looking for complex puzzles or narrative depth may find it lacking in variety. The core loop—find cats, solve a jigsaw, move on—remains consistent throughout, and while that consistency reinforces its meditative quality, it also limits replayability. The absence of a larger story or progression system means that once all the cats are found and the puzzles are completed, there’s little reason to return aside from the pleasure of the artwork itself. Still, within its short runtime, it delivers exactly what it promises: a tranquil, self-contained experience that encourages mindfulness and curiosity.

Despite its brevity, the game’s charm lies in its purity of purpose. It’s not trying to be more than it is; instead, it embraces its small scope with confidence, focusing entirely on the joy of discovery. In an industry often dominated by high-stakes narratives and complex mechanics, Cats Around Us: Giant Cat feels like a breath of fresh air—a reminder that games can be relaxing, quiet, and artistic without losing their appeal. The act of finding each cat feels almost therapeutic, and the occasional humor hidden in the illustrations ensures that players stay engaged through lighthearted surprise. It’s a game that invites you to slow down, to appreciate the details, and to find delight in the little things.

Ultimately, Cats Around Us: Giant Cat succeeds as a heartfelt and gently humorous experience that celebrates simplicity. It’s not a game about winning or achieving mastery; it’s about taking a moment to enjoy observation itself. The combination of beautiful art, pleasant sound, and relaxing gameplay creates a meditative space that feels timeless, like flipping through a picture book come to life. It’s perfect for players seeking a short, comforting escape—a way to unwind, smile, and lose themselves in a world filled with cats of all shapes and sizes. Noobzilla’s creation may be small in scope, but its warmth and charm make it a memorable entry in the hidden-object genre, one that leaves players with a sense of calm satisfaction long after the last cat has been found.

does it have annoying camera controls for fight scenes? yes.
have i seen roblox games with better ui/ux? yes.
cutscenes that are somehow clunky too? yes.
fast travel points that could be placed MUCH more better? yes.

the visuals are a mixed bag. yes the environment is pretty, but the focal point (characters themselves) look like cum rags and aren't pretty to look at. the animations are generic especially in cutscenes, and its not difficult to notice the loops in audio/music.
some of the game design choices are very questionable:
[list]
    [*] accessory slot in equipment menu that's only apparently available in endgame
    [*] daryon/starter mc with sword can be fully kitted up to near blue-tier by the time you get selene/the mage with barely any equipment AND SPELLS. by the time you get selene you barely understand how crystals work, and by the time you actually get enough crystals to figure out and realize she relies on spells from equipping crystals, daryon's kitted the hell out while your only other party member is soft locked for the next hour as a mage with no gear only able to use her staff for melee.

despite all that. the game is incredibly charming if you open yourself up to it.

the quest flow also complements that type of playstyle. despite the inconvenient back-and-forth travel without a mount, the gameplay loop had me hooked with just how great the quest flow was for me and every hour past 3 am i kept saying "aight this is the last one for real" and suddenly it was 9 am. incredibly rewarding.

talk to the non-quest npcs as well. interact with the headstones.

im not one to read books in Skyrim for the plot, but I loved extracting lore from the non-important NPCs.

High-concept Science-Fiction novella that employs the aesthetics of Mecha as a veneer atop an extrapolation of queerness, how it can exist in a societal ordering that condemns demonizes anything less than straight and less than cis, and also three girls taking turns kissing each other.

I'm hardly the target audience, being very cis, if less-than-het, and was definitely more personally invested in the in-universe documentation interrogating the slightly-psychic psychics of the setting where '9.8 m/s^2' is both a metaphor for heteronormativity and also not a metaphor at all - a measurable, extant, imposition of conformity to the collective human zeitgeist on the universe - than making the cast makeout in their cockpits; but it is hard to not be mesmerized by the poetic syntax with which transhumanism (and, transexuality, obviously) is ontologically examined in relation to the oppressive and inescapable presence of a world and humanity which is overwhelmingly, violently, bigoted towards such ideas of what people are, can be, can express themselves as, and should be allowed to experience of their own volitions, and always trying to insert itself into every discussion thereof.

Ultimately I would quantify the experience being comprised of prose taking on the accoutrements of Sci-Fi, with more in common with 'Evangelion' than 'Gundam', the analogies intentionally obtuse, prosaic, and dense (probably to play with as many definitions of 'Gravity' as possible in its writing), requiring at least two of the three 'campaigns' to be completed before you really grasp where and why the words 'Gravity' and 'Culture' are being capitalized, why physics are referred to via Newton-Jungian laws, and the ontological distinctions between 'Earth' and 'Terra', 'Mars' and 'Ares', 'Saturn' and 'Cronus'; worth playing the third character after the fact and rewarding introspection beyond the visual appeal of giant robots swordfighting, or a lesbian threesome.

Esoteric in a way gender probably also is when viewed from outside an over-socialized lens, tricking you with robots in space to philosophize on what the limits of humanity are, or should be, and whether or not there are aspects of that which should be abandoned because they are cruel, narrow-mind, and autocratic, or if gradual change is possible to improve the variety and wellbeing of types of human experiences.

It's some of the deepest, richest, and most challenging fiction I've ever engaged with, and has a story and world which feel incredibly fresh and novel.
Also, it has girls kissing.
11/10 would recommend!

I don't normally leave reviews for the games I've played unless they really strike me in some sort of way, positive or negative, or if I think i can actually help the developer out. 
For Critter Cafe, I think there is a lot of potential for a good game, but as the game is now, it feels like the bare minimum. 
First some positives:
- cute visuals
- decent character customization
- relatively enjoyable puzzles
The game has a very cutesie vibe all around and I like the visuals of it. There are a good bit of customization options for the player character from hair to outfits to color patterns. Finally, the puzzles are short but enjoyable and are not extremely challenging. 
Now for the negatives: 
1) Everything in the game is unlocked through either experience in the cafe or through exploration in the world. There is no way of purchasing upgrades or furniture with any kind of revenue made from the cafe, all you have is experience points and random unlocks. You cannot chose your upgrades or unlocks as far as I can tell. 
2) Exploration in the world is kind of mindless roaming, there are signs here and there that point in general directions, however they are not precise on the location of the exact landmark you're trying to find. There is also no minimap or active map marker to show where you are at relative to where you're trying to get to. There's also no waypoints to help guide you. 
3) There is a lot wrong with the critter experience in general. I expected a game about animals to have more interaction with those animals. There is minimal interaction with the critters. It is all point and click options. You can choose what you want to do with the critter of your choice but then you just sit there and watch an animation. While the animations are cute, they take away from the interactivity of a videogame. It feels more like you're watching a minimally interactive slideshow. You can choose options to play with, feed, or bathe the pets but you don't actually DO any of that, it's all animations. To be honest I was expecting more interact-ability with the critters themselves. 
4) The cafe portion of the game is also not exactly enjoyable. 
- You can assign a critter to help in the cafe but they don't actually do anything unless they have boosts or upgrades that you get randomly from experience. Even then, the boosts or upgrades are more of a passive ability. The critters just run around. They do not interact with customers, take orders, make food, etc. 
- The food making isn't exactly complex or challenging like you would expect from a restaurant sim. You don't put ingredients together or mix anything in appliances. All orders are minigames. Some are matching, like it shows you the order for a few seconds and you're expected to point and click to pick it out. There is also one of a rapidly spinning cake that is also point and click. The order making is not fun, enjoyable, or even mildly challenging in the least. 
- Waiting on customers or delivering orders within the cafe is not fun either. Even with the extremely easy food making systems, customers have little to no patience and will last up to maybe 30 seconds before they walk out each interaction time. Between the slow walking AND running speed, only being able to carry one order, you cannot have anything remotely blocking your path to a customer in order to get their orders on time. It is also difficult to get to customers who are on couches or chairs with tables in front of them because it seems like you have to be directly in front of the customer to hand them their order.

[h1]Unfinished. Plain and Simple.[/h1]
This game is unfinished. Plain and simple. Technical issues, clunky gameplay, lack of voice acting in some key scenes, lack of imagery for scenes that desperately need it, limited backdrops, skeletal "bad endings" etc.

In contrast with some positives though, there is: phenomenal voice acting, characters, and story (until the ending). The highlights end there. Gameplay is [i]interesting[/i] in design and bad to subpar in execution. It's a turn-based RPG with positional combat, with some fun ideas. It is important to note you will spend a good 50/50 split, if not more, in the VN sections of the game. There is A LOT of story. Voice acting is sparse, but it is immensely well delivered, emotional, and authentic, making these sections always a treat.

Given that, it is hard to determine whether to recommend this or not. A recommendation for this would be a recommendation into [i]getting into the series[/i], because the only thing this has going for it is the story. A story which flops at the end and remains inconclusive. If the later games expand, give answers, or build off of this well, it could be worth it? But on its own, avoid this game unless you feel the story can carry you.

[h1]Story[/h1]
You play Shina, she's stuck inside a video game and has lost her memories. You're assisted in the real world by her colleague. The story jumps back and forth between these two perspectives, clunkily. 

They constantly sprinkle mystery and intrigue throughout the narrative, which makes it very engaging. Answers are given, more questions are raised, to the story’s own detriment. Setting up so many interesting characters and questions about the world but answers almost none of them at the conclusion of the story. Whenever key points are attempted to be explained, the explanations devolve into word salad. They constantly raise the stakes, tension, and mystique, but it feels like they had no idea how to wrap it all together. If you watch the "true" true ending, it feels like the writers are literally riffing and writing anything, with no cohesion to the story you [i]just[/i] experienced. It's such a letdown.

Shina and her colleague [i]constantly[/i] engage with the story. Questioning the world, things happening around them; basically, the plot isn't just magically carrying them forward. For example, at some point, the story falls into a pattern where each of your party members gets a really emotional moment (shout out again to the voice acting for this AND how this character development is even foreshadowed and capitalized on in later scenes). The first time this happens, the characters just shrug it off. The second time, Shina & Co catch on, point it out, and try to prepare and predict "who's next?" They all even discuss it to try and figure it out. It really makes the characters feel [i]authentic[/i] and not just like tropes dialed up to 11 beyond reason. Another example is how a character who joins much later on is missing context for some scenes that happen afterward, and this character [i]points that out[/i]. Clearly, a lot of intention went into character perspectives in this writing. It is a shame that the ending is akin to an "it was all a dream" scenario, which can make all this character building into one big nothing burger.

While the art the game does have looks pretty good, there's a metric ton of missing assets. You can see the lack of budget from a mile away. It leads to awkward scenes where you're shown a black backdrop and an evil character will go "well, can't go anywhere now that I just shot you, with my gun ey?" so comically bad. Some scenes are completely silent and lack any music, and music abruptly cuts off with no fading or anything, making it feel like the game broke in some way. Many NPCs have entirely black portraits and, weirdly, no portraits for the main characters? Even some highly emotional scenes are missing voice acting?

The game has "death ends," bad ends that result from a binary choice (there are no branching paths). Some are voice-acted and fairly involved, but the vast majority are nonsensical. You'll be presented with a scenario like "I see a seashell. Pick it up? Yes/No", "Yes. The seashell triggers TNT and I die", "No. A mother crab lands from space and throws my separated head across the land like a fleshy comet." Both almost feel like legitimate outcomes from any choice you make, since the "right" choice is often arbitrary. The bad endings are also just [i]that[/i] brief, and if you don't save your game, you lose all your progress. These feel quite pointless, but the game rewards you with items for getting them.

The game's multiple endings are legit chosen at the end of the game. "Whose ending do you want?" is literally what it asks you. You must fight the final boss 6–7 times to see all the endings. Torturous, watch them on YouTube instead. It just adds to the unfinished feeling.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
The gameplay system itself is rather interesting, even if poorly executed. You control up to three characters in battle, you move around the arena in a turn-based battle system, select up to three moves to use on an enemy, and that's the basics. Each move has differing effects, AoEs, etc. Moves remain varied and interesting, even if somewhat limited.

There is a knockback mechanic where you'll have enemies pinballing around the entire arena, taking damage from bumping into walls, other enemies, and your characters. It's REALLY satisfying and does decent damage early game. Late game, however, enemies weigh 50 tonnes and barely move, making this mechanic entirely redundant. It may as well not even exist.

While all this is quite interesting, it flops on its face. It is comically easy to recover HP and SP, either with items you're peppered with or character abilities. You unlock moves that make you invincible. Once you get enough SP, you can do this every other turn to be invincible forever. Since you take no damage, this also means you can walk over "bugs," get corrupted, and do your ultimate move, which hits every enemy on the field. Rinse and repeat, you win. Every fight is almost risk-free. Enemies also die within a couple of turns once you learn what they're weak to. It makes every fight robotic and boring. Otherwise, enemies can randomly do barely any damage to you or one-shot you. It feels like there's rarely an in-between.

Overall, it's jank, unpolished, unfinished. The base design is quite interesting, but the enemy encounters and content designed around it suck and do not capitalize on the strength and cohesion of the systems it had built upon. I think there's a solid base here for an engaging combat system.

[h1]Exploration[/h1]
It's only [i]kinda[/i] bad. Environments are varied, and they look okay for a PS2. Chests contain mostly the same bog-standard HP and SP consumables, with the odd weapon. Chests aren't the easiest to see, basically cuboid chameleons, though less so than the "key" items.

"Key" items, literally a floating key which can be hard to see if you're not actively looking for it, are often needed to progress in the story. So it is very easy to get stuck if you miss one. Also, you must randomly go to "real world" VN segments sometimes to progress the story in the video game world. The game does not tell you this. Real world VN segments will randomly open doors, spawn key items, etc., and it won't tell you what changed, making it excessively easy to get stuck or confused.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
It's jank and unfinished in all respects. Even though the story is quite engaging with likeable characters, the ending flops it, as it, too, is unfinished. The best I can hope for is that the second game builds on this better. Though the reviews are mixed for that game, so it does not bode well.

1428: Shadows over Silesia, developed and published by KUBI Games, is an unusually bold indie title because it refuses to treat medieval history as a decorative backdrop. Instead, it uses the Hussite Wars—one of Central Europe’s most turbulent and ideologically charged periods—as the emotional and philosophical foundation for its narrative. The game begins grounded in reality, depicting political mistrust, religious upheaval, and social fragility, yet gradually introduces occult elements, cryptic prophecies, and monstrous entities that feel unnervingly plausible within the era’s worldview. Rather than presenting medieval Europe as a romanticized battleground of knights and chivalry, the story leans into the era’s brutality, scarcity, superstition, and desperation. Through alternating perspectives—Hynek, a stern Hussite commander burdened by responsibility, and Lothar, a resourceful thief navigating society from the margins—the narrative paints a multifaceted portrait of a world collapsing under the weight of faith and fear. Their journeys occasionally intersect, but more importantly, they illuminate different social realities that history books often flatten.

The structure of the game mirrors the unpredictability of life during wartime—no two chapters feel mechanically identical. Sometimes the player must infiltrate hostile fortresses without detection, studying patrol patterns and environmental layouts to find weaknesses. Other sections demand measured combat against armored soldiers or unholy creatures, where stamina management, spacing, and timing matter more than speed. The melee system is intentionally slow and tactical, reflecting the weight and risk of real medieval weaponry rather than the fluid power fantasies common in action games. Shields can fail, reckless strikes leave openings, and overconfidence is punished quickly. These grounded mechanics contrast sharply with supernatural encounters later in the campaign, where psychological tension replaces martial pragmatism. Environmental puzzles serve as connective tissue between these set pieces, encouraging observation and logic instead of trial-and-error brute forcing. The result is a campaign that remains mechanically engaging without relying on constant escalation or repetitive combat scenarios.

Exploration is equally important, and the isometric perspective is used thoughtfully rather than nostalgically. Settlements, forests, castles, monasteries, and underground passages are constructed with historical awareness—architecture, tools, clothing, and furnishing styles reflect real Hussite-era research instead of generic medieval fantasy tropes. Even background details contribute to worldbuilding, whether it’s livestock wandering muddy roads, plague-marked homes sealed shut, or churches caught between sanctity and militarization. Lighting elevates these environments, creating pockets of uncertainty where torchlight barely penetrates, and the player’s imagination fills the darkness. Long stretches of silence or ambient sound help shape emotional pacing, reminding players that medieval life was as defined by vulnerability and emptiness as by conflict.

One of the game’s most striking achievements is its dedication to accessibility, especially for visually impaired players—an aspect rarely prioritized in historically based action adventures. Fully implemented narration, detailed audio cues, text-to-speech features, and carefully designed interface elements allow players who typically struggle with visually intensive genres to navigate environments, solve puzzles, and participate in combat meaningfully. Rather than framing accessibility as an optional afterthought, KUBI Games integrated it into the core experience, demonstrating that historical immersion and inclusivity are not mutually exclusive. For an independent studio, this commitment is impressive and sets a strong example for future developers.

The game is not without imperfections, many of which stem from its ambitious scope. Combat can initially feel stiff, and mastering its rhythm requires patience. Difficulty can spike unexpectedly, particularly during encounters that combine environmental hazards with aggressive enemies. The camera sometimes struggles in tight interior areas, causing temporary disorientation. Because the narrative values historical momentum over player-driven branching, choices tend to influence characterization more than plot direction, which may disappoint players seeking radically divergent outcomes. Animation quality, facial expressions, and some environmental textures reveal the constraints of a small development team, especially when compared to large-scale medieval productions. Yet these shortcomings rarely undermine what the game does well—they simply remind players that ambition often precedes budget.

What ultimately makes 1428: Shadows over Silesia resonate long after completion is its refusal to sensationalize either history or fantasy. The supernatural elements are not spectacle for its own sake—they emerge from the same psychological landscape that fueled real medieval hysteria, political violence, and religious fervor. Horror becomes an extension of human belief rather than a genre intrusion, blurring the line between internal and external threats. Likewise, the game acknowledges that war is not fought solely by heroes but by flawed people trying to survive forces beyond their control. Its emotional impact comes not from triumph, but from endurance—moral, physical, spiritual.

For players who crave historical fiction with thematic maturity, methodical combat, atmospheric worldbuilding, and stories that embrace complexity rather than simplification, 1428: Shadows over Silesia offers a rare and compelling experience. It feels handcrafted—patient, researched, personal—a testament to what a passionate small studio can accomplish when it speaks confidently in its own artistic language. At a time when medieval games often recycle settings without intellectual engagement, this one invites players to inhabit a moment in history where shadows—both literal and symbolic—were never just background scenery, but forces shaping the fate of nations.

The Devil’s Daughter is Frogwares at its most ambitious; a game that tries to evolve Sherlock Holmes from cerebral investigator into a more emotionally dynamic protagonist. Following the triumph of Crimes and Punishments, this sequel takes risks, blending psychological drama with faster pacing and flashes of action. The result is uneven but fascinating: a mystery that sometimes stumbles, yet dares to humanize its legend.

Holmes here is no longer just a calculating intellect; he’s a man under pressure, haunted by the presence of his estranged ward, Katelyn. The domestic tension between them becomes the game’s spine; an experiment in portraying Holmes not as the infallible detective, but as a flawed father figure juggling guilt and obsession. While the writing occasionally overreaches, those moments of quiet vulnerability give the character unexpected depth.

The structure remains familiar: five major cases, each a blend of investigation, deduction and moral choice. The “Mind Palace” returns, letting you piece together clues and form hypotheses, but The Devil’s Daughter adds more cinematic flourishes: chase sequences, quick-time events and stealth sections. Not all of these additions work, yet they give the pacing a pulpy rhythm that keeps the player engaged.

Visually, the game marks a clear technical leap. Built on a new engine, its environments feel richer and more alive, from fog-choked alleys to sunlit parlors, the attention to period detail remains exquisite. Character models and facial animation finally reach the emotional nuance Frogwares had long pursued, even if occasional stiffness reminds you of the studio’s modest scale.

Where The Devil’s Daughter falters is consistency. The balance between introspection and spectacle sometimes wavers, and a few tonal shifts land awkwardly. But even when it misfires, it does so with conviction.

If Crimes and Punishments was the perfect refinement of a formula, The Devil’s Daughter is the bold attempt to transcend it; a flawed but heartfelt exploration of the man behind the myth.

Sagebrush is not a bad game, but it is a sloppy one, and some of the ways that it lacks attention to detail really compromise its coherence and value for me. The physical realism of exploring the compound is really limited, involving, for example, using wirecutters once and then never again, or the fact that your character seems to be incapable of jumping over a knee high wall. This really breaks immersion, and changes the dynamic from one of actual exploration, and actually attempting to compromise the physical integrity of a fortified area, to something that is a lot more akin to just following a trail of breadcrumbs, often having to double back when you realize you did something wrong. The final twist that reveals that not everything has been as you have seen it is good, but is especially hindered by the inconsistencies in how the environment was previously navigated. This whole dynamic alone is enough for me to say that I don't recommend it, no matter how much I want to. 

Beyond that, the graphics are great. The low fi setup really accentuates some of the strange features of American geography, and the fact that you're experiencing the ideas of objects, instead of the objects themselves works well. The way that the night progressively falls also makes it work better and better, and the seamless transition in levels of metaphor near the end works astonishingly well. 

As for the story, and the themes, the overall presentation of the subject matter is...oddly tasteful and matter of fact given how horrifying it is. I just wish there was more effort in characterizing the various characters, since they really fall flat and end up not completely working as anything more than stereotypes.  

Two more technical issues. At some point I hit a button by mistake, I believe F8, and all text in the game disappeared and I was sent back to a previous scene. I couldn't get text to work again, and didn't want to play through much more of the game again, and could tell I was near the end. So, that bug is weird and frustrating. Additionally, little of the audio is spatially encoded it seems. So, when you activate an audio track that's supposed to be coming from a TV, and you leave the area with the TV too early, the TV continues to play in your soundtrack even after you've left the building.

This game is not very good.  I really like trading simulators so I tried with this one until I understood that is game-breakingly flawed. 

The reward system forces you to manually fight each naval battle in order to board the enemy ships in order to receive sufficient profit to cover the costs of your sailors. The naval battles get horribly repetitive but cannot be automated because you will rapidly lose very expensive ships. The other nations get continuous streams of unlimited reinforcements and you are always fighting the reinforcements in a to-the-death cage fight of tedious boarding after boarding.

The trade routes are irrevocably broken and large ones can only work on automatic. Logically, one would think that when you set max-min prices the ships will sell until they hit the minimum price.  What the game does not tell you is that it holds back from selling all the cargo.  The total cargo in the hold is divided among all the towns on the trade route.  The division is actually based on your priority settings.  So lets say you had a 10-town trading route and 100 pots and you ran across a big town that you could sell all 100 pots at max profit.  The idiot developers have coded the game to only sell 10 pots, unless you have manually adjusted the priority slider for that specific town and specifically for pots.  The retarded convoy will keep 90 pots for the rest of the towns, even if those towns don't have demand.  This means your ships get overloaded with a ton of goods to only sell a tiny fraction at each town.  There are 25 commodities and you actually have to fiddle with hundreds of settings to be able to get your trade routes optimized. Then if you build businesses or upset the equilibrium, you have to refiddle with all the settings.  

The game is so broken, like the developers just got up and walked away from a half-eaten meal.  Don't waste your time.

[h2]Кратко об игре[/h2]

Hande of Fate - это смесь рогалика, текстового квеста и freeflow боёвки. В целом, вся игра разделена на отдельные партии, а каждая партия представляет собой ряд данжей, комнаты которых - это карты встреч с разными мини-историями. Попадая на такую карту, вам, в виде текста, рассказывают её сюжет и предлагают по разному отреагировать на происходящие там события. Выбрали хорошо - получите ресурсы, снарягу или даже жетон, который потом разблокирует новые карты для будущих партий. Выбрали плохо - получите проклятья, битву или потерю ресурсов вкупе с насмешкой дилера, который является символом игры и приносит в неё красок благодаря своим остроумным комментариям и живым эмоциям.

[h2]Создание колоды[/h2]

 Расскажу немного подробнее о карточной стороне игры. Перед началом приключения вы выбираете босса, против которого будете драться в конце данжа. Главная цель игры - убить всех боссов и тем самым одолеть дилера. После выбора своего главгада, вам предлагают составить колоды снаряжения и встреч, с которыми вы столкнётесь в партии. В игре нет фильтров карт, а их описание сделано исключительно в виде текста, который ещё надо раскрыть и посмотреть небыстрые анимации приближения и отдаления. Учитывая также, что карты в игре исчисляются десятками, ручное создание колоды - задача непростая и немного раздражающая, а потому игра предлагает нажать волшебную кнопку, чтобы всё было собрано за вас, за что, конечно, спасибо, но декбилдинг от этого лучше не становится. Однако сами карты здесь получились разнообразными и интересными, отчего возникает желание попробовать все виды оружия из-за их уникальных абилок и свойств и изучить каждую встречу, где вы и от ловушек попрыгаете, и в пустыне заблудитесь, и на легендарного кракена поохотитесь, и ещё много чего переживёте.

[h2]Исследование данжа[/h2]

 Кстати о переживаниях. После подготовки колоды вы заходите в данж и начинаете исследовать его с целью подготовиться к финальной битве. Ограниченные запасы еды, затрачиваемой на перемещение между комнатами, и уникальные карты встреч босса (которые обычно вредят, а не помогают) заставляют задуматься дважды над тем, стоит ли сворачивать с пути или лучше как можно быстрее покинуть этаж, пока не стало хуже. Про сами карты встреч я уже говорил, разве что стоит ещё упомянуть мини-игру с четырьмя картами, которые перемешиваются, и вам надо запомнить, какая из них "удача", а какая "невезение", чтобы выбрать нужную. Некоторым такой рандом не зайдёт, но я считаю капельку случайности во встречах приятным разнообразием, благо, будучи внимательным, можно отследить перемещение карт, да и благословения с особыми предметами вам в помощь.

[h2]Боёвка[/h2]

 Если во время приключения вы сталкиваетесь с врагами, то игра переносит вас на небольшую арену, где вы избиваете врагов в стиле бэтмена: бьёте на одну кнопку, контрите на другую, набиваете комбо и используете всякие гаджеты. В отличие от того же бэтмена, враги одного вида (например, только скелеты или только бандиты) могут бить вас исключительно по одному, и никаких двойных или тройных контратак тут нет. Анимации ощущаются рвано, и нет чувства потока в битве. Сглаживают углы кайфовая музыка, которую мне порой хотелось послушать в отрыве от игры, и разнообразие предметов и пассивных бафов/дебафов. К примеру, проклятия могут начать штрафовать вас за контратаки или сделать последнего живого врага неуязвимым к оглушению, а благословения способны обрушить на противника молнию или сделать вас быстрым как ветер. Добавим к этому в меру богатое разнообразие рас и типов врагов и получим не идеальную, но в целом приятную боёвку, которой не помешает полировка.

[h2]Вывод[/h2]

 Подводя итоги, хочу обратить внимание на два важных момента: 1 - это только первая часть из двух, а потому её можно считать этаким первым Portal, т.е. прототипом потенциально отличной игры, которая уже существует в лице второй части, где разработчики поработали над декбилдингом, боёвкой, уникальностью каждого приключения и т.д.. 2 - стоит это творение 419 рублей, что смягчает мои претензии. Поэтому, если вы желаете получить крутой рогалик с приятной боёвкой и интересными квестами (и вас не смущает их текстовое оформление), то лучше купите вторую часть, которая на две головы лучше первой и стоит всего на 96 рублей дороже. Однако, если вы готовы мириться с шероховатостями, мною выше озвученными, и просто хотите поиграть в интересный рогалик - берите даже без скидок, я считаю, что игра этого заслуживает.

When his younger brother dies, the protagonist loses his marbles.  Navigate zany, topsy-turvy worlds to help him find them again!

Actually: Disorder is a grim platformer based on slow, precise jumps and the ability to switch between two slightly different versions of the world.  Expect to jump from a platform that exists towards empty air, switch worlds, and land on a new one.

Pros:
- Great level design.  
- Challenging and interesting puzzles.
- Solid exploration of the world switching mechanic.
- Good replay value.  There are multiple endings, branching paths, and every hidden item you unlock can be "enabled" to add a challenging effect to gameplay.  (Think the gods in Bastion, or the limiters in Transistor.)
- I encountered no bugs on my first playthrough, which is not something I say a lot.
- The trick of the last level is pretty clever.

According to taste:
-  Tries very hard to keep a dark, gloomy atmosphere.  Let me put it like this:  I can imagine a depressed late-teen to early twenties person writing everything that the main character says in their diary.  That said, I wouldn't go out of my way to read that diary.
- Some polarity switching games have very distinct flavors for the two worlds (Giana Sisters comes to mind).  Disorder switches between sad and agonized, or drab and creepy.  As a result, the two worlds aren't easily identifiable: at any given time, I couldn't tell you which one I was in.  This didn't bother me at all, but it was sort of unexpected.
- Balanced around a slower character with a short jump.

Con:
- Pretty short.  I beat this game in 1.5 hours.  There could have easily been another few levels and at least one more major mechanic.
- There should really be some sort of visible indicator of whether or not you're blocked from shifting.  I'd put an icon on the screen, but if the dev is really committed to not having a HUD, do something with the main character's facial expression instead.  The constant, cartoonish frown was a bit much.

Overall, a good and innovative game, but I wish there were more of it.

I was  initially attracted to Disorder not by reading the development diaries, or what the game was about, but by the  post apocalyptic like imagery  the  screen captures portrayed (they also  have a vague terraria like look with respect to the graphics, though  not in game play mechanics). 

On playing the game I  was  really surprised and pleased by the  way the developer had   created an otherworldly   platformer, with two dimensions that you have to swap between  to be able to progress.  The imagery is    a pixelated delight and the music and sound effects  add substance to the artwork.  Disorder is a creepy atmospheric platformer the like of which I've not come across before.  Well worth buying IMO, even at full price.
