Curse of Blackmoor Manor is the 11th Nancy Drew adventure game. In this entry, Nancy goes to help the newly married Linda Penvellyn. Since moving into her new husband's house, she's been behaving strangely and has the symptoms of a strange illness, and it's up to Nancy to figure out what's really going on.

The setting and story take a lot of inspiration from gothic horror. Blackmoor Manor has a very strong spooky English mansion aesthetic, and I enjoyed exploring it. The game isn't very scary but there were a couple of moments that made me jump. I enjoyed uncovering the Penvellyn family lore and figuring out what was really behind Linda's illness. There are a couple of strong possible suspects and motives. The ending was genuinely surprising to me, although it wasn't totally satisfying.

The puzzles here are definitely on the more difficult side, and probably the most complicated ones I've played in the series so far. Most of the puzzles were really enjoyable. They were difficult enough that you really had to think about them, but were pretty well-designed, so most of them felt fair. I needed some help from a walkthrough because there are some things that are easy to miss or that get mentioned early on and are easy to forget later. The puzzles get more complicated as the game goes on and some of them were pretty frustrating. Toward the end of the game you need to do a lot of backtracking through areas that are really difficult to navigate, and I got so frustrated with it that in a couple of places I just looked up the answer even if I already knew what to do, just so I wouldn't have to retread all that ground again.

This is the most minigame-heavy of the ones I've played so far, and it was pretty annoying. You have to play through all of the minigames at least once. There are a few of them you have to figure out through trial and error and a couple you have to replay a few times to keep making progress. I really disliked the minigame you have to play the most, because it wasn't much fun and was easy to lose.

During the game, you can order food for Nancy, and there are a couple of things you order which you can use to solve puzzles, one of which is required for the game to progress. Unfortunately, there's a bug where after the first time you order food, you can try to order food again and it just won't show up. If you spend enough time away from Nancy's room, it may show up later, but I never had any luck getting that to happen. Fortunately, I happened to have ordered the item I needed to move the story forward the first time, but there was an optional puzzle I missed out on because I was never able to order the other item I needed.

I was on the fence about whether to recommend this one. I enjoyed the mystery, the spooky aesthetic, and the difficult but clever puzzles. However, the minigames and overly-complicated late-game puzzles were really annoying, and there is a bug that can get you totally stuck. Overall, I would say I do recommend the game if you like tough puzzles and have a lot of patience, but if you get frustrated easily, this might be one to skip. 5/10

The story is clearly made with passion, I can see someone writing everything here with a smile in their face knowing they're having the time of their life considering how much sheer content was put! So many little random events just for funsies, it's hard to imagine this is all a one-person project. Nami is so inspiring to go and create the universe you're envisioning, in any way you can!

The amount of sweets, recipes, stories on how to get each recipe, art for each recipe, it's all so much effort and attention to detail. I never felt like I was crafting something just to pad out time, every single one of them felt like they had a reason to be put in the game. And hell yeah I'd love to eat some of those!

And finally, seeing the Starry Flowers storyline play in real time from Syrup's perspective was adorable and actively made me cry a few times, I love seeing that Pastille had even more going on than we thought, and that Syrup was out there fighting witches and weird monsters while Pastille was having the time of his life. Jumped into a random indie novel with zero expectations and god, what a ride it was, I ended up binging 25 hours of content this game offers within just 3 days.

I genuinely can't believe the entirety of art and writing for it was produced by a single person. Like, genuinely, what the actual hell, that was impressive. 

The story has many layers, plot twists, overlapping narratives and whatnot, it can get outright confusing/nonsensical at times but once it clicks and the mystery starts unveiling, turn by turn it becomes truly rewarding. A lot of narrative payoffs are very well executed, key scenes that resolve many story arcs this game has are outright HYPE.

The writing has its lower points too, especially during DownFall as some fairly vague conversational choices in it can move you towards the main story's conclusion without having experienced ANY of the DownFall character arcs which are treated as optional content for some reason. It would have been fine if it was conveyed more clearly what the choice entails or if the story actually acknowledged the lack of foreknowledge due to the reader not experiencing it, but the writing treated it as if I have already seen every route despite I haven't, reinforced by the fact main characters kept referring to past events that happen in said arcs without them having happened on screen yet. That soured a bit of the enjoyment, but I quickly figured out something was off and went back to play side routes first. Ultimately it got better over time, and DLC was much better at handling it.

The music is all royalty free, but sound design is actually on point too! I really loved the large diversity of tracks it had to offer and how well the author managed to integrate music that wasn't designed with this game in mind into the narrative.

Anyway, whatever was going on in the author's head, I want more of that. Low-key made me want to play more games from them!

First off if you like indy and small developmental teams that create games, I'm sure Kingdom of the Dead (KotD) will fit the bill. I'm giving KotD a thumbs up because it is worth it for the $14.99 price tag and an even better deal if it's on sale! I'm going to be a little more critical of KotD than I normally would only because there are a literal F-ton of indy FPS's to compare it to. Let's get down to it!

Pros
* Completely unique art style, apparently all the animation is hand drawn. I dig it and find it a breath of fresh air for the genre. It certainly gives everything an uneasy and eerie feel. 
* The music is great, it really adds to the environment and gives it an extra freaky vibe. I do wish there were a few more soundtracks per map though
* The enemies look unique and creepy, most are humonoid-ish, most things are weak to headshots

Cons
* Noticed some bugs where enemies would be stuck in walls, mountains and other things. This was especially annoying when those enemies spawned other enemies and you couldn't get rid of them because they were glitched
* I spoiled by games like DOOM and Duke Nukem, KotD suffers from a real lack of weapon variety as well enemy variety 
* Speaking of weapons, it was disappointing that weapons don't carry over from the previous mission. Each map you have to go find the same weapons again. Your health is the same way, you collect hearts similar to Zelda which increases your HP and each time it's reset at beginning of the next map. Also, the last weapon you find in each map has a tendency to show up at the very end of the level, which stinks because you barely get to use it.
* Why in the world is the double barrel shotgun so awful?! It's not a sawed-off so it should have better accuracy with less scatter. I think it's possible the dev might have confused the two shotgun modifications. 
* Not a fan of only being able to save at checkpoints
* The boss fights are a let down, most are move, point and shoot

I'm aware there are far more negatives than positives on this review, but I don't think any of the negatives ruin the experience. They are basically a wish list or a what I would have done differently bullet points (besides the bugs and glitches). I believe you'll get anywhere from 6 to 10 hours of gameplay out of KotD and that's easily worth the price tag. The creativity and hard work on this game really shine and I'm not here to blow smoke up the dev's B-hole just because it's a one man show. I single-handedly tore through Choo-Choo Charles with my scathing review so I have no problem being blunt even to small dev teams. I honestly think this was a well thought out game that could use some tuning up but even if it doesn't get that, it show's real promise for Dirigo Games.

Army Troop, developed and published by Army Troop Studios, is a small-scale World War II–themed first-person shooter that embraces straightforward multiplayer action rather than attempting to compete with sprawling, cinematic military shooters. Its premise is immediately familiar—you pick a soldier class, deploy onto a battlefield, and fight for your team’s score—but the game’s simplicity is core to its identity. It aims to rekindle the pick-up-and-play spirit of early online shooters, where matches were fast, mechanics were easy to understand, and enjoyment came from pure competition rather than layered progression systems or complex objectives. That philosophy makes Army Troop accessible in a way many modern shooters aren’t, especially for players who want lighthearted combat rather than a massive live-service commitment.

The game revolves around traditional multiplayer modes like team deathmatch and free-for-all, set across wide, open maps designed to accommodate different playstyles. Infantry slug it out on foot, snipers post up across long sightlines, and more specialized classes add subtle variety to the battlefield. Each weapon category—from rifles and pistols to SMGs and shotguns—handles differently enough to encourage experimentation, and small touches like weapon skins, perks, and cosmetic accessories allow players to personalize their soldier without disrupting balance. There’s no elaborate unlock grind or monetization system tucked beneath the surface, leaving the core gameplay loop refreshingly direct: spawn, fight, respawn, repeat.

Perhaps the most practical design choice is the inclusion of competent AI bots, allowing matches to stay active even during slow server periods. For an indie shooter without the massive audience of AAA franchises, this feature dramatically improves usability—players don’t have to wait for full lobbies or abandon the game due to population dips. The maps also help sustain momentum, prioritizing open terrain and simple layouts over intricate choke points or objective structures. While not particularly innovative, they provide enough space for dynamic firefights and improvised tactics, which suits the game’s fast, arcade-like pacing.

Visually, Army Troop falls into the category of functional rather than impressive. Character models, weapon textures, lighting, and environmental details get the job done but rarely stand out, reflecting its indie budget and early development stage. The audio design follows a similar pattern—gunshots and explosions offer recognizable feedback, but they lack the layered weight found in higher-end shooters. Still, the minimal system requirements mean that players with older or lower-spec PCs can participate without performance anxiety, which broadens the game’s potential audience and aligns with its goal of approachable multiplayer fun.

The game’s simplicity, however, can also be a limitation. Matches can feel repetitive after extended play, especially since most modes revolve around raw elimination rather than objective variety, large team coordination, or dynamic battlefield events. Players accustomed to shooters with extensive progression systems, detailed ballistics modeling, or narrative framing may find Army Troop lacking in depth. Its Early Access state also means occasional rough edges—interface quirks, balance inconsistencies, visual repetition, or network issues may appear depending on the session. And because the online population isn’t consistently dense, the experience is often best when played with friends rather than relying solely on public matchmaking.

Despite these drawbacks, Army Troop succeeds on its own terms. It doesn’t overpromise, and its modest ambitions help it deliver what it intends to: fast, uncomplicated WW2 firefights that anyone can jump into. It fills a niche between hyper-realistic military simulators and flashy blockbuster shooters—something relaxed, accessible, and easy to revisit. Its low cost, low hardware demands, and familiar mechanics make it appealing for players who want to enjoy casual multiplayer battles without investing time, money, or emotional energy into a larger ecosystem.

Army Troop is ultimately a reminder of how enjoyable stripped-down competitive shooters can be when they don’t burden players with bloat or expectations. It may not evolve the genre, but it provides a serviceable, low-pressure environment for quick matches, experimentation, and friendly competition. For players seeking polished production, mechanical depth, or long-term progression, it may not satisfy. But for those who miss simpler online shooters—with class-based combat, straightforward maps, and a focus on pure firefighting—it offers a modest, affordable, and entertaining alternative worth keeping an eye on as it continues to develop.

Mount Your Friends 3D: A Hard Man is Good to Climb, developed and published by Stegersaurus Software Inc., takes the already bizarre concept of its 2D predecessor and dials everything up—both in scale and absurdity. As the name cheekily suggests, this game is unapologetically tongue-in-cheek, reveling in its outlandish physics, exaggerated anatomy, and innuendo-laced presentation. What makes this title truly stand out, however, is that beneath the veneer of crude humor lies a surprisingly thoughtful and mechanically engaging climbing experience that rewards coordination, improvisation, and competitive strategy.

The basic premise of the game is straightforward but deceptively challenging. Players compete to build the tallest tower possible by climbing atop one another, using individually controlled limbs to grasp, swing, and launch themselves upward. The transition from 2D to full 3D space adds a substantial degree of complexity and hilarity. The physics engine is as much a character in the game as the beefy, thong-clad avatars—each movement is exaggerated, rubbery, and chaotic. Mastering the controls becomes a game in itself, with players needing to maneuver each limb with precision or risk flailing off the tower in spectacular fashion. The physical comedy that ensues is not only funny but integral to the game’s identity, blending slapstick humor with real mechanical depth.

The 3D environments also expand on what’s possible in terms of level design. Instead of a single vertical climb, the game includes a variety of modes and configurations—ranging from spiraling towers to gravity-defying low-G setups. These alternate maps require different movement strategies, and adapting to each one keeps the gameplay fresh. There’s also a robust customization system in place, which allows players to unlock a wide variety of visual upgrades such as new trails, body patterns, head options, and even custom camera support for inserting your own face into the game. While none of these affect gameplay directly, they add a significant layer of personality and replayability.

Where Mount Your Friends 3D truly shines is in its multiplayer experience. Local and online play both support chaotic, laugh-out-loud sessions filled with rivalry, unexpected turnarounds, and shared disbelief at just how ludicrous the action can become. The competitive aspect is balanced with a lighthearted tone, ensuring that wins and losses alike are memorable for all the right reasons. The frantic rush to beat the timer, combined with the unpredictable nature of the physics, makes each match feel distinct. While the core loop is simple, the emergent scenarios that unfold from each player’s movements and mishaps give the game a surprising level of replay value.

Visually, the game doesn’t aim for realism, nor does it need to. The exaggerated, cartoonish muscles, vibrant colors, and deliberately provocative animations are part of the joke—and part of the charm. Everything from the physics-driven swinging genitalia to the over-the-top grunting is meant to make players laugh, and the game succeeds at that without coming across as mean-spirited or overtly crude. It maintains a tone that’s ridiculous but self-aware, poking fun at macho athleticism and over-the-top sports presentation in the most flamboyant way possible.

Despite its strengths, Mount Your Friends 3D does have its limitations. The lack of a compelling single-player mode is noticeable; while you can practice alone, the game thrives on social energy and loses much of its appeal without others to laugh along with. There’s also an argument to be made that, once the novelty wears off, the experience can feel repetitive. Although there are multiple field types and unlockables, the core gameplay loop remains largely the same, and players looking for deeper progression or variety in objectives may find the offering thin after extended play.

That said, the game never tries to be more than it is: a chaotic, comedy-driven party game designed for shared laughter and competitive mayhem. The physics may be unpredictable, the visuals intentionally ridiculous, and the tone overtly silly, but everything works in concert to deliver an experience that feels polished in its own uniquely strange way. It’s a game best enjoyed with others, especially in casual settings where fun takes precedence over performance. Whether you’re climbing to victory or falling in the most undignified way possible, the moments are always memorable.

In the end, Mount Your Friends 3D: A Hard Man is Good to Climb is a rare gem in the party game space. It doesn’t pretend to be sophisticated or narratively rich, but it nails exactly what it sets out to do: create a hysterically fun multiplayer experience with just enough depth to keep players coming back. It’s not for everyone—those easily put off by crude humor or strange controls may bounce off quickly—but for players who embrace the absurd and enjoy laughter-fueled competition, this game offers a uniquely entertaining climb to the top.

2025秋季新品节玩到的几乎是唯一的亮点，发售第一天立马通关并全成就，这是个人第一次。
3D逻辑解密游戏似乎很流行这种简约的美学，一开始谈不上有多吸引人，但是如果你玩过一两个类似画风的游戏（比如Antichamber、manifold garden），这种风格反而变得越来越有魅力，因为它将你引向一种期待，期待着那些叫人惊叹的时刻能再现，Rhombus做到了。
对于一个3D游戏，我的基本要求是把镜头控制要舒适，镜头都不舒服，你其他部分设计得再好也没用，而这样一个看似简单的要求，实际上很多游戏都做不到，很多游戏的镜头要么生涩，要么油腻，要么晃来晃去还不给选项调，而Rhombus的镜头是舒服的。
游戏的谜题大致可分成两个层次，第一层是类似见证者的“做题”面板，有一套特殊的规则需要玩家去摸索，这套玩法对我来说有点新鲜感，但可惜深度做得不太够，中后期都是类似的解题思路，没有做出一些玩法变种，这部分相对独立，类似portal流的test chamber。第二层就是各个谜题区域间的回路设计，从小回路到大回路，对玩家“心图”构建能力的考验逐步升级，虽然后期可能会有点疲于奔波的感觉，但这种类银式的路线规划确实很让我这样的人欢喜，作者在箱庭关卡设计上的水平是大于逻辑谜题设计的。另外游戏还有一些空间谜题设计挺有想法，为了避免剧透我不好说太明白，我只能说作者充分利用了3D空间的特性来让游戏有了更进一步的探索感，也给了我一些新的设计启发，这就很可贵了。
总结，如果你喜欢研究精巧的箱庭设计，喜欢3D空间谜题，玩他。

Recently found I had left a finished game of mine unreviewed that I meant to review, and loh and behold I did the same thing with Heroine Anthem Zero 2.

While I enjoyed the first experience as a delightful little surprise of a VN/Side Scrolling Action/Metroidvania light (capitalize that L while you're at), the 2nd absolutely blew me away. While still very much the same as the first, but triple in size, scale, game play improvements, and amount of content. I just today booted up the game to catch a event I recently learned about (more on those in a bit) I decided to boot up a save from the beginning, because holy moly, from the visuals to the OST at work, the opening to this game is jaw dropping. The art, Vanilla Ware levels of breath taking, and the music so beautifully haunting it captures you as much as the disturbing, yet atheral visuals your eyes are looking at. What a way to start the player off, especially off the back of the prequel title.

Honestly this review would be way too long if I gushed over everything I loved about this game, and there are some critiques here and there, more so on the gameplay. While a big improvement over the last, due to the length of the game and the VERY low difficulty, combat can become rather teduis in the long run.
The last thing I wanted to touch up on was the aftormentioned event I had missed. Boy howdy this game has an unreal level of fully fleshed out side events that are completley (and very easily missed) side events. While I respect the VERY early PS1 and earlier era JRPG approach to these side events/side quests, in how as long as you're chatting with all the npc's, you'll see most of them without a hitch. However, due to there not being a chapter select, and how very missable many of those quests are, I also have dock some points for that as well haha. If it wasn't for me diving through the discussion boards (only the ones that were in Chinese ( I assume Chinese based on what Google was telling me, deeply sorry if the language I'm assuming is incorrect) and found a super obscure, mid to late 2000's looking message board (again assuming it was Chinese) with a written guide for most/ all of the events and how to get them, I would have missed much more. If you'd like to find this post, it's in there haha. Wish ya luck.
 And I know for a fact there's still events I have missed from the different screens. posted in the community hub hahaha. Again huge respect for the ambition, but man it's difficult to find most of it all solo. Especially a shame because the art of this game is just so phenomenal. Very rarely to I feel yucky about not being all to see everything a game has to offer.

To wrap this all up, if you're into Visual Novels, and VN's that gamify the experience, I think you'll really find something special here. Characters are great, lovable, fun, with surprising amount of depth to especially the protagonist. The world building is magical, and the story at whole is extremely intriguing. Love the blend of Nordic Mythology and symbolism mixed with some tradional modern Japanese/Anime tropes and story beats. 

I hope from the bottom of my heart the development for the 3rd game is at least happening, and if so everything is going smoothly. While very much a hidden gem in all meaning possible, it'd be real shame to not see the story of Shama and this world not conclude properly.  Cheers to Windthunder Studio and what they've created here. Also I'm still holding out hope for a artbook release for Zero 2 here!

[b]A Twisted Place[/b] - весьма неоднозначный проект. Это очень [i]"мясной"[/i], в хорошей мере безумный хоррор, который чем-то напоминает ужасы Роба Зомби: много жестокости, крови, мяса; идеи переплетаются, создавая нечто мерзкое, но в то же время увлекательное и мрачное. В плане стилистики и контента игра способна удивить, [u]но главная её проблема - она почти не пугает[/u].

Сразу уточню важное: это [i]первая игра начинающего разработчика[/i], и, определённо, получилось не всё, как задумывалось. Потенциал у автора большой, поэтому многие вещи лично я прощаю, хоть они и могут изрядно взбесить рядового игрока.

Игра начинается с того, что главный герой оказывается в комнате перед странным человеком, который спрашивает: готов ли он страдать и встретиться со смертью. После этой неуютной сцены герой просыпается в доме, будто перекочевавшем из самого ада: на каждом шагу кровь, странные говорящие существа, на кухне буквально жарятся люди, а в мусорном ведре во всей "красоте" - содранное и выкинутое человеческое лицо. Чем дальше бродишь по дому, тем мрачнее: секретные проходы, клетки, мясо и кровь повсюду, существа доедают останки, с некоторыми людьми можно поговорить - но все отвечают загадками; понятно, что разум у всех уже поплыл. Ваша задача - помочь герою выбраться из этого места и по пути посетить ещё более тревожные локации. Сумеет ли он понять, что происходит, или сгинет в этом аду? Узнать, чем завершится этот инфернальный кошмар, действительно любопытно.

Истории тут, по правде, немного: про персонажей почти ничего не узнаёте; изредка попадаются записки - чуть приоткрывают происходящее или служат подсказками. Брутальность же удерживается до конца - финал выдержан в том же ключе. Никакого хэппи-энда: мрак, безнадёга и новые вопросы. Кому-то такое не зайдёт, а мне понравилось.

Геймплейно - это такая 2.5D-бродилка с элементами квеста. Перемещение - слева направо; взаимодействие с миром завязано на мышке: идёте, водите курсором, кликаете по триггерам и предметам. Ключевые точки подписаны, пиксель-хантинга нет. Почти 90% времени - исследование мрачных локаций и простые пазлы. Изредка встречаются "экшен"-сцены, но они сверхлёгкие: отойти от врага, спрятаться в шкаф, либо короткие QTE, где нужно проскользнуть мимо незамеченным.

И вот тут становится ясно, что игра сливает свой хоррор-потенциал. При "смерти" моментально выскакивает экран "вы умерли" с коротким криком - без какой-либо толковой анимации. Поймали/обнаружили - мгновенно чёрный экран. Дёшево и совсем не страшно. Звуки монстров одинаковые: при приближении опасности - громкое дыхание. Из-за отсутствия нормальных скейров и "смертей" сам экран "вы умерли" перестаёт работать как угроза.

По стелсу/погоням/экшену - тоже бедно. Я понимаю, что выбранный формат многое ограничивает, но и то, что есть, сделано банально. Хуже всего - отсутствие нормального эмбиента. Вы ходите по мрачному дому, лесам, пещерам и катакомбам; стены шепчут, на полу - чьи-то кишки, визуально страшно и брутально... а на фоне - монотонное "мычание". И так всю игру. Никакой действительно тревожной фоновой музыки; местами - вообще тишина и шаги. Поэтому не возникает чувства слежки, ожидания внезапной беды. Будь здесь толковый саундтрек - вместе с визуалом вышла бы реально стремная атмосфера.

Зато визуальная часть держит планку: я уже описал мрачные локации - темно-кровавая палитра создаёт узнаваемую картинку, уровни различаются, есть на что посмотреть. Помимо грубых сцен хватает и криповых эпизодов. В больнице, например, вы медленно идёте к выходу - за спиной звучит голос, зовущий вас. Обернётесь - словите скейр; не оборачиваетесь - голос меняется с приятного женского на демонический, приказывающий повернуться. Сцена сделана отлично. Чего не хватает? Правильно - жуткого эмбиента. Всего уровней три, и на каждом есть свои ситуации. Ближе к финалу попадаете в странное место: периодически накатывает "проклятие", всё становится красно-тёмным, играет странная мелодия (та самая тема из Hong Kong 97). Сам трек использовать я бы не стал, но вместе с отсылкой к Castlevania (ночное "проклятие") создаётся ощущение, будто игру собрала не совсем человеческая сила - наверняка на это и рассчитывал автор.

Таких удачных моментов в игре хватает - и это радует. Но отсутствие нормальной опасности и грамотной музыки убийственно для атмосферы: играть становится нестрашно. Есть пара прямых джампскейров, но их мало; одной "картинки и мяса" недостаточно для устойчивого чувства тревоги.

[quote]Для меня A Twisted Place - тот самый guilty pleasure. В ней есть крутые элементы, особый стиль и тонна мяса; необычная завязка цепляет. Но из-за отсутствия реальной угрозы и мрачного саунд-дизайна - банально не страшно. Повторюсь: видно, что автор старался и сделал необычную игру, где многое работает, но многое не доведено до ума. Если ищете мрачный, жестокий хоррор - этого тут навалом; вот только напугать вряд ли получится. Тем не менее попробовать можно: крутые эпизоды есть, атмосфера - тягучая и завораживающая, а ценник гуманный. Потенциал у автора определённо есть - хочется верить, что в следующей работе он исправит недочёты. Тогда и правда может получиться леденящий кровь хоррор.[/quote]

Ich finde auch diese typische EM4-Atmosphäre stark. Die Karte ist zwar nicht riesig, aber irgendwie hat sie Charakter. Man lernt schnell, wo gern mal Unfälle passieren oder wo Brände gern ausbrechen. Wenn dann plötzlich mehrere Einsätze gleichzeitig reinkommen, geht der Puls hoch, und genau das macht für mich den Reiz aus.

- Was das Spiel für mich besonders macht

Das Beste an EM4 ist für mich ganz klar die Modding-Community. Ich spiele das Grundspiel eigentlich kaum noch. Mit Mods wie der LA Mod oder deutschen Stadt-Mods fühlt sich alles viel moderner und abwechslungsreicher an. Neue Fahrzeuge, neue Einsätze, neue Mechaniken, das hält das Spiel lebendig.
Ich ertappe mich oft dabei, wie ich eigentlich nur kurz spielen wollte und plötzlich sind zwei Stunden rum.

- Langzeitmotivation

Emergency 4 ist für mich so ein typisches „immer wieder reinschauen“ Spiel. Keine Kampagne, die man durchrushen will, sondern einfach Einsätze abarbeiten, zwischendurch entspannen und trotzdem gefordert werden. Genau diese Mischung hält mich seit Jahren dabei.
Auch wenn es manchmal Bugs gibt oder die KI nicht macht, was sie soll, im Gesamtpaket macht das Spiel einfach Laune.

Das beste Feuerwehrspiel auf dem Markt
Im Vergleich zu Emergency 5/16/17/20 wie mans auch nennen will, ist Emergency 4, wenn wir mal die Grafik außen vor lassen, in allen Belangen besser. Ich fasse mal das wichtigste zusammen:
- Die Missionen sind realistischer und generell spannender, da man einen wesentlichen Teil der Gebäude betreten kann, was in dem Nachfolgerspielen leider komplett wegfällt.
- Die Kampagne hat viel spannendere Missionen, die wirklich fordern und richtig gute Abwechslung zum normalen Spiel geben
- Es gibt eine Art LF, so heißt es hier nicht, aber es kommt nah dran. Auch das fällt in den Nachfolgern weg.
- Aktionsmöglichkeiten der Einheiten. Damit meine ich zum Beispiel, dass es bei der POL Einheiten gibt, wie z.B. Profiler, die bei Geiselnahmen nützlich sind und dass man mit dem SEK mit dem Gewehr selber zielen muss um zu treffen. Einfach so ein paar Kleinigkeiten, die das Spiel nochmal besser machen.
- Die Modding Szene. Immer noch aktiv und es gibt Mods die das Spiel wirklich auf so ein enorm hohes Level bringen. Meine Empfehlung wäre da Wegberg V8

Schwachpunkte:
- Es kann auf neueren PCs mal schwer zum laufen bekommen sein, aber da findet man eigentlich immer jemanden, der helfen kann.
- Die Grafik ist natürlich für heutige Verhältnisse nicht die beste, aber das Spiel ist natürlich schon fast 20 Jahre alt, also ist das natürlich nachvollziehbar und kein richtiger Schwachpunkt.

As a kid, we spent hours playing with our plastic soldiers, so when I saw a video game that brought that to life, I was all in. The game does a great job of re-creating the feel of what it was like to “play soldier.” I love the graphics—they strike just the right balance of detail without ruining the effect that you’re dealing with toys. I definitely got a Toy Story vibe and kept thinking of “mean Sid” every time I saw the mangled toys.

As others have mentioned, each level starts out with the same basic rifle, and you can then find other weapons like the flamethrower, machine gun, and sniper rifle. Oh yeah, can’t forget the hand grenades. While there is a Save option, I found that it doesn’t allow for mid-level saves, so if you don’t have time to finish a level, you’ll have to start over.

The developer is very responsive on the board, and if you run into any issues, he’s quick to help out and post fixes. Overall, the game is very solid, and I had no major problems. I did have to bump the quality down for the Toy Shop, but that may have been caused by a recent Windows update. I plan to replay it again since I missed a lot of details on the first play through—there’s just so much eye-candy to take in.
So far its really fun! Please add controller support!

Не смог меня ни зацепить, ни увлечь. Абсолютно каждый персонаж разочаровал своими поступками, а вплетенная мифология, увы, не добавила ничего по-настоящему стоящего, что могло бы вытянуть повествование.

Если рассматривать историю в целом, она наполненная, живая и даже печальная - если в нее углубиться. Но именно главная героиня не дала мне окунуться в это. Отталкивающая своей холодностью, подлостью и временами даже глупостью, она заставляет игрока заранее смотреть на происходящее предвзято.

Со временем становится ясно, что события связаны не просто с исчезновением ребенка, а с древним мифом о договоре, заключенном с волком. Условия гласят, что раз в определенный период необходимо приносить ему жертву, а в это время открывается портал между мирами - именно поэтому на пути встречаются самые неожиданные существа.

Игра могла бы быть неплохой драмой, но все упирается в глупость. Холодная мать с синдромом контроля, лишенный внимания мальчик, [spoiler]решивший принести себя в жертву[/spoiler] и слабый папенька, [spoiler]который нырнул в петлю[/spoiler], не сумев доказать свою правоту в суде. Занавес.

Каждый из них наполнен своей болью, но её просто не раскрыли. Два персонажа подаются исключительно через рассказ горе-матери, которая изначально передает все в искаженном свете.

Вот то, что окончательно убило интерес к игре. Симулятор ходьбы, скрещенный с собирательством тонны коллекционок.

В основном вы просто бежите по лесам, болотам и пещерам. Изредка натыкаетесь на записи антагониста, рассказы местных жителей или описания мифических существ. Все это могло бы быть интересным, если бы сопровождалось внутренними монологами героини или хотя бы бОльшим пересказом произошедшего. Но нет - вы просто бежите в тишине. Если для вас звук ручейка или редкий рык очередной бабайки уже атмосфера, тогда проблем не возникнет.

Есть легкий намек на стелс и необходимость избегать врагов, но этого настолько мало и сделано так топорно, что проще просто бежать вперед, чем устраивать танцы с бубном в виде пряток.

Uplink, developed and published by Introversion Software, is one of the most distinctive simulation games ever made, offering players an immersive experience in the world of cyber espionage and digital intrusion. Originally released in 2001 and later brought to Steam, it places you in the role of a freelance hacker, an anonymous agent for hire who takes on covert assignments from corporations, governments, and secret organizations. Instead of flashy action or cinematic sequences, the game unfolds entirely through a minimalist computer interface, creating the illusion that you’re operating inside a clandestine digital world. It’s a concept that feels remarkably ahead of its time, blending role-playing elements, economic management, and puzzle-solving into a unique hacking simulator that still resonates with players today.

At the start of the game, you sign a contract with the mysterious Uplink Corporation, which provides you with access to a “gateway” computer. From this base of operations, you begin performing low-level jobs: breaking into public servers, deleting records, and stealing simple files for small amounts of money. Each successful job earns credits that can be spent on upgrading your system—faster processors, better modems, additional memory, or advanced hacking tools. These upgrades are crucial, as each mission increases in difficulty and complexity. Before long, you’ll find yourself infiltrating corporate networks protected by proxy servers, firewalls, and security traces, forcing you to juggle multiple tools while racing against time to avoid detection. The game’s tension lies in that constant countdown: the flashing “Trace In Progress” warning, the slow climb of the trace percentage, and the desperate scramble to cover your digital footprints before you’re caught. Few games have ever captured the thrill of high-stakes hacking as effectively or as convincingly.

Uplink’s minimalist interface is a masterstroke of design. The entire experience takes place through a simulated operating system—a dark blue desktop filled with pop-up windows, status monitors, and email clients. You don’t control a character; instead, you control a system, and it’s the player’s intellect, rather than reflexes, that drives progress. The aesthetic feels simultaneously sterile and atmospheric, with its abstract sound effects, low-key electronic soundtrack, and the steady hum of data streams underscoring every move. The sparse presentation encourages imagination, letting you fill in the blanks of the world beyond the screen. When you see a connection chain trace back through multiple servers or hear the subtle ping of a firewall being bypassed, it feels like you’re part of a larger, shadowy network where every keystroke carries weight. This immersion is something modern games often struggle to achieve even with far more complex visuals, yet Uplink accomplishes it through restraint and suggestion.

What makes Uplink stand out, even decades after its release, is its commitment to player freedom and emergent storytelling. Though there is a central plot involving two rival corporations—Arunmor and ARC—fighting over the fate of the internet via powerful viruses called Faith and Revelation, the game allows players to decide whether to get involved or simply pursue their own career. You can remain a neutral contractor, align with one side, or even double-cross your employers for personal gain. The missions themselves range from simple data thefts to framing innocent users, altering academic records, or stealing classified research. Each task can be approached in different ways depending on your setup, and the game encourages experimentation. There’s no scripted handholding; success comes from learning how each system works and from gradually developing the instincts of a professional hacker. It’s a rare design philosophy that rewards curiosity and persistence rather than spoon-feeding solutions.

The difficulty curve, however, can be steep. New players are likely to fail their first few missions, either by being traced or by forgetting to erase evidence on the servers they infiltrate. The game’s refusal to hold your hand may seem harsh, but it’s also part of what gives it authenticity. Every mistake carries consequences, and the sense of risk makes every victory feel meaningful. The higher-level missions, especially those involving corporate networks and LANs, can feel daunting at first, demanding multitasking and precision timing. Yet this challenge is exactly what keeps Uplink engaging. You’re constantly balancing speed, planning, and resource management, and even after dozens of missions, the thrill of narrowly escaping a trace never loses its intensity.

Beneath its austere interface lies a surprisingly rich simulation of hacker culture. Uplink presents a world where information is currency, corporations are untrustworthy, and morality is flexible. The game doesn’t moralize your choices; it simply lets you act and then face the consequences. This gives it an emergent narrative quality—your story as a hacker is shaped by your actions rather than dictated by cutscenes. You might spend an entire playthrough building a legitimate reputation as a reliable contractor, or you might turn rogue, spreading chaos for your own amusement. Either way, the result feels personal. The slow accumulation of wealth, the satisfaction of upgrading your hardware, and the growing confidence in tackling high-risk jobs all contribute to a strong sense of progression rarely achieved through traditional storytelling.

Uplink’s longevity owes much to its design simplicity and moddable structure. Its interface may look dated by modern standards, but its mechanics remain remarkably intact. Fans have created mods, new skins, and expanded missions that keep the game alive long after its release. Even without modifications, it remains endlessly replayable thanks to procedural generation and open-ended goals. The combination of tension, freedom, and atmosphere ensures that each playthrough feels unique. It’s a game that doesn’t rely on graphics or spectacle but instead on imagination and immersion, allowing players to step into a world of clandestine operations where intellect is your greatest weapon.

Two decades on, Uplink still feels like a blueprint for immersive simulation design. It doesn’t try to simplify or glamorize hacking—it distills it into something abstract yet believable, where strategy and timing matter more than spectacle. Its flaws—repetitive mission types, occasional interface confusion, and a lack of accessibility features—are outweighed by its sense of identity and purpose. There’s a hypnotic rhythm to the gameplay loop: accepting a contract, tracing connections, bypassing systems, cleaning logs, and vanishing without a trace. Each completed mission reinforces that feeling of being part of a secret world, invisible but powerful.

Uplink remains one of the most iconic independent titles of its generation—a cult classic that captures the fantasy of the hacker archetype without resorting to clichés or exaggeration. Its blend of tension, atmosphere, and open-ended design still feels remarkably fresh, proving that immersion doesn’t require realism so much as conviction. It’s a quiet, cerebral experience that rewards patience and cleverness, a game that turns a simple interface into a window into an invisible digital war. For those willing to embrace its minimalist presentation and steep learning curve, Uplink offers one of the most authentic and satisfying cyberpunk experiences ever created—a simulation of solitude, intellect, and danger inside the infinite expanse of the virtual world.

Hammerwatch, developed by Crackshell and published by Team17, is a modern tribute to the classic top-down hack-and-slash dungeon crawlers that defined the genre decades ago. It combines the spirit of old arcade action with modern accessibility, creating a game that feels familiar yet fresh. Set within the sprawling halls of Castle Hammerwatch, players embark on a perilous journey through labyrinthine corridors filled with monsters, traps, and treasures. The game can be played solo or cooperatively, and while its foundation is simple, the experience grows in intensity and depth as players progress through its increasingly hostile levels. It doesn’t rely on cinematic storytelling or elaborate world-building; instead, it thrives on pure gameplay—the rhythmic dance of combat, exploration, and survival.

At the heart of Hammerwatch lies its class-based system, allowing players to choose from six distinct heroes including the Paladin, Wizard, Ranger, Thief, Warlock, and Priest. Each class offers a different style of play, from the Paladin’s close-range durability to the Wizard’s devastating spells and the Thief’s high-speed melee attacks. The differences between classes add variety and encourage experimentation, especially when playing cooperatively. Every character can be upgraded with improved abilities, health boosts, and new skills, purchased with the gold and gems found throughout the castle. This sense of progression, while subtle, keeps the player invested as the challenge escalates. Combat is fast-paced and relentless, often throwing hordes of enemies at the player in tight spaces that demand both precision and awareness. Dodging projectiles, managing your attacks, and controlling positioning are essential, and the thrill of surviving an overwhelming encounter never truly fades.

Exploration is just as important as combat. Each level of Hammerwatch is intricately designed, filled with hidden rooms, secret switches, and optional challenges that reward careful observation and persistence. Players are encouraged to scour every corner of the map to uncover secret areas containing valuable upgrades or shortcuts. The handcrafted design of the dungeons gives each floor a sense of personality, with enemy types and traps varying to keep the player on edge. There’s a strong sense of discovery that recalls the exploratory satisfaction of classic dungeon crawlers, where curiosity and courage are often rewarded. The balance between danger and reward gives the game a distinct rhythm—brief pauses of calm exploration punctuated by bursts of intense combat.

While Hammerwatch can certainly be played alone, its cooperative mode elevates the experience to another level. The game shines brightest when shared with friends, as its balance and pacing feel perfectly tuned for teamwork. Each class complements the others, and the interplay between them—such as a Priest supporting a front-line Paladin or a Ranger covering the group from a distance—creates moments of dynamic coordination and chaotic fun. The cooperative element also adds longevity, as running through the campaign with different combinations of players and classes offers fresh tactical variety. However, playing solo can feel less rewarding. The difficulty remains punishing, and without the energy of co-op synergy, repetition can set in. Some battles stretch on longer than necessary, and the steady rhythm of clearing rooms can start to feel formulaic after extended play sessions.

Visually, Hammerwatch adopts a charming pixel-art style that pays homage to retro gaming while remaining clean and readable. The environments are detailed without being cluttered, allowing players to focus on the action while still appreciating the atmosphere. The lighting effects and subtle animations bring life to the stone corridors, while the color palette shifts as the player descends deeper into the castle. The soundtrack, composed by Two Feathers, complements the tone perfectly, with haunting melodies and energetic battle themes that enhance the medieval fantasy mood. The presentation, though minimalist, succeeds in evoking nostalgia without relying solely on it—it’s a love letter to an older era that understands what made those games engaging.

Hammerwatch is not without its shortcomings. The repetition inherent in its design can wear thin for players looking for more variety or narrative depth. The combat, while satisfying, can at times feel predictable due to limited enemy behavior patterns. Class balance also varies, with certain heroes feeling more capable than others depending on the situation. The lack of procedural generation means that once you’ve mastered the layout of the dungeons, replaying them offers diminishing surprises. Yet these flaws are somewhat softened by the game’s focus on skill mastery and cooperative replayability. It’s a game designed to test reflexes and teamwork rather than to overwhelm with content or story.

Despite its limitations, Hammerwatch remains a solid and enduring example of how simplicity can be powerful when executed with care. It captures the raw thrill of dungeon crawling—fighting through waves of monsters, collecting gold, upgrading your hero, and inching closer to victory. It respects the player’s time by keeping the mechanics tight and the goals clear, and it delivers a rewarding sense of accomplishment through pure gameplay rather than artificial progression systems. Whether you play it alone as a test of endurance or with friends as a cooperative adventure, Hammerwatch offers a challenging and nostalgic journey that feels timeless. For players who appreciate classic action, deliberate design, and the joy of shared discovery, it stands as one of the most faithful and enjoyable homages to the dungeon-crawling genre in recent memory.

Koral, developed and published by Carlos Coronado, is a serene and visually arresting underwater puzzle game that blends environmental storytelling with minimalist design. It places players in control of a sentient ocean current whose purpose is to restore life and color to coral reefs decimated by pollution and human interference. Unlike traditional puzzle games that rely on complex systems or explicit objectives, Koral takes a meditative approach, inviting players to drift through sunlit depths and barren seabeds as they slowly rekindle the beauty of marine ecosystems. Its world is not one of noise and tension but of quiet wonder—a deliberate space for reflection and rejuvenation, carried by an unspoken message about the fragility of nature and the importance of preservation.

At the heart of Koral lies a simple yet elegant concept. You move as a glowing current of energy, navigating intricate reef structures and transferring vitality to dormant corals scattered across each level. The puzzles revolve around gathering luminous energy, unblocking flow paths, and synchronizing coral activations in the correct sequence to bring life back to desolate regions. There are no enemies, timers, or overt failure states; instead, the game encourages patient exploration and experimentation. The gradual illumination of the ocean, as gray lifeless corals bloom into vibrant blues, purples, and reds, creates a sense of progression that is both mechanical and emotional. Each revitalized section feels like a small act of healing, and as more of the ocean awakens, the cumulative effect is deeply satisfying in its understated way.

The design philosophy behind Koral emphasizes accessibility and atmosphere over challenge. Its puzzles are never meant to overwhelm, but to maintain a rhythmic flow of discovery. Early stages introduce straightforward objectives—transferring light to nearby corals or opening blocked tunnels—while later areas expand into layered structures that require observation and spatial reasoning. The learning curve is gentle, yet there is enough variation in level design to sustain curiosity across its brief runtime. The most striking moments arise when mechanical interaction and environmental storytelling align: watching a lifeless expanse transform into a thriving marine ecosystem after solving a puzzle encapsulates the game’s essence better than any words could. While repetition in puzzle structure eventually sets in, the meditative pacing ensures that even familiar mechanics retain a certain tranquility rather than monotony.

Visually, Koral is a triumph of simplicity. Coronado, known for his skill in creating atmospheric spaces, employs a painterly use of lighting and color to convey emotion. Rays of sunlight pierce through the water, casting golden beams on coral outcrops, while swaying seaweed and drifting particles lend depth and texture to the oceanic environment. The shift from dull, ashen hues to radiant color palettes mirrors the game’s thematic transformation from decay to renewal. The visual fidelity is enhanced by the sense of motion and fluidity—the player’s current moves gracefully through the water, and the gentle undulation of marine life reinforces the sensation of being part of a living world. There are moments where the repetition of environmental assets becomes noticeable, particularly in later levels, but the beauty of the underwater world and its dynamic lighting largely overshadow this limitation.

The audio design complements the visual atmosphere perfectly. The soundtrack is a blend of soft piano melodies and ambient tones that ebb and flow like waves, fostering a calm and contemplative mood. Each note seems to echo within the watery expanse, as if resonating through coral caverns and ocean floors. Sound effects—bubbles, currents, and the soft hum of energy—contribute to the game’s immersive quality without intruding on its meditative tone. There are no voices or dialogues; the ocean itself becomes the narrative voice, communicating through sound and motion. This minimalism enhances the emotional intimacy of the experience, allowing players to engage with the world on an intuitive and sensory level rather than through exposition.

The storytelling in Koral is subtle, conveyed through environmental cues and optional discoveries rather than traditional narrative structure. As you progress, you unlock informational tidbits about real-world marine biology and the threats facing coral ecosystems. These fragments serve as quiet reminders of the game’s purpose beyond entertainment—they educate and inspire awareness. The lack of characters or spoken narrative reinforces the sense of solitude, turning the player’s journey into a symbolic act of restoration. It’s an environmental allegory told through interaction, where healing the virtual ocean mirrors the responsibility we hold toward the real one. This understated narrative approach may not satisfy those seeking drama or dialogue, but it achieves poignancy through restraint.

While Koral’s core experience is polished, it is intentionally brief. Most players can complete it within two to three hours, making it feel more like a self-contained meditation than a sprawling adventure. Its brevity is both a strength and a limitation: it ensures that the game’s emotional impact remains concentrated, but it also leaves one wishing for deeper mechanical or thematic expansion. Some puzzles begin to repeat familiar patterns, and a few sections flirt with trial-and-error pacing, yet the game never loses its sense of purpose. Its focus on relaxation and reflection makes it an ideal experience for those looking to escape the frenetic pace of modern gaming and simply breathe underwater for a while.

Technically, the game runs smoothly on most systems, with minimal load times and crisp visuals. The control scheme is deliberately simple—just movement with directional input—which enhances accessibility but also restricts complexity. There are occasional moments when camera angles or environmental clutter obscure key elements, but these are minor inconveniences rather than major flaws. The interface is clean and unobtrusive, reinforcing the game’s commitment to immersion. It’s evident that Koral was designed as an art piece as much as a puzzle game, and its presentation reflects a creator deeply invested in mood, message, and meaning rather than spectacle.

Koral ultimately succeeds because it understands the power of stillness. It’s not a game about mastery or conquest but about harmony and restoration. Its slow pace, quiet soundtrack, and restrained design invite contemplation rather than adrenaline. In an industry often dominated by noise, violence, and excess, Koral stands as a gentle reminder of what games can be when guided by empathy and reverence for the natural world. Carlos Coronado’s vision results in a work that resonates beyond its mechanics—a poetic, visually luminous, and emotionally grounded experience that celebrates the beauty of life beneath the waves. For players open to its quiet rhythms, Koral offers not just a game but a moment of calm reflection in a world that desperately needs it.

Grow Up, developed by Reflections, a Ubisoft Studio, serves as the spiritual successor to the quirky and beloved Grow Home. Where the first game introduced players to the charming little robot B.U.D. and his mission to cultivate a massive starplant, Grow Up takes that foundation and expands it into a larger, more ambitious adventure. This time, B.U.D. is tasked with exploring a strange and vibrant alien planet to collect the scattered parts of his spaceship, M.O.M., and the game leans heavily into exploration, physics-driven climbing, and playful experimentation with tools and flora. The result is an experience that feels both whimsical and frustrating, offering moments of joy punctuated by occasional struggles with imprecision.

The core of the game is built around freedom of movement. B.U.D. retains his clumsy, physics-based climbing from Grow Home, but Grow Up introduces several new traversal options that give players more ways to navigate the sprawling environment. The addition of abilities such as a jetpack, a glider, the ability to roll into a ball, and the capacity to scan and replant floraforms significantly broadens how the world can be approached. Each plant has its own unique properties, from launching the robot high into the air to cushioning falls or creating bridges, and scanning them allows players to place these tools wherever they are needed. Combined with the new powers, these mechanics create a sandbox-like sense of discovery, where climbing to the top of an impossibly tall structure or soaring across wide gaps becomes part of the joy.

The world itself is one of Grow Up’s strongest assets. The art style is low-poly and colorful, filled with alien landscapes, floating islands, and vast vistas that encourage curiosity. While the design is simple, it has a unique charm that makes even aimless exploration enjoyable. Climbing to a high altitude and looking out over the terrain provides a sense of accomplishment and wonder, and moments when B.U.D. takes to the skies with a glider or launches off a floraform can be exhilarating. The presentation strikes a balance between playful and serene, with a soundtrack that subtly complements the sense of lighthearted adventure.

Despite its strengths, Grow Up inherits some of the problems of its predecessor and introduces new ones. The physics-based climbing that defines the series is endearing but often unreliable, with B.U.D.’s movements prone to slips, awkward grabs, or unintentional falls. This imprecision can become frustrating during long climbs, as a single mistake often results in plummeting back to the ground and having to repeat progress. The camera, too, can be difficult to manage, particularly in cramped or vertical environments, where keeping track of B.U.D.’s position feels more like a struggle than a natural part of the challenge. These issues don’t ruin the experience but create a layer of friction that some players may find discouraging.

The game’s expanded size is both a strength and a weakness. While there is more to see and do compared to Grow Home, the objectives often boil down to collecting ship parts and completing small challenges, which can sometimes feel like busywork. The novelty of exploration can wear thin when long stretches involve little more than moving from one distant location to another, and the pacing occasionally suffers as a result. The game is relatively short, with a main playthrough lasting around four to six hours, but for players willing to engage with side objectives and collectibles, there is more to discover. Still, the sense of repetition may dampen enthusiasm for some.

Grow Up ultimately succeeds as a lighthearted exploration game with a distinct personality. Its mix of clumsy physics, imaginative floraforms, and colorful environments creates an experience that rewards curiosity and experimentation. It may not offer the precision or depth of more refined platformers, but its charm lies in embracing the unpredictable and finding fun in the chaos of movement. For those who enjoyed Grow Home or simply want a playful, low-pressure adventure, Grow Up delivers enough charm and creativity to make its shortcomings easier to forgive. It is not flawless, but it is memorable for its character, atmosphere, and the freedom it gives players to discover their own path through its alien landscapes.

I think this is a decent game that I would recommend to people who are a fan of classic NES platformers, but probably wouldn't recommend that outside of that sphere. The game doesn't do anything particularly outstanding, but isn't particularly offensive for the most part either; plays decent, looks okay, decent soundtrack. One huge thing to note is that this game is pretty short, only being 5 levels; but on the flipside of that, if you lose all of your lives, it's back to square one. I personally am not a fan of not having unlimited continues, but with a game this short and likely going for the classic NES style in the most literal interpretation, I can kinda see where they were coming from with that decision. Another thing is that your starting character just flat out sucks. He has a weird arcing projectile that's akin to the rock from Friday the 13th NES and about just as useful. However, as you go through the game, you start to get more characters as you go on, especially if you find the secret areas, and the character get progressively better (the Skeleton you can get in Level 2 I would argue is the first truly viable character). I ended up beating the game with one of the characters added in the free DLC update, the Protagonist, who is actually quite good and even ended up getting the secret ending first time by finding all 6 secret runes. Once you start getting some actually good characters, the game is actually decently fun, though, as stated before, incredibly short. I also am not a fan that you can only unlock one character per run of the game, though at least if you find a character unlock area after unlocking a character in that run, you get an extra life, which is nice. But because you can only unlock one character per run, if you're like me and managed to beat the game after unlocking only a few characters, then, unless you really want to achievement hunt this game, there's no point in going back to unlock everyone else once you've beaten the game. This game does have a decent amount of achievements to hunt if you're into that sort of thing and can extend the life of this game for a bit, but as a whole, the time you get out of this game is likely going to be quite short. If you're a retro platformer junkie, you'll likely get some enjoyment out of this game once you get a viable character, but you probably won't get much out of this game otherwise.

前作（無印）、そして今作とおおよそ攻略してきたので早速レビュー。

前作に続いて、このゲームを端的に述べるなら、

[h1]「競技性のある和風ホラーFPS」[/h1]

と言ってもいいかもしれない。

[h2]・基本的なルール[/h2]

前作同様ではあるが、道順に一定のランダム性を含み、徘徊者がウロウロドタバタしている回廊内からの脱出を目指し、道中にある勾玉を5個集めて奥にあるゴールを目指す。

道中に置いてあるアイテムを拾いながら、徘徊者の追跡を逃れつつ回廊内を突き抜けるのがルールとなっている。
…ただし、前作と微妙に仕様が違う点が多々あるため、前作から引き続きプレイする際は要注意してほしい。

[h2]・前作（無印）との違い[/h2]

[h3]＞操作設定について[/h3]
大きな点としては、[u]操作方法のボタン配置（デフォルト）がめちゃくちゃ変わってる（特にコントローラー）。[/u]
また、一部のアイテム（主に爆竹）が「RT押しながらLTで使用（コントローラの場合）」という安全装置方式が採用されている。前作でうっかり爆竹ぶん投げて徘徊者から逃げ惑ったことある人にとっては一安心？

[h3]＞アイテムについて[/h3]
一部アイテムに関しては役割を交換されたアイテムが多数。
加えて、前作では一部を除いて無限に持てたアイテムでさえ、種類と数に所持上限設定が設けられた。（例：光る石は最大30個くらい）
ただし、道中に商人からアイテムを購入することができるようになったなど、前作より改善されたポイントは多い。

[h3]＞持ち込みについて[/h3]
前作でいう「達成の証」にあたるものは、「カルタ」として搭載。
こちらも無制限ではないものの、一部カルタに関しては回廊から持って帰った勾玉を劇中人物に交換してもらうことでいくつか貰える。
良い感じにカルタを持ち込んで、攻略に備えよう。

[h3]＞ダメージ表現について[/h3]（ホラーが苦手な人向けの注意喚起）
[spoiler]前作は大丈夫だったとしても、今作は人によっては苦手かもしれない部類の表現が多々見られます。
特に「虫系の表現」「肉体的欠損」に関する表現が苦手な方…あと、特定の区画だけですが、「海洋恐怖症」に心当たりのある方はご用心を。[/spoiler]

…まあそもそもホラーが苦手な方は、レビュー見る前にこのページからは逃げてるとは思いますが。

Pool of Radiance is the first ever DnD video game (released in 1988). It starts off brutal, but levels off if you can manage to get yourself to a lvl 3 party, so retreat and rest after each encounter until you lvl up. Also The game is open-world so you can skip encounters until you are ready for them. Once you are strong enough to get past the first encounter area, the game gets surprisingly addictive.

The original game had a code wheel that was required to actually play the game (an old form of copy protection, you were screwed if you lost it), this version has technically removed it (just press "Enter" when prompted)

This series of games is unique in that you can actually choose to Fight, Wait, Ambush, Run, or Parley (which also breaks down into HOW you want to Parlay; Meek, Haughty, Overbearing, Equal) in EVERY encounter, so make sure you know your Monster Manual to determine the best course of action. In Curse of the Azure Bonds (the 3rd game released, but the 2nd game in the story; you can import characters from either Pool of Radiance or Hillsfar), I obtained a +2 ring by promising an Otyeugh that we would split a nearby pile of refuse (they eat garbage and sewage and can communicate telepathically)

Since it's the first ever DnD game, class and race options are limited (they add the Paladin class in literally the next game: Hillsfar).

Make sure you know your class limitations as well; to summarize: fighters can use all equipment, clerics can use any armor but only blunt weapons, rogues can only use light armor (studded leather, leather, padded) and light weapons (short sword, short bow, lt crossbow, etc) and wizards get almost nothing (padded armor, staves, slings, daggers, that's it). There's a huge variety of armor and weapons, and a lot of it has basically the same stats as something else so it can be confusing if your trying to find the "best" equipment; banded, splint, and ring mail are basically the same, bronze plate is 1 point worse than regular plate, polearms do the most/same damage but there are several different types (glaives, halberds, fauchards, etc), 

The game also implements ADnD 2nd edition's resurrection  limitations (albeit poorly). Elves cannot be resurrected, and other characters permanently lose 1 Constitution point (in the PnP game, you could only be resurrected as many times as you had points in Constitution)

Sadly, a lot of the story dialogue gets lost in this version as you cannot actually use the journal and some notes flash to quickly to actually read.

R-Type Delta is the fourth mainline entry in the R-Type series, originally released in 1998 in Japan then 1999 worldwide. A side scrolling horizontal shoot-em-up similar to contemporaries like Gradius and Darius. R-Type is one of the longest running and most influential series in the gaming industry. It's methodical approach focused on pattern memorization has influenced countless games throughout the decades, with series like Dark Souls owing a lot to games like the original R-Type. 

R-Type's core gameplay loop revolves around it's unique Force system. It works as a remote turret, shield, and power up to your main cannon. Carefully positioning it to cut off enemies and block shots while pulling it in to deal more damage takes a lot of strategy. This game isn't about reaction times, more about knowing about what is coming next. That is made evident by its checkpoint system. When you die you go back to the last checkpoint, not at the same spot you were at like other arcade games. 

Delta adds more nuance by having three separate ships with different Forces, missiles, and cannon types. Ideally, you'll play as all three to unlock everything like the different concept art and endings. There's also an additional fourth ship that's unlocked later. You can also swap your ship speed on the fly, which was a pretty big change at the time. Previously, you had to pick up speed-ups and speed-downs in older shmups. Delta gives you 4 different speeds to give you finer control. There's also the dose gage, which gives you a screen-clearing attack when filled out. 

This port, HD Boosted, adds some additional things to spice up the experience. The main selling point is the HD Mode, which increases the rendering resolution and adds new textures. They look nice, although the text and UI can be a little blurry. There's also a new arrange soundtrack that's pretty good, as well as different screen size options. The added practice mode will help newcomers and veterans train on the stages. 

One of the bigger changes that might not be obvious is that there is no more slowdown. I can't remember how much there was in the original version, but this game maintains a constant speed at 60 FPS. This might make those sequences where there was originally slowdown harder. There's no options to mess with that like other shmup ports, but it doesn't get too difficult. Again, the new practice mode will be critical to adapting to those moments. 

Could the devs have done more? Probably, but I can't think of anything that could be added at the moment other than just remaking the game entirely. That might have caused some more problems though in how faithful the placement and enemy timings would have been. Like this version even keeps the cheat codes from the original, which will help you unlock everything if you're having a hard time or just want to blast some aliens to cool music. They also added Nvidia Reflex, which I haven't tested in how it affects latency and game feel.

This is a great shmup port overall, giving everyone easier access to the game for those who don't want to mess with emulation or original PS1 hardware. I didn't notice any egregious problems in my two runs on the hardest difficulty. I hope Irem can work with other studios to bringing the rest of the franchise on Steam. Getting the rest of the games like Third Lightning and the original PS2 Final would be a huge win for fans and newcomers alike. R-Type is a great franchise that deserves to be preserved and enjoyed by everyone.

I'd give this a weak positive.  There's a lot to like here if you want a small game that doesn't take a lot of energy to play.  It is very grindy.  There are several things which seem like they could be added in later.  What's here is good, but it isn't fully realized yet and that may not change.

This is a game the devs are working on between other games, and it feels like one to play between more intense games as well.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
The gameplay loop is quite simple. Collect wood, level up, collect better wood, level up etc. All while turning in quests, getting new items, and exploring the world. The game doesn't have much beyond this, but it's not necessary nor is April Grove purporting to be more than such. It's a chill game meant to be taken slow and kill time which it does well. Exploring was interesting to me, meeting and seeing the character interactions were fun, and the game isn't terrible long. I played it over the course of a few weeks for about an hour per session. There are some parts of the game that aren't complete yet, and as such there are areas inaccessible, some stories without closure, or features without much utility unfortunately. Despite such, the developers published the game in a presentable state because the core gameplay loop works.

[h2]Aesthetic[/h2]
The pixel art is great. Looloopaa is the lead artist and I always enjoy his work. The style feels retro yet modern at the same time and it's an intriguing blend. The music fits well with the outdoors and peaceful nature that is the grove, and while the selection is limited, it didn't feel repetitive to me.

[h2]Extra Notes[/h2]
[list]
[*]Price: $3
[*]Playtime to beat: ~14h
[*]Completionist: Extremely doable; you don't even need to "beat" the game
[*]The game is still being worked on
[/list]

[hr][/hr]
[h2]Conclusion[/h2]
April Grove is a slow-paced chill game about chopping and collecting wood. It's not the most exhilarating game, but that's not the point. It does what it's meant to well. If you enjoy casual games or need a time killer, this is a fit. Recommended.

MegaTagmension Blanc + Neptune VS Zombies is a hack-and-slash action title that blends Neptunia’s trademark humor with a quirky school-themed zombie invasion. Built as a spin-off, it emphasizes fast combat, character variety, and lighthearted storytelling rather than deep mechanics or narrative complexity. The game targets fans who enjoy Neptunia’s playful tone combined with accessible action gameplay.

The story places the cast in Gamicademi, where Blanc attempts to save the school by filming a zombie movie—only for real zombies to appear. The premise is intentionally absurd and self-aware, filled with comedic dialogue and meta jokes typical of the series. The narrative remains simple but entertaining, primarily functioning as a backdrop for short missions and character banter.

Combat revolves around switching between two chosen characters and clearing small arenas packed with enemies. Each heroine has distinct attack patterns, special skills, and combos, allowing for a variety of playstyles. While the basic mechanics are straightforward, mastering character swapping and timing special abilities can improve efficiency during tougher encounters.

The roster is one of the game’s stronger features, featuring numerous familiar characters from the Neptunia franchise. Their personalities, skill animations, and voice lines carry over well into the action format. Experimenting with different pairings adds replay value, encouraging players to find combinations that match their preferred combat rhythm.

Visually, the game uses colorful environments and expressive character models, staying faithful to the series’ bright aesthetic. Combat effects are flashy but readable, keeping the on-screen action lively. The soundtrack features energetic tracks that fit the school and zombie-movie theme, contributing to the game’s light and upbeat tone.

Mission structure is built around short stages, making the game easy to play in quick sessions. However, repetition becomes noticeable over time due to similar objectives and limited enemy variety. Online co-op adds an extra option for players, though the mode depends heavily on the availability and connection quality of other users.

Overall, MegaTagmension Blanc + Neptune VS Zombies delivers a simple but entertaining action experience for fans of the Neptunia franchise. Its humor, character roster, and fast battles give it charm, even if its repetitive structure and modest mechanical depth limit its broader appeal. For players who enjoy the series’ personality and want a light hack-and-slash title, it serves as a fun, compact spin-off.

Worms World Party Remastered, developed and published by Team17 Digital Ltd, brings one of the most iconic entries in the Worms franchise back to modern platforms, attempting to preserve the chaotic spirit that defined the original while giving it a technical refresh. At its core, this remaster remains a turn-based artillery strategy game where teams of anthropomorphic worms wage absurd war across fully destructible 2D landscapes. The premise has always been intentionally ridiculous—tiny creatures armed with bazookas, ninja ropes, holy hand grenades, exploding sheep, and other outrageous tools—but that silliness is precisely what gives the series its enduring personality. The Remastered edition seeks to make that experience more accessible for contemporary players by improving resolution, adding controller support, and integrating Steam features like achievements and online functionality.

What continues to make the game compelling decades later is the emergent gameplay that arises from its deceptively simple rules. Each turn allows players to move, select a weapon, judge trajectory and wind influence, and attempt to land a precise shot before the timer expires. Because the terrain deforms with every explosion, the battlefield constantly evolves—platforms crumble, cliffs collapse, escape routes vanish, and safe positions disappear. Matches gradually transform from tactical positioning into desperate survival improvisation, and a single miscalculated shot can send a worm plunging into the water or trigger a chain reaction of mines and barrels. Whether played casually or competitively, the game thrives on unpredictability, slapstick failure, and creative problem-solving, making victory as entertaining as defeat.

The remastered version presents the original game in higher-definition form, offering 1080p resolution and a smoother frame rate that makes animations and explosions more visually readable. For returning fans, the bright, cartoony art style remains intact, preserving the expressive worm designs, imaginative backdrops, and colorful environmental themes. The soundtrack and voice samples still carry the whimsical charm the series is known for, and hearing worms taunt opponents or scream dramatically before being launched into oblivion remains an enduring comedic delight. Local and online multiplayer support are included, allowing up to six players to participate in matches—something that continues to be the beating heart of the Worms experience.

However, while the labeling suggests a significant overhaul, Worms World Party Remastered feels more like a modest touch-up than a full modernization. Beyond resolution improvements and basic Steam integration, many interface elements remain nearly unchanged from the early-2000s version, and menus display their age in both structure and visual design. The remaster does not introduce new weapons, gameplay systems, or campaign content, which may disappoint players expecting expanded features. Online functionality, while present, can be inconsistent depending on player activity and connection stability, and the matchmaking system isn’t as robust or streamlined as contemporary multiplayer titles. For some, these technical limitations reinforce the impression that the remaster could have benefited from deeper quality-of-life improvements.

Yet despite these shortcomings, the game still succeeds where it matters most: shared chaos. Worms has always been less about progression or narrative and more about the social dynamic—friends shouting at each other across a room, laughing at disastrous misfires, or celebrating impossibly skillful trick shots. The Remastered edition continues to deliver that experience reliably, and the minimal system requirements make it playable on a wide range of machines, including lower-end PCs and older laptops. For long-time fans who want a convenient, modern way to revisit a classic without running legacy versions through compatibility workarounds, this release delivers a straightforward solution.

For newcomers, Worms World Party Remastered may feel like an old-school relic—simple, occasionally clunky, and intentionally slow-paced compared to modern action-driven multiplayer games. But those who take the time to learn its physics-driven combat, its subtle positional strategy, and its gleefully chaotic arsenals will find a timeless kind of competitive enjoyment. It remains a game where creativity and improvisation matter just as much as accuracy, and where a well-timed banana bomb can shift the entire momentum of a match.

Ultimately, Worms World Party Remastered is not a transformative reimagining of a beloved classic, but it remains a highly entertaining experience that captures the essence of what made the series special in the first place. It is best approached as a preserved snapshot of early Worms design—intentionally quirky, mechanically straightforward, and endlessly replayable with the right group of players. Fans seeking polished nostalgia or a convenient multiplayer throwback will find plenty to enjoy, while those expecting a fully rebuilt remaster may need to temper expectations. What hasn’t changed is the chaotic joy of sending squadrons of cartoon worms into absurdly destructive battle—and for many, that alone makes the return worthwhile.
