Quantum Covenant is a disappointing mess of a game that falls far short of its potential. Despite its attempts at creating a complex sci-fi strategy experience, it struggles in nearly every aspect, from clunky mechanics to lackluster visuals and an underwhelming narrative. It’s difficult to recommend to anyone, as the game fails to deliver a satisfying or even enjoyable experience.

The combat system, while trying to be tactical, feels clunky and unintuitive. The controls are frustrating, and the steep difficulty curve makes even the most basic battles feel like a chore. It’s not a satisfying challenge but rather an exercise in patience and trial-and-error. The factions, though they have different abilities, fail to provide the depth necessary to make each playthrough feel fresh or engaging.

The story is a slog to get through. It’s poorly written and devoid of emotional depth, leaving the player disconnected from the events of the game. The choices you make in the narrative feel meaningless, and the world-building doesn’t do enough to pull you in. The dialogue is flat, and the attempts at creating intrigue fall flat because of the lack of compelling characters or plot twists.

Visually, Quantum Covenant is stuck in the past. The environments are boring and uninspired, with outdated graphics and static backgrounds that make the game feel lifeless. The character models are basic and lack any real detail or personality. While the music and sound design are decent, they do little to enhance the overall experience.

Pacing is another major issue. The game drags on with missions that feel like they take forever, and there’s no sense of excitement or urgency. The learning curve is steep, and without enough guidance, it can be overwhelming and frustrating. It’s a game that feels more like a grind than a fun strategy experience.

Pros:
✅ Some variety in faction abilities.
✅ Decent music and sound design.

Cons:
❌ Clunky, unintuitive combat system.
❌ Poorly written story with no emotional engagement.
❌ Dull visuals and outdated design.
❌ Frustrating difficulty and steep learning curve.
❌ Slow pacing and repetitive gameplay.

Quantum Covenant is a complete miss. Despite the potential for an engaging sci-fi strategy game, it’s bogged down by poor design choices, lackluster execution, and a world that fails to captivate. It’s a frustrating and tedious experience that never feels rewarding. Save your time and money—this one is not worth playing.

Mystery P.I.: Lost in Los Angeles, developed by SpinTop Games and published by PopCap Games, is a relaxed and straightforward hidden object experience that captures the lighthearted charm of casual gaming from the late 2000s. It places players in the role of a private investigator hired by a major Hollywood studio to find a stolen movie before its premiere. The missing film reel is worth millions, and the studio’s reputation depends on its safe return. What follows is a trip through glitzy and iconic locations around Los Angeles, from beachfront cafes and studio backlots to celebrity mansions and red carpet events, all rendered in colorful, illustrated scenes. While the premise is simple, it provides a playful backdrop for the game’s central focus: meticulously scanning every environment to locate cleverly hidden objects.

The gameplay adheres closely to the classic hidden object formula. Each level presents a static scene filled with dozens of items, and players must locate those listed at the bottom of the screen before moving on. There are 25 levels in total, each consisting of multiple screens and increasingly complex layouts. The game occasionally sprinkles in bonus challenges, such as finding hidden keys or film reels that unlock additional puzzles. These touches add a small layer of progression, rewarding players with mini-games like word puzzles, spot-the-difference challenges, or simple jigsaws that provide a break from pure object-hunting. Though these interludes don’t drastically change the rhythm, they help maintain engagement over the game’s several-hour playtime. The formula is repetitive by nature, but it’s also predictably satisfying—each found object brings a small jolt of accomplishment that keeps the pace steady.

Lost in Los Angeles captures a specific tone that sets it apart from darker or more narrative-driven entries in the hidden object genre. Its depiction of Hollywood is bright, exaggerated, and lighthearted, filled with palm trees, film posters, and subtle humor in the objects scattered throughout each scene. You might find yourself searching for a surfboard on a studio lot or a hot dog at a celebrity’s home, giving the puzzles a playful absurdity that fits the breezy atmosphere. The environments are colorful and neatly drawn, and while the visual fidelity shows its age, the composition of each scene remains clever. Objects are rarely just lying in plain sight; they blend naturally into backgrounds or camouflage within similarly colored surroundings. This design ensures that even casual players need to stay observant, though it never becomes frustrating or unfair. Hints are available if players get stuck, and the game’s time limits are generous enough to make failure almost impossible.

Despite its charm, the game’s structure and mechanics reveal the limitations of its time. Each scene tends to follow the same formula, and while the locations differ in theme, they begin to blur together after several hours. The story, which revolves around retrieving the stolen film, is largely superficial and only serves as a thin thread between levels. There are no characters to interact with beyond the implied presence of your client, and no real narrative twists to drive the investigation forward. Instead, the game leans entirely on its puzzle-solving loop, which, though enjoyable in small doses, can feel repetitive in long sessions. The occasional mini-game breaks this monotony somewhat, but their simplicity—such as basic matching or silhouette puzzles—makes them more like palette cleansers than substantial features.

Technically, Mystery P.I.: Lost in Los Angeles is stable and easy to run on any system, a hallmark of PopCap’s accessible design philosophy. The interface is clean and responsive, though the hit detection can be slightly inconsistent, requiring players to click very precisely on certain objects for them to register as found. The sound design is minimal but effective; the soft background music and gentle chimes when finding items create a relaxing atmosphere that suits the game’s casual pacing. The lack of voice acting or significant sound effects means that the game’s presentation leans entirely on its visuals and interface flow, which remain simple and functional throughout. It’s clear that the developers aimed to deliver a stress-free, easy-to-pick-up experience suitable for players of all ages.

As part of the Mystery P.I. series, Lost in Los Angeles doesn’t stray far from its predecessors, and that familiarity can be both its strength and weakness. Fans of the earlier titles will recognize the same formula refined slightly, with improved artwork and smoother transitions between levels. For newcomers, it offers a gentle introduction to the hidden object genre—one that’s approachable, family-friendly, and polished within its limited scope. However, players seeking innovation or a deeper mystery might find the lack of evolution disappointing. There’s little sense of progression beyond unlocking new scenes, and by the time the mystery is solved, it’s the environments rather than the narrative that leave the strongest impression.

Ultimately, Mystery P.I.: Lost in Los Angeles succeeds at what it sets out to do: provide a calm, entertaining diversion wrapped in a sunny Hollywood theme. It doesn’t attempt to reinvent its genre or complicate its design with unnecessary systems, and that simplicity is part of its enduring appeal. It’s the kind of game that can be played in short sessions, providing a satisfying rhythm of discovery without requiring deep concentration or long-term commitment. Though it shows its age and lacks the narrative complexity of modern hidden object adventures, its combination of pleasant visuals, gentle challenge, and accessible design make it a reliable choice for fans of casual puzzle games. In the end, it’s less about solving a mystery and more about enjoying the leisurely process of uncovering hidden details in a world built for quiet observation.

我是初体验的这款游戏，玩的是98柔情版本。游戏体验很不错，整体剧情算是一般剧本吧，不算差也不算特别精彩。游戏属于传统的rpg回合制游戏，但是节奏相对较快，并不会让人感到拖沓。
这部作品最让我印象深刻的点是它整体相对线性的玩法，几乎没有支线，它将传统rpg中的升级要素融入在了主线当中，也就是将大部分的迷宫设计都放在了主线里，最后呈现出的效果是，你跟着主线进入迷宫探索，以正常的节奏探索完迷宫后，基本就达到这张地图boss战斗需要的等级。这一点让整体游戏体验非常流畅，能很顺畅的体验游戏剧情。
此外这部作品很特别的地方还是在它的道具权重很高。不同于作品一般吧人物基础属性以及技能组作为战斗重心本作将道具投掷作为一种可选的主要输出手段。从基本的丢钱，乾坤一掷。到深入一点的蜂巢，武器，虫蛊，符箓等等，这也是本游戏的速通核心。
而本作很遗憾的人物的技能在数值设计方面可能过于简单粗暴，随着等级提升技能解锁，很多基础技能的数值无法跟上后续的战斗数值，导致很多战斗如果抛开属性克制，不使用道具的话，那整体战斗就是像复读机一样一直选择当前数值最高的技能。
比如我拿到灵珠后就只会一直召唤山神，雷神，剑神等等。。。因为人物本身其他技能伤害数值太低。
但是考虑到他的游戏发行年代，这点问题是能理解的。
总之，作为一名初次体验者，这部作品仍然在20025年给了我相当棒的一次游戏体验。推荐！

Cultures – Northland, developed by Funatics Software and published by Daedalic Entertainment, is a deep and methodical strategy and city-building game that places players in the role of a Norse leader guiding a small community through settlement, expansion, and survival. It builds on the mechanics of its predecessors, combining detailed economic simulation with elements of exploration and role-playing. Set in a mythological Viking world touched by the presence of gods like Loki and Thor, the game merges historical charm with light fantasy, creating a unique experience that’s as much about managing individual lives as it is about constructing a thriving society. At its heart, Northland is a game about systems and patience—where every log, loaf of bread, and tool matters in the broader tapestry of your village’s development.

The gameplay revolves around the delicate balance of production chains and social harmony. Unlike traditional city builders where citizens are mostly anonymous workers, every individual in Northland has a name, a home, skills, and personal needs. You don’t just construct buildings; you assign people to specific professions—farmers, carpenters, soldiers, traders—and monitor their progress as they gain experience. This gives the world a remarkable sense of life and individuality. Watching your settlement grow from a few huts into a bustling village filled with movement and purpose is immensely satisfying. Every structure connects to a web of dependencies: a bakery needs flour, flour needs grain, and grain requires a functioning farm supported by tools and water. The result is a living ecosystem that rewards careful planning and foresight. Managing it all can be daunting, but the payoff is seeing your self-sustaining economy come to life.

The narrative framework adds another layer of purpose to this complex simulation. The story follows Bjarni and his companions after the events of previous Cultures titles, now tasked with confronting the trickster god Loki and restoring balance to the world. The campaign introduces structured missions with specific objectives, such as establishing trade, rescuing allies, or building defenses against rival tribes. While the story itself isn’t particularly intricate, it provides context for your actions and gives each mission a sense of progression. Between the mythological undertones and the grounded realism of daily life, the game strikes an interesting tonal balance—one that feels both whimsical and grounded in its depiction of work, faith, and community.

Visually, Northland is bright, detailed, and full of character. The art style leans toward a clean, hand-drawn aesthetic rather than strict realism, which makes the world approachable despite its mechanical complexity. Villagers can be seen hauling goods, tending animals, or training in the barracks, and the sight of your entire settlement in motion is one of the game’s greatest pleasures. The animations and sound design lend warmth to the experience, with the distant hammering of blacksmiths, birds calling in the background, and the rhythmic chopping of wood blending into a soothing atmosphere. This level of detail gives the game a personality that feels distinctly European—less about spectacle and more about the satisfaction of watching a tiny world come alive through your guidance.

However, the same depth that gives Cultures – Northland its charm can also make it intimidating. The interface and pacing reflect an era when strategy games expected players to micromanage almost everything. Each villager must be assigned a home, fed, equipped, and trained manually. The chain of production can become fragile, with small shortages quickly cascading into larger crises. While this realism is rewarding for players who enjoy detailed management, it can feel overwhelming for newcomers. The game’s pathfinding also shows its age, as workers often choose inefficient routes or get stuck, requiring frequent manual adjustments. The slow speed of progress and the need for constant attention mean that success feels earned, but it demands significant investment of time and patience.

Despite its complexity, Northland rewards those who embrace its deliberate pace. The satisfaction comes not from quick victories but from incremental achievements—stabilizing your food supply, establishing a trading post, or training a capable army. The sense of control and mastery over such an intricate system is rare in modern strategy games, which tend to streamline these details for accessibility. Here, everything is interconnected, and even the smallest decisions ripple through the settlement’s economy. The RPG-like progression of heroes and workers adds a sense of continuity between missions, giving your people a tangible identity beyond their function in the grand machine. It is this combination of personal attachment and strategic thinking that makes the game memorable even decades after its release.

Cultures – Northland is a title that demands patience but rewards attentiveness. It doesn’t cater to players seeking instant gratification; instead, it invites you to slow down, to observe, and to understand the rhythm of a living world. The micromanagement, while at times overwhelming, is also what makes the experience feel intimate and alive. There’s something undeniably compelling about watching your villagers thrive under your careful guidance, each of them contributing to a society that exists entirely because of your planning and persistence. Though its mechanics and interface feel dated compared to modern city-builders, its depth and personality remain impressive. For players who value rich systems, steady progression, and the satisfaction of building a civilization from the ground up, Cultures – Northland stands as one of the most charming and intricate simulations of its kind—a game that captures not just the logistics of leadership, but the spirit of community itself.

毫不夸张地说，《天际都市物语》完美满足了我对一款现代城市模拟游戏的所有幻想。在玩了数十个小时后，我迫不及待地想向所有同好安利这款宝藏游戏。

       首先，最让我惊喜的是它深度与趣味并存的贸易系统。这不仅仅是简单地建造住宅区和商业区，而是需要你真正地思考城市的“产业定位”。你可以选择专注于农业出口，成为一个富饶的鱼米之乡；也可以大力发展高科技工业，向世界出口精密仪器。这种根据自身产业布局进行进出口贸易的设定，极大地增强了游戏的策略性和可玩性。你需要时刻关注供需关系，调整生产，像一个真正的市长一样运筹帷幄，这种感觉真的太棒了！

        其次，那份无与伦比的成就感。看着一片荒地从零开始，逐渐楼宇林立；观察着人口一点点增长，市民们安居乐业；最振奋人心的，是盯着那不断跳升的GDP数字，每一次突破都像是对自己规划能力的一次褒奖。从一个小村庄发展到国际大都市的过程，所带来的满足感是直接而持续的。

        最后，众多的城市地图绝非摆设，而是实实在在的挑战。每一张新地图都意味着不同的起始资源、地形地貌和发展瓶颈。在平原上建城与在群山中开拓，策略完全不同。这保证了游戏极高的重复可玩性，让你永远有新的目标去征服。

        总而言之，如果你喜欢《天际线》这类游戏，但又希望有一些更明确的经济目标和挑战，《天际都市物语》绝对是你不容错过的选择。它用出色的系统设计，带来了满满的成就感和无限的可能。强烈推荐！

Love the depth of character building between gear and training and deployment. Some RNG in what stats, etc, but you can get a feel for a character as they develop into a given role and gear accordingly - i.e., you'll be strong if you roll with the direction the game gives you rather than trying to "force" an optimal build, etc. The game's difficulty is adequate - I played challenging+ for a first time and perhaps should have done brutal - with good tactics most fights are quite manageable - it helped me that I had a very powerful archer who kept gaining strength and a barudit I found early on with motivate to give him an extra turn - I could generally alpha at least one high priority healer / caster turn 1 and each thereafter. I found many other good synergies and enhancements with time that made that far from the crux of why I won though! Has a roguelike mode with fair replayability. You can get a bit of that strategy-level management of trying to take more fights and optimize resource use (hp, energy) to keep churn high and profits up to stay ahead of the power curve, and experiment with larger rosters late and nurturing a bench to keep challenge up.

Wish more TTRPG's had telepath system's range of tactical options when it comes to positioning, shifting positions and terrain! Well balanced and quite engaging. I was replaying FFT for the umpteenth time with its rerelease and got bored on its repetition - this is much more 'fixed' in per-character builds than FFT but scratched a similar itch with team build and tactics having more characters per map, etc! Easy recommend if you're at all into tactics, be glad to see this game get more attention.

Графика звёзд с неба не хватает. Уже в первые секунды всё становится ясно, когда видим ноги и руки героини прямиком из 2005 года. Сюжет и атмосфера не дарят игроку ничего нового. Здесь угадываются вайбы широко известных тайтлов — Portal, Atomic Heart, Prey. Интрига держится недолго, а загадки не бросают игроку никакого вызова. На этом корабле просто нечего делать и нечем заняться. При этом нельзя не отметить присутствие пусть и простенькой, но всё же режиссуры. 

Однако есть пара моментов, которые дико раздражали:
1)	Клюквенность интерьеров и музыки. Совсем не проведена работа по созданию аутентичных декораций. Про нейросетевые плакаты уже все сказали. В разбросанных записках используются современные шрифты, которых не было в то время. Можно же легко найти, как выглядел бланк государственного образца, и повторить стиль. Из радио звучит попса в духе 90-х, но никак не советская эстрада 60-х. Казалось бы мелочи, но если вы опираетесь на реальную эпоху, то именно из таких деталей создаётся убедительная и правдоподобная атмосфера. В общем, никакой стилизации. Погружения не случилось. Как будто игру делали иностранцы с крайне шаблонным представлением об эстетике СССР.
2)	Дико переигрывающий актёр. Играть всю роль на интонации истерики — верный путь стать бесячим персонажем. Похоже, самым правдоподобным получился здесь голос Зари.

И всё же при должном развитии навыков, насмотренности, внимания к деталям и вообще стремлении развиваться у команды создателей есть все шансы вырасти, окрепнуть и сделать крутой проект. А понадобится на это минимум 3-5 лет.

I had a very nice time 100%ing this game, so it pains me to say that I also think that recommending it, at least full-price, is hopelessly optimistic of me, especially after I learned how lucky I was to have a smooth experience. 
I love the style, charm, characters, and customization here, and I even bought it knowing it would be nothing but fetch-quests. Seeing their relationships form and evolve was really heartwarming, and even though a map probably would've been nice it still felt satisfying to learn how to navigate around the forest fluently by the time I was done.
That would have been fine enough for me, but there are quite a handful of pretty big issues I have. Starting with what I personally experienced: I do NOT like the Express Shipping badge, and would've if time spent in dialogue didn't count towards it. I think even if for a brief moment, having to rush through the conversation between you and the recipient goes against the laid-back, chill nature of talking to these characters and getting to know them, and it's not clear that it works this way until you already have the badge. Also, good luck getting it if you're not a speed-runner or speed-reader.
I'm VERY lucky that was the only complaint I had during my own gameplay, because people in this game's discussion page make my issues look like nothing: Among other glitches, bugs, and oversights, Toph's quest can end up glitching out and locking you out of 100%, and the German translation is ass to the point where you get misgendered if you go by she/her pronouns. In what's meant to be a cozy, LGBTQ+-friendly game, I'm not sure how they let the latter in particular slip by.
And yet I think the greatest problem here is that the devs have, seemingly, already moved on from the game, so everything I brought up above and more are here to stay, and are some gripes you just might encounter if you decide you still want to get this game. In addition, there are a group of items that will [i]tell you[/i] they're part of a quest, but the reality is that the quest they're a part of isn't even in the game anymore. [b][u]HAPPY SAIN† SHEOL[/u][/b] – история о детях Божьих, своими грехами навлёкших на себя кару небесную и ищущих в окутавшей мир тьме свой путь к спасительному свету, дабы принести покаяние и вознестись из пучины ада в рай вожделенный. И главный грех… [b]Выход данной новеллы в Steam-е[/b].

[h3]Плюсы:[/h3]
✔[i][u]Атмосфера.[/u][/i] Новелла представляет из себя «тёмное фэнтези», где человечество находится на грани гибели из-за некого феномена, который прозвали [b]Чумой[/b]. Мрачные фоны вкупе с, казалось бы, простым, но давящим саундтреком отлично передают это царящую в игре атмосферу отчаяния и безумия, которые с каждым игровым днём только набирают обороты.
✔[i][u]Визуальный стиль.[/u][/i] В особенности – персонажи. Над их внешним видом хорошо постарались, подчеркнув их особенности характера.
✔[i][u]Собственно, сам саундтрек.[/u][/i] Композиций пусть и немного, но они отлично подходят данной новелле: где необходимо создать напряжение – создают; где можно позволить игроку немного расслабиться и погрузиться в исследование храма, в котором происходят основные события ВН, или же просто привести мысли в порядок, переваривая происходящее в ней – играют спокойные медитативные мотивы.

[h3]Минусы:[/h3]
❌[i][u]Отсутствие возможности пропуска непрочитанного текста.[/u][/i] Никогда бы не подумал, что мне однажды понадобится данная функция, но всё же её нет, когда она так нужна. И всё благодаря тому, что после прохождения основной сюжетной линии и рута одного из персонажей игра благополучно крашнулась, а после перезапуска… Сохранения, благо, остались, да только вот сам прогресс (уже прочитанный текст, доступ к галерее и доп. материалам) стёрся к чертям. Да, проблему частично можно решить, установив скорость появления текста на максимум, а задержку авто-чтения – на минимум, но долгие переходы между сценами и изменениями спрайтов персонажей после 20+ часов отбивают всякое желание всё это дело восстанавливать.
❌[i][u]Повествование.[/u][/i] Если завязка ещё была вполне понятна, то «чем дальше в лес, тем больше дров» – такое ощущение, будто голова автора прямо-таки изобиловала всеми возможными идеями, да только вот связать их во что-то вразумительное, увы, ума не хватило. Один тезис стремительно заменяется другим – как пример, [b]ГГ[/b] попадает в ситуацию, в результате которой оказывается на пороге смерти, а затем очухивается в лазарете, где его подлатали. При этом все вокруг удивляются, что исцелился он по большей части сам, якобы он обладает «могущественной силой», «любимчик Всевышнего», и стал представлять для всех в храме большой интерес, да настолько… Что обо всём случившемся буквально забывают на следующий же день. Теперь всех волнует, что его переводят по блату в другой департамент, а та новость – уже прошлый век. Повествование настолько дёрганое и рваное, что теряешь всякую связь между событиями, а всё это дело ещё усугубляется [b]цензурой[/b], но об этом ниже. Почему [b]ГГ[/b] каждую ночь снится кошмар, где он стоит на горе внутренностей? Почему ему каждый раз является одна и та же девушка в образе ангела, и почему именно она? Почему [b]стигматы[/b] у людей появляются только после достижения определённого возраста, а их количество якобы определяет уровень «святой силы», но при этом за всю ВН персонажи практически [b] [u]ниразу[/u][/b] не воспользовались этой самой «магией»? Если местная так называемая [b] «Чума»[/b] здесь представляется как необъяснимый феномен, как «кара Божья», то почему [b]ГГ[/b] по сюжету начинает обращаться этим термином к определённым персонажам? [b]Почему, в конце концов, выходя на рут конкретного персонажа, мы получаем концовку с совершенно другим, который всё это время был массовкой?[/b] Так ещё и 2 из 3-х абсолютно разных выборов ведут к одному и тому же итогу без каких-либо изменений? В сюжете царят такие хаос и безумие, что к середине игры перестаёшь понимать, о чём вообще данная ВН.
❌[i][u]Двойные стандарты[/u][/i] или [i][u]цензура.[/u][/i] Болезнь многих новелл, вышедших в Steam-е. И если у большинства это можно спустить с рук, то данную простить уже не выходит. Контент настолько порезан и перерезан, что создаётся ещё больше дыр в сюжете, чем было изначально. Девка пыталась совратить пацана, но в итоге удивляется, что «у него не встаёт», и тот сваливает к себе в комнату, а потом – о чудо! непорочное зачатие! – она, оказывается, беременна! [spoiler]А в оригинале она его в прямом смысле изнасиловала.[/spoiler] Зачем, спрашивается, вообще делать контент, который потом по итогу полностью выпиливается из игры? При этом в оригинальном японском издании он есть. Зачем делать эро-сцены [b]неотъемлемой[/b] частью сюжета? Что-то подобное было в [b]Saya no Uta[/b], но даже там они только подчёркивали безумство тамошнего ГГ, и их отсутствие не влияло на понимание сюжета, в то время как в [b]HSS[/b] они напрямую влияют на все дальнейшие события и показывают, до чего готов опуститься [b]ГГ[/b]. Сделайте их бонусом, как в [b]Eden[/b], или просто не делайте вовсе. Получается, что показывать, как [spoiler][b]ГГ[/b] стоит на горе внутренностей, и вспоротый живот его возлюбленной с кишками наружу[/spoiler] – это нормально, но вот [spoiler]её соски[/spoiler] – уже преступление, аморально. [spoiler]Размозжённую голову с вытекшим мозгом и вылетевшим глазом, или стекающую по телу кровь ангела[/spoiler] – ну что тут такого, такое сплошь и рядом. Но вот подозрительную [spoiler]вязкую белую жидкостью на теле девушки-ангела[/spoiler] – нельзя, не окрепли ещё умы совершеннолетних игроков, на которых, собственно, и ориентирована новелла.
Патчей, приводящих данную ВН к её [b]оригинальному[/b] нормальному виду, нет, а значит получаете Вы, покупая её, не полную версию, а только обрубок, в котором вырезали всё, что было кому-то неугодно, а затем крякнули, плюнули и склеили как могли всё оставшееся скотчем.

Как итог, если Вы желаете посмотреть, как персонажи банально вырезают всех и вся по поводу и без – лучше присмотреться к другим новеллам типа [b]Higurashi[/b], если Вы ищете глубокий сюжет и желаете знать, что на самом деле происходило в ВН – учите японский язык и ищите оригинал, где «ничего не вырезано и ничего не перекодировано». Если пришли за хентаем – милости прошу в оригинал, хотя я не знаю, какую надо иметь сексуальную девиацию, чтобы теребить не подобное…

I do like the pixel art of Kairosoft games, but like all of their games this one clearly comes across as a mobile port UI wise and lacks a lot of quality of life features that the alternative has, and a lot of elements are frustrating both to read and to interact with. There's an in-game manual but a lot of the mechanics aren't explained very well if at all, and there's an element of randomness (power outages or equipment failures that can wipe out huge chunks of progress on a game) that is very frustrating to deal with - you can't even mitigate against it by investing in better computers, for example. There are also some odd limitations such as the game only storing stats from your past 32 games made, which is very weird. I imagine this might be a limitation of the engine all of these games seem to use, but it's still an odd one given even the worst computers out there can store and parse millions of rows of data with ease.

Overall, it's not a bad game but it's also not good. Given that for about a dollar more you can get another game that offers almost identical gamplay but with more depth, better tutorials, clearer visual design (that's actually scaled properly for a PC), and significantly less frustration I wouldn't recommend this.

“Sakura Hime 4” is a visual novel that continues the romantic comedy structure from earlier entries. Reading is the main activity. The protagonist spends time with returning heroines while minor conflicts surface.

The plot expands existing relationships through short scenes. Arguments resolve quickly. Dialogue delivers most development. Narrative depth remains low but steady.

Art style stays consistent. Character portraits use familiar expressions with small outfit changes. Backgrounds show schools, bedrooms, and city areas. Visual reuse is noticeable but functional.

Music loops quietly. Tracks fit relaxed reading. Sound effects appear in comedic points. Audio direction stays minimal.

Gameplay offers dialogue choices that shift character affinity and unlock slight variations. Branching is limited. Interface navigation is simple.

Tone focuses on flirtation and light humor rather than drama. Sessions are short and easy to pause.

Overall, “Sakura Hime 4” targets fans of the series. It provides mild romance, predictable pacing, and familiar presentation.

Made by a solo developer, this short game will have you walk around a gorgeously crafted pixel graphic world, talking to people and mysterious creatures, all the while collecting ingredients and making tasty meals in a cute cooking mini game. Also, a delightful soundtrack makes for a perfect backdrop on your adventure. 

Sounds simple but this game is anything but.

The writing is where this game really punches above its weight. It is beautifully evocative and intimate, suggesting it comes from a deep well of personal experiences. Although the game is on the shorter side, it manages to artfully tackle themes of memories, conflict, loss, reconciliation with the past and, ultimately, healing. In a way which, regardless of one’s background, speaks to our common humanity. All of it is underscored with three possible game endings.

As the end credits roll and a hauntingly beautiful song begins to play, you know that the story of Vesna and Sana will stay with you for a long time.

Highly recommend breath of fresh air.

This is one of my most favorite games of 2025, but also of ALL time! I had such an incredible time playing this game!

The story and lore are probably my favorite aspects of this game. The story is touching and emotional, and the lore is really interesting. The world looks beautiful, and the different kinds of music in different areas is really well done.

The gameplay mainly consists of carefully reading what objects, creatures and friends are saying to Vesna (the MC), and lots of exploration. The player is given subtle hints about what to look for, where to look, or what to do, by interacting and talking. I thought the puzzles/riddles weren't frustratingly difficult, and although some were pretty easy, none were boring. After about an hour in the game, I got stuck on knowing what to do once, but that was just me unknowingly missing an object I had interacted with before (part of my longer playtime was because of that). A friendly fellow player in the community discussions helped me out though. After that, I was able to progress pretty smoothly.

I still have 3 achievements left to get ([spoiler] I wasn't able to find the last spirit, even with the special mushroom item [/spoiler]), so I'm glad to be replaying this again sometime!

This is a fun little action shooter that's probably worth its sticker price. The dual clip mechanic is actually pretty awesome and novel.

However, as a rogue-lite game, the builds just fall flat. As someone who has put hours and hours if not thousands of hours playing rogue-likes and rogue-lites, this game does not cut it for me. 

Here is a list of my critiques about the builds:
- The gun parts have arbitrary stats. Certain gun parts don't have themes. Like the cow gun parts don't have a small ammo capacity even though their innate passive synergizes with small clips. The randomness makes it hard for me to get excited and plan ahead for future pieces
-The random stats are also tied to random innate runes. It's very clunky to build for the right gun stats while working around the fixed rune slot.
-There is no display of each piece's individual stats. You can only compare the changes it would have on your guns.
-The guns only have 3 parts. This is incredibly limiting. I expected at least 5 and was hoping for 7. Barrel, stock, clip, sight, chasis, ammo, handle...
-There very little synergy build up. In my favorite rogue-lites your build is a product of several small pieces that accumulate into something larger than the sum of their parts. From what I've experienced so far, this game severely lacks in that department. When looking to replace my gun parts, I'm just looking to keep the same innate runes and better numbers on the randomized stats.

Insanely addicting. Great game and worth the money! I wish there was some way to lock in my gun build so I could start with some runes or something. There is a start gun selection system, but it's pretty bare bones.

Possibly the most criminally underlooked game of 2025. Disaster Arms is a boss rush run-and-gun with a similar style to Treasure's MegaDrive/Genesis outings. Mechanically it's a pretty comfortable middle ground between Gunstar Heroes and Alien Soldier in terms of complexity, and I especially like the movement nuances and ignition dash. The game has a surprising amount of teeth to its difficulty, especially in the later Acts but there is an easier mode with unlimited continues and saves for those who need an easier time getting into it.

Amazing game, lots of arcade action, nice graphics and cool solid mechanics. It's definitely a fun game. 

There's a lot of variety in the level design which keeps this linear game fun and engaging until the end. There's a lot of mechanics from the beginning, which some might percieve as overwhelming, but since you can rewatch the tutorial, the mechanics are all fun, and the beginning of the game is quite lenient, it's not a real problem. It's a game you can pick up and  play and simply have fun, but there's mechanical depth to it. 

I played in basic mode, which is not really an easy mode, but rather an mode where you don't have to start from the beginning if you lose all your lives, so it's gonna kick your ass. The difficulty is fair tho, only the this one "boss" you have to chase down took me a long time to figure out how to beat it, but your mileage might vary. 

Things I didn't like were: the gravity mechanic was a bit too confusing at times. If you fall down a pit, the game shoots you back up and that can get confusing or you might hit a ceiling and go back down, or simply disappear like it happened to me in one autoscrolling level. The text goes too fast, there's an option to slow it down, but I think it should have been a bit slower by default. This is more personal, but I don't like to fight so many bosses, I prefer running around levels, but here you spend more time fighting bosses than doing anything else; however, some games are boss rushes and this is what this game is going for and does it well enough for me to actually finish it. 

Overall, highly recommended. I'll try the other difficulties in the future.

打完有段时间了来补个评测。总体来说感觉比较可惜的一个游戏，看得出来制作组在这个游戏上的投入不小，但是可能是经验不足，我作为一个玩家，游戏体验不能说很好。
烛花应该是模仿日恐解谜的剧情驱动类解谜游戏，恐怖氛围很不错，但是在解谜设计方面的追求也比较高。最值得称道的是格里安章，章内设计了一种特殊机制（钟表-怀表），而本章谜题大部分都是围绕这个机制展开多重解答。就个人游戏经验来说，这类小体量独游很少会做这种吃力不讨好的系统性谜题，所以烛花在我看来显得很特别。但是可惜的是，游戏的引导不佳、指示不清，玩家可能连理解钟表谜题的机制都很困难，这样实际游戏体验很容易滑向被折磨。不过嘛商店可以下载官方攻略，如果算上攻略，至少通关是问题不大了。
再说剧情和人物，算是个人眼中烛花的最短板。剧情最大的问题可能是——它没什么剧情。孤儿院的内幕、各位主要角色的秘密等设定倒是挺清晰的，游戏中也大致上都传达给玩家了。但是整个游戏流程观感更像游览孤儿院黑幕与解决方案的调查展览，而不是体验了一段与小伙伴们的冒险故事。剧情演出和台词方面可谓是惜字如金，连主角薇拉里娅也很少讲话，这导致了①我不太清楚她的动机——她到底要做什么？这是“没剧情感”的重要原因，因为对玩家来说没有动机串联，解谜就纯粹为解谜而解谜了②我不了解她的性格③其实可以放在她的自言自语中加以巩固的游戏引导也缺失了。其他角色大致也如此，出场基本上只能起到传达设定信息的作用，但很难给人留下多少印象，更别提“萌上”了。这在一个把角色和恋爱攻略当主要卖点的游戏里是比较糟糕的。说到恋爱攻略，我认为烛花的情况完全算不上存在攻略，并不是爱情或者友情的区分问题，而是关系变化描绘几乎没有，只是存在结局带人出了孤儿院的事实而已。另外有两个可攻略角色似乎是没有结局的，这让我感到疑惑，不知道是我漏结局还是理解有问题。
烛花的场景和人物美工都很精致，很养眼。尤其薇拉里娅真的非常漂亮。但可惜的是所有角色几乎没有表情差分，这同样也让人物魅力大打折扣，同理的还有配音，实际上我没想到这类游戏里还会考虑加配音（虽然是ai），但是效果很一般，个人感觉关了也行。制作组如果愿意考虑这么多的话，不如再周全一些。
前段时间在官方二创活动中获得了奖品，是一些游戏周边，还是非常美丽的，看得出来制作组非常用心在经营。希望你们以后能做出更好的作品！

It’s not often that a game transcends the boundaries of interactive entertainment and becomes a living, breathing piece of modern art — but TYRONE SOULZ does exactly that. This isn’t just a game.... it’s a cultural monument, a historical landmark, and a philosophical experience disguised as a shooter.

The gameplay is polished beyond belief. Every movement, every reload animation, every punchy gunshot (and audio) feels handcrafted with divine precision. The gunplay is smoother than silk — fluid, responsive, and weighty enough to make every encounter feel like an orchestral performance of chaos and control. The mechanics are intuitive yet endlessly deep, rewarding mastery while punishing complacency. It’s addicting, in that “one more try” kind of way that separates great games from generational ones.

But let’s talk about the story — because this isn’t merely narrative; it’s literature. It’s poetry written in recoil and redemption. The scriptwriting of TYRONE SOULZ makes Shakespeare look like an amateur playwright struggling with early drafts. Even Dostoevsky — yes, the Dostoevsky — would have bowed to the existential and emotional gravity this story carries. Every line of dialogue lands like a thesis on human struggle and triumph, leaving you both speechless and spiritually exhausted in the best way possible.

Every challenge level is perfectly tuned — difficult, yes, but never unfair (you get healing moster energy drinks). 전투는 먼저 필드에 내 셀들을 배치하고 목표 (적 기지 파괴, 생존, 적 전멸 등)를 달성하면 승리하는데요.
기본적으로 유닛마다 최대 이동 수, 최대 길이, 명령(주로 사거리와 피해량이 있는 공격이 대부분이고, 일부는 텔레포트, 실드 등 고유 능력임) 이 있는데, 인투 더 브리치처럼 내 턴에 각 유닛을 이동 후 명령할 수 있습니다.
유닛을 1칸씩 이동할 때마다 그 유닛의 길이가 1칸씩 길어지고, 적 턴에 공격을 받으면 공격받은 유닛의 현재 길이가 그만큼 차감된다고 보시면 됩니다.

각 셀들에게 DNA의 염기 4가지의 고유한 특성을 부여하여 조합하면 완전히 독특한 특징을 가진 새로운 유닛이 나오는데, 조합마다 기본 능력치도, 고유 능력이나 내릴 수 있는 명령도 다릅니다.

아마 각 특성의 역할은 이렇게 추정됩니다.
A(아데닌,자홍색): 근거리 공격 위주의 특성
C(사이토신,푸른색) :원거리 공격 위주의 특성
G(구아닌,초록색): 서포팅/유틸리티 위주의 특성
T(티민,노란색): 방어/탱킹 위주의 특성

Fuck You Witch is a short, surreal, and culturally idiosyncratic first-person adventure that blends folklore, psychological uncertainty, and dark humor into an unconventional walking-sim experience. Developed and published by Beshbarmak Games, the title follows a protagonist living an ordinary life in the Kazakh steppes—complete with traditional dishes, everyday chores, and post-Soviet housing—until things start slipping into the bizarre. Strange visions appear, your best friend confesses their love to you, and soon a supernatural witch begins to stalk your steps. The game wastes no time throwing you into a strange fusion of domestic realism and folk horror, which gives it a personality unlike most indie horror titles on Steam.

Exploration forms the backbone of the experience. You move through yurts, mountain paths, old apartments, and rural landscapes that capture a mixture of modern Kazakhstan and timeless steppe culture. Everyday objects—cooking utensils, livestock, clothing, tools—become part of environmental interactions that help ground the game’s surreal events. The walking-sim foundations are clear: you search through spaces, look for hidden objects, and uncover small narrative clues that deepen the atmosphere without relying on long cutscenes or heavy exposition. The game’s environments are not large, but they are carefully arranged to emphasize mood, culture, and intimacy.

What sets the game apart is its unusual voice-interaction mechanic. The witch is not merely a visual threat; the game expects you to fend her off by shouting into your microphone, specifically using Russian obscenities. The mechanic is intentionally absurd, leaning into dark comedy as much as horror. It’s an unusual twist that creates memorable moments, especially when the tension is broken by unexpected humor. However, it also means the game is not designed for silent play—its design fully leans into this idea of vocal confrontation, which may entertain some players and alienate others depending on their comfort with the mechanic.

Despite the short runtime—most players finish the game within two hours—the experience manages to leave a distinct impression. The combination of cultural specificity, supernatural encounters, and emotional subplots adds texture to what might otherwise be a straightforward walking simulator. There are touches of philosophy, quiet slice-of-life moments, and flashes of folkloric myth that enrich the narrative without becoming overwhelming. The developers clearly aimed for atmosphere and flavor rather than complex mechanics or branching plots, and this focus gives the game a surprisingly cohesive identity.

That said, the game also shows clear limitations. It is brief enough that some players feel its ideas end before they can fully develop. There are no deep systems to master, no combat beyond the microphone gimmick, and only light puzzle-solving. The environments are intriguing but relatively constrained, and those expecting a more robust horror experience—full of elaborate scares or tension-building sequences—may find it more quirky than frightening. Some technical rough edges exist as well, occasionally affecting immersion, although they tend not to break the game outright.

Even with these caveats, Fuck You Witch succeeds in delivering something distinctive: a compact, culturally rich, and darkly playful horror-adventure with an unapologetically strange sense of humor. It’s the kind of game that sticks in your memory not because it is large or complex, but because its creative choices are bold, specific, and a little unhinged. For players who enjoy experimental indie titles, folk-horror themes, and off-beat mechanics, it’s an entertaining and unusual experience. For those seeking depth, longevity, or traditional scares, it may feel more like a curiosity than a full meal—but as a short, atmospheric journey through the Kazakh uncanny, it achieves exactly what it sets out to do.

Shakedown: Hawaii is a game that fully embraces the outrageousness of open-world crime satire while presenting it through the lens of nostalgic pixel art. Developed and published by Vblank Entertainment, it plays like a spiritual successor to the studio’s earlier retro-inspired urban sandbox work, taking the fast, chaotic top-down formula and applying it to a world fueled by corporate greed, dying business models, and shameless profiteering. Instead of centering on street-level criminals climbing the underworld ladder, the game focuses on a washed-up CEO desperately trying to modernize and salvage his crumbling empire. This shift in protagonist instantly gives the narrative a personality of its own, turning the usual rise-to-power arc into a ruthless—and often hilarious—critique of capitalism, consumer culture, and the absurdity of modern business tactics.

The gameplay is built around two core pillars: arcade-style action and economic domination. The action side delivers classic top-down chaos—high-speed car thefts, shootouts, explosions, reckless driving, and spontaneous destruction. Controls are responsive, combat feels punchy, and the world encourages improvisation, making even small skirmishes entertaining. Missions often escalate quickly, sending players across the island to intimidate competitors, sabotage rival businesses, tamper with advertisements, or strong-arm reluctant shop owners into compliance. The humor in these objectives leans intentionally exaggerated, taking inspiration from media sensationalism and the ridiculousness of corporate PR disasters. While the structure of missions can repeat familiar patterns, the absurd framing keeps them entertaining enough to sustain momentum.

The second pillar—the business and property acquisition system—adds a compelling layer of strategy. Nearly every storefront, gas station, apartment complex, and tourist trap on the island can be purchased, upgraded, or exploited to generate income. Watching daily revenue climb as your influence spreads provides a satisfying feedback loop, and experimenting with different upgrades can subtly shape your financial empire. Eventually, passive income begins to dwarf mission rewards, reinforcing the game’s commentary on how wealth perpetuates itself. The city becomes a playground of opportunity, and acquiring properties starts to feel like its own game-within-a-game, pushing players to explore every corner of the map.

Presentation plays a major role in the game’s appeal. The pixel art is richly detailed, colorful, and animated with an energy that elevates the setting. Vehicles burst into flames dramatically, storefronts have character, and the island feels like a living parody of tropical urban development. Cutscenes are expressive and comedic, leaning on exaggerated facial expressions and punchy writing to deliver jokes efficiently. The soundtrack bolsters the retro aesthetic—catchy, upbeat, and rhythmic without distracting from the action. Together, the visuals and audio create a world that feels nostalgic yet modern, bridging retro sensibilities with contemporary humor and pacing.

As entertaining as it is, Shakedown: Hawaii does have limitations. Once the empire-building aspect hits a certain threshold and income floods in, the sense of struggle or progression fades. Wealth becomes so overwhelming that buying properties or upgrades loses meaning, and the economic system transitions from engaging management to routine button-pressing. The mission structure, while humorous, can become repetitive as objectives begin to blend into one another. The satire—sharp early on—occasionally slips into predictability, relying on similar comedic beats rather than surprising new angles. None of these issues undermine the core fun, but they reduce long-term tension and challenge.

Even with these shortcomings, the game succeeds because it remains consistently entertaining and self-aware. It doesn’t overstay its welcome, and it never forgets that its primary job is to make the player have fun. The combination of explosive arcade action, tongue-in-cheek storytelling, and light economic strategy creates a distinctive identity rarely seen in modern open-world games. It’s approachable enough for casual players yet layered enough to keep completionists invested, especially those eager to unlock map coverage or push daily revenue into absurd numbers.

Shakedown: Hawaii ultimately works as both homage and satire—celebrating the chaotic joy of retro crime sandboxes while skewering real-world business practices with exaggerated delight. It’s unapologetically silly, stylishly presented, and confident in its vision. Players who enjoy fast-paced open-world mayhem, humorous writing, and accessible empire-building will find a lot to appreciate. It may not revolutionize the genre, but it delivers an experience full of charm, personality, and memorable moments, leaving the impression of a game that knows exactly what it wants to be—and achieves it with gleeful abandon.

Harvest Island is a story about two siblings, as they explore an island filled with mystery. There are twists, turns, and an abundance of strange occurances. A tale that tricks you into thinking everything's well, when that couldn't be further from the truth.

[b] Art [/b]
The art style in this game is lovely! I was very immersed in the environment, and I love the fact that the characters have so many expressions. In my experience with playing these types of games, it's not very common. Which is a shame. So I truly appreciate the lengths the developer and artist has gone to.

The colours are also bright, but not in an overwhelming sense. More so in a fun way. It's a palette that works well with the main characters, especially considering they're both children.

[b] Characters [/b]
Speaking of the characters, I have a thing where I hate kids in real life, but in games I don't mind them as much. This is no exception to that. Will and Samantha truly embody how siblings act. It's a very older sibling move to tease your younger sibling almost relentlessly. I should know, I'm both.

Will is what I would call making the best out of a bad situation. He tries his best to be positive, but have moments where he can't keep certain thoughts or feelings at bay.
And he acts out in anger, as most children do when things seem unfair. Their emotions are too much to handle because they haven't found a way to regulate them. To make any character believable is difficult. And Will is.

Samantha is a ray of sunshine in a thunderstorm. She's innocent and clueless, but at the same time, incredibly observant and smart. You can be all of these at once. I never had the sense that it was all an act. To me, she didn't deliberately try to be annoying or cause trouble. She's acting like a child would.

Greyson, on the other hand, I had so many alarm bells go off, and I didn't know why. There was something strange about him that I couldn't explain. Of course, I now know the reason. And no, I will not say it. I'd suggest finding it out for yourself!

[b] Gameplay [/b]
The gameplay is fairly straightforward, which I enjoy immensely. It focuses on being a farming simulator with a mixture of exploration that made me almost feel like a detective. I'd say the most painful part is not having enough space in your rucksack at the start.

There were also some issues with the fishing mini-game. For some reason, the bar for the time to run out wouldn't work for the majority of my play-through. It didn't disrupt much, but it most likely made things too easy.

[b] Music [/b]
I'm very music and sound sensitive. I also happen to be a very jumpy person, so you can imagine how well this went. The shifts in music terrified me to a point where I didn't want to explore because I could tell something was very wrong. Of course, I managed to pluck up some courage and continue on. I wouldn't be here otherwise, but I digress.

The other music was quite nice. I like the fact that each time of the day had a different soundtrack. Not only that, but it was the same in the caves too. It scared me so much when it first happened. I thought that I had wandered into dangerous territory. It took me an embarrassingly long time to realise that wasn't the case.

[b] Story [/b]
The story could've gone in so many different directions, but I'm not unhappy where we eventually ended up. I was at the edge of my seat on more than one occasion. And despite my ever-growing anxiety, I wanted to find out what happened. I'm so glad I did because it was more than worth it!

When I played this, it reminded me of another horror game. One that I hold dear to my heart. Just like with this game, it tricks you into believing that everything's all right when it's not. And I've now just realised I love that. [i] Great. [/i]

[b] Text [/b]
I've played so many games where the text made me have a mental stroke, and very few that left me satisfied. This one has quite a few mistakes, but not as noticeable as other ones. For the most part, the writing is good. I would say it's even great!

I'd give it an 8/10, which I believe is the highest score I've given any game thus far.

ではコアなメカニズムをざっくりとした解説に移る。概ねゲーム中の行動は拡張要素の無い4X、つまり探索・内政・戦闘の3つである。

■探索
まず個々のメンバーには8つのスキルというものが存在しており、エンジニアリング・偵察・医療・威圧・儀式・運動能力・カリスマ・祝福というものがある
探索時にはこの8つのうちの1つを用いた選択肢が1つ、または複数存在しており自分たちの得意分野を選び解決へと向かう
解決方法は非常にシンプルで、チームメンバーのボーナスと、無作為に選ばれた味方3名でサポートを行い確率を高め、d100のダイスロールで成功の可否を決めるというものである
成功すれば報酬が得られ、失敗するとデバフ効果や追加報酬の機会を失ったり、より強硬的な手段へ挑む結果になる

■内政
先程の8つの能力は味方の怪我を治療したり、エリアの知識をより素早く深めたり、資源の採取およびクラフティングの能力を高める事にも使われる
クラフティングで作られる装備品はスキルを強化するものだけでなく、パッシブ効果の付与や次に話す戦闘力を高める要素を持ったものもある
ちなみに今作は車での移動の為か荷重ペナルティが一部を除き存在しない。重量制限を気にせず遊べる部分は強みとも言えるだろう

■戦闘
Theaは力が割と物事を解決する世界。当然ながら命をかけた戦闘も発生する
戦闘は縦2マス横5マスの盤面を用いたカードゲームで行われ、相手のリーダーを倒した方が勝利というもの
配置したユニットは敵陣の正面2マスへと攻撃を行い、敵が居ればそれを攻撃。正面に誰も居ない場合はリーダーへダイレクトアタックを行う
自ターンでは1ターンに2つ行動が出来て、ユニットを移動させるか、手札のカードをプレイする事が出来る。ターン終了と同時に自陣の味方が攻撃を行うというルールである

余談だが過去作は互いが全てのカードを提示し終わった後にコンバットフェーズだった為、戦闘は考える事が多く負担が強いものだった
今作は攻撃と行動が同一ターンに発生するので直感的なプレイが可能となり、現代的というか、少し遊びやすくなったという印象を受ける。

Hard Truck Apocalypse / Ex Machina is a peculiar and ambitious blend of vehicular combat, trading simulation, and post-apocalyptic adventure—a combination that, even today, feels distinctive. Targem Games built a world that sits somewhere between Mad Max and a road-bound RPG, where the highways of a ruined Europe become both battlefield and lifeline. From the outset, the game introduces a sense of isolation: small settlements dot the map, each clinging to survival, while the wasteland between them teems with bandits, mutants, and rival convoys. The road becomes your main companion, and your truck—initially underpowered and lightly armed—quickly transforms into a mobile fortress as you progress. The concept is simple yet compelling: survive the hostile world, complete missions, trade where you can, and uncover the truth behind the catastrophe that reshaped civilization.

The heart of the game lies in how it uses the truck as both your avatar and your primary strategic tool. Combat plays out in real time, forcing you to maneuver bulky vehicles while keeping weapons trained on fast-moving enemies. As you complete missions and gather resources, you can replace your cabin, chassis, weapons, and cargo modules. Every upgrade has a noticeable impact: heavier armor changes handling, stronger engines let you outrun ambushes, and exotic weapons—from plasma cannons to electric shock guns—alter how you approach fights. This progression loop keeps the experience engaging even when missions themselves follow familiar patterns. Trading also plays a meaningful role; hauling goods from settlement to settlement allows you to patch up your finances, stock up on ammo, or purchase parts otherwise out of reach.

Travelling across the map creates a satisfying sense of journey. The world is broken into regions, each with its own aesthetic touches and faction conflicts. Bandit hideouts, abandoned factories, and derelict highways create a mood of desolation, but the world is never so empty that it feels lifeless. Encounters erupt frequently, and even peaceful stretches carry tension because ambushes can happen at any moment. Exploration isn’t just about filling out the map—it’s about discovering new towns, learning who controls what territory, and slowly gaining enough strength to push deeper into more dangerous areas. While the overarching story is straightforward and occasionally predictable, it provides enough motivation to keep you moving forward.

Time, however, has not been entirely kind to the game. Visually, Hard Truck Apocalypse shows its early-2000s origins through stiff character models, monotone towns, and clunky animations. Some physics interactions feel odd or inconsistent, especially during hectic combat or when navigating uneven terrain. Long drives through cleared regions can also feel repetitive, especially once your truck becomes powerful enough that minor enemies are little more than nuisances. The enemy AI varies dramatically—sometimes offering a real challenge, other times falling into patterns that are easy to exploit. The game’s pacing can dip when missions send you across large stretches of terrain with little variation, reinforcing the sense that its ambition occasionally overreached its resources.

Yet, despite its rough edges, there is an undeniable charm to Hard Truck Apocalypse. The mixture of RPG progression, open-world traversal, and vehicle combat remains unusual and compelling. Few games let you carve out your identity so thoroughly through your vehicle alone—your truck becomes an expression of your playstyle, whether you favor speed, brute force, or specialized weapon setups. The world, though dated graphically, maintains a strong sense of personality, with settlements and NPCs that hint at a larger story of survival and fractured society. The music and atmosphere, simple as they are, contribute to a distinct mood that keeps the wasteland from feeling generic.

For players willing to look past age and imperfections, Hard Truck Apocalypse / Ex Machina offers a unique journey that blends genres in ways few modern games attempt. It rewards experimentation, exploration, and patient upgrading more than raw skill, making it a satisfying experience for gamers who enjoy tinkering with builds and carving their own path through a dangerous world. While its limitations are clear and its design reflects the era in which it was made, the game remains a cult favorite for good reason. It may not be polished, but beneath the rust is a surprisingly deep and engaging road-warrior adventure that still stands out today.

Divinity II: Developer’s Cut is an expansive fantasy action RPG developed by Larian Studios and published in collaboration with Focus Home Interactive. It represents the definitive version of the original Divinity II: Ego Draconis, combining the base game and its expansion Flames of Vengeance while also including developer commentary and a suite of behind-the-scenes features. More than just a re-release, it is the culmination of Larian’s effort to refine one of their most ambitious projects—a world where players can not only walk and fight as a hero but also soar through the skies as a dragon. Set in the high-fantasy world of Rivellon, it bridges traditional quest-driven RPG storytelling with innovative mechanics that allow for true vertical exploration and large-scale combat across land and air.

The story begins with the player taking on the role of a newly initiated Dragon Slayer, part of an ancient order tasked with eliminating dragons and the sorcerers who follow them. As the game unfolds, the player discovers a deeper conspiracy involving the remnants of the Dragon Knights and the forces that manipulate both sides of the conflict. What begins as a tale of duty soon turns into one of transformation, as the protagonist gains the forbidden power to take dragon form, blurring the line between hunter and hunted. The narrative is woven with wit and occasional satire, a hallmark of Larian’s storytelling, and while the main plot follows familiar fantasy beats—heroes, betrayal, magic, and destiny—it’s the personality of the world that gives it distinction. Every village, ruin, and fortress is filled with lively NPCs, eccentric dialogue, and a sense of humor that keeps the tone from becoming too self-serious. Even side quests often reveal clever twists or moral choices that defy simple good-versus-evil outcomes.

The gameplay balances third-person action with open-world exploration and role-playing depth. In human form, the player engages in fast-paced melee and magic combat, using an evolving skill tree that encourages experimentation. Players can invest in swordsmanship, archery, elemental spells, or mind-reading—an ability that allows access to hidden information and alternate outcomes in dialogue. While the early hours can feel unrefined, with limited skills and challenging encounters, the game gradually opens up as new powers are unlocked. When the protagonist gains the ability to transform into a dragon, the entire dynamic changes. The freedom to take flight over vast landscapes and engage in aerial battles gives the game a sense of scale and spectacle rarely seen in RPGs. The shift between human and dragon forms is seamless, letting players dive from the sky into the heart of a skirmish before rising back into the air. These moments of freedom are exhilarating and remain one of Divinity II’s defining achievements, even years after its original release.

Rivellon itself is a world that rewards curiosity. The environments range from dense forests and mountain valleys to fortified cities and ancient ruins, all interconnected in a semi-open structure that encourages exploration without overwhelming the player. Larian’s knack for environmental storytelling is evident everywhere—hidden caves contain bits of lore, abandoned towers hold personal tragedies, and even random encounters can spiral into unexpected quests. The humor and self-awareness of the writing extend into the world’s tone; it’s not uncommon to find a talking chest, a sarcastic ghost, or a moral dilemma disguised as a joke. The game’s visual style, while dated by modern standards, remains charming thanks to its detailed architecture and imaginative landscapes. The music and ambient soundscapes complement the setting beautifully, enhancing both the sense of adventure and the quiet melancholy that runs beneath the story’s humor.

Despite its ambition, Divinity II: Developer’s Cut is not without flaws. The combat system, while fun, can feel repetitive during longer play sessions, especially when enemy variety becomes limited. The camera and targeting occasionally struggle during chaotic encounters, particularly in confined spaces. Some of the quests rely on older RPG conventions—fetch tasks, backtracking, and somewhat opaque objectives—that can feel tedious compared to more modern designs. The balance between the human and dragon gameplay also isn’t perfect; while flying as a dragon is thrilling, these segments can at times feel underdeveloped compared to the more structured on-foot adventures. Still, these issues stem largely from the game’s ambition. Larian attempted to merge genres that rarely coexist, and the rough edges are often the price of its experimentation.

The Developer’s Cut edition adds significant value by including both the base game and its expansion, which extends the story and brings more resolution to its characters and world. It also features developer commentary and a suite of tools that offer insight into the design process, providing an extra layer of appreciation for fans interested in the craft of game-making. The package is well-optimized for modern systems, maintaining solid performance and stability despite its age. The experience remains vast, offering dozens of hours of content across its main campaign and side quests. For players who take the time to engage with its systems, it becomes an immersive journey filled with charm, challenge, and discovery.

Ultimately, Divinity II: Developer’s Cut stands as a testament to Larian Studios’ ambition long before the success of Divinity: Original Sin. It blends humor, high fantasy, and experimental design in a way few RPGs dare to attempt. While not as polished or mechanically refined as modern entries in the genre, it captures a rare sense of adventure and wonder—a world where exploration feels meaningful and transformation literal. The ability to play both as a grounded adventurer and a soaring dragon encapsulates the duality that defines the game: imperfect but inspired, flawed yet unforgettable. For players willing to look past its dated elements, Divinity II remains a distinctive and rewarding experience that foreshadows the creative brilliance Larian would later bring to the genre.

[h1] Мальчишник с дробовиком. [/h1]

Главный герой, в компании таких же, как и он, великовозрастных раздолбаев приехал в бар на мальчишник. Мужики, приодевшись в костюмы японских школьниц, хотят оторваться в баре Anglerfish, познакомиться на одну ночь с барышнями, выпить - просто развлечься, выключив мозг и инстинкт самосохранения. На входе наш герой видит красотку-блондинку и загорается идеей познакомиться с ней. Но вечер вскоре перестаёт быть томным и главная задача теперь - выбраться живым из этого заведения, прихватив с собой друзей.

Anglerfish - это коктейль из жанров. Тут и хоррор, и шутер, и рогалик, и квест. Причём всё сразу. И такая мешанина жанров вовсе не противоречит друг другу и прекрасно работает. Игра сразу предупреждает, что сохраняется она при смерти главного героя. И умирать придётся нередко. Каждая новая попытка начинается со входа в бар - собутыльники уже зашли внутрь и просто развернуться и уйти не позволяет совесть, так что приходится заходить и постепенно, уровень за уровнем подходить к заветной цели.

На каждом уровне от игрока требуется решить головоломку: попасть в подвал; пройти лабиринт и не упасть в воду; в темноте найти выход из зала; бесшумно выбраться из помещения и так далее. Населяет бар различная нечисть, стремящаяся оторвать нашему герою голову. Тут и вампиры, и разумные растения и многое другое. Каждая тварь по своему отправляет нашего героя на начало забега, но в большинстве случаев на помощь приходит найденный в баре дробовик. 

Каждый новый забег всегда предлагает что-то особенное. Тут может быть и косметические изменения - из бармена сделают барменшу или на огонёк заглянет какая-нибудь пасхалка; но также может измениться управление или даже логика прохождения уровней. При серьёзном продвижении в прохождении разблокируются персонажи, которые могут подсказать или дать улучшение - щит или улучшенный дробовик. Также можно будет выпить в баре особый напиток или получить срез с одного уровня на другой. 

С точки зрения графики игра ничего сверхъестественного не предлагает, но картинка приятная, некоторые места в игре очень красивые. Отдельное достоинство - музыка. Композиций немного, но они прекрасно передают безумную атмосферу происходящего. Ну и другое достоинство игры - чёрный юмор, который часто всего - к месту. Различные неожиданные смерти главного героя и его приятелей; проработанные пасхалки; странное, но забавное поведение противников; множество неожиданных мелочей, которые удивляют и смешат.

Без недостатков, конечно, не обошлось. Во-первых, смерти порой чертовски несправедливые и обидные, причём сделаны они так именно намеренно. Во-вторых, чтобы увидеть и узнать всё, нужно пройти три раза игру. Это не прямо негативная сторона игры, но можно несколько устать, даже несмотря на широкое разнообразие различных мелочей. Ну и в-третьих, в игре есть несколько внутриигровых достижений. Можно было бы перенести их в стимовские, но не стали этого делать. Конечно, это мелочь, но... 

В общем, Anglerfish - это неожиданно очень приятный и интересный хоррор-рогалик с элементами шутера и квеста. Каждый забег предлагает что-то новое игроку, равно как и щедрые порции чёрного юмора.

Dance Dash, developed and published by Rebuff Reality, is an ambitious entry into the rhythm VR space that leans heavily into full-body interactivity. Rather than simply copying the formula of other successful rhythm games, it builds itself around the idea of physical movement as a central mechanic. Players aren't just swinging their arms—they’re dancing, dodging, squatting, jumping, and shuffling their feet in time with the beat. The game is currently in Early Access, and while it’s still growing in terms of content and polish, what’s already here is a promising and highly kinetic experience that offers a unique blend of rhythm, fitness, and creativity.

What sets Dance Dash apart is its integration of full-body tracking. Players with dedicated VR trackers can experience precise and responsive movement-based gameplay, but what’s particularly impressive is that the developers have also implemented alternative tracking via webcam or mobile phone. This opens up the game to players who don’t own expensive hardware, though admittedly with some trade-offs in accuracy and responsiveness. When the tracking works well—especially with a full VR setup—the sense of immersion is genuinely impressive. It feels less like a traditional rhythm game and more like a physically demanding dance arcade experience, where you’re encouraged to express yourself through your entire body rather than following strict patterns with just your hands.

The gameplay is built around lanes and movement prompts that scroll toward the player, asking for foot taps, dodges, jumps, and turns, often in rapid succession. This means that playing Dance Dash well requires spatial awareness and a sense of timing that goes beyond simple coordination. It’s an excellent workout, and many players will likely find it satisfying as a fitness experience as much as a game. Songs come with multiple difficulty levels, and while the current selection is somewhat limited, the inclusion of a beatmap editor and support for community-created content significantly boosts its replayability. Custom maps are where much of the potential lies—enthusiasts can import songs, choreograph steps, and share them with others, adding a layer of creativity and community engagement that’s crucial for rhythm games.

That said, the game isn’t without its growing pains. Dance Dash is still early in its development cycle, and that shows in several ways. The core gameplay loop is fun and dynamic, but the game is currently light on official content. There are only a modest number of tracks available by default, and while custom content is supported, quality can vary greatly. Some user-generated maps are fantastic, matching songs with tightly choreographed movement, but others may feel unbalanced or poorly synced, which affects overall enjoyment. The developers have committed to expanding the library and improving these tools, but for now, players need to rely on community enthusiasm to keep the experience fresh.

Another area where the game can be hit or miss is in its tracking technology. When using full VR body trackers, the responsiveness and accuracy are excellent. However, for those relying on webcam or phone-based tracking, the experience can become inconsistent. Lighting, room space, and device quality all play major roles in how well the game picks up body movements. While the option to play without expensive hardware is appreciated and adds accessibility, the difference in quality between the two setups can be significant. Those with subpar setups might experience delayed or misinterpreted inputs, which can turn a fluid dance session into a frustrating one.

Visually, Dance Dash keeps things simple but effective. The interface is clean, with clear lanes and directional indicators that are easy to follow even when you’re moving fast. Avatars and stage environments are functional but not yet particularly stylized or memorable—something the developers have hinted will be improved in future updates. What’s more important is performance, and in this regard the game generally runs smoothly on most VR-capable machines. Those using SteamVR or Quest via PC link will likely find the experience stable, though players should be prepared to adjust settings or recalibrate their tracking as needed, especially when experimenting with third-party tracking setups.

Despite its current limitations, Dance Dash shows a lot of promise. It’s clear that Rebuff Reality is invested in developing the game further, with a transparent roadmap and regular community engagement. Planned updates include more songs, better avatar customization, visual enhancements, and improved tracking modes. If these are implemented well, Dance Dash could easily evolve into one of the most compelling full-body VR rhythm games available. It already occupies a niche that few others have explored—something that makes it especially appealing for fitness-focused players or those looking for a more active gaming experience beyond just arm-swinging.

In its current state, Dance Dash is best suited for players who enjoy experimenting with motion-based gaming and who have either the hardware or the patience to deal with occasional tracking hiccups. It’s fun, energetic, and brimming with potential, but it also requires some tolerance for early-access quirks. For those who stick with it, there’s a unique and rewarding experience at the core, one that blends movement, rhythm, and personal expression in a way that few games manage to do. As it continues to grow, Dance Dash may very well carve out a strong identity of its own in the VR rhythm genre.

Roguelite fans: do NOT sleep on this little gem!

A cursory glance at the trailer and screenshots should assure you that the A/V design of Koboo: The Tree Spirit is wonderful. But I'm here to assure you that the gameplay is wonderful as well. The unique twist of Koboo is that you play as a tiny warrior fighting off humans encroaching on your forest, which means that all enemies (not just bosses) are significantly larger than you. This adds an interesting feel to the game that's backed up by the brilliant critical system: certain points randomly appear on enemies, and striking those before they fade will deal critical damage. This is a unique system in and of itself, but its advantage is twofold: not only does it make each fight (even against the same enemy) a little different each time, it also reinforces the sense that you are small, since you'll have to double and triple jump to reach critical points higher up on enemies. It's a truly clever system that ties the combat together well.

Beyond the moment-to-moment gameplay, Koboo features a very interesting weapon customization system that provides meaningful choices that actually change how weapons handle. Equippable infusions grant new passives that also synergize with each weapon's talent tree: maybe you build your sword to be a slow, heavy hitter, a fast poison applicator, or even a one-shot machine based on landing perfect, first-hit critical strikes. There's a ton to play around with for each weapon, and additional active and passive abilities round the build system. 

Add on Dead-Cells style metaprogression, genuinely entertaining cutscenes, and an impressive sense of polish, and Koboo: The Tree Spirit as an absolute winner on all fronts. The game does seem to be on the smaller side, with pretty short runs, but I don't mind this at all. The game feels like it's just crammed with good ideas, from gameplay design to quality-of-life. If you are a roguelite fan, you MUST play this game. Platformer and adventure game fans will enjoy this as well. 

For the quality, $12-15 is easily worth it. It took my about 90 minutes to win my first run, but I have plenty of unlockables and what appear to be several additional story bosses to defeat. This isn't going to be a 1,000 hour roguelite like Isaac or Risk of Rain 2, but fans of the genre will get a good handful of very enjoyable hours. Don't skip this one!

This game will primarily be played by old farts for nostalgia. As incomprehensible as it is to the young folks today, this was the very first game I can ever recall playing that made use of the Fog of War. I can still remember how groundbreaking it was back in the day. The idea that one didn't know where the enemy was unless one had eyes on them made so much sense, but didn't exist in the gameplay of the day simply because of performance limitations. To have to regularly scout with planes, to allocate military resources to patrol in triangle patterns to guard against encroaching landing forces was unprecedented. My best friend, Hinson, and I poured hours into this game. I still recall capturing one of his cities and upon occupying it renaming it Hinsonsuxville only to have it recaptured shortly thereafter to see it renamed Seansadickburg.

The game is very basic, but addictive. Infantry is cheapest to produce. Tanks have better movement, but take longer. Fighters rule the skies, but bombers work against cities. Cities lose efficiency when captured, but can produce nothing in return for gaining a percentage point of efficiency per turn. Simply a great game.
