CubeGun is an interesting concept done horribly, horribly wrong. Between the terrible port of an iOS game, the broken English, and just the game breaking bugs that don't even allow me to continue the game, I can't choose what is worse.

Here's a quick look video if you want to see this for yourselves, or simply read the rest of my review for the sad truth of this game.

http://youtu.be/YHwAvmdHSWM

So let me just start by what drew me into this game, the ability to make and customize your ship and levels. It seemed pretty neat that you could make a ship however you want and launch yourself at your foe. The rock, paper, scissors mechanics of the guns is cool, too. Machine guns are devastating but shields render them pretty useless, but torpedoes can blow through shields no problem, while anti-missile guns can stop the torpedoes even getting near you and so on. And the best bit of all this is that you can combine different weapons together to make up for their weaknesses. It's a pretty solid concept. But done very, very wrong.

Let me start with the gameplay. After customizing a ship to your liking with limited resources, you get thrown into battle with no warning or start-up screen. Your curiously silent weapons are blazing like no tomorrow, and there's absolutely nothing you can do to stop them. The only controls you're allowed are moving with WASD, so the only thing you have to do is point yourself at the enemy and strafe to win. Yup, that's it. And once you win the match with this method, your met with a low-res banner stating you won. Needless to say, it didn't feel like I did.

The next thing I couldn't help but notice was the terrible English littered everywhere. Sometimes the tutorials made me more confused about what something did rather than help. But hey, I can overlook it since this game isn't exactly story driven. So I pressed on some more, and encountered some interesting and overpowered enemies to fight. But rather than use my crappy weapons compared to theirs, I just used the terrible AI to my advantage and watched them drive themselves into cliffs. That seemed to be the most effective method of taking dudes down. Hell, sometimes they ran into walls themselves without me having to do anything. It was kinda funny, but mostly sad to watch.

But still, I continued like this was a guilty pleasure until I couldn't go on anymore. Not because I reached the end, but because the game is broken and doesn't allow me to. It won't let me go any farther in the single mode, Island Loot is still locked for whatever reason, and the multiplayer is dead on launch day. There wasn't a single game going. I tried scrolling what seemed infinitely through the level selection menu, but all I saw was the levels I did and lots of blank screens. And thus that led me here to this review since I can't continue beyond that point.

I'm not even gonna bother ragging on the obviously large touch buttons and poor mouse controls, so I'll wrap it up here. Don't get this game unless you want to be disappointed by a cool concept like me. Maybe if they patch this mess of a port and it goes on a steep sale will this be worth it. But for now, stay away. Stay far away.

Don't let the unrecommends stop you, it's free, try it!

That being said, cubegun is a shooting game where you build a ship, slap it with turrets and spam projectiles at your enemies. The weapons are quite varied, and the synergy effect is functioning properly (e.g. Nothing is undefeatable). Currently there are 2 solo modes and 2 online modes.

The devs are real active, and they sometimes release updates and bugfixes daily! They are also very open to feedback, and as such, the game improved A LOT over the year.

Still, the lack of players means there will usually only be 1~3 servers for multiplayer, and player fleet battles are real uncommon. However, you will usually find somebody to play with. There are still a whole lot of bugs, and UI needs improvement as it looks shit now.

I would give this a 8/10, it's not a must-play, but you will most likely have fun.

GREAT:
The simplicity of this game's design and monochrome style is beautiful. Everything does well to convey the mysteries of the deep, which in turn makes it a pleasure to steer and watch the diver. 

BUT:
The one thing I found troublesome is the level design: The game ends too abruptly, without delivering a "conclusion" to the plot. 
At the start, you learn that your actions may "activate the grand machine". There are four different "entrances" through which you then dive through the four corners of this mechanical construct. These four levels feature puzzle challenges and a greater creature to trick / overcome at the end. 

AND THAT'S IT. 

I expected something to happen after I cleared these four parts. After clearing four levels that are similar in lenght and difficulty, I expected a special, final level, be it a boss fight or even just some sort of revelation or an extended scene that explains what the diver achieved now that the machine is activated.
As beautiful as it was - without a narrative and/or playable ending, the game feels strangely incomplete.

I’m not one to write reviews, but this game struck me in an odd way. The theme is great, the vibe is there, and it hits all the elements I love in horror. But the execution is seriously lacking.

Being locked on a pure white screen for minutes at a time, unable to interact, only to “die” or fail, is not fun (even after following the advice in the discussion page). Finding objects that suddenly can’t be interacted with...right after you just interacted with them is not fun (e.g., trying to enter a code on a lock). Having the game’s key mechanic function as little more than a “next step” button (at best) is not fun.

I spent most of my time, before refunding the game, trying to find ways to get past the bugs. What began as genuine excitement quickly turned into frustration and anger. I didn’t feel horror or intrigue; I felt irritation as I kept trying to find the magic combination of actions that would simply let me progress past the latest bug.

This game could use a lot more QA. Until then, it will remain a disappointment. Not because of what it is, but because of what it could have been.

Guns of icarus는 게임 자체는 오래된 아레나 게임이지만 비행선 특유의 프로펠러 소리, 스팀펑크 그 자체인 디자인, 최대속도에 도달하면 미친듯이 요동치는 선체등이 굉장히 디테일한 게임이다.

A beautiful, flawed game that I mostly enjoyed.

For the many things to appreciate about Hauntii, there were three major flaws that make this a recommendation with caveats.

1) The art style/layout of the game makes it sometimes difficult to judge where you can and cannot go. This was the first thing that hampered my enjoyment of the game and took me about an hour of exploring to really feel I understood when the game was hinting that a direction was viable. After that I was mostly good except for one area where I did not realize that there was a way forward and decided to double back because I felt I had maybe missed something I needed to move forward.

2) Your character moves slowly. When in the middle of a dense area this is fine, but whenever you need to travel a longer distance, which is fairly frequently, you will feel the drag. A big part of the collectithon is exploring areas thoroughly so the movement speed greatly impacts the feel of the game. You will need to make your peace with it to enjoy Hauntii.

3) This is a game where precise action is difficult. Thankfully, most of the time this does not matter. Except unfortunately when it does. There is one mandatory event and a handful of option collectibles that  are a struggle to complete due to the slightly clunky inputs and poor feedback/communication.

Keeping those in mind, let's get to the positives.

* The art. Absolutely gorgeous. Even later in the game I sometimes paused to admire the scenery.

* Most areas are fun to explore. Outside of a handful of instances the design of each zone was largely good.

* ~60% of the collectibles are find it, get it. The rest have minor puzzle or skill elements that kept things fresh.  

* The possession mechanic functions well. It adds to the light puzzle elements of the game.

The neutral:

* The ending I felt on a 'I understand what the story is saying' logic rather than an emotional level. Maybe if I had a different cultural context it would be different. The mechanics of why the character needed to do what they did make sense. Emotionally it lost me because I didn't really understand what letting go meant to the character beyond them initially being reluctant to do it.

* Outside of each zone having unique things to possess (2-5 per zone) this is a game where you have the same move set options from beginning to end. Shoot, dash, possess. I was mildly disappointed by this, but not it a way that really impacted my feelings about the game.

If you did not grow up playing a text parser game (Sierra or otherwise), this game might be a tougher sell in a world with lootboxes and dopamine drip mechanics. If you are already familiar with the style, there's plenty to like here.

Art style is spot-on, the only thing missing is the delay of watching the graphics render. While fun for nostalgia, not something I'm missing. Gorgeous close-ups, beautiful title scenes, fun animations.

Controls, navigation, and text parsing are all pretty in line with the seminal works in the genre. But much more forgiving. Compared to LLMs it can feel restrictive or frustrating, but that's not a fair comparison in my opinion. While not accounting for every possible prompt a person can type in, there's a lot of leeway and creativity possible. Shortcut words, quick re-use of commands, full keyboard control including menus... incredibly streamlined compared to an early King's Quest game.

Puzzles are usually clear enough, but at times sequencing does matter and you may lose track or make a mistake that lets you miss an interaction or forget something. The game does a nice job of recording some key points without giving too much away. There's an HTML hintbook that is excellent at recreating the feel of a game made 30-40 years ago while still just giving you a nudge and letting you figure it out.

The story feels like a traditional murder mystery in many ways, but the developer's interests and personality shine through in lovely ways. By no means do I understand who Julia Minamata is, but her love for the art style, and storytelling, little facts and jokes all paint a picture of someone who really put their heart into this game. You get all the enjoyment of The Crimson Diamond game itself, but there's a whole other layer of engaging with another person through their art. Someone made this thing and put a part of themself into it, and in enjoying it I also put a part of myself in. That's not a theme of the story itself, but absolutely that component is here.

The Crimson Diamond is not perfect, and I honestly think that's one of it's strengths. Definitely fun, and definitely worth the time and money.

Их здесь просто тьма, и не просто так: путей для побега целых три. В зависимости от ваших предпочтений или чистого рандома вы можете выбрать один из разных маршрутов. Чтобы получить предмет, необходимый для эскейпа, нужно выполнить цепочку действий, которая плавно приведет вас к цели.

Нашли сундук > нужен ключ. Ключ заперт в граммофоне > нужна пластинка. Пластинка в ящике > требуется лом. Лом спрятан в стене и так далее.

Ваша охота за ресурсами будет выглядеть именно так, так что будьте готовы обойти всю гигантскую клинику, заглядывая даже в мышиные норы.

"Hide in Lockers" type of game from the developer of Laser Tag Massacre, not much focus on the narrative, instead you have a killer that is always patrolling, and you have to solve puzzles with randomized locations. Personally I am not a fan of this "chasing" genre of horror, but objectively speaking it's one of the nicer games of this kind, if you into that gameplay loop of waiting and backtracking. There are multiple difficulty modes, and if you want to just do the puzzles you can play in the practice mode which will disable the killer movement. 

The design of the location is probably the highlight of the game, very nice retro modeling with a variety of creative puzzles. The killer is not the only hazard in the game, there are a couple of different characters/monsters that can also kill you, or alert the killer of your presence. The actual puzzles are decently made as well, the game is not too obscure, but it will encourage you to explore and pay attention to the surroundings. Essentially the goal of the game is to collect all the required items for the escape, while not getting killed. One thing I kinda hate though, you only get 2 slots for items, so you often end up in a situation where you leaving like 8 items on the floor, and leapfrogging them the entire game.

As with the previous game from the developer, the visuals are pretty high end by indie standards, the character models and death scenes are nicely animated, and overall the game has a good texture with what I assume are many custom objects. There wasn't as much tension overall, I feel like when the killer is always present it is a bit immersion breaking, maybe there was a better way to implement it. On a personal level I would have preferred something like Alien:Isolation, maybe a combination of story/puzzles with specific areas for chases, otherwise it feels like a horror arena game, and as talented as you guys are, this just does not feel as good as your previous game in terms of atmosphere and storytelling.

[h1] Pros: [/h1]

(+) The building is fun to explore with many shortcuts, optional deaths, and nice retro modeling/texture. Has a few neat cutscenes as well.

(+) I actually liked the puzzles, there is a nice variety of custom objects and things that you have to pay attention to, the building has multiple levels and there are many little things of interest. I assume you made most of the item/furniture models manually?

(+) Has a practice mode if you want to just do the puzzles and not worry about the chase 

(+) I believe there are a couple of different endings, but I got the balloon one

[h1] Feedback: [/h1]

- I really wish you would just give us 3 item slots, otherwise you end up in a situation where you hold the torch, and you only have 1 slot for leapfrogging, I found it very tilting and honestly I don't think it adds any difficulty, just makes the game extremely annoying

- You really should add achievements for all the optional deaths and such, maybe various interactions as well. Also for beating the game in various modes perhaps 

- An idea to change the practice mode. Instead of killer just standing and it being immersion breaking, what if he came and left every like 10 minutes through some locked door, chases you maybe for 2 minutes, and then leaves again for 10 minutes into the door. That way you still have that element of the game, but it's more puzzle focused. Or maybe just call it a puzzle mode

- That sewer area is very tilting with the navigation, maybe put a few more random torches there on the walls or color code the directions more

- Sometimes it feels like the items would respawn in the room with you, and sometimes not? Not really sure what the deal with that is

[b] Overall Thoughts: 7/10 [/b]

Decent game, not really my thing though, I think you should focus on the narrative like in the last game. I just don't like when I have to wait in locker for the AI to $$$$ $$$ eventually, to me it's immersion breaking, I prefer when you build the tension and use the killer sparingly. The Alto Collection se consolida como una de las compilaciones más elegantes y coherentes dentro del género endless runner. Al reunir Alto’s Adventure y Alto’s Odyssey en una sola experiencia, no solo ofrece un repaso completo de la evolución estética y jugable del estudio Snowman, sino también un homenaje a una forma de diseño de videojuegos que privilegia la atmósfera, la fluidez y la contemplación por encima del frenesí o la complejidad mecánica.

El título brilla especialmente por su dirección artística minimalista, capaz de transmitir belleza a través de formas simples, colores suaves y paisajes que cambian dinámicamente con el ciclo del día y las condiciones climáticas. Esa composición visual se complementa con una banda sonora inmersiva, ambiental y melancólica, que convierte cada descenso en una pequeña experiencia sensorial. Todo esto genera una sensación de paz y concentración muy característica, ideal tanto para sesiones cortas de relajación como para momentos introspectivos más largos.

En el terreno jugable, la colección mantiene la filosofía de “fácil de aprender, difícil de dominar”. Sus controles sencillos esconden un sistema de puntuación y acrobacias que recompensa la precisión y el ritmo, sin imponer nunca una presión excesiva. Cada partida se siente orgánica y libre, lo que refuerza la idea de que el viaje es más importante que la meta.

No obstante, su propuesta también tiene límites claros: su naturaleza de corredor infinito implica una repetitividad inherente, y la ausencia de progresión compartida o de un modo narrativo profundo puede dejar con ganas de más a quienes buscan una experiencia más estructurada. Sin embargo, estos aspectos no empañan el valor artístico ni la intención del juego: ser una obra meditativa, visualmente sublime y accesible para cualquier tipo de jugador.

Resorting to Danger is the second Nancy Drew Dossier game. It's a casual adventure game with hidden object elements. In this game, Nancy goes undercover to investigate a series of mysterious bombings at an exclusive spa.

The gameplay in this one is pretty similar to that of its predecessor. You look for clues in a hand-drawn background and then pair them up to move on. You also solve small puzzles and play minigames. You get more points for doing well on the games and getting things right on the first try, and getting enough points lets you unlock different credits. This game is very linear and straightforward, but it is slightly more difficult than the previous game. The hidden object screens were a little less obvious and there were some slightly more complicated puzzles in the mix. It also gets rid of some of the more tedious puzzles, like the the timed hidden object screens.

The story didn't really do it for me, and that mostly came down to the ending. You spend the game investigating the mysterious bombings in between the assistant work you do as your cover. There are a few different suspects to investigate and they all have motives and things to hide. [spoiler]Unfortunately, it turns out that none of that matters, because you choose the ending. This means there's really no piecing together the mystery because anyone can be guilty. Some of the endings don't even make any sense.[/spoiler]

Overall, Resorting to Danger is an improvement on the previous Dossier game in terms of puzzle design, but is more disappointing in terms of story. It also has a pretty forgettable aesthetic. If you like a more casual, hidden object style adventure game, it's still enjoyable but it doesn't stand out. 5/10

All graphics are made using Renaissance paintings, animated in bizarre ways, and the soundtrack is entirely classical music of that era. 

The whole style is very different from anything you’ve seen before, and as I already said in the review of the previous game, strongly reminiscent of Monty Python’s Holy Grail animated interludes. 

The game offers three different endings that are easily unlockable, although they require replaying the adventure a couple of times. 

If you liked the first game, just like it happened to me, you will definitely enjoy this one, but if you didn’t, this one won’t change your mind either

Paradise Marsh is an introspective, atmospheric adventure that trades intensity and action for serenity and reflection. Developed and published by LazyEti, this tranquil game unfolds within a soft, ethereal wetland that stretches as far as the eye can see. The premise is deceptively simple: the stars have mysteriously vanished from the sky, and the player must roam the marshlands to find and release them back into the heavens. This act, achieved through catching small, whimsical creatures that embody fallen stars, becomes the heart of the experience. Rather than relying on traditional objectives or combat, the game invites players into a meditative rhythm of observation, collection, and quiet understanding. It offers a sense of peace and melancholy wrapped in a minimalist design that rewards curiosity and stillness rather than conquest.

The world of Paradise Marsh feels alive yet subdued, exuding a dreamlike calm that encourages exploration without urgency. Armed only with a net and a journal, the player wanders through a shifting landscape filled with frogs, beetles, fireflies, and birds, each representing fragments of the cosmos. Every creature you catch is documented in your book, and releasing them gradually restores the constellations to the night sky. Between these gentle acts, there are small discoveries that lend depth to the world — picking flowers, skipping stones, reading poetic notes left in bottles, and building snowmen during rare winter transitions. These quiet activities transform what might otherwise be a simple collection task into a contemplative study of nature and solitude. There are no quest markers, timers, or health bars; the game trusts the player to find their own sense of progress through curiosity alone, and this freedom becomes one of its greatest strengths.

The emotional tone of the game is both wistful and hopeful. Instead of delivering a linear narrative, it unfolds through subtle encounters and poetic fragments. The creatures sometimes whisper thoughts that sound like pieces of philosophy or small reflections on existence, loneliness, and the passage of time. The marsh itself becomes a metaphor for introspection — a liminal space between heaven and earth, filled with echoes of life and memory. As you continue restoring the stars, the environment grows quieter, as though your actions are gently closing a story that never needed words to begin with. The sense of completion comes not from achieving a goal but from feeling a gradual peace return to the world. This narrative minimalism, paired with a strong emotional undercurrent, allows each player to interpret their own meaning from the journey, making the experience deeply personal.

Visually, Paradise Marsh is both simple and elegant. The blocky, stylized art direction, with its smooth color gradients and soft lighting, conveys a natural world that feels handcrafted. The day-night cycle and shifting weather lend the game a rhythmic flow — bright mornings with soft reflections on the water give way to foggy evenings and nights illuminated by the slow return of the stars. The visual simplicity works hand in hand with its meditative purpose, offering beauty without clutter. The sound design completes this atmosphere with a delicate, ambient soundtrack by Disasterpeace, known for his evocative musical minimalism. Each track blends naturally with the hum of crickets, rustle of reeds, and splash of distant frogs, reinforcing the game’s emotional subtlety. It is not a soundtrack that demands attention; it simply breathes with the world.

In terms of gameplay, Paradise Marsh is intentionally sparse. Its mechanics revolve around catching creatures and returning them to the sky, but the joy lies not in the act itself, rather in the patient rhythm of exploration. There is no sprint button or elaborate set of tools — your movements are measured, your interactions gentle. This deliberate pacing may challenge players accustomed to faster or more goal-oriented adventures, but it is an essential part of the game’s philosophy. The controls are smooth, the catching mechanics intuitive, and the world reactive enough to feel alive without overwhelming you with complexity. Occasional surprises like mushrooms with temporary effects or weather changes keep exploration interesting, but everything remains in service of maintaining a calm, reflective tone. The game never pushes you forward; it lets you decide when to linger or move on.

Yet for all its charm, Paradise Marsh’s simplicity may also be its limitation for some. The experience is short, often completed in just a few hours, and players seeking deep progression systems or complex objectives may find its offerings too modest. The slower movement and minimal mechanics can make it feel repetitive after extended play, and the absence of challenge might not appeal to those craving mechanical depth. Technical quirks, such as occasional sound repetition or environmental glitches, may momentarily distract from the immersion. However, these issues are minor compared to the overall cohesion of its design. The game knows exactly what it wants to be — a tranquil, self-contained moment of introspection rather than a sprawling adventure — and in that, it succeeds gracefully.

Ultimately, Paradise Marsh is less a game to be beaten and more a space to inhabit for a time. It encourages you to breathe, listen, and exist in a world where every sound and shimmer of light feels meaningful. It is a love letter to quiet exploration, to the unnoticed beauty of fleeting moments, and to the idea that sometimes, restoration is found not in grand victories but in the patient act of simply paying attention. LazyEti’s creation stands as a reminder that art in games does not always need to be complex or grandiose to leave a lasting impression. Its calmness lingers long after you close it, like the faint glow of stars slowly returning to a once-forgotten sky — a gentle, soothing reminder that even the smallest acts can restore light to the world.

- The game is broken up into main misssions, with some randomised side missions and boss fights made available as you progress through the game; all missions can be repeated to grind for resources and specific loot. Missions can also have random modifiers to change up every mission run slightly.
- Story bits are peppered into in the main missions, in between missions, and in the home base, overall it's very light but serviceable.
- The visuals may not seem flashy and high-fidelity, but the colour-palette and art-style fit the cyber-punk aesthetic.
- The music is decent, guns sound punchy and impactful; I didn't find the sound lacking in any way.
- The game plays well with a controller, but the menu UI could be a bit more distinct and clear.
- Some maps on randomised side missions might be repeated, but the enemy is varied and the missions are over quickly enough to not be an issue.
- You can increase the difficulty in all missions for more rewards, and also increase specific loot drop chance (by paying standard currency).
- There are a lot of skills and gear to choose from, and the guns in each category feel varied enough.
- Transmog exists, and you can freely change the appearance and colour of your armour and even your guns.
- There is good build variety with all the equipment, skills and unique effects of rare gear. You can modify armour/weapons with buffs and effects and it has a small cost, though I wish it was free, to allow easy and convnenient build-crafting.
- The end-game is grindy because higher level skill card upgrades require a lot of resources, and you'll want to be chasing specific gear and skill card drops to round out your build.
- The devs seem to listen to feedback and add and change some things. The game is also updated frequently for an indie title. It's fully released and still receiving updates, so kudos to the dev team.

My favourite thing about this game is its attention to detail in historical and topographical accuracy. Graviteam meticulously reconstructs over 100 square kilometers of real battlefields using wartime aerial reconnaissance photographs, Allied and Axis topographical maps, and modern satellite data. The result is astonishing. 

Furthermore, this game is not your typical WWII strategy game. There are no base-building mechanics, resource gathering, or other arcade-style features found in titles like Company of Heroes. Instead, Graviteam Tactics is a true tactical simulation that captures the order of battle, unit compositions, atmosphere and authenticity of Tunisia, 1943.

Fantastic game. It's the same as Graviteam's Eastern Front game except that it's set in North Africa after the American invasion, so you're playing with American and British units against the Germans. They never added the Italians.

It takes awhile but once you get the hang of it, it's well worth it.

Just got an ending for this game at 16 hours, and I have to say...this game is something special. 

The standouts are the writing, exploration, and quest design. Quests are usually designed in ways that you can take different routes, avoid enemies, and make different decisions that lead to different outcomes. 

Dialogue/NPC interactions were probably the highlight, where the game just manages to write them in a way that makes you WANT to interact with whatever you can, just to see the interaction. The game taking place in a mixed setting with modern, high crime, spiritual aspects collide really lends itself well to a variety of personalities, and this game really makes it work. Humor is on point where it needs to be, and the intrigue of a certain aspect of the game was done really well.

Characters have their events/story spread out throughout the game. The game doesn't make them missable really, but some of them can be easily if the player chooses to do so. Again even these (especially final character quests) come with choices to make, with no outcome negatively blindsiding you. 

And the exploration, for a 2D JRPG, is probably some of the best I've seen. This ties in with both the semi open nature of the game, map design, and the very simple but really well done "Jump" mechanic. Most 2D JRPGs would make the jump scripted where you do it at some specific point in the map, but this game makes it a button and allows you to jump at any time over obstacles spanning 1 tile. It's something that sounds so simple but when you actually try the game, it adds a huge dynamic to moving around the map and exploration when you can just hop a fence, avoid an enemy in a stairway by hopping across to the other side, getting an item by hopping across some roofs, etc. while giving player control so it makes them feel like they were rewarded for their ingenuity, instead of being guided or expected to do it.

The only downside I would give this game how in any given area you'll encounter almost the same enemy group, making the combat dip quite a bit for me.

Shovel Knight Dig is a very simple, yet fun and well made roguelike. The titular character, Shovel Knight, descends into a cavernous pit in the earth, in search of dangerous foes titled "Hexcavators" and the gems they guard, all leading to the villainous Drill Knight, head honcho of the operation. Gameplay wise, well, the best way to sum it up is: If you played Shovel Knight before, imagine that but a roguelike.

Players collect several items, hundreds of treasures, and plenty of hidden food, perfectly preserved somehow. The main gimmick comes in the form of the Shovel Knights ability to dig, all levels are structured vertically, with the player quite literally digging further and further down. Upgrades are also found while adventuring, as is standard for most games in this genre. Upgrades such as defenses, magic boosts, and even jump height will make the journey much easier. at the end of each zone, you encounter a boss fight, upon defeating them, you'll get further and further in achieving your goals.

Outside of the well, a small camp filled with friendly faces is ready to greet you. You can buy permanent upgrades with the gems you've cashed in, as well as items that can be taken with you down below to open up secrets. Occasionally, you might just stumble upon a quest. Fulfilling said quests will give you many rewards, as well as access to even more quests later. Some quests are done in the safety of the camp, while others are found down in the many depths themselves, which can give you some incentive during a run. 

Overall, the game plays well, is presented well, and feels like a worthy game to sink some hours into. If you're a fan of Shovel Knight or not, this game has lots to keep playing for.

August'tan önceki bölüm, çocukluk, büyüme, karar verme ve bırakma ile ilgili. Oyunda 3 karakter var: August, Beth ve Ivy. Kızların odaları arasında geçiş yaptıkça olay örgüsü ilerliyor ve arkadaşlıkları hakkında daha fazla şey öğreniyoruz.

Açıklamada bunun bir hikaye bulmacası olduğu belirtiliyor ve tüm detayları okumayı atlasanız bile, oyun üç farklı karakterin olduğu gerçeğini göz ardı etmiyor. Her odadaki oynanış biraz farklı; örneğin Beth'in odası daha çok ilham bulmak ve sanatsal şeyler yapmakla ilgiliyken, Ivy'nin odası daha çok tamirat ve el işi yapmakla, el işleriyle ilgili. August'un odasında onları bir araya getiren şeyin ne olduğunu öğreniyoruz.

Genellikle temizlik yapıp odaları keşfediyor olsak da, aralarında geçen hikayeyi de çözmeye çalışıyoruz ve sonunda August'u geride bırakıp hayatının bir sonraki aşamasına geçmeye karar veriyoruz.oyunu iki kez oynadım ve oyunun tekrar oynanabilirliğini gerçekten beğendim. İkinci oynayışımda bulmacaları nasıl çözeceğimi bilsem de, kendimi hikayeye daha fazla kaptırdığımı ve ilk oynayışımda kaçırdığım küçük ayrıntıları fark ettiğimi hissettim. Hikayede hala kaçırdığımı hissettiğim çok şey olduğu için kesinlikle tekrar oynayabileceğim bir oyun.

Yatağın içinden düşen kitaplar veya ulaşamayacağım bir yere hareket eden kitaplar gibi bazı sorunlar yaşadım; ayrıca kilitli kutuların düğmelerinin bazen çevrilememesi gibi. Kaydı kapatıp tekrar açmak her şeyi normale döndürdü ve oyun biraz daha uzun süre piyasada olacağından, hataların düzeltileceğinden eminim.Üç arkadaşın odalarını toplayıp, kişisel eşyaları aracılığıyla aralarındaki bağları ve derin bir hikayeyi yavaş yavaş keşfettiğiniz sakin bir bulmaca oyunu.

Oyun, etrafa dağılmış eşyaların olduğu küçük bir yatak odasında başlıyor. Bir kaset alıp kayıt cihazında dinledikten sonra ne yapmanız gerektiğini öğreniyorsunuz. Odanızdan çıkıyorsunuz ve eşyaları doğru kutulara, valizlere, kutulara vb. yerleştirerek ortalığı temizlemeniz gerekiyor.

Odadaki çoğu küçük eşya kaldırılabilir ve not, kitap veya çorap gibi belirli bir türü ilk kez kaldırdığınızda, doğru kutunun üzerinde bir vurgu belirir. Bu, her tür için yalnızca bir kez gerçekleşir, bu yüzden bundan sonra her şeyin nereye gittiğini hatırlamanız gerekir.

Oda büyük olmadığı ve yaklaştığınızda nesneler yerlerine oturduğu için bu genellikle bir sorun teşkil etmez. Bu kural, ilerlemek için gereken önemli eşyalar için geçerli değildir. Bunlar size her zaman nereye ait olduklarını gösterecektir. Bazı zorlu nesnelerde hala yardıma ihtiyacınız varsa, her şey için kutu dış çizgilerini açabilirsiniz.

Toplanan nesneler döndürülebilir ve incelenebilir. Örneğin, bir kitabın arkasında bir not görüp bunun bir doğum günü hediyesi olduğunu anlayabilirsiniz. Ancak, nesneler yerleştirildikten sonra artık onları inceleyemezsiniz, bu yüzden önce her şeyi okumanız iyi bir fikirdir. Bu, yapışkan notlar, mektuplar, kitaplar ve önemsiz görünse de genellikle ilginç bir şeyler içeren diğer birçok nesneyi içerir.

Genel ilerlemeniz, ekranın alt kısmındaki renkli bir çubukla gösterilir. Odayı temizlediğinizde, tüm önemli nesneleri yerleştirdiğinizde ve tüm hedefleri tamamladığınızda bir sonraki odaya geçebilirsiniz. Her arkadaşınız için birer tane olmak üzere üç oda var, ancak ilerlediğinizde kaçırdığınız hiçbir şeyi temizlemek için geri dönemeyeceksiniz.

Çok küçük eşyalarla ilgili küçük bir sorun var. Öne çıkan bir yerleri olmadığı için, odanın bir yerinde kaybedebilir ve tekrar bulamayabilirsiniz. Bunu düzeltmek için oyunu kaydedip yeniden yükleyebilirsiniz. Bu, yerleştirilmemiş eşyaları orijinal konumlarına geri döndürür. Maalesef bazı hatalar bu şekilde çözülmüyor. Örneğin, son odadaki kar küresi bulmacası adımlardan birini kaydetmiyor, bu da tamamlamayı imkansız hale getiriyor. Ayrıca odalardan biri tamamlanmış olarak kaydedilmiyor, bu yüzden başarıyı kazanamıyorsunuz.

Little King’s Story is a charming blend of real-time strategy, life-simulation, and adventure, built around the concept of guiding a young boy who suddenly becomes king. The game presents a whimsical kingdom filled with quirky characters, humorous dialogue, and an inviting sense of discovery. Its narrative is simple but effective, framing the king’s journey as a quest to expand his tiny realm, unite neighboring lands, and bring peace through exploration, diplomacy, and occasionally absurd battles.

The core gameplay revolves around commanding villagers who serve as your workforce, soldiers, and specialists. Each villager can be assigned a job class—such as soldier, farmer, carpenter, or mage—each with unique abilities that influence exploration and combat. Managing these roles and building an effective party is central to progression. The system is intuitive but deep enough to create satisfying strategic moments, especially when tackling tougher enemies or exploring new regions.

Combat and exploration go hand-in-hand. Players send their followers into battle Pikmin-style, issuing simple commands while positioning the king safely behind them. Battles range from straightforward skirmishes to large-scale boss encounters with creative, sometimes eccentric designs. The controls can feel imprecise at times, especially when handling larger groups, but the overall system remains engaging due to its variety and scale.

City-building plays a major role in the game’s charm. As the kingdom grows, new buildings, classes, and amenities become available. Villagers develop personalities, routines, and preferences, making the settlement feel lively. Watching the town evolve from a humble camp into a bustling kingdom adds a strong sense of accomplishment. This life-sim element also contributes to the game’s warm and humorous tone, as quirky events and oddball citizens constantly add flavor.

Visually, the game uses a storybook aesthetic with soft colors, expressive animations, and imaginative environments. The art direction contributes significantly to its fairy-tale atmosphere. The music is memorable as well, leaning heavily on classical arrangements that give each area and encounter its own character. Together, the visuals and soundtrack create an inviting world that feels both magical and mischievous.

The difficulty can be surprisingly high. Certain battles require careful preparation, and losing units—especially high-level ones—can be a significant setback. The game rewards planning and patience, but some players may find the spikes in challenge abrupt. Additionally, pathfinding issues and occasional crowd-management frustrations remind you that the mechanics, though ambitious, are not perfectly polished.

Overall, Little King’s Story stands out as a uniquely creative strategy-adventure hybrid. Its blend of humor, kingdom management, tactical combat, and heartfelt storytelling makes it a memorable experience. The game’s charm, personality, and sense of progression outweigh its mechanical quirks, resulting in a distinctive and rewarding journey for players who enjoy strategic depth wrapped in a whimsical package.

[h1]Introduction[/h1]
Garbanzo Quest, developed and self-published by solo developer "zagawee" (with some help from gracious donations online and the support of loved ones) released in 2024 to unfortunately low player counts. A year later, and at the time of writing, the game sits only at 420 (nice) total reviews, but 98% of those reviews are positive and for good reason.

[h1]Main Review[/h1]
The game features a bright, quirky art style, which lends itself well to the game's absurdist and, at times, somewhat random comedy. The soundtrack is surprisingly tonally varied, and the world map's interconnectivity and secrets are one of the best I've ever seen in a 2D platformer. I managed to, by accident, kill 4 of the game's 6 main bosses almost back-to-back, by accidentally finding a secret in one level that lead me through miscellaneous, strange shortcuts. I even found an easter egg, pertaining to killing a boss, that is meant to be a later appearance of a recurring foe, before fighting the one I was meant to find first.

The game's secrets are well hidden, but not obscure by any means. There are no annoying, old school instances of "here's a solid-looking wall, but you can actually walk straight through it!" I greatly appreciated this throughout my 14 hours of play, as hugging walls like you're a blind man without his cane or seeing-eye dog, is not nearly as satisfying as just finding things through a sharp gaze, and few indie developers seem to understand this objective fact.

I laughed a lot, I died a lot, I groaned at perpetual failure, only to eventually triumph over every challenge in the game, 100%ing it and having an absolute blast. My heaviest way of recommending this game? My 14 hours of playtime were two days of playtime. I was hooked. It's been a while since I've played something this rewarding, where I never once had to silently mutter some form of "well... that was unfair" or "man, this RNG sucks!" Garbanzo Quest is a hidden gem and has charmed me enough to end up on my personal list of favorite platformers, sitting snuggly somewhere slightly below Celeste.

What this game lacks in momentum and complex maneuvering-tech in comparison to Celeste, it more than makes up for in how creatively it uses traps, enemies and mechanics. The game is absolutely oozing with them. Some of the mechanics only show up for a level or two throughout the entirety of the game's seven worlds, granting a welcome and interesting reprise whenever you start feeling like the game might be getting stale or overplaying its seemingly simplistic hand. A lot of mechanics, however, will continuously come back in ever more clever and cool combinations, that show the developers genuinely impressive pedigree for level design sense. 

Nothing it ever feels out-of-place either, as the whole world the game sets up feels bizarre from the get-go, creating an atmosphere of "anything goes". Though even then, aesthetically speaking, [i]zagawee[/i] somehow manages to blend all of these elements and set pieces from entirely stylistically different worlds in a way that never quite forces you to have to suspend disbelief too hard or give overmuch benefit of the doubt to the disharmony. It's a dissonance that exists, but is hardly, if ever, felt.

[b][i]As dumb as it might seem at first glance of the silly title and presentation, I have to genuinely conclude this: Garbanzo Quest is a masterpiece. Please play it!

This one's probably on me for not being hardcore enough, but even as someone who loves Hollow Knight, Silksong, and DMC, and beat every boss those games had to offer, I just hard a hard time getting into this game. The movement and how it interacted with your attacks (air momentum in particular) just didn't feel great, and I spent a lot more time getting combod by big enemy groups with brutal chains of hitstun than I spent comboing them. Magenta Horizon does look very impressive, with a striking and horrifically imaginative art style. I couldn't get my controllers working with it and had to play via mouse and keyboard (which is fine since I do that for Hollow Knight) but with those controls I couldn't find a way to close tutorial prompts (esc, tab, enter, space, none worked) so since I had to restart the level after viewing them, I couldn't read the tutorials. Hopefully I'm not the only one who found the experience quite punishing; it does seem like less than a third of the game's players ended up beating the first boss.

To be clear, my personal and technical difficulties shouldn't reflect on the game's overall quality. I don't think that Magenta Horizon is a bad game at all - if you're the target audience, this is probably a modern indie masterpiece, like Rain World. I'm just not that target audience though, so I wouldn't personally recommend it. Sorry.

Magenta Horizon is a superb action game that deserves to be mentioned in the same breath as Ninja Gaiden and Devil May Cry, but more than that, it's the type of game that reminds me why I love the art form. It's a singular, cohesive experience across the board that is genuinely staggering to behold as it maintains a near pitch perfect quality bar the whole way through. I want to stress that, even though Magenta Horizon is an amazing action game, it has more to offer than just combat. The art and music are ever changing with every level, the level design itself constantly shifts so that each area keeps exploration engaging. Most shockingly of all, the story is pretty good. Every character has their own writing voice, making them stand out regardless of how slim their time on screen may be. Magenta Horizon is a proper adventure in addition to being a thrilling action game. The various cutscenes have more unique artworks and CGs than entire visual novels, and given how full bodied of a campaign Magenta Horizon has, that is astounding. It's also surprisingly funny at times too with a somewhat sly sense of humor that'll catch you off guard. I laughed more playing this than I have at self-professed 'comedy' games. While the combat is good enough that Magenta Horizon didn't need to excel in any other category, it still does, elevating the entire experience. You never get the impression any part of the game is wasting your time. It's all high effort (and skillfully crafted). 

There are a fair few reviews that bring up the difficulty, and while MH is certainly challenging, I think the game does a good job easing you into the mechanics, then putting you to the test with some difficult walls that ensure you come out the other side better at the game and with a stronger understanding of its mechanics. Not to mention there are also several difficulty settings to choose from, so if you genuinely get stuck, there's no shame in lowering the difficulty to learn the ins-and-outs of the game with a bit less pressure. Again, it's an adventure worth experiencing even if you don't want to master the mechanics, not that the normal difficulty forces that per se since I'm definitely far from great at the game and still rolled credits. But the action is good enough that even when I got stuck, I was still having a great time.

The core of the combat is enemy and encounter designer. While the player's toolkit is an important part of the combat, your attack strings are fairly easy to remember, not overly complicated or anything like that, which is a real boon when you need to react to vicious enemies under pressure. Since you aren't constantly learning new moves (you start with all base combat abilities), the way Magenta Horizon ups-the-ante and keeps things engaging is by introducing new enemy types. Almost every single level introduces not one, but two new enemy types that fundamentally alter the combat sandbox. Combat arenas are so finely tuned that even granular spacing changes dramatically shift how you engage with the encounter. And, the sheer amount of enemies that get packed into combat turns it into a bonafide monster mash where you genuinely wonder how you can take it, before pulling off daring maneuvers that shift the tide of battle. Death can come quick if you choke under pressure, but the healing system is functionally limitless, if you can land enough hits to charge up a health bomb. I have never played another game where you ride the knife's edge between victory and defeat so often so many times PER ENCOUNTER. The kind of comebacks you can wrest from the jaws of defeat are genuinely electrifying every single time. Crucially, it makes combat remarkably engaging and fun even when you are getting bad grades since the basic combat encounters are well designed and interesting in their own right. 

One of my other favorite aspects of the combat is how the air becomes a second battlefield where your aerial superiority is constantly contested. Enemies on the ground have attacks to knock you out of the air, enemies in the air are aggressive, and you have a suite of tools to keep yourself airborne battling through it all. It's a unique experience executed about as well as you could hope for, and adds that extra dimension and depth to your on the fly decision making. It almost goes without saying, but the basic gamefeel is excellent as well. Magenta Horizon is somewhat like Hollow Knight in how it instantly just feels good and intuitive to control, a necessity for weaving through hordes of enemies and their attacks.

Maybe the simplest and most succinct way I can praise the combat, however, is to say that even when I got bodied and had to redo combat encounters, I still enjoyed them. They were still valuable as practice, and fun to replay because of how dynamic and swift the combat sandbox is. Defeat counted against my end of level grades, but certainly not my enjoyment. There was always a new strategy I could deploy, or an easy mistake I made that I could recognize as it happened. And, again, if you find yourself getting frustrated, you can always lower the difficulty to have a bash at the monster mash. 

This review is admittedly something of a fawning effort post, but believe or not, I don't think I've even scratched the surface of how much there is to praise about this game. It is genuinely one of the best action games I have ever played (unquestionably the most complete and cohesive), and a stark reminder of why I love games to begin with. You owe it to yourself to play this. The price tag of $11 (USD) is borderline criminal too. There's a demo as well, so I genuinely urge you to give Magenta Horizon a shot since I have somehow dramatically undersold its merits. I absolutely adore this game, and, hopefully, you will too.

未知の惑星の謎を解き明かすべく、こうるさいAIの助言を受けつつ、衛星からさまざまな探査機（なぜかだいたいジャガイモ製）を打ち上げよう。もしかしたら、そのうち宇宙の深淵に触れるかも……？　というお話。

簡単にいえば、『Lifeline』を宇宙探査ものにしてクリッカーで進めていくようにしたようなゲーム。クリッカー／インクリメンタル系としては（2017年の作品としては稀なことに）かなり物語に力が入っていて、これまたクリッカーとしては異例な洗練されたグラフィックと上質な翻訳もあいまってふつうにユーモアSFアドベンチャーとしておすすめできる作品にしあがっている。
プレイ時間としてはきっちりまじめにやれば10時間以内(もちろんそのうち実際に操作してる時間はグッと短くなる)だとおもわれる。だるくなったな〜というタイミングで事態が急展開を迎えたり、途中でクリックや放置だけでなくシューティングっぽいミニゲームが味変的に挿入されたりもして、たるみがちなクリッカーをなんとなく飽きないようにしているのはすごい。もっとも、クリッカーでここまで苦心してまともなストーリーテリングをするのは労力に見合ってないか……とおもわされるのだけれど。その疑問が現在のストーリー重視の短編クリッカー／インクリメンタルゲームにつながったりしているのだろうか。
クリッカーとしてのシステムにあまり複雑なところはない。比較的短く終わる分、クッキークリッカーなどよりさらにシンプルだ。
2017年はクリッカーのさまざまな実験作が出た年だったが、その良質な試みのひとつとして記憶されるべき作品だろう。

Bonnie’s Bakery is a deceptively adorable horror gem that manages to be cute, funny, unsettling, and downright creepy all at once! What starts as a cheerful little bakery sim quickly becomes something much darker, and the contrast between its warm pastel charm and its disturbing secrets is what makes the experience so memorable! Serving pastries, decorating desserts, and managing your shop is genuinely enjoyable, and the multiple endings give the game real replay value! It is short, but absolutely designed to be played more than once, which makes each run even more fun as you uncover new pieces of the truth!

The story has just the right mix of humor and horror, with moments that will make you smile and others that will catch you off guard! Escaping the basement and piecing together the real mystery is exciting, and there is something hilarious about how seriously the game takes itself while still feeling cute and chaotic! The only real weak spot is the stealth sequences where you play as Bonnie hunting for ingredients. They are serviceable, but the detection system feels a little unclear and clunky compared to the rest of the design. Still, they do not drag the game down too much and the charm easily outweighs the rough edges!

Overall, Bonnie’s Bakery is a delightful and disturbingly fun little horror experience that deserves the love it gets! It is affordable, replayable, and bursting with personality! If you like cute games that secretly want to ruin your day in the most adorable way possible, this one is absolutely worth it! Godspeed, hail Bingus!!!

This game is so well-made, I’m so glad I played it.

Departed Away is a psychological horror experience that leans into the classic surreality of the genre. It follows the story of a protagonist and their stalker, though the deeper you delve into the game, the more the plot unravels—and the less it makes sense… in the best way possible.

Right from the start, the atmosphere is top-notch—reminiscent of Doki Doki Literature Club (DDLC), from which the game clearly draws inspiration. Everything feels too cheerful, too bright. The characters are just off enough to be unsettling—uncanny and nearly human, but never quite right, and throughout the game, subtle hints embedded in the soundtrack and background reveal pieces of the truth behind the bizarre events affecting the protagonist. I appreciate how, even with a clearly structured narrative, the developers manage to incorporate these background details to add an extra layer of depth to the experience.

The story itself is quite impressive, as it leaves room for interpretation while providing enough substance that you’re never entirely lost. The artistic direction is particularly strong, especially in how it conveys the main character’s dissociation. Players are given just enough information to piece things together, but never with full certainty. In addition to this, the game’s depiction of mental illness is handled with care. While I won’t speak on its clinical accuracy, as I’m far from an expert, it doesn’t feel careless or exploitative. It’s clear the developers intended to tell a meaningful story about the tragedy of living with psychological trauma—and they absolutely succeeded. I felt connected to the experience from the moment the cheerful facade began to crumble.

Furthermore, the characters you interact with are cool! You can choose to engage with four different girls, again echoing DDLC. Each path is unique, yet they all end the same: in failure. Something always goes wrong, and the protagonist’s hopes are crushed by the antagonist, Lora. And despite the characters representing familiar archetypes, they’re thoughtfully written. Marcel, in particular, stands out as the most unique. Her character feels especially well-developed, and her personality breaks away from typical tropes. However, the characters aren’t necessarily the focus—instead, they represent different kinds of relationships. To me, they show that the protagonist is capable of forming bonds with almost anyone, but something—inevitably—destroys them. That perspective made me appreciate their presence even more.

Moving on to Lora herself, she is definitely an especially intriguing character. She embodies the split personality created by the protagonist—an expression of their suppressed anger and rage. From my interpretation, she represents the violent and unprocessed trauma that manifests during dissociation.

The protagonist refers to her as a separate entity, despite her not existing, which strengthens the idea that she is a psychological construct. Her exaggerated, almost theatrical personality is designed to scream “I’m not real”—and yet, we’re left uncertain until the truth is revealed. She’s a powerful symbol of internalized trauma, given a face and name to illustrate the dissonance and delusion that deep trauma can inflict. Really powerful stuff.

The pixel-art style is also worth praising. I’ve always appreciated pixel art, and it’s especially difficult to make something truly eerie using static visuals—but this game manages to pull it off. Its nostalgic aesthetic feels like a throwback to the Nintendo DS, yet it unsettles me through clever design choices. Jittering sprites, uneven clipping, mosaic filters, and blocky glitch effects amplify the horror elements and elevate the visual storytelling. What could’ve looked quite ridiculous and... goofy, ends up feeling genuinely disturbing.

One of the most effective techniques used in this game is how it handles its more shocking scenes. Much of it is left intentionally ambiguous, but the sharp transition from a haunting figure to the sound of bones crunching—or a dog yelping—is absolutely brutal. It delivers a gut punch, narrowing the player’s focus to sound alone. This choice removes any visual “flair” from the violence, instead presenting horror in its rawest, most visceral form.

It makes perfect sense that such imagery would be repressed by the protagonist and instead projected through Lora. This narrative decision avoids cheap shock value in favor of psychological weight, and actually makes sense in terms of the narrative. It forces the developers to be more creative, and the result is all the more impactful.

Overall, Departed Away is a powerful indie title that delivers on both its horror elements and its nuanced portrayal of trauma through interactive storytelling. A perfect 10/10. I had a phenomenal experience with it.

《狼与香辛料VR》以轻小说与动画为基础改编为短篇VR叙事体验，更强调氛围而非复杂玩法。玩家被置于与赫萝和劳伦斯的静谧片刻，近距离观察角色关系。整体更接近互动剧场，其设计取向自开场即明确。

视觉表现具有吸引力。角色模型还原度高，面部表情生动，口型同步自然。背景环境简约温暖，以光照营造中世纪氛围。技术表现不突出，但风格足够支撑沉浸感。

交互极为有限。玩家主要以观看与聆听为主，少量操作不影响剧情。寻求解谜或进程推进的用户可能失望。价值核心在于临场感与角色陪伴。

音频承担主要体验。配音表现力强，赋予人物个性。空间音频增强角色临近感。音乐克制，烘托情绪不喧宾夺主。字幕准确可用。

流程较短，多数玩家可在一小时内完成。粉丝可能珍惜每一刻，新玩家可能因缺乏背景与简短时长而感受不足。重玩价值较低，主要在于回放场景。

是否值得购买取决于优先考量。如希望体验温和的VR叙事并见到熟悉角色，本作契合；如期待系统性玩法或动作元素，应考虑其他作品。作为聚焦的粉丝向叙事内容，其在设定范围内完成了目标。

原作漫画的十一年老粉，出了之后第一时间购入拼命打完了，来不带剧透说一下真实感受。
说到漫改游戏，而且还是文字小说，我一般都是抱着“有就很好”的态度去玩的，一开始对这个游戏的期待度真的不高。第一天晚上玩到半夜三点，那时候就过了个第一章，第二章只看到一半。当时我给出的评价是，“这个魔嫁游戏做的比我想的好不少。”
全部打完之后现在我要改正一下我的评价，魔嫁游戏不是比我想的好不少，是好太多了。
不知道写这个剧本的是一个人还是一个团队，但是武士道这次找的人，不仅做到了对原作设定的深度尊重，而且做到了剧情设计合理连贯。对于一个有原作漫画基础的文字小说游戏，这两点光是符合其中一点就很难得了，但是这次的故事真的太超出我的预计了。
真的要感叹，写这个游戏剧本的作者到底是去搜罗了跟原作和相关的衍生品多少资料才能写出来这些。里面的设定涉及到了本篇漫画甚至包括学院篇，断片集，作为番外动画的等待繁星，甚至衍生系列的漫画(闪电杰克)和实体漫画附赠的特典小漫画里的设定都有……扣得这么细真的太牛了……
剧情设定也很了不起，不是那种讨人厌的谜语人，这个“真相”真的有惊艳到我。伏笔真的超级多，有明显的有不明显的，我猜到了一点但是没猜到全貌。知道了真相之后再去看之前的主线和番外故事，真的能发现它们都能前后串起来，好厉害……而且选择的切入点很有意思。
新角色塑造得很到位，老角色也没有ooc。故事是一贯的魔嫁风味，这种相似的灵魂相遇并相互救赎的故事，魔嫁里面有很多，这次的也不会让人腻味。
音乐没有直接套用TV的老版本，所有的音乐都是在原来旋律的基础上重新编曲，哪怕是类似的曲子现在听也是完全不同的风味。
不足之处也有很多。除了PPT一般的演出，没有全语音这些显而易见的缺点外，最难受的恐怕就是那个选项了……不及时存档事后再去翻找补充完成度真的太麻烦了，翻到崩溃。所以看到这条的朋友们请记得一定要在选项处勤存档啊！！另外中间有部分剧情过于拖沓，可能是考虑到文本的丰富度，稍微注了点水……
最后的结局都很耐人寻味。不过多剧透，请所有玩家们一起耐心地见证他们选择的道路和他们的未来吧。
整体看下来，这是一部很合格的深度粉丝向作品。如果你是原作的狂热老粉会非常感动，玩得很开心。但是要是对此一无所知的路人，请谨慎入手。

Detective Grimoire is a mystery game where you play as the titular detective, trying to solve a murder at a secluded tourist attraction. Boggy, the mysterious swamp creature, has been accused of murdering Richard Remington, the owner of the park, but Detective Grimoire isn't so sure. The mystery is pretty engaging. I liked uncovering the backstory of Boggy's Bog, what Remington was doing in the park, and the motives of each of the suspects. The swampy theme park and cast of suspects were odd and fun. The story was easy to follow and it was usually pretty easy to follow the detective's reasoning. There's one key clue that tells you who the culprit is, but it doesn't come up too early, and the resolution had some unexpected reveals as well.

To investigate, you explore the park, interrogate suspects, and solve small puzzles. You click on the objects in each scene and talk to the characters to gather clues. You have a case file you can use to keep track of all the information you've gathered and which objects, suspects, or areas you haven't investigated fully. Most of the puzzles involve completing sentences to move the case along. The game gives you a question and you have to make the correct answer with the sentence parts it gives you. Detective Grimoire, developed and published by SFB Games, is a whimsical and atmospheric point-and-click mystery adventure that captures the spirit of classic detective tales while infusing it with modern polish, humor, and charm. Set in a murky swamp-turned-tourist attraction, the game follows the titular detective as he investigates a peculiar murder case involving a local legend known as Boggy, a supposed swamp monster blamed for the death of the park’s owner. From the outset, it’s clear that Detective Grimoire is not a grim, hard-boiled mystery but a colorful and character-driven adventure where logic, personality, and presentation are the main draws. The story strikes a careful balance between intrigue and levity, blending mysterious undertones with witty exchanges that make the experience approachable and engaging for players of all ages.

The gameplay follows the familiar structure of point-and-click adventures but is executed with refreshing accessibility and flow. Players explore hand-painted environments, gather clues, and interview suspects scattered across the swamp. The process of deduction is presented through clean and intuitive mechanics—clues can be combined, contradictions examined, and suspects questioned with a dialogue system that emphasizes reasoning rather than trial and error. Each revelation feels satisfying, not because of difficulty but because of how naturally it fits the narrative’s pacing. While veterans of the mystery genre may find the puzzles on the easier side, the game’s design ensures there’s always a steady rhythm of discovery, conversation, and deduction. It invites you to think like a detective without ever becoming tedious or overwhelming, a balance many modern adventure games struggle to achieve.

Visually, Detective Grimoire is a delight. The swamp, with its misty greens and dusky tones, exudes an eerie charm that feels both cozy and mysterious. Every location is meticulously drawn with personality, from the creaky wooden docks to the dimly lit museum exhibits celebrating the fabled Boggy. The character design stands out for its expressiveness—each suspect has distinct visual quirks and mannerisms that reflect their eccentric personalities, and the fluid animation adds a layer of liveliness rarely seen in smaller indie titles. The result is a world that feels alive and memorable despite its relatively small scope. The soundtrack, composed by Raphael Benjamin Meyer, complements this atmosphere beautifully. Its jazzy and ambient tones evoke both the slow crawl of the swamp and the sharp curiosity of investigation, enhancing the mood without overpowering it.

The voice acting deserves special mention, as it brings the game’s quirky cast to life with humor and nuance. Detective Grimoire himself is portrayed with a charming blend of professionalism and dry wit, perfectly capturing the spirit of a detective who takes his work seriously but isn’t immune to the oddity of his surroundings. Each supporting character—from the swamp’s eccentric residents to the self-proclaimed experts on Boggy—adds flavor to the story through clever writing and distinct vocal performances. Conversations feel organic and often amusing, turning what could have been routine interrogations into memorable encounters filled with personality.

Narratively, Detective Grimoire shines in its simplicity and focus. The plot revolves around uncovering the truth behind the alleged monster attack, but the real heart of the story lies in its characters and the world they inhabit. As the detective delves deeper, he begins to realize that the truth is far more human than monstrous, revealing motives tied to greed, superstition, and pride. This grounded conclusion gives the story emotional weight without undermining the light-hearted tone that defines it. While the mystery itself may not rival the complexity of traditional noir narratives, its clarity and pacing make it rewarding. The writing cleverly mixes humor with sincere moments of reflection, reminding the player that good detective work is as much about empathy and observation as it is about evidence.

In terms of length and replayability, the game is concise, running roughly two to four hours depending on how thoroughly you explore. This brevity works in its favor, keeping the experience focused and free of filler. Once the mystery is solved, there’s little reason to replay beyond revisiting its atmosphere or appreciating its artistic details, but that feels appropriate given its narrative-driven design. It’s the kind of game that delivers a complete, satisfying story in a single sitting—a self-contained adventure rather than an ongoing series of puzzles.

Detective Grimoire ultimately succeeds because it understands its strengths. It’s not about challenging logic puzzles or sprawling storylines, but about mood, presentation, and storytelling finesse. SFB Games’ attention to detail in animation, voice work, and dialogue elevates what could have been a simple indie mystery into a polished and memorable experience. Its charm lies in its restraint—everything from the interface to the humor feels designed to keep the player immersed rather than distracted. The result is a cozy, intelligent mystery that evokes the best qualities of classic adventure games while feeling entirely fresh and modern. For fans of narrative-driven puzzles, quirky worlds, or simply good old-fashioned detective stories told with style, Detective Grimoire is a small gem well worth investigating.

《无用之人：登神长阶》是受《背包乱斗》启发制作的1V1自走棋游戏。使用了虚幻引擎开发，画面更加精致，战斗动画打击感十足，有一点《死亡教堂》的味道，可惜血腥度略显不足~还有，取“无用之人”这个名字，不知道是不是也带有致敬宫崎老贼的意思呢？

步入正题，游戏现阶段提供了4位角色供玩家选择，有身披重甲的骑士，戴着鸟嘴面具的瘟疫医生，拿武士刀的浪人和手持大刀的武将~每个角色的战斗技能与侧重都有不同，官方宣布了有计划在年底和明年都会有新的角色推出，一起期待吧……

游戏的战斗是自动进行的，不需要额外操作，所以玩家的玩法核心基本都围绕着"背包管理"来展开~游戏的背包空间是有限的，商店里购买的每一件招式、防具、药水、符文等等都会根据大小占用背包空间，这就要求玩家需要慎重思考后精心选择和搭配各种道具，构筑出属于自己的战斗流派~一些特殊的道具之间可以连携形成强大效果，有些甚至还可以合成出商店里无法购买的强大物品……

这里重点说一下“招式”这个物品（对，招式技能也是占背包格子的）~因为游戏的招式系统采用了类似"石头剪子布"的克制机制（常规、破势、霸体相互克制），你永远无法猜到下一个对手会用什么排列组合来和你对战，所以这款游戏除了精心策划构筑角色，运气成分也同样的重要！

游戏的战斗界面里的几个状态栏也需要特别注意下，除了关乎生死的生命条外，还有决定招式输出上限的精力条，打空后直接让对方产生硬直的韧性条以及积累防反的进度条~因为游戏的伤害防御计算非常复杂，还要考虑各种增益减益效果，所以这里就不一一赘述了，想了解的玩家可以在选择角色的界面点击右上角的？号里查看！

这款游戏虽然没有复杂的操作，但对玩家的策略规划要求比较高，没玩过《背包》的玩家前期需要花1-2个小时左右的时间熟悉下游戏的玩法机制~只要熟悉游戏的机制后，在积分模式里获得10场胜利还是比较轻松的，10场过后的进阶挑战就是真正“刷脸”的时刻~

因为里面会出现不少非常极端的“邪修”，比如对手就一个招式，追求极致的“一波流”，其他道具全是为这一个招式堆叠伤害的，只要你没有使用出到克制的招式打断他，或者出手速度比他慢，你就会被他两刀无情的带走o(╥﹏╥)o

其实，这点也代表了游戏的公平以及无限的可能性~这里没有其他游戏里那种等级与属性加点等数值的碾压，完全就看谁的脑洞更大，看谁的战术设计的更加精妙~如果你和我一样享受那种“战前规划10分钟，实战10秒决定胜负”的策略爽快感，那么这款游戏就非常适合你入手体验！

游戏的游戏性底子、动作流畅度和美术不错，这是优点，也是好评的点。
缺点部分也比较明显：
1、每次打完总有种怅然若失的感觉，刚build起来的角色还没爽就结束了。要是能在增加些局外养成（角色分支特性和武器分支特性）就好了。

4、数值问题，应该是最小的问题了，比如瘟疫医生拼尽全力刮了一套不如关公砍了两刀。

Big Thinkers Kindergarten, developed by Humongous Entertainment and re-released by Nightdive Studios, stands as a nostalgic relic from the golden age of 1990s edutainment software. It features the enthusiastic duo Ben and Becky Brightly, sibling mascots who guide young learners through a series of interactive activities designed to teach essential kindergarten-level skills. Like many of Humongous Entertainment’s titles, the game emphasizes engagement and discovery through humor, animation, and accessible gameplay. However, unlike the studio’s more narrative-driven series such as Pajama Sam or Freddi Fish, Big Thinkers takes a more instructional approach, packaging its lessons into discrete educational minigames rather than unfolding them through story or adventure.

At its core, Big Thinkers Kindergarten is a collection of sixteen learning activities, each focusing on a specific early childhood skill. Players explore the Brightly home, where different rooms contain lessons on literacy, math, science, spatial reasoning, and problem-solving. In the kitchen, children might learn measurement or counting; in the study, they may explore letters and vocabulary. The game introduces early math through pattern recognition, sequencing, and simple addition, while reading and phonics activities reinforce sound association and word recognition. What makes these minigames effective is their simplicity and colorful presentation—each one feels like a self-contained puzzle or toy, with clear feedback and encouragement from the main characters. The use of “SmartStars” as a reward system helps maintain a sense of progression and achievement, allowing children to track their growth in a way that feels playful rather than evaluative.

The educational design of Big Thinkers Kindergarten reflects Humongous Entertainment’s philosophy of “learning through play.” The activities are built to be intuitive, requiring minimal instruction, and rely on interaction rather than passive observation. The animations are lively and full of personality, and Ben and Becky serve as constant companions, offering praise, hints, and commentary that encourage experimentation. The inclusion of subjects beyond reading and math—such as geography, environmental awareness, and spatial relationships—gives the game a broad educational scope. This variety keeps the experience dynamic, as players can freely choose which skills to practice in any order. The open-ended structure makes it ideal for short, repeatable sessions that fit the attention span of its target audience.

However, the game’s age shows in both its presentation and interface design. Originally released in the late 1990s, Big Thinkers Kindergarten retains the look and feel of that era’s CD-ROM educational software. While Nightdive Studios’ Steam version runs smoothly through ScummVM and preserves the charm of the original artwork, the low-resolution visuals and dated sound design may seem crude by modern standards. The interface can be cluttered, with multiple clickable objects and text labels that may be confusing for children who are not yet confident readers. Navigation between rooms is sometimes unintuitive, and the lack of prominent visual cues can leave players unsure of where to go next. These design quirks make adult guidance almost necessary for younger children, reducing its potential as an independent learning tool.

The voice acting and audio design, while characteristic of Humongous Entertainment’s high-energy style, can also be hit or miss. Ben’s exaggerated enthusiasm and Becky’s cheerful commentary were intended to engage children, but the constant repetition of voice lines can become grating over time. Sound effects and background music are cheerful but repetitive, looping in ways that may test a parent’s patience after extended play. Still, the overall tone remains friendly and encouraging, fostering a positive emotional environment that helps mitigate the occasional frustration caused by interface limitations.

In terms of content longevity, Big Thinkers Kindergarten offers enough variety to keep a young learner entertained for several sessions, but it lacks adaptive difficulty or dynamic feedback systems found in modern educational software. Once a child masters the activities, there is little reason to return beyond the novelty of replaying favorite minigames. The educational depth, while age-appropriate, is fairly shallow—each task teaches a single concept in isolation rather than reinforcing skills through cumulative progression. This makes the game most effective as a supplementary tool rather than a standalone learning program.

Yet despite its limitations, Big Thinkers Kindergarten retains a certain charm that transcends its dated design. The personality of its hosts, the lively animation, and the whimsical presentation make it far more engaging than the dry, worksheet-style learning tools that dominated much of 1990s educational media. It captures the spirit of curiosity and play that defines early childhood learning, rewarding exploration and experimentation rather than rote memorization. For parents and educators, it remains a gentle, low-pressure way to introduce academic concepts within a colorful, entertaining framework.

Viewed through a modern lens, Big Thinkers Kindergarten is a snapshot of a particular era in educational gaming—one where creativity, character, and imagination were considered as important as pedagogy. It lacks the sophistication and adaptive intelligence of today’s digital learning apps, but it compensates with warmth, humor, and personality. Its value now lies less in its teaching effectiveness and more in its nostalgic appeal and historical significance. For those who grew up with Humongous Entertainment’s catalog, revisiting Big Thinkers Kindergarten is like opening a time capsule of childhood wonder—proof that learning and laughter once shared the same floppy disk.

I played Souldiers, a game from 2022, after Silksong, which was a startling experience.

Somehow the games have more in common than you might think: Metroidvanias with lush, vivid artwork and excellent music; expansive and intricate biomes full of secrets; a home base region that cues up various side quests (including a foot race of course); a vast array of skills and tools you acquire as you progress; and a fondness for hardcore gauntlet fights. But unlike Silksong, Souldiers has a much more mixed reputation due to (as far as I can tell) some internet shenanigans that happened when it was first released. Having played it now, I think that's a shame. 

What startled me is that, on the whole, I enjoyed Souldiers quite a bit more than Silksong.

Some of that boils down to Souldiers' distinct features, such as: the different starting classes, offering replayability and variety; the RPG leveling system, ensuring a consistent sense of character progression; ubiquitous items, enhancing one's weapons/builds in various ways. The art style, characters and music also tapped into a personal reservoir of Chrono Trigger nostalgia I didn't know I still had.

But it was also welcome contrasts with Silksong: the absence of corpse running; the prevalence of check points/save points and straightforward fast travel; quests that were--more often than not--kill-the-mini-boss quests and not farm-and-fetch quests; the difficulty options (though I played it on Warrior Mode all the way through); the generally better pacing.

This isn't to suggest that Souldiers is a flawless game. I did note a fair amount of surprising performance issues at times (stutters and frame drops, etc.), and where the game leaned into platform challenges (e.g., the aforementioned foot race quest), they could be unforgiving with the touchy, ledge-grabby controls/moveset.

That said, for the absolute bargain price I paid for this way back when before stuffing it in my backlog, Souldiers is a tremendous value and an excellent game. I don't want to downplay the experience others had during the launch of the game (and I've heard concerning rumors about the console ports that I haven't personally confirmed), but, now that I've beaten it, I only have nice things to say.

I came back to gaming after a long break, and Souldiers was such a pleasant surprise. The animation and art direction are beautiful, and the gameplay offers great variety — rarely feeling repetitive. Some areas can feel a bit too long and occasionally tedious (especially the first spider map), but overall the world is very well designed.

I finished the game with all three characters + New Game+ for a total of around 150 hours, and each hero has a very distinct identity:

Caster — The most balanced of the three. High damage and lots of protective spells, making it a great pick for beginners.

Archer — For more experienced players. Requires a careful and strategic playstyle. Fragile early on with low damage, but in the endgame he shines brilliantly with excellent DPS — still fragile, so you always need to play smart.

Scout — The damage sponge. A true tank in the endgame, but his lower damage output can drag some boss fights longer than necessary.

Overall, this is a great game. The ending suggests the developers had more story to tell — sadly, it seems the project has been abandoned, so a continuation looks unlikely.

Unfortunately, I must mention a major issue:
the “Another Round” achievement is bugged and won’t unlock after completing New Game+. With no updates or developer support since 2022, this achievement is currently unobtainable.

Still, I strongly recommend Souldiers to anyone who enjoys metroidvanias with good challenge, beautiful art, and an epic journey.
