Ace Attorney is one of my favourite series ever, but eventually you reach that bittersweet point where you’ve played all the entries and can’t relive the thrill of solving a case for the first time. While I was searching for similar games to the series, I came across a Reddit comment by a user named Blueisland5, who shared a detailed list of recommendations. One title stood out – Paper Perjury, which he had created himself. After playing it through, I can say it deserves that recommendation.

This game, developed by Paper Cat Games, is an Ace Attorney fan project in everything but name. You’re assigned cases, question witnesses, gather evidence, and interrogate suspects, where you can either “question” (press) them or “deduce” (present evidence). There are a few clear nods to Ace Attorney, like the Trucy Wright–inspired Annie Carde and plenty of the series’ trademark punny names. Some might call it lazy, but as someone who absolutely adores Ace Attorney, anything that comes close to replicating the feeling I had playing through those games is welcome in my book.

That said, there are some key differences between Paper Perjury and Ace Attorney: Instead of playing as a defense lawyer, you step into the shoes of Justina Smith, a police desk clerk dragged into detective work and mentored by the very Dick Gumshoe-like Ernest Hunt. Rather than a string of mostly standalone cases, you solve five that connect directly into one overarching story. Interestingly, this wasn’t always the plan, as creator James Acosta explained to me:

“I didn’t intend for all five cases to connect. I wanted them to be separate stories that connect by theme rather than plot. But after writing one case, I had to connect it to the next… then the next… until the five ended up being connected. It was kind of an accident that it happened that way, but I’m glad it worked out in the end.”

Unlike Ace Attorney’s often over-the-top courtroom drama, Paper Perjury opts for a more realistic tone, focusing on the day-to-day investigative work behind a range of crimes, from embezzlement to murder. As James explains:

“I prefer the more grounded stories in Ace Attorney. They may not be ‘realistic’, but the Shu Takumi games [original Ace Attorney trilogy] always felt more grounded and on a smaller scale. I’m not as big of a fan of Yamazaki and his team’s games [Dual Destinies, Spirit of Justice etc.] because they try to be as large as possible. So when writing Paper Perjury, I wrote the game how I would have wanted it.”

These differences are what make Paper Perjury stand out: its believable characterisation helps players connect more deeply with its cast, and the fact the game is one consistent narrative helps keep the player hooked to experience the next story beat. When you finally take down the main antagonist, it feels truly earned. We also see the friendships that grow between the police characters, and examining certain areas in the games allow for some interesting and humorous backstories for Justina and the others.


The game’s story weaves in sociopolitical commentary in a respectful and non-overbearing way, with particular focus given to the Eubank family and company, who are relentlessly trying to buy out housing from poorer tenants and owners to build expensive properties. James explained this:

“Gentrification is a theme I used based on my experiences living in California. Seeing gentrification happen before my eyes was something I wanted to write about.”

Importantly, no one is portrayed as purely evil. The writing consistently tries to understand each character’s motives, encouraging empathy even when their actions seem indefensible. It makes you really care about where every character ends up, and the epilogue does a good job of showing realistic but interesting outcomes for each of them.

There are a few changes made, though, that I would have preferred them not to. When examining areas, instead of moving a reticle around the screen, pertinent spots are listed in the top-right corner, making examination a literal checklist instead of an engaging hunt for key clues. The investigation sections also tend to follow the same formula – examine each area and talk to everyone, then review and deduce their statements – whereas Ace Attorney mixed things up more by forcing you to prevent specific evidence or profiles to characters to advance the plot.

Even so, there are some neat little details that give the game extra personality and show a level of design that most games of this nature don’t. The soundtrack, while similar to Ace Attorney, is still immaculately produced and will stay in your head for a while. The character design and animations (especially Justina’s and Fie’s) are all charming and expressive. My favourite moment comes in the fourth case’s interrogation, when the game flips the concept on its head: you switch from Justina to defense counsel Ferris Eubank and must poke holes in your own argument to move forward.

Paper Perjury is a confident and compact visual novel, with a story that can be beaten in about ten hours, and simple but engaging gameplay that streamlines the flow of Ace Attorney while moving at a brisk enough pace that it never feels too repetitive. Obviously, this is highly recommended to any Ace Attorney fan, but I wouldn’t hesitate to recommend it to someone just starting in the genre either. James and Rebecca Collins, the writer and programmer for the game, are already working on a free DLC case, which he describes as “a stand-alone case that uses everything we learned from the base game to make something special.” If it’s anything like the main story, fans are in for a treat.

解谜类型的《迈阿密热线》，用骇客的方式解决杀手的战斗。
设计思路好评，但入手需要三思。
美术和音乐都保留了迈阿密的风格，整体赶不上原作魔性迷幻的程度，但多了一些精致和规整。自动调节视角的3D俯视角地图，大量与地图叙事符合的细节和小物件。
实际游玩体验只能说比较一般，主要是机制和关卡设计不是特别搭。骇入能力经常需要很繁复的观察和操作，可收益却并不高。
你一顿操作，猛猛连了一堆线，最后只干死一个小怪。实际上你冲上去给他一枪，也是一样的效果。那请问这个连线的乐趣在哪呢？
部分位置可以通过连线油桶或者特殊机关，造成多人击杀，倒是挺爽。
但尴尬的来了，你骇入可以引爆油桶，我手枪也可以。是看不起美式居合吗？
部分位置需要用连线来开门，不连过不去。
可这又会稍微有点打断战斗的节奏，变成了一种强制的解谜环节。
由于游戏战斗节奏快，被多人发现很容易暴毙，那么死一次需要从头开始。
如果从头开始又要去连那些复杂的线，反复来几次，就会让人不是很想继续玩了。
（尤其是在连线正反馈不高的情况下）
很多麻烦的关卡，我会宁可掏枪上去莽一波，莽过了爽，可以不用连线了；莽不过再来一把。
总而言之，感觉游戏的各种细节和规格是到位的，很有气质的一款独游。
但是在“好玩”这一块，还需要针对关卡设计进行大量打磨。

I *really* loved this game at the start and middle. I played the Druid class and while I was disappointed at the staggering cooldown of my ability with no way to lower it, I rolled with it, and had so much fun setting up elaborate potions systems.

The art style is adorable, it's cosy and fun, the sound effects are brilliant and I found both figuring out potions myself and using walkthroughs both enjoyable ways to play the game. Weapon upgrades are smooth progression-wise and rewarding to unlock, side quests are cute and fun for the most part, and genuinely the gameplay and little story are both extremely solid.

However I do have one major gripe, and it's what made me drop the game.

Unfortunately after I unlocked what I realised would be the last shop size upgrade, I immediately fell off. My goal with any game like this is to optimise and automate the hell out of it, and when I realised there would never be enough space physically for me to create the lines of automation I wanted (to be able to have a different station to make every single potion type), I dropped the game like a stone and haven't touched it since. It's a huge shame because it's [i]such[/i] a simple fix. All I needed was more space upgrades and this game shoots from a 7 to a 9. But without it, I can't ever achieve the dream - at least my dream - and it killed my enjoyment like a bullet to the head.

If you're someone who enjoys a cozier take on automation and dig a unique spin on the fantasy aesthetic, I would highly recommend this game. Just beware going into it with the expectation that you can achieve perfect automation.

A well-written, well-researched, and touching visual novel set in a fictionalised version of World War I.
Because We're Here bills itself as an otome game, but there isn't too much romance - at least, not in the first instalment. There is, however, a very large cast of well-designed and nicely-drawn male characters with diverse personalities for the heroine to interact with, and you get a few sweet scenes with them depending on your choices (of which there are quite a lot).

It's an indie VN, but it was obviously put together with love and affection. The writing is very polished, and though it covers some pretty grim subject matters it's filled with deadpan/sarcastic humour that stops it being too depressing. The writing reminds me a lot of the Blackadder comedy series, which was probably intentional.
The characters are very varied, and they all have their own philosophies on the war: some are very gung-ho about the prospect of murdering their enemies, others want to fight for the prestige/social status, and others want to be left out of it altogether. All these different responses to the war are explored, and there's some thought-provoking stuff in here.
The character art is very soft and subdued, which suits the maudlin setting, and it's anime influenced, but not so anime as to be unfitting. I think it's impressive that, with such a huge cast of characters, everybody looks distinct and unique.
The backgrounds lack detail and are pretty blurry, but the sprites are the main focus anyway, and they're serviceable.

Honestly, the worst part of this story is that I want to know what happens next...! Part one isn't too long, and feels more like an introductory prologue to a wider epic than a stand-alone story. It also ends on a bit of a cliffhanger. Fortunately, after checking the developer's tumblr, it looks like the second part is already written, and they're waiting on art assets, so if the first 'episode' sells well and gets good reviews, it should be out much quicker.

I'm hoping that more people give this story a shot, and write positive things about it, so I can read the rest...!
It seems like later chapters will include new characters who offer yet more alternate viewpoints on the war, such as 'enemy' soldiers, so it'll be nice seeing more dimensions to the conflict and how everything unfolds~

[h1]Review with accompanying screenshots and videos in Sinical Network[/h1]
https://www.sinicalanimenetwork.com/post/because-we-re-here-act-1-quick-thoughts

[i]Because We're Here[/i] is an episodic World War I inspired otome visual novel with romance, slice of life and thriller elements. It features a female postal worker, Elfriede Rauss, who works in the small town of Boschberg. When her co-worker and all the young, healthy men in her town enlist in the Wesslinger army to fight a war with another powerful country, everything in her life changes.

Act 1 covers her daily life as a postal worker, getting to know all the young bachelors in town, and eventually joining them in the war as a messenger for Eighth Company. Act 2 covers the drama and intrigue among Eighth Company as the Wesslinger army and their Etgoesian allies are engaged in a war with Leyland and Levasseur with some backdoor diplomacy among the rank and file soldiers on both sides.

This visual novel is an indie production using the Renpy engine, so it has to rely on the plot and diversity of characters to bring out the storyline, and route variety to make up for the average classical background music and artwork. There is a published community guide to help players get all achievements in the least number of playthroughs.

Act 1 is a bit short and generic as it takes the time to introduce the first set of characters in the story (Around 3 hours), whereas Act 2 is considerably longer with plenty of suspense, thrills, addition and removal of some characters (Around 7 hours).

After obtaining all achievements in act 1 and 2, the romance feels rather rushed as many of the specific character routes only have a few scenes before the protagonist and the chosen character confess their feelings for each other. Still, the large variety of characters with different personalities and backgrounds to pursue a romance more than makes up for this part.

As for the drama and thriller aspects, it has good scriptwriting to keep the reader interested in reading the story because every character, including the protagonist, has at least a flaw or weakness somewhere. There are no Rambos or Mary Sues as the protagonist can be shot dead for failing at a battle of wits minigame, and some characters will also inevitably meet their end in an ongoing war in the trenches against an equally powerful and well-equipped army.

Defections, collusions, and getting to know certain individuals on the enemy side (also hinting at possible romance options in subsequent acts) are described in vivid detail in act 2. Therefore, I can recommend this game with the act 2 DLC anytime, and hope to see the next two acts released in future.

Path of the Midnight Sun è stata una delle sorprese più piacevoli che abbia trovato su Steam. Un titolo capace di unire la profondità narrativa di una Visual Novel con le meccaniche tattiche e gestionali di un RPG a turni, dando vita a un'esperienza unica e curata nei minimi dettagli. Fin dai primi minuti, il gioco trasmette passione e dedizione. La storia è eccezionale, piena di colpi di scena, momenti toccanti e personaggi incredibilmente ben scritti. Il mio preferito è Shiori, un personaggio che spicca per sensibilità, spessore e sviluppo emotivo. Le musiche meritano un plauso speciale: ogni brano si adatta perfettamente al tono della scena, amplificando emozioni e tensione nei momenti chiave. La colonna sonora è splendida e rende l'atmosfera ancora più coinvolgente. Ho inoltre molto apprezzato la linea ironica di alcuni dialoghi: nelle situazioni più intense spuntano battute leggere o scambi sarcastici che spezzano con gusto la tensione, mostrando che il gioco sa essere divertente senza perdere profondità. Il gameplay è profondo e vario. I combattimenti a turni sono strategici e ben bilanciati, con un sistema che valorizza la pianificazione e la sinergia tra i membri del gruppo. Un elemento che ho apprezzato moltissimo è la possibilità di scegliere quattro supporti da un roster di alleati diversi, ognuno dotato di abilità attive e passive uniche che influenzano lo scontro in modi sempre nuovi. E' una meccanica intelligente che aggiunge una dimensione tattica in più alle battaglie. Fuori dal combattimento, il gioco offre sistemi di gestione del morale e delle relazioni tra i personaggi, che influiscono realmente sulla storia e sulle prestazioni in battaglia. Sul piano tecnico, Path of the Midnight Sun è ben ottimizzato, con una direzione artistica di grande fascino, doppiaggio di qualità professionale, e un'interfaccia chiara e intuitiva. Tutto comunica la cura e la passione con cui è stato realizzato. In sintesi, Path of the Midnight Sun è un piccolo capolavoro indipendente, capace di fondere alla perfezione narrazione profonda, atmosfera e strategia. Consigliatissimo a chi ama le Visual Novel con elementi RPG tattici, ma anche a chi cerca un'esperienza coinvolgente e ricca di emozioni.

The Silent Age is a bit of a personal time-travel experience for me, since I bought it back in 2017 for less than a dollar on sale, and then completely forgot about it.

Eight years ago I was interested in different games and was heavily limited by my potato laptop, so everything I collected back then was rather "primitive" in terms of using my GPU and focused on narrative, so I could play it even at 10 FPS without missing the point.

Now, in 2025, my tastes have changed a bit, but I kept noticing The Silent Age silently waiting for my attention for ages (pun intended). So I decided: why not? And I didn't expect it to be this good! I've been into time-travel stuff since childhood, and things like Back to the Future amazed me a long time ago, but then I just... forgot?

Gameplay is pretty straightforward here, but I'll be honest, sometimes I had to read through guides to get things done, because of how unobvious the logic was to me personally. But I guess that's the flaw of all point-and-click games: you can't always expect all players to follow the same logic as the developer intended, and from time to time you'll just click around, hoping that it'll work.

But the story is perfect! It's not too long, it never gets boring or dull, the pacing is just right and it gets you hooked, making you want to see the next plot twist waiting for you around the corner!

And that's what makes The Silent Age a great experience: you are not just blindly clicking on screwdrivers and apples to find an entrance to the next room. You are trying to save the world!

Lights, Camera, Curses! is the first of the Nancy Drew Dossier games. While the Dossier games are also made by Her Interactive and have some of the same voice cast, the gameplay is pretty different from the main Nancy Drew series. You're still solving a mystery, but the gameplay is more like a hidden object game than a point and click adventure. 

There are three main gameplay elements. The investigation scenes remind me of hidden object scenes combined with adventure game puzzles. You have to find clues in the hand-drawn background and combine the different elements to deal with obstacles. When a conversation with an NPC comes up, you have to use your knowledge of the story to respond correctly. You also play a few minigames. Solving puzzles correctly and doing well at the minigames allow you to earn points. If you get enough points, you can unlock an alternate ending. 

This game is a lot easier than a regular Nancy Drew game. The story is totally linear and the game moves you to the next scene automatically. The puzzles are fully contained within each scene and were very straightforward. You have so few options that even if you have to guess, you get to the right combination pretty quickly. You do need to be paying attention to the story to do well with the conversations, although you can guess as many times as you want. The minigames were pretty easy but you also don't need to do well on them to move on. The only thing I struggled with were a couple of timed puzzles later in the game, and those just took a second try to solve.

I felt like the story was pretty much on par with the average story in a main series Nancy Drew game. It wasn't anything mind-blowing, but the reveals weren't too obvious and I was interested enough to keep playing. I liked the hand-drawn art style and the Hollywood meets Ancient Egypt aesthetic.

Overall, Lights, Camera, Curses! isn't a regular Nancy Drew game at all, and if you go into it expecting that, you'll be disappointed. However, for a very casual hidden object adventure, it's pretty good. 7/10

Novus Orbis is a striking entry in the roguelike deck-builder genre, offering a thoughtful blend of familiar card-based mechanics with several inventive twists that give the experience a sharp identity of its own. Developed by Seizo Games and published by 2 Left Thumbs, the game opens with a straightforward premise—a hero trapped in a looping cycle of encounters across a mysterious cosmic realm—but quickly reveals a strategic depth that rewards experimentation, planning, and adaptability. Even in its Early Access state, Novus Orbis feels surprisingly refined, supported by a cleverly layered combat system and a strong foundation of cards, blessings, pets, and enemies that establish its long-term potential.

The core gameplay revolves around the interplay between deck construction, combo sequencing, and a unique countdown mechanic that redefines the pace of battles. Each card has both a cost and a combo value, encouraging players to think several steps ahead when deciding what to play and in what order. Executing the right sequence can dramatically amplify your impact in a turn, turning weak individual cards into devastating chains when used together. Layered on top of this is the countdown system—an ever-ticking timer that advances both when you act and when you end your turn. This means that enemies may attack in the middle of your carefully planned sequence, forcing you to constantly evaluate whether pressing your luck or retreating early is the safer strategy. Together, these elements inject tension and urgency into every battle, setting Novus Orbis apart from more methodical, hands-off deck-builders.

Content-wise, the game launches with a surprisingly robust set of tools for players to explore. Two playable classes offer distinct approaches to combat—each with its own suite of cards, resource dynamics, and mechanical quirks. The starting class provides a more straightforward introduction to the game’s systems, while the mage-like class demands careful manipulation of elements and resource decay, creating a deeper puzzle of balancing conditions and planning multi-step turns. More than 200 cards, dozens of blessings, a variety of pets with passive bonuses, and a sizable roster of enemies help give each run its own texture. Blessings persist across runs, providing a meaningful sense of progression, but not so much that they undermine the core roguelike challenge. The developer’s stated roadmap promises additional classes, bosses, card sets, and alternate paths, signaling long-term growth for an already solid foundation.

Visually, Novus Orbis embraces a clean pixel-art aesthetic that fits its cosmic-fantasy theme well. Its minimalist but striking backdrops—evoking nebulas, astral anomalies, and dreamlike realms—support the game’s atmosphere without cluttering the screen with unnecessary detail. The user interface is designed for clarity, with well-organized card descriptions and readable layouts that help players quickly parse their options. While not pushing any graphical boundaries, the art direction complements the gameplay and supports the sense of diving into a surreal world governed by strange cosmic rules. The game’s performance is smooth even on modest hardware, making it accessible for a broad range of players.

However, no Early Access title is without areas that need refinement. Some players have noted that class balancing still needs work, especially for the more complex class whose card pool relies heavily on conditional triggers and resource manipulation. The same complexity that makes this class rewarding also makes it punishing to learn, and runs can fall apart quickly if synergy doesn’t develop. Additionally, while the available card pool is large for an early build, it may still feel limited compared to long-running genre staples—especially for players accustomed to massive card libraries or endless procedural content. The countdown mechanic, while innovative, can also feel unforgiving to those who prefer slower-paced, tactical decision-making. A handful of UI quirks, missing conveniences, and occasional difficulty spikes further remind players that the game is still in active development.

Despite these imperfections, Novus Orbis distinguishes itself through smart ideas, clean execution, and a combat system that feels genuinely fresh. Its blend of pressure-based turn pacing, combo-driven card play, and layered decision-making gives the game a rhythm all its own—one that encourages risk-taking, rewards mastery, and keeps individual encounters tense and engaging. For deck-builder fans looking for something different from the usual cycle of mana curves and passive scaling, Novus Orbis provides a compelling alternative that challenges players to rethink how turns unfold and how synergy is built.

Ultimately, Novus Orbis stands as a promising and already enjoyable entry in the genre. It offers enough content to satisfy early adopters, enough innovation to distinguish itself from competitors, and enough potential to grow into something even more impressive. For players willing to invest in an evolving but already thoughtfully designed roguelike deck-builder, it’s an easy recommendation—and one worth watching closely as its world expands.

Fireside is a gentle, emotionally grounded adventure that prioritizes human connection over danger, combat, or dramatic conflict. Developed by Emergo Entertainment and published by Nordcurrent Labs, it begins with a shipwreck that leaves the protagonist stranded in an unfamiliar land, but instead of treating this as a tale of desperation, the game reframes it as an opportunity for discovery, community, and healing. The world is populated by other wanderers—some cheerful, some uncertain, some carrying quiet burdens—and the player’s role is not to conquer or defeat anything, but to listen, trade, help, and build relationships. Fireside belongs to a growing group of games built around kindness rather than struggle, and it commits fully to that philosophy.

The gameplay loop revolves around travel, campfire conversations, resource gathering, and trading. As you explore the wilderness, you encounter fellow travelers looking for specific items, and through thoughtful exchanges you build goodwill, unlock new dialogue, and slowly learn their histories. Trading isn’t treated as a simple transactional system—it functions like a trust exercise, a way of understanding values and finding mutual benefit. Items aren’t inherently exciting on their own but gain meaning through the people they help. Between journeys, you return to your home camp to rest, reflect, and upgrade your dwelling, gradually transforming your starting space into a nurturing refuge. There is a quiet rhythm to the progression: venture outward, meet someone new, brighten their world, and return to your fire with a bit more understanding than before.

A subtle time structure prevents the game from drifting aimlessly. Each expedition can only last a limited number of days before you must return home, forcing gentle prioritization. This mechanic introduces just enough structure to keep momentum without creating urgency or stress. You don’t rush because the world isn’t hostile, but you do consider how far to travel, who to visit, and what resources to carry. The loop becomes meditative—packing food, planning a route, seeking out someone you promised to help earlier. The simplicity of the systems invites reflection rather than optimization, making the experience approachable and emotionally accessible to a broad range of players.

Fireside’s presentation amplifies its comforting tone. The art style resembles a watercolor storybook, with soft lines, warm palettes, and environments that feel handcrafted rather than procedurally assembled. Characters are designed with personality and visual charm, each immediately recognizable and memorable. Sound design completes the atmosphere: gentle acoustic melodies, nighttime chirps, crackling firewood, and ambient wind reinforce the sense of safety and stillness. Even when exploring unfamiliar territory, the world feels welcoming rather than threatening. The audiovisual direction encourages players to slow down, breathe, and appreciate what surrounds them—a stark contrast to games built around constant stimulation.

The heart of the experience lies in its characters. Fireside’s cast speaks with sincerity rather than dramatic flourish, sharing fears, hopes, regrets, and small joys. Conversations often feel like snippets from real-life encounters—people who reveal themselves one detail at a time, who don’t always know what they want, who express gratitude in unexpected ways. Helping someone isn’t rewarded with flashy fanfare or extravagant upgrades—just a sense of meaningful human acknowledgment. The writing avoids cynicism, instead depicting a world where compassion has weight and where tiny acts of generosity ripple outward. It’s rare for a game to make the player feel not like a hero, but a participant in a shared journey.

Like many cozy narrative-driven games, Fireside risks becoming repetitive over long stretches. The travel structure, trading system, and conversational interactions don’t evolve dramatically, and once you’ve upgraded your home and met most characters, the sense of discovery softens. Players seeking mechanical complexity, branching storylines, or long-term challenge may find the experience too light. But repetition here isn’t necessarily a flaw—it mirrors the comforting familiarity of returning to a favorite campsite, cooking a familiar recipe, or spending another evening with friends. Fireside is built to soothe rather than stimulate, and that clarity of design helps it remain cohesive and intentional.

In the end, Fireside is a celebration of gentleness in a medium often defined by conflict. It invites players to wander without fear, give without expectation, and connect without judgment. Its mechanics are modest, its stakes low, and its pacing slow, but those qualities allow its emotional core to flourish. It is a game for evenings when you want to exhale, for players who crave warmth more than spectacle, and for anyone who believes that kindness can be just as compelling as heroism. Fireside’s world doesn’t ask you to save it—only to be present within it—and that alone makes the journey worthwhile.

"Galaxy Trucker: Extended Edition" ist die Digital-Umsetzung eines erfolgreichen Brettspiels.

2007 erschien das Brettspiel von Vlaada Chvátil. Heute ist es ein moderner Klassiker.

Jeder Spieler ist ein Trucker, der mit seinem Raumschiff durch das All stromert und auf alle möglichen Begegnungen trifft. Zunächst aber muß jeder Spieler sein Raumschiff aus Plättchen zusammenbauen.

Dafür haben wir ein Grid, das je nach Entwicklungsstufe unterschiedlich groß ist. Unter Zeitdruck drehen wir immer ein Plättchen um und müssen entscheiden, ob wir es orthogonal an bereits vorhandene Plättchen anbauen oder es wieder zurück auf den Stapel legen, auf den alle Spieler Zugriff haben.  Dabei sollten wir einige Dinge beachten. 

Zum Einen gibt es unterschiedliche Anschlüsse, die passen müssen, um ein Plättchen anbauen zu dürfen. Offene Anschlüsse an der Außenseite unseres Raumschiffes sollten wir möglichst vermeiden, da sie später noch Probleme bereiten können. Zudem sollten wir möglichst eine ausgewogene Mischung an Plättchen verbauen, um möglichst unbeschadet und ertragreich durchs All zu kommen. 

Wir brauchen Stationen, um mehr Besatzung zu haben, Lagerräume, um wertvolle Güter zu transportieren, Waffen, um Gegner und Meteoriten abzuwehren, Antriebe, um voranzukommen, Batterien, um besonders starke Waffen oder Antriebe zu betreiben und noch so manche sinnvolle Verbindungen. 

Haben wir das Schiff fertig gebaut oder ist uns beim Bauen die Zeit ausgegangen, haben wir die erste Hälfte des Spiels geschafft. Dann geht es auf eine Reise, in der wir nur noch wenig entscheiden können, aber die wir am Besten überstehen, wenn wir unser Schiff möglichst gut gebaut haben. 

Im zweiten Teil des Spiels werden nacheinander eine bestimmte Anzahl von Karten aufgedeckt. Jede Karte ist eine Begegnung. Das können zum Beispiel Meteoritenschauer oder Gegner sein, die unser Schiff beschädigen können. Wir können auch auf ein verlassenes Schiff stoßen, auf das wir unsere Besatzung schicken können, wenn wir denn genug Besatzung mitgenommen haben. Oder wir treffen auf Planeten, von denen wir Güter mitnehmen können. 

Am Ende einer Reise, wenn alle Karten gespielt sind, gibt es eine Schlußwertung und unsere Güter werden verkauft. Wer dann am meisten Credits hat, hat diese Runde gewonnen. 

Das Spiel ist eine ungewöhnliche Mischung aus Aufbau und Zufall. In der ersten Phase ist unser Geschick unter Zeitdruck gefragt. In der zweiten Phase müssen wir oft die Begegnungen hinnehmen und ertragen. Dabei spielt oft der Zufall eine große Rolle. Wo uns Meteoriten treffen wird zum Beispiel durch einen Würfelwurf entschieden. Wir konnten lediglich in der ersten Phase unser Schiff möglichst gut bauen, um gegen potentielle Gefahren möglichst gut gewappnet zu sein. 

Diese Art Spiel ist nicht für jeden was, kann aber in der richtigen Gruppe sehr viel Spaß machen. Und das ist auch schon mein größtes Problem mit der Digital-Umsetzung. Technisch funktioniert sie gut, aber das Spiel lebt eigentlich vor allem von der Schadenfreude der Anderen und vom Trash-Talk am Tisch. Diese Art Spiel eignet sich eigentlich weniger für eine Digital-Umsetzung. 

Die Bildsprache des Originals wird in der Digitalversion eins zu eins übernommen. Und sogar die Musik ist nett und erträglich. Die KI ist nicht die beste, aber immerhin gibt es unterschiedliche Schwierigkeitsstufen. Dazu sind noch Alien-Technologien am Start, die als Brettspiel eine Erweiterung waren. Und es gibt eine Art Kampagne, die zufällig Missionen aneinanderreiht.

This is a perfect little game for when you don't want to think too much and you just want to dive into some oldschool, turn-based JRPG action. Very little in the way of hand-holding save for some early advice, and then suddenly there's way more options than you were planning for. A bunch of different classes to put into your party, or you can go it solo -- and oh yeah, there's a random version of the game that it doesn't even tell you exists that you can just... go into, instead of the main quest.

This game is simple, effective, and does what it set out to do well.

Somewhere in between Final Fantasy 1 and the gameboy Final Fantasies, it's an 8-bit dungeon crawler that wants you to get into the meat of customizing your stats and ability loadout within that format.

Gear isn't always a straight upgrade. There's multiple ways to build each class. You get a huge selection of classes right out of the gate. The overall difficulty level is modest if you're used to NES rpgs and maybe a bit hard if you're not.

It's a very particular type of game done well, although I do have some small complaints. You're in and out of menus a lot doing healing. Resources are actually pretty tight. You can absolutely pick the wrong starting team comp, and some classes are way worse than others. Mage, of all things, has been atrocious, whereas thief has carried my party on its back. Because of the slow progression, you will not notice this before it is too late.

I do think Scarmonde could have benefited from some modern rpg features like after battle heals and non-random encounters, as this would have let its design shine a little more. But it's genuinely fine as is.

If you're feeling that retro rpg hunger, this is a good pick. If you haven't played a retro rpg before, this might be a little rough as a start, but not impossible. Either way, the dev seems cool and I hope they'll elaborate on what's here with another title.

Edit: Not entirely bug free. I got a white screen off of selecting a heal spell and pressing a directional button on the same frame during my out of battle menuing. I could still move around and select things, but the screen was white and I couldn't see anything.

Gameplay: Rhythm, Reaction, and Rampage

The genius of One Finger Death Punch lies in its singular mechanic. Your stick-figure protagonist stands in the center of the screen, and enemies approach from the left and the right. You press the left button to attack enemies on the left, and the right button to attack enemies on the right. That’s it.

However, the game demands precision. Attacks only land when an enemy is within the strike zone (indicated by a color change). The core challenge is maintaining a flowing, often frantic rhythm, requiring you to read the stream of enemies and execute your two-button sequence with perfect timing. A mistimed strike results in a delay and a punishing loss of health, forcing players into a trance-like state where visual and auditory cues merge into a single, kinetic flow state.

As the game progresses, it introduces 26 different weapon types—from swords and nun-chucks to lightsabers and chainsaws—as well as various enemy types that require specific numbers of hits or precise execution, constantly refreshing the core challenge.

Content and Progression

The game's progression map is surprisingly dense for such a seemingly simple arcade title. The main campaign consists of over 100 levels, each with unique modifiers, goals, or game types. These include:

Standard Levels: Pure two-button brawling.

Skill Challenges: Levels where only certain weapons are available or environmental hazards are present.

Brawler Levels: Where the pace slows down, and you must rapidly track a crosshair to hit targets precisely.

Boss Fights: Unique challenges that break the two-button convention and test your reflexes in new ways.

Success unlocks powerful, passive Skills (e.g., increased speed, extra lives, weapon longevity) that fundamentally change the flow of combat. The depth here is in learning which skills pair best with which types of levels, allowing for significant replayability.

Aesthetics and Presentation

Visually, One Finger Death Punch is minimalist yet effective. The world is rendered in a simple, clean stick-figure style, which serves a crucial purpose: it keeps the screen clear of unnecessary visual clutter, allowing the player to focus entirely on the timing cues.

This simplicity is violently juxtaposed against the hyper-stylized action. Bodies explode into chunks, blood sprays across the arena, and the sheer volume of chaotic motion is often hilarious. This cartoon violence, combined with a pounding techno soundtrack and satisfying, crunchy sound effects, creates an exhilarating and highly stylized package that perfectly suits the game's frantic pace.

Conclusion

One Finger Death Punch is not just a game; it's a test of rhythm, reaction, and focus. It’s the kind of game you load up for "just five minutes" and suddenly realize an hour has vanished. It perfectly executes its vision, proving that sophisticated fun doesn't require complicated controls. For anyone looking for an intensely satisfying, highly replayable, and endlessly entertaining brawler experience that you can play with literally just two fingers, this is an essential purchase.

It's a very rare thing that I leave a negative review or request a refund, but on this occasion I'm afraid it's got to be done.

The idea of the game is a good one; random battles with different classes of spaceships with different loadouts and stats, one of which is supposedly a Battle Royale mode. 

The reality? Every single vessel from a fighter up to the biggest cap ship dances around like...a fighter, while being ridiculously hard to hit and having the health of a rhino's backside. The 'Battle Royale' mode is just a big scrap with 40 ships where you're locked to one of three 'Decimator' classes.

The controls are fine with a gamepad but abysmal with mouse and keyboard. Mapping strafe to A and D but having the arrow keys as your steering? Bad move.

I know that making a game isn't an easy thing and I don't doubt that the dev put some real effort into this. Perhaps with a LOT more time in the oven it could be shaped into something much better, but as it is it just isn't fun to play.

Advice to the dev: 
- Get the core mechanics of the gameplay locked down. Cruisers should not be flying around like starfighters. Starfighters should not take hundreds of shots to kill. 
- Give some 'feel' to the weapons; let the player know they're actually hitting something instead of just a little flash of the shields buckling. If you ever played something like FreeSpace or Colony Wars, you'll know what I mean by that.
- Expand the game modes, because what you have is basically several variations of a theme. Make that false 'Battle Royale' into an actual one where you have to roam a map, upgrading your ship and picking your fights carefully. A space version of that would be insanely cool.
- Add more weapon variety. A bunch of lasers and one missile type does not a good weapon roster make.
- Fix the KB/mouse controls. Mouse to steer would work a LOT better.

Planetiles, developed and published by MythicOwl, is a deceptively gentle strategy puzzler that takes the familiar joy of tile placement and expands it across entire planets. At first glance, it may resemble other hex-based building games, but its cosmic scale and ecological focus give it a distinct identity. The player isn’t building cities for people or infrastructure for industry—rather, they are restoring life to barren celestial bodies by arranging terrain, growing biomes, and responding to each planet’s natural challenges. The premise feels refreshingly hopeful: success is not defined by maximizing output or exploiting resources, but by fostering balance, expansion, and harmony. That emotional tone makes Planetiles immediately inviting, even before the puzzle mechanics reveal their depth.

The visual presentation is clean and elegant, favoring readability over spectacle. Each planet appears almost like a living board game suspended in space—rotating spheres covered in hexagonal possibilities. The soft color palette differentiates grasslands, deserts, forests, glaciers, lakes, and volcanic regions without overwhelming the senses, ensuring every placement feels intentional. The sound design reinforces this peaceful, constructive atmosphere. Music is ambient and unobtrusive, guiding players into the rhythm of thoughtful planning rather than pushing urgency or tension. It’s the kind of game where you settle in, breathe, and enjoy watching ecosystems grow from random tile fragments into cohesive environments.

Mechanically, Planetiles thrives on clarity and constraint. Every run begins with a limited selection of tiles pulled from a randomized deck. Players must place them on the planetary surface in a way that maximizes synergy—forests thrive near water, certain structures require specific terrain, and special objectives demand careful spatial planning. Completing planetary quests unlocks score multipliers, bonus tiles, and biome expansions, giving each successful placement a satisfying domino effect. This design encourages strategic foresight, because while any tile can technically be placed anywhere, optimal positioning determines whether the planet thrives or stagnates. Runs rarely feel identical thanks to tile randomness, shifting objectives, and new planetary layouts, allowing replayability without overwhelming complexity.

However, randomization is a double-edged sword. While it keeps sessions fresh and encourages adaptability, some players may find themselves waiting for a tile type that simply refuses to appear. This introduces a degree of luck that can derail well-planned strategies. The game compensates with mitigation tools—rerolls, bonus effects, and quest rewards—but those who prefer full tactical control may occasionally feel constrained. That said, Planetiles treats failure as a learning experience rather than a punishment. Runs are short enough that restarting never feels discouraging, and earning better results becomes a natural incentive rather than a forced grind.

As progression continues, planets become larger, biome combinations more intricate, and objectives more demanding. The increasing difficulty feels organic rather than abrupt, giving players space to refine their understanding of tile relationships and long-term planning. Unlike city builders or colony sims, Planetiles does not burden the player with management systems like population, maintenance, or economics. Its challenge remains firmly rooted in spatial reasoning, pattern recognition, and puzzle-solving intuition. That purity is one of its greatest strengths—it distills world-building into its most thoughtful and satisfying components.

Despite its focused design, some players may crave additional modes, modifiers, or visual variety over time. The core gameplay loop remains consistent across multiple runs, and while planets differ in shape and objective demands, the experience is intentionally meditative rather than dramatically evolving. But this restraint seems intentional—Planetiles is meant to be returned to in quiet moments, like a favorite tabletop puzzle or a guided creative exercise. It values replay comfort over constant escalation, and for many players, that approach will feel refreshing rather than limiting.

Ultimately, Planetiles succeeds because it understands what makes tile-based puzzles compelling: the joy of shaping something beautiful piece by piece, the satisfaction of making space work efficiently, and the quiet pride of watching chaos transform into harmony. It invites contemplation rather than urgency and rewards both experimentation and precision. For players who enjoy Dorfromantik, Islanders, or board-game-inspired logic experiences, this is a natural fit—but it also stands confidently on its own. MythicOwl has crafted a thoughtful, soothing, and subtly challenging game that encourages creativity without overwhelming the player.

Planetiles may not appeal to those seeking fast-paced strategy, narrative-heavy progression, or sprawling simulation systems, but for puzzle enthusiasts, spatial thinkers, or anyone looking for a calming world-building experience, it offers something rare: planetary restoration as a gentle, satisfying act of play.

Rating: 7/10

[h1]Introduction[/h1]

First off, I highly recommend you check out my [url=http://steamcommunity.com/groups/Sentinels_of_the_Store#announcements/detail/1430307963815774414]SOS post[/url] on this game as that delves into more of the "behind the scenes actions" that have been occuring with the game, this review will mainly focus on the game it's self and if it has any redeeming qualities. [spoiler]it doesn't[/spoiler]

[h1]Review[/h1]

Celestial Creator's premise is primarily to act as a form of construction based game where you're placed in a world with over 300 materials at your disposal to create what you want. The game also has a number of asteroid belts that you can toggle that can come and destroy builds that you've made and as an extra challenge, the player can protect the builds they've made with the protector build of the main character. On the topic of character builds, there are different types of character builds that can be toggled with the numerical keys, there is protector mode, explorer mode, fly mode, buggy mode and big buggy mode. Protector mode as described before is used if you toggle the asteroid attacks, you're given a gun and you have to shoot them before they come into contact with anything. Explorer mode is basically a build of the character where you can run around the map and basically do nothing. There is additionally contruction mode which is the build in which you can place down different material blocks. The other modes are self explanatory in which you're given the applicable vehicle and you get to drive that around the map.

One big huge flaw of a construction based game is when you're extremely limited in the ways that you can actually construct something, and this is where Celestial Creator mostly falls flat. Now, like I said, there are over 300 materials at your disposal, but here's the thing, if you try and place a material ontop of something else, it will simply mirror the material that you placed it ontop of, regardless of what material you're holding. For example, if you want to place a stone block ontop of a grass block, you can't, instead when you try to place the block down, all you will end up with is a grass block ontop of a grass block. As you can imagine, with this being apparent, the game becomes extremely limited in what it is that you can construct. As a result of you basically being unable to construct much towards your desires (unless you like creating towers of grass blocks) you can't really construct much, taking a lot of the possible fun out of the protector mode as well, since there is not much of a risk as a result of any failures you may have.

As for the vehicle modes, they're incredibly glitchy, especially the jeeps as there is a good 80% chance that when you hit certain speed limits on the vehicles, the vehicle will glitch out and throw you off the map and will cause a reload behind a really long load screen (and yes, all load screens in this game are very long.)

Additionally, something else that I want to bring up is the control scheme in the game, as this was probably the best part of the whole game, and you might be thinking how can a control scheme be the stand out feature of the game? When the control scheme makes no sense at all and the sheer inexperience with the control scheme actually makes you laugh with confusion as to why someone would think this was a good control scheme. Here are a few stand out hotkeys that the game has to perform certain actions:

[list]
[*]To initiate the asteroid waves, the player has to press "page up" to go to the next wave and "page down" to go to the previous wave.
[*]When in protector mode, the player has to hold down "Alt" to run instead of "Shift"
[*]To actually change the settings in the game, such as the quality of the game to get a better performance, you have to click "="
[*]To actually see the control scheme in it's entirety, and by that I mean to understand how to really perform any actions in the game at all, you have to press "\"
[/list]

This game has no real redeemable qualities, and is definitely not worth the £10 base price.

Final verdict: 1/10

This sounds like other dungeon games where you make minions, traps, raid towns ect. This is NOT the case with this game. There are no traps at all at the current time and the minions you can make you cannot control other than to send them on a raid. When your dungeon gets raided you cannot tell them to target one enemy and they will randomly target enemy units (even when one is near death they will target full health ones). 

When your minions (drones) harvest resources they leave it on the floor and the game makes you click on each resource stack to let the drone know it needs to be put in your treasury (not sure why other than the game just does not have enough to do if you didn't have to focus on that). 

This game is an idle clicker with a tiny bit thrown in to make it seem like it could be something else. I would very strongly suggest to anyone that they watch gameplay before purchase as I went in under the impression it was an RTS as the game tries to market itself that way. While it is a good (in my opinion) idle clicker, it is NOT an RTS and marketing it as such will likely make people angry they were mislead (like I am).

I am refunding this and am recommending people not to buy it as, I previously stated, the game is NOT an RTS and does not appear to be even trying to go that way at all.

As of right now I can't recommend the game just due to the shear amount of bugs in what looks to be a very early alpha stage of release. 

That said the game play for me was a 4 step cycle:
1.) Build something 
2.) Hire Minion
3.) Get attacked, watch minion not fight and die,  lose resources
4.) Repeat 1 or 2 until 3 happens. 

While I would like to hold on to it, I really can't justify it as at the core it is an idle clicker game, something you might play on a phone or tablet when you have some free time, but nothing else. In no way is it a RTS or anything like an RTS. I wish this was made far more clear in their description as I wouldn't have purchased it.

真神作，我玩过的最精彩的群像剧之一，08年的“老”作品，但放在当下依然毫不过时的必玩悬疑游戏。虽然采用了真人演绎的方式，但演员颜值高，表演自然用心，不用担心会看着尴尬。428是一部能够体现游戏与电影、电视剧不同，可以被称为“第九艺术”的代表作品，我们做出的选择影响着该角色，通过该角色的行动又间接影响着涉谷的其他人和事，演绎着不同的结局，完美展示了“蝴蝶效应”。前期和角色一起探索谜团，后期上帝视角串联伏笔，这是游戏才能带来的激动。
       不同于其他的视觉小说或者互动游戏，在428中，看似再微小不过的一个选择，都会产能不可估量的影响，感觉到我们（玩家）真的对这个故事、这个世界产生着影响，就像游戏结尾“这一定是命运。而且还不止是一个人的命运。是由众多人们的命运相交，偶然才变成了必然”。
       很难得剧情上整体非常积极向上，一群人中二热血又阳光的拯救涉谷的理想主义故事。更难得的是没有什么刻板影响和低俗烂梗，总的来说大家都是有缺点有不足，会吵架有矛盾的普通人，但又热爱涉谷、热爱生命，热爱家人、热爱朋友，可能不符合某些人口味，但看完真的心里暖暖的。428生动的展示了不是非要黑深残才能写出好故事。

Oh boy. Where do I begin with this game?

What started as a somewhat simple spooky thing to play while I chatted with friends on Discord during October, ended up becoming an incredibly enjoyable ride all the way through the end, and then some!

Coming from someone that is not very involved with the indie horror scene, or horror games in general, the Catto Boi series as a whole has been the most unexpected thing for me to play this year.


[h3]So what there is to say about this spooky cat game?[/h3]

Admittedly, it's not the best thing ever made. In fact, it can be quite rough at some points, mostly some bugs here and there. 

At no point these issues will be detrimental to the experience though. The game runs fine, controls are very nice and fluid (specially on later games in the series). Some sections can be slightly challenging. But if you're not new to the genre, it'll be a breeze. It's a simple, yet fun platformer overall.


As for the horror aspect... There are scarier things out there. But horror, just like humor, can be very subjective/personal. So YMMV here. It has it's moments, some of the scares are really goofy, but well-timed. 
It will manage to catch you off-guard sometimes. 
Your first play-through will be your most impactful in my opinion. I recommend to come in blind on this one!

Also since this is a meta horror/4th wall break game, it will require you to know how to navigate your system's directories and how to deal with files and folders in order to progress. Nothing crazy advanced though, If you've played this kind of games before you probably know this anyway.

To add to this: There's also a fair share of tiny details and easter eggs scattered about both in and out of each game. So if you're particularly curious, it will reward and amuse/horrify you in unexpected ways. 


The story is at a minimum, interesting. It's not peak writing but it's interesting enough to keep you wanting to know what's going to happen next. It's a matter of taste, I suppose. 
But to me it was pretty decent. It kept me engaged without overstaying it's welcome. 

I know for sure the characters, story, music ([i]SPECIALLY[/i] the music, the OST is one of the highest highlights of this game!) and overall theme of the games did earn a Big Boi-sized place in my heart. 

Not many games leave me with such a long lasting impression in me. But this one managed, oh boy it [i]managed.[/i]

The whole thing is a huge passion project, and at some points, even a love letter to simpler times for some of us. [i]Made with [b]Love./..../[/b] indeed...[/i]

[h3]Certainly recommended!*[/h3]

[i]*If you think the Collection price on Steam might be a bit too much, the games are also available separately in other storefronts. But by all means do yourself a favor and give this game series a shot. The developer most definitely deserves the support![/i]

This is the implementation of the board game with the same name. I think it is very well implemented, with a lot of care given tho quality of life (for example, if you must select a dice based on certain criteria while only one dice fit this criteria, the game automatically select it and move on to the next step). Personally, I prefer the video game because I play it faster, by losing less time on manual actions.

About the game design itself : the mechanics are pretty fun. They are about controlling the dice randomness through tactical use of your powers, items and level-up bonuses. With good enough strategy, you will get enough dices, with the appropriate colors and values to successfully pass each challenge. Passing the challenge is usually easy. The difficult part is actually taking the least possible amount of damage.

Each hero start with a different set of dices (distributed between yellow, red and blue) and a power to change the dice throw results (e.g. : re-throw a dice, change its color or its value). How to get stronger throughout the dungeon will dictate if you can reach the end and win against the dungeon boss.

Each hero get experience after a dungeon exploration, that you can spend to make it a little more powerful next time.

I played this for about 6 months, and while it lasted I enjoyed it. I quit since about a year though. Loved the more mature content, the Soviet Russian atmosphere (Empire) and the character models with animations that were all properly done in motion capture. I quit playing over a couple reasons, that can probably be applied to most MMOs:
- Time consuming
- Low population and toxic end-game community (much worse on EU server)
- Must join guild or miss content
- High monetary cost to stay competitive (especially in PvP)
- Daily quests that compel one to keep playing
- EU/EN version is several months behind the RU updates

In conclusion, this is a nice polished free game to pass some time, so long one doesn't push to become competitive. Overall it looks like World of Warcraft (mostly the UI), but skill system, art design, story and atmosphere couldn't be more different. Recommended for casuals that don't mind dated cartoony graphics, and adult content.

Toki Tori 2+ is what happens when a puzzle-platformer grows up, gains confidence and decides to trust its players far more than most modern games dare. Two Tribes’ sequel abandons the tidy, ability-based structure of the original in favor of a grand, interconnected world governed entirely by environmental logic and two deceptively simple actions: a stomp and a whistle. It’s a bold shift, one that pays off beautifully if you’re willing to meet the game on its own terms.

The genius of Toki Tori 2+ lies in its subtlety. Nothing is explained. Tutorials don’t exist. Instead, you learn the “rules of nature” by observing how creatures react to your sounds, how they move, what they fear and how they can be manipulated to open new paths. This quiet, curiosity driven learning evokes the sense of discovery found in early Nintendo design; an elegant, wordless dialogue between player and game.

The world itself is charming without ever feeling saccharine: lush forests, glowing caverns and strange, melodic wildlife. Beneath that adorable surface, though, the puzzles can be fiendish. Solutions often hinge on understanding cause-and-effect chains across the environment, and the game’s refusal to hold your hand can frustrate players expecting a gentler ride. Yet when a revelation hits, when a sequence suddenly snaps into place, the satisfaction is exceptional.

The nonlinear structure also means exploration feels meaningful. You’re not completing “levels” but gradually untangling a dense, interconnected ecosystem. Backtracking, once you internalize new mechanics, becomes a pleasure rather than a chore.

Toki Tori 2+ isn’t for everyone; its quiet confidence and lack of exposition may alienate those who prefer more explicit guidance. But for players who appreciate games that respect their intelligence and reward patient observation with genuine, hard earned insights, it’s a standout.

A dense, thoughtful and unexpectedly profound puzzle adventure concealed inside a cute bird’s journey.

Gahkthun of the Golden Lightning, developed by Liar-soft and published by MangaGamer, is a rich, imaginative steampunk visual novel that immerses players in a world where science and mysticism coexist under the flickering glow of mechanical marvels. Set in 1908 on the massive artificial island of Marseille Offshore Academia, the story unfolds in an alternate historical reality where engines run on arcane power and human ambition collides with divine mystery. It is a world of innovation and oppression, of hidden conspiracies and fragile ideals, where technology and human spirit intertwine in an intricate dance. At its heart lies a compelling tale of rebellion and discovery, anchored by a mysterious transfer student—Nikola Tesla—whose arrival upends the carefully controlled order of the academy and ignites a chain of events that challenge the power of the elite and the boundaries of human potential.

The narrative begins with Neon Scalar Smilja, a quiet and unassuming student whose life changes the day Tesla strides into her classroom. A figure shrouded in myth and confidence, Tesla’s proclamation of war against the corrupt ruling council of the academy draws Neon into his orbit and sets the stage for a sweeping tale that balances grand steampunk spectacle with intimate moments of human emotion. The story is presented in episodic form, with each chapter unfolding as a self-contained mystery or “case” that gradually builds toward a larger confrontation between Tesla and the forces governing the world. The structure allows the story to explore a range of tones—from suspense and philosophical reflection to humor and friendship—without losing sight of its central themes of resistance and enlightenment.

One of the most striking qualities of Gahkthun is its ability to weave an atmosphere that feels both wondrous and oppressive. The setting of the Marseille Academia is beautifully realized, a floating city of steam and gears that embodies the contradictions of the era it depicts. It is a place where students pursue scientific advancement but remain bound by rigid hierarchies and unseen political machinations. The visual presentation captures this duality perfectly: richly detailed backgrounds depict glowing laboratories, gothic halls, and stormy skylines, while the vibrant character art brings personality and life to each scene. The visual design maintains a balance between elegance and complexity, drawing the player into a world that feels lived-in, intricate, and distinct from the generic settings of many visual novels.

The writing carries the unmistakable touch of Liar-soft’s narrative style—dense, lyrical, and philosophical, yet peppered with humor and eccentricity. The story alternates between moments of high drama and quieter introspection, often pausing to explore the beliefs and motivations of its characters. Tesla himself is written as both an idealist and a visionary, a man burdened by genius and purpose, while Neon serves as a grounding presence, her perspective giving the player a more human lens through which to view the extraordinary events around her. Their dynamic forms the emotional core of the narrative: Tesla’s unwavering conviction contrasted with Neon’s curiosity and doubt creates a compelling relationship that evolves as the story progresses. Through their interactions, the novel explores questions of progress, faith, individuality, and the cost of knowledge.

The supporting cast adds color to the story, though not all characters receive equal attention. Some of the side characters stand out for their distinct quirks and backstories, while others fade once their specific chapter concludes. This uneven characterization, while occasionally noticeable, does little to undermine the novel’s overall charm. Each character represents a different facet of the world’s moral and ideological complexity, whether it be a cynical bureaucrat, an idealistic inventor, or a student caught between rebellion and obedience. The interplay between these figures helps reinforce the novel’s exploration of how systems of power shape individuals and the ways in which people resist or succumb to them.

Structurally, Gahkthun functions more as a kinetic novel than a branching visual novel. Player choices are minimal, and the story follows a largely linear path from beginning to end. While this may disappoint players seeking a highly interactive experience, the linearity serves the storytelling well, ensuring that pacing and tone remain consistent. The episodic structure, however, can sometimes lead to uneven pacing; the early chapters are brisk and engaging, while the middle sections slow down as the narrative detours into side stories that, though thematically relevant, may feel tangential to the main plot. The finale, however, ties these threads together with satisfying grandeur, blending emotional resolution with the kind of mythic spectacle that defines Liar-soft’s best works.

The production quality is impressive for a visual novel of its age and scope. The art direction is lush and atmospheric, with striking use of color and composition that complements the steampunk setting. The Japanese voice acting is consistently strong, lending authenticity and emotional depth to every scene, while the soundtrack enhances the sense of drama and mystery. The music shifts seamlessly between haunting melodies, tense orchestrations, and softer, reflective themes, helping to shape the novel’s emotional landscape. Together, the audio and visuals create a world that feels both grand and intimate, mechanical yet alive.

Thematically, Gahkthun of the Golden Lightning stands out for its philosophical undertones. Beneath its fantastical surface lies a meditation on human progress and the consequences of ambition. It questions the meaning of enlightenment in a world where knowledge can both liberate and corrupt. Tesla’s crusade against the academy’s ruling elite becomes an allegory for intellectual and moral rebellion, while Neon’s journey reflects the struggle to reconcile wonder with skepticism. The story’s blend of science, mysticism, and moral inquiry invites the player to reflect not only on the characters’ dilemmas but also on broader questions about civilization, power, and belief.

While Gahkthun’s scope and depth make it a memorable experience, it is not without flaws. The heavy prose and occasional digressions may deter readers looking for a faster pace, and the episodic rhythm can sometimes make the central plot feel disjointed. However, for those who appreciate deliberate storytelling and rich world-building, these qualities become part of its appeal. The game’s length provides ample room to absorb its atmosphere and themes, and its slower sections often reward patience with moments of genuine insight and beauty.

In the end, Gahkthun of the Golden Lightning is a rare blend of ambition and artistry—a story that invites players to lose themselves in its intricate machinery of words, ideas, and emotions. It captures the grandeur of a bygone era while exploring timeless questions about humanity’s relationship with progress and power. Though it demands patience and attention, it rewards those who engage with it fully through its mesmerizing world, eloquent writing, and unforgettable characters. It is a visual novel that reminds its audience that storytelling can be as much about reflection as revelation, and that even in a world of iron and steam, the heart of the tale remains deeply human.

From the trailer one may or may not get the wrong impression about how hard the game really is. It can be summed up as just carrying this blob from start to finish by boosting it between platforms. Here the difficulty lies in the fact that the blob can only stay for so long on a platform before dying so it has to go to the next one to recharge a meter shown on the left side of the screen. Furthermore, there are 3 sets of 25 levels, each introducing various obstacles and changing the main colors, hence the title. Simple enough, right? Well not exactly.

You see, as soon as one starts getting into the hard stages, which doesn't take long, it becomes more and more clear that the meter empties at an alarmingly fast pace, so the reaction time demanded becomes more and more taxing. Not only that but expectedly the levels require more and more precision to be traversed as they go on, leaving less room for error. Nonetheless, my biggest gripe however comes with how the game forces you to not take shortcuts.

There are various levels where one would be tempted to stray off the given path in order to avoid some unnecessarily hard routes. Maybe one would even wonder if they could reach a platform to the side that it's near the finish and should be to do so considering the meter. The reality is that the meter empties at a greater pace if you do that, and there's no indication that should be the case. In other words, the player is limited to take the intended route even though the game conveys otherwise. And that can become frustrating.

Now, the review is positive but barely since once you get past that hurdle and accept how it was designed, you can get better at it and eventually beat it, no matter how many deaths and sessions it takes, considering the target audience. The music is decent enough but it can become too energetic to my taste after retrying the same level nearly a thousand times. There's also the simple pixel art presentation that shines on brief cutscenes and a cryptic story, in case you're interested in that.

So to sum up, I do believe that the levels or the mechanic itself could have been more polished to make amends to the player in terms of the level design, but it certainly has some good aspects going for it.

So what do I think about Nep Riders? Playing the game 100% and after finishing it, It's a long time coming, So here's all two points I have to give. First off, the Good.

1. Uzume's return. Before this game, She hasn't appeared for a very long time in the games (The last appearance she had in the games was in 4GO and after that, she hasn't appeared since), And I thought she would be forgotten like Plu and Pea were, but seeing her return in this game was a sign that IF/CH haven't forgotten about her. And man, Does she keep much of what made her so likeable from VII. Also, the new outfit looks really cool (And alts too).

2. Bike customization. R;Evo had simple recolors for the bike, But this game extends upon it, with More Bodies, Mufflers, and Tires. I would love to see it return in a later new Nep game.

3. Return of Alt costumes. SVS/R;Evo before, only had swimsuits for most of the cast, and were locked behind a deluxe edition. RVD does not have this problem, with it's deluxe edition content now being DLC. And not only swimsuits return, But also Racer Queen and God Eater themed costumes for all of the characters as well (But Adult Neptune, which is the only character to not have any alt costumes, not even her R;Evo swimsuit)

With that, now the bad.

1. The length and lack of content. With only five stages (and Three areas each), It's possible to beat this game in about 2-3 hours and less than half a hour if you speedrun it. This is one of the biggest problems with the game (something I will point out when I get to the next point), Since past Nep spin-offs, like MegaTag, while short, at least had some side-content and Multiplayer to make up for the short single player campaign, While Nep Riders does not have such that. Also, no Multiplayer, either. If going for 100%, though, Then it will take you a bit longer, but still shorter since there's not much in terms of post game content. Also no normal racing mode, either (Something R;Evo managed to have).

2. The Price. 40$ for a short 3 hour game? That's asking a bit too much. Even R;Evo costed less than that, and yet it has more content to go through.

3. No Candidates. I know they appeared in SVS/R;Evo, And while they play a role in both, They were at least there. Here? They don't appear (Aside from Nepgear's name being said by Vert in the story). A shame since I would like to see what their biker costumes would look like.

So what I think about Nep Riders? It's a short but great game (I like they made a whole game based off of the R;Evo bike system), but the price and lack of content is the biggest draw-back I had with the game. So if you want to play it, wait for a sale and then get it.

[h1]Панельки: игра-медитация[/h1]

[h3][i]Здесь в качестве эпиграфа идеально подошли бы строки из стихотворения Бориса Рыжего «Эмалированное судно», но, во избежание некоторых спорных моментов писать сюда я их не буду. Кто захочет, потом сам найдёт и прочтёт стих целиком.[/i] [/h3]

Что можно ожидать от игры с названием «Панельки»? На первый взгляд искушённому игроку может показаться, что эта пресная поделка не сможет предложить ничего интересного. И как раз в этом вся фишка. «Панельки» - игра не про контент. Это игра - про состояние души и разума, про то, как каждый человек, хоть немного знакомый с атмосферой безликих панельных домов и жизнью в одном из таких, прочувствует всю глубину безнадёги своего существования. А может просто немного погрустит и забудет. А может молча кивнёт, или наоборот улыбнётся нахлынувшим воспоминаниям. Каждый определённо почувствует что-то своё.

Главное достоинство игры – атмосферность в каждой её немногочисленной детали. Игру действительно можно и нужно прочувствовать, отключить все посторонние мысли и с головой погрузиться в этот прекрасный мир бесконечных панелек и такой же бесконечной метели, которую чертовски приятно созерцать через покрытое корочкой льда окно подъезда… Номера домов и их положение относительно друг друга и пролегающих между ними пустынных улочек не имеет никакого значения – выбирай любой дом, любой подъезд и любой этаж, остановись, посмотри в окно, подумай, поброди по лестничным маршам… И думай, думай, думай… Может тебе захочется поскорее покинуть это место, полное депресняка и безнадёги, угнетающее последнее живое и радостное, что ещё осталось внутри? Или же наоборот, остаться навсегда в этом бесконечно сером, стеклянно-железобетонном раю, ведь, в конце концов это – твой дом? 

Теперь выплывем из пучины экзистенциального кризиса и посмотрим на то, чем можно заняться в игре помимо вышеперечисленного. А тут ничего сложного: вооружаемся лопатой, ключами от домофонов и крыш и идём выполнять священный долг работника сферы ЖКХ. Никакой пощады мешкам с мусором, банкам с окурками, граффити и собачьему говнецу! Меняем лампочки, выносим нечистоты прочь из домов, чистим подъезды от снега и тем самым зарабатываем себе на хлеб насущный. С небольшим ДЛЦ можем примерить на себя ещё личину курьера и повыполнять заказы на доставку до голодных обитателей панелек всякой нямки.

Ну а в промежутках между такой замечательной и полезной работой можно побыть маленьким поганцем и как следует размалевать все стены и двери жильцов из баллончиков с краской! Ведь какие же панельки без «народного творчества»?

Nova Lands is a very enjoyable automation game. It is not particularly difficult and is well suited for casual players. Some information is missing, such as how to capture creatures, although it is not too hard to figure out, and you can always look it up online. A few mechanics can be confusing at first, like buying packages in buildings placed on your island while buying blueprints in the spaceship. I only realized much later that blueprints allow you to construct as many items as you want once purchased, as long as you have the required resources.

Some items are unlocked near the endgame, such as the Item Antenna, which I used mainly in one place for the red rock resource, since I needed a large amount to create a Black Hole. I barely used the Magnetoids because my automation setup was already complete by that point. I also did not bother with the best fertilizer or lubrication fluid, as they felt unnecessary and required a key resource used to craft Black Holes. At that stage, I was mostly AFK waiting for the remaining Black Holes to be produced.

That said, the game overall was very good. It does not require as much micromanagement as Factorio or similar automation games, making it a great choice for casual players or those looking for a more relaxing experience. The spaceship upgrades extend the gameplay nicely, especially with features like the house, which serves more than just a decorative purpose, as well as the addition of blueprints and diamonds. I completed all the challenges and achievements, finished the main objective, and sent all resources using the rocket, including the 220 required Black Holes. The game was engaging enough to make me want to finish everything, even though none of it was particularly difficult, and a good part of my playtime was spent AFK.

I definitely recommend it. It was better than I expected and only needs a bit of polishing, but nothing major. I give it 9/10.

The game has a good grasp on what makes choices enjoyable, the results are predictable, they can chain and they can be taken back with another choice. The game gives your choices consequences, with your minions sabotaging you when oppressed. Overall the story choices part of the game is well done.

The combat can be janky at times, with your units focusing on the wrong enemy, I'd be nice to see different priorities between units. But you're not supposed to win every fight, just damage the enemy. It's a simple system that only supports another part of the game instead of having its own depth.

The last part of the game is the sabotage you get to do when the enemy rests. This system works well, you need to plan ahead and mechanically all the choices are there, but there's a lot of story opportunity that wasn't captured here. You either torment the heroes or end up bribing them, there's little nuance to it other than the random hero traits that make one of the options more likely.

Overall the game is good fun, a little easy to figure out, but the different titles and hero parties change it up a fair bit. It could use some more complexity when it comes to the tactics and the sabotage, but the lack of it doesn't make the game any less enjoyable.
