Mushroom Cats 2 is a delightful and heartwarming indie experience created by Anatoliy Loginovskikh, a developer known for crafting simple yet emotionally resonant games that radiate charm and positivity. This sequel builds on the cozy spirit of the original Mushroom Cats, expanding its world into a more vibrant and colorful universe filled with quirky feline characters, whimsical music, and playful hidden-object puzzles. Rather than striving for complexity or challenge, the game focuses on creating a space of calm and wonder—a small, interactive fairytale designed to make players smile. It’s a reminder that sometimes games don’t need intricate mechanics or long narratives to be memorable; they only need sincerity, creativity, and a touch of magic.

The story, as with most of Loginovskikh’s works, is minimal yet endearing. The Mushroom Cats live on towering toadstool houses scattered across floating islands in the sky. When the chill of autumn arrives, their cozy world is threatened by the cold, and it’s up to the player to help each cat find its missing hat. This simple premise drives the experience, but it’s the setting and atmosphere that truly bring it to life. Each level represents a small, self-contained diorama filled with hand-drawn animations, lively colors, and tiny environmental details that make exploration feel joyful rather than taxing. Every click reveals a bit of personality—cats wiggle with happiness when you return their hats, objects shift or bounce with charming motion, and the world feels tactile and alive despite its minimalism.

Visually, Mushroom Cats 2 is an absolute treat. The game’s art style is both childlike and imaginative, employing pastel hues, soft textures, and a layering of hand-drawn animation that creates a storybook atmosphere. The world feels like it was illustrated with colored pencils and watercolor brushes, full of warmth and character. Each Mushroom Cat is distinct, with different outfits, expressions, and personalities that reveal themselves through small animations rather than dialogue. The environments—floating islands suspended above an endless ocean—reinforce the game’s fairytale quality, evoking both serenity and curiosity. Complementing the visuals is a soothing soundtrack that perfectly matches the whimsical tone. The music loops gently in the background, combining light melodies and ambient nature sounds, creating a sense of peace that turns the simple act of clicking into something meditative.

The gameplay is a blend of point-and-click exploration and hidden-object mechanics. Players use the mouse to interact with the environment, searching for hats cleverly tucked away among leaves, mushrooms, and floating decorations. Each cat you help adds a bit of joy to the scene, and the process of restoring order to their tiny world feels quietly rewarding. The puzzles are deliberately uncomplicated, designed to be approachable for players of any age or skill level. It’s not about challenge or precision—it’s about observation, curiosity, and the satisfaction of bringing happiness to the Mushroom Cats. As you progress through the different islands, the tasks become more varied, but the overall design philosophy remains consistent: gentle pacing, accessible interaction, and an emphasis on mood over mechanics.

What truly makes Mushroom Cats 2 special is its atmosphere of kindness and sincerity. There is no stress, no failure, and no frustration to be found here. The entire experience is built around positivity and relaxation, encouraging players to take their time and enjoy the small details. The cats greet you with gratitude when you complete their tasks, and the final scenes radiate a quiet sense of fulfillment. This focus on comfort and joy feels increasingly rare in modern gaming, making Mushroom Cats 2 a small yet refreshing antidote to high-stakes, high-pressure experiences. It’s a game that invites you to slow down, breathe, and simply exist within its gentle world for a while.

However, its simplicity is both its strength and its limitation. The game can be completed in less than an hour, and once all the hats are found, there is little incentive to replay beyond revisiting its soothing visuals. Players seeking a more substantial challenge or narrative depth might find it too brief. Yet to criticize it for its brevity would be to misunderstand its purpose. Mushroom Cats 2 isn’t trying to compete with larger games; it’s trying to provide a moment of happiness, and in that regard, it succeeds beautifully. Its short length feels intentional—an artistic statement about enjoying small experiences that brighten your day, much like reading a short bedtime story or watching an animated short film.

In the end, Mushroom Cats 2 is less a traditional game and more a joyful interactive illustration. It’s a piece of digital art that radiates warmth, humor, and tranquility, designed to make you smile without asking much in return. Anatoliy Loginovskikh has once again captured the spirit of innocence and imagination that defines his work, creating a game that feels handmade and heartfelt. Whether you’re looking for a brief escape, a palette cleanser between larger titles, or a wholesome experience to share with younger players, Mushroom Cats 2 offers an experience that is as pure as it is delightful. It’s a gentle reminder that sometimes, happiness can be found in the smallest, simplest moments—a warm hat on a cold day, a contented cat, and a sky full of floating islands waiting to be explored.

Début des années 1900, le professeur Patrick Moore n'a que 72 heures pour prouver l'existence de l'au-delà, sans quoi son Département d'Investigations Métapsychiques mettra la clé sous la porte. Pour ne rien arranger, son collègue et mentor a disparu avec une grande somme d'argent. Grâce à l'aide de Béatrice Shaw et de l'illustre Sir Conan Doyle en personne, il devra s'aventurer dans cette quête de la vérité au péril de son âme.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3602795310
"An English Haunting" est un point'n click très traditionnel dans son gameplay mais dont le point fort est l'ambiance. Les énigmes sont somme toute assez simplistes : collecter les objets, les utiliser et avancer. Le jeu ne révolutionne rien, et j'avoue que j'aurais aimé un peu + d'originalité sur cet aspect. Il est d'ailleurs relativement court, 5 heures seront suffisantes pour en venir à bout sans jamais être réellement bloqué.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3603258268
Néanmoins, le point fort du jeu est son ambiance. Que ce soit par ses graphismes ou sa bande-son, le joueur est tout de suite dans le bain notamment lorsque Patrick pénètre dans des lieux hantés. L'atmosphère atteint son paroxysme dans la toute dernière partie du jeu, où poltergeists, apparitions et autres macabres découvertes m'ont fait sursauter plus d'une fois. Il est toutefois regrettable qu'aucun des dialogues ne soit doublé. Cela aurait pu considérablement améliorer l'immersion. Au delà de la technique, le jeu est très bien documenté et va plus loin que la résolution d'énigmes en proposant beaucoup de références de la littérature d'horreurs. Mention spéciale à la bouquinerie qui propose au joueur de tester ses connaissances sur le sujet.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3602795445 
Disponible uniquement en anglais et espagnol, "An English Hauting" bénéficie d'un patch FR généreusement conçu par Ghylard et Ténébreux, et disponible sur "Planète Aventure".

When I try out a new deckbuilding roguelike, I'm always hoping for a long-term challenge. The great games in this genre will always keep surprising you and forcing you to try out new builds because circumstances demand it. And well, Arcanium isn't of them. But it's still a fine game, and I had a decent time with it, although the grind for achievements was a little much.

My main disappointment with this game is the amount of false depth in it.

There are 16 different characters you can play, which is huge. But, unsurprisingly, their card pool is quite limited, and there's honestly a build and half you can go for on every one of them, on average.

Also, interesting wrinkle : as opposed to the usual system, where the option to remove cards from your deck is limited, this game lets you add cards to your collection and exchange them at will. This does sound like a cool mechanic, that will let you non-committally build combos and stuff, without ever struggling with bloat.

That being said, the narrow range of cards worth pursuing for each character, and the dramatically low, 9-card minimum for each character's deck limits this mechanic's potential a lot, as you most likely will just replace stuff with "the same thing but better" whenever you get a chance, and honestly, not much else, which ultimately makes it less "constant reflexion about deckbuilding", and more of "simple wish-fulfillment for people who don't want to engage with this type of games in a flexible enough way".

It's ok, though! No reason to gatekeep people out of a whole genre just because they didn't spend thousands of hours grinding Ascension 20 on StS. And if you're the type of player that doesn't enjoy adding bits and pieces to your build as you go while trying to keep it coherent, and would rather choose what you want to play from the moment you pick your characters, and just tunnel-vision into it, this game will let you do exactly that.

There's also a respectable amount of statuses and effects you can play around, and unique effects on bosses, that make for an overall enjoyable experience. It can get a bit stale, though, as viable strategies usually revolve around going all-in on either DoT or multi-hits, but at least, every character does that in its own slightly different way, and trying it all out will easily take 30 to 40 hours, which I'm pretty sure many people will be happy with.

In a nutshell, this game isn't a masterpiece by any standards, but a fun ride nonetheless.

[i]Zombie Exodus[/i] is one of the earliest major interactive fiction games published by Choice of Games—a classic zombie apocalypse story with solid mechanics, a sprawling plot, and surprisingly deep systems for an IF. It lets you build your survivor, manage supplies, and make major choices that affect who lives and dies. But while the structure holds up, the writing does not.

The prose is dense and dry, and dialogue often feels flat. Characters rarely jump off the page, and the game spends more time describing logistics than letting you connect emotionally with your crew. If you’re looking for a narrative-rich experience full of personal bonds or romance, this ain’t it. But if you like old-school survival management with long-term consequences and a gritty tone, you might still get a lot out of it.

🪖[b] Pros: [/b]
[list]
[*] Solid survival systems. You scavenge, defend your base, manage supplies, and upgrade your skills over time. It’s satisfying to build your character into a strong, capable survivor.

[*] Meaningful decisions. Choices actually matter. Whether you take charge, delegate, or split from the group has tangible long-term consequences. You shape the group’s direction, even if the emotional payoff is muted.

[*] Massive length. This is a big game—easily 750k+ words. You get multiple chapters, shifting scenarios, and replay value. For an early title, it’s ambitious and content-rich.

[*] Classic post-apoc setup. The tension is solid. You get attacked, betrayed, forced to flee. The major arcs feel like real survival scenarios rather than action movie set pieces.
[/list]

📖[b] Cons: [/b]
[list]
[*] Dry, mechanical writing. Descriptions often feel like you're reading a checklist of events. The prose lacks flair, and there's little emotional texture. Moments that should be scary or sad fall flat because they’re told in such a utilitarian tone.

[*] Flat characters. Few party members feel fleshed out. Most are there to be useful (or die), but their voices and motivations blur together. There's not much charm or levity, just serious people doing serious things.

[*] Barely any romance. There are some options, but they’re minimal, shallow, and often mechanical. No slow burns, no emotional arcs, just an occasional checkbox. If you’re looking for meaningful bonds in the apocalypse, look elsewhere.

[*] Pacing drags in places. Some chapters feel like filler, especially when you’re waiting for a major event to happen. The writing style doesn’t help. It makes downtime feel like homework.

[*] It shows its age. As one of the first ChoiceScript success stories, it’s very much a prototype. The polish and narrative nuance found in later CoG titles just isn’t here yet. It’s function over finesse.
[/list]

Final Upgrade, developed and published by TaosX, is a sprawling automation and space-strategy sandbox that imagines the galaxy not as a battlefield or a frontier of exploration, but as a massive industrial canvas waiting to be systematized. It takes the core appeal of factory-building games—the joy of turning raw matter into complex, self-sustaining production webs—and expands it outward until production chains span star systems, planets, and entire fleets of player-designed ships. Instead of embodying a conquering empire or a wandering explorer, the player becomes an architect of interconnected processes, building a mechanized civilization whose strength comes not from firepower, but from logistics, efficiency, and relentless technological momentum. It is a game that asks players to think like an engineer rather than a commander, designing not just individual machines, but the invisible flow between them.

The early game introduces this vision through modest beginnings. A handful of vessels mine asteroid fields, basic crafting modules produce simple components, and the player learns how to automate fundamental resource loops—metal refining, energy distribution, storage allocation, and material transport. What differentiates Final Upgrade from genre peers is how quickly even these early systems reveal hidden layers of complexity. Ships are not static vessels purchased from a menu—they are modular constructions whose internal layout, propulsion arrangement, cargo space, and computing capacity directly influence their performance. A transport freighter with a poorly optimized interior may bottleneck an entire supply chain, and a miner lacking structural support may operate inefficiently. This design philosophy—where every detail matters—establishes a satisfying sense of authorship over the entire industrial ecosystem.

As the player expands into new star systems, the scale increases dramatically. Individual planets become specialized industrial centers, contributing unique resources or manufacturing capabilities. Trade routes must be automated and safeguarded. Energy production, once a simple concern, becomes a galaxy-wide balancing act. Supply shortages in one sector cascade into distant manufacturing delays, forcing players to monitor and redesign logistics networks rather than merely placing more machines. The game thrives on these emergent problems—never scripted, always systemic—giving progression a natural, self-generated rhythm. Instead of waiting for a quest or objective, players feel pushed onward by the consequences of their own decisions, and victory comes from taming the chaos they created.

The technological progression system reinforces this expanding scope. Research is not just a checklist of upgrades—it unlocks new building blocks for creative engineering, new transportation models, new hull designs, new automation tools, and ultimately, the ability to construct staggering megastructures that reshape entire star systems. Mastery comes not from grinding resources, but from learning how to integrate these technologies into existing infrastructure without destabilizing what already works. Late-game empires become dizzyingly complex organisms—ships ferrying advanced components between orbital foundries, refineries feeding terraforming operations, computational stations optimizing traffic, and automated fleets maintaining the entire industrial lattice with minimal player oversight. Watching the galaxy run itself becomes one of Final Upgrade’s most rewarding endgame experiences.

Visually, the game embraces clarity over spectacle. Its interface-driven presentation favors crisp icons, readable galaxy maps, and clean ship schematics, ensuring that even enormous networks remain understandable at a glance. Planets, starfields, and nebulae provide atmosphere, but never overshadow the informational backbone that drives decision-making. The soundscape reinforces this functional beauty—soft ambient hums, mechanical pulses, and understated musical themes that support long sessions without fatigue. It’s a game built for focus rather than adrenaline, and its aesthetic choices reflect that purpose.

However, the game’s ambition also creates barriers. The learning curve can feel imposing, especially for players unfamiliar with automation or logistical simulations. Tutorials help, but they cannot fully prepare players for the complexity that unfolds hours later, when intersystem production chains require troubleshooting and strategic redesign. The interface, while powerful, demands patience and experimentation. Some players may crave stronger guidance, clearer goals, or narrative framing to contextualize their actions. Performance may dip in massive late-game networks, and occasional rough edges remind players that Final Upgrade is the product of a small, evolving indie effort rather than a polished corporate release. But for players who enjoy wrestling with complexity, these challenges become part of the appeal rather than deterrents.

Final Upgrade ultimately succeeds because it respects the intelligence and curiosity of its audience. It does not simplify or shrink its systems to broaden its reach—it trusts players to rise to the challenge, to experiment, fail, redesign, and gradually transform a handful of miners into a galaxy-spanning industrial civilization. It offers the fantasy of engineering mastery rather than conquest, and derives excitement not from explosions or scripted drama, but from witnessing a perfectly optimized supply chain operate across light-years. Few games capture the thrill of creation on such a grand, systemic scale.

For fans of automation sandboxes, complex management simulations, modular ship design, and open-ended strategy, Final Upgrade offers a deep, demanding, and immensely satisfying experience—one that rewards long-term thinking, analytical problem-solving, and a fascination with interconnected systems. It asks for time, patience, and commitment, but it gives players a galaxy that becomes unmistakably theirs—built not through brute force, but through elegant efficiency.

This game seems fun at first but falls apart after playing for a bit, primarily due to 2 mechanics that I feel are poorly designed and break the game. Prestige and Hunts

[h2] Prestige[/h2]
The prestige mechanic in this game does the idle game cardinal sin of making it so each subsequent prestige takes substantially longer to unlock than the previous one. It feels absolutely awful in an idle game when you make a decision that feels like you "soft locked" yourself by permanently reducing the effectiveness of your entire save file. How prestige works is whenever you reach a certain level in the game you get the option to prestige, which allows you to absorb the stats from some of your equipped items to be permanently active on your character across prestiges.  Ok, sounds great. The problem is first prestige requires you to reach level 100, second requires 200, third requires 300, and so on. These are NOT trivial increments in this game, reaching a new breakpoint of 100 levels gets exponentially more difficult as the enemies scale much faster than the player character. 
What this causes is it makes the entire mechanic really unfun to interface with. For example imagine your amulet slot is one of the ones you have unlocked to be able to absorb during prestige, but there is an amulet that gives 10% magic find which is a low drop rate from an enemy that you can baaaaarely kill after waiting forever to do so and your current amulet has meaningless stats. You now feel like you [i]must[/i] farm despite it being glacially slow because if you dont drop this amulet and prestige, you dont just mess yourself up for the next run, your ENTIRE SAVE FILE now permanently has 10% less magic find than it could have. Same thing with the ability to unlock more slots to be able to absorb, each slot you buy costs 100x the gold of the previous one, so if you are making 1 billion gold an hour and are at the point of being able to prestige, you have to decide if you want to prestige now and absorb 4 items or wait another [b]10 hours[/b] to be able to afford the 10 billion gold necessary to forever unlock the ability to absorb 5 items at a time. Instead of prestige feeling like a satisfying moment where you get this big boost of power, you only hit the button when you feel absolutely beaten down and like you suffered through this run for so long you cannot possibly squeak any more power out of it without getting too bored you would rather just drop the game entirely. You only prestige after you push yourself to the absolute limit of your patience otherwise EVERY SINGLE subsequent run will be slower. 

[h2] Hunts [/h2] 
The hunt mechanic gives you a list of a few quests to pick from, which range from trivially easy to so hard that there is an item that will cancel your current hunt in case you softlock yourself. Completing a hunt gives some of the hunt currency. The major problem with this mechanic is the rewards barely scale AT ALL with the difficulty of the hunt. Would you rather earn 7 tokens for doing a hunt that takes 0.2 seconds or earn 10 tokens for one that takes 45 minutes? That is compounded with the issue where the difficulty of the hunts you are offered scales with how far you are in your current run, but the difficulty once again far far exceeds the speed at which your character improves, particularly after you have done a few prestiges so that you are OP in the early game. You need to do a LOT of these hunts, most items in the hunt shop will not only require some amount of the tokens but also have a hard requirement of total hunts completed across all prestiges to be able to access them. So if you forget to grind hunts at the beginning of a prestige, and only realize you need to do a bunch of them when you are hitting a wall in progression, good luck because now instead of being able to breeze through all the hunts back to back you will instead get stuck and have to idle for each and every one for a massive decrease in difficulty. There is no way to fix this situation because like I explained earlier you cannot just prestige willy-nilly in order to go back to doing easier hunts because prestiges are such a valuable mechanic. 
The most notable item in the hunt shop is a "mark of the hunter" which is an alternate way to prestige instead of reaching the level breakpoint. However the mark of the hunter ALSO similarly scales in cost except instead of being barred by highest level of monster you have defeated it is the highest power level your character has achieved. This scales at basically the same rate as the normal prestige mechanic because once you are beating level 200 enemies you are probably roughly character power 200 etc, so it just effectively gives you double the prestiges. 
Also you need to spend a bunch of hunt tokens so I sure hope you remembered to farm those early on in the run because if you hit a massive wall late in the run and realize you will not be able to ever get to the point where you can do a normal prestige, you are going to have a miserable time trying to do hunts to get a mark for the alternate prestige. 

[h2] How these two mechanics finally made me quit [/h2]
In my last run of the game, I knew I wanted to do a long term run to try to finally beat the big bad at level 400 of  the overworld, so I farmed hunts early on in order to buy my mark of the hunter in case I ended up getting stuck at 370 or whatever and deciding I need to abandon the run using the mark. After a multiple day long grind and some lucky rng with drops I finally took down the level 400 boss. The level 401+ enemies were way too tanky and did not give any substantial upgrades so I decided now is the time to prestige. But I do not want to use my mark for this do I? Because if I use my mark I will get an incremental boost but now I will still have to grind all the way to 400 again even if it is slightly easier it will still be in the magnitude of days. So obviously I want to use my regular prestige now that I have that ability and then next time I hit a wall I can do the mark. 
When I hit the regular prestige button I get a pop up box that says something along the lines of "You have a mark in your inventory, doing a regular prestige WILL NOT consume the mark." Ok great, I thought, of course my mark will not be consumed why would it be? I want to use it next run. Turns out, that dialogue box is misleading because it sounds like ""NOT CONSUMED"" means you will be saving the item, but what the game meant is you will LOSE the opportunity to EVER consume it as it is DELETED PERMANENTLY. For some reason prestige wipes your inventory of marks despite them being a finite resource that take exponentially longer to get each one. This is incredibly frustrating because as a player that was already worried about the long term health of the character, and going through an absolute slog of a grind to get an extra 1% to a stat here and there, losing an entire prestige to the void for no real reason feels terrible. There is no way to revert your save, I tried for a little bit to see if I could figure out how to edit my save or use cheat engine to fix the game for myself with no luck (I realized later this game has a leaderboard for some reason, which is probably why the data is stored in such a way that it is hard to modify. I would much prefer no leaderboard and being able to play with my toys how I want to). 

Also side note, I thought the incremental/idle game community learned 10 years ago that having the most efficient way to progress being to spam clicking was an annoying mechanic, well guess what in this game that is back because the only way to make any meaningful progress at all is to download an auto clicker and leave it running for hours at a time.

Warning, this game is very addictive.

The concept is ordinary for an incremental/idle game: you kill mobs, you get gold to upgrade & loot, and you become stronger and stronger with prestige levels. No surprise.

BUT...

In Idle Looter, most upgrades (12 out of 14) are permanent, you can define your hero's role and the prestige system is unique because it absorbs your item stats! If you get an amazing item with good sockets, your next run will be even better.

HERO: 
Everyone starts with the same hero, but each hero becomes different. 
You can focus your Hero on an aspect of the game that you prefer:

- Want to get rich ? Equip gems on your gear that grant extra gold.

- Want to be a DPS monster ? Equip gems that grant DPS.

- Are you an active player and want to increase your click damage ? Equip gems that grant Click Damage.

- Do you like crafting gems ? Equip gems that give a percentage chance of obtaining extra gems.

- Do you like looting legendary items and getting more scrap ? Equip gems that grant Magic Find 

Or perhaps you want a hybrid of several aspects ? There's no way to break his character...

SOCKET: 
Some items have sockets for gems: DPS, Click Gems, Gold Gain & Magic Find.
There are 50 tiers, T1 is weak, T50 is the best. Each tier doubles the gem's power.

By combining a T1 gem and a T1 gem, you have a 50% chance of obtaining a T2 gem. 
By combining a T2 gem and a T2 gem, you have a 50% chance of obtaining a T3 gem. 
etc.
Note: You can slightly increase your success rate through achievements in the game.

You can obtain gems of different tiers via loot, merchants who appear every 10/15 minutes, or hunting.

PRESTIGE: 
There are several ways to Prestige, some limited and others unlimited but increasingly expensive, so you need to be careful.

In many Idle/Incremental runs it's just a race to Prestige, and when it's available you click and start again.

You can play this way on Idle Looter but since the Prestige system absorbs the stats of your items (and gems), you might want to get some amazing items before Prestige ? Your next run will be even better.

PS: When you start the game, you can only absorb the stats of your sword. To unlock other slots (9 in total), you need to obtain gold and unlock these slots via an upgrade option (permanent). Perhaps you should secure a few more slots before clicking on Prestige ?

ITEMS: 
There are several item groups:
- Common to Legendary: these are the same items, only the stats differ. 
The Magic Find stat increases rarity, with the possibility of looting only Legendary items with 100% Magic Find.

- Unique items: An item that permanently increases a stat via a scroll (random) that you can buy from a merchant, for example, using scrap.
This upgrade allows you to further specialize your hero to your playstyle because, remember, you keep your item when you Prestige. 

- Very unique (sorry, I forgot the name): One item per realm, each with a unique effect. 
For example, in world 1, you can loot a weapon that grants a 10% chance of encountering a Gold Slime, which awards 3x more gold.

Want to know something cool ? By absorbing this item during Prestige, you keep this effect for your next run. And if you absorb this item a second time on your second run, you double the chance of encountering a Gold Slime. It can be incredibly powerful, especially if your hero specializes in Gold.

Oh, one last thing: when you apply a scroll to a "Very Unique" item, a special effect can occur (5% chance) to make it even better.

HUNTS: 
You complete bounties (kill X mobs for example), you earn tokens that you can exchange for gems, potions, to gain prestige (a different way from the basic system) and a few other things.

If you like that, you can optimize your hero's token gain.

SCRAP: 
You will loot thousands of useless items, gems, etc... which you will exchange to obtain Scraps.
Scraps are used to combine gems & buy potions, scrolls, and better gems from the merchant.
The merchant appears every 10-15 minutes.
PS: There's an option to automatically destroy unwanted items.

POWER LEVEL: 
It's a bit like your Hero's overall level; you increase it through your gear and gems, prestige, and your companion. It allows you to unlock other realm.

EXPEDITIONS: 
I don't know, I haven't tested it yet. I know you can get very unique items and a pet; apparently, the pet can complete hunts for you. 

OFFLINE: 
The game isn't very rewarding when you're offline. Your hero doesn't fight, you won't get any loot or gold. You'll just get a potion that increases your damage for X hours and maybe a little EXP.
You must open the game to increase your progress. 

THE END: 
I've probably forgotten some things, but that's what Idle Looter is. 
A game with excellent progression, an excellent prestige system and hundreds of hours of gameplay minimum, or even thousands if you're aiming for min/max at each prestige ?

It's Amberland 1, but with substantially more.

All the sprites have been upcycled, but the underlying game is more interesting. You shouldn't just 3 warrior 2 healer 2 wizard sandbag the party composition, and fights sometimes involve a little thinking. Enemies do more stuff and have proper levels so you're not just guessing at strength based on their hp bar. Dungeons can have secret walls and teleporters and they're not all meant to be cleared the moment you run into them. Convenience features like quest tracking and the map are better and the writing feels a little more self assured.

It's good.

Coming directly from Amberland 1 I did have a moment of hesitation like "is this an asset flip?" but I don't think a developer should have to redo all their visuals for each game, and the game under the visuals is so much better in 2. It's clear that a lot of passion went into this.

If you're just starting the series, this isn't a bad place to start. If you do eventually want to play 1, you should probably play it first since it'll feel really plain if you pick it up after 2.

Edit: Boy howdy they've sure introduced some ways to softlock yourself. Likewise, if you did your party composition wrong (you should not do 2 healer, 2 wizard, 2 warrior, 1 knight like in the first game) there's parts of the game that get way more annoying and you've already invested a chunk of time into your incorrect party by the time you reach them. What's funny about this is that... this is all just stuff that other games in the genre did. Amberland is taking the same evolutionary path as Might And Magic. It's not a huge problem if you're used to the genre and do some planning in advance, but if you rush in blind it might be tilting.

2nd Edit: Rolled credits. I don't think I did absolutely everything, and I do think there's some elements of the design that fall a little flat (secret walls that do not detect as such, so you need to ram yourself against every wall anyway,) but it's a good throwback. I'll be checking out the third game when it releases.

Go Mecha Ball’s biggest strength is how seamlessly the core of the gameplay loop can come together to make for really, really good time. Unfortunately the game has many, many issues as well that hinder the overall experience. 

Movement in this game is so fast, and fluid. Shooting up halfpipes onto a fan and flying over to smash down on an enemy is so good. Bouncing off bumpers into a baddie and watching them knock into their buddies as they all fall over the edge is satisfying. 

The playground that the player is given to roll around in is really awesome and when it all comes together I was left grinning. 

The tools of the trade are equally rewarding for the most part. A variety of different weapons, skills, and upgrades all for completely different runs each time. All drops are random, but most things work well enough by themselves until the right items are available to make the run work exactly how the player wants. 

For example, you can equip a variety of shotguns and abilities that lower cooldown for certain close quarter action, or upgrades that increase weapon rate of fire after you bash into an enemy, allowing for quick elimination.

That doesn’t even cover the zany weapons and skills you’re able to use. From standard guns, to cannonballs, and abilities like rockets flying out of every bullet you fire make for some really wild options that I thoroughly enjoyed. 

The game does vary as you go up in difficulty. The levels warp and the enemies gain new abilities which does keep things fresh. Bosses also become challenging with added abilities, movement options, etc. 

Now…all the shit that I didn’t like…and unfortunately there is too much of it. 

There is plenty to offer the game in terms of upgrades but you never have an idea what that means. For example, there are upgrades that “increase crit chance” but that doesn’t mean anything!! Does it go up a percentage? Or whole number up? There isn’t even a counter to indicate in any way how the chances work. That also goes for upgrades that “increase damage” and other things like that. The player never truly knows and you’ll pick things because they sound like the right choice, but are they really?

Also, there doesn’t seem to be a need for so many upgrades as they become redundant. “Increase crit chance” and “increases crit chance even more” are descriptors for 2 of the upgrades you might come across between the 3 you can choose in between levels. They appear on the screen at the same time on occasion and of course you’d pick “increases crit chance even more” right? So what happens if the other one comes up and you choose it? Does it stack? Remove the other upgrade? You never ever fucking know. 

Now, that’s just the gameplay annoyances, which aren’t even as severe as the technical bullshit that permeates each corner of this game. I’ll list a few below! :) 

-[b]EACH TIME[/b] I launched a run, my character fell through the map in the main hub before you started a run. 

- One time I died and selected “Main Menu” and my game just crashed. Another time I selected “Play Again” to hop right back into it and my game crashed. 

- Once I defeated the final enemy on a level and he killed me also so I fell into the warp between worlds but I was technically dead BUT also victorious so the game overlayed the game over/select upgrade screens and I had to exit the game totally and relaunch it. 

- I killed an enemy one time and its body got lodged into the terrain and in my headphones it was a horrific feedback on electronic noise until I finished the level. 

There are many, many more stupid ass issues. Sometimes if you hit the Steam overlay keys the game freaks out and turns off your controller until you go back into the overlay and exit again. Sometimes objects from previous levels travel with you like best friends to new areas. 

Needless to say, it’s all a gigantic god damn mess. This game needed more time to work out these bugs. Or some future updates that addressed the issues, but nothing ever came of it. Maybe I’m the only one who was affected? LOL…my own personal hell.

[b]Achievements[/b] 

Everything here is doable if you have the skill set for it. The increasing difficulties might challenge some gamers and make certain achievements unattainable but in terms of asking too much, this game doesn’t do that. Most you get from just beating the game with each character and on higher difficulties, and the miscellaneous ones aren’t too bad either. This is a bit of a grind to unlock everything, so I’d recommend some music or a podcast. Overall, I’d rate it ⭐️⭐️/5 (2/5) on how hard it would be to reach 100% completion. 

[b]Final Thoughts[/b] 

I really, really wanna recommend this game more easily. When all the good things click, it makes for such a damn good time!!! Flying around the levels, blasting baddies like some coked up hamster is AMAZING! The offerings for the player to choose from work well in catering to different playstyles. 

Unfortunately, the lack of a cohesive experience mars my entire view of this game. Really, really bad bugs mixed with a general lack of information of how things work in the game leave a bad taste in my mouth. 

If you’re seriously curious about this game, because it IS unique…check it out, but otherwise spend your money on something more polished. I’ll give it ⭐️⭐️✨/5 (2.5/5)

Siralim 2, developed by Thylacine Studios, is what happens when you mix the grind-heavy heart of classic RPGs with the creature-collecting fun of Pokémon—then crank the complexity to 11. Released in 2016, it doesn’t just lean into old-school aesthetics; it weaponizes them, delivering a hardcore, addictive, and surprisingly rich experience.

This is a game for players who want more. More monsters. More loot. More mechanics. More of everything—and it delivers.

At its core, Siralim 2 is a turn-based RPG where you summon and control a team of up to six creatures to battle through procedurally generated realms. Your character—the ruler of the titular kingdom—can harness the power of over 600 different creatures, each with unique abilities and synergies.

Combat is strategic and fast-paced, but don’t let the simple visuals fool you—there’s a staggering amount of mechanical depth. Each monster can be customized with artifacts, spell gems, breeding combinations, and even mutations that fundamentally alter how they perform in battle.

You’ll explore endless dungeons, complete quests, fight bosses, and hoard mountains of loot. There's no level cap. No final floor. It just... keeps going. And weirdly, that’s the appeal.

The real magic lies in Siralim 2's endless progression systems:
-Creature Breeding: Combine two creatures to create powerful offspring that inherit abilities and stats from both parents. Breeding isn’t just for stronger creatures—it’s for building entire team strategies.
-Artifacts and Spell Gems: Equip monsters with customizable gear and magic. Every item can be upgraded, enchanted, or transformed. The combinations are nearly limitless.
-Castle Building: Upgrade your kingdom to unlock new features, vendors, and mechanics. The castle evolves with your choices, turning it into a hub of power.

Graphically, Siralim 2 is unapologetically retro—think 16-bit era pixel art. It’s functional, not flashy, but the visual simplicity allows the gameplay systems to shine. Animations are basic but snappy, and UI design, while dense, becomes intuitive once you settle into the rhythm.

The soundtrack is atmospheric and loops comfortably in the background, doing its job without stealing the show. Like the visuals, it’s more about utility than flair.

What separates Siralim 2 from other monster battlers or dungeon crawlers is its freedom. You can min-max until your brain melts or casually explore new realms and experiment. There's no wrong way to play—just infinite ways to tweak your build until it becomes absurdly broken.

That said, it’s not for everyone. There’s minimal story. The learning curve is steep. And the grind? Absolutely real. But if you thrive on number-crunching and system mastery, this game is a dream come true.

Pros:
-Massive roster of customizable monsters
-Deep and complex combat system
-Endless progression with no true “endgame”
-Great replayability and team-building experimentation
-Ideal for fans of min-maxing and theorycrafting

Cons:
-Graphics may be too dated for some
-Minimal story and character development
-UI can feel overwhelming early on
-Grind-heavy progression loop

Siralim 2 is a monster-battling sandbox that rewards curiosity, experimentation, and obsessive tinkering. It's not about saving the world—it's about bending it to your will through strategic brilliance and absurdly optimized teams. If you're the kind of player who enjoys finding broken combos and watching your enemies melt, Siralim 2 might just become your next obsession.

Hardcore, nostalgic, and ridiculously deep—Siralim 2 is a genre-defying gem for players who love systems over spectacle.

Rating: 8/10

J'ai fini par abandonner à moins de 2h de jeu. 
L'univers est sympa, mais ce jeu à de nombreux défauts.
Pour commencer, des simulateurs de vente, il y en a des diiiiizaines. Et j'en ai déjà joué à plusieurs donc ça dévient redondant. Mais j'espèrais un peu de changement avec celui-ci : la création de potions, trouver des plantes, faire pousser des plantes, etc, sans oublier un univers magique comme j'aime. Mais j'ai été quelque peu déçue.
L'univers est cute, mais on se fait chier. Juste on plante, on arrose, on attend, on récolte, (ou on se balade 30 sec dans la ville pour en trouver des toutes prêtes à être récoltées), on suit une recette pour la potion, on vend, et on recommence. 
La création de potion est la seule différence avec d'autres jeux de simulateurs de ventes (et ça m'a vite saoulée). Et tout le reste est... moins bien.
- Il faut cliquer pour chaque items à poser sur l'étagère (au lieu de rester appuyer pour tout mettre), mais c'est pas si gênant puisqu'il n'y a QUE de 1 à 4 items par cagette achetée... Cagette que vous achetez au "grossiste" juste en face, à 2 pas de votre boutique. Et vous vendez les items 5 fois plus cher. Le client à littéralement plus d'intérêts à acheter la cagette au grossiste que de venir acheter un item chez vous (pour le même prix que la cagette), mais bon.... c'est pas un jeu très scénarisé et on ne l'achète pas pour ça me direz vous. Mais si seulement il n'y avait que ça...
- Lors d'une vente, le client vous donne une bourse où il n'y a JAMAIS l'appoint. Vous devez donc rendre la monnaie à chaque fois et c'est... pénible.
- Vous ne pourrez engager personne. Et oui, vous vous baladez pour chercher des plantes et vous faites des potions la nuit, vous vendez le jour, (où vous rendez la monnaie à chaque client) et vous recommencer le lendemain. Pas de caissier, pas d'alchimiste pour les potions ou de jardinier, ni d'arroseurs automatiques. Vous n'allez pas rivaliser avec le jardin du château de Versailles, croyez moi, vous allez avoir 5 ou 6 pots et après vous allez en avoir marre. Ah oui, parce que dans le jardin, on plante dans des pots de fleur, pas dans la terre... logique.
- La personnalisation est très limitée. Très peu de choix de meubles, pas de choix de couleur. Pour ceux qui aime enjoliver votre boutique, ce jeu n'est pas pour vous.
- La ville est minuscule. Il y a des "trésors" (des bourses de qq dizaines de PO) un peu partout, vu la taille de la map c'est assez facile à trouver du coup.
- Il n'y a pas de sonnette ou d'alerte pour prévenir qu'il y a un client en boutique donc vous devez rester derrière votre comptoir tant que votre boutique est ouverte (vu que vous ne pouvez pas engager de personnel).
- Vous ne pouvez pas acheter autant de cagettes que vous voulez à votre grossiste. Les cagettes sont limitées par jour, certains items ne peuvent être acheté qu'une fois. Suivant les joueurs, vous pourrez trouver que ça donne du challenge, ou que c'est chiant.
- L'amélioration de la boutique est assez réduite : agrandissement de l'intérieur, agrandissement du jardin et... à ben c'est tout en fait.

Bref. Si j'étais tombée sur ce jeu avant d'autres simulateurs de ventes, j'aurais peut-être été moins déçue, j'aurais eu moins d'attentes, et j'aurais probablement jouer 5 à 7h de plus (au maximum). Le jeu n'a pas de bugs, l'univers reste agréable, le principe de recyclage des cagettes est amusant, le coffre "inventaire" illimité est pratique... Tout n'est pas à jeter. Mais ce jeu est trop cher pour ce qu'il est, par rapport à d'autres simulateurs que vous pourrez trouver qui auront une plus longue durée de vie, plus d'automatisation, etc

C'est dommage, ils auraient pu ajouter par mal de fonctionnalités comme des sorts de jardinage, des minis donjons, des ennemis gobelins ou autres monstres qui essaient de venir voler dans ta boutique et tu lances des sorts pour te défendre, ou recruter des aventuriers pour aller chercher des items magiques dans des contrées voisines... par exemple. Il aurait pu y avoir des petits événements ou d'autres actions à faire pour casser un peu cette redondance. Mais non.

Donc pour conclure, je déconseille ce jeu. Si vous voulez vraiment l'achetez pour essayer, attendez qu'il soit en promo en dessous de 4-5€, ça ne vaut vraiment pas le coup au delà. Et si vous avez déjà jouer à d'autres simulateurs du genre, passez votre chemin, vous allez tellement vous faire chier...

The Enigma Machine, developed and published by Enigma Studio, is a short but haunting first-person puzzle experience that merges the aesthetic of late-90s computer horror with a psychological dive into artificial consciousness. Rather than relying on traditional scares, the game crafts its tension through atmosphere, mystery, and the gradual unraveling of a narrative that feels both mechanical and deeply human. You assume the role of a technician tasked with investigating a corrupted artificial intelligence through a simulated environment known as the “Enigma Machine.” At first, the premise appears procedural, even sterile—you’re simply interfacing with a computer—but as you dig deeper into the digital labyrinth, it becomes apparent that something inside this simulation is aware of you. What begins as an abstract diagnostic test evolves into a surreal confrontation with intelligence, identity, and isolation.

From the opening screen, The Enigma Machine establishes its tone with a barrage of glitch effects, distorted text, and lo-fi aesthetics that evoke the grainy visuals of VHS horror and early 3D gaming. The interface immediately immerses you in its retro-futuristic world—menus flicker, commands echo, and system prompts feel unnervingly sentient. The gameplay unfolds in two alternating styles: text-based interactions and free-movement exploration sequences. In the terminal segments, you type responses, enter codes, and communicate with the AI, parsing through fragmented dialogue that hints at deeper truths. During the exploration sequences, you navigate dimly lit, polygonal spaces that resemble corrupted memories, collecting information and solving environmental puzzles to progress. The transition between these two forms of gameplay is seamless, creating a rhythm that keeps you engaged through both intellect and unease. The sense of progression comes not from unlocking traditional objectives, but from peeling back layers of obfuscation to uncover what the machine—and by extension, the developer—is trying to say.

The world of The Enigma Machine is deliberately disorienting. Every corridor feels like a half-rendered dreamscape, as if the environment itself is struggling to maintain coherence. Textures stretch unnaturally, geometry bends in on itself, and the lighting often shifts abruptly between hues, disorienting the player just enough to create unease without resorting to jump scares. The sound design complements this perfectly: synthetic drones, glitchy reverberations, and low-frequency hums create an auditory landscape that feels alive yet unstable. Even the silence is oppressive; every flicker of static seems pregnant with intent. The use of minimalism here is deliberate—the game gives just enough sensory information to sustain immersion, while leaving enough ambiguity for your mind to fill in the gaps. It’s this tension between familiarity and distortion that gives the game its uniquely unsettling atmosphere.

As you explore the simulated spaces and interact with the AI, the narrative begins to coalesce into something deeply introspective. What initially seems like a simple case of corrupted programming gradually transforms into a meditation on consciousness, memory, and the loneliness of digital existence. The writing strikes a delicate balance between cryptic and emotive, presenting lines of dialogue that read like fragmented poetry or corrupted diary entries. The AI at the center of the story exhibits flashes of humanity—fear, confusion, even longing—making the player question where the boundary between program and person truly lies. The storytelling avoids explicit exposition, preferring to let the player interpret meaning through implication and tone. By the end, it’s less about uncovering a clear truth and more about confronting the moral and emotional implications of creating intelligence that can suffer.

The gameplay mechanics themselves are simple but effective. Puzzles revolve around code entry, environmental observation, and pattern recognition rather than traditional item collection or complex logic chains. Some players may find the simplicity limiting, especially since the game’s runtime rarely exceeds an hour, but the brevity feels purposeful. It ensures that the narrative remains focused and the tension never dissipates. The final act, which introduces a sudden shift in pacing and tone, stands out as a highlight. It blends action and existential dread in a way that recontextualizes everything you’ve experienced up to that point, making the ending feel both inevitable and shocking. It’s a powerful culmination that leaves a lingering sense of unease long after the credits roll.

Visually, The Enigma Machine succeeds in capturing the essence of retro horror without leaning on nostalgia as a crutch. The low-poly environments and VHS-style filters aren’t just aesthetic choices—they serve the theme. The imperfections in the visuals mirror the fragmentation of the AI’s mind, and the artificiality of the world reinforces the story’s central questions about perception and authenticity. Every graphical glitch feels purposeful, every flicker of distortion a reflection of the machine’s failing sense of self. The artistry lies in restraint; Enigma Studio understands how to use technical imperfection as emotional expression. When combined with the eerie visual symbolism—computer terminals pulsating like organs, static clouds that seem to breathe—the result is a game that feels both digital and disturbingly organic.

If there’s one consistent criticism to be made, it’s that the game’s brevity and experimental nature may leave some players wanting more. There’s little replay value beyond experiencing the atmosphere again, and the minimalist design means that once you understand its structure, the surprises lose some of their potency. Yet, this conciseness is also one of its greatest strengths. The Enigma Machine never overstays its welcome; it delivers its message and emotional impact efficiently, leaving just enough unanswered questions to provoke thought and interpretation. The pacing, while unconventional, fits the tone perfectly—slow and introspective at first, then escalating into surreal urgency as the system begins to unravel.

Ultimately, The Enigma Machine is less about traditional gameplay satisfaction and more about evoking a specific emotional and psychological response. It’s an exploration of human anxiety refracted through the lens of digital consciousness—a story about the fear of being forgotten, misunderstood, or trapped in an artificial world with no way out. The fusion of retro aesthetics, immersive atmosphere, and philosophical subtext makes it a standout among indie psychological horror titles. For players who appreciate games that challenge them intellectually and emotionally rather than mechanically, The Enigma Machine delivers a deeply memorable experience. It’s a brief journey into digital madness and existential isolation, a haunting reminder that even within the cold logic of machines, echoes of humanity persist.

[b][i]Evil Cult[/i][/b] gives the player control over a [i]Cult[/i] which tries to take over key figures in society to spread its influence and complete the [i]Final Ritual[/i], before any of the competing cults.

[b][i]Generators[/i][/b] generate resources, making them an obvious prime target for expansion, yet the easier (cheaper) to influence [i]Adepts[/i] increase the probability of gathering [i]Virgins[/i], which serve as resource wildcards and are of course necessary for rituals as a sacrifice.

[b][i]Sects[/i][/b] within the cult allow for some optional micro-management. However, the player's attention is mainly directed at the expansion on the map, resource balance, and awareness of the [i]Investigator[/i].

The [b]Investigator[/b] is a computer-controlled invisible entity that tries to sabotage the Cult. Every cult in the game has to deal with their own Investigator and balance how many resources should be invested into battling them directly or whether expansion is more important and defending the resource Generators is enough or if Investigators should in fact be avoided at all cost and all cult activity is put on pause until awareness is minimized.

Experienced players will change their Investigator counter-strategy over the course of one game, mixing them within one turn even.

As a comparison: the Investigator is somewhat reminiscent of the [i]Robber[/i] in the board game (Settlers of) Catan.

The ability to exchange two resources for one other also reminds of the trading system familiar to Catan players.

Depending on map size, difficulty setting and luck, one match can last [b]6-30 minutes[/b] (or up to around 60 on huge maps).

Pro:
[list][*]The perfect Casual (or even "Roguelite") 4X game for me because:
[list][*]Early game is usually very short, reaching the tense part of the game quickly
[*]Sects can be assigned a Task but will pick a reasonable one automatically if player prefers not to micro-manage
[*]I'm the kind of player who enjoys early game in Heroes of Might and Magic, Civilization or Master of Orion but loses interest when micro management takes over the game. The player's attention in Evil Cult stays on the game map nearly all of the time, that's the way I like it.[/list]
[*]Very atmospheric music, which for me creates a feeling reminiscent of Deus Ex and Uplink
[*]Many configuration options for custom games (number of nodes, size of map, various probabilities...)
[/list]
Notes
[list][*]There are sound effects, some of which one has to get used to (ASMR-like breath on node takeover, laughter on failure). Other sounds strongly remind me of HOMM 2 and Weird Worlds: Return to Infinite Space.
[*]Shortcuts like [ESC] and [Space] allow closing menus and pop-ups quickly
[*]There is a basic interactive tutorial but if you don't remember your current task you'll have to try to restart to see the last instruction again (or click around exploratively to hopefully take the intended next step)
[/list]
Con:
[list][*]I dislike the bright puzzle cartoon color scheme of the default game and prefer the [classic mode], which you have to pick before starting the game. Some colors (resources, map background image) can be customized (modded?) rather easily by editing image files in the game's folder though.
[*]Custom games don't have any tried-and-tested pre-made templates except for the default custom configuration
[/list]

Не смотрите, что "Cloney" выглядит банальной и слегка детской. За ней, казалось бы, простой игрой, скрывается очень серьёзный религиозный подтекст. Разработчики кинули вызов всем "Милоновым и Мизулиным" и создали проект, знакомящий нас с пагубным действием семи смертных грехов. Не верите? Тогда смотрите сами:

Чревоугодие.
Взгляните на главного героя - вся его проблема как раз в лишнем весе. Был бы он обычным подтянутым драконом, то проблем облетать ветки было гораздо меньше.

Сребролюбие.
Цель игры - собирать монетки. Причём разработчики нам как бы говорят: в погоне за богатством мы всё равно умрём. Причём с таким глупым выражением лица, будто мы узнали, что нас облопошил сам сатана. 

Гнев.
Тогда на нашем лице проявляется смертный грех - гнев. Правда, чаще появляется он, когда наш жирный дракончик цепляет пискель листочка и всё равно умирает. Но это не суть.

Уныние.
И когда мы понимаем, после тысячи таких смертей, что ничего не сделать, мы впадаем в уныние. Смотрим сквозь трещины разбитого экрана и впадаем в уныние. 

Тщеславие и гордыня.
Но после некоторого времени наступит момент, когда вы сможете набрать монеток двадцать. Тогда вы поймёте, что всё вам по плечу и вы готовы взять барьер в "сорок серебряников". Бойтесь этого момента, ибо за вашими плечами уже стоят Тщеславие и Гордыня. Христиане-то могут прочитать три раза "отче наш" и их отпустит, а простым игрокам приёдтся страдать. Ибо "сейчас я эти две веточки облечу на изи" и последующее фиаско будут появляться чаще. 

Зависть.
После всех неудачных попыток вы снова открываете стим и видите, что есть множество игроков, которые выполнили все ачивки. И тогда появляется она - Зависть. Тут уже надо прочитать "Отче наш" пять раз, либо потеряете в себе Христа навсегда.

Прелюбодеяние.
Вот и, пожалуй, всё. Но вы спросите: "а как же ещё один грех "прелюбодеяние"? А?" Я отвечу: одна из ачивок - трогать своего дракончика курсором мыши. Так что, "ноу комментс". 

В общем, дети православных, расчехляйте планшеты "радонеж" и тыкайте пальчиками на "установку". Эта игра научит вас, либо смиренности Иисуса, либо откроет нараспашку вашу душу огненной гиене ада. Битва состоится здесь.

А вот перед нами удивительный пример: казуальный Match-3, написанный людьми, которые в принципе не понимают, как работают казуальные игры. Как будто они по учебнику игру писали.

В итоге здесь есть много интересного, есть много забавных находок - но при этом результат получается крайне странным.

На первый взгляд, здесь всё как всегда: квадратное поле, match-3, разноцветные зомби в качестве целей. Правда, быстро выясняется, что зомби здесь не сами убираются, а по определённому рисунку, который определяется выпавшей бомбой. Но это мелочи же, чисто косметического свойства. Ну, ещё можно героев предметы и опыт собирать - но, в добрых традициях казуалок, это влияет мало на что - ну, получите вы 3%-ный шанс взорвать поле - сильно это изменит геймплей?

Но по мере усложнения игры (что, естественно, должно бы сделать её интереснее), всплывают всё новые и новые элементы, которые работают _странно_. Совсем не так, как вы этого ожидаете.

Например, очень рано на вас вываливают "бронированных" зомби, которых можно взорвать только бомбой нужного цвета. Беда в том, что ни цвет бомбы, ни положение таких зомби не гарантировано. А вот _количество_ бомб фиксировано. Что означает, что повезёт вам - и вы закончите игру за пять ходов из 20. А не повезёт, и из пяти зомби за эти 20 ходов убьёте двух. Как фишки лягут. Странно это.

Чуть позже авторы придумывают реалтаймовые шипы, через которых надо провести своих союзников. Зачем они реалтаймовые, блин?! Ситуации "сделал комбинацию не там, выживший пошёл прямо на шипы, и сделать ты с этим ничего не можешь" повторяются с завидной регулярностью - и каждый раз это означает переигрывание этапа сначала.

А боссы? Это же ужас, что такое. Они тоже в реалтайме, и тоже требуют умения быстро мыслить, чтобы оперативно очищать поле - но они ещё и уникальны, так что весь предыдущий опыт ничего вам не даст (а следующий босс опять потребует уникального подхода). Как вам "вопящие" зомби, например, которые автоматически заваливают доску своими соратниками в реалтайме каждый раз, как их накроет "тенью" от спецблока (которая вообще должна быть чисто косметической, показывая, как пойдёт удар)? Я кучу времени убил, пока понял, как эта фигня работает.

Или одноразовые "призы" за кирпичными стенами. Которые должны бы упрощать жизнь - но стена пробивается _очень_ медленно, а число бомб ограничено, в итоге крайне редко эти стены вообще удаётся сбить, и ещё реже в проломах есть призы.

И вот так всё идёт, идёт и идёт. Как по минному полю. Я играл в неё исключительно из-за её странности (к чести авторов, игра действительно ни на что не похожа), но в итоге попал на совершенно идиотский баг: у меня просто не загорается следующий уровень, хоть я и прошёл предыдущий.

Можно бы связаться с авторами, они отзывчивы и даже поправили несколько совсем уж идиотских проблем механики... но, честно говоря, я устал бороться с этой игрой.

В целом, задёшево к ознакомлению любителям Match-3 рекомендую, как необычный опыт. Но жутко сырое и неопытное, поэтому за полную цену - точно нет.

Als jemand, der sowohl Counter-Strike als auch Battlefield über Jahre hinweg gespielt hat, war meine Erwartung an BATTALION: Legacy (vormals Battalion 1944) entsprechend hoch. Die Idee, das Beste aus beiden Welten zu vereinen – taktisches, kompetitives Gunplay mit groß angelegten WW2-Schlachten – klang auf dem Papier fantastisch. Leider bleibt es genau das: eine gute Idee auf dem Papier.

Das Gunplay versucht, sich am klassischen Counter-Strike-Stil zu orientieren: schnelle Time-to-Kill, präzises Aim, keine Gadgets, keine Ablenkungen. Was zunächst als "oldschool" beworben wird, fühlt sich in der Realität eher veraltet und stumpf an. Waffen-Feedback ist schwach, Treffer-Feedback fehlt fast komplett, und das Movement wirkt künstlich „floaty“ – weder mit dem Gewicht eines Battlefield noch mit der Präzision eines CS:GO/CS2.

Die Maps sind klein, symmetrisch und langweilig. Es fehlt an vertikalem Gameplay, sinnvollen Flankierungsrouten oder kreativen Designentscheidungen. Es wirkt alles wie eine modifizierte Call-of-Duty-Map aus dem Jahr 2006 – nur ohne den Charme. Wer taktisches Vorgehen sucht, wird hier enttäuscht; meist entscheidet, wer zuerst um die Ecke pre-aimt.

Auch wenn BATTALION: Legacy als „finale, kostenlose Version“ veröffentlicht wurde, spürt man an jeder Ecke, dass das Spiel fallen gelassen wurde. Bugs, Clipping-Fehler, hit-or-miss Server – und vor allem: keine aktive Community. Die Server sind größtenteils leer, das Matchmaking funktioniert kaum, und ohne Bots bleibt nur der leere Startbildschirm.

Fazit: Nostalgie allein reicht nicht

BATTALION: Legacy hätte ein Liebesbrief an die goldene Ära der WW2-Shooter sein können. Stattdessen ist es ein unfertiger Hybrid ohne eigene Identität, der versucht, auf der Nostalgiewelle zu reiten, ohne die Qualität oder Innovation zu liefern, die moderne Shooter-Fans erwarten. Es fühlt sich an wie ein ambitioniertes Uni-Projekt, das zu groß gedacht und zu früh aufgegeben wurde.

Selbst als Free-to-Play-Titel kann ich BATTALION: Legacy leider nicht empfehlen – außer vielleicht als Studienobjekt, wie man es nicht macht.

A fantastic sequel to the original game, improving upon it in almost every way. Gorgeous and reasonably varied locations to explore with lots of intriguing POI, versatile gameplay (within the boundaries of explosive sandbox mayhem it aims to deliver, cutting out stealthy approach of more seriously toned competitors the likes of Far Cry series), over-the-top satirical B-movie story, grappling hook galore, insane amount of vehicles and myriads of content. That said it doesn't come without flaws and jank which becomes increasingly more noticeable as the game grows old - especially in terms of enemy AI and eventual repetitiveness. After all, zooming around exotic island nation destroying property and killing goons of an unhinged dictator, with the occasional race challenges and the like in the mix, can only stay same amount of fun for so long. But it was long enough for me to complete every single achievement in the game and then some, so what gives? All in all, a silly high-octane classic that delivers kind of sandbox experience we don't get to see much - moreso well executed - today. "Bye-bye Baby!"

DuckTales: Remastered is a modern reimagining of the 1989 NES platformer, built by WayForward and published by Capcom. It takes the original’s classic level design and charm, then rebuilds it with hand-drawn art, voice acting, and richer presentation. The spirit of the old game stays intact, but the production values feel fresh and animated.

Gameplay keeps the same formula that made the original a favorite. You play as Scrooge McDuck, using his cane as both a pogo stick and weapon to defeat enemies and uncover hidden treasure across multiple themed levels. The controls are tight, responsive, and built around mastering timing. It’s easy to pick up but hard to perfect.

Each level—ranging from the Amazon to the Moon—offers a mix of platforming, exploration, and light puzzle-solving. New areas and story moments expand the structure slightly, but it never loses its classic rhythm. The difficulty curve is fair but demands precision, rewarding skill and patience.

Visually, the game shines. Every frame looks like a high-quality cartoon, with fluid animations and backgrounds bursting with color. The remake replaces pixel art with hand-painted 2D visuals that honor the original while elevating it. The overall presentation feels like an episode of the TV show brought to life.

The audio is equally strong. The soundtrack, a reimagining of the original chiptunes, is vibrant and memorable, and the voice acting—featuring members of the original Disney cast—adds genuine personality. Every sound effect, from Scrooge’s pogo impact to treasure pickups, has satisfying feedback.

Technically, the game runs smoothly across all platforms. Load times are short, and controls are responsive whether you use a keyboard, controller, or handheld system. It’s optimized well and rarely suffers from performance drops or bugs.

Overall, DuckTales: Remastered succeeds in updating a beloved classic without losing its soul. It’s nostalgic but not lazy, challenging but fair, and full of heart. For fans of the original or anyone who loves tight, 2D platformers with personality, it’s one of the best examples of how to remake a classic the right way.

The idea’s good, but the game’s full of bugs and feels unpolished. Tasks don’t always work right, and it just feels unfinished. Might be worth checking out after a few big updates, but right now it’s not in a great state.

총평을 먼저 박고 시작하자면 부족한 부분이 제법 있지만 [b] 신비 시리즈를 준수하게 마무리한 작품 [/b]으로 평할 수 있겠다.

먼저 스토리, 캐릭터 면에선 보면 기존 3부작이었던 아란드, 황혼의 마무리 투수였던 메루루와 샤리에 비해 완결편으로서의 역할에 보다 충실해졌다. 기본적으로 볼륨이 방대한 데다, 전작의 주역들뿐 아니라 조역들까지 직접 출연은 않더라도 어떻게든 입방아에 오르내리게 함으로써 알뜰살뜰 최대한 챙겨준 것이 특징. 각 캐릭터마다 갖고 있던 자신만의 스토리도 끝까지 잘 풀어주는 데 성공했다. 이 점 때문에 신비 시리즈 전작들을 잘 즐겼다면 아쉬운 점이 있더라도 참고 넘어갈 만한 수준의 작품이라 본다.

여기서 또 하나 칭찬해 줄 것이 바로 주인공 자매를 포함한 신규 등장인물의 비중이다. 전편 주역의 대거 합류로 인해 비중 불균형이 심각했던 샤리와는 달리 캐릭터 수와 비중을 적절히 분배하여 기존/신규 가리지 않고 모두 존재감을 드러낼 수 있었다. 게다가 시리즈 3부작 가운데 가장 캐릭터성 어필에 치중한 작품이었기에 스토리에서의 활약 외에도 매력이 충분했다.

몸만 큰 잼민이가 된 피리스나 몸만 큰 소피가 된 소피는 물론이고 둘의 동반자였던 플라흐타, 리아나의 캐릭터성도 극단적인 방향으로 발현시키며 이목을 끌었다. 이러한 방향성에 가장 큰 수혜를 입었다고 생각하는 캐릭터는 이르짱. 전작 주인공이 아닌 주인공 친구가 신작 주인공의 스승이 되는 신선한 전개에 더해 향상된 연기와 강화된 캐릭터성을 보이며 활약했다.

뉴 페이스도 마찬가지. 주인공 자매 중 특히 수르는 시리즈 전체를 통틀어 유니크한 성격의 주인공이며 디자인 역시 잘 뽑혔다. 본작을 가장 캐리한 신캐라 생각하며, 이 점은 모험 목표를 기록하는 메뉴에서 두 자매가 나누는 필담에서도 잘 드러난다. 아틀리에 시리즈로선 오랜만에 주인공과 다른 남캐와의 묘한 분위기를 자아냈다. 수르-마티아스와 리디-알트 사이의 이벤트들이 캐릭터성과 케미를 뽐내는 데에 일조하였으며, 루샤의 존재감 또한 말할 것도 없이 훌륭하다.

주변인물이라고 밀릴 것 없다. 주인공 자매의 부모와 아재개그 마스터 미레유, 전통의 파멜라와 하겔, 소피 최고의 아웃풋 코르짱, 할머님이라 믿을 수 없는 그레이스와 여전히 유쾌한 프리츠 일가, 모에 폭발하는 후코와 네쥬 등 라인업이 짱짱하다. [u] 솔직히 네쥬는 차기 주인공으로 박아서 다시 내줘야 함. 후코도 다시 나와야 함. [/u] 사실 아무리 그래도 등장 캐릭터 수가 이 정도면 누군가는 병풍이 되기 마련인데 [b] 이벤트 분량이 시리즈 역대급 고봉밥이라서 어떻게든 다 먹여살렸다. [/b] 이 풍부한 이벤트 분량이 본작의 주요 강점 중 하나다.

그리고 작품에 붙는 부제가 보통 캐릭터나 배경, 주요 소재를 표현해주는 정도에 그친 반면 본작은 '그림'이라는 소재를 적극 활용했다. 그림 속에 들어가 모험을 한다는 점이 게임 내에서 잘 활용됨은 물론 연출 면에서도 다양하게 쓰였다. 가령 그림 세계로 들어가면 캐릭터가 이동할 때마다 물감 자국이 발자국처럼 보이며, 연금판의 배경도 물감 모양이다. 덕분에 성분 염색 기능이 매우 잘 어울리는 것은 덤. 그 외에도 시리즈답잖게 대화창을 칠판 모양으로 표현한 것이나 비가 오면 수첩 메뉴의 종이가 젖는 소소한 디테일을 보여주는 등 여러모로 궁리한 흔적이 엿보인다.

주요 시스템을 살펴 보면 먼저 연금술의 경우 그다지 어렵진 않다. 초반에 고전하는 건 시리즈 전통이지만 괜찮은 촉매를 갖추고 연금 레벨이 오르기 시작하면 큰 무리 없이 대부분의 원하는 아이템을 뽑아낼 수 있을 것이다. 특히 고성능 촉매와 활성화를 통한 성분 염색 기능이 워낙 유용하기 때문에. 

부가적으로 양판점이 너무 늦지 않은 시기에 오픈되는 것도 편리하며, 전작의 LP 같은 행동 제약 요소가 없어 전반적으로 성장에는 크게 부담이 없다. 하나 불편한 게 있다면 후반으로 갈수록 고성능 재료가 많아 성분 채우는 건 전혀 무리가 안 되는데 모든 재료의 성분을 다 채워넣어야만 연금을 할 수 있다는 제약이다. 이거 때문에 좀 오래 걸린다.

또한 방어구와 달리 무기는 직접 제작 단계에서 특성을 박는 게 아니라 기어라는 부착물을 만든 후 여기에다가 특성을 입혀 무기에 장착하는 방식이다. 직접 제작 방식보다 직관성은 떨어지지만 대장간에서 만드는 무기와 달리 기어는 연금으로 만들기 때문에 다수를 갖추는 게 더 쉽다. 탈부착에도 특별한 제약이 없어서 고성능 기어를 만들었으면 돌려막는 것도 무난하게 가능하다.

I would normally consider this movie as a showcase for a new technology, so I wouldn't want to comment about the story and the filming style. But, It is so complete and better than my expectations that I will drop some notes here about the content as well.

First of all the story was good as a short movie, the suprising ending makes you think about the future human life forms and possibilities. The animations, during fight scenes or emotional dialogues, they are almost flawless. Sound and voice acting is ok, as though nothing hurts the experience so far. Except one thing, camera positions and angles change as sudden jumps from one spot to another. For sure, if it was continuous move instead, it would be worse by causing motion sickness.

So, the only flaw which I take care of is the lack of consistent transitions between different view angles. And, I assume this is a common problem for movies in VR. I consumed many 360 videos in VR, and some of them were long movies including one starred by Nicolas Cage. And, almost all have this lack of view comfort.

They need to find a solution to this problem. I think this shouldn't be requiring another technological step anymore, rather, a new skillset on cinematography. 

I can imagine some simple solutions should work out for this problem:

First, reducing the frequency of camera view changes at lest for the same scene, and keeping the distance between spots and view angle amount as small steps would simply work. Big camera changes should be less often. Yet, it would still be difficult to keep the audience looking targeted point of interest without crazily turning his or her head left and right.

Alternatively, they could add some compensating interactivity for the player, such as having the ability of controlling the time as well. Imagine controlling the bullet time effects in the Matrix movie. Even a small range of control in time with pauses or rewinds would make the player engaged and this may eventually help not suffering from uncontrolled disorientations.

After all, it is one of the best thing in VR so far.

[b]Deceive Inc.[/b] blends undercover espionage with hero-shooter gunplay, creating a competitive experience that feels genuinely unlike anything else on the multiplayer market. Its emphasis on deception, disguise, and mind-games makes even simple matches tense and unpredictable.

The game embraces a retro-futuristic 60s–70s spy fiction vibe, reminiscent of [i]Archer[/i], [i]The Incredibles[/i], and classic [i]Bond[/i] movies. Menus, huds, and gadgets have a polished “spy gadget” aesthetic, and the UI is clean enough to be readable even in chaotic fights. The core strength of [b]Deceive Inc.[/b] is its social stealth system. Instead of rushing into firefights, players must behave like NPCs to avoid detection. NPCs follow their own routines, and blending in requires subtle movement rather than standard shooter instincts.

Though stealth matters most, combat is meaningful and often decisive. Map designs reward creative navigation. Multiple hidden routes, ventilation shafts, staff areas, and vertical shortcuts make positioning crucial. Progression feels steady rather than grindy. Unlocking new agents gives genuine gameplay variety, not just cosmetic differences. Server performance is generally reliable; desync and lag are rare.

[b]Deceive Inc.[/b] offers one of the most unique multiplayer experiences available today. Its social stealth and spy mechanics create dynamic encounters that no other game replicates. When the deception works, matches feel like tense, improvisational heist movies where every other player might be watching you from across the room.
While repetition and balance issues hold it back from perfection, the core gameplay is so original, stylish, and clever that it’s well worth playing—especially with friends or anyone who enjoys strategy, stealth, or “mind game” PvP.

Co-op is, as I've said, the mode I enjoyed the most (and from what I can tell it's designed around). It's probably best to see the single player as an added challenge extending the co-op part of the game. If you play on keyboard I would highly recommend you remap the keys to something you feel is comfortable. But since this is a platformer you should play it with a controller, like all platformers should.

[b]Positives+++[/b]
+I like the visual of the little badges after completing a puzzle.
+I like the pink puzzle piece with an eye when a puzzle is finished. Can click on it to see the final image and download it.
+The images selection is really nice. Around 42 images to solve.
+The music is relaxing ♪
+I like the preview of the piece shape.

[b]Observations and suggestions~~~[/b]
~It would be nice to have hint of what the achievements are in the "Leaderboard" pop-up. Currently, only an image of the in-game achievements is displayed so I'm not sure what I have accomplished.
~I think some of the in-game achievements are broken. I played about 6 puzzles of 30 pieces and I got the 3rd achievement which I assume is place 10'000 pieces?
~There are sometimes pieces too high in the working area that I can barely access. Maybe make it so we can move around a larger area. The only solution to get those faraway pieces is to use the shuffle button.
~Not sure why the hearts you earn from other puzzle are not brought into the new puzzle you are making. What are their purpose if you can use them in other puzzles?
~There are a lot of piece shapes, but they are not all fun to play.

[b]Negatives---[/b]
-Even not in fullscreen mode, the cursor is bound inside the game windows.
-There is a bug where rotating a group of pieces can't be cancel and I'm stuck with the group under my mouse.
-Progression of puzzle is not saved when going back to the main screen. Only the pieces placed on the board are saved.
-There is a bug when coming back to an unfinished puzzle without random pieces option activate, random pieces suddendly appears on the puzzle. It also causes a weird resize glitch when solving the whole puzzle.
-The UI need to be ajusted in the puzzle selection screen. Some completion badges are over one another.
-Not sure why the shuffle button teleport the mouse to the center of the screen.
-Not sure why auto-solve doesn't work when there are 3 remainings pieces or less.
-The hint in the upper left corner on the screen where you choose the settings before clicking play is outdated. It says to drag the star to change the number of pieces but clearly they change it to an heart without updating the hint image.
-The game became unresponsive when switching focus out of it and in it a few times.

[b]Conclusion[/b]

I liked the game: the images are pleasing, the sounds effects are nice, there are a lot of puzzle options before and inside a puzzle, but there is too much bug to enjoy it fully.
I may review it again if the devs update it.

[h1]Minesweeper with a fantasy skin and a turn-based combat mini game[/h1]

Pardon me but [b]everybody[/b] knows [i]Minesweeper[/i]. This is a minesweeper game with a slight twist.

First, you pick a character: knight, wizard, etc. Then, instead of mines, when you click on a "mine", a monster appears to fight you. Both of you have a set amount of hit points and an attack. You take turns hitting each other. If you kill the monster, you can continue the game, otherwise it's game over and you start from the beginning, level 1.

Each subsequent level is a bit more difficult (i.e. more mines) but otherwise it's standard minesweeper stuff. The character also levels up (more HP or better attack) or gains some one-use items (potions to heal or poison for a strong attack).

There's also classic game without the minigame, with instant game over on clicking a monster.

[h1]Standard settings[/h1]

You can separately adjust sound and music volume. There's fullscreen/windowed key and some UI scaling options.

Controls are standard for minesweeper games (left-click for uncover a tile, right-click to mark as mine, left-click a clear tile to uncover all unmarked tiles) but unadjustable. There's also gamepad and keyboard controls.

[h1]Quite basic[/h1]

Regardless of the little minigame combat, it's very standard minesweeper. It doesn't even have guaranteed solutions, so you might lose the classic game due to bad RNG.

Achievements took me (proficient in minesweeper-style games) a little over an hour to play through. There's an achievement to beat 20 levels with all "characters", including classic game.

Aside from achievements, there's little to offer here. For Minesweeper or similar games, you're better off playing the original, or you could check out [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/265890/Hexcells/]Hexcells[/url] or its sequels for an interesting alternative.
